file: 1,000 Chinese Journalists Call For Greater Freedom of Press.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the strongest appeal so far for freedom of the press in China, more than 1,000 journalists from official news organizations signed a petition that was presented to the Government today calling for talks with China's leaders.
The goal of the talks would be to discuss independence of the press, broader coverage of major events like the recent student demonstrations, and the dismissal of the editor in chief of a Shanghai newspaper.
''The reason we are calling for such a dialogue is that our press coverage has attracted criticism at home and abroad,'' said Li Datong, an editor at the China Youth News. 
''We think that the press in Beijing has failed to be comprehensive and fair in its coverage. 
And we think this is the direct result of our current press system.''
The petition, which was presented to the All-China Journalists Association by about 100 journalists, criticized press censorship in coverage of the recent student demonstrations and demanded a change in the Communist Party's role in press coverage.
Â 
'Some Reports Were Distorted'
''Some reports of the demonstrations were extremely distorted and they have severely damaged the reputation of China's press both here and abroad,'' the petition said.
Because domestic news organizations have been restricted in their coverage of the demonstrations, many Chinese people have learned of the recent events from foreign reports, such as those on the Voice of America and the British Broadcasting Corporation.
During the big student protest last Thursday, about 300 reporters from leading publications demonstrated at the headquarters of the official New China News Agency. 
Several newspapers also printed articles, albeit brief ones, on the event the next day.
''We saw more than you did, but you wrote and published more than we did,'' Yuan Xiaolu, a journalist at China Youth News who signed the petition, told a foreign reporter.
Several reporters said they did not know whether their newspapers were going to publish articles about the petition today. 
But a reporter at the Science and Technology Daily, which was forced to delay distribution of an issue recently because it included articles about the demonstrations, said the newspaper planned to cover the event.
The single action that seems to have aroused the greatest dissatisfaction among journalists is the dismissal two weeks ago of Qin Benli, who was the editor in chief of China's boldest newspaper, the Shanghai-based World Economic Herald. 
Mr. Qin, 70, seems to have become a symbol of the need for more press freedom.
Journalists for the newspaper said the authorities have again intercepted the Herald and delayed its publication. 
They said officials refused to allow the current issue of the weekly newspaper to be printed because of a front-page letter declaring Mr. Qin's dismissal improper. 
The letter was removed and the newspaper was printed 36 hours late, they said.
Zhang Weiguo, a reporter in the Herald's Beijing bureau said the staff members also intend to sue the Shanghai Communist Party leader for his decision to dismiss Mr. Qin and reorganize the newspaper.

file: 10,000 in Hong Kong Rally for a Free China.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 10,000 people staged a noisy but peaceful demonstration today in support of democracy in China.
The rally took place outside the offices of the official Chinese press agency, Beijing's quasi-official representative in this British colony.
Demonstrators shouted slogans and carried banners that said, ''We Love China, Not Communism'' and ''Today Rumania, Tomorrow China.''
They also voiced support for the overthrow of Communist governments in Eastern Europe.
The protesters earlier rallied in downtown Hong Kong before marching the several miles to the office of the New China News Agency.
The demonstration was organized by the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of the Patriotic Movement in China, which has been accused by Beijing of trying to use the British colony as a base for subversion in China.
China has pledged to retain Hong Kong's capitalist and legal systems for 50 years after the territory reverts to Chinese rule in 1997.

file: 100 Chinese Defy a Ban.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 100 Chinese today defied a Government ban on ''English Corner,'' a glade in a Beijing park where people have gathered for years to practice English-language skills with foreigners. 
Cordons sealed off the glade, in the Purple Bamboo Park, which has served as a Sunday venue, and official notices nearby proclaimed that ''English Corner has been withdrawn.''
But defiant students and workers said they would continue to hold the conversation sessions until they are forcibly driven away.

file: 115 Killed in Quake in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
An earthquake rocked China's western region of Qinghai late Thursday, killing 115 people and flattening more than 1,000 homes, officials said today. 
Officials from Qinghai's seismological bureau said by telephone from the provincial capital, Xining, that the quake, measuring 6.9 on the Richter scale, also damaged a labor camp and that more than 200 convicts had escaped in the confusion. 
Officials said 120 people were in the hospital.

file: 13 Are Charged in Violence Tied To Queens Gang.txt
text:
ï»¿
Federal authorities charged 13 people yesterday with operating a murderous gang headed by a man in China who wielded power on New York streets through a violent group of enforcers.
Seven murders, three kidnappings and many cases of extortion were among the charges cited in a racketeering indictment. 
The defendants were identified as leaders, members and associates of a gang called the Green Dragons. 
Investigators called the group one of the most violent gangs in the city, with operations based in Queens since January 1986.
"This indictment, for all intents and purposes, destroys the Green Dragons and their leadership," said Andrew J. Maloney, the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York. 
He said some members were cooperating with the authorities.
The heavily armed gang resorted to murder more quickly than Chinese gangs that had been in the United States longer, Mr. Maloney said. 
"They put a lot of weight on terror," he added.
Among the murders were those of a woman and a man who were kidnapped from a restaurant in Queens last year and shot in their heads while kneeling with their hands tied behind their backs, investigators said. 
The woman had testified in a case against some Green Dragons, they said.
Â 
'Deep Within' China
A 35-year-old man, Kin Fei Wong, was charged with being the founder and leader of the gang. 
The authorities said he was born in China, lived in the United States for a time and then operated the Green Dragons from "deep within" the Fujian Province of China. 
He was accused of being a major heroin trafficker who conducted extensive criminal activities and used the Green Dragons as an enforcement arm to maintain his authority in this country.
Investigators said the Green Dragons, most of them in their late teens or early 20's, carried out extortions, robberies and other crimes to finance their activities and sometimes graduated to more important criminal roles for their leader in China. 
Eleven of the 13 defendants are in custody, several of them since November, when initial charges were filed. 
Kin Fei Wong is one of the two not arrested.
"We don't have a treaty with China that would cause his extradition," Mr. Maloney said. 
But the prosecutor said he thought that China would turn over the suspect to American authorities.
Mr. Maloney said wiretapped telephone conversations showed that the leader in China regularly sent orders to the gang leader in New York, identified as Chen I. Chung, 22, who "recruited new gang members from the schools and playgrounds of Queens, promising them money in exchange for their loyalty."
Mr. Maloney said the gang extorted payoffs of up to $2,000 a week from Chinese restaurants in Queens. 
He hopes, he added, that the indictment will send a message to the growing Asian community that "the police and Federal authorities are ready and willing to help them rid themselves of these lawless gangs."
If convicted, each defendant could face 20 years in prison for racketeering, and those named in murders could face life in prison.

file: 150,000 March in Defiance of Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
More than 150,000 demonstrators openly defied official warnings and a concentration of troops today to march for 14 hours through the capital, repeatedly and effortlessly puncturing lines of policemen and soldiers sent to stop them, in one of the biggest displays of dissatisfaction in 40 years of Communist rule.
The student-organized demonstration in support of democracy and against corruption was a stunning humiliation for the Government, which responded this evening by agreeing conditionally to the students' demand for discussions with officials.
Most worrying for the authorities was the fact that crowds of cheering workers lined the entire route and hailed the core of student marchers almost as a liberating army. 
Workers vigorously applauded the students, waved encouragement from office windows, and frequently sent them food and drinks to show support.
Soldiers Are Surrounded
On at least three occasions thousands of workers surrounded hundreds of soldiers and and prevented them from approaching student marchers.
Workers sometimes pushed aside police blockades even before the students drew near, and the marchers in the four-mile-long parade were easily outnumbered by supporters who walked and bicycled along with them for at least part of the way.
Beijing residents said the security forces, including army troops called in from surrounding areas, had made their greatest show of force in recent memory, but it was dwarfed by the sea of demonstrators.
Including the onlookers who waved and cheered as the parade went by, perhaps half a million people took part one way or another, often climbing trees and lampposts when there was no ground to stand on.
The only comparable protest came in the first week of April 1976 when angry crowds gathered in Tiananmen Square to mourn the death of Prime Minister Zhou Enlai and oppose the ''Gang of Four'' then in power. 
Several Chinese who took part in both demonstrations said the one today involved more people and more general defiance of the authorities, who had warned of a crackdown on demonstrators.
Â 
New Themes Are Raised
For the first time, the pro-democracy movement, which in the past has been overwhelmingly limited to students and intellectuals, seemed to draw fervent support from others. 
The students encouraged this not only by pressing their previous demands, like freedom of the press and more money for education, but also by raising populist themes like official corruption and inflation.
The perception of Government impotence was most vivid when the crowds burst through the last police barricade to get to Tiananmen Square in the center of the capital. 
Nearly 1,000 soldiers in 20 trucks did not flee quickly enough and mobs swarmed around them, clambering onto the hoods and sides of the vehicles and appearing ready at first to lynch the troops. 
But when it became obvious that the soldiers were terrified and thinking only of retreat, the mobs cleared a way for them to escape.
Shouts of ''Brothers, go home and till your fields'' could be heard from the crowd as the trucks raced off.
Aside from some shoving, there was no violence. 
Indeed, students once rescued soldiers sent to block their march. 
Several truckloads of troops were surrounded by angry mobs, who allowed them to leave only when persuaded to do so by students waving their university identification badges.
Â 
An Appeal to the Workers
''We're deeply moved by the students' audacity,'' said a young Government ministry official who came out of his office to applaud as the students passed. 
''They say what is in our hearts.''
The procession was full of signs and banners, ranging from ''Vive la liberte,'' erected by French-language students, to a large black banner aimed at workers: ''You work but you get nothing; your life is bitter.''
The students were far better organized than they have been in the past, and some with megaphones were assigned to rally worker support. 
When the march passed a large factory, whose gate was promptly locked, a student made a small speech:
''Dear workers, we are all citizens, and we all have the right of free movement. 
If anyone stops you from getting out and joining us, that's against the Constitution.''
Of the 150,000 or more marchers, about half were organized students carrying banners and the rest were workers or students taking part on their own. 
One worker who marched was Zhou Jingping, a library clerk, who said he was an enthusiastic supporter of the students.
''Inflation has given us a lot of difficulties because prices rise but salaries don't,'' Mr. Zhou said. 
''Students voice that desire of ours to suppress the inflation. 
And then there's corruption. 
Bribery is evident everywhere, and people are sick of it. 
Education is another reason - the Government hasn't paid enough attention to education.''
To many workers, the students seemed to represent not a focused, alternative agenda, but simply a cry of discontent that struck a deep chord.
''They represent people's thinking, the sense that we the people are in control,'' said one of the marchers, Lin Yulin, a 52-year-old worker wearing a Mao Zedong button as a sign of his discontent. 
''The leaders cover everything up. 
People don't know anything, and we are no longer the masters. 
That's why there is this uprising.''
The outpouring of support for the students was humiliating for the entire leadership, but for no one so much as the senior leader, Deng Xiaoping. 
In the last 10 days of protests, the students have often expressed contempt for Mr. Deng, and he more than anyone appears to have been behind the hard line that the Government has taken in the last few days. 
Harsh Words From Deng?
Chinese with close Communist Party connections say the Politburo raised the matter of student unrest this week and asked Mr. Deng for his views. 
He is said to have answered particularly harshly, saying that if necessary some blood could be spilled and that repression would not seriously harm China's image in the world.
The students said tonight that they would continue their boycott of classes and some predicted that there would be more demonstrations on May 1 and May 4. 
It was not clear how the students would regard the Government's offer of discussions, which was a major concession but which appeared to be linked to the students' willingness to avoid street demonstrations.
The Government appeared dumbfounded by the size of the day's demonstration, and the television news did not mention it tonight. 
The official New China News Agency mentioned it briefly and suggested its effect only indirectly when reporting that it had caused ''huge traffic tie-ups'' affecting 300,000 people.

A1 & 6)

file: 2 CHINA DISSIDENTS DETAINED IN MAY.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities have recently detained at least two democracy advocates, including one who spent a decade in prison for political beliefs, Chinese familiar with the cases say.
Students at Beijing University said a fellow student, Peng Rong, was detained on Friday, one day after President Bush recommended the renewal of most-favored-nation trading status for China.
Two weeks ago, Liu Qing, a leader of the Democracy Wall movement in 1978-79, was picked up and accused of not having a valid permit to live in Beijing, associates said.
One of the most prominent dissidents in China, Mr. Liu was freed from prison at the end of 1989 after having served 10 years for advocating democracy and human rights and also for publicizing prison conditions.
After his release, Mr. Liu steered clear of overt political activity.
Fellow students said they were not certain why Mr. Peng had been detained or whether he might be released. 
But they said they suspected the reason was that he signed and put up a poster on May 11 urging an end to foreign economic sanctions against China.
Â 
Exact Charges Unclear
Although the poster echoed the official position, it is illegal to put up posters or petitions without approval. 
A year ago, posters at Beijing University helped set off student demonstrations.
University authorities deny that Mr. Peng was detained because of the poster, students said. 
They attribute the action to ''counterrevolutionary'' activities. 
Three other students who also signed the May 11 petition have not been arrested so far. 
But one or more other students were also detained in connection with the incident, two university teachers said.
Mr. Peng took part in the students' demonstrations a year ago, but he was not detained in the months after the army's June 4 suppression of the demonstrations and he was not on the list of 21 students sought after the violence.
No other arrests of students have been reported since 211 political prisoners were released this month, apparently as a gesture to the United States.
Still, the authorities are worried about unrest on the anniversary of the military action or before Beijing plays host to the Asian Games in the fall.

file: 2 Chinese Businessmen Get Death Sentences for Theft.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two businessmen were sentenced to death today for theft and embezzlement, as part of the Government's crackdown on economic crimes.
Tonight's television news programs showed the sentencing before a large public meeting held in a gymnasium. 
Both the publicity and the stiffness of the penalties seemed intended to discourage such corruption.
The ways business and Communist Party officials have illegally used their jobs to amass wealth were a major concern of the democracy movement this spring.

file: 2 From Hong Kong Expelled From Chinese Charter Panel.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today expelled two Hong Kong members from a committee drafting a constitution, known as the basic law, for the British colony after it returns to Chinese rule in 1997.
The two were outspoken supporters of the pro-democracy movement last spring, which the army crushed in June with heavy loss of life.
The official New China News Agency said the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the Parliament, had expelled Szeto Wah and Martin Lee because of ''their antagonistic stand against the Chinese Government.''
The announcement of their dismissal was widely expected in Hong Kong and came on the last day of the last consultation period for the basic law. 
The charter is to be examined by Parliament at its annual session in March.

file: 2 in Race Disagree On Defense And Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
With a troublesome economy and social issues as focal points of their rancorous race for the United States Senate, Senator Alfonse M. D'Amato and Attorney General Robert Abrams have virtually ignored any discussion of foreign policy issues.
Even on those rare occasions a foreign policy issue has been raised, like military budgets and the future of Russia, their answers have been framed in domestic concerns, like the impact on jobs and trade possibilities.
But a broader examination of their positions on world affairs reveals a striking difference between them despite their relative agreement on narrow issues like favoring improved relations with Israel after the periods of strain through the last four years.
In essence, Mr. D'Amato, a Republican seeking his third Senate term, and Mr. Abrams, a Democrat in his first bid for national office, embrace fundamentally different visions of the future, in that Mr. Abrams sees a world less threatening to the United States than Mr. D'Amato does.
Â 
Quick-Strike Force
The disparity emerges through the role they see the United States playing in the near future and the degree to which they would reduce the current national defense budget of $290 billion over the next five years.
While both envision the kind of mobile, quick-strike military force used in the Persian Gulf war in 1991, with a strong presence in Europe and other strategic places, Mr. D'Amato's force would be larger. 
He favors reductions of $85 billion in the defense budget over the next five years, and a decrease of 400,000 troops, to 1.5 million. 
Mr. Abrams would cut spending by more than three times as much, $280 billion over the same period, and require only 1.1 million troops.
Both see the need for reducing the 300,000 troops stationed in Europe -- Mr. Abrams to 75,000 to 100,000; Mr. D'Amato, to about 100,000.
In a recent interview, Mr. D'Amato assailed the continuing presence of Saddam Hussein in Iraq and the ethnic wars in Yugoslavia, citing them as reasons for slower defense reductions. 
He said the demise of the Soviet Union and Communist governments in Eastern Europe was no guarantee military threats had evaporated. 
He called North Korea "still a military threat" and said he worries about countries like Iran and China buying weapons on the open market.
Â 
Similar Concerns
Mr. Abrams cited similar concerns in a separate interview but not to the degree expressed by Mr. D'Amato, who he said "hasn't yet realized the cold war is over."
Mr. Abrams argued that the cuts and troop levels he advocates, drawn from a recent study by the Brookings Institution, would be sufficient to safeguard the interests of the United States.
While he would keep the United States military advantage over other countries, he played down the need for the United States to act as "the world's policeman," saying he preferred what he described as the "collective action" of the gulf war.
In an election year in which voters are far more focused on domestic concerns, Mr. D'Amato's approach of seeking smaller cuts in military spending is tied to jobs. 
He says slashing the military further would not only undermine national security but also devastate New York's economy by eliminating hundreds of thousands of jobs from defense contractors like Grumman on Long Island and General Electric in Schenectady.
But Mr. Abrams argued that the longer-term economic stability of New York requires conversion of military production to consumer businesses and reallocating dollars saved from military spending into programs to rebuild the nation's infrastructure. 
Mr. D'Amato favors the same kind of programs but a more gradual conversion rate.
Â 
'Responsible Reductions'
"With the end of the cold war, we cannot bury our head in the sand and miss this opportunity," Mr. Abrams said. 
"We can remain the strongest military power in the world, but at the same time get the benefit of the end of the cold war with responsible reductions in the military budget."
On trade issues, Mr. D'Amato favors approval of the North American Free Trade Agreement with Canada and Mexico, which means he supports the measure as written.
Like Gov. Bill Clinton in the Presidential race, Mr. Abrams supports the agreement in principle but would prefer amendments or parallel legislation to require Mexico to enforce its environmental standards and insure worker safety and the United States to provide retraining programs for Americans losing their jobs when their employers move to Mexico.
Both candidates contend that trade relations with China, specifically most-favored-nation status, should be tied to improved human-rights policies in China, especially in the wake of the Chinese Government's crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in 1989.
But Mr. Abrams takes a harder line against the Chinese Government than Mr. D'Amato, saying "the furthering of democratic principles and human rights should be at the cornerstone of foreign policy" with China.
The Senator called China a "very, very difficult situation."
In July 1991, he voted against granting most-favored-nation status to China because of Tiananmen Square. 
Less than two years later, when the issue came before Congress a second time, he voted with the minority to grant most-favored trade status as a way to encourage the Chinese leadership to adopt more democratic principles.
But a month later, after the President vetoed Congressional rejection of favored-nation trade status, the Senator joined 59 other senators in an override vote that fell 7 votes short.
Mr. Abrams contended that Mr. D'Amato's change in position represented either an inconsistency in position or political opportunism, in that it never appeared that the Senate would gather enough votes to deny China the preferred status.
The Senator disagreed, saying his initial support in 1991 was based on the President's satisfying concerns of Congress through an executive order that, among other things, protected Chinese students living in the United States by not forcing them to leave. 
His override vote, he said, was cast in the spirit of supporting human rights.
Both candidates chided the Bush Administration for reacting too slowly to help Russia toward democracy and a market economy. 
Both would encourage investment to further open Russia to American products.

file: 2 Skulls in China_ Early Humans Outside Africa_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Anatomically modern human beings, believed by many scientists to have first evolved in Africa, may have independently evolved in China and other parts of the world, a joint American-Chinese anthropological team has concluded.
That finding, being reported today in the British journal Nature, is based on the sizes and features of two very old skulls excavated from a site in China's Hubei Province.
The scientists, led by Dr. Li Tianyuan of the Hubei Institute of Archeology and Dennis A. Etler, a post-graduate student in anthropology from the University of California at Berkeley, believe the skulls are at least 350,000 years old and may represent a transition between Homo erectus and Homo sapiens. 
They describe the crania, or brain cases, of the two skulls as the most complete ever found in Asia for fossils of such great age.
Other scientists say the age of the skulls has not been determined precisely enough to support the conclusion that their owners actually lived at about the same time Homo sapiens appeared in Africa. 
But one matter on which paleoanthropologists appear to agree is that if the great age of the Chinese skulls can be confirmed, those specimens will be extremely valuable in helping to decipher the history of human evolution.
Â 
More Modern Features
The two skulls and other contemporary fossils were excavated by Dr. Li and a Chinese team in 1989-90. 
Although Chinese authorities have not allowed either the skulls or plaster casts made from them to leave China on loan, Mr. Etler, who speaks Mandarin, was permitted to work with Dr. Li in a collaborative study.
From the structure of rock sediments in which the skulls were embedded and from the remains of other animals in the same sediments, the scientists inferred that the human skulls date from the middle Pleistocene epoch some 350,000 or more years ago. 
More precise dating by measurement of ratios of radioactive isotopes has not been completed, Mr. Etler said in an interview.
Dr. Li and Mr. Etler evaluated 28 characteristics of the skulls, comparing them with comparable characteristics of other fossil human skulls. 
The best preserved of the two Chinese fossils has a long, low cranial vault, parietal bones that converge in a characteristic way, and other features that mark it as belonging to the species Homo erectus, the precursor of Homo sapiens. 
Homo erectus appeared in the fossil record some two million years ago and survived until less than 500,000 years ago.
But Dr. Li and Mr. Etler found other characteristics in the Chinese fossils not typical of Homo erectus but more similar to those of Homo sapiens -- the immediate ancestors of modern man (which is designated Homo sapiens sapiens). 
The more modern features include a rather flat face and sharply angled cheek bones. 
The Chinese skulls thus appear to the two scientists to represent a transitional blend of Homo erectus with Homo sapiens.
Paleoanthropologists are in broad agreement that Homo erectus originated in Africa and later migrated to other parts of the world. 
Among the first fossils scientists discovered of that species (formerly called Pithecanthropus erectus) were those unearthed before World War II in Java and China, and Homo erectus has also been found in Greece and elsewhere in Europe.
But there is little agreement among anthropologists as to where Homo sapiens started out.
"Dr. Li and I believe that alternatives to the idea that Homo sapiens originated in Africa are possible," Mr. Etler said. 
"We believe that modern man may have developed independently in various parts of the world from Homo erectus ancestors, migrating, intermingling, and finally fusing together as a kind of amalgam that we call Homo sapiens. 
Another possibility is that Homo sapiens actually began in China and radiated from there."
Dr. Philip Rightmire of the State University of New York at Binghamton is one of the scientists who sharply disagree.
"This is a controversial subject," he said, "but I do not believe in a multiregional origin for Homo sapiens."
The history of the human genus is one of movement, which for Homo erectus, began from Africa about one million years ago, he said. 
The hypothesis that modern man might have evolved first in Asia is not supported by any evidence, including the fossils studied by Dr. Li and Mr. Etler, he said.
Dr. Rightmire, who has examined photographs of the fossils, believes they are those of early Homo sapiens, not Homo erectus, and that their estimated age of more than 350,000 has yet to be proved. 
The features that Dr. Li and Mr. Etler believe mark the fossils as those of Homo erectus are so badly distorted, Dr. Rightmire said, that no conclusions can be drawn from them.
"Paleoanthropology is always controversial, even when specimens are well preserved, which these skulls are not," he said. 
"Neither the dates of the fossils nor their original shapes, which are squashed and crusted with some of the rock in which they were embedded, are yet known with any accuracy."
Mr. Etler acknowledged that the bones are too distorted to make definitive measurements, but said their general forms are suggestive.
Â 
Role of Ethnic Pride
"Others may disagree with our interpretation, and that's fine," he said. 
"But we felt it was important to bring this great Chinese material to the attention of scholars in the West."
Some scientists, including Dr. Rightmire, suggest that Chinese ethnic pride might color contentions by Chinese scientists that modern human beings might have evolved in China rather than Africa. 
Dr. Etler counters that a similar but opposite bias may color the theorizing of British and American paleoanthropologists who work exclusively with African fossils.
The recent discovery of a 1.6-million-year-old Homo erectus jawbone in the former Soviet republic of Georgia suggests that that species migrated from Africa much earlier than was formerly believed, and that modern man therefore had plenty of time to develop from his primitive ancestors in many parts of the world besides Africa, Mr. Etler said.

file: 2 Student Leaders in U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two leaders of the Chinese democracy movement who escaped to France last month arrived in the United States yesterday, and they are to announce the formation of a new opposition movement at a conference in Chicago this weekend.
The two leaders are Wuer Kaixi, a 21-year-old organizer of the student demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, and Yan Jiaqi, 47, a political scientist who was a close adviser to Zhao Ziyang, ousted General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Mr. Wuer and Mr. Yan escaped to Hong Kong and traveled secretly to France after being put on the Chinese Government's most-wanted list after the Communists suppressed the protests in Beijing on June 4.
A State Department official said the Administration had approved visas for the two men despite the likelihood that the action will prompt protests by Chinese Government officials, already enraged over the refuge granted in the American Embassy in Beijing to another leading dissident, Fang Lizhi.
Mr. Wuer and Mr. Yan plan to attend a meeting at the University of Chicago tomorrow through Sunday. 
There, they are to announce the establishment of a new umbrella group, another of the five founding members, Su Shaozhi, said.
As envisioned by its founders, the worldwide umbrella group will give impetus to the fragmented Chinese opposition, which includes Communist intellectuals in China and abroad and anti-Communists living in the United States and Taiwan.
While the Chinese Government has publicly admitted the arrest of about 2,000 people, Mr. Su said they were told that 10,000 people have been arrested in Beijing alone, with 120,000 arrested nationwide.
Correction
An article yesterday about the arrival of two Chinese student leaders in the United States misidentified the campus where a congress of Chinese students is to begin today. 
It is the University of Illinois at Chicago.

file: 2 U.S. Officials Went to Beijing Secretly in July.txt
text:
ï»¿
The White House said today that the national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, made a secret trip to China in July, shortly after President Bush suspended high-level meetings with the Chinese Government over the June crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators. 
Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger also went on the trip.
Word of the July visit came as the White House was still fielding criticism about a more recent visit to Beijing by Mr. Scowcroft and Mr. Eagleburger. The two men went to China 10 days ago to mend relations after hundreds of students died in June at the hands of the Chinese military in Tiananmen Square. 
That crackdown stirred deep anger and calls for sanctions among the American public and in Congress.
The second trip was announced by the White House only after Mr. Scowcroft and Mr. Eagleburger arrived in Beijing. 
July's trip had been kept secret, and it was made public by the White House today after it was reported by Cable News Network.
The pictures of Mr. Scowcroft during the visit this month, toasting Chinese leaders by candlelight ''as friends to resume our important dialogue,'' set off a wave of criticism in the United States. 
Many critics responded strongly again today to the news of the July visit, saying Mr. Bush has misled the American people.
Senator George J. Mitchell, Democrat of Maine, the majority leader, said he was ''astonished'' to learn that Mr. Bush had sent the two officials to China on ''another midnight mission, barely a month after the brutal killing of pro-democracy student demonstrators.''
''At that time, the President was saying there could not be business as usual with a Government that took such actions,'' he said. 
''Yet this is increasingly what seems to be happening.''
He said the trips ''make a mockery of our profession of concern for human rights and the stated ideals of our democratic system of government.''
Mr. Bush has been annoyed by the criticism of his policy in an area where he considers himself an expert, and he responded today in an interview with news-agency reporters, saying:
''I notice now that some of the critics who were so opposed and using this fantastically, diabolically anti-me language, they come up now saying, 'Well, if you get A, B and C, then it will be all right or then we'll understand.'
Let them just stay tuned in.''
The President would not say whether China had offered any gestures of good faith in return for his decision to make the diplomatic overtures after the June killings.
Mr. Bush also said he did not know when the Chinese dissident Fang Lizhi would be able to leave the United States Embassy in Beijing, where he has taken refuge since the crackdown.
The July visit came a month after the violent assault by Government forces on pro-democracy demonstrators, mostly students, and days after Mr. Bush directed on June 20 that there be a ban of all high-level exchanges of American officials with Beijing.
Â 
Statement by White House
In a statement today on the July visit, the White House said: ''General Scowcroft did undertake a mission to China for President Bush in July to personally underscore the U.S. shock and concern about the violence in Tiananmen Square and to impress upon the Chinese Government the seriousness with which this incident was viewed in the U.S. 
The President felt this face-to-face mission, like the one recently completed by General Scowcroft, was necessary to show the sense of purpose and direction of the U.S. 
Government.''
But if the purpose of the trip was to criticize the Chinese action, it is unclear why the White House did not make it known at the time.

file: 5 Countries to Meet on Reviving Cambodia Peace Talks, Paris Says.txt
text:

Amid new concern over stepped-up attacks by Khmer Rouge guerrillas, the United States, the Soviet Union, China, France and Britain are to meet here on Monday to discuss ways of reviving stalled peace efforts on Cambodia.
Announcing the meeting today, a French Government spokesman said the five Governments would give special attention to an Australian plan to put Cambodia under a temporary United Nations administration pending free elections.
Diplomats said the meeting was proposed by Washington and immediately endorsed by Moscow. 
As permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, the five powers have special responsibilities for international peace and security under the United Nations Charter.
''There has been a lot of talk of an enhanced role for the U.N. in Cambodia,'' a United States official said. 
''The situation on the ground makes it more urgent. 
The United States has been trying to get the diplomatic track going again for some time.''

Talks and a Surge in Fighting
A monthlong 19-nation peace conference on Cambodia ended in failure here in August amid sharp differences between the Vietnamese-backed Government of Prime Minister Hun Sen, which controls Phnom Penh, and three loosely allied rebel groups, including the Khmer Rouge.
At the time, officials said they did not expect new peace talks until after the warring factions had tested their strength anew during the current six-month dry season and, in particular, in the wake of the withdrawal of Vietnamese troops last September.
But diplomats said peace efforts are now being renewed in response to a surge of fighting and assertions of major victories by the Khmer Rouge, which brought terror to Cambodia during the rule of Pol Pot from 1975 to late 1978.

The Australian plan, modeled after a similar formula that enabled Namibia to hold free elections and end its occupation by South Africa last year, has been welcomed by the United States, France, Britain and the Soviet Union.

file: A 6-Foot-3, Blue-Eyed Taiwanese-American Is China_s Top Rocker.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dressed in a sequined jacket and white slacks, a slender blue-eyed, black-haired singer swivels his hips around the stage under the light of a flickering strobe as a crowd of 15,000 Chinese youngsters, officials and even grandparents watch the spectacle in fascination.
The singer's troupe of agile Chinese dancers - the women sometimes wearing no more than skimpy bathing suits - pranced about the circular stage in twos or threes, posing as butterflies or silver robots or rotating their hips in time with him.
The rock star is Fei Xiang, a dashing 28-year-old American who has dazzled about half a million Chinese around the country in a six-month tour that ends tonight. 
He has sold more cassette tapes than any other singer in China, the Culture Ministry says, and his murmuring love songs and glitzy stage shows have made him perhaps the most popular singer on the Chinese mainland.
Mr. Fei, whose American name is Kris Phillips, has an American father and a Chinese mother from Beijing. 
He was born in Taiwan, where he grew up until he moved to California to attend Stanford University. 
He speaks both Chinese and English without an accent, but he sings only in Chinese. 
He plans to leave the Chinese music world and begin a career as an actor in New York.
Â 
'Not So Much His Singing'
His stardom here is partly the result of his looks and his American connections. 
Fans invariably comment on Mr. Fei's 6-foot-3 frame and his blue eyes, and on his links with the United States.
''It's not so much his singing,'' said a young Chinese man who attended a concert the other day. 
''It's because he's from America and because to Chinese women he's like a prince riding up on a white horse.''
At one of his farewell-to-China performances, the audience chuckled when he dressed in gaudy robes, sang a modern version of Beijing opera, then stripped down to a T-shirt and swimming trunks for a song about summer. 
Some viewers looked mildly embarrassed when Chinese dancing girls appeared in scanty silver costumes.
Since the crackdown on the democracy movement in May, the Chinese authorities have banned some Western-style films and books and may have blacklisted some popular Chinese singers. 
One of those in disfavor is Cui Jian, who was becoming one of Beijing's hottest singers, with lyrics that expressed an inner struggle and cried out for change and freedom. 
Other popular singers, like Hou Dejian, who was affiliated with the democracy movement, are staying out of sight.
Â 
'Not a Bourgeois Liberal'
Mr. Fei, on the other hand, has been given a free rein. 
Not only has he been allowed to go ahead with his tour despite the campaign against ''bourgeois liberalization,'' or Western influences, but one of his performances is to be shown on national television. 
One reason for the distinction is that Mr. Fei is less overtly political than other singers; another is that he is perhaps excused in part because he is American.
''He's not a bourgeois liberal,'' said Lu Hongsheng, a director of art and literature at the Culture Ministry. 
''His singing and his acting are very natural. 
And his attitude is earnest. 
He is very hard working.''
While Mr. Fei does not write his own lyrics, some of his songs subtly challenge Chinese tradition:
''Listen to me, Dad, give me the freedom to grow up,'' he sings in a song called ''Say No More, Dad.''
''I don't want to listen to all that you've arranged for me.''
From the moment he gave his first concert in Beijing on May 19, the evening martial law was declared in the capital, Mr. Fei has seen his reputation soar in 63 performances in 12 cities. 
Throughout the tour, the house has been packed for every performance except in the southern city of Canton, where Cantonese songs are preferred to Mandarin ones. 
Ticket prices ranged from $2.15 to $10.80, considerable sums in a country where a month's salary is typically $40.
Â 
An Overnight Star
Mr. Fei began to sing in Taiwan after graduating from the Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theater in New York City. 
In 1985, he abandoned Taiwan for the Chinese mainland, partly because the mainland was a larger market and partly because his career was not doing as well as he hoped. 
He had the good fortune to be picked for a Chinese New Year program that was broadcast on national television.
''That show established everything overnight,'' Mr. Fei said. 
''When it counts, I am considered a foreign guest, but the audience doesn't treat me as someone from outside.''
Since his debut, Mr. Fei has recorded five cassettes - most of them in recording studios in Canton - for the Chinese market, and this has brought him the equivalent of about $200,000 for each of the three years he has worked in China. 
Ten percent of his earnings go to the Government as royalties, and the rest, after taxes, is paid in local currency. 
He says he converts the money to dollars with private businessmen, a common practice.
Â 
Aside From Money
Mr. Fei's three-day farewell engagement in the capital this week brought in $152,838 in ticket sales alone, although he says he loses money on his concerts because of the high costs, including importing the sound system, stage, lights and mixing board.
Mr. Fei's income in China may be less than he could earn as a popular singer in Taiwan or even Hong Kong, but his ascent to the top of the Chinese market, he says, became a personal challenge mixed with a desire to contribute to China's fledgling entertainment industry.
''It's important in China to develop a popular culture,'' Mr. Fei said. 
''In China, the Government has gotten by with filling the people's lives with five-year plans, and now that is no longer going to happen. 
People aren't going to fill their minds, their days, their lives with that stuff anymore.''

file: A Bid for Power In Motion for Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
When members of the International Olympic Committee vote later this week on several changes to the executive board, the 11 officers and members who virtually run the organization, He Zhenliang of China is widely expected to gain a position as vice president.
Attaining such an elevated status among the 92 individuals who maintain and shape the Olympic Games is an honor unto itself. 
In He's case it also carries an implicit vote of confidence that Beijing can successfully stage the 11th Asian Games next year, despite concerns over more clashes like those last spring in Tiananmen Square between Government troops and members of a pro-democracy movement.
The disturbances caused minor disruptions in preparations for the Games when crews were unable to deliver construction materials to various sites and some workers wandered off the job to watch or participate in the demonstrations.
'Not So Serious'
''I can't say the turmoil had no affect on things,'' said He, a 59-year-old vice minister for physical culture and sports in Beijing and an I.O.C. member since 1981. 
''But it was not so serious. 
The disruption was only for a few days, and all the preparations went on without one day of stopping.''
Just as the 10th Asian Games in 1986 enabled Seoul, South Korea, to prove it could successfully stage the Olympics, which proceeded free of incident last fall, the next Asian Games play a critical role in Beijing's attempt to show itself as a worthy Olympic host. 
Chinese sports officials envision Beijing bidding for the summer Games of 2000, which the I.O.C. will award in 1993. 
A final decision by Chinese authorities, He said, would be made after the Asian Games.
Meanwhile, the Chinese Goverment and the municipal government of Beijing have demonstrated their support of the next year's Games by allocating more than $600 million for the renovation of 11 existing sports facilities, the construction of 16 new ones and other capital improvements. 
Altogether, He said, the athletes from as many as 39 countries will use 33 different competition venues and have access to 46 training facilities.
Ultimately, however, the success of the 1990 Games and Beijing's viability as a host for the Olympics a decade later are more likely to be measured in political terms, a prime consideration since 1972 in Munich, where members of the Israeli team were murdered by terrorists.
Â 
Constant Fears
In Seoul, preparations for the 1986 Asian Games and the 1988 Olympics continued under constant fears of disruptive activity by North Korea and by the occasional student demonstrations in Seoul that turn violent. 
Not all the fears were unfounded: A week before the Asian Games, a bomb exploded in Seoul's Kimpo Airport, killing five people, and 10 months before the Olympics, a bomb exploded aboard a South Korean airliner in mid-flight, killing 115.
North Korea denied involvement in either incident, but that did little to reduce the anxiety level in South Korea. 
Nor did the periodic clashes between students and the police in Seoul, which continued as the Olympics were under way.
While the present calm in and around Beijing would seem to indicate a return to normalcy in the aftermath of events last spring, the president of the Olympic Council of Asia, Sheik Fahad al-Ahmad al-Sabah of Kuwait, was concerned enough about next year to raise the issue of security and the current state of martial law in meetings with Chinese government leaders on a recent 10-day visit.
Â 
Strong Sense of Support
''The safety of the participants in the Games is the first thing I discussed with the Chinese people,'' al-Sabah said in an interview today. 
''I wanted to make sure there would be no military or political interference, and I was assured by the highest authorities that everything would be as normal.''
During his visit, al-Sabah said that he sensed nearly unanimous support for the Asian Games by the people he met, including students. 
The only opposition he has encountered since June, he said, was from Chinese students living in Hong Kong and the United States.
''They wrote me letters saying that Beijing should not have the Games,'' he said. 
''My reply to them was that I would listen to the Chinese people living in Beijing and China, not those living outside.''
By the end of the year, sports officials in Beijing will have a better sense of where they stand with regard to the Asian Games, which open in 13 months. 
The last of regional championships in 10 sports will have been held, giving the system and facilities a test run, with almost a year to rectify any remaining problems.
''Thailand has had the Games three times, India twice and China never,'' said He. 
''Our people are keen to see the Asian Games succeed, not only for themselves but for all the people of Asia.''

file: A Developer_s Big Gamble on the New Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
At the ribbon-cutting ceremony for a customs station on the China-Hong Kong border, Gordon Y. S. Wu was patiently listening to an address by a senior Chinese official. 
It was one of Mr. Wu's first China ventures, and all his profits from building the station were to come from public tolls.
Suddenly, Mr. Wu's face went red. 
The deputy mayor of Shenzhen, a special economic zone on the border, was saying that no tolls would be charged.
"He took me by surprise," said Mr. Wu, a short, blunt-talking man who is principal owner and managing director of Hopewell Holdings Ltd., a property development company that is one of the largest foreign investors in China. 
" 'Hey, there's supposed to be a contract,' I said. 
But he said he wanted to take care of the Hong Kong people and charge no toll."
Mr. Wu complained to Zhao Ziyang, Prime Minister at the time the project was finished in 1985. 
Mr. Zhao agreed with Mr. Wu but would not overrule the deputy mayor. 
Finally, China agreed to buy Mr. Wu out of the contract.
Since then, doing business in China has not gotten much easier. 
But Mr. Wu, one of Asia's best-known developers, is stubbornly plodding ahead.
Indeed, while many of Hong Kong's taipans, or "big bosses," are trying to relocate their empires to Western countries before Britain cedes control of the territory to the Chinese in 1997, Mr. Wu is rolling the dice in the other direction -- toward China itself.
Mr. Wu is betting that dramatic growth in China and other developing countries in Southeast Asia will provide a steady stream of profits for at least the next decade or so.
The bets are enormous. 
Mr. Wu's company is building a 188-mile superhighway connecting Hong Kong, Macao and the city of Guangzhou in southern China's Guangdong Province. 
He is proposing to build a multibillion-dollar road and rail network in Bangkok, Thailand. 
And he is planning to erect a 91-story hotel in Hong Kong.
Not everyone thinks Mr. Wu will emerge a winner.
"Gordon Wu is trying to reduce his exposure in Hong Kong, but he's getting more exposed to Thailand and China," said Edward Chan, an analyst at ChinTung Research International Ltd. 
"They will continue to be fraught with political risks."
Mr. Chan says Hopewell has capital commitments in Asia of an estimated $6.8 billion over the next 10 years. 
It already has $250 million invested in China, according to Mr. Wu.
But others say that Mr. Wu's projects in southern China could not only change the landscape but could mean a giant economic leap for Guangdong and Hong Kong -- and, of course, for Hopewell Holdings.
"He may have too many ideas in his head at one time, and many people think Gordon Wu is talking too big, given the resources he has," said Steven So, an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities in Hong Kong. 
But if he can succeed with the superhighway, "then more governments will have confidence in Hopewell to do construction in their countries."
For his part, Mr. Wu is characteristically confident. 
"I always deliver on what I say," he said. 
"Maybe not in the time I want."
Mr. Wu, the seventh of nine children, began his company in 1969 with a $2 million loan guaranteed by his father, who had owned a taxi fleet. 
In the early 1970's, when Mr. Wu was still a relative unknown, the Government objected to him putting up a 66-story headquarters building outside Hong Kong's traditional business district. 
Mr. Wu took the case to Hong Kong's Supreme Court and won.
For a decade, his building was the tallest in Hong Kong until the Bank of China surpassed it in 1990. 
Mr. Wu is now planning to construct the Tower Hotel, which would take back the title.
Mr. Wu and his family own at least 51 percent of Hopewell Holdings, which earned the equivalent of $93 million in the year ended June 30.
Along the way, Mr. Wu, who is 55 years old and holds a degree in civil engineering from Princeton University, has earned a reputation as the quintessential Hong Kong entrepreneur, an ambitious man who takes on enormous risks and challenges.
To get his bankers on board, he often sinks in large chunks of his own capital and then persuades them to lend more money without a guarantee. 
Repayment comes only from the cash flow generated by the project. 
This way, Hopewell, which is traded on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, can limit its exposure to its share in a joint venture with a foreign partner.
Nowhere is this combination of risk-taking and limited exposure more at play than with Mr. Wu's biggest project to date: the superhighway connecting Hong Kong, Macau and Guangzhou, which is expected to cost $1.2 billion.
During the past several years, Hong Kong has shifted its manufacturing base to Guangdong Province, but the infrastructure there, while better than elsewhere in China, is still quite poor.
Trucks and cars transporting merchandise or raw materials between Hong Kong and Guangzhou must take narrow winding roads, stopping at times to let farmers cross with their chickens or pigs. 
The 75-mile trip takes seven hours by bus; Mr. Wu hopes to cut that to 90 minutes.
"I first proposed the superhighway in 1979, and that's when people said I was a dreamer," said Mr. Wu. "I saw it as a parallel to the New Jersey Turnpike."
"Deng Xiaoping had just announced an open door and reform and so I said, 'Hey, let's go in there, sweet talk them into giving us a franchise and do something meaningful,' " Mr. Wu said. 
"They all believed in railways. 
I told them railways belong to the 19th century, and I went on to explain Henry Ford."
The project took a great deal of sweet-talking, but finally Mr. Wu was able to break ground in 1987, operating through a joint venture with the Guangdong authorities. 
The project has been delayed numerous times, and construction was halted for three months after the 1989 military crackdown in Beijing.
Because of political demonstrations in China, and jitters in the financial community toward the mainland, Mr. Wu had to cancel plans to raise almost $500 million through a stock rights issue scheduled for May 1989. 
Instead, Mr. Wu put up $150 million of his own capital before he went to the banks to raise $800 million last year. 
Despite the political uncertainty, the banks supported him. 
The Chinese are expected to contribute more than $100 million to the financing.
Mr. Wu plans to earn his return through tolls, charging the equivalent of about $12 for cars from Hong Kong and less for Chinese cars. 
Mr. Wu will get 40 percent of the profits for the first 10 years and 30 percent for the next 20 years, with the remaining profits going to his Chinese partners.
By the year 2000, Mr. Wu could make annual profits of $170 million from the tolls, according to James Capel (Far East) Ltd. 
This would be on top of recovering his equity and repaying bank loans.
The first phase of the project, to link Hong Kong to Guangzhou, is scheduled for completion in mid-1994. 
But Mr. Wu hopes to complete it a year ahead of schedule so that he can collect early toll profits as a bonus agreed to by the Chinese authorities.
Some analysts are skeptical that Mr. Wu can finish ahead of time, given the difficulties he already has had, but Mr. Wu has beat the clock before.
In 1987, he completed a coal-fired power station for Guangdong in 22 months, about one year before the projected completion date. 
He collected about $50 million in bonuses.
While doing business in China is not easy, it is no more difficult than in many other parts of the developing world, Mr. Wu said.
"It's like pulling teeth, but the Philippines is just as difficult," said Mr. Wu. "They have the Filipino bureaucracy."
Mr. Wu recently completed a $42 million power plant in Navotas, north of Manila. 
He signed the contract in November 1989 and brought in his shovels and bulldozers, only to confront a military coup attempt against President Corazon Aquino at the end of December. 
After that settled down, there was a flood, an earthquake and two typhoons. 
By August 1990, Mr. Wu sent out the first bit of electricity and everyone congratulated him.
Now, he is negotiating the construction of a $710 million coal-fired power plant in the Philippines, which he hopes to complete in 1994, and another power plant in Guangdong Province, which is expected to cost $1.4 billion.
This summer, Mr. Wu raised about $725 million through a rights issue, mainly to finance the power plants, some hotel development and the grand transportation scheme he is planning for Bangkok.
"A fellow walking the tightrope at the circus to me is very dangerous," Mr. Wu said, in discussing the risks he takes. 
"You pay me a million dollars and you'd never get me up there. 
But to the fellow who knows, it's easy, isn't it?"
Â 
Â 
Â 
THE ROAD TO BANGKOK
When asked whether his company might be too dependent on China, Gordon Y. S. Wu points to a pile of maps of Bangkok and launches into his favorite topic these days: his proposed $3.2 billion double-decker elevated road and railway system for the Thai capital, which has a population of about 6 million.
"It's big, innovative, profitable," he said.
The project began a few years ago, when Mr. Wu found himself in heavy traffic on a business trip to Bangkok, long known for its congested streets and roads.
"I got stuck like everybody else on Sukhumvit Road," he said. 
"A lot of people start cussing and swearing about the traffic. 
I look at it and say, 'Here's an opportunity. 
Let's crack that problem.'
"
Using Tokyo's transportation system as a model, Mr. Wu has proposed tearing up Bangkok's current railway and turning it into an elevated system with shops below. 
He would then add a second level over the railway to accommodate a six-lane highway.
There are two big advantages to this approach, he said. 
There is no need to demolish any housing, because the proposed system would follow the existing rail route. 
And profits would come not so much from passenger tickets -- which could sell for as little as 25 cents -- as from the shopping malls, restaurants and other properties that Mr. Wu would develop underneath the 37 miles of railway line.
Just as final contract negotiations for the project were taking place in February, however, Thailand was shaken by a military coup.
Now, Mr. Wu is embroiled in negotiations with the new Government over development rights and tax concessions. 
While he still must overcome some local opposition, Mr. Wu says he is optimistic he will soon be able to sign a contract.
He is hoping to send in his bulldozers before the end of the year. 
If all goes smoothly, he says, the project should be completed in 1999.

text:
ï»¿
So often in Japanese business life, success comes to those who avoid risks and follow the well-trodden paths. 
Then there are people like Kazuo Wada, chairman of the Yaohan Department Store Company, who personifies another Japanese type: the devoted renegade.
The avuncular Mr. Wada, a trim 61-year-old man with a ready smile who prefers plain gray suits, is an unlikely radical, but in his genteel but determined way he has built one of Japan's most unusual retailers by breaking just about every rule of the game as it is played here.
His guiding business philosophy, he said, has been ''to give my company a special character that nobody else had.''
He has clearly succeeded.
Atypical Geography
Where the economic and Government center of Tokyo has been the focus for most big Japanese retailers, the Yaohan supermarket chain has eschewed the capital for the provinces. 
While most Japanese companies expanding overseas have gone to the wealthy nations of Europe or the United States, Yaohan has focused on Hong Kong, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan and Brunei.
Instead of renting landmark locations, Yaohan generally searches for less glamorous but practical sites -the kinds of places where you might find a vegetable stand, which is how Yaohan got started in a provincial town outside Tokyo.
And most Japanese companies have only one ideology: work hard and be loyal. 
But Mr. Wada and his mother, Katsu, who helped found the company, are leaders in a new Japanese religion, known as Seicho No Ie, which is loosely translated as House of God's Children. 
It is an amalgam of Shinto, Buddhism and Christianity, which stresses the Confucian ethic of respecting authority and of seeking harmony. 
Nearly all of Yaohan's managers are members of the sect.
Yet no step has been more unusual, or risky, than the one Mr. Wada announced late last year to move Yaohan's international headquarters from Japan to Hong Kong, the politically fragile British colony that is to revert to Chinese control in 1997.
Many Chinese professionals are fleeing Hong Kong because of concern over how the Communists on the mainland will manage the prosperous capitalist enclave. 
But where they spot trouble, Mr. Wada says he spots opportunity. 
As he noted, from his new home in the prestigious Peak district of Hong Kong island, he will look out over the largest potential market in the world.
The headquarters move is partly a matter of thrift. 
Hong Kong has some of the lowest taxes in the world, and land prices there are considerably cheaper than the inflated levels of Japan.
''Taxes and land are one consideration,'' Mr. Wada admitted. 
''But more important was that I see big possibilities in Asia and China in the future. 
This is the era of Asia.''
Of China, he states bluntly that it is not rich enough yet to support his supermarkets, but that will come. 
He said that over the next few decades he plans to develop along the country's relatively prosperous coastal regions a huge network for buying goods as well as for a chain of stores. 
It will all add up to one of the most extensive, if not the largest, distribution systems connecting all of Asia.
''Yaohan has developed into an interesting story, in part because they have realized that there is clearly a higher profit potential overseas than in Japan, given the costs you face here,'' said Mike Allen, a retailing analyst at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, a securities house.
Mr. Allen said he is somewhat skeptical of Mr. Wada's ability to pull off his plan. 
Two problems are the store's middle-brow image, which may make it hard for it to distribute higher margin goods later, and some labor problems that he said it has had in the United States, reportedly because of its insistence that employees follow the company's rigid tenets. 
That may make it tough for Yaohan to maintain consistent service outside of Japan. 
Nonetheless, Mr. Allen said the strategy is potentially attractive in the long run.
Although Mr. Wada's unusual vision is distinctly Asian, it is not being applied only to this part of the world. 
Yaohan operates six stores in the United States, including a large supermarket in Edgewater, N.J., just across the Hudson River from Manhattan. 
The store sells Japanese and Asian foods almost exclusively.
In New Jersey, Mr. Wada plans to build Yaohan's first hotel, which will have some unusual features, by Edgewater standards. 
Its roof will be equipped with a traditionally Japanese pool-sized communal tub. 
After taking the cedar-scented waters, guests will be able to relax in Japanese cotton robes, yukata, on the traditional straw tatami mats, eating Japanese food and sipping sake as the lights of New York City blink in the background.
In Japan, Yaohan has 55 company-owned stores and another 35 franchised stores around the country. 
In addition, it has 22 stores overseas, including a big new wholesale distribution center in Singapore.
About a third of the $1.2 billion in sales it registered in the fiscal year that ended May 20, 1989, come from its international business. 
But it expects the overseas sales to match the domestic sales by 1992. 
The company reported a profit of $18.5 million in the last fiscal year, a 32 percent jump from the previous year.
Â 
A Folk Hero
As different as it is in many ways, Yaohan is very much a creature of Japan. 
Mr. Wada's mother has become something of a folk hero here, with a life story that could have been written by an Asian Horatio Alger. 
Her tale was told, in fact, in one of the most popular television series ever broadcast in Japan, which gave her the fictional name, Oshin.
It told of how she came from a family so poor she was put to work before she was 10 years old, and of how her hard work and persistence brought her business success and, eventually, a good husband. 
Together, they started a greengrocer that eventually became the chain of stores in the hands of her dedicated and pious son. 
It is the sort of tale of struggle and success against long odds that the Japanese immediately identify with.
Although Yaohan is publicly held, members of the Wada family dominate the management and maintain the largest shareholding. 
One younger brother, Terumasa, is president, and another, Mitsumasa, is senior vice president. 
Together, the family members own about 13 percent of the company's stock.
For his part, Mr. Wada concedes that, in many ways, he was forced to take the international route. 
''The main reason was high land prices'' in Japan, he said. 
''If land had been more reasonable, I wouldn't have gone overseas.''
Â 
Low-Rent Neighborhood
In an interview in the decidedly modest office his company keeps in a low-rent Tokyo neighborhood, he also said: ''I had the choice of opening stores in Osaka, Tokyo or overseas. 
Given the situation with land prices, I chose overseas.''
After an initial failure in 1971 in Brazil, which has a large Japanese community, he persisted and began to open successful stores around Asia. 
Yaohan's first American location, at Fresno, Calif., was opened in 1979. 
Now Yaohan has stores in California in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Costa Mesa and Torrance, as well as the New Jersey store. 
Mr. Wada admitted that the largest, in Edgewater, was not profitable yet, but he said it was meeting all his projections.
Although the American stores show promise, Mr. Wada said Asia still offers the best prospects for growth because of the region's explosive accumulation of wealth and rising standard of living. 
He rattles off precise figures of the national income of the nations of Southeast Asia, and clearly specifies Yaohan's prospects in each.
Once he moves to Hong Kong in a couple of months, Mr. Wada will be giving up his new $7 million home on a spectacular seaside site in Atami, a hot spring resort 55 miles southwest of Tokyo. 
But, as he put it, ''All of Asia will become my home.''

text:

China faces a difficult battle in Congress this summer to retain its preferential access to the United States market, but you would hardly know it from the unconciliatory remarks being made by Chinese officials.
Ambassador Zhu Qizhen, in a speech last week outlining his Government's position in the coming debate, took a hard and at times menacing line. 
China has not violated any human rights, he said; it does not have a problem trade surplus with the United States, and it keeps adequate controls over its exports of arms and nuclear technology.
Â 
Retaliation Is Likely
China will also use high tariffs to drive American companies out of its markets if the United States does not renew the current trade privileges, Mr. Zhu added. 
Billions of dollars in contracts and thousands of jobs in industries from aircraft manufacturing to agricultural chemical production would be at risk, he said.
Mr. Zhu's remarks were only a little more strident than other policy statements by Chinese officials. 
For China has pursued a pugnacious four-pronged lobbying strategy here that has dismayed its friends and gladdened its foes.
Mr. Zhu's comments were not what members of Congress had hoped to hear. 
The massacre at Tiananmen Square in 1989, along with reports in the last month by a human rights group and a Congessman that political prisoners are being forced to produce goods for export, have so stained the reputation of China's leadership that diplomats' assurances carry little credibility.
A growing number of American lawmakers say they want China's "most favored nation" trade status revoked outright. 
"The Ambassador's threats will strengthen their case," said Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat who opposes renewal unless it is linked to human rights improvements.
Â 
Bush Decision Due by June 3
President Bush must notify Congress by June 3 if he wishes to renew for one year China's most-favored status, which is due to expire on July 3. 
A motion of disapproval, which seems likely to be introduced, would have to pass both houses of Congress within 90 days, and it probably would provoke a Presidential veto.
When President Bush renewed China's trade status last year, the House voted to disapprove the renewal. 
The Senate considered similar action but did not take a vote before the 90-day time limit expired, so the renewal stood.
Several lobbyists who favor renewal expect that this year President Bush will recommend a renewal of the special status, that both houses of Congress will disapprove it, and that the President will veto the disapproval. 
It is possible, though unlikely, that Congress will then override the veto.
Another possibility is that Congress will pair its disapproval of the status for China with approval of a renewal for the Soviet Union, said one lobbyist who favors a renewal for China. 
In that case, the President would face a particularly difficult dilemma, because the Soviet Union is in desperate need of certain trade subsidies and other credits that indirectly depend on a renewal of its status.
Â 
Tariff Would Rise to 47.48%
The U.S.-China Business Council, a Washington-based group of American companies with investments in China, has estimated that the average tariff for the 25 biggest categories of American imports from China will rise to 47.48 percent, from 8.35 percent, if most-favored status is not renewed. 
With this status, Chinese products enter the United States at the lowest rate available to any American trading partner for each category of goods.
The test of China's strategy will come soon. 
Congress appeared increasingly likely last week to authorize the Administration to negotiate a free-trade agreement with Mexico and another round of reductions in global trade barriers. 
At the same time, China's trade status was moving quickly toward the top of the agendas of Washington's economic policy makers.
An eclectic alliance of trade protectionists, anti-Communist conservatives and liberal human rights advocates opposes an unconditional extension.
The strongest of China's four lobbying themes has been that Congress and the Administration should value the United States' strategic relationship with China too highly to risk endangering it for the sake of human rights or trade surpluses. 
President Bush, a former chief of the American liaison office in Beijing, is widely seen as particularly influenced by this argument.
Â 
Overestimation by Chinese
But the Chinese consistently overestimate how much weight is given to such long-term considerations on Capitol Hill, said Warren W. Williams, the president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong. 
Mr. Williams has led a delegation to lobby Washington in support of the Chinese.
"Their fundamental lack of understanding of how things work in Washington, D.C., is a continuing surprise," he said.
Another Chinese lobbying tactic is to insist that China guarantees different human rights, including rights to food and shelter, than the the United States does. 
American officials, by this argument, should not judge a foreign country by their own standards.
Chinese officials also criticize American trade statistics showing that China shipped $15.1 billion worth of goods to the United States last year while importing products worth only $4.8 billion. 
Excluding Chinese exports that pass through Hong Kong, the trade is nearly in balance, Mr. Zhu contended. 
But this argument has not been persuasive in Washington, Mr. Williams said.
Â 
Attempt to Intimidate U.S.
The last of China's four approaches to lobbying in Washington has been intimidation. 
"I have a fondness for the American people," Mr. Zhu said after his speech on Tuesday. 
"I really don't want to see West German or Japanese people there, taking over."
Business conditions for Americans in China are said to be deteriorating already. 
For three weeks, Chinese negotiators have been stalling in contract talks with American companies, said an American businessman with extensive contacts there, who spoke on condition that he not be identified. 
He said the Chinese negotiators were acting on Government instructions.
But in a possible change of tack, the New China News Agency said Saturday that China would send a buying mission to the United States, Reuters reported.
Some people in Washington question the credibility of Chinese threats to exclude American businesses and products. 
"They may not love capitalism; they may not love human rights, but they love money," Representative Pelosi said.

text:
ï»¿
IN the pottery and porcelain of most of the world, there are few developments that do not have some relation to Chinese ceramics. 
An exhibition that gives some sense of the evolution and highlights of Chinese ceramics, as well as a shorter history of Japanese ceramics, can be seen at the Asia Society in Manhattan through Sept. 
3.
The show covers five major periods of Chinese ceramics: the Tang dynasty (618 to 907), notable for glazed earthenware; the Song dynasty (960 to 1279), known for its stoneware and the green glaze known as celadon; the Yuan dynasty (1279 to 1368), when porcelain began to appear; the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644), associated with blue and white wares, and the Qing dynasty (1644 to 1912), notable for rich floral porcelains.
The first object the viewer sees is a striking glazed earthenware horse about 30 inches long. 
The realistically modeled cream and tan animal is a tomb figure from the Tang dynasty, dated around the eighth century, as is a glazed sculpture of a court lady playing cymbals. 
She was probably one figure in a funerary set that would have constituted a whole burial orchestra.
Celadon ware from northern China in the Song dynasty is not as familiar as the pale, rich jadelike celadon of southern China. 
The olive-hued glaze on several small northern pieces in the show is incised with stylized leaves and flowers.
Chinese ceramics were traded over much of the world. 
A 17th-century platter showing a gazelle in a garden belonged to Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal.
The exhibition, in which all the work is from the Asia Society's permanent collection, includes a number of Ming pieces in blue and white porcelain. 
On many dragons cavort among waves or clouds. 
The Chinese section ends with a few examples of fruit and flower paintings on porcelain, a technique perfected under the Manchus in the Qing dynasty.
The Japanese work that makes up the rest of the ceramics exhibition covers a shorter but important stretch of time: the 17th and 18th centuries. 
This era saw the development of porcelain in Japan, the expansion of the Japanese export market, the emergence of legendary potters like Ninsei and Kakiemon and the continued creation of pieces for the traditional tea ceremony.
Among the stoneware tea-ceremony objects on display is a modern-looking square dish with a broad ceramic handle used as a food tray. 
There is also a tea storage jar boldly painted with black birds on a cream glaze by Ninsei, a mid-17th-century potter known for his masterful painting on earthenware.
Among the porcelain pieces are several figures. 
Two guardian lions, about 10 inches high, are elaborately patterned and colored in the style of Kakiemon. 
The first potter named Kakiemon, or his son, is credited with establishing overglaze painting on porcelain in the last third of the 17th century.
Also on view at the Asia Society, 725 Park Avenue (70th Street), is a continuing exhibition of Korean porcelain of the Yi dynasty (1392 to 1910). 
Since both Korean and Chinese ceramics influenced Japanese work, it is interesting to compare all three.
