text:
ï»¿
The only fact that everyone agrees on is that some gangsters visited Tang Rimei's home in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen one day last year and beat her brother to death in front of her.
Miss Tang, a slender 23-year-old woman, says the reason is simple: she was a whistle-blower, calling attention to a web of corruption involving senior officials at the company she worked for. 
The easiest way to silence her, after threats failed, she said, was to murder her and her brother, adding that the killers became frightened and ran away before they got to her.
The authorities offer little comment. 
They hint that the killing may have been the result of a street quarrel or a misunderstanding over Miss Tang's use of a company-owned apartment. 
But they do not explain why the trial of the accused killers was abruptly suspended a month ago when one of them reportedly stated in court that the company chief had ordered the attack.
"This case shows that the reforms in China haven't been carried out correctly," said Yang Zhenguo, a co-worker of Miss Tang who backs her up on every detail. 
"And it shows that there are no human rights in China."
Â 
Window Into Corruption
The case offers a remarkable window onto the web of corruption in southern China, the most prosperous part of the country. 
Shenzhen, which is nestled next to Hong Kong, is probably the richest city in China and is known for a freewheeling atmosphere.
It is impossible to confirm independently the accusations that Miss Tang and Mr. Yang make, but the general portrait that they paint of widespread graft fits with accounts from many other Chinese. 
The only unusual aspect of this case, aside from the killing, is that Miss Tang and Mr. Yang have escaped to Hong Kong and are willing to be quoted by name.
Miss Tang first went to Shenzhen in 1989 and eventually found work at the Yellow River Corporation, a successful trading company that spent large sums of money cultivating support from party and government officials. 
She said she was appalled when the company chief, a man named Wang, asked her to forge contracts that would be used to defraud the banks.
The executives at Yellow River specialized in defrauding banks and out-of-town companies, said Miss Tang and Mr. Yang, who also worked there.
Â 
Writing a Thousand Letters
Miss Tang said that when she tried to report her allegations about Yellow River, local officials simply laughed and reported her to Mr. Wang. According to her account, Mr. Wang cut off her salary and sent thugs to harass her. 
This only outraged Miss Tang even more, and she took an extremely rare course in China: she fought back.
She began writing letters to officials all over China, more than 1,000 letters in all. 
She also pasted posters around the city denouncing the corruption.
Her older brother, Tang Richeng, came to Shenzhen to protect her. 
Because Shenzhen is a special economic zone adjacent to Hong Kong, it is illegal for outsiders to enter without permission, but Miss Tang said she and her brother bribed soldiers and police to get working papers.
According to Miss Tang's version of events, a gang of hoodlums led by two Yellow River employees came to Mr. Yang's company-owned apartment in which she had found refuge, and announced that they were going to kill her on orders of "Boss Wang."
She quotes them as saying that a deal had been worked out for them to serve a few months in prison and then be released.
"My big brother tried to protect me, so they hit him with their iron bars," she recalled. 
"I was screaming, 'Help!
Help!'
They hit me a little bit, but because my big brother was protecting me they mostly hit him. 
Then some people came by, and they got scared and ran away."
The accused killers were arrested a few days later, but Miss Tang said that when she demanded that Mr. Wang be arrested as well, the police detained her and threatened her. 
After what she described as two more attempts on her life, which she says she foiled by barricading herself inside the apartment so that the hired killers could not get to her before she had raised the neighborhood with her screams, she fled China. 
Now she is applying for a visa to resettle in the United States.
The trial of the accused killers was held in late February. 
But after the reported confession of one of the Yellow River employees that Mr. Wang planned the whole operation, the court suspended the trial indefinitely.
"Some things are still under investigation," Chen Zongyi, the Deputy Chief Judge of the Intermediate People's Court in Shenzhen, said by telephone.
But an official of the Yellow River Corporation, who would identify himself only by his surname, Sha, said Mr. Wang was still employed and receiving his paychecks, but was not coming to work.
Mr. Sha said Yellow River officials had merely been trying to force Tang Rimei from the company-owned apartment when a fight resulted in which her brother was killed.
"This incident has been exaggerated," Mr. Sha said. 
"It was all a misunderstanding."

text:
ï»¿
BRINGING DOWN THE GREAT WALL
Writings on Science, Culture, and Democracy in China.
By Fang Lizhi.
Edited by James H. Williams.
Translated by James H. Williams and others.
Introduction by Orville Schell.
336 pp. 
New York:
Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95.
Fang Lizhi, the Chinese dissident, likes sometimes to present himself as the very model of the absent-minded intellectual, a man so wrapped up in his own thoughts that he has little consciousness of the world around him. 
In middle school, he tells us in "Bringing Down the Great Wall," a moving collection of his essays, interviews and speeches, "I was so absorbed with the daydreams that my teachers aroused in me there that at times I would walk right into utility poles on the side of the road."
But he at once adds a gloss to this fairly conventional metaphor, one that shows the mischievous and pragmatic side of his character: "So hard did I bump into them, in fact, that I can still remember the numbers that were written on those poles."
It is not the pain he wants us to know he remembers, but the numbers.
As one of China's leading scientists, first in astrophysics and later in cosmology, Mr. Fang is very good indeed both at dreaming and at remembering the numbers. 
But as an incorrigible freethinker, who has seen with mounting anguish the hopeless state into which Chinese society is drifting, Mr. Fang also has become an accomplished expert at deliberately walking into immovable objects -- in this case, the hard-liners in the upper echelons of the Communist Party's political and educational bureaucracies.
Fang Lizhi is now one of China's best-known dissidents. 
He was accused by the Chinese Government of being one of the ringleaders of the huge spring 1989 demonstrations in Tiananmen Square; and, after the mass slaughter of civilians in Beijing on June 4 by the People's Liberation Army, he and his wife sought shelter in the United States Embassy. 
Allowed to leave the country in the summer of 1990, he has since received academic sanctuary in Cambridge University and in Princeton.
Mr. Fang's popularity and notoriety have been due in part to his visibility: as an internationally prominent scientist and the vice president of the important University of Science and Technology at Hefei in Anhui Province, he was at the forefront of those trying to train China's youth to participate successfully in the front ranks of the international scientific community. 
Mr. Fang has also got attention because he has been through a lot: he was purged and deprived of his Communist Party membership in the antirightist campaign of 1957 for his outspoken critique of the sterility of Communist party discussions; he was rehabilitated in 1978, after the Cultural Revolution; he was deprived once more of his party membership in early 1987, as the hard-liners struck back against the late 1986 student demonstrations; and he brought the Government's anger down on himself again in January 1989 when he appealed to the Party to release Wei Jingsheng, the foremost protester of China's long-crushed democracy movement of 1978, who had by then spent 10 years in jail. 
But, above all, Fang Lizhi has been listened to because he is witty, passionate, tenacious and articulate. 
Students have loved his speeches; whether he had prepared carefully or spoke off the cuff, he could hold an audience in the palm of his hand.
The rhythms of Mr. Fang's life as a highly visible protester against his Government's stupidity, greed and cruelty have inevitably led to his being compared to Andrei Sakharov in the Soviet Union and to Vaclav Havel in Czechoslovakia. 
But in various interviews Mr. Fang has always dodged all parallels with Sakharov, and has explicitly rejected those to Mr. Havel. He emphatically denies that he is a political leader and insists that he does not want to be one. 
It is one of the weaknesses of China, he explains, that the Chinese reject one leader only to submit themselves to another. 
It would be far better, he says, for the Chinese "to learn that democracy requires a confrontation of ideas and not a leader who says one thing and everybody follows. 
. . . If the Chinese people are expecting the appearance of a hero, it had better not be me. 
This expectation in itself is very unhealthy."
In "Bringing Down the Great Wall," James H. Williams, a scholar on science and technology in China, and a few of his colleagues have translated and compiled an admirably comprehensive selection of Fang Lizhi's written and spoken words,focusing on his works since 1979 and ending with some of the pieces he wrote after being allowed to leave China in 1990. 
Mr. Fang's writings are divided into sections corresponding to what they see as four sides of his nature: the cosmologist, the cosmopolitan, the democrat and the dissident. 
The translations are fluent, and the introductions to each section, along with Orville Schell's long introduction to the book as a whole, are intelligent and pertinent. 
The Fang Lizhi who is thus introduced to us is humane in an immediately accessible way: decent, courageous, sometimes evasive, sometimes sarcastic, urbane yet emotional, a socialist and an elitist, opinionated and impatient of official cant.
Readers today are likely to have trouble remembering just how "unsayable" so many of Fang Lizhi's thoughts were in the contexts in which he uttered them. 
His courage is thus not obvious to an outsider. 
The fervor of the students' responses came from the fact that they had never heard such words before, certainly not from a senior figure in the establishment. 
As Mr. Fang says in a beautiful essay, "The End of Forgetting History," this does not mean such things had not ever been said in China -- they had been said spiritedly in 1957 and in 1978 -- but the Chinese state had erased them from the record, replacing the vanished voices with a void that could be filled only with whispers.
In the mid-1980's, as Mr. Fang hit his stride as a social critic, a host of other Chinese were also trying to give their own versions of truth, not just in essays and speeches but also in films and paintings, novels and poems. 
But whereas most of them chose to be indirect to some extent, there was little that was indirect about Mr. Fang. He suggested to his audiences that the best global parallels for China were to be found in the zealotry of Iran, the economic stagnation of Poland and the terrible poverty of Chad; he told them "Marxism has become ossified," that the Government's habit of continually shifting its policies was "an infantile way of running an economy," and that the philosophical pronouncements from the Office of National Dialectics in the Chinese Academy of Social Science merely perpetuated "the image of a Chinaman with a long pigtail, clad in a Western suit."
During the 1980's, Deng Xiaoping and the Chinese Communist Party were trying to make people subscribe to the "Four Upholds," : the Socialist road, the dictatorship of the proletariat, Communist Party leadership and the leading role of "Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought."
Mr. Fang countered these by saying that he believed a university should have its own four upholds: "a spirit of science, democracy, creativity, and independence."
Told by a reporter that his four upholds" might be seen as "a little dangerous," Mr. Fang replied that perhaps he could clarify things by relating his four upholds to what the Government's four really referred to -- namely, superstition, dictatorship, conservatism and dependency. 
To give some idea of Mr. Fang's bravado, this particular speech was delivered to about 3,000 students and faculty at Tongzhi University in Shanghai in November 1986.
Commentators on China's various democracy movements, those of 1978, 1986 or 1989, have stated that there never seems to be any content to Chinese discussions of democracy, and that this makes the whole movement seem elusive. 
Mr. Fang, however, has offered frequent, crisp and intelligent analyses of what he means by democracy -- definitions that even those comfortably raised within such democracies might find hard to improve upon. 
Democracy, Mr. Fang told his Chinese audiences, means genuine pluralism rather than personalized attacks on the opposition; it means controlling corruption through public scrutiny and accountability; it means upholding the right to complain about injustice of all kinds; it means supporting the fundamental idea of shared human rights; it means governmental responsibility to its citizens; it means not relying on informers and not taking punitive action on the basis of casual suspicions; and it means refusing to quote as wisdom the observations of political leaders who know nothing.
Chinese and foreign journalists and Mr. Fang's student audiences have often asked how such values might be introduced into China. 
Mr. Fang has no easy answers. 
Perhaps change could come from within even if the external structures of government remain the same, he suggests, illustrating his point by using the words of a homely traditional Chinese metaphor: "In front of the shop the sheep's head keeps dangling, but inside the shop one sells dog meat."
But, he says, before that happens the people must make it clear to the party that they want change. 
And that will not be easy, since the Chinese, unsure about what to do, are "like a swarm of headless flies, buzzing around in every direction."
But Mr. Fang suggests two ways out of this box. 
First, it is possible that the Government, faced with the strength and determination of the democracy movement in China and abroad, might be forced to change constructively, "just as a bandit gives in when he meets a stronger force."
Secondly, it is possible that current global changes themselves might force the issue: "The greenhouse effect, the population explosion, are issues that cannot be solved without a global solution. 
If China cannot catch up with the rest of the world, the world will make China catch up with it."
Fang Lizhi may reject comparisons between himself and Andrei Sakharov or Vaclav Havel, but others will continue to make those comparisons for him. 
As Mr. Williams succinctly puts it in his introduction to one of the sections of this moving and intelligently orchestrated collection, Mr. Fang's great skill is that, "like Sakharov in the Soviet Union, he used the prestige of science to ferry ideas from beyond the margins of political permissibility into the general discourse on reform."
We might supplement that comment with an idea that Mr. Havel expressed in his books "Disturbing the Peace" and "Letters to Olga": in the grim world of Communist dictatorship, where optimism seems too facile an idea, there is always a deeper force, something we can term "hope."
Hope to Mr. Havel is the power that enables us to keep alive the belief that one day things will again make sense. 
This making sense of experience is one of the things that gives us courage as we pursue what Mr. Havel calls our "entirely obscure task" on this planet. 
Mr. Fang, this book shows, has the mental strength to keep that hope alive and to maintain the faith that one day all that he, his contemporaries and his country have gone through during the last half-century will somehow make sense. 
On the day that happens, the Great Wall will truly come down.
Â 
Â 
Â 
INTELLECTUALS UP FRONT
"For the democracy movement, of course, China needs leaders," said Fang Lizhi, the Chinese astrophysicist and dissident, during a telephone interview from the University of Louisville, in Kentucky, where he was visiting. 
Yet Mr. Fang refuses to be considered one of those leaders. 
"I do not like that job," he replied rather wearily. 
"I like teaching and telling people things. 
I'm a sparrow leader."
What Mr. Fang calls a sparrow, Americans call a gadfly. 
Indeed, it was Mr. Fang's outspokenness that forced him to seek refuge in the United States Embassy in Beijing before going into exile. 
He is now working on the topology of the universe at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J.
Mr. Fang may not hope to govern, but he does believe intellectuals belong at the forefront of any functioning democracy -- quite the opposite of the situation in China. 
There, he said, "the party's first, the intellectuals last."
Mr. Fang assembled his speeches, letters and essays in "Bringing Down the Great Wall" so they would be on hand for debate. 
The first step toward reform, he said, is freedom of speech and freedom of the press. 
But how, aside from the book, does he hope to contribute to the conversation about China while living in New Jersey?
"It's difficult," he said. 
"I am quite far from China. 
I have joined the Chinese students, I have joined some international organizations for human rights. 
I can still do something, but it is limited, obviously, to the issue of human rights."
-- JUDITH SHULEVITZ

text:
ï»¿
The pigs amble lazily among the mud-brick houses and the grinning children play Ping-Pong on flat bits of ground, for an almost picture-perfect image of bucolic contentment. 
But villages like this one in central China still have their secrets, perhaps dark ones, as something is missing in these hamlets: several million little girls.
Newly released data from China's 1990 census support previous suspicions that 5 percent of all infant girls born in China are unaccounted for. 
It is not clear what has happened to them.
Are they killed at birth, drowned in a bucket of water by the midwife, on instructions from parents who want a son rather than a daughter?
Or are they given up for adoption?
Or perhaps they are raised secretly to evade the one-child policy?
Some evidence suggests that a combination of these factors accounts for the missing girls, although officials usually insist that very few are killed.
"There's no infanticide here," said Jin Mingai, the Mayor of Daijiawan, a remote hillside community accessible only by foot trail. 
Mr. Jin squirmed on his stool and acknowledged that every couple in the village had managed to produce a son, despite family planning restrictions, but he added firmly, "The peasants here would never drown their own daughters."
Villagers overwhelmingly give the same answer, and perhaps they are right. 
But one of the great mysteries of China is what happens to about half a million infant girls who are born alive each year but then vanish.
Â 
Sons Inherit Family Line
The girls almost certainly disappear because of the traditional preference, common in many parts of Asia, for sons rather than daughters. 
But in a larger sense, they are the unintended casualties of China's 12-year-old "one-child policy."
While Chinese couples are limited to having one or two children, as is now the case, they are sometimes reluctant to "waste" their allotment -- or risk heavy fines and stiff punishments if they exceed it -- on a daughter. 
They fear that if they go ahead and raise a girl, they may miss the chance to have a son later on.
"If they have a son, most couples will usually be satisfied and stop," said a local official here in Hubei Province. 
"But there are some couples that think they absolutely must have a son, and they keep on trying no matter how many daughters they've already had."
Boys are preferred partly because they customarily do more farm work. 
But the most important reason is that in Chinese families, girls "marry out," and the family line passes only through sons. 
Couples also want boys as a kind of social security, because it is sons who are charged with caring for their parents in old age.
For now, the question of the missing girls is such a puzzle that even the number of those missing is only an inference, based on skewed sex ratios of newborn infants.
Data released in May from the 1990 census indicate that for every 100 girls aged less than one year there were 111.3 boys. 
This disparity was not a fluke: a survey conducted in 1989 found 112.5 boys, while one in 1987 found 110.5.
Â 
Suspiciously Large Gap
All around the world, male births outnumber female births, but in China the gap is suspiciously large. 
In countries with good statistics -- and where female infanticide is not considered an issue -- the ratio is constant at about 105 or 106 boys to 100 girls.
If the true ratio at birth in China is about 105.5 boys to 100 girls, but so many girls were not reported that the official ratio jumped to 111.3, then something happened to more than 600,000 infant girls last year alone.
Chinese officials sometimes dispute such calculations, and suggest that it is a bit arrogant for Westerners to claim that birth ratios of 105 or 106 to 100 are universally valid.
"It's hard to say why, but in Asia some nationalities have higher ratios," said Li Honggui, director of the general office of the State Family Planning Commission. 
"Every country is different."
Â 
Normal Ratio About 106 to 100
Yet there is considerable evidence that China, too, has a natural sex ratio at birth of between 104 and 106 males for every 100 females. 
The sex ratio for newborn infants in the 1964 census was 103.8 to 100, and in the 1953 census it was 104.9. 
It was beginning with the 1982 census, after the one-child policy was implemented, that the figure surged.
Moreover, even now, for first-born infants, China has a fairly normal sex ratio of about 106 to 100. 
It is only the second-born, third-born, fourth-born and fifth-born infants that are disproportionately male. 
Among fifth-born children, the ratio is more than 125 males to 100 females.
Presumably this is because couples will accept a daughter if she is their first child, because they expect that they can find a way legally or illegally to have another child.
With later births, parents may feel that this is their last opportunity to have a son. 
In addition, they know that they may well be fined heavily if they flout the policy and raise the child, while if they declare that it is stillborn, they will not get in trouble.
"They may think, 'If it's a boy, I'll own up and pay the fine, but if it's a girl then I won't pay a cent,' " said Huang Baoshan, a spokesman for the State Family Planning Commission.
There are various ways that parents can evade the fines, and some evidence suggests that many of the missing girls are informally given up for adoption. 
They are not registered at birth but are left bundled on the doorstep of an official or someone else who will take care of the infant.
Two Swedish experts working in conjunction with a Chinese demographer concluded recently on the basis of an extensive survey that up to half of the 500,000 infant girls who go missing each year are in fact adopted informally. 
Some villagers confirm that this is a common course for households that have unauthorized pregnancies and give birth to girls.
A second possible explanation is that parents, unwilling to pay fines for their daughters, send the infants to be raised by relatives in other areas. 
A third possibility, in areas where family planning supervision is lax, is that parents simply raise their daughters at home without registering them.
Of course, a fourth alternative is infanticide. 
Most Chinese -- including those who are critical of the Government -- say they believe that infanticide is uncommon, but with as large a population base as China's, even a tiny proportion of infanticides would equal a large number of killings.
If there are killings, they apparently take place primarily in remote villages, like Daijiawan, where women give birth at home and the midwife is a neighbor and probably a relative. 
In these villages, there are no police stations or autopsies, and babies are quietly buried without anyone taking a close look.
Zeng Yi, a Chinese demographer, argues that the missing girls are hidden rather than killed, except in rare cases that do not affect the overall statistics. 
One indication that some of the missing girls are merely hidden is that population surveys have sometimes found more five-year-old girls than there were female births registered five years earlier. 
That presumably means that they were hidden from the authorities at earlier ages.
The latest census data arguably support that hypothesis. 
While the sex ratio for newborn infants was a highly abnormal 111.3 to 100, it dropped to about 108 for toddlers and declined further to 107 for elementary school-age children.
"At a young age, the girls are hidden," Mr. Zeng said. 
"Then when they grow up they are reported, perhaps because they go to school."
Â 
Ultrasound Testing
While most Chinese believe that infanticide is rare and declining -- partly because more births are taking place in hospitals, where it is not so easy to drown a newly born infant -- another trend may result in an even more skewed sex ratio. 
That trend is the growing use of ultrasonic testing to determine the sex of the fetus. 
If it is a girl, the parents can abort the pregnancy and try again.
Since 1987, doctors have been forbidden by law from telling parents the sex of their fetus, but it is widely acknowledged that the law is frequently violated. 
A carton of cigarettes apparently is a typical bribe to be told the sex of the fetus, and sometimes the information is offered gratis.
"It's quite normal to tell the parents the sex of their child," said a doctor in Beijing. 
"And anyway, there are no secrets in China."

text:
ï»¿
Success, Amy Tan has learned, is never what you expect it to be.
"In some ways it's like being a kid in a candy store," the 39-year-old best-selling author says, pouring coffee in her suite at the Carlyle Hotel. 
"But there's also the loss of privacy. 
I'll be getting up from a nap on an airplane, and someone will come over to me and say, 'You're Amy Tan.'
And I'll realize that I look like everybody else does when they've just awakened on a plane, and I want to say, 'No, I'm not.'
"
Three years ago, Ms. Tan was a freelance technical writer living in San Francisco and working on her first novel. 
That book turned out to be "The Joy Luck Club," a tale of Chinese-American women and their immigrant mothers. 
It jumped onto the best-seller lists in the spring of 1989, and a few weeks later its paperback rights were sold for $1.2 million.
Ms. Tan's second novel, "The Kitchen God's Wife," is being published this month by G. P. Putnam's amid much promotional fanfare. 
Early reviews have been glowing and it would be surprising if the novel, in which an elderly immigrant woman tells her daughter the story of her harsh and oppressive life in China before the revolution, did not wind up on the best-seller list.
With money sometimes comes celebrity, a status that Ms. Tan says has affected her life on the ground as well as in the air. 
For one thing, she has had to move. 
"I was determined at one point to keep everything the same," she says. 
"Which is a very idealistic, romantic notion. 
We lived in a very nice house, but we were on the first floor, and every day there were people walking by and pointing at it. 
My mailman would tell everybody what mail I had received. 
I felt very exposed."
So she and her husband, Lou DeMattei, a tax lawyer, packed up and headed a couple of blocks away, to the third floor of a condominium. 
As she speaks, Ms. Tan carefully rearranges a shimmering orange-gold cape that is wrapped around her shoulders. 
Her legs are crossed, and much of the time so are her arms, as if she is shielding herself from public prying. 
She is trying very hard to be outgoing and cheerful, but her nervousness shows. 
She seems, surprisingly, a little shy. 
It is not that she is still a novice at interviews; it's that she really doesn't like them.
"I have a different personality in public than I have in private," she says. 
"I put on the public personality. 
I ironed these clothes for you this morning. 
Otherwise what I would be wearing would be really grungy."
Â 
Different in Private
She is a lot sillier in private, she says, "and a lot bitchier."
She is more comfortable, she says, "when I'm walking around back home with my husband, or when I'm having a conversation with him, and he's sort of drifting off trying to read the paper, and I say: 'Well, this is good; I'm as boring as I always was.'
"
"The Kitchen God's Wife" didn't come easy, she says. 
While she was writing it, she was very much aware of another aspect of success: the fear that the second book will not be as good, or as well received, as the first.
"I see all the faults," she says. 
"I know what's been put in and what's been taken out. 
I know where the mistakes are, and I'm always afraid someone's going to catch them and say, 'You put the wrong emphasis on this,' or 'You used the wrong angle on that.'
"
She also didn't want to be typecast. 
"I didn't want to be pegged as the mother-daughter expert," she says. 
So at first she tried writing something very different from "The Joy Luck Club."
But that something wasn't working, and there were a number of false starts. 
"It was an attempt at rebellion," she says. 
"And I realized that rebellion was not a good reason to write what I was writing."
Then, suddenly, her mother provided the inspiration. 
"My mother kept complaining about how she had to tell everybody she was not the model for the mother in 'The Joy Luck Club,' " Ms. Tan says. 
"She told me that next time I should write her true story. 
And then one day she said something that I thought was remarkable.
"I knew she had lived in China during World War II, that she had been married to someone else before my father, and I asked her what the war had been like. 
I expected to hear all these exciting tales, and instead she told me, 'I wasn't affected.'
"But then she mentioned that maybe two or three times a week, when the bombs fell, she would have to run to the east gate or the west gate. 
'We were always running,' she told me. 
'We were always scared that the bombs would fall on top of our heads.'
So I said to her: 'Wait a minute. 
You told me you weren't affected by the war.'
And she replied: 'I wasn't. 
I wasn't killed.'
"
For Ms. Tan, the statement was a remarkable revelation about the difference between her own perspective on life and her mother's. 
"I decided I wanted to try to capture the shock of that difference," she says.
She changed many details, but the novel keeps close to the basic outlines of her mother's life in China before, during and after the war: "Everything from her horrible marriage, to her children dying, to being in jail, to escaping right before the revolution in 1949."
Â 
An Effort at Understanding
Her goal, she says, was to try to understand her mother. 
"She is such a strong person," Ms. Tan says. 
"And I could never understand why she lived with such a horrible man for 12 years of her life. 
She once told me that she might even kill him if she ever saw him again. 
If she hated him that much, why didn't she leave him?"
But Ms. Tan came to learn more and more about the subservient role of women in that Chinese society. 
"My mother was repressed so much by her family, by the society she lived in," Ms. Tan says. 
"And then I started thinking about all the different myths we grow up with, all the assumptions and the expectations. 
There are these things that form and control our lives that we never question."
The novel's title, Ms. Tan says, is a reference to a Chinese tale about a man who wronged his wife and was then elevated to the status of a deity -- "a perfect metaphor," she says, for those unquestioned governing myths.
Ms. Tan wrote the novel in 1989, while the student demonstrations were taking place in Tiananmen Square in Beijing. 
"People would always say that the students were so brave," she says. 
"I wanted to understand what it is like to live a life of repression and to understand the fear that one has, and what you have to do to rise above that fear."
Ms. Tan says she has already done research for her next novel, and expects to begin writing it as soon as she has finished promoting "The Kitchen God's Wife."
And with the writing, she knows, will again come the pressure.
"If I get an award, I look at it and I thank somebody and I give it to my mother," Ms. Tan says. 
"And if my mother wants to throw it away, she can throw it away. 
I don't keep that stuff around. 
I don't keep my books on my coffee table. 
I don't want to see any reminder of them. 
There's an unreality about it. 
My life with the last book ended when I made the final corrections."
She takes a sip of coffee and looks up expectantly. 
Is the interview over?
Yes, she is told, it is. 
She laughs, the carefree laugh of a schoolchild at dismissal.
"Great," she says.

text:

Sir Run Run Shaw, the Asian tycoon who tried to help Macy avoid bankruptcy by offering a $250 million loan, was turned down in part because board members hardly know him. 
Some members heard his name for the first time in March 1991, when he bought a 10.3 percent stake in Macy.
Yet in Hong Kong, where he has dominated the movie business for decades, Sir Run Run is a highly visible billionaire known to virtually every household.
Even at age 84, Sir Run Run politely pauses for photographers at the elite social gatherings he frequents, sometimes with a movie actress on each arm. 
He often wears the black gown of a traditional mandarin, a gesture to the educated backround into which he was born in Shanghai in 1907.
Sir Run Run is credited with making China's first film in 1924, but he left Shanghai before long for Singapore, where he and his brothers produced hundreds of low-budget kung-fu movies. 
In 1959, Sir Run Run brought his growing fortune to Hong Kong, where he earned a reputation for careful, shrewd real estate investments.
"He is a very, very conservative investor," said Terry Fok, research director at Kim Eng Securities in Hong Kong, who tracks Sir Run Run's flagship company, Shaw Brothers. 
"He's got vast personal wealth, but is unlikely to ever do anything dramatic with it."
Shaw Brothers, now valued at about $255 million, includes movie studios, theaters and a 30 percent stake in Hong Kong's largest television station. 
Sir Run Run's 66 percent stake is worth about $172 million.
His private holdings, however, are estimated to be worth somewhat more than $1 billion. 
He owns sizable tracts of land and high-rise buildings in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Vancouver, British Columbia, as well as a share of Shangri-la International Hotels.
Like other Hong Kong financiers, he has shied away from other United States investments because of corporate taxes, which do not exist in the British colony. 
Sir Run Run has never disclosed his full holdings, and prefers to conduct business with people whom he knows personally. 
In the Macy case, he was persuaded to invest by Myron E. Ullman 3d, now Macy's vice chairman, who had done business with Sir Run Run in Hong Kong.
"He's very secretive about his investments," said Alan Ng, an analyst at S.G. 
Warburg in Hong Kong. 
"He seems to keep a lot in cash, but we haven't seen him spend much in Hong Kong in the past 10 years."
Despite his frequent public appearances, Sir Run Run protects the secrecy of his private life, often telling interviewers only that he is a widower who likes to rise before dawn to practice Chinese shadow-boxing.
Even the source of Sir Run Run's unusual name, different from his given name in Mandarin Chinese, Shao Yifu, is a mystery. 
An elder brother was called Run Me Shaw, and articles in the gossipy Hong Kong press have credited the boys' father with choosing English-language nicknames that played on the similarity of 'Shaw' to the word 'rickshaw,' the hand-pulled taxis of old China that were at once a symbol of aristocracy and exploitation.
"Run Run" was the name that the financier used when he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth of Britain in 1977, largely for his philanthropy in Hong Kong, where he donates some$20 million each year to hospitals, charities and schools.

file: A Return to Pakistan.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHEN British India shuddered on the faultline of religion and split apart at independence in 1947, a new nation for Muslims, which they called Pakistan, was born.
But Pakistan, washed in the sun-seared south by the Arabian Sea, and fringed at the north by the soaring, snowy peaks of the Hindu Kush and the Karakorams, was new in name only. 
This narrow land, enclosed on three sides by India, China, Afghanistan and Iran, was where much of the subcontinent's culture originated.
India may have taken the name, but Pakistan got a lot of the history -- prehistoric, Hellenistic, Persian, Buddhist and Mogul. 
Alexander the Great rode into its valleys. 
So did the Emperors Darius and Cyrus the Great. 
Archeological sites at Mohenjo-Daro in Sind and at Taxila in the North-West Frontier Province reveal sophisticated cultures thousands of years old. 
Museums at the sites preserve their artifacts and tell the stories of the ruins.
Pakistan also has good samples of the Indian subcontinent's dramatically varied geography. 
There is an undeveloped seacoast, quiet mountain valleys with cool, clear streams, deserts - camels loom over cars at traffic lights in Karachi - and fertile agricultural plains that bloom and die and bloom again in rhythm with the rains.
The Indus, the river that gave life to the subcontinent's earliest civilizations, flows nearly the full length of Pakistan, from mountains to sea.
One of the world's great overland journeys can be made from the north of Pakistan to China along the recently completed Karakoram Highway, a contemporary addition to the ancient Silk Route, which opened West Asia to the Orient.
What Pakistan doesn't have is tourists, at least not many of them, not yet. 
The country, emerging from more than a decade of military domination, returned to democracy recently and exuberantly, and now hopes to welcome more visitors, while considering how to develop its tourist attractions, and what kind of tourists it wants.
Pakistan remains at heart a pious, though not fundamentalist, Islamic nation. 
Women are dressed modestly in trousers and tunics - the comfortable shalwar-kamiz suit that Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto is helping to raise to new fashion heights. 
No alcoholic drinks are served or consumed in public places, though non-Muslim foreigners may buy local beer, whisky, gin and rum from room service menus in international hotels. 
Bringing alcohol into the country is illegal and gambling is forbidden by both law and religion.
Most Pakistanis, however, are friendly and tolerant people. 
Outsiders who understand and generally respect their customs - avoiding shorts or other skimpy clothes in public places and removing shoes in mosques - feel little or no hostility or sense of opprobrium. 
Service, if sometimes unpracticed or erratic, is never disingenuous or slick. 
Accommodation is adequate to excellent in most towns and all cities, where good cars can be hired for free-lance trips.
Urdu is the national language, but all the regions have their own languages and English is sometimes used as a link. 
English will be spoken in all tourist areas and in most hotels. 
The best time to travel is in the spring, when snows melt in the north and temperatures are pleasant. 
Summer is hot almost everywhere except high in the hills. 
Temperatures in Pakistan's cities, especially in the south, can rise above 100 degrees, and the desert sun is punishing. 
After October, snows close the mountain passes, including those along the Silk Route, which reopens for the season on May 1.
Pakistan used to be accessible overland from Kabul to the west and Delhi to the east along the old Grand Trunk Road until war in Afghanistan and separatist unrest in India's Punjab state closed those routes to most travelers.
The country is now most easily reached by air, and perhaps in the future will be served by cruise ship. 
Pakistan can be sampled as a side trip to an Indian vacation, or as a stopover on the way to Southeast Asia or China. 
Pakistan International Airlines, which is both a domestic and international carrier, is one of South Asia's most pleasant travel surprises, with efficient service and clean, well-cared-for aircraft. 
Flying inside Pakistan is cheap and safe, and most tourist destinations can be reached by plane from larger cities.
There are two international gateways to Pakistan by air: Karachi in the south and Lahore (or on some days Islamabad) farther north. 
Karachi, Pakistan's largest city and a busy seaport, is the best base for exploring the lower end of the Indus River valley and the archeological ruins of Mohenjo-Daro.
Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, called the Indus civilization the precursor of all later cultural periods in India. 
At Mohenjo-Daro, connected to Karachi by air, a metropolis with educational institutions, civic buildings and a drainage system flourished before 2500 B.C.
Like another apparently large and highly developed city at Harappa, in Pakistan's Punjab state to the northeast, Mohenjo-Daro appears to have vanished into history, leaving no clues to its language and thus locking away its secrets. 
The site was not unearthed until 1922, and restoration work since then has been sporadic. 
But some of the city's street plan is visible, and a collection of pottery, weapons, toys and household objects can be seen in the museum at the site.
From Karachi, tourists can also go west to the country's largest and most remote province, Baluchistan. 
The Baluchi capital, Quetta, like Peshawar to the north, is a frontier town populated by fierce-looking, often armed, men true to the past. 
It is not a city of either charm or historical interest, since much of it was destroyed in an earthquake in 1935 that killed 23,000 people. 
But it serves as a base for hiking and for drives into mountain passes and valleys. 
Its bazaars are full of colorful Baluchi handicrafts, including embroidered clothes and jackets and pillows decorated with tiny mirrors.
The city of Karachi is not regarded as a tourist attraction, but it is not without its points of interest. 
In the seaside suburb of Clifton, where the Bhuttos and other wealthy and influential Pakistanis - as well as a few oil sheiks from the Persian Gulf - have homes (or minor palaces), there are camels to ride along the beach. 
Families come out to stroll on Fridays, the Pakistani day of rest, when children don their finest clothes. 
Curbside, makeshift shooting galleries are popular here, a reminder of Pakistan's long fascination with guns.
A visit to Karachi should include a stop at the tomb of Pakistan's founder, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, known as Quaid-e-Azam, or Father of the Nation. 
The white marble, domed mausoleum stands on a hill, visible from some parts of the city. 
It is set in a large public park where families come to relax or picnic. 
Jinnah, whose Karachi home has also been made into a small museum, is Pakistan's most revered leader, and a hero on whom politically fractious Pakistanis agree.
The National Museum of Pakistan is in a garden off Dr. Zia-uddin Ahmed Road in Karachi, the country's first capital. 
Open every day but Friday from 10 to 4, the museum offers a panoramic look at Pakistan's history and regional cultures. 
Like several other exceptionally good museums found in Pakistan - two others are at Lahore and Peshawar - the National Museum is housed in a building erected during British colonial times. 
A Muslim Gallery in the museum is devoted to the rich Islamic cultures that converged in Pakistan.
It is the northern part of Pakistan, rather than Karachi or the southwest, that is most popular with tourists, who can travel easily and comfortably along the Lahore-Rawalpindi-Peshawar route, making as many side trips as time and interest permits.
Lahore is a classic Mogul city with added elements of Victorian brick and stone. 
Its character is intellectual and political. 
Rawalpindi, four or five hours away by road or rail or less than 45 minutes by air, is the military center of Pakistan, and a thriving commercial city. 
Peshawar, near the entrance to the Khyber Pass, is vintage frontier, embellished now by millions of Afghan exiles who walk the streets selling carpets, or lay out tables of chunky Turkoman jewelry and fine woolens hand-knit by refugee women.
These three cities have three of Pakistan's four oldest hotels: Faletti's in Lahore, Flashman's in Pindi and Dean's in Peshawar. 
The fourth in the chain, now owned by the Government, which toys now and then with the idea of tearing them down, is the Cecil in the hill town of Murree, east of Islamabad.
Rawalpindi or Islamabad, Pakistan's new capital city only a few miles away, is the takeoff point for trips by road or air to the remote regions of Gilgit, Balistan and the Pakistani part of Kashmir. 
From here, the trip along the Silk Route to China can also begin. 
The Chinese Embassy in Islamabad issues the necessary travel documents in three to seven days, for a nominal fee of about $3.50.
For people who prefer to travel in a group, Pakistan Tours, with offices at Flashman's Hotel in Rawalpindi and at the Chinar Inn in Gilgit, offers 8-day and 15-day trips into and back from China across the 16,500-foot Khunjerab Pass. 
The tour costs about $70 a day, including all transportation, meals and accommodation, from Rawalpindi to China and back. 
Trips begin in mid-May with one a month minimum.
The tour operator has vans equipped with oxygen for high altitudes, tourism officials say. 
Privately hired cars may go only as far as the Chinese border. 
Further information is available from Pakistan Tours, 23-24 Flashman's Hotel, The Mall, Rawalpindi; telephone 65449 or 64811.
A trip through the Khunjerab, however, is not necessary to get a sense of the majesty of Pakistan's northern mountainous frontier. 
In good weather, travelers can fly to the towns of Skardu or Gilgit, or drive into the northern valleys, known for their good hiking and climbing terrain, fishing streams, clear air and solitude. 
By jeep, the trip to Gilgit can take between 12 and 20 hours; most car-rental companies recommend breaking the journey into two or more day trips. 
There are small inns and rest houses of varying quality along the way. 
Flying to Gilgit, however, is subsidized, and costs only about $12 from Pindi. 
This means the daily flights are often full. 
Buses also make the trip from Pindi for under $15.
The towns in Pakistan's northern territories are in high mountain valleys, Gilgit-Hunza at 4,770 feet and Skardu, to the east, at 7,500 feet. 
Skardu has the more dramatic scenery. 
Backed by some of the highest mountains in the world, the Skardu Valley has lakes, sand dunes and an old mountain fort. 
There are more than half a dozen approved hotels and lodges in Skardu.
From a base at Rawalpindi, a day trip can be made to the archeological sites of Taxila, most of them an hour or less away by car.
Taxila, at the heart of the Gandhara civilizations of the North-West Frontier, is a collection of several excavated sites that together document an extraordinary confluence of religions and cultures. 
There are Hellenistic influences - Buddha figures in Greekstyle robes, for example - as well as Bactrian, Scythian and Persian.
India's first Emperor, Chandragupta Maurya, was crowned at Taxila; here his grandson Ashoka later ruled as viceroy. 
During Ashoka's time, in the third century B.C., Taxila became a center of Buddhist learning and pilgrimage. 
Some of the finest of early Buddhist art has been found here, including the startling, skeletal Fasting Siddharta, often called the Gandhara Buddha, now on display in the Lahore Museum.
A visit to the Taxila sites takes a visitor into the hearts of poor, dusty Pakistani villages, a poignant contrast to the glories of the past, when the land was kinder to the people who lived here. 
One word of caution: villagers have become adept at reproducing Gandhara artifacts, which they offer to tourists as originals ''dug up over the hill.''
Government guides at the archeological sites say that no metal or pottery items are found these days, but that occasionally a coin will be genuinely old.
However, the reproductions of tiny bronze pots or jewelry are often so pleasant to look at that visitors buy them, once the price has been bargained down from antique to trinket level.
West and northwest of Rawalpindi lie more beautiful mountain valleys: Swat and, beyond that, Chitral. 
The capital of the Swat region, named for its river, is Saidu Sharif, the seat of the Kings of Swat, who ruled until 1969. 
Good small hotels begin here and dot the villages - Miandam, Bahrain and Kalam - to the north. 
Over these towns tower the mountains of the Hindu Kush. 
Across the border to the west is Afghanistan.
It is forever-unruly Afghanistan that has dominated the life of Pakistan's most fascinating city: Peshawar. 
Now the capital of the North-West Frontier Province - and the headquarters of seven Afghan resistance armies trying to overthrow the Soviet-backed Government in Kabul - Peshawar is a town full of energy and intrigue.
The bazaars hereabouts are legendary, so a traveler might be wise to look around ahead of time in other cities to get a working knowledge of fair prices, but then save the shopping for Peshawar. 
Here there are warrens of markets with copper and brass, woolens and leatherware. 
Afghan carpets - some with latter-day symbols like automatic weapons or Soviet tanks woven into them - and colorful Afghan dresses with trousers to match are sold in shops run by exiles.
There are beads and powder horns, camel bags and icons stolen from Russian soldiers who died across the border in a war that must have baffled them. 
Soviet officer's hats and decorations are also available, along with a smuggler's cornucopia of imported foods and luxury goods seen nowhere else in South Asia. 
Trekkers can stock up here on comforting home-town goods like real chocolate bars and mustard.
In the past, travelers who came to Peshawar from the east almost invariably took a day trip through the Khyber Pass and back. 
Lately, however, that trip has been off limits because of fighting around the Afghanistan-Pakistan border town of Torkham on the other side of the pass. 
Hotels in Peshawar keep in touch with local authorities, and can tell visitors whether the route, with its wild mountain scenery and fortified villages behind mud walls, is open or not.
Meanwhile, it is possible to drive west of Peshawar far enough to pause at the large Afghan refugee colonies to see first-hand the overwhelming human tragedy Pakistan has on its border.
When traveling in isolated valleys or through mountainous terrain, tourists should avoid being on lonely roads after sundown, when armed bandits sometimes stop and loot vehicles, particularly in regions near the Afghan border. 
Roads are also dangerous at night because of the mix of animals, unlighted farm wagons and speeding cars, trucks or buses, usually elaborately decorated. 
For both reasons, it is a good idea to settle down early in the day, and plan an evening around the hotel, whether in town or countryside.
Peshawar is not a dangerous city because of the Afghan war. 
But it is a city with spies, gunrunners and narcotics agents where weapons are abundant, demanding circumspection on the visitor's part. 
It is also the home of some of the most conservative Muslims in Pakistan or Afghanistan. 
Western women, who almost universally don Pakistani attire here, sometimes say they feel uncomfortable in Peshawar. 
But hundreds of them are working happily with more than three million refugees from Afghanistan, and have come to understand, as have their Western male counterparts, the ways of this barren frontier.
Â 
FOR REAL AND ARMCHAIR TRAVELERS
Because Pakistan has not been a major tourist destination, not many travel books have been written on the country. 
But those that are available are excellent, partly because they assume a certain unfamiliarity on the reader's part.
Â

Pakistan: A Travel Survival Kit, by Jose Roleo Santiago (Lonely Planet Publications, Post Office Box 2001, Berkeley, Calif. 
94702; $7.95; about $12.50 in international hotel bookshops in Pakistan). 
Like its companion guides to other little-known countries, this Travel Survival Kit begins with ancient history and moves through almost every topic of interest - food, vocabulary, accommodations and so on - to descriptions of places and attractions detailed enough to help a traveler plan a tour.
A Traveler's Guide to Pakistan, by Hilary Adamson and Isobel Shaw (The Asian Study Group, Post Office Box 1552, Islamabad; about $6.95 in bookshops in Pakistan). 
A private project, thoroughly researched by two Westerners who lived in Pakistan for several years, this guide with its many hand-drawn maps covers nearly every corner of the country.

Mr. Moorhouse, a skilled travel writer with a gifted eye for detail, describes his own first, solo encounter with Pakistan. 
No shopping or accommodation details here, except when part of the narrative. 
But there is enough atmosphere to make Pakistan memorable, even for those who may never visit it.

text:
ï»¿
When foreign journalists asked Li Ruihuan three years ago about his prospects for promotion, he mischievously cited a Chinese proverb: ''Men dread fame as a pig dreads fattening, for both can be a prelude to slaughter.''
But these days, Mr. Li - now the youngest member of the six-member Standing Committee of the Politburo, the most powerful body in China -seems to be risking both prominence and political extinction. 
In a series of remarkable public speeches, he has positioned himself in recent months as the prime opponent of the hard-liners and of the ideological blizzard that envelops the country.
''The people are like water,'' Mr. Li told the official New China News Agency, in a clear warning to the hard-liners. 
''They can support a ship. 
Or they can sink it.''
A onetime carpenter, the 55-year-old Mr. Li (whose name is pronounced approximately lee ray-HWAHN) is stepping into the vacant position as leader of the faction that supports returning to the policies that preceded the military crackdown on the democracy movement in June 1989. 
Chinese officials say they believe that if the hard-liners are defeated in the continuing power struggle, Mr. Li will be the leading candidate to replace Li Peng as Prime Minister.
On the other hand, some Chinese believe that unless Li Ruihuan is more discreet, he is the one likely to be dismissed. 
Indeed, he is said to have told friends, ''I can always go home and become a carpenter again.''
Does He Have a Mentor?
The prime question among many diplomats and Chinese officials these days is whether Mr. Li is acting on his own or as the front man for a more powerful sponsor.
''He's very daring, for he's the only one challenging the hard-liners right now,'' said a Chinese Government official who greatly enjoys watching Mr. Li enter the fray.
''But I don't understand it,'' he went on. 
''Sometimes a flock of birds will push one in front to lead the way, and I hope that's what's happening. 
But I'm afraid he's alone, blindly flying this way and that, with no one behind him. 
In that case, he'll end up in a bad way.''
Some other officials say Mr. Li has the backing of Deng Xiaoping, the 85-year-old senior leader, and of Wan Li, the 73-year-old head of the National People's Congress.
Chinese officials say that another top Politburo member, Song Ping, recently met with Mr. Li and told him that some ''old comrades'' were unhappy with his comments. 
Mr. Li is said to have responded, ''Well, there is one 'old comrade' who approved everything I said.''
He was referring to Mr. Deng. While Mr. Li has not openly attacked the hard-liners, his speeches have a completely different tone from those of other leaders. 
In an implicit rejection of the repression and harsh language that has prevailed for more than a year, Mr. Li said last month, ''Making human relations tense is not the original intention of Marxism, nor is it inevitable under the socialist system.''
''We must respect people, understand them and care for them,'' Mr. Li told the staff of the People's Daily newspaper at a meeting in April. 
''Ideological and political work cannot be effective unless the people are receptive to it. 
How can you do your work if people run away as soon as they see you?''
Â 
Remaking Marxism
Mr. Li criticized Chinese propaganda for ''wavering from one extreme to another'' and said an ''urgent, formidable and gigantic project'' is to make Marxism more practical. 
On some occasions, he has seemed impatient with the army-sponsored campaign to glorify Lei Feng, the legendary soldier-hero of Maoist days.
''We should talk about things that people are interested in and things that can help people erase their worries,'' he added. 
''Our slogans should be practical. 
Anything not practical will eventually separate us from the people.''
In addition to his speeches, Mr. Li has taken other measures that distance himself from the hard-liners. 
When student protests broke out in April 1989 in the city of which he was then Mayor -Tianjin, the nation's third most important city after Beijing and Shanghai -Mr. 
Li neatly solved the problem by allowing university students free train tickets to the capital. 
Most of the students traveled to Beijing and became someone else's problem.
After being put in charge of ideology and propaganda last summer, Mr. Li took charge of the national campaign against ''bourgeois liberalization.''
Many intellectuals feared they would be the target, but Mr. Li deftly redirected the campaign into an assault on pornography.
When Mr. Li was promoted to the Politburo's Standing Committee a year ago, he was not generally expected to step to the front in the way he has. 
While he had achieved a reputation as a powerhouse who overwhelmed the bureaucracy and got things done, he was not known as a backer of democracy.
Indeed, Mr. Li was a fierce critic of the 1978-79 Democracy Wall movement, and in Tianjin he clamped down immediately on 1986-87 student demonstrations.

text:
ï»¿
From images of life in rural Africa, the Middle East, Southeast Asia or large cities in North America, 2- to 12-year-old artists are guiding both the young and the old viewer to places they will probably never see.
The work of the young artists, who represent 29 countries, make up a traveling exhibition, "A Child's World," now at the Cork Gallery at Lincoln Center. 
The show, organized by the Children's Museum of the Arts, offers more than 100 drawings, paintings and self-portraits on themes like daily life, neighborhoods, cultural traditions and fantasy.
All the works share a common trait unique to children: innocence. 
"Kids tend to paint an idealized world; that is the beauty of children," said Laurie McGavin Bachmann, the public affairs director for the show.
As children who visit the show glimpse life in Pakistan, Tibet, China or Australia, they can listen to accompanying music at the touch of a button. 
For Lisa Lee, 12, of Flushing, Queens, who likes hard rock, it was an opportunity to hear Lebanese and Japanese music for the first time.
In "Chinese New Year," Lisa painted a festive carnival in her native Taiwan. 
"It reminds me that I am still Chinese," she said with pride. 
Lisa said all the works reinforce the importance of maintaining personal tradition and customs. 
She last visited her country seven years ago.
In "The Neighborhood Where I live," Adama Kandeh, also 12, offers a tour of a faraway village of huts in Sierra Leone where children climb on coconut trees and women carry water buckets on their heads.
While country scenes dominate, urban settings are well represented. 
Bianca Nieves, 9, of Nanuet, N.Y., created happy swimmers in "Orchard Beach"; Divya Awal, a 9-year-old native of India who now lives in Manhattan, drew a huge field of grass with tall buildings in the background, and Sarah Graves, 10, of North Adelaide, southern Australia, focused on environmental and industrial problems in "Dim City."
All the work is hung at child's height, along with mirrors and magnetized noses, eyes and mouths that allow young visitors to put portraits of their own on the wall. 
They can also hang their own spontaneous drawings, which will become part of the permanent collection of the Children Museum.
The exhibition also turns into a course in world geography when visitors, who each receive a "passport" with various activities on it, place miniature versions of the paintings on a world map. 
"Due to the Gulf war, the only nation they seem to recognize with ease is Saudi Arabia," said Kathleen Schneider, the museum's founder and executive director.
Most stops on the tour will also include a display of housing materials that children can identify, including reeds, bamboo, concrete, bricks and roof tiles.
"A Child's World" will be at the Cork Gallery in Avery Fisher Hall until Feb. 
18. Admission is free. 
Telephone: (212) 941-9198. 
The show will be in the Fifth Avenue Gallery in the Empire State Building March 1-April 30 and at the Museum of the City of New York from May 11 into September. 
The Children's Museum is also organizing other stopsfor the show, which opened three weeks ago at the A.I.R. 
Gallery in SoHo.

file: A View of Communism, as the Chinese See It.txt
text:
ï»¿
A university teacher described this scene in his home the other day: As the television announcer bragged about the economic gains since 1949, his father-in-law nodded approvingly and said: ''My, just look at that progress!''
That was when the teacher threw up his hands and protested: ''There's been no progress!
Just think what has happened in Japan in that time.''
Such exchanges seem to be repeated all over China these days, and they reflect what is emerging as a prime battleground in the struggle for the hearts of the Chinese people: the standard of comparison for judging the Communist Party.
The Government-controlled television and newspapers are full of accounts of the improvements since 1949 - the increases in grain output, railroad tracks, steel production and so on. 
The ''sick man of Asia'' is now an international power, the Government boasts.
By comparing life today to the poverty and chaos before ''liberation'' in 1949, the Communist Party comes off looking excellent, for it has accomplished a tremendous amount in its 41 years in power. 
But for many young people, all that is history. 
They note that their capitalist neighbors - particularly Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan - have accomplished far more in the same period. 
Moreover, these countries are not only richer than China but have become more democratic and have also done more to raise standards of education and technology.
By that standard of comparison, the Communist Party looks miserable; Taiwan, for example, now has a per-capita income more than 25 times that of the mainland.
Thus, the way in which China's progress is assessed - compared to the past or compared to its neighbors - determines people's views of the Communist Party's performance. 
The Government, therefore, is ever more vigorously promoting its version of history, in which every aspect of the ''new China'' is contrasted to the poverty and lassitude that used to prevail. 
Even in playing host to the Asian Games a few weeks ago, the Government emphasized that such an event in Beijing showed how much China had progressed since 1949.
Yet there are signs that on this battleground, the Government is losing ground. 
The principal problem is that many young people dismiss the official news media with a shrug, but pay considerable attention to what they see around them. 
The propaganda about China's achievement as host to the Asian Games, for example, was perhaps outweighed by the tide of South Korean sports fans who arrived for the Games lugging video recorders and other luxuries that most Chinese only dream of.
''In the 1960's, it wasn't possible to reach a conclusion about whether socialism or capitalism worked better, and many Westerners favored socialism,'' a young Chinese economist said. 
''But now it's very clear which system works better.''
''The best comparisons,'' he added, ''are with East Germany and West Germany, North Korea and South Korea, and China and Taiwan.''
Just over three-quarters of China's population was born after the 1949 revolution, and such younger people are impatient with lectures about the horrors of life before then.
Government officials concede they have a problem, and that their own children sometimes ''do not understand the correct situation.''
But they say that more political training about the virtues of Communism will reverse the trend. 
Young people themselves overwhelmingly say that while ''political education'' was sometimes effective in the past, it has little effect today.
''The difference is that China has opened up,'' a businesswoman in her 20's said. 
''We used to look around and see that everybody else lived in dreadful, crowded housing, and so we figured we could put up with it, too. 
And we knew that we had it better than our parents' generation. 
But now we understand how backward we are. 
Sure, we've developed over the past 40 years, but so have other countries, and the gap is enormous. 
What are we to think?
What hope is there?''

file: About New York_A Fortune Will Greet You In an Endeavor Faraway.txt
text:
ï»¿
Thanks to the Brooklyn-based Wonton Food company, China will soon have fortune cookies.
Until now the cookies, which cap off just about every meal served in most of America's 30,000 Chinese restaurants, have been unknown and gone untasted in China. 
Like hot dogs, pizza and more particularly, chop suey, they are essentially American concoctions.
But Wonton Foods, which produces a million fortune cookies a day in New York, has decided that the time is propitious to go east with the fortune cookie. 
"We just signed a joint venture agreement with the Guangzhou Municipal Foodstuffs Machinery Corporation to build and operate a fortune cookie plant," said Donald H. Lau, the company's vice president. 
He said he expected production to begin in about eight months.
He sounded as pleased as a man, who, having cracked open a cookie, found a message saying, "Greater success is in the days ahead," this being just the kind of thing you want to read when you are establishing a beachhead in a market of more than a billion cookie-eating people.
Mr. Lau said he did not believe that the fortunes needed to be passed by Government or party censors. 
"Those days are over," he said. 
Still, he noted, in terms of style, the Chinese fortunes are more elliptical than the American variety, which essentially foretell good health, growing wisdom, increasing riches, much love and ever greater sexiness in a straight-forward manner.
He offered a few of the Chinese fortunes picked at random: "True gold fears no fire," "Heaven never seals all exits," "The only way to catch a tiger cub is to go into the tiger's den" and "Constant grinding can turn an iron rod into a needle."
Asked whether turning rods into needles was good or bad, he replied, "I don't know."
Â 
'Fortunes on Floppy Disks'
Even before its entry into China, Wonton Foods had been moving boldly to reshape and dominate domestic fortune cookie production. 
Traditionally, the industry, centered here and in California, had a few large bakeries and several dozen tiny workshops where, typically, family members made cookies largely by hand.
"We have put all our fortunes on floppy disks," said Mr. Lau as he showed off an automated assembly line. 
"We were the first to offer chocolate fortune cookies on the East Coast and to sell cookies in retail outlets. 
We also do special jobs, customized messages for birthdays, anniversaries and sales promotions. 
We did the Democratic Convention and now are doing a two-million-cookie job to promote a new Chinese ginger liqueur."
The standard noncustomized fortunes have been collated from many lists. 
Some, Mr. Lau said, were acquired about 10 years ago when Wonton, branching into cookies from noodles, bought a Queens bakery from its elderly Japanese founders. 
Some have been sent in by customers, among them teachers who had assigned classes to compose lists of fortunes as writing exercises.
Mr. Lau took a few such examples from his briefcase. 
"You will never go to jail," one fifth-grade boy in Virginia had written. 
"You will find money on the couch where your father sits," wrote a girl from Maryland.
"I even wrote fortunes myself, but after about 500 I got burned out," said Mr. Lau, a former banker. 
All the fortunes the company uses are upbeat, but Mr. Lau said he had heard of a New England business calling itself the Unfortunate Fortune Cookie Company that offered dismal forebodings, presumably for misanthropes, masochists or what some might regard simply as realists. 
"I think they went out of business," he said.
In anticipation of starting up in Guangzhou, Wonton's partners in the booming south Chinese city have sent many hundreds of fortunes to Mr. Lau to be translated into English. 
The idea is to have each cookie contain a fortune printed on one side in Chinese and the other in English, because the first customers are expected to be hotels and restaurants in China and Hong Kong that cater to foreigners and overseas Chinese.
While it is generally accepted that the first fortune cookie was made in this century by Chinese immigrants to the United States, some writers have contended that the development here echoed an ancient event in Chinese history. 
This occurred in the 12th century, when, during a revolt against the Mongols, rebel monks passed conspiratorial plans in moon cakes. 
Moon cakes, however, look more like cinnamon buns than fortune cookies.
A more specific account, altogether ignoring any notion of a culinary subconscious, credits George Jung with inventing the fortune cookie at the Hong Kong Noodle Company, which he founded in Los Angeles in 1916. 
According to "Madam Chu's Chinese Cooking School," a book by Grace Zia Chu, Mr. Jung came up with the cookie either to cheer up customers depressed by World War I or to keep them amused while they waited for their orders.
Three years ago, an entrepreneur in Hong Kong began importing fortune cookies and selling them as luxury items in a chain of fancy delicatessens. 
They were advertised as "Genuine American Fortune Cookies."

file: Adrift, Taiwan Loses Urge for Firmer Footing.txt
text:

The people of Taiwan might like to attach a huge outboard motor to the end of their island, rev it up, and move Taiwan several hundred miles farther away from the Chinese mainland.
That would reduce the risk of a Chinese attack and give Taiwan more options for deciding its future. 
But while physical relocation is impossible, there are signs that Taiwan is drifting politically and socially farther from the mainland.
The Nationalist Chinese Government here used to speak of "gloriously recovering the mainland," but it is now far from clear that Taiwan would take China back if it were offered.
Political candidates here issue furious denials when rivals accuse them of favoring rapid reunification. 
Even Taiwan's leaders seem to be trying to keep their options open by pushing reunification off into the distant future.
"We want eventual reunification, but not immediate reunification," said Ma Ying-jeou, vice-chairman of the Government's Mainland Affairs Council.
Jason C. Hu, the chief Government spokesman, seemed even more ambivalent when asked what Taiwan would do if the mainland Government collapsed tomorrow and the people of China asked the Nationalists to return. 
"That's an unfair question," he protested.
The stakes are enormous because Beijing repeatedly threatens to use its military to keep Taiwan from becoming an independent sovereign state.
The island of Taiwan lies just 100 miles off the Chinese mainland. 
For four decades it has been the bastion of the Nationalist forces that lost the Chinese civil war to the Communists.
These days, some dissidents want Taiwan to declare itself the independent Republic of Taiwan. 
But the opposition Democratic Progressive Party did unexpectedly poorly a year ago when it made independence a major issue, muting the calls for independence.
Paradoxically, at the same time there seems to be diminishing interest in reunification.
Tim T.Y. 
Ting, a poll taker in Taipei, said his most recent survey suggested that only about 15 percent of the public favors immediate independence. 
That figure has been fairly stable for years, he said. 
But another survey found for the first time that less than half the public favors eventual reunification, seeming to prefer the status quo.
"When people think about reunification, they think: 'What's in it for us?
You want to equalize incomes with the mainland?'
" said Chang Liang, president of Shearson Global Financial Services in Taipei.
Another businessman, one with close links to Government leaders, said: "We should go on telling Beijing that we want to reunify, even though in our hearts we don't mean it. 
As long as we don't give them a timetable -- and we won't -- then we can postpone the issue indefinitely."
Curiously, the diminishing enthusiasm for reunification comes as Taiwan is rapidly expanding its economic links with the mainland. 
Trade may reach $7 billion this year, up from $1 billion in 1986. 
One million Taiwanese visit the mainland each year.
Leaders in Beijing are anxious about Taiwan in part because the Nationalist refugees from mainland China who used to rule Taiwan are gradually being replaced by native Taiwanese. 
Legislative elections held last week may accelerate the process. 
The Nationalists did poorly, winning just 53 percent of the vote.
The new generation of Taiwan-born leaders, including President Lee Teng-hui, is often considered more sympathetic to eventual independence than the mainland emigres were.
President Lee insists that he favors reunification, but just a few days ago he raised eyebrows by seeming to back away from the expression "one China."
Mr. Lee said that Chiang Kai-shek had never referred to "one China" but simply to the "Republic of China," the official name of the Government here.
"You can see what Lee Teng-hui thinks in his heart," said Antonio C.N. 
Chiang, a magazine publisher in Taipei. 
"He wants to sustain the separation with the mainland, because that's the reality."
He added: "Reunification is the state religion here. 
But ordinary folks are atheists."
