text:
ï»¿
GOLDEN INCHES
The China Memoir of Grace Service.
Edited by John S. Service.
Illustrated. 346 pp. 
Berkeley:
University of California Press. 
$19.95.
The foreign Christian presence in China in the first 40 years of this century increasingly appears to have been an important contributing factor in the slow development of the Chinese revolution between 1911 and 1949. 
Some sense of this can be gathered from John Hersey's fine novel ''The Call.''
Yet that book and most others on the subject remain focused on the men who lived for their ''call.''
Grace Service's memoir, ''Golden Inches,'' helps us understand that often behind those men, making their work possible, were equally extraordinary women.
It is a wonderful, sad, moving memoir by an indomitable American who went to China with her husband. 
Inspired like so many others by the brilliant and charismatic John R. Mott of the Student Volunteer Movement, Bob Service and his wife arrived in China in 1905, before the end of the empire, before the beginning of the revolution. 
They lived there until 1934, 30 of the most turbulent years in Chinese history.
Service was a Y.M.C.A. secretary based in Sichuan, and, from the image presented here, he was saintly. 
Completely dedicated to the Y, he labored long and hard to build an indigenous self-help movement in China. 
Indeed, like many others, he came to feel that ''he had no place in America.''
Behind and beside him, and making his life possible, was his highly intelligent, reflective, well-read and artistic wife, a woman who was self-disciplined rather than overtly pious.
The point of view in the memoir remains hers; the book is only secondarily about successes and failures in bringing the Y's programs to China. 
The revolution itself is something that happens to her, and must be dealt with like a natural event. 
''Golden Inches'' is not a book to read for a new interpretation of the early stages of the Chinese revolution. 
Rather, it is about the support that men like Bob Service had to have in order to be able to carry out their vocation.
And what support it was - a kind of marriage that seems to have all but disappeared in our time. 
''I thought I had given you certainty when I brought you to China,'' Service remarked apologetically to his wife in 1934, after being ''demobilized'' by the Y.M.C.A. in response to economic pressures. 
Such a vision of ''certainty'' could only be that which a shared sense of vocation can bring. 
By the time the Services had reached Chengdu (by boat, up the Yangtze) in 1905, their first-born, an infant daughter, had died of dysentery and Bob had contracted a severe case of malaria; within a year, Grace had at least one miscarriage. 
They still knew no Chinese.
But the Services endured - through civil war, battles, disease, riots - because in a way almost unspoken, but nonetheless absolutely firm, they had each other. 
After one episode outside their compound wall, Grace Service remarked: ''We heard that there had been some 150 to 200 executions, but soon the whole episode was merely an incident in the course of daily life.''
The Services came to love China and drew strength from it. 
Their three sons were born in Sichuan.
If the Services tried to accept China as it presented itself to them, they had more trouble with other foreigners. 
Again and again there are telling passages about the standoffish, almost imperial attitudes of fundamentalist missionaries who put doctrine above love, in contrast to the attempts of the Y to develop a Chinese-based organization. 
It is interesting to note that the Protestant churches in China are currently trying to follow the pattern of development set by the Y. The Services were people equal to the turbulence of the times in which they lived. 
''Golden Inches'' not only gives many fascinating glimpses of historical events; more important, it shows us what it meant to live through those events and deal with them without rancor, resentment or facile anger and enthusiasm. 
It reads fluidly and plainly. 
Like most of her generation, Grace Service was not introspective, but her memoir is all the more powerful for not being so: it extends our concept of what can be ordinary.
John S. Service, a Foreign Service officer in China from 1933 until 1945 and one of the first United States Government officials to have understood the nature of the developing Chinese revolution, has expertly edited and annotated his mother's memoir. 
He has filled in necessary historical information, and he shows just enough filial rebellion in his footnotes to give the reader an added sense of the family.

file: AFRICANS IN BEIJING BOYCOTT CLASSES.txt
text:
ï»¿
African students at a Beijing language institute began boycotting classes today to protest what they feel is racism in China, and interracial clashes were reported in another city after two weeks of racial unrest.
On Tuesday, about 2,000 Chinese students at the Beijing Languages Institute boycotted classes and held a march to protest what they said were attacks on Chinese women by African men. 
Most of the Chinese returned to classes today, but the institute's 500 African students began boycotting classes themselves to protest what they described as racist attitudes and policies.
The African students said they did not dare hold a demonstration in the current tense atmosphere, but that they would continue to boycott classes until the police released African students in the eastern city of Nanjing who have been charged with starting a Christmas Eve fight in which 11 Chinese were injured. 
That brawl touched off demonstrations in Nanjing that have spread to other cities.
Â 
Students Urged to Return
The president of Hehai University, the school in Nanjing where the troubles started called on the African students today to return to the institution. 
''We have made full preparations to welcome foreign students to return to school to study,'' Liang Ruiju, the official, was quoted by the official New China News Agency as saying.
About 40 or 50 of Hehai's African students remain locked up in a Government guest house outside Nanjing. 
The authorities will allow them to return to school but not go anywhere else. 
The students say they feel unsafe in Nanjing and want to leave.
Meanwhile, a dozen African students in the central Chinese city of Wuhan have been isolated after an attack on them Saturday by hundreds of Chinese students, according to reports reaching Beijing. 
The Associated Press also quoted sources in Wuhan as saying that a Sri Lankan student had been beaten up, apparently because of his dark skin.
Liu Wu, a Government spokesman in Wuhan, denied that any racial unrest had occurred. 
He said a child had broken a window and that a Sri Lankan student cut himself picking up the glass. 
The African students have not been isolated, he said, but are on a special holiday trip.

file: AFRICANS IN CHINA ARE FINALLY FREED.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 45 African students who had been held against their will by the authorities in the eastern Chinese city of Nanjing for the last 10 days were released today. 
Most plan to leave China as soon as possible.
''We are damned in China,'' said M. T. Wills, a 25-year-old student from Zambia. 
''Definitely we're not safe here.''
Three students are still detained of the 130 Africans whom the police took to a Government guest house on Dec. 
26 after racial clashes in Nanjing. 
The three have been accused of injuring Chinese in a racial brawl on Dec. 
24 that touched off the unrest initially in Nanjing and since then in several other Chinese cities.
While China has invited some 1,500 Africans to study in China, most of them on scholarships much more generous than those awarded to Chinese students, many of the Africans interviewed tonight sounded bitter about their experience of the last two weeks.
''Even in South Africa, blacks are treated better than they are in China,'' said Abdul Sankoh, a 22-year-old engineering student from Sierra Leone. 
''At least there, innocent people are not tortured and shocked because they are black.''
#3 Chinese Also Reported Held In Beijing today, the Foreign Ministry again denied charges that the police had tortured the African students, and also announced that three Chinese were being held along with the Africans for their role in the initial fight that touched off the disturbances.
The racial confrontations in Nanjing, Wuhan, Beijing and Hangzhou have in some cases taken on a political character and have thereby presented the Government with the most serious challenge since student pro-democracy demonstrations were crushed two years ago.
In the eastern Chinese city of Hangzhou, African students appeared today to end a 10-day boycott of classes that began after their university telephone operator was said to have told callers the Africans had AIDS. 
The confrontatation appeared to be resolved by an agreement under which the university will write a letter certifying that they do not have AIDS and will provide them with a direct telephone line.
Â 
Nanjing Boycott Continues
But in Nanjing, African students interviewed by telephone said they would continue to boycott classes until the remaining Africans are released.
The Nanjing authorities have repaired the Africans' dormitory after crowds of Chinese attacked it on Dec. 
24 and again the next day, demanding that the Africans be punished for their role in a fight in which two Africans and 11 Chinese were hurt.
The official New China News Agency reported late tonight that the three Africans still detained have admitted to breaking the law. 
It said two of the students, Alpha Robinson of Gambia and Dossoumou Boni Lodovic of Benin, would be detained for 15 days. 
The third, Alex Dosoo, of Ghana, will apparently face criminal charges for what the authorities say was the beating of a university employee.
In Ghana, the official radio reported today that Ghanaian students in China may be recalled. 
Most African countries have been hesitant to criticize China's handling of the racial clashes, partly because of the historical friendship and assistance provided by China, and perhaps partly because China subsidizes many of the African embassies.

file: After the Cold War -- Views From Japan_Tokyo in the New Epoch_ Heady Future, With Fear.txt
text:
ï»¿
No country prospered more during the cold war than Japan, and perhaps no country is more wistful for that era's comforting certainties. 
While the United States and Europe were preoccupied with throw weights and satellite photographs, Japan was able to focus almost entirely on building an economy that became the envy of the world, largely undistracted by, and often profiting from, the superpower rivalry.
For several years now the Japanese have known that those heady days were coming to an end. 
Nonetheless, the cold war's demise caught this country strangely ill prepared, forcing it to recast its dealings with its main ally, the United States, and break out of a four-decade stalemate in its diplomatic relations with its most powerful Asian neighbors.
Though still bound to be dominated by economic issues, the 1990's will also be a test of Japan's ability to overcome its reflexive isolationism, to become an independent political power without arousing those who are already deeply anxious about its economic might.
Â 
New Security Rationale Sought
For the United States, Japan's search raises a question that officials on both sides of the Pacific are just beginning to discuss publicly: What is the new rationale for a security alliance intended to give Japan protection in return for America's biggest, strongest Pacific outpost against Communism?
Though the Bush Administration insists that it remains deeply committed to a forward deployment here, especially as long as tensions remain on the Korean Peninsula, many here believe that it is only a matter of time before America's 56,000 troops here are reduced to a largely symbolic force.
"What we are concerned with is an America turning inward, politically and economically," said Takakazu Kuriyama, a former Deputy Foreign Minister and now Ambassador to the United States.
Others share his fear, not least because America's presence reassures Japan's neighbors.
Â 
Is Japan Next U.S. 
Rival?
But the prospect of a reduced American role in the Pacific is only part of what leaves the Japanese uneasy. 
In the Japanese press and on television it often seems the conventional wisdom that America has a psychological need for a rival, and that Japan is next in line. 
Such views may be more widely repeated than deeply held; polls show that while there is a deepening distrust and disillusionment with the United States, Japanese still regard America as their closest -- and perhaps only -- true friend in the world.
But it is a measure of Japan's insecurity on this point that books with titles like "The Coming War With Japan" are always much bigger sellers here than in the United States, and a recurrent theme in manga, the thick comic books read by millions of Japanese workers on the subways, is an American military once again at battle with Japanese forces.
Without question, such popular views have a subtle effect on the way Japanese view their own future relations with the rest of the world, making them feel that they are increasingly being cast out to fend for themselves. 
But some believe that such a change is overdue, that America's domination of Japanese security policy has delayed Japan's maturation as a truly independent state.
"In a sense we are politically in transition, from being dependent on U.S. policy to an independent status," said Saburo Okita, a former Foreign Minister. 
"But our politics have been so dependent that we still cannot make our own decisions."
Nothing has made that clearer than the two continuing debates that have seized Japan this year: whether to demand a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council and whether to create a peacekeeping force that could be sent on United Nations missions, violating a taboo against "collective security" arrangements that dates to the end of World War II.
The Tokyo Government has not wanted to appear to be openly seeking the Security Council seat, even though countries with far less economic power sit there today. 
But there is also an underlying fear that Japan, if given a bully pulpit, may have little to say. 
"We might be ashamed to raise our hand," Seiki Nishihiro, a former Deputy Defense Minister, said during a recent conference.
Â 
Peacekeeping
Fear of Sending Troops Abroad
The debate over a peacekeeping force has been marked by ambivalence of another sort. 
Ever since the Persian Gulf war, the Government has tried to push through a bill that would create a lightly armed organization that could be sent out entirely under United Nations command. 
From the outside it appears innocuous. 
Yet twice the bill has been defeated, and Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa's tenure in office may depend on his ability to pass it in the next few months.
While few will say so explicitly, the debate over the peacekeeping bill seems to be motivated by a broader question: Does the Japanese public yet trust its Government enough to send the military abroad, without fear that it could once again veer toward the expansionist militarism that got the country into World War II?
Over the last year, it has become increasingly clear that the Japanese public does not share the political leadership's enthusiasm for post-cold-war self-assertiveness. 
In surveys, on television and just in conversation, many Japanese say that while they agree that Japan must find new ways to contribute to the world, they are deeply uncomfortable with the idea of breaking the taboos that have kept their military forces at home and focused the Government on economic development, not geopolitics.
Such questions are arising only now because for four decades Tokyo's foreign policy has followed Washington's so closely that Japan has developed few of the institutions needed to chart its own course -- a powerful foreign ministry, an independent intelligence network, a confident military. 
Unlike Germany, Japan in the postwar era never entered regional collective security arrangements, even with other American allies like South Korea.
As a result, many Japanese leaders concede that the country still finds itself almost paralyzed diplomatically. 
Though it has tried to help bring about a settlement in Cambodia, not long ago the Japanese who is running the United Nations peacekeeping operation there, Yasushi Akashi, accused his country of moving too slowly and helping too little in sending personnel and logistical assistance to the area. 
To get the peacekeeping bill through Parliament, the governing Liberal Democratic Party may have to agree to send no one for several years, presumably until after the Cambodia peacekeeping operation expires. 
Or the Government may bow to demands from the opposition that forces be sent on a case-by-case basis, meaning a parliamentary debate each time.
Such domestic deal-making may be the biggest impediment to Japan's broader international role. 
The constant factional struggle in the Liberal Democratic Party has led party leaders to talk about the direction of the country's foreign and security policy in only the vaguest of terms. 
Japan's neighbors say the clubby, often secretive ways that political decisions are made in Japan add to their distrust of a broader global role for the country.
"The prerequisite for taking a larger political role," said Gerald Hensley, the Defense Minister of New Zealand, "is whether they can clean up their own political system, thus commanding more international confidence. 
And they must learn to act more generously."
Â 
Security
Dependence on U.S. 
Begins to Crumble
When he commanded the American occupation of Japan, Gen. Douglas MacArthur described his vision of the country as a "Switzerland of the Pacific," a neutral nation that took no sides in the region's many conflicts. 
It was an image that still resonates deeply with many Japanese, who associate the country's 40-year territorial expansion -- first into Sakhalin and Korea, then into China and Southeast Asia -- with phenomenal destruction and crushing poverty.
General MacArthur's vision of neutrality was quickly jettisoned in reaction to the Communist takeover in China, the growing confrontation with the Soviet Union and the wars in Korea and Indochina. 
Soon a new bargain was struck: Japan would provide the United States with bases on Japanese soil in return for American protection. 
Though the security treaty was the subject of violent street protests in 1960, it has since come to be the fabric underlying Japanese foreign policy.
At America's urging, Japan used the prospect of invasion by the Soviet Union to justify the buildup its own military forces, reinterpreting its Constitution to allow defensive forces. 
As Japan geared up a military budget that now tops $30 billion a year, making it among the largest in the world, Japanese industry profited greatly, building ships and aircraft under American license and gaining considerable technology and manufacturing experience.
"In reality no one really believed there was much of a Soviet threat," a senior Japanese diplomat said recently. 
But it was a "convenient arrangement," he said.
It was particularly convenient for Japanese businessmen, who always enjoyed hearing the American Ambassador to Tokyo throughout the 1980's, Mike Mansfield, repeat that Japan and America had "the most important bilateral relationship in the world."
They knew it meant that the security relationship would almost always overshadow American concerns about economic competitiveness.
"When you read some of the history, it is incredible how much of Japan policy for 40 years centered around making sure that Japan didn't go to the other side, the side of military neutrality," said James Fallows, who is completing a book about Japan and Asia. 
"As a politically relevant fact, that only ended a year ago."
The first concrete evidence that the traditional thinking was crumbling came in 1989, when Congress objected to technology transfers to Japan for the co-development of a new fighter jet, called the FSX. 
That began a spiral of resentments that reached a zenith when Japan rejected requests that it provide personnel -- not necessarily military personnel -- in the gulf war.
To Washington that constituted evidence that the alliance was one-sided. 
"Japan lost a lot of supporters here," a senior American military official said several months ago.
Â 
U.S. Presence
New Threats Seen As Old Ones Ease
Critics of America's military presence here say the military is simply inventing missions to justify the presence, overstating threats and magnifying the power of potential rivals.
But whenever American military officials travel through the region, they insist that Japan has taken on renewed importance in the Pentagon's strategy, especially after the loss of Clark Air Base and Subic Bay Naval Station in the Philippines. 
Potential threats, they argue, are real and plentiful.
"Russia is still one," said Lieut. 
Gen. Richard E. Hawley, who commands all the American forces in Japan. 
"You don't see the same changes in the Russian military structure when you sit in Japan and look west as you do when you sit in Berlin and look east."
"China is a major power center," he continued, "and that alone is simple justification for continued U.S. presence in this part of the world."
Perhaps the most unpredictable threat of all, and the one cited most often these days, is North Korea. 
Its suspected efforts to build nuclear weapons have rattled Japan's leadership and become the focus of what may be the closest political cooperation between Tokyo and Washington in years, as the two try to convince North Korea that the price it must pay for economic aid and recognition is abandonment of its nuclear ambitions.
"To talk about an American decline of interest here is both wrong and dangerous," James R. Lilley, a former Ambassador to China and now Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs, said during a recent Asian tour. 
"It gives potential predators a false sense of opportunity and an inducement to be aggressive."
"Let's not give Kim Jong Il any ideas," he said, referring to the heir-apparent in North Korea.
Â 
Militarism
Fear of Revival Of Adventurism
American and Japanese officials are more hesitant to talk about the other, rarely stated benefit of keeping American troops posted here: It reassures Asian nations that worry about a revived Japanese military.
But as the peacekeeping bill demonstrates, the concern seems overblown. 
There is virtually no detectable appetite for military adventurism in Tokyo, and little support, except from the Japanese right wing, for building anything other than purely defensive ability. 
Year after year, the Japanese military has been unable to win support for refueling planes or for small aircraft carriers, both of which Japanese fear would be viewed as potentially offensive weapons. 
Japan does not even have its own surveillance satellites, a source of considerable frustration in Tokyo since the North Korean nuclear scare began.
Most vocal in support of an American presence to keep a check on Japan are countries like Singapore, where this year schoolchildren were herded through an exhibit at the national museum with graphic images of Japanese atrocities during the occupation of the city 50 years ago. 
Singapore's Defense Minister, Yeo Ning Hong, said recently that should the United States gradually reduce its presence in the Pacific, "Japan may feel compelled to re-arm to safeguard its trade routes beyond the 1,000 nautical miles south of Tokyo," the current limit for Japanese forces.
That could prompt the Chinese and the Koreans, Mr. Yeo said, to "build up their respective armed forces to counter and contain any Japanese rearmament," setting off "a whole chain reaction of destabilization."
But the true concern about American withdrawal from the region involves a far more subtle form of Japanese influence. 
With newly built factories stretching from southern China to Indonesia, Japan is already the overwhelming economic power in the region. 
Japanese-style capitalism and Japanese work habits rival the Sony Walkman as Japan's most conspicuous export. 
The United States, in the view of many Southeast Asians, plays a critical if economically unrewarding role, assuring that Japan's influence stays on the factory floor.
"The more respectable argument is not that Japan will re-militarize in the absence of America but simply that if America pulls back, the Japanese will slowly move to fill the gap," said Mr. Hensley, the New Zealand Defense Minister. 
"Everyone will feel uncomfortable. 
Not because of memories of World War II -- most people are too young to remember it -- but because America and Great Britain, while they have made mistakes in Asia, have thought and acted globally. 
They pay into the system as well as take out. 
And so far, the Japanese have not paid in."
Â 
Old Disputes
New Relationships Are Elusive
In their dealings in Asia, the Japanese have also seemed oddly hamstrung by their older cold-war habits.
Many Tokyo officials say they are embarrassed that smaller nations like South Korea managed to break free of traditional anti-Communist restraints over the last two years, forming new relationships with Russia, China and even the hard-line Communist regime in North Korea. 
But Japan still seems locked in its old disputes.
Its longtime territorial dispute over four northern islands, taken by the Soviet Union in the last days of World War II, has virtually frozen any prospect of anything but grudging Japanese economic aid to the former Soviet republics. 
Relations with China and South Korea, always on a knife's edge, are once again being colored by new charges that Japan is ducking responsibility for war atrocities -- this time by deflecting demands that it compensate Korean and Chinese women who were forced to provide sex to Japanese troops. 
It now appears unlikely that Emperor Akihito will take a long-expected trip to China this year, the first ever by a Japanese emperor.
Not everyone is unhappy keeping the Japanese slightly off balance in Asia.
"No matter what kind of nice face they put on it, people are still suspicious as hell of the Japanese," said K. S. Sandhu, a Malaysian who heads the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies in Singapore. 
"The fact is that they are perfectionist about everything they do, and if they decide again to become influential politically or militarily, they will do it to a fine art."
The Japanese have their own complaints about the new era, and the chief one is that if an American comes to visit Japan these days, someone has to lock the treasury door. 
Though Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d chastised Japan last year for what he called its inability to break out of "checkbook diplomacy," Japanese say a check is all America really seems to want, whether the project is the liberation of Kuwait or the building of the superconducting supercollider in Texas. 
In each case, they complain, Japan is often excluded from the critical moments of decision.
Some fear that Japan is heading into a Faustian bargain, that a more assertive Japan will mean the abandonment of the postwar military restraints that have become the core of the country's self-image.
Many Japanese recognize, however, that their political re-engagement is now inevitable, the logical conclusion to a particularly mercantile phase of Japanese history.
"Since 1945, the whole country was directed to bringing a recovery to the Japanese economy," said Akio Tanii, the president of the Matsushita Electric Industrial Company, the world's largest consumer electronics company. 
"We have come to the point where we are not the student any longer. 
We have something to teach. 
The problem is we don't know where to start."

file: After the Summit_The Soviets and South Korea_ At Odds Since Day 1.txt
text:
ï»¿
By meeting yesterday, Mikhail S. Gorbachev and Roh Tae Woo underscored an anachronism of cold-war history.
Since it was established after World War II, South Korea has had no formal diplomatic ties with the Soviet Union, and few unofficial contacts. 
The first Soviet tourist ship to dock in a South Korean port since World War II - the 13,000-ton Mikhail Sholokov - did not drop its gangplank until Sept. 
4, 1988, 43 years after Korea was partitioned into northern and southern halves by the victorious Allies.
Russia was interested in Korea as far back as the mid-19th century. 
Russian merchants traded there in lumber and metals. 
The Russian Orthodox church began sending missionaries to the peninsula.
The Japanese Influence
Japanese and Chinese competitors wanted similar access and exports, and the rivalries led to war - first between Japan and China in 1894 and 1895, then between the Russians and Japanese in 1904 and 1905. 
Japan won both times, and the Russian influence in Korea waned. 
Japan set up a protectorate over Korea and in 1910 annexed the country.
Several attempts by Korean nationalists to overthrow Japan's harsh rule were crushed. 
After World War I, a Korean Government in exile was established by Syngman Rhee in Shanghai.
Japanese investment led to major social and economic changes, particularly through the industrial development of the northern half of the country, which adjoined the Japanese industrial complex in Manchuria. 
The southern half remained mostly agricultural.
In World War II the Allies called for the restoration of an independent Korea ''in due course'' during the Cairo Conference in 1943. 
After the fighting stopped, the major powers divided Korea in two for occupation purposes, with Soviet forces in control north of the 38th parallel and American forces south of it.
Â 
Deadlock Between Superpowers
The details of unification and independence for Korea were left to the two superpowers. 
As the cold war broke out, the two sides soon deadlocked on the establishment of a provisional government and in 1947 sent the issue of Korea's future to the United Nations General Assembly, where a temporary commission was set up to schedule elections and establish a national government.
But the Soviet occupation authorities refused. 
Elections in the southern sector, with United Nations observers on duty, took place in 1948, and the Republic of Korea was established south of the 38th parallel. 
A separate Communist-controlled Government was set up in the north, which renamed itself the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
Soviet troops withdrew from the north at the end of 1948, and United States forces went home from the south in mid-1949, a few months before Secretary of State Dean Acheson outlined an American retrenchment in Asia with a Pacific ''defense perimeter'' that did not include Korea.
Â 
Invasion Leads to Korean War
But on June 25, 1950, North Korea invaded the south, and United States troops were sent back to the country, where they were joined by contingents from many other nations under the United Nations flag. 
After three years of fighting, the battle lines stabilized close to the frontiers before the war.
Under a 1953 truce agreement at Panmunjom a demilitarized zone was established near the 38th parallel.
Soviet-North Korean relations have had their own difficulties. 
After the Chinese-Soviet split of the early 1960's, President Kim Il Sung of North Korea tried to avoid complete identification with either side. 
But since the mid-1970's North Korea leaned more toward China. 
Mr. Kim visited Beijing in 1975, a year after he welcomed Hu Yaobang of the Chinese Communist leadership to Pyongyang.
Â 
North Korean Overtures
Soviet-North Korean trade declined by 10 percent between 1982 and 1983, and in 1984 Mr. Kim visited Moscow, for the first time in nearly 20 years, looking for economic aid.
During Mr. Kim's visit, Mr. Gorbachev's predecessor, Konstantin U. Chernenko, said that reunification of the two Koreas should be worked out peaceably. 
South Korean officials later said that North Korea had proposed secret talks on unification with the United States. 
But the Reagan Administration refused, insisting that such negotiations involve only the two Koreas.
With the 1988 Olympics in Seoul, the South Korean Government began trying to turn its economic boom to its political advantage. 
In part, this involved setting up diplomatic relations with countries in the Soviet bloc. 
So far, South Korea has opened embassies with all the Eastern European nations except East Germany and Albania.
The south's economic strength and its diplomatic successes have put it in a commanding position, said Gari Ledyard, a professor of Korean history at Columbia University and the director of the Center for Korean Research there. 
''They've already won, even if they can't agree on anything,'' he said. 
''Just the fact that a Korean president met with the Russian is a severe blow'' to the North Koreans.
Indeed, Professor Ledyard said, the meeting appears to have created a no-win situation for North Korea. 
''Presumably, their relationships and agreements with the Soviets will continue in force, just like ours do with China,'' he said, ''but the spirit's just not there anymore. 
There has been talk in South Korea about using Siberian development as a possible way for North and South Korea to cooperate, but it's something that South Korea would be able to dominate.''

file: AFTER THE WAR_Bush May Seek U.N. Ruling For Force in Kurdish Zone.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Bush said today that he was willing to seek Security Council authority to create a United Nations security force in northern Iraq that would pave the way for the withdrawal of American and allied military forces from the Kurdish region.
The announcement came a day after the Secretary General of the United Nations, Javier Perez de Cuellar, indicated that his envoy in Baghdad was making progress in negotiating conditional Iraqi support for such a security force. 
The State Department spokesman, Richard A. Boucher, also said today, "There may be some preliminary agreement on some type of guard arrangements to be associated with the U.N. humanitarian effort."
A compromise on the security force issue that is acceptable to Washington and Baghdad could spare Mr. Bush a stalemate in northern Iraq, a development that could turn the humanitarian effort into a political liability at home.
Also, a compromise security force that won Iraq's approval would defuse a potentially bruising dispute between Mr. Bush and the Security Council, where the Soviet Union and China have expressed strong reservations against a United Nations military role in Iraq that is not approved by the Iraqi Government.
In a sign that Mr. Bush may be courting Security Council votes, the President also stated publicly today that he favored renewing China's most-favored-nation trade status, linking his decision to China's cooperation at the United Nations during the Persian Gulf conflict.
Last fall, when Mr. Bush needed critical Chinese and Soviet votes to authorize the use of force against Iraqi troops in Kuwait, the President broke his own ban on high-level visits by Chinese officials imposed after the Tiananmen Square crackdown.
The United Nations police force, if it is approved, would provide protection for the relief operation under way in the Kurdish security zone that stretches from Zakho on the Turkish border to the outskirts of Dohuk, a major Iraqi provincial capital. 
More than 8,000 American, British and French forces occupy the zone and thousands more are stationed in Turkey and the Eastern Mediterranean as a "quick reaction" force.
Responding to a question about the United Nations police force proposal, Mr. Bush told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House, "We're contemplating going to the United Nations on that to get further authority."
Â 
Compromise Possible
Mr. Bush added that, in his opinion, the authority to create such a police force has already been granted "under existing resolutions" of the United Nations that require Iraq to cooperate with humanitarian relief efforts.
But his public remarks indicated that Mr. Perez de Cuellar's negotiations with Baghdad may have produced a formula that the United States and its allies will be able to accept.
On Tuesday, Mr. Perez de Cuellar said that his special envoy, Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan, was negotiating approval from Iraqi officials to add an armed United Nations security force of 400 to 500 men to the United Nations relief workers already in northern Iraq.
A permanent reconciliation between the Kurds and the Iraqi Government is the subject of separate negotiations now headed by the Kurdish guerilla leader Massoud Barzani. 
Mr. Bush also said today that these talks "could offer some hope."
But Mr. Bush emphasized that until relations between the Kurds and the Iraqi Government are normalized, the United States will adhere to its security commitment. 
"I don't think we can entrust the fate of the Kurds to the word of Saddam Hussein."
At the State Department, Mr. Boucher said "we don't have the details" of the security force proposal that is emerging from the talks in Baghdad. 
"But we understand that discussion will continue this week between the U.N. and Iraqi authorities."

file: Aided by U.S. Waiver, China Launches First Foreign Satellite.txt
text:
ï»¿
China launched a foreign telecommunications satellite tonight, setting off a national celebration to mark its entry into the international launching business.
As television viewers watched, a Chinese Long March 3 rocket carrying the American-made satellite blasted off from a launching pad in the central province of Sichuan. 
It is the first time that China has launched a foreign satellite.
The launching took place around 9:30 P.M. after being delayed for more than an hour and a half because of bad weather, officials said.
The launching of the satellite, Asiasat, built by the Hughes Aircraft Company and owned by a consortium based in Hong Kong, was made possible when President Bush temporarily waived a ban on weapons exports to China to allow the export of the satellite in February. 
The ban was imposed in June in response to China's military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing.
Â 
U.S. to Export 2 Others
Although President Bush said he was exercising the waiver for the sake of ''national interest,'' the move was viewed by many diplomats and politicians as a conciliatory gesture to Beijing.

Asiasat has the capacity to relay television, telephone and facsimile signals to about 2.5 billion people in more than 30 Asian countries. 
Many live in remote areas with little access to telecommunications services.
A Chinese company, the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, is a partner in the consortium, but apparently has no control over the satellite's operations, which will be monitored from Hong Kong. 
Other partners are Cable and Wireless P.L.C. of Britain, and Hutchison Telecommunications Ltd. of Hong Kong.
It was the second time that the 2,732-pound satellite, formerly called Westar-6, was launched into space.

text:
ï»¿
A report that 146 peasants from Yunnan Province on China's southwest border used dirty drug needles and infected themselves with the AIDS virus has sent shivers throughout China.
It was the first sign of a large incidence in China, where officials asserted previously that most AIDS cases involved foreigners. 
In addition to the discovery, announced in February, more than 100 other samples from Yunnan peasants have been sent to Beijing for additional testing to see whether they are infected with the virus, officials here said in interviews.
The more the Government investigates, the more cases the Government fears it will find, deflatingthe notion that China faces neither a drug problem nor an AIDS problem.
''The news was explosive,'' a Chinese official here said of the discovery of the AIDS virus. 
''We were shocked.''
Â 
Comparatively Tiny Number
So far the numbers are tiny compared with the tens of thousands of AIDS cases in Western countries, but they are a cause of great concern in China. 
China had previously reported that 41 foreigners and 7 Chinese carried the virus, of whom only 3 actually developed the disease. 
The latest confirmed findings brought China's total number of publicized cases to 194.
The spread of the virus here in Yunnan Province, in a temperate corner of China, points to what officials acknowledge is an increasingly severe problem of narcotics trafficking. 
Hard drugs like heroin are transported through China to the West from bordering countries like Burma, Thailand and Vietnam, the officials say.
Most of the drugs pass through China, rather than being consumed here. 
But a growing number of people are using the drugs, and the discovery that most of those with the AIDS virus are from ethnic minorities could affect the sometimes fragile relationship between the Government and some minorities.
''Those farmers have the impression that if you take drugs, they'll have pleasant illusions,'' said Wang Wenxin, a doctor of infectious diseases at the office for AIDS prevention and control here. 
''These people are poorly educated and relatively ignorant.''
Â 
Victims Used Heroin
The 146 cases were discovered after testing of peasants living in Ruili County, along the border with Myanmar, formerly Burma. 
Health officials say all the victims, including one woman and young men in their late teens, were infected with the AIDS virus when they injected heroin with shared needles.
Provincial oficials said that so far they had not linked any AIDS-related cases to foreigners or contaminated blood, and tests on 500 Kunming residents proved negative.
For China, the role of intravenous drug use in AIDS brings back painful memories of the nation's suffering in the last century and in the first half of this century because of widespread opium addiction. 
Many Chinese attributed the widespread opium dependency to the country's weakness as it fell victim to foreign invaders and domestic warlords. 
About 20 million people - nearly five percent of the population at that time - smoked opium, and a sizable portion of the cultivable land in China was used to grow poppies, according to Chen Cunyi, deputy director of the provincial public security division against drugs.
When they took control in 1949, the Communists virtually wiped out opium smoking, and for several decades China was considered a drug-free country. 
But Mr. Chen said drug activity had not only resurfaced but had also shifted from smoking opium to smuggling and intravenous use of heroin.
Â 
Heroin Seizures Double
Last year, the amount of heroin seized in Yunnan Province rose to almost 600 pounds from about 260 in 1988, while seizures of opium declined to about 300 pounds from 340 in 1988. 
The heroin seized, however, is highly concentrated, and one kilogram can be reformulated into 12 kilograms in Hong Kong.
Mr. Chen declined to estimate what portion of the drug traffic is intercepted, although some estimates have put it at 10 percent.
The discovery that narcotics use is leading to the spread of the AIDS virus has made the problem much more compelling in China, which has long been concerned about the disease.
In Chinese clinics most hypodermic needles are reused, although disposable needles are being introduced, and the hygiene and frequency of blood checks before transfusions is worse than in the West.
Chinese officials have therefore been very aware of the risks of AIDS, and so far they have focused their efforts on screening foreigners. 
All foreigners who live in China for a year or more must have an AIDS test, and even short-term tourists are sometimes asked questions intended to determine if they have AIDS.
Â 
Diplomatic Ties Involved
The border trade in drugs is a delicate matter for China because of its effect on diplomatic relations with China's neighbors. 
Mr. Chen insisted that the drugs came from the bordering countries, and that China was only a conduit because of its geographic position between the drug-producing areas and transportation hubs like Hong Kong.
''It is absolutely not grown here,'' Mr. Chen said. 
So far the China connection is not nearly as significant as other sources of the West's heroin - such as Latin America or other Asian transit points - even though officials here acknowledge that it is a growing problem.
The authorities have stepped up their efforts, spending about $1 million on narcotics control in Yunnan Province, but they acknowledge that it is not enough.
The public security staff has added 1,300 officers to combat the drug problem, but this is a fraction of the number believed necessary to monitor the porous, 2,500-mile southwestern border.
''It's impossible for us to station guards, one by one, along the border, because we don't have such manpower,'' Mr. Chen said.

file: American on Their Own Terms_The Complete Other Side of the World_.txt
text:
ï»¿
TYPICAL AMERICAN
By Gish Jen.
296 pp. 
Boston:
Seymour Lawrence/Houghton Mifflin Company. 
$19.95.
Migration and mutation form a persistent, characterizing theme of our unsettling time. 
In her first novel, "Typical American," which explores the transformation of Chinese immigrants in the United States, Gish Jen has engaged this theme with distinction. 
More than that, she has given us "natives" (that is, the less recently settled) back to ourselves with a jolt of sharpened self-recognition.
"It's an American story," so the tale begins. 
"Before he was a thinker, or a doer, or an engineer, much less an imagineer like his self-made-millionaire friend Grover Ding, Ralph Chang was just a small boy in China, struggling to grow up his father's son."
The novel charts the progress of "Ralph" (an Americanization of Lai Fu -- "Come Fortune"), who leaves China in 1947, amid the "wreckage, and inflation, and moral collapse" that follow the war with Japan. 
Ralph's aim is to pursue engineering studies in New York.
He has six subsidiary goals, carefully listed. 
Two are resolutions to cultivate virtue and bring honor to his family. 
The succeeding four, culminating in a resolve to have nothing to do with girls, are abandoned without recall as Ralph comes to realize that he is alone, that he has journeyed "to the complete other side of the world."
It is during his first year abroad that Manchuria falls to Communist control -- the opening in a series of moves that will utterly transform China, sundering Ralph's link with his parents and ancestral traditions and leaving him unmoored, adrift in a new world.
Then, one day, Ralph is found slumped on a park bench, in the depths of despair. 
The finder is none other than Theresa, his long-lost older sister, who had emigrated before him. 
" 'Was miracle.'
This was Ralph's version of the story. 
'Miracle!'
" There's yet another miracle in store: Theresa happens to be rooming with a beautiful young Chinese woman named Helen, who is destined to become Ralph's wife. 
Together Ralph, Helen and Theresa set up housekeeping and, as they progress from permanent residents to citizens, each -- in his or her own way -- begins to undergo a sea change.
It is greed that most powerfully transforms Helen and Ralph. 
From their former playfully defensive recital of "typical American" characteristics ("typical American no-manners," "typical American no-morals," "typical American use-brute-force," "typical American wasteful") comes a new chant. 
Helen's is a litany of enraptured consumerism; Ralph's, of high-venture capitalism. 
Hers: "Double garage with separate entrance. 
Finished basement. 
Sliding glass doors. 
. . . breakfast nook with built-in benches. 
. . . wall unit. 
. . . extras galore."
His: "Got to spend money to make money. 
. . . What you can conceive, you can achieve. 
. . . The whole trick is. 
. . . Sky's the limit. 
. . . Can do, can do, can do!"
And, in time, as his own restaurant -- Ralph's Chicken Palace -- takes tangible shape, Ralph's dream of America as "every wish come true" seems to be realized.
I won't reveal what comes next, although no mere plot recital could possibly spoil the rest. 
No paraphrase could capture the intelligence of Gish Jen's prose, its epigrammatic sweep and swiftness. 
There's no pause, no underlining, no winking aside to the reader to signal how clever this is, how humorous that is. 
The author just keeps coming at you, line after stunning line. 
Even her incidental description seems new-minted -- purely functional, bone clean yet lustrous -- whether it's focused on the wilting of an elaborately curled hairdo in a discouraging social situation, or on children facing their first move, kissing the walls of their old apartment goodbye, or on death threatening one of the family members as "a man to sit at supper and never eat -- a man with his eye on everyone."
Here is Theresa, succumbing to the seduction of a pair of highly colored, voluptuously curved new shoes:
"These shoes had snagged her -- so vital, there in the store window, that they did not look like shoes so much as some highly adapted life form, mimicking shoes the way lizards mimicked desert rocks. 
Whereas the shoes she'd had on were plainly the real thing: worn out, dried up, cracking. 
Like their owner -- her reflection in the window was spindly and stiff, separated just this way, by a pane of glass, from some more vibrant world. 
At the center of her image, the red shoes had seemed to pulse, like her own true heart."
My only quarrel with this book is a backhanded tribute to its virtues, to the interest created in character and situation. 
There were times when I wanted to know more -- deeper and more -- moments when Helen and Ralph's capitulation to all-American greed seemed too easy, too headlong, verging on the simplicity of fable. 
This simplicity is clearly not wrong in itself, but it struck me as fundamentally at odds with the complexity, the multifaceted richness, of the novel as a whole.
Were there no contending forces?
No dim remembrance of Confucian harmonies or Buddhist detachment before Ralph's obsession gained full sway?
Wouldn't even passing reflection on the austerities of life under a Communist regime in China have raised a little point-counterpoint, exerted a chastening influence?
There were numerous references to church (Ralph, unconverted, attending with Theresa), rosaries, prayers, parochial school for the Chang children, yet not a word of admonition, not a whisper, concerning thralldom to material things. 
Was the church completely captive to culture, then?
It would seem so. 
Two perfunctory lines -- slogans, really -- from a homily ("Risk faith. 
Doubt doubt.") would suggest that the priest speaking was well attuned to typical American one-sound-bite attention spans. 
I wanted to know more.
It may be that this reader's lingerings and wonderings stem, in large part, from just plain reluctance to close the book on the Changs. 
For I came to care about all of them -- Theresa at first meeting, Ralph belatedly. 
And as the Changs seemed so hopelessly to drift apart, each one off in pursuit of some bright fragment of the American dream, I waited eagerly for them to return -- quan jia tuan yuan, the whole family together -- quite as if they had become my own family.
Â 
Â 
'I DREW ON WHAT I KNEW'
Gish Jen was once asked if the publishers of her first novel, "Typical American," had pressured her to change her name to something sounding less Chinese. 
"My real name is Lillian," she said, laughing, in a telephone interview from her home in Cambridge, Mass. 
She playfully adopted Gish -- as in the actress -- in high school. 
"It was part of becoming a writer," she said, "not becoming the person I was supposed to be."
That person was the dutiful daughter of Chinese immigrants, who expected her to get a practical job. 
Ms. Jen did attend business school briefly, and even took a typing test after marriage and house renovation had led her to put fiction aside. 
But before she became a secretary, Ms. Jen, an alumna of Harvard and the Iowa Writers' Workshop, successfully applied for a fellowship at Radcliffe's Bunting Institute. 
Her submission -- a story about the immigrant Changs -- grew into "Typical American."
"I drew on what I knew," she explained. 
"But even though I can see the elbows and knees and noses of people from my past, the relationship is like that between a dream and life. 
It's similar, but highly transformed."
Ms. Jen, who is 35 years old, once lived in Yonkers, where her family was called names and pelted with stones. 
But the experience, she said, did not define her childhood, and she refuses to emphasize it. 
In fact, the comedy of "Typical American" came most naturally. 
"I felt like a stereo with no bass," she said. 
"I had to learn to hit the low notes."
Although "Typical American" does include sadness, Ms. Jen still feels it is upbeat. 
"Not everyone has to be like Ralph," she said of her hero. 
"You can use the freedom of America differently."
When asked if she was working on a new book, Ms. Jen, who is now pregnant, replied simply: "I'm hatching."
-- LAUREL GRAEBER

In a plain stadium where a loudspeaker boomed out rousing Chinese folksongs, the United States women's soccer team defeated the German team tonight, 5-2, and won the right to take America into its first world championship soccer match.
Having reached the final of the first women's soccer championship, the United States team now has a chance to bring home a new trophy, and create a new image for American soccer.
"If we win this championship, I think the win will give us an international identity," said Anson Dorrance, coach of the United States women's team.
Dorrance, whose women's team garnered 49 goals to 0 for its five opponents during the qualifying matches for this tournament, said that while soccer is a very popular sport in the United States, "it's a sport with an inferiority complex. 
It's a sport most Americans feel is better played abroad."
But, he added, "The statement we're making is that we can play soccer in the United States."
Â 
Good Publicity for World Cup
Moreover, American soccer officials believe a championship women's team would focus attention and interest on the sport as the United States approaches 1994, the year it will be host to the World Cup soccer championship for men.
The championship match, which will be played Saturday in this sprawling, prosperous city in southern China, will pit the United States team against its archrival, Norway.
Norway has defeated the American team the last two times they were matched. 
In its semifinal game today, Norway beat Sweden by 4-1.
The United States women's team, which has played aggressive, entertaining, high-scoring soccer throughout the competition here, has "captured the attention of even the old stodgies here," said one soccer official, referring to some of the officials of FIFA, the organization governing world soccer, who are attending the event.
Â 
Making Up for Deficits
April Heinrichs of Littleton, Colo., the captain of the United States women's team, said that while the Americans might lack "the sophistication and the subtlety of the European players who grew up watching soccer on TV, we make up for that lack with speed, guts and determination."
Heinrichs, who is now head women's soccer coach at the University of Maryland, said that winning the world championship would be a watershed event for women's soccer in America.
"Females play soccer more than any other sport in America and I think this championship could draw attention to the sport, increase enrollment, sponsorship and audience interest," she said. 
"I think in four to eight years, soccer could dominate women's sports in America."
America's growing interest in soccer comes at a time when women's soccer is beginning to come into its own around the world, with 65 of the 165 countries involved in FIFA now sponsoring women's teams, officials said.
Â 
Sport Maturing in U.S.
The interest in soccer that began with boys and girls in America's suburbs and small towns in the mid-1970's is now maturing, bearing fruit in the form of the very players on the United States women's team here.
Carin Jennings, from Palos Verdes, Calif., said she had been playing soccer since she was 8 years old. 
Jennings scored three of the goals tonight against Germany, the defending European champion. 
Heinrichs scored the other two.
If they have impressed the other soccer teams and officials here, the 18 American players, aged 19 to 26, have also impressed the local Chinese.

file: An Empire Run Amid Rice Paddies.txt
text:
ï»¿
Retailers in bankruptcy?
A crumbling real estate market?
A global recession?
The problems might as well be happening on Mars, as far as Zhang Guoxi is concerned.
While gnarled old peasants slog barefoot behind water buffaloes in the rice paddies here, Mr. Zhang, apparently China's richest private businessman, has found a better way to make a living.
A balding 39-year-old who dropped out of school after the sixth grade, Mr. Zhang runs an international business empire based on furniture exports, property development and stock trading from his 10-story corporate headquarters, which juts above the paddies. 
From this remote country town he has emerged as an entrepreneur with assets worth tens of millions of dollars.
Â 
Defining the Limits
Mr. Zhang (whose full name is pronounced JAHNG gwaw-shee) is one of the best measures of how much capitalism the Communist authorities are prepared to tolerate in their drive for national prosperity. 
For 15 years, he has more or less defined the frontier of what can be tolerated, and despite the hardline oratory from Beijing in the last few years, he continues to thrive.
"Sure, I live very well," he said, grinning, when he was asked how many homes he owns. 
"Very well!"
After a pause, he added with a mischievous gleam in his eye: "So I should say, 'Long live Comrade Xiaoping!'
" The reference was to Deng Xiaoping, the 87-year-old paramount Chinese leader, who since January has led a new drive to carry out further capitalist-style changes in the economy.
In a society where peasants earn cash incomes of about $150 a year, Mr. Zhang is rich in a way that can scarcely be fathomed, rich in a way that the Rockefellers are rich. 
He sips Remy Martin cognac, and he has a chauffeur-driven car waiting for him in each city where he has an office. 
The state even provides him with his own police station of a dozen officers solely to protect his company and serve as his bodyguards.
Mr. Zhang may be leading the pack, but there are many other business tycoons emerging across China, capturing the spirit of the times. 
In the 1970's, many Chinese wanted to be revolutionary; today, they want to be rich. 
Most private businesses are only about a dozen years old, but they are expanding rapidly and branching across the nation and even the world. 
By the end of the century, China's private industrialists may be far more numerous and powerful than they are today.
"Deng Xiaoping has always said that China should let some people get rich first and let these people pull the economy along," said Christine Wong, an associate professor of economics at the University of California at Santa Cruz. 
"Now that Deng Xiaoping has reasserted his dominance in trying to formulate economic policy, I expect that things will look up for people like that."
Already the wealth and power that Mr. Zhang has gathered are jarring, partly because his base is not Beijing or Shanghai, but this small county seat of Yujiang in Jiangxi Province. 
Jiangxi is a poor, landlocked area that early in the century was a Communist guerrilla base. 
Most of the buildings around Yujiang are dilapidated brick homes with propaganda slogans proclaiming "Socialism is Good!" or calling on people to have just one child.
Â 
Touches of Modernity
Mr. Zhang's corporate headquarters rises abruptly from these surroundings, 10 stories of gleaming modernity with international direct dialing and fax service, in a sprawling compound that also includes a goldfish pond and two marble arches -- "I'm an artist, after all," he explained. 
His buildings have their own slogans, but they are not political: "Guard against fires!" the banners warn.
Financial success carries political risks in China, and for that reason Mr. Zhang prefers to refer to his enterprise not as "privately run" but as "people run."
But he does not dispute that his company is privately owned -- after all it is called the Guoxi Group, named after him -- and Government ministries have publicly referred to it as a private company.
Mr. Zhang is also discreet enough to dodge questions about his personal spending habits and about his net worth, but he finally acknowledges that $30 million or more might be a good estimate.
"More or less, more or less," he repeats, each time accenting the word "more."
Â 
Some Special Skills
Entrepreneurs in China often run into trouble with grasping officials, who arbitrarily impose huge taxes or who force the owner to sell to the Government. 
Mr. Zhang has had few such problems, and his methods offer a window into the skills that business tycoons need to succeed in China.
One of the most crucial skills is cultivation of Government and Communist Party officials, a task that the gregarious Mr. Zhang assumes with ease. 
He is a good friend of the provincial governor and of county officials, and he has contributed more than $1.5 million in recent years to local charities and public causes.
"He is a good party member and an excellent businessman," Gov. Wu Guanzheng said of Mr. Zhang at a recent public meeting. 
"For many years he has loved the party and the people, and done many good deeds."
The latest good deed -- and the purpose of the meeting -- was Mr. Zhang's contribution of $200,000 to endow a new Zhang Guoxi Education Foundation. 
Everything he contributes to seems to bear his name: the Zhang Guoxi Big Bridge is being completed to link Yujiang with the other side of a broad river.
"Boss, three cars can pass at a time on the bridge, no problem!"
Luo Genshen, the head of the construction team, says obsequiously as Mr. Zhang stands in the middle of the bridge and inspects the work. 
After asking a few questions, Mr. Zhang returns to his Nissan Cedrick to be chauffeured to his next spot on a round of inspections.
Â 
Providing Services
Mr. Zhang also helped pay to bring running water and international telephone service to Yujiang. 
In addition, he contributed the only other structures in Yujiang that rival his headquarters in height: a television relay tower to improve local reception and a seven-story science tower at the local school.
Perhaps because of the philanthropy, local officials regard Mr. Zhang as a great hero rather than an evil capitalist. 
"We hope that more Zhang Guoxis will emerge!"
The Jiangxi Daily News declared in a front-page headline. 
And local Communist Party officials have formally called on the entire community to "learn from Comrade Zhang Guoxi."
In some parts of China, including Beijing, Communist Party organizations have officially banned wealthy entrepreneurs from joining the party. 
But Mr. Zhang joined the party in 1972, long before he struck it rich, and he not only remains in the party but serves as party boss of his enterprise group, while also holding down the posts of chairman and general manager.
Zhang Guoxi's name means fruit of happiness, because at birth he was only a bit more than four pounds, the size of a small fruit. 
His mother died when he was 2, and after finishing elementary school he dropped out and began work as a carpenter. 
A few years later, in 1973, he sold his family home for $250 and used the money to start his company.
Initially, the company made carved wooden chests, when it was not fighting off criticisms and investigations by Communist Party ideologues who denounced it as the "tail of capitalism."
Â 
Recalling Rough Times
"I'm fine now, and people see me going abroad and praised in the papers, and so on," Mr. Zhang said soberly. 
"But back in 1973 to 1977, it was really rough and I was often hungry. 
If I told you about those years, you'd be in tears."
After Mr. Deng came to power in 1978, the company prospered and began to export the wooden chests and other carved furniture to Japan. 
Then it branched into the manufacture of gold-plated Buddhist altars, which in Japan sell for about $10,000 each.
As business grew, Mr. Zhang opened offices in three Chinese cities, as well as Japan, Hong Kong, Canada and Germany. 
The Guoxi Group became a general international trading company, with interests ranging from stock trading in Hong Kong to Chinese restaurants in Germany. 
The company is about to open a new trading office in Thailand and is building a nine-story hotel in the southern Chinese resort of Sanya.

file: Angel Island Journal_Saving Voices of the Other Ellis Island.txt
text:
ï»¿
Paul Q. Chow re members that when he first learned in school of the great flow of immigrants from Europe to America through Ellis Island, he went home and asked his mother where their people arrived in this country.
He recalls how she became upset and replied in a hushed tone: "Angel Island. 
Shhhhhh."
For a long time, the small boy believed there was a place called Angel Island Shhhhhh where 175,000 people of the ancient Pearl River villages were welcomed to the new land they called "Golden Mountain."
It would be many years before he learned about the immigration station on this island in San Francisco Bay that was not a reception center but rather a place of detention and potential deportation from 1910 to 1940. 
It was here that officials and immigrants played out a complex dance, tens of thousands of times: the officials charged with enforcing laws aimed at keeping most Chinese out, and the immigrants trying to circumvent those laws.
The immigration station was closed 50 years ago this month. 
Mr. Chow and other Americans of Chinese descent are trying to raise money to restore it as an important if painful history lesson. 
Their task is made more urgent by their wish to preserve hundreds of Chinese poems written on or carved into the walls of the men's barracks by anonymous authors expressing their anguish.
"The generation that went through it wants to forget it," said Mr. Chow, a 62-year-old retired worker with the state transportation department. 
"It's the first and second Chinese-American generations that says, 'This was shameful and you put my parents or grandparents through this and it should not be forgotten.'
"
The first wave of Chinese immigration occurred after the discovery of gold in California 141 years ago. 
Here they worked for 12 cents an hour laying the tracks of the Central Pacific Railroad and reworking the gold claims abandoned by white miners.
Dismissed from their jobs on completion of the transcontinental railway in 1869, they were bombed and lynched by people who blamed them for the high unemployment that followed the Civil War. 
The racist fury culminated in the passage of the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1882: the first law denying naturalization to members of a specific ethnic group.
But a window reopened when the fire that followed the 1906 San Francisco earthquake consumed records of the births and businesses of Chinese. 
Residents of Chinatown came forward to claim fictitious children in China and received documents that allowed whole villages of relatives and strangers, the "paper sons and daughters," to come to America.
But when they arrived at Angel Island, they were separated by sex and penned in into cramped barracks, then subjected to intense questioning. 
Some were kept here for a year or more, and stories, not confirmed by island records, say some hanged themselves rather than face deportation.
Mr. Chow's father arrived in 1922 with his own mother, who had been born in the United States but had lost her American citizenship because she married a Chinese national. 
They were detained on the island for six weeks and were freed after paying a bribe of $550, Mr. Chow said.
The 750-acre island became part of the state park system in 1965, and the immigration station was scheduled for demolition until a park ranger noticed the Chinese characters inscribed on the barracks walls. 
Asians pressed for preservation of the inscriptions, and the State Legislature created a study commission headed by Mr. Chow.
Other Asian-Americans have worked to keep the memories from dying. 
In 1980, 135 of the poems were translated and collected by Him Mark Lai, Genny Lim and Judy Yung in a book, "Island," and in 1988, Felicia Lowe made a documentary film, "Carved in Stone."
The poems show that some of the detainees considered returning to China. 
Others spoke philosophically of their detention. 
And there are rare sparks of anger. 
A poem signed "One From Taishan" reads:
It is unbearable to relate the stories accumulated on the island slopes.
Wait till the day I become successful and fulfill my wish!
I will not speak of love when I level the immigration station!
"We are happy with the idea of having money to restore it," said Gregory Picard, chief ranger for the Marin District of the State Department of Parks and Recreation, which administers the island. 
But with a $16 million projected shortage in their budget this fiscal year, "if money doesn't come from outside sources, it won't come at all," he said.
It is this reality that helped turn Mr. Chow into what he calls "the poor man's Lee Iacocca," attempting to raise $3 million to rehabilitate the station in a low-budget version of the Chrysler Corporation chairman's efforts on behalf of Ellis Island.
He is also driven by the memory of bringing his father to the station in 1975. 
He said his father, then 75 years old, entered the gutted men's barracks and walked immediately to the place where his bunk had been.
"It was the first time I ever saw my father cry and the first time I ever put my arms around him," Mr. Chow said.

Ancient Chinese bronzes, aglow with brilliant green patinas or polished to mirror brightness, are combined with less pristine vessels encrusted with mud or corrosion in a new exhibition at the China House Gallery, 125 East 65th Street. 
The unorthodox mix of the glorious and the gross can be seen in "Ancient Chinese Bronze Art: Casting the Precious Sacral Vessel," through June 15. 
The exhibition documents how bronzes were made between 2205 and 256 B.C. and how they are restored.
The show's emphasis on metal technology determined the selection of the 41 period bronzes lent by 21 collections in the United States. 
The surface decorations of the vessels range from minimal cord markings to bold mythological images, calligraphic symbols, malachite chips or inlays of copper wire.
To illustrate the casting processes developed in China 4,000 years ago, the Shanghai Museum sent facsimile molds, photographs showing metalworking techniques and reproductions of ancient bronzes. 
From other sources came fragments of original molds, several elaborately restored vessels and two forgeries.
"If you want to understand the evolution of these vessels and why they look the way they do, you have to understand how they are made," said the show's guest curator, W. Thomas Chase, who is head conservator of the Freer Gallery of Art and the Arthur M. Sackler Gallery of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. 
An owl-shaped wine jug, described until 1982 as a work of the Song Dynasty (A.D. 960 to 1279) in the Shang style, was re-identified when the bronze it is made of was tested and found to be from the Shang Dynasty, which is 2,000 years earlier.
The chronological organization of the show reveals much about the evolution of bronzes. 
The first object, one of the earliest known such vessels, is a roughly crafted, three-legged pitcher, made between the 19th and 16th centuries B.C. The raised lines belting the waist were carved into a ceramic mold before it was filled with molten bronze. 
From the 13th century B.C. came a more gracefully shaped pitcher, its surface enhanced by masks and scrolls, its handsomely curved spout flanked by knobs and its tall tapered legs engagingly raked.
Knowing which comes first -- the vessel or its surface decoration -- may pique the curiosity of some people, but it is not necessary to enjoy these bronzes. 
A case in point is a remarkable narrow-necked flask with copper fretwork on the front and back. 
According to Mr. Chase, tests revealed that the fretwork was placed in the mold first and the vessel was then affixed by casting it to the wafer-thin sheets. 
"If you want to do things just by casting," Mr. Chase said, "this is amazingly elegant solution."
Several objects show varying degrees of corrosion. 
Mr. Chase suggests that the red splotches in the bright green patina of a large jar from the sixth or fifth century B.C. may have developed when acid was used to remove corrosion from the lacelike ribbons banding the surface. 
Whatever the cause, the color from the copper oxide heightens the delicacy of the decoration.
When deterioration is far advanced, it can be less pleasing, as is seen in a wide-mouthed Shang pot made between the 13th and 11th centuries B.C. This vessel is dull gray, and its surface, eaten away by time and the elements, is full of holes. 
In sharp contrast to the elaborate restorations probably made in China before World War II by a skillful artisan, the images on the unrestored half of the pot are fuzzy or totally erased. 
The piece was lent by the Art Museum at Princeton University, a gift from a collector who discovered the modern repairs only after he bought the vessel and had it X-rayed.
An even more audacious fabrication -- at least to Western eyes -- is a trumpet-shaped beaker, 85 percent of which is new. 
The forgery includes only five original fragments that form the base. 
The rest of the beaker, made of brass and lead, may date from the early 20th century.
"The reconstruction, most certainly done in China, shows the extent to which the Chinese will go to restore an ancient bronze," Mr. Chase said.
According to J. May Lee, director of the China House Gallery, the concept of museums is very new in China. 
"Displays are educational, and the Chinese want to show as many types of objects as possible," Ms. Lee said. 
"They use reconstructions and facsimiles side by side with unrestored works in their museums."
The gallery's exhibition was financed by the New York State Council on the Arts, the Asian Cultural Council, the Corning Foundation, Grumman International, the Henry Luce Foundation and the Starr Foundation. 
The paperback catalogue ($28) was written by Mr. Chase with Ms. Lee.

text:
