file: Baker Denounces Executions of Chinese Protesters.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d joined a chorus of Western leaders today in denouncing China's execution of three men for their role in political demonstrations in Shanghai. 
But he said the Bush Administration was not planning any additional actions against Beijing ''at this time.''
''We deeply regret the fact that these executions have gone forward, notwithstanding appeals from the United States, appeals from the Federal Republic of Germany, and perhaps other countries, for clemency,'' Mr. Baker told reporters at a briefing at the White House. 
The briefing followed a meeting between President Bush and Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher of West Germany.
The United States, Mr. Baker added, ''is not contemplating any additional action at this time.''
''I ought to also say that there is an important relationship here which we should seek to preserve if we possibly can,'' Mr. Baker said.
Â 
Thatcher 'Utterly Appalled'
Reacting to the events in China today, Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain said, according to Reuters, that she was ''utterly appalled'' by the executions, and said she and Prime Minister Bob Hawke of Australia were discussing possible sanctions against China.
The Associated Press reported that Foreign Minister Roland Dumas of France told the National Assembly in Paris: ''What is happening in China is atrocious. 
The totalitarian machine, in all its horror, is rolling. 
It turns what should be judicial decisions into veritable murders.''
The A.P. quoted a Dutch Foreign Ministry spokesman as saying the executions were expected to be discussed at next week's European Community summit meeting in Madrid.
As with many other decisions on China, the actions Tuesday to suspend high-level exchanges between American and Chinese officials and to postpone consideration of new loans to China by international financial institutions were made by the President and the Secretary of State, along with a tight circle of aides. 
It took not only many White House staff members by surprise but many in the State Department as well.
Â 
Events in China
While the move obviously had a heavy domestic political component, aimed to demonstrate that the Administration was not being indifferent to the suppression of pro-democracy demonstrators, it also seems to fit with the overall analytical framework with which Mr. Baker and Mr. Bush are understood to be operating.
A senior Administration official said President Bush and Mr. Baker are acting on the assumption that events in China will go through several stages in the coming years.
The official described the first stage, encompassing the present situation, this way: ''The Chinese leadership is entirely focused on their short-term survival. 
They determined that their basic system of authority was being challenged by the pro-democracy movement and they were ready to pay any price - both foreign and domestic - to preserve that system.''
The official said of this stage: ''There is nothing that the United States can do or say that will really influence the behavior of the Chinese leadership. 
They are motivated by basic impulses of survival.''
The moves the Administration took Tuesday were done with the full awareness that they would have no immediate restraining effect, officials said. 
Rather, they were aimed at the next stage in developments in China, when the authorities in Beijing consolidate their rule and try to restore the economic modernization program they were on before and then confront the full domestic and international price of their repression.
That includes the postponement of loans, the halt in military sales from the West, the decrease in Western investment in China, the falloff in tourism, international diplomatic isolation and, maybe most important, the passive resistance of their own people.
That passive resistance, as Administration officials see it, could take a variety of forms, from sabotaging of production in state-owned factories, to work stoppages, to decreases in productivity, to sporadic demonstrations.

file: BAKER FAILS TO WIN ANY COMMITMENTS IN TALKS IN BEIJING.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two days of talks between Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and China's top leaders have yielded none of the gestures on human rights, arms control and trade sought by Washington as requirements for improved relations with Beijing, a senior American official said today.
Mr. Baker, making the first public high-level visit to China by an American official since Beijing's violent crackdown on democracy advocates in 1989, has one more scheduled meeting with the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, on Sunday. 
The American official said Mr. Baker hoped that at this session the Chinese would be more forthcoming than they had been up to now.
Â 
A Last-Ditch Appeal
This evening's briefing by the State Department official seemed at times like a desperate, last-ditch appeal to the Chinese to respond before Mr. Baker departs with the kind of specific concessions he had anticipated in making the visit, which has already bestowed some much-sought legitimacy on the Chinese leadership. 
If Mr. Baker goes home empty-handed, the Bush Administration is likely to face growing domestic criticism of its China policy and greatly increased pressure in Congress for sanctions against Beijing.
"We cannot want an improved U.S.-China relationship more than the Chinese," the official said after today's six hours of meetings. 
"There are obviously certain things that need to transpire for that to move forward. 
For whatever reasons, if there is anything they have to say to the Secretary, it will be said tomorrow. 
They know when we are leaving, they know that we have that meeting tomorrow, and I think I will leave it right there."
The official said Mr. Baker came here expecting at least some firm commitments from China on human rights, missile proliferation and trade.
He was understood to be seeking the release of some of the 800 political prisoners rounded up by Beijing after the Tiananmen Square killings in 1989, a halt to the transfer of Chinese missiles and nuclear technology to Middle Eastern nations and an end to restrictive trade practices, which have created an American trade deficit with China of about $13 billion.
Up to now, the official said, Mr. Baker has received neither positive nor negative commitments from China in any of these areas.
Mr. Baker met today with China's Prime Minister, Li Peng; the Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin; the Minister of Justice, Cai Cheng, and President Yang Shangkun.
The American official said that in the meetings Mr. Baker repeatedly emphasized to the Chinese that they had been asking him to come to Beijing for two years and that now he was here they would be making a big mistake to send him home with nothing to show for his politically risky trip.
The Chinese presented a somewhat different view of today's talks. 
The common theme running through their comments to the Secretary, judging from the briefing given by the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman, was that the Chinese greatly value their ties with Washington and want them improved, but not on Washington's terms alone.
Each of the Chinese leaders emphasized to Mr. Baker that they would not respond to any pressure from Washington, that the United States had to learn to continue dealing face-to-face with China, despite differences in the relationship, and that Washington should appreciate more the strategic value of Chinese-American ties. 
If it did, some of the differences in the relationship could be more easily muted or overlooked.
For instance, President Yang was quoted by the official New China News Agency as having told Mr. Baker: "Some problems can be solved through discussions, while others need several rounds of discussion. 
Those which cannot be solved for the time being can be shelved. 
We call this 'seeking common ground while reserving difference.'
"
Â 
A Warning on Pressure
So long as both the United States and China can adopt such an approach, Mr. Yang continued, it will be easy to solve the problems between them. 
But he added that "the practice of exerting pressure can only lead to tension in the bilateral relations, and is of no use in solving problems, " the official press agency reported, that
The Chinese President went out of his way during his opening comments to Mr. Baker -- while American reporters were in the room -- to praise President Bush and talk about what good friends they were.
With Mr. Baker at his side, President Yang recalled that he first went to the United States at the invitation of Mr. Bush when he was Vice President.
"After our meeting, we had a long and pleasant talk," he said. 
"We didn't use diplomatic language. 
We talked about a lot of things about China. 
Actually, Mr. Bush asked me a lot of questions concerning China. 
Though we had a long talk, time was passing very quickly. 
Actually, we had this long talk on a boat, and when we finished the boat tour it was already very late. 
So Mr. Secretary, when you return to Washington, please convey my greetings to my friend Mr. Bush."
When the Foreign Ministry spokesman, Wu Jianmin, was asked whether Minister of Justice Cai responded to Mr. Baker's appeal for the release of imprisoned democracy advocates he responded brusquely, "Actions that the Chinese judicial organs will take are entirely something that the China side shall decide."
His remark seemed to suggest that if China did release some prisoners in response to Mr. Baker's appeal it would not be during this visit.
Another issue high on Mr. Baker's agenda is arms proliferation. 
China is believed to have provided help to the nuclear programs of Iran and Algeria, among other nations, raising concerns that it is helping third world countries develop nuclear weapons. 
Beijing is also believed to have pursued sales of medium-range missiles to Syria and Iran despite pledges not to sell such weapons in the Middle East.
What seemed to have distressed the American delegation was not only that Mr. Baker received no concrete commitments from the Chinese leaders, but also that the same was true for the experts he brought along. 
These went over the human rights, arms control and trade issues in detail with their Chinese counterparts.
When the senior American official was asked to characterize the talks that the Assistant Secretary of State for Human Rights, Richard Schifter, and the Under Secretary of State for International Security Affairs, Reginald Bartholomew, held with their Chinese counterparts, she said curtly, "The only characterizations I would give is that they were meetings between experts."
The Chinese press omitted all references to Mr. Schifter's presence in the American delegation.
During Mr. Baker's talks with Prime Minister Li, the Chinese leader told the Secretary that while there were some problems between the United States and China, they could not be solved if the two sides did not sit down and talk "face to face," the Chinese press agency reported.
Mr. Li was quoted as adding: "China may share the same view with you on some questions and have different viewpoints on others, but this is very natural. 
The Chinese nation, with a history of more than 5,000 years, has a strong sense of national dignity. 
For more than 100 years we the Chinese people suffered very much from foreign aggression and humiliation, so we cherish so much our independence and sovereignty. 
We hope to see gradual restoration and improvement of the bilateral relations through contacts."
Jiang Zemin, General Secretary of the Communist Party, used his meeting with Mr. Baker to emphasize that "it is very abnormal and not in keeping with the interests of our two big countries that you don't have high-level contacts with us," the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
Â 
Nixon's Approach Recalled
Mr. Jiang explained to Mr. Baker that "the world is a colorful one which has various kinds of social systems, cultural heritages and ideologies, so it is dangerous to model such a colorful world on one form."
The Communist Party leader recalled fondly for Mr. Baker the approach to relations taken by former President Richard Nixon and former Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger with Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai, the late Chinese leaders. 
He seemed to be trying to encourage Mr. Baker to harken back to those days, when the United States and China supposedly did not seem to worry so much about questions of human rights, but focused on the global game of nations in which Washington viewed China as a critical counterweight to the Soviet Union.
Mr. Nixon and Mr. Mao, he said, "came to realize that the common interests count most for both sides."
Mr. Jiang concluded by telling Mr. Baker: "I remember two lines of an ancient Chinese poem. 
It says that if you want to have a longer vision you should move to a higher level. 
We should look further by moving to a higher point, and have our eyes on the future and in this way we should surely be able to restore Sino-American relations."
In all of his meetings today, Mr. Baker was never photographed shaking hands with any Chinese officials. 
Before each meeting, reporters and photographers were kept out of the room until after Mr. Baker and his Chinese hosts had greeted one another, and were ushered in only when the Chinese and American delegations were seated stiffly around the conference table.
Chinese officials told American reporters that Mr. Baker's delegation had requested such arrangements, although American officials denied this.

file: Baker Warns China Against Selling New Missiles.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d warned China today that there would be "profound consequences" for Chinese-American relations if Beijing sold newly developed ballistic missiles to Syria and Pakistan.
China's arms exports have become a matter of controversy as Congress considers President Bush's proposal to renew Beijing's preferential trade status. 
Mr. Baker said the United States had no "evidence or any indication" that China had actually shipped surface-to-surface missiles to Syria, despite a recent press report suggesting that a deal was near completion.
He said the Bush Administration had also cautioned Beijing against sending sophisticated new missiles to Pakistan, asserting that this "would constitute grave threats to the region and could have bilateral consequences."
Mr. Baker did not elaborate further.
A group of Republican and Democratic senators is seeking concessions from the Administration in exchange for legislative support for President Bush's decision to renew trade privileges for China for another year.
Â 
Bitter Rift With Lawmakers
The White House and Congress are bitterly divided over how to handle relations with China. 
Many Republican and Democratic lawmakers are concerned that Mr. Bush has reacted too mildly to Beijing's crackdown on the democracy movement two years ago.
Mr. Bush prevailed last year in extending trade privileges to China, but he faces stronger opposition this year in both the House and the Senate. 
The renewal of China's trade status has become one of the most contentious foreign policy and trade issues facing Congress this summer.
At a meeting this morning with Mr. Baker and Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser, Senator Bob Dole, Republican of Kansas, presented a proposed letter to Mr. Bush that was drafted by Senator Max S. Baucus of Montana and co-signed by three other Democratic senators.
The letter calls for five concessions from the Administration, a participant in the negotiations between the White House and Congress said. 
The biggest concession would be for the United States to end its opposition to Taiwan's immediate entry into the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
Such a move would infuriate China, Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger told a House panel today.
The letter also suggests that the Administration take legal steps to fight China's import barriers, insure that Chinese products made with prison labor are kept out of the United States market, block loans to China by multilateral agencies until the country's human rights record improves, and enter negotiations to curb the spread of ballistic missiles in the third world.
"My understanding is they are willing to make virtually all the concessions I've asked for in my letter," Senator Baucus, the chairman of the Senate's International Trade Subcommittee, said in an interview today.
Â 
Risking China's Anger
Several Administration officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that no final deal had been struck. 
They said White House officials were divided on whether to risk China's anger by supporting Taiwan's application to GATT.
Senator Baucus said he had not decided whether he would support the renewal of China's so-called "most-favored-nation" status if the Administration refused to grant the concessions.
A Congressional resolution canceling the renewal of China's trade privileges is considered likely. 
To sustain a Presidential veto of such a resolution, Mr. Bush would need the votes of nearly a dozen Democratic senators led by Senator Baucus who strongly support free trade but are troubled by China's human rights record.
The participant in congressional negotiations with the Administration said that Senator Dole was asking other Republican senators to co-sign Senator Baucus's letter, which is to be released on Thursday.
Senator Baucus said that 8 to 12 Democratic senators and 25 to 30 Republican senators were likely to support the renewal of China's preferential trade status if the Administration granted the concessions.
Such a tally would not prevent the Senate from approving a resolution rejecting renewal of China's trade status, he said, but it would insure that a Presidential veto could not be overridden.

file: BAKER WILL VISIT CHINA THIS MONTH.txt
text:

After several months of secret negotiations, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d announced tonight that he would visit China this month, a trip that is bound to revive the debate over the Bush Administration's stance toward the hard-line Beijing Government.

On a street where hardware, electronics and shoe stores competed for space 10 years ago, a gleaming new glass obelisk juts above the squat buildings. 
Each block, it seems, has a new type of tenant -- with sleek gray steel, polished brass and tinted windows suggesting an international financial center.
Seven banks crowd into just two blocks in the din and traffic of Main Street in downtown Flushing, Queens, and the incongruous glass obelisk will make eight. 
Wander down the side streets or nearby Roosevelt Avenue and Northern Boulevard and the number of banks multiplies to at least 35 -- American, Chinese, Korean, British, Indian, Pakistani and Colombian.
As thousands of immigrants, particularly Chinese and Koreans, have settled in Flushing in the last decade, the banks have followed, tailoring their strategies to serve the savings-minded workers and flourishing small businesses.
Many are branches of the big American banks, which continue to dominate business in Flushing. 
But small AsianAmerican banks, with headquarters in Flushing or Chinatown, also compete fiercely for customers, and the latest arrival is a branch of a large Taiwan-based bank.
The China Trust Bank -- the largest private bank in Taiwan, which has its American headquarters in lower Manhattan -- opened its doors four weeks ago in a temporary office that was once a vegetable stand at 40-36 Main Street. 
Just a few steps away are the Hong Kong-Shanghai Banking Corporation, Amerasia Bank and Golden City Bank, which will open soon in the new glass obelisk on Main Street. 
Across the street is Manufacturers Hanover, and a block away are Green Point Savings and Citibank. 
Around the corner is Asia Bank, the oldest Chinese-American bank in Flushing, which opened in 1984.
In its first two weeks, the China Trust branch took in $6 million from 400 depositors, said the manager, Frank Lin. 
"It's fantastic," Mr. Lin said of the new business, and a state banking official described the total as "pretty darn good."
China Trust officials say they expect business in Flushing to keep growing, and they are spending $13 million to build a new three-story office just down the street.
The banks have in part been lured by the booming businesses in the area, where scores of restaurants and flashy boutiques have helped transform Flushing into the fourth-largest retail center in New York City. 
Pauline Chu, a Community School Board member who is running for City Council, said there are 200 stores in a three-block area and 800 restaurants in the neighborhood. 
A new 175-room Sheraton hotel will open in November.
But business executives and state banking officials say another big reason for the influx of banks and capital is fear over the Chinese takeover of Hong Kong in 1997. 
Uncertainty over the future of the British colony has prompted a flight of people and money from Hong Kong and Taiwan into the area since the early 1980's.
"The scare over 1997 is definitely one of the factors," said Clare E. Sykes, a spokeswoman for the State Banking Department. 
"Flushing is a fast-growth, healthy area, a good bankable area. 
It is faster growing than Chinatown."

Separate From Chinatown
Ms. Chu said about 140,000 Chinese and Korean immigrants now live in the Flushing area, which had few Asian residents 10 years ago.
Many residents and business owners envision Flushing as a flourishing international community, separate from Chinatown in Manhattan and uniquely positioned between New York City, Long Island, New Jersey and Connecticut, said Ho Pei Lee, a developer and builder.
A study comparing banks in Chinatown and Flushing convinced China Trust Bank to open its new Main Street branch, Mr. Lin said.

A Mix of Strategies
The study found that American banks still have the greatest share of deposits in the area, and many have tailored their banking strategies to the community.

Service and Interest Rates

Joy Xu, 25 years old, arrived in the United States two years ago and banks at Asia Bank.

file: BARCELONA_ DIVING_China and U.S. Divers Make Different Splashes.txt
text:
ï»¿
The men's 10-meter platform diving competition teetered today between moments of sublime perfection and frightening failure.
A disastrous plunge that will make the year's highlight films showed the possibility of what happens to a dive out of control from three stories up.
"It was definitely agony and it was definitely defeat," quipped an aching but intact Matt Scoggin of Austin, Tex.
In the standing, his dive was at the other end of the point spectrum from the spectacular closing attempt by the soon-to-be champion, 16-year-old Sun Shuwei of China. 
On Sun's final dive, trying to keep his first-place lead over Scott Donie of Fort Lauderdale, Fla., the Chinese diver refused to play it safe. 
He produced one of the highest scores in Olympic history -- four of the seven judges awarded him perfection, a 10.
Sun wound up with 677.310 points, scoring seven perfect 10's on his 10 dives, and finished comfortably ahead of Donie's 633.630. 
China ended up with three golds in the four men's and women's diving events. 
Donie's silver medal, meanwhile, gave the United States its third diving medal over all. 
Xiong Ni of China took the bronze.
"I've been diving great all my life, but no one's noticed," said Donie. 
It was an ironic statement, coming on a day when everyone noticed his teammate, who didn't dive great but who survived.
Scoggin's memorable Olympic moment came on Dive 7, a back 3 1/2 somersault tuck. 
Dives are scored in part by their degree of difficulty, and for Scoggin, this was his most demanding of the day with a difficulty of 3.3.
He stood ramrod straight, back to the water, outlined against the blue-gray Barcelona sky and the city's skyline, high above the outdoor pool atop Montjuic. 
Then Scoggin, at 28 the oldest diver in the competition, took off. 
If you looked up at him, you would have thought he was soaring over the city. 
The dive called for him to grab his knees and tuck them under his chest. 
He leaped backward off the board, somersaulted once, and reached for his knees with both hands. 
His right hand latched onto the right knee. 
But the left hand missed.
"It slipped," Scoggin said afterward. 
He started to spin like a broken helicopter, going sideways. 
The water was coming fast and he was out of control.
"I tried to find the water," he said.
Â 
Shadows Cause Problem
But there was another problem. 
The pool is laid out east to west, and the shadows of the late afternoon played havoc with some divers' perceptions. 
It was so dark on the water they couldn't tell which was the bottom of the pool and which was the water.
He hit the water on his back. 
The water splashed, the only tidal wave of the day.
"That was the worst hit I ever had," Scoggin said.
The crowd moaned, seemingly feeling his pain. 
Despite the sickeningly loud splatter, he didn't swallow any water and pulled himself out of the pool quickly.
"I started to run," he explained, "hoping to run off the pain."
He was taken to an emergency medical room, but released within a minute.
"It hurt for 20 or 30 seconds," he said. 
"I don't think I ever felt pain like that. 
Ever."
His coach, Mike Brown, a former Dartmouth diver, described Scoggin as "being in shock."
"It was like running into that wall over there," Brown said.
Scoggin was, essentially, out of the competition now. 
He had started the dive in sixth place, not far removed from medal contention. 
Instead, it was recorded as a "failed dive" -- the only one of the competition, and worth zero points.
Still, he returned.
"It never crossed my mind not to compete," he said. 
"I came here, I gave it a shot. 
All athletes know it can happen, that's why winning is so great -- you know you overcame danger."
His next dive was a forward 3 1/2 somersault pike. 
He mounted the platform to growing applause, took off, and completed the dive without a hitch, producing a decent score of mostly sevens.
How did he feel about going up again?
Did he want to get right there and do it?
"I could definitely wait," he said.
Despite his failed attempt, Scoggin beat out two divers and finished 10th.
"I'm happy that I don't have to do that again," said Scoggin, who is going to sell real estate and retire. 
"I don't have to do that dive again. 
Or any other dive."
Brown predicted that Scoggin's fall will make a lasting Olympic impression. 
"I think Matt will make the new 'Agony of Defeat' poster," he said.

When Lin Li of China hit the contact pad tonight in world-record time of 2 minutes 11.65 seconds in the 200-meter individual medley, the spin doctors went to work again.

file: BARCELONA_Chinese Beam With Pride.txt
text:
ï»¿
If bicyclists are swerving even more than usual these days, if factory workers are nodding over the assembly lines, if Government officials are excusing themselves from evening banquets, the problems have less to do with the sultry weather than with collective pride at the leaps and plunges of a few pint-sized teen-agers 7,200 miles away.
Many Chinese, who can barely tell a shot-put from a discus, have been transfixed by the Olympics -- and that makes them insomniacs. 
Because of the seven-hour time difference from Barcelona, Spain, the live television coverage lasts well into the night, but many are alternately delighted and impatient to watch the triumphs of their Olympic athletes.
"It's about time we picked up some gold," said a shopkeeper in his 20's. 
"With 1.1 billion people, we should be winning all the golds. 
Hey, did you see Li Xiaosahuang?
Stunning. Absolutely beautiful."
Li Xiaosahuang, whose name translates as "Little Twin," earned a gold medal for the floor exercise in men's gymnastics. 
His twin brother, Li Dasahuang, or "Big Twin," also competed but did not win a medal.
Â 
15 Gold Medals
China has done much better than anybody expected in the Olympics, excelling in diving, swimming and gymnastics. 
It won only five gold medals in the 1988 Olympics in Seoul, but already it has earned 15 in the 1992 Games, including three of the four golds in diving.
In a nation that has been deeply divided politically in the last few years, the Olympics have provided a rare occasion when everyone from Communist Party bosses to student dissidents can join together and cheer China's performers. 
The nation's newest heartthrobs include Lu Li, the bright-eyed 15-year-old who earned a perfect 10 as she won the gold medal for uneven bars in gymnastic competition, and Fu Mingxia, the 13-year-old sensation who dominated in women's platform diving.
For three years, the Government has tried to find a way to unite the nation. 
It tried to win support with the Asian Games, which were held here in the fall of 1990, but those games annoyed many people who were forced to contribute money and labor for the preparations.
But the daily news from Barcelona of the rising medal count, which stood at 48 after today's events, has functioned as a nationalistic adhesive to rally the nation.
Whatever they think of their Government, many Chinese bristled at the way American journalists were reported to have treated the swimmer Qian Hong after she won the gold medal in the women's 100-meter butterfly. 
When Qian, 21 years old, was asked what her mother did, she replied "environmental sanitation."
As reported in the Chinese press, the American reporter pressed Qian with another question: "Does that mean she collects garbage?"
The room filled with raucous laughter and Qian ended up crying.
"Those American reporters really have no manners," the report said, a statement that was echoed in many conversations with Chinese about the Olympics.
Â 
Stir Over Steroid Issue
Allegations that Chinese athletes may be using steroids -- a charge that is not backed by any clear evidence and that the Government denies -- also have caused an uproar.
Chinese appear to be divided on the issue, with some convinced that their athletes have learned from Eastern European coaches how to take steroids. 
Some say that the athletes probably take Chinese herbal medicines to improve their performance.
One instance of the use of Chinese medicine was confirmed today in Barcelona when Wu Dan, a Chinese women's volleyball player, was banned after she tested positive for strychnine. 
The official New China News Agency said she had absorbed the strychnine in a Chinese medicine after she was feeling ill.
Wu's case, the first positive result after 1,080 tests, was a clear embarrassment for the Government. 
The news agency indicated that Wu took the medicine of her own volition, apparently without realizing that it contained a forbidden substance.
Official television and radio news programs did not report the test results this evening, and so Chinese were not aware of the violation. 
In any case, the positive test for strychnine does not shed light on whether Chinese athletes take steroids -- a suggestion that offends many people in Beijing.
"Are you kidding?" said a Chinese clothing salesman. 
"If it were discovered that Chinese athletes were really taking steroids, think of all the heads that would roll at the National Sports Commission. 
The Government definitely wouldn't let them take the stuff."
Â 
Wide TV Coverage
The Government has given the Games extensive publicity. 
For the last week, national television has broadcast about 19 hours a day of Olympic coverage.
By the end of the Olympics, China will have aired about 250 hours of Olympic programs. 
Replays of events in which Chinese athletes have won gold medals occur throughout the day, along with commentary and interviews of the athletes.
Companies, radio stations and newspapers have sponsored Olympic guessing games, with prizes that range from cars to televisions and refrigerators, and free trips to Hong Kong or Singapore.
To encourage athletes, the National Sports Commission will give about $14,000 to each winner of a gold medal, The China Youth Daily reported last week. 
The article added that companies, factories and other sponsors have also made contributions so that each gold medal winner could bring in about $37,000, or 95 times the annual salary of an average factory worker.
One company, Jianlibao, which makes a sports drink, said it would give a gold can, worth about $6,500, to each gold medalist. 
It had already prepared 30 cans of gold, partly in expectation that the Chinese women's volleyball team would win a gold medal. 
But the team lost to Brazil.
"The volleyball players were too proud and thought they would get the gold without having to try," said a private businessman, who said he stayed up regularly throughout the night to watch the live coverage.
The Government is hoping that its performance will enhance its chances to win the right to be host to the Summer Olympic Games in the year 2000. 
A Chinese sports official expressed the thought cautiously: "We hope the achievements of our athletes in Barcelona will leave a very deep impression on the decision-makers."

''If the United States population were five times its current size, it would be fairly easy for members of Congress to agree on China's family planning policy,'' Mr. Qian said.
Mr. Qian's comments reflected the increased strains in relations over the last month, principally on human rights. 
China has always been touchy about such matters, regarding criticisms as interference in its internal affairs. 
Lately it has been particularly sensitive, as its internal situation has grown more delicate with some people openly calling for greater democracy as well as for independence in Tibet.
Â 
Incident During Bush Visit
The strains began when President Bush visited China a month ago and invited Fang Lizhi, the astrophysicist and dissident, to a banquet. 
The police kept Mr. Fang and his wife from attending the banquet, and Mr. Bush expressed ''regret'' over the incident.
Early this month pro-independence rioting broke out in Tibet, and the United States Senate approved a resolution condemning China's use of violence in Tibet.
China has also long been sensitive about charges that it forces women to have abortions as a part of its family planning policy. 
It denies the accusations and says that in any case family planning is China's own concern and a necessity given its population pressures.
Mr. Qian said today that the Fang incident ''reflects the fact that there are some people in the United States who always support those who are dissatisfied with the Chinese Government.''
He added, ''Such petty conduct is not in the interest of the friendly relations of our two countries.''
Aside from calling for mutual trust, and criticizing what he said was interference in China's internal affairs, Mr. Qian did not specify what the ''new pattern'' in Chinese-American relations would consist of.
While Mr. Qian called on the United States to help improve relations between Washington and Beijing, he also suggested that there were some difficulties in Chinese-Soviet relations. 
Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, is scheduled to visit China in mid-May to mark the formal end of the three-decade split between the two countries.
Mr. Qian said the obstacles to improved Chinese-Soviet relations had been reduced but not yet eliminated. 
The remaining problem is the Vietnamese presence in Cambodia, and Mr. Qian suggested that the Soviet Union could do more to achieve a solution to that conflict.
The Cambodian conflict will be a key topic at the Chinese-Soviet summit meeting, Mr. Qian said.

file: Beijing Frees 97 Held in Protests To Try to Ease Domestic Tension.txt
text:
ï»¿
China announced today the release of 97 people who had been involved in last year's pro-democracy movement, including two student leaders, in a move that diplomats described as an attempt to ease domestic tensions and win favor in Western countries.
The announcement came two days after the anniversary of the crackdown on the democracy movement, and some diplomats said it reflected a mild reduction in tensions now that the Government does not have to worry about protests on the anniversaries of last year's key protest dates.
China said that 76 prisoners were released in Beijing, while 21 were released in Shanghai.
The action brought the total officially reported to have been released in the last six months to 881, but it is unclear how many remain behind bars.
Â 
Releases Last Month
In mid-May, when it released 211 prisoners, China said only 431 were still ''under investigation.''
After today's announcement, that would leave 334 people in detention, according to the Government figures.
Most Western diplomats say, however, that there are probably more than a few hundred being held, and some estimates run into the thousands. 
Partly because of the uncertainty about how many dissidents are still being held, diplomats interviewed were cautious about judging the significance of the releases.
''Whether it is a loosening remains to be seen, but it was a good gesture,'' said a foreign diplomat in Beijing. 
''This is something that they must have planned some time ago. 
They wanted to do it after June 4 passed.''
An Asian diplomat said that while China probably had carefully timed the releases, the fact that it waited until after June 4 indicated that China did not want to bow to pressure from Western countries.
Â 
'The Humanitarian Way'
''They are showing that they are releasing people as they finish the investigations,'' the Asian diplomat said, taking a more generous view than most Westerners. 
''It shows the inquiries are genuine, and that's the humanitarian way to do it.''
Among those released was Zhou Fengsuo, a 23-year-old student who ranked fifth on a wanted list of 21 student leaders publicized by the Government last June. 
Xiong Wei, a 24-year-old student who had ranked No. 20 on the list, was also released, according to the announcement by the official New China News Agency.
The release is one of the latest examples of mixed signals by the Chinese leadership. 
In recent days, China has detained a small number of students and dissidents who were speaking out against the Government. 
The security forces have also beaten foreign journalists and students as recently as this morning in the university district in the western part of Beijing.
The group released today apparently did not include three dissidents who were believed to have been detained last week. 
The three are Hou Dejian, a Taiwan folk singer, and two of his friends, Zhou Duo and Gao Xin, who had both been arrested after the June 1989 crackdown and subsequently released. 
All three were detained when they tried to publicize a petition calling for the release of political prisoners.

file: Beijing Invites Chinese Abroad to Return Home.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government today invited Chinese living abroad to return "to serve the construction of the motherland," but it also hinted that it might bar Chinese students from returning if they oppose Communism.
The issue has arisen because the authorities are refusing to allow Gong Xiaoxia, a Chinese student at Harvard University, to return to China for a visit. 
Ms. Gong, who has been critical of the Government, is waiting in Hong Kong, hoping that the Chinese Government will relent and allow her back.
Two weeks ago, the Chinese Government barred Dai Qing, a prominent journalist holding a fellowship at Harvard, from flying back to Beijing for the summer vacation. 
But a few days later -- after the June 4 anniversary of the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown -- the authorities reversed themselves and allowed Ms. Dai to return.
Â 
Fate of the Outspoken
In fact, thousands of Chinese have been allowed to return to China without difficulty after trips abroad, and there seems little chance that a loyalty test will be imposed. 
But Beijing might refuse to allow outspoken dissidents to return, forcing them into exile.
To be sure, many Chinese students would be delighted to stay in the United States. 
More worry about getting in trouble after returning to China than about the possibility of being turned back at the border, although that risk could concern those who have spouses or children in China.
Some 40,000 Chinese, including the children and grandchildren of many Chinese leaders, are studying in the United States. 
Many took part in demonstrations in June 1989 against the army crackdown on the Tiananmen Square democracy movement, and the Chinese Government reportedly has maintained files on militants and monitored their activities in America.
Wu Jianmin, the Foreign Ministry spokesman, said at a briefing today that he was unfamiliar with the details of Ms. Gong's case. 
But he added that the Government welcomed Chinese students abroad to return, notwithstanding the views they used to hold.
Mr. Wu was then asked whether the Government would allow the return of Chinese students who currently oppose the "four cardinal principles."
Those principles are socialism, the people's democratic dictatorship, leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism, Leninism and Mao Zedong thought.
"Whatever their past political views," Mr. Wu responded, emphasizing the word past, "we welcome them back to serve the construction of the motherland. 
If you study these words, you will get the correct answer."
That response suggests that China could refuse to readmit students whose present views it finds offensive.
China has more students in the United States than does any other country, and their presence has often been a source of tension in the two countries' relations. 
Americans have been indignant at the reported harassment by Chinese Embassy officials of Chinese studying in the United States, while Beijing has been outraged that the United States has extended the students' visas to avoid forcing them to return to China.
In a sign of the Government's enthusiasm to lure students back, at least if they do not oppose Communism, the Government is drafting a new policy that will give important privileges and better jobs to Chinese who return from foreign universities.
The new measure will allow returned students to choose any job they wish. 
It nullifies the agreements that many of the students were obliged to sign promising that they would return to their previous employers.
As an extra lure, the returned students will be able to move with their families to any city they want, including Shenzhen, a special economic zone next to Hong Kong. 
Normally, residence permits for desirable cities -- like Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen -- are extremely difficult to obtain, and even if an outstanding scholar finds a job in a major city and obtains a residence permit, it may take years to get a residence permit for a spouse.
Since 1978, some 150,000 Chinese have left the country for study abroad. 
Only 50,000 have returned.

file: Beijing Journal_A Weekly Bath, and a Good Brain-Scrubbing Too.txt
text:
ï»¿
It is less verdant and spacious than Beijing University, and far more isolated and gloomy than Tiananmen Square: a guarded compound in the southwest part of the capital that may be the next home for many leaders of China's democracy movement.
Surrounded by 13-foot walls topped by an electric fence, Beijing No. 1 Prison is a gray and dilapidated compound built in 1908, in the dying days of the Ching Dynasty. 
Its cells have been home to thieves and rapists and political idealists, and it leaves its mark on all of them.
There are eight hours of political education a week, intended to make inmates acknowledge their guilt and inspire them to support the Communist Party and the Government.
''The political education is effective,'' said Wang Hehao, a 25-year-old man serving an 18-year sentence for killing a man in a fight. 
''Before we did not understand anything about the law, but now we know about the need to respect the law and society.''
Â 
Where Minds Are 'Cleansed'
Beijing No. 1 Prison is for felons who have been convicted and sentenced to terms of more than 10 years, and so far it has not received any prisoners from the democracy movement. 
But in the coming months, as those people are brought to trial, some will end up behind the jail's walls, left to struggle for self-respect and the faith of their ideals in a system that aims not only to isolate criminals but above all to cleanse their contaminated minds.
Wei Jingsheng, an electrician serving a 15-year sentence for leading the 1978-79 democracy movement, was kept in solitary confinement early in the decade before being transferred to a prison camp in the desolation of Qinghai Province, in western China. 
The official press says he has a bad attitude and refuses to repent.
Xu Wenli, another leader of the Democracy Wall movement of a decade ago, remains in a cell here. 
Prison officials do not much like to talk about him, although when asked about his ideological progress they say it is ''about average.''
Â 
Bleak and Austere
No one knows how many people have been detained or arrested throughout China in connection with this year's democracy movement. 
Most estimates by diplomats range from 10,000 to 20,000. 
Some people are released after several days of interrogation, but arrests continue.
A visit to the No. 1 Prison offered a window into the life that many dissidents can anticipate for the next decade or two. 
It presented glimpses of an existence that is bleak and austere, but perhaps not so harsh as might be imagined.
In part, this may be because No. 1 Prison is a model institution, in contrast with places like the Gongdelin Prison, in the north of Beijing, where the guards are said to torture inmates by manacling them so tightly that they are unable to use their hands for days afterward.
And there is Qincheng No. 1 Prison, in the northern suburbs, where some intellectuals are believed to be confined behind an arched entrance known as the Atheists' Gate to Hell.
Still less accessible are the labor camps in remote areas of the far west and far north. 
Two Chinese officials with access to high-level information say a senior leader has proposed that new labor camps be built in the areas along the border to accommodate large numbers of those deemed counterrevolutionaries.
Â 
Bunk Beds and Guitars
Xu Jizhuang, the lean, affable warden of Prison No. 1, led the tour of the prison, showing how a dozen inmates are packed into six bunk beds in a room the size of a large American bedroom - crowded, but not strikingly so by Chinese standards. 
Many prisoners have guitars, which they play in their free hour each evening or on their day off each week. 
A few have books: some political or inspirational, but also a few novels.
About 2,000 prisoners live here, including 100 women and 30 people serving sentences for counterrevolutionary offenses. 
Inmates work eight hours a day, six days a week, in two prison factories, making socks and plastic objects like sandals and lunch boxes. 
They are paid about $1 a month, and the state turns a $300,000 annual profit on the operation.
Mr. Xu said 5 percent of former inmates were arrested for new crimes in the three years after their release. 
He attributed the rate to political education, along with technical and academic training programs.
The prisoners are allowed some access to television news and newspapers, and they were aware of the democracy movement when it was happening. 
But if there was any thrill at seeing the anti-Government demonstrations, it is dead now.
Â 
'Stable Environment'
''During the unrest, we were very indignant,'' said Liu Xuewen, a 23-year-old man serving a 12-year sentence for robbery. 
''What we want most is a stable environment.''
Of course, Mr. Liu was speaking not only to a foreign reporter but also to a half-dozen prison officials eyeing him with apprehension. 
While the reporter selected Mr. Liu at random for the interview, it was hardly a realistic probing of his attitudes.
Mr. Liu and the other inmates interviewed in these circumstances expressed considerable enthusiasm for prison conditions, sometimes with such apparent sincerity that it seemed they might be reluctant to leave. 
But three former inmates interviewed independently confirmed that while the No. 1 Prison is hardly idyllic, it is bearable.
The worst aspect is the winters, they said, because the prison is not centrally heated and the small stoves never raise the temperature enough to be very comfortable. 
In addition, they noted that some political prisoners have been kept in isolation -even guards are not allowed to talk with them - and that this takes an enormous toll on the prisoner's well-being and sanity.
Â 
One Bath Each Week
Ordinary prisoners, who appeared relatively healthy and well fed, are usually allowed to receive mail and to write two letters a month. 
They bathe weekly and receive one family visit a month. 
Particularly well-behaved prisoners are even allowed outside to visit their families on the Chinese New Year, and 15 percent have their sentences reduced for good conduct. 
Some have their sentences lengthened for fighting or other misconduct.
Inmates and officials say that torture and fighting are rare in the No. 1 Prison, and that brutality or rape among inmates is much less common here than in the United States.
But the official press has indicated that torture and wrongful imprisonment do occur on a large scale in some parts of the country. 
China Legal News reported that in the first half of 1986, 949 people were known to have been detained illegally, and 140 of them were killed or injured by ''cruel and vile methods.''

file: Beijing Journal_Army_s Business Sideline_ These Guns for Fun.txt
text:
ï»¿
It is a lazy afternoon on the outskirts of China's capital, in the hills near the majestic tombs of the Ming emperors. 
Little breaks the stillness except occasional birdsong, a quiet conversation barely overheard and, every so often, the convulsions of a heavy machine gun sending tracer bullets slamming into a hillside a half-mile away, then ricocheting hundreds of feet in the air.
The gun's fierce bark grows quiet, but just as the ears stop ringing the harsh report of an AK-47 assault rifle shatters the calm.
"Too high."
Another shot rings out.
"Missed."
Everyone relaxes for a moment, soft sunlight leaving the dun-colored hills in a pleasant haze, when everything seems to jump two inches with the terrific kaboom! of a rocket-propelled antitank weapon exploding against a bluff a couple of hundred yards away.
"It's only 490 yuan if you want to try that, too," says the young businessman handing out weapons to the customers, noticing the stunned look on the face of the amateur AK-47 marksman.
Â 
An Average Business Day
No, this is not a training ground for some people's liberation front, but one of the faces of China's economic reform program, an average business day, in fact, at the China North International Shooting Range.
Anyone with a bit of cash willing to make the 38-mile trip to the northwest of the city center, on the road to the Great Wall, can relax over a mortar (150 yuan, or about $27, a round), light and heavy machine guns, a few pops with a mounted 14.5-millimeter antiaircraft gun or a number of sidearms available in a showroom bristling with armaments.
The firing range is more than just an unusual way to kill an afternoon; it is one of the more colorful means devised by the People's Liberation Army to transform its traditional assets into money-making enterprises, in keeping with China's national policy of turning to the markets rather than the central Government for future growth.
That policy has been particularly important to China's military, which is often referred to as a state within a state by experts. 
It has its own hospitals, factories, banks and markets. 
Since military strength was a national priority in the tense years of the cold war, the army generally has among the best installations in the country, giving it an edge in developing money-making enterprises today.
For instance, China has become a major arms exporter. 
It has sent its high-powered missiles and other heavy weapons to the Middle East, angering some Western governments.
According to David Shambaugh, a professor at the University of London and a specialist on the Chinese military, the army has also retooled some of its factories to produce consumer products, from electric fans to construction equipment and trucks. 
In addition, some military units are starting to charge local governments for civil engineering projects they once did free, like bridge building and flood-control work.
"There were explicit orders that the military was to diversify its revenues by getting involved in civilian production and other kinds of activities, and they've been doing it," Mr. Shambaugh said. 
"The story is that they are developing a more visible military industrial complex."
But one of the darker sides to these activities is that they have given the military far more money to spend with even less oversight, Mr. Shambaugh said. 
Few seem to know how much the army is earning or how it is using what is believed to be billions of dollars from these businesses.
"It's all off-budget revenue," Mr. Shambaugh said. 
"I couldn't give you an estimate on how much accrues to them. 
But it's got to be mammoth."
The China North International Shooting Range is a sign of what might be called the market's acceptance of some of these capitalist strategies -- and the political pragmatism of what has traditionally been one of the world's most politicized armies.
The customers shoot at black silhouetted targets -- or just hillsides with the serious weaponry -- without a single running dog capitalist target in sight. 
In fact, the area is conspicuous for its lack of political content, save for the odd comment by a visitor noting the irony of Western thrill seekers being offered potshots with weapons that once symbolized attempts to destroy capitalism.
The operation is bare bones, with a lounge to sip soft drinks next to the armory. 
It is doubtful the operators did any market analysis, but they seem to have focused on the things its audience really wants: a large area in back where the blasting is done and an array of weapons in front where the casually attired soldiers of fortune can take each other's pictures with rocket-propelled bombs and various guns hoisted on their shoulders.
Wang Gui Ying, the smiling round-faced technician who helps visitors choose their weapons, offers expert tips on the relative merits, for instance, of tracer bullets or hand-held versus mounted machine guns. 
She says that on weekends the range gets as many as several hundred visitors.
And these are not just foreigners; newly affluent Chinese, she says, are willing to pay to blast away with Chinese-made M-16's, Uzis and the other guns available. 
The range advertises on Chinese television, Ms. Wang said, sponsoring the weather report. 
There are a few limits on what children are permitted to shoot, but otherwise the market's invisible hand appears to be the guiding spirit.
On a recent afternoon a group of Japanese tourists who arrived in a bus leaned towards extremes; while some took turns firing the antitank bombs, the most expensive weapon offered, the rest stuck mostly to small handguns.
By the end of the day, after many of the visitors had posed out front with AK-47 assault rifles or other weapons, the haul was not bad. 
The Japanese group had paid about $500 for less than an hour's worth of teeth-jarring fun, leaving Ms. Wang wearing an infectious smile as she obliged a visitor by posing briefly with a shoulder-fired rocket launcher in the spreading coolness of a Beijing evening.

file: Beijing Journal_As Daily Toes the Line, Readers Turn Their Backs.txt
text:
ï»¿
Behind the armed guards at the grand main gate of the compound, beyond the cafeteria in a pleasant park-like setting, is a building that is identified as No. 5, but which might better be labeled as a battleground for the future of China.
It is the editorial office of People's Daily, the most important of the 1,459 newspapers published in China. 
In a nation where power struggles are constant and camouflaged, People's Daily functions for people here and abroad as a window - heavily frosted - into the minds of the Chinese leadership.
During the democracy movement in the spring of 1989, the walls of building No. 5 were plastered with posters in which many of the newspaper's 1,900 staff members endorsed the movement, and expressed embarrassment at the pablum they felt they were writing.
Now it seems that the battle for People's Daily has ended in a remarkable stalemate: The hard-liners have gained clear control of the newspaper, but many people no longer read it.
Â 
Mood at Paper Seen as Bleak
''It's so boring that I don't look at it anymore and neither do my friends,'' an economist in Beijing said. 
''We would rather read other papers, which at least contain some social news and crime news.''
The new publisher of People's Daily, Gao Di, a 63-year-old former provincial party secretary who lives in the same compound on Wanshou Road as Prime Minister Li Peng, declined to be interviewed. 
But other editors who spoke in officially arranged interviews asserted that stabilityI had returned to the newspaper.
''Last year the newspaper had some incorrect guidance, and we had to rectify our errors,'' said Zhang Yongwen, a senior editor. 
''Some people made mistakes. 
But with some political study they were able to improve their understanding and raise their consciousness. 
Some had unrealistic ideas. 
But once they had a proper understanding, they could return to work as normal.''
Other People's Daily reporters -interviewed privately in defiance of a ban on unauthorized contacts with foreign journalists - said the mood in the newspaper was bleak.
Â 
Promoting Hard-Liners' View
''Most people are quite depressed,'' said a reporter for the paper. 
''And there's little sense of hope that conditions will improve.''
But the reporter said that as the investigations and political study wind down, life is returning to a routine and that the new editor in chief, Shao Huaze, an army man, had proved to be more reasonable than some people had expected.
Under the newly arrived editorial team, including not only Mr. Gao and Mr. Shao but also a fresh deputy editor and deputy publisher, People's Daily has taken the lead in promoting the hard-liners' view that only Communism can save China. 
A typical front page carries articles about the activities of top leaders, along with a call for unity, a few items about improved economic performance, and perhaps an inspirational account about a model worker.
If gloom and frustration are the primary emotions in the People's Daily compound these days, it is not for the first time.
''There's only one thing that's accurate in People's Daily each day -the date,'' a former top editor once said to a group of friends, according to a Chinese who was there. 
And a poll in 1988 of 1,800 Chinese journalists found that only 1.1 percent thought that the public believed the press.
Â 
Role of 'Positive Propaganda'
One of the ways in which People's Daily has tried to build credibility is by soliciting letters to the editor. 
Each day the newspaper receives about 1,000 letters, and those are carefully scrutinized by a staff of 54 people for possible publication.
''Those letters we publish are those reflecting what people most care about and what people most want to read,'' said Li Youchun, the first vice director of the Masses Letters Department of People's Daily. 
Some of the published letters criticize traffic jams, pollution, rude clerks and other problems. 
But no attacks are permitted against Government policies.
''Criticism is an aspect of our jobs,'' said Wang Yongan, a deputy director of the Masses Letters Department. 
''But it's just a part. 
The main function is still positive propaganda.''
One problem for People's Daily is that the propaganda zigs and zags along with China's policies, and the newspaper's editors tend to be get in trouble at each twist. 
According to a book about People's Daily published last year, Chairman Mao Zedong warned the editor in chief in 1957 that in taking the job he should accept the risks of dismissal, expulsion from the party, divorce, imprisonment and even execution. 
So far no one has been executed, But Mr. Gao is the fourth publisher in the last seven years.
Because People's Daily is published by the Central Committee, the paper's editor and publisher have ministerial rank - along with perhaps 1,000 other current and former office holders in China - and the publisher in the past has been entitled to sit in on expanded meetings of the Politburo.
With a claimed circulation of 3.5 million, based overwhelmingly on subscriptions from offices rather than individuals, People's Daily is probably the most widely circulated newspaper in the country. 
The closest competitor is Reference News, a digest of positive news reports about China from abroad, which claims a circulation of 3.3 million. 
Because it has such a large circulation, People's Daily is able to charge foreign advertisers $40,000 for a full-page advertisement - insuring the newspaper a measure of prosperity.
''The People's Daily used to be very prestigious, and young journalists wanted to work there,'' said a reporter who turned down the chance to join People's Daily and now works for a rival newspaper. 
''Now smart young people would rather look elsewhere for jobs, because the People's Daily is absolutely inflexible. 
Rigor mortis is setting in.''

file: Beijing Journal_At Work Where the Cold War_s Ice Still Lingers.txt
text:
ï»¿
A fault line rarely makes a cozy nesting spot, but for more than a year J. Stapleton Roy has occupied precisely the spot where the American and Chinese tectonic plates come grinding together.
As Ambassador to China, Mr. Roy is periodically scolded by the Foreign Ministry here because of disputes related to human rights, arms sales and other concerns. 
Chinese police guard the embassy, intimidating some Chinese from approaching, and security agents still sometimes follow American diplomats.
Diplomatic homes and most parts of the embassy are assumed to be bugged, while Chinese-dug tunnels run somewhere deep beneath the fenced embassy compound. 
A mysterious windowless building, said to be the C.I.A. station and communications center, looms over the embassy backyard as a constant reminder of the security concerns at the last American embassy in a hard-line Communist country.
Mr. Roy, a 57-year-old career diplomat and fluent Chinese speaker who was born in China as the son of missionaries, seems to relish his posting despite the official pressures.
Â 
Cycle Rides in the Capital
Each Sunday he escapes from the world of neckties and diplomacy by cycling through the back alleys of the capital, chatting informally with those Chinese he meets. 
While Mr. Roy owns a locally made Flying Pigeon, he mostly uses his 21-speed Peugeot to whizz by Beijing cyclists on their single-speed Phoenixes and Golden Lions.
But while Mr. Roy has proved adept at managing relations with China, these days the entire embassy seems a bit disquieted about a challenge from the other side of the Pacific: the prospect of Gov. Bill Clinton becoming President and adopting a tougher policy toward China.
"I have no expectations," Mr. Roy said when asked what would happen to him if Mr. Clinton wins. 
"I'm a career diplomat, and you serve at the pleasure of the President."
The problem is that ever since Chinese troops opened fire on pro-democracy protesters near Tiananmen Square in June 1989, United States policy toward China has been highly politicized. 
Mr. Roy and other embassy officials have been effective spokesmen for President Bush's policy of constructive engagement, rejecting economic sanctions as counterproductive, but if Mr. Clinton wins the embassy may have to switch course.
"There's no question that one of the major consequences of Tiananmen was the shattering of the bipartisan consensus in favor of improved relations with China," Mr. Roy acknowledged in a recent interview in his home, over coffee and brownies prepared by his household's six-member staff. 
But he also suggested that some consensus remained at a deeper level.
"While there have been disagreements on specific questions about how we should advance our human rights and other objectives in China, I don't think there has been a shattering of the understanding that China remains an important country."
Mr. Roy arrived in Beijing as Ambassador only in the summer of 1991, but in some ways he seems to have spent his life preparing for the post. 
His first memories are of Japanese bombs exploding near his home in Sichuan Province. 
And he grew up speaking the Sichuan dialect of Chinese with his playmates.
After passing most of his boyhood in China, Mr. Roy and his family were among the few Americans who remained in China for the first year after the Communist revolution in 1949. 
In the fervor after "liberation," Mr. Roy learned to sing a few Chinese songs, like "The East Is Red" and "We Workers Are Strong," that are not normally part of a diplomat's repertory.
The United States Embassy, with 161 American officers and staff members, is the largest foreign mission in China. 
Other Western diplomats and resident foreigners praise it for having an excellent staff and for cultivating specialists on various topics and regions. 
But they also sometimes criticize it for its rapid turnover of diplomats -- many stay only two years -- and for persisting in a cold war-style disapproval of close friendships with Chinese.
In a city where Chinese are far more likely to talk openly over a beer or a game of mah-jongg than in a formal meeting, diplomats from Australia and several European countries have a reputation for cultivating warmer friendships with Chinese than do the Americans. 
Indeed, at least two European diplomats are having romantic relationships with Chinese women, while American diplomats rarely shed even their neckties during meetings with Chinese.
"We encourage our officers to go out and make as broad contacts as they can," Mr. Roy said. 
"But because this is a Communist country, we discourage intimacy."
A reminder of the risks came in 1988, when an American diplomat fell in love with a Chinese women. 
State Security agents reportedly burst in with cameras when they were in bed together, and tried to blackmail the American into spying for them. 
He immediately reported the incident to the embassy's security officer and was quietly whisked out of China the next day.
For all the lingering tensions, there is far less hostility in the air now than in the summer of 1989, shortly after the Tiananmen crackdown. 
The previous Ambassador, James R. Lilley, was then hiding a famous dissident, Fang Lizhi, in the embassy's medical clinic, and Chinese troops with submachine guns patrolled outside the compound. 
Fearful that the troops would invade the compound, the embassy destroyed its confidential files to avoid the risk of their falling into Chinese hands.
Almost overnight the atmosphere in the embassy changed from considerable optimism to deep pessimism about China. 
Those diplomats who were present during the killings have long since left China, however, and now the mood has swung back to one of relative optimism.

file: Beijing Journal_China Is Fighting for Its Soul_ Its Looted Antiques.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was not drugs the peasant was selling under the cover of darkness, but something just as restricted, and he was very careful as he displayed his wares on a quiet street before dawn.
"Ming Dynasty," the peasant, a thin man in his 40's, nervously told a dealer, who was crouched down, scrutinizing the blue-and-white porcelain vases. 
If they really did date from the Ming Dynasty, which collapsed in 1644, then they were probably dug from a tomb and are barred from leaving the country.
Smuggling of antiques can be punishable by death in China, but such transactions are nonetheless very common. 
The Government estimates that 40,000 tombs were robbed in 1989 and 1990 alone, and gangs manage to smuggle out huge statues 1,000 years old or more.
Some smugglers show Western collectors photos -- even faxes -- of important pieces in Chinese museums, which often have poor security. 
If they receive an order, the smugglers steal them from the museum and whisk them secretly to a boat waiting somewhere along China's 11,000-mile coastline.
Â 
Joy and Heartache
Encouraged by China's push toward a market economy and by the piles of money they believe Chinese art fetches, smugglers have refined a business that is causing a mixture of joy and heartache on both sides of the Chinese border. 
Art-starved Western collectors -- even some large museums -- have been able to fill their yearning for a neolithic pot or a Song Dynasty ceramic, as Chinese smugglers fill their pockets with money.
But the Government is horrified that national treasures are being stolen. 
Archeologists and historians are also distraught that troves of information are being erased by rampant, careless excavation of tombs.
"A nation's antiquities are a nation's soul," said Kwang-Chih Chang, a professor of Chinese archeology at Harvard University. 
"Antiquities are destroyed every day all over the world by natural disasters, by floods, by construction. 
But when we can control the destruction, it behooves us to do so."
These days, the Government is fighting back harder than ever. 
In the last couple of years it nearly tripled the amount of money spent on protecting its relics. 
This year it coordinated a nationwide crackdown, bringing together museum officials, customs agents, police chiefs and even two Politburo members to publicize the crackdown.
A result is that the smuggling of antiques, especially first-rate ones, seems to have declined. 
In previous years, antiques shops in Hong Kong displayed shelves of glazed pottery, jades, bronzes, clay horse heads and silver objects. 
But now the shops look depleted.
Still, grave robbers and smugglers are clinging to work. 
Late in October in Shaanxi Province in northern China, where Chinese archeologists have discovered the tombs of 72 emperors and 1,240 royal families, a gang of robbers used explosives, searchlights and guns in digging up a tomb from the Tang Dynasty, which reigned from the seventh to 10th centuries.
This year thousands of villagers openly plundered a group of tombs in Shaanxi, Chinese press reports say. 
Tomb robbery has been especially severe in the provinces of Shaanxi, Henan, Gansu and Jiangsu, as well as in the city of Shanghai.
Museum robberies are also a problem, in part because the museums cannot afford adequate security systems. 
About four years ago, when Sotheby's was planning to auction an ancient bronze vessel, perhaps 3,000 years old, an art expert who had read the catalogue wrote to the Chinese authorities asking them to check whether the piece had been smuggled from China.
Â 
Beauty Comes First
The authorities discovered that the vessel had been stolen from a small county museum in Hubei Province and they had the photographs and documents to prove it. 
The owner returned the vessel to China, and the Chinese thief was caught and sentenced to death.
Local Chinese authorities are often much less concerned with preserving their culture than the central Government. 
Some prefer to have money instead of what they regard as old pieces of pottery that only clutter up warehouses.
James J. Lally, a Chinese art dealer based in New York, explained how a businessman was able to take six 16th-century Ming Dynasty stone sculptures out of China. 
What was remarkable was that these sculptures -- horses, rams and tigers -- were all life size.
Local officials evidently let him take the carvings across the border because they regarded them as little more than a pile of stones that farmers kept bumping into when they planted.
But the appetite for rare antiques means that the vigorous debate about how they reach the West is likely to persist among lovers of art. 
Archeologists are often outraged by the smuggling while dealers and collectors say that bronzes and statues that get out of China are often better preserved than those that remain, and that such pieces help arouse public awareness of Asian art.
"The way the art market regards works of art is first and foremost for their beauty," Mr. Lally said. 
"The hierarchy of what's important to know is sometimes the reverse for an art lover than it is for an archeologist."

A university professor sighed as he described the long self-criticism that he had written painstakingly in a small notebook and then read aloud to a critical audience of colleagues and Communist Party officials at a political meeting.
''I was humiliated, but I had to do it,'' said the professor, whose self-criticism detailed his involvement in the democracy movement this past spring.
Now, he says, he feels a deep loneliness, an emptiness that grows when he recalls the violent crackdown in June. 
To fight his depression and to cleanse away his anger, he is pouring his energy into teaching, nearly tripling his number of hours in the classroom, to 26 a week.

Students are nervous about a new guideline that would require them to work for as much as seven years in China before they are allowed to study abroad. 
Their lives have also changed enormously this academic year, with new ideology sessions, new mandatory labor in the ''grass roots'' after graduation, and at some institutions a new requirement of military training.

Â
