file: Beijing Journal_Chinese Cartoonist Is the Master of the Fine Line.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a country where bold is bad, artists sometimes think more about diplomacy -- about tiptoeing on a thread of silk -- than they do about drawing. 
Ding Cong is such a diplomat: he is a consummate political cartoonist who never raises the topic of politics.
At a time when people are thrown in jail for openly criticizing the Government, Mr. Ding's black and white drawings stand out because they dare to satirize the leadership and the tensions in Chinese society. 
But these days, Mr. Ding has mastered tact and subtlety, a far cry from his younger days when he would paint scrolls streaming with flashy evil-doers, distorted and contorted, to portray his views of the Chinese Nationalists.
Like poetry, his drawings now often convey layers of meanings, but the most sensitive meaning is usually masked behind an image of everyday experience. 
For that reason, by American standards, Mr. Ding's cartoons are tame. 
They never explicitly portray any of China's current leaders. 
Instead, they sometimes draw on allusions, plucking out characters from way back in China's history to illustrate a point relevant to current events.
"He's a very slippery cartoonist," said a Chinese writer who is a fan of Mr. Ding's works. 
"How can the leaders catch him?
If they point to a cartoon and say, 'This is critical of the Government,' all he needs to ask is, 'Where is it critical?'
And he'd be right, because you can't pin his cartoons down."
Â 
A Difficult Social Climate
Mr. Ding's drawings often capture the alienation of intellectuals in society, or the chasm between the leadership and the people, or the system's corruption. 
Sometimes, the political zap is so veiled that a political explanation seems far-fetched, but Mr. Ding's background is rooted in politics and many of his cartoons have a bitter edge. 
To Mr. Ding, cartooning is wedded to politics.
"In China, all cartoons are political," Mr. Ding said with a loud, nervous laugh. 
"To be a cartoonist, if you want to satirize something, it's political."
And then with another laugh he added, "But because our social climate is not so good, there are not too many political cartoons these days."
In many ways, his demeanor and personality mirror his style of cartooning. 
Physically, the 74-year-old Mr. Ding is a plump, bubbly man whose features are bold and accentuated, like many of his cartoon characters. 
His manner of conversation -- winding and dodging around a point -- resembles his style of cartooning.
Part of the reason he is careful is simply that he wants to keep drawing. 
His cartoons have always contained critiques of society, often with severe consequences. 
After the Chinese-Japanese war broke out in 1937, Mr. Ding's cartoons so offended the Japanese that in 1938 he had to flee to Hong Kong. 
In 1945, Mr. Ding worked for an underground unit of the American armed forces based in the southern city of Kunming. 
He and his colleagues would sneak out at night, rip down posters put up by the Japanese troops, change them subtly so they poked fun at the Japanese, and then stick them up again.
Â 
10 Books of Cartoons
During the next couple of years, some of his most biting satire was aimed at the Chinese Nationalist regime of Chiang Kai-shek, and in 1947 he fled to Hong Kong once again to escape persecution. 
He returned to China to support the Communist revolution, but then in 1957 he was labeled a "rightist" and sent to the countryside to do manual labor. 
For the next 22 years, Mr. Ding did not draw a line.
Since 1979, when he was rehabilitated and allowed to draw again, Mr. Ding has published 10 books of cartoons. 
He has not been active in the democracy movement, but in early 1989, before the crackdown, he signed a petition calling for greater freedoms. 
He was not punished for this.
Even though Mr. Ding is probably the best-known cartoonist in China his drawings are rarely published in the official national newspapers. 
These days, Mr. Ding knows how far he can stretch a point before he must stop. 
But this is the hard part of his work, he says.
"It may take me only a few hours to draw, but days and days to think about what to draw," Mr. Ding said. 
"As soon as you look at a cartoon, one meaning jumps out at you immediately. 
But if you draw so that the real satire can be seen right away, ah, then you're finished."
Many ordinary people simply do not catch the underlying point of his cartoons. 
In a cartoon that appears completely nonpolitical, an obese woman is holding a picture of a young woman with a flowered dress. 
The woman is wearing an exact replica of the dress that her tailor just completed, but after looking at the slim shapeliness of the woman in the dress, she complains to him, "You didn't do it exactly according to the picture."
Â 
A Political Meaning
Mr. Ding, who published the sketch more than four years ago, says the cartoon has a political meaning as well. 
The obese woman can be thought of as the Government, slovenly and out of shape. 
No matter how many people it orders around to help dress it up, it cannot hide its bulges and mistakes.
A much more recent drawing portrays a string puppet in the image of a fierce general, Cao Cao, in the third century A.D. The cartoon derives its satire through interplay with an accompanying poem, "An Ode to a Puppet," which Mr. Ding did not write:
With pieces of string, it dances gracefully,
Yet, few people see through the small trick.
Black-haired, white-faced, it looks the image of Cao Cao
Without a soul behind the curtain, it's a good-for-nothing.
The crucial question is this: Does the puppet represent Prime Minister Li Peng, manipulated by China's octogenarian leaders?
Some intellectuals look at the cartoon and immediately say that it must be Prime Minister Li. 
Others take a look and are sure it does not refer to Mr. Li. Mr. Ding denies he had any intention of referring to the current leadership.
"I just drew a picture according to the poem," he said. 
"Where is it critical?"

file: Beijing Journal_Counterfeit Train Ticket_ No Problem. It_s China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Lin Liangxi, a budding tycoon, saw his manufacturing venture collapse early this year after he tried to get a refund for three train tickets.
The clerk at the train station suspected that they were forged, and the police seized Mr. Lin and confirmed that the tickets were fakes. 
In Mr. Lin's hotel room, the authorities found 254 more fake tickets hidden in two packages of instant noodles.
That was just the beginning. 
China Daily, an official newspaper, reported that the police found that Mr. Lin had set up a ticket-making factory in his hometown, Wenzhou. 
The factory was stocked with a printing press, a paper-cutting machine and 1,200 pounds of the cardboard used to make tickets, which are almost always in short supply.
The episode underscores the point that the train-ticket industry, like most in China, is thriving and profitable. 
More fundamentally, the black market for train tickets offers a peek at the usually hidden underbelly of China: increasingly brazen entrepreneurs, growing webs of corruption and the state's decreasing power to do anything about it.
Â 
The Manchurian Scalper
The laws say ticket counterfeiting and scalping are illegal. 
But the scalpers, known as huang niu, or "yellow cows," openly solicit business at the Beijing train station.
"How many tickets do you want?" asked a short young man of about 25. 
"I can get you as many as you want. 
No problem."
He quoted a second-class sleeper to the southern city of Guangzhou at $90, compared with an official price of $27. 
"Just tell me when you want to go and how many tickets you want," the yellow cow urged, speaking Chinese with a Manchurian accent.
"The police won't interfere," he said. 
"We know the cops. 
They know us. 
In fact, they buy their tickets through me, too."
With China's hard-liners now in retreat, the Communist Party is aggressively trying to build what it calls a "socialist market economy."
Clearly the leaders do not approve of scalping, but in some ways the ticket industry is a perfect illustration of this emerging socialist market economy: the scalpers create their own market economy, they depend on the backdrop of socialist fixed prices to create shortages, and their efforts turn bribery into the lubricant for Communist-run capitalism.
Â 
Rail Travel Is Booming
"Cadres and crooks are all part of the same family," the father of a railway policeman explained to a friend the other day. 
He said his son gets a share of the scalping profits from the yellow cows he is supposed to arrest.
The yellow cows can earn thousands of dollars a year -- huge amounts in China -- because train tickets are scarce. 
With the economy booming at a growth rate of nearly 10 percent per year, far more Chinese than ever can afford to travel both for business and pleasure.
Traditionally in Communist countries, central planners kept up output of heavy industrial products like rail cars while neglecting consumer products. 
In China, on the other hand, the markets are exploding with sweaters and stuffed animals, while the stock of rail passenger cars increases by only about 5 percent each year -- much less than the demand.
A result is that it is often impossible for Chinese to get a train ticket anytime soon among major cities like Shanghai, Guangzhou and Beijing.
"When do you want to go to Beijing and how many tickets do you want?" asked a yellow cow in the central Chinese city of Hefei. 
The ticket office had just said that no seats were available, but the yellow cow -- a man in his late 20's, equipped with a beeper to stay in touch with his business contacts -- promised that all he needed to do was make a phone call.
Some of the scalpers get their tickets in the traditional way, by lining up, but many order them in bulk through friends in purchasing offices of large companies or Government ministries. 
Others bribe ticket sellers to get a bundle of tickets each month at the official price.
Still other yellow cows simply forge train tickets. 
As China has loosened up in recent years, it has become possible for crooks as well as entrepreneurs to buy printing equipment and travel around the country making sales.
"We're very concerned by this," said Jin Wanjian, an official in the Foreign Affairs Department of the Railways Ministry. 
But Mr. Jin said the authorities are cracking down on scalping, and he noted that in Beijing alone the police have detained 3,300 yellow cows so far this year.
Mr. Jin denied that scalpers have frequent links with the police or with official ticket sellers. 
He said that in any case the rail ministry is increasing its efforts to educate employees not to sell tickets on the sly, and that the Government is also considering raising ticket prices to reduce the shortages and put the yellow cows out of business.
Many of the yellow cows are organized into gangs, and they frequently diversify into a related growth industry: marketing blank receipts so that officials can pad their expense accounts. 
When one train ticket salesman was told that his prices were too steep, he offered to throw in a receipt so that the purchaser could claim the difference as a restaurant meal.
Outside the Xizhimen Train Ticket Booking Hall in northwest Beijing, a dozen street vendors openly sell hotel and restaurant receipts with the amounts left blank. 
A traveler on official business could, for example, stay at a $4-a-night hotel while turning in a receipt for a $20-a-night hotel.
To be sure, only a small proportion of officials appear to pad their expenses. 
But the brazenness of the yellow cows reinforces a deep popular outrage at the growing corruption, as well as the sense that the Government is losing control and that the police are on the take.
"If the cops come over, then we just run away," said a receipt vendor, a young man of about 25 in a gray sports jacket. 
"And even if they grab you, things can be worked out. 
If you're also selling cigarette lighters, maybe the policeman will grab five of them and say to you: 'I've confiscated four of your lighters, right?'
Then you say, 'Four, that's right,' even though you know he's got five. 
So instead of hauling you in, he returns four lighters, pockets one and lets you off."

text:

A class of 40 nervous students looked blankly at the teacher who had just asked a sample question on an English test, about the purchase of shoes from a catalogue. 
''Class, what is a catalogue?'' the teacher asked.
Several students squirmed in their seats, for none of those in the cold, damp classroom had ever heard of buying from a catalogue. 
Shoes were bought in shops, not catalogues. 
They shrugged, and hoped that the issue would not come up in a test of English as a foreign language.
They had signed up for this series of English classes to prepare for the test, which is required of foreign students by American universities. 
Many young intellectuals, thrown into a depression after the military suppression of the democracy movement in June, regard study abroad as the best escape hatch out of China.
The more the Chinese authorities attack the United States, the more many intellectuals perceive the political climate to be worsening, and the more fanatically they study English to try to get to the United States.
''We are all trying to get out,'' said a young Chinese man planning to study abroad. 
''There is little hope for us here.''
Â 
Pointless to Remain, They Say
It is not so much that they are afraid of being arrested; rather, they say they believe there is no point in remaining, for they will be given no opportunity to use their talents in China.
Paradoxically, the biggest obstacle for many is not permission from the Chinese authorities, at least for the moment, but American immigration law. 
The United States Embassy here is reluctant to give visas to those who cannot show a good reason why they must return, such as a spouse who is remaining behind, and so a large number of single men and women who have been accepted at universities abroad find that they are denied visas.
''I don't think I'll be able to go abroad because it's nearly impossible to get a U.S. visa,'' said a young Chinese woman who was taking a class to prepare for the English test.
Because of their passion for getting away, many Chinese with only an inkling of English are brushing up on their Americanisms. 
In Shanghai, novice English-speakers boldly walk up to foreigners and offer to be their guides, just for the sake of speaking English to a foreigner.
Â 
Some Use Connections
Those hoping to take the English test are not just from the universities. 
Technicians, physicists, philosophers and computer programmers are among the thousands flocking to English classes and standing in line to register for the test, which is given four times a year.
The next test date is in January, and some people lined up for two days to insure a spot on the registration list at one of about a dozen locations in the city.
Yet the authorities have already started to make it difficult for Chinese people to prepare for and take the test. 
Late in October, the authorities closed down the English Corner, an officially designated area in Purple Bamboo Park in Beijing where people could go to practice English. 
About 100 Chinese gathered in the English Corner last Sunday in defiance of the Government ban.
It has also been hard for Chinese who work in units that are being scrutinized because of the pro-democracy demonstrations this spring. 
Most Chinese must obtain permission and a letter of introduction from their work unit to register for the test, and some Chinese without connections say they have been denied that permission.
''This Government controls nearly every aspect of our lives, down to the very food we eat,'' said a young woman who, like many Chinese, lives in a dormitory and eats at a cafeteria run by her work unit. 
She also planned to take the English test, but was denied permission.
Â 
Rumors of a Rules Change
One Chinese worker infuriated officials when they found out he had used a letter of introduction written months before for an earlier test date to register for the January test.
The rush to study English has been fanned by rumors that the Government will change the regulations for studying abroad sometime next year.
Among the fears is that the Government will not allow Chinese people over 35 years old to go abroad for study, although they may make an overseas trip as part of a business delegation or other work. 
Others fear that the Government will not let students who have just graduated from college go overseas to study until they have worked in China for four to seven years.
Â 
A Fear of Rejection
Some Chinese are confident they will obtain passports, a process that sometimes can take as long as six months, but are concerned they will be rejected by foreign embassies.
But a United States Embassy official said the visa approval rate for study, now about 50 percent or higher, has remained essentially the same as it was before June.

But figures for visas issued from April to September at the United States Embassy suggest that fewer lecturers and researchers have applied to go to the United States since June. 
The largest drop in applications was in the category of business travel.
''This category had grown 20 to 30 percent a year,'' the official said. 
''It's usually a barometer of the state of economic relations.''

text:
ï»¿
With "counterrevolutionaries" said to be afoot at home and abroad, the task of keeping China safe for Communism is giving new prestige to a Government ministry so mysterious that even its official address is phony.
Known as the State Security Ministry, it represents the acme of secrecy in an already secretive bureaucracy. 
While the ministry says it is situated in a compound next to Tiananmen Square, Chinese say its headquarters are really in a large walled compound in northwest Beijing.
The nation's spymaster, Jia Chunwang, who is Minister of State Security, is a 53-year-old English-speaking engineer who is said to be a great admirer of the Central Intelligence Agency. 
But even though Mr. Jia is associated with the liberal wing of the Communist Party that is now in disgrace, State Security is thriving as one of the main institutional beneficiaries of the military crackdown on dissent in 1989.
While the police and the army were stumbling over themselves during the Tiananmen student protests, State Security undercover agents kept up their intelligence work even during the height of the protests, even when they were detained by unsuspecting soldiers along with members of the groups they had infiltrated.
Â 
Improving Benefits
A memorandum went out in September 1989, three months after the Tiananmen crackdown, providing for improved benefits for the State Security staff, and the ministry has been riding high ever since. 
While the C.I.A. and the K.G.B. sometimes have to scrounge for enemies to justify their existence, State Security faces a target-rich environment since the Chinese Government believes that enemies are everywhere.
While State Security also sends spies abroad, its main task is to ferret out foreign spies in China as well as dissidents and counterrevolutionaries. 
Its staff runs in the many tens of thousands, posted in all major cities around the country, as it keeps an eye on political troublemakers, religious figures, applicants for travel abroad and foreigners, just about every kind of foreigner.
"Foreign diplomats are open spies," declares a Chinese book on espionage, intended for circulation only to specially approved people. 
"They have used a thousand means, including bribes and sex, to recruit agents, including more than 10 of our Government staff."
The book also suggests monitoring foreign journalists, scholars, business executives, overseas Chinese, tourists and even athletes. 
The book cites many examples, including an American woman who it says was a C.I.A. spy while teaching English in Beijing. 
The book asserts that she used sex to trap four Chinese into giving her 200 Government documents.
Â 
Seen as Humane
In running intelligence operations, Mr. Jia is supervised by Qiao Shi, a senior Politburo member who oversees the police and courts as well as spying. 
Mr. Qiao, who is 67 years old and has a daughter studying in the United States, is said by Chinese who have met him to be cool-headed, ambitious and affable, and artful in avoiding revealing his own stand.
Remarkably, State Security has a reputation in China as a generally humane and liberal organization, at least compared with the police and the army. 
State Security staff members, many of them graduates of the ministry's own university, the Institute of International Relations, tend to be younger and better educated than most Government officials and complain to friends just as much as anyone else about the Government, sometimes more so, because no one is watching them.
"It's not like it used to be, when police were assigned to State Security work," said a former Public Security official who worked for many years with State Security colleagues. 
"Now almost all State Security staff are college educated, and they're much sophisticated than the police."
The former Public Security official says, with just a trace of jealousy, that the State Security officials always got better equipment than the police. 
Typically there are several thousand State Security staff members in all the provinces, reading mail, listening to phone calls, monitoring dissidents and deciding whom to allow abroad, he said.
Â 
Diplomats as Spies
While many of China's spies abroad are from the military's intelligence agency, many also come from the State Security Ministry, principally pretending to be diplomats or journalists. 
In the mid-1980's, however, morale apparently suffered when Wu Xueqian, then Foreign Minister and now Deputy Prime Minister, tried to reduce the ranks of spies posing as Chinese diplomats.
State Security suffered another major blow in 1985 when one of its department directors defected to the United States, and apparently gave evidence that led to the arrest shortly afterward of a mole in the Central Intelligence Agency, Larry Wu-tai Chin. 
Mr. Chin committed suicide, and some Chinese say there was a strong resentment in State Security that Deng Xiaoping, the senior leader, did not push for a deal with the United States to get Mr. Chin released to China.
In any case, these days State Security has recovered its prestige and established new influence. 
It has triumphed in the bureaucratic wrangling over the Foreign Ministry and is widely believed to be expanding its spy networks abroad.
China's spies abroad are believed to focus on monitoring Chinese dissident groups, obtaining military technology and gathering intelligence about Taiwan. 
The counterintelligence work within China has always focused on rooting out spies for foreign countries or for Taiwan -- just this week China announced the arrest of five people for spying for Taiwan -- but lately has also sought to counter American bugging of Chinese communications.
Â 
Secret Phone Lines in Doubt
Staff members in army and Communist Party offices have been warned that Western countries have used high-tech equipment to intercept secret phone calls. 
In the 1980's China received Western help in replacing hard-wire telecommunications lines with microwave systems that are said to have facilitated American intelligence-gathering because they are easier to tap.
While it is difficult to judge, State Security leaves the impression of being the most efficient ministry in the Chinese capital. 
Most Government offices are lackadaisical even when they are not on tea breaks, but State Security manages on a moment's notice to rustle up teams to pursue correspondents even in the middle of a rainy night or, most startling of all, at dinnertime.
In 1988 State Security even trapped an American diplomat who was having a sexual relationship with a Chinese woman and tried to blackmail him into spying for China. 
Instead the diplomat immediately told embassy officials, who hustled him out of the country.

text:

Hou Xiaotian's face brightens with an innocent grin as she weaves her bicycle through the traffic. 
But her girlish demeanor belies a life these days composed more of tears than smiles, more of prison than family, and of memories of a husband whom she is not scheduled to be reunited with again until the year 2002.
Ms. Hou, 28 years old, has become virtually the only person in Beijing now who dares to speak out for human rights to the foreign press. 
She assumed the role after her husband, Wang Juntao, was sentenced in February to 13 years in prison for his role in the Tiananmen Square democracy movement.
"Why am I doing this?" she asked. 
"If I can speak freely, if this can take place in China, then it shows that China is making progress. 
I am nudging the Government. 
This is an opportunity and I must not abandon it."
Since April, her husband has been confined alone in a small jail cell where he eats, sleeps, and uses a toilet, Ms. Hou said. 
A scholar of economics, with a passion for democracy, he can barely read because of the dim light. 
His family said he suffers from hepatitis B, a potentially fatal ailment of the liver.

Husband on Hunger Strike
Last week, Mr. Wang began a hunger strike as a protest against his treatment and in response to the authorities' decision not to allow Ms. Hou to visit him this month. 
Normally she is allowed one monthly visit for 30 minutes, but this month the session was cancelled -- apparently because the authorities were annoyed at Ms. Hou's contacts with foreign journalists.
For more than a year, Ms. Hou's battle has focused on improving prison conditions for her husband, and she has repeatedly approached various officials in different Government departments to solicit help. 
She brought cakes and gifts to the prison doorsteps on his birthday, their wedding anniversary and the new year, but both she and her gifts were turned away.
The setbacks, she said, have taken a toll on her emotional and physical health. 
Earlier this summer, she became weary and severely depressed, crying every day, and she spent more than a month in the hospital.
"They are really villains, trying to exploit the love a woman has for her husband to attain to their means," Ms. Hou said in an appeal printed earlier this year by a human rights organization. 
The authorities wanted to know what she had told foreign reporters, threatening to reject the presents she had brought for her husband, she said.
Â 
Served 5 Months in Prison
"I knew the life inside prisons because I had been inside one, and so I was very concerned about my husband," the appeal continued. 
"How dare they blackmail me using this relationship and my feelings. 
They are really not human beings at all."
Ms. Hou was jailed for five months until April 1990 in a jail cell separated from the outside world by eight layers of doors or gates. 
The authorities charged that she helped her husband attempt to escape the law in the months after the June 1989 crackdown. 
She insists, however, that she did not help him. 
But now she suggests that she wished she had.
"I was full of despair and thought I would never come out," Ms. Hou said of her time in prison. 
"I know what my husband must be going through. 
He must be losing his respect. 
I have wronged him. 
In jail I thought that if I got out, I would help my husband."
Mr. Wang is just as concerned about his wife. 
When he first decided in July to begin a hunger strike, he told his parents in confidence, but not Ms. Hou, for fear she could not bear the news. 
After his trial in February, he sent a letter to his lawyers and closed with a request that they look after his wife for him.
Â 
Allowed to Provide Medicine
"Please help me comfort Xiaotian," he urged in the letter, which was later published by newspapers in Hong Kong. 
"Let her calm down, not to get into any more trouble, not to break any law, especially not to become impolite to those who are handling my case. 
I still need her to help me in many things on the outside, so she must take care of herself."
For a long time, the authorities denied that Mr. Wang was ill, but finally in June, they admitted to his family that he had hepatitis and allowed them to bring him some medicine.
But the family has not been allowed to give him medicine regularly, and earlier this month the Government denied to a visiting United States Congressional delegation that Mr. Wang was sick. 
Mr. Wang apparently contracted hepatitis while he was being treated by injection for a toothache during his detention in Qincheng prison, family members said. 
In April, he was moved to Beijing No. 2 prison, as was another dissident, Chen Ziming, who was also sentenced to 13 years. 
The two men were detained in 1989, two years before their trial, and this period will count toward their jail terms.
"I speak about the most basic right of man, what God gave man -- even though I don't believe in God -- and I tell them that you must give back what man is born with," Ms. Hou said. 
"This is what I fight for."
Â 
'I Can Be Taken In Anytime'
She talks little about the shortcomings of socialism or of the need for freedom of the press and political reform, and says she believes that this may be one reason why the authorities have been relatively tolerant of her outspokenness. 
She is still concerned, however, that she could be detained or arrested at any moment, and one stark reminder of the risk came when Zhang Weiguo, a prominent journalist who spoke openly against the political system, was detained for three weeks this summer in Shanghai.
"I've been waiting for them to come get me," she said. 
"When Zhang Weiguo was detained, it made me realize what a thin tightrope I am walking on. 
I can be taken in anytime."
Eased out of her job in an employment center, she has no means of livelihood and no place to live. 
Instead, Ms. Hou, who has a graduate degree in psychology, moves from place to place, relying on handouts from friends who dare to help her as she continues to fight for her husband so that she can go on with her life.
"What I really want is a family, to be a housewife -- a virtuous wife and a good mother," Ms. Hou said. 
"I want a child, but now I can't have one."

In the 10 years since China opened up to the world, most Chinese encountered enough Coca-Cola, television, disco dancing and sunglasses to make them blase about most exotic imports from the Occident - until Beijing opened an exhibition of nude art.
''Oh, I'm so embarrassed,'' stammered Chen Hong, a medical student, when a reporter asked her why she came to see the exhibition. 
Miss Chen blushed and hid her face with her hands while hastily adding, ''This is the first time I've seen this kind of thing.''
A mix of curiosity and prurience drew record crowds of 10,000 people a day for 18 days in a row to the exhibition at the Beijing Art Gallery. 
The exhibition, which closed today, was one of the most successful art shows ever held in the capital, and it seemed to reflect public interest not only in naked bodies but also in forms of culture arriving from the West.
Each visitor paid the equivalent of 60 cents admission, 10 times the normal ticket price in China and a sum equivalent to half a day's wage for most workers. 
The exhibition is scheduled to travel to the United States and Japan later this year.
Â 
Nude Art as Clash of Cultures
Crowds of men and women elbowed each other aside to get a closer look at the canvases. 
Some stood gaping at the most realistic and sensuous of the paintings; others hurried quickly by in horror. 
Most of the paintings were of women, and some were so realistic they seemed almost like photographs. 
Others were so abstract that it was difficult to discern the human figure.
China has almost no tradition of nude paintings, and over the centuries virtually the only curves in Chinese art have been those of the hills and waterfalls in traditional decorous landscapes. 
Human figures were sparse and small, and they were usually wise old men encased in traditional gowns.
Yet Chinese painting, like much of Chinese culture, is reeling from the encounters with sharply different Western artistic traditions. 
Chinese opera, calligraphy, story-telling and music all are grappling with the task of adaptation and survival in the presence of so much Western influence. 
The clash of cultures is rarely more visible than in the current craze for nude art.
While art schools have been using nude models for about the last five years, the resulting paintings have been shown publicly only for the last year. 
Shanghai, Tianjin and Guangzhou all held exhibitions of nude art last year, and Beijing's - with 120 canvases - is by far the largest held in China. 
At least three publishing houses have brought out books recently on nude art, and one theoretical work on the subject (illustrated) has become a best-seller.
Â 
Models' Fear of Ridicule
''This isn't just an artistic matter,'' said Ge Pengren, the artist who organized the exhibition. 
''This is a sociological phenomenon.''
Yet for all the evident public enthusiasm for such art, nudity remains a taboo in Chinese society. 
Though China lacks a Judeo-Christian tradition linking sex and nudity with immorality, it has a long Confucian tradition in which nudity is - if not immoral - at least highly improper and perhaps vulgar.
That prudishness, which some officials have publicly condemned as feudalistic, has led to some unexpected problems. 
The official press reported last year that a 19-year-old woman who worked as a nude model had been driven mad after relatives accused her of being no better than a prostitute. 
And the models depicted in the paintings on display in Beijing have protested bitterly that they will be ridiculed if friends or relatives recognize them.
Two of the models have hired lawyers and plan to sue the art gallery, an extraordinary move in a society where lawsuits are almost as scarce as nude paintings. 
The models complain that the painters should have made their faces unrecognizable, and they have already succeeded in having five paintings in the show exchanged. 
Many of the models apparently had been too embarrassed to tell family members, even their spouses, about their jobs.
Â 
At Least the Pay Is Good
China Youth News reported that one of the models was with her husband when the television news broadcast a segment about the exhibition. 
When the woman casually asked her husband what he would do if she happened to be a model, his answer came quickly: divorce.
Some of the models are demanding that the portraits should be shown only with the model's permission. 
Others say the paintings can be shown, but argue that the model is part owner of the painting and is entitled to a share of the ticket sales or proceeds from the sale of postcards or catalogs of the exhibition.
The artists say the models should have known that the paintings might be exhibited, and they note that they were paid what in China is an astronomical wage of about 65 cents an hour for modeling nude.
''That's more than a professor of art earns,'' said Meng Luding, a painter whose work is in the exhibition.
Â 
A Certain Chinese Flavor
Not only are the paintings of nudes, but the Western influence is also evident in the medium - they are all oil paintings or mixed media instead of traditional water colors - and in the composition. 
Most are not noticably different from American paintings.
''Except that the models are Chinese, these could be Western paintings,'' Mr. Ma said. 
But he added that he and the other painters do try to inject an undefinable Chinese character in the works.
Americans will have the chance to judge for themselves if there is a Chinese element in the paintings because the organizers are now arranging to take the paintings to Japan for a show and then to the United States. 
The paintings will be shown in Seattle, and Mr. Ge is now looking for other galleries in the United States.
It is not clear to what extent visitors to the show were seeking titillation instead of enlightenment, but artists said they thought both were important reasons for the show's success. 
Until recently, China had regarded all nudity as improper, and even partial nudity is banned in China's magazines and films. 
However, attitudes are changing, and a movie with a discreetly filmed sex scene was shown last month in southern Guangdong Province.
''As our society develops, it is natural to have this kind of show,'' said Chen Qun, a film student who came to see the exhibition. 
He paused and added, ''The more the better.''

file: Beijing Journal_Marxism Died and Left a Big Hole in Their Lives.txt
text:
ï»¿
A secular age of faith appears to have collapsed in China, turning into a time of despair and doubt in which many people have no heroes and nothing to believe in.
When Chinese bare their souls to foreigners these days, they sometimes speak of a ''spiritual crisis'' that they blame for increases in petty crime, as well as for a disintegration of social values and cohesiveness.
This sense of emptiness and purposelessness has been on the rise in recent years, but many Chinese, interviewed in different parts of the country, say it has become particularly acute since the suppression of the democracy protests last June 3-4.
''We used to believe that Chairman Mao or Deng Xiaoping could solve our problems,'' said a disgruntled Communist Party official in Beijing. 
''But now we've lost hope. 
Now there's nothing for us to believe in.''
'We Feel an Emptiness'
In the central Chinese city of Chengdu, a young university teacher searched for a way to explain her malaise. 
''There's nothing left,'' she said. 
''We feel an emptiness.''
A university student in Beijing said some of his friends were turning to Christianity and Buddhism, as a new source of moral values.
''Without doubt there's a spiritual crisis in China,'' he said. 
''I don't have any friends who believe in Marxism now. 
Even my parents don't believe in Marx or Deng anymore. 
There's a vacuum.''
''This also existed in the 1980's,'' the student added. 
''But then we could live by our dreams. 
My friends and I dreamed of studying abroad, of working for joint venture companies, of going south to make more money. 
Since June 4, those dreams have died, and now we have nothing to live by.''
Not everyone is so melancholy, and many people continue to be absorbed by the challenges of daily life rather than by existential crises. 
For all the concern about the effects of nihilism on society, the impact so far has been confined mostly to petty vandalism, thievery, a relatively minor drug problem and an aggressive discourtesy.
Â 
Life Seems Grayer
China's family structure is intact, crime is low by Western standards, and people continue to marry, find jobs and go about their daily lives pretty much as ever. 
But the texture of life seems grayer, and gloomier, particularly in the cities.
In the countryside, where about three-fourths of Chinese live, peasants are usually more absorbed by fluctuations in weather than in politics, and in any case regarded Mao and Mr. Deng as rather remote deities. 
Moreover, while many peasants and workers have lost their faith in political leaders, they can still sound quite reverent when speaking of new consumer goods or ways to earn the money to buy them.
''These days we don't believe in political leaders,'' a worker in his mid-20's said. 
''But we still believe in something. 
The new god is money.''
Chinese say that just 25 years ago, almost all of their compatriots believed in Mao, and just a few years ago, there was overwhelming support for Mr. Deng. These days, it is difficult to find a young person who believes passionately in anything or anybody, and despair is more common than faith.
Â 
Disparaging a Legacy
The loss of faith has been complicated because it has not only discredited China's political leaders but also the value of the Chinese cultural legacy itself. 
Whatever their political beliefs, Chinese used to share a common pride in a 4,000-year-old heritage, but now more and more intellectuals worry that China's poverty and authoritarianism are rooted in the culture itself. 
They disparage their historical legacy and stress the need to turn to the West for help in modernizing China.
A university teacher in his 30's, who like many others is trying to find a way to the United States, described what to him is one of the most painful aspects of the present society: the obligation to take part in meetings where everyone is forced to profess beliefs they do not feel.
''In the West, if you lost faith in Christianity, you could still believe in yourself, or in existentialism, or in whatever you wanted to,'' the teacher said. 
''But here you are forced to say you believe in what you don't: in the party, and in the 'glorious crackdown.'
''
China was also swept by a great wave of disillusionment in the late 1970's, after the Cultural Revolution. 
But many Chinese, as well as foreign specialists, say the situation is worse now - partly because people see no way out of the nation's difficulties and because there is no obvious candidate to lead them to safety, as Mr. Deng seemed to do after his return to power in 1978.
Â 
Campaigns to Build Spirit
''I sense greater despair this year than in my 11 previous years of visiting China,'' said David L. Shambaugh, a China scholar from the University of London. 
''In the reform period, people at least had a sense of the future, for there was progress and social mobility. 
Now, most of those who benefited from the reforms are losing hope.''
The Chinese leadership seems to be aware of the malaise, for there have been a series of campaigns recently to build national spirit by emulating the legendary soldier Lei Feng, who died in 1962, and other Communist heroes. 
Those campaigns seem to be greeted with indifference by most of the population, and by resentment among intellectuals.
''It's very serious when people don't believe in anything,'' said a business executive in his 30's. 
''Even my friends who are foreign-trained intellectuals do nothing but play the game mah-jongg all day. 
It's disastrous for the long run, and the central leaders know it.''

text:

Of all the names being bandied about these days as potential prime ministers, one evokes a special tingle -- depending on your vantage point -- of either hope or horror.
Zhu Rongji, a former rightist who has spent more years in disgrace than in power, is the fastest-rising star in China's political firmament. 
But Mr. Zhu, a fluent English-speaker and aggressive advocate of economic change, faces a horrendous image problem within the party leadership: admirers abroad have affectionately dubbed him "China's Gorbachev."
This helps Mr. Zhu about as much as it would benefit President Bush for China's hard-liners to hail him as "America's Mao Zedong."
"You're not going to write a story saying how great Zhu Rongji is, are you?" a Chinese official who likes Mr. Zhu asked reproachfully. 
"Because whenever there's an article like that, he gets whacked politically."
Â 
Specter of Gorbachev
Vice President Wang Zhen, an acid-mouthed octogenarian who peppers his conversations with village expletives, is said to have warned colleagues last year that "there is a Gorbachev sleeping beside us."
Mr. Wang did not mention any names, but that's the kind of comment that would have Politburo members craning their necks to look at Mr. Zhu.
Still, the 63-year-old Mr. Zhu (whose name is pronounced joo rong jee) has managed to survive both the attacks and the compliments. 
In his spacious, air-conditioned second-floor office, just inside the north gate of China's park-like leadership compound of Zhongnanhai, Mr. Zhu has amassed prestige and authority along with the calligraphy that he hangs on the wall.
Named a Deputy Prime Minister last year, Mr. Zhu is one of several contenders hoping to replace Prime Minister Li Peng when his five-year term expires early next year. 
It is unclear, however, if the position will be vacant; Mr. Li is a skilled tactician who is fighting for a second term.
"Zhu Rongji is doing really well right now," said a family member of a top official. 
"But in China, the better things look for you, the worse your prospects really are. 
It's the bird in front of the flock that gets shot."
Some officials say the present fragile consensus at Beidaihe, the beach resort where China's elderly leaders are playing bridge and deciding the nation's future, is to allow Mr. Li to retain the post of Prime Minister. 
But they say that even according to this plan, Mr. Zhu would become first deputy prime minister in charge of the economy, so that he would be breathing down Mr. Li's neck.
"Even if Zhu Rongji isn't made Prime Minister, it may not matter so much," said a party member who has discussed policy with Mr. Zhu. "Because in any case, he'll be in charge of economic policy."
When summoned to Beijing last year from his previous post as Shanghai's Mayor, Mr. Zhu was given the task of unsnarling endless debt chains among state-owned companies. 
Partly because he was more successful than most people expected, he was named head of a new department called the Economic and Trade Office. 
It is emerging as a super-ministry with overall responsibility for managing the economy.
Â 
Nominal and Real Power
Officials say that a deal has been struck for Mr. Zhu to vault onto the Politburo's standing committee, the nation's top policy-making body. 
It is exceeded in authority only by the so-called sitting committee of octogenarians who are nominally retired but continue to hold ultimate power.
The key to Mr. Zhu's success is that Deng Xiaoping, the nation's 87-year-old senior leader, is acting as his campaign manager. 
Mr. Deng has gone out of his way to praise Mr. Zhu's understanding of economics.
Mr. Zhu is disliked not only by some hard-liners, however, but also by many midlevel and senior officials. 
They find him a terror to work for. 
Extremely demanding, Mr. Zhu scolds people publicly in a society where it is considered more polite to stab them in the back.
"Some comrades are kind of muddled, and even when you point out some problems they figure they're in the right," Mr. Zhu said in a recent confidential speech, defending his style. 
"Even their self-criticisms are superficial. 
So then you've got to criticize those laggards by name.
"I also encourage everyone to criticize me," Mr. Zhu added in the speech, parts of which appeared in a restricted-circulation publication for party officials. 
"A couple of times, the criticisms were pretty nasty, and they weren't entirely fair. 
But I listened. 
Whether or not the complaints are correct, it's good for them to let off steam."
Mr. Zhu still speaks Chinese with a trace of a Hunan Province accent, reflecting his childhood there, but he studied electrical engineering at Qinghua University in Beijing and has spent most of his life in the capital. 
He took up Mao's invitation in 1956 to offer the party constructive criticisms, and a year later he fell victim, along with others who spoke out, to the "anti-rightist campaign."
By a fluke he escaped with extremely lenient punishment: he was allowed to hold on to a job in the central Government, but in disgrace. 
In 1978, when Mr. Deng came to power, Mr. Zhu was rehabilitated and climbed onto the fast track.
Â 
An Embarrassing Encounter
While many Chinese believe that Mr. Zhu is different from other leaders, the last thing he wants is for this to be pointed out. 
When he once found himself seated beside an American correspondent at a dinner, he studied the reporter's name card and then asked accusingly, "Weren't you the one who wrote that article?"
The journalist asked if he meant an article that had appeared 10 months earlier, reporting that Chinese like Mr. Zhu much more than other leaders. 
"Yes, that article," Mr. Zhu said coolly, and he switched to English and quoted the headline word for word.
When the reporter acknowledged writing the article, Mr. Zhu paused for a moment in horror, and then pivoted. 
For the rest of the dinner he engaged in conversation exclusively with the person on his other side.

text:
