At one of Beijing's elite universities not long ago, students were subjected to another of a series of propaganda films intended to insure the reindoctrination of China's future leaders along the correct Communist road.
These same students had led ''the counterrevolutionary rebellion'' crushed so brutally in June, and they have since been subjected to steady, numbing sessions of political education.
The film that evening, ''Wei Wei Kunlun,'' which translates roughly as ''Towering Mountain,'' depicted China before the Communist takeover in 1949. 
A scene of a demonstration being violently broken up brought cheers because unlike the case in June no tanks were used.
Party officials asked the students why they had applauded. 
''Because it was such a good film,'' they said.
Â 
Common on the Campuses
Stories of quiet mockery of this sort are common on the campuses. 
The familiar slogan ''Only socialism can save China'' has been slightly altered to become, ''Only without socialism can China be saved.''
Freshmen at Beijing University have been sent off to Hebei Province for military and political training for a year; older students say that when the freshmen return they will practice ''peaceful evolution'' on them -the party catch phrase for the supposed capitalist strategy to undermine Chinese Communism through the introduction of alien cultural influences. 
One upperclassman, a party member, said, ''We will pass on to them their proper education in the four evils'' - excessive eating, drinking, gambling and promiscuity - and he seemed to be quite serious about the task.
The rapid changes in Eastern Europe, and especially the overthrow and execution of Nicolae Ceausescu, the Rumanian leader who was a longtime ally of the Chinese leadership, have brought a few daring gatherings and posters. 
Like the mockery, they are indicative of a lasting disgust and a resoluteness of spirit largely untouched by the ideological corset being tightened everywhere in intellectual and academic life.
But while the investigations are winding down and students and teachers await the party's judgments on punishment, there is wariness and mistrust everywhere and a general depression about the future that argues against any rapid re-emergence of the sort of demonstrations that electrified the world last spring.
Â 
A Sense of Caution
The unexpected death of a prominent figure like Deng Xiaoping or Zhao Ziyang, the party leader who lost his job after showing some sympathy with the June demonstrations, could create a pretext for students to gather and march, but few believe the leadership would react a second time with so much confusion and delay.
Students and teachers interviewed over the last three weeks described caution and lack of purpose. 
Among many students there is a self-imposed cap on political discussion and an aimless escapism. 
There are increasing experiments in casual sex and alcohol abuse. 
''We're watching trashy movies and reading trashy novels,'' one student said. 
''Sidney Sheldon is very popular now, and so is 'I'll Take Manhattan.'
''
Students speak of a sense of isolation from the larger society. 
''The campus is a very small world,'' one said. 
''It's like living in a cage, and you feel watched all the time.''
People are ''depressed and discouraged,'' she said. 
''Life seems meaningless now, and they are cynical. 
They feel bored. 
Life is boring if you're in school or out, boring if you have a boyfriend or not, boring if you work or not.''
Students still speak of politics to their closest friends, ''but that gets boring, too,'' the student said. 
''We don't disagree about anything. 
We all want change. 
But politics once again seems like empty talk.''
Â 
Something to Hide
The analogy of Rumania frightens the Government right now, another student said. 
''All the killing frightens us, too. 
We don't think the Chinese Army will crack so quickly as in Rumania, and many more could die.''
Most students, one said, had made less than fully forthcoming self-criticisms and protected their friends, and there is a feeling that many teachers and deans are also protecting students from the authorities. 
''But there are a lot of people who participated and have something to hide,'' he said. 
''So people don't trust one another. 
It is one of the biggest successes of the Government.''
Some students said many wanted either to go abroad or to make a lot of money and live an easy life. 
Everyone seems to be learning English and trying to pass the language examinations required to study abroad. 
But freshman are now judged too young to study abroad, and graduating students are told they must stay in China and work off their debt to society. 
''It's a way of keeping people here,'' a teacher said.
Teachers describe relatively open political discussion in the faculty rooms, but they are under strict orders not to discuss politics in class or with students. 
''The party tells us, 'If you have your own views, O.K., but don't pollute them,' '' a teacher said.
Another described a faculty meeting with the party secretary, who complained that while some students had informed on others, no teachers had done so, behavior that set a bad example. 
The party secretary was particularly outraged because he had received anonymous letters purporting to inform on him. 
''We felt he had no sense of shame,'' the teacher said. 
''Only the die-hard leftists or the careerists pursue this witch hunt.''
Â 
Caution Is Still Needed
One must nonetheless be careful, another teacher said. 
She was teaching a night class in English to adults who were behaving passively while she was trying to explain the prefix ''octo.''
''So I finally said: 'Why don't you talk?
You're as stubborn as octogenarians!'
''The class laughed, but the next day she was called in by the party secretary and asked why she had made fun of the party leadership, which is largely composed of elderly officials. 
''I said that it was in the textbook,'' she said, ''and that was that, but it worried me. 
Someone obviously made a report.''
Another teacher said that while he understood his students' anger and shared it, he tried to caution them that the situation could get worse, as it did in the 1950's and '60's.
''The students are impatient, of course, and want rapid change, and they have their own ideas. 
But I don't want them to get into trouble or waste their lives. 
We've all been inspired by a few demonstrations and by Rumania, but I tell them: 'Right now, your lives are more important. 
Don't throw them away.'
''

file: Beijing Journal_Stilled by the Unthinkable, a Singer Tries His Voice.txt
text:
ï»¿
Like a thick carpet of snow, silence has settled over China. 
In muffled voices, among friends, some people still mock their leaders and dream of change, but despite the lifting of martial law last week they are quiet in public, or they are in jail.
Everyone except Hou Dejian. 
Seven months after violence erupted around him on Tiananmen Square, five months after he came out of hiding in the Australian Embassy in Beijing, Mr. Hou has decided that it is time to shatter the silence.
''I hate violence,'' Mr. Hou, one of China's best-known pop singers and songwriters, said in an interview in his apartment here. 
''I don't think it's good to take a gun and shoot Deng Xiaoping, or to use violence to overthrow the Li Peng Government. 
But I can't keep quiet. 
I want peaceful change in China, and I want to help that process.''
Â 
The Rumania Factor
''There has to be change,'' Mr. Hou added somberly. 
''Otherwise we will face what happened in Rumania.
''If nobody speaks out, and the economy deteriorates, and the Li Peng Government goes on treating the people as if they're enemies, then the people will be turned into the enemies of the Government. 
In Chinese, we have a saying: 'You force us to overthrow you.'
So now I'm telling the Li Peng Government, 'Don't force the people to overthrow you.'
''
In private, many young Chinese are bitterly critical of Mr. Deng, China's senior leader, and especially of Mr. Li, the Prime Minister. 
But what makes Mr. Hou unusual is that in the last few days he has decided that he is willing to voice criticism publicly, even to foreign journalists.
Â 
'I'm Prepared for This'
When a reporter asked him if it was really possible to quote him saying such things, he scarcely paused.
''I'm afraid to die, and I would hate to be imprisoned,'' he said. 
''But I'm prepared for this. 
I've made up my mind to make noise.''
A lean 33-year-old with an easy laugh, Mr. Hou has always been an iconoclast. 
A native of Taiwan, he defected to the Chinese mainland seven years ago, and his songs were promptly banned on Taiwan. 
His independent way of thinking wore out his hero's welcome from the Communist authorities, and these days his works are banned here - although they are again allowed on Taiwan.
In a song written during the democracy movement last spring, Mr. Hou referred to the oppressive political atmosphere and asked:
What is the weather today?
The sky drops lower and lower. 
Why is it stil not raining?
What is the weather today?
Tell us, how can we breathe?
Â 
Account of Tiananmen Events
On the night of June 3 and June 4, Mr. Hou was in the center of Tiananmen Square, in a hunger strike with three other intellectuals to galvanize opposition to martial law. 
When tens of thousands of army troops battled their way to Tiananmen Square, killing hundreds and wounding thousands of protesters along the way, Mr. Hou negotiated with the troops to allow the students in the center of the square to leave.
According to Mr. Hou's account, much of which is confirmed by others who were there, he and other protest leaders first appealed to those around the monument to give up anything that might be used as a weapon. 
After 20 minutes, one worker was finally persuaded to give up a machine gun with which he had planned to defend the square from troops. 
Mr. Hou said Liu Xiaobo, another hunger striker who now is in prison, smashed the gun to make it inoperable.
And so, at about 5 A.M. on June 4, the 3,000 students remaining in the center of Tiananmen Square marched out. 
Mr. Hou said that he was in the rear and did not see anyone remaining, but that a small number could have stayed without his necessarily seeing them.
Â 
Refuge With Australians
Two days later, Mr. Hou learned that his friend and fellow hunger striker, Mr. Liu, had been arrested. 
So Mr. Hou sought refuge in the Australian Embassy, and stayed for more than two months. 
He finally left after receiving a written guarantee that he would not be punished and that he would be allowed to travel freely to and from China.
Immediately after he left the embassy, Mr. Hou gave interviews to the official press in which he asserted that he had seen no one killed in Tiananmen Square. 
The interviews were used by the Chinese Government to back up its assertion that there had been no massacre in the square.
Some young Chinese felt betrayed after seeing those interviews, and there was speculation that Mr. Hou bought his freedom by backing the Government line. 
In his defense, Mr. Hou says that Communist officials told him he had to give the interviews, and that in any case he told the truth.
Shortly after June 4, there were reports of a massacre of thousands of students in the center of Tiananmen Square. 
Now those reports are widely though not universally discounted, partly because of the testimony of Mr. Hou and others who were there. 
The consensus is that while troops fired on crowds in many parts of Beijing, including the Avenue of Eternal Peace, at the north end of the square, and that hundreds were slain, there was little or no killing of those students gathered in the center of the square.
Mr. Hou says he has no idea whether anyone died in the center of Tiananmen Square. 
Asked about reports that students were killed shortly after leaving the square, he says he was told by a witness that 11 were killed several hundred yards to the west, as they tried to make their way home. 
What is important, he said, is not where people were killed but that they were killed at all.
Â 
Cannot Give Concerts
These days Mr. Hou is unable to give concerts or make records, and despite assurances from the authorities, he has been told to ''wait for a while'' before leaving China. 
So Mr. Hou spends his time with his music, singing blues and writing songs. 
In one written on June 3, just before the troops attacked, he says:
Â 
Everything can be changed.
Nothing is too far away.
Let's prick our ears like a dog,
And nobody can lie to us any more.
Let's pry open our eyes, and
Nobody can distort the truth again.
''Before June 4, I wasn't a dissident or protester,'' Mr. Hou said. 
''Now I'm training to become one.''

file: Beijing Journal_Tiny Counterrevolutionaries Facing Reform From 200,000 Fly Swatters.txt
text:
ï»¿
A few months ago, the authorities started noticing something very strange, scratched their heads and called in specialists who also scratched their heads but couldn't come up with an explanation to the mystery: why, all of a sudden, does China have so many flies?
No one seems to know the answer, but with the same Communist zeal that the Government hunts down "counterrevolutionaries," it has launched a grand campaign to wipe out flies.
"To build a 'City of No Flies' is a requirement of a highly civilized modern city," a senior official, Tie Ying, was quoted as saying recently in the official Beijing Daily. 
"It is a requirement of reform and openness and a means to push the economy to a higher stage."
China's leaders are calling on the masses to make greater contributions in the front against the flies, and the expression "City of No Flies" has become a rallying cry. 
Front-page news articles describe the latest battlegrounds of the fly war, the different tactics used and the successes in diluting the density of flies per room.
Â 
A Bid for the Olympics
A major reason for the campaign, which began in March, is to boost Beijing's chances of being host to the Olympics in 2000. 
The International Olympic Committee will decide on the location of the games next year, and the Chinese Government believes that if it stamps out flies -- in part by cleaning out hidden repositories of squalor and feculence -- it will be more likely to be chosen.
"Our goal is to create a city of no flies," said Gao Yukun, a senior health official in Beijing's Eastern District. 
"But we won't just kill flies. 
We want to create clean cities."
As part of the campaign, Beijing, which has a population of about 10 million people, purchased 130 tons of pesticides and held training courses to teach people the most advanced methods for eradicating flies.
Officials hold high-level meetings to discuss strategy and exchange status reports. 
Everyone is urged to study models of cleanliness, like the Foreign Ministry, which won praise from Beijing's Mayor, Chen Xitong.
Â 
Even in the Wonton Soup
Early in the summer, when the authorities sent their work teams into the dirty bowels of China's cities, they were alarmed to discover that flies were buzzing all over: in the gutter, in the toilet, in the dusty rooms, in the wonton soup.
"By June, we found that there were significantly more flies than before," said Zhang Xizeng, a senior health official in the Beijing Government. 
"It was this way all over the country. 
We don't know why."
The campaign bored deeper and the city held special "attack weeks," or cleaning festivals. 
Citizens posted banners bearing the slogan, "Mobilize the Masses to Build a City of No Flies," and distributed two million pamphlets to publicize the campaign.
Scores of children and elderly citizens joined special swat teams. 
They swatted flies, sprayed and sprinkled poison and cleaned out the garbage cans and bathing areas.
During one of the "attack weeks," the city distributed about 15 tons of pesticides, along with 200,000 fly swatters. 
In mid-July, after the first blitz, the density of flies had dropped 20 to 30 percent from the previous month. 
During another "attack week" in August, 1,000 teams of elderly people and young children hunted down flies, using 17,600 pounds of poison.
As in any major political campaign, citizens throughout the nation feel obliged to declare their support. 
Privately run restaurants post the slogans on the walls, hotels hang red banners and senior officials, like the Mayor, go on inspection tours.
A group of Beijing sixth-graders wrote a letter to Mayor Chen to propose that they use their summer vacations productively by swatting flies and cleaning up alleys filled with garbage.
To an outsider, Beijing does not seem to be particularly plagued by flies any more than, say, New Delhi or New York. 
But China is still trying to hold its cities to a tough standard for its showcases to the world: out of every 100 rooms, only one room is allowed to have two flies. 
In some parts of Beijing, the density was as high as 33 flies per room in June.
Â 
The Dry- Dish Test
Aside from taking aim at flies and rats, the campaign also promotes other ways of improving hygiene. 
Restaurants must pass a three-step dish-cleaning test that includes using water hot enough that it evaporates on the plates after rinsing. 
One joint-venture hotel, the Tianlun Dynasty Hotel, was fined about $735, partly for failing the dry-dish test.
Officials say that statistics on flies and rodents are difficult to collect. 
A few decades ago when the Government wanted to clean up the city by promoting campaigns against rats, it had citizens cut the tails off the rats they killed and mail them to the unit that collected the statistics. 
But then the Government discovered that children were picking up diseases from handling the dead rats.
Now, one of the rat tests consists of sprinkling piles of powder in several parts of a room, waiting 24 hours, then checking how many footprints there are. 
If two out of three piles have prints, then the room fails the permissible standard.
The campaign is producing some clear results. 
According to official statistics, the city of Beijing alone has cleaned up 26,000 dirty areas that bred flies and disposed of 270,000 tons of garbage that had been left on the streets or in vacant lots. 
Workers installed screens for 300 public toilets and cleaned 47,000 dustbins.
Â 
Dissent Even on This Issue
The Government knows it is up against extraordinary odds. 
When the weather is hot and damp and there is plenty of garbage for fly food, female flies can lay batches of 100 to 150 eggs every 18 days, according to Yang Jianmei, an entomologist at Beijing University.
Most citizens agree with the aims of the campaign and are fond of pointing out that even the United States and European countries still have flies. 
But for some people, the Government propaganda is nettlesome.
"A cleaner city is something that no one would normally oppose," said a young Chinese researcher. 
"But the Government turns everything into a political campaign. 
I don't like flies, but the way the Government forces you to kill flies, I'm almost tempted not to side with the Government."

file: Beijing Journal_Whatever the High Walls Hide, It Isn_t Opulence.txt
text:
ï»¿
Behind 15-foot walls in the center of the capital is a vast and lovely park called Zhongnanhai, which was once a playground of the emperors and their concubines and which today doubles as the Communist version of a Forbidden City and the most exclusive retirement home in the world.
Mao Zedong moved into a Ming Dynasty pavilion in Zhongnanhai on the triumph of the Communist Revolution in 1949. 
Ever since then, Zhongnanhai has been the headquarters of the Communist Party and Chinese Government, as well as the home of high leaders.
"It is the new Forbidden City," a Chinese woman said with a laugh the other day. 
The original Forbidden City, the residence of the emperors, is next door and is now a public museum visited by thousands of people every day.
Zhongnanhai (pronounced joong-nahn-high) is shrouded in secrecy. 
The aura of mystery is magnified by the periodic rumors of the sybaritic way of life that is supposedly enjoyed on the other side of the wall.
Â 
Charges of Hypocrisy
Because of their egalitarian language, Communist leaders are particularly vulnerable to charges of hypocrisy when they they begin to ride in limousines and drink from crystal glasses. 
Yet, as Milovan Djilas, the Yugoslav dissident, noted in a classic 1957 analysis, Communist governments tend to create their own privileged "new class" to replace the one swept aside. 
In China, resentment of the corruption and extravagance of this Communist "new class" helped prompt the democracy protests of 1989, and is a continuing source of popular indignation.
Yet a visit inside Zhongnanhai -- in the more relaxed days of early 1989, when it was possible for a foreign reporter to offer a senior official a ride and then drive him through the gate and drop him off inside -- suggests that it is not nearly so splendid as many people think.
Conversations with Chinese who have worked or lived inside, or who have visited the homes of leaders there, also suggest that Zhongnanhai is beautiful and comfortable but that the leaders' lives are not nearly as extravagant as those of top officials in many other countries.
"If a foreigner's home in Beijing ranks 7 on a scale of 10 for comfort and convenience, then the homes in Zhongnanhai rank about 3," said a Chinese who lived briefly inside the compound. 
"It's very spacious, but everything is old. 
You should see the kitchen: sure it's big, but there's nothing modern."
Â 
'It's Nothing Special'
Another Chinese official recalled his visit to a leader's home inside Zhongnanhai and said, "It's nothing special, just a lot of sofas and a bit more comfortable than average."
But he added with a laugh that he would gladly move inside.
To be sure, the homes have excellent cooks, air-conditioning -- which is banned for ordinary Chinese -- and satellite television. 
During the early morning hours of June 4, 1989, as army troops were firing on pro-democracy demonstrators outside, the family of at least one leader was glued to the television, watching Cable News Network as machine-gun fire reverberated outside.
Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, lives outside Zhongnanhai, but his circumstances suggest the oddities of the leadership's comfort level. 
Mr. Deng has a stable of vehicles, including a Mercedes-Benz 500 SEL and a bullet-proof Cadillac, but his home has hot water only briefly each morning and two evenings a week.
After hearing all the fanfare about Zhongnanhai, most visitors find on entering the main Western gate that the vista is almost disappointing. 
There are simply a series of dowdy red-brick and gray-brick buildings, with pleasant but not spectacular gardens and various maintenance men strolling around in old clothes.
Security is relatively light, but appears to have been tightened since the 1989 crackdown. 
Chinese tourists are no longer admitted to Mao's former residence, and meetings with Westerners are now often held at other sites instead of Zhongnanhai.
Â 
A Dormitory for Workers
About a dozen senior leaders live in Zhongnanhai, but the compound is no longer quite as exclusive as it used to be. 
In the Maoist period, virtually all top leaders lived inside except Lin Biao, the Defense Minister, and Jiang Qing, Mao's estranged wife. 
These days, in contrast, more than half the highest leaders, including Mr. Deng, Prime Minister Li Peng, and Vice President Wang Zhen, live outside the compound.
Those who live inside -- mostly along a narrow lane in the southwestern part of Zhongnanhai -- are predominantly retired leaders in their 70's or 80's.
To add to the ordinariness of Zhongnanhai, some cooks and nurses live with the leaders in their courtyard homes, and there is even a dormitory for young workers from the Communist Party General Office.
Some officials suggest that it is best to live outside Zhongnanhai because it has bad "fengshui" -- a traditional Chinese belief that some locations are plagued by bad spirits and ill fortune. 
Certainly Zhongnanhai has been the scene of much plotting and scheming and tragedy over the last century.
Chinese officials remember that the Emperor Guangxu, who was ousted in a coup in 1898, was confined to an island in South Lake in Zhongnanhai until he died, probably slain, a decade later.
"It brings bad luck," a midcareer Chinese official said. 
"I don't know why any leader would want to live in Zhongnanhai."

file: Beijing Marks 40 Years of Tibet_s _Liberation_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Somewhere in the far west of China, nestled in the Himalayas, is a Shangri-La brimming with contentment and human rights -- or so say the Chinese newspapers these days.
It is Tibet, although it does not entirely resemble the Tibet that Western visitors describe. 
The Chinese newspapers are full of reports about progress there, as China on Wednesday celebrates the 40th anniversary of what it calls "the peaceful liberation of Tibet."
China is using the 40th anniversary celebrations to spread its own perspective on Tibet: that the "roof of the world" has always been part of China, that the life there has improved dramatically in 40 years of Communist rule, and that the overwhelming majority of Tibetans are delighted with socialism.
"Only after Tibet conducted democratic reforms did the masses truly become the masters and life become better with each passing day," People's Daily declared today at the top of the front page. 
"With life this good, the masses are very angry at the few people stll festering for Tibetan independence."
Li Tieying, a Politburo member, has arrived in the Tibetan capital of Lhasa to lead a delegation to attend the celebrations. 
Scores of Chinese journalists have also arrived in Lhasa, but no China-based foreign reporters have been allowed to visit Tibet for the festivities.
Duan Jin, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, explained that the Tibetan authorities were limited in their capacity to host foreign journalists, and that in any case Western reporters were not always fair in their coverage.
For the last few years, the Chinese Government has only rarely permitted foreign reporters to visit Tibet, apparently because the journalists invariably report that the population would prefer independence to the current regime. 
While diplomats and scholars are often skeptical of some of the assertions and criticisms made by the Dalai Lama, the exiled spiritual leader of the Tibetan people, his photo is everywhere in Tibet and there is little doubt that he is still revered and supported by virtually all Tibetans.
The nature of the celebrations on Wednesday has not been revealed, perhaps for security reasons. 
Separatist demonstrations, often led by Buddhist monks and nuns, have occurred regularly in Tibet for four years, and martial law was lifted in Lhasa only last May. 
Martial law was imposed in March 1989, after clashes that left at least 16 people dead.
"They must be taking a lot of precautions" to insure that there will be no unrest, said an Asian diplomat in Beijing. 
He noted that there have been reports that the army and police presence in Lhasa has been bolstered substantially in recent months.
A Tibetan court sentenced three Chinese, all members of the Han ethnic majority, to death last month for killing a Chinese soldier and stealing guns and ammunition. 
A Tibetan newspaper said the three planned to sell the weapons to "rioters and rebels in Lhasa."
The three men, who presumably have been executed by now, had attacked a government armory in late March, killing the guard and stealing 19 pistols and 869 bullets. 
The incident was a reminder that while the opposition to Chinese rule has been largely peaceful so far -- partly because it is backed by Buddhist monks who profess pacifism -- it is not impossible that protesters will increasingly turn to violence.
The celebrations on Thursday will mark the 40th anniversary of the signing of a 17-point agreement between the Communist Government and representatives of the Dalai Lama. 
Tibetan exiles say that the agreement, which concedes that Tibet is part of China, was achieved by threats and coercion. 
In any case, they say, Beijing has not abided by the promises in the agreement.
The topics of a seminar in Beijing on the 40th anniversary suggest the way that the commemorative activities are unfolding. 
Themes included "Tibet being an inseparable part of China" and "the great achievements made in Tibet in the last four decades since the region was peacefully liberated."

file: Beijing Memo_As the Crackdown Continues, China Starts to Seem Just Like Old Times.txt
text:
ï»¿
Swept up in liberalization and a mood of relaxation until a few weeks ago, China suddenly seems more familiar to people who lived here or visited 10 or 20 years ago than to those who may have arrived recently.
It is not that China has returned to the days when the population was awakened at 6 A.M. by propaganda loudspeakers or when it was an offense, punished by a ''struggle'' meeting, to wrap garbage in a newspaper bearing a photograph of Mao.
But the repression sweeping China has brought back many once-common practices and controls - from the numbing repetition of a few authorized statements to a modest cult of personality.
The televised reports of trails of ''thugs'' who were said to have attacked troops during the crackdown two weeks ago illustrate the point.
Â 
'Open' Trials Now Closed
For a time, China made efforts to open up its criminal procedures. 
Trials were attended by foreign journalists and other observers. 
A system that for decades had been shrouded in secrecy emerged into the open.
But this week, when journalists asked the authorities if they could attend one of the ''open'' trials of people involved in the recent protest movement, they were told that it would be ''inconvenient at present.''
The near absolute management of information and the practice of conducting ostensibly public affairs behind closed doors are the sorts of practices that seemed to be falling into abeyance in the recent past.
To observe them again provides a shock of recognition to the Chinese and foreigners alike whose memories stretch back to the 1960's and 1970's, when China was not only far more secretive but also more closed in on itself than it has been in recent years.
''This is a place I recognize,'' an Italian journalist, absent from China for several years, said on his return after the crackdown two weeks ago. 
The journalist had read accounts of a country far different from the one he knew when he lived here in the early 1980's. 
It is, he said, far less different now.
''After these few relaxed years, these changes will have a deep psychological impact,'' one analyst said. 
''People will think that China is moving backward, no longer forward.''
Â 
Some Gains Still Stand
In fact, the backward move does not represent a wholesale reversion to the Maoist era when the very right to a private sphere of life went unrecognized. 
It is not yet forbidden in China to do things like listen to foreign radio broadcasts, play Beethoven, try to become wealthy or get married without the permission of the local party secretary.
The situation of the last two weeks is perhaps well represented by the anchorwoman on the evening news broadcast. 
She is chicly coiffed and dressed in a pink silk blouse, a style that would have been condemned as ''bourgeois'' in the worst of days past. 
But she presides over news broadcasts reminiscent of the saturation propaganda campaigns not known in this country for years.
In today's broadcast, for example, a coal worker from China's northeast was shown expressing his anger at those who conducted the ''counterrevolutionary disturbance'' in Beijing. 
The disturbance, he said, was aimed at ''overthrowing the Communist Party and the socialist system and at beating, smashing, looting, burning and killing.''
Two minutes later, the television anchorwoman read a statement by a local party leader. 
Word for word, right up to the ''beating, smashing, looting, burning and killing,'' the statement was the same.
Â 
End to Freewheeling Talks
The incident reminded some who first came to China in the early to mid-1970's that, in those days, practically all Chinese felt constrained in public to utter only a few correct phrases and little else - a stark contrast with the freewheeling discussions of recent years.
China specialists attribute some of the restorations of past practices to the current prominence of the group of aging revolutionary veterans who, in the face of the recent challenge to their authority, fell automatically back on older, familiar ways of doing things.
The ceaseless repetition of the same small number of phrases is, in this sense, a sign of the revival of another once-common technique that had fallen into abeyance in recent years, the use of a mass propaganda campaign to establish the leadership's authority.
The overall changes could be described as ones of mood and degree. 
Propaganda and sloganeering, Government secrecy and political intimidation, have never entirely ceased in China. 
But those with long memories here say the intensity of the present repression has not been reached since the moderate party faction, led by Deng Xiaoping, returned to power in the late 1970's.
Â 
Speech as Gospel
Analysts here, for example, say they cannot remember a time since the death of Mao and the arrest of his closest followers in the Gang of Four when the speech of a leader became the basis for a mass campaign.
But some remarks made by Mr. Deng to the Military Affairs Commission more than a week ago have not only got much publicity - even though Mr. Deng's actual words have not been released - but have become the objects of a national study campaign being promoted every day in the state-controlled news media.
The emerging pattern of political life also bears striking resemblances to a pattern that had virtually disappeared for more than a decade, that of a new unpredictability at the top.
One of the clear goals of Mr. Deng's leadership was to establish a kind of schedule of government, to run things according to clear rules. 
And so, since about 1983, key meetings of the party or of the National People's Congress, China's parliament, have been announced in advance and held on schedule.
Â 
Behind-the-Scenes Maneuvers
Now, for the first time in several years, the leadership seems likely to return to its older method, which was to hold meetings in secret and to announce them only later.
This week a scheduled meeting of the National People's Congress was postponed indefinitely. 
The assumption is that the leaders wanted to hold a meeting of the Central Committee before the congress. 
But while rumors have circulated for a week about a Central Committee meeting, there is no indication yet when or if it will be held.
The point is that after several years of apparent stabilityII, the leadership has returned to a pattern when behind-the-scenes maneuvers were so intense and difficult that it was impossible to keep schedules. 
Analysts say that the business of the party and the Government are likely to become, as they were in previous decades, enshrouded not only in secrecy but in uncertainty.
In this sense, one of the most conspicuous aspects of an earlier era to reappear is the spectacle of an aging leadership clinging to its power.
Â 
Comparing Deng With Mao
Some Chinese are quietly comparing the current period of Mr. Deng, who is 84 years old, to the last years of Mao, which were marked by an ever more intense personal tyranny.
The saturation campaign to advertise Mr. Deng's speech is the sort of thing that used to surround Mao's pronouncements. 
In a subtle but perhaps telling shift, Mr. Deng is being referred to as Chairman Deng - he is chairman of the Military Affairs Commission but not of the Communist Party.
To be sure, the modest cult of personality growing up around Mr. Deng falls far short of the mass adoration of Mao, during which his statue and picture were ubiquitous and his every word was given Delphic authority.
And yet, one of Mr. Deng's stated goals when he returned to power more than a decade ago was for the old leaders to step aside in favor of younger ones. 
Like Mao, however, Mr. Deng has destroyed the younger figures that he himself anointed.
Â 
'Love the Party'
In allowing a cult to grow up around himself now, Mr. Deng seems, in the view of analysts, to be returning to an effort to re-establish the authority and prestige of the party as the sole source of wisdom and legitimacy.
One result is the constant repetition of slogans that had almost disappeared. 
''Without the Communist Party, there would be no new China'' is one incessantly repeated lately. 
Another is ''Love the party, love the socialist motherland.''
In the last few years, particularly in speeches at party congresses, such slogans have been occasionally spoken, particularly by the veterans of Mr. Deng's generation, but they have not become parts of intense campaigns to build up the party's authority.
Since the mid-1980's, the party was something certainly to be obeyed; but the people have not for many years been called on to ''love'' it.

file: Beijing Memo_Is the Crackdown a Legacy of Traditional China or of 20th-Century Communism_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Musing bitterly over the recently televised spectacle of a woman who turned her own brother in to the police, a Chinese scholar reached into the treasury of ancient lore and came up with an old saying.
Roughly translated, the saying was ''For the sake of the great cause, destroy your loved ones.''
The expression - used in Imperial China to persuade people to inform on traitors - shows that the repression of the democracy movement, which has included, among other techniques, public exhortations to denounce students and other leaders, has its precedence in China's long history.
Indeed, it seems fair to ask whether the events in China of the last few weeks stem from the Chinese tradition itself, or whether they represent a new turning in this country's history. 
Is the harshness of the crackdown a product of 20th-century totalitarianism?
Or does it represent a continuation of this country's authoritarian tradition?
#2 Traditions in Conflict In many ways the protest movement and its violent repression can be seen as a re-enactment of an age-old conflict in this country. 
In the distant past, there were two enduring traditions.
One was legalism, whose great forebear was a Machiavellian practitioner named Li Si, a believer in the need to control the citizenry by an unsparingly harsh system of laws and punishments. 
The Communist rulers who sent the army against students and have already sentenced 11 workers to death for their involvement in the protests seem to be the inheritors of the legalist tradition.
On the other side were the humanist scholars, the Confucianists who, in principle at least, believed in government, not by laws and punishments, but by moral example and virtuous rule. 
There was also an escapist tradition in Taoist mysticism, which has been interpreted by some scholars as an effort to gain a spiritual liberation from the harshness of China's dictatorship.
The humanist tradition in China was not democratic. 
It accepted the right of the emperor to rule autocratically. 
But it placed a high value on the responsibilities of intellectuals to criticize the emperor when his rule became too harsh. 
It stressed the notion that the emperor could lose his moral right to rule - the mandate of heaven - if he were cruel or incompetent.
Â 
Humanists Rarely Win
The protesters who occupied Tiananmen Square in Beijing for a month before the crackdown in early June seemed to be saying to the Communist rulers that they had lost the mandate, in part because they were undemocratic - a relatively new and modern concept in China - and because they were mired in corruption. 
What was new was that the democracy movement was just that, a democracy movement, brandishing notions of human rights and free speech.
But the crushing of the students seems to echo a basic fact of Chinese history: the humanist tradition has rarely prevailed in specific conflicts with the emperor. 
The scholars, while retaining the respect and admiration of the people, have been buried alive, sent into exile and disgraced, their books burned and banned.
''What happened in the past few weeks was a democracy movement,'' a diplomat here said, ''but the student movement was also of a kind of rebellion that has happened many times in Chinese history before.''
A rebellion, the diplomat said, is not the kind of thing that can be accommodated by rulers of China; it must be suppressed.
''Authority figures should not and could not be challenged,'' John K. Fairbank, a senior historian of modern China, has written of the country's political tradition. 
''Criticism endangered authority and was therefore unacceptable,'' Mr. Fairbank said in his book ''The Great Chinese Revolution: 1800 to 1985.''
In suppressing this latest rebellion, China's Communist leaders have also reflected both tradition and novelty.
The almost nightly television scenes of arrested people, their arms held by two policemen and their heads forced downward in a kind of bow to the interrogators, seem - like the denunciations that have sometimes put them into that position -cruel both to Westerners and to the many Chinese who sympathize with them.
Â 
Punishment Old and New
But the treatment of the ''thugs,'' as many of those involved in the protest movement are being called, could also be seen as a variation on the traditional Chinese handling of criminals. 
A standard punishment in past centuries was to lock around the criminal's neck a wooden disk known as a kang. 
The device, which was heavy and painful to wear, exposed the criminal's face to public scorn and shame.
The Chinese police, in picturing arrested suspects on television held in a kind of airplane position, looking bruised and unkempt, their heads pushed downward, seemed to be trying to dehumanize them before the public in the way the kang did in past centuries.
But there is a clear difference, too. 
The kang was used on common criminals. 
Those being hauled before police interrogators in the continuing manhunt in China were participants in a movement demanding greater freedom. 
The effort to portray them as common ''thugs'' being advanced by an entirely modern campaign of incessant propaganda on television and in the newspapers seems to be drawn from 20th-century totalitarian practice.
The notion here is that any opposition to the Government is not just wrong; it is criminal, treasonous, counterrevolutionary, and those who led it deserve neither respect nor humane treatment.

file: Beijing Orders 2 More Americans to Leave China.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign of continuing diplomatic tensions, two Americans have been ordered to leave China, presumably because of their activities during the recent pro-democracy demonstrations, an American official here said today.
The two Americans, Mark Radicia, 25 years old, a teacher at Nankai University in Tianjin, and Helen Qubain, 21, a student at the same univesity, were given until the end of the month to leave, the official said.
The two are believed to have maintained close ties with pro-democracy demonstrators in Tianjin, a large industrial port in northeast China.
An official at Nankai University said in a brief telephone interview that the university was ordered by the Tianjin public security bureau to tell the two Americans to leave China. 
He gave no reasons for the order.
Peace Corps Program on Hold
An American official said Mr. Radicia, who is from Omaha, and Ms. Qubain, from Buena Vista, Va., were now in Beijing. 
They are expected to leave the country within the next day or two, the official said.
The expulsions bring to five the number of Americans ordered expelled from China since the violent crackdown on the protest movement more than three weeks ago. 
Three journalists have also been expelled.
The order to the two Americans to leave followed notification by China that it was putting off a Peace Corps program that had been due to start this fall with the arrival of 20 American teachers in Sichuan Province. 
A United States official said today that the Chinese had given no reason for postponing the program, which would have been the first of its kind in any Communist country. 
The program was agreed to in April.
The official said the Chinese move, which was announced by the China Education Association for International Exchange, a Government organization, did not mean that the program would not eventually go ahead.
''We're not reading anything retaliatory into it,'' the official said. 
''It's not by any means canceled.''
The indefinite postponement of the Peace Corps program, however, seemed almost certainly to be linked to Chinese irritation with the United States, both for imposing sanctions against China after the crushing of the protest movement and for providing shelter in the American Embassy here for China's best-known dissident, the astrophysicist Fang Lizhi.
Â 
Visa Requests Are Up
But in one sign that China is allowing some aspects of relations with the United States to continue, American officials reported today on a rapid rise in the number of visa seekers already holding newly required exit permits. 
The Government said after the crackdown that all Chinese would have to have exit permits issued by the Public Security Bureau before they would even be allowed to enter foreign embassies to apply for visas.
An American official said that on Monday 100 people came to the embassy seeking visas, compared with just a handful in previous days. 
The English-language China Daily reported today that 8,520 of the newly required permits have already been granted.
A Chinese here said that the permit can generally be obtained when an applicant furnishes the Public Security Bureau with a letter from his workplace testifying that he had no part in the recent demonstrations. 
#24 Killed in Train Blast The Chinese also announced today that 24 people died when dynamite exploded on a passenger train traveling near Shanghai late Monday night.
While the explosion seemed to be an act of sabotage, it was unclear whether it was related to the protest movement or to the sweeping repression that has followed it.
The explosion recalled an incident three weeks ago when a train in Shanghai ran into demonstrators who were blocking tracks to protest the crackdown in Beijing. 
Six people were killed in the incident, and some protesters, apparently angered by the failure of the train to stop, set fire to the train. 
China later announced that three ''ruffians'' were executed for setting the fire and for burning police motorcycles.
While that incident made it seem possible that the sabotage Monday night was an act of retaliation, diplomats here pointed out that acts of vandalism on trains, including the setting of explosions, were known to take place in the months before the outburst of protest. 
Moreover, even if the sabotage Monday night was an act of retaliation, it seems unlikely that such acts of terrorism will become widespread here.
''China is just not a very likely place for that sort of thing,'' a diplomat said, referring to the tight control and pervasive surveillance here.
A television report on the incident showed a gaping hole in the side of a green passenger train, which was making the trip from Hangzhou, a major tourist city about 100 miles southwest of Shanghai. 
It said 11 people were seriously wounded in the blast.
Â 
Draft of New Law Approved
As details of the blast were announced, China's State Council today approved the draft of a new law on rallies and demonstrations. 
The draft is in preparation for a meeting of the standing committee of the National People's Congress, China's parliament, which is due to meet on Thursday.
There were no details of the law, but it is widely expected to impose formal restrictions on the rights of Chinese to hold demonstrations.
The laws being drafted by the State Council, which is a kind of Government cabinet, have been under discussion for months. 
When the discussions began, many analysts were expecting the laws to expand citizens' rights. 
Since the protests, however, the mood has changed dramatically.

file: Beijing Orders Its Ambassadors Home for a Meeting.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has summoned home its ambassadors for a meeting next week as the crackdown on dissent continues to evoke condemnations and sanctions abroad.
Western diplomats and Chinese officials overseas said the ambassadors were being summoned to a meeting here on July 7. 
The exact purpose of the meeting is unclear, but the newly reshuffled Chinese leadership may want to instruct its diplomatic corps on ways to respond to the worldwide criticism, aid cutoffs and embargoes on military sales that have followed the repression of the pro-democracy protest movement here this month.
The recall of the ambassadors coincides with a widening purge of intellectuals and officials loyal to the ousted party chief, Zhao Ziyang.
Report of Departures
The Foreign Ministry neither confirmed nor denied reports that ambassadors were being summoned home, but bureaus of The Associated Press in 10 countries, including the Philippines, Australia, Spain, West Germany, and Bahrain reported that Chinese ambassadors there had left for home or would soon leave.
Chinese officials in an Asian country and in Western Europe confirmed that all the country's ambassadors were being summoned back for a meeting, but they said the gathering was a routine annual event unrelated to the recent events here.
But diplomats here said that they could recall no such meeting taking place in the past. 
They said the move underlined the seriousness with which the leadership here views both the reaction abroad and the outbreak of the protest movement itself.
Â 
Similar Move in Late 1960's
Though analysts could only speculate on the attitudes toward the protest taken in China's embassies abroad, the recall of ambassadors may be a first step toward extending the purge into the diplomatic corps.
The only other time China summoned all of its ambassadors home was in the late 1960's, in the first years of the Cultural Revolution, when a major portion of the Chinese Government bureaucracy was dismissed and sent to labor in the countryside. 
Only one Ambassador, Huang Hua, the Ambassador to Egypt, returned to his post, while China remained diplomatically isolated from most of the world. 
Mr. Huang later became Foreign Minister.
Since the army's violent crackdown on June 3 and 4, some 20 Chinese diplomats abroad have requested political asylum, according to figures tabulated by The Associated Press here. 
One topic of discussion at the meeting next week may be the problem of defections.
In addition, the suppression of the protest movement has led other countries, particularly in the West, to undertake a variety of measures against China. 
On Tuesday the 12-nation European Community called for a suspension of World Bank loans to China and an embargo on military sales. 
Japan has also suspended talks on loan packages estimated to total more than $5 billion.
Â 
Action by Bush
The Bush Administration has also canceled military sales to China and has suspended high-level visits between Washington and Beijing.
The intense propaganda campaign that has been going on since the crackdown continued today with the public release of the text of a speech by China's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, that has been the subject of mandatory study in the country.
Mr. Deng's speech, which has become a kind of official justification for the army's crackdown on protesters, was read in its entirety on all the television news programs today and published in full in all the newspapers.
Mr. Deng gave his speech to the Military Affairs Commission five days after the army's bloody assault on pro-democracy protesters who had been encamped in Tiananmen Square. 
In it Mr. Deng congratulated the army for its suppression of the protest movement, but he also vowed that China's policies of economic reform and openness to the outside world would not change.
Even though Chinese news organizations for weeks have been urging everyone in the country to study Mr. Deng's ''important speech,'' today is the first time that it has been released to the public.
In the speech, Mr. Deng appeared to issue a kind of definition of the protest movement that has become the basis of the saturation-point propaganda campaign that has been waged ever since.
He called the student protest a ''counterrevolution rebellion'' whose actual aim was the overthrow of the socialist system and the Communist Party. 
And he called for greater ''ideological education'' and a resolute stand against ''bourgeois liberalization,'' China's code word for Western-style political ideas.

file: Beijing Ousts Governor Tied to Zhao.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign that Beijing is trying to crack down on freewheeling economic policies in the provinces, China today announced the dismissal of the Governor of the nation's most experimental economic region.
The official, Liang Xiang, the Governor of Hainan Province in southern China, is a close associate of the ousted Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang. 
Mr. Liang is the highest-ranking official to be purged in connection with the Government's recent campaign against corruption.
The former Mayor of Shenzhen, the bustling city adjacent to Hong Kong, Mr. Liang, 71 years old, is a symbol in China of economic restructuring. 
Like many local officials, he put his faith in capitalist-style incentives and foreign investment rather than Marxist orthodoxy.
Accused of Corruption
The Chinese authorities accused Mr. Liang of ''serious mistakes by abusing power for personal interests'' and said he allowed his wife and son to profit from illegal business dealings. 
Mr. Liang is also said to have close ties to Mr. Zhao's second son, who has repeatedly been criticized for corrupt commercial practices.
The announcement said that Mr. Liang was replaced by Liu Jianfeng, a deputy party secretary of Hainan and former deputy minister of the electronics industry. 
In a dispatch by the official New China News Agency, the 53-year-old Mr. Liu said that Hainan's policies of restructuring and opening to the outside world would not be changed and indeed would be ''stepped up.''
Some analysts say they believe the dismissal of Mr. Liang is part of a broader attempt by hard-liners to clamp down on local officials who were closely associated with Mr. Zhao's style of economic change.
''It ties in with the overall politics of China and the overall attitude toward south China,'' a foreign official in Canton said of the dismissal. 
In a telephone interview tonight, he said the new leadership ''is going to try, as every political movement does, to reinforce itself and cut down opponents.''
He said a test of how far the purge would go may be the treatment of the party leader of Hainan, Xu Shijie, who has also been a vigorous proponent of foreign investment and economic restructuring. 
Mr. Xu was quoted extensively this week in the People's Daily, suggesting he is not in political trouble for the moment.
Â 
Other Discharged Officials
The most recent senior Government official to be discharged was Wang Meng, the Minister of Culture, although there was some question about whether he had previously requested to step down. 
Mr. Wang was considered too lenient on ''bourgeois liberalism,'' an official code word for corrupt Western values.
Another important figure in economic policy making, Liu Hongru, the vice governor of the People's Bank of China and an alternate member of the Central Committee, was dismissed from his post at the bank.
Unlike Mr. Liang, Mr. Wang and Mr. Liu were not explicitly discharged in the campaign against corruption.
Mr. Liang developed a national reputation as Mayor of Shenzhen, which expanded rapidly in recent years and is one of the most capitalist Chinese cities, partly because of foreign investment. 
Mr. Liang has also held numerous senior posts in the Guangdong provincial party and government apparatus at a time when the province was undergoing some of its most dramatic economic transformations.
Â 
Symbol of Economic Goals
Formerly under the administrative arm of Guangdong, Hainan was declared a separate province in 1988, and Mr. Liang was named its first Governor. 
The entire province is a special economic zone, and Hainan is regarded as the least regulated region in China. 
While the area is not important in the national balance sheet, it is a symbol of the nation's drive toward a more market-oriented economy.
The announcement on national television this evening did not cite specific crimes of corruption committed by Mr. Liang, but it said he violated regulations when he allowed a local company to import cars. 
His son, the announcement said, profited enormously from the deal.
Unlike some Chinese officials, Mr. Liang did not have a reputation for corruption, although he was sometimes accused of nepotism. 
There was no indication that criminal proceedings would be started, but the announcement today said the case was still under investigation.

file: Beijing Puts Khmer Rouge on Shorter Leash.txt
text:
ï»¿
As a new round of civil war threatens Cambodia, diplomats here say China finds itself in the awkward position of wanting the Khmer Rouge troops it supports neither to win nor lose.
The Khmer Rouge, which brutally ruled the country from 1975 until the Vietnamese invasion in December 1978, is China's most dependable ally in the region, partly because no one else wants anything to do with the Khmer Rouge.
Yet Western and Asian diplomats say China would be alarmed if the Khmer Rouge enjoyed a major string of victories after the Vietnamese troop withdrawal under way. 
In part, the reason has to do with China's suppression of the democracy movement in June, which created a storm of outrage that has made Beijing reluctant to face a new barrage of international criticism for pushing the Khmer Rouge back toward power.
'Watching and Waiting'
China will continue to arm the Khmer Rouge, but may counsel it toward restraint on the battlefield, diplomats say. 
It is unclear how effective China's counsels would be, or how far China would go to avoid a Khmer Rouge victory, but the diplomats say there are signs of renewed flexibility in its Indochina policy as the principal arena of confrontation moves from the conference room to the front lines.
''China is waiting and watching,'' an Asian diplomat said. 
''This is the chance to test each faction on the battlefield.''
The diplomat and others interviewed said China's principal goal was not to secure a military victory, but to put sufficient pressure on the Vietnamese-backed Government in Cambodia that it will return to peace talks in about six months willing to make further compromises with the Khmer Rouge.
At the same time, specialists say, China will not allow relations with Vietnam to improve. 
Only when there is a settlement of the Cambodia issue will diplomatic and economic relations be normalized, the Chinese have told diplomats here.
China regards the future of Cambodia as a matter of paramount importance, partly because of a traditional hostility between China and Vietnam. 
With Vietnam enjoying support from the Soviet Union, China is alarmed at the possibility of its Soviet-backed rival forming a sphere of influence on its southern flank.
Â 
Skepticism of Vietnam Pullout
Reflecting the official line here, the Chinese press has been extremely skeptical over taking the Vietnamese troop withdrawal at face value. 
A report carried today by the official New China News Agency said that while ''several groups of Vietnamese troops'' rode to gathering points in army trucks, no tanks or heavy weapons were seen. 
The implication was that the tanks and tank crews were remaining behind.
On Thursday, China's Foreign Ministry spokesman said that Vietnam was not sincere in searching for a political settlement and was ''playing tricks'' on the international community by pretending to withdraw.
Early this year there was some sign of a diplomatic warming, when the Vietnamese Vice Foreign Minister came to Beijing twice for talks. 
But the Chinese Foreign Ministry concluded that the Vietnamese official was unwilling to compromise, and so it decided not to allow further such visits.
The distrust of Vietnam, coupled with the feeling that the Khmer Rouge is the most effective fighting force against Vietnam, seems to be the primary explanation for China's ties with the Khmer Rouge. 
The embarrassment about being associated with a group held responsible for more than a million deaths under its rule seems to have grown in recent years.
''They don't love the Khmer Rouge for itself,'' a Western diplomat said. 
''They love the fact that each dollar they put in Khmer Rouge hands produces a dead Vietnamese.''
Â 
No Reduction in Aid
Because ties to the Khmer Rouge are also based on its past friendship and loyalty to senior Chinese leaders, diplomats say, China's economic difficulties will not mean a reduction in aid to the Khmer Rouge and to the other two anti-Government factions: one led by Prince Norodom Sihanouk and the other by Son Sann, a former Prime Minister.
China has complained privately to some Asian diplomats that the Soviet Union is increasing its military assistance to the Hun Sen Government now in power in Cambodia, and so some diplomats expect that China could provide a matching increase in funds for the three Cambodian guerrilla factions.
Chinese officials earlier this month called in officials from Asian countries for a meeting on Cambodia, and some were struck by one sign of movement in China's position. 
A year ago, China was unhappy about some wording in a United Nations resolution that in an indirect swipe at the Khmer Rouge called for a ''nonreturn to the universally condemned policies and practices'' of the recent past. 
But in the meeting this month, China seemed content with such wording.

file: Beijing Regime to Fall, Student Leader Asserts.txt
text:

Wuer Kaixi, the Chinese student leader who fled China after the Government crackdown on the democracy movement in June, said yesterday that he believed the Chinese Government would fall within two to three years but that student leaders still welcomed dialogue and contact with Beijing.
''We need to put an immediate end to the fascist regime now in power,'' said Mr. Wuer through a translator.
Speaking at a news conference at the offices of Asia Watch, a human rights organization based in New York, he called for the overthrow of the Government, but added that he welcomed recent moves by Beijing to curb nepotism and abuses by high-ranking officials and members of their families.

Mr. Wuer traveled from a three-day conference of Chinese students in the United States that was held at the University of Illinois at Chicago over the weekend. 
He said the newly formed group unifying overseas Chinese student groups would remain independent of all government organizations.
Later yesterday afternoon, with the Statue of Liberty as a backdrop, Mr. Wuer and several other students who had participated in the protests at Tiananmen Square in Beijing before the crackdown addressed a small crowd of supporters and called upon Chinese abroad to continue the fight for democracy.
