The controversy surrounding Britain's refusal to allow holders of British passports in Hong Kong to settle here has fed a long-running debate over this nation's policies toward immigrants.
Since the Communist repression of the pro-democracy movement in China last month, London has reaffirmed several times its decision not to give Hong Kong's 3.25 million Chinese who hold British passports the right to live in Britain after the colony's scheduled reversion to China in 1997.
Sir Geoffrey Howe, British Foreign Secretary repeated this last week. 
He told the House of Commons that the Government would be as ''generous as possible'' in admitting people from the colony but that a commitment to take in all of them was ''impossible.''
''It would be wrong to raise expectations we could not possibly meet,'' Sir Geoffrey said, adding that the authorities were working on a plan to admit some people from both the private and public sectors on the basis of the value of their service to Hong Kong, as well as their connections with Britain.
Both Conservative politicians and their Labor opponents have supported the Government's decision. 
But The Sunday Times, in a recent editorial, accused the authorities of not standing by the colony's people.
''To most British politicians, Hong Kong is a place out of sight, out of mind,'' the newspaper said. 
''On both sides of the House their attitude is, at best, clouded by ignorance; at worst, warped by racism.''
Opinion polls suggest that the public is divided over the immigration issue.
Under the headline ''No!
No!
No!''
The Sun, a national tabloid, published a survey recently that indicated that 65 percent were against a mass immigration of people from Hong Kong.
A Gallup Poll published last month in The Daily Telegraph, just after the Chinese Army crushed the pro-democracy protest, showed that the crackdown had not changed attitudes on giving the colony's people the right to settle here.
The poll indicated that 42 percent of Britons favored extending the right, 46 percent opposed it and the rest were undecided. 
When Gallup asked the same question in November 1983, it got almost identical results.
Behind the statistics is the reality of Britain today. 
In the early 1950's, the nation had 35,000 nonwhite residents, compared with 2.5 million today out of a total population of 57 million.
Huge waves of immigrants, many of whom were encouraged to settle here to fill the lowest paying jobs, arrived in the 1950's and 60's from Africa, India, Pakistan and the West Indies.
They settled in a class-oriented country that had previously known the newcomers only as colonial subjects. 
Sociologists say Britain remains socially and politically uncomfortable as a nation of diverse cultures and cannot easily contemplate a commitment to accept a new influx of immigrants.
Government figures show that a total of about 49,000 immigrants were allowed to settle in Britain last year and, in the last four years, fewer than 1,000 a year were allowed in from Hong Kong.
Critics of the Government position say it should undertake research before embarking on its stated course of asking the rest of the world to help Hong Kong residents in the event that the colony's people are forced to flee.
Paddy Ashdown, leader of the Social and Liberal Democrats, has condemned the political consensus over the Hong Kong issue. 
In a letter to The Independent newspaper, Mr. Ashdown said Mrs. Thatcher had added to the impression that concessions to Hong Kong would greatly strain the nation by giving Parliament a ''savagely simple'' answer to a question about the hardships that families faced when immigration regulations caused them to be separated.
''Her case, she said, rested on the fact that we are already admitting 40-50,000 immigrants per year and could not absorb any more,'' Mr. Ashdown wrote. 
''In other words, issues of justice and morality are overruled by the numbers game.
''This fawning before unstated popular prejudice does no credit to our leading politicians. 
It may not in itself be racist - but it feeds off and adds to the already dangerous level of racism within our society.''

file: British Foreign Secretary Is Booed By Angry Crowds in Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
In an outpouring of fear and anger unusual for this British colony, crowds jeered Sir Geoffrey Howe, the British Foreign Secretary, when he arrived today on a visit intended to restore Hong Kong's confidence in its future.
''To turn over six million people to a Communist Government after the massacre in Beijing is despicable as well as dishonorable,'' said K. T. Poon, an advertising executive, addressing one of the groups of demonstrators. 
Other protesters lining the streets outside Kai Tak Airport booed and shouted ''Shame!'' as Sir Geoffrey was driven by in a Rolls-Royce.
In a brief statement on his arrival, Sir Geoffrey said, ''You have no stauncher friend than Britain.''
But the Foreign Secretary offered no details on what steps Britain might take to insure political and economic freedoms in Hong Kong after the territory's scheduled reversion to China in 1997. 
He also said nothing about the widespread demand here that Britain provide an ''insurance policy'' for Hong Kong by allowing the 3.25 million Chinese who are British citizens the right to live in Britain after 1997.
'Hong Kong Has No Future'
When he refused to answer reporters' questions on the subject, he was loudly booed in a sign of how emotional people have become since the Communists' repression of the pro-democracy movement in China last month.
This evening, after a crowd of 15,000 protesters marched past the Governor's residence where Sir Geoffrey is staying during his three-day visit, a group of about 400 people sat down in front of the main entrance and refused to leave, despite the pleas of the rally's organizers and the police.
''If Britain doesn't help, Hong Kong has no future,'' said Jennifer Leung, a 26-year-old secretary, explaining why she was taking part in the sit-in. 
''Before the Tiananmen massacre, I had no interest in politics, like most of my friends, but now I think we have to let the British know what they are doing.''
Under the agreement to return the colony to Chinese rule, China promised Hong Kong autonomy for 50 years to practice capitalism. 
But the agreement is now widely viewed here as just a scrap of paper. 
Under it, for example, China's National People's Congress would have the right to amend or interpret laws affecting Hong Kong and the right to declare martial law, as it theoretically does in China. 
But when martial law was imposed in Beijing, it was done by a group of Communist Party elders. 
The congress was ignored.
Â 
Earlier, 600,000 Marched
The demonstrations today were far smaller than ones earlier this month, including a march of 600,000 people through Hong Kong's central business district to mourn the victims in Beijing. 
Leaders of several of the new political groups that have sprung up here in the last few weeks said they believed that some people were afraid their activities would be monitored by the Communists while others had become convinced London would not help.
''There were rumors that Chinese spies would take pictures and my family urged me not to participate,'' said Miss Leung.
Anger at Britain was heightened by a parliamentary report issued Friday in London that rejected giving Hong Kong's British citizens the right to live in Britain. 
It is a right they had, as colonial subjects, until it was stripped away by Parliament in the 1960's.
Rosanna Tam, a member of the Legislative Council, said the report ''will probably go down as one of the most dishonorable statements ever made about Hong Kong.''
Dame Lydia Dunn, the senior member of the Executive Council, which serves as a cabinet for the British-appointed Governor, said she feared that Hong Kong would now become ''ungovernable.''
''I fear that without assurances of a home of last resort, this community will lose its will and there will be a loss of talent'' as qualified people increasingly emigrate, she said.
Â 
'The Issue is Right or Wrong'
Many people here believe that Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Parliament are unwilling to restore the right for Hong Kong's people to live in Britain because they fear a mass migration of Chinese and are racially prejudiced. 
One protester's sign today alluded to this. 
''The issue is right or wrong, not white or Wong,'' it said.
Privately, British officials here acknowledge they made a major miscalculation in trusting that China was on its way to becoming a stable country no longer subject to periodic upheavals and that the Communists understood Hong Kong's economic importance to them enough so that Beijing would avoid upsetting the territory's confidence. 
''I confused my hopes with analysis,'' said a senior official who helped negotiate the 1984 reversion agreement with China.
Fear about what will happen in 1997 led 46,000 people to emigrate last year, many of them the highly trained professionals Hong Kong most needs, like factory managers, police officers, teachers and accountants. 
Since the killings in Beijing, the number wanting to leave has skyrocketed.
An American banker said that of the 150 Chinese working in his company, every single one has been to see him over the past month about leaving, including his driver and his messengers. 
''We can't keep operating in Hong Kong if this goes on,'' he said. 
He is now looking at Singapore as an alternative location.

file: Briton Pledges Hong Kong Changes.txt
text:
ï»¿
The British Foreign Secretary wound up a four-day visit here today, saying Hong Kong wanted to see the pace of democratic changes quickened as the colony moves toward its return to Chinese control in 1997.
The Foreign Secretary, Douglas Hurd, said that if London and Beijing could not agree on reforms here, Britain would proceed on its own.
While the visit produced no concrete announcements on changes, Mr. Hurd said Britain would announce within weeks how many seats in the largely appointed 60-member Hong Kong legislature it would open to direct elections.
He said the number would be considerably more than the 10 Britain had suggested in its original reform proposal two years ago, a number that had been widely criticized from the beginning as too few.
Chinese 'More Suspicious'
He also repeated his assessment that ''the first prize'' would be a political arrangement that would continue after the Chinese takeover. 
But he said if that were not possible, if Britain could not reach agreement with the Chinese, ''then we have to take our own decisions'' on reforms and their pace up until 1997.
He acknowledged that since the military crackdown on the democracy movement in Beijing last June the Chinese leaders ''have been difficult because they feel somewhat defensive.''
He added, ''They are more suspicious than before.''
But Mr. Hurd insisted there was also a ''powerful Chinese incentive'' to integrate Hong Kong successfully under the ''one country, two systems'' formula.
The new Foreign Secretary, who once wrote a novel about the Chinese takeover of Hong Kong that he said had a happy ending, has been visiting the territory at a time when confidence in its future is critically low, with many of the most successful residents lining up to emigrate to avoid life under the Chinese Communists. 
Many have criticized the British for their failure to set up a strong, functioning democracy before the Chinese take control.
Â 
A Liberal's Complaint
Mr. Hurd said he had come to Hong Kong to ''assess opinions here'' on reforms. 
Most politicians who met with him politely described the discussions as useful.
But Martin Lee, an outspoken liberal legislator, said it had been months since Hong Kong people, repelled by the killings in Beijing on June 4, began to demand more democracy and ''the British Government is still listening without doing anything.''
A wide range of Hong Kong politicians and pressure groups now support a political plan that calls for 20 directly elected seats next year and 30 seats -half of the legislature - directly elected by 1997.
But China, which controls the drafting of the Basic Law that will govern Hong Kong after 1997, has said it wants only 18 directly elected seats by 1997. 
Currently, members of the legislature are appointed by the colonial government or elected by constituency groups such as lawyers and social workers.
Â 
Advice From Beijing
A conservative pressure group of Hong Kong entrepreneurs, who returned today from a meeting with top Chinese officials, including Prime Minister Li Peng, said they had been told that Hong Kong must proceed cautiously and only gradually increase the ratio of directly elected members.
Vincent Lo, the businessman who headed the delegation, said senior officials in Beijing had told them that ''to increase gradually will help Hong Kong's stabilityI and prosperity, and avoid having the radicals make use of the situation.''
At a news conference at the end of his trip today, Mr. Hurd also reaffirmed Britain's intention of continuing the forced repatriation of Vietnamese boat people screened out as non-refugees.
Robert Van Leeuwen, the head of the Hong Kong office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, which monitors the screening process, said he shared the concern of Amnesty International and other relief agencies that the screening procedures were dangerously flawed.
Â 
'We Don't Have the Resourcs'
In the process, immigration officers interview boat people to determine if they are ''genuine'' refugees fleeing religious or political persecution. 
Asked if the United Nations monitoring program was an effective safeguard and could prevent genuine refugees from being sent back, Mr. Van Leeuwen said, ''No, we don't have the resources to provide a safety net.''
He added, ''We are not able to insure, with confidence, that people who might be mandatorily repatriated in the future might not be refugees, that there might not be refugees among them.''

file: BRITON, IN CHINA, CALLS TIES NORMAL.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister John Major of Britain said today that relations between Britain and China were generally back to normal, but he also emphasized that in two days of talks with Chinese leaders he had pressed for improvements on human rights.
While the focus of his trip was to discuss Hong Kong matters, Mr. Major also sought the release of a number of political prisoners. 
When he raised the topic of human rights, however, he seemed to receive a mild rebuke from Prime Minister Li Peng.
Mr. Major, the first Western European leader to visit China since the army crackdown on the democracy movement two years ago, signed an accord that will govern the construction of Hong Kong's new airport. 
The two sides also issued a joint communique on matters relating to Hong Kong.
Mr. Major, who has been criticized for coming to China to meet the leaders of the hard-line Communist Government, described his discussions on human rights with Chinese leaders as "free, frank and forthright."
Â 
Tibet Situation Raised
He said he mentioned individual rights cases, including four detainees from Hong Kong and several prisoners singled out to him by Amnesty International, the human rights organization.
"I raised the situation in Tibet, I raised the treatment of religious believers in Tibet and elsewhere, and I raised the detention of people in China for expressing the freedom of expression, predominantly student demonstrators," Mr. Major said at a news conference tonight. 
"I asked Prime Minister Li Peng to take a personal interest in all these cases."
"Our discussions today are not the end of the matter," he added later. 
"I intend to follow the matter up."
Mr. Major also mentioned a letter he had received from an opposition party member urging him to raise human rights in his talks with Chinese leaders. 
Mr. Major said he had used this to illustrate to Chinese leaders that the concern for human rights in China cut across party lines in Britain.
Mr. Li seemed to reproach Mr. Major for scolding China on human rights matters.
Â 
'China Was Humiliated'
"I also received a letter, from a Chinese historian," Mr. Li said, according to the Foreign Ministry spokesman, Wu Jianmin. 
"He reminded me not to forget that for more than 100 years, China was bullied and humiliated. 
For 100 years, foreign powers totally disregarded the human rights of the Chinese people."
"China and Britain have different social systems, and their value systems, ideologies and historical traditions are different," Mr. Li said, according to a paraphrase by the Foreign Ministry spokesman. 
"So, regarding the problem of human rights, the two sides definitely will have differences here and there. 
This is natural. 
However, the two sides can exchange opinions on this and can enhance mutual understanding."
Mr. Major appeared cautious when characterizing relations between the two nations, and the Chinese side seemed similarly vague. 
In contrast, when Prime Minister Toshiki Kaifu of Japan came to China last month, the Chinese side said Chinese-Japanese relations had been restored to normal.
Today, the Foreign Ministry spokesman, Mr. Wu, said, "Prime Minister Major's visit marks the resumption and development of relations between China and Britain."
Â 
A Qualified Normalization
In his remarks tonight, Mr. Major said, "There is a general normalization of relations."
He qualified his statement, however, by emphasizing that while the day-to-day contacts between the two countries were essentially normal, Britain still regarded the issue of political and human rights in China as important.
"Because normal commercial and political traffic continues, does not mean we have withdrawn our concerns or that we cease to express our concerns either about past events that caused such a rupture in our relationship in 1989 or the human rights or arms sales problems that have been the subject of frequent discussions between our two countries," he said.
Earlier today, in a tour of the Forbidden City, Mr. Major attempted an impromptu walkabout to meet ordinary Chinese people, but he barely shook a hand before guards ushered him back and the Chinese people aside.

file: Buddha and Genghis Khan Back in Mongolia.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a makeshift temple at the foot of a rocky cliff in the Gobi Desert, four aged lamas in saffron robes sat cross-legged on carpets before a shrine to Buddha. 
They were fasting, meditating in silence and perusing sacred texts of Tibetan Buddhism.
Outside under a harsh sun lay the crumbling mud-brick ruins of the Ulgii Khiid Monastery, which once held more than a thousand monks. 
It had been sacked by the repressive Communist Government that ruled Mongolia for 70 years, a Government that destroyed more than 700 monasteries in the 1930's, burning books and executing thousands of lamas.
Now some surviving lamas are returning to occupy Ulgii Khiid and several dozen other monasteries. 
They live and worship in yurts, the customary dome-shaped dwellings of Mongolian nomads. 
They are teaching younger men to be monks and making plans to rebuild the temples.
Â 
Resurging Nationalism
The scene of religious revival amid revolution's ruins illustrates the extraordinary changes under way in Mongolia. 
In yet another reverberation from the collapsing Soviet empire, the dictatorship tied to Moscow was ousted in March 1990 and replaced with a more reform-mined Communist Government and a Parliament that includes increasingly assertive democratic opposition parties.
With that new political freedom has come a resurgence of Mongolian nationalism.
One of its most fundamental expressions is the official and popular support for Buddhism, the traditional religion of Mongolians for centuries.
In an interview in his private reception room at the Gandan Monastery here, the Khama Lama, the country's ranking Buddhist cleric, said, "This movement is very strong, not only among Buddhists but all people."
Other religious leaders, officials, intellectuals and diplomats agreed. 
Although few Mongolians may have a deep knowledge or belief in Buddhism, they said, anything from the pre-Soviet days is encouraged and celebrated.
That goes also for Genghis Khan, the legendary 13th-century warrior who united the Mongol tribes and set out with the Golden Horde to conquer much of Eurasia. 
The empire controlled by him and his immediate successors included China and Russia and extended all the way to Hungary.
Since Communists came to power in a revolution here in 1921, the Soviet Union had tried to suppress the name and memory of Genghis Khan, in part because no national hero could be allowed to eclipse Lenin but also because of residual embarrassment over being one of the conqueror's victims. 
But now Genghis Khan rides again.
Within months of the fall of the Soviet-backed Government last year, Mongolian scholars convened an international conference to commemorate the 750th anniversary of "The Secret History of the Mongols," the epic describing the glory days of Mongolian power and influence.
In a message to the conference, President Punsalmaagiyn Ochirbat endorsed the rehabilitation of the national hero and spoke of the importance of "The Secret History" for "the renewal of the Mongolian society, consolidating of their national integrity and social progress and for the restoration and development of their historical and cultural heritages."
Â 
Statue of Stalin Removed
At a diplomatic reception a few months ago, Mr. Ochirbat came up to an American military officer and congratulated him on the victory in the Persian Gulf war.
"Our countries now have one thing in common," he said. 
"We both have conquered Baghdad."
A statue of Stalin in the capital is gone, and billboards bearing Lenin's likeness have been painted over. 
But the image of Genghis Khan is everywhere, on banners at a trade fair and postcards and in souvenir shops. 
A vodka is named for him, and a local rock group sings his praises.
A Japanese-Mongolian expedition is spending its second summer in the nearby mountains searching for Genghis Khan's grave. 
If it is found, a museum will be built at the site.
Dr. Shagdaryn Bira, secretary general of the International Association for Mongol Studies and a member of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, said the expedition had found several hundred tombs, including some from the 13th century, but not the one they were looking for.
"I'm against making Genghis Khan a demigod," Dr. Bira said. 
"He was neither a devil nor a god. 
He was a man."
Even so, Dr. Bira said, efforts were being made to enlist international support for archeological excavations at Khara-Khorum, Genghis Khan's capital. 
The ruins, west of Ulan Bator, are a regular tourist stop. 
But research there was suspended years ago, when Mongolians were discouraged from studying their early history, and so the country has a shortage of archeologists.
Officials of the Academy of Sciences, reaching out for contacts with the West, are capitalizing on their paramount scientific asset: dinosaur remains. 
A group of French and Italian paleontologists arrived in early July to examine the rich fossil beds of the Gobi. 
Paleontologists from the American Museum of Natural History in New York, working with Mongolians, have begun a planned three-year campaign of fossil hunting.
Â 
Found Monastery Ruins
It was when the members of the American-Mongolian expedition were crossing the broad, desolate landscape between the towns of Saynshand and Dalan Dzadagad that they found the monastery ruins.
Cresting a dusty ridge, they caught sight of what appeared to be some "lost city" of archeological legend. 
It was the ruins of a small monastery known as Khonchiyn Khural. 
On the ground the Americans found spent cartridges and a flattened Buddhist statue with bullet holes, legacies of the sack. 
The place was utterly abandoned.
Most of those monasteries were destroyed in 1936 in what Renchingiyn Otgon, director of the State Central Library, likened to China's Cultural Revolution in the 1960's. 
He said more than half of the country's books, many of them priceless hand-printed religious works in Sanskrit and Tibetan, vanished.
In a few more hours of cross-country travel, the expedition came upon Ulgii Khiid, where the white cloth of yurts glistened among the earthen ruins.
The American scientists were given a taste of Mongolian hospitality, tea with camel's milk, and a few were allowed a brief visit inside the temple yurt. 
The lay leader of the settlement, a young man named Sandag, told them that 12 lamas and several young monks had taken up residence at the ruins late last year. 
With help from local herdsmen, they hoped to begin rebuilding the temple next year.
The Khama Lama said that some 100 monasteries have been reoccupied in at least a symbolic form, but that their restoration would be slow because of a lack of money and a shortage of monks. 
Many of them are old -- the Khama Lama is in his 80's -- and only recently have younger men started joining the monasteries.
Michael Sautman, an American businessman here and a practicing Buddhist, expressed concern that "the whole tradition of Tibetan Buddhism, with its scholasticism and deeper meditative arts, have been lost in Mongolia."
Many of the lamas, he pointed out, had to spend years outside the temple, living as laborers and herdsmen. 
Only the Gandan Monastery in Ulan Bator was permitted to reopen earlier, in 1944, but more as a showpiece than as a vibrant religious center.
Mongolians are adherents of the Gelug sect of Tibet, commonly called the Yellow Hat Buddhists for the yellow caps worn by monks to symbolize their rigid rules on learning, discipline and celibacy, and followers of the Dalai Lama. 
Indeed, Dalai is a Mongolian word meaning "ocean of wisdom."
Â 
New Generation to Train
Kushok Bakula, considered a living Buddha and India's Ambassador to Ulan Bator, agreed that it would take years to train a new generation of monks. 
He and other Buddhist leaders are hoping that a visit from the Dalai Lama would set off a wave of religious fervor, bringing back more people to worship and inspiring the young to take up the monastic life.
But the issue of the Dalai Lama's visit has exposed the limits of religous freedom in Mongolia and served as a reminder that this country of two million people is landlocked between two giants, China and the Soviet Union.
With its withdrawal of most trade, military forces and economic aid, the Soviet Union has left the once-dependent Mongolians to fend for themselves. 
Food and gasoline shortages are spreading, and Mongolians fear that conditions will worsen. 
They have made overtures for new trade ties with Japan, South Korea and the West, but they are restricted because their only transportation links are through Soviet and Chinese territory.
Under the circumstances, the Mongolian Government has sought to cultivate relations with China. 
And since Beijing looks with disfavor on any show of respect for the Dalai Lama, who disputes China's sovereignty over Tibet, cautious Mongolian officials withheld permission for the religious leader's planned visit here this month.
Not that the monks at Gandan are sitting still, waiting for a visit from the Dalai Lama. 
At noon one day in early July, they were out inspecting the construction of a new temple, young monks lending a hand to the old ones as they leaned over the foundation trenches. 
One of the few other construction projects in the city is the imposing glass edifice for a luxury hotel to open next year -- the Genghis Khan.

file: Building a Voice for Chinese in the U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
After the Chinese Army shot down pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing two years ago, I. M. Pei, the Chinese-American architect, found himself besieged with calls from people wanting to know how Chinese-Americans felt about the crackdown. 
So, too, did other leading Chinese-Americans, including the cellist Yo-Yo Ma.
Mr. Pei and Mr. Ma were not sure how to react. 
And they were concerned that the China experts who were quoted on television and in newspapers were not Chinese-Americans.
"There was no organization to turn to," Mr. Pei said. 
"There isn't any spokesman for Chinese-Americans.
"That seemed a pity," he added.
So Mr. Pei, Mr. Ma and Shirley Young, vice president of General Motors for consumer market development, began putting together a group of distinguished Chinese-Americans, called the Committee of 100, to try to represent Chinese-Americans the way lobbying organizations for other minority groups have long done.
The committee, which recently held a national meeting in San Francisco, is finishing the work on its operating rules and membership list.
Â 
Well-Known Members
Among its other well-known members are Bette Bao Lord, the novelist, David Henry Hwang, the playwright, T. D. Lee, a professor of physics and Nobel laureate at Columbia University, and Chang-Lin Tien, the chancellor of the University of California at Berkeley.
The formation of the Committee of 100 is seen by some Chinese-Americans as an important breakthrough, because Chinese have historically avoided politics in the United States and have not organized outside the family structure. 
Also, the Chinese community in the United States was long riven by bitter disputes between backers of the Chinese Nationalists and those of the Communists, as well as divided among immigrants who came from Hong Kong, Taiwan or different parts of the mainland.
The establishment of the committee also comes at a time when Asian-Americans have emerged as the fastest-growing minority in the country, with the population up 107 percent in the last decade to a total of 7.3 million, according to the Census Bureau. 
And Chinese-Americans, who numbered 1.6 million in the 1990 census, make up the largest single block of Asian-Americans.
In California, Asian-Americans constitute 10 percent of the population, surpassing the number of blacks. 
Although the state has two United States Representatives who are Japanese-American, Norman Y. Mineta and Robert T. Matsui, there is no Asian-American in the California State Assembly or Senate.
Â 
Effort on Elections
This disparity between Asians' numbers in the population and their lack of political clout has given impetus to a quiet effort in California to elect more Asian-Americans.
In San Francisco this year, Tom Hsieh, an architect born in Beijing, is one of four candidates for Mayor. 
In Monterey Park, a Los Angeles suburb whose population is 57 percent Asian, a former Mayor, Judy Chu, is leading a campaign to create a seat that could be won by an Asian in the current reapportionment of the State Legislature.
And in Los Angeles, Michael Woo, a member of the City Council, is being touted as a possible successor to Mayor Tom Bradley.
Each candidate has benefitted from major financial support from Chinese-Americans around the country; many of them are newly affluent business executives or professionals.
Â 
Vow to Be Nonpolitical
But it is unclear how active the Committee of 100 will be in supporting Asian-American political candidates. 
Nor is it certain whether it will play a critical role in relations between the United States and China, as other lobbying organizations for some ethnic and racial groups do.
Within the newly formed group, there is disagreement about the role it should have, as well as disagreement on individual political issues.
Mr. Pei, who came to the United States to study at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1935, insisted in an interview that the committee would be "absolutely nonpolitical."
Referring to the debate over President Bush's decision to extend most-favored-nation trade status to China again this year, he said, "We will not take a position on issues like M.F.N."
Mr. Bush has been criticized by liberals and conservatives in Congress who wanted the trade status issue used to pressure China to improve human rights and curb foreign arms sales.
Instead, Mr. Pei said, the members of the committee would offer themselves as a resource for Chinese-Americans in this country and, if needed, as a go-between for either the United States or Chinese Government.
Â 
Chinese Government 'Suspicious'
"The Chinese Government is very suspicious of Chinese-Americans," Mr. Pei said. 
"They think our views are warped, that we are no longer Chinese. 
But they know about the Committee of 100, so I like to think they will come to us. 
In fact, I'm sure they will."
As an example of the committee's potential influence , the United States Ambassador to China, James Lilley, and the Chinese Ambassador to this country, Zhu Qizhen, spoke at the organization's meeting in San Francisco in March.
The committee's lack of a clear-cut agenda has prompted some criticism. 
Asian Week, a San Francisco-based newspaper for Asian-Americans, compared the group to "a high school student without a date, all dressed up with no place to go."
The committee's founders "have yet to articulate a clear purpose for the organization or its methods for accomplishing its goals," Asian Week said.
Mr. Hsieh, the candidate for Mayor of San Francisco, said of the committee: "I don't think they know where they are going yet. 
I think they should be more assertive, more active. 
Without that, it just becomes an academic approach."
Mr. Pei acknowledged that the committee may have a problem in not being more politically committed. 
"Maybe that makes it difficult for us to be really effective," he said. 
"Is it possible to generate enthusiasm without a cause?
All we know is, we are here, and we are Chinese-Americans."
Mr. Ma said there had been "some passionate talk from some people" in the group about taking stands on issues like M.F.N., China's role in Tibet and Beijing's human rights record. 
For now, Mr. Ma said, the committee as a whole would not take policy positions. 
But if another crisis like the crackdown on the demonstrators should erupt, "then we would act quickly."
Correction
Because of an editing error, An article on June 22 about a new organization of Chinese-Americans gave an incorrect name in some editions for a Chinese-born candidate for mayor in San Francisco. 
He is Tom Hsieh.

file: BURMESE WARNING ON ARMS BUILDUP.txt
text:

U Sein Win came to Washington last week to remind the Bush Administration that his popularly elected Government in Myanmar, formerly Burma, remains powerless because of a military dictatorship that is building an alarming weapons arsenal with the help of China.
A year and a half after winning a sweeping majority, Mr. Sein Win's provisional Government is still barred from power by the State Law and Order Restoration Council, which has hounded, imprisoned or driven underground many of its victorious candidates.
Â 
Seeking Sanctions
"There is only one superpower left in the world," Mr. Sein Win said in an interview on Saturday. 
"We want the United States to use its influence to get other nations to cut links with the military regime and impose sanctions."
That China is heavily arming the law and order council, known by its acronym Slorc, has caused concern in other Asian nations, particularly India, said David I. Steinberg, a Georgetown University Asian specialist who has written several books on Myanmar.

Mr. Sein Win is the Prime Minister of the National Coalition Government of the Union of Burma, an administration-in-waiting operating from rebel-held territory near the Thai border, trying with scant resources to get the attention of the democratic world. 
A 48-year-old mathematics professor educated in Hamburg, Germany, Mr. Sein Win has been more successful in gaining support in Europe, where the European Parliament has pledged help and the Swedish Government has sponsored a resolution on the restoration of rights in Myanmar to be considered in the next week or two by the United Nations General Assembly.

Mr. Sein Win, who has the backing of several ethnic rebel groups long opposed to military governments in Myanmar, is the cousin of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, the leader of the national democracy movement and the winner of the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize.

He said that the country of 40 million people was being run by "uneducated criminals."
Mr. Sein Win fled to Manerplaw, in an ethnic Karen enclave of Myanmar, in October 1990 as the Slorc's forces under Gen. Saw Maung were closing in on leaders of the democracy movement.

'Great Concern in India'
Mr. Sein Win and other exiles are asking that the democratic world not only help in installing the Government the people elected, but also pay attention to the Slorc Government's militarization, which could soon pose a regional threat.
Professor Steinberg said in an interview Saturday that after the collapse of the Chinese-backed Communist Party of Burma insurgency and the improvement of relations with Beijing, Slorc has bought about a dozen F-6 jet fighters, six Hainan-class patrol boats, armored vehicles and a variety of guns. 
He said that the military Government was spending from a quarter to half its national budget on weapons, in a country that has been impoverished by 30 years of dictatorship.
"There is great concern in India about this," Mr. Steinberg said. 
"India is very interested in making sure that Burma is not too much in the Chinese camp because it would be outflanked on its northeast frontier."
He said the Chinese were also making substantial inroads into the Burmese economy, challenging Thailand in supplying cheap consumer goods and in the lucrative smuggling trade in timber, gems and narcotics. 
The Thai military, now Thailand after a February coup, is one of the main beneficiaries of commerce with Myanmar, legal or illegal. 
The two armies have had very close relations.
Pakistan and Bangladesh, friendly to China and wary of Indian intentions in Myanmar, are also becoming military suppliers to Slorc. 
South Korea and Singapore are also reported to be trading in strategic materials. 
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, to which Singapore and Thailand belong, has refused to be drawn into criticism of the military Government.

text:

Handing President Bush a major defeat, the House of Representatives today overwhelmingly reaffirmed legislation protecting Chinese students in the United States from deportation. 
The Senate is expected to vote on Thursday, and the outcome is too close to predict.
The Administration's setback in the House came in the form of a 390-to-25 vote to override the President's veto of a bill allowing Chinese students to remain in the United States, with 145 House Republicans joining 245 Democrats. 
Only 25 Republicans and no Democrats sided with the President.
When he vetoed the bill Nov. 
30, the President argued that he could protect the Chinese students with the same effectiveness as the legislation through administrative measures that would be less offensive to the Beijing authorities.
Extensive Lobbying Effort
The vote marked a direct, but not unexpected, repudiation by the House of Mr. Bush's handling of relations with China, despite what has probably been the most extensive lobbying effort by the White House on any foreign policy issue since Mr. Bush was elected.
At a news conference this morning, Mr. Bush acknowledged that he was ''a little late'' in trying to block a two-thirds majority of House members from lining up against him and that he was focusing his energies on trying to prevent a similar majority in the Senate. 
If a two-thirds majority there also votes to reject the veto, the bill will become law.
In today's floor debate, Congressmen repeatedly criticized the President's decision to send two top aides on two secret missions to Beijing, despite his public claim to have banned all high-level exchanges, and his willingness to ease many sanctions on Beijing in the absence of any significant improvement in human rights. 
They said these steps caused them to lose confidence in Mr. Bush's judgment on China and convinced them that a different approach must be mandated by legislation.
''Make no mistake about it, this vote is a referendum on human rights that will be heard around the world,'' said William S. Broomfield of Michigan, who is the ranking Republican member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. 
''I appreciate the difficulties President Bush finds himself in. 
America cannot always choose the foreign leaders it has to deal with. 
Yes, we should deal with the Chinese Government. 
However, let's do it on our terms. 
America should be remembered for providing a launching pad for Chinese leadership of the future and not for providing crutches for its tyrants of the past.''
The President had breakfast this morning with a group of Republican Senators in an effort to convince them that he has fully protected all 40,000 Chinese students who want to remain through administrative measures he implemented through the Immigration and Naturalization Service. 
Therefore, he argued, the legislation was both unnecessary and provocative.
Opening his news conference this morning, the President warned that Congress ''will have only itself to blame'' if it overrides his veto, because, he added, the authorities in Beijing have threatened to stop all Chinese students from coming to the United States if the bill is passed.
Â 
Called a Question of Pride
The President did not explain, though, why the Chinese would retaliate for the legislation and not for what the President ordered, if his executive orders were identical to the legislation. 
The only explanation, say many Congressmen, is that the Chinese know that a law cannot be easily changed, while an executive order can be reversed or amended by the stroke of the President's pen.
An Administration official said it was a question of pride. 
The Chinese, he said, can live with a ''quiet'' administrative order but not an open, and embarrassing, repudiation by Congress.
Mr. Bush said today that immediately after the crackdown on democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square last June, ''I moved to protect the Chinese students in this country.''
''Not one was sent back,'' he said. 
''They were safe then, and they are safe now, and they will be safe in the future. 
If I signed the bill, the students would still be safe, but China would retaliate and cut off future student exchanges. 
I want to keep contact. 
I do not want isolation.''
Since the Bush Administration imposed sanctions on China in the wake of the killings in Tiananmen Square last June, Beijing has allowed more than 7,000 Chinese students to come to the United States. 
There are currently about 40,000 Chinese students in this country, 32,000 of them holding visas that would require them to return to China before applying to change their American visa status.
Â 
Congress Not Impressed
Most members of Congress simply were not impressed by Mr. Bush's argument. 
They countered that if the Beijing leaders want to punish themselves and their country by stopping all Chinese students from benefiting from an education in the United States, they can go right ahead.
Speaking in the House debate before the vote, Stephen J. Solarz, the New York Democrat who heads the House Asia subcommittee, argued: ''If the President can send some of the highest foreign policy officials in his Administration to Beijing at the same time as he is telling the American people that he has suspended all high-level contacts then he simply cannot be relied upon not to rescind the executive order at some time in the future.''
Judging from the vigor with which Democratic House members denounced the President's approach in the floor debate, they relished not only repudiating his China policies, but also delivering him a political blow at the very start of the Congressional new year. 
Their rather assertive start to the second session of the 101st Congress seemed to signal that despite the President's soaring approval ratings, Democrats would not shrink from challenging his policies on a broad front.
Â 
Defense of Administration
Republican House members who voted with the President cited this, and other arguments, in trying to defend the Administration in the floor debate. 
Lamar S. Smith, Republican of Texas, said: ''I think the real question here is if the students are protected, what is the rush to override the veto of the President?
It sounds rather suspiciously that the bash President Bush brigades are on the prowl.''
Robert H. Michel of Illinois, the House Minority Leader, said: ''President Bush knows China as well, if not better, than any member of this House. 
He knows their people. 
He knows their special traits and he must be given the room to make the foreign policy moves he feels are in the long range best interest of our country.'
According to The New York Times/CBS News Poll, the American public is about evenly divided on the question of the proper approach to dealing with China. 
Asked on the weekend of Jan. 
13-15 whether it was more important to criticize the way China suppresses human rights, as the Congress seems to favor, or to avoid criticism in order to maintain good relations with China, 42 percent favored outspoken criticism, while 46 percent said their priority was maintaining good relations. 
The survey questioned 1,557 Americans by telephone and had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.
Trying to sway Senate Republicans this morning, Mr. Bush said the Chinese authorities have permitted Peace Corps volunteers to work in China, have accredited a correspondent from the Voice Of America and muted hostile propaganda against Americans.

''I think that will certainly convince people, those that might be skeptical, that I have every intention of keeping my word,'' Mr. Bush said in a question-and-answer session with members of the American Society of Newspaper Editors.
After vetoing the bill on Chinese students in December, Mr. Bush said he was issuing an executive order to make it easier for students fearing persecution by the Beijing Government to remain in the United States. 
An executive order is a formal document that is printed in the Federal Register and has the force of law.
Called 'Technical Matter'
Mr. Bush and his staff repeatedly said afterward that he had issued the order. 
But in fact the President only issued an ''executive directive,'' which does not carry the power of law and can be amended or revoked without public notice.
Mr. Bush said today that the difference was ''a technical matter.''
''But I did say 'executive order,' so this will formalize it in an official executive order fashion,'' he said.
Mr. Bush's measures to protect Chinese students were taken in response to the nationwide crackdown on dissent in their homeland last year that ended with the violent suppression of demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in June.
In vetoing the legislation on Chinese students, Mr. Bush said the law infringed on his executive powers. 
He also suggested that it would interfere with his efforts to improve relations with Beijing, a policy that spawned a storm of protest on Capitol Hill after the disclosure of two secret missions by top American officials to China.
The White House said the executive order would probably be issued next week.
Â 
Expands Previous Action
Mr. Bush said it would expand his previous actions on behalf of Chinese students in these two ways:
* It will extend until Jan. 
1, 1994, an order that the Justice Department suspend all deportation proceedings against Chinese students. 
The earlier directive ran only through June 5.
* It will waive a regulation under which Chinese students whose passports have expired or have been revoked by Beijing are barred from changing their legal status in the United States. 
The waiver would allow a student to change his status to temporary worker, for example.
Mr. Bush also said the executive order would include these provisions of his earlier, less formal, instructions to the Justice Department:
* An ''irrevocable waiver'' of foreign residency requirements for Chinese nationals who were in the United States as of Dec. 
1, 1989. 
The waiver would be valid through Jan. 
1, 1994.
* A work authorization for all Chinese citizens in the United States as of June 5, 1989.
* Special consideration to refugee applications from Chinese citizens who have expressed ''fear of persecution related to family planning policies of forced abortion or sterilization.''
An aide to Representative Nancy Pelosi, the California Democrat who sponsored the Chinese students' relief bill vetoed by Mr. Bush, said Mr. Bush's promise to issue the executive order ''is precisely what we've asked the President to do.''
But the aide expressed concern that some provisions applied only to Chinese citizens who were in the United States as of last June, which would not include students who took part in the Tiananmen Square demonstrations early that month.

FULBRIGHT EXCHANGE TO RESUME
BEIJING, April 6 (AP) - China has agreed to resume the Fulbright scholar exchange program with the United States, but on a smaller scale, a United States Embassy official said today.
