file: Business Wary About End Of Martial Law in Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
While foreign companies welcome the lifting of martial law in the capital, the action is unlikely to have an immediate effect on their commercial or investment activities here, officials of a dozen companies said today.
The foreign business executives in interviews described the lifting of martial law, effective today, as a necessary condition for a better business climate. 
But they added that except for improving the prospects for the tourism industry, the move would be largely cosmetic and symbolic.
''The Chinese can, of course, put soldiers at will overnight back where they were before, and we all know that,'' said an American businessman who asked not to be identified. 
''The same problems remain whether or not they move a few people dressed up in fancy uniforms from one particular, visible location to one that is not so visible.''
Deteriorating Economy
For most companies, the dominant concerns are the result of China's deteriorating economy: tight credit, reduced demand and shortages of raw materials and foreign exchange.
''A lot of people were experiencing problems well before June 4 due to recentralization and a credit squeeze,'' said Matthew D. Bersani, an associate at the Beijing office of the American law firm of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison. 
''None of those problems go away, even if Sino-American relations were perfect.''
The tourism industry stands to gain the most from the lifing of martial law, which was imposed in certain areas of the capital on May 20, and hoteliers say the change will allow tour operators to offer more travel packages without insurance restrictions. 
Many insurance companies either raised their prices or were reluctant to give insurance for companies offering tours to China as long as martial law was in effect.
The cold winter has been a particularly bleak one for the tourism industry, and some hotel managers say they believe this year's tourist season, which begins in March, will start slowly.
Â 
Unlike a Faucet
''You can't just say there is no more martial law, and then have everyone willing to come to China,'' said Gerhard R.E. 
Schmidt, general manager at the Palace Hotel, which he said is currently operating at 50 percent occupancy. 
''It's not like a faucet you can switch on and off.''
Many companies hope for a softening of tensions between China and the United States, Japan and other Western countries. 
Once bilateral relations improve, their logic goes, Government lending will follow, paving the way for more trade and better business opportunities, greater confidence, and then more commercial lending and investment.
American businesses still say they are looking to the resumption of lending by the World Bank, and particularly the Japanese Government, for a stimulus to their commercial activity. 
In some cases, such loans are expected to provide the financing for a number of big-ticket imports that companies in China say they cannot afford without outside financing.
For the World Bank, the lifting of martial law will not directly lead to a change in its lending policy, but there will probably be an indirect effect if the action substantially improves the view of China taken by the World Bank's pivotal shareholders, like the United States.
Â 
Change Is Needed
Commercial banks, however, will not necessarily jump into the market once the World Bank resumes lending. 
Foreign bankers say a great deal more substantive change is needed before the capital market for China resumes its former scale and vibrancy.
For a lending market to re-emerge, a sizable number of banks must be willing to share the risk of underwriting or participating in China loan syndications, and at least some of the preconditions for this are that the World Bank and the Japanese Government resume their lending programs.
''Lifting martial law is a small step in the right direction,'' said an American banker in Beijing. 
''The World Bank loans being re-established is a little bit of a bigger step in that direction, and an official position by the Japanese banks toward China is another pretty big step in that direction.
''When there is a large enough universe of banks that are prepared to go back to China and take China risk, then we can do our business.''

file: By the Sea, China_s Leaders Chart the Nation_s Path.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Chinese worker circled a small pavilion tucked among the sleepy hills here, and when the guard wasn't looking, he stole a peek at the red-tile roof of a mansion that for the next month may be the most important building in China.
Under the roof of the mansion, which is surrounded by trees, Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, is taking counsel on whom to promote and dismiss, and on how to redefine the Communist road.
Each summer, when the political heat follows the mercury upward, China's leaders retire to this seaside resort to debate the nation's future alongside the sand and salty water of the Bohai Gulf. 
Although their movements are never announced, Chinese say that Mr. Deng arrived in mid-July and that most of his associates have joined him to occupy the adjacent mansions on the hillside.
"That's where it's all happening," a foreign diplomat said, referring to Beidaihe (pronounced bay-dye-huh).
Â 
The Place for Negotiating
In a nation where the most important decisions are made not by a parliament or even a politburo but by consensus among a handful of old men, Beidaihe is usually the forum where the bargaining takes place and an agreement is thrashed out.
This year the Beidaihe meeting will be even more important than normal. 
Even the winds off the sea have an unusual whistle to them.
The party elders will have to determine the new roster of leaders and set the agenda for the 14th Communist Party Congress, which meets this fall to select a new Central Committee. 
A party congress takes place only once in about every five years to set the nation's direction and pace.
Many Chinese intellectuals expect the congress to legitimize a bold program for liberalization. 
Even Chen Yun, the elderly hard-liner who is Mr. Deng's most powerful rival, recently endorsed special economic zones and other new methods for economic reform.
Â 
Many Changes Are Expected
"We expect a lot of changes at the 14th Party Congress," a university lecturer said. 
"Next year will be much more open than this year."
Another urgency probably nags at Mr. Deng these days: his mortality. 
Three of his close revolutionary colleagues have died this year, so Mr. Deng, who is 87 years old, must be anxious to complete the task of deciding on succession.
"Deng is in a tough spot," a Chinese journalist said. 
"It all requires a delicate balance, to accommodate all the different groups and factions. 
And all this is being sorted out at Beidaihe."
Those holding formal positions often commute to Beijing for meetings, but most of the octogenarians remain in Beidaihe in the July and August heat. 
Since they have arrived, Beidaihe has gushed with gossip about who has come and who has not come, who will step aside and who will step ahead.
The fate of Prime Minister Li Peng may well be determined in Beidaihe this summer. 
Mr. Li's five-year term expires early next year, and there are whispers that Mr. Deng would like to move him aside into a less powerful post, like the largely ceremonial position of the presidency. 
Mr. Chen and other hard-liners are unlikely to agree to that without a tussle.
Mr. Chen, who apparently rarely comes to Beidaihe, may retire at the party congress from his job as chairman of the Central Advisory Commission, which Mr. Deng has been trying to dissolve for years.
Mr. Deng is believed to have arrived in mid-July, followed a few days later by Yang Shangkun, China's President, and then Prime Minister Li.
Bo Yibo, another elderly leader, and Wan Li, Mr. Deng's bridge partner and chairman of China's legislature, are also believed to be here.
Â 
Tight Security for Deng
"Deng came on a special train with three cars," said a local driver who has been inside Mr. Deng's compound. 
"He rode in the middle car, and army men were in the front and the rear ones. 
When he arrived, none of us were allowed to be at the station. 
They shooed away the buses and the taxis."
Tight restrictions are imposed when leaders come to town, and Mercedes-Benzes snake through the tree-lined streets in the hills. 
The police have set up checkpoints around town, and at night they sometimes refuse to allow cars to pass.
One minibus was stopped three times in the middle of the night and told to take a detour to its destination, said a Chinese business executive who was in the bus. 
The policemen beamed a searchlight at the bus, searched the luggage of the passengers and asked if anyone had knives.
Mr. Deng stays in Lianfengshan Park in Mao Zedong's old house, part of a compound of villas where several elderly leaders stay. 
The Deng villa was apparently renovated a few years ago, said a Chinese who visited the compound.
Â 
Summer Brings Life
Two town workers said separately that Mr. Deng's children spend most of their time on a large red-and-pink brick estate built into the cliffs of the Jinshan peninsula, where the streets wind through patches of pruned poplars and red roses.
Beidaihe sleeps in the winter and then booms all summer. 
Yellow-sand beaches are crowded these days with screaming children, old cadres and young couples who come in droves under the guidance, and expense accounts, of their Government ministries.
Almost all Government departments operate resorts here for employees. 
Along the beach are the State Council Resort, the Beijing Old Cadres Sanitarium, the Public Security Resort and the People's Daily Resort. 
Beidaihe, a town of 50,000, also has local bureaus of the New China News Agency and The Guangming Daily.
Some of the buildings are high-ceilinged colonial houses built by foreigners early in this century, while others are modern round-windowed compounds partly hidden behind high hedges. 
Brown-eyed Susans peer out of flower gardens and darkened windows appear through tufts of trees.
Nobody knows what happens inside.

file: Calls for Economic Changes Rise Among Chinese Officials.txt
text:
ï»¿
After a two-year freeze on the process of opening China's state-controlled economy to market forces, a growing number of Chinese economic officials are openly calling for a wave of changes, arguing that without further liberalization China's march toward development may reverse.
For several months, China's leaders have acknowledged a need to ease the austerity measures imposed in the fall of 1988 to battle soaring inflation. 
Now, momentum is building for more basic changes, like those of the early 1980's, when China was a leader among Communist countries in experimenting with market-oriented policies to revitalize its state-run economy.
''In China, without real reform, the economic situation will become hopeless,'' Ren Junyin, deputy director of planning at the nation's central bank, the People's Bank of China, said in an interview in Beijing. 
''It is only a matter of time and the conditions before we undertake serious reform.''
No Changes in Policy
Chinese officials and some Western experts say the tolerance being shown for opening the market of economic ideas suggests some easing of the tense political climate that has existed since tanks were sent into Tiananmen Square in Beijing last June to crush the democracy movement. 
They add that it also shows some acknowledgement of the depth of the current problems on the part of the leadership.
Finance Minister Wang Bingqian has described the economic situation as fairly grim, and Prime Minister Li Peng recently acknowledged that the economy was fragile. 
Still, the leadership has produced no changes in policy in response to the calls for change.
Dwight H. Perkins, a China expert at Harvard University who recently con-ducted research with the State Planning Commission in Beijing, said: ''I don't think there's any real commitment for reform now. 
What I see is lots of ad hoc thinking about administrative intervention in the economy, but no real plan. 
Most of the people at the top have no real understanding or confidence in how markets work.''
Yet the calls for change have grown louder.
Zheng Hongqing, head of an important Government research center, was quoted on the front page of The China Daily newspaper last week, saying the Government has too much control over bloated state enterprises. 
He proposed a shareholding system for companies and the introduction of competition among banks.
In fact, China's first organized stock exchange is scheduled to open near here in Shenzhen within a few months. 
It will be closely watched as a sign of how tolerant the authorities will be.
Other proposals being floated are the creation of a national stock market, an easing of price controls and an opening of banks that make loans based on the prospect of getting repaid rather than on Government policy. 
Even with such ideas being widely circulated, China's current leadership is still expressing its suspicions about market-oriented changes, making the prospects for fundamental change uncertain.
Li Guixian, president of the People's Bank, recently told a financial conference in Shenyong, in northeast China, that banks ''are supposed to provide lending mainly in light of the state policies rather than for profit.''
Â 
Alert to Conspiracy
And a broadside was recently issued by Communist Party officials insisting that China would maintain its vigilance against ''peaceful evolution,'' code words here for what is believed to be an American conspiracy to transform the Communist planned system into a capitalist system.
The mood was expressed well by Rong Yiren, one of Chinese Communism's best-known capitalists. 
Mr. Rong is chairman of the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, known as Citic, a multifaceted Government-owned merchant bank in Beijing born of the open-door policies a decade ago. 
Citic has survived by deftly sensing and conforming to the prevailing winds.
''My view is that we should adopt a very gradual, stable reform policy that does not proceed hastily,'' Mr. Rong said, seated in his modern office under a picture of himself with Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader.
Â 
Expression of Disapproval
Nonetheless, it does not appear that the debate or the pressure for change will be halted. 
''China's economy is too large to be run efficiently on the basis of commands from the center,'' the World Bank said in a recent report. 
In blunt language the report stated the case for pushing ahead with liberalization, saying disapprovingly that China's leadership seemed to believe that ''problems encountered in the course of reform,'' like inflation, could be fixed by resorting to the same inflexible mechanism ''responsible for the distortions the reform was designed to correct.''
Nicholas R. Lardy, an expert on the Chinese economy at the University of Washington, observed: ''They are at a critical point. 
The underlying economy is much softer than most of the figures suggest.''
The profits of state-owned enterprises plummeted 60 percent in the first half of the year, cutting even further into state revenues already depleted by heavy Government price subsidies. 
Industry is suffering from nagging shortages of basic commodities like energy and water because state-fixed prices are too low and promote inefficiency, economists say. 
And there could be an even more severe slowdown in foreign investment, which has tumbled 22 percent this year.
Â 
Enormous Changes
Before the economic liberalization ground to a halt two years ago, enormous changes had been wrought. 
Farmers were freed to grow more of what they wanted and to sell in more open markets; some central Government functions were taken on by the provinces; the economy was opened to a limited amount of foreign investment and trade, and the seeds of a real banking system were sown.
The changes put China far ahead of most Communist countries in liberalizing its economy, and they brought a large measure of prosperity to the countryside.
The region around Canton was a major beneficiary of the reforms. 
Farmers' incomes rose, and a flood of investment from Hong Kong caused a boom in factory and hotel construction. 
The region then suffered as the austerity measures and renewed emphasis on state control forced thousands of newly formed small businesses to close.
Â 
Some Positive Economic Signs
''This is like rowing a boat upstream,'' said Gao Xiqing, a graduate of the Duke University School of Law who is the general counsel of a new body trying to establish China's first formal stock exchange in Beijing. 
''You can't stand still. 
You have to go ahead or you go backwards.''
There are some positive economic signs, like vibrant exports this year. 
Inflation has fallen to about 3 percent. 
After a recession last year and earlier in 1990, industrial activity perked up modestly in the last two months. 
Urban store shelves are filled, and streets are lined with merchants sitting atop hillocks of watermelons, as city dwellers enjoy a bumper harvest.
After negative growth in the first months of this year, the Government has reported that the economy had an annual growth rate of 1.6 percent in the first half, compared with the first half of 1989. 
In the crucial area of industrial production, growth at state-owned enterprises rose 2.7 percent, less than half the 5.6 percent growth rate at more freely operated collectively run enterprises and a fraction of the 54.3 percent growth rate of foreign-financed ventures in China.
Â 
Experts' Recommendations
To put the whole economy on a more stable growth path, the experts advocate a number of changes:
* Creating broader markets for determining prices. 
To avoid jolting consumers too harshly, the World Bank and others have proposed phasing in market-determined prices.
* Permitting a greater element of private ownership. 
To many, this step is the most important and the one that seems to be the slowest in moving ahead.
* Freeing the financial system so that banks make their lending decisions on the basis of their likelihood of getting repaid.
''It boils down to a political question of what you can sell the people,'' said Mr. Lardy of the University of Washington.''There has to be some pain before they can really move ahead.''

file: Cambodian Factions to Meet Today.txt
text:
ï»¿
A new round of talks on Cambodia begins here on Monday, with at least limited success already insured for their Japanese hosts who have stepping gingerly into regional peacemaking for the first time.
The leaders of all four rival Cambodian factions will attend and all of them have already initialed a memorandum, including a symbolic cease-fire agreement, worked out by the Defense Minister of Thailand, Gen. Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.
While American officials are said to want a stronger document, one calling for a comprehensive settlement and providing a greater monitoring and administrative role for the United Nations, Washington will applaud anything that looks like an agreement.
The memorandum, according to Thai officials and Western and Asian diplomats, calls for an immediate cease-fire, military ''self-restraint'' and a cessation of foreign military aid, though without effective monitoring. 
That lack will render it largely symbolic. 
In any case, the rainy season has already imposed a sort of cease-fire.
A Transitional Council
The agreement also calls for the formation of a Supreme National Council made up of six representatives from each of the two rival governments. 
The council would serve as the repository of Cambodian sovereignty until a new government is formed, presumably after a final settlement and elections.
By itself, the agreement will do little to end the war in Cambodia but, unless derailed here, it will represent the first agreed understanding among all the four factions. 
And it does resolve a few vexing issues.
Prime Minister Hun Sen of Cambodia, whose Government was installed by Vietnam when it drove the Khmer Rouge out of Cambodia in January 1979, is opposed by an uneasy, three-part coalition: the Khmer Rouge guerrillas, who are supported and armed by China, and two non-Communist factions, headed by Prince Norodom Sihanouk and a former Sihanouk Prime Minister, Son Sann, backed by China and the United States.
Â 
Sihanouk and Hun Sen to Sign
While all four factions are represented here and separately initialed General Chavalit's memorandum, Japanese officials say it will be signed by Mr. Hun Sen and Prince Sihanouk as leaders of the two rival governments.
That fact itself, combined with equal representation for the two sides on the Supreme National Council, represents a concession on the part of China and the Khmer Rouge, which have long insisted on equal representation for all four factions.
Vietnam and Mr. Hun Sen have opposed equal treatment for the Khmer Rouge, which was responsible for the deaths of more than a million Cambodians between April 1975 and December 1978, when Vietnam invaded Cambodia. 
But Hanoi and Phnom Penh have agreed that the Khmer Rouge can participate on the Council as members of the opposition coalition headed by Prince Sihanouk.
The Thais have long been pushing for a step-by-step settlement to Cambodia, beginning with a cease-fire, an approach criticized by Washington, which fears it favors Mr. Hun Sen.
The Japanese have been pushing quietly for a diplomatic role on Cambodia, in part as a sign of their postwar stature and influence. 
They are also expected to pay the bulk of the costs.
Thai officials say that Tokyo urged them to invite Japan to play host to this meeting. 
The Thais, whose boom is largely dependent on Japanese investment and aid, were happy to oblige, at the same time co-opting the Japanese.
But this meeting might not have happened without progress in other forums concerned with Cambodia. 
The five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council - Britain, China, France, the Soviet Union and the United States - have been meeting regularly on Cambodia. 
Also, China has opened talks with Vietnam, after a long period of inaction, on the level of Deputy Foreign Ministers.
Dinh Ngo Liem of Vietnam met his Chinese counterpart, Xu Dunxin, in Beijing in early May. 
Another meeting is scheduled. 
Western and Asian diplomats suggest that the new flexibility on the part of Mr. Hun Sen and the Khmer Rouge stems from these meetings.

file: Cambodian Rivals Said to Accept U.N. Peace Plan.txt
text:
ï»¿
Today also marked the first meeting of an official American representative, John Monjo, Ambassador to Indonesia, with Hun Sen, the Prime Minister of the Vietamese-installed Government in Cambodia. 
Washington announced last week that it would begin direct talks with Phnom Penh, a dialogue that was begun last week at the ambassadorial level in Vientiane, Laos.
Mr. Hun Sen, speaking after a 40-minute meeting with Mr. Monjo, said that he accepted the United Nations plan as ''the framework for a comprehenive solution.''
He said that the plan, which calls for thousands of administrators under United Nations auspices leading to new elections in Cambodia, had to be elaborated upon in negotiations, a fact also emphasized by Mr. Alatas and the French co-chairman, Edwige Avice, a Deputy Foreign Minister, in their formal opening remarks.
But Mr. Hun Sen said he was now optimistic that the talks here, which quickly broke into meetings of the co-chairmen with the individual factions, would have a successful outcome.
He said the meeting with Mr. Monjo was a very good and important one. 
''It is a first meeting but very valuable,'' he said. 
''We have the same intention, the same understanding with the Americans.''
Mr. Monjo said only he brought ''no special messages - just exchanging views.''
The United Nations plan has already been accepted by the three-party opposition coalition fighting Mr. Hun Sen's Vietnamese-installed Government. 
The coalition, led by Prince Norodom Sihanouk, is made up of his followers, those of another non-Communist, former Prime Minister Son Sann, and the Communist Khmer Rouge, during whose rule, from 1975 to 1979, more than one million Cambodians died by execution and famine. 
Vietnam invaded the country and installed a pro-Hanoi, anti-Khmer Rouge Government in 1979.
Khieu Samphan, the Khmer Rouge representative and vice president of the anti-Government coalition, said today that he was also optimistic. 
''Peace is closer than ever,'' he said. 
He had ''no reservations'' about the United Nations plan. 
The plan would establish a national governing council, under United Nations supervision, to administer the country. 
The United Nations would also set up and monitor free elections, and sending a military force as peacekeepers. 
The four factions must negotiate the details of the plan, and it is expected that there will be disagreements.
Khieu Samphan's comments were echoed by Prince Norodom Ranariddh, Prince Sihanouk's son and representative here.
Â 
Sihanouk's Status Unclear
But the status of Prince Sihanouk, who said in a statement Saturday that he was too ill to come here and who was communicating with Jakarta by fax, remained unclear, adding a note of uncertainty.
Senior Western and Asian diplomats said today that the Chinese Prime Minister, Li Peng, had urged Prince Sihanouk to come here, but that the Prince refused at the last minute, because he was offended by some remarks of Mr. Hun Sen.
The diplomats said that Prince Sihanouk and the Chinese Deputy Foreign Minister, Qi Huaiyuan, then had a long and bitter discussion, which ended with the Prince saying that he was packing his bags to go to his second home, in Pyongyang, North Korea.
China has been the main sponsor of all the opposition factions and the sole sponsor of the Khmer Rouge. 
Prince Sihanouk is provided a home in the old French Legation building in Beijing.
Â 
A Break From Diplomacy
Prince Sihanouk remained today in Beijing. 
But in a hallway interview, Prince Ranariddh said that his father had decided to take ''a five- or six-month break'' from diplomacy because of his health, and would issue a statement to that effect today in Beijing. 
No statement was issued, however, and some diplomats suggested that if this meeting turns out to be a success, Prince Sihanouk may yet arrive.
Although Prince Sihanouk has said in the past that he would not serve as chairman of an interim national leadership, the Supreme National Council, he is now said to want the position.
In a statement Saturday, Prince Sihanouk said the coalition would accept a council made up of six members from the coalition and six from Phnom Penh, as Mr. Hun Sen has demanded. 
The Khmer Rouge had been demanding that all four factions have an equal number of seats, giving the coalition three-quarters of the seats.
In his statement, the Prince said the council could elect a chairman as a 13th member. 
But Mr. Hun Sen is said by diplomats to be insisting that Prince Sihanouk, if he is to take part in the council, be one of the 12.
Â 
A Demand for Consensus
Diplomats said, however, that Mr. Hun Sen is willing to accept Prince Sihanouk's demand that the council operate by consensus, rather than by majority voting.
Still, Prince Sihanouk has been reluctant to allow himself to be put on the same footing with Mr. Hun Sen, only 39 years old, whom he has called ''a Vietnamese valet.''
Mr. Alatas, appearing buoyant after a process in which he has been so intimately involved, said that the bilateral meetings would continue Monday ''to start talking about forming the Supreme National Council,'' a necessary first step for peace.
After getting the factions' commitment to the United Nations framework, he said the main priority of the meeting will be to ''finalize the process of the formation'' of the Supreme National Council, including ''its nature, composition, functions and related aspects.''
If that could be accomplished here, senior Asian diplomats said, the peace talks might then return to Paris, where a formal international conference on Cambodia broke up in disarray in August 1989.
The talks here are taking place under the aegis of that conference. 
''If nothing else goes wrong, which it probably will,'' one Asian diplomat said, the conference could be reconvened in late October.
The United Nations plan envisages the Supreme National Council taking Cambodia's seat in the United Nations in the upcoming General Assembly. 
It would then cede to a special United Nations authority the right to ''supervise or control'' the five key ministries of state - foreign affairs, interior, finance, defense and information.
The United Nations authority would in this way insure the neutrality of the Government in the year or so before new elections can be organized and held.
Diplomats say the five permanent members foresee the appointment of United Nations officials at the top levels of the ministries, working through Cambodian bureaucrats of both rival administrations. 
If the Council agrees on particular decisions, the United Nations would go along. 
If not, the United Nations officials would decide.
''But how does Hun Sen understand 'supervise or control'?'' an Asian diplomat said. 
This was the thorny sort of issue still to be worked out, he said.
The United Nations would also be responsible for monitoring a cease-fire and the cessation of external aid to the combatants, for disarming the rival armies and repatriating the 300,000 or so Cambodians displaced after the Vietnamese invasion.
Phnom Penh is reluctant to cede too much control to the United Nations, but it may do so if it does not mean the dismantling of the administration that is now in place. 
Cambodian officials say dismantling would allow the Khmer Rouge to intensify the war, but some admit it would also undermine the Government's chances in an election.
Mr. Hun Sen has worries, too, that the Khmer Rouge will take advantage of a cease-fire and continue its war for power by political as well as military means. 
The Khmer Rouge might not hand in all its arms to the United Nations, for instance, or tell many of its fighters to go underground rather than group themselves in cantonments for disarming, as the United Nations plan suggests.
Â 
The U.N. Plan For Cambodia
Â 
These are the major requirements of the United Nations peace plan under which the Vietnamese-backed Cambodian Government would share power with three guerrilla groups it has been fighting for 11 years.
Â 
U.N. administration of the Cambodian Government until elections are held.
Â Â U.N. supervision of disarmament of rival factions.
Â 
U.N. supervision of elections.
Â 
Human rights guarantees.
Â 
International guarantees regarding the neutrality of a restructured Cambodia.

file: CAMPUS LIFE_ Berkeley_Scholars in China Discover a Meal By Early Man.txt
text:
ï»¿
Finding human teeth marks on a million-year-old elephant ankle made waiting a lifetime to dig in China worthwhile for an anthropology professor at the University of California at Berkeley.
A team of American and Chinese anthropologists led by Emeritus Prof. Desmond Clark -- who in 1981 in Ethopia was a co-discoverer of some of the oldest human remains found to date -- recently received the first grant for non-Chinese to conduct excavations in China since before World War II.
Professor Clark said team members in China are examining a pile of old broken bones and stones that were discovered this summer in the Nihewan Basin, northwest of Beijing, hoping to find clues of how early hominids lived.
"It was difficult during the Cultural Revolution for foreigners to research in China," Professor Clark said. 
"We could look at the site with our Chinese colleagues but could not participate in excavations. 
This is truly exciting and has finally happened."
Â 
A Find After Days of Sifting
The Chinese-American team began excavations and surveys in July, a month after its permit was issued.
After four days of sifting through fine-grained sands, a team member uncovered an ankle bone belonging to an elephant dating from more than a million years ago, said Dennis Etler, a Berkeley anthropology graduate student from Lakewood, N.J.
Human teeth and cut marks on the bone indicated that humans, not large mammals like as hyenas, had been gnawing on the bones, Professor Clark said.
The cut marks could have been caused by sharp-edged rocks or flakes, many of which were found alongside the bones, Mr. Etler said. 
"These flakes were possibly used as tools to scrape loose the meat," he said.
But finding beautifully fashioned tools or the remains of early humans -- million-year-old hominid fossils have already been discovered -- is not what the team is after. 
"We not only want to establish early presence of homo erectus, but we want to figure out how they behaved," said Kathy Schick, an archeology professor at the University of Indiana at Bloomington who is on the China team.
Â 
Techniques New to Chinese
In addition to the excavations, Frank Brown, a team member and geology professor at the University of Utah, taught seminars for Chinese scientists.
Modern excavation and survey techniques introduced by the American scientists were new to the Chinese scientists, Professor Clark said. 
"Because the Chinese Government forbade foreigners from excavating, the Chinese were not exposed to these modern techniques now used internationally by archeologists."
Professor Clark's Chinese counterpart on the team, Jui Lanpo, pressured the Government to ease its restrictions, Mr. Etler said. 
(Mr. Lanpo was working on the excavation site when the 450,000-year-old remains of Peking Man, the first hominid remains found in China, were unearthed in the 1920's.)
Lifting the ban, however, has reciprocal advantages, Professor Clark said in a recent interview. 
Until now, foreigners have not had the opportunity to dig in undisturbed sites like the Nihewan Basin.
Â 
Educating Chinese Scientists
As part of the effort to educate the younger Chinese scientists in the group, Professor Schick arranged for two of them to work this semester at the University of Indiana as research scholars. 
In June 1992 Professor Clark is scheduled to teach for a semester at Beijing University.
The $60,000-a-year a year project, financed by the Henry Luce Foundation in New York, will resume in April and continue over the next three summers.
The 15 team members include scientists from the Chinese Academy's Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing and Nicholas Toth, an anthropology professor at the University of Indiana at Bloomington.

file: Campus Life_ M.I.T._Officials Seeking Grant to Establish Course in Chinese.txt
text:
ï»¿
Five days a week during the academic year, Andrea Li boards the No. 1 bus at the steps of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's main building for a 15-minute ride to Harvard University, where she is studying Chinese.
Like 16 of her M.I.T. classmates, Miss Li, a senior from Stony Brook, L.I., who is majoring in brain and cognitive sciences, must take Chinese at Harvard because M.I.T., where students of Asian heritage account for 19.3 percent of the student body, does not offer the language. 
Four other M.I.T. students studied Chinese at Wellesley College last fall, making the 45-minute commute four times weekly.
But that situation may change, perhaps as soon as this fall.
Last month, M.I.T. applied to the Chiang Ching-kuo Foundation in Taiwan for a three-year, $300,000 grant to establish a Chinese language program at M.I.T., said David L. Lundberg, director of development for the School of Humanities and Social Sciences.
Â 
Satisfying Language Needs
The newly established, private foundation has an endowment of $100 million. 
Its function, Mr. Lundberg said, is to give grants ''exclusively to Americans to promote Chinese culture and things related to Chinese culture in America.''
Should M.I.T. be awarded the grant, the language classes would satisfy the needs of many, from students who want to talk to relatives in their native tongue, to others with a general interest in Asian cultures, to others who may find knowledge of Chinese useful in business. 
Mr. Lundberg expects a reply within two months.
For Miss Li, whose parents were born in Hong Kong and speak Cantonese at home, she wanted to study Chinese to learn about the culture.
''Since I am Chinese, I feel the need to be familiar with the language,'' she said. 
''There are a lot of people in my position, brought up understanding Chinese, but not fluent.''
Â 
Survey of Student Interest
Yet most like her do not have time to commute, said the vice president of the Chinese Students Club, Min-yuan Tung, a senior in the department of electrical engineering and computer science, from St. Clairesville, Ohio.
The club, representing a group that makes up the larger part of M.I.T.'s 800 Asian undergraduates, distributed surveys to several hundred students during the first week of December, asking about their interests in studying Chinese. 
One club member, Rebecca Kao, a senior from Framingham, Mass., who is majoring in electrical engineering and computer science, said the survey results indicated that a large number of students would be interested in studying Chinese if classes were taught at M.I.T.
''Our long-range goal,'' Mr. Lundberg said, ''is to establish an area studies program for Asia.''
''We've got lots of bits and pieces,'' he said. 
''But a big gap is that we don't teach the Chinese language.''
M.I.T. offered courses in Chinese from 1976 to 1980 jointly with Wellesley, but the program was discontinued after a disagreement. 
Several M.I.T. groups, including the Chinese Students Club and the Asian Working Group, have since sought the reinstatement of the Chinese classes.
The Asian Working Group is made up of faculty members like Richard J. Samuels, who directs the M.I.T. 
Japan science and technology program, and Tunney Lee, head of M.I.T.'s urban studies and planning department, who are interested in promoting awareness of Asian cultures and values.
Last fall, the Chinese Students Club members met with various administration officials, including Ann F. Friedlaender, the dean of the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. 
As acting head of the foreign languages and literature section, Mrs. Friedlaender would be responsible for the establishment of the Chinese classes.
''Institutionally, if you were to ask anyone if Chinese should be taught at M.I.T., the answer would overwhelmingly be, 'yes.'
'' she said. 
''But M.I.T. is in a budget deficit. 
In that situation there is a reluctance to start new programs.''
If M.I.T. receives financing from the Chiang Ching-kuo Foundation, it may take up to a year for the institute to find and hire faculty members to teach the courses, Mrs. Friedlaender said. 
In that case, M.I.T. may accept help from Wellesley College's Chinese department, which would provide instructors until M.I.T. hires permanent ones.
Miss Li, whose parents speak Cantonese, said she wanted to study Chinese to learn about the culture. 
(The New York Times/Rick Friedman)

file: Can Choosing Form of Care Become Neglect_.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Juliet Cheng was called in to Newington Children's Hospital in July, she thought it was for a final consultation about the health of her 7-year-old daughter, who suffers from severe juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, before they returned to China for medical treatment there.
Instead, a security man and social workers charged her with neglect and placed her daughter, Shirley, into temporary state custody.
The allegation of neglect rests with Ms. Cheng's refusal to agree to surgery for her daughter's legs. 
Without it, the hospital says, Shirley will never be able to walk. 
But Ms. Cheng, who was born in China and is a naturalized United States citizen, says she does not trust American doctors. 
She wants to return to her native country to try other, more traditional and familiar, options first, like physical therapy and herbal medicine.
A juvenile court judge has authorized surgery on the child's hips, knees and ankles, but the procedure has been twice scheduled and postponed as Ms. Cheng's lawyer, George Athanson, takes the case through state and Federal courts. 
He is seeking a full hearing, with testimony by Asian as well as Western physicians.
The case is now in Federal District Court in Hartford, where Judge T. Emmet Clarie is deciding whether it is a Federal matter and, if so, whether to grant a temporary restraining order. 
''If he grants the order,'' Mr. Athanson said, ''we'll have a full hearing on a preliminary injunction, and then we'll bring in the doctors.''
Ms. Cheng, 39, moved to this country in 1980. 
She has a mother and a sister living in the Poughkeepsie, N.Y., area, where she lived until moving to Newington for her daughter's treatment. 
She is separated from her husband, whom she met in the United States.
Although the case recalls medical confrontations over the rights of parents to withhold treatment from their children, this incident deals with what Ms Cheng and her lawyer say is the right of a parent to choose a particular form of treatment.
Ms. Cheng says she is not opposed to medical intervention and has consented to physical therapy, the use of casts and anti-inflammatory medication prescribed by specialists including her physician, Dr. Lawrence Zemel. 
Newington doctors, for their part, have permitted Ms. Cheng to continue to administer Chinese medication and to have her daughter treated by a practitioner of homeopathic medicine.
Â 
Agency Is Said to Be Insensitive
The dispute comes at a time when the State Department of Children and Youth Services, which has temporary custody of Shirley Cheng, has been criticized for what people have called a series of inadequacies and is being rebuked in hearings throughout the state. 
A three-member panel is hearing testimony in a class action suit that the Connecticut Civil Liberties Union brought nine months ago on behalf of nine children.
At a hearing in the class action suit, Carolyn Richter, a lawyer for Connecticut Legal Services, offered examples Wednesday night of what she said were the agency's overbearing and insensitive operations. 
After the hearing, she said the Cheng case ''is an example of the medical establishment deciding they have the truth of the matter and totally disparaging alternate forms of medicine.''
Ms. Cheng ''only wants to try other options first,'' Ms. Richter said. 
''What is outrageous is that powerful people, the institutions and the doctors, are throwing away a brand of medicine practiced by two-thirds of the world. 
That's cavalier.''
''If there is still time, as we understand it, the state should not have stepped in,'' Ms. Richter said. 
She was referring to testimony that Dr. Zemel was said to have given in juvenile court, where proceedings are closed to the public, that the operation need not take place for two years. 
Mr. Athanson said he had a transcript of Dr. Zemel's testimony to that effect.
Â 
Hospital's View
Mr. Athanson also argued that ''Western medicine has made great advances, but we don't harbor all medical knowledge in the world. 
Some of the things that have been used in China for thousands of years may be helpful here.''
Dr. Zemel, a specialist in pediatric rheumatology, has declined to discuss the case or to respond to the statement that Mr. Athanson said he made in closed court, but Dr. Julius Landwirth, vice president for medical affairs at Newington, spoke for him and for the hospital.
''When Shirley was referred to us, she was absolutely crippled,'' Dr. Landwirth said. 
He said that physical therapy and medication had proved unsuccessful ''because her joints were so contracted, so frozen, that it was impossible to straighten them out using the usual procedures.''
''The problem arises when the only opportunity to prevent this child from living with a lifelong crippling condition is being denied her,'' he said. 
''It is then appropriate, when either a life-threatening condition or a condition with lifelong crippling implications exists, that a physician and an institution need to raise the question of possible medical neglect.''
''It's not up to us to decide that,'' he said. 
''It's up to the child protection agency and the court to answer that question.''
Dr. Landwirth also asserted that it was ''not the same as saying we have a culture gap because the child has been receiving care with nontraditional medicines in addition to the traditional ones.
Â 
Best Interests of the Child
''Nor is it an issue of physicians and the hospital overriding the rights of a mother to make decisions. 
The question is, given a serious lifelong irreversible handicapping condition that will preclude this child from ever getting out of a wheelchair and with treatment available to relieve that condition, does a parent have a right to deny that or is that denial a form of medical neglect.''
He said the surgery would relieve the tightness around the girl's joints. 
''We don't really go into the joints; it's a matter of releasing the tension on the ligaments and tendons that surround the joint. 
They are all tightened up and shortened; they need to be released and lengthened.''
A spokesman for the Department of Children and Youth Services, Tom Moriarty, said, ''What the Newington doctors and we are saying, and the courts have so far agreed, is that what the mother wants to do is not in the best interests of the child.''
Ms. Cheng, who visits her daughter twice a day, said: ''Shirley is very upset in the hospital. 
Every time she sees me she asks me to take her out of her chair. 
She doesn't want to do the surgery. 
I just want her back so we can return to China.''

file: Canton Journal_The Pastor_s Good for a Sermon, Even in Prison.txt
text:
ï»¿
The floors creak, the stools sway, and a peasant mother soothes a baby tired from the two-hour trek they have taken to this dilapidated house-church. 
But the congregation sits rapt as the Rev. Lin Xiangao bellows out his sermon on Elijah.
This cramped two-story tenement is Pastor Lin's home as well as an illegal church. 
Every week, 700 to 1,000 Chinese workers, peasants and students file through a narrow lane and climb the steep and dark stairway to join one of a dozen services or prayer meetings.
Because of his religious beliefs, Pastor Lin, a frail 66-year-old with sparkling eyes, has been jailed twice, for a total of more than 21 years. 
His wife and mother died while he was doing prison labor.
But even in prison camp in the Cultural Revolution, while hooking up rail cars in a coal mine in Shanxi Province, Mr. Lin dared to preach to his fellow convicts.
"I've been in prison twice," said Mr. Lin, a Baptist pastor who also goes by the English name of Samuel Lamb. 
"I'm ready for a third time."
Â 
Number of Conflicts Grows
China officially says it has 5 million Protestants and 3.5 million Catholics, and it generally allows them to worship freely if they follow certain guidelines and support the Government. 
Many other Chinese profess Christianity but want to have nothing to do with the officially established church. 
As a result, there has been a growing number of conflicts over the last two years.
On one side are the religious leaders who believe that church and state should be separated. 
On the other side is a Government that fears the spread of a belief that it cannot control and that might challenge Communism.
Pastors like Mr. Lin who are practicing without Government approval have been drawn into a long battle with the authorities. 
The United States State Department estimated in its report on human rights that as many as 50 Christian leaders in China had been detained or imprisoned by the end of last year.
While there are no figures on the underground church, various reports in China have suggested that both the Protestant and Catholic followings have been growing steadily, and some estimates put the real number of adherents at many times the official number.
"The Government doesn't like our church because we preach according to the Bible, including the second coming of Christ, and they don't," Mr. Lin said. 
"Our faith is controlled by God, not by man, especially not by nonbelievers. 
As a civilian, I am controlled by the Government. 
But my faith is controlled by God."
Many senior religious officials in China are Communist Party members and are therefore not allowed to belong to any religious congregation. 
While they say they sympathize with religious men, they cannot understand why people like Mr. Lin will not abide by Government rules.
"Why must he practice his own religion when there are already so many places for him to go here in China?" said Liu Wenyan, director of religious affairs in Guangdong Province, of which Canton is the capital. 
"We just can't allow this kind of citizen. 
But we aren't arresting him."
The Government insists that Mr. Lin register with the official church organization, the Three-Self Patriotic Movement Committee, which is China's independent church and which is founded on the principles of self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating. 
Officials have offered him a nice, large church, which would allow him to expand his following. 
They also detained him briefly in February 1990, and have interrogated him nearly a dozen times in in the last two years.
Mr. Lin responds that registering would give the Government too much control over what he can preach. 
He says the regulations in the official church are too restrictive and sometimes relate Communism to the church. 
Moreover, he says, they would dictate how long his sermons should be and what topics he should avoid discussing. 
Mr. Lin sometimes preaches for two hours at a time.
Â 
Prejudiced, Officials Say
But officials say Mr. Lin is prejudiced against the Government, and this presumably makes them uneasy about his sermons. 
They add that Mr. Lin is a bit crazy.
"There is something wrong with his thinking," said Mr. Liu, who says he has never met Mr. Lin. "When some followers get sick, he tells them not to go to a doctor."
Indeed, Mr. Lin preaches that he has been cured of illness by God and not by medicine. 
He says that one of his most striking memories from childhood is his recovery from an illness when doctors predicted he would not survive. 
He was cured, he says, when his father, also a Baptist pastor, gathered family and friends together to pray through the night for him.
Nonetheless, Mr. Lin has a solid following, and each week people crowd into his tiny quarters to listen to his sermons or come for a chat, a baptism or some religious advice. 
He has followers who visit from Hong Kong, and even Billy Graham stopped by Mr. Lin's church three years ago. 
Wealthy visitors have made contributions to Mr. Lin's church, including a sound system.
Â 
'I Preached to Them'
In the past, Mr. Lin used Bibles supplied by a Hong Kong churchgoer, but last year the authorities confiscated all his religious texts, hymn books and other materials. 
Now he uses Bibles furnished by the Three-Self Movement, which he says are complete versions of the Bible.
Each time there is a crackdown on religion, he says, he expects to be harassed. 
One time he was asked whether he took part in the Tiananmen democracy movement and he said he had not. 
On another occasion, he was asked whether there was truly a resurrection of Christ.
"They asked me, 'Is there a real God?' and I preached to them," Mr. Lin said. 
"They asked me, 'Was Jesus really resurrected?' and I preached to them again."

file: Capital Flees an Edgy Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
The signs of fear are everywhere in Hong Kong, economists, bankers and brokers say, from the Chinese women crowding into little shops to buy small bars of gold, to the thousands of residents patiently lining up in the hot June sun for immigration forms from the Canadian, Australian or American consulates.
''In one day, our bank received $25 million in new business, most of it attributable to the China situation,'' said one foreign banker. 
Another Western banker estimated total new business at $5 million.
From the bustling Chinese street stalls of Mong Kok to the glittering skyscrapers of the central business district, the British colony of Hong Kong has become anxious and edgy because its future is so closely tied to the repressive Chinese regime just across the border.
In the last few weeks, as the tumultuous events in China have moved from a student rebellion to a military crackdown, overseas investment and property brokers have reported a surge in requests from residents who want to get their money off the island.
Â 
Sharp Stock Market Decline
One measure of the disquiet is the decline in the Hong Kong Stock Market since May 18, the last stable trading day before the Chinese turmoil. 
The Hang Seng Index at that market has fallen by 922.47 points, or 28 percent, to 2,355.10, in that period. 
Brokers say that most small investors here have been dumping stocks, and that foreigners have also been selling.
One broker said, ''Unless they like gambling in a casino, locals won't put money back in the market in the near future.''
Foreign banks also report increased business from Hong Kong Chinese who want to open offshore accounts.
''There are no statistics on this subject, just vague estimates and gut feelings about what is happening,'' said one American banker. 
''And my feeling is money is moving. 
But we're talking about personal accounts of wealthy Chinese,'' not pullouts by major businesses. 
Investment capital, he said, ''isn't that mobile, and it takes more time to detect movement there.''
Â 
'Money Is Moving'
Just how much capital is fleeing Hong Kong is anyone's guess. 
The Government, celebrated for its laissez-faire approach to business, places virtually no controls on the movement of money into and out of Hong Kong, and banks here respect secrecy laws that rival those of Switzerland.
Robert Broadfoot, a consultant, said, ''Much of the direct investment capital here now will stay because it is tied up in big projects, but I think new capital investments will slow down. 
Business money will be looking for overseas opportunities, hotels in Canada or the United States, that kind of thing.''
He added, ''I think foreign institutional investors will be liquidating their stock holdings here with each slight rise in the stock market.''
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control in 1997, and as China continues its violent repression, residents here are losing faith that officials in Beijing will abide by their pledges to leave the colony's economic and political freedoms intact. 
Moreover, half of the 5.7 million residents here are Chinese immigrants who fled the violence and persecution of the Communists in the 1950's and 1960's, many losing homes and profitable businesses.
Stephen Yu, vice president and branch manager of the National Bank of Canada, said the recent repression in China had made some of his depositors so edgy that ''they insisted we redomicile their deposits, even though these were Canadian dollar accounts in our bank.''
He added, ''We are a branch of the main bank, not even a subsidiary, but they wanted that money moved offshore because they were so worried the Chinese Army might march in and seize it here.''
Â 
Outflow Started in '84
Since 1984, when Britain agreed to return Hong Kong, businesses here have been moving large blocks of their capital overseas, but offsetting that move have been investments in Hong Kong by ompanies, which are anticipating trade and business opportunities in China.
''While substantial capital has been leaving Hong Kong, that outflow has been balanced by an inflow of foreign money from Japan, Europe, the United States, and I am not certain now that that balance will continue,'' said Miron Mushkat, director of economic research at Baring Securities. 
''In light of the events in China, I think the outflow is intensifying, and I think there is a chance the inflow will diminish.''
''There is a lot of panicky conversion going on now among wealthy Chinese, and while some of that will taper off when there is stabilityI, even negative stabilityI in China, it won't stop,'' he added.
Mr. Broadfoot, who is managing director of Political and Economic Risk Consultancy Ltd., said he thought the Chinese were ''liquefying all their assets now - stocks, houses, cars.''
He added: ''They are putting their deposits in offshore accounts, making significant movements into gold. 
They are poised for flight, but I don't think it has really started yet.''
Alex Fung, manager of the investment department of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, said that in the last few weeks, the Hong Kong Chinese had been moving ''a substantial amount'' of money, transferring it out of the colony through offshore accounts, bond purchases or other short-term foreign investments.
Â 
'Confirmed the Worst Fears'
''The events in China have confirmed the very worst fears of many Hong Kong people, and if they were even thinking of leaving or sending their money out, their decision is now definite,'' said Mark Michelson, vice president of Business International Asia/Pacific, a consulting firm.
Another Hong Kong banker said a number of local Chinese were so fretful that ''they have been breaking into fixed-deposit accounts and accepting the penalties.''
He added, ''They want to move their money right now, because they are very uncertain about the future.''
Last year, the Government estimated conservatively that 45,000 people emigrated from Hong Kong, taking their assets with them. 
Most went to Canada, Australia or the United States. 
And experts expect those numbers to be even more dramatic now.
Richard Grams, a manager of overseas investment and migration, said: ''Calls about emigrating have increased fourfold. 
Yesterday alone, we received 273 phone calls or visits from people interested in emigrating.''
He added: ''The people who leave Hong Kong take with them substantial amounts of money, plus their own business expertise and skills.''
And residents who once thought they had time to make more money in Hong Kong before they left, ''now want out as soon as possible, and they want their money out too,'' Mr. Grams said.

file: Capitalist-Style Layoffs Ignite Sabotage and Strikes in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Worried by layoffs and rising prices, many Chinese workers seem increasingly disenchanted by the capitalist-style changes taking hold in shops and factory floors around the country.
As a result, for the first time since China began liberalizing its economy more than a dozen years ago, many ordinary citizens seem to be no longer agents of change but obstacles to it. 
Workers in several cities have attacked factory directors who have tried to introduce market-oriented changes, and there are growing reports of strikes and acts of sabotage.
Those incidents suggest that opposition to fundamental change is increasingly coming not only from octogenarian Communist hard-liners but also from many ordinary blue-collar workers.
Â 
Fear and Fury?
Similar tensions have erupted throughout the former Communist bloc. 
While China has been able to avoid deep social upheavals associated with "shock therapy" in other countries, the experience here suggests that even a gradual weaning away from central planning can lead to widespread fear and sometimes fury.
"There's enormous frustration out there with the reforms," a Chinese economic official said. 
"The leaders are running scared."
What alarms the leadership is cases like that of Huang Chuanying, a bank director whom the official Chinese press hailed as "a daring reformer."
Mr. Huang tried to curb the Maoist-style labor practices that have crippled state-owned enterprises all over China, and he began dismissing bank employees considered incompetent and unproductive.
One dismissed staff member, Cao Weihua, responded by firebombing Mr. Huang's house, severely wounding Mr. Huang, his wife and their two children. 
Mr. Cao was sentenced to death recently, but the incident seemed to reflect a broad concern among many Chinese that while a market economy may be more prosperous and efficient than a Communist one, it may also be less cozy.
The contrast is profound with the mood in most of the last dozen years, when ordinary Chinese were ardent backers of change. 
In those years, they often took the initiative and pushed liberalization more quickly than the Politburo intended.
"Reform used to be very easy and rewarding," a Chinese journalist said. 
"In the 1980's, it meant dividing up the land, and starting up free markets, and opening new businesses, and everybody loved it."
But in the 1990's, the agenda is different. 
While virtually all Chinese endorse "reform" as a general slogan, many workers worry about what it will mean: higher rents, rising rice prices, and destroying the "iron rice bowl" system that guarantees workers stable employment and steady incomes.
Â 
The Changing Rice Bowl
According to a folk ditty now making the rounds among workers: Before liberation, we had a clay rice bowl. 
Then Chairman Mao gave us an iron rice bowl. 
Deng Xiaoping poked a hole in it. 
Since reform, we've had a porcelain rice bowl.
"A porcelain rice bowl looks rather elegant," a manual laborer in her 40's explained dryly. 
"But it's no more sturdy than one made of clay."
A 26-year-old woman who works in a factory said that when she was in the university, she believed that most Chinese wanted more economic liberalization. 
But now she figures that aside from intellectuals, many people are against fundamental changes.
"We need housing reform and price reform, but nobody wants them," she said. 
"Who wants to pay more?
I figure that in my factory, 80 percent of the workers believe in the iron rice bowl system."
That may well be exaggeration, for most workers interviewed seem to be not so much hostile to change as worried by it. 
And while some are openly opposed, there also is a significant proportion that favors dog-eat-dog capitalism and believes that economic liberalization should be speeded up.
Â 
Weaning From Subsidies
Many of the problems arose because China's leaders have finally taken Western advice and moved to impose a market discipline on state-owned enterprises, one-third of which lose money. 
Exasperated by continuing inefficiency in those enterprises, China's leadership has waged a campaign since last year to wean factories from subsidies and expose them to market pressures.
As a result, a few factories began to dismiss workers considered unproductive, a practice that almost never occurred in the past. 
There is also talk of layoffs to trim the 26 percent overstaffing that the Government admits exists in state enterprises.
While many Chinese, particularly the university educated, say that such changes are essential, blue-collar workers are less enthusiastic. 
For the first time, a significant sector of the population, though probably not a majority, seems to be siding with Communist hard-liners in discouraging rapid market-style changes.
Early this year, a laid-off driver at a toothpaste factory drove his truck over his boss, a pioneering manager who had shaken up his factory by adopting Western-style management practices. 
The central Government suggested that the factory manager be hailed as a "martyr" for reform, but the factory workers refused to nominate the manager for the honor, said the official who related the incident.
In another case, reported in the official press, a 27-year-old factory worker was sentenced several weeks ago to 15 years in prison for shooting at his boss at a factory in Shanxi Province. 
The worker, who failed to wound the manager, had been dismissed last year.

Machinery Smashed
Factories in Xian, Tianjin and Dalian were reportedly also disrupted by angry workers, and in some cases machinery was smashed. 
After a watch factory in Tianjin temporarily laid off 2,400 workers early this year, rumors of suicides, sabotage and military intervention rapidly spread throughout Beijing. 
The official Economic Daily recently denied the allegations, and said the factory had retooled and reopened, providing jobs for all but 300 of the previous workers.
"The Government's talking about smashing our iron rice bowls, and making us pay for our own medical care," said a 29-year-old worker in Beijing. 
"Companies are even beginning to lay off workers!
Of course folks are angry."
To be sure, apprehension of market-style changes is common around the world, from Russians who fear rising bread prices to New Yorkers who worry about lifting controls on rent.
"We're very different from the former Soviet Union," said a Chinese Government economist who has studied former Communist economies. 
"We already have a foundation of a market, and people can get jobs on their own if they have to. 
The changes may not be pleasant, but we can take it. 
But in Russia, there's no real market to speak of, the economy is shrinking, and all the changes have been introduced very abruptly."
Han Dongfang, an independent labor organizer who was released a year ago after serving two years in prison, argues that the Government is caught in a dilemma.
"To raise living standards, the Government needs to go ahead with economic reform," Mr. Han said. 
"But reform will involve trampling on the rights of workers, and a lot of people won't be very happy about it. 
These contradictions will grow in the next few years."

file: Changes in China Offer Lessons for East Europe.txt
text:
ï»¿
When China specialists think about how Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union can reorganize their economies, they tend to agree on one point: transforming socialist countries into market competitors will be a far more complex and painful task than is often acknowledged.
The Chinese experience is relevant, diplomats and academics say, because China generally has a richer and more successful experience in economic liberalization than its socialist brethren. 
While political changes, symbolized by the Russian word glasnost, lag here, few experts dispute that China has the upper hand in the economic restructuring known as perestroika.
''If Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union do as well in the next 10 years as China has in the last 10 years, they will have done extremely well,'' said Gregory Chow, an economist at Princeton University.
Even after a dozen years of economic change, China is still grappling with some Herculean problems. 
But its achievements are also Herculean: until 1989, China's real growth rates averaged nearly 10 percent a year, among the highest in the world; shops and free markets are as bountiful as the Soviet Union's are bare; lavish joint-venture hotels and international direct-dial telephones are found in major cities; agriculture has been de-collectivized, and the state sector's share of industry has fallen to about 60 percent.
Â 
Successes and Mistakes
Thomas M. H. Chan, an economist at the Hong Kong Baptist College, observed, ''China may not be a solution for Eastern Europe, because it still has to find a solution for its own problems, but its examples of successes and its mistakes may be useful for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.''
Mr. Chan noted that one of the main engines of China's economic growth in the last decade has been the township and village enterprises that have sprouted in coastal areas. 
More flexible and tuned to the markets rather than state-run behemoths, these small factories produce goods ranging from sweaters to plastic flowers. 
Mr. Chan suggested that Eastern Europe might study such enterprises to see if they could increase production there as well.
One area in which China has been most successful is in cultivating exports and integrating itself into the world economy. 
Nicholas Lardy, a China scholar at the University of Washington, said the Soviet Union should note China's relatively realistic valuation of the yuan and its use of currency swap markets to allocate $8 billion in foreign exchange last year.
For some economists, there is another lesson in the Chinese experience: national leaders should resist advice to free prices immediately. 
While these experts agree that irrational prices are a major burden for the economy, they suggest that decontrolling prices overnight will hurt the public and turn them against the entire liberalization program.
Â 
A Crucial Lesson
''The most important lesson of the Chinese experience is that price reform is not essential to reform,'' a Government economist said. 
''The most essential reform is that of the fundamental economic system, of ownership and management.''
Hua Sheng, a Chinese economist now studying at Oxford University, put it more strongly, ''It seems to me that to start with price reform is a very stupid idea, because the Government will become very unpopular.''
Mr. Hua noted that the Soviet Union had to back off earlier this year from a radical proposal to free prices, just as China had to retreat in the summer of 1988 from a plan to decontrol prices.
That 1988 proposal in China was followed by waves of panic buying and a steep rise in inflation. 
It also marked a watershed, for since then some urban residents have been soured on the whole idea of economic restructuring, and the Chinese leadership has been reluctant to push much further with any major initiative for economic change.
Delaying price decontrols is not a universal prescription, and there is still a camp of Chinese and foreign economists who believe that price liberalization is an essential starting point. 
They say that the chaos that began in the summer of 1988 in China was a result not of price decontrols but of an easy monetary policy. 
Without a prompt if painful adjustment to rational prices, they say, there is no way out of the economic quagmire.
Â 
An Impossible Task
Mr. Hua, who left China for Oxford early last year, said that the task that he and other economists faced in socialist countries, to combine public ownership with a market mechanism, was virtually impossible to complete satisfactorily.
''For the Soviet Union, the most important lesson is that public ownership doesn't work,'' Mr. Hua said. 
''If you want to carry out reform seriously, you have to carry out ownership reform, and denationalize industry on a large scale.''
Mr. Hua urged governments to sell off state factories and other assets to reduce their budget deficits and raise funds. 
He said those funds could then be used to sweeten the process and soothe the pain when prices were freed.

Americans may have missed it, but they are engaged in a bitter and deceitful conspiracy of sabotage and infiltration called "peaceful evolution," aimed at subjugating the Chinese people under the horrors of capitalism and imperialism.
That, in any case, is the view presented by the Chinese leaders to their people. 
The harsh language does not usually appear in China's English-language publications, which still maintain a smiling face to the outside world. 
But in the Chinese-language news media, the alarms are shrill, vehement and growing.

He added that if all Chinese rally together, "we can surely defeat the criminal designs of domestic and foreign hostile forces as well as peaceful evolution."

Western 'Power Politics' Seen

Diplomat's View

file: Changsha Journal_In China_s Cities, the Busybodies Are Organized.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Wang Xingzhou's wife threatened to divorce him, he ran down the block to the street committee. 
Soon a team of elderly women filed into his tiny apartment and showered his wife with a dozen reasons why the couple should stay together.
Their foreheads wrinkled with concern, the women offered to buy winter coal for the wife whenever the husband had to be out of town. 
They pleaded that, for the sake of the three children, the couple not separate.
"They always help out whenever there is a conflict," said Mr. Wang, a construction worker. 
"Unfortunately, the street committee couldn't solve this problem and we got divorced."
In cities all over China, street committees, quasi-governmental, quasi-civilian groups that sprang up after the Communist revolution in 1949, are the central Government's nimble tentacles, winding around corners, climbing up stairwells and peering into people's homes and private lives. 
The street committees have become the main link between the leaders and ordinary people.
Â 
Many Functions
Sniffing and snooping, these energetic busybodies -- often retired men and women who work as volunteers -- poke into all kinds of family disputes and tussles between neighbors. 
In some cities, residents snidely refer to them as the "xiaojiao zhenjidui," or tiny-footed inspection teams, after the old women with bound feet who were originally on the street committees' staffs.
At times these committees function as therapist, at times as utility company, at times as patrol unit, always trying to prod, scold, nudge and push the Government's policies down to the masses.
For instance, street committees are instrumental in carrying out China's family planning policies, and on the walls of street committee offices hang charts describing the child-bearing profile of the neigborhood: how many women are taking contraceptives, what kind of contraceptives they take, who has had an abortion and how many women must be monitored for family planning.
If a woman is pregnant, then the street committee also keeps track, trying to insure that the newborn will be the first and only child of the family. 
If the mother becomes pregnant a second time, the street committee will notify the woman's work unit in case it does not already know.
"We don't force them to have only one child," said Luo Ping, the director of a street committee here in Changsha, in Hunan Province in southern China. 
"We do ideological work and sometimes go to their house to spread our views."
Â 
Food Coupons Distributed
Ms. Luo heads the street committee in Wang Jiazhou, a tree-lined neighborhood of new apartment buildings in Changsha. 
Some 700 families live in the area monitored by the street committee, which has Ms. Luo as its only paid employee and 12 other core members. 
In addition, a network of representatives lives in each building.
Like other street committees throughout China, this one distributes grain and food coupons every month to the residents, and sometimes it works closely with Government departments, like the Health Department, when it needs to notify children's parents of a vaccination schedule.
Street committees also help take care of hygiene, running water and public security. 
In Wang Jiazhou, the patrol guards work in teams of two or three, scouting for robbers or more mundane threats. 
The guards say they have never encountered a robber, and often the patrol encounters nothing more alarming than a sock that has fallen from a clothesline.
"I spotted a little girl picking a branch from a tree, and I told her that we need to protect the trees and she shouldn't cut down the branches," said Yang Zhiqing, a 52-year-old retired woman, as she described her morning patrol in Wang Jiazhou. 
"I also mediated a quarrel. 
Two kids were fighting and I stopped them."
Â 
Mechanisms of the State
In the past, these street committees were viewed as control mechanisms of the state, putting into effect Government campaigns, registering late-night visitors to the house of a resident, or reporting on other unusual behavior of any of the residents. 
This control function remains, but many street committees have expanded their scope and taken on practical tasks, like setting up bicycle parking lots or local businesses to earn money.
They also preserve the Communist life of the neighborhood and hold political study sessions and stage activities to promote the pantheon of Communist heroes, like Lei Feng, a soldier. 
A few miles away, in the Chaoyang No. 1 Village -- a misnomer because it is actually a neighborhood of intertwining curvy lanes and boxy streets in Changsha city -- the street committee plans a campaign in March to "study Lei Feng."
Most urban residents are already closely monitored by their "work units," so the street committee particularly scrutinizes those few people -- like private entrepreneurs and the unemployed -- who have no work unit. 
Still, the members and their volunteers keep their eyes and ears open all the time; they keep tabs on residents, know where they work and what their habits are like.
If two neighbors are yelling at each other, a street committee member is likely to hear about it and step in. 
Large disputes get recorded in a log in the street committee office. 
Last year, for example, the Chaoyang No. 1 Village recorded 26 conflicts among its more than 1,000 households.
"Our political goal is to educate people to live harmoniously and act peacefully," said Liu Zhenming, a district official that oversees the Chaoyang No. 1 Village. 
"In America, if you don't have a street committee, where do you go when you have a problem?"

Israeli officials have strongly denied such technology leaks since reports about them came to light last week. 
Speaking to reporters after meeting Mr. Cheney, Mr. Arens repeated the denials and said Israel had agreed to cooperate with American experts who will travel to Israel to investigate the claims.
The State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, told reporters today that Israel had agreed over the weekend to accept inspectors.
