text:
ï»¿
The streets of this provincial capital are paved not with gold but with a layer of asphalt topped with dust, mud and decaying cabbage leaves, but still the peasants troop here in search of jobs and a new life.
''You can make a lot more money in the city,'' said Gao Jingru, a lithe 53-year-old in a Mao suit. 
Mr. Gao brings odd-shaped stones and fossils from his village 50 miles away to sell to the residents of Chengdu, and in a good month he can earn the equivalent of more than $32 - 10 times as much as he would earn in his village.
The market street in Chengdu and many other Chinese cities is full of migrant laborers like Mr. Gao, and they pose a growing challenge to the Government. 
About 50 million people in China, nearly 5 percent of the nation's population, are migrants, and increasingly they are beyond the tight control of the Government.
The economic slowdown, particularly the closing of millions of rural enterprises, could add to the number of migrants. 
Official figures indicate that China's countryside has about 80 million surplus laborers, including 10 million here in Sichuan Province. 
Many seem to be remaining in their villages rather than swarming to the cities, where jobs are also tough to find, but their movements are difficult to predict.
Â 
Ignoring Restrictions
Unlike most developing countries, where peasants have always rushed to the cities and put up shantytowns on the outskirts, China has tried to control people's movements through a complex household registration system. 
Chinese citizens are not supposed to move without getting their registration changed, but these days many people simply ignore the requirements and move anyway.
''If the city needs my things, then I'll be here selling,'' said Chen Kailie, 47 years old, who moved to Chengdu from a village 20 miles away to sell flower pots. 
''If I can't make ends meet, then I'll go back to my hometown.''
The swelling tide of migrant laborers is one of the clearest signs that China's old command structure is wearing down. 
In major cities like Chengdu, Beijing and Shanghai, more than 10 percent of the inhabitants are migrants who come and go largely as they please. 
China has a complex web of ''street committees'' to watch over urban residents and make sure they do not cause political problems or have unauthorized children, but this system of scrutiny does not succeed in controlling those who do not belong in the first place.
The existence of this large ''floating population,'' as the Chinese call it, helps explain how student leaders of last year's crushed democracy movement have been able to elude the security apparatus for months. 
Five or ten years ago, most Chinese say confidently, the student leaders would have been arrested promptly; these days, they can simply blend in with the flow of other wanderers.
Â 
Enlivening the Economy
The migrants also present a more direct challenge: Like Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping and other Chinese revolutionaries, they are peasants who go to the cities and risk picking up dangerous political ideas. 
In last year's rioting in cities like Beijing, Changsha and Chengdu, migrants played a significant role, perhaps partly because they were less likely to be identified and caught than permanent residents.
Government officials, like Yan Cheng, the deputy secretary general of the Chengdu municipality, acknowledge that the floating population creates some difficulties for family planning and for public security, but he adds that on the whole it is a good thing because it enlivens the economy.
''This is an economic phenomenon, not a political problem,'' said Mr. Yan, who noted that the peasant migrants fill an important niche by selling farm products and filling jobs in service industries in the city. 
In Beijing, always the most security-conscious of Chinese cities, the police have made periodic efforts to round up migrants and send them home, but in other cities officials point to the services they provide and seem to regard them as a blessing.
''It's reality beating ideology,'' said Aprodicio Laquian, who recently completed a term as country director in China for the United Nations Fund for Population Activities. 
''The migrants will really be the salvation of China, because they solve needs that central planning can't.''
That also seems to be the view of most urban residents, who are sometimes contemptuous of the migrants' unkempt appearance and uncouth manners but appreciate being able to find a business where the service is attentive and the hours are long -even if it consists only of cabbages in a cart or old magazines spread on a blanket on a sidewalk.
''We think the floating population is terrific,'' said the owner of a small business in Chengdu. 
''Why?
Because we can exploit them. 
They're willing to work hard in exchange for just enough money to buy some food. 
We need them and they need us. 
It's a great partnership.''

file: Children_s Books.txt
text:
ï»¿
A YOUNG PAINTER
The Life and Paintings of Wang Yani --
China's Extraordinary Young Artist.
By Zheng Zhensun and Alice Low.
Illustrated. 80 pp. 
New York:
A Byron Preiss/
New China Pictures Book/
Scholastic. $17.95.
(Ages 8 and up)
DOTING parents tend to see promise in even the most muddled brushstrokes of a beloved toddler. 
But while most must eventually acknowledge that their child is not Picasso in Pampers, Wang Shiqiang, a painter from Gongcheng, China, had a different experience. 
Mr. Wang's daughter, Yani, who was born in 1975 and began drawing at age 2, proved to be indeed a prodigy: when she was 4, her art was shown in several Chinese cities, and one of her early monkey paintings, "Scratching an Itch for Mother," was reproduced as a postage stamp. 
Now 16, Yani has had solo exhibitions in Japan, Hong Kong, Germany, Britain and the United States, including a display at the Smithsonian Institution two years ago.
"A Young Painter" by Zheng Zhensun, a Chinese journalist and photographer, and Alice Low, an American children's-book author and art teacher, is the story of Yani's career, told in both words and pictures. 
Not surprisingly, the latter are more effective in revealing Yani's artistic evolution. 
Filled with beautifully reproduced examples of her paintings -- some in foldouts for greater detail -- the book shows how Yani has progressed from droll portraits of monkeys and cats to bolder, more abstract renderings of people and landscapes. 
The accompanying text often gives her explanation of the works, revealing a child with tremendous imagination. 
One painting done when she was 4, "Is There a Moon on the Water?," depicts a baby monkey and its mother, searching the sky reflected in the river.
But though young readers will be thoroughly familiar with the artist's work when they finish the book, it is less likely that they will feel they know Yani. 
Except for commentary on specific paintings, her voice is strangely absent. 
Even many of the observations about her art seem to be her father's. 
And the authors offer little in the way of reflections from Yani on her personal life, seeming content to describe her rather than allowing her to portray herself.
Granted, extremes of self-revelation are hardly prized in Chinese culture, and Yani is characterized as both modest and somewhat shy. 
But since she is now an adolescent whose metier is self-expression, it seems odd that she has not played a greater role in this book. 
At times, a reader gets the impression that this is more her father's book. 
While the child's mother and brother are mentioned only in passing, Mr. Wang appears on virtually every page.
A related problem is the authors' uncritical appraisal of Yani's upbringing. 
While it is impossible to know how much of the writing is Mr. Zheng's and how much is Ms. Low's, the text implicitly endorses a child-rearing style that will strike many Westerners as rather rigid. 
Although no one can question the sacrifices Mr. Wang has made for his daughter -- he has even given up his own successful career -- it is disingenuous to claim, as the authors repeatedly do, that he has allowed her almost unlimited artistic freedom. 
Once, for example, Yani began to paint a bridge, only to be told by her father that "a bridge is not pleasing to the eye."
ON another occasion, Mr. Wang criticized Yani harshly for becoming upset when she was giving a demonstration and a stranger knocked over a cup on her worktable. 
He told her that she must stop painting if she could not be serious. 
Not bad advice, except that Yani was all of 4 1/2 at the time. 
It is hard to believe that American children will find this vignette sympathetic, much less inspirational.
While Mr. Zheng and Ms. Low ignore cultural differences in child rearing, they do examine them in relation to art. 
Wang Yani paints in the age-old Chinese style, and a helpful appendix describes both the tools and the techniques used to achieve it. 
Interestingly, her choice of techniques is very different from that of her father, who opted for oil painting instead of traditional ink and pigments. 
We can only wonder how she feels about the large role he plays in her life and career. 
But if the authors' portrait of Yani could use considerably more detail, her own work beckons and intrigues. 
It is testimony to her talent that we would like to know so much more about her.

text:

In the most tangible sign so far that China is retreating from its decade-long commitment to sending students abroad, new restrictions will make it virtually impossible for most university graduates to study in other countries unless they work first for five years.
The rules, which had been anticipated since early this month, took effect on Feb. 
10. They have not yet been widely disseminated, although a copy was obtained here.
''If enforced as written, it's going to have a big impact,'' a Western diplomat in Beijing said. 
''There have been competent Chinese graduate students going to the U.S. that won't be going there anymore.''
But many experts, noting that Chinese students have been adept at evading previous restrictions, said much would depend on how the new restrictions are put into force. 
End to an Academic Exodus?
On their face, the regulations would considerably reduce the annual stream of about 12,000 students to the United States that had been one of the most remarkable aspects of China's former open-door policy.
The basic change in the new rules is a requirement that university graduates work for five years before they go abroad to study, although students with relatives overseas can pay for an exemption from the work requirement.
The regulations seem to be motivated by Government alarm over the large number of top students, educated essentially for no charge at China's best schools, who go overseas and fail to return to contribute to their country.
''It is a continuation of their concern over the brain drain,'' said Karen C. Stanton, consul at the United States Embassy in Beijing. 
''They are losing their best and their brightest, and the reality is that past efforts have failed to control this flood.''
Although Chinese officials agree that the policy is aimed mostly at preventing an exodus of top minds, the new rules come at a time when China is again emphasizing ideological devotion over professional ability in hiring and promotion.
Â 
Socialism's 'Gravediggers'
Chinese and Western officials say the authorities are also concerned by the support lent by students abroad to the democracy movement at home.
''The Government does not want to help educate the gravediggers of socialism,''a Chinese teacher said.
The document describing the new rules was circulated by the state Education Commission. 
It states that only students who have not yet reached their final year in a university, or students with Chinese relatives overseas, can win exemptions from the work requirement.
Students seeking the latter exemption must apply for identification papers from a provincial Government office indicating that they related to a Chinese person overseas.
''I think there are going to a lot of fake relatives,'' a Chinese intellectual said. 
''The authorities can't possibly check into everyone's background.''
Students eligible for the exemptions must pay for each of the years of university-level schooling they completed. 
Graduates must pay the equivalent of about $530 for each of their college years; students at the masters level, $850 per year, and students at the doctoral level, $1,275. 
If they return to China within eight years, their money will be refunded.
Â 
Few Can Afford Exemption Fees
Most students and their immediate families could not afford such fees, although some will be able to take advantage of loans from relatives abroad.
Several Western diplomats said the loopholes softened the impact of the rules. 
They noted that similar regulations were used in Eastern European and some Western countries. 
France, for example, has a work requirement for students educated at state universities.
''The pressure to go abroad is so strong, and it's on everyone's mind right now,'' a Western official said of China. 
''If they just stonewall, then the rules would be called restrictive and coercive, like the old policies before. 
They open a small hole so people won't say they're not reasonable.''
Consular offiials say they will be unable to gauge the effect of the rules on visa applications before May or June.
The new regulations were announced to university officials earlier this month, less than two weeks after President Bush vetoed a bill that would have relaxed visa restrictions on Chinese students in the United States.
Beijing's new rules, which apply to students applying on their own as opposed to scholars sponsored by the Government, appear to be part of an overall tightening of control over university students.
Students sponsoring themselves have been receiving an increasing proportion of visas for study in the United States. 
Their applications are multiplying more rapidly than those of Government-sponsored students, who will not be affected by the new rules.

file: China Again Cuts Off TV News Transmission.txt
text:
ï»¿
In their second reversal in as many days, Chinese officials yesterday abruptly halted the transmission of foreign television news reports from Beijing. 
They also barred foreign broadcasters from recording and transmitting news reports by China's state-run network.
Some television news transmissions continued to be available to American viewers yesterday as network news organizations skirted the Chinese decrees by sending videotape reports to Hong Kong for transmission. 
The networks were also picking up reports from the Chinese state network, Central China Television, in Hong Kong, and sending them to the United States from there.
Reversals and Power Struggle
Network executives said they were perplexed by the repeated reversals regarding television news coverage. 
The successive policy reversals may mirror continuing shifts in power between competing factions of China's leadership.
Television coverage of the protests in and around Tiananmen Square was first halted on Saturday (Friday evening in the United States) as the Government said it was imposing martial law in parts of Beijing. 
But the ban was lifted without explanation on Tuesday evening in Beijing.
Foreign news organizations in China, including the three major American broadcast networks and the Cable News Network, were allowed to resume transmitting reports, but only through the satellite of CCTV, the state-run network. 
The American television news organizations resumed sending reports on Tuesday.
Last night in Beijing, however, the networks were told by CCTV officials that their access to the CCTV satellite would be halted at midnight, or 11 A.M. Eastern time yesterday. 
They were also forbidden to rebroadcast the CCTV reports.
Â 
CBS Shows Last Live Report
Network officials said they were given no reason for the reversal, and they could not determine the source of the order. 
The ban may have been resumed for political reasons, they said, or it may simply have been that the request for satellilte time by more than 100 foreign news organizations had overwhelmed the modest CCTV staff.
CBS News interrupted its regular programming yesterday morning with its chief anchorman, Dan Rather, in New York, introducing the network's last live report from Beijing. 
The report, filed by John Sheahan, a CBS correspondent in Beijing, concluded at about three minutes past 11 A.M., as a Chinese technician was shown pulling the plug on the transmission.
Executives at other networks accused CBS News of overdramatizing the situation because the news organizations had learned of the ban several hours earlier. 
But Lane Venardos, the executive producer of special events for CBS News, defended the report. 
''It was an accurate representation of what was happening in Beijing,'' he said.
The television news organizations have not been prevented from videotaping the events in Beijing, and the networks are continuing to do so.
Â 
'Unbelievable Nightmare'
The television correspondents in Beijing have also been broadcasting audio reports by telephone. 
But television executives, dependent on live video images, are increasingly frustrated by the lack of pictures. 
All of the American networks have devoted major resources to covering the events unfolding in China. 
ABC News, NBC News and CNN each have about 30 employees in Beijing, including correspondents, producers, cameramen and technicians. 
CBS News has more, though it would not say how many.
''It's an unbelievable nightmare,'' said Eason Jordan, the acting international editor of CNN. 
''The fate of China is being decided, and we're caught in the middle just trying to report the story.''

file: China and Indonesia Agree to Renew Ties Suspended in 1967.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Indonesia agreed today to normalize relations, 22 years after they were suspended over allegations that China supported a Communist coup attempt against the Indonesian Government.
President Suharto of Indonesia and the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, reached agreement after meeting for more than two hours at a Tokyo hotel, said Max Lapod, spokesman for the Indonesian Embassy in Tokyo.
''We are going to go through the process of normalizing relations based on the five principles of noninterference, nonaggression, mutual respect, beneficial relations and peaceful coexistence,'' Mr. Lapod said in an interview.
President Suharto and Mr. Qian are in Tokyo to attend the funeral for Emperor Hirohito.
Indonesia suspended relations with China in 1967, two years after an attempted Communist coup in Jakarta that Indonesia said had Chinese backing. 
In 1985 the two countries resumed direct trade.
President Suharto and Mr. Qian accepted invitations for the Indonesian and Chinese presidents to exchange visits, Mr. Lapod said.
China's state-run press agency reported that Mr. Qian and President Suharto ''agreed upon future efforts for normalization of bilateral relations.''
The meeting with the Indonesian leader marked the beginning of the normalization process, the New China News Agency quoted Mr. Qian as telling reporters.
''They agreed that the two countries should make further efforts toward the normalization of bilateral relations,'' the agency quoted an unidentified official as saying.
China long has been pressing for normalization of relations with Indonesia. 
But Jakarta has held back largely because it fears China would use its influence among Indonesia's ethnic Chinese to foment unrest. 
About four million of Indonesia's 168 million people are ethnic Chinese.

file: China and Indonesia Sign a Pact To Restore Ties Severed in 60_s.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Indonesia signed an agreement today to restore diplomatic relations next month, ending a 23-year rift between the two most populous nations in East Asia.
Both sides described the agreement as of ''historic significance'' and said they hoped it would contribute to peace and stabilityI throughout the Pacific region. 
The new agreement is expected to lead to increased trade between the two countries, to further discussions aimed at resolving the war in Cambodia, and to an accord to establish diplomatic relations between China and Singapore.
Prime Minister Li Peng will travel to the Indonesian capital, Jakarta, to mark the resumption of relations on Aug. 
8. For him and for China's diplomacy as a whole, the agreement is a rare bright spot in a year that has been characterized by isolation and invective since the army crackdown against the democracy movement in June 1989.
The accord also puts the seal on China's repudiation of its onetime program to export revolution to other parts of Asia and the world. 
It was accusations of support by China for a Communist-backed rebellion in Indonesia in 1965 that led to relations being suspended two years later. 
Until then, China and Indonesia had enjoyed close relations.
Â 
'Turning of a New Page'
It was partly because of the rift with Indonesia that China reconsidered its attempts to spread revolution, and today Foreign Minister Qian Qichen seemed much more interested in exporting goods than revolution. 
He said at a news conference that he had no idea whether Indonesia still had a Communist party - and his tone seemed to imply that he did not much care, either.
Ali Alatas, Indonesia's Foreign Minister, said at the news conference that a new trade agreement was already under way to bolster two-way trade, which was valued at $920 million last year.
''I believe it is no exaggeration that what we have achieved today is a significant development and in fact signifies the turning of a new page in our bilateral relationship,'' Mr. Alatas said.
People's Daily had earlier called Mr. Alatas's visit - the first by an Indonesian Foreign Minister since relations were suspended in 1967 - a ''great event.''
The Chinese press has not explained the reason for the rupture of relations in the 1960's, attributing it only to ''some complicated historical causes.''
Â 
Surprise Meeting in Tokyo
The agreement today comes after more than 16 months of negotiations that followed a surprise meeting between Mr. Qian and President Suharto of Indonesia in Tokyo on Feb. 
23, 1989. 
The two men then agreed to work toward normalization of relations.
Singapore is widely expected to follow Indonesia in establishing formal ties with Beijing. 
Singapore already has good ties with Beijing, and runs a trade office here. 
But it has not formally established relations with either China or Taiwan.

file: China and South Korea Planning To Establish Diplomatic Relations.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and South Korea signaled today that they would establish diplomatic relations in the next few days, turning their backs on decades of enmity dating to the Korean War and raising the possibility of a new pattern of economic and security relations throughout the region.
South Korea's Foreign Minister, Lee Sang Ock, will visit China on Sunday for three days of talks to discuss "the normalization of relations," officials announced today. 
The visit and other signals strongly suggest that the two sides will soon establish diplomatic ties, perhaps as early as Monday.
Taiwan, China's rival, angrily responded by saying that it would cut its ties with Seoul.
Â 
Increases in Trade Seen
While expected, the formal end to one of the last cold-war rivalries may stimulate sharp increases in trade and investment between China and South Korea. 
But the change would also raise fundamental questions about the prospects for security and peace in this region: Will the new ties further isolate North Korea, an unpredictable nation with almost no close friends in the world besides China, and drive it to intensify an effort to build nuclear weapons?
Or will China, which sent more than a million troops to fight on North Korea's side in the Korean War, now be willing to act as a broker between the Koreas, pressing the North more forcefully to forsake its ambitions of becoming a nuclear power?
Beijing and Seoul have both officially refused to confirm the prospect of new relations. 
But lawmakers and officials in Taiwan, which South Korea now recognizes as the legitimate government of China, said Beijing and Seoul would establish ties as early as Monday.
At a news conference in Taipei, Taiwan's Foriegn Minister, Fredrick F. Chien, harshly attacked the South Korean President and immediately announced that Taiwan would break relations with South Korea.
"The Government of Roh Tae-woo has violated the trust and trampled on international justice," Reuters quoted Mr. Chien as saying.
Both Taipei and Beijing claim to be the legitimate government of all China. 
China does not allow nations to maintain diplomatic relations with both Taiwan and itself.
China will continue to recognize North Korea after establishing relations with South Korea, but North Korea has strongly opposed its allies' recognition of what it calls the "puppet regime" in the south.
The North Korean Embassy in Beijing refused to comment today.
Some diplomats warn that a more isolated North Korea could be more dangerous. 
China has discouraged North Korea from developing a nuclear bomb, and it may lose leverage if it builds closer ties with South Korea.
Other diplomats say that Seoul may be able to enlist more help from China in persuading North Korea to abandon its nuclear ambitions. 
South Korea may also hope that China will encourage North Korea to agree to international inspections of more nuclear installations or at least to reduce its forces and stop digging tunnels at the border with South Korea.
Â 
Apology From China Mentioned
Press reports from Seoul suggest that China may have apologized to South Korea for helping the North during the Korean War. 
But so far China has given no indication of a change in its position that its participation with the North in the Korean War was a noble effort to combat American aggression.
The war began in 1950 after North Korea launched a surprise attack on the South. 
But the Chinese version of history is still that it was the South that began the conflict.
In the fall of 1950, Beijing sent forces to join North Korea in the fight against the South, embroiling the newly Communist China in a three-year war. 
Under the auspices of aiding a fraternal socialist country, China battled American-backed South Korean forces to a stalemate that led to the division of Korea into the North and South.
China sometimes has described its relationship with the North by saying it is "as close as lips and teeth."
Partly because of that closeness, China is likely to continue to emphasize its friendship with North Korea despite the recognition of Seoul.
Still, China will have to make a small but symbolic change that North Korea will not like: the redrawing of its maps. 
Current Chinese maps show one Korea with the North Korean city of Pyongyang as its capital, but presumably China will have to issue new maps showing a divided Korea with two capitals.
South Korean officials, who spoke on condition that they not be named, told reporters today that President Roh planned a visit to Beijing in October and that a return visit by a top Chinese leader was expected next January.
China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, is believed to have encouraged ties between South Korea and China. 
His youngest son, Deng Zhifang, who is a businessman, has visited both North and South Korea and may have played a significant diplomatic role.
For decades, China's ties with North Korea, and Taiwan's relations with South Korea, were built on ideological similarities. 
But now, the new ties seem to be dominated by pragmatism.
Economic trade between China and South Korea has surged, reaching $5.8 billion in 1991, far more than China's trade with North Korea. 
The new ties offer even greater potential, particularly in the Chinese coastal province of Shandong where South Korean investment has already developed. 
South Koreans are also likely to pour funds into Jilin Province, where many ethnic Koreans live.
Â 
Businesses Had Been Hesitant
In the past, South Korean businesses were hesitant to invest large amounts of money in new factories because of political uncertainty between the two countries. 
In contrast, trade between South Korea and Taiwan was slightly more than $3 billion last year, and China's trade with North Korea was far less than that.
Although Taiwan still expects to maintain strong economic ties with South Korea, it complained of betrayal and apparently will halt -- if only temporarily -- direct flights and eliminate or reduce trade preferences to South Korea. 
Severing ties with Seoul would leave Taiwan with formal ties with only 29 countries.
South Korea had been consistently denying to Taiwan that it would establish relations with China, and last year it discouraged Taiwan from selling consulates in South Korea and the land under its embassy, which some estimates say is worth $1.9 billion. 
The embassy and the land will now apparently be given to China.

file: China and U.S. Agree on Prison-Export Curbs.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and the United States have reached a tentative agreement to prevent the export to America of goods made in Chinese prisons.
A memorandum of understanding, which was reached Thursday by teams of negotiators in Beijing, could resolve a long-running dispute in Chinese-American relations.
The United States bans the import of goods manufactured by prison labor, but for years Chinese prisons have quietly exported tea, pipes, engines, leather clothing and other products made by convicts.
The Chinese Government at first denied that such exports existed. 
More recently, it has said that while prison exports are against national law they may have occurred occasionally through the connivance of local prisons and foreign importers.
Â 
Prison Visits Denied
It is not clear whether the agreement, which requires the approval of Washington and Beijing, will be more effective in curbing the exports.
The principal stumbling block in the negotiations, which have been under way since late last year, was an American demand that United States officials be allowed to visit prisons to check accusations that they are exporting. 
China refused, saying such visits would violate its sovereignty.
Lorraine Toly, a spokeswoman for the United States Embassy, declined to say if the draft agreement would permit prison visits, and she said she could not discuss other elements of the memorandum. 
Ms. Toly said the United States team had been headed by Sandra Kristoff, Deputy Assistant Secretary of State. 
The Chinese team included delegates from the Ministries of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade, Foreign Affairs and Justice.
Export of prison goods is not an issue among Chinese dissidents, who assume that if exports are halted prisoners will still have to work just as many hours making goods for the domestic market.
Â 
Congressional Opposition
In the United States, however, the exports have inflamed Congressional sentiment against China because of the perception that Chinese prison labor is costing American jobs. 
Because of rights abuses and other issues, Congress has tried to impose conditions on the renewal of trade privileges for China. 
The efforts have failed, but a new attempt is planned when the trade privileges come up for renewal next year.
Former prisoners have said that labor programs vary among jails, but that sometimes convicts are beaten if they do not meet production quotas.

file: CHINA AND VIETNAM REPORTED IN PACT.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Vietnam have agreed on a broad outline for a Vietnamese troop withdrawal from Cambodia by the end of September, a Vietnamese diplomat here said today.
Several important aspects of the plan have yet to be decided, and rival Cambodian factions apparently still must reach some agreement among themselves. 
But the reported accord between Vietnam and China appears to bring Southeast Asia a step closer to resolution of one of its most persistent and bloody disputes, the one arising from the 10-year Vietnamese intervention in Cambodia.
The agreement came last week in meetings in Beijing between a Vietnamese First Deputy Foreign Minister, Dinh Nho Liem, and ranking officials of the Chinese Foreign Ministry. 
The visit had been intended to be secret, but officials on both sides later confirmed that it had taken place without detailing the nature of the talks.
The Vietnamese diplomat, who asked not to be identified by name, said that the two sides had agreed that all countries should steadily reduce their support to Cambodian guerrilla groups. 
Such aid would completely end in September when Vietnam completes its troop withdrawal.
Â 
'International Body' Urged
That would mean that China would stop its support for the Khmer Rouge, militarily the strongest of three groups fighting against the Vietnamese-backed Government in Cambodia.
Prime Minister Li Peng of China and his Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, had previously indicated that aid to Cambodian factions could be reduced during Vietnam's troop pullout. 
But the agreement appears to go further than previous comments in guaranteeing that as Vietnam withdraws, China will cut off its support to the Khmer Rouge.
Chinese officials had refused to discuss the content of last week's talks about Cambodia.
In addition, the Vietnamese diplomat said China and Vietnam had agreed that ''an international body'' should be sent to Cambodia to serve three purposes: monitor Vietnam's troop withdrawal, insure that other countries stop their support of opposition factions and supervise the selection of a new Government.
In Washington, the State Department said it had no independent confirmation and noted that it came from ''diplomats,'' not official statements by China or Vietnam. 
Charles E. Redman, the State Department spokesman, said the United States was encouraged by the ''very intensive level of diplomatic activity'' surrounding Cambodia, but he would not comment on the report from Beijing.

file: CHINA ANNOUNCES RELEASE FROM JAIL OF 211 DISSIDENTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today announced the release of 211 people jailed for taking part in the democracy movement last year, including several of the most prominent supporters of greater democracy. 
Diplomats described the action as an attempt to improve Beijing's relations with the West.
The Government also said ''431 law-breakers involved in the turmoil and rebellion'' were still under investigation. 
The implication was that only 431 people remain behind bars in Beijing, of the thousands who were detained after the military crushed the protests last June. 
It was the first time the authorities had given a figure for pro-democracy protesters in prison. 
[In Washington, the Bush Administration welcomed the release of 211 prisoners, but it urged Beijing to disclose the number and names of all the others who remain in detention.] Fate of Prisoners Unclear ''This is important,'' a Western diplomat here said of the prisoners' release. 
''This is a message to Western countries, and it should be welcomed.''
But a diplomat from another Western country was more cautious. 
While stressing that the announcement was good news, he said he wanted to know what restrictions had been placed on those released, as well as a clearer indication of who remained behind bars and what would happen to them.
The diplomats said the principal reason for the release, or at least the timing, was Chinese concern that the United States might revoke most-favored-nation status for Chinese exports. 
President Bush must decide by June 3 whether to recommend continuing most-favored-nation status, which gives Chinese exports the same relatively low tariffs that the United States levies on goods from almost all other countries. 
An end to the low tariffs would be a significant blow to China's export sector.
Â 
Writer Is Among Those Freed
Among those released today was Dai Qing, a prominent writer in her mid-40's, who apparently offended the leadership with a speech in Tiananmen Square in which she praised the student demonstrators but also called on them to leave the square. 
Also freed was Cao Siyuan, 44, a lawyer who was heavily involved in a campaign a year ago to use constitutional procedures to revoke martial law and perhaps unseat Prime Minister Li Peng.
''Coming back home was like a dream,'' The Associated Press quoted Miss Dai as saying in a telephone interview. 
''After 10 months my kitchen is like a stranger.''
The A.P. quoted Miss Dai as adding that she could not say more, for fear of rearrest.
This evening Miss Dai's husband said that she was out and that in any case it was better that she not take a call from a reporter. 
A woman who answered the phone in Mr. Cao's home said he could not take a reporter's call. 
The announcement, by the official New China News Agency, said that among other prominent figures released were Li Honglin, former president of the Fujian Province Academy of Social Sciences; Zhou Duo, an employee at a computer company who was one of four hunger strikers at the time of the crackdown last year; Yang Baikui, a political scientist in the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, and Li Nanyou, an editor at a Beijing publishing house.
No Word on Many Dissidents There was no word on other prominent dissidents, like Wang Dan, the scrawny history student from Beijing University who became probably the most important leader of the student movement. 
Mr. Wang, along with other important figures in the movement, is believed to be held at Qincheng Prison in the outskirts of the capital.
The brief announcement said little more than that ''211 law-breakers involved in the turmoil and counterrevolutionary rebellion last year have been given lenient treatment and released upon completion of investigations.''
The statement added that those who confessed and showed repentance would be dealt with leniently, while those who ''continue to do evil will surely be punished strictly in accordance with the law.''
In January, the Ministry of Public Security announced the release of 573 people who had been involved in the democracy movement in Beijing. 
But there is little doubt that many more people were detained after the crackdown - most estimates by diplomats are in the range of 5,000 to 10,000 in the capital alone - and that most of these were released one by one in the late summer, fall and winter.
Â 
Uncertainty of Estimates Cited
One dissident estimated in an interview recently that the number still in prison probably was in the hundreds rather than in the thousands.
But he emphasized that such calculations are fraught with uncertainty. 
While many intellectuals have informal networks to pass around information about each other, little is known of the workers who were arrested in the crackdown and its aftermath.
In addition to those still in prison for their involvement in the 1989 democracy movement, dissidents say that about 10 people are still incarcerated for pro-democracy activities in the Democracy Spring movement of a decade ago.
The Government also has not relented, so far, in the case of Fang Lizhi and Li Shuxian, the dissident couple who remain in refuge in the American Embassy in Beijing. 
Allowing Mr. Fang and Miss Li to leave China would improve the chances that China could retain most-favored-nation status, but some Chinese officials worry that such a concession would make the Chinese lose face internationally.

file: CHINA ANNOUNCES RELEASE FROM JAIL OF 211 DISSIDENTS_U.S. Welcomes Move.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Bush Administration today welcomed China's release of 211 prisoners arrested for involvement in the pro-democracy demonstrations, but urged Beijing to disclose the number and names of all the others who remain in detention.
Administration officials said they viewed the Chinese move as an attempt by Beijing to improve its image in American eyes at time when President Bush is considering whether or not to extend most-favored-nation trade status for China. 
The trade status would enable China to continue exporting products to the United States at the most advantageous tariff rates.
A bipartisan coalition is taking shape in Congress to challenge the President if he renews China's trading benefits.
Administration officials insisted that they did not specifically request that the Chinese make such a prisoner release at this time, but rather have been telling Beijing for months through diplomatic channels that it will be impossible to improve relations unless those who were arrested for the sole crime of demonstrating for political freedom were set free.
Â 
More Information This Time
''Officially we welcomed the move,'' an Administration official said. 
''We don't want to spit in their eye when they do something positive for whatever reasons they might have done it. 
This was certainly better than the announcement that they released 573 in January, which did not include a single name or any proof.''
With the latest release, the names of six prominent democracy movement leaders were included by the Chinese.
''The fact that they did it while the President is considering M.F.N. is obviously not unrelated,'' the official added. 
''Nobody has to hit them over the head with it. 
They understand from every conversation we have had with them that a key determinent in the United States' willingness to improve relations is the release of prisoners. 
But I don't think M.F.N. is the only reason. 
When they make decisions of this nature internal security is the prime factor.''
Last year United States-China trade reached $18 billion, including $13 billion worth of Chinese exports to the United States. 
In fact, the United States is now China's biggest trading partner, even larger than Japan.

file: China Arrests a Student Leader Back From Exile in the U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
The police today detained a prominent Chinese student leader who had returned from exile in the United States and was preparing to meet with foreign reporters to discuss his plans for setting up a chapter in China of the pro-democracy organization he heads.
The security forces seized Shen Tong, a 24-year-old graduate student at Boston University, at 12:30 this morning at his family home in Beijing. 
Two other Chinese, Qi Dafeng and Qian Liyun, were taken away with Mr. Shen at about 4 A.M. and none of the three have been seen since.
Three French television journalists were escorted from Mr. Shen's home and then expelled today.
Ross G. Terrill, an American writer of several books on China, was detained at his hotel room for a few hours in connection with Mr. Shen's press conference, but he was allowed to move freely after United States Embassy officials intervened.
Â 
Embassy Expresses 'Concern'
"I was pushed into my room and then I tried to get out and was stopped," said Mr. Terrill. "They said I was in violation of the rules."
Several guards were posted outside his room during the day. 
The American Embassy submitted a protest on Mr. Terrill's behalf to the Foreign Ministry. 
It also expressed "concern" over the detention of Mr. Shen, who holds a Chinese passport.
The detentions seemed to arise from Mr. Shen's plans to hold a press conference to discuss his decision to set up a local chapter of the Democracy for China Fund, which he heads. 
Mr. Terrill, who is on the fund's advisory board, tried to preside over the conference instead, until the police detained him.
Mr. Shen's mother, Li Yixian, said the police passed her a note written by her son that said he was being questioned at a hotel, but did not give the location. 
The police gave no reason why Mr. Shen was detained, but they confiscated his computer disks, notebooks and other materials collected during travels throughout China this past month.
"They didn't show us any identification," said Miss Li, his mother. 
"Then one of the policemen took my son away."
Â 
Visit Kept Quiet
Mr. Shen was one of the top leaders in the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement and then fled to the United States and became active in lobbying for more attention to human rights violations in China. 
He also wrote a book about his experiences in China.
Although Mr. Shen returned to China about a month ago, he kept his visit quiet. 
He apparently is the most prominent democracy leader to return to China from exile.
Mr. Qi, who lives in China and was jailed for 20 months after the Tiananmen Square military crackdown, traveled with Mr. Shen and worked closely with the Democracy for China Fund. 
Miss Qian, the wife of another student leader, Xiong Yan, was apparently also helping Mr. Shen.
The materials confiscated could presumably be used to incriminate other Chinese whom Mr. Shen met during his journey. 
In a statement released to the press before his detention, Mr. Shen said he conducted interviews with intellectuals, workers, peasants and bureaucrats across the nation on behalf of the fund.
Mr. Shen apparently also met with dissidents belonging to underground pro-democracy groups that the Government bans outright. 
The authorities gave no indication whether they detained him for the materials he gathered or solely for his plans to hold a press conference.
Whether the Government knew he had been traveling and interviewing people across the country is not clear. 
Mr. Shen flew from Hong Kong to the southern city of Guilin and then traveled freely to cities and the countryside.
Â 
Others in Danger
"In four weeks I have seen things which encouraged me and others which made me sad," Mr. Shen said in his statement.
Mr. Shen and his assistants had notified official Chinese news organizations about the press conference. 
This may be how the authorities discovered his plans.
Robin Munro, a researcher at Asia Watch, a division of Human Rights Watch, said that the authorities were likely to be much harsher toward Mr. Qi and other less-well-known figures than to Mr. Shen himself, who is partly protected by his prominence in the United States.
"There's a fear that the real victims of this debacle are the lesser-known people involved in the Shen Tong project," Mr. Munro said.

file: China Austerity Cools Economy.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's tough austerity policies have cooled off the overheated economy but have made few inroads in solving basic flaws in the system, the Government said last week.
In a report on economic performance through September, Zhang Zhongji, spokesman for the State Statistical Bureau, said the year-old austerity program had held the gross national product to $30 billion, up 5 percent from a year earlier.
Mr. Zhang said consumer demand was down, the rise in retail prices had been brought under control and ''the whole economy is taking a favorable turn.''

But he acknowledged that

file: CHINA BACKS PACT ON NUCLEAR ARMS.txt
text:
ï»¿
China announced today that it had decided "in principle" to sign the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, becoming the last major nuclear power to commit itself to the terms of the agreement to curb the spread of atomic weapons.
The announcement came during a summit meeting today between Prime Minister Li Peng and Prime Minister Toshiki Kaifu of Japan, whose nation last week marked the 46th anniversary of the two American atomic bomb attacks. 
Mr. Kaifu, who arrived today for three days of talks, is the first leader of any industrialized country to visit China since the Tiananmen crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in June 1989.
Â 
'Things Have Changed'
"On many occasions in the past, China made clear its reasons for not acceding to the treaty," Wu Jianmin, China's Foreign Ministry spokesman, said tonight. 
"Now things have changed. 
This is for the purpose of attaining the complete prohibition and thorough destruction of nuclear weapons."
In recent months, China had hinted it might join the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, and today's announcement, while not entirely a surprise, is expected to be a boost to the international effort this year to curtail the spread of nuclear and conventional weapons, particularly to trouble spots like the Middle East.
The Foreign Ministry spokesman did not say when China would sign the treaty, nor did he say whether "in principle" meant that there were any issues China still wanted to discuss before it signed. 
He did say, however, that China has not "imposed any conditions" for signing the treaty.
China was the last of the five major nuclear powers to hold out against the accord; on June 3, France committed itself to the terms of the treaty, although it has not yet signed it.
Only a handful of countries -- including India, Pakistan, Israel, South Africa, Argentina and Brazil, which are thought to possess advanced nuclear technology -- have yet to sign the accord. 
But among the nations that have accepted it are countries like Iraq and North Korea that are believed to have ambitions of developing nuclear weapons.
[The Bush Administration welcomed China's announcement, saying the move was something the United States had long sought. 
"We welcome this development and we look forward to early ratification by China of the treaty," the White House spokesman, Marlin Fitzwater, said in Kennebunkport, Me., where President Bush is vacationing.]
Mr. Li's announcement appeared to be a friendly gesture toward Japan, which has been more eager than Western countries to re-establish normal ties with China.
Â 
Ties 'Returned to Normal'
In the last two years, Japan and China have rebuilt strong economic, commercial and even diplomatic ties, without focusing on the Tiananmen crackdown or human rights abuses. 
Some Western countries, particularly the United States, continue to have frosty relations with China because of concerns about Chinese violations of human rights and weapons sales.
Prime Minister Li suggested to Mr. Kaifu, in a comment repeated by the official New China News Agency, that China regarded the summit meeting as an indication that Chinese-Japanese relations are now back to normal.
"We are pleased to see that our bilateral relations have returned to normal," Mr. Li said. 
"We hereby express our appreciation for the positive efforts the Japanese Government and Prime Minister Kaifu have made to restore and develop the bilateral relations."
Â 
Treaty Took Effect in 1968
One of the aims of Mr. Kaifu's visit was to encourage China to play a more active role in controlling weapons sales and the proliferation of nuclear arms.
Mr. Wu today did not explain why his country had long opposed the treaty, but China in the past has suggested that the pact was an effort by the superpowers to dominate other countries. 
Beijing has said the treaty discriminated against developing countries and hindered international cooperation for peaceful uses of nuclear energy.
The treaty, the subject of intensive negotiations between the United States and the Soviet Union in the mid-1960's, bans the export of nuclear weapons and nuclear-arms technology. 
It went into effect in 1968.
The treaty was controversial because it sought to make permanent the nuclear-weapons monopoly of those nations that then possessed such weapons -- the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China -- and sought pledges from other countries nt to acquire any. 
The treaty also committed the nuclear powers to work toward total nuclear disarmament and to help nonnuclear nations that sign the accord to develop peaceful uses of nuclear energy.
Arms control experts say China's nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of the United States, Soviet Union, Britain or France. 
According to a report by Jane's Information Group, China has a nuclear arsenal that consists of 1,455 devices, both strategic and tactical. 
Many of those include warheads on land-based missiles, but China also has bombs, submarine-launched ballistic missiles and mines and shells.
The Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control has reported that China has transferred sensitive nuclear material or technology to Pakistan, India, South Africa, Algeria and countries in South America.
In addition to seeking Chinese acceptance of the nonproliferation treaty, the United States has been pressing Beijing in the last year to curb its missile sales. 
Nevertheless, China went ahead recently with the sale to Pakistan of a package of M-11 missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. 
It is apparently considering the sale of M-9 missiles to Syria.
China indicated recently that it was considering joining the Missile Technology Control Regime, an international agreement to curb the spread of missiles, but the issue was not raised at today's meeting, according to a Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman, Sadaaki Numata.
Â 
Issue of Arms Transfers
Mr. Numata said Prime Minister Kaifu had pressed China for support in Japan's effort to sponsor a United Nations resolution calling upon countries to report weapons transfers. 
But China said only that it was willing to discuss the subject and gave no commitments.
Japan is now offering low-interest loans to China, and the Chinese have made a request for more economic assistance. 
But the only announcement of economic aid today was a new donation, worth $1.5 million, in disaster relief for Chinese regions devastated by flooding last month. 
Japan already had given $500,000 worth of aid.
One reason bilateral ties have improved relatively smoothly is that Japan has tended not to criticize China's human rights abuses harshly. 
In today's meeting, Mr. Kaifu seemed to touch lightly on human rights issues, referring to the concerns expressed at the recent summit meeting of the seven major industrialized countries about China's process of democratization.
Mr. Kaifu did not seem to win any assurances from China that Communist North Korea would allow international inspection of its nuclear installations.

A reconciliation between the two Communist neighbors, after a dozen years of enmity and occasionally armed conflict, would reflect the steps taken toward resolving the civil war in Cambodia. 
A reconciliation would also improve the chances that a lasting peace could be achieved in Cambodia.

file: China Bans Pro-Student Newspaper.txt
text:

In its firmest action so far to stem the growing student campaign for more democracy, the Communist Party today banned an issue of a popular newspaper that published comments openly supporting the demonstrators.
As the paper was banned today, tens of thousands of university students in the capital began an indefinite boycott of classes to press their demands for more democracy and a freer press. 
It appeared that almost all students at Beijing's universities were honoring the boycott, and student leaders said they would send delegations to factories to solicit support from workers.
The latest issue of the banned weekly newspaper, The World Economic Herald, had already been printed and contained some of the boldest criticisms of the Communist Party ever published in a major Chinese newspaper. 
But the party today prohibited the distribution of the newspaper, according to Chinese familiar with the order.
Qin Benli, the editor in chief of the Shanghai-based newspaper, which has a circulation of 300,000, was not in the office this afternoon. 
The deputy editor in chief, Zhu Xinqun, confirmed in a telephone interview that the newspaper was not distributed today as it normally is on Mondays. 
Mr. Zhu declined to say why it did not appear.
Â 
Apparently a One-Time Ban
Several people familiar with the banning said that a Politburo member, Jiang Zemin, who is also party leader in Shanghai, gave the order that The Herald could not be distributed. 
It was not clear if the order originated with him or someone higher.
It appeared that only this issue was affected, and that the newspaper might be reprinted later in the week with the offending articles removed. 
Mr. Qin, who is 70 years old, was nearly forced into retirement early this year after The Herald published an essay criticizing the Communist Party, and there were fears that the latest episode might speed up his retirement.
A copy of the paper, obtained today despite the ban on distribution, made clear why the authorities were upset. 
The first six pages are about Hu Yaobang, the ousted party leader whose death on April 15 set off the pro-democracy demonstrations that have continued ever since. 
Perhaps the most sensitive section is a selection of reminiscences and comments by prominent friends of Mr. Hu, who was criticized and forced to resign in disgrace in 1987 after nationwide student protests.
''The main problem China has had, up to today, is the lack of democracy,'' the newspaper quotes Yan Jiaqi, one of the nation's top political scholars, as saying.

Â 
'Stabbed Him in the Back'
Mr. Yan expressed strong sympathy for the student demonstrators and their demands. 
In an apparent reference to two senior party officials, Deng Liqun and Hu Qiaomu, Mr. Yan said: ''Some people who were in charge of ideology have no right to mourn Hu. 
They stabbed him in the back. 
They should be tried by history.''
Dai Qing, a prominent writer, was quoted as saying about the forced resignation: ''It was a total violation of our organizational principles and procedures. 
Besides, he was forced to make a self-criticism against his will. 
In my opinion, that was the most miserable thing in his life.''
Wu Mingyu, an official in China's State Council, or cabinet, was quoted by The Herald as saying that Mr. Hu had acknowledged two regrets in his life. 
The first was his failure to protect a colleague who was wrongly accused in the 1950's of being a rightist. 
The second was his self-criticism when he stepped down.
In a sign of the importance that the leadership places on support from the press during the unrest, Hu Qili, one of five members of the Politburo standing committee, met Wednesday with editors of major papers to advise them not to cover the student demonstrations lest they inflame the situation, according to journalists who said they heard about the meeting from people who were there.
In addition to The World Economic Herald, at least one Beijing newspaper ignored the warning. 
The Science and Technology Daily printed a long and sympathetic article about the demonstrations as well as six photos.

file: China Called Top Copyright Pirate.txt
text:

Companies producing books, records, films, computer software and other so-called intellectual property contended today that 12 countries, headed by China, are depriving the United States of more than $1.3 billion a year of foreign earnings through piracy of copyrighted material.
The International Intellectual Property Alliance, representing 1,600 companies that generated $270 billion in revenues in 1988, placed losses in China, with a population of a billion people and no copyright law, at $418 million, or about a third of the total of the 12 countries.
In a report to Carla A. Hills, the United States trade representative, the group said the problem was particularly acute in textbooks.
Â 
Collier Macmillan Loss in China
One example the report cited was English 900, a Collier Macmillan basic textbook used extensively around the world. 
It has had print runs in China of more than one million copies, yielding no income for Collier Macmillan, the report said.
American book publishers put their losses in China ''conservatively'' at $100 million a year, the report said.
In Saudi Arabia, the report said, 16 companies specialize solely in the distribution of pirate copies of Michael Jackson's music.
The alliance, which makes periodic assessments of piracy losses for the trade representative, named these other countries as the leading offenders: South Korea, India, the Philippines, Taiwan, Indonesia, Brazil, Egypt, Thailand, Nigeria and Malaysia.
Although the group has been providing data since 1984 on its members' losses, this year's report is getting unusual attention because of a requirement in the new United States trade law that the worst violators of intellectual property rights be identified for special Government action that could result in trade sanctions.
Trade officials noted that most of the countries named by the alliance are in some form of negotiation with the trade office to try to prevent their designation as a ''priority'' country under the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988.
Mrs. Hills is required to inform Congress by May 30 of what countries she has designated. 
After the designation, her office must enter intensified talks with those countries. 
If the situation has not improved in a period of 18 months, the President may curb imports from those countries.
The United States has already taken action against one of the countries for intellectual property violations. 
On Jan. 
19, the last day of the Reagan Administration, President Reagan denied duty-free entry to $165 million of Thai imports because of what he said was Thailand's failure to protect copyrighted works.
Most of the 12 governments have agreed to try to correct abuses. 
''The question is how quickly or how resolutely,'' said Eric H. Smith, general counsel of the alliance.
China, for example, is working on the 19th draft of a copyright law, American officials said, and hopes to have one completed by year-end. 
Saudi Arabia is also drafting a law.
Â 
Statement by Chinese Embassy
''China is now actively accelerating legislation for the protection of intellectual property,'' a spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said. 
He noted that not long ago in the port city of Sheng Chen, a company that was found to have infringed on trademarks of the International Business Machines Corporation had been required to pay the highest such fine ever in China.
South Korea's Minister of Trade, Sung Soo Han, said at a news briefing here that his country had ''drastically overhauled and strengthened'' its intellectual property laws and had engaged 900 additional prosecutors and police officers to enforce them.
A report by the alliance in 1984 called Singapore ''the world's capital of piracy,'' but in the current survey Singapore is described as a ''success story.''

file: China Calls TV Tale Subversive.txt
text:
ï»¿
Television programming has been blamed for many things, but China is perhaps the first country to accuse a program of helping sow the seeds of a counterrevolutionary rebellion.
The Chinese Government has ferociously denounced a previously acclaimed television series, ''River Elegy,'' whose six parts were broadcast twice last year on the Government-run national network.
'' 'River Elegy' was a propaganda coup for bourgeois liberalization,'' Hong Minsheng, the deputy director of China Central Television Station, said in a blistering self-criticism broadcast on the evening news. 
''The broadcast of 'River Elegy' provided theoretical and emotional preparation for the recent turmoil and rebellion.''
The attacks on ''River Elegy'' represent the latest front in the century-old debate about whether traditional Chinese culture should be glorified or scorned, whether the nation's poverty is best diagnosed as the result of foreign imperialism or of a rotting indigenous civilization. 
Oddly, the Communist authorities are firmly on the side of ancient tradition, the defenders of the honor of the ''old China'' that they rebelled against in seizing power 40 years ago.
Â 
A Heretical Strain
Most Chinese are taught in school that theirs is a glorious cultural inheritance, but since late in the last century a heretical strain of intellectual thought has attributed China's lack of economic and democratic development to flaws in its culture.
''River Elegy,'' which suggests that Chinese civilization is stagnant and needs to be refreshed by foreign influences, is the most powerful statement of this heretical strain so far. 
It has come to symbolize the debate about how China should modernize and whether it should cherish or discard certain values and symbols of the nation's past.
The television series takes its name from the Yellow River, a potent symbol of China, which is portrayed as violent, erratic and stagnant. 
What is needed to revive China, the film suggests, is the influence of the Pacific Ocean: trade, exchanges and the West.
''Those who are now criticizing it as being a rejection of China's national culture and a need for complete Westernization - that criticism is well founded,'' said Andrew J. Nathan, a professor of political science at Columbia University, in a telephone interview.
The television series was firmly backed by Zhao Ziyang, the Communist Party leader who was ousted in June after the suppression of the democracy movement, and its principal scriptwriter, Su Xiaokang, was a leading dissident and the object of a nationwide manhunt before he escaped to Hong Kong. 
The criticisms of the series thus have a political dimension, and the attacks on it have been on the airwaves and front pages since late July.
Â 
'Bourgeois Liberalization'
'' 'River Elegy' distorts Chinese history, entirely negates the fine traditions of Chinese culture and vilifies the Chinese people,'' the national television news declared, after convening a panel to castigate the program. 
''The essence of the film is to negate the socialist system, oppose the leadership of the Communist Party and propagate all-round Westernization. 
'River Elegy' is the product of bourgeois liberalization, in collusion with the doctrine of 'peacefully transforming China' as peddled by the international reactionary forces. 
We should see that behind the series there is a life-and-death struggle for the Chinese nation and the socialist system.''
In another sign of the Communist Party's effort to rebuild its legitimacy by presenting itself as the defender of traditional culture, a Politburo member, Li Ruihuan, called for more emphasis on the study of China's cultural heritage. 
Mr. Li said that while it was wrong to copy indiscriminately from ancient culture, China should devote more attention to ancient books and other emblems of the civilization.
The role of defender of traditional culture is a somewhat delicate one for the Communist Party, which had scarcely taken over China when it ordered the dismantling of the city walls and many other ancient sites in Beijing. 
The desecration of ancient culture reached its peak in the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976, when anything old was considered fair game for the Red Guards, who destroyed ancient temples, books, vases and furniture with equal abandon.
Â 
Horror and Applause
''River Elegy'' tried a more intellectual approach. 
The series - which aroused an immense reaction of both horror and applause throughout the Chinese-speaking world - complained that the Chinese take such pride in their past achievements that they obscure their present failures.
''The fact remains that our civilization is moribund,'' Mr. Su asserted in the series.
''River Elegy'' even criticized the Great Wall, which it labeled ''a symbol of confinement, conservatism, impotent defense and timidity in the face of invasion.''
The television series made some of the same points as the book ''The Ugly Chinaman,'' written by a Taiwanese social critic, Bo Yang, five years ago. 
That book has been banned in China but remains in demand among young intellectuals. 
Its popularity and that of the ''River Elegy'' series reflect the struggle among Chinese intellectuals to account for their nation having been left behind as the rest of the world industrialized in the last two centuries.
'' 'River Elegy' crystallizes in the 1980's an issue that's been around China since the 1880's,'' said Harry Harding, a China scholar at the Brookings Institution in Washington, ''and that is the degree to which Chinese culture provides the basis for modernization, or conversely, the extent to which Western culture provides that basis.''

file: CHINA CHIEFS SEEM EDGY AND DIVIDED.txt
text:

Two months after the collapse of Soviet Communism, China's leaders seem increasingly edgy and divided, and there are signs that they have responded to the events in the Soviet Union by deciding to tighten their grip on the nation further.
Chinese newspapers have carried more statements about "class struggle," there are calls for intensifying Marxist education, leaders of many work units have recently warned employees not to meet foreigners without permission, and officials at one Beijing university even called on staff members to report on colleagues who have contacts with foreigners. 
The officials insisted that even private correspondence with Westerners should be reported to the authorities, a Chinese who was present said.
That person, and many others, characterize the situation as "nei jin, wai song" -- tranquillity on the surface, repression within.
The tighter controls are imperceptible at first glance, for the streets of Beijing abound these days with mountains of cabbages rather than crowds of police, and the free markets spill out as much as ever with bright jackets and lacy underwear and other emblems of free enterprise. 
But members of the urban middle class, especially those in sensitive work places or with foreign friends, are feeling the political cold front.
"I can't help worrying if my leader is going to call me aside this afternoon for seeing you," a scholar in his 30's said, laughing nervously as he bid a foreigner goodbye. 
He said the staff members of his work unit had been banned from seeing foreigners and had been warned that the Central Intelligence Agency was trying to step up spying in China.
Â 
Gates Statement Cited
The talk of the C.I.A. stems from a statement by Robert M. Gates, President Bush's nominee to be Director of Central Intelligence, in his Senate confirmation hearings. 
In answer to a question about China on Sept. 
17, Mr. Gates said, "I think more can be done through expanded human intelligence collection."
The statement was scarcely noticed in the United States, but it has been published in secret news summaries for Chinese officials. 
Already nervous after the Soviet events, some hard-liners are taking it as proof of their fears of a secret American conspiracy of "peaceful evolution" that would lead to replacing the Communist Government. 
The leadership takes this supposed plot so seriously that it is said to have formed an "Anti-Peaceful Evolution Working Group."
Another indication that the leaders are jittery, according to one knowledgeable Chinese, is a shuffle in the command of the Chengdu Military Region. 
Zhang Taiheng, the commander of the region, is said to have been summoned to Beijing for "study" and retirement, and will be replaced by an officer from the General Logistics Department in Beijing.
The reason for the shuffle apparently is a helicopter crash last spring in Tibet in which a number of senior military officials died.

"Normally it would be a minor matter, but the center is very fearful now of generals who don't obey orders, and so it wants to take a very stern action," said the Chinese who recounted the episode. 
Government spokesmen in Chengdu could not confirm whether there had been a change in the command.
It is difficult to gauge the tension in cities outside Beijing -- partly because the authorities are so tense that they are denying permission for American correspondents to travel virtually anywhere outside the capital. 
The Government has refused permission lately to visit even innocuous places such as Jilin and Hebei Provinces, where there are no known political problems.
Â 
Official Press Is Split
One sign of a split in the leadership lately is the divided nature of the official press. 
One line of articles recently has focused on the financial problems of state-owned enterprises and has emphasized that the main task in China is to boost economic reform and raise the standard of living. 
This line of reasoning appears to have the backing of the nation's patriarch, Deng Xiaoping.
The other line of articles in the official press argues that the most serious threat comes not from economic problems but from political enemies at home and abroad.
In a recent People's Daily article, a patron of the hard-liners, Deng Liqun, called for more "class struggle" -- a term that for many intellectuals has frightening associations with the brutality of the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976.
