file: China Cracking Down on Sale of Women as Wives.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Miss Zhao, a junior high school student, was sold as a wife to a peasant in Shandong Province, she infuriated her husband by repeatedly trying to run away. 
Finally he came up with a way to keep her: he gouged out her eyes.
Miss Zhao's plight, which has been publicized here, is one of the more bristling examples of what some experts believe is a growing problem in China: the abduction and selling of women. 
In a sign of official alarm, the Government this month opened a campaign against the practice, declaring it one of ''six evils'' that must be eradicated from contemporary society.
There are no official statistics on how many women are sold to become wives, but unofficial estimates are in the tens of thousands at least. 
A book published this year about the practice - Miss Zhao's photo appears on the cover - reported that in Xuzhou, in Jiangsu Province, more than 48,000 women have been sold in the last few years. 
A recent Chinese news report estimated that some 30,000 women have been sold in Shandong Province.
The practice has surfaced in more than 20 of China's 30 provinces and autonomous regions, another article this week in the official Legal Daily said. 
It is particularly rife in villages in mountainous and remote rural areas of provinces like Sichuan, Shandong, Hebei and Henan.
Â 
Officials Avoid the Issue
Local authorities acknowledge that some peasants buy wives, but they are reluctant to discuss the practice and suggest that it is rare in their area. 
Officials refused to arrange interviews to discuss the issue on recent visits to Henan and Shandong Provinces.
''The city and the countryside all have this problem, but it is infrequent,'' said Ma Yingjun, a senior official in the Luoyang City government in Henan Province, when the topic came up in an interview about other matters. 
''We can't say the problem is solved, but the state is cracking down on it.''
Some Chinese say the sale of wives has its roots in traditional rural values about men and women. 
Earlier in this century, it was not uncommon for parents to sell their daughters to help support the family and raise a son. 
Sometimes the women are willing to be sold if it means they can escape poverty for a better life elsewhere.
How many women are sold voluntarily is unclear, but most Chinese say the great majority of those sold do not understand the perils they might face. 
Usually they are not kidnapped, but are deceived by offers of good jobs in the city. 
Too late, they find that they are being sold as wives. 
Some try to escape, but most accept their lot, Chinese say. 
In part this may be because the women are far from home and have neither money nor friends to help them get away. 
In addition, many may believe that it would be difficult to get another husband if their fate became known.
Â 
A Chain of Abductors
While many urban Chinese say they disapprove of the practice, and it is strictly illegal, the sale of wives is reported to have increased as social controls in the countryside are eased and more people search for ways to make money during the transition toward a market-oriented economy. 
Often, wife-selling involves a chain of abductors, with each one passing on the woman to the next link in their intricate network throughout the country. 
An essay published in September in a confidential Government document called ''Nei Can Xuan Pian,'' or ''Selected Reference Articles,'' explains some reasons for the phenomenon. 
In many areas, the rising cost of traditional rural weddings, which frequently exceeds $2,500, makes marriage expensive. 
Purchasing a wife generally costs only $500 to $800.
''Buying a wife saves money and trouble,'' the article said. 
''Peasants regard women as tools for carrying on their lineage from one generation to another.''

file: China Cracks Down Harder on Christian Activities Outside Official Church.txt
text:
ï»¿
Just before church began one recent Sunday, nearly a dozen plainclothes security policemen swarmed around the courtyard, scrutinizing the churchgoers and eavesdropping on conversations.
"Don't create trouble!" an elderly minister whispered sternly to a young religious leader who had held illegal Bible-study sessions in his home. 
"They're all around."
The minister was nervous because only a few months earlier, he had been stripped of his right to preach and was worried that he could be expelled from his position and his church punished if a member were to get in trouble with the authorities.
Such scenes have been repeated recently in churchyards throughout China as the authorities increasingly clamp down on Christian activities not sponsored by a Government-affiliated church.
Â 
Students Are Warned
Just in the last few weeks, some secondary schools have disseminated a circular issued by the State Education Commission warning students against practicing religion. 
Seventh graders at one Beijing school were told that it would interfere with their studies.
The tighter control appears to be a response to a surge of interest in Christianity across the nation. 
Growing numbers of people, from peasants in the countryside to workers and intellectuals in the big cities, are turning to religion, with much of the increased interest focusing on Christianity.
The Communist Party asserts control over all religions in China, and there is a strong Muslim and Buddhist following in China, but Islam is largely confined to the northwest region and the Government finds Buddhism ominous mainly on the Tibetan plateau. 
In both areas, security officials have maintained a tight rope around the religious communities.
But partly because it believes that Western influences are trying to subvert Communist Party authority, the Government finds Christianity especially threatening. 
Religious groups in Hong Kong say the Beijing Government is particularly concerned about the role the church played in the revolutions in Romania and Poland and other Eastern European countries.
Â 
Overseas Ties Fought
In the anti-Christian campaign the authorities seem to have expanded a hunt for unauthorized pastors, bishops, evangelists and religious worshipers with ties to overseas Christian organizations that China views as threats to its sovereignty.
"There is an inherent conflict between Christianity and Marxism, and this will mean a confrontation sometime in the future," a Protestant believer said, as he sat with other members of an illegal Bible discussion group in an apartment in Beijing. 
"Christianity is a new faith, a new force in China. 
Now it is small, but our numbers will grow, and change will come from this force."
In the last five years, the number of official Protestant churches grew to 7,000 from 4,000 and the number of official Bibles circulating has tripled to 6.5 million, according to the official China Daily newspaper.
Deng Zhaoming, editor of Bridge, a Hong Kong-based periodic report on Christian activities in China, said: "The number of Christians, both Catholics and Protestants, is on the rise. 
There's no question about that."
Â 
At Most, 5 Percent of Nation
To be sure, the number of Christians in China is still minuscule in proportion to its population of 1.1 billion, and many older Christians are the products of the efforts of thousands of Western missionaries who left after 1949, when China became Communist. 
According to China's statistics, there are nearly 3.7 million Catholics and 5 million Protestants affiliated with the official churches.
Overseas religious groups say the total number of Christians, including those who do not register with the official churches, could be 20 million to 60 million, or at most about 5 percent of China's population.
The most recent effort to control religion was systematized in February 1991, when the Chinese Communist Party and the Government issued Circular No. 6, calling for stricter control over religious practices and punishment for offenders.
"The crackdown has been stepped up since 1989 and it's widespread," said Marianne Spiegel, a researcher on religion at Asia Watch, a human rights organization based in New York. 
"There is definitely a movement afoot, and it's been very intense since the end of 1990 -- to make sure that religion is clearly under the control of the Government."
Â 
Some Signs of Leniency
Circular No. 6 applies to all religions, but less is known about the crackdowns on fervent Buddhists and Muslims. 
As for Christians, treatment varies from minor harassment to imprisonment. 
In some areas, officials ignore the orders from above and tolerate the underground church. 
In others, the victims may be physically abused.
There are also signs of leniency, perhaps because of disagreements with the leadership over how religion should be treated, says John T. Kamm, an American businessman who has lobbied successfully for the release of Christian prisoners. 
Moreover, there seems to be a movement among some Government officials to promote the release of elderly bishops and religious figures who are in jail, according to Mr. Kamm.
Even so, a 72-year-old bishop, Paul Li Zhenrong, is said to have been missing or detained for more than a month, according to various Hong Kong accounts. 
According to Asia Watch, there are at least 70 Christians across the nation who are believed to be under detention, and the figure may be as high as 195.
China's Constitution guarantees the right to religious freedom, so long as it does not undermine the Communist Party or the Government, but preachers are not allowed to hold services at unregistered locations or use unauthorized tapes and reading materials from overseas. 
Military officers and workers are banned from practicing religion, says a cadre in a military unit.
"We must be aware that hostile forces abroad have been using religion as an important means of promoting their strategy of 'peaceful evolution,' " Circular No. 6 warns, as translated by Bridge. 
"And they are continually carrying out activities of infiltration and sabotage."
Â 
Bishop Is Detained
After the Vatican announced in May that the former Bishop of Shanghai, Ignatius Gong Pinmei, had been secretly elevated to Cardinal 12 years earlier, China detained Bishop Joseph Fan Zhongliang in June, in what religious groups say was retaliation against the Vatican.
China does not allow its Catholic Patriotic Association, the organization that runs the Catholic Church in China, to establish any ties with the Vatican.
"There is no difference from the West in our belief in God, but what differs is that we administer our church affairs independently and autonomously," said Laurence Shi Yukun, a pastor at the Catholic Cathedral, the largest in Beijing. 
"The Vatican also sends in many underground cardinals and underground priests to wage secret religious acts. 
They try to undermine the Chinese church."
While Catholics like Mr. Shi run the churches, the Government officials who supervise the churches are nonbelievers, and many of them are in fact party members who are required to attend regular study sessions on Marxism.
Â 
Clergy May Be Limited
One way the Government may control the growth of Christianity is by limiting the number of clergy.
There are now 1,000 official priests in more than 3,600 official Catholic churches, according to Mr. Shi. The Catholic Cathedral in Beijing has trained only 10 priests in the last 10 years, and there are only about 700 seminary students across the nation. 
The number of Protestant ministers has remained at about 1,000 during the last decade, according to the China Daily.
Even these ministers and priests are often regarded with suspicion by the faithful, because some regard the clergy as operating with the blessing of the Government rather than God.
"We never tell the minister our real thoughts, what we believe in our hearts," a Chinese Christian said. 
"We know he must report back to the authorities."

file: China Denounces Petition Drive For Political Prisoners_ Amnesty.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign of Government concern at growing calls for human rights, China's official media today attacked a dissident petition drive for an amnesty of China's political prisoners.
But in a sign of the more relaxed political atmosphere here, the dissidents reacted by immediately organizing a news conference to respond to the Government charges. 
They also announced the establishment of a four-member working group called ''Amnesty 1989'' with an office in a local hotel and a telephone that was billed as a 24-hour hot line for democracy.
They said they would put out a weekly newsletter on human rights issues. 
Such a newsletter would apparently be illegal, since it would not be licensed by the authorities.
Â 
First Such Campaign in 10 Years
Such open campaigning for human rights in China has not been seen in nearly a decade, since the ''Beijing Spring'' political thaw of late 1978 and early 1979. 
That thaw was followed by a crackdown in March 1979, which included the arrest of Wei Jingsheng, an electrician whose essays had called for China not only to modernize its economy but to nurture democracy as well. 
Mr. Wei was subsequently sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Thirty-three Chinese intellectuals last week opened the petition drive for an amnesty of political prisoners, particularly Mr. Wei. More than 70 other mainland Chinese have also signed the petition, and in the United States more than 700 people, mostly Chinese nationals, have also signed their names in the last few days, organizers say.
In Taiwan, 32 scholars have also signed a letter supporting the appeal.
Â 
Dissidents Invited to Bush Dinner
Moreover, at least two of the most prominent supporters of the amnesty have been invited by President Bush to a banquet in Beijing on Sunday night where they may brush shoulders with senior Government officials. 
The two are Su Shaozhi, a political theorist who was one of the 33 intellectuals who signed the letter, and Fang Lizhi, China's best-known dissident, who initiated the call for the amnesty with a personal letter to China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, in January.
The petition drive appears to have alarmed the Government. 
Official newspapers carried a dispatch today from the Government-run New China News Agency that sharply condemned the appeal for amnesty. 
The dispatch quoted a Justice Ministry official as saying that Mr. Wei had been fairly sentenced by an independent court, and that the Government had no power to intervene in its sentence.
The article singled out Chen Jun, a 30-year-old manager of a private bar in Beijing, for criticism. 
It said Mr. Chen was the chief sponsor of the letter.
Signers say, however, that the main organizer of the letter was Bei Dao, a 40-year-old poet and author who is regarded as one of China's best writers today. 
Bei Dao, whose real name is Zhao Zhenkai, held a press conference today with Mr. Chen in which they complained that the Government published only the criticism of their letter and not the letter itself.

file: China Detains Two Dissidents During Baker Visit.txt
text:
ï»¿
With Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d visiting here in part to press for the release of hundreds of Chinese dissidents, two more of them were detained over the weekend as the Beijing authorities apparently sought to prevent them from meeting with Mr. Baker's aides.
Before Mr. Baker arrived in Beijing on Friday for a three-day visit, American officials had tentatively arranged meetings between his deputies and several dissidents in Beijing.
But tonight one dissident, Hou Xiaotian, the wife of a prominent democracy advocate now serving a 13-year prison sentence, said she was awakened at 1 A.M. Saturday, taken briefly to a police station and then driven to a Beijing suburb. 
There she was kept in a comfortable guest house, where she was allowed to watch television but was not permitted to leave or to make telephone calls.
Ms. Hou said her guards were reasonably cordial and indicated that she had been detained because of Mr. Baker's visit. 
The authorities drove her home tonight, a couple of hours after Mr. Baker left Beijing.
"I had hoped that through his efforts, Wang Juntao and Chen Ziming and other political prisoners would be released, but I know this requires a long time," Ms. Hou said when asked to discuss what she would have told Mr. Baker. "But before then, I think there are practical needs that should be met, problems such as improving their health care."
Mr. Wang, who is Ms. Hou's husband, and Mr. Chen were sentenced to 13 years for their reputed roles in the Tiananmen democracy movement that was crushed in June 1989.
Dai Qing, a journalist who had been denied an exit permit to take up a fellowship at Harvard University this fall, also reportedly was detained this weekend because of tentative plans to visit with American officials. 
Her telephone number produced a busy signal all night, and it is not clear if she has been released yet.
Mr. Baker was asked at a news conference before his departure about the detention of Ms. Dai. He said, "If it's true, it would be distressing news."
Â 
Churchgoers Barred
It was not clear how the Chinese authorities knew of the tentative meetings, which apparently were not arranged on the telephone. 
But Chinese officials knew that there had been suggestions that Mr. Baker or his assistants might meet with dissidents.
Earlier this morning, when Mr. Baker attended a service at a local church, seven or eight regular Chinese churchgoers were denied entrance because the authorities suspected that they were troublemakers, one of them said.
"For some reason, they didn't let me into church today," the churchgoer said. 
"I even went to the service when President Bush was here. 
It's my right to go to church, and when they didn't let me in, I felt very shaken and disturbed."
One of Mr. Baker's aims in his talks with Chinese officials was to achieve the release of some Chinese dissidents. 
China so far has not released any, but it did give information on about 800 dissidents whose names were on a list presented by American officials to Beijing.

file: China Dismisses Culture Minister, An Advocate of Artistic Freedom.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese Government said Monday that it had dismissed Culture Minister Wang Meng, a noted novelist who was exiled during the Cultural Revolution and whose rise to government power three years ago was hailed as a sign of renewed literary freedom.
Mr. Wang was the most prominent of several high Chinese officials removed at the end of a meeting of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Monday. 
According to today's issue of the People's Daily, the committee also dismissed Yuan Chongwu, the deputy director of the State Commission on Science and Technology, and Lin Hongru, the deputy director of the nation's central bank.
Â 
Campaign Against Liberals
In addition, three judges of the Supreme Court were removed. 
The newspaper identified them as Zhang Ming, Yue Qide and Gai Fengqi.
Mr. Wang is the highest-ranking official to be ousted since the crackdown on the student democracy movement in June, and since China began a campaign against the ''bourgeois liberalism'' of the West. 
Just before the crackdown, Zhao Ziyang, the General Secretary of the Communist Party, was removed for sympathizing with the student protesters.
There have been persistent reports in Hong Kong that the Governor of Hainan province, Liang Xiang, has also been relieved of his post and is under investigation for corruption. 
Mr. Liang spent five years as party secretary in Shenzhen, China's first special economic zone, and was deeply involved in China's market forays with foreign nations. 
He was also considered closely tied to Mr. Zhao, whose political allies are now all under suspicion.
Mr. Wang, who is 54 years old and was recently rumored to be ill and away from Beijing, was replaced by He Jinzhi, a poet who had been a high-ranking official in the propaganda department of the Communist Party. 
His appointment appears to signal a further campaign to keep a firm hand on books, plays, films, painting and virtually every other sphere of the arts, all of which fall under the Culture Minister's control.
While the official press here said outright that Mr. Wang had been dismissed, the Chinese television also said Monday night that he had ''repeatedly asked to be relieved of his official posts to concentrate on his writing.''
While that could not be independently confirmed, in 1986 Mr. Wang had resisted his appointment as Culture Minister, but acceded when the party leadership decided that his appointment would signal its intention to follow far more relaxed policies.
Mr. Wang has long been a powerful symbol in China. 
He was denounced in 1957 in the Communist Party's anti-rightist campaign because of a short story he had written. 
The story, called ''The Newcomer in the Organization Department,'' was about apathetic Communist Party cadres in an inefficient factory after the Communist revolution in 1949.
Accused of writing ''destructive, anti-party, anti-socialist work,'' he was assigned to manual labor on a farm outside Beijing. 
He was briefly reprieved, then banished in 1963 to a remote desert area in northwestern China, where he remained for 16 years and was forbidden to write.
The man who restored Mr. Wang's reputation and his typewriter is the same man who, presumably, was involved in his downfall: Deng Xiaoping, China's foremost leader. 
While Mr. Deng has not been seen in three months and is often rumored to be ill, he is still believed to be in firm control of the Government.
Mr. Deng invited Mr. Wang back to Beijing in 1979, allowing him to write a series of novels and short stories based on his experiences in exile. 
The novels were broadly popular, not only for their portrayals of frontier life, but also because they depicted the enormous costs of the Cultural Revolution.
Mr. Wang's appointment as Culture Minister in 1986 was hailed as a permanent turning away from the repression of the Cultural Revolution. 
Just before he was appointed, he told fellow writers that a ''golden age'' was at hand, and that writers should not ''go with the tide or follow the wind,'' but instead should follow their consciences. 
At the same time, he warned that writers could not stray too far off the socialist path or question the legitimacy of the party to rule over China.
Â 
Permissiveness Criticized
Presumably, he was removed for allowing literature that led to just that. 
While there is considerable debate here over what lay beneath the democracy movement - officially described here as riots intended to overthrow the Government - many in the Government have suggested recently that it was encouraged by the air of permissiveness in the society in recent years.
Under Mr. Wang's tenure, at least until the crushing of the student movement on Tiananmen Square, there was a resurgence of artistic expression. 
A far wider variety of literary works were published, and Beijing even saw a few avant garde art exhibitions. 
Mr. Wang said early in his tenure that ''neither administrative measures nor propaganda are effective in defining what is true, good and beautiful.''
But in recent months, such views have become far less tolerable within the party. 
Mr. Wang's dismissal was foreshadowed recently when he was replaced as the head of the Communist Party within the ministry.

file: China Disputes Western Accounts Of Secret Trials of Demonstrators.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today denied reports that it had held secret trials of those involved in last year's democracy movement and also appeared to deny that it had arrested as many as 10,000 people in connection with the movement.
The official New China News Agency quoted a senior Chinese judge, whom it did not identify, as sharply criticizing a foreign news account that some 800 Chinese had been sentenced recently for their role in the democracy movement.
The article, which appeared in The Washington Post last week, attributed the report to Communist Party members.
The judge said this was ''sheer fabrication'' and in particular denied that any protesters had been tried secretly. 
But the dispatch did say that there had been some cases ''arising from the anti-Government riots'' that were tried openly.
Â 
Post Stands by Its Reports
The Post said it stood by its reports by Daniel Southerland, its Beijing correspondent.
Mike Getler, the Post's assistant managing editor for foreign news, said, ''The attack on Southerland's reporting by Chinese authorities contains no actual evidence to discredit his reports.''
The authorities have released almost no information about those arrested or the disposition of their cases. 
This was the first time an official denied that the number of protesters detained had been as high as generally believed in the West, where most estimates start at 10,000 and go higher, although some have been released. 
In the past, Communist Party and Government officials, including General Secretary Jiang Zemin, have declined to comment on questions about arrests and detentions.
The Government's denial, like other recent measures such as the lifting of martial law earlier this month, seemed aimed at improving China's image abroad, particularly before the United States Congress deliberates on sanctions against Beijing.

file: China Dissidents Lose Sway in Exile.txt
text:
ï»¿
Teacher Fang and Teacher Li, as their admirers know them, still carry Chinese passports, and it is not impossible that they would return to a changed China. 
But many Chinese here say, with regret, that one lesson of the last year is that exiles can have little impact on the motherland and that distance makes them almost irrelevant.
Â 
From Heady Days to Reality
After the military crackdown on the democracy movement a year ago, many refugees who escaped abroad joined with other overseas Chinese to form organizations that they hoped would press the battle for democracy that was lost in Tiananmen Square. 
In the breathless days of international sympathy and endless press coverage, one of the parallels often made was with Sun Yat-sen's campaign at the beginning of the century to overthrow the emperors. 
Sun Yat-sen succeeded in fomenting revolution from abroad in 1911 and was able to return to become President of the new Chinese republic.
It has not been so easy this time. 
The overseas democracy movement, particularly the Paris-based Federation for a Democratic China, faces a task that is far more difficult than the one Sun Yat-sen encountered in the dying days of the Qing Dynasty. 
Now the Government is strong and the Communists seem able to regulate the flow of information and prevent infiltration by the overseas organizations.
''Their influence is extremely small,'' said the admirer of Mr. Fang and Miss Li, speaking of the exiles in general. 
''We can't read their publications, and we can't have any contact with them. 
We're afraid to join any underground that might be linked with them.''
Â 
A Darkening View
Of course, the Government may gradually ease the intimidation, and that may lead to greater access by dissidents based abroad. 
Likewise, informal contacts with foreigners and the flow of information from abroad seem to sow dissatisfaction with the present leaders, but this happens mostly by itself rather than by design of the overseas democracy movement.
Hua Sheng, a prominent economist who left Beijing a few months before the protests and is now studying at Oxford University in England, said that at first there was optimism among the exiles that they could help bring about change in China and then return, in some cases to take up important positions. 
That optimism has dissipated, he said in a telephone interview.
''Especially recently, most Chinese students have become pessimistic about their influence on China,'' he said. 
''The longer they are away from China, the less confident they feel.''
Scholars like Mr. Hua face a painful choice. 
They can return to China and struggle for change while suffering poor living conditions, suspicion from rivals and the risk that they will be denounced or denied the chance to do meaningful work, or they can remain in foreign countries where it is difficult to find the jobs they want and where they are cut off from their avowed aim of saving the motherland.
Â 
Overseas Movement's Problems
The overseas Chinese democracy movement had barely begun when it was beset with credibility problems and internal conflicts. 
Moreover, the overseas movement has found it very difficult to penetrate China's armor.
For example, there were several efforts to send information into the country by fax machines, but the Government immediately warned owners of the machines that they would get in trouble if copies of the faxes were passed around. 
As a result, intellectuals sometimes heard about the fax campaign, but overwhelmingly from Voice of America accounts rather than from bootleg copies of the faxes.
The exiles have also been hobbled by a lack of support from foreign governments, particularly those of Hong Kong and Taiwan. 
The British-run Government in Hong Kong has refused to let the exiles visit, much less run their offices in the territory.
One project that might have given the overseas groups a major platform for their views was the Goddess of Democracy, the radio ship they planned to use to broadcast to China. 
That plan collapsed in May when Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan responded to pressure from China by refusing to allow the ship access to their ports.
What most surprised many Chinese intellectuals was that Taiwan, the traditional anti-Communist bastion among overseas Chinese, appears to be giving up that role. 
Diplomats say that as Taiwan becomes more democratic, its Government has become less preoccupied with activities to sow discord or democracy on the mainland and more concerned with winning votes by keeping the peace and nurturing business ties with the mainland.
The 50 million Chinese around the world have been enormously important in helping China open up over the last dozen years, and ethnic Chinese from Hong Kong, Taiwan and elsewhere have supplied more than 60 percent of foreign investment.
These links between China and the outside world, including the growing number of Taiwan tourists on the mainland, may well hurt the Government more than a boycott. 
Few if any of the overseas Chinese are evangelists for democracy, but they often speak scathingly of the Communists' economic performance and of their political campaigns.

file: CHINA ENDS PURGE OF PARTY_S RANKS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A year after the Communist Party announced a purge of members who were involved in the democracy movement, party members say, with relief and a bit of surprise, that the purge has fizzled.
Hard-liners who ordered the purge succeeded in making life miserable for many of their opponents, and in forcing a significant share of the nation's 48 million Communist Party members to go through a complex process of ''re-registration'' that was intended to weed out those who ''deviated from the correct political stand.''
But after months of meetings, self-criticisms and essay writing, virtually everyone has managed to stay in the party.
The ineffectiveness of the purge suggests the extent of the deadlock that has brought the Chinese political system to a virtual halt, officials say. 
The hard-liners have been pre-eminent for more than a year, but they have been unable to consolidate their gains by eliminating large numbers of their antagonists.
A Stalemate in the Party
''Neither side can overcome the other,'' said an official with first-hand experience in China's power struggles. 
''There's a sort of agreement reached now: you don't do anything, and I won't do anything either.''
The leadership called for the purge on June 25 last year, and the entire party membership in Beijing was obliged to re-register to retain party membership. 
Outside the capital the process was far looser and generally involved only party officials, party members say.
The re-registration is now completed or nearing completion in most work units, and party members say that the vast majority - perhaps 99 percent or more - have been approved to remain in the party, even in certain sensitive departments under the Central Committee that are hotbeds of quiet opposition to the hard-liners.
Officials say privately that only a few prominent liberals have been prevented from re-registering so far. 
Among them are Zhu Houze, a former director of the Central Committee's propaganda department; Du Runsheng, the head of an influential research center, and Li Rui, Li Chang and Yu Guangyuan, all members, along with Mr. Du, of the party's powerful Central Advisory Commission.
Â 
Five Left in Limbo
Although these five people have not been allowed to re-register, they have not been expelled from the Communist Party either. 
Nor has there been a definitive judgment on their cases; instead they have been labeled ''registration postponed,'' officials familiar with their cases said. 
The result has been to leave them in limbo.
Despite reports to the contrary, another prominent liberal - Yan Mingfu, nominal head of the Central Committee's United Front Department, who has been removed from decision-making - has tentatively been allowed to re-register, an official said. 
And the most prominent person to fall from power last year, Zhao Ziyang, the General Secretary, remains in the party although investigations into his conduct are continuing.
Even those in the ''registration postponed'' category may receive a favorable decision soon. 
Chen Yun, the 85-year-old mastermind of central planning, has recently argued against expelling people from the party for political reasons, Chinese officials said. 
Mr. Chen is said to have cited the case of Wang Ming, a rival of Mao Zedong. 
Mr. Wang lost a power struggle with Mao in the 1930's but not only kept his party membership but also retained a seat on the central committee.
Holding onto party membership can be important for senior officials who still hope to make a comeback. 
Deng Xiaoping, the senior Chinese leader, was dismissed from all his posts in 1976, but his return to power a couple of years later was facilitated by the failure of his enemies to strip him of his party membership.
Â 
'The Purge Isn't Working'
''The conservatives would like to kick out a lot more people,'' a young worker said. 
''But they are too high up, and they don't control the re-registration at the grass roots. 
That's why the purge isn't working.''
Others say the purge fizzled because the hard-liners lost their nerve and were afraid of creating enemies of large numbers of people by expelling them.
''What could they do?'' a university teacher asked. 
''Expel all intellectuals?
That would just make them more unpopular than ever.''
Of course, with 48 million members, the expulsion of even a tiny fraction adds up to a large number of individuals. 
In 1989, 33,400 party members were expelled - a modest increase over the figure in previous years, but still less than one-tenth of 1 percent of the national membership.
Those who have not been allowed to re-register seem to fall into several categories. 
Some are party members whose involvement in the democracy movement was so flagrant that it could not be overlooked, as in the case of people who were imprisoned. 
Others tried to resign from the party, but found themselves expelled instead. 
Some people have also been purged for reasons that have little to do with politics: they took bribes, engaged in sexual misconduct or were otherwise judged unfit.

file: China Ends Silence on Deal U.S. Rescinded.txt
text:
ï»¿
When President Bush voided the sale of a Seattle aerospace supplier to a Chinese Government agency, the company's executives and employees saw themselves caught in political crosswinds stemming from the killings of demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in June.
For two weeks, the Chinese Government did not comment on Mr. Bush's action, but today the silence ended. 
The official New China news agency asserted that the deal by the China National Aero-Technology Import and Export Corporation, or Catic, to buy Mamco Manufacturing Inc. was entirely legal and did not pose any threat to the United States, the Reuters news agency reported.
The Chinese said the United States would be responsible for any financial losses that resulted from President Bush's order. 
The statement did not specify what recourse Beijing might seek.
In Compliance With Laws
An official of Catic was quoted by Reuters as saying the acquisition ''is solely a commercial activity in the area of civilian aircraft manufacture, the whole procedure of which was in full compliance with the Federal and local laws and regulations of the United States.''
The official added, ''This acquisition does not involve any high-technology leakage, nor does it impair or threaten the national security of the United States,'' Reuters reported.
Roger Bolton, a spokesman for the Treasury Department, said: ''We are going to withhold comment until we hear directly from the Chinese Government. 
We haven't heard from them yet.''
On Feb. 
2, Mr. Bush had ordered Catic, a Chinese agency that exports military and civilian planes, to divest itself of Mamco, saying Catic's continued control of the airplane parts maker might threaten the national security of the United States. 
A panel comprising officials of eight agencies and headed by Stephen Canner, the director of the Office of International Investment in the Treasury Department, had recommended that the purchase be rescinded. 
Catic had acquired Mamco on Nov. 
30.
Mr. Canner has declined to comment on the reasons for the panel's recommendation.
Â 
Boeing Is Main Customer
Mamco supplies small mechanical parts, built to customer specifications, for commercial aircraft. 
Its largest customer is the Boeing Company, and it reported sales of $19 million in 1989.
''I find it hard to believe we pose a threat to national security,'' Kenneth A. Keller, president and chief executive of Mamco, said in a recent interview. 
''We're no different than literally hundreds of other machine and job shops around the country.''
Mr. Keller said officials of the Chinese agency had attempted to persuade United States officials to rescind the ruling, which requires that Catic divest itself of Mamco by May 1, unless an extension of up to three months is granted.
Mr. Keller said Catic was ''exploring all other avenues'' to prevent the divestiture. 
But if those attempts are not successful, he said ''we'd probably talk to Catic about a re-acquisition of the company.''
''It is just too early to speculate what will happen,'' he added.
Mamco makes no parts for export. 
In addition to Boeing, its customers include McDonnell Douglas, Bell Helicopter and Cleveland Pneumatic. 
Mamco does not employ full-time designers or engineers and does not own the rights to the designs of its products. 
None of its products are on Government lists of militarily significant high-technology parts. 
205 Employees A 50-year-old company that had been privately held before its sale to Catic, Mamco operates in an industrial area of Seattle. 
Its 205 employees work two shifts on weekdays and one on Saturday and Sunday.
Catic is responsible for much of China's imports and exports, and some American officials have contended that it has close ties to China's military. 
The Seattle Times, quoting unidentified Congressional sources, has reported that Catic provided two General Electric jet-turbine engines to the military, which dissassembled them for study, breaking agreements that the engines would be for civilian use only and would be left intact.
The order involving Mamco is believed to be the first in which a President has ordered a foreign corporation to sell an American company it had already purchased. 
President Bush acted under a 1988 trade bill that authorized the President to block sales of companies to foreign interests if the sales are seen as threats to national security.
Mr. Keller, who is 45 years old, a certified public accountant from Oregon, purchased Mamco in 1988 with two partners, James Young and Barry Allen. 
The three men had met and worked together for six years at Security Properties Inc., a Seattle real estate company, where Mr. Keller was chief financial officer. 
They left that company with the intention of buying a number of businesses in the Pacific Northwest at a rate of one a year. 
Mamco was their first acquisition.
Â 
Joint Venture Sought
Mr. Keller said that as the partners searched for other companies to acquire, they decided to bring in joint-venture partners. 
In early 1989, an accounting firm introduced them to officials of the Chinese agency.
''Catic was not interested in our proposals, but a few months later offered to buy Mamco instead,'' Mr. Keller said.
After the deal was concluded in November, the company's managers stayed on to insure that it remained under American management. 
Catic did bring two executives to the operation, including Shan-Jun Xiong, Catic's chairman of United States operations. 
He is not involved in day-to-day operations of Mamco, Mr. Keller said, but oversees Catic's other interests in the United States, including its dealings with Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.

file: China Enlivens Hong Kong_s First Direct Vote.txt
text:
ï»¿
For the first time in the 150-year history of Hong Kong, people here will be able to vote directly for some of their legislative representatives in an election scheduled for Sept. 
15. And in the final days before that vote, the most compelling, most emotional campaign issue in this British colony is China.
While the 54 candidates competing for the 18 directly elected seats in the legislature have been discussing pollution, traffic and crime, their positions are often interchangeable and their debates dull -- until the subject of China is introduced. 
Then, voices are raised, tempers flare and charges and countercharges fly.
One candidate told voters that he had publicly opposed China's crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989, but that his opponent was "scared to death when dealing with China."
Another candidate accused his opponent of trying to pretend now that he had taken part in demonstrations against China in 1989.
With Hong Kong scheduled to revert to Chinese control in 1997, many here would like to see a strong, independent local government set up before then.
"The main political issue here is the growing influence of China," said Anthony Cheung, a political commentator and a senior lecturer in the City Polytechnic's Dept of Public and Social Administration. 
"Voters want to know how candidates have reacted to that."
While only 18 seats are up for direct vote in the legislature of 60, which has largely been a rubber-stamp body, voters and politicians are taking this election seriously, hoping that if it is a success, they can press Britain for further reforms.
In Hong Kong, where officials are often criticized for bowing to pressure from China, polls show that two of the most popular candidates are Szeto Wah and Martin Lee, both outspoken critics of China who have been publicly branded as "subversive" by Beijing.
Newspaper polls indicate that Mr. Lee's party, United Democrats of Hong Kong, may take more than half of the directly elected seats. 
The party's 14 liberal candidates have been critical of China's abuse of human rights and its interference in Hong Kong affairs.
Several other parties are fielding a few candidates, but most contestants are running as independents.
While pro-Beijing groups are supporting several candidates, and half a dozen other candidates are known for their mainland sympathies, Mr. Cheung said, "Today, in Hong Kong, to be branded pro-Beijing is a liability."
Indeed, one candidate endorsed by a pro-Beijing trade group has complained that his posters have been defaced with slogans like "running dog of the Chinese Communists."
The apparent popularity of the United Democrats and their allies has made both China and the British Government anxious, political experts say.
Recently, China's semi-official China News Service advised Hong Kong voters that "apart from considering the political platform of each candidate, they should also take into consideration the attitude of each candidate towards Hong Kong's relationship with the mainland."
"Without a good relationship with the mainland, there will be a great impact on Hong Kong's prosperity and stabilityI," the agency said.
The 18 popularly elected legislators will take their seats in the Legislative Council alongside 21 Government-appointed lawmakers, and 21 indirectly elected representatives from constituency groups defined by the Government, including doctors, lawyers and teachers.
Francis Ho, of the Government's Constitutional Affairs office, said that of the four million potential voters, about half were registered to vote.
And no one maintains that Hong Kong's six million residents are in the grip of election fever.
The local television and radio stations do not cover the campaigns on their regular nightly news programs, for fear of violating tough equal time laws laid down by the Government. 
And the Government does not permit political advertisements to be carried on radio or television.
Campaigning is largely a matter of handing out leaflets and knocking on doors.

text:

China expelled a British journalist today amid some indications that the Government is tightening control over foreign journalists.
The Briton, Andrew Higgins of The Independent, said he had been summoned to the Public Security Bureau today and ordered to leave China within 48 hours. 
The authorities did not give a reason, but in June Mr. Higgins reported on a confidential Chinese document that discussed the suppression of a nationalist movement in the Chinese region of Inner Mongolia.
Security officials found the document in his luggage while he was on a trip within China. 
The Chinese Embassy in London later advised The Independent's head office to transfer Mr. Higgins. He had already been planning to leave China in the next few months.
Â 
Wrote About '89 Crackdown
Mr. Higgins, who is 33 years old and speaks fluent Chinese, is co-author of a book about the military crackdown on the democracy movement in 1989.
"I'm saddened and disappointed," Mr. Higgins said this evening. 
"I've spent a good part of my life involved with and interested in China, and so to have it all sealed off to me so unceremoniously is very distressing."
Mr. Higgins is the first Beijing-based correspondent to be expelled since John Pomfret of The Associated Press and Allan W. Pessin of Voice of America were ordered to leave in June 1989, 10 days after the crackdown at Tiananmen Square.
The state security apparatus appears to have tightened surveillance of foreign journalists in the last few weeks, possibly as a reaction to the upheaval in the Soviet Union. 
Security agents seem to be following more foreign correspondents than usual, and sometimes interrogating those Chinese who dare to meet with them.
In addition, at least four American correspondents were contacted by an unknown Chinese last week and asked to take some materials and pass them on to Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, who was visiting China. 
The correspondents declined, fearing that they were being set up for a charge of spying, and in at least one case security agents were seen hovering in the background taking photos.
In another sign of a harsh line, the Government refused today to allow Hou Xiaotian to visit her imprisoned and hospitalized husband, Wang Juntao, a prominent dissident. 
Ms. Hou was scheduled to have her monthly meeting with her husband today, but for the second month in a row the authorities refused to admit her, said a Chinese with firsthand knowledge.
The prison officials did not give a reason, but they had earlier asked Ms. Hou to write a self-criticism and to promise that she would cut off all contacts with foreign journalists. 
Ms. Hou declined, fearing that a self-criticism might be used as the basis for legal action against her and concerned that her husband's treatment might worsen if she pledged not to tell anyone about it.

file: China Fights an Academy Award Nomination.txt
text:
ï»¿
The nomination of the Chinese film "Judou" this month for an Academy Award might have been a tremendous triumph for a nation that has long sought respect from the West. 
Instead, in a move that says much about the state of the arts in China today, the Government has tried to suppress the film and withdraw it from consideration.
"Judou," a beautifully filmed tragedy portraying a dye factory and the family that runs it, has become the centerpiece of a bitter drama about politics and art in China. 
If "Judou" is a symbol of the best in Chinese films, the Government's treatment of the film and of the Oscar nomination is a stark measure of the cultural repression that continues to haunt Chinese intellectuals and artists some 20 months after the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown.
Throughout China, cultural life has gone through a recession: the most acclaimed authors are in exile or are writing only for their desk drawers. 
Experimental art has been effectively banned. 
The country's most famous rock singers are tightly restricted. 
The film world, however, is perhaps the most tightly controlled of all.
"Films are the most effective way of reaching the people, and now the Government wants more films that promote socialist values," said a Chinese writer, who has seen the film. 
" 'Judou' leaves one with a sense of tragedy, of sadness. 
The Government doesn't like unhappy films."
Â 
Bleak Themes, Sad End
"Judou," set in a the countryside in the 1920's, is a vivid depiction of the dye factory's aging owner, who takes on a young and unwilling wife to bear a son. 
He beats her ferociously when she fails to become pregnant, and she finds solace in the arms of her husband's adopted son. 
The two young lovers produce a boy, a strangely quiet, cold-blooded child who ends up killing both the old man and his mother's lover, his real father. 
The film was directed by one of China's most talented young film artists, Zhang Yimou.
The Chinese Government's attempts to suppress the film may prevent it from being considered for an Academy Award. 
While "Judou" was one of five nominated for best foreign film, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences could reconsider the nomination if pressed to adhere strictly to eligibilty requirements. 
Academy rules require films to have been released publicly to a paying audience in their own countries between Nov. 
1, 1989, and Oct. 
31, 1990. 
But, while "Judou" has won acclaim overseas, including the Luis Bunuel Award at the Cannes Film Festival in France, the film is effectively banned in China.
"Judou," the first Chinese film to be nominated for an Oscar, is the latest in a line of artistic Chinese films since the 1980's that have appealed not only to Chinese audiences but have captured interest abroad also. 
Such films included "Yellow Earth," "Red Sorghum" and "Hibiscus Town" and were dramatically different from the propaganda films characteristic of earlier periods.
Â 
Who Has Seen It
Last summer, during a brief period of cultural relaxation, "Judou" began to attract attention with reviews and commentaries in the official press telling readers that it would soon be released. 
But hard-liners in the film industry regained control and have blocked the film's release, Chinese and foreign film experts say.
In recent weeks, the Chinese Government has asked twice to have the film withdrawn from consideration for an Oscar, and reportedly even contested the film's eligibility. 
So far, the academy seems to have stood by its nomination.
Many Chinese intellectuals and officials have managed to see a video copy of "Judou" or to attend private screenings that are sometimes held for films that are deemed too sensitive for the masses to view. 
It is to open in New York on March 15.
"Aside from videotaped copies of the film or other special circumstances, the film has not been shown here," said a Chinese film official. 
"I suspect it hasn't been approved because of something to do with the sexual aspects in the film."
While the prurient interest of most Americans would doze during "Judou," for there is no depiction of sex or nudity, it is a bit racy by Chinese standards. 
The young wife bathes, her bare back to the camera, and her adulterous relationship with her lover is central to the plot.
Â 
China's Image Abroad
Foreign diplomats and other Chinese who have seen the film suggest that the Government may not be happy with the film's bleak delineation of rural life and its pessimistic ending. 
One Chinese connected to the film industry said the China Film Bureau is considering stricter guidelines for films made with foreign cooperation and will not tolerate extremely anti-traditional films or films that portray only the dark side or the backwardness of China to the rest of the world. 
"Judou" received Japanese financing.
The Chinese Film Bureau declined to be interviewed. 
The film's director, Mr. Zhang, said that film officials had asked for modifications but added that he had not had a chance to talk with them about specifics.
Even if the film does not win an Oscar or even retain its nomination, Mr. Zhang, who spoke cautiously in a phone interview from Tokyo, says he will not be discouraged.
"Those of use who have been through the Cultural Revolution can bear a great deal, for we have already endured many great storms," he said.
"But I still hope that someday my film can pass the censors. 
I made the film so that 1.1 billion Chinese people could see it."

file: China Gains in Mideast Crisis But Loses Cold War Benefits.txt
text:
ï»¿
Less than a year and a half after China's leaders sent tanks and machine guns to crush the Tiananmen democracy movement, Western sanctions are being dismantled and China is regaining status in the international community.
Japan is resuming subsidized loans to China. 
The European Community last month lifted economic sanctions against China. 
A group of American Congressmen is expected in Beijing this month for the first time since the crackdown. 
Countries like Saudi Arabia and Singapore have in the last few months established diplomatic relations with Beijing.
"China has withstood the international anti-socialist environment and safeguarded the socialist system," crowed the official New China News Agency.
While most of the world has suffered from the gulf crisis, China has been a beneficiary. 
Scholars, diplomats and Chinese themselves say China benefited in two ways: Saddam Hussein's behavior gave the West a new enemy and China won gratitude for its cooperation in imposing sanctions against Iraq.
Â 
'Best of All Worlds'
"The gulf crisis accelerated a process that was already under way, of them waiting us out," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"It's the best of all worlds for them, because they'be been able to reintegrate themselves with the West without sacrificing any third world credentials to do it."
Yet there are signs that over all China is a loser in the geopolitical reordering that has accompanied the end of the cold war. 
China has lost the leverage it had in playing the Soviet Union and the United States against each other, and its leaders may also be at a disadvantage in an environment in which nuclear weapons matter less than economic strength.
"People don't pay much attention to China any more," a European ambassador said the other day. 
Most experts agree that China matters less than it used to -- a proposition that drives some Government officials here to alternate between despair and fury. 
Visiting Americans these days are sometimes greeted with almost obsessive explanations of why China is still of fundamental importance to American interests.
Â 
Never Much of a Threat
The West's sanctions were never threatening to China in any fundamental sense. 
The sanctions included delays in new World Bank loans, a freeze on most military cooperation, and a halt to most high-level exchanges. 
Ordinary imports from China were never curbed, and in fact they have risen sharply: China's trade surplus with the United States could exceed $10 billion this year, up from $3.5 billion in 1988, before the crackdown.
Military cooperation remains on ice, but World Bank loans are gradually being resumed, and high-level exchanges are increasing. 
Zhu Rongji, Shanghai's mayor, visited the United States this summer; Wan Li, the head of China's legislature, will tour Great Britain this month; and Wu Xueqian, a politburo member, is leaving in a few days for Tokyo.
"The pace is very slow, but I can see that the direction is toward improvement in relations" with the West, said Yuan Ming, an international relations expert at Beijing University.
In any case, sanctions affected China's relations with only a relatively small number of countries. 
Most of China's neighbors were uncritical of its behavior and continued to do business with China as before.
In some respects, China now has broader international support than ever: Saudi Arabia and Singapore have newly established diplomatic relations with China, while Indonesia has resumed ties. 
South Korea will open an office in Beijing very soon, and would like to establish diplomatic relations.
"We were never so upset about the crackdown," said a diplomat from an Asian country that has its own human rights problems. 
"It's their business."
Â 
Communist Legitimacy Eroded
This is not to say that the crackdown on the democracy movement was painless, for the killings of peaceful protesters deeply eroded the Communist Party's legitimacy at home and among Chinese overseas as well as in the West. 
But some Chinese officials say the hard-liners probably regard the foreign sanctions as an acceptable price to pay, given that their alternative may have been loss of power. 
The price may be acceptable even if, as many believe, the Government's relations with the West will never again be as warm as before.
"Things will return to business as usual, but that emotional enthusiasm for China won't come back any time soon," a Western diplomat said.
One reason is that while the Bush Administration is gratified by China's cooperation in the Security Council, China's critics are less impressed. 
Their quarrel with Beijing was not about diplomacy, but about human rights, and they see no fundamental easing of the domestic repression.
While the Bush Administration is expected to favor further dismantling of sanctions, Congress may have other ideas. 
John T. Kamm, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, expects Congress to make a new attempt next year to end China's Most Favored Nation status. 
He also is bracing for an effort to establish a code of conduct for American corporations dealing with China.
"We may well find ourselves in a position where Japan and the European Community are lifting sanctions, and we're adding sanctions," Mr. Kamm said.
Â 
Mutual Resentment and Suspicion
China wants a resumption of cooperation with the West, but it is wary that too much interaction might again lead to unrest. 
The resentments and suspicions are mutual and may slow the reconciliation on both sides.
A classified Communist Party document, obtained from a well-connected Chinese in Beijing, conveys these apprehensions. 
The document, an analysis of international affairs published at the end of last year by the Central Committee Propoganda Department, warns that "the struggle between the two systems" will be prolonged and intense.
"Since the appearance of the first socialist state in 1917, this kind of struggle has never ceased," the analysis reads. 
"It only varies in its form, intensity and the tactics employed. 
Now the struggle has entered a new stage, and the struggle will be sharper, more complex and more intense than before. 
We must be highly vigilant."
While most nations are celebrating the end of the cold war, China has been saying, even before the invasion of Kuwait, that the new environment is not so wonderful after all.
Â 
Emerging Regional Powers
One difficulty for China is that a multipolar world is likely to see the emergence of new regional powers including Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, India and Indonesia. 
China has had wars or bitter disputes with each of these countries in recent decades.
"They've always hailed, in theory, the emergence of a more multipolar world," said Harry Harding, a China scholar at the Brookings Institution in Washington. 
"But now that it's finally happening, the problem for China is that its relations with many of these emerging poles are rather strained."
Chinese leaders are most anxious about the rise of Japan, which they remember fighting in the 1930's and 1940's, and they often regard Americans as naive in playing down Japan as a military and strategic threat. 
Some Chinese are even warning that the Soviet Union and Japan could form a threatening alliance in the Pacific, creating a reason for cooperation between the United States and China.
China has clearly lost leverage in that it can no longer play the United States and the Soviet Union against each other. 
But Mr. Harding says that in a larger sense China has fewer cards to play in a world in which money increasingly seems to matter more than guns.

file: China Gives Light Sentences To Advocates of Democracy.txt
text:
ï»¿
China said today that it had handed down relatively short sentences for 11 protesters tried recently in connection with the Tiananmen Square demonstrations of 1989 and subsequent democracy protests.
These are believed to be among the last cases of people who have been held without trial for more than two years after the military crackdown on June 4, 1989. 
The sentences, reported in Ta Kung Pao, a Hong Kong newspaper controlled by Beijing, ranged from immediate release to five years in prison. 
Sketchy details on some of the convictions were provided earlier this week in Beijing by people familiar with some of the defendants' families.
By the standards of the hard-line Government, which earlier sentenced two prominent democracy advocates to 13 years each, the sentences reported today were mostly on the mild side.
The disclosures come as Beijing officials are calling for faster economic change and seem to be a sign that China is finally willing to resolve many of the cases in which dissidents have been held without trial. 
Such cases have figured prominently in its discussions on human rights with Western nations.
Â 
Public Barred From Trials
While the relative leniency, by hard-line standards, is probably a response to Western pressure on China, there is not necessarily a specific link to the vote by the United States Senate this week to add conditions on an extension of low tariffs for Chinese exports.
The trials were held at various times, effectively closed to the public and the press, and the timing seems mostly to reflect the aim of resolving the Tiananmen cases by the time the national legislature convenes for its annual session, around March 20.
Wu Xuecan, a former editor at the official People's Daily who was arrested for distributing a leaflet during the demonstrations, was sentenced to four years. 
Zhai Weimin, whose name appeared in 1989 on a list of 21 most-wanted university students and who later tried to organize an anti-Government underground movement, was given three and a half years.
Sentences begin from the day of detention, so those who were taken into custody at the time of the 1989 crackdown have already served more than two and a half years. 
The sentences were also released in a State Council letter to John T. Kamm, a Hong Kong-based American businessman active in promoting human rights.
One dissident, Bai Chunxiang, about whom little is known, was released without punishment. 
Peng Rong, a Beijing University student who was arrested for organizing a survey about demonstrations, was sentenced to two years and is expected to be released in May. 
Li Minqi, a student arrested for his role in a commemoration on the first anniversary of the military crackdown, was also given two years and will presumably be released in June.
The Hong Kong report suggested that China had now closed all of the cases raised by the State Department in its human rights report this year. 
In fact, a number of cases remain unresolved. 
China has not given information on about a dozen other dissidents whose names appeared on a list presented to Beijing in November by Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d.
Moreover, Bao Tong, a top aide to the former Communist Party leader Zhao Ziyang, was officially arrested in January and is expected to be tried soon. 
Wu Jiaxiang, a party official as well as a writer and researcher, was also arrested recently and is awaiting trial.
Little is known about the six other people sentenced, but presumably they were workers who had taken part in the demonstrations: Li Baoqin and Wang Guoqing, five years each; Dong Huaiming, four years; Wang Zhong xian and Wei Ren, three years each, and Wang Lidong, two years.

file: China Imposes Tighter Curbs on Foreign Reporters.txt
text:
ï»¿
China imposed new restrictions on foreign journalists today and banned articles that in the view of the authorities ''distort facts'' or violate ''the public interest.''
The rules, signed by Prime Minister Li Peng on Friday, took effect today on their publication in People's Daily.
''Foreign correspondents and news agencies must observe journalistic ethics, and must not distort facts, fabricate rumors or use improper means in their reporting,'' read the most sweeping of the new rules. 
''Foreign correspondents and news agencies must not engage in activities that are incompatible with their status, or those that endanger state security, national unification, or the public interest of Chinese society.''
In serious cases, journalists who are found to have violated the regulations could be expelled from China.
The rules specified that they were to be interpreted by the Chinese authorities, so the practical effect was not immediately clear.

file: CHINA IS SOFTENING ITS ECONOMIC LINE.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a strong sign of shifting political winds in China, the official press is abruptly attacking the hard-line attitudes it espoused for the last two years and has instead started to call on the nation to emphasize economic growth and even adopt useful elements of capitalism.
The pirouette was reflected in a front-page essay today in People's Daily, which in the past carried mostly dour warnings against Western subversion. 
Today's article, headlined "Opening up to the world and using capitalism," was the boldest in a monthlong flurry of signals that change-minded leaders may be gaining the upper hand over ideologues.
"All of modern Chinese history has demonstrated that China can travel only the socialist road, not the capitalist road," the article began. 
"At the same time, recent world history shows us that economically backward nations -- especially those with long histories of feudalism -- must correctly use capitalism, rather than rejecting it out of hand. 
Only by critically absorbing those elements of Western culture that are useful to us, rather than disdaining them, can we prosper and flourish."
The wave of recent editorials apparently reflects a push by Deng Xiaoping, the 87-year-old paramount leader, for China to devote more energy to becoming prosperous and less to remaining ideologically pure. 
The Politburo is believed to have confirmed this moderate line, and the new articles indicate that the hard-liners are losing control even over the newspapers that they have dominated for more than two years.
Still, political fashions in China often change quickly, and it is unclear whether the recent articles reflect a major and irreversible trend to speed up economic liberalization. 
Even if economic growth is back at the top of the agenda, there is no hint that the regime will release political prisoners or tolerate challenges from Tibetan separatists or underground Catholic priests or disgruntled university students.
Calls for ideological vigilance and tributes to model Communists generally filled the front pages in the two and a half years after the June 1989 crackdown on the Tiananmen democracy movement. 
The crackdown, in which the army killed hundreds of protesters and wounded thousands, was accompanied by the rise of hard-line leaders who installed their lieutenants as editors of the major newspapers.
The People's Daily article appears days before the United States Senate's vote, scheduled for Tuesday, on renewing most-favored-nation trade status for China. 
The Administration is urging the Senate to renew the favorable tariff treatment, continuing President Bush's policy of trying to change China's behavor on human rights, arms sales to the third world and other issues by contact rather than by confrontation and punishment.
Â 
No Shift on Rights Seen
While there is no evidence of any major change by China on human rights, on economic topics there is no doubt that a switch has taken place. 
The People's Daily article published today called for tolerating a measure of capitalism in the Chinese economy, and gave a ringing endorsement of stock markets and other practices associated with the West.
On Saturday, People's Daily carried a front-page editorial calling on the nation to focus more attention on economic development -- and, by implication, give less attention to the Marxist ideology that the same newspaper has emphasized since the rise of the hard-liners in June 1989.
Also on Saturday, the official Guangming Daily filled most of the top two-thirds of the front page with a call to "liberate our thinking, deepen reform, open the door more widely."
It was a dizzying change in emphasis for a newspaper that just last month carried a front-page appeal for universities to select students more on the basis of loyalty to Communism.
Mr. Deng began the new drive for reform with a trip last month to the southern Chinese special economic zone of Shenzhen. 
He called for more rapid change and went out of his way to praise Shenzhen, a symbol of economic experimentation that has shown spectacular increases in prosperity but also in prostitution and drug abuse. 
The tide shifted apparently in part because Mr. Deng and other leaders determined that the best way for China to avoid the fate of the Soviet Union is to make people richer, and in part because other octogenarians who take a harder line are too feeble to fight back.
Today's article in People's Daily carried the byline Fang Sheng, which is almost certainly a pen name of an individual or a group of people in the central leadership. 
The fact that it was published on a Sunday -- when almost no one reads the newspaper, which is delivered to offices and factories rather than homes -- suggests that a Politburo member may have ordered the top editors to publish it but that they did their best to insure that as few readers as possible would notice it.
Â 
Adapting Capitalism
"Using capitalism includes developing an appropriate capitalist economy within our country, as a useful supplement to the socialist economy," the article said. 
"As our country is in only the preliminary stage of socialism, it is impossible to wipe out capitalism completely, and some exploitation will linger for a long while. 
So the important thing is to improve our guidance of these phenomena, and direct them onto a course where policy allows them."
Many elements of today's long article had appeared previously in one place or another, but they had not been combined with such force or clarity. 
The tone throughout sounded like a rebuke to the hard-liners. 
In particular, the article indicated that most Communists now acknowledge the need to use foreign capital and technology.
"On other matters, it seems that there are still some differences," the newspaper said, in a clear reference to hard-liners who are wary of capitalist influences. 
The article added that instead of fearing contacts with the West, China should expand exchanges "to enrich our culture."
Â 
Defining Socialism
"In the past we took the tortuous path of sealing ourselves off from the world and refusing to use capitalism," the essay declared, in a reference to the Maoist era. 
"Leftist errors and other factors were behind this, but they have nothing to do with socialism. 
On the contrary, in principle socialism means an open system and a reform-oriented economy."
A People's Daily editor said by telephone that the essay today was not an editorial or a commentary, but simply an "article."
He said he did not know the identity of the author.
Wu Guoguang, a former People's Daily editorial writer now studying at Princeton University, said he could recall only one other case in the last 15 years in which the newspaper carried a front-page commentary with a byline that was a pen-name. 
The other one was arranged by Mr. Deng's family and published last year, and Mr. Wu said an essay like today's would have to have the approval of a top leader.
While recent commentaries have been short of specifics, their tone is important because officials at every level are what the Chinese call feng pai -- weathervanes. 
In other words, they watch for hints of prevailing political winds before taking any action.

file: China Offers Cautious Economic Plan.txt
text:

China's Communist Party Central Committee concluded a major six-day meeting today, after approving a moderate, cautious new blueprint for the 1990's and warning that the next decade could determine the rise or fall of the nation's Communist system.
