The official New China News Agency said Ms. Leung had bribed a Government employee into obtaining a "most confidential" document, a copy of which she then forwarded onto her Hong Kong headquarters.
On Oct. 
5, Ms. Leung's newspaper published the entire text of the keynote speech by the Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin. 
The speech was delivered at an important Communist Party Congress that was held in mid-October.
The New China News Agency said Ms. Leung had destroyed her copy of the speech by burning parts of it in her hotel room bathroom, before discarding the remains in several trash cans on the streets. 
The dispatch added that Ms. Leung had obtained many secrets from the Government employee in exchange for a "large sum of money."
Patrick W. T. Wong, deputy editor at The Express newspaper, did not deny that Ms. Leung had obtained an advance copy of Mr. Jiang's speech. 
Asked if she had paid for a document, Mr. Wong said he had not seen her and so could not comment, but he added that his newspaper did not approve of paying money for information.
Â 
An Apparent Confession
National television this evening showed Ms. Leung, calm and steady, affixing her fingerprint to what appeared to be a signed 15-page confession. 
She was filmed answering several questions and then the camera displayed a bundle of money, suggesting that it had been found as evidence.
Until Ms. Leung is released, it will be impossible to confirm this account. 
Chinese Government versions of events have not always been noted for their accuracy.
The authorities say they treated her with leniency because she confessed to her crimes and was acting under the direction of her editor. 
The report said her editor had given an apology and promised that such a case would not happen again. 
The New China News Agency did not say what would happen to the two Chinese who obtained the document and provided it to her.
In May, Chinese State Security authorities searched the office of the Beijing-based reporter for The Washington Post, Lena H. Sun. They confiscated documents and issued a stern warning that she was involved in activities "incompatible with her status," but there have been no further repercussions.

file: China Orders Students Going Abroad to Pay Fees.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has issued new rules that would toughen restrictions on young people planning to study abroad, including a requirement that they first work for five years in China or pay large sums of money to the Government as deposit, officials say.
The new guidelines, issued by the State Education Commission last week and effective beginning Saturday, are apparently a result of months of deliberation on how to revise the program for overseas study, and to insure that greater numbers of students return.
The pronouncements were disclosed by several different Chinese officials and foreign diplomats, and they were confirmed by a spokesman at the State Education Commission.
Chinese officials have admitted privately that they are highly concerned that so few of their students have returned from studying overseas. 
Yet, the number of students preparing to apply to schools in the West has risen significantly since the military crackdown in early June, and word of the new rules, particularly the staggering amounts of money required for deposit, has worried many of them.
Despite assurances from Chinese leaders, many students say they fear that this new rule may represent a retreat from China's 12-year-old policy of promoting study in the West.
Two weeks ago, China's Education Minister, Li Tieying, told a group of returning students that ''the policy of sending people abroad to study will not, and has no reason to, change,'' according to the official People's Daily, which paraphrased Mr. Li's remarks.
The guidelines would require college graduates, who want to waive the work requirement and go abroad immediately, to pay the equivalent of about $530 for each year of college they attend. 
A student with a master's degree would have to pay the equivalent of $850 for each of the years in a master's program, and a doctoral student would need to pay about $1,275 a year. 
#2 Categories of Students It is not clear if graduate students would also have to pay for each of their years spent in college. 
The students would presumably get their money back if, and when, they returned to China. 
In contrast to these sums, a typical worker earns a salary of about $32 a month, and would need to save his entire salary for more than five years to pay for his child's college fee.
The Education Commission spokesman who confirmed the rules refused to elaborate on whether they applied to self-sponsored students or Government-sponsored students. 
Most students who study in the United States, for example, receive tuition assistance from the American university, but can be regarded by Chinese authorities as Government-sponsored students for visa purposes if the Government picks up at least a part of the educational bill.
Currently, however, self-sponsored students are not as strictly monitored as are sponsored ones, presumably because the Government has greater control over students it agrees to send overseas. 
According to the Chinese definition, the number of sponsored students tends to be higher than self-sponsored students, but in the last few months there are indications that the proportions have switched.
According to the United States Consulate in Beijing, there has been a marked decline in visa applications from Government-sponsored students, while those from self-sponsored students have risen. 
It is unclear if these new stipulations represent fundamental changes in an overall policy or merely stricter versions of a policy or regulation previously in place.
In China, the effectiveness of policies often depends on how thoroughly they are carried out. 
It is not clear if other ministries besides the State Education Commission are subject to similar rules, and even universities that fall under the jurisdiction of the Education Commission may not wish to carry out all parts of the regulation.
One Western diplomat suggested that, since the rule applies only to college graduates, students who had not yet received their bachelor's degrees may apply to study abroad and thereby circumvent the retroactive school fee and the five-year work requirement. 
''It's a possible loophole,'' he said.

file: China Ousts 2 Aides and Raises Drug Penalties.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government replaced its ministers of public security and trade today at a closing session of the legislature's standing committee. 
It also established the death penalty for serious traffickers in narcotics and pornography.
Chinese officials and foreign diplomats had expected the Cabinet shuffle, and the changes did not give any clues to the status of China's power struggle. 
Few Cabinet changes have taken place over the last year, and they have been announced with little fanfare because China still appears to be trying to preserve an image of political stabilityII.
Wang Fang, 70 years old, the minister who presided over public security during demonstrations in Beijing in June 1989, was replaced by his deputy minister, Tao Siju, 55, the official New China News Agency reported today.
The Public Security Ministry initially adopted a lenient approach to controlling the pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in 1989. 
But that approach failed, and ultimately the military was brought into the capital to crush the protests.
Â 
Reasons for Removal Unclear
In choosing such a strategy, Mr. Wang probably followed guidelines from China's senior leaders, and it is not clear whether his removal is related to his performance in 1989 or whether he is retiring because of his age.
Zheng Tuobin, the Minister of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade, was also removed from his post. 
No reason was given.
Mr. Zheng, who is 66, was replaced by his deputy minister, Li Lanqing. 
The 58-year-old Mr. Li speaks English and Russian and is a former Deputy Mayor of the nearby city of Tianjin.
The legislative session, of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, also passed resolutions that decree life imprisonment or the death penalty for serious crimes relating to the spread of pornography or narcotics.
Since the rise of the hard-liners in June 1989, the Government has waged a campaign against pornography, and recently it has also become increasingly concerned about the return of opium and other narcotics to some parts of China.
"The resolution is aimed at safeguarding social order and promoting advanced socialist culture by punishing pornography pushers," the press agency reported.

Mr. Terrill was an adviser to Shen Tong, a leader of the 1989 pro-democracy protests who was arrested Tuesday as he was preparing to meet with foreign reporters.

file: CHINA OUSTS ZHAO AND PICKS LEADERS TOUGH ON DISSENT.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Communist Party dismissed General Secretary Zhao Ziyang from all his posts today and named a new set of leaders who are likely to favor somewhat new directions in the nation's economic and political development.
The new leaders advocate economic relations with the outside world and aggressive economic development, but their past suggests that the emphasis will be on the planned economy rather than the market, and that they will be ready to crack down harshly on any sign of political protest.
The new Communist Party General Secretary is Jiang Zemin (pronounced jeeahng dzuh-meen), a 62-year-old engineer who has been Mayor and Communist Party leader in Shanghai in the last few years during efforts there to modernize the economic base of China's largest city.
Â 
Erudition but Not Fervor
A friend says that Mr. Jiang can recite passages from the American Declaration of Independence - in English - but that in Shanghai, he acted firmly to quell the pro-democracy movement.
The most important reason for choosing Mr. Jiang, according to Chinese familiar with high-level decision-making, was that China's elderly leaders believe he will improve the Communist Party's image and help rebuild the confidence of foreign business. 
They regard Mr. Jiang as being among the smarter officials in the Politburo, a cosmopolitan and well-educated politician.
Mr. Jiang speaks English, Russian and Rumanian and can read Japanese and French. 
He has met many foreign business executives, and his son is now studying in the United States. 
All of this has created for him a reputation for a certain dynamism among a leadership with the reputation of being dowdy, doddering and out of touch. 
A Wider Party Problem?
Nonetheless, diplomats and others suggested that the selection of Mr. Jiang may have been a sign of the leadership's being out of touch, if it believed him to be popular abroad. 
Mr. Jiang is generally credited with having done an acceptable but not outstanding job in Shanghai, and earlier this year he outraged many Chinese and foreigners by dismissing the most outspoken newspaper editor in the country.
The leadership reshuffle was approved today at a full meeting of the Chinese Communist Party Central Committee, but the decisions almost certainly were made earlier by the senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, in consultation with other elderly leaders.
The changes in the leadership announced today will reshape the highest level of decision-making, the Standing Committee of the party Politburo. 
Two members have been dismissed from what used to be a five-member panel and three new members have been appointed.
The dismissals, which had been expected, appear to end the careers of both Mr. Zhao and the propaganda chief, Hu Qili. 
Three new members have been appointed: Mr. Jiang; Li Ruihuan, a former carpenter who rose to become Mayor of the industrial city Tianjin, and Song Ping, a party official with long experience in economic planning.
The dismissal of Mr. Zhao, the second General Secretary to be ousted in two years, is another sign of the perils that Mr. Jiang will face. 
Since the Communist Party came to power in 1949, every party leader except Mao Zedong has been dismissed from the job. 
While Mr. Jiang had been a possibility mentioned for the position, he was not the front-runner, and it is not clear how much power he will really have so long as elderly leaders like Deng Xiaoping are alive.
''I don't think Jiang will be the real leader,'' a United States Government analyst said tonight. 
''He will be weaker than Zhao. 
Power doesn't come from the position one holds. 
It all depends on prestige, clout, personal connections and seniority, and Jiang doesn't seem to have much of these. 
He is a junior member of the Politburo, and has only been on it for less than two years.''
Neither Mr. Zhao nor Mr. Hu was widely liked or respected, at least until it became clear that they had been purged. 
But both were associated with the vigorous and sometimes carefree patterns of economic growth of the last decade.
Mr. Zhao worked early in his career in bustling Guangdong Province, and won fame for his economic experiments in relatively poor Sichuan Province, and he was comfortable relying on markets and small businesses to increase competitiveness in the economy.
Mr. Zhao also associated with some of the nation's most respected and iconoclastic economists and political scientists, and if he had remained in power, it is considered possible that he would have instituted major changes after Mr. Deng died. 
Instead, he has been disgraced, perhaps in part for favoring conciliation with student leaders but probably most for defying Mr. Deng on the issue and for using the difference of opinion to mount a bid for paramount power.
Mr. Zhao, who is 69 years old, is still a party member and could perhaps make a comeback in a few years. 
Mr. Deng, after all, was purged toward the end of the Cultural Revolution at the age of 71 and restored to power at age 74.
''There is a possibility of a comeback so long as he lives,'' an Asian diplomat said of Mr. Zhao tonight.
But his status is uncertain. 
No self-criticism has been announced, which suggests that he has refused so far to admit serious error despite weeks of strong pressure from the leadership. 
In addition, he was dismissed, suggesting that he refused to resign, which is probably how Mr. Deng would have preferred to handle the matter.
''At the critical juncture involving the destiny of the party and the state, Comrade Zhao Ziyang made the mistake of supporting the turmoil and the splitting of the party, and he had unshirkable responsibilities for the development of the turmoil,'' a statement approved by a full meeting of the party Central Committee said.
Â 
Unanimity in Question
The official media did not mention if the voting was unanimous, suggesting that there may have been some ''no'' votes. 
But Chinese television showed one vote that appeared to be unanimous, though it was not clear what the members were voting on.
The Central Committee statement said that the party would ''look further into his mistakes'' - which may be a warning that if Mr. Zhao complains, he will be expelled from the party or even face criminal charges.
In an apparent attempt to reassure the West, the statement said that China would maintain an open-door policy.
''The policy of reform and opening to the outside world, as the road to lead the country to strength and prosperity, must be implemented as usual in a steadfast manner,'' the party said. 
''The country must not return to the old, closed-door path.''
Â 
New Faces, Old Goals
But the party also outlined four major tasks for the future, and the first three of those were not calculated to reassure the West: first, quell the ''counterrevolutionary rebellion''; second, continue the economic retrenchment policy begun last year, and third, encourage ideological work and oppose ''bourgeois liberalization.''
The fourth was to improve the party image and punish corruption.
Mr. Jiang is friendly with China's former President, Li Xiannian, as well as with another senior figure, Chen Yun, and these connections must have helped him.
And he came to know a Politburo member, Wan Li, in the 1950's, when Mr. Wan was Deputy Mayor of Beijing and responsible for several major construction projects, including the Great Hall of the People. 
Mr. Li was a ''model worker'' and carpenter who took charge of the construction, which went extremely quickly.
Both men ran major industrial cities - Shanghai and Tianjin - and encouraged foreign investment and pragmatic economic policies to spur growth. 
In both cases, the emphasis was on industry and economic planning, perhaps because the foundation of the urban economies was already state-owned industry.
The final person to rise today is Ding Guangen, whose main fame is as Mr. Deng's regular bridge partner. 
Mr. Ding, who now is an alternate member of the Politburo, in addition to the 14 full members, is said to be an excellent bridge player whose friendship and access to Mr. Deng constitute a major political advantage. 
Mr. Ding was appointed today, along with Mayor Li, to a position in the Secretariat, which handles day-to-day matters of the party.
One man who did not rise, but who had been expected to, is Qiao Shi, the Politburo Standing Committee member in charge of security matters. 
Mr. Qiao had been the leading candidate to succeed Mr. Zhao as party leader, but instead there was no change in his position.
One account going around is that Mr. Qiao did not want the position, fearing that whoever took it would not last long. 
It is also possible that if the party wanted to refurbish its image, it did not want to elevate a man with close connections to the security agencies.
In addition to Mr. Zhao and Mr. Hu, two other men lost power. 
One is Rui Xingwen, an ally of Mr. Zhao who lost his job in the party Secretariat. 
The other is Yan Mingfu, a protege of Mr. Deng himself who had favored conciliation with the student demonstrators. 
Mr. Yan was also dropped from the Secretariat, but one account is that he has been depressed lately by the turn of events and himself chose to leave the post.

file: CHINA PARTY CHIEF APPEARS TO GAIN IN POWER STRUGGLE.txt
text:
ï»¿
An unannounced Politburo meeting has endorsed the moderate line of the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang, toward student demonstrators, including more discussions with the students and limited steps toward greater democracy, Chinese with high party connections say.
The situation remains extremely unsettled, as the debate over recent student demonstrations continues to reverberate through the leadership and exacerbate the power struggle here. 
However, three Chinese familiar with the Politburo proceedings say that the result of a tense meeting held on Wednesday and Thursday in the capital was to strengthen Mr. Zhao's faction, favoring more rapid economic and political change over one preferring a more cautious path.
The result, at least for now, is a reversal in the fortunes of Mr. Zhao, whose influence had slipped greatly over the last year and reached its nadir at the beginning of the student protests last month. 
Many of the students had worried that their demonstrations might lead to his dismissal.
Students Begin Hunger Strike
The eventual outcome of the party's internal conflicts remains uncertain, however, and officials say that further student demonstrations might affect the competition and possibly hurt Mr. Zhao. Today, students continued their protests by taking a new tactic and going on a hunger strike to back their demands for more democracy and a meaningful dialogue with the nation's leaders.
More than 20,000 spectators watched in Beijing's Tiananmen Square as more than 1,000 university students staged the strike in the middle of the square. 
Some students said they would remain until Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, arrives on Monday for the first Chinese-Soviet summit meeting in 30 years.
If present trends continue, Mr. Zhao may be emboldened to press for further economic and political liberalization and greater democracy. 
In a sign of that attitude, the People's Daily newspaper on Friday published on the top of the front page a long article calling for democracy, human rights and Government by balance of powers.
The People's Daily article attracted special attention as a sign of the rise of the more moderate grouping. 
It was one of the few times that the official press has mentioned the phrase ''human rights'' in a favorable light. 
In addition, the article's endorsing a system of ''balance of powers'' raised eyebrows because such a system had previously been implicitly criticized by the senior leader, Deng Xiaoping.
''This is a breakthrough,'' a young intellectual said, pointing to the newspaper. 
''This hasn't been written before.''
Â 
Deng Seems to Back Zhao
Mr. Deng did not attend the Politburo meeting, but he did send a statement in which he seemed to support the moderate approach. 
He also indicated that his earlier warning on April 25, calling for a crackdown on student demonstrators, was based on misleading information apparently supplied by the Beijing City Communist Party authorities, a party official said.
The support of Mr. Deng and the Politburo - actually an enlarged meeting of the Politburo, including some provincial leaders - is a crucial respite for Mr. Zhao. But party officials said that the struggle continues and noted that there are rumors that Mr. Deng will make major personnel shifts after the Chinese-Soviet meeting next week.
Â 
Struggle Isn't Over Yet
''The worst stage of the fire appears to be over, but there is still danger,'' the party official said.
In one move to shore up support, Mr. Zhao submitted to the Politburo a letter offering to have two of his sons investigated for their commercial dealings. 
Some of the harshest public criticisms in recent weeks have been against corruption, especially against the way children of high officials abuse their positions to make money. 
Although there is no clear evidence, Mr. Zhao's sons are widely believed to have made large sums by abusing their family positions.
It is not the first time his sons have given him difficulties. 
In 1981, Mr. Zhao reportedly made a self-criticism to the Politburo because of the aggressive business activities of his children.
The disagreements on how to handle the student demonstrators seemed to have accentuated the existing tensions within the leadership.
Mr. Zhao was on a visit to North Korea during some of the early demonstrations, and so he was not tainted by the Government's harsh line and threat of a crackdown on April 25 and April 26.
Â 
Zhao Seeks Dialogue
After his return, Mr. Zhao made a conciliatory speech on May 4, in which he said that the students and the party had similar aims and that a dialogue was desirable between them. 
The major student demonstrations then ceased, and Mr. Zhao received some credit for his handling of the matter.
The next battleground may be a meeting of the Politburo scheduled to take place after the summit meeting. 
In addition, the Central Committee is scheduled to meet at the end of the month and a leadership fight is possible.

file: China Party Chief Visits Japan Amid Tensions in Relations.txt
text:
ï»¿
The head of China's Communist Party, Jiang Zemin, arrived in Tokyo today, seeking what the Beijing Government still seems unable to get from most other industrialized nations: technology, aid and at least the formalities of a welcoming reception.
Mr. Jiang is the first senior Chinese leader to visit Japan since the democracy movement was crushed in June 1989, and his visit here is part of a careful effort by the two countries to rebuild economic ties gradually. 
Last summer, Toshiki Kaifu, when he was still Prime Minister, was the first leader of an industrial power to visit China since the killings in Beijing.
Though Japan is easily China's largest source of aid, in recent months relations between the two countries have been strained by a variety of new conflicts. 
They include arms control, a territorial dispute over a small island chain, and growing demands in China for Japanese compensation payments for damage involving World War II.
Â 
Unofficial but Major Visit
The ostensible reason for Mr. Jiang's trip -- which is officially described as a "good will visit" because he has come here as a party chief, not a Government official -- is to mark the 20th anniversary of the restoration of diplomatic relations.
"Japan has achieved a level of economic development that has attracted attention from the rest of the world, and has had many experiences China can learn from," Mr. Jiang said on arrival for the five-day visit.
At a time when the Chinese leadership is struggling over how much capitalist influence in its economy to allow, Mr. Jiang seemed to be dwelling on those qualities of Japan that China most admires: the mixture of free markets and a strong central Government long dominated by a single ruling party.
Chinese officials have repeatedly asked that Emperor Akihito visit their country this year to mark the diplomatic anniversary. 
But Tokyo has yet to respond officially.
At a meeting today at the Akasaka Palace, Japan's official guesthouse, Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa declined to make a commitment about whether or when the Emperor might visit.
News reports said Mr. Miyazawa did not dwell on many of the irritants that have recently developed between the two countries. 
There were apparently few discussions about nuclear proliferation in Asia or Japan's objections to China's thriving trade in conventional weapons. 
In addition, Japanese officials have viewed China as being slow to press North Korea to abandon nuclear-weapons development.
There was some discussion of the Senkaku Islands, a small chain in the East China Sea that is claimed by Japan, China and other nations. 
China calls the island group the Diaoyutai. 
In recent weeks, the Chinese leadership has indicated that it would probably not press the issue, leaving the question of the islands' sovereignty for a future generation to decide.
Tensions have also grown over claims by some in China for war reparations. 
Beijing formally waived those claims 20 years ago, but it has hinted that it may not block individual Chinese from seeking reparations.

file: China Party Chief_s Son Keeps Low Profile at a U.S. School.txt
text:
ï»¿
The son of the new Chinese Communist Party leader has spent the last three years as a graduate student in electrical engineering at Drexel University here.
The student, Jiang Mianhang, the son of Jiang Zemin, the new General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, is characterized by the head of his department as ''a likable guy.''
But the younger Mr. Jiang prefers to keep out of the public eye in light of the recent events surrounding his father's appointment.
''I hope you will understand why I prefer not to comment,'' he said when contacted by phone at his West Philadelphia apartment near the Drexel campus. 
''My father is my father, and I am me.''
When asked to clarify that statement, he said, ''I believe it is self-explanatory.''
Â 
No Comment on Turmoil
Mr. Jiang said he liked Drexel and enjoyed being in the United States. 
He would not make any comment on the events of recent weeks in China or on the protests that have taken place in Philadelphia and the rest of the country.
''He is due his privacy,'' said a fellow Chinese graduate student who asked not to be identified. 
''It is difficult to say anything at all about Chinese politics for fear of what might happen to your family. 
I admire him for keeping his profile low, and even those who do not agree with his father respect his preference to stay far from the controversy.''
''He is a likable guy - everyone seems to like him a lot,'' said Dr. Bruce A. Eisenstein, head of the electrical and computer engineering department at Drexel. 
''He is a good student. 
He is well thought of in the department and does well in school. 
It was known to us through other sources about his father's position, but that had nothing to do with his admission in 1986.''
Dr. Thomas Canavan, Drexel's interim vice president for academic affairs, said: ''There has been no furor at all at Drexel about this. 
I really don't know how many students knew he was here and I'm sure most of the university administration had no knowledge of him.''
''He is a student in course and doing well,'' Dr. Canavan said. 
''At the time of his admission, I'm sure it was noted that his father was Mayor of Shanghai, but it would have created no special sensation. 
I believe it will create no special sensation now.''
Â 
Many Students From Asia
Dr. Eisenstein, the head of Mr. Jiang's department, said about 80 of the 110 full-time graduate students in his department were foreign, the great bulk of them from Asia. 
He said he had no firm count about how many others are from China.
Drexel also has 350 part-time graduate students and 1,400 undergraduates in the electrical and chemical engineering department, almost all of them Americans, Dr. Eisenstein said.
''Most Americans with undergraduate degrees in engineering are able to get high-paying jobs, so if they go to grad school it is usually part time,'' he said. 
''Foreigners like Jiang come to Drexel and the rest of the schools in America to do research work that they can't do at home.''
Dr. Eisenstein said that Mr. Jiang was doing research toward his Ph.D. this summer, but that he did not want to comment on the nature of the research.

file: CHINA PARTY PLANS PARLEY ON ECONOMY.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Central Committee of the Communist Party will meet next month to ratify a detailed policy of economic retrenchment that will last through 1991, Chinese officials and foreign diplomats say.
The meeting will also deal with the case of the ousted Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, officials say. 
While Mr. Zhao's fate has not been entirely decided by the small circle of Chinese leaders led by Deng Xiaoping, most people in the central party apparatus expect that Mr. Zhao will be vigorously denounced but will not face a criminal trial.
Although there has been no official announcement of the Central Committee meeting, officials and diplomats say that the agenda has been largely worked out and that officials are hammering out details of an economic plan to be approved at the meeting.
'Turning Point for China'
''This will be a very important meeting, because it comes at a turning point for China,'' an Eastern European diplomat said.
In the present environment of uncertainty and instability in China, with no clear political or economic direction, the meeting will be a closely watched indicator of who is in control and of what kind of policies are likely in the coming years.
The meeting will be the first by the Central Committee, which includes 174 full members and 110 alternates, since a session in late June that formally dismissed Mr. Zhao and elected a new set of leaders. 
Officially, the meeting will be called the Fifth Plenum of the 13th Communist Party Central Committee.
It will issue a ringing endorsement of the need for a continuation of China's open-door economic approach and other policies of change, Chinese officials say. 
But they add that aside from professions of reform, the main economic task will be approval of a detailed three-year retrenchment plan beginning this year and lasting through 1991.
While the retrenchment began a year ago and was expected to be maintained for several more years, the focus on consolidation instead of change is unlikely to raise confidence among foreign investors.
In part to reassure the world that China is maintaining its commitment to liberalization, some specific new changes are likely to be approved, officials say. 
Among them are price adjustments in some sectors, changes in the tax system and a realignment of the banking system.
''We think that reform and retrenchment are inseparable,'' said Liu Guoguang, the vice president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and one of the nation's most influential economists. 
''If we can't control inflation and the health of the economy, then we can't introduce new reforms, especially price reform.''
Â 
No Major Changes Seen
Mr. Liu, who is an alternate member of the Central Committee, said in the interview that he had no information about the meeting or what policies would be adopted, but he suggested that there would be no major changes introduced in the next few years.
''Right now we can't take a big step toward reform, because of the risk of inflation,'' Mr. Liu said. 
''During the period of adjustment, only small steps can be taken. 
Then afterward we can take bigger steps.''
The retrenchment program will stress the need to reduce inflation, control investment and consumer spending, and increase roads and bridges and energy production, officials say. 
The central Government will try to regain some power and funds from the provinces and local governments, and a new system of taxation or financial quotas from local authorities is likely to raise funds for the central Government.
The official Chinese-language newspaper Economic Information also suggested that the plan will involve some steps that most Western economists would regard as a retreat from the economic restructuring plan of the last decade. 
The newspaper said China would adjust the ratio of state companies to collective enterprises. 
This apparently means that the number of state-owned corporations will increase rather than diminish, as it has steadily in the last decade.
Â 
No Bank 'Commercialization'
The newspaper also said the Government would prevent the ''commercialization of banks,'' which seemed to mean that banks would be obliged to lend to state-owned companies instead of collectives, regardless of judgments about profitability and credit-worthiness.
It was not clear from the article if these elements would be formally announced at the meeting, or if they would simply take shape over the next few years.
Little real decision-making is expected during the meeting. 
The principal decisions will almost certainly have been made by the Politburo and by retired leaders well before the session opens.
A Western diplomat said the meeting was also likely to be significant as a benchmark and a signal that the latest wave of repression could be eased somewhat. 
He said he planned to try to make contact with his Chinese friends after the meeting for the first time since the democracy movement was crushed in early June.
There has been some speculation in Beijing, but no evidence, that Mr. Deng might use the meeting to announce his resignation from his last formal position, chairman of the Central Military Commission. 
Such an announcement, and in particular the decision about who would replace him, would be of enormous significance, but so far the talk seems to be more rumor than anything else.

file: China Plans Big Layoffs Of Coal Mine Workers.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has laid off 100,000 coal workers and will lay off hundreds of thousands more in the coming years, as part of a broad effort to modernize its energy industry, an official report said today.
The layoffs suggest that the Communist Party is finally grappling directly with the enormously complex and painful problems of industrial revamping.
Until now, the Government has resisted such layoffs for fear of provoking worker unrest -- the same kind of anxieties and outrage that erupted in Britain in October when the Government there proposed laying off 30,000 coal miners.
The Communist Party here sees the problem the same way that the Conservative Party perceives it in Britain: some mines cannot be operated economically at current prices. 
But the British Prime Minister, John Major, was forced to scale down his program in response to the public outrage, while the self-professed leaders of the Chinese working class seem determined to expose the miners to the discipline of the market.
The official China Daily said the China National Coal Corporation, a huge state-owned conglomerate that employs three million people, would close 30 inefficient mines in 1993 alone and lay off 30,000 miners and 70,000 workers in related jobs.
The newspaper said the company planned to reduce the number of its coal workers by 400,000 by the time the current five-year plan ended in 1995. 
The report added that another major state-run coal company, which it did not identify, also planned "massive layoffs to increase efficiency."
The China Daily also said that 100,000 coal workers had already been laid off, although it did not say when that had happened. 
It said that most had found other kinds of jobs, and the Government apparently also will help employees laid off in the future to find jobs in new companies in the service sector.
The Energy Ministry refused to comment today. 
The coal corporation directed phone calls to Tan Enli, its director of policy research, and he declined to discuss specifics. 
But he did say that the article in China Daily was premature and should not have been allowed to be published.
"We'd like to do these things," Mr. Tan said, referring to the prospective layoffs for 1993 and subsequent years. 
"But first we need approval. 
In January the company will hold a conference to decide whether to go ahead with these plans."
In China, if a conference is called to debate a topic, that usually means that the aim is to build a consensus and legitimacy for a decision that has already been made.
Â 
Â 
A Big Headache
State-owned corporations like the coal company have been a big headache for China's leaders. 
While the overall economy is booming at a 12 percent growth rate this year, the main beneficiaries are private and collective enterprises.
Among state companies, which account for about half of industrial output, only a third are earning profits, with another third showing losses and the rest breaking even. 
Coal mines have particularly suffered, because their costs have gone up while the price of the coal they sell is fixed at artificially low prices by the state.
The solution is twofold: to raise coal prices and to lay off surplus workers. 
But the Government has worried that consumers might protest rising prices for coal, which is used for both heating and cooking, and that miners might protest the layoffs.
Now the authorities appear to be moving on both fronts, not only in the coal industry, but throughout the economy.
Â 
Price of Coal to Be Raised
In addition to laying off surplus coal workers, China has said it is raising coal prices gradually so that they will reach market levels within the next few years. 
This year, for example, the National Coal Corporation is allowed to sell 20 percent of its output at market prices, and in 1993 the figure will rise sharply.
Elsewhere in the economy, state-owned companies are also revamping and laying off workers.
In the central Chinese city of Chongqing, for example, the local Foreign Affairs Office says a state-owned knitting mill was declared bankrupt in September, costing 3,000 workers their jobs. 
At the time, it was the biggest single bankruptcy ever allowed in China, the local officials say.
Until recently, the state normally bailed out such money-losing factories indefinitely, because of the fear of worker unrest. 
In the spring of this year, the Government was deeply worried by a series of wildcat strikes and attacks on change-minded factory managers.
As a result of those incidents, the leadership cooled down the talk about how beneficial layoffs were for economic efficiency. 
And now, while going ahead with the restructuring, it appears to have decided to provide as many sweeteners to the workers as possible.
Each laid-off coal worker will be eligible for a no-interest loan of up to $1,720 to help start a business or find work elsewhere. 
The Government will also give the coal corporation a $340 million loan to allow it to start service companies that can absorb some of the laid-off employees.

file: China Pledges to Keep Close U.S. Ties.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Foreign Minister said today that despite normalization of relations with the Soviet Union, China will maintain a special and closer relationship with the United States for the foreseeable future.
The Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, said that relations with the Soviet Union would grow, but that it would be difficult to challenge the great lead in economic, cultural and educational contacts between China and the United States.
In a rare interview this afternoon, Mr. Qian also said relations with the United States were likely to flourish in the Bush Administration, partly because of President Bush's experiences in China, when he lived here from 1974 to 1975 as head of the United States mission in Beijing. 
Mr. Qian also said President Bush's visit to China this weekend, after the funeral of Emperor Hirohito in Tokyo, will be ''of great significance.'
'
''He is paying this working visit soon after assuming office, and I believe the timing of the visit shows the importance he attaches to relations with China,'' Mr. Qian said.
On Issue of Taiwan
But Mr. Qian also said there were various obstacles in Chinese-American relations, principally disagreements about Taiwan. 
In addition, he called on the United States to assist in the process of reunifying Taiwan with the Chinese mainland, something the United States has always refused to do.
Mr. Qian, a 61-year-old veteran diplomat who became Foreign Minister almost one year ago, spoke in Chinese in a Foreign Ministry conference room at the 35-minute interview. 
He apparently granted the interview because of the imminent visit by President Bush.
A suave man who speaks fluent English and Russian, Mr. Qian has sometimes been regarded as sympathetic to warmer relations with the Soviet Union. 
Like Prime Minister Li Peng and many other officials of their generation, Mr. Qian studied in the Soviet Union in the 1950's when relations were close between the two Communist giants, and some Chinese and foreign analysts believe that the Soviet-educated officials are more likely than others to favor renewed ties between China and the Soviet Union.
But in the interview Mr. Qian dismissed that idea. 
''State-to-state relations are unrelated to the experience of the national leaders, or to the places where they have lived,'' he said. 
''State-to-state relations are different from personal relations.''
Â 
Broad Range of Issues
Mr. Qian said the talks between President Bush and Chinese leaders will cover the broad range of international issues and bilateral relations. 
He said he doubted that they would focus on any particular topic.
Discussing Taiwan at length, however, he cautioned that some Americans both in Government and in the private sector incorrectly believed it was in the United States' interest to keep Taiwan and the mainland apart.
Mr. Qian also appeared to suggest that the United States should do what it could to oppose Taiwan's recent adoption of ''flexible diplomacy.''
By using its considerable economic influence, Taiwan has persuaded a number of countries in the last six months to exchange offices or in other ways increase official or semi-official contacts.
''In reality, such a practice aims to create a political concept of 'two Chinas,'' or 'one China, one Taiwan,' '' Mr. Qian said. 
''We are absolutely against it.''
Â 
Critical of Taiwan's Diplomacy
Strongly critical of Taiwan's flexible diplomacy, Mr. Qian said it was unlikely to be successful and thereby unlikely to have a major influence on Chinese-American relations.
Mr. Qian's comments appeared designed to serve two purposes. 
On the one hand, he reassured the United States that the Chinese-American friendship would not suffer from normalization of Chinese-Soviet relations, which is expected to follow the visit to Beijing of the Soviet leader, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, in May. 
On the other hand, Mr. Qian seemed to wish to caution the United States against encouraging Taiwan to seek a future separate from that of the mainland.
While he said that American trade interests had a large headstart over Soviet exchanges, Mr. Qian also noted that the Soviet Union had some trade advantages, such as proximity. 
And his assessment that Chinese-American relations would continue to outstrip Chinese-Soviet relations for the foreseeable future seemed based more on a cool assessment of economic advantages rather than on any intrinsic judgment about the merits of each superpower as a friend.
In discussing attempts to resolve the conflict in Cambodia, Mr. Qian strongly criticized Vietnam and called on other countries to pressure Vietnam to pull its troops from Cambodia by the end of September.
Â 
Vietnam Is Criticized
''Vietnam is not trustworthy,'' Mr. Qian said. 
''We cannot believe its words, and the international community should exert more pressure on it.''
Mr. Qian said he believed that Pol Pot, the Khmer Rouge leader whose regime ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1978 and killed more than a million inhabitants, is still in Cambodia today. 
Many Western and Asian diplomats suggest that China may offer Pol Pot refuge as a way of withdrawing him from the scene.
Mr. Qian said, however, that no one has asked for refuge and that in any case it would be inappropriate for China to encourage anyone to seek political asylum here.

Police officers attacked 140 foreign students with truncheons and cattle prods today in five hours of unrest near a house where the foreigners, mostly Africans, were isolated after a week of racial violence, witnesses said.
Officers moved in to arrest a student from Ghana in connection with a campus brawl a week ago that led to five days of anti-African protests in this eastern Chinese city, a student said.
About 300 to 400 police officers surrounded the restaurant of the guest house 60 miles northwest of Nanjing to arrest Alex Dzabaku Dosoo, a student at Hehai University accused of beating a university employee in the fight.
The police ordered the students to come out, then burst into the building, striking them with truncheons and shocking them with electric cattle prods, two African students and a Nepalese student said.
The 140 students were taken to a field near the guest house, and the police demanded they get on buses. 
The witnesses said that when the students resisted by holding onto each other, the police divided them into groups according to the college they attended.
''They were taking them by force and beating them,'' an African student said. 
''When we walked out, I personally saw one Congo student being beaten by - I don't know - six or seven policemen.''
Â 
Fear for Their Safety
Police officers used loudspeakers to order the students to return to their schools. 
''We tried to tell them that it was not safe to go back,'' an African said. 
He said the students were waiting for diplomats from their countries, with whom they had met at the guest house last Tuesday.
The police forced 16 students to return to their colleges, nine to Hehai and seven to Nanjing Polytechnic Institute, the witnesses said. 
Seven or eight others were isolated as ''troublemakers,'' the witnesses said. 
It was unknown where they or the rest of the students were taken.
Last Monday, the 140 foreign students had fled to the railway station in Nanjing to try to leave the city, but were forced by police to move to the factory guest house outside the city.
Liang Ruiju, president of Hehai University, said today that the students had ''turned the guest house into an independent kingdom.''
He said students barricaded the entrance to the building since Wednesday to prevent Chinese officials from entering.
But an African student said: ''That's crazy. 
There was nothing like that. 
We were completely isolated from the outside.''
The initial fight, which broke out Dec. 
24 when African students brought young Chinese women to a dance, was followed by violent protests in which thousands of Chinese youths destroyed property in the students' dormitories and marched through the streets chanting racist slogans.

file: CHINA PREPARING FOR PARTY PARLEY.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's leadership is beginning preparations for a Communist Party congress next year that is expected to provoke a major power struggle among officials hoping to serve on the next Politburo and Central Committee.
Already, the hard-liners appear to have taken the initiative to insure that the 14th Party Congress goes as they would like. 
Two Chinese knowledgable about party activities said that a committee had already been formed to begin work on the congress, and that two hard-liners were heading it.
No date has been set for the congress, but it is expected some time between next spring and fall.
Song Ping, one of the six members of the Politburo's standing committee, heads the committee to prepare for the congress, the Chinese say. 
They said his deputy is Lu Feng, an associate of Mr. Song's who heads the party's organization department.
Mr. Song and Mr. Lu are said to be charged with helping localities and provinces arrange their own party congresses, where delegates to the national congress will in theory be chosen. 
In fact, almost everything is decided from the top down, and their work will give Mr. Song and Mr. Lu an excellent opportunity to select hard-line local officials to be delegates.
A party congress is supposed to be held every five years, bringing together about 2,000 delegates to determine national policy and choose a new Central Committee. 
The Central Committee then chooses a new Politburo and General Secretary.
In fact, nearly everything is decided ahead of time among various factions in the party. 
While the congress would be an opportunity for the Communist Party to change course, few people now believe that that will happen. 
General Secretary Jiang Zemin and most members of the Politburo standing committee are expected to retain their posts.
The last party congress, in 1987, was a disaster for the hard-liners, who were outmaneuvered in the preparations for it by Zhao Ziyang, then the General Secretary.
It set the tone for the next year or two as a time of unparalleled political and economic liberalization in China. 
That was reversed when Mr. Zhao was ousted at the time of the army crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in June 1989.

China imposed martial law in the Tibetan capital on Tuesday, and thousands of soldiers were reportedly deployed throughout the city early today to begin a crackdown after three days of violent protests against Chinese rule.
The nationally televised nightly news announced the imposition of martial law Tuesday evening, saying the Government in the capital, Lhasa, had been authorized to take ''any measures necessary to restore order.''
''Any person who defies martial law or who instigates others to do so will be severely punished,'' said the order, approved by the State Council, China's cabinet, and signed by Prime Minister Li Peng. 
[Experts on Tibet say the anti-Chinese unrest is the most serious challenge to Beijing's rule since a bloody uprising 30 years ago. 
Page A11.] The official New China News Agency said martial law had been imposed because ''separatists have been constantly causing disturbances in the city over the past few days.''
Since Sunday, at least 12 people have been killed and more than 100 wounded in clashes between protesters and the police, according to official accounts.

The press agency said the city and parts of two adjoining counties would be ''cordoned off'' and ''all meetings, parades, strikes, petitions and any other gathering are banned.''
The order also gave security forces vast powers to stop vehicles and pedestrians in the city of 70,000 people.
An American tourist in Lhasa, reached by telephone from Beijing, said that at midnight Tuesday, jeeps carrying loudspeakers ordered residents to stay inside and informed them that martial law had begun.
Soon thereafter, 31 trucks carrying Chinese soldiers sped into the city, said the American.
The soldiers were deployed at ''designated places,'' the press agency said early today.
Earlier Tuesday, Tibetan protesters attacked Chinese, ransacked their stores and stoned government buildings as part of demonstrations calling for an end to Chinese rule.
Until the soldiers arrived, the police had been trying to keep order, clearing the streets and threatening to shoot anyone found in the central square.
''There's a lot of sirens going and a lot of troop movement outside,'' said the American, who spoke on condition that he not be identified, citing the fear of reprisal by the police. 
''I can hear soldiers pounding on doors,'' he added.
The order declaring martial law said that no foreigners would be allowed to enter Lhasa without permission, and those in the area without permission were required to leave. 
The American, who said he had not been informed of the rule, estimated that there were about 80 foreigners in Lhasa.
Â 
Unofficial Account of 75 Dead
On Sunday and Monday, clashes between the police and Tibetans left 11 Tibetans and one Chinese policeman dead, along with 100 wounded, official reports said.

file: China Puzzle_ Why a Panel Doesn_t Meet.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a famous Sherlock Holmes case, the key clue was a dog that did not bark. 
These days, sleuths who follow China are focusing on a similar indication that something is amiss: the clue this time is the Central Committee that does not meet.
The evidence is mostly circumstantial, but it points to significant disputes among China's top leaders. 
The jostling seems to be about power, succession and the political and economic directions the nation will take in the 1990's.
The hardest of the hard-liners in the Government seem to have gained influence in the last few months, but are unable to win a consensus for the changes they want in personnel and policies, Chinese officials and foreign diplomats say.
Thus the stalemate continues at the pinnacle of the leadership, and the Communist Party Central Committee is unable to meet and ratify the changes or the five-year plan that is to begin in January.
The Central Committee meeting was expected to convene in September or October, but a Politburo member recently told a Japanese visitor that it would not meet even in November. 
Prime Minister Li Peng said today that the committee would meet before the end of the year, so December seems to be the current target.
Â 
'Fighting Among Themselves'
"During the Asian Games, the leaders concentrated on the games and there was some cooperation and unity," said a Chinese with close ties to senior officials. 
The Asian Games, a miniature Olympics, ended on Oct. 
7.
"But now they're fighting among themselves to get their way on a whole range of issues, and until they reach some agreement, the Central Committee can't meet."
A Western diplomat was blunter, saying, "We think it's a battle."
The traditionalists have been able to score some gains because the pivot of the political system, Deng Xiaoping, appears to have withdrawn from daily involvement in political affairs. 
Mr. Deng appears to be staying at home and enjoying an apolitical life as patriarch of a family of 16 living together in one courtyard.
Mr. Deng, who is 86 years old, has not been seen in public since July -- a gap that normally results in rumors that he is seriously ill. 
But these days, Mr. Deng is said to be in satisfactory condition, and his youngest son, Deng Zhifang, is planning a trip to the United States, which also suggests that his father is getting along.
The octogenarian hard-liners -- whose patriarch is Chen Yun, an 85-year-old who has not been seen in public in more than a year -- are said to be pushing for a major promotion for Deng Liqun, 75, a retired head of the Communist Party Propaganda Department.
Â 
Guidance to Journalists
Some party elders are also ignoring their lack of formal positions and are quietly issuing hard-line instructions on whatever catches their attention. 
Deng Liqun, for example, is believed to be meeting with newspaper editors and advising them on what to write.
Former President Li Xiannian, 81, was recently outraged to read in a news summary that the city of Shenyang in northeastern China was planning to sell stakes in several dozen companies to foreigners. 
A Chinese with high-level associations said Mr. Li scrawled "reckless" on the report and issued instructions that the sale be halted.
The octogenarians have also curbed the influence of Li Ruihuan, who is a protege of Deng Xiaoping. 
Mr. Li appeared in July to win a turf battle with the traditionalists over control of the Culture Ministry.
Mr. Li's victory immediately rippled throughout the Government: At the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, hard-liners became much more friendly to the scholars, whom they were subjecting to grueling Communist Party study sessions.
But in August, the group of octogenarians began to complain that Mr. Li was making statements that went beyond the party line. 
Deng Xiaoping did not come to his defense, and Mr. Li's influence has diminished.
Â 
Centralized Planning Continues
Another sign of hard-liner dominance is the five-year plan, drafts of which have circulated among senior officials. 
Economists and others who have seen it say that it includes general calls for further reform, but that as it stands, it is primarily a document of central planning.
But if the reformists are lying low these days, they have not given up the battle. 
At the end of last month, the leaders of China's provinces were summoned to Beijing to study and approve an outline of the five-year plan. 
Instead, the governors rebelled, a major embarrassment to Prime Minister Li, and refused to approve the plan.
According to accounts by knowledgeable Chinese, the governors complained that the draft transferred too much power and wealth from the provinces to the central Government. 
Some governors, including Ye Xuanping of Guangdong province, dared to interrupt Prime Minister Li, and the meeting reportedly ended in tumult. 
Now the draft is being re-examined and is expected to be modified after negotiations with the governors.
The one item on the Central Committee's agenda that has already been agreed upon, Chinese officials and diplomats say, is the fate of the ousted Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang. 
Mr. Zhao was formally dismissed from all his posts in June 1989 and has been under investigation since. 
But the leadership is now believed to have agreed to end the investigation and allowed him to remain in the party.

file: China Ready to Try (and Forget) Dissidents.txt
text:
ï»¿
Perhaps what is most remarkable about Zhu Jianbin is not that he has spent the last nine years in prison for trying to promote democracy, but that he has been so totally forgotten in the labyrinth of the Chinese penal system.
Mr. Zhu is evidence that repression sometimes works, for the authorities have locked him up without attracting any significant criticism or tarnishing their image.
His very existence has been virtually obliterated, for most democracy advocates here and abroad have neverheard of him, and even in this city where he worked and dreamed of democracy, people shake their heads and say they have never heard his name.
The Chinese leaders appear ready to go ahead soon with criminal trials of some major figures in the 1989 democracy movement, and the Government may well believe -- based on the evidence of Mr. Zhu and countless others -- that the harm to its image will be slight and transitory.
Beijing may well believe that such a temporary setback is an acceptable price for making an example of some activists and frightening the rest intosubmission.
Hundreds, and perhaps thousands, of people remain in Chinese prisons and labor camps for their involvement in the 1989 democracy movement. 
Last week, the Government formally charged two editors of an economics journal, Wang Juntao and Chen Ziming, with counterrevolutionary crimes because of their participation in the movement. 
They and others are expected to face trial soon, and perhaps prison sentences of up to 15 years.
The result has been a flurry of foreign indignation -- just as there was a burst of outrage a decade ago when China imprisoned the leaders of the1978-79 Democracy Spring movement. 
But that outrage gradually dissipated, and only Wei Jingsheng is much remembered now, in China or abroad. 
Mr. Wei, an electrician and essayist, is now in the 12th year of his 15-year prison sentence. 
He is said to be in solitary confinement, with even the guards ordered not to speak with him.
Mr. Zhu's case never attracted much attention, partly because he lived and worked here in Wuhan, where there are no resident diplomats or foreign journalists. 
Mr. Zhu, who is now 35 years old, was a worker at a big steel mill in Wuhan and an editor of a journal about democracy, "The Bell Tolls."
"We've been sending letters, but we've never heard anything," said Barbara Krasnoff, a member of an Amnesty International group in New York that has "adopted" Mr. Zhu as apolitical prisoner. 
"We never found out if he has any family."
"It's very hard not to lose interest in a case," Ms. Krasnoff added in a telephone interview. 
"We're human and if you don't hear anything from somebody for so many years he becomes almost fictional. 
Every once in a while we have to take out his picture and remember that this is a real person."
The way in which Mr. Zhu has been forgotten, except to the Amnesty group, raises larger questions about the democracy movement in China. 
Nelson Mandela managed to inspire many South Africans while he was in prison, and in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union dissidents kept alive the memories of many who were in labor camps.
But Chinese intellectuals say that the tendency here has been to forget thosewho are locked away. 
Many of the students involved in the 1989 Tiananmen movement had never heard of the leaders of the Democracy Spring Movement a decade earlier -- names of men like Xu Wenli and Wang Xizhe, who are serving 15- and 14-year prison sentences, respectively.
Fang Lizhi, the Chinese dissident now living in England, wrote in an essay this year about "The Chinese Amnesia" -- the tendency for society to forget and ignore past repression -- as a factor inhibiting the emergence of greater democracy in China.
While Professor Fang argued that the Communist "Technique of Forgetting History" was losing its effect with regard to the 1989 crackdown, there is no sign of greater interest in those who remain in prison for their efforts a decade ago to promote democracy.

file: China Rebuff Seems Unlikely to Hurt Trade Status.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese rebuff to Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d over human rights and arms sales last weekend drew little initial criticism in Congress tonight and appeared unlikely to spur action on legislation to limit China's trading status.
President Bush said of the trip: "I think it was worthwile. 
I think when all of it's out, I think people will think some progress is made."
He declined to disclose details of Mr. Baker's successes, and said, "Now we sit down and figure out what's the next step."
Senator George J. Mitchell of Maine, the majority leader and the chief Senate sponsor of legislation to make China's most-favored-nation trading status contingent on changes in human rights, trade and arms-sale policies, told reporters he would await details from the State Department before responding.
But Nancy Pelosi, the California Democrat who led the House effort on similar legislation, said in an interview that the visit provided additional evidence of the "failure of the Bush China policy."
She said Mr. Baker tried hard but did not succeed because China "did not take seriously any messages from the United States because the President wasn't a part of them."
Senator Claiborne Pell, the Rhode Island Democrat who heads the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement, "I know Secretary Baker has been working immensely hard and am sorry the results so far are disappointing to him and to all of us concerned about U.S. relations with China."
Mr. Mitchell's bill was passed by the Senate on July 23. 
But the 55-to-44 vote was so far short of the two-thirds needed to override a threatened veto that no House-Senate conference has yet been held to reconcile differences with the Pelosi bill. 
That measure was adopted on July 10 by a vote of 313-112, easily a veto-proof margin, but the Senate total was 12 votes short of the 67 needed when all Senators vote.
The conferees may meet this week, but Congressional aides said it was unlikely that a conference agreement would come to the floor before Congress adjourns for the year, which it hopes to do next week. 
But there are likely to be floor speeches in the Senate on Tuesday criticizing Chinese policies on arms and human rights.
But today there was evident reluctance in the Senate to attack the Baker mission because of a sense that he had pressed the Chinese for change in the areas that Congress was most concerned about.
Representative Pelosi was more aggressive. 
She said it was "ridiculous" for China to demand concessions in the form of computer and satellite export licenses as the price of a commitment not to export missiles to Syria, Pakistan and other countries.
Her bill would end most-favored-nation trade status next year unless the President certified China had made "significant overall progress" in human rights, religious and press freedom and prison conditions. 
The bill would also require China to end coercive abortion or sterilization, assure the United States it was not exporting ballistic missiles to the Middle East or spreading nuclear technology, and end the export to the United States of products produced by prison labor.
Mr. Mitchell's bill covers similar ground, but does not give Mr. Bush as much of an opportunity to clear China by certifying that progress is being made, as the Pelosi bill does.
On Friday, while Mr. Baker was in China, the Senate passed another resolution condemning China's human rights policies. 
It specifically complained about the case of Dai Qing, a journalist awarded a Nieman Fellowship at Harvard University, but denied a passport to use the fellowship.
Ms. Dai, who was detained during Mr. Baker's visit and prevented from meeting him, was praised in the Senate as courageous. 
The resolution, passed without debate, called on President Bush to tell Beijing of "the urgent concern of the Congress and the citizens of the United States for the rights of all political prisoners in China and urge the Government of the People's Republic of China to recognize the right of Dai Qing and all Chinse writers to free expression and travel."

file: China Rebuffs U.S. Scrutiny Of Policy on Family Planning.txt
text:
ï»¿
China rejected American scrutiny of its family-planning programs today, saying it was a nation's sovereign right to determine its own population policy.
The comments by a Foreign Ministry spokesman, Li Zhaoxing, at a weekly news briefing were nominally directed at the United States Congress. 
But they also appeared to be intended to caution the Bush Administration, which will soon have to take a stand on whether the Chinese family-planning program includes forced abortions.
After reports that China's rigorous family-planning policy was resulting in female infanticide and forced abortion, Congress in 1985 approved a law requiring the Administration to determine annually whether the program includes forced abortion. 
If it does, aid to the United Nations Fund for Population Activities is halted on the ground that the agency is helping such policies.
The Reagan Administration concluded each year that the Chinese program included forced abortion, but the Bush Administration has so far not made a determination. 
In June the United States will have to decide whether to approve a new population plan for China when it is presented to the agency's governing council, to which the United States belongs.
Â 
Correcting the Overzealous
''It is a country's sovereign right to decide its own population policy,'' Mr. Li said. 
''China's population policy is formulated according to its own national conditions. 
China's pursuance of a family-planning policy that prevents excessive population growth and raises the quality of its population not only serves China's own development but also contributes to the population stabilityI and economic development of Asia and the world as a whole.''

file: China Reports Release of 573 Held in Revolt.txt
text:
