The Government said today that it recently released 573 people who had been imprisoned for taking part in the democracy movement last year.
It was the first official announcement since a Government order at the end of June that banned the publicizing of information on arrests and punishments.
The action seemed to be part of an effort by the Chinese authorities to improve their image before the United States Congress reconvenes next week and considers sanctions against Beijing.
The lifting of martial law in the capital last week was also widely seen as an attempt to improve China's international image and reduce the possibility of new sanctions.
Â 
Flurry of Arrests and Executions
The official New China News Agency said the lawbreakers had been released ''because during investigations, they pleaded guilty and showed repentance.''
The brief report quoted an unidentified police spokesman as saying, ''Our policy is to educate anyone who can be educated and temper punishment with leniency.''
The report said the spokesman ''hoped that those who took part in the turmoil and counterrevolutionary riots, broke the law and obstinately stuck to the wrong course would understand the situation, repent immediately and plead guilty for leniency.''
The authorities detained thousands of students, workers and intellectuals in June and July, after the military crackdown in early June.
There was never an announcement on how many were arrested, but most estimates started at 10,000 and some were far higher.
After an initial flurry of arrests and executions were reported on television and led to an international outcry, the Chinese leadership circulated an internal document ordering that information about detentions and punishments no longer be publicized.
Since then there have been very infrequent reports, mostly in provincial Chinese newspapers, of arrests or executions.
Â 
Mistreatment of Prisoners
Some of those arrested were released in the late summer and early fall, and a significant number of students and intellectuals were released beginning in December, say dissidents who maintain an unofficial network among themselves.
The announcement today appeared to refer to those released beginning in December. 
Most of those released were not beaten by the jailors, and in some cases the guards showed a measure of admiration or respect for the political prisoners, friends say.
But some prisoners are said to have been mistreated in other ways.
One intellectual, for example, was kept in handcuffs constantly for the first 35 days of his imprisonment, a close friend said.
The intellectual had to rely on other prisoners to help him eat, dress and use the toilet.
After his release, his former employer refused to take him back, and no other concern would hire him. 
Since employers provide housing, the dissident had no place to live, no money to live on and no prospects for a career.
It is not clear how many people are still imprisoned for their role in the democracy movement, but nearly all estimates are in the high hundreds and probably the thousands.
The most prominent prisoners, like Wang Dan, a student leader; Ren Wanding, an essayist, and Liu Xiaobo, a literary theorist, all remain behind bars and nothing certain is known of their condition or treatment.
Almost all that is known about prisoners concerns intellectuals and students.
Very little is known about the many workers who played important roles in the movement, because they and their families were not part of a dissident network that could help them and spread the word about their circumstances.

file: China Revives Its Test of Capitalism.txt
text:
ï»¿
After the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown, China's bold experiment in fusing socialism and capitalism in this South China city stalled. 
By last summer, Shenzhen's mayor lost his position, economic reforms were halted, and the city's 10th anniversary celebration was postponed.
But now Shenzhen has talked its way back into Beijing's favor, and many leaders again point to it as a model for the nation's development.
Shenzhen officials, though wary of the power struggles in Beijing, are seeking a nearly open border with Hong Kong. 
A primitive stock market that has operated, literally, over the counters in small buildings around the city is about to expand into a modern, computerized exchange.
In a single decade, Shenzhen has developed from a barren patch of grassland into one of China's most modern metropolises. 
But the transformation has been marked by a battle between China's ardent central planners and those who envision a national economy far more open and free.
Shenzhen, a special economic zone in Guangdong province, is a product of China's effort to prove that a capitalist economy can thrive under a socialist government. 
Many central officials still fear that Shenzhen is becoming too capitalist and too unwieldy for the Government to control.
Local leaders say they have strong reasons for continuing to support the Beijing Government, which has allowed Shenzhen and other special economic zones to prosper. 
While some of Shenzhen's students protested in May 1989, the demonstrations were much smaller than in other big cities, as many citizens saw that protests would only stand in the way of making money.
Some say Shenzhen is turning into a mini-Hong Kong. 
Already, the Hong Kong dollar is Shenzhen's semiofficial currency, accepted by hotels, taxis and restaurants, which refuse the foreign currency exchange certificates required of foreigners everywhere else in China.
Â 
Rapid Industrial Growth
Industrial growth over the last decade averaged 69 percent annually, among the fastest of any city in the world. 
For a while, Shenzhen's tiny, nascent stock market was more free-wheeling -- and scandal-ridden -- than Hong Kong's.
While some Shenzhen officials agree about the increasing resemblance to Hong Kong, they insist that there is one major distinction: Shenzhen is still socialist, with most businesses run by the state.
"It is not impossible for Shenzhen to become a Chinese Hong Kong," said Wang Xinkuo, a senior manager at the Catic Shenzhen Enterprise Group, whose member companies include a maker of simple electronic components. 
"The biggest difference is that Hong Kong is a capitalist system, while in Shenzhen, public ownership is the main path."
Besides Shenzhen, with nearly 1.9 million people, there are four other special economic zones -- Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen and Hainan Island, all also in southern China. 
While officials still describe these zones as socialist, not everyone agrees that socialist planning will dominate these export-oriented cities.
Â 
Prices Set by Market
Almost all their prices, including those for raw materials, are set by the market. 
The rest of China buys many materials, including coal and oil, at subsidized prices.
"Only postage and bus fares are set by the Government, and that's because they are uniform for the whole nation," said Liang Wensen, a professor of economics at Shenzhen University.
"There is even a market in people's labor," Mr. Lian said, with most of Shenzhen's wages also determined primarily by market forces.
Partly because of its location next to Hong Kong, Shenzhen has attracted major foreign investments. 
Some 3,000 of Shenzhen's 7,000 companies have some foreign capital. 
Total foreign investment in Shenzhen amounts to about one-seventh the foreign investment in all of China, according to official statistics.
Â 
A Bumpy Ascent
But Shenzhen's ascent has not been smooth. 
When China's economic liberals had the upper hand in the late 1980's, Shenzhen was developing into a virtually free market. 
But when hard-liners took over two years ago during the Tiananmen crackdown, it seemed that Shenzhen's best years had ended.
Beijing refused to allow Shenzhen's modernized stock exchange to open; Li Hao, a reformer, was relieved as mayor, although he remained party secretary, and the city's 10th anniversary celebration, scheduled for last summer, was put off for nearly four months.
But now, Shenzhen seems to be back on the reform track. 
Once more, national leaders tout Shenzhen as a model, and again provincial officials from throughout China are visiting to learn how to help their own economies. 
Shenzhen has adopted an aggressive, 10-year growth plan, and a new airport is scheduled to open in the fall.
Shenzhen's leaders are sufficiently confident of their futures to press for more dramatic changes. 
Shenzhen is said to have sought Beijing's permission to establish its own currency and relax border restrictions with Hong Kong while tightening them with the rest of China. 
Already, other Chinese need special permission to cross the "second border" into Shenzhen.
Â 
Beijing's Concerns
Shenzhen's leaders apparently want to merge their economy into Hong Kong's, but it is unclear how far the hard-liners in Beijing will go along.
The central Government worries that Shenzhen will become too self-sufficient or closely integrated with Hong Kong, widening its economic lead over the rest of China.
"By the year 2000, Shenzhen's per capita G.N.P. should reach or almost reach the present level of typically developed countries," said Zheng Liangyu, Shenzhen's new Mayor, in a recent report. 
"The more profoundly we reform, the more contradictions and problems we shall face. 
This thus requires us to explore and experiment more bravely than we did 10 years ago, so as to really act as the pioneer and testing ground."
The saga of Shenzhen's stock market exemplifies the perils of economic revamping. 
For nearly a year after the stock market opened at the end of 1989, workers, clerks, taxi drivers and other residents viewed buying stocks as a sure way to riches because the market only went up.
Â 
Began With 5 Stocks
The stock market started with only five stocks, and the Government limited daily price changes to 5 percent. 
A lively black market developed where investors traded stocks at large premiums over official prices.
With no comprehensive securities law, there were no restrictions on Shenzhen officials owning stock. 
Many had bought stocks both to promote the new market and to make profits.
But in October, rumors circulated that to avoid conflicts of interest, Chinese officials would soon be banned from owning stock, and stock prices would be frozen. 
Many officials apparently tried to dump their stocks, and the black market crashed. 
Shenzhen had its first stock market scandal.
Â 
City Is Rebuked
The scandal soon came to Beijing's attention. 
In late November, the Government cracked down on the black market and reduced the limits on daily price changes to five-tenths of 1 percent.
Officials said privately that Vice President Wang Zhen, a hard-liner, circulated a memo among top leaders that criticized the chaotic Shenzhen market.
In response, Prime Minister Li Peng dispatched a team from Beijing to investigate. 
In a rebuke to Shenzhen, the central Government decided to allow Shanghai to become the first Chinese city to open a modern, computerized securities exchange.
The Shanghai market opened in December, and officials say that Beijing has now also approved the opening of a unified Shenzhen exchange, which is preparing to list an additional 10 stocks. 
Shenzhen, it seems, is supposed to develop and prosper, but in an orderly manner that does not alarm the central planners.
Local officials have learned to be more tactful in discussing stock markets and other initiatives.
"For some time we considered stock exchanges as something capitalist, but that is not right," said Lei Yu, the deputy mayor of Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, as he commented on Shenzhen's market. 
"It's just a good way to raise funds."

file: China Rushes From Mao to Markets.txt
text:
ï»¿
Perhaps the best-performing financial instrument in the world in 1992 has been a slip of white paper entitling the bearer to buy newly issued stocks on the Shanghai stock exchange. 
Sold early in the year for $5.50, by the summer these forms fetched nearly $300.
The soaring prices reflect the growing enthusiasm, bordering on desperation, of ordinary Chinese to become shareholders -- preferably rich ones.
After six years of on-and-off experimentation with shares, China is accelerating the development of a modern stock market. 
New companies are being listed each week, the number of investors is surging and hard-line critics have been muzzled.
Â 
Making a Transition
"The ideological problems are basically resolved," Wei Wenyuan, the executive director of the stock exchange, said in an interview in an alcove above the trading floor.
A local stockbroker put it more bluntly. 
"We're in a transition to capitalism, conducted under the leadership of the Communist Party," he said.
That is hyperbole, for the number of stock companies make up only an infinitesimal proportion of the economy. 
But the stock market is emerging as a central element of the nation's economic reorganization, and popular support seems boundless.
In early August, more than a million would-be investors waited in line -- some for days -- to buy applications for stocks being issued in the southern city of Shenzhen. 
The applications cost $20 and had only a random 10 percent chance of being approved to buy shares. 
Even so, the potential investors rioted when the applications ran out.
Some 50,000 people rampaged through the streets, attacking police cars and shouting anti-Government slogans. 
The police fired tear gas and some gunshots, and there were unconfirmed reports that two people were killed.
Â 
Leadership Meets
The clamor of a riot was not the kind of boom that reformers had hoped for. 
The Cabinet is said to have been worried as it met in the Zhongnanhai leadership compound in Beijing to watch secret police videotapes of the rioting, but so far there is no sign of a big slowdown in the move toward stocks.
"The Shenzhen incident was a problem arising at a technical level," said Wang Poming, the American-educated vice president of the Stock Exchange Executive Council of China. 
"It doesn't have anything to do with policy, or with the market itself. 
I don't see any major retreat from the shareholding system."
Mr. Wang said the rioting would probably lead to the establishment of a type of Securities and Exchange Commission to provide improved oversight.
China began to get excited about stocks late in 1986, and Shanghai and several other cities quickly set up rudimentary trading systems. 
A prominent economist, Li Yining, urged then that most of the nation's state-owned factories be turned into shareholder-owned companies.
Â 
A Popular Trend
Progress was slow, however, partly because of the rise of the hard-liners at the time of the Tiananmen crackdown in June 1989. 
Shanghai opened a much more credible stock exchange in December 1990, and Shenzhen formally opened its own a few weeks later. 
Now other cities are frantically trying to get Beijing's approval to open exchanges, but the authorities are refusing on the basis that Shanghai and Shenzhen should be national markets.
Foreigners have also been invited to buy Chinese stocks through special "B shares" listed on both the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges. 
Early this year, B shares were all the rage as investors dreamed of getting in on the ground floor of one of the most vibrant economies in the world.
Since then, the B share market has stalled, in part because the shares are relatively expensive and thinly traded.
"These are the ups and downs you get at the beginning of any emerging market," said Timothy Beardson, chairman of Crosby Securities Ltd. in Hong Kong. 
"China is going to have a very large stock market, one of the largest in the world, in our view. 
As the market gets bigger it'll get broader, and I think it's here to stay."
Â 
Foreigners Show Interest
About 20 stock funds have been set up by Crosby and other foreign brokerage firms to buy Chinese equities, and Chinese companies are also trying to list directly on exchanges in the United States, Hong Kong and Australia.
The Shanghai market now lists 17 A share issues, for Chinese investors, along with 8 B shares. 
Mr. Wei, the exchange's head, says that by the end of the year there will be 50 A shares and 10 B shares.
Likewise, the number of seats on the exchange has risen to 212 from 46. 
Soon, there will be 600 seats.
Mr. Wei estimates that 1.2 million people -- a bit more than two-thirds from Shanghai and the rest scattered around the country -- have bought shares through the exchange. 
Among them are 10,000 to 20,000 professional investors, known as the dahu, who have $100,000 or more in their brokerage accounts.
Â 
Some Fortunes Made
Some dahu -- the most famous is a Shanghai resident who goes by the name Millions Yang -- have made fortunes. 
For while B shares have been stagnating, the A shares traded by Chinese have been soaring.
"A fellow in my office put 5,000 yuan into Gold Cup Company shares a few years ago, and now it's worth 80,000 yuan," an envious official in Beijing said. 
Eighty thousand yuan is a bit less than $15,000.
These success stories have enticed more people into the market and created what is known here as "stock fever."
Books about stocks are selling wildly, night schools on how to trade stocks have been set up in major cities, and newspapers are running columns on how to invest.
Â 
Ignoring the Fundamentals
The only tactic that has not been tried has been analysis of fundamentals. 
Partly because of the unreliability of Chinese accounting, and partly because fundamentals do not matter as long as no one else looks at them either, trading often seems a bit divorced from reality. 
Price-earnings ratios exceed 100 for most Shanghai A shares, compared with a bit more than 10 for stocks in the less risky Hong Kong market.
Chinese investors seem to have a much clearer concept of upside potential than downside risk, even after a speculator lost $730 and committed suicide by electrocuting himself.
"What a numbskull," a Shanghai journalist said. 
"If he'd just waited, the market would have gone up again and he would have got his money back."
Restrictions on upward and downward movement of Shanghai stocks were lifted in May, and prices now generally follow the market. 
The first collapse came in Shanghai in August, with stocks abruptly plunging by nearly half. 
Some experts said the sharp selloff was a good thing, because it burned a few fingertips and chastened investors.
Â 
Talk of Intervention
Officials insist that the authorities did not intervene in the market collapse, but the word among Chinese brokers and journalists is quite different. 
They say the Communist Party General Secretary, Jiang Zemin, telephoned the Shanghai party leader and asked for smooth trading in advance of a party Congress this fall.
When stock prices continued to slump, the exchange apparently halted trading for 20 minutes -- under the guise of a computer breakdown -- and ordered brokers to buy and support the market. 
The intervention worked, and prices have returned to their earlier range.
"Privatization" is still a taboo word in China, sending shivers down the spines of Communist hard-liners. 
But some younger officials use the term "going public" to suggest that share issues are just another form of public ownership.
Â 
Pace of Change Is Disputed
"The key thing is that the Chinese have done it right," said William H. Overholt, executive director of the Bankers Trust Company in Hong Kong. 
"They've taken the time to create the institutional mechanisms for privatization before doing the privatization."
Some economists are impatient with China's relatively plodding steps, compared with the rapid changes in some former Communist countries. 
But others, including Mr. Overholt, say that China has prudently established a suitable foundation for capital markets.
"The East Europeans have done it utterly wrong, which is to rush pell-mell into reallocating the whole ownership and management of national productivity without having the institutional mechanisms in place to manage it properly," he said. 
"China will come out looking good."

The Chinese Government has agreed to pay $25 million to stage a boxing match between the heavyweight champion, Mike Tyson, and the former champion George Foreman, Tyson's manager and the fight's promoter said yesterday.

A Rookie Promoter

Aiming for a Championship

file: CHINA SAID TO PLAN NEW ARMS SALES_ U.S. IS CONCERNED.txt
text:
ï»¿
Western diplomats and experts are concerned by indications that China is seeking to increase its share of the world market for missiles.
The Chinese military, the experts say, may begin shipments of two new kinds of missiles to Syria and Pakistan, and perhaps to other countries as well. 
The new missiles, which are said to be more accurate than the Soviet-designed Scuds used by Iraq in the Persian Gulf war, are thought to be at the end of the development stage and could be deployed soon.
Short of money and therefore eager to sell weapons, China, the experts say, may be on a collision course with Western nations that say they want to slow the international arms race.
With the decline of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as arms merchants, China, in the view of some, is emerging to fill the void.
Â 
What of U.S. and Soviet Sales?
For its part, China points out that it sells far fewer weapons than either the United States or the Soviet Union. 
If Washington can sell arms to the Middle East, it asks, why can't Beijing?
Still, China's weapons sales are becoming a growing source of friction with the United States, and a factor in the debate about whether to cut off China's most-favored-nation trade benefits. 
In a sign of American concern, Reginald Bartholomew, the Under Secretary of State for Security Assistance, is scheduled to visit Beijing June 17 to 19 to discuss weapons proliferation.
Apparently intending to ease the friction and improve its image, China has reportedly accepted an invitation from President Bush to attend a July conference of major powers to discuss limits on arms sales to the Middle East.
Â 
For China, Business as Usual
But whether China will agree to do more than talk may depend on the outcome of disagreements between China's Foreign Ministry, which would like to curtail proliferation to improve the nation's image, and the army, which wants to raise funds through the sale of weapons, and regards the Foreign Ministry as weak-kneed.
Diplomats and experts say that the new international interest in China's arms sales reflects changes not so much in China as in the rest of the world. 
For most of the last decade, the Chinese Army eagerly pursued arms deals, but now there is far less sympathy for China than before. 
In addition, the United States and other Western nations are talking about curtailing the arms race in the Middle East and elsewhere, and China could upset such plans.
"They are doing things that they've been doing all along, but we have a lower level of tolerance than we did a few years ago," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"In addition, what they were doing all along now seems to be coming to fruition in a number of cases."
What is coming to fruition appears to be the development of the M-9 and M-11 missiles, and plans to sell them to Syria, Pakistan and probably other nations as well.
The missiles apparently have not been delivered so far, but launchers for the M-11 have been spotted in Pakistan and diplomats expect that the missiles themselves will follow. 
The M-11 is said to have a range of about 180 miles and can carry a nuclear warhead.
Â 
Pakistan and Nuclear Arms
Pakistan is widely believed to be close to achieving a nuclear bomb. 
If Pakistan were able to build a nuclear device in the form of a warhead for the M-11 missile, it would be able to launch a nuclear strike that India could not easily defend against.
The Western diplomat said he doubted that China could be prevented from transferring the M-11 missiles to Pakistan, but that there was a somewhat better chance of preventing shipments of the M-9 to Syria. 
The M-9 is thought to have a range of about 375 miles, and so would be able to hit targets throughout Israel.
There have been some indications that China struck a deal several years ago to sell M-9's to Syria, and the missile may have been developed in part with Syrian financing.
When the national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, visited Beijing in December 1989, he received pledges that China would not sell medium-range missiles to the Middle East, and that "at the present time, China is not planning any sales of the M-9 missile to Syria."
These days, Beijing is no longer repeating that "at the present time" it will not sell the M-9, and the promise not to sell medium-range missiles may not be useful because of the way Beijing defines medium range.
Â 
A Question of Definition
The Missile Technology Control Regime, an agreement that China has not joined, defines medium-range missiles as those that go about 188 miles. 
But a Chinese military encyclopedia defines a medium-range missile as one that can travel 625 miles. 
If that is the definition that it is using, its promise not to sell medium-range missiles would cover neither the M-9 nor the M-11.
Diplomats are also concerned about China's capacity to transfer nuclear technology, and there was concern recently when China was found to be building a nuclear reactor in Algeria that experts suspected might be used to produce plutonium for nuclear weapons. 
China and Algeria responded by saying that the reactor was intended only for research, and Algeria has now indicated that it will allow international inspections, alleviating much of the concern.
China is also widely believed to have assisted Pakistan with its nuclear program, although there is no firm public evidence to confirm allegations that Beijing provided Pakistan with a design for a bomb. 
There is also evidence that some Chinese provided India with "heavy water" for its nuclear program, but this may have been an unauthorized profit-making venture that did not have the central Government's approval.

"It raised the whole debate about how best to bring the Chinese along -- by stiff-arming them or by coaxing them when they make a few moves in the right direction."

When asked at a briefing today whether an announcement to lift sanctions was imminent, a State Department spokesman, Joe Snyder, said that once the two Governments completed the agreement reached during Mr. Baker's meeting in November, "the Administration plans to take the steps necessary to lift the June 1991 sanctions."
"We have no set timetable for lifting the sanctions," he said.
Â 
Divisions in Administration
There are deep divisions in the Administration over the wisdom of lifting the sanctions. 
Many intelligence officials and some senior Pentagon officials oppose any easing of restrictions, while the White House is clearly in favor of such a move.
The State Department notified Congress in a letter in mid-December that it intends to lift the sanctions. 
But resistance by Chinese leaders to an American demand that they put their oral promise to Mr. Baker in writing has contributed to a delay, Administration officials said.
Some non-proliferation experts in the Administration are convinced that the recent sales to Syria and Pakistan would constitute clear violations of the agreement, known as the Missile Technology Control Regime, which was devised by the United States and other powers to limit the supply of ballistic missiles to the developing world.
But other officials use a broader interpretation, saying it is nearly impossible to determine whether the transfer of certain technology that might have dual uses is a violation.
The suspicion felt toward China in some quarters of the Administration was reflected in remarks by Defense Secretary Dick Cheney after a speech in Wisconsin this week. 
Mr. Cheney said that his "prime concern" with regard to China was proliferation.
"They have in the past, on occasion, been less than scrupulous in their concern for maintaining control over that technology," he said.

China's Policy 'Worrisome'
Similarly, in testimony before the Senate Armed Services Committee last week, Lieut. 
Gen. James R. Clapper Jr., Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency, called Chinese arms sales and proliferation policies "worrisome," adding, "China is currently assisting many of the nations that we estimate will acquire a ballistic missile capability by the end of the decade."
China has vigorously denied selling entire missiles or warheads to Syria, Pakistan or any other country in the Middle East or Southwest Asia. 
Indeed, American officials say there is no proof Beijing has shipped such weapons.
Many American officials and independent non-proliferation experts have expressed growing concern, however, that China is circumventing the spirit of missile-control agreements by selling missile components. 
Such transfers are significant because developing countries can assemble the parts and, in some cases, market the technology themselves.
"These transfers would help both Syria and Pakistan develop a manufacturing capability for their own missiles and would even allow them to proliferate missiles to other countries," said Gary Milhollin, director of the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control, a private group. 
"It happens at the very time that China is promising to change its behavior."
Â 
Limitations to Guidelines
A senior Pentagon official acknowledged the limitations of the missile control guidelines, saying they were "a way to keep a lid on things, but not strictly control" proliferation.
American intelligence reports over the last few years have also shown that China has discussed with Iranian officials the possible sale of M-9 missiles.
Launchers and M-11 training missiles were delivered to Pakistan last year, despite Beijing's pledges not to sell medium-range missiles in the Middle East and Southwest Asia. 
The Chinese view the M-11, which is said to have a range of about 180 miles and can carry a nuclear warhead, as a short-range missile, although the United States considers it a medium-range missile covered by the missile technology agreement.

Limited Context

Two of the officials added that those reading the document were told to say that it expressed their own views, apparently as a way of allowing the leadership to distance itself from the comments.

file: China Says Taiwan Is _Buying Hearts_ Abroad.txt

China suspended formal relations with Liberia on Tuesday, a day after Taiwan restored ties with the West African nation. 
It was the second diplomatic face-off between China and Taiwan since July, when Taipei re-established ties with Grenada.
The quarrel comes as Taiwan is pressing a diplomatic offensive in the third world seeking to gain influence and respectability - and, particularly, diplomatic recognition. 
Taipei, like Beijing, claims to be the legitimate government of all China, but only 25 countries recognize Taipei while 134 recognize Beijing. 
$150 Million to Liberia With its enormous foreign exchange reserves and acknowledged expertise in economic development, Taiwan is in a good position to offer aid to developing countries. 
Reports in Taiwan have said Liberia would receive about $150 million in coming months, after its decision to normalize relations with Taipei.
''The Taiwan authorities use silver bullets in the name of cultural, economic, trade and technological exchanges to buy the hearts of the people, and to develop diplomatic relations with certain countries,'' the official People's Daily declared in a front-page commentary on Wednesday.
Relations between Beijing and Taipei had improved sharply in the last two years, since Taiwan allowed its citizens to visit relatives on mainland China. 
Taiwanese businessmen also began investing in China, and prospects for closer ties were greatest in May, when a senior Taipei official attended an Asian Development Bank meeting in Beijing.

Â 
Taiwan's Two-China Policy
Taiwan's diplomatic campaign has not focused on getting countries to switch their diplomatic recognition from Beijing to Taipei. 
Instead, it has sought to have countries recognize both governments at the same time.
In the past, China and Taiwan have pursued a policy of ''sole recognition,'' although in the last year, Taipei has adopted a more ''flexible diplomacy'' that would allow dual recognition of both China and Taiwan by a third country. 
China has rejected this approach.
''The authorities on Taiwan should understand that on the question of 'one China' and 'unification of the motherland,' there is no flexibility to speak of,'' the commentary on Wednesday said.
Beijing's suspension of relations with Liberia, a step short of severing ties, was the same response as to Grenada's normalization of relations with Taiwan in July.

file: China Seeks New Image as Asian Games Host.txt
text:

With an edge of nervousness, a few sharp warnings and a flurry of activity counter to the usual languid summer pace of the Chinese capital, Beijing is preparing for its biggest diplomatic event in years - the 11th Asian Games.
Though technically a sporting event, the 16-day Asian Games, which start here on Sept. 
22, have become a major public-relations and political exercise. 
The last host, South Korea, used them and then the Olympics to make diplomatic breakthroughs with former enemies in the Communist world.

file: China Sees a Greater Role For Free Market in 1990_s.txt
text:

More Slogans Than Specifics

file: China Sentences 8 Leading Dissidents.txt
text:

A Chinese court today sentenced the nation's leading human rights advocate to seven years in prison and its foremost student leader to a four-year term for "counterrevolutionary propaganda and incitement" during the Tiananmen democracy movement.
Six other democratic militants were sentenced to terms ranging from two to five years, the official New China News Agency said, while 66 others were apparently released. 
By Chinese standards, the sentences were relatively lenient as counterrevolutionary offenses can bring the death penalty.
"The court, after hearings, confirmed that some of the eight defendants, resorting to various means, wantonly conducted public agitation to subvert the people's Government and the socialist system during the 1989 turmoil and rebellion, and others made Molotov cocktails to attack the armed forces enforcing the martial law and helping safeguard public order," the press agency said.
Ren Wanding, an accountant and determined spokesman for human rights, received the seven-year sentence, the stiffest handed out in the latest wave of trials. 
Mr. Ren played a relatively minor role in the 1989 democracy movement, but the leadership regards him as a troublemaker because he refuses to admit wrongdoing and because he has a history of agitation for democracy.
Â 
Student Is Given 4 Years
Wang Dan, the Beijing University student who was No. 1 on a most-wanted list published after the crackdown, was sentenced to four years in prison. 
The press agency said he had committed serious crimes but showed repentance.
Another student leader, Guo Haifeng, was also sentenced to four years. 
Bao Zunxin, a historian and advocate of greater democracy, was sentenced to five years. 
A person named Yao Junling, whose background is unknown, was sentenced to two years in prison.
Mr. Ren was a leader of the 1978-79 Democracy Wall movement, and while others called for democracy it was Mr. Ren who focused on human rights. 
His efforts won him a four-year spell in prison, from 1979 to 1983, but this had no effect on his iron will.
Prisoners are normally expected to write self-criticisms while in their cells; instead, Mr. Ren wrote a two-volume attack on the Government, etched painstakingly with the nib of a pen on his supply of toilet paper.
In the fall of 1988, Mr. Ren emerged in public again to call for greater democracy and human rights. 
He acknowledged the risk to himself and to his wife and daughter in an interview at the time.
Â 
'Frightening Experiences'
"I went through some very frightening experiences," he said then. 
"But China has no democracy and no human rights, and its living standard is too low. 
These are even more frightening."
Mr. Ren was arrested shortly after the crackdown on June 4, 1989, and since then has not been allowed to see his wife or daughter, now 14 years old.
In explaining the sentence, the New China News Agency said that Mr. Ren "was found guilty of grave crimes and showed no repentance."

And in the immediate aftermath of the June 1989 crackdown, some very harsh sentences were announced.

Trials Called a Sham
The sentences run from the time of detention, which for most of those sentenced was the summer of 1989, the press agency said.

Many ordinary criminal offenders in China have up to half their sentences reduced for good behavior, but this provision is not normally applied to political prisoners.
Hu Ping, chairman of the New York-based Chinese Alliance for Democracy, said in a telephone interview that the trials were a sham and that the punishments could not be regarded as lenient.
"The arrests and entire judicial process were closed and arbitrary, reflecting the caprice of the authorities, so that they can terrorize the population," Mr. Hu said.

Not since the Gang of Four were tried for their role in the Cultural Revolution has the Government prosecuted such a senior political figure. 
Mr. Bao was convicted of leaking state secrets and spreading counterrevolutionary propaganda.
Mr. Bao was a member of the Communist Party Central Committee who had been one of younger men and women in the leadership trying to restructure China economically and politically. 
A tall, lean man with gold-framed glasses, Mr. Bao had been the right-hand man to Zhao Ziyang, the Communist Party leader who was ousted from his post after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in June 1989. 
At that time, Mr. Bao was political secretary to the Politburo Standing Committee and head of a high-level Party institute to examine political change.
The trial, which began at 9 A.M. this morning, was videotaped but closed to the general public, even his family. 
Family members were allowed to attend the 10-minute sentencing shortly after 2 P.M., the only time they were allowed a glimpse of Mr. Bao.
He walked into the courtroom at a slow gait, turned to face the panel of judges -- his back to the audience -- as the verdict and sentence were read and then was escorted out again, according to his daughter, Bao Jian. 
She said that her father wore a T-shirt and dark-colored slacks, and he appeared to have had a haircut recently.

Right of Appeal
Mr. Bao appeared calm, and he nodded when he was told that he would be allowed to appeal the court's verdict, his daughter said. 
The family members said that they were given a place to stand in the middle of the courtroom and that because they were surrounded by many people, it is unlikely that Mr. Bao saw them.
The authorities said that about 200 members of the public were given tickets to attend the trial, but some of these members of the public arrived at the courthouse in cars belonging to the Public Security Ministry and others returned to work after the sentencing in offices within the courthouse.
Mr. Bao was sntenced to five years for leaking state secrets, although the verdict did not explicitly mention what secrets he is accused of leaking. 
He was then also given four years for inciting and spreading counterrevolutionary propaganda, but the sentences were merged for a total of seven years.

Many people had been looking to Mr. Bao's trial as a barometer for political change in China.

He spent five years in prison for street fighting, but after his release, with few friends and no work prospects, he decided to start a small vendor business.

While foreigners tend to regard entrepreneurs as heroes of the Chinese restructuring, many are social outcasts, and they are frequently accused of acquiring their goods by bribing factory managers. 
Their immense wealth also breeds growing resentment among many ordinary Chinese.
Partly because of such resentment, and perhaps because of its suspicion of private enterprise, the Government has begun a program to control the nation's 14.5 million individually owned businesses and raise their taxes. 
The Communist Party recently announced that ''exploiters'' would not be allowed to become members, and many believe this was a reference to wealthy entrepreneurs.
Â 
Drive Against Steet Traders
The authorities in Beijing also concluded a 100-day campaign against ''illegal street traders,'' including cigarette and clothing vendors, hair salons and food and drink outlets. 
The official English-language China Daily said the campaign had exposed 110,000 unauthorized businesses and produced more than half a million dollars in unpaid taxes and fines.
Official newspapers have said that much of the money made by the entrepreneurs is never reported to the tax collectors and that the majority of vendors have been in prison. 
A prison background apparently is common because released inmates have difficulty finding new employers, so they are forced to strike out on their own. 
On the other hand, most Chinese are reluctant to forsake their jobs and plunge into business, with its economic and political risks.
As a result, some former felons have been among the greatest beneficiaries of the economic restructuring policy of the last decade. 
There are no statistics on average incomes among private vendors, but it is certain that they earn many times China's average monthly wage of about $40.
The income disparities are creating discomfort for the Government, which prides itself on socialist egalitarianism. 
Since the new leadership took office in June, there have been ''cleanups'' in some of the capital's free markets. 
Police have closed down stalls of those vendors who do not pay rent, who evade taxes, who sell pornography or who ignore other regulations.
The Government complains that wealthy entrepreneurs are inflating prices, aggravating shortages and ''dampening the enthusiasm'' of state employees and intellectuals. 
Many of these vendors also contributed vast sums of money to the students during the democracy movement.
Â 
The Fastest-Growing Sector
It is not clear how far the Government will pursue its harsh line, partly because it needs private enterprises to help absorb a growing number of unemployed people. 
The authorities recently announced a tax break for private businesses that employ jobless workers in certain trades.
While private enterprises in the cities and rural areas are a minuscule portion of the overall economy, employing fewer than 27 million people, they constitute the fastest-growing economic sector. 
Their wealth is highly visible, for they can afford such conveniences as washing machines and video recorders, and they also have money to spend at wine bars and discos. 
Mr. Zhao complains about not having a Mercedes-Benz and an apartment large enough for his possessions.
Younger vendors also tend to dress better than most Chinese. 
One of their biggest problems is where to keep their money. 
A man selling athletic wear says he has four different bank accounts in the names of his wife, child and parents. 
He also keeps a large amount of money at home.
Small entrepreneurs pay rental and management fees for their stalls, and the total expenses including taxes could run to more than $160 a month. 
Normally, profits cover the expenses many times over, but since the violent crackdown on June 4, some vendors say earnings have been down by more than one-half. 
This is partly because of the shortage of foreign tourists. 
Even now, however, the vendors still earn much more than factory workers.
For all the anticipation of greater state control, the concern does not seem to show in their attitude.
Â 
'It Won't Rattle Us'
''They will put more controls on us,'' said a vendor selling women's blouses. 
''But we have already been through the worst. 
We've survived the Cultural Revolution, so no matter how tight their policy is, it won't rattle us and it won't last long.''
The Cultural Revolution, started by Mao in 1966, was a period of rigid Communist orthodoxy lasting 10 years.
Li Binglu, a 25-year-old former public relations manager, opened a restaurant and bar this fall. 
She paid $8,100 in capital, borrowed from friends, and pays the same in annual rent along with $270 in monthly taxes.
''My friends warned me that society was not stable and that the Government is severely controlling private enterprise,'' she said. 
''But if I make $27 a month from the state, it's just not worth it. 
I'd rather use a year's savings and get the experience, even if the Government shuts me down.''

file: China Threatens Contracts Reached by Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
China significantly raised the stakes today in its dispute with Britain over Hong Kong by declaring that all contracts signed by the territorial Government and not approved by Beijing will become invalid when London ends its rule there in 1997.
The Hong Kong Government responded immediately that the declaration violated the Chinese-British Joint Declaration of 1984 and the Basic Law, the documents that govern the transition period and guarantee economic and political freedoms to the territory for 50 years.
"According to the Basic Law, contracts which are valid under Hong Kong's existing laws will continue to be valid and recognized and protected by the Hong Kong special administrative region, provided that they do not contravene the Basic Law," the Hong Kong Government said in a written statement.
It was the first substantial step taken by China to retaliate against British plans to bring greater democracy to Hong Kong, plans that Beijing says violate the agreements it signed with Britain. 
But China's international standing and credit-worthiness could be reduced if its retaliatory steps are widely construed as violating the agreements.
Â 
Confusion and Concern
Even if the announcement does not derail the plans for a peaceful transfer of control over the territory, it is certain to cause confusion and grave concern among a wide variety of local and international companies that do business with the territorial Government. 
The Hong Kong Government has signed thousands of contracts that could be affected.
"The implications could be very broad," said an American businessman in Hong Kong who refused to be identified. 
"If you've done business with the Hong Kong Government, which is itself a large contractor, you have to ask yourself: What is the validity of that contract?"
By undermining Hong Kong's authority to issue contracts extending beyond 1997, the Beijing statement seemed particularly intended to prevent Britain from continuing its efforts to build a new airport and a new container port in the territory.
The Hong Kong Government recently announced that it would pursue plans to build a new airport even if China did not give its final approval to the proposed financing arrangements, and the Hong Kong legislature approved an initial allocation of funds last week by a narrow margin.
"It's horrific," Emily Lau, a Hong Kong legislator, said of the Beijing move in a telephone interview. 
"They're intimidating the Hong Kong people. 
They're trying to bring Hong Kong to its knees. 
They will resort to anything."
The Chinese announcement was made after the Hong Kong stock exchange was closed for trading today. 
The stock market index lost 2.9 percent of its value today in reaction to a far more limited Chinese threat made on Friday -- that it might not honor contracts relating to the new container port.
Today's statement said: "According to the Sino-British joint declaration, Britain's administrative power over Hong Kong will terminate on June 30, 1997, and it will then have no right to handle any affairs after the date. 
Accordingly, all contracts, leases and agreements signed or ratified by the Hong Kong British government will be valid until June 30, 1997."
The statement added that aside from certain land leases, "other contracts, leases and agreements signed and ratified by the Hong Kong British Government which are not approved by the Chinese side will be invalid after June 30, 1997."
Beijing said it would "take a positive attitude in examining and approving contracts, leases and agreements after June 30, 1997."
Today's announcement reflects the extreme irritation that China feels toward new British proposals to make the territory a bit more democratic, coupled with Britain's increasing willingness to make decisions about Hong Kong without Beijing's approval. 
Since the new Hong Kong Governor, Christopher Patten, took office in July, Britain has taken a much more confrontational approach in dealing with China.
Mr. Patten proposed in October that election rules be changed to expand the number of people who can vote for legislative seats representing Hong Kong industries. 
China disagrees with the proposal and is infuriated that it has not been given a veto over the changes.

file: CHINA THREATENS HONG KONG TREATY.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has sharply escalated its dispute with the British and Hong Kong authorities by threatening to scrap the 1984 agreement that promised Hong Kong continued political and economic freedom for 50 years after the colony returns to Chinese control in 1997.
The threat was made on Monday night by Deputy Prime Minister Zhu Rongji, who was in London for talks with British officials.
"People cannot help but ask whether we still have to stick to the joint declaration between us, whether the important understanding and agreement that we have reached should go with the wind," the official New China News Agency quoted him today as saying.
China itself would suffer enormous diplomatic harm and economic damage if it repudiated the agreement, so such an action is widely regarded as unlikely. 
Instead, the threat appears intended to put new pressure on Hong Kong and force Britain to back away from its recent proposals to introduce more democracy in its final years of rule over the territory.
Still, the bluff -- if that is what it is -- is so threatening to the existing economic order in East Asia that it creates fundamental new uncertainties that may hang over the region for years to come. 
Mr. Zhu's remarks sent share prices tumbling by more than 3 percent on the Hong Kong stock market, where the Hang Seng Index fell 206 points to close at 6,089.
If the threat were carried out, Hong Kong, a British colony for 150 years, would still revert to China on July 1, 1997. 
A 99-year lease on most of the territory expires then, and Britain has decided that it will return the entire colony at that time. 
In its negotiations with Beijing, London tried to get the best conditions it could for Hong Kong's residents, but the decision to hand over the territory is considered final.
A Chinese takeover without the international guarantees for Hong Kong's future would have a devastating impact on confidence and investment in the territory, would trigger waves of emigration by the middle class, and would crush the spectacular economic boom in both Hong Kong and southern China.
Given the enormous stakes, the threat is an indication of the outrage that Beijing feels over the British-backed proposals that would make Hong Kong more democratic -- and thus more difficult for China to govern -- at the time of the handover in 1997.
The proposal that most irritates Beijing calls for a vast expansion in the number of people who can vote for certain kinds of legislators. 
China is also opposed to a proposal to lower the voting age to 18, and is infuriated that it has not been given a veto over the changes.
The joint declaration confirms that Hong Kong will be returned to China on July 1, 1997. 
But it says that the territory will have "a high degree of autonomy" and that Hong Kong people can continue to practice capitalism and enjoy freedom of speech and other civil rights for at least 50 years.
The agreement is the framework and guarantee for Hong Kong's future, and paradoxically for China's as well, since China gets about 55 percent of its foreign investment from Hong Kong and nearly 35 percent of its trade passes through the territory's ports. 
China does not want to scare off investors and businesses.
In addition to the joint declaration is the "basic law" that China has promulgated for Hong Kong after 1997. 
The basic law, a mini-constitution, promises that Hong Kong can enjoy its autonomy and prosperity after the handover, but there is deep apprehension in the territory about whether Beijing will honor the basic law after the takeover.
The Hong Kong Government had no official reaction to Mr. Zhu's remarks, but a Government official who asked not to be identified said, "It's a new ball game now, and quite a serious one."
Martin C. M. Lee, a Hong Kong lawyer who for years has been the leader of the territory's democracy movement, said in a statement today, "Any threats made by the Chinese Government not to honor the joint declaration will cause the international community to doubt China's commitment not only to this agreement but to all its international agreements."
"Threats of this nature by the Chinese Government often have a countereffect, in that they serve only to encourage the people of Hong Kong to stand up for their interests," Mr. Lee added at a news conference in Hong Kong.
The comments by Mr. Zhu came as a surprise to many in Hong Kong because he is one of the most pragmatic of China's top leaders.
"We want cooperation, not confrontation, but no one should expect confrontation to force us into concessions from our stand on the matter of principle," he was quoted as saying by the New China News Agency, which released a translation. 
He reiterated the Chinese argument that the proposed steps toward democracy violate British promises, threaten Hong Kong's prosperity, and run contrary to the desires of the people in the territory.
In fact, public opinion polls show overwhelming support for the steps toward more democracy.
Britain for years did what it could to suppress the indigenous democracy movement in Hong Kong, but since the middle of this year has been far more assertive in supporting democracy despite objections from Beijing.
The change came when Prime Minister John Major appointed Christopher Patten, the former leader of the Conservative Party, to take over as Governor of the territory beginning in July.

file: China Ties New Demand to Dissident_s Fate.txt
text:

Stiffening resistance to American efforts to free the dissident Fang Lizhi, China has made new demands on the United States in discussing terms for his release, American officials said today.
The United States tried again recently to arrange the release of Mr. Fang, who has taken refuge at the American Embassy in Beijing, but China still refuses to let him leave the country, the officials said.
Indeed, they said, after the United States met one of China's original conditions for Mr. Fang's release, allowing the resumption of some World Bank loans, China issued another demand: that the United States resume exports of military goods and high-technology products to China.
State Department and White House officials said they saw no prospect that Mr. Fang would leave the Embassy in the near future because Chinese authorities were tightening their political control over the country to prevent protests and demonstrations as several important anniversaries approach.
'He Is Not Isolated'
Chinese authorities have demanded that Mr. Fang write an ''admission of guilt,'' acknowledging that he helped organize the demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in May and June last year. 
American officials said Mr. Fang was unlikely to admit guilt now after having railed against the Chinese Communist Party, complaining of arbitrary, dictatorial rule, corruption and nepotism for several decades.
Mr. Fang, an astrophysicist, continues his work and study at the American Embassy and is able to correspond with scientists all over the world, Administration officials said. 
''He is not isolated,'' one official said.
Another American official said of the Chinese: ''It's in their interest to resolve the case, to regain the confidence of intellectuals in China, to gain the respect of the world community, to revitalize scientific exchanges with the outside world and to improve bilateral relations with the United States.''
A program assistant at the National Academy of Sciences, Derek S. Wilson, said the Academy suspended scholarly exchanges with China after the Tiananmen Square crackdown. 
Most of the programs are still suspended, although the Academy has sent several social scientists back to China in the last few months, he said. 
Chinese Deported by U.S. 
On a separate matter, Administration officials confirmed today that President Bush had not issued an executive order to protect Chinese students in the United States, even though he says repeatedly that he has issued such an order.
Administration officials said the difference between an executive order and the President's action was one of semantics, not policy.
The term ''executive order'' refers specifically to a Presidential proclamation with the force of law published in the Federal Register. 
On Nov. 
30, when he vetoed a bill to allow Chinese students to remain in the United States, Mr. Bush said he had directed the Attorney General to ''insure that no nationals from the People's Republic of China be deported against their will.''
Mr. Bush's directive has not been published in the Federal Register, does not have the force of law, can be changed without public notice and protects only those Chinese who were ''present in the United States on June 5, 1989.''
Chinese who took part in the Tiananmen Square demonstrations in early June were obviously not in the United States at that time. 
Immigration lawyers said the Immigration and Naturalization Service had arrested, detained and deported some Chinese who supported the student demonstrators, came to the United States and sought political asylum after June 5.
Â 
Assertions on Executive Order
Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, the author of the bill vetoed by Mr. Bush, said he should issue a formal executive order if he truly has no intention of sending Chinese students back to China.
In a television interview broadcast by NBC News on Feb. 
28, Mr. Bush bristled at criticism of his China policy. 
''I put into effect an executive order that's broader than the legislation that was so touted,'' he said.
Likewise, in a news conference on March 13, Mr. Bush said, ''The approach I took, accomplishing something by executive order that the Congress wanted to do dramatically later on through legislation, was the proper approach.''
In a handwritten letter to Senator Connie Mack, Republican of Florida, on Jan. 
24, Mr. Bush said, ''The executive order, in my view, protects the Presidency and does better by the students.''
But White House and State Department officials confirmed that Mr. Bush had not issued an executive order. 
Asked why the President continually boasted of having issued an executive order, Douglas A. Davidson, a White House spokesman, said: ''He is the executive, and he ordered it. 
These distinctions are semantic. 
It has the same effect. 
It doesn't really matter how it's done, by a Presidential memorandum, directive or executive order.''

file: China to Deal In Futures.txt
text:

China will open what it says is the first futures market in a socialist country this summer, an official newspaper reported today.
The market will open in August in the central city of Zhengzhou in Henan Province and will handle wheat transactions, The China Daily said.
If the market is successful, the Government may open futures markets for corn in the northeast city of Changchun, rice in the central city of Wuhan and pigs in southwest China's Sichuan Province, the paper said.

A futures market allows traders and producers to negotiate a set price for a commodity at a specified future date. 
The seller is guaranteed that price regardless of subsequent fluctuations in the market.
Although most Chinese agricultural products must be sold to the state for a set price, an estimated 65 million tons of agricultural commodities circulate in the free market every year.
Poor regulation of the free market has led to wild price fluctuations for produce and livestock and serious gaps in supply and demand.
The paper said foreign dealers will not be allowed to participate in the Zhengzhou market at the outset.

file: China to Raise Arms Spending Again.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's leaders announced a sharp increase in military spending today, despite a rising budget deficit and economic challenges that will mean slower growth in the economy this year.
The increase in military spending, the second in two years, apparently reflects the rising status of the People's Liberation Army since the army-led crackdown in 1989. 
The Chinese military is gaining influence at a time when a transition of generations in the nation's leadership is likely before long, and greater financial resources are expected to bolster that influence.
Â 
Chagrined by Comparison
In addition, Western diplomats and Chinese with ties to the military leadership say that during the Persian Gulf war, the Government was deeply distressed by the remarkable display of Western weapons, which are far more advanced than Chinese military systems. 
The military leaders have apparently lobbied hard for more money to modernize weapons systems.
Finance Minister Wang Bingqian said arms spending this year would rise by nearly 12 percent, to the equivalent of $6.25 billion. 
An itemized military budget is not made public, and it is unclear what is included in this amount. 
In addition to this money from the Government, the Chinese military presumably also raises substantial amounts from weapons sales and from civilian factories that it operates.
The budget increase, which followed a rise in military outlays last year of 15.5 percent, was announced at a session of the National People's Congress. 
The congress, a rubber-stamp parliament, convened Monday for a session that will last less than three weeks and is expected to approve a new 5-year plan and a 10-year economic program.
The economic plans were marked by bitter negotiations between the provinces and the central Government, which is experiencing a severe shortage of money and wants local areas to pick up more of the burden.
Mr. Wang announced a nominal budget deficit for this year equivalent to $2.56 billion, down slightly from last year's estimated deficit of $2.89 billion.
But those figures were calculated using the Chinese practice of including borrowed funds as revenue. 
Using Western accounting practices, the budget gap would reach $9.34 billion this year, compared with $9.15 billion in 1990. 
In addition, the 1991 deficit is expected to exceed Mr. Wang's forecast, as a year ago he had forecast a deficit much lower than the actual amount.
Still, the adjusted deficit last year amounted to only 2.6 percent of the gross national product. 
The Government acknowledges that a deficit is likely to persist.
The state enterprises, one of the Beijing Government's main sources of revenue, have become a cash drain, Mr. Wang acknowledged. 
He provided figures indicating that losses at the state enterprises exceeded profits by a ratio of nearly 8 to 1. 
The Government is afraid to close factories losing money because of the risk of provoking unrest among workers. 
And subsidies to such factories absorbed nearly a third of revenue in 1990.
Â 
Maldistribution of Wealth
Mr. Wang also reported that in some areas throughout the year, public institutions were unable to pay salaries on time. 
He indicated that another "glaring issue" was the uneven distribution of income, which has widened as the economies of southern provinces, like Guangdong, expand faster than those of other provinces.
The budget proposal for this year also included an increase of 9.7 percent in funds for culture, education, science and health; a 12 percent decline in price subsidies, and a slight decrease, to $10.1 billion, in subsidies to state enterprises. 
It is unclear if these plans will be realized.
China's economy, which has been governed by an austerity plan since the fall of 1988, was forecast to grow even more slowly this year.

file: China to Reward Army With 13_ Increase in Military Budget.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government announced today that it would give the army a 13.8 percent budget increase this year, apparently a reward for helping to keep the Government in power.
The rise in the military budget is bigger than any other increase in a major spending category and comes on top of a substantial boost in army spending in each of the last few years. 
The new military budget is more than 50 percent bigger than the one for 1989.
The decision to increase military spending, particularly at a time when the threats along the nation's borders are diminishing, is sure to raise eyebrows and anxieties among some of China's neighbors. 
Not only has the principal threat to China, an attack from the Soviet Union, virtually disappeared for the time being, but tensions have also been considerably eased between China and two other neighbors with which it has fought border wars: India and Vietnam.
The announcement today by Finance Minister Wang Bingqian in a speech to the National People's Congress, the rubber-stamp Parliament now holding its annual session, did not give any clues on how the allocation to the 3.1 million-member army would be spent. 
But the military has been focusing lately on acquiring high-tech weapons and on gaining equipment to project an image of power at sea.
A stronger navy would threaten Taiwan, which China insists is an errant province that it has the right to invade. 
It would also worry several Southeast Asian nations that have competing claims with China over islands in the South China Sea.
Ever since the army was called upon in June 1989 to suppress the democracy movement in Tiananmen Square, the military has played an important role in internal security. 
Domestically, the army is particularly concerned about the possibility of unrest in ethnic minority regions like Tibet and Xinjiang.
The official military budget, which in 1992 is projected to be $6.85 billion, includes only some of the money actually made available to the military, but no more comprehensive figure is available. 
Mr. Wang put the 1992 increase at 12 percent, but that was because military spending in 1991 was over budget. 
The increase in the budgeted amount is actually 13.8 percent.
In contrast, agriculture spending will rise 7.2 percent this year, education funds are increasing 11.3 percent, and science expenditures are rising 7.4 percent.
One revelation in Mr. Wang's speech today was that the leadership plans essentially to abolish the grain subsidy this year. 
That would be a major stride to restructure prices along market lines, and it also suggests that the authorities feel comfortable that they can handle any protests over such an unpopular move.
Â 
Raising Both Prices
"The State Council has decided to raise the purchase and selling prices of grain at an appropriate time in 1992, basically unifying the two prices," Mr. Wang declared.
The purchase price refers to the price that the Government pays farmers for rice, wheat and other grains. 
The selling price means the price that the Government charges consumers in the cities for rice, bread and flour.
The retail prices are well below the real cost of the grain, but until now the Government has picked up the difference for fear that higher prices might provoke unrest.
The Government raised grain prices a year ago, causing grumbling but no serious protests, and the authorities announced this month that prices would rise again on April 1. 
But so far the price increases have only reduced the subsidy, and today's announcement is the first indication that it will be almost entirely abolished this year.
While the abolition of the grain subsidy would be welcomed by economists as an important reform measure, the basis for the move apparently is not so much enthusiasm for economic liberalization as it is alarm over rising Government spending. 
Mr. Wang has acknowledged that it will be difficult to avoid exceeding budget deficit targets this year.
