The Government acknowledged today that it faced grave budgetary difficulties, but at the same time proposed a budget for 1990 that includes a sharp increase in military spending.
The National People's Congress, now meeting in Beijing for a 15-day session that will give pro forma approval to the budget and other proposals from the leadership, also agreed today to accept the resignation of Deng Xiaoping from his last formal post, as chairman of the Government's Central Military Commission. 
Mr. Deng announced in November that he would retire from the post, and today's move was a formality.
The Congress did not name a new chairman, but it is widely expected to be Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader and Mr. Deng's choice to succeed him as China's paramount leader. 
In November Mr. Jiang succeeded Mr. Deng as chairman of the Communist Party's Central Military Commission, which in practical terms is the same as its Government counterpart.
The military spending increase, by $6.2 billion, or 15.2 percent, had been expected as a signal of the leadership's appreciation of the role of the People's Liberation Army in crushing democracy protests last year.

''The condition for the state budget this year is grim,'' Finance Minister Wang Bingqian told the congress in an address. 
He presented a draft budget that included a nominal deficit of $1.89 billion, down slightly from last year.
But those figures were calculated under the Chinese practice of counting borrowed funds as revenue. 
Using Western accounting practices, the budget gap this year reaches $9 billion, up 14.5 percent.
Most Western and Chinese economists agree that China's economic difficulties are related less to the military crackdown last June than to the 18-month-old austerity program. 
The economic slowdown has made it more difficult for the central Government to raise funds, and has meant increased subsidies to money-losing state enterprises.
The budget proposal also included a 9.9 percent increase in education spending and a 7.9 percent increase in funds for agriculture. 
It is not clear how such numbers are derived or how reliable they are, and some university faculties have been told that education spending would drop this year.
Most Western diplomats regard the figure for military spending as a significant understatement of the total, partly because the budget allocation apparently does not incorporate sums the army earns from weapons sales and from civilian products produced by army-owned factories.
China's leaders have given strong hints - particularly after seeing the Romanian Army help topple a Communist Government in December - that they want to insure the loyalty of the army. 
In addition, the leadership has been trying to give the army a greater role in maintaining domestic security.
According to the Finance Minister's report, the two largest allocations, each amounting to about $14 billion or about 20 percent of the budget, are for capital construction and subsidies to money-losing enterprises.
China has tried to cut spending for inefficient enterprises by introducing a bankruptcy law, but the Government has been reluctant to allow money-losing companies to go bankrupt.

file: China_s Babies_ Better _Elegant_ Than _Red_.txt
text:
ï»¿
While there are no free elections in China to use in judging the popular mood, one gauge of the people's sentiment is the names bestowed upon children.
By that standard, the hard-liners who run China are in trouble. 
Names with political meanings, redolent of the Communist past, are decidedly out of fashion. 
Almost no self-respecting parents now name their children Red, which used to be the most common name of all. 
Today's babies often get names that have an association with prosperity or the West, like Xiu, a name now common that means Elegant.
"These days people don't want political names like Red that are reminiscent of the Cultural Revolution," said Zhang Shuyan, a senior researcher in China's State Committee for Reforming the Chinese Written Language. 
"Now many names are unusual. 
Parents search the dictionary for a character that has a good meaning and is uncommon."
These days, parents strive for names that sound more cultured or cosmopolitan. 
Some children born in September, for example, were named Yayun, meaning Asian Games, after the mini-Olympics of which China was host at the time -- an international event that symbolized sophistication.
For baby girls, the character na, often used in transcribing Western names into Chinese, is common. 
It has little meaning, but because of its use in transcriptions it has the allure of associations with the West.
Almost all Chinese names have a meaning and are plucked from daily life.
For example, tens of thousands of people are named Li Jianguo (Build-the-Country Li), Zhang Hong (Red Zhang) and Wang Jun (Army Wang).
Those names proliferated during more orthodox moments of Communist history, and it used to be that a name offered an instant clue to when the person was born.
Anyone named Build the Country was probably born in 1949 or 1950, around the birth of the People's Republic. 
Yuanchao, meaning Assist Korea, is a common name of people born during the Korean War. 
Many who were born in the late 1950's, when Mao Zedong began an effort to catch up with Western industry, are named Chaoying, or Surpass England. 
And someone named Weidong, meaning Protect Mao Zedong, probably was born in the Cultural Revolution.
China's official newspapers reported approvingly that one soldier named his child Pingbao -- Suppress Rioting -- in honor of the crackdown against the democracy movement last year. 
In past years, that kind of name would have been ubiquitous, but in an indication of changing attitudes the newspaper report caused only mirth and ridicule.
A vast study of names by Ms. Zhang found that the single most common character used for names in the Cultural Revolution was Red. 
But since then, she says, the most common character in names has been hua, meaning magnificent and prosperous, and also signifying China.
Feng Yingshu, a sculptor, said, "It used to be that the time period provided a context, a frame in which to come up with a name for a child."
His own name reflects a drought at the time when he was born in 1948. 
The last character, shu, means a timely rain and includes the symbol for water.
Fortunetellers and astrology are still sometimes used in Hong Kong and Taiwan to derive names, but this is not common on the Chinese mainland today. 
Superstition is still evident in villages, however, where the desperate desire to give birth to a son leads to names for daughters like Zhaodi, Yindi and Ladi. 
All can be translated as 'Bring a Younger Brother.
As the Cultural Revolution generation enters adulthood, some people are changing their revolutionary names for more mundane ones -- as did many of the Soviet children who received similar names, particularly in the 1920's and 1930's, when Traktor, Elektrifikatsiya or Vladlen, for Vladimir Lenin, were not uncommon. 
A Chinese who deals regularly with Taiwan or Hong Kong business executives, for example, might feel a bit embarrassed if he was named Dongfeng, meaning East Wind, or Dajun, meaning Great Army.
While names are becoming more bourgeois, the names are still different from those that preceded the 1949 revolution. 
At that time, villagers often used ordinary characters from daily life. 
A child might, for example, be called Yuliang, meaning Surplus Grain, in the hope that he would always have enough to eat. 
Very feminine names, based on varieties of flower or jade, were common for girls before the revolution but have not made much of a comeback.
Mao Zedong's name meant Anoint the East. 
Deng Xiaoping's name is a common one and means Little Peace. 
Mr. Deng's partner and rival, Chen Yun, has a name that simply means Cloud.
One of the biggest changes in selecting names is that more and more people are getting names with only two syllables, consisting of one character for the surname and one for the given name. 
Chinese say that two-syllable names make it easier to hail somebody. 
But officials are concerned that a proliferation of two-character names will worsen the problem of large numbers of people having the same names.
Of the 1.1 billion people in China, about 100 million bear the surnames Wang, Chen, Li and Zhang. 
There were lots of mix-ups even when most people had three-character names, and with the popularity now of two-character names officials expect a good deal more duplication and confusion.

file: China_s Communists Prepare Party Congress.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Communist Party is preparing for a rare congress that will convene next week to shuffle the national leadership and establish a party line that is supposed to last for the next five years.
The party congress, the first to be held since 1987, is expected to confirm the rise of more pragmatic, change-minded officials within the leadership and to launch a new slogan: the building of a "socialist market economy."
No one knows just what a "socialist market economy" is, and that may be part of the attraction: the term is vague enough to be acceptable to all groups, while still sounding bold and reform-minded.
The authorities have given few details about the party congress, the 14th since the Chinese Communist Party was formed more than seven decades ago, except that it will begin on Monday. 
Still, they have hailed its importance, with Prime Minister Li Peng describing it last week as "a major event in our country's political life."
"We are sure that it will give a fresh impetus to reform, opening up and our economic development, and become an important milestone in the history of the Chinese Communist Party and China's socialist modernization," Mr. Li said.
The party congress will approve a work report that is supposed to set the tone for the next five years, and it will also choose a new Central Committee. 
The Central Committee, in turn, will choose a new Politburo.
In fact, all the crucial decisions have been made in advance by the handful of octogenarians who hold ultimate power in China, and the congress is less a forum for decisions than a platform for self-promotion -- a Chinese version of a national political convention in the United States. 
Among the key differences are that party congress speeches can last for hours, many of the proceedings are secret, and there is no election afterward to put it all in perspective.
The 14th party congress is expected to be important in that it will presumably anoint the team of leaders who will preside over the transition after the death of Deng Xiaoping, the ailing paramount leader. 
But the same was said of the 13th party congress in 1987.
Â 
Deng Not Expected to Appear
Mr. Deng appeared at the 1987 congress but there is no sign that he will turn up this time. 
He is 88 years old and rarely appears in public now.
Since the beginning of this year, Mr. Deng has been pressing behind the scenes for more rapid economic growth and restructuring, to the point of borrowing some elements from capitalism. 
The congress may be his last hurrah, and it is expected to endorse his preferred combination of free markets and one-party rule.
"There seems no question that the congress is intended to be a strong reaffirmation of the Deng Xiaoping line of reform and openness," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"We expect that the new Central Committee and the new Politburo in particular will basically reflect that, in the sense that there will be a strengthening of the reform and moderate forces."
While the personnel decisions have presumably already been made, the rumors about who will be promoted vary considerably. 
By almost all accounts, the Politburo will be expanded from its present membership of 14, and most of the likely candidates are relatively young and enthusiastic about markets -- for goods if not ideas.
The most powerful rulers of China, all octogenarians like Mr. Deng, are nominally retired and will not be shuffled. 
Among the younger leaders who hold formal positions, the two most important -- Prime Minister Li and General Secretary Jiang Zemin -- are generally expected to hold onto their posts, at least for now.
Â 
Small Role for Delegates
The 1,991 delegates to the party congress, which will last about a week, will be entrusted with a minor role in addition to approving decisions already made. 
They will elect a Central Committee from a list of names that is a bit longer than the number of positions, so that a small percentage of candidates will lose the election.

file: China_s Credit Rating Downgraded by Moody_s.txt
text:
ï»¿
Signaling uncertainty about China's political stabilityII, Moody's Investors Service Inc. today downgraded the country's long-term credit rating.
While the move reflected the likely difficulty China will have in returning to the financial marketplace since suppressing the democracy movement in June, bankers say China will still be able to raise money - though at higher prices than it is used to paying.
The downgrading of the debt rating from A3 to Baa1 is unlikely to have an immediate impact on China's borrowing costs since China has raised only about $5 billion in foreign currency bonds, none of it in United States markets. 
Bonds rated A are considered ''favorable'' and are one step above those with a Baa rating, which are considered medium grade.
Moreover, foreign banks are more concerned about when the World Bank will resume lending to China than they are about ratings.
The lower rating reflects the general assessment that China will have to pay more for its conventional loans than its previous typical margin of one-quarter percent above the London interbank offered rate, or Libor, a standard benchmark.
Indeed, bankers here and in Hong Kong say that since June, rates for trade credits and occasional other loans have generally risen by half a percentage point, and sometimes even more. 
The higher interest rates, for bank loans or bonds, will raise China's borrowing costs and put new pressures on an already strained economy. 
China is to begin repaying larger amounts of its $43 billion foreign debt next year, and higher interest rates will increase the difficulties of refinancing these loans.
The rating change could have been more severe and the fact that it was not is one indication that financial analysts and bankers are being careful not to overestimate the impact of the June crackdown on China's creditworthiness. 
Moody's may also have been particularly careful since its initial rating last year of A3 was lower than had been expected.
''We think there is a lot of rhetoric accompanying the economic adjustments, but the inference that this is a complete return to the old operating method is not necessarily valid,'' Roger B. Arner, director of Moody's Japan K. K., said today in a telephone interview from Tokyo.
Two American banks have arranged loan syndications for Chinese borrowers that are expected to be signed this month. 
Both were five-year loans for $50 million, by the Hong Kong merchant banking arms of the Bankers Trust Company and the Chase Manhattan Bank.
In each deal, the Chinese borrowers were successful in obtaining pricing below Libor in return for a currency risk.
The Bankers Trust loan syndication, to the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, or Citic, offers three-quarters of a percentage point above Libor to its syndication partners. 
The loan was oversubscribed.
The more recent Chase Manhattan deal has had greater difficulty attracting participants. 
The loan was made to China Resources Holdings and offers partners three-eighths of a percentage point over Libor for the first three years and one-half of a percentage point for the remainder. 
So far, about $25 million has been sold to other banks.

file: China_s Divided Economy.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 60 percent of China's labor force is engaged in agriculture, where farmers essentially grow and sell their produce on the principle of private enterprise.
In 1990, agriculture accounted for about 33.3 percent of national income. 
Farmers do not own the land but since the early 1980's they have been given the right to use individual plots. 
They must sell a certain part of their produce to the state, but then can sell the rest on a relatively free market.
About 17 percent of the work force is involved in industry, which produced 46.5 percent of 1990's national income. 
The state sector is the largest category in industry, producing about 53 percent of industrial output in 1990. 
But private and collective enterprises in the countryside -- which are often far more efficient than state enterprises -- are gradually producing a larger share of the nation's industrial output.
Collectively owned enterprises sometimes blur the distinction between state and private sectors because they sometimes are run partly by village or township governments. 
In any case, they tend to operate on market principles and are much more entrepreneurial than Government-run enterprises.
Other parts of the economy, such as construction and retailing, are split between the private and state sectors. 
For example, large department stores are largely Government-owned, but in recent years, there has been a proliferation of small free markets and private stores and stalls. 
A growing number of collectively-owned construction companies also are now competing with large state companies for contracts to build homes and small buildings.

file: China_s Films_ More Propaganda, Less Art.txt
text:
ï»¿
Any good Communists attending the recent premiere of China's grandest propaganda film, "Decisive Battles," had to have been disappointed with the audience reaction.
The scene was from China's Civil War, and a vast army of the enemy Nationalist Chinese forces filled the screen and were marching on the heroic Communist soldiers. 
At the most suspenseful moment, when it seemed the Communists were going to be annihilated, there was a burst of applause in the cinema.
The incident captured something of the spirit of Chinese cinema in the 1990's: blatant propaganda on the screens and cynicism and yawns in the audiences.
This summer the propaganda films are everywhere, and Chinese workers are being organized to see them in the hope that the movies will improve attitudes toward the Communist Party. 
But with politics replacing art as the raison d'etre of Chinese film, some Chinese see the billboards for the new epics as tombstones for the golden era of Chinese cinema.
In the 1980's, a new generation of Chinese film makers won international respect for works that were innovative and visually stunning, among them "Ju Dou," which was nominated for an Academy Award this year. 
But this summer's movies, particularly three that are strongly backed by the Government and the army, have a Maoist tinge that apparently is the wave of the future in Chinese arts, at least as long as the present leaders are in power.
The most important of the movies is Part 1 of "Decisive Battles," probably the costliest film ever made by a Chinese studio. 
Parts 2 and 3 are to come out later this year. 
The trilogy, depicting battles in 1948 and 1949 that let the Communists take power, is said to be the pet project of China's 84-year-old President, Yang Shangkun. 
Not surprisingly, Mr. Yang is a dashing young man in the movie.
Â 
125,000 Extras
Part 1 is three and a half hours of battle scenes interspersed with glowing portrayals of most of China's present leaders. 
There are no compelling characters, but there are a lot of non-compelling ones: the Army provided 125,000 soldiers for battles scenes. 
The trilogy is believed to have cost the Army more than $15 million -- reportedly more than all the 100 other films that China produces annually.
A shorter summer epic is "Kaitian Pidi," which was officially translated as "An Epoch-Making Event" but which translates more literally as "The Creation of the Heavens and the Earth."
The topic is the Communist Genesis: the forming of the Chinese Communist Party.
The third of the trio is "Mao Zedong and His Son," which deals with Mao's grief when he lost his son to an American air raid in the Korean War. 
The film is unusual in that it portrays Mao as a human rather than a god. 
Though it is clearly propaganda with anti-American overtones, it leaves many Chinese in tears. 
For all his unchallenged political power, Mao is unable to break the news of his son's death to the son's wife.
"The new trend is for these historical, political movies," a young Chinese journalist said regretfully the other day. 
Speaking of the earlier artistic films, he said: "That era has ended."
Â 
Arty Movies Are Still Made
But Geremie Barme, an Australian scholar of Chinese culture, said in a telephone interview that it was far too early to say that.
"These party epics that are sucking up huge amounts of money have tended to overshadow other developments in Chinese film," he said. 
"But still each year there seem to be a handful of arty movies still being made."
Mr. Barme cited "Li Lianying," a film about a famous imperial eunuch, and "Bloody Dawn," about the murder of a village schoolteacher who is suspected of having an affair with a local woman.
Moreover, Mr. Barme and others noted that internationally respected film makers like Chen Kaige and Zhang Yimou continue to shoot movies in China, but now with foreign financial backing and foreign audiences.
A Western diplomat who follows the film industry said incipient capitalism is also hurting art films. 
With declining subsidies for culture and uncertain attendance for highbrow films, studios are afraid that artistic films will lose money.
From the point of view of the studios, an important advantage of political films is that no matter how awful they are, they make money because the great majority of tickets are bought in bulk by offices and factories. 
Employees are encouraged to see the films during normal work hours.

file: China_s Frontier_ The Search for Development.txt
text:
ï»¿
This is the ''other China,'' a land of poor peasants and occasional smokestacks, where for some households upward mobility means nothing more grand than moving out of their cave and into a house.
As China develops, the caves are giving way to brick or mud homes, and most people in northwestern China have basic clothing and enough food to eat. 
But there is still none of the sense of economic vibrancy and rapid change that permeates the coastal areas of southeast China.
The peasants here in Gansu Province earn an average of just $100 a year, the lowest of any province in China. 
Their basic needs have mostly been met, but economists and other analysts say that the people of Gansu have probably benefited less than other Chinese from the restructuring of the last decade.
''In recent years, the country has had a policy of regional favoritism,'' said Chai Zhuqing, an official of the provincial planning commission. 
''The coastal areas developed very quickly, with the help of the state and foreign investors. 
But we're in the hinterland, with long distances to transport goods.''
A recent survey suggested that the gap between China's rich and poor areas is continuing to grow. 
In the first half of this year, the survey found, per capita incomes of peasants were $49 higher than a year earlier in southern Guangdong Province, the wealthiest part of the country. 
In the poorest parts, like Gansu and Tibet, incomes grew by just $5, compared with those of a year earlier.
''The gaps have increased and I can't see that trend changing anytime soon,'' Nicholas Lardy, a China scholar at the University of Washington, said in a telephone interview. 
Professor Lardy said that the central government is no longer redistributing resources among regions the way it once did, and that this will limit Gansu's ability to bridge the gap.
Under Mao, China's economic planners milked rich areas such as Shanghai for the benefit of other parts of the country. 
The planners also tried to build up the industrial capacity of the interior, partly for national security reasons, so that the country could continue to produce if it were attacked.
Even so, China's industry is geographically lopsided. 
Of the nation's 500 largest industrial enterprises, 111 are either in Shanghai or in northeastern Liaoning Province, while only 25 are in the six provinces and autonomous regions of China's west.
The Government in recent months has expressed increased concern about the plight of the hinterland, and there is no longer as much conviction as there used to be that some areas should get rich first and then spread the wealth to the interior. 
But there is still not much of an economic strategy for China's interior.
''Opening the door on the northwest frontier'' read the headline of a front-page editorial in the semi-official China Economic News last month, but the article contained few specific ideas for how to develop the frontier. 
While rich in mineral resources, the northwest lacks the entrepreneurial tradition of coastal areas, as well as their wealth of overseas relatives and other links.
The People's Daily and other official publications have recently called for developing overland trade with other Asian countries and even rebuilding a ''land bridge'' to Europe. 
This revived form of the old Silk Route will take shape around the end of next year when China completes a rail link across its northwestern border with the Soviet rail system.
Officials here in Gansu Province are optimistic that the rail link will allow them to export their products to European ports, so that Gansu too can participate in the opening to the outside world that has left the coastal region so flush with wealth.
Much of China is now alarmed at the prospect of recession, because of an economic retrenchment, but Gansu seems less worried. 
In September, industrial production in the province was 8 percent higher than a year earlier, while in cities such as Shanghai production actually fell. 
Officials note that the local economy was never particularly overheated, so the slowdown will not be very painful.

file: CHINA_S INDUSTRIES QUITTING THE HILLS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A postscript to the cold war is being written here: a missile factory has been converted to make refrigerators.
Just as important, the refrigerators are rolling off assembly lines not in the company's old location in the mountains of south-central China but in a new industrial zone here in the provincial capital. 
As the people here say, the tiger has come out of the mountains.
The tiger is China's so-called Third Line of industry, built mostly in the 1960's. 
Fearing attack by the United States or the Soviet Union, Mao Zedong ordered 2,000 companies representing a large share of China's industrial and military capacity removed from vulnerable coastal areas to remote hillside towns in the country's interior. 
Mao thought that the Communists could rely on that Third Line of industry even if an enemy attacked the coast.
It was an extraordinary scheme, the most daring and perhaps the most ill-considered industrial relocation plan that any country had ever attempted. 
From the mid-1960's to the mid-1970's, nearly half of China's budget went to Third Line construction, but the new factories tended to be inefficient because of poor infrastructure and supply lines.
Â 
Moving Back to Cities
In this post-Mao, post-cold-war era, the Third Line companies are now moving back to the cities, and in many cases retooling to make consumer goods instead of weapons. 
Across the nation, enterprises that once produced tanks and missiles and other military products are now making 650 kinds of civilian goods. 
Here in Guiyang, the capital of Guizhou province, two new industrial zones are filling up with Third Line factories making everything from transistors to automobile headlights.
"Intellectuals are very happy with the move, after being in the mountains for two decades," said Wang Quan, director of the Guiyang office of the Zhenhua Electronics Industry Corporation, one such enterprise. 
"Life is better here, there is entertainment and culture, and there's better education for the kids."
Of the 700,000 industrial workers in Guizhou Province who work in Third Line enterprises, about a third have already moved to the cities or are in the process of doing so, according to Hu Lun, chief economist of the Guizhou Province Planning Commission.
Â 
Efficiency and Location
"We plan to move all our workers to Guiyang," said Mr. Wang, of Zhenhua, which has 30,000 employees at 21 factories scattered across Guizhou. 
"But that will depend on economics and on how efficient the factories are here."
One of the factories that already has moved and started operations in Guiyang is the Jianxin Machine Factory, a unit of Zhenhua that makes stone cutters, drill presses and other industrial equipment. 
In the past it exported some goods to Eastern Europe and now the managers are hoping that the improved location will improve exports to the West.
"It's much more convenient here," said Feng Yisong, a senior engineer of the factory. 
"Transportation is much easier, and it's far simpler to make contacts and get a hold of people. 
So our efficiency is much better now."
The factory shop -- emblazoned with huge red characters across the wall declaring: "Socialism is Good. 
The Communist Party is Good" -- is spacious and is taking advantage of a tax break to install some brand-new equipment in addition to assembly lines brought in from its old location near the town of Duyun.
Â 
Creating a Society
The director of the nearby New Cloud Equipment Factory, Long Hanmin, said that though there is a hefty cost to moving the plant and all of its employees to Guiyang, the move will soon pay for itself in improved efficiency and reduced transportation costs.
"We used to be a company town and had to create our own society," said Mr. Long. "We had to provide schools, restaurants, a movie theater and a hospital. 
In Guiyang, we don't have to do any of that."
Mr. Long's factory used to make electronic components for the army, but it shifted a half-dozen years ago to manufacturing similar civilian products, like transistors and capacitors. 
These days, the transition from military production to civilian production is well underway, not just in Guizhou but throughout China.
For Guizhou Province, one of the poorest in China, that switch -- coupled with the emergence from the mountains of the Third Line "tiger" -- also offers an important opportunity to lure foreign investment.

file: China_s Intense Love of Education Cools Off.txt
text:
ï»¿
The director of a research institute here made a novel proposal the other day: he suggested that full professors receive the same salary as waitresses at the nearby Shangri-La Hotel.
There is little chance that the Government will approve the proposal, which would involve huge pay increases for the professors. 
But his idea underscores the humble circumstances of teachers in China, contributing to what is widely perceived today as a crisis in education.
At the annual session of the National People's Congress that adjourned on Tuesday, one of the topics that generated the most complaint was education. 
The outpouring of criticism appears to have galvanized top officials to acknowledge the problem and take action.
Prime Minister Li Peng said at a news conference Monday that he would convene a special committee to examine the nation's education problems. 
He also said he agreed with Deng Xiaoping's remarks on education.
''Our biggest mistake in the last 10 years has been that education has not been developed sufficiently,'' Mr. Deng, the senior Chinese leader, told Uganda's leader, Yoweri Museveni, who was visiting in the opening days of the legislative session.
In another sign of official recognition of the problem, Li Tieying, the Minister of Education, told reporters late last month, ''Our education is backward, our people's attainments fall short, and the low level of education has become a major constraint on our country's modernization and reform.''
While the Government is cutting spending on most programs, it has pledged to raise education expenditures by 15.4 percent to the equivalent of $10 billion. 
But some delegates said that sum is not enough. 
In some areas, children trudge hours each way through fields to classrooms in dilapidated shacks, or they learn from teachers with barely a high school degree, or are forced to share ragged books. 
In Beijing, some children bring their own chairs to school. 
Even in top universities, students often live six to a room that snugly fits one desk and three bunk beds.
Some rural children attend school in converted Buddhist temples or abandoned buildings, where conditions are often unsafe. 
Ninety percent of primary schools and 60 percent of junior high schools lack proper buildings and books, according to official figures.
Across the country, 220 million people are illiterate in a country with a population of 1.1 billion, and the average adult has only five years of schooling. 
While virtually all children enroll in primary school, one-third do not continue on to junior high school. 
High school enrollment has plunged by 27 percent over the last decade.
With China's rapid economic development, the symbols of achievement are no longer a college diploma or the rank of a scholar, but a new color television or a videotape player. 
While students still covet a scholarship to an American university - a possible route to permanent residency in the United States - the value of a local education is diminishing.
Â 
Professors Average $39.50
''If I had to make the decision again, I wouldn't become a graduate student,'' said a doctoral candidate in computer science at Beijing University. 
The student, who began his program six years ago, said that now not only the students but even the professors are going elsewhere.
A professor in China averages $39.50 a month, a bit less than the average for employees in Chinese business enterprises, and much less than taxi drivers or waitresses at international hotels.
When a college student advertised for a wife recently in a local newspaper, a young woman responded with a sarcastic scolding.
''Of what use is studying?'' she wrote. 
''Scribblers are not even as good as beggars. 
You can't eat culture, and you can't put ideals in the bank.''
The delegates to the National People's Congress admitted that the small increase in state funds will do little to improve the situation. 
The Education Ministry has suggested a school tax and higher tuition fees.

file: China_s Newspapers, After Crackdown by Beijing, Revert to a Single Voice.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's newspapers today show little trace of the independence and pluralism that they displayed last month before the Government cracked down on pro-democracy demonstrators.
Now the newspapers have reverted to a single voice, with little reliable domestic news, and if the reporters and editors are not satisfied, the only hint of it is the absence of bylines and an occasional indirect jab at the Government in articles on foreign news.
In the week after the military crackdown in China on June 4, a prominently placed headline in People's Daily read, ''The North Korean Labor News Criticizes Roh Tae Woo's Fascist Regime, Which Indiscriminately Kills Innocent Students and Citizens.''
Â 
Finding a Hidden Message
The reporter criticized Roh Tae Woo of South Korea, saying, ''The state of affairs makes clear that if Roh Tae Woo's military fascist regime is not overthrown, then the South Korean people will have no way to break away from bloodshed and death.''
But it was not farfetched to imagine that many Chinese would find a hidden message: that China's own military Government, which killed innocent students and civilians, needs to be overthrown, too.
Chinese newspapers have habitually been rife with such subtleties as reporters and editors try to work around the curbs ordered by the Government.
Â 
News More Constrained
The course of press freedom in a sense illustrates the trajectory of the entire democracy movement. 
There were tremendous initial gains, resulting in a relatively independent press, but then there was a crackdown that left news organizations even more constrained than before the protests.
Before the crackdown, criticisms were a bit more obvious and political analysts did not have to examine the international news so carefully.
About two months ago, readers found the front pages blanketed with national articles written by a newspaper's own correspondents, with perhaps a Government news item or two written by the official organ, the New China News Agency. 
But now, as part of a chorus of Government indoctrination, newspapers have yielded the front page to the official propaganda committee so that page 1 of each newspaper looks practically identical.
In bolder moments in the student movement, multiple perspectives were printed on the front pages, and some editors were openly sympathetic to the hunger-striking students. 
Just as the students had pushed their demands further than anyone expected, so, too, it seemed that news organiations had achieved much more independence and ''toumingdu,'' or ''openness,'' than anyone anticipated.
Â 
Propaganda Committee
But the swiftness with which the Government seems to have wrested control again over news organizations raises the concern that perhaps the newspapers will be indefinitely muzzled and that ordinary people will again have almost no source of information other than the official line.
For now, at least, newspapers are tightly controlled by a special propaganda committee that was formed after martial law was declared. 
In the absence of such committees, top editors and chief advisers, many of whom are elderly, were usually prestigious enough to defend a paper's decision to publish a particularly bold article.
''The passing of that generation might have several effects, and one is that people with very distinguished histories within the party are going,'' said Lynn T. White, a professor of Chinese politics at Princeton University.
''The independence or the social prestige of that kind of person can be very important in determining whether committees like this can make everything uniform,'' said Professor White, who is now doing research in Hong Kong.
Â 
'Concerned About Events'
''I'm concerned about the recent events because they might result in a structural change to some extent in the Chinese press by making the heads of newspapers less prestigious at least in normal times and so less able to have published what they feel is O.K.''
In the large protests at Tiananmen Square, where hunger-striking students had camped out before military soldiers forced them out on June 4, many journalists demonstrated to support the students and to demand greater press freedom.
Reporters at many large newspapers, including People's Daily, marched under their own banners. 
Moreover, thousands signed a petition to the Government protesting the dismissal of the editor in chief of China's boldest newspaper, World Economic Herald, based in Shanghai.
Journalists have been forced to abandon their demonstrations, and now they seem to be concentrating on retaining their jobs. 
While no reporters are known to have been arrested, there are fears that many will be.
Â 
'Subtle Passive Resistance'
If journalists are more careful now, that does not mean that they are satisfied, and there are signs they are resisting.
One possible indication of resistance is simply the near absence of staff-written articles in most newspapers. 
While it could mean that editors are ordered to publish mostly articles by the New China News Agency, that is not what the newspapers were originally intended to do. 
If it were, there would be no point in having so many newspapers, or in the newspapers having so many reporters of their own.
''There is obviously some kind of subtle passive resistance,'' said Byron S. J. Weng, a China scholar at Chinese University in Hong Kong. 
''I'd be surprised if there were none.''
In one sign of the continuing uncertainty at People's Daily, the Communist Party newspaper, a spokesman turned down a request to interview the editor in chief, Qian Liren.
Â 
Contacts Are Impossible
''Mr. Qian is in the hospital,'' the spokesman said. 
''And everyone else is too busy to receive you now.''
In China, when a senior official is unreachable because he is in the hospital, it usually means he is in political trouble, at least for the moment.
Before, it was relatively easy for foreign journalists to get to know counterparts on People's Daily and other newspapers; now it is impossible.
Recently, People's Daily has been publishing a string of articles that seem to be intended as subtle rebukes of the leadership.
The newspaper wrote about about President Raul Alfonsin of Argentina, ''President Alfonsin announced today that in order to prevent the nation from falling into a deeper crisis and to prevent the people from further suffering, he would leave his post early.''
Â 
Comparison With Argentina
The reporter for the newspaper continued: ''Now, the Alfonsin Government has already completely lost administrative ability. 
The majority of people in the ruling party propose that he should retire early from his political post to prevent the entire party from further loss of reputation.''
The suggestion seemed to be that China's Prime Minister, Li Peng, should resign.
When Prime Minister Nikolai I. Ryzhkov announced changes recently in the Soviet bureaucracy, a bold headline in People's Daily read, ''Three special characteristics of the new Government: Number of ministries and commissions reduced; Experts increase to some extent; The average age is 55.''
The subtle hint appeared to be that the Chinese Government bureaucracy could use similar trimming, more expertise and younger people.
Â 
Signs of Resistance
The article itself was written by the official New China News Agency, the Government organ through which most of the print propaganda has been disseminated. 
But the editors of People's Daily placed the article in the main position and wrote the headline.
There are also signs of resistance at other newspapers.
An article a few days ago in the China Youth News reflected on the death of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, saying, ''After the Iranian leader died on June 3, he left behind him a nation of feudal subjects in a state of utter stupefaction.''
In referring to the Iranian leader, the article seemed to be really describing Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader: ''Whenever a contradiction of political power suddenly became apparent, all that was required was a few words by him and calm would be restored.''
In another reference, the article said, ''The new Iranian leader was also decided by the word of Khomeini.''

file: China_s No. 2 Didn_t Invoke Jack Kennedy.txt
text:
ï»¿
If Dan Quayle ever gets annoyed at the jokes made about him, he should hear what is said about China's Vice President.
Wang Zhen, the 82-year-old Vice President, has emerged as one of the most outspoken hard-liners in the Chinese Government, and that makes him the target of some of the most bitter invective that is quietly muttered among young Chinese.
In the last few weeks, when rumors started to go around that Mr. Wang had fallen and broken his leg, many intellectuals expressed regret that he had not fallen on his head.
Â 
Not Seen in Public Lately
There is still no confirmation that Mr. Wang was injured, but he has not been seen in public since Aug. 
5. The account making the rounds among knowledgeable Chinese is that Mr. Wang arranged a private meeting with another hard-liner, 88-year-old Peng Zhen. 
When it was over, Mr. Peng reportedly tugged on the door and then lost his balance when it suddenly sprang open. 
He tumbled backward on the slight Mr. Wang, and the two leaders, with a combined 170 years on this planet, collapsed in a heap.
Whether or not this version is true, the satisfaction it evokes among intellectuals is palpable.
Mr. Wang is not the leader of the hard-liners. 
That title probably goes to Chen Yun, the 85-year-old head of central planning, who has not been seen in public for more than a year. 
But Mr. Wang is among the most outspoken, combative, energetic and persistent of the octogenarian hard-liners.
The position of Vice President is largely symbolic in China, but Mr. Wang has used it as a bully pulpit to push his vision of socialism, and this has won him attention and influence.
One example of Vice President Wang's influence reportedly came in August, when he read in Dongtai Qingyang, a classified news summary for the leadership, about chaotic and unauthorized stock trading in the southern city of Shenzhen. 
According to a Chinese with direct knowledge of the incident, Mr. Wang promptly wrote a memorandum denouncing such stock trading and circulated it to the Politburo.
Â 
Opening of Exchange Delayed
Prime Minister Li Peng was less aroused than Mr. Wang but agreed to investigate the matter and send an inspection team to Shenzhen. 
The upshot is that the Shenzhen Stock Exchange has had to delay its formal opening indefinitely.
By contrast, Mr. Wang's son, Wang Jun, is a highly regarded business executive in China's leading Western-style investment company, the China International Trust and Investment Corporation.
Even Mr. Wang's enemies generally acknowledge his sincerity and determination, even if they disagree with his views.
''Whatever you think of him, he's one of the most persistent people around,'' said a Western diplomat. 
''He hasn't changed his tune over the years.''
Two years ago, for example, Mr. Wang was the only leader who took strong exception to a television series called ''Death of a River.''
The series criticized the Yellow River, a symbol of China; to develop itself, the series suggested, China had to look outward to the blue ocean that symbolized the West.
Mr. Wang condemned the series on the ground that it profaned China's rich cultural heritage. 
For a time his was a lonely voice, but now his view has prevailed and the series is banned.
Â 
Defender of Mao Icon
When some younger people proposed in early 1989 that the portrait of Mao be taken down from Tiananmen Square, it was Mr. Wang who threw down the gauntlet. 
''If the portrait is removed,'' he is said to have declared in a meeting with other officials, ''I will never again go to Tiananmen Square.''
After the crakdown in June 1989, a widespread rumor reported that Mr. Wang was calling for special prison camps along China's northern border, where disgruntled intellectuals could be locked up for years. 
There is no evidence that the rumor was true, but it suggests how Mr. Wang is viewed -and feared.
Although he only has a third-grade education, Mr. Wang has taken a keen interest in literary and cultural affairs, which explains his frequent clashes with younger intellectuals. 
Particularly since the 1989 crackdown, he has tried to make writers and artists use their works to win support for socialism.
Mr. Wang's impetuousity seems to go way back. 
As a 16-year-old boy, he reportedly was dismissed from his first job, as a fireman on a locomotive, when he slapped the wife of a foreign employee of the railroad. 
Perhaps the incident helped to radicalize him, for within three years he joined the Communist Party and soon began rising through the Red Army to power and prominence.

file: China_s Open-Door Stock Policy.txt
text:
ï»¿
Nearly a year after China's two securities exchanges opened with fits and starts, demand for stocks is so strong that people line up on the streets to buy them. 
Now, the Government is planning to let foreigners in on the action.
China's two stock exchanges, in Shanghai and in Shenzhen, a special economic zone on the southern border, are working furiously to bring out special shares for foreigners in the next few weeks.
But the process of issuing these shares, called B shares, has caused clashes between authoritarian-minded Chinese officials and Western financiers, who are helping to underwrite the deal. 
Moreover, a headshake of disapproval from one of China's octogenarian leaders could mean another delay or even a cancellation of the deal.
Still, compared with other emerging exchanges, like Taipei and Seoul, which have loosened their rules for foreign investors slowly, China's socialist Government is racing ahead.
"China has actually proceeded quite fast compared to Eastern Europe, for example, or even compared to some other Asian countries," said Rolf Gerber, managing director at SBCI Finance Asia Ltd., a Swiss Bank Corporation subsidiary that is coordinating the foreign underwriters of the new shares. 
"In this way they are very progressive, although they understand very little about the habits of how such transactions are done internationally."
China's bid to sell stocks to foreigners, without first developing the domestic stock markets more fully, underscores its appetite for ways to raise foreign capital.
Shanghai's exchange is still in its infancy and currently trades only eight stocks, with a total market value equivalent to about $430 million. 
At the end of November, Shenzhen listed 11 new companies, in addition to the six already traded, that have a total market capitalization of about $100 million. 
All are state-run enterprises.
Stocks are so popular that price-to-earnings ratios go as high as 428, many times those of even the most promising American and Japanese companies. 
But the authorities seem ambivalent. 
The Government has restricted listings and tried to curtail speculation for fear of subverting socialism.
The Government had not allowed any other new companies to be listed on the Shanghai exchange during its first year of operation, until 10 more won approval earlier this month, according to the English-language China Daily. 
Companies must wait at least three months before they are formally listed.
"The central Government is being very cautious," said Zhang Ling, a spokeswoman at the Shanghai Securities Exchange. 
"They think that if the market develops too quickly, there will be harmful effects. 
If there are no clear results or if the results are poor, then they will be even more careful."
Â 
Conflict Among Aging Leaders
The slow development of the markets also appears to result from indecision or conflict among China's octogenarian leaders, like Deng Xiaoping and Chen Yun, who are nominally retired but still hold real power.
Earlier this year, when Chen Yun and Li Xiannian, two of these octogenarians, were traveling in Shanghai during the Chinese New Year holiday, they happened to notice that many people were poring over the stock market pages of a local newspaper that prints the results of the week's activity. 
Apparently believing that the market's rapid growth was contrary to socialism, the two complained to Zhu Rongji, then Mayor of Shanghai.
Subsequently, the exchange's original plan to issue foreign shares as early as April was delayed until now. 
Foreign participation will be controlled and limited.
Just as China has separate currencies for foreigners and for local Chinese, there will be two kinds of shares: A shares for Chinese and B shares for foreigners, both in local currency. 
Foreigners will have to pay in foreign exchange for their local currency shares but will earn dividends in foreign exchange. 
Asian investors, particularly in Hong Kong and Taiwan, are expected to be among the major buyers of the B shares.
In Shenzhen, the Governmentsigned underwriting agreements last Thursday with 10 Hong Kong-based brokerages to market about $34 million in B shares issued by 10 Shenzhen enterprises.
But Shanghai, where the process began earlier, is likely to sell the first equity issue directly to foreigners. 
The Shanghai Vacuum Electronic Device Corporation, a state-run television picture-tube maker, has signed agreements with foreign underwriters to place about a million B shares, raising about $74 million.
The company has already issued two million shares domestically to individual investors and other Chinese companies, although it is restricted as to how many shares over all can be sold to individuals. 
On Dec. 
12, the price for A shares was 863.40 yuan.
The deal has been an eye-opener for both the Western underwriters and the Chinese officials. 
China hemmed and hawed for nearly a year before it gave final approval to the issuance of B shares, but then it expected the deal to be done immediately. 
Early in November, China abruptly asked a syndicate of six foreign underwriters to fix the share price at 420 yuan -- about $72 at the essentially free-market rate that will be used instead of the official exchange rate.
Â 
Chinese in "an Enormous Hurry"
The Chinese proposal included a tight timetable and a demand that the foreign firms respond by the end of the day. 
In the West, underwriters carefully negotiate the timing of a deal, fixing the price of shares around the time of the placement. 
But in this case, the price was to be set months in advance.
The foreign firms had not even had a chance to examine the financial condition of Shanghai Vacuum Electric. 
Arthur Andersen & Company, the accounting firm, was not allowed to begin its review of the company until early November, and even then, Shanghai Vacuum Electric executives complained that the accounting firm was scrutinizing the books too thoroughly.
Four of the six original participating firms found the terms of the deal unacceptable and withdrew. 
The Chinese "were in an enormous hurry," said Ted Rule, director at Standard Chartered Asia Ltd., one of the underwriters that stepped down. 
"They wanted things to get done in a period of time which I thought was unrealistically short."
Â 
A Replacement Syndicate
Before he even knew what the company's earnings were, Mr. Rule said, he was asked to commit to a price at which the underwriters would buy the shares. 
Part of the reason for the hurry appears to be the company's desire to issue the B shares -- representing a 33 percent interest -- before the end of the year to qualify for lower tax rates as a joint venture.
After the other underwriters left, Sun Hung Kai & Company, a Hong Kong securities firm, and SBCI Finance Asia, the Swiss Bank unit, remained. 
Salomon Brothers (Hong Kong) Ltd. joined to form a new consortium that completed the deal. 
The new consortium signed an underwriting agreement on Nov. 
30, with the price fixed at 420 yuan. 
The foreign underwriters insisted on a safety clause that would allow them to pull out or renegotiate the price if they found something in the company's books that they did not like. 
Now, the shares will probably be marketed in the first quarter of next year, in January at the earliest.
Â 
Swiss Bank's Examination
Recently, Swiss Bank was allowed to examine the company closely for the first time, touring its factory and talking with the company's managers. 
Discovering how China's planned economy meshes with the free market was a bit of a revelation, Mr. Gerber of Swiss Bank admitted, but he remains committed to the deal.
"I haven't seen any shocking things that would prevent us from doing it," he said. 
"But we're all used to a free market, so we had to revise our understanding in terms of how the Chinese economy works."
The Shanghai company has also agreed to allow Swiss Bank to become the 16th and only foreign member of its board, so that the Chinese can gain advice on how to adjust to a free market economy. 
Foreign underwriters will place 80 percent of the issue, while three Chinese securities firms will place the rest.
Â 
Takeovers Highly Unlikely
So far, China's rules do not limit the shares a Chinese individual can buy, nor is it expected that the regulations will limit the B shares a foreigner can buy. 
Theoretically, a foreign and a Chinese investor could team up to purchase more than 50 percent of a listed company.
But the Government is unlikely to allow such a move. 
"Takeovers?" a Chinese official exclaimed, laughing at the idea. 
"They may not yet have any rules that prevent this, but they don't need them. 
They just won't let it happen, at least for now."

file: China_s Peasantry Takes Measure of Its Prosperity.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ignoring a light drizzle, the women emerged from their houses carrying small plates of potatoes, goose livers and pickled cucumbers, and placed them on tables clustered outside a shiny white three-story house.
The focus of attention was a tiny boy bundled up like a bushy red ball and cradled in the arms of his new mother. 
He had just turned one month old, a magic age in the hardscrabble Chinese countryside, traditionally signifying that a baby is likely to survive, and nearly a hundred peasants had come with gifts of little red packets bulging with money.
"He's the first son," said Mai Shunjing, the scrawny grandfather, as he let out a smile filled with broken teeth and big aspirations. 
"This is an important day for our family."
Half a dozen years ago, there would have been a similar celebration, but without the food, the money or the wine. 
Life has overwhelmingly improved over the last six years, even the last six months, for the 440 people in Pan Shi, a village in a land of rich, rolling rice paddies in southern China's Guangdong Province.
Â 
Well Off and Typical
Pan Shi (pronounced pahn sher) is a bit wealthier than the average Chinese village, but customs and conditions here are still fairly indicative of how China's 900 million peasants -- three-quarters of the nation's population and nearly 17 percent of the world's -- go through life.
The great issues that absorb residents of Beijing, and through them catch the attention of the West, are of subdued interest here. 
The peasants seem little interested in challenging the Government on freedom of expression, for instance, preferring to put their energies into defying Government limits on having children.
They do not seem intrigued by macroeconomic questions, like whether China's economy now trails only that of the United States and Japan, but rather by such mundane matters as whether they will be able to afford running water instead of having to fetch water from a well.
Yet even here, the peasants feel vulnerable to what happens 1,000 miles away in the capital. 
The Communist Party's policies may change tomorrow. 
Or some official may arbitrarily decide to ruin one family or another.
"Our life is so much better now than before, but in China, you never can tell what the Government will do," said a young entrepreneur who runs a factory in another village. 
"I don't know how long this economic policy will last. 
So whenever I get the chance, I'm going abroad. 
Life is stable in America."
Â 
Knowing When to Clam Up
While they may not know much about politics, the peasants here in Pan Shi know enough to clam up when the topic comes up. 
As the festivities for his grandson continued over a 10-dish banquet by the porch, Mr. Mai turned sheepish when asked what he thought about the growing gaps between the rich and the poor.
He managed a faint smile before mumbling something about there being no gaps at all. 
Immediately, however, his son came to his rescue, and Mr. Mai slipped away.
"We don't talk politics in this house," said Jinsheng, his 29-year-old elder son. 
"My father has suffered too much in his life, from the Cultural Revolution, from this and that movement.
"He is old and afraid. 
I don't want anything to happen to him again because of politics. 
I have to protect my father. 
If it weren't for him, I wouldn't be here today."
Â 
Politics Is Passive
For most villagers, politics is not an interactive process but a passive one. 
A new political movement means that they must change the slogans on the village walls, or -- worse yet -- attend silly meetings instead of working the fields.
To be sure, the Government now holds elections for village chief, but only one person runs. 
That is partly because villagers cannot quite imagine a political race, and partly because it is no longer a very attractive position.
"Most people don't want to do that kind of work," said Chen Qiumei, a 33-year-old woman with two children, both boys. 
"The Government wants you to do a lot of work that offends other people."
A few others echoed her view. 
In a place where much of life is lived outside, there are few secrets. 
The village leaders often have take sides with one villager over another.
Â 
Spying for Family Planning
The worst part is reporting on mothers who get pregnant for a second, third or fourth time. 
The village chief risks being regarded as a traitor for turning in his friends.
Mai Ruiqian, a 46-year-old sturdy fellow with a rounding stomach, became the new Mayor this year. 
He is a member of the Mai clan that dominates the village: nearly all men are named Mai, and only their wives, who came from other villages, have other surnames. 
It is common in China for a village to be made up of a single clan, and many villages are known only by the surname of the people who live there: the Mai Village, the Wu Village, and so on.
One sign that the job is not as enviable as it was in the past is that the last chief declined to run for a second term. 
Still, Mayor Mai says he has found a way around the difficulty of picking on his neighbors: He leaves the troublesome tasks to his superiors in the township government a few miles away.
"The township sends its family planning people here," Mr. Mai said, expressing relief that he does not have to worry much about it. 
"They have the family planning rosters."
Â 
A Phone but No One to Call
Mr. Mai enjoys a few perks, like lunching in the township with officials nearly every day. 
But there are problems: arranging for water for crops and for more electricity to meet the growing demands of modernization. 
In a small triumph, the village also got a public phone recently; the only problem is that since few peasants have a phone, there is no one to call.
The phone, however, is a sign that the peasants are pretty well off in Pan Shi. 
Indeed, in addition to the public phone, two families have their own phones -- not including the Mayor.
Being moderately well off, in Pan Shi's case, means that peasants here earn an average of about $175 per person per year, instead of the national average for peasants of about $125. 
The figure may be a bit misleading because the peasants grow most of their food themselves and have few expenses.
Another reason they are doing well is that people throughout this region called Taishan have many relatives in Hong Kong, the United States and Canada. 
Taishanese is still a common dialect in Chinatowns in the United States, although in the last few decades it has been partly eclipsed by Cantonese and, more recently, Mandarin.
The gates to Pan Shi itself are a reminder of the overseas connection, having been built with money sent home from migrants abroad and carrying a tablet with the names of dozens of contributors.
Â 
Plastic for the Crops
Still, it was only when someone here introduced a new farming technique -- protecting the vegetable crops with plastic covers -- that life for everyone seemed to get better. 
The plastic serves to keep moisture in the soil and protect the vegetables from freezing, and the practice has since become widespread throughout China.
Mai Caidong, 26, is among the new entrepreneurs who are branching in new directions. 
Not content simply to spend her days wading in the rice paddies or bending over the cabbages, she is taking advantage of opportunities to go into business.
Up at 3:30 A.M., she and her husband roar off on their motorcycle to the Taishan city center every day to sell fruit and vegetables, a business that brings them about $2,600 a year. 
Last year, they saved $1,700 of that in the bank, although Ms. Mai recently diversified her assets by investing some of that in a gold necklace from Hong Kong and other jewelry.
"They let us go into private enterprise, and most people don't feel bad if they stay behind in the village," said Ms. Mai, sitting in her clean, spacious living room. 
"Of course, my husband wants to go to Guangzhou and set up a rice shop."

file: China_s Premier Sees Progress on Cambodia.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Li Peng said today that significant progress had been made in reaching a political settlement in Cambodia and that Beijing was ready to repair ties gradually with Vietnam.
The Prime Minister, speaking at a reception on the eve of China's National Day celebrations, held out hope for an early settlement of the 11-year Cambodian civil war.
''We hope that Vietnam and the Phnom Penh regime will show sincerity by taking positive steps towards the political settlement of the Cambodian question,'' he said. 
''Along with such a settlement, China is ready to gradually improve its relations with Vietnam.''
Chinese-Vietnamese relations became hostile when Hanoi invaded Cambodia in 1978 and early the next year set up a pro-Hanoi Government there to replace the Khmer Rouge, which China had backed; China and Vietnam fought a brief border war in 1979.
Today China backs a coalition of three guerrilla groups, including the Khmer Rouge, that oppose the Hanoi-backed Phnom Penh Government in the Cambodian civil war.
Vietnam's Communist Party chief, Nguyen Van Linh, visited China early this month, and Vice Prime Minister Vo Nguyen Giap went to Beijing this month to attend the Asian Games there.

file: China_s Premier Talks Of Economic Distress.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Li Peng acknowleged in a speech made public today that the Chinese economy faced severe difficulties, and he called for greater restructuring of prices and enterprises and the elimination of export subsidies.
In his speech, which was given on Dec. 
1 at a National Planning Conference but published only today in The People's Daily, Mr. Li spoke more openly than in the past about the economy. 
But while he made many proposals, he was vague about when and how they would be carried out.

file: China_s Premier Urges Tighter Control.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Li Peng opened the annual session of China's legislature today with a call for tighter control on what he described as ''hostile elements at home.''
The speech lasted more than two hours and was the equivalent of a state of the union message. 
It signaled the Government's plans to ease its 18-month economic austerity program. 
Mr. Li suggested that monetary policies would be loosened somewhat to revive the stagnant economy, which has become a focus of discontent recently.
Despite several vague assertions that China will go further with economic and political liberalization, the speech took an unmistakable hard line on almost every topic it touched upon. 
Mr. Li called on officials to ''redouble ideological and political work,'' and he called for vigilance against ''some factors leading to social instability.''
Tightening of Public Security
''While fostering socialist democracy and the socialist legal system, we must intensify dictatorship by the socialist state apparatus,'' Mr. Li said. 
''Prosecutors and judges should fully perform their duties and be on the alert so that they can promptly crush attempts at infiltration and subversion by foreign hostile forces, and so that they can crack down on all sabotage by hostile elements at home.''
The speech, which also called on governments at all levels to build up police units so as to tighten public security, is not the work of the Prime Minister alone. 
Drafted by a brain trust and circulated among senior officials for suggestions, the address is regarded as representative of the general views of leaders - some of them retired and occupying no formal position - now making crucial decisions.
In reviewing events of last year, Mr. Li hailed the suppression of the democracy movement last year, saying:
Opium War Anniversary ''China's victory in quelling the turmoil and the rebellion has foiled the vain attempt of the international anti-Communist and anti-China forces to subvert China's legitimate Government and socialist system.''
The speech included warnings about foreign subversion, and it also called on school authorities to mark this year's 150th anniversary of the Opium War with Britain.
''They should make use of the occasion to expose the crime committed by imperialists in their aggression against China and to educate about the history of the Chinese people's traditional patriotic struggles against imperialism, so as to heighten their vigilance against the imperialist strategy of peaceful evolution,'' Mr. Li said.
The Government often refers to ''peaceful evolution,'' which it describes as the West's plan to achieve the gradual displacement of Communism in China.
Â 
Most Leaders on Rostrum
Most of China's top leaders were on the rostrum today for Mr. Li's speech and the formal opening of the National People's Congress. 
But for the second year in a row the paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, did not attend. 
Mr. Deng, who is 85 years old and feeble, is nominally retired. 
[The Congress accepted Mr. Deng's resignation from his last government post, as chairman of the state Central Military Commission, The Associated Press reported on Wednesday.] In recent years, the National People's Congress, whose nearly 3,000 delegates meet annually for a session of about 15 days, has occasionally sought to offer more than simply a stamp of approval for the leadership's decisions. 
Government proposals always pass, but they have occasionally been delayed, and last year for the first time a measure attracted a significant minority of no votes.
The assertiveness came to a peak last May, when about one-quarter of the 159-member standing committee called for an emergency session to repeal martial law, against the wishes of Prime Minister Li. 
These days the Congress is expected to be more compliant, partly because one of the organizers of the May effort, a lawyer named Cao Siyuan, is still in prison. 
Another backer of the emergency session, Hu Jiwei, a former editor of People's Daily, was dismissed last week from his positions in the Congress.

file: China_s Prime Minister Arrives in India.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a visit that portends major realignments in Asia, China's Prime Minister, Li Peng, arrived here today. 
It was the first trip by a Chinese head of Government in more than three decades.
India, long allied with the Soviet Union, has been thrown off balance by the calamitous disintegration of its former ally and has struggled to find a handhold in a changing world order. 
Now, presented with overtures from China -- like India an enormous, largely rural, developing country -- India sees the potential in establishing a new structure of international relations involving a newset of alliances.
Not since Zhou Enlai met with India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, 31 years ago, has a Chinese leader set foot on Indian soil. 
Since Mr. Zhou's visit in 1960, relations between the two Asian giants, which together embrace some 40 percent of the world's population, have wavered between outright belligerence and merely chilly. 
In that time, India, for decades an ally in all but name with the Soviet Union, and China have fought a vigorous border war, have jousted verbally over international disputes in Cambodia and Afghanistan and have differed over India's granting refuge to the exiled Tibetan leader, the Dalai Lama.
A major concern for India in discussions with Mr. Li is China's traditionally close and supportive relationship with Pakistan, with which India has fought two wars and which India insists is the major sponsor of separatist militancy in Kashmir. 
Indian officials, according to a Foreign Ministry official, are hoping to extract some assurance from Mr. Li that China will not provide Pakistan with surface-to-surface missiles as part of its weapons sales to Islamabad.
Â 
Concessions Unclear
It was unclear this evening, from either officials at the Chinese Embassy or from Chinese journalists, what concessions China was willing to offer India in its dealings with Pakistan.
Mr. Li's visit was greeted with outrage and protests by Tibetans who have taken refuge in India from China's occupation of their homeland. 
Just hours before the Chinese leader's arrival, the police detained hundreds of Tibetans protesting his visit and engaged in bloody clashes with thousands of others attempting to march on the Chinese Embassy.
But now, China and India find themselves adrift and isolated amid the rapid changes in the Soviet Union and Europe. 
China, still ostracized internationally because of its human-rights record, and India, stranded by a self-imposed economic isolationism, are struggling to find new partnerships in an emerging global order neither appear to like very much.
"It is historic," said a Western diplomat watching the visit from the sidelines. 
"It is important. 
The Indians are feeling a bit lonely in the world. 
This visit holds a whole lot more for India than for China. 
The only thing the Chinese have to gain is to pick up an ally in terms of issues like human rights and to find a friend to resist U.S. hegemony."
Â 
International Scrutiny
India has reacted sharply in recent months to Washington's efforts to raise a whole range of bilateral and regional issues -- from nuclear proliferation to intellectual property rights -- which it regards as evidence of American efforts to erode Indian sovereignty. 
Similarly, China has been vocal in its resentment of Washington's pronouncements on the issues of human rights, Beijing's weapons and nuclear technology sales and on trade issues. 
To that degree, some senior Western diplomats here said, the leaders of both nations feel beseiged.
China and India face international scrutiny over their behavior in Tibet and Kashmir respectively, both territories where there is widespread sentiment for independence. 
Diplomats here said that the Chinese and Indian leaders would likely seek support from each other that neither issue be the subject of debate in international formus, particularly the United Nations.
Yet, there remain serious differences between the two countries. 
The most visible source of tension between the two countries is China's continued occupation of Indian territory it took in the 1962 border war.

text:

The number of private businesses in China has fallen for the first time since 1981.
Â 
The Farmers Daily reported
Friday that at the end of June the country had 12.34 million private businesses employing 19.43 million people, a drop of 2.19 million and 3.57 million respectively from the end of last year.
Output value of private business in industry, construction and transportation - three of the biggest sectors apart from restaurants and retail shops -fell 29 percent in the first six months of the year from the corresponding period last year, it said.
