file: China_s Private Businesses Face Inspection.txt
text:
ï»¿
China announced today that it was initiating an inspection of the nation's 14.5 million individually owned businesses, the great majority of which are accused of evading taxes, and concern is growing that the Government is adopting a more hostile attitude toward private enterprise.
The announcement appeared in an article on top of the front page of today's People's Daily. 
The article said 70 percent to 80 percent of individual enterprises were evading taxes, and indicated the inspection would last two months.
''Tax evasion not only causes losses to state revenue,'' the official New China News Agency quoted Jin Xing, director of the State Administration of Taxation, as saying, ''but also disturbs the normal economic order and aggravates social problems caused by the distribution gap.''
Over the last 10 days, there have repeatedly been articles in The People's Daily and other newspapers accusing private enterprises of evading taxes, engaging in illicit activities like selling pornography, and causing growing income disparities in China.
Few people seem to expect a campaign to uproot private enterprises, which employ more than 26 million people for whom the state would then have to find other employment. 
But some foreign economists worry that the leadership could make life much more difficult for private enterprises.
''It does seem to be another step away from the reform direction,'' a Western diplomat said today. 
''The central leadership may just want to clear up some of the abuses. 
But without a clear line of support from Beijing to private enterprises, there is the potential that low-level officials will see this as a chance to settle scores: to impose new taxes, to demand kickbacks and in general to make life more difficult for them.''
Â 
Backing for Democracy Effort
Private enterprises in Beijing were deeply involved in the democracy movement this spring, and a crackdown could be a way of reducing their influence. 
Such enterprises, ranging from clothing shops to restaurants to small factories, gave student demonstrators money, food and equipment, and those entrepreneurs with motorcycles raced around the city to alert citizens about troop movements.
Economists and diplomats say that any crackdown would be difficult to enforce. 
Most private enterprises are family owned, and with bookkeeping still something of a novelty, it is very difficult even for China's 500,000 tax inspectors to prove tax evasion. 
Many enterprises, like the watermelon vendors now found throughout Beijing, are not even registered.
Likewise, the fate of the private enterprises will depend at least as much on the attitude of local officials as on the policy in Beijing. 
Those enterprises that have worked out mutually beneficial arrangements with local authorities are unlikely to face difficulties.
Â 
A Growing Private Sector
The private sector is the fastest-growing part of China's economy, but it is also by far the smallest. 
Officially, private enterprises account for only 3.5 percent of industrial production, compared with 63 percent from state enterprises and 33.5 percent from collectives.
But those figures underestimate the size of the private sector, both because many private enterprises call themselves collectives in the belief that it is safer politically, and because many entrepreneurs are involved in retailing and other services that are not measured in the industrial production statistics.
Formally, China distinguishes between privately owned enterprises employing eight or more people, of which there are 225,000 employing 3.6 million, and ''self-employed'' or ''individual businesses'' that employ fewer than eight people. 
There are 14.5 million of these businesses, with a total employment of 23 million people. 
Informally, both categories are normally referred to as private enterprises, and although the new tax inspections are said to be directed at the self-employed category, most experts expect all private enterprises to be affected.
Â 
An Easy Target
A Western economist working in Beijing cautioned that if the Government is trying to appease public anger about widespread corruption, it could find private enterprises an easy target. 
They are a tiny constituency without political muscle, and everyone believes that they, like other enterprises, are often corrupt.
''For now, I don't think any serious policy decisions have been made,'' he said. 
''But I think it's worth watching this space very carefully.''
There is no indication that a crackdown on private enterprises would directly affect foreign interests. 
Those officials who have been promoted to top positions since the democracy movement was crushed in early June have long histories of supporting joint ventures and welcoming foreign investment.
These officials - particularly the new Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin, and a new member of the Politburo standing committee, Li Ruihuan - are generally viewed as supporters of continued economic change and development. 
But their background suggests that they are most comfortable with growth that is centrally planned and subject to strict control and that they may have reservations about private businesses.
Â 
Warning by New Party Leader
''Self-employed traders and peddlers cheat, embezzle, bribe and evade taxation,'' Mr. Jiang wrote in an article published in today's China Daily newspaper. 
His article warned against rising disparities in income distribution because of the wealth in the private sector, although he also cautioned against rigid egalitarianism.
Businesses that employ eight or fewer people are supposed to pay 52 percent of their profits in taxes, to reinvest 30 percent of the profits, and to pay only 18 percent to the owner. 
Businesses that employ more than eight people have 10 different tax rates, and many of these enterprises are supposed to pay a majority of profits in taxes.
On Saturday, the New China News Agency warned that ''China will soon inspect and clean up all individual businesses and private enterprises in the country.''
The dispatch warned that the Government would crack down on private businesses that produced pornography or shoddy or dangerous merchandise, or that were engaged in speculative investments that drove up commodity prices.

file: China_s Showcase Company.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Gold Cup Automobile Company is China's pride: a behemoth corporation that embodies China's hopes of transforming its state-owned factories into efficient, market-oriented enterprises.
Gold Cup manufactures minibuses and trucks, but just as important in a country where many state-owned concerns lose money, it has been making ever-larger profits. 
Tugged into the unfamiliar world of market economics by an aggressive chairman hailed as one of China's shrewdest industrialists, Gold Cup has become a laboratory for change and an inspiration to those who believe in the future of Chinese industry.
One of the experiments that has attracted the most attention is Gold Cup's effort to sell shares that are listed on the Shenyang stock exchange. 
The company is the largest in China to issue stock. 
What's more, the shares are sold nationwide instead of just to the company's employees. 
Gold Cup's shares can be freely transferred and, at least in theory, the shareholders could vote to oust the management.
''To me, it's basically an attack on the socialist ownership system,'' said Carl Eugene Dorris, the United States Consul General in Shenyang. 
''Because it's a state company with 50,000-plus workers, it's perhaps the most important experiment in the northeast, or in all of China. 
There are a lot of people watching, and if it succeeds, it will perhaps be a new direction for China.''
A look at Gold Cup provides a peek into the murky world of Chinese industry: the cozy links between Government and business, the travails of management in a system that relies on an uneasy mix of socialist principles and market mechanisms and perhaps the hope that at least in some situations, daring management can make a big difference for China's state-owned companies.
It is not coincidence that Gold Cup is based in Shenyang, a drab northeastern city that has become the nation's laboratory for restructuring state-owned industry. 
Gold Cup has license from Beijing to tamper with tradition. 
The result is a work environment different from that in most Chinese factories.
In a way, it is misleading to refer to China's state-owned companies as businesses, because they are so different from American businesses. 
For one thing, they are owned by ''the whole people,'' which is so vague that nobody really knows who owns them. 
And because nothing terrible happens if they lose money, they tend to maximize not profits but revenues or bonuses to workers. 
Their raw materials are often not purchased on the free market but supplied by the state. 
And prices for what they sell are also often controlled.
Even in its origins, Gold Cup suggests how different Chinese companies can be from their American counterparts. 
Five years ago, officials simply turned Shenyang's Auto Industry Bureau into a company consisting of the city's auto plants. 
The regulators suddenly found themselves in charge of 58 factories that previously had little or no connection - indeed, some had been collectively owned instead of state owned. 
(Collectively owned businesses are typically owned by the employees.) The former head of the auto industry bureau, Zhao Xiyou, suddenly became head of the Shenyang Auto Industry Corporation, which last year changed its name to the Gold Cup Auto Industry Corporation. 
Gold Cup is the brand name of one line of minibuses and trucks that the company manufactures.
Gold Cup makes 35,000 vehicles a year, providing one-fourth of China's domestic pick-up trucks and half of the minibuses made in the country. 
It reported profits last year of about $40.5 million on total income of $375 million. 
While Chinese accounting methods are far from rigorous, the reported numbers reflect a 25 percent rise in profits and a 27 percent increase in revenues from a year earlier.
By 1993, the company hopes to be earning more than $120 million a year and producing much higher quality vehicles. 
''Our goal is that we want people not to be able to tell whether our vehicles are imported or local,'' said Bi Wenjie, chief of Gold Cup's auditing division.
Almost no one outside Gold Cup seems to think that is realistic. 
So far, the pick-ups and minibuses are obviously cheaply made and are not generally regarded as very reliable. 
''Nobody would get one if they could afford a Japanese model,'' acknowledged a Government official.
Still, most people seem to think that the quality has improved and that high import duties will continue to restrict competition from Japanese vehicles. 
Principally because of duties, a Japanese minibus or pick-up costs three or four times as much as a Chinese vehicle of about the same size, though the Japanese model is also likely to be better made and include extras like air-conditioning.
Gold Cup has attracted attention in large part because of Mr. Zhao, its manager. 
A 54-year-old native of Shenyang, he has studied economics and is regarded by both Chinese and foreigners as a man who ignores ideology and aims to make money for his company.
One of the main reasons for Mr. Zhao's success, and his company's, seems to be his longtime association with a kindred spirit, Liaoning Province Governor Li Changchun.
Governor Li, who was mayor of Shenyang at the time that Gold Cup was made a company, is an aggressive advocate of economic restructuring and an ally of Communist Party General Secretary Zhao Ziyang. 
That alliance led to Shenyang's becoming a laboratory for economic change; Gold Cup has often played the role of guinea pig.
In 1985, for example, Beijing sent one of its most unorthodox economists, Hua Sheng, to Shenyang, where he worked with Gold Cup as part of an effort to make Chinese industry more efficient. 
Mr. Hua now says he has a high regard for what Gold Cup is doing, but adds that it is inadequate because strong ties remain between the Government and companies like Gold Cup. 
Mr. Hua has achieved some fame here with his solution: that China must abandon its state-ownership system.
Under Mr. Zhao, Gold Cup has taken several initiatives to make itself a more efficient state enterprise. 
By Western standards, they may seem ludicrously tame, but are very bold by the standards of China's other state-owned industrial corporations.
The company picked a board of directors, consisting of experts on law, economics and industry, to oversee the management. 
A board of directors is a novelty: most companies are directed by the company manager and Communist Party secretary, with vague supervision from various Government departments.
Gold Cup's party secretary, He Zhongbin, also is unusual in that he disavows any competition with Mr. Zhao. While party secretaries and company managers in China are often at each other's throats, Mr. He is an enthusiastic supporter of the changes that are taking place. 
He also is deputy manager of Gold Cup, while Mr. Zhao is deputy party secretary, which perhaps reduces party-management conflicts. 
''I don't think there are a lot of companies organized like this in China,'' Mr. He said, ''We have a lot of cooperation here, and that is one factor behind the company's development.
Paradoxically enough, another initiative to make Gold Cup more efficient was bankruptcy. 
A collectively owned factory under the parent corporation several years ago, it became the first company in China formally to go bankrupt since the Communist Revolution in 1949.
Wages also became more flexible, to encourage workers to be more industrious. 
Large monthly bonuses were initiated in 1987 as incentive payments; they can now add up to four times the regular monthly wages. 
Bonuses were also linked to the company's profitability. 
The system of incentive payments has extended to Mr. Zhao, who nominally earns $42 a month, about twice as much as an ordinary worker. 
Of course, like other senior officials in business or government in China, he enjoys many perquisites, such as use of a car and housing, that permit a much higher standard of living than his income would suggest.
The board of directors set a target of $36.1 million of profits in 1988 and said that if it was met, Mr. Zhao would earn a bonus of almost $500 - not much by American standards, but about a year's salary to him. 
If profits fell short of the target, his pay would be docked. 
He met the target and took home the bonus.
Bad workers at Gold Cup have already had their wages docked, and a very few have even been fired for violating regulations. 
''Everybody noticed when workers were docked,'' said Shen Chuanjian, a secretary at the factory's office.
After last year's share issue, Gold Cup is now about 50 percent owned by the state, 40 percent by various companies, 7 percent by corporate stock purchasers - including other state-owned and collectively-owned concerns with cash to spare - and 3 percent by individual stock purchasers. 
And if another large stock issue goes ahead as planned in several years, the state share in the company would drop below 50 percent, a sensitive demarcation in a nation that has not yet decided whether the state should give up its majority interest in companies it owns.
Gold Cup also plans to issue $4 million in United States dollar-denominated stocks to help raise hard currency to finance imports of needed equipment. 
So far, however, the country's central bank has not given approval for the sale of dollar-denominated stock, which would be issued both to foreigners and to Chinese holding foreign currency. 
In the meantime, Gold Cup has lost the chance to be the first corporation to sell to foreigners; a company in the southern city Shenzhen issued Hong Kong dollar-denominated stocks in December and January.
Mr. Bi said the biggest problem for Gold Cup is simply getting hold of the raw materials it needs. 
Buying steel, for example, often depends less on the price than on the ability to cultivate good relations with a steel plant somewhere. 
And raw materials that come from abroad must be paid for in hard currency, which is scarce.
''Right now we want to import steel boards costing $3 million, but we only have $1.5 million in U.S. currency,'' Mr. Bi said. 
He added, however, that he expected more hard currency to turn up soon, from the state or from Gold Cup's exports to southeast Asia.
One of the most crucial raw materials that is in short supply is electricity. 
Gold Cup has had to stop Saturday production because of electricity shortages, and there is the possibility of further cutbacks.
But such problems would be far worse were it not for Mr. Zhao's connections with the locality. 
These have been an enormous boon to the company. 
Shortly before Gold Cup issued shares last year, for example, it was able to convince Shenyang that its tax rate should be lowered. 
The company argued that the state, as half-owner, would get half of the stock dividends and that these should count in lieu of taxes. 
The Government obligingly cut the tax rate for share-issuing companies in Shenyang from 55 percent to 35 percent.
City officials seem to think they should do their part to help a local company make good. 
Guan Weiguo, executive director of Shenyang's economic restructuring commission, proudly explained: ''Gold Cup is experimenting not only for Shenyang, but for the entire country.''

file: China_s Students Seek To Avoid Ban on Travel.txt
text:
ï»¿
Sometimes Wang Jie dreams of achieving her goal and making it to America, but there is just a hint of apprehension about what will happen if she is admitted to an American prep school and later to an American college.
"I think of myself surrounded by all these people with blond hair, and my parents too far away to help," Miss Wang said with a laugh, adding that her parents share her trepidation.
"My mother is a typical Chinese woman," Miss Wang added. 
"Whenever she sees some hope of me getting a scholarship abroad, she smiles. 
And then she cries."
Miss Wang, a 17-year-old student at one of China's best high schools, the Shanghai Foreign Language School, is part of a growing number of Chinese high school students who are trying to earn their undergraduate degrees in the United States.
The surge in younger applicants reflects improving standards of English among Chinese high school students. 
But most of the applicants say the prime reason is a requirement instituted a year ago that prevents Chinese from going abroad for at least five years after they graduate from a university.
While the Government has used the five-year requirement to make it more difficult for Chinese to go abroad for graduate study, it has not prevented high school students from applying to undergraduate programs abroad. 
Because the rule applies only to those who have graduated from a Chinese college, some college students are dropping out and applying to American colleges as transfer students.
Miss Wang plans to go first to a prep school, essentially repeating the last year or so of high school, but most high school graduates are trying to go directly to American colleges.
Â 
More Undergraduate Applicants
China already has more students in the United States than in any other country, and they are almost all graduate students. 
Only now are significant numbers of high school students applying for undergraduate programs.
Political discontent does not seem to be a factor in the yearning to go abroad; rather, some students cite a general pessimism about the future and resentment at the stifling orthodoxy and lack of academic freedom that they say now prevails at Chinese universities.
In the 1986-87 school year, 1,500 Chinese took the Toefl (Test of English as a Foreign Language) exam to apply to American undergraduate programs. 
By the 1989-90 school year, the number had soared to about 9,750. 
It is unclear how many of these are high school students and how many are college students trying to transfer to American institutions.
Only a tiny number of the high school students obtain the scholarships and the visas they need to go abroad to study. 
But their determination is sometimes staggering.
"The five-year rule makes them all the more desperate to go, to avoid the rule," said M. Elizabeth Barr, a Shanghai resident who conducts interviews for Wellesley College.
Many young people, and their parents, seem to believe that unless they escape to earn their undergraduate degrees, they will be destined to spend the next decade, and perhaps the rest of their lives, in uninspiring curriculums and careers at home.
"My niece is trying to go abroad to earn her B.A.," said a newspaper editor in Beijing. 
"It's her last chance, because otherwise she'll have to do a year of military training at the beginning of university, then four years of college, then a year after graduation working at the grass roots, and finally five years of work before she can get her passport. 
What's the point?
Why wait?"
Chinese students have grown more and more resourceful in their efforts to evade the five-year rule.
One first-year student at a Chinese university, now undergoing a compulsory year of military training, smuggled her application materials from the military camp through friends who acted as couriers. 
A student at Fudan University in Shanghai refused to go through the graduation ceremony so the requirement would not take effect.
Another student, an 18-year-old applicant to an Ivy League university, said sourly, "I refuse to take the Chinese college entrance examination, because there's nothing I can learn at a Chinese university."
If the determination of some of the students to leave is striking, so is their brilliance. 
Shen Jie, for example, is a top student at the Shanghai Foreign Language School who is applying to Princeton University and other schools.
Because China does not offer the Scholastic Aptitude Test, he took the Graduate Record Examination. 
Competing mostly against students who are already completing their American undergraduate programs, Mr. Shen earned the highest score possible in the mathematics section.
But Mr. Shen and most other Chinese applicants need more than an admission slip. 
Admission to an American university is often useless to a Chinese student without a full scholarship, and some students also need financial help even to buy the airline ticket to the United States.

file: China_s Tranquillity Is Seen as Only Skin Deep.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government assures foreigners that life in China has loosened up, but lately many Chinese are shaking their heads, whispering: ''Nei jin, wai song'' - ''tranquillity outside, repression within.''
The expression has also been used internally by the Government to describe its policy of managing China's image, Chinese officials say.
The result of this attitude, Chinese intellectuals say, is that there is a divergence between the texture of life on the surface and the inside reality. 
Moreover, as the Government tightens its control on certain groups, contours of repression emerge to separate the largely unaffected ordinary Chinese from those under special scrutiny.
''When they lifted martial law, they announced to the world that everything was smooth and peaceful,'' a Chinese worker said, referring to the lifting of martial law in Beijing in January.
''But the troops are still here hiding indoors,'' he said. 
''To the outside world, they say life is normal. 
In Beijing, they drill the troops even harder.''
What goes on in the army is often a mystery to many Chinese. 
But particularly after noticing the army's role in the collapse of Nicolae Ceausescu's Communist Government in Romania, China quietly tightened control over its army, and there is talk about changes among regional commanders.
China's leadership has also explicitly distinguished between doctrine for domestic consumption and face-saving propaganda for the outside world. 
In closed meetings, the party has criticized the Soviet President, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, implying that he is not a true socialist, but officials have told Chinese not to publicize the criticism.
''They explained to us why Romania collapsed, and why China was different from Romania and the rest of Eastern Europe,'' a teacher said. 
''They also told us not to discuss this with outsiders, especially foreign reporters.''
Chinese intellectuals say the Communist apparatus, with its strata of rank, bureaucracy and secrecy, has many ways to tighten control over clusters of people without influencing the rest of society. 
For instance, party members are now facing greater pressures because they must re-register in a new screening procedure intended to weed out problem members.
Tension is growing at the higher echelons, partly because of power jockeying over major decisions before the National People's Congress, which convenes on March 20. 
China's security agencies have issued orders to restrict the flow of information about China's internal matters to the outside world.
The state has also managed the press and broadcasting more tightly.

file: Chinese Aide May Seek U.S. Refuge.txt
text:
ï»¿
A senior Chinese official who disagreed with the military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators last spring has quietly arrived in the United States, apparently seeking refuge, American officials said yesterday.
The arrival of the official, Xu Jiatun, who until last fall served as China's top representative in Hong Kong, could further strain United States-Chinese relations, which are already upset by American outrage at the killing of protesters in Beijing last June.
Mr. Xu arrived in Los Angeles with two relatives around May 1, traveling on a tourist visa arranged by the United States Consulate in Hong Kong, Administration officials said yesterday. 
They said Mr. Xu has not applied for political asylum, but they said they believed that he left China to escape attacks by hard-liners.
'Just a Tourist'
Mr. Xu could not be located for comment, and his plans remain unclear.
A spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said it had been told by the official New China News Agency in Hong Kong that Mr. Xu had come to the United States ''for a rest,'' and was in this country ''just as a tourist.''
He said the embassy had no information on how long Mr. Xu would remain.
Mr. Xu, 74 years old, was a member of the Communist Party Central Committee, and if he does seek asylum he would be the highest-ranking Chinese leader to ask for refuge in the United States.
Mr. Xu was serving as director of the New China News Agency in Hong Hong. 
The position made him China's unofficial governor in the British colony, which in the eyes of many residents gave him greater power than the British Governor.
Â 
Movie Stars and Nightclubs
As an indication of Mr. Xu's status, when he took over the job in 1983, Hong Kong was effectively elevated to the provincial level in China. 
Mr. Xu reported directly to the central Government in Beijing, Chinese analysts say.
Mr. Xu was a veteran Communist revolutionary who served as a political commissar in the Red Army before the Communists' victory in 1949 and rose to be first party secretary of Jiangsu Province.
When he arrived in Hong Kong he was regarded as a hard-liner, an impression he confirmed during a speech by banging his glasses on the lectern and warning that China would not tolerate steps toward democracy in the British colony.
But Mr. Xu rapidly underwent a change, hobnobbing with wealthy Hong Kong business executives and escorting movie stars to Hong Kong nightclubs. 
He wrote articles suggesting China should learn from capitalism.
This may have been in part his mission in Hong Kong, to reassure the colony about China's intentions as Hong Kong faces a return to Beijing's control in 1997. 
Mr. Xu's actions may also have reflected the market-oriented economic changes then being carried out in China by Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang.
Â 
High-Level Connections
Mr. Xu often boasted of his close connections to both Mr. Zhao and Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader.
Last spring, when student protesters called for greater democracy in Beijing, Mr. Xu is said to have urged a conciliatory solution as the only way to maintain Hong Kong's confidence.
But this January, Beijing announced that Mr. Xu's ''request to retire'' had been accepted. 
He apparently hoped to stay on in the new city of Shenzhen, just across the border from Hong Kong, but in April the Hong Kong press reported that Beijing had ordered Mr. Xu to return to his hometown, Nanjing, in central China.

file: Chinese Aide, Visiting U.S., Sees Room for Compromise.txt
text:
ï»¿
A top Chinese official met today with Vice President Dan Quayle and Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and said there would be no bloodshed in Beijing if the demonstrators continued to exercise restraint, an Administration official said.
The Chinese official, Wan Li, the chairman of the National People's Congress, the legislature, told Mr. Quayle that the students' ''reasonable demands'' could eventually be met and that army troops had been deployed around Beijing to maintain order, not to suppress the students.
The Administration official said Mr. Wan seemed to position himself carefully between Prime Minister Li Peng and the demonstrators. 
Mr. Wan was reported to have said China must have internal stabilityI if it is to continue liberalizing its economic system, and must end the student unrest before it can take further steps toward democracy.
Â 
Broadcasts Are Jammed
At the same time, the Voice of America said today that the Chinese authorities had begun jamming its broadcasts to China for the first time since 1978, shortly before the United States and China established diplomatic relations.
Administration officials said Mr. Quayle had emphasized several themes: the need to avoid violence and the United States' interest in promoting human rights and democracy around the world.
Mr. Baker, repeating the Administration's cautious stance toward the demonstrations, said he had told Mr. Wan, ''The United States appreciated the restraint which at least so far the Government of the People's Republic has shown.''
Speaking to reporters, Mr. Baker said, ''The United States supports freedom of speech'' and reported he had urged Mr. Wan ''that there be no resort to violence or bloodshed on the part of both sides of this problem.''
Mr. Wan, who is 73 years old, is a longtime ally of Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, and is considered a key figure in the current political crisis in Beijing. 
As head of the Congress, he could play a critical role in reported efforts by supporters of the protesters to get the Congress to revoke martial law and remove Prime Minister Li Peng.
Â 
No Public Comment
Reflecting the seriousness of the situation in Beijing, the normally genial and outgoing Mr. Wan declined to make any public comments today after his meetings with Mr. Quayle and Mr. Baker. After his talk with the Vice President in the Old Executive Office Building next to the White House, Mr. Wan maintained a stony stare as Mr. Quayle read a prepared statement, and Mr. Wan's interpreter refused to translate several questions from reporters about the demonstrations.
Mr. Wan is believed to be caught in a difficult position by the power struggle in China. 
For he is both a close friend of Mr. Deng - sometimes serving as Mr. Deng's bridge partner - and is a leading exponent of China's changes in recent years.
In the late 1970's it was Mr. Wan, then the Governor of Anhui Province in central China, who first began to decollectivize agriculture by allowing peasants to farm their own land in an effort to increase productivity. 
His action, then a breathtaking break with Communist orthodoxy, was later copied nationwide and forms the basis of Mr. Deng's political changes.
Mr. Wan has also been an outspoken supporter of more political openness, having made a major speech in 1986 advocating a greater role for China's intellectuals. 
These actions have placed him on the liberal side of the Chinese political spectrum.
Â 
Bush Meeting Scheduled
Mr. Wan, who arrived in Washington after a trip to Canada, is scheduled to meet with President Bush on Tuesday, Defense Secretary Dick Cheney on Wednesday and receive a honorary degree from Johns Hopkins University on Thursday. 
On Saturday he is to visit Disney World in Florida.
A scheduled tennis match between Mr. Wan and President Bush was canceled because ''it would be inappropriate at this time,'' Roman Popadiuk, a White House spokesman, said. 
Mr. Wan is an avid tennis player and had played with Mr. Bush when the President was the American envoy in China in 1974 and 1975.
In his 55-minute meeting with Mr. Quayle, Mr. Wan said that before he left China 10 days ago, the Chinese rulers agreed that no violence would be used against the student demonstrators. 
But Mr. Wan said that he was not fully aware of all the decisions that might have been made since then.
A statement issued by the Vice President's office said that Mr. Quayle expressed a hope that the Chinese authorities ''could resolve the situation without resorting to violence.''
Richard W. Carlson, director of the V.O.A., said that there was ''jamming on three of the five V.O.A. 
Mandarin Chinese frequencies.''
The jamming was apparently designed to cut off the flow of information to Chinese students and others demonstrating for greater democracy.
Many demonstrators had been relying on V.O.A. broadcasts to keep informed during the five weeks of pro-democracy protests.

file: Chinese Aim to Harness Yangtze and Yellow Rivers.txt
text:
ï»¿
DISCONTENT with the way the heavens have arranged its rivers and rainfall, China is embarking on a program to build huge waterworks that could have a colossal impact on the nation's development in the 21st century.
The Yellow River, so thick with silt that it sometimes seems a flowing yellow mud pie, courses past timeless villages in northern China whose peasants are constantly threatened by floods from the same waters that sustain them in irrigating their fields.
Farther south, Asia's mightiest river, the Yangtze, drains an area inhabited by 380 million Chinese, or 8 percent of the world's population, leaning against ancient dikes that would release a flood that could kill one million people if they burst in the middle of the night.
The new waterworks projects, which are intended to ease the threat from the country's age-old cycle of devastating floods as well as transfer water hundreds of miles to revitalize dry areas of China, have been under discussion for three decades or more. 
Collectively they would represent the country's most significant development projects since the Grand Canal was completed in the 13th century to transport hundreds of thousands of tons of grain each year to Beijing.
Preliminary approval has already been given to one project, a proposed 730-mile canal that would pump water from China's south, where rainfall is plentiful, to northern areas around Beijing that are running dry. 
The $10 billion channel is the first of three that are planned for the next century to reinvigorate a broad swathe of northern China with southern water. 
Government officials have warned that Beijing could not remain the nation's capital without a new supply of water to sustain it.
Much more controversial is an $11 billion project called the Three Gorges Dam that is proposed for the Yangtze River. 
Supporters note that the project, which would be bigger than any existing hydroelectric station, would sharply reduce the risk of a potentially disastrous flood. 
But critics point out that the price is immense: 1.1 million people would have to be relocated from a 375-mile long area that will be flooded, some of China's most beautiful scenery would be marred, and a rare porpoise would be threatened with extinction.
Â 
A Waterway Called 'Sorrow'
Preparatory work is already under way on the third major project, the Xiaolangdi Dam on the Yellow River. 
That $2 billion dam will generate electricity, control silting, make irrigation easier and reduce the risk of a catastrophic flood on a waterway that is known as "China's sorrow" because of its propensity to overrun its banks. 
Since 602 B.C., the Yellow River has changed course 26 times, sometimes by hundreds of miles, each time wreaking immense havoc.
In addition to these projects, China is planning to build more than 60 substantial hydroelectric projects in the 1990's to fuel industrial growth in the next century.
Such efforts to refashion nature would be important in any country, but they are particularly significant in a country like China, whose culture and history are inextricably linked with water. 
One of China's legendary heroes, a father-of-the-nation figure, is Yu the Great, who 4,200 years ago coordinated flood-control projects along the Yellow River where Chinese civilization was born.
"Water looms larger here," said Roy D. Morey, the representative in China of the United Nations Development Program, which is assisting China in its many water projects. 
"Historically, what rivets people's attention is the fact that you either have too much or too little. 
One is either lamenting the ever-shifting channel of the Yellow River, or you're talking about the arid or semi-arid regions of China that have never had enough water."
Floods are a special risk in China because in some places the rivers are actually higher than the surrounding ground. 
In these areas the water is held in place by dikes, and if a dike is breached, the river spills out and forms a new channel on lower ground.
The rivers' elevation is linked to the tremendous amount of silt they carry. 
A result of soil erosion upriver, silt is suspended in the flowing water and is gradually deposited on the river bed, raising the level each year. 
In the case of the Yellow River, the bed has been built up as many as six inches, leading the peasants to raise the dikes correspondingly, and over the centuries the river has risen higher and higher. 
In the lower reaches of the Yellow River and in part of the middle section of the Yangtze, the water flows as many as 30 feet higher than the surrounding terrain.
"People walk under water," goes a folk saying, "and the river flows overhead."
Â 
Debate on Projects Is Missing
Some scholars argue that despotism was born in water-based cultures like ancient China's because of the need for centralized organization of irrigation and flood control. 
In any case, there is no doubt that authoritarianism lives on in China, and some believe that that is one of the fundamental problems of all of these projects: they are not subject to the checks of democratic debate.
"Information from those opposed to constructing the dams usually doesn't get up" to the leadership, says William Y. B. Chang, an expert on Chinese water issues at the National Science Foundation in Washington. 
Mr. Chang says he is concerned that the decision-making has been based more on political than scientific reasoning and that the new water projects may not reflect the best value for the money.
He notes, for example, that many areas of China are short of water -- in rural Shaanxi Province, peasants may have to hike miles to the nearest well -- but that the enormous effort to divert water to the north will feed the political and industrial centers of Beijing and Tianjin, where people already are relatively well off.
The project has already received preliminary approval, and the construction is expected to get fully under way within the next few years. 
The canal will begin at the Yangtze River and pump water up a slight gradient to the Yellow River, and then pass in a tunnel beneath the Yellow River and from there flow downhill to Tianjin and Beijing. 
There is not enough water in the Yellow River to supply the project, so the canal must start at the Yangtze much farther away.
While pumping the water uphill will use enormous amounts of electricity, which is scarce, the advantage of the route is that the channel is, for the most part, already in place: the Grand Canal, begun in the year 600 by at least two million laborers and extended in the 13th century. 
Parts of the Grand Canal are still in use, although others were blocked when the Yellow River shifted channels in 1855.
The impetus behind the project is simply that nature lavishes water on the southern part of the country but is much more stingy in the north. 
Some 180 million Chinese in the north are short of water and the situation is becoming more desperate.
Â 
Effects of Bargaining
The diversion project will take 11.76 billion cubic yards of water from the Yangtze each year. 
Most will be used to irrigate farmland along the route, with only 1.3 billion cubic yards reaching Beijing. 
The project had to be designed to supply substantial benefits to the provinces along the way in order to win their approval. 
Jiangsu Province, in particular, bargained hard to get a large share of the water in exchange for its participation.
Eventually, the Government intends to build two additional systems to carry water to the north from the Yangtze, but they will have to wait until the next century.
Over one of the routes, in the center of the country, the water would run downhill, so this system would not require pumping stations, but it is extremely complex technically and would require extensive tunneling through mountains. 
The other route would involve construction in remote areas on the Tibetan plateau. 
In this project, water would be pumped uphill from tributaries of the Yangtze to the headwaters of the Yellow River, and in conjunction with the other two routes this plan is expected to encourage development in the poor and parched areas of northwestern and north-central China.
The intensity of the bargaining with the provinces to win approval for the "south waters north" and the Three Gorges Dam projects is reflected in the many compromises made in the plans.
"There are few things that tell you as much about the politics of a country as where it builds its dams, because dams create big winners and big losers," said Kenneth G. Lieberthal, a political science professor at the University of Michigan.
For example, as Professor Lieberthal noted, the Three Gorges Dam is to be almost 607 feet high, with a normal water level of 574 feet. 
That level will create a reservoir that will just reach the city of Chongqing. 
The Communist Party leaders in Chongqing had insisted that the reservoir reach their city, to give them a year-round river port for large vessels. 
But the leaders rejected a higher dam, even though this would have helped in flood control efforts, because part of the city would have been submerged.
The dam would have a hydropower station with a capacity of 17,680 megawatts, making it the largest in the world except for a proposed Russian project that has been put off.
One of the greatest problems with the Three Gorges Dam and other water projects in China is how to deal with the silting. 
Each year about 520 million tons of silt is carried down the Yangtze past the site of the Three Gorges Dam, and skeptics argue that in a few decades the reservoir will become an unnavigable pool of mud.
Backers of the project have conducted extensive tests, some of them using a half-mile-long laboratory version of the Yangtze, and they insist that siltation would not be a major problem. 
In the summer, when the river is the muddiest, they plan to lower the reservoir level and flush the silt through, while in the fall, when the river is clearer, they would build the water level.
Government officials seem to be pushing hard for a final go-ahead on the Three Gorges project in March, at a meeting of the National People's Congress. 
As evidence of the danger, they cite devastating flooding last summer in which 3,000 people were killed and 3.2 million were left homeless, and they emphasize that the sooner work begins on the dam, the less onerous the relocation requirements will be, partly because of the rapidly rising population.
"The sooner Three Gorges starts functioning, the better," said Su Qianqing, an official of the Ministry of Water Resources in Beijing. 
"It's going to be more difficult for us to solve the problem of relocation if we don't start now."
The Three Gorges Dam has been under discussion since the 1920's and is by far the country's most controversial construction project. 
In the relatively open environment of the late 1980's, an incipient environmental movement seemed to have defeated the plan for a dam when a Politburo member announced a postponement of further consideration until at least 1995.
But over the last 18 months the project has been resuscitated, and in the aftermath of the crackdown in Tiananmen Square in 1989 most environmentalists and critics of the project have been cowed into silence. 
Dai Qing, a prominent writer who is one of the dam's foremost opponents, was arrested after the crackdown, and Li Rui, a party elder and water specialist who also opposed the project, was placed under tight restrictions.
"I still have some hope that the Three Gorges Dam won't go ahead," Ms. Dai said last month, shortly before she was allowed to go to the United States to accept a fellowship at Harvard University. 
"If we devote so many resources to the Three Gorges, then everything else will have to wait. 
Education and science spending will slow, and China's backwardness and burden on the world economy will grow."

China warned today that it would "react strongly" if France or any other country sold jet fighters to Taiwan, but the French, the United States and possibly other Western nations seem to be quietly pushing ahead with military sales to the Chinese Nationalists.
Taiwan newspapers, including the semi-official Central Daily News, reported today that the authorities in Taipei, Taiwan's capital, signed a contract on Wednesday to purchase 60 Mirage 2000-5 fighters and 1,000 or more short- and medium-range missiles. 
French officials would not confirm the report, and by some accounts they plan not to make an announcement of the deal in hopes of lessening Beijing's anger.
Because China claims sovereignty over Taiwan, it has always denounced such weapons sales. 
But diplomats say that almost any measure the Beijing authorities could take would have repercussions at home, and whatever steps it takes against France, it might feel compelled to take, as well, against the United States.
Washington signed an agreement with Taiwan on Nov. 
11 to provide its air force with 150 F-16 jets, worth as much as $5.8 billion. 
The formal signing drew little attention, because it had been expected since Sept. 
2, when President Bush announced the sale during a campaign stop at a Fort Worth plant of the General Dynamics Corporation, the F-16's manufacturer.
The Chinese sharply criticized the United States at that time and suspended their participation in international talks on curbing arms sales. 
They also rejected a proposal to establish a two-nation human rights commission and have hinted at further action.

Wu Jianmin, the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman, said today that Beijing had noted the Mirage sale reports. 
"We firmly oppose the sale of military weapons to Taiwan by any country," he said, "whether it does it openly or secretly, or whether it announces it or not. 
We strongly demand the French Government refrain from approving such a contract. 
If it ignores the strong opposition of the Chinese side and insists on having its own way, the Chinese side will react strongly."
He gave no indication of what retaliatory measures Beijing might take, but said, "China lives up to its word."
The United States office in Taipei today confirmed newspaper reports there that Washington is sending Carla A. Hills, the President's trade representative, to Taiwan for a conference early next month, the first official trip by a Cabinet-rank official since Washington broke diplomatic relations with Taipei more than a dozen years ago.

file: Chinese Apparently Halt Rights Talks With U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a rebuff to President Bush and a warning to President-elect Bill Clinton, China appears to have suspended its discussions with the United States on human rights issues, including American inquiries about specific political prisoners.
The action by the Beijing authorities halts a process that began in December 1990, when the Bush Administration hailed the talks as a sign of progress on human rights following the violent suppression of the democracy movement in June 1989.
The dialogue on rights was never especially productive, but it gave American diplomats and visiting officials a basis for raising inquiries about specific political prisoners. 
These on-again, off-again discussions, about broad human rights topics and individual cases, sometimes drew minimal Chinese responses and occasionally led to real improvements in people's lives.
For all the frustrations, the discussions meant that China at least acknowledged that human rights were a valid topic of discussion. 
Now, even that much seems to be in jeopardy.
Mr. Clinton sharply criticized China for human rights abuses during the Presidential campaign. 
Since the election, he has eased up a little on that criticism, but indicated that he would continue to take a tougher line on the issue than the Bush Administration.
Â 
Throwing Down the Gauntlet
In effect, then, the Beijing authorities were laying down a challenge to Mr. Clinton as he and his advisers fashion a China policy.
Their action also comes as disagreements are expected in coming months on trade and other issues.
The Chinese approach in the wake of the American election is still being developed, however, and may permit discussions about human rights with legislators and others who are not part of the Administration.
In a significant step, China is welcoming a delegation of five Senators next month, a visit in which rights concerns are certain to be raised.
The latest Chinese decision seems to be a response to Mr. Bush's announcement in September that the United States would permit the sale of F-16 fighter jets to Beijing's adversary, the Chinese Nationalists on Taiwan. 
The Government here was outraged by the sale, which appeared to violate American pledges, and some diplomats expect further retaliatory action.
"The United States Government decision to sell F-16 fighters to Taiwan has seriously hurt Sino-U.S. relations," the Foreign Ministry said in an oblique statement today, 24 hours after it was asked for details about the suspension of the human rights discussions. 
"The Chinese Government has expressed its solemn and just stance on this."
The United States is not without leverage. 
Beijing, for instance, is worried that if it reacts too strongly, it will lose its low-tariff access to the American market, known as most-favored-nation status. 
Mr. Clinton has said that he favors linking China's trade with its human rights situation, but much will depend on how this principle is drafted into legislation on extending this trading status.
A Western diplomat explained: "You're talking about the U.S. taking 30 percent of their exports, and their exports to the U.S. are growing 40 percent this year. 
And they're counting on this to continue to grow. 
It's something that their entire reform package is based on."
Mr. Clinton's changing tone in recent weeks leaves his intentions unclear. 
During the campaign, he said that President Bush had failed to win concessions from China on rights and trade issues, but last week he said that "in the last several months" China had begun to moderate its policies.
"We have a big stake in not isolating China, in seeing that China continues to develop a market economy," Mr. Clinton said. 
"But we also have to insist, I believe, on progress in human rights and human decency."
The Foreign Ministry did not directly respond to the questions about whether the rights discussions had been terminated. 
By avoiding a direct response, the ministry seemed to be offering tacit confirmation without painting itself into a corner.
In a sign of the sensitivity of the issue, the United States Embassy in Beijing took two days to provide this terse response: "We believe an active dialogue on the issue offers the best chance of furthering both countries' interests. 
We continue to press China on human rights at every opportunity."
The embassy declined to comment further, but at a meeting earlier this month, American diplomats are believed to have tried to give the Chinese Foreign Ministry an unofficial though written inquiry on political prisoners.
The Chinese refused to accept it, so the Americans left it on a chair as they packed up and prepared to leave the room. 
The Chinese picked it up and said that there would be no response. 
The Americans were apparently heartened that they at least picked it up.
China's growing trade imbalance with the United States, in which its exports far exceed its imports, is another prickly issue. 
The surplus, now second only to Japan's, amounted to $13.4 billion in the first nine months of this year, more than in all of 1991.
The Beijing leadership has also been slow to carry out an agreement with Washington on curbing the export of goods made with prison labor.
If that were not enough to worry about, the Chinese Government's fierce opposition to democratic changes in Hong Kong may cause further tensions with the United States.
There have been significant improvements in other areas. 
China seems to have curtailed its arms sales, and it has allowed many, if not all dissidents to leave the country. 
It has released some prominent Catholics from prison and sharply toned down its Communist propaganda.
Last month, Beijing caved in on American demands that it open its markets to more American goods, and it is taking other steps to allow parts of its economy to be run on market lines. 
And, in a bouquet to Mr. Clinton, the Chinese announced shortly after the election that they would buy two million tons of American wheat, the first such purchase this year.
The suspension of human rights discussions was apparently decided at the highest level. 
The leadership informed various Chinese ministries that they should not discuss rights issues with American officials.
A test of how the Chinese will apply the suspension is expected during the Senators' visit. 
According to current plans, the delegation is to be led by Senator David L. Boren and to include Senators Bob Kerrey, Carl Levin, Claiborne Pell and John W. Warner.
In an important suggestion that it wants to be conciliatory, China plans to let the Senators visit Tibet. 
It ordinarily controls access to Tibet very tightly, effectively barring Western journalists from visiting the region.

file: Chinese at the U.N. Seeking to Keep Jobs.txt
text:
ï»¿
The union of United Nations civil servants has asked Secretary General Javier Perez de Cuellar to extend the contracts of several Chinese workers at the Secretariat who the union says have been asked to leave their jobs under ''pressure from the Chinese Government.''
The Chinese Government says it has exerted no such pressure, describing its actions as merely routine staff rotations.
The president of the union that represents three of the at least six staff members in question said the Chinese Government was seeking to end their work at the Secretariat although they had been recommended for career appointments by their section and departments.
He suggested that the staff members were being penalized for their participation in protests against the Government after the student democracy demonstrations in China were crushed last summer, and for refusing to turn over parts of their paychecks in keeping with Chinese Government regulations.
Appointed to Fill Posts
''They have excellent performance reports,'' said Lowell L. Flanders, the president of the staff union. 
''They're intelligent, bright young men. 
They've done an outstanding job. 
If they were any other nationality, they would be entitled to a career appointment after five years of satisfactory service.''
Most staff members join the Secretariat on probationary appointments of two years, which lead to career appointments. 
But, as in the case of the staff members in question, some countries appoint their civil servants on the basis of secondment, a policy under which workers are loaned by their governments to fill posts in the Secretariat for a limited period of time.
The staff union, the Staff Council of the Secretariat, has taken up the cause of these language staff members as part of a campaign against abuses of secondment as a government way of controlling Secretariat employees.
Under the United Nations Charter, any nation that tries to influence the Secretariat - and any Secretary General who yields to such pressure - is in violation of the Charter. 
Nevertheless, experts say member nations have considerable influence over appointments.
Â 
Called Standard Procedure
In a recent unanimous resolution, the Staff Council suggested that the United Nations denied Chinese staff members new contracts as a result of ''undue pressure being exerted upon it from external authorities,'' an apparent reference to the Chinese Government. 
Mr. Flanders said five employees in New York and one in Vienna were affected, but that there might be more.
Mr. Flanders said he had discussed this issue with Mr. Perez de Cuellar at least three times.
Mr. Perez de Cuellar's spokesman, Francois Giuliani, said the situation was nothing more than standard procedure. 
''The contracts came to an end,'' Mr. Giuliani said. 
''That's it. 
The extension of contracts is not an automatic thing. 
There are many other cases like this. 
I don't know of any case when we've extended secondment once the government finished it.''

Chinese banks have offered $108 million in loans to hundreds of foreign-financed enterprises that face money shortages because of China's austerity program.

text:

In its most sweeping declaration of policy since leadership changes in June, the Communist Party acknowledged some mistakes today but called for vigilance against what it described as efforts by the West to subvert the Chinese Government and institute capitalism.
''Hostile forces, international as well as internal, are still engaged in activities of sabotage and subversion against us,'' Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader, warned in an 80-minute address shown on national television. 
The speech, part of the commemorations of the 40th anniversary of Communist rule on Sunday, had been circulated among the leadership and reflected not only Mr. Jiang's views but also those of all other top officials.
Giving a methodical if vague survey of China's economic, political and ideological policies, the speech was generally harsher than expected. 
While it reaffirmed the need for economic changes, some of the phrasing was more reminiscent of the 1960's and '70's than of the last decade of the open-door policy.
Maoist Phrase Resurrected
Mr. Jiang said China was engaged in ''a serious class struggle,'' a term that has occasionally been used in recent months but that has generally been out of favor since the Maoist era ended 13 years ago. 
In the past, use of the phrase often accompanied repression. 
Mr. Jiang said Beijing would ''isolate and attack the handful of hostile elements'' behind the democracy movement this spring that ended with a crackdown in Beijing on June 4.
''The disturbances stirred up by hostile forces, both internal and external, were aimed at overthrowing the Chinese Communist Party's leadership and subverting the socialist system, at turning China into a bourgeois republic and reducing it once again to a dependency of the Western capitalist powers,'' Mr. Jiang said. 
A 63-year-old technocrat who was appointed Communist Party General Secretary in June, Mr. Jiang has been designated by Deng Xiaoping, the nations' senior leader, to be the next paramount leader of China. 
The speech was perhaps his most significant opportunity yet to gain credibility and authority by speaking on behalf of the entire leadership.
China's new leadership has given mixed signals since it took power after the violent suppression of the democracy movement. 
The speech does not resolve the uncertainties, but it suggests an outline of China's directions: vigorous repression of any sign of dissent, economic retrenchment, increased central planning, but apparently modest extension of some economic restructuring programs.
Â 
A Split Is Acknowledged
In the most explicit statement so far of the divisions within China, Mr. Jiang warned that ''two completely different views exist on the issue of reform and opening.''
One view, he said, was the correct one, which would result in modernization and perfection of socialism. 
The other aims for ''total Westernization'' and ''constitutes transformation into capitalism and brings China into the orbit of the capitalist system of the West.''
By declaring that those who favor more aggressive change are effectively agents of Western capitalism, the party was escalating the accusations against them and serving notice that favoring ''bourgeois liberalization'' is an extremely serious offense.
With members of the Politburo and other top leaders seated behind him to underscore unity, Mr. Jiang acknowledged that the Party had made mistakes that had cost support.
''After we became the party in power, some phenomena of bureaucratism, petty tyranny, abuse of power for personal gains, corruption and degeneration, which result in alienation from the masses of the people, have gradually emerged,'' he said. 
The problems became worse in recent years, he added, and he called for extensive new ideological education to restore the Communist spirit and faith in the party.
Â 
Small Role for Private Sector
The struggles against foreign and domestic rivals ''will continue for a long time,'' Mr. Jiang said.
In economic matters, Mr. Jiang called for more central planning and suggested that China for the next three years at least would have to pursue its policy of economic retrenchment. 
During this period, he said, China should increase centralization and the proportion of revenue controlled by the central Government.
Apparently in response to concerns about attacks by the Government on the private sector, Mr. Jiang vigorously stressed the need for private enterprise. 
But he emphasized that it would always occupy a small role in the economy and suggested higher taxation of entrepreneurs as a way of avoiding rising disparities in incomes.
Mr. Jiang denied that the economic retrenchment amounted to a slowdown in the policy of economic change, and he said that China would maintain and further develop policies related to special economic zones and open areas along the coast. 
Apparently in a reference to China's fledgling stock markets, he said that China would continue to experiment with various ''pilot reforms.''

He was reading from the communique of the party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, adopted on Saturday and released today. 
The communique suggested that the selection of a new party leader and other top officials on Saturday may not produce a new calm or an end to the searches for supporters of the democracy movement, or the ''counterrevolutionary rebellion,'' as it is now known here. 
#47 Million in Party No new arrests or executions were announced today, and the newspapers and television news were full of enthusiastic declarations of support for the new leadership, rather than the triumphant arrests of ''thugs'' that were the main news story last week.
Yet the communique on discipline suggested that the restructuring at the highest level of the leadership - expelling two members from what used to be a five-member Standing Committee of the Politburo, and adding three new members - might now ripple through lower levels in the 47-million-member party.
It is unclear how successful such an attempt at purges would be, since the hard line that is the new orthodoxy may not enjoy majority support within the party, but it is likely to be a new source of contention and conflict in the coming months.

Such a stringent approach to rectifying the party fits in with the relatively harsh treatment given to the ousted party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, who was formally dismissed on Saturday. 
In 1981, Hua Guofeng was forced to resign as party chairman, but he has been able to keep his Central Committee seat all these years. 
Two years ago, Hu Yaobang was forced to resign as General Secretary, and he was allowed to keep not only his Central Committee seat but even his position on the Politburo until his death earlier this year.
The continuing presence of both men in the leadership was meant to be a sign of a new civility within the Communist Party, an indication that losing a power struggle no longer meant loss of all offices and even imprisonment.

Fang Sees a Double Standard

Face-Saving Measure
Although they were initially released to Britain, apparently as a face-saving response to Chinese concerns that Mr. Fang not go to the United States, there is no known agreement that prevents them from moving later on.
And while Beijing might regard Mr. Fang's speaking out against the Government as a breach of his pledge not to conduct ''anti-China'' activities while in exile, Mr. Fang was careful not to rule out criticism of the Chinese Government, as opposed to criticism of the nation itself.
In the wide-ranging interview, Mr. Fang, whose full name is pronounced fahng lee-jur (rhyming with burr), gave details of negotiations involving the United States Embassy in Beijing and the Chinese authorities that led to exile for him and his wife, who is also a physicist and a prominent dissident.

Urges Sanctions Against Beijing
Appearing relaxed and cheerful at his office at Cambridge University's Institute of Astronomy, Mr. Fang also touched on the state of the democracy movement in China, the need he saw for continued economic sanctions against the country and the role the Bush Administration could play in bringing about change.
Mr. Fang, who is here doing research into the structure of the universe, said that the Chinese authorities had allowed one of his sons, who had remained behind when the couple left, to travel to Britain a week ago and that the family, including a second son, had now been reunited.

Mr. Fang was asked whether he would meet Chinese dissident leaders while in the United States, where he would have a broader platform for his views.

But he said that whether he would be willing to serve as the leader of exiled dissidents would ''depend on the situation.''
Mr. Fang said he might make his home in exile in the United States because it ''is very large and very easy to spend a longer time'' there than in Britain. 
He said he would visit various parts of the United States and had already received invitations from universities and institutes in California, Chicago, Colorado and New York.

Chose to Go to Britain
He said the Chinese authorities, for reasons that were unclear to him, had not wanted the United States to be his first stop after leaving Beijing. 
He said he had told the authorities he was willing to go to any developed country, and ultimately chose Britain, where he conducted research in 1979.
Mr. Fang and Miss Li flew to exile in Britain on June 25 after having been in the United States Embassy in Beijing since June 5, 1989. 
They took refuge in the embassy the day after the Communist leaders sent troops into Tianamen Square and after pro-Government demonstrators burned Mr. Fang in effigy.
Mr. Fang said he believed that the Government had allowed him to leave largely because it was feeling the pressure of economic sanctions. 
But the authorities also wanted to improve their image, he said, because ''intellectuals don't believe them and students don't like them.''

Â 
Long-Term Optimism
Mr. Fang said that world trends made him optimistic that democracy would be achieved in China but that ''we'll be waiting until the old generation'' of leadership is gone. 
He said it was difficult to determine which of the country's current leaders would become ''China's Gorbachev,'' because the autocratic system made it difficult for them to reveal ''what is really in their minds.''
For the first couple of weeks of their stay in the embassy, Mr. Fang said, he and his wife feared that the authorities would come and take them away, ''because there were still shots'' being fired.

Â 
Life in the Embassy
Mr. Fang said he had spent most of his time in the embassy doing research and writing five scientific papers.

Mr. Fang said he would go back to China if the Government guaranteed ''all my rights as a citizen.''
He said he still kept his Chinese passport and would never apply for political asylum. 
''In our Constitution, citizens have many rights, including freedom of speech,'' he said. 
''If they will guarantee that, I will go back.''
Â 
WOULD BE WELCOME IN U.S.
WASHINGTON, July 13 - A senior State Department official said today that Mr. Fang would be welcome in the United States. 
Any plans he might have for a prolonged stay, the official said, would not contradict the terms of the agreement reached with Beijing.

THREE times a week, 19 Chinese dissidents meet in Albert Einstein's former lecture hall to discuss how to bring democracy to their homeland.
Many of them fled to the West after the bloody crackdown in Tiananmen Square two years ago. 
Now they work from a safe haven inside the ivy-covered walls of Jones Hall at Princeton University, where Einstein, a refugee from another regime, Nazi Germany, once taught.
"We carry so much blood," said Su Wei, a 38-year-old writer and literary critic.
"I don't want to be a political leader," he said. 
"But there was so much blood we spent at the square, so big a price for the democracy hated in China. 
So we have to say something, do something."
The dissidents helped bring about the student democracy movement that ended June 4, 1989, when the Government ordered soldiers to fire on the crowd in Beijing, killing hundreds.
Â 
'They Need Our Voice'
"All we gained before 1989 we have lost," said Liu Binyan, 66, a former journalist for the Communist Party newspaper People's Daily, who left China before the student protests. 
"The freedom of the people has become less. 
The people now, they need our voice."
More than 100 Chinese dissidents applied for positions as visiting scholars at Princeton under a program financed by a $1 million donation from an alumnus, John Elliott. 
The school chose 23, some of whom have since moved on.
The scholars receive stipends to work in their own fields while researching and writing a book together about the 1989 movement.
On their own time, they are waging a war against Communism through freelance articles published in Hong Kong and American newspapers and magazines that are smuggled into China. 
Some are working on plays, poems or books they hope will find their way into the hands, minds and hearts of the Chinese people.
Â 
Memorizing, Not Analyzing
Surrounded by Chinese calligraphy about human rights in the office of the Princeton Chinese Initiative, the scholars described their campaign over a constant stream of cigarettes and warm Coke, both reminders of home.
Bai Meng, 28, the poet who drafted the "Declaration of the Hunger Strikers" for the student protesters, said that before democracy could work in China the people's minds needed to be reshaped.
He said that in China, students were taught to memorize, and not analyze, the Government's version of history. 
They are exposed only to acceptable theories like Communism, he said.
At Princeton, Mr. Bai said, the scholars are learning to open their minds to new theories and ways of formulating ideas. 
They use their writings to teach the Chinese back home to do the same, he said.
Zhang Langlang, 48, is a painter, writer, philosopher and humorist. 
He tries to educate the people he left behind about Western ideas through humorous stories in publications subscribed to by companies in China. 
He says he places his messages between the lines, where the Government cannot find them.
"My articles don't make the Government nervous because they don't focus on politics," he said with a laugh. 
"China's leaders are very stupid and can't understand my articles."
Â 
'Democratization Is Difficult'
Su Xiaokang, 41, a journalist and film maker, made the 1988 documentary "River Elegy," which questioned China's authoritarian tradition and encouraged the Government to open itself to the outside world. 
He is studying television in the United States with the goal of using the medium to change the Communist system.
"Democratization is difficult, and television is a strong tool," he said through an interpreter.
The scholars hope that by combining their different experiences, professions and ideas, they can figure out what has caused successive democracy movements to fail. 
Only by understanding the problem can the scholars solve it, they say.
But they are running out of time.
The donations that finance the Princeton program are expected to dry up in June, forcing the scholars to scatter. 
They will have to put earning a living before helping China, said Ruan Ming, 60, a political scientist and journalist who was expelled from the party because of his ideas.
The scholars have only now overcome the culture shock of living in the West and learned enough English to communicate their ideas, he said.
"We're finally at the stage where we can do things and the program is ready to be resolved," Mr. Ruan said. 
"There isn't enough time."
