text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities staged a public execution today of three young men who were accused of taking part in a violent political protest in Shanghai.
The executions were the first to be reported of anyone in the democracy movement since the military crackdown on June 4. 
[Another seven people, described as ''rioters,'' were executed in Beijing Thursday for various acts of violence during the military crackdown on the democracy movement, Reuters reported from Beijing, quoting the official New China News Agency.] The United States and other countries had pleaded with the Chinese Government not to execute political protesters. 
[Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d joined a chorus of Western leaders in denouncing the executions.
But he said the Bush Administration was not planning any additional actions against Beijing ''at this time.''
Page A10.]
A Hard-Line Attitude In another sign of a hard-line attitude here, the Beijing radio announced tonight that 45 people had been sentenced to death or imprisonment in the eastern city of Jinan, in Shandong Province, for ''seriously endangering public order.''
The announcer said they had been sentenced after an open trial attended by 10,000 people, but did not indicate how many had been sentenced to death and how many to imprisonment.
Such large gatherings to humiliate political criminals have been rare in recent years, and the trial in Jinan seemed to mark another example of reversion to methods that had largely disappeared since the end of the Mao era in 1976. 
#6 Convictions in Shanghai An editor at Jinan Daily News said in a telephone interview that 17 of the 45 had been sentenced to death, and that 9 others had been sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve at hard labor - intended to give convicts a chance to reform and win commutation to life imprisonment. 
The others were sentenced to various prison terms, the editor said, but he cautioned that at least some of the 45 were convicted of offenses unrelated to the political unrest.
The authorities in Shanghai also announced that six more people had been convicted in court today, apparently of taking part in the same protest as the three who were executed. 
These six are expected to be sentenced in the next few days.
Â 
Bush's New Measures
The three young men in Shanghai were presumably executed in the Chinese way, with a bullet fired in the back of the head at close range.
The executions, as well as the new death sentences, followed the Bush Administration's announcement on Tuesday of new measures to protest China's suppression of the democracy movement. 
These included a suspension of high-level contacts between American and Chinese officials and a declaration that the United States will try to postpone consideration of new loans to China by international institutions.
The Administation also appealed to China to grant clemency to those sentenced to death and to pardon those who were arrested for their role in pro-democracy demonstrations. 
Carrying out the death sentences ''could only deepen the wounds of the past few weeks,'' the White House spokesman, Marlin Fitzwater, said Tuesday.
China had no direct response today to the new steps announced in Washington, but the executions and announcement of new death sentences could be interpreted as an indirect response. 
#1,500 Known Arrests More than 1,500 people are known to have been arrested throughout the nation for taking part in the seven-week democracy movement, but it is not clear how many may face the death penalty.
In addition to the three executed in Shanghai, eight people in Beijing are awaiting appeals on their death sentences. 
Except for the sentences announced in Jinan, no other people are known to have been sentenced yet for taking part in the democracy movement.
The death penalty is relatively common in China, and hundreds of people are believed to be executed each year for violent crimes or large robberies or corruption cases.
Normally, the execution is carried out at an execution ground and the public is excluded. 
But on this occasion, several thousand people were reported to have attended the execution, apparently to make more of an example of the punishment. 
Occasionally during anti-crime campaigns in the past, executions have been shown on television, but that did not happen today.
Â 
Firefighters Attacked
The three men in Shanghai - Xu Guoming, an employee of a Shanghai brewery; Bian Hanwu, who is unemployed, and Yan Xuerong, a worker at a radio factory - were sentenced to death last Thursday but had appealed.
They were accused of helping to set fire to a train on June 6 and then attacking firefighters who arrived to put out the fire. 
No one was killed, but some firefighters were beaten up and nine rail cars were burned, forcing the closing of the rail line for two days.
The Government has not mentioned the circumstances in which the crowd attacked the train. 
The crowd had gathered to block the rail line, in protest of the killings of hundreds of students and workers in Beijing two days earlier by the army. 
A train rammed its way through the human blockade, killing six people who lay on the track, and only then did the outraged crowd attack the train and set it afire.
It is not known what evidence existed against the three men, who appeared to be in their 20's or perhaps early 30's, or even exactly what role each was accused of having played in the incident. 
Nor have the authorities indicated how they caught the three, who were apparently arrested several days later rather than on the scene.
Â 
Called Mentally Retarded
A diplomat in Shanghai said that Mr. Yan was mentally retarded, and that others who were facing trial in connection with the burning of the train were also mentally impaired. 
This could not be confirmed, and it is not clear whether this would be a factor in their arrest or a coincidence.
People's Daily reported today that the Supreme People's Court had issued a notice urging that ''punishment without leniency'' should be extended to those who engaged in violent protests, who planned the ''chaos'' and who organized the ''counterrevolutionary propaganda.''
''Major or typical cases could be publicized through television, radio and newspapers so as to frighten criminals into submission and encourage the masses to fight the counterrevolutionaries and criminals,'' the newspaper said.
The radio tonight also reported the arrest of Zhou Chifeng, a student from the central city of Wuhan, whom the authorities identified as a liaison officer in the student occupation of Tiananmen Square in Beijing. 
The radio report accused Mr. Zhou of stirring up unrest against the Government.
Â 
On U.S. 
Relations
So far, no students are known to have been sentenced, and it is not clear if those who were not directly linked to violent protests could be sentenced to death simply for planning the democracy movement, known here as the ''counterrevolutionary rebellion.''
Prime Minister Li Peng appeared tonight to make some indirect comments about the growing tension with the United States.
''When China is in difficulties for the time being, it sees clearly who are true friends and who are false ones,'' Mr. Li told visiting the Pakistani Foreign Secretary, Humayun Khan. 
''Now some countries have exerted diplomatic and economic pressures on China and tried to interfere in China's internal affairs. 
This is short-sighted and unreasonable, and we believe that more people will change their opinions so long as they get to know the facts.''
Mr. Li said China would not bow to external pressure, but he added that China would maintain its open-door policy and its program of change. 
He also emphasized that the authorities would punish only a small minority of the participants in the democracy movement, although he did not specify how many people this might consist of.
Â 
'According to Law'
''The tiny minority of criminals will be punished according to law, and the Government will be lenient in dealing with most of the people who took part in parades and demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes, even those with extremist opinions,'' he said.
Earlier today, the Government announced other arrests, including 44 ''ruffians'' who were accused of taking part in protests in the capital and then fled south to nearby Hebei Province. 
The Shanghai authorities announced that 65 people had surrendered there, and that some, having been persuaded of their errors, had later informed on others.
Four others were arrested in connection with an attempt by two women to flee the country by boarding a Paris-bound flight with false passports. 
It was not clear how they had obtained the passports or if they were also sought for other reasons.
The official newspapers called today for more ''ideological education'' for college students around the nation. 
The State Education Commission ordered local governments to arrange the educational sessions and in particular to stress the study of a recent speech by Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, that included the official account of the ''counterrevolutionary rebellion.''

text:

Chinese exiles and opposition figures from around the world ended an inaugural meeting today establishing the Federation for Democracy in China, an umbrella group that aims to coordinate worldwide opposition to the Beijing Government.
The 150 Chinese, in one of the most important meetings of the Chinese opposition since the crackdown in Tiananmen Square in June, elected Yan Jiaqi, an intense 47-year-old political scientist, as president of the federation. 
Late in July, 1,100 Chinese students from across the United States met in Chicago to press their cause.
In an interview, Mr. Jiaqi said he was confident that economic problems in China and a power struggle among the leadership would fuel a public clamor for democracy that would lead to a rehabilitation of the democratic movement.

Wuer Kaixi, an outspoken leader of the student protesters in Beijing, was elected vice president of the federation. 
Other founding members were Wan Runnan, one of China's most prominent entrepreneurs; Su Xioakan, a writer and intellectual, and Chen Yizi, a former adviser to Mr. Zhao and the highest-ranking Chinese official known to have gone into exile.
Â 
Influence Asserted
The federation's leaders asserted that they could exert effective pressure on China's Government even though they are outside the country. 
They say they expect to obtain funds from Chinese living in Hong Kong, Singapore, the United States and elsewhere.
''There are 56 million Chinese living abroad,'' Mr. Chen said. 
''We hope to unite them.''
Mr. Wan, who had headed a computer company, said: ''We can have a great impact even though we're all in exile now.

In its founding statement, the federation, which will be based in Paris, said it opposed a monopoly of power in China and supported human rights, democracy and an economy that responds to market forces.
Mr. Yan, who had been director of Beijing's Institute of Political Science, was not optimistic about Jiang Zemin, the new party leader and the man chosen by Deng Xiaoping to succeed him as China's paramount leader.
''Jiang is not a reformer, and he is not a democrat,'' he said. 
''He is a bureaucrat. 
What he is gifted at is navigating his way politically. 
He is a puppet of Deng.

Â 
Battle to Come
Federation leaders said they foresee a power struggle between Mr. Jiang and Li Peng, the hard-line Prime Minister who was instrumental in the crackdown in June.

file: Chinese Face Epochal Wait For Housing.txt
text:
ï»¿
At an electronics company here, 20-year-old employees face a 73-year waiting list to get housing.
In Shanghai, a household of 12 people in three generations has devised its own solution to the housing shortage. 
The family has divided its 12-foot-by-12-foot apartment horizontally into two levels. 
The women of the family live in the upper crawl space, the men below.
Then there are China's less lucky citizens who get no housing at all and must live, according to a Government report, ''in warehouses, offices or even toilets.''
Goaded by growing dissatisfaction, the Government is undertaking a national campaign this year to turn China into a nation of homeowners.
Â 
To Be 'Mainstay' of Change
''We must gradually make housing reform one of the mainstays of the national economy,'' the Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, said recently. 
So far, ''gradually'' has indeed been the watchword: 100,000 people attended a housing fair recently, but the fair featured only 13 apartments for sale.
The decision to privatize home ownership was not taken lightly, for it challenges the underpinnings of society as it has been interpreted here. 
For the last 40 years, virtually free housing supplied by one's ''work unit,'' or employer, has been as much of a staple of urban Chinese life as rice or noodles.
''Housing used to be a kind of welfare system,'' said Tong Naiwen, the deputy director of the General Pharmaceutical Factory, which in January became one of the first companies in the nation to privatize its apartments. 
''We used to rent out very cheaply, but there was a terrible shortage. 
Now we're encouraging workers to buy houses.''
Wang Tong, a 33-year-old clerk at the same factory, which is in the northeastern city of Shenyang, said in an interview that she and her husband were delighted to buy a two-bedroom apartment for the equivalent of $1,350. 
Even though the price has been heavily subsidized by the Government and the factory, it still dwarfs Miss Wang's monthly salary of just under $30.
Â 
Discussed for Years
Housing reform has been discussed for several years in China, and already many farmers own their own houses. 
But privatization of urban homes has been very slow, and it seems to be taking off nationally only this year.
''Gradually, more and more people will own their own homes,'' said Ma Jinlin, director of Beijing's housing exchange center, which began operations this month and acts as a broker between developers and buyers.
As officials describe it, the method is twofold. 
First, work units will try to sell apartments to employees instead of renting. 
Second, new apartments will be built and sold on the open market to those who can afford them. 
Technically, people are buying only the right to live in the apartment, rather than the apartment itself, but in practice this seems to make little difference.
Â 
Protection Against Landlords
In most areas there still are restrictions to prevent the emergence of a landlord class, including the requirement that the owner also occupy the apartment and a prohibition on resale within five years. 
Even so, there are political objections.
The practical difficulty of managing a transition to the market is not so different from the challenge that faces American cities with rent control. 
Raising rents creates new incentives to build and maintain housing, but it is difficult to convince people that they are better off paying higher rents.
Yet the consensus seems to be growing in China that rents are too low. 
Rent for a family of four averages the equivalent of 60 cents a month, which covers only half the Government's maintenance expense. 
As a result, there is little money to build new apartments and shortages are acute. 
In China's large cities, per capita living space including bathrooms and kitchen is about the size of a king-sized bed.
Young couples usually must look forward to the distant day when their work unit will assign them their own apartment, even if it is tiny. 
Until then, the new employees must live with their parents - who, in some cases, are still living with their parents.
Beijing began this month to sell apartments on the open market for the first time, but the prices were so high that only a small number of entrepreneurs or those with overseas relatives could afford them. 
The 400 apartments ranged in price from about $13,000 up to $41,000, momentous sums in a country where the monthly wage averages about $25 a month.

text:

About 1,200 people, most of them graduate students from China, rallied in Manhattan yesterday in support of pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing.
The twin themes of the gathering at Dag Hammarskjold Plaza, near the United Nations, and subsequent march to the Chinese Consulate at 12th Avenue and West 42d Street were denunciation of China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, and its Prime Minister, Li Peng, and support of the democracy movement challenging the Beijing Government.
The protesters' carried colorful banners and placards, including a poster depicting Mr. Deng as the ghost in the logo from the movie ''Ghostbusters.''
There were delegations from Princeton, Rutgers, Yale, the University of Connecticut, and Penn State, among others.
As the march began, some people began singing the spiritual ''We Shall Overcome,'' substituting lyrics like ''China will be free.''
Â 
Shouting to Consulate Staff
When the marchers arrived at the consulate building, they broke into chants of ''Li Peng, Step Down.''
When they saw consulate staff members peering down from upper-story windows, some using binoculars, the protesters began to shout, ''Come down, if you're Chinese!''
At one point, a student identified as Haitao Zhang cut his hand and used the blood to write a four-character slogan that translates as ''An eye for an eye'' on a cloth banner. 
Mr. Zhang tried to give the banner to consulate officials, but they would not accept it, other protesters said. 
Mr. Zhang was taken to a hospital for treatment.
Most students said they agreed with the decision of their counterparts in Beijing to leave Tiananmen Square. 
''We can't achieve everything in one night,'' said Yiming Tang, a graduate student at Columbia University and one of several coordinators of the march.
Students who head back to their homes and universities will spread their fervor for democracy among more people that way, he said, adding: ''We have to go step-by-step. 
Perhaps we should say this is the end of the beginning, like Sir Winston Churchill.''

file: Chinese in U.S. Lament Bush Victory.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the student union at the University of Wisconsin, Jian Tang wore a sweatshirt emblazoned with the slogan ''We Have a Dream: Freedom, Democracy -China, China, China.''
The 31-year-old graduate student in nuclear engineering has made no secret of his disdain for the Government of China. 
And he said that if he was forced to return, he had a good idea what his future would hold.
''A labor camp, perhaps,'' he said. 
''Or imprisonment. 
Or execution.''
Sadness and Disappointment Chinese students in the United States have voiced sadness and disappointment over the Senate's upholding of President Bush's veto of a bill permitting them to remain in the United States after their visas had expired. 
There are about 40,000 Chinese enrolled at American universities, with one of the largest groups, about 450 students and visiting scholars, here at the University of Wisconsin.
President Bush has said he will order administrative measures to protect all Chinese in America from forced deportation. 
While students said they did not fear being asked to leave the country, many of those interviewed here and at other American schools insisted that their concerns were more than symbolic. 
They argued that an administrative order would leave them more vulnerable than they would have been if the legislation had passed.
''Without protective legislation, we are in danger every day,'' said Ma Yong Sheng, who is studying for a doctoral degree in biology at City College of New York, adding that the veto ''doesn't hurt the democracy movement but it sends the wrong message to the Chinese leadership.''
Students said they had reason to question Mr. Bush's credibility on issues involving policy toward China, especially in light of recent disclosures that two top Administration officials visited the Beijing Government soon after the massacre in Tiananmen Square last June.
''It's hard for us to believe that what he says is reliable,'' said Mr. Tang, a native of Chong Qing.
Â 
Students Remain Wary
But even among those who remain skeptical of Mr. Bush's intentions, few seriously believe that the President would quickly do an about-face and send the Chinese home.
''But down the road these things can change,'' said Michael Dean, director of the Wisconsin Office of International Students and Faculty. 
''It was just this January, for example, that the U.S. 
Government would no longer issue an extension on voluntary departures for students from Uganda. 
And many people still believe that Ugandans might face a danger if they return.''
At the University of California at Berkeley, Zhang Ruizhuang, a political science doctoral student, expressed an unease shared by many students: ''If that law had been passed, we'd be feeling safer, because the law is more stable.''
The legislation that Mr. Bush vetoed would have changed existing law requiring that most of the students, who hold visitor's visas, return to China before applying for new visas or permanent residence in the United States.
Another theme repeated by student after student was frustration, because they believed that the 62-to-37 Senate vote on Thursday to sustain Mr. Bush's veto was driven not by the merits of the bill, but by a partisan desire among Republicans to protect the President from an embarrassing defeat. 
Although the House voted against Mr. Bush on Wednesday by a vote of 390 to 25, two-thirds majorities in both houses of Congress are needed to reverse a veto.
Â 
'Matter of Saving Face'
''It came down to a matter of saving face - the President's face,'' said Yongchuan Liu, president of the Independent Federation of Chinese Students and Scholars, a group founded in Washington after the crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in China.
After the crackdown, the Chinese group at Madison changed its name from the Chinese Students and Scholars Association to the Chinese Independent Union, a shift intended to show support for the protesters in Beijing.
Like students at many American colleges, the Chinese here have openly protested against the Beijing Government, fully aware that such criticism would make them easy targets of persecution if they return home.
While the students had been encouraged, indeed moved, by the expressions of solidarity among most Americans, they worry that Mr. Bush might ultimately see them as a bargaining chip in the broader foreign policy scheme.
''Why does the President want flexibility?'' asked Xingyu Chen, the 29-year-old leader of the Chinese Independent Union. 
''Because he wants to be able to negotiate with the Chinese Government. 
What will be used as bargaining chips in the negotiations?
The Chinese students.''
A 37-year-old graduate student in political science at the University of California, who did not want to be identified because he plans to return to China, said Mr. Bush's veto ''won't substantially influence the future of Chinese students in the U.S.''
''Every Chinese student can make full use of Bush's administrative order,'' he said.
But ''I don't believe Bush is really pro-democracy,'' he said. 
''He just passed that order to deal with the political situation, not with Chinese students or human rights.''
Â 
Overthrow Seen as the Answer
While President Bush has embarked on a strategy that seeks changes in the Beijing Government, the Chinese students contend that freedom can come to China only through the overthrow of the current rulers. 
In trying to placate Deng Xiaoping and his colleagues, the students argue, the United States is unwittingly knocking the wind out of the pro-democracy movement in China.
''The bill is more important in terms of sending a message to China than it is in terms of protecting the students,'' Mr. Tang said. 
''We think this Government will not survive. 
It will fall in the near future. 
President Bush should not help it keep from falling.''
For the students, the deepest fears center on their families in China. 
They worry that the authorities there might retaliate for the treasonous words and acts of their sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, on college campuses in the United States.
In letters and telephone conversations with their families, the students are careful to avoid any discussions that could be deemed subversive, and they try to decipher any messages about the political atmosphere at home.
Zhongdang Pan, another student, said that earlier this week he talked with his parents, who teach at a junior college in Anhui Province.
''They said, 'We are fine. 
Don't worry about us,' '' Mr. Pan said. 
'' 'And don't come home.'
''

A Chinese jumbo jet bound for New York was hijacked today and forced to land in western Japan, Japanese authorities said.
The Boeing 747 with 223 people aboard was on a flight from Beijing to New York when it deviated from its course and flew toward South Korea, a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.
Â 
Tried to Land in Seoul
Flight 981 of the Civil Aviation Administration of China, China's flagship airline, tried to land in South Korea but was rejected by South Korean authorities, said the Foreign Ministry official, who by custom would not be identified by name.
South Korea and China have no diplomatic relations, and there are no commercial flights between the two nations.

They were imprisoned for less than a year and resettled in Taiwan, where they received heroes' welcomes.

file: Chinese Leadership Names 2 Deputy Premiers.txt
text:

The Chinese leadership has tentatively decided to name two new Deputy Prime Ministers, including the reformist Mayor of Shanghai, in a move that is expected to give a lift to the faction that favors more rapid economic change.
The promotions, which have circulated as rumors and speculation for some time, have been formally put in writing and circulated among leading officials and the "Democratic Parties" that cooperate with the Communist Party, an official said.
"Unless one of the octogenarians gets up and starts objecting, the promotions will go through," the official said. 
"Something unforeseen might come up, but as of now the plan is to elevate them."
The appointments would be formally presented to the delegates of the National People's Congress, a rubber-stamp Parliament now holding its annual session, and approved over the next week.
The most important appointment would be the selection of Zhu Rongji, the 63-year-old Mayor and Communist Party Secretary of Shanghai, as the Deputy Prime Minister. 
Mr. Zhu, who was denounced as a rightist in 1957, is an engineer who has been Mayor of China's biggest city since 1988.
A protege of China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, Mr. Zhu has risen extremely rapidly in the last few years and would be well positioned to replace Prime Minister Li Peng if Mr. Deng and the other octogenarians who hold ultimate power can reach a consensus on replacing Mr. Li.
Mr. Zhu is one of the few senior Chinese leaders who is generally admired by young Chinese, as well as by foreign business executives. 
He has a reputation as a practical official who leans toward market mechanisms and is far more concerned with invigorating the economy than with Marxist ideology. 
But the central-planning faction in the leadership also deems him acceptable, partly because Mr. Zhu worked under the Planning Commission from 1952 to 1975 and so is regarded by them as a central planner as well. 
Mr. Zhu would replace Yao Yilin, a 74-year-old leader of the central-planning faction. 
Mr. Yao has been seriously ill for many months, Chinese officials say.
The other new Deputy Prime Minister is said to be Zou Jiahua, the 65-year-old head of the State Planning Commission. 
He has a reputation as a moderate, but one Chinese who knows him says he leans toward the reformists.
Mr. Zou is the son of a famous Communist journalist and the son-in-law of the late Marshal Ye Jianying, who was an ally of Mr. Deng and an important figure in China until the mid-1980's.

file: Chinese Lose_ U.S. Boat Sinks.txt
text:
ï»¿
The 14th annual Hong Kong international dragon boat races ended today with Indonesia dethroning the heavily favored Shun De team from China in the men's final. 
The False Creek Canoe Club of Vancouver, British Columbia, took the women's title from the similarly favored Chinese women's team.
The United States men's team from Philadelphia, which won its opening heat Saturday and its semifinal this morning, suffered the ignominy of sinking and placing last in the eight-boat final.
The American boat had high hopes going into the championship. 
Based on its semifinal victory, the United States was assigned lane 5, next to the other semifinal winner, Indonesia, which was in the fourth lane. 
Shun De, which won the Hong Kong championship the last four years, was in lane 6.
Â 
Perfect Position
It was an ideal draw for the United States, making it tactically possible to race the co-favorites placed on either side of the American boat.
The wooden craft used for dragon boat racing are 38 feet long, weigh close to 4,000 pounds and use a crew of up to 20 rowers plus a coxswain to steer and a drummer, seated in the bow, to beat out the racing cadence.

text:

The police arrested several Chinese today as they tried to mark the third anniversary of the army's attack on democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, and detained and roughed up foreign journalists covering the incident.

file: Chinese Region Uses New Law to Sterilize Mentally Retarded.txt
text:
ï»¿
The provincial government in this poverty-stricken region of northwestern China is aggressively enforcing a new law requiring the sterilization of mentally retarded people.
So far this year, officials here say, more than 1,000 people have been sterilized under the law, which requires people with significant mental retardation to be sterilized if they are married or intend to be married. 
If the couple evade the law and the woman becomes pregnant, she must have an abortion.
The law was approved by the provincial Parliament a year ago and took effect at the beginning of the year here in Gansu province, where it directly affects about 30,000 retarded people out of a population of 21 million.
Law Receives Wide Praise
The law has been hailed nationwide, and officials say that the national Legislature and half a dozen provincial governments are thinking of adopting similar legislation. 
Several provinces have sent delegations here to study the measure as they consider drafting their own laws.
''The purpose of the law is to raise the quality of our population and of our nation,'' Miao Xia, the deputy head of the Gansu Province Family Planning Association, said in an interview. 
''We want to solve the poverty problem in part by raising the quality of the population.''
As Miss Miao acknowledged, however, the new law raises questions of morality and the role of legislation: Does society have a right to force people to be sterilized?
If a citizen has committed no crime, but happens to be retarded, can the state intervene to the point of forcing sterilization or an abortion?
Â 
Different Views in the West
The law is an echo of the eugenics movement in the West earlier in this century. 
Tens of thousands of ''mental defectives'' were sterilized across the United States, mostly between the 1920's and the 1950's.
In Virginia, which kept records, about 8,300 were sterilized between 1924 and 1972 under a state law providing for compulsory sterilization of the mentally disabled. 
The law was upheld in a landmark Supreme Court ruling of 1927 in which Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes made a now notorious comment: ''Three generations of imbeciles are enough.''
In Nazi Germany, a system of eugenic health courts ordered the sterilizations of more than half a million people from 1933 to 1940. 
They were judged by the courts to be suffering from mental retardation, physical deformities, schizophrenia and other illnesses.
In most Western countries, such sterilization programs have been sharply curtailed in response to public furor. 
The Chinese sterilization law could escalate longstanding complaints by the United States Government over China's population control policies, which seek to limit the number of children born and impose penalties on couples who violate the rule. 
[President Bush vetoed a $14.6 billion foreign aid bill Sunday night, objecting specifically to an allocation of $15 million for the United Nations Population Fund. 
Foes of abortion in the United States have opposed its financing on the ground that the agency performs work in China, whose population program includes abortion and sterilization.] Individual Vs. 
Society But in China there has been almost no public reaction to the sterilization law. 
Some Chinese intellectuals observe that their nation is inspired not by the notion of an individual's rights, or theories of social contract that limit the state, but by a Confucian heritage in which the individual is subordinated to the good of society.
Before the law was approved, the discussion centered not so much on ethics as on practical questions such as how the law would be enforced, and whether the mentally retarded were likely to have mentally retarded children.
''Some people said that ordinary people can have an idiot for a child, while two idiots can have an ordinary child,'' said Wang Jian, the Secretary General of the Gansu Population Studies Association. 
''But we explained that even if their child is normal, it will carry a gene for idiocy.''
The degree to which mental retardation is hereditary has been vigorously debated in the West, and no clear consensus has emerged.
Â 
How the Law Applies
The Chinese provincial law applies to people with moderate or serious mental retardation, such as those with an IQ of 49 or below. 
The retardation must be congenital and must be confirmed by a doctor.
The law has initially been put into effect in four particularly poor counties in Gansu, and has been accompanied by a major publicity campaign to convince people of the measure's importance. 
The arguments are not aimed at the mentally retarded themselves, for they are deemed insufficiently aware to react much one way or another, but at their families.
Many of the mentally retarded are married to people of average mental ability, and their spouses have not been enthusiastic about the law, some officials acknowledge. 
While their partners would not have to be sterilized themselves, they would be prevented from conceiving children within the marriage.
Â 
Policy Is Criticized
Two leading American geneticists say that the number of mentally retarded children would not be significantly reduced by sterilization of mentally retarded people.
''There are many causes of mental disease and deficiency - some genetic, some environmental, some simple and some complex,'' said Dr. James F. Crow, emeritus professor of genetics at the University of Wisconsin. 
''The Chinese program as described seems exceedingly crude.''
Scientists said it was likely that less than half of the mentally retarded acquired their disability genetically.
''For a good many of these sterilizations, there would be no genetic basis,'' said Dr. James V. Neel, professor of human genetics at the University of Michigan.
About 1 percent of the world population suffers from mental retardation. 
Dr. Neel estimated that it would take approximately 20 generations to reduce the frequency of a gene from 1 percent of the population to one-tenth of 1 percent.
Although scientists said the Chinese plan had little scientific merit, they suggested that sociological arguments could be made for such a plan. 
For example, ''one can argue that affected persons do not provide a good environment for their children and should not have them for that reason,'' Dr. Crow said.

file: Chinese Seem to Be Risking More Open Protests.txt
text:
ï»¿
The campaign by Deng Xiaoping and other Chinese leaders for faster economic change seems to be having an unintended effect: Dissidents and ordinary citizens are becoming a bit bolder in challenging the authorities.
Partly because the hard-liners appear to be losing ground as the airwaves fill with calls for reform, many Chinese say they find the atmosphere looser and less ominous. 
Some say that the fear that has gripped the country for the last three years, since the Tiananmen Square crackdown of June 1989, is gradually easing.
Consequently, some dissidents are no longer hiding their activities. 
They now openly meet with foreign reporters, write for foreign publications and denounce human rights abuses in their country.
Â 
Overseas Publication
Zhang Weiguo, a Shanghai journalist whose newspaper, The World Economic Herald, was closed during the Tiananmen democracy movement, is one of several democracy advocates who seem less afraid of the leadership than it is of him.
"I'm writing more articles now than when I was at The Herald," Mr. Zhang said in a recent interview in Shanghai. 
Since his articles cannot be published in China, he writes about China for leading newspapers in Taiwan and Hong Kong, and he has given telephone interviews to the BBC's Chinese-language service.
The security apparatus is clearly alarmed about such growing boldness, but it seems at a loss how to react. 
So the authorities settle for harassing Mr. Zhang, summoning him periodically for interrogation, as well as threatening him and refusing to allow him to leave Shanghai. 
But Mr. Zhang, who spent more than 20 months in prison after the 1989 crackdown, continues to speak.
Perhaps the only effective way to silence someone so fearless would be to re-arrest him and sentence him to a long prison term. 
But this might provoke a furor abroad, reinforce the image of China as a brutal and repressive place and increase the chance of American trade sanctions.
Â 
Order vs. Freedom
The treatment of Mr. Zhang is relatively lenient compared with the repression of a few years ago -- in 1989, for example, a marine biology student named Chen Lantao was sentenced to 18 years simply for speaking against the Government.
As fear diminishes, China may be becoming a more open country -- but perhaps also a less stable one. 
For the three years after the army's crackdown, in which hundreds were killed, thousands hurt and many more imprisoned, the peace was preserved through a balance of terror: The people were afraid of the Government and the Government was afraid of the people.
Some of that fear lingers on both sides, but less than before. 
Some in the Government acknowledge their apprehension that people could eventually take to the streets and overthrow the Communists, but there is a clear division within the leadership about the nature of the threat.
Hard-liners say the risk comes primarily from the dissidents and from contact with the West, and so they favor harsh repression. 
But others -- including Mr. Deng, the 88-year-old senior leader -- suggest that dissidents will get nowhere as long as the economy is booming, and so the leaders fear trade sanctions perhaps more than outspoken critics.
Still, there are several indications that the greater boldness has affected not only dissidents but also ordinary Chinese, although in ways that are not overtly political.
When application forms to buy stock ran out in the southern city of Shenzhen last month, some 50,000 would-be investors accused the Government of corruption and rampaged on the streets.
"That rioting would never have occurred in the immediate aftermath of the Tiananmen crackdown," said a Chinese journalist in Beijing. 
"But this year, with all the new talk about reform, people are feeling more hopeful and braver than before."
The journalist added, however, that most people are still afraid of openly criticizing the Government. 
For now, a repeat of large-scale pro-democracy demonstrations is impossible, he said.
"Lots of people are willing to be followers," he said. 
"But no one wants to be the first to say anything. 
There's a saying: the first bird in the flock is the one that gets shot. 
So there are plenty of birds that want to fly, but not in front."
The greater public boldness reached Beijing late last month, when China's normally docile soccer fans stormed out of Workers Stadium in Beijing after a loss to South Korea and marched angrily down the middle of the street. 
They shouted curses at the Chinese team, the head coach and the police.
It was the third outburst in a week from soccer fans, and the authorities were quick to arrest a few people and denounce the behavior.
The official Beijing Daily wrote, "These riotous acts, totally alien to China's long-noted politeness and courtesy, smeared the image of Beijing as well as our country."
Chinese soccer hooligans may seem like paragons of obedience compared to the more violent British soccer rioters, but in one sense the disruptions here are much more significant than in Britain.
The glue that keeps most Western governments together is public support for the system; in China, according to many foreign diplomats and Chinese, the adhesive is fear. 
So if Chinese soccer fans dare to march on the streets because of dissatisfaction with a sports competition, there is at least some chance that they may dare to protest the form of government.
Â 
Pitfalls in Leniency
Recent history also suggests that a diminishing fear of the authorities might eventually lead to political protest.
Throughout the last four decades, the times when Chinese have protested against the Government have not generally been the periods of greatest discontent. 
Rather, they have occurred when people perceived -- usually incorrectly -- that the atmosphere was sufficiently lenient that they could get away with it.
To be sure, the authorities do their best to let people know that they will not get away with it. 
Some democracy campaigners, though not the most prominent ones, reportedly were quietly arrested over the last few months, and political prisoners in northeastern China recently smuggled out a letter complaining of continued beatings in their jail cells.
The latest police move occurred today, when the authorities detained Shen Tong, a democracy advocate who had returned from exile in the United States, as he prepared to hold a news conference. 
If Mr. Shen's return was a sign of the dissidents' new boldness, his detention was a signal that the authorities are willing to fight back.
So far, however, the Government has not reacted to another recent development that may cause security officials to furrow their brows. 
Three prominent independent-minded Chinese openly joined the board of a New York-based organization, Human Rights in China, that is often critical of the Beijing authorities. 
While the Government has not punished the three, it is not clear that it will allow them to leave China to attend a board meeting in the fall.
This relative restraint is having an unintended effect: It is skewing the incentive structure for dissidents. 
A few years ago, any Chinese knew that denouncing the Government would mean immediate dismissal, arrest and incarceration. 
But now, some critics suffer only harassment, and they achieve international renown and invitations to be visiting scholars at foreign universities.
Likewise, relatives of political prisoners used to believe that they were best off keeping quiet so as not to offend the authorities. 
But in several recent cases, family members have concluded that they are better off causing a fuss or at least speaking to the foreign press. 
In part they believe that attention in the West may result in shorter sentences for their loved ones, and in part they seem to feel more daring and assertive than they used to.
"With all the talk about reform, the Government has been telling us to be bolder in our actions," said a worker in his 20's, flashing a mischievous grin. 
"And so that's what's happening. 
We're bolder."

file: Chinese Set Off Their Biggest Nuclear Explosion.txt
text:

China today set off the largest underground nuclear test it has ever conducted, the State Department said. 
The explosion was thought to have a yield of about one megaton, equivalent to a million tons of TNT.
The blast, which took place about 1 A.M. Eastern daylight time, had 70 times the explosive power of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima, and exceeded the 150-kiloton limit observed by Washington and Moscow under a 1990 treaty, scientists said.
The Bush Administration said it regretted the action by Beijing and urged restraint.
Â 
Limit on Underground Tests
There were sharp condemnations of China in Congress. 
Legislators from both major parties have been critical of what they see as an unacceptably conciliatory policy toward China by President Bush.
[The Chinese Foreign Ministry issued a statement confirming that Beijing had held a nuclear test. 
The statement said China was in favor of "complete prohibition on nuclear tests within the framework of effective nuclear disarmament."]
The Chinese test was only one-fifth as powerful as the largest underground test by the United States, a five-megaton blast in Alaska on Nov. 
6, 1971, the most powerful underground nuclear explosion on record. 
A megaton is 1,000 kilotons.
The largest underground test by the Soviet Union was a 2.8 to 4 megaton blast on Oct. 
27, 1973, a year before Moscow and Washington signed a treaty limiting the size of those explosions to 150 kilotons. 
The pact was ratified in 1990.
The Chinese test comes on the heels of persistent reports that Beijing is selling missile technology to Middle Eastern nations, and at a time when Beijing is rejecting all criticism of its human-rights record.
Arms-control experts also seized the chance to criticize the Bush Administration for its opposition to a comprehensive international test-ban treaty.
China's last and largest previous underground test, an explosion of between 50 and 200 kilotons, was on Aug. 
16, 1990.
The United States set off two underground nuclear explosions this year in Nevada, on March 26 and April 30. 
Both were reported to be less than 150 kilotons.
Large underground tests, even on the scale of today's blast in China, are considerably smaller than the atmospheric explosions of the 1950's and 1960's. 
On Feb. 
28, 1954, the United States tested a 15 megaton bomb at Bikini Atoll in the Pacific. 
The largest atmospheric test on record was conducted by the Soviet Union, a 58-megaton explosion on Oct. 
30, 1961.
Atmospheric tests were prohibited by the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty, signed by more than 100 countries.
Today's Chinese underground explosion was situated in Xinjiang Province in northwestern China by Scandinavian seismologists, according to reports from Stockholm. 
In Hong Kong, scientists at first thought they were registering an earthquake.
"This suggests that the Chinese must be trying to develop large yield, offensive nuclear warheads for long-range missiles," said Gary Milhollin, director of the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control. 
"This is a city-buster."
But he emphasized that China was still no threat to the United States in the development of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
Richard A. Boucher, the State Department spokesman, said, "We regret that the Chinese have conducted this test and that they are not demonstrating the same restraint as shown by Russia, ourselves, or the other nuclear weapons states."
Â 
Cold-War Mentality
China is not a party to the Threshold Test Ban Treaty between the former Soviet Union and the United States, which came into effect in December 1990. 
Under that pact, underground tests are limited to 150 kilotons.
"It is rather ironic that the United States would criticize other countries for testing," said Dunbar Lockwood, senior analyst at the Arms Control Association, a private research organization. 
"The United States under the Reagan and Bush Administrations has been one of the major impediments to progress toward a comprehensive test ban."
Mr. Milhollin described the Chinese test as illustrative of a cold-war mentality in Beijing. 
He added: "This is the price we're paying for not having a worldwide comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty. 
It means China can improve its ability to destroy U.S cities at long range by testing."
Leonard S. Spector, a nuclear-weapons expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace who has recently been in China, said in an interview that Beijing's test could take the pressure off the Bush Administration to agree to a comprehensive test ban. 
Pressure has been growing internationally and in Congress for that action.
Â 
Moratorium on Tests
In October 1991, the former Soviet President, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, announced a one-year moratorium on the testing of nuclear weapons. 
Boris N. Yelstin, the Russian President, has suggested in public remarks that he is preparing to resume testing this fall if there is no reciprocal movement from the United States.
The French have also stopped testing to encourage international action on a comprehensive ban.
"Thoughtful advocates of testing restraint think that a comprehensive test ban might draw in India," Mr. Spector said.
Senator Alan Cranston, Democrat of California and chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on East Asia, reacted to reports of today's test by calling China a "renegade nation."
"This test will strongly reinforce Congressional efforts, which I once again will help lead, to deny China most-favored-nation trade staus unless China complies with international non-proliferation standards," Senator Cranston said in a statement.

The new tactic represents a major expansion of the far-flung smuggling networks that for years have brought small groups of Chinese laborers to the United States through Canada and Central America.
International Chinese crime syndicates, many with roots in ancient secret societies called triads or tongs, have begun to add their resources and muscle to the enterprise of human smuggling, Mr. Nicholl said.
The immigration service is barely keeping pace, and even in cases where immigrants are caught here they often are released pending hearings, or for lack of detention centers, and simply disappear into an underworld of forced labor, drug dealing and crime.
"This is kind of 19th-century stuff now where the tongs are not just shipping illegals but trafficking in people as human slaves," said Peter Kwong, a professor of political science at the State University of New York College at Old Westbury.
For a price of $25,000 to $30,000, part of which goes to bribe Chinese officials, poor farmers and laborers from southern China are following earlier immigrants in search of prosperity in America. 
And like their predecessors who helped build the nation's railroads, most are destined for years of servitude as they labor to pay off the cost of their passage.
"Most of them end up in pretty squalid conditions as indentured servants in restaurants and packing houses and garment factories," said Mr. Nicholl, who is the immigration service's expert on Chinese smuggling. 
Others "can end up actually enslaved to the triads as prostitutes or enforcers or drug runners or pickpockets."
He said as many as 25,000 Chinese have entered the country illegally, mostly smuggled in by air, in the last three years; the ocean routes appeared to have been put into operation about a year ago.
Most of the new immigrants come from Fujian, a southern coastal Chinese province with a history of migration and human smuggling, and most are headed for the Fujianese enclave of New York's Chinatown, he said.
Â 
Kidnapped and Beaten
There, Mr. Kwong said, they are subject to exploitation and to a growing wave of violence by the syndicates enforcing the repayment of their debts with torture, kidnapping and sometimes murder.
"Mostly they are handcuffed within an apartment and severely beaten with anything from claw hammers to sticks," said Lieut. 
Joseph Pollini of the New York City Police Department. 
"They are told they have to pay $10,000 or $15,000 above their original fee, and a lot of drastic things take place."
Just today, he said, the last of eight men was convicted of kidnapping in the first such incident to have been uncovered, in November 1990. 
Since then, arrests have been made in seven similar kidnappings.
Partly because of the violence surrounding the smuggling operations, the department is forming a new unit to deal with Asian organized crime.
"The tragic thing is that these illegals are so desperate to get money that they are willing to work at any price," Mr. Kwong said. 
"So the situation in Chinatown is that wages are getting lower and lower."
A Fujianese service economy has sprung up in New York, including "travel agencies" that help coordinate contacts and payoffs to the smugglers.
"I heard of one woman on East Broadway who emptied her village, which was about 2,000 people," Mr. Kwong said, "and she was not the only one doing that."
The Fujianese are known as tough and hard-working, he said, and those who have paid off their debts after several years of labor are beginning to enjoy the rewards of their rough passage by opening Chinese takeout restaurants, mainly in poor areas of New York City.
Â 
Dreams of Success
Dreams of such success inspired the 84 men packed for 50 days into the fetid hold of the 150-foot Taiwan-registered trawler Jinn Yin No. 1, which was seized off the California coast last month.
"It was my goal and my dream to come to the United States," said G. Ling, a 22-year-old student who comes from a family of truck drivers and who is now being held at an immigration service detention center in Long Beach pending a hearing on his status. 
"But we suffered so much: so crowded, so cold in the ship, not enough food, no water to drink, no place to wash."
C. Chen, 31, a professional diver who, like Mr. Ling, declined to give his full name, said the terrified passengers wept, prayed and vomited as the rusting boat, with its crew of seven, struggled through a typhoon and survived two fires.
He said many people from his grandparents' village near the Fujianese city of Fuzhou had come to America and prospered and that some of these had returned home for visits, tempting others to follow with stories of prosperity.
"Since the day I was born I wanted to come to America," Mr. Chen said, speaking through an interpreter. 
"We wanted to apply to the United States government to come the legal way, but too many people want to come. 
With so many people in China how long would it take us?
The rest of our lives?"
In 1990, the most recent year for which figures are available, 31,800 people succeeded in immigrating legally to the United States from mainland China, putting that country in sixth place as a source of legal immigration.
Gu Kechen, a 21-year-old carpenter, said he had made a $2,500 down payment in China and that relatives in New York had guaranteed the balance of his $25,000 passage. 
"I don't know how I will pay them back," he said. 
"The important thing was to get to America."
Though they are now subject to deportation, the men under detention here still stand a chance of completing their journey to New York. 
Many will be released on bond either because of overcrowding at detention centers or because they apply for political asylum, officials and immigration lawyers said. 
When that happens, the chances are that they will simply disappear.
The results are hundreds of millions of dollars in profits for the traffickers, who operate what Mr. Nicholl called "the most sophisticated and largest and most expensive smuggling operation that exists in the world today."
As of last year, he said, "We have identified as many as 30 different smuggling routes coming into the United States."
People who cannot pay the full price for passage, Mr. Kwong said, sometimes travel as couriers on a drug-smuggling run from Fujian through Burma and Thailand, with stops in Latin America.
"Every time we get a handle on what they are doing and how they are doing it, things change," Mr. Nicholl said. 
When the first shipload was captured off Los Angeles last September with 118 smuggled passengers, he said, "We were sort of in a state of shock."

file: Chinese Students in U.S. Say Beijing Has Harassed Them.txt
text:
ï»¿
Since the Chinese Government began its crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators last month, Chinese students and scholars in the United States who took part in similar demonstrations in this country say they have been harassed by anonymous callers as well as by Chinese consular officials.
The harassment has taken several forms, from a man watching for hours from a car parked outside a house outside Boston where Chinese graduate students operate a communications center, to telephone calls that warn students to look out for their futures, to visits by officials to university campuses, looking for names of students involved in pro-democracy activities.
Incidents have been reported from California to Long Island, and several have been reported to the Federal Bureau of Investigation and to the State Department.
Representative Tom Lantos, Democrat of California, met with Chinese students from the San Francisco area this month. 
As a result of their complaints, which included reports of telephone harassment, the Congressman sent a letter July 11 to Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d, asking for an investigation of the Chinese Embassy and its five consulates around the country, an aide in his office, Bob King, said.
Denial From Consular Official
An official at the Chinese Consulate in New York, Ye Qiping, said keeping in touch with students was ''part of our normal work,'' and said no one had sought names of students who demonstrated for democracy.
''The students have no clear picture about the situation that happened in China, so they took part in demonstrations in the States,'' Mr. Ye said. 
''We can understand their feelings.''
Liu Yuan, a Brandeis University graduate student in anthropology who volunteers at the China Information Center, part of the Walker Center for Ecumenical Exchange in Newton, Mass., said the center received three or four calls a day from Chinese-speaking callers until last week, when they dwindled to one a day or less. 
An article about student harassment was published in The Boston Globe last week.
Â 
'A Lot of Detailed Questions'
Some of the anonymous callers ''just ask a lot of detailed questions about what we are doing,'' Mr. Liu said.
Other callers warn the person who picks up the phone to be careful, Mr. Liu said. 
''They would say things like, 'Don't do too much,' or 'Be careful about your future,' '' he said. 
They hang up quickly and never identify themselves, he added, so it is difficult to tell whether they are Government officials making veiled threats or just people worried about the students.
Gordon J. Schultz, executive director of the Walker Center, said he received several calls on July 14 in which the caller growled like an animal. 
At the end of one such call, the person snarled, ''Shut up!'' in Chinese, he said.
Other calls suggested that the students buy guns for their movement, and some were placed to students' homes, warning them to ''stop right away, we know what you're doing.''
One student was terrified when the caller said he knew many details about the student's life, Mr. Schultz said.
Â 
A Visit to Stony Brook
''I'm not sure I was expecting it,'' Mr. Schultz said. 
''And we don't know where it's coming from. 
It doesn't have to be the Chinese Government. 
It could be a right-wing kook, or a kook being used by the Chinese Government.''
Lan Yishen, a historian doing graduate work at the Stony Brook, L.I., campus of the State University of New York, said a Chinese consulate official named Zhao Lingshi appeared suddenly at Stony Brook last month.
''He asked about my activity,'' said Mr. Lan, who helped organize a group called Human Rights in China. 
''He asked somebody else about me, and he wanted to get the names of the students who had been taking part in the demonstrations.''
Dr. Wang Zhaozhang, 43, a researcher in physics at Princeton University, asked permission late last year from the Chinese Academy of Science to stay three more years. 
The academy said it would arrange to have his student visa extended through the consulate in New York.
Â 
Visa Application Pending
Shortly after students and workers were shot to death by Chinese troops in Beijing, Dr. Wang said, he helped organize a Princeton student protest over the killings. 
The group published a statement on June 13 that said in part that they no longer recognized Prime Minister Li Peng's Government.
On June 16, Dr. Wang said, his wife received a telephone call from Wang Haozhong, the educational consul in New York. 
According to Dr. Wang, whose wife taped the call, the official said:
''If you are one of the organizers of this group and you do not recognize the Chinese Government, well, we are the Chinese Government. 
You do not need us to help you do anything. 
If you have any questions, any problems, any difficulties, we will not help you.''
Dr. Wang's visa application is still pending. 
He said he did not know what would happen. 
''There are some people, I don't know who, in Princeton who reported this to the consulate,'' he said. 
''I am a scientist. 
I do not want to take part in too much politics. 
But after June 3 and June 4, I cannot keep quiet. 
I presented my political attitude.''
He is also friendly with Fang Lizhi, the astrophysicist and dissident who took refuge in the American Embassy in Beijing after the killings, and believes that may account for the Government's singling him out.
Mr. Ye, the education consul, said he had ''no clear idea'' about Dr. Wang's situation and could not comment.
Some students have not been harassed, and they theorize that those doing the harassing only bother with people they think they can intimidate.
''They dare not to call me,'' said Tang Yiming, a Columbia graduate student and poet who coordinates student groups in the New York area. 
''They maybe think I am too counterrevolutionary so it's no use to call me.''

file: Chinese Tale of Betrayal, With a Twist.txt
text:
ï»¿
One of the most searing images of the crackdown on the democracy movement in China was the scene of a young woman being praised on national television for turning in her younger brother to the police for his role as a student leader.
The student leader, Zhou Fengsuo, had fled to his sister's home in this city in central China, hoping to avoid arrest. 
The television footage related that the sister and her husband allowed him to stay with them, but then on June 13 reported him to the authorities.
The incident was widely regarded as a symbol of the relentlessness and ferocity of the Government's crackdown. 
It recalled the Cultural Revolution, when Red Guards denounced their parents as counterrevolutionaries. 
It provoked soul searching among Chinese intellectuals, who pondered how, in a society where family ties have traditionally been so important, someone could deliver her own brother to the police. 
The answer may be that she didn't. 
The scuttlebutt in the city where it happened is that the sister, Zhou Wenrong, did not intend to alert the police. 
Moreover, it seems that the vast majority of people still do regard family ties as paramount, for Miss Zhou has become the pariah of Xian.
New Version of Events
The account that is circulating everywhere here is that Miss Zhou confided to her boss in the hope that the boss could visit her home and persuade the young man to turn himself in. 
It was the boss who notified the police.
Mr. Zhou was shown on television in handcuffs that evening, but there has been no subsequent indication that he has been tried or sentenced. 
Most knowledgeable Chinese doubt that he would be sentenced to death, but they say a sentence of 10 years to life in prison could well be handed down for student leaders at his level.
''She just meant to get her brother some counseling,'' said a 39-year-old worker. 
''All the neighbors knew he was staying here, and she was afraid one of them would report him. 
That would have been terrible for her career and her husband's, so she wanted Zhou Fengsuo to turn himself in.''
If all the neighbors did indeed know that Mr. Zhou was staying with the family, but did not report him despite an appeal on television for information about him, that suggests a surprising lack of cooperation with the authorities. 
It is the opposite of the impression that the authorities were trying to convey.
Â 
'Everybody Hates Her'
Those accounts of what happened are impossible to confirm. 
Local authorities refused a request to interview Miss Zhou, saying she was ill.
Nevertheless, nearly everyone here gives the same account of what happened. 
Likewise, the contempt and dislike for Miss Zhou seem widespread.
''Everybody hates her,'' a woman in her early 30's said. 
''She is afraid to go out on the street because of all the threatening letters she has received. 
People say she is going crazy. 
If she does go mad, her parents will have lost both children.''
The ostracism of Miss Zhou might suggest that everyone here is a staunch supporter of the student movement. 
In fact the situation is more complex, partly because the intense propaganda on television has had an effect on residents here. 
People here do not believe the Government accounts of what happened, but the images of bloodied soldiers have persuaded them that the democracy movement was not as pure as they had thought.
Â 
Modestly Successful Propaganda
''We are all Chinese,'' a young woman said. 
''It's wrong to kill the students and it's just as wrong to kill the troops. 
It's all very bad.''
To the extent that people have any sympathy for the crackdown, it is not founded on the Government's justification of protecting Communism. 
On the contrary, it is based on the belief that only when order is restored can people make money.
The propaganda has been modestly successful in portraying the democracy movement as responsible for the turmoil that threatened China's modernization policy. 
Those who expressed reservations about the movement said that while its aims were good, its later stages reminded them of the turmoil of the Cultural Revolution.
''I went through those 10 years of chaos,'' said a middle-aged worker. 
''Nobody in my generation wants to go through that again.''
Â 
Few Tourists, Little Disruption
Xian is one of the tourism capitals of China because of the tombs and other historical sites from the time when it was the cultural, political and commercial center of Asia during the Tang dynasty more than 1,000 years ago. 
These days, however, there are scarcely any tourists in town. 
The best hotel in the city, the Golden Flowers, is running at just over 30 percent occupancy, compared with nearly 100 percent a year ago, and it has slashed its rates from $115 a night to just $50.
There is no military presence, and no obvious threat to tourists. 
At least 43 ''counterrevolutionaries'' have been arrested in Xian, and investigations are under way in many Government departments and in the local Academy of Social Sciences to ferret out others. 
But for most people, life seems to be going on pretty much as before.
