file: Chinese Trade Practices Raising Concern in U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's growing trade surplus with the United States, expected to be surpassed only by Japan's next year, is emerging as an important irritant in relations between the two countries.
Administration officials and some members of Congress say China's surplus, which is expected to overtake Germany's and Taiwan's, is in part a result of unfair trade practices.
The Americans complain that the Chinese are "dumping" products, or selling them at below cost, and are circumventing United States import quotas by shipping goods through other countries.
"The surpluses mean we're headed for trouble with our economic as well as political relations with China," said Senator John Heinz, Republican of Pennsylvania.
"And when you engage in unfair trade practices, you lose friends fast," said Mr. Heinz, a member of the Senate Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over trade issues.
The growing trade gap is expected to figure prominently in the Congressional debate next year on trade with China. 
The issue before Congress is whether to strip China of commercial privileges and raise tariffs on billions of dollars of toys, apparel and other Chinese exports here. 
Chinese textiles represent one-fifth of its United States surplus, and China manufactures about half the toys imported by the United States.
Each June, China's "most favored nation" treatment, which keeps its tariffs as low as for most other countries, is subject to review by the President. 
President Bush decided this year to continue the special treatment.
On Oct. 
18, the House, still mindful of the crushing of the democracy movement at Tiananmen Square in 1989, voted to punish Beijing by removing the trade privilege the Chinese have enjoyed since 1980. 
But , the House's 247-to-174 vote was short of the two-thirds that was needed to override the President's decision.
Next year, lawmakers say, the concern over trade surpluses and trade fairness could tilt the balance. 
Chinese surpluses have soared from $6 billion last year to an expected $11 billion this year, with Japan expected to come to more than $40 billion and Taiwan and Germany to around $12 billion each. 
Next year, a $15 billion surplus is forecast for China.
In an increasing number of cases, the Chinese are being accused of dumping, or selling exports below cost, in the United States in order to raise market share. 
Under American trade law, duties on dumped products can be raised to offset the unfair advantages.
A number of cases have been brought by the textile industry, which has taken the brunt of the Chinese export offensive. 
China shipped two billion square yards of textiles here last year -- everything from cotton nightwear to wool sweaters -- compared with 325 million square yards in 1980.
The textile industry has won dumping duties against products like cotton print cloth and industrial wiping cloths. 
Other dumping cases involved axes and sledgehammers and small electric fans.
Â 
Using Other Countries
Textile industry and customs officials insist that the Chinese are circumventing American textile import quotas by moving goods to the United States through Macao, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines and other countries.
"In our opinion, the Chinese are engaged in massive quota fraud," said Carlos F. J. Moore, executive vice president of the American Textile Manufacturers Institute, an industry trade association.
What makes the issue potentially explosive is that China is one of the few remaining non-market economies. 
Far from reflecting a lack of American competitiveness or supply-and-demand forces of the marketplace, its trade surpluses result from targets, quotas, administrative guidance and other calculated decisions by Beijing authorities.
"This is somewhat alarming," noted Roger W. Sullivan, president of the United States-China Business Council, "because until recently, China was making the point that it was not a mercantilist nation and not seeking to pile up foreign exchange."
Â 
Restatement of Doctrine
Mr. Sullivan, whose organization represents American companies doing business in China, said the change in Beijing's thinking could be seen in a recent statement by its Soviet-educated Prime Minister, Li Peng, that China's policy was not only to push exports but also to limit imports and bring in only necessary goods. 
In effect, it was a restatement of the old Communist doctrine of economic self-reliance.
Before the 1989 crackdown, more liberal policies had allowed for a rapid increase in imports and resulted in a large drain on hard currency reserves.
American officials say they have raised the issues of surpluses and trade unfairness in virtually all recent discussions with the Chinese.
The latest was a meeting in Washington on Dec. 
10 and 11 of senior Chinese trade officials led by the Vice Minister for Trade, Gu Yongjiang, and Americans led by the Under Secretary of Commerce, J. Michael Farren.
Â 
Warning of Political Problem
American officials say they warned the Chinese that the surpluses could become a significant political problem if not addressed.
"Our objective," said a senior Administration official, "is to get the Chinese to go back again to reforming their trading system toward more market-oriented operations."
American officials raised both the issues of creating trade surpluses -- through quotas, import substitution programs, export subsidies and other measures -- and of circumventing textile and apparel quotas through third countries.
Although the Chinese officials promised to investigate the accusations of irregularities, one American official said the Chinese were "not very sympathetic to our problem."
This official added, "They will pursue their interests and get away with anything they can."
Tien Mingwang, Minister Counselor at the Chinese Embassy here, denied that his Government was trying to create trade surpluses by closing its market to imports. 
He cited a special mission to the United States last October that bought $700 million of wheat, chemical fertilizers, timber, and other products.
"This was the first purchasing mission in our history," he said, adding that others may follow. 
"This is to show our desire for further expansion of imports from your country."
He said his Government would investigate all the trade accusations. 
"We would like to put the trade in textiles on a healthy basis," he stressed.

file: Chinese Trials End_ Fate of Hundreds Unclear.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a wave of trials ending Tuesday, Chinese courts sentenced 18 of the nation's best-known dissidents to prison for terms ranging up to 13 years. 
But while those trials have ended, almost nothing is known about the hundreds of others who are in prison for taking part in the Tiananmen democracy movement.
The Chinese have never given an accounting of those arrested in the crackdown beginning in June 1989, but most estimates are that more than 1,000 people are still in prison, detention centers or re-education camps for their involvement in the Tiananmen Square protests.
"Just the cases that will serve their purposes are announced, and the rest are never reported," said Robin Munro, a Hong Kong-based researcher for Asia Watch, a human rights organization. 
"We certainly believe these trials are the tip of the iceberg."
Among the others are such people as Han Dongfang, a 28-year-old railway employee who led a Beijing workers group in support of the students; Wu Jiaxiang, a Communist Party researcher who sympathized with the students and was arrested in July 1989, and Chen Ting, a worker arrested forhelping to organize protests in the central Chinese city of Hefei.
Asia Watch has compiled a list of 960 names of people believed imprisoned, and many others have been quietly sentenced without their cases coming to public attention. 
Family members often say they dare not seek help from foreigners.
"In our hearts, we feel terrible for not speaking out," said a relative of a young man who is serving an eight-year prison sentence. 
The family decided not to report the prisoner's name to foreign human rights workers for fear that the family members themselves would get in trouble."Some day, things will change," the relative said, "but for now we must keep silent."
The stiffest sentence in the latest trials was 13 years. 
But in occasional trials in the provinces, local leaders of protests were given even harsher punishments. 
In Shandong Province, for example, a 22-year-old worker named Zhang Jie was officially reported to have been sentenced to 18 years in prison for making a speech denouncing the army crackdown in Beijing.
Workers are typically given much longer sentences than intellectuals, and often face a more physically punishing prison regime. 
Although intellectuals may risk serving their terms in solitary confinement, workers are more likely to risk beatings, freezing nights in unheated cells, and near-starvation rations.In addition to those formally tried, a large number of protesters were sent to re-education camps. 
The police are allowed to send people to such camps for up to three years without going through the courts. 
The United States State Department report on human rights, issued this month, says that just two re-education camps near Beijing housed more than 800 youths detained extrajudicially for involvement in the Tiananmen protests.
So far, there has been no public reaction within China to the trials, and most Chinese express relatively little outrage or even interest. 
Some attribute the muted reaction to a yearning by people to withdraw from political affairs, which they say are burdened with painful memories and a feeling of hopelessness.
"People noticed the sentences, but itwasn't a big thing," said one Chinese who is moderately critical of the Government. 
"People are much more interested in the gulf war."
Family members of political prisoners have been warned not to talk to foreign journalists, and this places them in an agonizing position: do they disclose what they regard as outrageous injustices, if the consequence will only be further punishment inflicted on them and their loved ones?
"They are really villains, trying to exploit the love a woman has for her husband," Hou Xiaotian, wife of one of the dissidents who was sentenced to 13 years, wrote in an open letter last month. 
In the letter she described how prison guards refused to accept items she had brought for her husband unless she disclosed her contacts with correspondents.

file: Chinese Upheaval Shakes Italy_s Communists.txt
text:
ï»¿
The explosive events in China have sent shivers through Italy's faltering Communist Party, the largest in the West, and have emboldened Socialists who hope to emerge soon as the country's dominant left-wing group.
Communists here are bracing for what may prove to be unusually important elections for the European Parliament on June 18.
It clearly troubles party elders that because of China's turmoil Italians will vote with fresh memories of a Communist government that ordered its soldiers to shoot citizens demanding democracy. 
As a result, they have gone to considerable lengths to denounce Chinese leaders and to organize demonstrations of solidarity with the student-led democratic movement.
Perhaps more significantly for the future of Communism in Western Europe, the party secretary, Achille Occhetto, has gone further than ever to align himself with European social democratic movements in his continuing campaign to stop a decade-long slide at the polls. 
His efforts have even rekindled a public debate that arises periodically over whether it is time for the party to change its name. 
''We are not part of an international Communist movement,'' Mr. Occhetto said in a newspaper interview this week.
''In the East, communism is a term that has no relation any longerto its historic origins, and constitutes a political framework that is completely wrong,'' he said, adding, ''There is absolutely nothing left of communism as a unitary and organic system.''
Today, he called on the Government to freeze economic relations with China.
If Mr. Occhetto's damage-control strategy fails, the Socialist leader, former Prime Minister Bettino Craxi, is standing by to pick up the pieces.
Â 
Craxi Weary of Junior Role
Throughout the 1980's, the Socialists have been junior partners to the more numerous Christian Democrats in a series of coalition Governments, but Mr. Craxi is growing weary of the role. 
His ambition is to command an Italian left restructured under a single umbrella, but first his Socialists must overtake the Communists, who though weakening, have been second only to the Christian Democrats throughout the postwar era.
Thus, for him, the European parliamentary elections are far more critical than simply who will wind up going to Strasbourg. 
To drum up interest in the campaign, Mr. Craxi went so far as to help bring down the Government, through relentless badgering that finally impelled Prime Minister Ciriaco De Mita to resign three weeks ago.
While Mr. De Mita remains in office as caretaker over the shell of a Government, senior politicians have held endless consultations to figure out who should lead next. 
Their talks drag on and on, but a solution seems likely to elude them until after the so-called European elections.
Mr. Craxi was heartened last week by the results of local elections in 165 municipalities. 
For the first time, Socialist candidates won a bigger share of the vote than the Communists, 19.1 percent to 16.9 percent. 
In 1987 parliamentary elections, by comparison, the Socialists drew only 14 percent to the Communists' 22.6 percent.
The balloting in a relatively small number of localities was hardly conclusive. 
Mr. Occhetto dismissed it out of hand, saying his party lost primarily in Mafia-dominated towns in the South.
Nevertheless, political commentators say that if the results are duplicated on June 18, they may have a broad impact on the balance of party power, and could even trigger early national elections. 
At the least, it is said, they are likely to determine the shape of the next government.

file: CHINESE VISA BILL MAY FACE A VETO.txt
text:
ï»¿
Congress has passed a bill allowing Chinese students to stay in the United States after their visas expire. 
But Administration officials said today that President Bush might veto it at Beijing's request.
Chinese students active in the democracy movement overseas say they would face political persecution if forced to return to China.
Administration officials maintain that the bill is unnecessary because there is already an American clemency program for Chinese students. 
They say China dislikes the bill so much that Chinese authorities might end student exchanges with the United States if it becomes law.
'Planted the Seeds of Democracy'
Senator Alan K. Simpson, the assistant Republican leader in the Senate, said that on Nov. 
15 ''the Chinese Foreign Minister advised our Ambassador in Beijing that if this legislation is enacted, the Chinese Government will terminate outright the Fulbright scholarship program, as well as all other educational and cultural exchange programs with the United States.''
Such programs ''planted the seeds of democracy in China,'' the Wyoming Republican said.
In Beijing, a Chinese Government spokesman said today that the bill was unacceptable.
And a spokesman for the State Department said it opposed the bill.
Mr. Simpson said Mr. Bush would probably veto the measure.
Administration officials said Mr. Bush was aware that a veto would shock millions of Americans who sympathize with the Chinese students. 
But they said Mr. Bush, a former chief of the American mission in Beijing, did not want to offend the Chinese leaders if he could avoid it.
Â 
Warning on the Consequences
John H. Sununu, the President's chief of staff, said the Administration was still evaluating the bill and was concerned that it might have the ''unintended negative consequence'' of reducing opportunities for Chinese students to come here in the future.
The bill, introduced by Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, was approved in the House of Representatives on Sunday by a vote of 403 to 0 and in the Senate on Monday by voice vote.

Chinese Army troops crushed China's democracy movement and killed hundreds of protesters in Beijing on June 4. 
Since then, students at Chinese universities have been required to attend classes on party doctrine and ideology.

Chinese students in the United States said they hoped that Mr. Bush would not be swayed by Beijing's threats.

text:

P. V. Narasimha Rao and Li Peng, the Indian and Chinese Prime Ministers, concluded two days of talks here this week with China gaining an Indian statement of support for Chinese sovereignty over Tibet, and India apparently getting little in return.
Mr. Li, who left here on Friday, was the first Chinese Prime Minister to visit India in 31 years. 
The trip raised high expectations in the Indian Foreign Ministry, coming at a time when India, long a close ally of Soviet Union, and China are both ill at ease with the collapse of Communism in Europe. 
Both say they are seeking to create a new structure of relations in Asia and among developing countries generally.
Yet after two days of conversation, Mr. Li on issue after issue secured accommodations from the Indians without yielding on any significant points of his own.
The talks also brought some angry oratory against the United States and other wealthy nations. 
The two sides denounced what they called "the emerging international oligarchy," in the words of an Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman, and called for the creation of a world order where no country can "manipulate world affairs and play power politics."
Mr. Li, facing international opprobrium for his Government's policies toward Tibet, elicited an unequivocal Indian declaration that Tibet was a part of China. 
In the past, India has provided asylum to hundreds of thousands of Tibetan refugees.
For the Chinese Prime Minister's visit, though, Mr. Rao's officials rounded up hundreds of Tibetans and forcibly -- at times brutally -- halted protest marches to the Chinese Embassy. 
The harshness of police action against the Tibetans provoked an outcry in Parliament, and late Friday the Supreme Court ordered that all detained women and children be released from jail by today.
Even with that, India, which has been seeking support for its policies in Kashmir, a predominantly Muslim northern region seeking independence, obtained no commensurate declaration from the Chinese. 
Mr. Li merely repeated China's position that India and Pakistan, which also claims Kashmir, should resolve the issue peacefully.
Even India's concern about China's close relationship with Pakistan evidently did not come up in the two days of talks. 
The New Delhi Government, which charges Pakistan with arming Kashmiri separatists and harboring aggressive intentions, did not raise the matter of Beijing's significant weapons shipments to Pakistan, according to a Foreign Ministry spokesman.
Likewise, India failed to extract any concessions from the Chinese over its territory occupied by China after a fierce border war in 1962. 
The Government, Indian newspapers report, had been seeking some movement on the dispute, but Mr. Rao and Mr. Li simply agreed to let talks between lower-level working groups continue.
Mr. Rao did raise the issue of human rights with the Chinese leader, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said. 
But even then, he couched his remarks in terms that implied no criticism of China.
"The Indian Prime Minister said we give central importance to the issue of development," the spokesman, Aftab Seth, related at a briefing. 
"We pointed out that India's system was fully transparent, open and democratic with an independent judiciary. 
He said it was not desirable to use the question of human rights as a condition for denying aid to developing countries."
A senior Foreign Ministry official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, expressed frustration. 
"We don't know how to deal with the Chinese," he said. 
"We've always been a little afraid of them. 
Remember, Rao learned at the knee of Nehru. 
We Indians have never learned the art of tough negotiations."
Mr. Seth rejected the idea that the Chinese Prime Minister got the better of Mr. Rao. "The visit should be seen in a broader context," he said. 
"It is a factor for progress and stabilityI."
Three agreements were signed: one calling for resumption of some border trade, a second establishing consulates in Bombay and Shanghai, and the third providing for greater cooperation in space-related research and technology.

file: Chongqing Journal_China_s Dismal Truth_ 100 Million Out of Work.txt
text:
ï»¿
A score of grubby, lanky men marched into the cavernous and crowded Big Sheep Gully market, hauling buckets of potatoes, bricks and cloth on poles across their shoulders.
These men, who earn 64 cents a day for winding through the tangle of carts and peddlers and pungent smells, are part of the human migration of millions of Chinese peasants.
For the sake of a livelihood, they stream from their rural villages to cities far and near, like Chongqing, a sprawling metropolis on the Yangtze River in Sichuan Province.
"There's no need for me to work in the fields so much, and you can't produce money anyway, just grain," said a bucket carrier who must support his wife and three children.
Â 
100 Million Jobless Peasants
Throughout China's countryside, where three-fourths of the nation's population lives, there are an estimated 100 million jobless peasants, looking for odd tasks, chatting among each other, or standing around watching their crops grow.
Peasant restlessness has not led to major unrest in China in recent years, but serious underemployment in the countryside, let alone the vast numbers of those underemployed in China's state-run enterprises, poses a significant threat to social stabilityII. 
China's history is full of peasant rebellions, including the Communist revolution of 1949.
Peasants have a number of legitimate complaints, for despite the revolution's rural origins the Chinese Government discriminates in a number of ways against villagers. 
Most fundamentally, the Government pays an artificially low price to farmers for their grain, and then gives it at a subsidized price to urban workers -- who already have a substantially higher standard of living than the villagers.
Moreover, peasants generally do not receive financial support from the Government, while city dwellers are given subsidized food, health care, housing and many other benefits.
More and more peasants seem to realize that their work is helping the city slickers enjoy a comfortable life, and they resent it.
"The city folk get so many subsidies, and so do the cadres in the countryside," said a peasant doctor from the eastern province of Shandong. 
"But we get nothing. 
We even lose money when we grow grain."
Costs for farming, school and medicine are rising in the countryside, and if there is a bad harvest, if the economy falters, or if the Government goes so broke that it cannot afford to pay farmers for their grain, then a huge army of peasants could descend upon the cities in demand of jobs.
Â 
Projection of 300 Million Idle
According to some accounts, by the end of this century China will have 300 million idle peasants scouring the towns and cities for work outside their farming tasks. 
Already, peasants from China's relatively poor areas who migrate in giant waves to the cities are creating numerous headaches for the authorities. 
More than three million peasants, for example, have already come from other areas to work in the Pearl River Delta in southern China, according to a Chinese press report.
"We are under a lot of pressure," said Xiao Yang, Communist Party Secretary of Chongqing, a city with 14.5 million people. 
Mr. Xiao said the workers put it this way: "You give me a job. 
If you don't, how can you call yourself the people's government?"
There is virtually no labor mobility in China, and the Government restricts unplanned migration by forbidding its citizens to live in a place unless they have residence permits or official consent. 
But peasants flout the rules, and young women who want to become maids, young men seeking construction work, or people simply seeking a better life trickle out of the countryside into the cities.
Sichuan, China's largest province, with 108 million people, is particularly sensitive to unemployment problems because about a third of its rural work force -- 14 million farmers -- are idle, "surplus" laborers.
Â 
Unemployment Officially at 4%
China officially says its nationwide unemployment is about 4 percent, but those statistics exclude underemployment both in the cities and among the more than 800 million people in the countryside.
While jobs are tough to find, peasants say it is still worthwhile to go to the cities to look for work. 
There they join the "floating" population of workers without permanent residence permits.
In Bao An Village, about 60 miles north of Chongqing, Fang Qiong, 28 years old, does the family farming and child rearing on her own because her husband has gone off to the remote, northwestern province of Xinjiang to look for a job.
"About a dozen of the men went together to Xinjiang," Ms. Fang said as she was weeding her field. 
"He wanted to go, and I let him. 
What can I do about it?"
At a neighbor's house, four of the family's five daughters have gone to Shenzhen to work, while the parents look after their grandson.
"My daughters send money," said Yang Shengui, the 48-year-old mother. 
"Otherwise, we couldn't survive."

file: Citicorp_s Hong Kong Deal Called Vote of Confidence.txt
text:

Citicorp, the largest banking company in the United States, yesterday gave Hong Kong one of the strongest votes of confidence it has received since the upheaval in China in June shook its markets.
Citicorp said it would arrange $5.2 billion (Hong Kong), or $667 million (United States), in loans to build two office towers in the territory's central district and may take an equity stake in the project. 
Citicorp plans to buy office space in the complex, and one tower may bear its name.
''We wouldn't have made the announcement at this time if we did not want to display in a dramatic way a vote of confidence and the fact that we intend to stay,'' said Steven Baker, Citicorp''s chief corporate officer in Hong Kong and division executive for East Asia.
Analysts noted that this also is a time to find property bargains in Hong Kong.
Â 
'A Very Good Price'
''Now is not a bad time to pick up assets,'' said Cheah Cheng Hye, head of research at Morgan Grenfell (Hong Kong) Securities. 
''If you don't think Hong Kong is going to fall apart after 1997, you're going to get in at a very good price.''
The invitation to participate in the project came from the Great Eagle Company, a major Hong Kong property developer that recently bought the last prime building site in the downtown business district.
The price Great Eagle paid at a Government auction, $2.7 billion, was well below expectations and about half the valuation placed on the site when Hong Kong's market was at its peak.
The territory's real estate market has been hard hit since the Chinese Government, which is scheduled to assume control of Hong Kong in 1997, suppressed pro-democracy demonstrations in June.
Â 
Completed in 1993
This is not the first time fears over Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty have contributed to slumps in the local property market. 
Prices were notably weak in the early 1980's.
The high-rise project on Garden Road is to be completed in 1993. 
The site is next to the towering new Bank of China building, a highly visible reminder of Beijing's presence in the territory.
Citicorp's involvement in the development could be three-pronged: arranging a $1.9 billion bridge loan and a $3.3 billion term loan; possibly taking a 5 percent equity stake, which could be about $250 million dollars at the estimated development cost, and purchasing up to 400,000 square feet of office space.
At market rates for the district, that space would cost about $22 million, but Lo Ka Shui, managing director of Great Eagle, said office space in the development would be sold or leased to Citicorp below the going price.
Â 
Three Major Locations
Citicorp is one of the busiest foreign banks in the territory, with about 2,200 employees. 
But Hong Kong represents a small percentage of its worldwide business.
The bank now has three major Hong Kong locations: the stylish Exchange Square complex next to Victoria Harbor, Citicorp Center in Causeway Bay and Hopewell Center in Wanchai.
Mr. Baker said the planned move to Garden Road fits a ''two-building strategy'' that would group the bank's operations while expanding its existing Hong Kong office space of about 300,000 square feet.
Under the plan, the bank would have operations in one building in the central business district to house corporate and private banking businesses and a second, less-expensive site out of the central district to house its retail banking and credit-card operations. 
One alternative is to keep its Hopewell Center offices for that purpose.
In addition to the equity stake offered to Citicorp, Great Eagle said it had offered a 10 percent equity interest in the new project to the Singapore-based Robert Kuok Group, 5 percent to Wing Tai Exporters Ltd., 10 percent to Manhattan Garments Ltd., 7 percent to Sung Foo Kee Ltd. and 5 percent to a Japanese conglomerate.
Great Eagle will maintain about a 60 percent interest in the project, Mr. Lo said.

file: Clamor in Europe_Czech Students Belatedly Assail China Crackdown.txt
text:

In a belated expression of sympathy, several thousand Czechoslovak students marched here today to protest the violent suppression of China's pro-democracy movement in June.
When troops attacked and killed demonstrators in Beijing, students here said they were horrified but powerless to respond. 
Their own repressive Government supported the Chinese authorities, thwarting any chance of a student show of solidarity.
But after their own Government sent troops in to violently disperse a peaceful student demonstration here on Nov. 
17, prompting a backlash of protest that has caused the collapse of the Communist regime, Czechoslovak students decided to hold the demonstration they were prevented from holding months ago.
''It's important to stand up and say that what happened in Tiananmen Square and what happened here on the 17th should never be repeated,'' said Vera Krincvajova, a 20-year-old journalism student, who said she learned of the Chinese student uprising and the crackdown by monitoring foreign news reports on the radio.
Â 
'Dialogue - Yes!
Tanks - No!'
The students gathered in the freezing cold under threatening gray skies in a square opposite the philosophy department of Charles University, a center of the student movement.
They carried banners saying, ''Freedom for Prague and Beijing,'' ''Democracy Is Not a Crime'' and ''Dialogue -Yes!
Tanks - No!''
They wore headbands, as the Chinese students had, bearing the same messages.
The example of China has haunted the students of Czechoslovakia ever since they declared a strike two weeks ago and began working with leading dissidents to organize daily mass demonstrations and a two-hour general strike last week to force change on the Government.
This was the first large-scale demonstration in Prague in more than a week, because mass rallies were temporarily called off after the opposition group Civic Forum began negotiating with Prime Minister Ladislav Adamec over the formation of a new Government. 
For 10 days those protests had brought hundreds of thousands of people to Wenceslas Square.
Â 
'Guilty That I Was Silent'
Disappointed by the Government restructuring announced today, Civic Forum has called for a mass protest rally on Monday, a move the students say they endorse.
Students here have also said it is difficult for them to ignore that what happened in China might happen here.
''The possibility is in the back of everyone's mind,'' said Vladimir Kropacek, an 18-year-old math and physics student. 
''In the spring, I did not have the courage to express my sympathy, and in truth, I feel a little guilty that I was silent.''
The students had originally planned to march from the square to the Chinese Embassy, but Chinese diplomats protested to officials here.
After discussions with the authorities and among themselves, the students decided to avoid a confrontation by marching from the square through the winding, cobbled streets of an old section of Prague called Mala Strana, or the small quarter, and to a compound of dormitories for foreign students of Charles University.
''The most important thing to us was to show students' unity,'' said Simon Panek, a 22-year-old biology student and one of the leaders of the Student Strike Committee, who addressed the students after their hour-long march. 
''The world has been standing up for us, and now that we have the chance -it is late, we know, but it is our first chance - we are standing up for our fellow students.''

Newspaper readers in China learned of the remarkable resignations of East German leaders this week, but they also picked up another bit of news: two East Germans who had fled more than a month ago to the West found the new society too disorderly and so returned home.
Chinese official newspapers have regularly, if sparingly, reported the developments within the East German leadership this week. 
But the brief reports included no explanations of the pressures that led to the unusual collective resignations. 
Lately, there has been little coverage of the mass demonstrations for democracy or the exodus to the West.
Such matters are presumably regarded as too delicate, too reminiscent of the democracy movement in China in the spring. 
Instead of giving in to some of the demonstrators' demands, as the East German leadership has done, the Chinese authorities called in troops and crushed the movement.
Today, there was no mention in the press or the national television about East Germany's opening of its borders to the West, although the trip to Poland by Chancellor Helmut Kohl of West Germany was reported.
Â 
'Period Full of Contradictions'
The recent articles - about one every two days, carried on the international news pages - have confined themselves to reporting excerpts from speeches by the new East German leader, Egon Krenz, about the necessity of reforming the party so that it can better exercise its leadership role.
''Democratic Germany is currently in a tense period full of contradictions,'' People's Daily today quoted Mr. Krenz as saying. 
''To make it through the difficult period, it is necessary to first carry out reform in the party itself.''
''The state economy is still the foundation of the socialist economy,'' Mr. Krenz was quoted as saying. 
''It is imperative to combine the superiority of the socialist planned economy with the regulation of the market.''
Chinese news outlets have tended to convey the impression that the ferment is coming from the top down, from a Communist leadership seeking to improve itself, rather than from a beleaguered party seeking to respond to enormous popular pressures. 
Still, many Chinese intellectuals listen to ''Voice of America'' or BBC radio programs, and often regard the changes in the Eastern bloc as a sign of the pressures that China could also face.
Â 
German Exodus Is Played Down
The newspapers have played down the exodus to the West, and have emphasized that some refugees found that capitalism was not as delightful as they had believed.
''When they first arrived, they were well treated,'' said a report in People's Daily early this week.

text:

President Mikhail S. Gorbachev has sent President Bush a message supporting the changes taking place in East Germany and expressing hope that the situation will remain ''calm and peaceful,'' the White House spokesman said today.
Marlin Fitzwater, Mr. Bush's press secretary, disclosed the message, which was received on Friday while the President was here to dedicate a memorial to soldiers killed in the Vietnam War.
The cable from Mr. Gorbachev was described by Mr. Fitzwater as ''an informal message.''
Although its text was not released, the spokesman said the Soviet leader spoke of ''the importance of the changes'' in East Germany and ''expressed the hope that the situation will remain calm and peaceful.''
Mr. Gorbachev also told Mr. Bush that he supported the actions of the new East German leadership to open its their country's borders.
Â 
U.S. Response Is Promised
Mr. Fitzwater said later that ''the President will respond, and he will repeat many of the things he said, as well as offering encouragement for the continuation of political and economic reforms.''
Mr. Bush, addressing thousands today at an emotional Veterans Day ceremony in which he dedicated a new Vietnam War memorial, said that the perforation of the Berlin wall shows ''a great truth shining brighter with each passing day.''
''The quest for freedom,'' he went on, ''is stronger than steel, more permanent than concrete.''
Recalling that his Administration had not foreseen the suppression of blossoming dissent in China, President Bush said in an interview published today that he has acted with ''prudence'' toward the developments in Eastern Europe because of concern that bolder action could ''contribute toward an unforeseen disorder'' in the Soviet bloc.
Â 
Inside View
In the interview, conducted on Friday with Texas reporters, Mr. Bush said he was prepared to discuss ''a wide array of economic questions'' with Mr. Gorbachev. But, in his first detailed response to the rapidly unfolding events of recent days in East Germany and other nations of the Warsaw Pact, Mr. Bush reflected the deep uncertainty within his Administration about how much the United States can become involved.
He seemed frustrated both at criticism that he has been reluctant to take the kind of leading role in Europe that the United States has pursued for four decades and at the limitations on American action created by the current upheavals.
Mr. Bush said his advisers believe that Mr. Gorbachev is irrevocably committed to his reforms. 
''They can't go back to Square One,'' the President said. 
But he and his aides are still uncertain, and debating among themselves, how the Kremlin will respond to the growing rift amomg its neighboring countries. 
What About Prague?
With Friday's change of leadership in Bulgaria, Mr. Bush went on, the Administration is eager to assess the possibilities for change in a remaining hard-line Communist country, Czechoslovakia. 
Mr. Bush said that Prague is now among ''the most egregious offenders of human rights, those that resist change the most clearly.''
Asked if he was concerned that the rapidity of events could lead to instability in Europe, he said, ''I think that's why I keep using the word like prudent.''
Still, he said, ''I am convinced, given not just the events of yesterday, but the cumulative set of events that have taken place, that this change is real.''
The President and his advisers have repeatedly insisted that China and Eastern Europe cannot be compared in political terms. 
But Mr. Bush would not disregard the Chinese crackdown on dissent that culminated in hundreds of deaths in Beijing in June, and he used that event to explain his seeming anguish over policy toward Eastern Europe.
Â 
'Keep Our Eyes Open'
''I think many of us felt that what happened in China set back the relationship there,'' he said. 
''I hadn't seen anybody predict that was going to happen.''
''And so we keep our eyes open, and we keep acting prudently so as not to exacerbate tensions but to encourage that democracy is whole and free. 
If we continue to do that, we can hopefully not contribute to an unforeseen disorder.''
Mr. Bush said he would like to return to Berlin ''to see it with the wall down, not just with holes in it.''
But he said he did not plan to stop there after his meeting with Mr. Gorbachev on ships off the coast of Malta on Dec. 
2 and 3 ''unless there were something that developed between now and then that would make the presence of the U.S. 
President catalytic for peace or for evolution of democracy.''
Â 
Possible Economic Help
Turning to questions about economic aid, the area in which the Administration has been especially reluctant to engage the Soviet Union, Mr. Bush said: ''I think the time is right, should the Soviets want to discuss how to improve their economy, that we do that. 
I'm perfectly prepared to talk to Mr. Gorbachev on a wide array of economic questions, and will be ready to do that.''
He added that he had had two ''interesting seminars'' with his advisers on economic issues to prepare for the meetings with the Soviet President.
Despite some conflicting statements in recent weeks about the Soviet-American relationship, Mr. Bush said he and his advisers agree on the substance of policy toward the East bloc. 
Still, they ''sit and argue back and forth - How quick will this happen?
Or, What will be next?
Or, what do you think is going to happen to Mr. A. or Mr. B.''
''Will Gorbachev remain committed to perestroika and indeed to glasnost?''
Mr. Bush said. 
''Absolutely.''

file: CNN Basks in Reaction to Its Beijing Coverage.txt
text:
ï»¿
These have been glory days for the Cable News Network. 
Its coverage of the upheaval in Tiananmen Square in Beijing has won praise from press analysts and attracted thousands more viewers, especially in the six days last week that CNN was able to transmit from its own satellite facilities in Beijing.
The network, its admirers say, was simply doing what it does best: showing a historic event unfolding - live. 
And being a round-the-clock all-news operation, it devoted many more hours to the story - 30 of them live that week - than could any of the three major networks.
''I think the Cable News Network really came of age,'' said Fred Friendly, a professor emeritus at the Columbia Graduate School of Journalism and a former CBS executive. 
''It performed a great national and even international service.''
Â 
Kudos for CBS
CBS, the only one of the three major networks to send an anchor, Dan Rather, and to set up its own satellite facility in Beijing, also performed ''an enormous service,'' he said. 
In an age when air time is enormously expensive and networks are cutting back, ''CBS did more than anyone else among the commercial stations,'' he said. 
''But they didn't have what CNN has, which is unlimited air time.''
CNN, a network of the Turner Broadcasting System, made its debut in June 1980, and has been turning a profit in recent years. 
It has grown rapidly, and now has 21 news bureaus, of which a dozen are outside the United States. 
It is seen in 83 countries besides the United States.
Its ''Prime News'' programs at 8 P.M. are normally watched by about 500,000 American households, roughly one-tenth the size of audiences for each of the three major networks' prime evening newscasts.
Â 
An Order on a Legal Pad
But 860,000 American homes watched CNN live last Friday night between 8 and 10:15 P.M., when a tense and curious exchange took place. 
Chinese officials told CNN to stop transmitting and CNN staff members asked for that in writing. 
A Chinese official complied on camera, writing the order on a legal pad. 
CNN members conferred with their network's headquarters in Atlanta, and the transmission ended.
That same night, 12.2 million viewers were watching CBS (and some called in to complain) as the network broke into the season's final episode of ''Dallas'' with a 21-minute special report that showed Chinese officials telling CBS to end its operations in Beijing.
During the past week, 400,000 American households tuned in daily to CNN on average - an increase of some 150,000 from usual.
Â 
'Logistical Nightmare'
The broadcasts from China were ''a logistical nightmare,'' said Eason Jordan, CNN's acting international editor, although events such as the 1988 Democratic National Convention required a larger staff.
CNN had 40 people in China last week, including the CNN anchor Bernard Shaw; Mike Chinoy, the Beijing bureau chief, and three other correspondents.
''They were working without sleep, as long as 20, 24 even 40 hours,'' Mr. Jordan said. 
''Even when they were told to get some sleep, they were too excited.''
In the view of Ed Joyce, a former president of CBS News, ''Bernard Shaw, and particularly Mike Chinoy, showed that nobody in commercial networks is doing anything better than they are doing. 
Chinoy, I thought, really seemed to have a grasp on the subtleties'' of the situation.
Â 
ABC and NBC 'Were Not Factors'
''What I found fascinating,'' Mr. Joyce said, ''was that the competition was between CBS News and CNN. 
ABC and NBC were just not factors'' - which he called a ''watershed'' development.
ABC and NBC were hardly in accord with this assessment.
''We're not at all ashamed - we covered it well,'' said Dick Wald, the senior vice president of ABC News. 
Noting that the original reason for the coverage was the Chinese-Soviet summit meeting, he said, ''The second story that captured the attention of the world wasn't part of anybody's planning.''
Comparing CNN to a wire story and the networks to newspapers, Mr. Wald said, ''The wire service is constant and constantly updating, but the newspaper creates a shape for things and a context.''
Joseph Angotti, a senior vice president of NBC News, said, ''I think its unfortunate that people have a perception that if your anchor is not there, you're not covering a story adequately.''
Â 
On the Camera's Presence
''The nature of CNN allows it to do things we simply can't do,'' Mr. Angotti added. 
Describing the coverage by CNN - and by all three networks - as ''terrific,'' he added that ''We think our pictures have been the best.''
Not everyone agrees on the impact of CNN's presence. 
Reuven Frank, a former president of NBC News, said the main point was that these days, ''the presence of the camera changes the nature of the event.''
Students, he said, were very much aware of the coverage, and timed their protest to the summit talks, just as antiwar demonstrators chose the Democratic National Convention to capture the cameras' eyes in Chicago in 1968.
And will CNN's achievement affect the way the commercial networks cover news?
''What I'm afraid of,'' said Mr. Frank, ''is that it may allow the networks to cop out. 
They could say, 'well, if you want it, it's there on CNN.''

file: Columbia Journal_Doolittle Raiders Recall 30 Seconds in History.txt
text:
ï»¿
Fifty years ago Jimmy Doolittle, then a lieutenant colonel in the Army Air Forces, flew to a small air base south of here seeking volunteers for a World War II mission that he described only as top secret and extremely hazardous.
Nearly 140 men base volunteered, and 80 of those were selected. 
Their mission: bomb Tokyo.
It was daring and seemingly suicidal. 
The five-man crews, aboard 16 heavily loaded B-25 bombers, were to take off from an aircraft carrier 450 miles from their target, knowing there was no turning back. 
The bombers could not land on the carrier; instead, after dropping their bombs they were to continue on, hoping to land at two primitive landing strips in Chinese territory that was not controlled by the Japanese.
On April 18, 1942 -- four months and 11 days after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor -- Colonel Doolittle's Raiders accomplished their mission.
Flying low, they approached Japan undetected and dropped 16 tons of bombs on factories and military installations in Tokyo and four other cities. 
The bombs caused little material damage, but they sent shock waves through Japan and lifted the morale of a dispirited America.
Somehow, 73 of the 80 crew members survived that historic mission. 
And on Thursday, 36 of the 40 who are still living will, for the first time, return to Columbia to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the raid. 
Their leader, who was promoted to general and awarded the Medal of Honor for the raid on Japan, is now 95 years old and living in Monterey, Calif. 
But he is unable to attend the three-day celebration.
Since World War II ended, the Raiders have met every year except one, said Brig. Gen. Richard Knobloch of San Antonio, the chairman of the Doolittle Tokyo Raiders Association.
As with all extraordinary events, the raid serves as the defining moment of their lives. 
They were young and, as one of the navigator-bombardiers, James Macia of San Antonio, said, "full of spit and vinegar."
They had been at the Columbia Army Air Base only two weeks when Colonel Doolittle sought their help. 
Few remember much about this city, but they did know the colonel, who had been a World War I flier and had a reputation as a daredevil.
Colonel Doolittle was counting on surprise. 
He knew the Japanese felt secure from an air attack because Japan was beyond the range of Army bombers.
"The old man," as his raiders call him, also knew that a B-25 could do the job from a Navy carrier. 
But his plans went askew on the rainy morning of April 18 when, some 800 miles at sea, a Japanese boat was spotted. 
The Americans sank the boat, but they did not know whether their whereabouts had been reported. 
The mission was quickly launched, but the Raiders knew they lacked the fuel to get to the landing strips in China.
They took off from the carrier Hornet at 8 A.M., hit their targets about noon and soared away to the west. 
They flew for nine hours more, but as the fuel tanks emptied, the crews of 11 of the planes parachuted out. 
Four other planes crash-landed near the Chinese coast, killing four crewmen, and the remaining plane landed in Vladivostok, Siberia.
Seven crewmen who parachuted out over Japanese-occupied China were captured, and three of them were executed. 
They were William G. Farrow, of Darlington, S.C.; Dean E. Hallmark, of Robert Lee, Tex., and Harold Spatz, of Lebo, Kan.
Columbia and local businesses have planned and paid for the $115,000 Raiders celebration, which includes a state dinner, a ball, an exhibit at the South Carolina State Museum and the premiere of a play about the raid.
But the raid has already been documented in the 1943 movie "Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo," which was based on the book by Ted Lawson, a pilot who died earlier this year.
"I would do anything for these guys," said Marvin Chernoff, whose Columbia-based advertising and public relations firm coordinated the reunion. 
"I got very emotional the first time I met them. 
I'm told in '42 they were crazy, and they're crazy now. 
They are a great bunch of guys."

file: Companies Expect Benefits From U.S.-China Trade Pact.txt
text:
ï»¿
Executives of several corporations expressed guarded optimism yesterday about the potential benefits of the accord signed by China and the United States to remove a broad range of trade barriers to American goods, including computers, chemicals and cameras.
"It sounds very encouraging to us," Paul Allen, a spokesman for the Eastman Kodak Company, said of the agreement, which was signed Saturday.
Kodak, based in Rochester, has three offices in China, where it has sold film for both consumer and professional uses for several years. 
Mr. Allen said he did not know the specifics of China's current restrictions on film and other Kodak products. 
Even so, he said, "it's welcome news."
His comments were echoed by other executives, who said that even though they were not sure precisely how the trade agreement would affect their operations, the agreement signaled an opening of the Chinese market that would more than likely represent added business.
"It gives A.T.& T. the opportunity to compete in the Chinese market," a spokeswoman for the American Telephone & Telegraph Company said. 
A.T.& T. is likely to benefit from an agreement by China to eliminate by next March 31 all restrictions on purchases of digital switching equipment made by American telecommunications manufacturers.
Many American businesses will be examining the complex agreement this week to learn exactly how their particular industries are affected. 
Many companies will probably be formulating strategies for the Chinese market from a standing start, Ira Wolf, the assistant United States trade representative for Japan and China, said yesterday.
"The Chinese market has been so closed and opaque for so long, nobody is going to sell something tomorrow because of this," he said.
Â 
Trying to Curb Huge Deficit
Under the agreement, China committed itself to eliminating a vast majority of the quotas, import-licensing restrictions and secret rules it has used to impede imports.
Michael H. Moskow, the deputy United States trade representative, said at a news briefing on Saturday that the accord would mean hundreds of millions of dollars in extra United States exports in the short term and billions more within several years.

file: Companies Speeding Beijing Exodus.txt
text:
ï»¿
More United States companies rushed to pull personnel out of Beijing yesterday as the Bush Administration urged all Americans to leave the embattled city.
Northwest Airlines, which has two flights a week to Shanghai, said its flight yesterday left about half full but that its flight scheduled to leave tomorrow was fully booked. 
The airline uses Boeing 747's with a seating capacity of 400.
United Airlines has three regularly scheduled flights a week from Tokyo to Beijing, with its flight on Mondays routed through Shanghai. 
It also uses 747's. 
Sara L. Dornacker, media relations manager, said that yesterday's flight left Beijing with 85 empty seats, but that the carrier expected all seats to be filled today.
Some companies were trying to arrange for charter flights to move large numbers of employees. 
McDonnell Douglas, which has had a joint venture since 1985 to produce MD-80 planes for commercial use in China, said yesterday that it was trying to evacuate 43 workers and their families from Shanghai, where it has a plant that employs several thousand workers. 
James Reed, a spokesman for the company, said he did not know the status of the plant, although he said there had been no problems reported at it.
The Chrysler Corporation said it was watching the situation in Beijing, where it has a plant employing 4,500 Chinese workers who manufacture Jeep Cherokees and BJ-212's, which are Soviet-style jeeps.
Â 
Supplies Arriving
Anne H. Lalas, manager of international public relations for Chrysler, said the plant operated on Monday and yesterday with two-thirds of its work force. 
She said supplies were arriving normally as of yesterday. 
The company evacuated its eight non-Chinese workers on Sunday.
At Coopers & Lybrand, Sue-Jean Lee, the accounting firm's China desk manager in Washington, said the manager of the Beijing office was scheduled to leave for Hong Kong, but there had been no confirmation that she had made the trip. 
The company had not been able to reach its personnel in Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, she said.
''Once the situation settles down a bit and we know who will be in charge, I'm sure we will continue our presence in China,'' Ms. Lee said. 
Most of the firm's business is with American, Canadian and British companies in China.
Richard M. Hammer, national director of international tax services for Price Waterhouse, said the firm had sent eight to ten employees to Hong Kong from Beijing in the last few days.
Â 
'Real Convulsion' Expected
''China is in for a real convulsion,'' Mr. Hammer said. 
''I don't think its leaders can put the lid on this.''
He added that he thought the situation was a disaster because companies that pull out now will not go back soon.
Peter P. Mullen, executive partner at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, said the international law firm had put on hold plans to open an office in Beijing in October. 
He described the situation in Beijing as ''highly charged and very dangerous at this point.''
Mr. Mullen said the Chinese companies represented by his firm were continuing yesterday with their business ventures. 
One, for example, which has bought a steel plant in upstate New York, continued to dismantle the plant and make arrangements for its shipment to Shanghai.
Another client continued the process yesterday of buying assets in the Midwest to ship back to China, while one actively pursued fund raising to make investments in the United States.
Yet another company, he said, that owns part of a plant that makes polypropylene, a plastic, is continuing to take shipments destined for China.
Â 
Insurance Coverage
In Washington, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, which insures American companies against expropriation, war damage and other political risks overseas, said it had written policies covering 29 projects in 15 localities in China, but that it was too early to know if it would have to make any payouts.
Among the projects are the Cabot Corporation's carbon black factory in Shanghai and a Warner-Lambert plant in Suzhou.
OPIC, which is a United States Government corporation holding $1.2 billion in reserves, said its maximum liability was $95 million.
Robert L. Jordan, director of public affairs, said, ''Whatever reactions we get in the form of potential claims will be down the road.''

file: COMPANY NEWS_China Will Launch U.S.-Built Satellite.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Hong Kong company signed a $30 million contract today to fire an American-built satellite into space on a Chinese rocket - the first time China will launch a foreign-built satellite.
''This marks China's first step in the international satellite business,'' said Terry Seddon, chief executive of the Asia Satellite Telecommunications Company, or Asiasat, which signed the deal with the state-owned China Great Wall Industrial Corporation.
Asiasat 1 is to be launched in April 1990, and China will be sending two other American-made satellites into space in July 1991 and February 1992 for an Australian satellite company, Aussat, Chinese officials said.
In addition, negotiations are under way for the Chinese to launch a second satellite from Asiasat and a weather satellite from Sweden. 
Asiasat 1 and the two Aussat satellites were made by the Hughes Aircraft Company.
The launchings on an unmanned rocket will provide China with much-needed foreign exchange and, if successful, help cement its position in the world of international aerospace.
Since 1984, China has successfully launched four of its own communications satellites. 
It started launching satellites in 1970 and has had 23 successful firings and one failure.
In December the United States agreed to allow China to launch American-built communications satellites after Beijing promised it would neither steal American satellite technology nor undercut private American companies.
China said it would limit itself to launching nine foreign communications satellites in the next six years.
According to some estimates, China's state-subsidized rocket industry charges 30 to 50 percent less per launching than its American or European competitors.
The Chinese launching will be Asiasat 1's second trip in space. 
In 1984, under the name Westar 6, it was sent up on the American space shuttle, but a rocket motor malfunctioned and the satellite was not delivered into orbit.
It was retrieved in a spectacular salvage operation in 1985 and sold to Asiasat, the company owned by a consortium consisting of Cable and Wireless of Britain, the state-owned China International Trust and Investment and Hutchison Whampoa, one of Hong Kong's biggest companies.

file: COMPANY NEWS_G.M. Sets Venture in China To Assemble Pickup Trucks.txt
text:
ï»¿
The General Motors Overseas Corporation announced today that it had formed a $100 million joint venture with a Chinese vehicle manufacturer to assemble pickup trucks for sale in China.
The joint venture represents General Motors' effort to enter a vehicle market that is expected to be one of the fastest growing in the world. 
China's 1.1 billion people now get around mostly on bicycles, but very rapid industrial growth rates are likely to mean enormous growth in the numbers of cars, buses and trucks on the roads in the future.
Volkswagen, Peugot and Chrysler are already active in China, mostly assembling passenger cars from parts imported from abroad. 
While there are enormous problems with quality control, high tariffs make imported vehicles frequently uncompetitive in China.
"We've been trying to do business in China since 1978," David Bodkin, a company spokesman, said in Beijing today. 
"We finally got an agreement."
The venture agreement, in which General Motors will take a 30 percent equity stake, will produce 600 to 1,000 trucks by the end of this year after the production line starts up sometime around June, Mr. Bodkin said. 
By 1998, the joint venture is expected to produce 50,000 trucks a year.
General Motors will provide mainly capital, while the Gold Cup Automobile Company will provide the production plant and about 5,000 workers. 
The workers, in the northeastern city of Shenyang, will assemble partial knockdown kits imported from General Motors S-class truck plants in the United States. 
These kits will be paid for in hard currency, a G.M. spokesman in Detroit said. 
Over time, the venture is expected to increase the portion of locally made parts.
There is also a provision in the agreement for G.M. to take profits out of China in a variety of ways including hard currency and currency exchanges, the spokesman said.
The agreement comes amid a recovery in China for automobile makers, including joint ventures, with the top seven or eight companies now turning profits after an austerity policy seriously hurt business in 1989 and 1990. 
Gold Cup lost the equivalent of about $11 million in 1990, according to an Associated Press report from Shenyang last year.
Â 
Company's Financial Innovations
Gold Cup, which in Chinese is known as Jinbei, attracted national renown a few years ago for its effort to become the first company in China to issue Western-style shares to domestic and foreign investors. 
Its shares were even peddled in a central Government compound, provoking sharp criticism from hard-liners that this practice was unbecoming in a Communist country.
Still, Gold Cup was better known for its financial innovations than for the quality of its trucks and mini-vans. 
Like most Chinese manufacturers, it is far behind Western standards.
Gold Cup recently spent $35 million to purchase a production line from the Toyota Motor Corporation to assemble 15-seat vans, and the two companies had considered further cooperation, according to a recent report in the official China Daily. 
It is not clear whether this cooperation will deepen, as had been intended, now that Gold Cup has formed the venture with G.M.
Â 
No Passenger Cars
Mr. Bodkin said there were no immediate plans to produce passenger cars, which several other foreign-financed operations, including Chrysler's well-known Beijing Jeep joint venture, have focused on. 
He added that the proposal to produce pickup trucks had come mainly from Gold Cup, which currently specializes in minivans and trucks and produced 20,000 light trucks in 1990. 
The two companies began discussions in 1988.
General Motors will have "operating and management responsibility," Mr. Bodkin said, and the president of the new company will be a General Motors representative. 
The joint venture will not have full autonomy in setting the prices of its cars, but it will make price proposals for approval by the Chinese Government.
General Motors currently is also installing an engine-manufacturing line that it has sold to the Beijing Engine Factory. 
These engines will be used in the pickup trucks.

file: Confrontation in the Gulf_China Gives Its View.txt
text:

Prime Minister Li Peng said today that China opposed any military involvement in the Persian Gulf by ''big powers,'' but officials reportedly told a visitor that it would not oppose a United Nations resolution allowing the use of force to back up the embargo of Iraq.
Sheik Sabah al-Ahmed al-Sabah, the Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister of the Kuwaiti Government in exile, said that China's leaders had assured him that if China did not support a United Nations Security Council resolution on policing the embargo, it would at least not veto it.

He has already been to Washington, London, Paris and Yugoslavia, and will next visit Moscow and Iran, he said.

It also said it would halt weapons sales to Iraq, and Sheik Sabah said today that he was sure that China would also halt all other trade with Iraq.
While supporting the trade embargo, China has also expressed unease at the American military buildup in the region.

file: CONFRONTATION IN THE GULF_Iraq Voted Out of Asian Games.txt
text:
ï»¿
Asian countries voted overwhelmingly tonight to exclude Iraqi athletic teams from the 11th Asian Games, a regional mini-Olympics scheduled to begin in Beijing on Saturday.
The vote in the 38-member Olympic Council of Asia was 27 for excluding Iraq and 3 against exclusion, with 5 abstentions and 1 invalid ballot. 
The decision was a particularly painful diplomatic defeat for Iraq because the members of the council are mostly third-world nonaligned nations, rather than Western powers whom Iraq blames for trying to isolate it.
As a result of the vote, Iraq has been suspended from the Olympic Council of Asia and lost its right to take part in the Asian Games, reportedly until it withdraws its troops from Kuwait. 
Iraq's soccer team had already arrived in China and had played Chinese teams, but now it will be unable to participate in the official athletic meet.
The Olympic Council of Asia has been particularly aggrieved by the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait because the council's president, Sheik Fahad al-Ahmad al-Sabah, was a Kuwaiti who was killed in the invasion. 
Some Arab countries from the Persian Gulf had said they might boycott the Asian Games unless Iraq was excluded.
Â 
China Sought Peacemaker Role
China had sought to reconcile the countries and had repeatedly said that it did not want politics to interfere with the Games. 
They form the biggest international conference ever held in China, and the leadership in Beijing has tried to use the event to mark its return to the international community after widespread criticisms of its military crackdown against the democracy movement last year.
For a time China succeeded in obtaining commitments from all 38 countries in the region to participate. 
But Jordan dropped out this week for unknown reasons and now Iraq will be excluded as well.
The Associated Press reported that Iraq, Yemen and the Palestine representatives opposed expulsion, and that Mongolia and Afghanistan did not vote.

file: Congress, Angry at China, Moves to Impose Sanctions.txt
text:
ï»¿
Members of Congress introduced amendments today that could severely curtail exports of computers, weapons, satellites and financing to China.
The legislators acted out of outrage over China's execution of pro-democracy demonstrators and disappointment with the Bush Administration's measured response.
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d, testifying before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, appealed to the legislators for restraint, reminding them that human rights concerns have to be balanced against the strategic and economic importance of the Chinese-American relationship. 
He also warned of the dangers of any split between the White House and Congress on how to deal with Beijing.
Baker Defends Bush's Response
''We've seen examples in the past where we have not spoken with one voice in the conduct of our foreign policy and we've always, almost without exception, failed in those instances,'' Mr. Baker told the legislators. 
''I believe that the President's response has been properly measured.''
Mr. Baker said the President had adopted ''carefully targeted actions, while not being inflammatory in his rhetoric and preserving his options for the future.''
He added: ''Human rights has got to be a fundamental keystone for American foreign policy, but there are also other considerations that must be taken into account. 
The geopolitical economic relationship between China and the United States is important.''
But the Secretary's remarks came at a time of a growing clamor on Capitol Hill for additional sanctions that would give substance to the outrage over the crackdown of the pro-democracy movement.
Â 
Anger on Capitol Hill
While none of the amendments being introduced may ever find their way into law, members of Congress said they are certain to increase the pressure on the President to adopt additional sanctions and more forceful language toward the Beijing authorities.
The anger on Capitol Hill was encapsulated by the Senate majority leader, George J. Mitchell, who issued a statement saying, ''I am saddened by the President's refusal to give outlet to the feelings of the American people about these executions which have now reached the point which can only be described as organized murder - terror by a Government against its own people, seeking to intimidate them, to permit that Government to remain in power.''
''I understand and appreciate the delicate situation in which the President finds himself,'' the Maine Democrat added, ''and I support his stated desire to maintain, if possible, some relationship with the Chinese Government. 
But I ask - I urge - the President to condemn these actions personally and in the strongest possible terms.''
To put teeth into those sentiments, a variety of amendments were introduced to the Foreign Aid Authorization Bill for fiscal years 1990-91 currently being debated on the floor of the House.
Â 
An Omnibus Amendment Planned
Representative Stephen J. Solarz, the Brooklyn Democrat who is chairman of the House subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific, said all the amendments will be sifted out, coordinated and then put together into one bipartisan omnibus amendment on China to the foreign aid bill, which should come up for a vote on Wednesday or Thursday. 
He said the Congress hoped to work closely with the Administration in forging the amendment.
Foreign aid authorization bills, however, often fail to be passed into law because they are weighed down with too many amendments, and no one could guarantee that will not be the fate of these measures as well.
The proposals introduced included these:
* Representative Mel Levine, Democrat of California, introduced an amendment that would cut off all high-technology exports to China for six months. 
Mr. Levine said he was moved to action after a meeting he and a bipartisan group of legislators held Tuesday with the Chinese Ambassador, Han Xu. 
Mr. Levine said he was ''deeply troubled'' by Mr. Han's remark that ''any country in the same situation'' would have behaved as China had.
* Representative Benjamin A. Gilman, Republican of New York, offered an amendment that would prohibit issuance of export licenses of items on the munitions control list.
* Representative Theodore S. (Ted) Weiss, Democrat of Manhattan, introduced an amendment prohibiting the Government-sponsored Overseas Private Investment Corporation, which provides risk insurance and financing for companies doing business abroad, from writing any new policies related to China.
* Representative Gerald B. H. Solomon, Republican of New York, brought an amendment prohibiting export licensing for American-manufactured satellites that are scheduled to be launched on Chinese rockets under an agreement reached last year.
* Representative Tom Lantos, Democrat of California, introduced a separate bill to end China's most-favored-nation trading status.
The House voted 416 to 0 to approve a resolution backing the President's call for clemency for pro-democracy demonstrators and calling on the Chinese Government to stop executing those arrested in its ''murderous crackdown'' adding, ''To the Government of China we say: You can muffle the voices of change for now, but you cannot silence them forever.''
Â 
THATCHER OPPOSES SANCTIONS
LONDON, June 22 (Reuters) -Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher ruled out trade sanctions against China today, telling Parliament that such action could cause great panic in Hong Kong.
The Labor Party Leader, Neil Kinnock, had asked Mrs. Thatcher to back up her condemnation of Beijing for executing pro-democracy demonstrators by leading a European sanctions drive.

file: Congressional Attempt to Impose Higher Tariffs on China Collapses.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Congressional move to impose higher tariffs on China involving billions of dollars of exports collapsed today when the Senate missed a voting deadline, thereby enabling China to continue getting low duties at least through the end of next June.
To protest the repression of pro-democracy student demonstrators, the House of Representatives voted 247 to 174 on Thursday to rescind President Bush's decision last May renewing for China the favorable tariff status known as most-favored-nation treatment.
Under a measure enacted in August, both chambers faced a deadline of midnight Thursday for action to reverse the Administration move.
In a statement early today, the Senate majority leader, George J. Mitchell, Democrat of Maine, officially pronounced the effort dead, but he said he continued to believe that given the current condition of human rights in China, Mr. Bush was wrong.
Â 
Bush Promised Veto
The Congressional move was largely symbolic, since Mr. Bush, a former Ambassador to Beijing, had promised to veto any resolution of disapproval, and most estimates said the two houses lacked the two-thirds voting strength to override a veto.
Mr. Bush said the higher tariffs would hurt American business and consumers, reduce American influence with China on global issues and damage the Hong Kong economy, which is heavily dependent on China trade.
Eliminating the favored status would mean up to a 10-fold rise in tariffs on the apparel, electronics, toys and other products that China sells here.
The two countries do about $18 billion in two-way business. 
Although China buys wheat, high-technology products and machinery and other capital goods from the United States, it has a large trade surplus with this country.
Signaling the importance of the Chinese market for American farmers, the Agriculture Department announced today that China has bought an additional 449,370 metric tons of wheat, its second purchase this week. 
At current prices the wheat would have a farm value of around $40 million.

file: Congressional Roundup_Senate Sustains China-Trade Veto.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Senate today sustained President Bush's veto of legislation intended to curb favorable trading status for China in 1993.
While 59 Senators voted to override the veto, 40 voted to sustain. 
That was eight votes short of the two-thirds majority. 
Fifty-one Democrats and eight Republicans voted to override. 
Five Democrats and 35 Republicans voted to sustain Mr. Bush.
The House had voted 345 to 74 on Wednesday to override the veto. 
It was the fourth time the House had voted to override a veto involving the nation's relationship with China, and the fourth time the Senate had followed with a vote to sustain.
This bill would have forced the President to deny most-favored-nation duty status to imports from state-owned Chinese industries unless he found that China had made improvements in human rights; had taken steps to halt exports of products produced with prison labor; had curbed the export of missile, nuclear and biological and chemical weapons technology and had helped account for American prisoners of war missing in Korea and Vietnam.
The bill was attacked in floor debates as likely to injure only American workers, since other countries would replace the United States as a Chinese trade partner. 
Senator Max Baucus, Democrat of Montana, said that trade was liberalizing China internally.
Senator George J. Mitchell of Maine, the majority leader and chief advocate of the bill, said the Bush Administration was making no progress in changing Chinese policies, because China's leaders "are immune to international criticism because they have a friend at the White House."

file: Congressmen, in China, Warn on Human Rights.txt
text:

Members of the first Congressional delegation to visit China since the military crackdown of June 1989 said today that they had warned Prime Minister Li Peng that unless China improved its human rights record, it risked losing important trade benefits.
The five House members said at a news conference that they thought they had conveyed to the Chinese Government the importance of rights issues in determining trade relations.
But while they were conveying their message, the Chinese authorities werebusy sending a very different message to the nation's people.
Film clips of the smiling Congressmen meeting Prime Minister Li and shaking his hand were the lead item on the television news, and an article about the meeting was published on the front page of People's Daily today.
Neither television nor the Communist Party newspaper indicated that the visitors had expressed any criticism or complaints, and the message to the Chinese audience seemed to be that Americans have returned and are happy to meet with Mr. Li.
"We are confident of the future of China," People's Daily quoted Mr. Lias telling his visitors.
The publicity, which was apparently intended to use the Congressional visit to bolster the legitimacy of the hard-line Government, also quoted Mr. Li as saying, "We Chinese should not observe the U.S. from the viewpoint of our own ideas and norms, while the Americans should not observe China's affairs according to their views and values."
Members of the delegation, which was led by Representative Michael G. Oxley, Republican of Ohio, said they were not particularly surprised by the Chinese attempt to put a "spin" on the visit. 
But they said the trip was worthwhile because they were able to impress upon Mr. Li that unless China improves its human rights record, it risks losing most-favored-nation trade advantages.
"We hope that our visit conveyed the strong message that there is a major concern about human rights violations," Mr. Oxley said.
Representative John J. Rhodes 3d, Republican of Arizona, said the group had emphasized that Congress would again consider at its next session whether to renew most-favored-nation status, and that an important factor would be China's handling of prisoners seized during the crackdown on the democracy movement last year.
"A final resolution of that situation is extremely important to future trade relations," Mr. Rhodes said. 
"I don't think they can have any doubt that thatlinkage exists."
Three of the five Congressmen said it was their impression from Mr. Li's comments that the fate of the prisoners would be resolved soon, but the two others said they did not have that impression.
The other members of the delegation were Representatives George Darden, Democrat of Georgia; Jim Lightfoot, Republican of Iowa, and E. Clay Shaw Jr., Republican of Florida. 
The delegation, which left Beijing today for Shanghai, is the first group of Congressmen to visit since the crackdown, although on two occasions, individual members of Congress have come for brief visits.
