text:
ï»¿
Administration officials today dismissed China's allegations that Washington was interfering in Beijing's internal affairs by harboring two Chinese dissidents, and the Speaker of the House declared that Washington should consider further sanctions if the Chinese crackdown on the pro-democracy movement continues.
Speaking of the death sentences handed down Saturday by the Chinese Government to eight pro-democracy demonstrators, and Beijing's denial that its army opened fire on students in Tiananmen Square, the Speaker of the House, Thomas S. Foley, told the NBC News program ''Meet The Press'': ''There are people who feel we ought to speak out more loudly and more clearly. 
I think the President probably needs to do that.
''We are outraged as a country about the death sentences, about the suppression, and about the enormous big lie that the Chinese Government is attempting to tell about this story.''
Mr. Foley, Democrat of Washington State, added that the Administration should consider further actions against Beijing ''if matters turn toward the worse, as they apparently are doing.''
Â 
Doubts of a Quick Resolution
Administration officials said that hopes have faded for a quick resolution to the case of the Chinese dissident Fang Lizhi and his wife, Li Shuxian, who have been in the United States Embassy in Beijing since June 4. 
Washington had suggested to the Beijing authorities that the couple be allowed safe passage to a neutral third country, but given the cool Chinese attitude, that is no longer a ''live option,'' and, as a result, the couple could find themselves staying in the embassy for a while, the officials said.
After several days in which the Chinese authorities seemed to be playing down the Fang affair, Beijing has once again turned up its polemics, with the official People's Daily newspaper for the first time accusing the United States today of breaking Chinese and international law by harboring the couple. 
The official New China News Agency also labeled as ''ridiculous'' recent White House condemnations of Beijing's military crackdown.
Reacting to these latest broadsides from Beijing, the State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, said, ''In 200 years, the United States Government has never shied away from speaking out for basic human rights, freedom of speech, freedom of association and freedom of the press.''
Administration officials say they now expect that it will be six months to two years before the situation in China stabilizes enough to get a clear picture of where the country is headed -whether it will continue on a course toward greater repression or return to its previous reform-oriented, open-door policy.
Â 
The Polish Example
Administration officials say they are hoping that events unfolding in China today will follow the same cycle as in Poland after the emergence of the Solidarity trade union. 
Solidarity began as a grass-roots pro-democracy movement, was suppressed by martial law in 1981, but eventually emerged in a more powerful and now officially sanctioned form several years later after the Communist authorities in Warsaw found that they simply could not rule, or maintain a sufficient level of economic development, without sharing power.
For now, the Bush Administration has decided to continue its low-key, wait-and-see approach toward Beijing.
The Chinese authorities ''are now as isolated in world affairs in some respects as they were eight to 10 years ago before their open-door policy began,'' said Michel Oksenberg, a China specialist at the University of Michigan who formerly worked on the National Security Council under President Jimmy Carter. 
''The hope is that once they face up to that fact, it will temper their behavior internally and they will recommit themselves to policies of economic and political reform. 
Having mass executions, though, is no way to begin.''

file: CRACKDOWN IN CHINA_In the Surface Calm of Beijing, What_s _Normal_ Isn_t Quite.txt
text:
ï»¿
Twelve days after soldiers machine-gunned civilians on the streets, the Government seems to have willed the capital back to normal life, with buses and bicycles rolling down streets and markets filled with the latest harvest of watermelons.
But beneath a surface of calm and behind the official story about the events of the June 4 massacre, there are small reminders that indicate it may take some time for a more profound peacefulness to settle on the capital.
''Martial law has had a drastic effect on our business,'' said a clothing vendor who awoke from an afternoon nap in front of his stall. 
''The Chinese come out only for work. 
A lot of people don't dare browse about the streets anymore.''
Few Customers Now
A few weeks ago, foreign tourists would have been wandering among the stalls, paying hefty prices for the clothing. 
But now foreigners are very scarce, since the evacuation ordered by many embassies.
''We must pay 300 yuan in taxes every month'' - about $80 - ''but because of martial law, we aren't making any money,'' the vendor complained bitterly. 
''How can we pay so much tax?''
Still, life is gradually returning to the way it was before. 
Ten or twelve days ago, stray bullets kept pedestrians off the streets, but now the main thoroughfares in the capital have begun to fill up again with cars and people.
There are other signs that daily life is almost normal: A crowd has gathered around one stall where a pretty woman in a rather revealing yellow dress is showing off tablecloths that she is trying to sell. 
A man dashes across Changan Avenue, the Avenue of Eternal Peace, his baby nearly spilling from his arms as a car passes by. 
Bicycles jam up at intersections, waiting for lights to turn green or for pedestrians to cross. 
Lines form at bus stops during rush hour, with people jockeying for the spot where the bus will open its doors.
Yet, for a city of about 10 million people, the streets are practically empty, the crowds are small, the traffic is too orderly. 
During a three-hour tour around the capital, only five foreigners were spotted on the streets - a pointed reminder that the capital is short of tourists, who normally pour out of their air-conditioned buses into popular sites like the Forbidden City or the Mao Zedong Mausoleum.
Now only troops march out of the Forbidden City, the old palace built in the early 15th century. 
The Mao Mausoleum is off limits to passers-by. 
More than 200 troops stand guard on Tiananmen Square, where students camped out until June 4 when they were forced out by soldiers who marched into the center of the city firing their submachine guns at crowds of demonstrators.
In places along the Avenue of Eternal Peace, where most of the shooting took place, soldiers are stationed about 10 feet apart, and at major intersections, sometimes 10 soldiers with submachine guns guard a single corner.
At many large crossroads, in fact, traffic officers direct what is normally a whirl of cars, buses, pedestrians and bicycles. 
Now, however, bicycles wait, almost too passively, at the street corners to be told when they may proceed.
People do not seem to push their way onto buses, many of which are surprisingly empty at rush hour. 
And their are fewer cars than normal on the streets.
''No one comes out,'' a bystander said sarcastically. 
''All the officials are inside studying the speech of senior leader Deng Xiaoping.''
The Avenue of Eternal Peace is bumpy, because of the tread marks left by tanks and armored personnel carriers. 
The lanes on many streets have been freshly painted white, and many dividers that had been damaged by tanks still have not been replaced.
Â 
Taxi Driver's Lament
There are almost no taxis on the streets, but there are even fewer people seeking rides. 
One taxi driver was disappointed this morning when a foreign visitor who emerged with his suitcases only wanted to change hotels. 
When the driver found that he was not going to be taking his passenger to the airport, he pleaded with the foreigner to hire the cab for the entire day.
''There's no sense in my waiting around at the hotel for a fare because I won't get one for another five hours,'' he complained.
A sports stadium has been taken over by thousands of soldiers. 
During the heat of the afternoon, crowds of the troops, all in dress uniforms, tried to rest under the shade of trees, and they played cards or just chatted.
''Long live the Communist Party,'' read one banner that hung outside a building. 
Just two weeks ago, pro-democracy posters seemed to hang on every major lamppost and public wall space. 
Now, throughout the city, official red banners with messages favorable to the Government hang outside hotels or other large buildings.
At Beijing University, the banners of mourning from last week have been torn down, as have all the pro-democracy posters that went up more than two months ago when the former Communist Party leader, Hu Yaobang, died on April 15. 
The triangle where students gathered to read posters and listen to broadcasts over a loudspeaker is empty. 
All classes have been canceled, and students have gone home for a lengthened summer vacation.
Authorities have transformed several spots in the city into memorials for soldiers, who are hailed for sacrificing their lives to fight the ''counterrevolutionary rebellion.''
A bridge in Chongwenmen district has been turned into a martyr's shrine to commemorate a soldier whom the Government said was beaten, thrown off the bridge, hanged and burned. 
Civilians have said that the soldier was killed after shooting a child to death.
Â 
87 Colorful Wreaths
Now, the bridge overflows with 87 colorful wreaths sent by large state enterprises and military units. 
In the center of the bridge, one work group set up a small offering of fruit and bread, tea leaves, cigarettes and rice wine.
Yet, if the shrine is to honor the soldier's death, it also inspires fear.
Several soldiers carrying AK-47 submachine guns patrol the bridge, as a platoon commander records the names of the work groups that have sent wreaths. 
Plainclothes Government workers wearing red armbands like badges of honor scrutinize the handful of people who come to the bridge.
Unlike the television scenes where weeping citizens come to lay their wreaths, many now seem to come out of curiosity, and they rarely utter a word as they examine the messages on the wreath.
Wreaths adorning an overpass from which soldiers were hanged during the recent violence in China are among the reminders of strife and confusion that penetrate the veneer of calm in Beijing (Agence France-Presse); soldiers from one of the units still occupying Tiananmen Square in Beijing jogging in formation yesterday (Reuters); map of Beijing (pg. 
4)

file: CRACKDOWN IN CHINA_More Chinese Diplomats Seek Refuge.txt
text:
ï»¿
A small but growing number of Chinese diplomats are reported to have sought refuge in the United States and several other countries as a result of the crackdown on the pro-democracy movement in their homeland.
As many as 13 Chinese diplomats in Canada, Japan, Australia and the United States were said yesterday to have asked for political asylum or refugee status in the last few days, Government spokesmen and news-agency reports said.
In addition, the United States, Britain, Canada and other countries have promised to look sympathetically upon requests by thousands of Chinese students for extensions of their visas or more permanent status as political refugees.
A day after China sentenced three protesters in Shanghai to death, at least two more Chinese diplomats were reported to have sought protection in the United States. 
Two officials of the Chinese Consulate in San Francisco were granted permission last week to remain in this country.
A State Department official confirmed yesterday that more Chinese diplomats had asked for protection in the United States. 
They did not ask for political asylum, but could do so later, he said.
The official declined to say how many Chinese diplomats had asked for refugee status and said he could not confirm a report that two Chinese Embassy officials in Washington had sought protection. 
Chinese diplomats are protected by President Bush's recent order granting any Chinese permission to stay here for at least a year.
In Canada, up to nine Chinese representatives were said to have defected. 
Officials in Ottawa, citing a fear of reprisals against defectors' relatives in China and Canada, declined to identify those seeking refuge, or even to cite their number.
Â 
Little Sympathy for Beijing
''I can confirm that there have been approaches by some officials of the Chinese Embassy indicating a desire to stay in Canada,'' the Minister of External Affairs, Joe Clark, told Reuters. 
China has 35 diplomats or consular officials in Ottawa, 14 in Toronto and 10 in Vancouver.
Since the killing of hundreds or possibly thousands of demonstrators in Beijing in early June, Canada has been sharply critical of China and has recalled its Ambassador, frozen $50 million in development projects in China, canceled all diplomatic visits and banned military trade with China.
Canadian immigration officials also say they have been flooded with inquiries from fearful Chinese students who want to stay as refugees, and Prime Minister Brian Mulroney has said that those completing their studies may remain as long as they wish.
In Tokyo, Japanese officials said yesterday that a Chinese consular official reported to have defected will probably be given asylum or a chance to leave for a third country. 
Foreign Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the case would be handled ''from a humanitarian viewpoint.''
The Japanese Government has refused to confirm that the 27-year-old consular official, Ma Qiuyun, a native of Beijing who has worked at the Chinese Embassy in Tokyo since March 1988, had asked for asylum. 
But Japanese newspapers say she was the first Chinese Embassy official in Tokyo to defect since the crackdowns in Beijing.
Australia granted asylum to a Chinese diplomat, Vice Consul Dong Qi, yesterday and said that because of the Beijing crackdown, none of the 15,000 Chinese in Australia would be deported, The Associated Press said.
Britain said it would grant a six-month extension to Chinese who do not want to return home while their country is in turmoil, Reuters reported. 
The Home Office said 6,500 Chinese citizens, 3,500 of them students, live in Britain.

file: CRAFTS_Sumptuous Silk Robes From China.txt
text:
ï»¿
EMBROIDERED serpents with long fangs prance and grimace on 19th-century silk robes from China in a dazzling exhibition, "Dragon Threads," at the Newark Museum.
The five-clawed dragon was designated as the official emblem of the emperor in 206 B.C. Through the centuries, this sign has been emblazoned on everything that belonged to the emperor and his immediate family. 
The Chinese regime became known as the Dragon Throne.
Although dragon robes were de rigueur for all court functions, only the imperial family could wear clothing with five-clawed dragons. 
During the last era of empire, the Ching Dynasty (1644-1912), the colors of the royal family's silks also signified their high rank: lemon yellow was reserved for the emperor, apricot yellow for the first-born prince and and golden yellow for the other sons.
One princely robe, in an apricot hue, is stitched with eight golden dragons, which twist and snarl across the front, back and sleeves. 
Other "auspicious symbols" include billowing waves and rocks along the lower border, to signify the earth and seas, while wispy blue and green clouds, bright blossoms and flames float across the heavens.
Iris Barrel Apfel, who collected the textiles in this exhibition, said that "this symbolism is only complete when the coat is worn" and that "the human body becomes the world axis and the neck opening, the gate of heaven."
At the time of marriage, even a village bride could become an "empress for a day" by wearing clothing emblazoned with a four-clawed imperial dragon. 
Brides represented yin, the female force that must combine with the masculine yang to insure human survival.
In this show, a wedding jacket is decorated with butterflies, the Chinese equivalent of Cupid. 
And these brides wore red, the color of virtue, joy and festivities.
During her engagement, a young women was secluded in her family home. 
What did she do?
Embroider, of course. 
A trousseau usually consisted of elaborate collars, 12 to 100 pairs of decorated shoes, and the cover and canopy for the bridal bed. 
Guests at the wedding felt free to critique a display of the bride's skill with needle and thread, Mrs. Apfel said.
After marriage, the embroidery tasks continued. 
Wives were expected to decorate their own wardrobes, wall hangings, tablecloths, canopies and covers for beds, the altar and mirrors.
If sons were born, their garments were usually bright and trimmed with grimacing creatures. 
The two tiger-head hats with fangs and flowery ears would entice even today's Ninja Turtle devotees. 
But a young girl's robe, trimmed with bunches of grapes and butterflies, is more refined. 
Her playtime activities must have been restricted, since this embroidered and appliqued silk dress is in perfect condition.
Antique textiles are fragile, so these sumptuous robes are rarely exhibited. 
"They need time to rest," Mrs. Apfel said.
Approximately one-third of the more than 100 robes and accessories on display have been donated to the Newark Museum's Asian Collections by Mrs. Apfel and her Attata Foundation (an acronym created from the words "antique textiles" in English, French and Italian).
Mrs. Apfel's search for these fabric treasures, which began in 1953, led her "into noisy street markets, dank cellars, dusty attics and into expensive auction rooms and elegant antique shops," she said.
A stylized version of a crimson Chinese garden pavilion with a royal yellow roof and short picket fence dominates the gallery. 
The atmosphere is of another place, another time, without the artifice of a re-created period room. 
Flat, headless figures display the robes with outstretched arms so that details are not hidden among the folds.
And these details are intriguing. 
The side closing, which always buttons under the right arm, is usually edged with a decorative border or two, replete with flowers or animals. 
Cuffs echo the symbolic motifs and colors of a robe. 
One processional robe is dotted with the "shou" character, meaning long life.
A patient and careful inspection can enrich the viewer's enjoyment of this exhibition. 
One woman's jacket features miniature scenes, no more than an inch and a half in any direction. 
Each one depicts a garden with one or two women holding a lute or potted plant. 
Others show courtiers crossing arched bridges. 
The perfection and charm of this minute workmanship is spellbinding.
Mrs. Apfel said that ancient Ching archives estimated the time required to complete a single robe. 
Drawing the designs took two weeks; 13 months were spent stitching the gold threads; another year passed before the embroidery was finished.
The legendary long fingernails of Chinese women did not interfere with their fine needlework. 
"They only had one or two long nails, and those were not on both hands," she said.
But another legendary account is true: about the age of 6, little girls did have their foot bones broken and bandaged. 
This torturous process produced grown women with "lotus bud" feet, which gave them social status. 
Although the practice was outlawed, it continued until the end of the Ching Dynasty. 
Some of the decorated shoes on display are barely four and a half inches long.
A group of jewelry, hair ornaments and a headdress all gleam in a heavenly shade of iridescent blue. 
The source of this exotic hue: feathers of the tiny kingfisher bird, which were cut to shape and set in gold and silver with semiprecious jewels. 
As with the egret, the popularity of the plumage of this bird nearly caused its extinction.
Displays of hand and stick puppets portray the nobility in their full regalia, plus some sweet-faced or evil-looking characters who must have added drama to the plots. 
Mrs. Apfel said that Ching puppeteers carved, painted and embroidered the clothing of their puppets and then performed all the parts. 
These artistic traditions and puppets were passed down from father to son.
A small side exhibition explains sericulture, the silk industry. 
Millions of Chinese were once employed in the raising and feeding of silkworms and the reeling and weaving of their precious filaments. 
There are cocoons, wound with the long delicate threads, and a skein of white silk strands.
There will be a Chinese Festival in the Junior Museum on Dec. 
30 from 1 to 4 P.M. "Claws and Panther Paws," for ages 3 to 15, will include hands-on workshops, noodle-pulling demonstrations and performances by the Asian American Dance Theater.
"Dragon Threads" will continue through Jan. 
3. The Newark Museum, at 49 Washington Street, is open from noon to 5 P.M. Wednesday through Sunday, but closed on Christmas and New Year's Day. 
Admission is free.

file: Critic_s Choice_An Opera In Chinese, With Titles.txt
text:
ï»¿
Probably every New Yorker has at some time, somewhere in the city, felt like a stranger in a foreign land. 
At the Chinese opera, for example. 
For years, any Westerner who attended its infrequent presentations and who did not understand the language and conventions of the genre was decidedly an outsider, not necessarily welcomed.
The Taipei Theater, administered by the Chinese Information and Culture Center, has changed all that with its regular presentations of opera. 
It supplies not only supertitles but also superbly informative program booklets and occasional demonstrations. 
This weekend and next, the theater is offering one of its most appealing productions to date, "The Monkey King Raids the Heavens," performed by Li Bao-chun and His Peking Opera Troupe.
The mischievous Monkey King, one of the most famous characters in Chinese folk tradition, has had other artistic representations in New York recently, including a production early this year at the same theater by the New Generation Drama Association of Taipei. 
But Mr. Li gives the tale the full operatic treatment, Chinese-style, with exquisite costumes, highly stylized drama and even acrobatics.
One scene in particular, "The Battle of the Gods," is as lavish and vigorous an exercise as could possibly be crammed onto so small a stage, with bodies hurtling in all directions. 
The music, too, offers rich rewards once the exotic idiom has begun to settle into the ear. 
This is truly something (to salvage a much-abused word) special.
"The Monkey King" will be performed today and tomorrow at 7:30 P.M. and Sunday afternoon at 2, at the Taipei Theater, 1221 Avenue of the Americas, at 49th Street, in the concourse level of the McGraw-Hill building. 
Performances will also be given the same times next weekend. 
Tickets are $8; $5 for students and the elderly. 
Information: (212) 373-1850.

file: CRITIC_S NOTEBOOK_Relax, but Don_t Leave Your Mind Behind.txt
text:
ï»¿
LET'S assume you don't want to hear another word about Kitty Kelley. 
Let's take it for granted that if this is your summer to finish "War and Peace," you're on your own. 
But in between overexposed gossip and obviously great works, you'll find the most engaging, entertaining and stimulating books of summer -- a lavish assortment of novels, biographies and both serious and satirical takes on politics. 
By coincidence, most focus on that nagging little issue, American identity. 
And they prove that beach reading is a state of mind. 
Any of these books is absorbing enough to block the sound of the radio on the next blanket or to give you a good excuse for ignoring pesky house guests, but they are also perfect for those of us to whom summer weekends mean a glorious escape into air-conditioning and a carefully cultivated library pallor.
THE KITCHEN GOD'S WIFE. 
By Amy Tan. 
G. P. Putnam's (mid-June), $22.95. 
Amy Tan combines the eloquence of literary prose with the irresistible narrative pull of commercial fiction. 
The Chinese-American family tale of "The Kitchen God's Wife" echoes her first novel, the 1989 best seller "The Joy Luck Club," but the new work is richer, deeper and more poignant.
Winnie Louie, an elderly San Francisco woman, tells the story of her past to her grown daughter. 
It is a heartbreaking but unsentimental remembrance of her life in China during World War II: a brutal first marriage, the deaths of children, escape from the Japanese bombings, an unexpected love, secrets kept and betrayed. 
Winnie's voice is perfectly pitched, veering comfortably between her belief in the slightly sinister Chinese kitchen god and her account of buying shoes at Macy's.
Winnie, Auntie Helen and Grand-Auntie Du are warm, triumphant characters, likely to make this one of the season's biggest novels.
O'KEEFFE AND STIEGLITZ: AN AMERICAN ROMANCE. 
By Benita Eisler. 
Nan A. Talese/Doubleday. $29.50. 
Despite the subtitle, this is less an American romance than an American merger, and a telling, absorbing one. 
The liaison between Alfred Stieglitz, the eminent photographer, and Georgia O'Keeffe, the young painter whose career he helped create, was what Benita Eisler calls an emotional and professional "collusion" from the start of their affair in 1917 through their marriage to his death in 1946. 
Ms. Eisler's clear-eyed, nonjudgmental portrait shatters the romantic myths without debunking the artists' accomplishments. 
She reveals Stieglitz's emotional cruelty to his first wife and daughter, and his manipulation of the press to inflate artists' prices. 
She does not flinch from noting O'Keeffe's increasingly "imperial" manner or taking on the controversial issue of her "varied sexual appetites" for both men and women. 
There are no surprises about art here, but the way these artists forged volatile lives and stellar careers is presented in vibrant, enthralling detail.
HUNTING MISTER HEARTBREAK: A DISCOVERY OF AMERICA. 
By Jonathan Raban. 
HarperCollins. $25. 
Yes, it's another travels-through-America book, but don't be put off. 
Jonathan Raban's is an unusually generous and sardonic view of the United States, like a vicarious summer vacation with a smart, pleasant English friend. 
He meets a Ukrainian emigre who sells bird whistles on Broadway and hobnobs with high-rise dwellers ("Air People") in New York City. 
But he is at his best when he rents a cabin and a dog and settles down in Guntersville, Ala., a place where, he observes, folks seem to be saying, "You want to find our town quaintly amusing?
We know how to play along with that."
Few writers are so savvy and witty about Americans' self-images, or so engaging.
THE COMMANDERS. 
By Bob Woodward. 
Simon & Schuster. 
$24.95. The latest book by the Watergate superstar Bob Woodward reads like the authorized biography of Gen. Colin L. Powell, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. 
That kind of inside information is its strength; the largely one-sided perspective is its weakness. 
Readers may want to dash through Part 1, about the 1989 invasion of Panama (intriguing, though not presented as high drama), to get to the book's second half, about the decisions that led the United States to enter the Persian Gulf war. 
That part is tailor-made for audiences primed by television coverage of the conflict. 
"The Commanders" turns into a lively behind-the-scenes docudrama featuring the familiar cast of Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and Gen. H. Norman Schwarzkopf, and of course General Powell, who emerges as the country's conscience and cautious voice of reason. 
As always with Mr. Woodward's anonymous sources, you either believe him or you don't. 
Filled with accounts of secret Pentagon meetings, political maneuvers, second guesses and roads not taken, it is a fascinating, accessible treatment of a story still coming to light.
PARLIAMENT OF WHORES: A LONE HUMORIST ATTEMPTS TO EXPLAIN THE ENTIRE U.S. 
GOVERNMENT. By P. J. O'Rourke. 
Atlantic Monthly Press . $19.95. 
Being a politically conservative baby-boomer and the White House correspondent for Rolling Stone magazine would guarantee P. J. O'Rourke a pretty strange perspective to begin with. 
Add to that his quirky, revealing turns of phrases and a healthy nonpartisan irreverence, and these collected articles are remarkably fresh, even when they're about the 1988 political conventions. 
The Democratic convention, he reminds us, was held in Atlanta, "that place where bad malls go when they die."
If the author doesn't quite decipher the misworkings of Congress, at least he goes a long way toward figuring out why the country's two-party system so often produces a mess. 
Democrats are "the party that says government can make you richer, smarter, taller and get the chickweed out of your lawn," he writes. 
"Republicans are the party that says government doesn't work, and then they get elected and prove it."
WOODY ALLEN: A BIOGRAPHY. 
By Eric Lax. 
Alfred A. Knopf. $24. 
This detailed biography is based on years of interviews and access to editing rooms, the kind of privileged insight authors dream of. 
Eric Lax faithfully, if uncritically, relates the facts, anecdotes and jokes that make up Woody Allen's life and career, from his babyhood in Brooklyn to his own baby with Mia Farrow. 
The best surprises come early on, when Allan Konigsberg was becoming Woody Allen: the youthful gags he ghostwrote for newspaper columnists, letters from Los Angeles (signed "Al") when he was a television writer for "The Colgate Variety Hour," and his miserable depression and stubborn determination while breaking in as a stand-up comic. 
The author wisely lets Mr. Allen speak for himself a great deal, so a Woody-ish voice runs through the book.
MAO II. 
By Don DeLillo. 
Viking. $19.95. 
This short, fluent novel is fraught with explosive implications about mass-produced art and society. 
The characters include an aging reclusive novelist, his caretakers -- a young male hanger-on and his girlfriend, a former Moonie -- and a famous middle-age female photographer. 
Although they seem mere vehicles for the author's ideas, they serve as a frightening distillation of American identity gone haywire. 
The title refers to an Andy Warhol portrait and to Mao Zedong's brilliant use of public relations, but nothing is quite so chilling as the novel's opening scene, the mass wedding of thousands of Moonies in Yankee Stadium.
Â 
Also Recommended
YOU'LL NEVER EAT LUNCH IN THIS TOWN AGAIN. 
By Julia Phillips. 
Random House. 
$22. Even if you already know the good parts, this is the perfect beach book: high-spirited, gossipy fun in which a Hollywood producer gets back at Steven Spielberg, Goldie Hawn and all the suits and drug-dealers who done her wrong.
IMMORTALITY. By Milan Kundera; translated by Peter Kussi. 
Grove Weidenfeld. 
$21.95. Written in the meditative style of "The Unbearable Lightness of Being," Milan Kundera's fanciful novel explores the nature of fame and immortality in a story that roams from a middle-aged Parisian woman to a heavenly meeting between Goethe and Hemingway.
LOS GUSANOS. 
By John Sayles. 
HarperCollins. $22.95. 
The film director's novel about a Cuban-American woman planning an anti-Castro rebellion in 1981. 
A half-dozen major characters, flashbacks to Fidel Castro's takeover, and snippets of untranslated Spanish (the title means "The Worms") create a peculiar blend of literary ambition and stock commercial style.
A LIFE OF PICASSO: VOLUME I, 1881-1906. 
By John Richardson. 
Random House. 
$45. A serious, elegantly written biography that follows the artist from his macho Spanish origins to the verge of creating "Les Demoiselles d'Avignon."
Profusely illustrated, unfortunately in black-and-white.
THE SUM OF ALL FEARS. 
By Tom Clancy. 
G. P. Putnam's (August). 
$24.95. For fans who can't get enough, nearly 800 pages in which the C.I.A. agent Jack Ryan tries to prevent a nuclear war set off by a crisis in the Middle East.
IF YOU CAN'T LIVE WITHOUT ME, WHY AREN'T YOU DEAD YET?
By Cynthia Heimel. 
Atlantic Monthly Press, $19.95. 
Sharp, smart comic essays by the author of "Sex Tips for Girls."
She hates Marilyn Monroe for playing "lamebrains" all the time, and she posits "Heimel's Law: Anything you fantasize about won't come true. 
So just cut it out."
MUHAMMAD ALI: HIS LIFE AND TIMES. 
By Thomas Hauser. 
Simon & Schuster. 
$24.95. Although written with the subject's cooperation, this is a rounded oral history told by family, friends, critics and men he has beaten up in the ring.
BEAST. By Peter Benchley. 
Random House (July). 
$21. It lives in the sea, it smells like ammonia, and when we're not watching it eat people in boats, we hear the creature's thoughts. 
This novel is goofier than "Jaws," but recognizably by the same author.

file: Crops Occupy Rural China, Not Unrest.txt
text:
ï»¿
Huang Dani giggled nervously at the mention of the turmoil in Beijing, and then inched her way as far back as she could against her living room wall near a large old portrait of Mao.
''Oh, it was very bad,'' said the 37-year-old woman, who says she was busy harvesting her wheat on June 4 when troops were firing on demonstrators in the capital, 400 miles to the northeast.
''Some bad people made revolution in Beijing. 
If the society is not stable, people will suffer. 
If the rebellion spreads, then we peasants can't farm the land and get the harvest.''
Here in Henan Province, in the heartland of China, where travel rarely takes a villager beyond the field and television is the only window to the world outside, Miss Huang's comments seem to reflect the only concern of many Chinese peasants: Will the Government be stable enough to pay for our grain and let us till the land?
Â 
Larger Stake in System
The word ''democracy'' is hardly ever spoken on these dirt roads that are shared by people, pigs and chickens alike, and few peasants here or elsewhere were involved in the protest movement.
But these peasants understand very well the language of money, corruption and even nepotism. 
In the village next door to Miss Huang's, the son of the village party secretary runs the lucrative carpet-making factory.
It is difficult to gauge peasant attitudes precisely because officials always accompany reporters on interviews. 
But most peasants seemed sincere when they worried aloud about instability, and it is noteworthy that since the land policies of the early 1950's and especially since the land distributions of the early 1980's most peasants have seemed to feel a larger stake in the system and have been a more conservative force in society.
Some peasants ventured to say they supported the students in calls against Government corruption. 
But they added, invoking the party line, that the students were manipulated by a small handful of people. 
If the terminology did not come from the Government's television propaganda, it probably came from the politically astute, fast-talking village leaders.
Â 
Rural Incomes Rise
''The students were not mature, and they were cheated by a small number of people,'' said Hu Zhonghe, the party secretary in the nearby village of Xia Zhuang.
There is less reason for peasants than for city residents to be dissatisfied with the Government. 
The authorities have given peasants the right to use their own plots of land, and rural incomes have risen even faster than those in urban areas.
What concerns peasants most now is whether their fall crops will turn out well and whether prices will remain stable so they can save quickly enough to build a new home and buy a cow or a pig. 
Many hope someday to be rich.
Hu Xianzhou, the only dentist for the township of Li Cun, is already rather wealthy. 
With a 14-room house, two television sets, including a color one, two pigs, a dog and several cats, he made more than $1,000 last year.
The gap in the living standard between the rural and urban areas is narrowing, according to official statistics. 
The average peasant earns the equivalent of $147 a year, or 45 percent of the average urban income. 
In fact, because the cost of living is far lower in the countryside, the real gap in incomes is much less than the figures would suggest.
Li Yukun, a 28-year-old peasant in Huai Shujie village in the northwest of Henan Province, admitted that the Beijing demonstrations were the talk of the village in early June, but added that since nobody really knew what happened the people believed it was best to stick to their farming or there would be nothing to eat.
He added, ''The Government's method in cracking down was correct.''

file: CROWDS IN STREET ASK DENG_S OUSTER.txt
text:
ï»¿
More than a million Chinese took to the streets of Beijing Wednesday in an extraordinary outpouring of support for more democracy.
The protests, amounting almost to a general strike, continued this morning and greatly increased the pressure on the Government to sacrifice one or more top officials and speed political liberalization.
In an attempt to defuse the situation, several of the nation's top leaders visited hospitalized students on a hunger strike early this morning to show their concern. 
But the crowds this morning seemed at least as militant as those on Wednesday, and many people said they would be satisfied only with the removal of the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, or Prime Miniser Li Peng.
Many Banners, Few Police
Some workers said their factories were on strike, and the crowds in the streets again turned the normally drab city into a kaleidoscope of banners demanding more democracy and urging support for the hunger strikers.
The police were nowhere to be seen, but the city reverberated with angry slogans demanding a more open political system and with sirens of ambulances carrying unconscious hunger strikers from the central square to nearby hospitals.
It was the 3,000 hunger strikers -like Wang Wen, a young man who turned 21 years old Wednesday and pledged to maintain the strike until death if necessary - who galvanized the support and often tears of people all over the city. 
On Wednesday, the fifth day of their strike, the students were visibly weakened as they lay on the ground sheltered from the hot sun by sheets and tents. 
But they saw their cause provoke a political crisis in China.
Â 
Party Leaders Visit Strikers
The Government televised this morning's hospital visit, in which Prime Minister Li and the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang, met with hunger strikers, and some of the television scenes included students making strong criticisms of Communist Party rule.
''Everybody thinks the nation has no hope, the Communist Party has no hope,'' a disheveled young man shown on national television told his visitors. 
''We should do things the way they do them in the United States, and thus restore people's confidence.''
The hospital visit seemed to have no impact in placating the hundreds of thousands of demonstrators who gathering again this morning in the center of the city to join the protests. 
More and more were high-school students and people from other cities who have poured into Beijing on trains and buses to show.
The demonstrators had little to say about the Soviet leader, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, whose visit to China continued to be disrupted by the protests. 
Many workers seemed little aware of Mr. Gorbachev, and though intellectuals said that they admired what Mr. Gorbachev had done in the Soviet Union, they emphasized that it was sympathy for the hunger strikers rather than Mr. Gorbachev's presence that brought them into the streets.
The demonstration Wednesday was the realization of one of the Government's worst nightmares - organized worker participation in what began as student protests. 
Furthermore, the workers included not only auto mechanics and railroad employees, but staff members of some of China's most respected and sensitive institutions.
Among the thousands of ''work units'' that paraded through the capital were organized groups representing pillars of the establishment like the People's Liberation Army, the Foreign Ministry, the Central People's Broadcasting Station, People's Daily and even the cadre school of the Communist Party Central Committee. 
Most of the marchers were young people who said they had taken the initiative to demonstrate, but many said that their bosses did not object when they painted banners and marched out the door.
''Dump Li Peng!
Dump Li Peng!'' shouted employees of the Government-affiliated Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, to roars of support from the crowd.
Demonstrations for democracy and in support of the hunger strikers were also held in 21 other cities around the country, the official New China News Agency reported. 
The agency, which like other official Chinese news outlets has reported extensively on the hunger strikers, said that in the cities of Shanghai and Tianjin, nearly 30,000 students rallied, while smaller numbers gathered in the other cities.
In calling for more democracy, the students are specifically demanding press freedom, an end to corruption and, in many cases, free elections to fill leading positions. 
The students' demands also include open-ended talks with the nation's leaders on a variety of issues and an official reappraisal of the student movement.
Â 
Weakening Support for Party Line
More and more prominent individuals and organizations also called on the Government to bend to the students' demands, in a sign of weakening support for the official party line. 
Among those appealing to the Government to heed the students were the presidents of eight universities and the central committees of the Chinese Communist Youth League, the All-China Youth Federation and the All-China Students Federation.
On Wednesday, the protest campaign seemed to complete its transformation from a student movement into a broad-based democracy movement that will be very difficult to squelch. 
The New China News Agency reported that the number of protesters in Beijing exceeded 1 million, corroborating Western estimates and making it by far the biggest demonstration in China since the organized rallies of Red Guards more than two decades ago, early in the Cultural Revolution.
Students and workers reported that small strikes were beginning at a number of offices and factories to show support for the students. 
The strikes compounded the urgency of the crisis and narrowed the options for top leaders.
Â 
Televised Debate Sought
A senior Communist Party official said he expected Prime Minister Li or Mr. Zhao to meet with students in an attempt to end the hunger strike and defuse the crisis. 
He said that while there were disagreements among top officials about how to handle the situation, the leaders are likely to bend to the students' main demands, for open-ended televised talks with the Government.
Further delays are likely only to hurt the Government's position, as the hunger strikers continue to weaken and inspire more and more sympathy from throughout the nation. 
China has had a long history of respect for scholars, and there is an enormous poignancy here in the situation of the youths who say they are willing to die on hunger strike to achieve more democracy.
''This is the fifth day of the students' hunger strike, so we have come to support them,'' Sun Yong, an engineer in the People's Liberation Army who marched with dozens of other members of his Army unit, said Wednesday. 
''The Government ignores the students, and so people hate the leaders. 
It is very dangerous for us to come, and we may lose our jobs. 
But every Chinese must speak out. 
If the Government doesn't answer the students' demands, we will keep coming.''

file: Crystalline Ice Fantasies In Frozen Manchuria.txt
text:
ï»¿
FAR north of China's Great Wall, a city of crystalline sculptured ice emitting colored light transforms long frozen winters into a fantasyland. 
The annual Ice Lantern Festival in Harbin, capital of the northeastern border province of Heilungkiang and once a city of many Russians, celebrates the lunar new year like no other place in China.
While the rest of the country frolics with paper lanterns, Harbin's vast Zhaolin Park is transformed into a city carved of ice. 
From Jan. 
1 through the end of February, fanciful creatures and giant animals inhabit a world of icy palaces and tall pagodas, snowy flowers, pavilions and frozen tableaus from Chinese legends. 
In daylight the scene takes on a silvery cast. 
At night it blossoms in rainbows of light that blaze from inside the sculptures. 
The peacock struts his multicolored tail, a volcano erupts with red light, the stout-hearted climb a bluish replica of an ice-covered Great Wall, and children scramble up the tail of an elephant to slide down its icy trunk.
Ice sculpture is a part of life in the Harbin (Harb-EEN), the industrial city and river port about 800 miles northeast of Beijing. 
Here, in the region still known as Manchuria, the largest Russian settlement outside Russia was established after World War I, and some of the city's architecture still reflects that time. 
Later, Harbin had one of the largest European populations in the Far East, until the Communists took over after World War II. 
And on a visit there last winter - before the harsh crackdown on pro-deomcracy demonstrators in Beijing and other cities - I noticed among the ice sculptures, along with other foreign themes, an exhibit inspired by Disney and a carved dolphin representing Alaska.
Throughout the city ice-covered pandas, prancing horses and tigers and creations of frozen falling water adorn traffic circles and the entryways of hotels and government buildings. 
In midwinter days that peak around zero degrees Fahrenheit, the high energy level of the Harbinese is noticeable, and perhaps it can be attributed to food portions fit for a giant, or to the fact that all buldings are superbly heated. 
Temperatures can sink to minus 20 at night yet no one seems to mind. 
The Harbinese leave their television sets and do what northerners everywhere do in winter - put on another layer. 
They stroll about eating ice cream clutched in mittened hands. 
They claim it melts too fast in the summer.
Reminiscent of a misty Oriental painting, a deceptively pleasing lavender pall hangs over city and countryside. 
Rather than bits of delicate cloud, the haze is a false curtain of polluting smoke from industrial coal and heating wood fires. 
''Black snow,'' said a visitor from Pennsylvania sweeping up a handful. 
''Just like Pittsburgh when I was a kid.''
The ice carvings are swept clean daily of snowfall and pollution.
A bustling city of some three million, Harbin is an exception in a land crammed with ancient sites. 
Until the turn of the century a mere village whose name meant ''where the fishing nets are dried,'' its character was forever altered by Russians and by Japanese. 
Russian architecture, especially old Orthodox churches and the railroad station, brought fame and the sobriquet, Moscow of the East. 
Japanese warlords imposed the birth of Harbin's thriving heavy industry.
The history of Heilungkiang plays a major role in the clamorous events of 20th-century China. 
In 1896 Russia negotiated a contract to build a railroad to Vladivostok through the province that has developed since into the Texas of China. 
(The nation's largest oilfields begin 62 miles northwest of Harbin. 
In 1914, following an agreement that extended Russian rights along the rail line to Britain as well, several European countries and the United States signed up for equal privileges, sending a swarm of foreign entrepreneurs to Harbin and turning it into an international city. 
In 1917 White Russian refugees surged into Harbin, which grew into alarge Russian settlement. 
Then in February 1932 Japanese troops occupied the city, renaming the province Manchukuo.
Throughout World War II, under the oppressive rule of Japan's Manchuria-based Kwantung army, the heavy industrial trend was begun with forced production in a province rich in coal and other largely untapped resources. 
The Soviet Army took back Harbin in 1945 and withdrew when Chinese troops were installed by agreement.
THE Russians are long gone from Harbin, leaving onion-domed churches and little trellised street kiosks that perk up the drab square buildings of newer vintage. 
The most interesting aspect of the provincial museum, built in 1923 as the commercial center, is outside, where symmetrical domes and spires rise at each end. 
The immense railroad station, built when the Russians projected a great northern transport hub in Harbin, is no longer large enough.
In the Daolichu district not far from Zhaolin Park, the skyline is studded with cupolas, spires and scalloped turrets. 
St. Sophia's Church is a fine example, its great onion bulb a tinge of old Moscow. 
While numerous churches were ravaged during the Chinese Cultural Revolution in the late 1960's and turned into warehouses, several remain. 
In the Nangang district the vaulted Orthodox church (Church of China Eastern Orthodox) is always open, and elderly devotees come and go. 
Services are conducted in Russian. 
The church was reopened in 1984. 
Nearby, the Gothic Church of the Christian religion (Lutheran), built in 1911, is locked except Sundays. 
Services are conducted in Chinese; the church was reopened in 1980.
The deep frozen Songari River is the soul of the Ice Lantern Festival. 
Winding through the northern part of the city, it provides the building blocks. 
Work begins in late November when metal stakes are driven into the ice. 
By hook, crane and truck, ice blocks are moved to the park where carpenters using electric saws slice them into smaller chunks. 
The last three weeks of December are a flurry of carving as more than 2,000 artisans and electricians leave factory jobs to apply skills and fancy to the ice.
By Jan. 
1 the entrance walk is lined with birds and animals on pedestals, leading to an icy cauldron with leaping red streamers simulating the Olympic torch. 
Pathways with whimsical creatures and ice railings curve toward a transparent Moorish palace with colored lights, a multilevel pagoda with 10 100-foot-tall pavonine spires, ice bridges and gardens, a frozen onion-domed church, or a glowing ice rink for dancing. 
Chinese and Western music hoots from speakers while frolicking lighted deer and rabbits, penguins, dragons and a phoenix accompany Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs.
Beyond a tall gateway of horseshoe-shaped ice blocks on the high road, the Sungari River turns into a huge playground. 
At an ice-walled slide that shoots down the steep bank, revelers sit on woven mats or stand in street shoes for careening descents to the frozen water. 
A bone-chilling wind accompanies merrymakers who hire ice boats to sail the wide river, or one-horse gigs mounted on sleds and decorated with colored streamers. 
Throughout the winter members of a little troupe of outdoor sports fanatics named the Harbin Penguins jump into the frigid water to swim where the three-foot-thick ice has been hacked away.
The festival, first held in 1963 in the tottering days of economic recovery from the Great Leap Forward, collided with the Cultural Revolution but restarted in 1978 and has been picking up size each year. 
International competition in ice carving began three years ago and in the winter of 1989, France took the gold. 
Circling a nearly full-scale Arc de Triomphe, shiny transparent sculptures included a glistening Liberte (first prize), a great fat sumo wrestler (third prize, Japan) and a fighting Australian kangaroo. 
Harbinese clustered at Alaska's entry, a totem-style dolphin with a placard in Chinese describing the Aleutian fairy tale of the dolphin god.
It's a sure bet that a visit to Harbin will include too much food. 
Winter meals are piled on platters in at least seven courses. 
The Chinese dishes are sour, mildly hot, fresh, salty and substantial; some are crisp and many are oily. 
Western fare has a bit of old Russia clinging to it, especially in pastries and braised dishes. 
The Harbinese favor sausage snacks - white-meat and red sausages are popular, stuffed in wheat buns, with pancake or steamed bread, or sauerkraut noodles. 
In street markets, fresh vegetables from southern provinces are kept under heavy quilts to prevent freezing. 
About the city, streamer flags on single poles announce restaurants - red for local, blue for Mongolian food and neither very clean. 
In addition to beef and mutton, pork is abundant. 
It is said that all leftovers go to the pigs and I believe it - the porkers wandering around country villages are enormous. 
Group travelers can arrange for a banquet serving the so-called four dainties of Harbin: stewed bear's paw, one of the oldest delicacies in Chinese recipes; braised moose's snout in brown sauce; fei-long (grouse) soup, and white houtou mushrooms served with shredded chicken.
Dancing is another diversion on winter nights. 
To Chinese popular music performed by a six-piece band and solist, throngs of dancers swirl around ballroom floors in a smooth adagio-like step. 
Western cassettes blast during the intervals when the dance floor takes on the look of a crowd of beginners trying to learn unrestrained disco movements. 
For an entrance fee of 6 yuan (50 cents), whether the music is live or canned, everyone dances (usually 200 to 300) - couples, men and men, women and women, threesomes and singles. 
(The regulars' boots were stashed neatly under tables.) There are about 20 dance halls in Harbin.
During Harbin's winter, Manchurians offer advisories on keeping warm outdoors. 
We wore the recommended down clothing, played amid frozen creations and always remembered the final admonition: after staying out for some time, don't drink hot water until your teeth get warm.
Â 
PLANNING A TRIP TO HARBIN
Â 
Getting There
Air China (formerly C.A.A.C.) operates many domestic flights to Harbin: from Beijing, Changchun, Shanghai, Shenyang and Guangzhou (Canton). 
Travelers can reach Harbin by rail from any province. 
The Chinese say that travel on the Trans-Siberian Railroad offers better service on the run from China to the Soviet Union, with Chinese staff, than in the other direction with Russian personnel.
Travel in China is controlled by China International Travel Service (C.I.T.S.), the government wing concerned with all foreign visitors. 
It provides English-speaking guides and has the final say in hotel choice. 
The best prices are in packages from travel agents specializing in mainland travel; they have Beijing branch offices. 
There are agencies in Hong Kong that arrange personalized itineraries and simplify the sometimes difficult visa procedures. 
They have a wide knowledge of hotels and arrange everything in 24 hours. 
An all-inclusive week in the north is about $1500 round trip from Hong Kong. 
One experienced agency is Lap Ming International Travel Service, East Ocean Center, 98 Granville Road, T.S.T. 
Kowloon, Hong Kong; telephone, 3-723-8803.
Â 
Currency and Customs
China's two-tier money system is confusing. 
Renminbi (R.M.B.) is People's Money and foreign exchange certificates (F.E.C.'s) are Tourist Money, both issued in denominations of yuan (pronounced wan). 
In exchange for cash or traveler's checks from international banks, visitors receive exchange certificates; a dollar equals about 3.71 yuan. 
Tourists must pay for purchases in F.E.C.'s; if you want to buy something at a street market, you'll have a small amount of R.M.B. 
Stay clear of the black market in currency; the penalties are stiff.
Â 
Where to Stay
Harbin is oriented to international trade and there is no shortage of hotels; reservations required. 
While cleanliness standards are not up to those in the United States , the hotels are are adequate, with restaurants and shops and English-speaking staff. 
Good are the Swan Hotel (Tian E Fandian), which was crammed with Russian buyers attending a trade fair when we stayed there (73 Zhongsang Road; telephone, 54041); and the Guoji Fandian (International Hotel, 124 Dazhi Street; 31441). 
Doubles with baths and TV from about $20.
Top of the line is the new wing of the Friendship Hotel. 
Full of marble, it is considered the best in Harbin. 
Doubles with baths and TV from $21 (57 Youyi Road; 47132). 
Opened this year, the new Milky Way Hotel charges from $21 for doubles with baths and TV.
Â 
Other Advice
Practical winter clothing is essential; fancy dress unnecessary. 
Take a down jacket, lined boots, warm slacks, a cap with earflaps, sweater, mittens and silk longjohns, which can be bought cheaply in China (though not in extra-large sizes). 
Women need warm slacks; a skirt or dress should be worn only indoors and not in transit.
The common cold with lingering cough is a hazard of China travel in any season. 
Known as Peking throat and caused by pollution, it happens anywhere, anytime. 
Take your own remedies and prescription drugs. 
Drink only boiled water (tea) or bottled liquids. 
No special innoculations are necessary for China, but a gamma-globulin shot to prevent hepatitis is recommended.
Â 
Dining and Shopping
Unless you have an iron stomach, hotel dining rooms are the safest bet, as well as restaurants recommended by C.I.T.S. 
It is said that Huamei in Zhongyang Street is the best in Harbin for Russian food. 
When you go to outside restaurants, don't plan on using the toilet facilities - they are not clean and flushes seldom work. 
Street markets are everywhere in the city, as well as two large department stores crammed with merchandise and always crowded. 
The Friendship Store, on the top floor of the Second Department Store, offers curios and toys. 
The Xiangyang Fur Store has a large selection of leather and fur, with coats of fox, squirrel or sable from $67; quality is mediocre.Â Â Â Â -Â M. 
T.
A bridge with pavilions and pathways all carved from ice is big enough for visitors to walk on. 
At night, a towering ice palace glows with the light of lanterns placed inside (pg. 
7); a palace courtyard of ice. 
An incense burner supported by carved fish; and a sumo from Japan (pg. 
8) (Moana Tregaskis)

The exiled spiritual leader of Tibet, the Dalai Lama, said today that his Himalayan homeland had been encouraged in its struggle for independence from China by Mongolia's experience in throwing off strict Communism.
Criticizing China's Communist leaders, he told reporters here, "These recent events clearly demonstrate their efforts are fruitless, useless."
There have been "so many restrictions, so much effort to eliminate the Buddhist faith in Tibet," he said, but "they will not succeed."
Earlier in the day, the Dalai Lama chanted prayers before a crowd of 15,000 people at Mongolia's national sports stadium.

text:

The Dalai Lama, the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader, says the arrests and executions set in motion by the Chinese Government will fail to wipe out aspirations for liberty and democracy.
''It will never work,'' the 55-year-old Buddhist leader said in an interview on Saturday in Manhattan. 
''It will never suppress real human determination.''
He was in New York on a one-day stopover on his way to a Costa Rican conference on the meaning of peace.
The Dalai Lama, who is venerated by Tibetans as a divine reincarnation with godly compassion, was himself chased from Tibet by Chinese troops when they crushed an uprising in 1959. 
Since then he has lived in India.
The Dalai Lama, dressed in his customary monk's robe during an interview at his hotel, said the Chinese invasion of Tibet in 1950 was followed by harsh repression and rigors that abated only in the last decade.
''You can see from what has happened in Tibet that violent suppression will not succeed,'' the Dalai Lama said, speaking in fluent, Indian-inflected English. 
''Today in Tibet there is more national feeling and more national cohesion than there ever was before the Chinese came.''
The Dalai Lama said he was aware of the reports from China of relatives turning in brothers and sisters for punishment, and he noted that this reflected ''an old Communist tactic.''
Â 
'Situation Has Changed'
''They really implement the policy of divide and rule,'' he said. 
''They brand people with suspicions. 
This has been the past experience, but now I think the situation has changed.
''In the last 10 years, Chinese people have had much contact with the outside world. 
There are a large number of sudents in the outside world. 
Also, these people have access to telephones and fax machines. 
They have much information. 
The regime will want to control this, but now it will be impossible to control.''
He observed that Buddhism teaches that every event and action has many aspects, both positive and negative. 
But he went on to say that the recent Chinese action was ''very negative, very harmful.''
''It is very bad for the Chinese themselves and for the Chinese Communist Party and very bad for the leaders,'' he said. 
''Without this their name would have remained in history signifying something wise. 
Now that has been damaged.''
Asked how the crackdown might affect initiatives by the Government to reach an agreement with him over the status of Tibet, he said that over the last two years the Chinese had rejected his proposal for negotiations on Tibetan autonomy.
''The Chinese disagreed with the proposal but at the same time they still insist they want dialogue,'' he said. 
''Just before the students were crushed they indicated that they still wanted to discuss the issue, sending me a message through the Chinese Embassy in New Delhi.
Â 
'Humans Love Freedom'
''But now, you see, we feel a bit reluctant to carry out dialogue because in a very real sense the Chinese Government may not be the people's government. 
Obviously we also want to remain in solidarity with those Chinese brothers and sisters who want to have more freedom.''
The Dalai Lama turned to a broader discussion of changes in he world that he said are causing totalitarian systems to place less reliance on force.
''Humans love freedom,'' he said. 
''Humans love democracy. 
Now at the end of the century this human spirit seems to be getting the upper hand, though of course in China for the time being there is a setback.''
After his visit to Costa Rica, the Dalai Lama is to return to the United States to officiate at Buddhist ceremonies in California and to receive the Raoul Wallenberg Human Rights Award from the Congressional Human Rights Foundation, the private-sector arm of the Congressional Human Rights Caucus.

file: Daqiuzhuang Journal_A Chinese Village Discovers the Road to Riches.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yang Yanru, a middle-aged woman who keeps her 11-room house spotless, could have been standing on a typical street in an affluent American suburb, bidding her guests goodbye after a luncheon.
Except for her crooked teeth, and a collar that suggested her man-tailored shirt was made in the 1960's, there was little to suggest that Ms. Yang was once a peasant who got her eggs from the chicken coop in the backyard. 
Now she is one of China's new rich, a woman who says she doesn't have to hold down a job because her husband makes so much money. 
She can spend her afternoons entertaining visitors, she said, or playing mah-jongg with friends.
About 45 miles down a narrow, bumpy road from the heart of Tianjin city, Daqiuzhuang has earned a reputation as a village that got rich through a strange blend of Communism and capitalism.
Factories here operate 24 hours a day, seven days a week, paying salaries of $800 to $900 a year to most village residents. 
Most of the rest of the money is plowed back into businesses or is spent on communal projects or perks for bosses and model workers.
"Even in my dreams, I never thought life could be so good," said Ms. Yang, who knits when she is not watching one of her three color televisions or talking on one of her two telephones.
Â 
Scores 0f Luxury Cars
This village of 4,400 people has 13 Mercedes Benzes and nearly 140 other imported luxury cars. 
In 1990, Daqiuzhuang's per capita income was $3,400, 10 times China's national average; last year, officials say, it soared even higher, to an estimated $8,400.
The village runs the factories that make the money -- 226 enterprises in all. 
Factory managers receive a share of profits in addition to their salaries, and their incomes can be enormous. 
In 1990, the last year for which figures are fully calculated, Ms. Yang's husband, who manages a construction business, was entitled to $9,300, though she said he took only a part of that and returned the rest to the enterprise.
No Daqiuzhuang citizen pays a cent for housing, electricity, hot water, gas, medical care or the 11 years of education to which every child is entitled. 
The village also invests about $3.7 million a year in building houses and apartment buildings for its 1,300 families. 
If an employee is rewarded as a model worker, as Ms. Yang's husband was, he receives one of 300 furnished, nicely painted two-story brick houses.
"Here we have reached the perfect form of socialism: Communism," said Sun Guiqiu, a senior official in the village.
But capitalism seems to be the major factor in the village's business success. 
Factories keep careful track of costs, pay their employees by the piece rate and use complex systems of incentives to increase production.
Despite detailed questioning, officials never made clear just how their village had managed do so much better than others. 
Perhaps there are further secrets here, or special benefits conferred by higher authorities.
One factor that surely helped is that Daqiuzhuang started earlier than most. 
More than a dozen years ago, the village established its first enterprise, a mill that processed rolled steel, and began selling the steel across the country.
Unlike most villages, which have a Communist Party Secretary as well as a village leader, Daqiuzhuang combined the two positions into one. 
That official is also chief executive of the holding company owning all village enterprises, suggesting that the village is actually one giant company.
Â 
$5.5 Million in Savings
The chief of Daqiuzhuang, Yu Zuomin, a 62-year-old native of the village, lives more like a tycoon than a Communist official. 
When his son married recently, the wedding and gifts, which included a beautiful new house, reportedly cost about $275,000.
After visiting the United States last year, Mr. Yu remarked that Daqiuzhuang residents were "much better off than the middle-class" of America, Mr. Sun said.
The village bank holds about $5.5 million in savings, the official said. 
As economic expansion has created work beyond what Daqiuzhuang's residents can manage themselves, the village has by official count added at least 7,000 laborers from across the nation; there may be many more.
These laborers are paid by the piece for their work. 
While they are also given housing, they have fewer opportunities for advancement than local people.
At Wanquan Industrial Company, a steel processing enterprise that reported earnings of nearly $5.5 million last year, 10 percent of the 2,100 employees are from Daqiuzhuang, and most of them hold positions in senior management. 
Liu Yunzhang, a villager who studied mathematics at Tianjin University and returned to become a senior personnel officer, is only 27 years old.
Mr. Sun is only 22 years old. 
While his annual salary is only $890, he negotiates high-powered business deals over elaborate lunches and lives in a spacious four-bedroom apartment.
Salaries are perhaps kept low to avoid taxes. 
Last year, the village's profits from its enterprises came to nearly $15 million, with one-fourth of that amount going to the Government in business taxes. 
Yet only a small handful of the 4,400 villagers paid any personal income tax, for a total of about $55,500. 
Income is sometimes distributed in the form of special perks like free cars for executives.
Perhaps because "guanxi," or business connections and relationships with powerful officials, are so important in China, the village also made big donations to flood-stricken areas last year. 
Such contributions may also be intended to ease criticism that Daqiuzhuang is too capitalist or too rich.

file: DE GUSTIBUS_Older Than Forks, Safer Than Knives.txt
text:
ï»¿
THIS is a plea for chopsticks. 
Chopsticks for pasta. 
Chopsticks for string beans. 
Chopsticks for french fries. 
Chopsticks for grilled chanterelles. 
Indeed, chopsticks for just about anything, except perhaps a thick hunk of meat. 
I have one friend who even uses them to eat ice cream.
I don't mean to be demanding. 
I know running a restaurant or arranging a dinner party is tough enough without having to worry about additional utensils. 
But I have long thought most food just tastes better when eaten with chopsticks, and I think diners should have the choice.
Let's face it: there is nothing sacrosanct about an eating utensil. 
It was not until the 18th century, after all, that most people in the United States even used a fork.
According to ''From Hand to Mouth,'' a history of the use of cutlery by James Cross Giblin (Thomas Y. Crowell, 1987), the wealthy began using forks in this country in the mid-1700's. 
Until that time, people got by with a spoon and a sharp-pointed knife. 
(Potatoes, like other food, were routinely stabbed and gulped off the blade.) Indeed, the fork met with resistance for centuries.
In ''Food in History'' (Crown, 1989) Reay Tannahill says that although small forks were first used in the 10th century by the Byzantines (the ancient Egyptians used large forks to display sacrificial offerings), it was not until 1533 that Catherine de' Medici introduced them to France, where they were for the most part ignored.
More than 100 years later, Louis XIV still ate chicken stew with his fingers and forbade the Duke of Burgundy and his brothers to use forks in his presence. 
The British did not start using forks until the 17th century. 
As late as 1897, Miss Tannahill writes, sailors in the British Navy were forbidden to use them ''because they were regarded as being prejudicial to discipline and manliness.''
In contrast, chopsticks have gracefully provided sustenance since as long ago as 1200 B.C.
Nina Simonds, whose book ''China's Food,'' a travelogue of food in China, is to be published later this year by Harper & Row, says that chopsticks (kuaizi in Mandarin, which is derived from the Chinese word for quick) have been in common use since the Early Han Dynasty, 206 B.C. to A.D. 8.
Simply put, Mr. Giblin writes, they appear to have provided a polite alternative to knives, which Confucius said reminded the diner of the violent act of slaughter. 
''The honorable and upright man keeps well away from both the slaughterhouse and the kitchen,'' Confucius wrote. 
''And he allows no knives on his table.''
I agree to a certain extent, although men do have their place in the kitchen these days. 
Chopsticks are serene instruments that permit diners to lift food to their lips rather than spearing it. 
They are elegant in both their simplicity and their singularity of purpose. 
But so far as I am concerned, their chief appeal is not their absence of violence. 
It is the opportunity they provide for gustatory involvement. 
In many ways, chopsticks are the culinary equivalent of the stick shift. 
They enhance the act of eating and make it more participatory, tactile, not to mention fun. 
They give a certain ceremony to consumption and force the calorie-conscious diner to focus on the ritual of gustation, and therefore on the amount of food being shoveled into the mouth at any time.
This increased awareness, in turn, enhances the attention paid to whatever is being eaten and encourages the diner to focus more on flavor.
But the advantages of chopsticks don't stop there. 
Chopsticks instantly promote a sense of community and conviviality at the table. 
Chopstick eaters are far less reluctant to lift up their individual plates and taste around. 
Even French foods like cassoulet, choucroute and ratatouille lend themselves, in part, to chopsticks. 
(Clearly a knife and fork are helpful for large chunks of duck.) But so do Indian beef curry, thick Tex-Mex chili and Greek souvlaki.
I know a lot of Westerners who do not use chopsticks. 
They either have little interest in them or have never learned how. 
Some have been exposed only to Japanese chopsticks, which are tapered, come to a point at the tip and are more difficult to maneuver than Chinese chopsticks.
Like sensible shoes, Chinese chopsticks - square at the head and thick at the base - are clunkier, perhaps, but far more functional. 
They are perfect for eating shish kebab, asparagus spears, shrimp, linguine with clam sauce or Chicken McNuggets.
Of course, anyone can learn to use chopsticks. 
Chopstick users outnumber fork eaters throughout the world by at least 2 to 1, some scholars of eating habits say. 
They simply require a desire to learn. 
But be forewarned: teaching someone to use chopsticks is a little bit like teaching someone to drive a car. 
It is best not to be related, and better yet not to be teaching someone who is hungry.
''Why can't I just use a fork?'' is obviously the kind of question best left unanswered.
Norge W. Jerome, director of the office of nutrition for the Agency for International Development in Washington and a professor of nutritional anthropology at the University of Kansas School of Medicine, is pessimistic about the future of chopsticks in the United States.
Knives and forks, she says, have a certain ''snob appeal'' and are too deeply embedded in the national sense of propriety. 
But I think it is time to re-evaluate this parochialism. 
Not that everyone should be forced to eat with chopsticks. 
Let fork eaters have their forks. 
But why should chopstick lovers always be made to feel like outcasts?
Why do they always have to feel left out?
Why can't they feel that they belong?
No question about it. 
Having to bring your own chopsticks to dinner, and to be instantly made a spectacle, is a form of discrimination - not the most heinous kind, but still a shame.
At a time when East and West are being merged more than ever before, isn't it time to reaffirm our sense of tolerance, to re-evaluate our table-setting habits and to give chopstick lovers a chance?
