ENOUGH of this kid stuff. 
Now that peanut butter is 100 years old, let's face facts and stop beating around the bush. 
Isn't it time for peanut butter to grow up?
It is almost embarrassing to admit. 
But this country is still serving most of its peanut butter with jelly when so many other parts of the world are using it subtly to enhance stews, thicken soups, or top grilled fish.
Isn't it time to start thinking of peanut butter in terms of finesse and fine crystal?
''Beyond the cookie,'' commanded Ellen Brown, a food consultant, who as part of peanut butter's 100th anniversary celebration, will be optimistically unveiling 30 new recipes on Friday at the International Association of Culinary Professionals in Atlanta in the hopes that a more sophisticated image will emerge. 
Her creations include recipes for peanut butter salad dressing, sauces, stews and soups.
There is disagreement about the origin of peanut butter. 
Some attribute its creation to a St. Louis physician whose identity is not known; others to a man named Joseph Lambert, who ran a nut business out of Battle Creek, Mich. 
But both are said to have emerged with their creations in the year 1890 and the process was patented seven years later. 
It became commercially available around the turn of the century.
George Washington Carver, who in 1925 published a paper at Tuskeegee Institute titled ''Bulletin No. 31, How to Grow the Peanut and 105 Ways of Preparing It for Human Consumption'' is credited with having been among the first to have concocted the peanut butter sandwich.
Now peanut butter is among this country's most popular foods with annual sales of an estimated 800 million pounds a year, said Mitch Head, a spokesman for the Peanut Advisory Commission, a trade association based in Atlanta. 
An estimated 85 percent of American households have a jar stashed away in a cupboard, according to the commission.
But to keep this in perspective, America is a mere child when it comes to the use of the peanut.
The peanut was believed to have been first cultivated 2,000 years ago in South America. 
It was eventually taken to Africa and Asia in the 16th century by the explorers of Europe.
Today the peanut and peanut butter are prominently featured in many cuisines. 
In Thailand, for example, they are used in the preparation of sauces and noodle dishes. 
In Indonesia, they are the base for a dipping sauce served with chicken and pork dishes. 
It is served in soups and stews in various African countries like Ghana where it is combined with tomatoes, onions, eggplant and okra in a stew-like chicken preparation and in Senegal where it is combined with sweet potatoes and cabbage. 
In the Sichuan province of China, it is commonly served in sauces that top noodles and cold chicken.
It is not that these more sophisticated uses of the peanut, which has long been appreciated as an inexpensive source of protein, never occurred to an American. 
Indeed, Evan Jones, the food historian and author of ''American Food: The Gastronomic Story'' (Vintage Books, 1981), said George Washington Carver tried valiantly to show Americans the many subtle joys of the peanut. 
But for some reason these uses never caught on. 
Americans resisted. 
Today the majority of Americans - 58 percent - continue to prefer their peanut butter on bread, according to consumer research done by CPC International, which manufactures Skippy brand peanut butter. 
Some 14 percent prefer it on crackers, according to the research, while another 10 percent eat it out of the jar.
It is not surprising then to discover that Dr. Peter McCann, a 37-year-old orthopedic surgeon living in Manhattan, an otherwise sophisticated diner and exacting food aficionado, prefers his peanut butter on white bread with jelly so thick it leaks through to the other side.
He only eats the creamy style, he said, because he doesn't like to chew peanut butter but instead prefers to be able to slosh it around with his tongue.
Interviews with peanut butter lovers around the country revealed that not unlike Dr. McCann, Americans share a similar, rather uninhibited childlike delight in the spread.
Larry Zisman, for example, who is co-author with his wife, Honey, of the ''The Great American Peanut Butter Book'' (St. Martin's Press, 1985), said he, too, often eats his peanut butter on bread. 
His favorite combination, he said, is ''putting some peanut butter in your mouth, adding chocolate chips and chewing them together.''
Frank Treadway, 61, of Fort Meyers, Fla., prefers it ''with meat loaf, bacon, cheese and cold baked beans.''
Norma Carpenter, a 45-year-old homemaker of Orofino, Idaho, routinely eats peanut butter mixed with margarine on popcorn.
''It's a sticky, gooey mess,'' she said. 
''But it's really good. 
You want to lick your fingers.''
Ethel Bonollo, who owns a telephone-answering service in Santa Barbara, Calif., keeps a jar by her desk.
''When you're working it's easier to stick a spoon in your mouth than to have to chomp on peants,'' she observed. 
''There's something smooth and settling about it.''
Other common ways of eating peanut butter in this country are with apples, celery sticks and bacon, and combined with mayonnaise, pickles, pretzels, corn chips, chocolate pudding, grilled cheese, graham crackers, saltines and whole wheat toast.
''When no one is looking, I simply stick my finger in the jar,'' admitted Sue Huffman, a former food editor, who now helps develop recipes for Best Foods.
There are, however, some Americans who do maintain some modicum of self-awareness and reserve about their passion for peanut butter.
David Haspel, for example, a 40-year-old film producer living in Los Angeles, admits to being addicted to crunchy-style peanut butter ever since he was sent away to summer camp. 
His wife, Jane, keeps at least one jar tucked away in a kitchen cupboard because he just ''needs to know it's there.''
''But I don't talk about it in public,'' Mr. Haspel said, pointing out that peanut butter and jelly on crackers is ''not like discussing French wines.''
All this may simply mean that peanut butter has just not been around long enough in America. 
Maturity, after all, has as much to do with experience as age; not to mention the desire to grow up.
Perhaps it should come as no surprise that one of the leading brands of peanut butter in this country is called Peter Pan.

text:

The opposition Democratic Progressive Party today expressed strong satisfaction with its showing in elections on Saturday, and said its performance would have been more impressive if it were not for vote buying and election fraud.
Final results available today showed that the party won 21 seats in the legislature, while the ruling Nationalist Party won 72. 
Independents won eight seats.
The Government denied charges of misconduct in the election, the first in which an opposition party was legally allowed to compete.
In the competition for 21 postitions of county magistrate and mayor, the Nationalists won 14 positions, the Democratic Progressives won 6, and an independent took 1.
There were no official results for the percentage of the popular vote received by each party. 
The Government spokesman, Shaw Yuming, estimated that the Nationalists had received 65 percent to 70 percent of the vote, with 20 percent to 25 percent going to the Democratic Progressive Party and the rest to independents and other parties.
Â 
Party Does Well at Local Level
But Tsai Shihyuan, deputy secretary general of the opposition party, said it had received 38 percent of the vote in the mayoral and county races and 45 percent of the vote when counting only those races in which it fielded a candidate. 
''It was a big victory for the opposition,'' Mr. Tsai said.
''They can say whatever they want,'' Mr. Shaw, the Government spokesman, replied later. 
He noted that the Nationalists still won a considerable majority of the votes and the seats.
A number of journalists and business executives, including some sympathetic to the opposition, said today in interviews that the Nationalist Party is so linked to the Government and to the press that the election was skewed. 
They asserted that vote buying, while practiced by candidates on both sides, is more prevalent among the Nationalists. 
But they said it was unlikely that significant fraud took place during voting or the counting of ballots.
Five members of the United States Congress who were here to observe the election gave it a qualified endorsement. 
''Our key judgment is that this year's election was the most free and fair in Taiwan's history,'' they said in a statement today.
But the delegation, which was led by Representative Stephen J. Solarz, Democrat of Brooklyn, added that Taiwan should take further steps to create fairness in the way that political parties can compete.
Â 
A More Benign Solarz
Mr. Solarz has sometimes offended officials here because of his support for dissidents, but on this trip it seemed that the authorities would be delighted with the contrast he drew with China.
''The entire world can see the contrast between Taiwan and the P.R.C.,'' Mr. Solarz said, referring to the People's Republic of China. 
''In the P.R.C., when the people ask for democracy, they are greeted with a hail of bullets, and Beijing is drowned in a river of blood. 
In Taiwan, when people demand democracy, they are given an opportunity to participate in an electoral process and can vote for the candidates of their choice.''
The Democratic Progressive Party's gains in the legislature are particularly significant because, for the first time, the party will have enough members to introduce legislation.

In the past, Taiwan's legislature has sometimes resembled a forum for debate less than a barroom. 
With no hope of either introducing or passing bills, frustrated opposition members have sometimes resorted to publicity stunts like smashing microphones and grappling with Nationalist legislators.
There has been a deep hostility between the two parties, with each regarding the other as untrustworthy. 
However, some Chinese here said they hoped that the election would mark the beginning of an evolution of the Democratic Progressive Party into the kind of loyal opposition found in the West.

text:

Unrepentant and defiant as ever, a well-known campaigner for democracy walked out of prison today after completing an eight-year sentence for editing a journal that called for greater human rights in China.
''I never gave in,'' Yang Jing told family members and friends who had gathered in his house to see him. 
''The officials said I had a bad attitude.''
During the ''Democracy Spring'' movement a decade ago, Mr. Yang was an editor of the ''April Fifth Forum,'' a mimeographed magazine that won acclaim as one of the most influential of the unofficial magazines calling for greater democracy and human rights. 
After some of his friends were arrested beginning in early 1979, Mr. Yang published numerous appeals for their release. 
In April 1981 he, too, was arrested.
Mr. Yang, who is 44 years old and was working as a steel worker at the time of his arrest, seemed in good health and fine spirits. 
He joked with the throng that crowded his home, including ''Democracy Spring'' dissidents who had been released from prison earlier, such as Ren Wanding and Xue Mingde. 
While prison was always grim, he said, the worst experience was an 11-month period early in his sentence when he was punished with solitary confinement for trying to get in touch with friends who were also in the prison. 
During that time, he was locked in a tiny, windowless cell, scarcely bigger than a bed, and for much of the time he was locked in handcuffs and leg irons, he said.
The left side of his body still suffers from a muscular ailment because of the conditions during that period, he said. 
But Mr. Yang, a slight man who wears black-rimmed glasses, seemed not at all daunted by his experiences. 
''I didn't shed a single tear during eight years in that place,'' he said.
Mr. Yang said he planned to find a job.
Some other ''Democracy Spring'' campaigners are still in prison, but Mr. Yang said he had little news of them. 
He said that he and other prisoners were not allowed to meet their most famous fellow resident of the Beijing No. 1 Prison, Xu Wenli. 
Mr. Xu, who is Prisoner 001, was the editor in chief of ''April Fifth Forum,'' and is serving a 15-year sentence.
Mr. Yang said that Mr. Xu, who apparently has been in solitary confinement since 1985 and has not been allowed family visits since then, has had two teeth knocked out. 
However, Mr. Yang said he did not know how the teeth had been knocked out.
While Mr. Yang's release was expected today on the expiration of his sentence, it was not certain. 
Mr. Yang said that he had been visited by four security officials two weeks ago and warned: ''You should change your attitude. 
Don't think we have to let you go.''
Â 
Yang Told to Avoid Friends
His family also was visited by security officials and advised that it would be best if he did not see his old friends.
Mr. Yang quoted one of the security officials as telling him: ''When we imprisoned you, it was for political reasons, and now that we release you, it also is for political reasons.''
On Friday, in another sign of the changes in the last eight years, China treated another dissident much differently than it treated Mr. Yang and his colleagues. 
Chen Jun, a 31-year-old democracy campaigner who in the last few months had openly confronted the Government and called for release of political prisoners, was escorted to the airport and put on an airplane to Hong Kong. 
The incident seemed to indicate both that open challenges will not be tolerated for long, and that the challengers at the moment may fare better than those who took on the system a decade ago.
In the meeting with security officials two weeks ago, Mr. Yang recalled, one of them said with a hint of reproach: ''You were ahead of your time; you thought too far ahead.''
''But if a nation has no one who thinks ahead,'' Mr. Yang told his friends tonight, ''our society would not progress and we would be finished. 
We would still be apes.''

text:

Results from the first direct legislative elections ever held here sent a resoundingly clear message to China and Britain today that Hong Kong's people want greater democracy as this British colony reverts to Chinese control in 1997.
Liberal pro-democracy candidates won 16 of the 18 seats contested on Sunday, according to the results announced today.
Not one pro-China candidate was a winner, despite a barrage of warnings from pro-China newspapers here and an impressive election effort by Beijing-backed unions and businesses.
Â 
Little Real Power
While little real political power was at stake in the voting for a largely rubber-stamp legislative council, the elections were seen as an important gauge of public sentiment as the economically powerful colony moves toward Chinese Communist control.
Buoyed by their victory, the liberal politicians vowed today to press their campaign for greater political freedom with both Britain and China. 
London has been embarrassed by the politicians' calls for democracy, and China has been angered by the demands.
"There is no doubt that the people wish to have democracy now, like any other people in the world," said Martin Lee, a leading liberal politician whose party, the United Democrats of Hong Kong, won 12 of the 18 seats.
China has had no official comment on the election results.
Only 39.2 percent of the 1.9 million registered voters turned out for the election, much less than the 50 percent predicted by Hong Kong officials. 
The elections were part of limited moves toward democracy promoted by Britain and China as 1997 approaches.
Britain and China signed an agreement in 1985 under which Hong Kong would be allowed to keep its capitalist system for 50 years after 1997, the year a 99-year British lease on Hong Kong territory expires. 
Calls for democratic safeguards against Beijing have grown in Hong Kong since June 1989, when China used troops to crush its own pro-democracy movement.
Â 
18 of 60 Directly Elected
The 18 directly elected representatives will be part of the 60-seat Legislative Council. 
All the other council members are appointed by the Governor or indirectly elected by constituency groups approved by the Government -- groups representing interests like the tourism, medical and legal professions.
Real power in Hong Kong resides with conservative businessmen and professionals, who counsel deference to China, and with officials of the New China News Agency, Beijing's representative here.
Looking at the results, Ian Scott, chairman of the political science department of Hong Kong University, said, "Voters have been pretty emphatic in declaring they want more say in the policy-making process here."
Mr. Scott said the election represented "a triumph for the Hong Kong middle class, which has been excluded from power by traditional business elites," who receive virtually all the key government appointments.
He said that "what we have now is a small, vocal opposition party whose members speak with moral authority" because they are the only ones in the legislature who are directly elected.
Â 
Waiting for Change in China
But he added, "Everyone knows nothing much will change about the way Hong Kong is governed or the amount of democracy here until the leadership in China has changed."
The voters' choices Sunday included leading liberal politicians like Mr. Lee and Szeto Wah, both of whom have been branded "subversive" by Beijing; Lee Wing-tat, a teacher and grassroots politician who made news in 1989 when he publicly rebuked a visiting British Foreign Secretary, and Lau Chinshek, a popular union leader whom one political analyst characterized as the kind of man "the Government would most hate to see elected because they don't think he will compromise with them."
Britain had vowed to help the colony establish a strong working democracy before it handed Hong Kong back to China. 
But many say Britain, yielding to pressure from China, has produced watered-down reforms, agreeing to permit only half of the legislature to be directly elected.
British politicians, including Prime Minister John Major, who visited the colony recently, have promised that if this first direct election is a "success," they might try to negotiate with Beijing for more democracy for the colony, though no one has defined what would constitute a success.
Mr. Lee, who has been persistently critical of Chinese interference in the territory, gathered the largest number of votes in the election, which saw 54 candidates vying for the 18 seats.
With its landslide victory, his United Democrats, the largest political party here, is already assuming the mantle of the "majority" party in Hong Kong.
Mr. Lee told reporters today that he had requested and been granted an interview tomorrow with the colonial Governor, Sir David Wilson. 
Many political analysts believe the Government will try to dilute the liberal victory by appointing very conservative members to the new lesilature. 
Those appointments will probably be announced within 10 days.
But Mr. Lee said the United Democrats and its allies had won the right to present their own list of candidates for appointed seats not only in the legislature, but also in the Executive Council, the Governor's top advisory body.
The two seats that did not go to the United Democrats and their liberal allies were taken by a conservative pro-business candidate and an independent.

file: Democracy_ In China, Write Morality.txt
text:
ï»¿
As 150,000 students filled the streets of the capital today, linking arms and singing revolutionary songs, it was still unclear exactly what they meant by the ''democracy'' they have been calling for in their 10 days of demonstrations.
The views of the students vary enormously, as do their sense of conviction and their ability to articulate a vision of democracy. 
Many students have scarcely thought about it, and in the last 10 days, they have marched to Tiananmen Square, the political center of the nation, to watch the spectacle and perhaps shout a few slogans along with the crowd.
''I don't know exactly what democracy is,'' said a 22-year-old physics student from Tianjin University. 
''But we need more of it.''
What emerges from interviews with several dozen students over the last few days is the feeling that democracy is as much a moral issue as a political one: that it would bring about a cleansing of the corruption that many people believe has become customary for Government officials in China.
Thirteen years ago, when tens of thousands of militant marchers protested after the death of the former Prime Minister Zhou Enlai, the people were asking for new leaders. 
Now, they are asking for a change in the system. 
Democracy, the students believe, would stamp out corruption and bring more equality to society because it would not bestow special privileges to those in power, nor to their sons and daughters.
Â 
'Many Officials Are Corrupt'
''Many officials in our society are corrupt,'' said a 24-year-old graduate student of journalism at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. 
''We are looking for a new way to reconstruct our society, and we are pursuing the separation of powers.''
''We need to set up a system to prevent officials from exploiting the people and the country's resources,'' added the student, who identified himself only as Mr. Hu. ''If a power is without supervision, it will commit crimes against its people. 
With democracy, we can punish people who commit such crimes.''
Many students are still vague about the kind of democratic system they want, but when they speak about democracy, most students think of the American system of government -even if they do not believe in wholesale importation of the American way.
''Ours must be different from the United States,'' said another journalism student, who gave his name only as Mr. Hou. He said the three-branch American system of government is unsuitable for China, apparently because gradual modification of China's system is more realistic than radical change.
The grievances of most students stem from personal experiences: the work allocation system, which prevents many from choosing their own jobs; the common practice of giving privileged positions to sons and daughters of senior officials; the censorship of the press, which has restrained coverage of demonstrations this week.
Â 
Avoid the Grand Questions
Because they start from their personal frustrations and experiences, many students seem to have thought much less about such grand questions as the ideal organization of government, or whether a multiparty system is feasible in China. 
Instead, they point to general areas they believe require change: elections to choose leaders, an independent judiciary, a legal system willing to punish officials as well as ordinary people, and supervision over Government through the press.
''Democracy means that all citizens have the right and the duty to participate in government policy making,'' said a 23-year-old student who gave her name as Miss Ma. 
''For example, not only should the representatives to the National People's Congress be able to express opinions, but those opinions should really represent the view of the people. 
We should be able to express our views to representatives who then carry the views to the leaders.''
The anger that characterized the demonstrations in 1976 seems to be missing today, say people who witnessed both, but the political awareness of the protesters has grown. 
This is partly because students have educated themselves through ''big character'' posters, unofficial open meetings on democracy, and even through participation in the protests.
The protests also have been marked by growing pragmatism, the realization that students may be more effective if they call for specific, moderate changes.
Â 
No Talk of Political Prisoners
They have not called for the release of political prisoners, because they say that is a sensitive subject that might provoke hostility among the nation's leaders and jeopardize what chances they have of being heard on other demands. 
For a similar strategic reason, they have for the most part refrained from complaining about inflation because they realize that it is a byproduct of economic liberalization policies they favor, say teachers and university graduates close to the student leaders.
Many students admit that there is little likelihood their demands will bring about immediate change. 
In some ways, the movement is an attempt to deepen their own understanding of democracy and to spread it among their fellow students. 
But they also hope to influence the leaders or at least the representatives to the National People's Congress, China's legislature, which meets once a year.
''For a long time, China has never had a system of law, so we don't know what rights we have,'' said A. P. Xia, 28, a graduate student of international studies. 
''So many students are struggling with the idea of what it means to have democratic rights.''
''Gorbachev perhaps has chosen the right way to begin with political reform, but it will still be a while before Chinese democracy will reach the stage of the Soviet Union,'' Mr. Xia said. 
''If China adopts a multiparty system as Hungary is doing now, it will be premature.''

Democratic leaders in Congress are divided over whether to deny China favorable treatment on trade or to fashion more moderate legislation that may prove acceptable to the Bush Administration.

Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, who has offered an amendment that seeks to toughen the House bill, said one reason for the rare difference of opinion between the Congressional leaders on an important foreign policy issue was the geographical location of the states Mr. Mitchell and Mr. Foley represent.

Mr. Foley worked behind the scenes last week to block the Rules Committee from allowing the attachment of amendments similar to Mr. Mitchell's approach for consideration by the full House. 
Mr. Mitchell's bill, widely supported in the Senate, is being considered by the Senate Finance Committee.

file: DENG CITES A NEED TO REPAIR U.S. TIES.txt
text:

China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, meeting the first high-level American officials to visit here since the June killings in Tiananmen Square, said today that the two countries must restore and improve their strained relations in the interest of world stabilityI.
''We share common desires and common needs,'' Mr. Deng told Brent Scowcroft, national security adviser to President Bush, and Lawrence S. Eagleburger, American Deputy Secretary of State.

The Chinese have regularly said that relations with the United States, deeply strained since the crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in June, could only be improved by American initiatives, and this daylong visit appears to have been such a gesture.

Steps Taken by Bush

He has also allowed Chinese students in the United States who fear reprisals on their return home to remain in America, an action that has drawn Chinese objections, most recently on Friday.
Mr. Deng, 85 years old, formally retired from his last official post last month, but he said it would be ''impolite and unreasonable for me not to receive a personal emissary of my friend President Bush.''
''I think we should say it is the common desire of our two sides to put an end as soon as possible to the disputes between China and the United States prevailing ever since June of this year,'' Mr. Deng added.

The Nixon Relationship

file: Deng Reappears to Cast Vote in Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Wobbly but beaming, China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, appeared on television tonight for the first time in five months, casting a vote in local elections conducted throughout the city.
More than five million people were expected to go to the polls today in Beijing to elect representatives to local councils, the only Government institution elected directly by the Chinese people.
At some polling stations, there was great fanfare, with firecrackers and streamers, but for the most part, many citizens privately expressed their indifference to the process.
"I'm sure there will be a lot of abstention votes this time," said a worker who helped organize voters in her district. 
"We are given so little information on the candidates. 
The people never meet them and so it's nearly impossible to tell them apart. 
None of them share my views, so I'm just going to abstain."
Â 
Complaints on Information
Indeed, many voters complained privately about the lack of information on the candidates and about their doubts that the candidates would ever voice the real views of the people. 
Still, the Government was promoting today's elections, which occur once every three years, as an example of China's political openness and democratic process.
The 86-year-old Mr. Deng was shown on television filling out his ballot and, escorted by his daughter, walking carefully over to the red ballot box. 
He gingerly stuffed his ballot into the box.
"That's all, right?"
Mr. Deng appeared to say, and then he walked away from the box. 
Mr. Deng was last seen on a publicity trip to the Asian Games village, where Beijing staged a mini-Olympics in the fall.
His television appearance at the polls today indicates that Chinese leaders want to stress the importance of the elections -- and perhaps rebut rumors that Mr. Deng is on his deathbed.
National television also showed the Communist Party General Secretary, Jiang Zemin, Prime Minister Li Peng and President Yang Shangkun casting their votes at the polls.
"The system of the People's Congress is the fundamental system of China," the official New China News Agency said in a paraphrase of comments by Prime Minister Li. 
"While continuing its economic reform, China will also carry out political reform."
Voters today elect representatives to the local People's Congress, which then elects deputies to a higher level people's congress. 
The congresses convene annually as a rubber stamp for the Government's legislation.
More than 90 percent of eligible voters were expected to turn out at the polls, but many people say they are going to the polls because it is their duty, and they do not want any repercussions from their work units, which keep a roster of the voters.
Â 
Biographies Are Posted
There are competing candidates in the election, normally four candidates for three positions, or three candidates for two positions. 
But all the candidates are officially approved, and often there is little difference among them.
At Beijing University, where brief biographies of the candidates were posted, many students still said they knew nothing about the candidates. 
The candidates apparently were carefully screened, and the popular former president of the university, Ding Shisun, withdrew his nomination, students at the university said. 
Mr. Ding was dismissed by the Government after the 1989 army crackdown on the democracy movement.
Some students scanned the biographies just before they entered the polling halls.
"I have no idea who these candidates are," a second-year student said. 
"It doesn't mean much anyway. 
Elections here are not like in America."
Candidates rarely appear at the polling stations. 
Most citizens vote through their work units, which distribute materials about the candidates.
At Fengsheng election district in west Beijing, the three candidates had videos of themselves distributed throughout the local work units, poll organizers said. 
But more than a dozen people approached at the poll today said they had not heard about a video.
At Jianguomen election district in east Beijing, poll organizers tried their best to portray the great respect that voters had for the election process.
But several voters said they selected candidates at random. 
One woman exclaimed to her friend that she did not know any of the candidates.
"Just put a mark next to any of the names," the friend said, as the woman began drawing a circle next to two of the names. 
The friend added, "It's all the same anyway."

text:

China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, told a small group of top officials that they should not listen to him if he starts to say ''crazy things'' as he gets older and becomes less clear-minded, according to a transcript of a speech he made in September.

4 in a speech that was recorded and is now being disseminated among party and Government officials.

A Time to Retire

file: Despite Rights Issue, Chinese Hope U.S. Trade Status Stays.txt
text:
ï»¿
As a battle looms in Washington over whether to end normal trade relations with China, many Chinese are finding themselves reluctantly siding with their hard-line rulers in hoping that the status is maintained.
While they appreciate the concern for human rights in their country and hope that the debate will force the Government to become less repressive, some worry that a cutoff of so-called most-favored-nation status would hurt their standard of living, harm the most reformist segments of the economy and prompt the hard-liners to restrict contacts with the United States.
It is impossible to be sure of public opinion in so vast and tightly controlled a country as China. 
But in informal conversations with dozens of Chinese in several parts of the country over recent months, most of those who were aware of the issue did not favor American economic sanctions and hoped that most-favored-nations benefits would be extended.
President Bush's annual recommendation on whether to renew the preferential trade status for China is required by June 3. 
He is expected to favor renewal, and opponents in Congress are expected to introduce legislation to overturn the decision.
In their first breath, urban Chinese intellectuals typically tell their trusted American friends how much they detest their leadership. 
In their second breath, they express affection for the United States and inquire about getting visas. 
And in their third breath, they worry that harsh American sanctions would hurt the Chinese people rather than their leaders.
"If I were President Bush, I would extend most-favored-nation status to China," said Zhang Weiguo, a Shanghai dissident who was unusual only in that he was willing to have his name published. 
"The U.S. should support China's economic development and social exchanges."
Mr. Zhang's anti-Government credentials are not in doubt. 
He was arrested after the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown and spent 20 months in prison before being released earlier this year, still unrepentant and fuming at the Government.
Mr. Zhang said the best result would be for a tough battle over Chinese trade in Washington, ending in an extension for another year. 
Such a close call would encourage China to make concessions on human rights and would leave the issue open for another fight next year, he said.
"Every year it's discussed, and that's very good," Mr. Zhang said. 
"It puts new pressure on China each year."
A downgrading of American trade links with China would mean a large rise in the tariffs imposed on Chinese goods shipped to the United States, and would hurt its thriving export sector. 
The south of China, which has the most developed private economy in the country, would be particularly affected, as would Hong Kong, through which Chinese goods usually pass for packaging or transshipment.
Many dissidents say they would like the United States and other countries to be even more outspoken in supporting Chinese human rights. 
Above all, they would like Prime Minister Li Peng and other hard-liners to lose "face."But they worry that economic sanctions are the wrong method.
"People are very torn inside," said a university student in Beijing. 
"They want pressure on the Government to change its policies, and they want the leadership to eat bitterness. 
But on the other hand, they're afraid that if sanctions are imposed, it's the ordinary people who would suffer. 
So we want America to threaten sanctions to pressure China, but we don't want sanctions themselves."
Â 
Peasants Seem Less Aware
Among Chinese peasants and workers, especially outside the capital, there seems to be much less awareness of the issue of sanctions, as well as less anger at the Government. 
Consequently, many people do not have clearly formed ideas on the subject, but frequently seem vaguely opposed to any sanctions that might compound the economic difficulties of the last couple of years. 
And some wealthier people fear that sanctions would make it more difficult to buy foreign products.
"The fear is that if M.F.N. were cut off, the price of a pack of Marlboros would go up," said an entrepreneur.
Â

Mr. Roy, 55 years old, of Bethesda, Md., is special assistant to Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and executive secretary of the State Department.

text:

Of all the criminal cases in China involving advocates of democracy, perhaps the most mysterious -- certainly the most titillating -- concerns a leading official here who was sentenced to four years in prison for engaging in an overly dynamic sex life.
Pan Weiming, the 42-year-old former chief of propaganda in Shanghai, China's largest city, was sentenced on Jan. 
24 for "hoodlum offenses."
"The defendant Pan Weiming, between August 1986 and February 1991, aimed to philander with women," the official Liberation Daily reported after the sentencing.

The disgrace of Mr. Pan, who had helped ease controls on artists and writers when he held the propaganda post in the late 1980's, was regarded as a triumph for China's hard-liners, and his escapades were widely reported.

Mr. Pan was detained a year ago in the central Chinese city of Chengdu. 
Even his friends acknowledge that he was in bed with a prostitute.
According to Mr. Pan's friends, however, it was a setup.

file: Diplomats Report China_s Premier Will Visit Soviet Union in April.txt
text:

Prime Minister Li Peng of China is scheduled to visit the Soviet Union in April, in an effort to improve relations between the two nations, foreign diplomats in Beijing say.
Moscow announced last month that Mr. Li would visit, but did not give a date, and the Chinese authorities so far have declined to comment. 
But the diplomats, from a Communist country and a Western country, confirmed that both Moscow and Beijing were now making preparations for a visit by Mr. Li at the end of April.
The visit would be the highest-level exchange since President Mikhail S. Gorbachev visited Beijing in May to normalize relations after the three-decade Chinese-Soviet split. 
Since then, Chinese-Soviet relations have not developed very rapidly, partly because of Chinese suspicions that the Soviet Union is straying from Communist orthodoxy and is inciting change in Eastern Europe.
Â 
Relations Still Cool
While border trade has increased and there is growing interest in cultural and business exchanges, relations between the two Communist parties are cool. 
Chinese hard-liners increasingly view the Soviets not as brothers in Communist solidarity, but as a potential source of instabilty. 
These days, for example, some Chinese seek independent news about Eastern Europe not just from Voice of America but also from the Moscow radio.
In December, the Communist Party circulated a document about the upheaval in Eastern Europe, and it said one factor was the change under way in the Soviet Union, the diplomats said. 
This was widely regarded as an implicit criticism of Soviet policy, and in political study sessions some officials apparently made this explicit. 
But foreign diplomats and other Chinese officials dispute foreign news reports that the party specifically rebuked Mr. Gorbachev and his policies.
Rumors of a power struggle, in which Mr. Li might leave the post of Prime Minister, have been circulating in Beijing for weeks, but the diplomats said planning for the trip did not shed any light on the rumors.

file: Dissident Chinese Gather in the West.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was 70 years ago that a movement of Chinese students and intellectuals, shocked by their Government's weakness in the face of Japanese aggression, engaged in a period of soul searching and re-evaluation known as the May Fourth Movement. 
A result was the formation of the Communist Party that now rules China.
The anniversary of the May Fourth Movement has been recalled in many ways these days, most spectacularly in large pro-democracy marches by students and others in Beijing and elsewhere.
The anniversary was also very much on the minds of some 30 leading Chinese writers, scholars, film makers, editors and journalists who met with a dozen or so Western experts on their country in an unusual conference in this small California town to talk about what virtually all participants saw as China's continuing 20th-century search for an identity.
The four-day conference, attended by some of the leading advocates of further democratic change in the country, in itself reflected the changes that have swept China under the leadership of Deng Xiaoping, the country's most powerful figure. 
Many of the Chinese participants flew here directly from China to attend the meeting, something that, they all acknowledged, has only recently been allowed.
Â 
A New Boldness
The meeting also reflected a new boldness on the part of many Chinese intellectuals. 
Among the participants were several figures who recently signed petitions to the Chinese leadership, demanding the release of political prisoners - something that has not happened before in China's recent history.
Indeed, even though the conference mixed genuine dissidents with several figures who are still members of the Communist Party, the near-unanimous tone was one of sharp criticism of the current leadership, both for failing to press ahead rapidly with democratic changes, and for allowing corruption to become rampant in the Government.
''We must get rid of the idea of one leader, one ism, one party,'' said Ruan Ming, who was once an official at the party school, where cadres are taught.
Another participant, Wu Zuguang, who at 72 is a leading playwright, said, ''In the May Fourth Movement, we called for democracy and science.''
The allusion was to the major slogan of the era of protest and re-examination 70 years ago, when China seemed to progressive intellectuals to be suffocating in superstition and tyranny.
''Now, 70 years later, we are still seeking the same things,'' Mr. Wu said.
Â 
Other Major Participants
Among the participants in the conference were several people who have been sharply criticized by Chinese leaders and the controlled press for their critical boldness.
Liu Binyan, a well-known investigative journalist who was expelled from the Communist Party two years ago after publishing articles on malfeasance in office, attended. 
So did Wang Ruoshui, a onetime deputy editor of the official Communist Party newspaper, People's Daily, who was dismissed from his post for writing that ''alienation'' still existed under Communism. 
Bei Dao, one of China's best-known poets, was a conferee, and so were Wu Tianming and Chen Kaige, two of the country's best-known movie directors.
Some of these figures, like Mr. Liu, were already in the United States. 
Others, like Bei Dao, which is a pen name, came just for the conference.
But five others, serving as reminders of continuing political difficulty at home, were refused permission to travel abroad. 
Among the five was Fang Lizhi, the astrophysicist who has emerged as China's leading human rights advocate.
Conferees at one point gathered round a television to watch a taped interview of Mr. Fang by Orville Schell, a writer who was the prime organizer of the conference, and his wife, Liu Baifang, another conference organizer.
Â 
A New Brand of Patriotism
They applauded as Mr. Fang explained his view of patriotism, saying that calls for democratic freedoms represented a higher form of love of country than did calls for party obedience.
But while disenchantment with the Government was a clear theme of the meeting, the conference also addressed underlying questions concerning China's identity, like whether there is a link between the country's culture and its economic backwardness and the authoritarian political system. 
Are the country's problems due to its traditions, or to the failures of Communism itself?
Many of the conferees maintained that the Chinese tradition, which always stressed collective and group interests over individualism, laid the basis for the suppression of individual rights under Communism.
Mr. Chen, the film maker, who was born after the Communist takeover in 1949, recalled how he grew up always hearing about ''the party'' as the representative of everybody in society, and that controlled everything about individual life. 
But, Mr. Chen maintained, this political system was close enough to Chinese tradition to gain widespread acceptance, even when a single individual, Mao Zedong, came to be worshiped as a kind of god.
As intellectual and cultural figures, many of the conference participants were persecuted, not only during the Cultural Revolution of the mid-1960's, but also during the ''anti-rightist campaign'' of 1957, when some 500,000 people, mostly intellectuals, were sent to labor camps. 
The conference thus mingled personal recollections with attempts to analyze why the intellectuals so meekly submitted to the party.
Â 
'The System Is the Problem'
Even as recent history and Chinese identity were discussed at the conference, lying in the back of virtually all minds were the student demonstrations. 
Chinese conferees frequently telephoned friends back home for the latest information, which was then conveyed to the conference as a whole.
Ge Yang, the 72-year-old editor of the official magazine New Observer, said at the conference's end:
''Corrupt governments have always been overthrown by the people in Chinese history, and this Government is certainly corrupt. 
There are many good people in the Government. 
It is the system that is the problem. 
It is the system that has to be reformed. 
Deng Xiaoping himself has said as much, but he has not been able to do it, and now he is too old.''

file: Draft Law for Chinese Rule Stirs Protest in Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
A committee in Beijing today ratified its final version of the constitution that will govern Hong Kong after the Chinese takeover in 1997, prompting an outcry from liberal and moderate politicians and angry protests by several thousand college students.
But even as the Hong Kong students demonstrated, burning a copy of the draft, some conservatives said they found the limited level of democracy included in the so-called Basic Law to be acceptable.
Hong Kong's local Government issued a statement saying the blueprint would ''allow for a smooth transition of Government in 1997,'' when the British colony will come under Chinese rule.
The constitution, which will be formally approved next month by China's national legislature, was drafted by a 51-member committee appointed and dominated by Beijing. 
Eighteen of its members are Hong Kong residents.
Far Short of Free Elections
The final version of the draft law was marginally more progressive than an earlier draft. 
But it fell far short of the proposal by local lawmakers and the Hong Kong Government for a fully elected legislature.
Although China says it will allow Hong Kong ''a high degree of autonomy'' after 1997, the large middle class here has demanded that a solid democratic framework be established to protect its rights and liberties. 
The calls for speedy adoption of democratic safeguards reached a peak here last June, when the Chinese Government brutally suppressed protests for democracy in a military crackdown.
As confidence in Hong Kong's future dwindles, thousands of educated professionals have been emigrating each year. 
The politicians who criticized the new draft of the Basic Law today said it would simply accelerate the exodus.
Hong Kong lawmakers, who are now appointed or indirectly elected, had united behind a plan that would permit half of the legislature to be directly elected by 1997, and all of its members by 2003.
But the final version of the Basic Law would mandate direct elections for only one-third of the 60 seats by 1997, and for half of the seats in the year 2003. 
It also would establish separate voting systems for bills introduced by lawmakers and legislation proposed by the Government.
Â 
'Indirect' Balloting
The draft constitution calls for some legislators to be indirectly elected through constituency groups such as doctors and lawyers, with others chosen by an electoral college whose members would be appointed by the Government.
The lawmakers chosen through this highly complicated system would vote in 2007 on whether Hong Kong should have a fully elected legislature.
T. L. Tsim, a leading political commentator, expressed the disappointment of liberals in Hong Kong who have marched and lobbied in favor of a more democratic system.
He said, ''I am reminded of what one of his friends once said about the movie star Errol Flynn: 'You know where you stand with Errol. 
He always lets you down.'
China is like that too.''
Thousands of students boycotted classes today to protest the future constitution. 
After demonstrations at colleges and universities, several thousand students gathered for a rally in Chater Garden, a park across from the legislative office building downtown.
Carrying red banners that denounced the draft law in bold Chinese characters, they marched later to the offices of the New China News Agency, China's de facto embassy here, which was heavily guarded by the police.
But Vincent Lo, a member of a conservative group of businessmen who had criticized an earlier version of the Basic Law, said the amended blueprint was acceptable.
Mr. Lo noted that the Governments of Britain and China had agreed on the Basic Law in private negotiations. 
''That can help insure a smooth transition,'' he said.
Â 
'A Shameful Act'
Martin Lee, a liberal legislator, denounced the blueprint as ''a shameful act of surrender'' by British officials, who accepted the latest version only after last-minute talks with Beijing.
''Could you imagine how the people of Czechoslovakia or even Lithuania would respond if their Governments told them they could not elect so much as half of their Parliament until 13 years from now?'' he asked.
A senior Hong Kong official who asked not to be identified said the Government was ''pleased with the draft, with reservations.''He said that Britain hoped to see ''at least 50 percent of the legislature directly elected by 1997, and that's what we will be working toward.
''We will continue our efforts to persuade the Chinese Government'' to change the plan, he added.
Hong Kong representatives on the drafting committee said that they found the final version acceptable for the most part. 
''It's the best we can get,'' said Li Ka-shing, a billionaire businessmen on the panel.
A statement issued by Omelco, a group that represent all of Hong Kong's legislative and executive counselors and and lobbied for a more liberal plan, said that the final decision on Hong Kong's political framework in 1997 ''will be made between the British and Chinese Governments.''
''For our part, Omelco have conscientiously reflected the views and wishes of the Hong Kong people,'' the statement said. 
''We have done this all the way to the British Prime Minister.''
Â 
'Everyone a Loser'
Joseph Cheng, a former professor of government at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said that the latest version of the draft constitution would leave ''everyone a loser.''
''Even China loses because the whole consultative and drafting process was suppose to legitimize the Basic Law, and it hasn't,'' he said. 
''This is not the government Hong Kong people said they wanted.''
In its statement, the Hong Kong Government also announced that it would permit 18 seats in the Legislature to be directly elected in 1991, two short of the 20 proposed in a consensus plan backed by most major political groups.
Britain, which proposed several years ago that 10 seats be opened to direct elections in 1991, promised recently to begin instituting democratic changes at a faster pace. 
During a visit to Hong Kong last month, Foreign Secretary Douglas Hurd said that Britain was prepared to enact safeguards alone if China would not agree to a faster pace of change.
One political analyst said that the proposal for limited direct elections in 1991 ''obviously has Beijing's stamp of approval. 
I don't think you would call this an heroic act on Britain's part.''
Students in Hong Kong protesting the law that will govern the island after it is turned over to China in 1997. 
The document, known as the Basic Law, was ratified yesterday in Beijing. 
(Agence-France Presse)

text:

With his friends in high places and a record as an influential theorist of the Communist Party, one might expect Wu Jiaxiang to be at the center of power in China.
Instead, Mr. Wu is in a cell of Qincheng Prison outside Beijing. 
For two years, the 35-year-old Mr. Wu has languished there without being charged with any crime. 
The Government has apparently been afraid to release him or sentence him. 
His Kafkaesque fate is an indication of how quickly a high-flying career in China can change trajectories and plunge into disgrace.
Perhaps more important, his case is a measure of the degree to which the hard-line Government has isolated itself from the younger generation of Communists. 
Mr. Wu is representative of a group of young and middle-aged professionals who sought to reform the party rather than overthrow it.
Â 
Many Are Alienated
A small number of such party members were arrested, and many others found themselves forced to pledge allegiance to a hard-line orthodoxy they found odious. 
By turning on such people, the hard-liners alienated a broad spectrum of mid-level officials in the central Government. 
The Government has not said a word about Mr. Wu since he was arrested on July 17, 1989, six weeks after the army assault on protesters in Beijing left at least several hundred dead and thousands wounded.
"I have not heard of this case," said a spokesman for the Beijing Intermediate Court, which is in charge of sentencing political offenders.
From interviews with Mr. Wu's friends and associates, it is possible to piece together an account of his career and of his present fate. 
But many are still puzzled about why he has been punished so harshly. 
"No one really knows why he's still in prison," said a Chinese with first-hand knowledge of the case. 
"People say that maybe it's because he knows too much."
While Mr. Wu clearly took a strong stand against Prime Minister Li Peng and the use of force to suppress the democracy movement, he was not a leader of the protests. 
His world was Zhongnanhai, the central leadership compound where he worked, rather than Tiananmen Square next door.
Wu Jiaxiang (whose name is pronounced approximately woo jyah shyahng) is a small, lean man who speaks the refined patois of Beijing intellectuals and yet conveys something of the earthy poverty of rural Anhui Province, where he grew up.
Â 
Backed 'New Authoritarianism'
A poet and graceful writer, Mr. Wu became a prominent essayist. 
In particular, he attracted attention for his promotion of "new authoritarianism."
This theory held that enlightened despotism was necessary for the time being to promote economic growth and prepare China for democracy later on.
Some young intellectuals were furious with these essays, regarding them as apologies for repression. 
Nevertheless, Mr. Wu shared their impatience for more rapid reform. 
When the Tiananmen democracy movement began in April 1989, Mr. Wu supported the students and opposed Prime Minister Li.
Mr. Wu is believed to be accused of "counterrevolutionary" slogans accusing Mr. Li of a "coup d'etat."
The difficulty for the courts in prosecuting him is that the first of his four slogans reportedly called for supporting the leadership of the Communist Party.

file: DYNASTY DEFIED_China_s Leaders Hear the Roar of the Crowd.txt
text:
ï»¿
ONE can only imagine the expressions on the faces of China's old revolutionary leaders as a cacophonous rendition of the Chinese national anthem wafted into the Zhongnanhai park where they live and work. 
''The peoples of China are in their critical hour; everybody must roar his defiance; arise! arise! arise!'' tens of thousands of voices sang defiantly during a vast illegal march on Thursday. 
Despite all the old guard's sniping about how the young Chinese today care only about money, it seemed that they had inherited a penchant for revolutionary ideas, after all.
Some Chinese see the demonstration as a turning point, the first time that students and workers truly joined forces to express dissatisfaction, and the first time in the history of the People's Republic of China that the people - lowercase ''p'' - defeated the People's Armed Police and the People's Liberation Army. 
The glee was unforgettable, and everybody jostled for a place in history: the ice cream vendor who gave her cart of popsicles to the marchers, the businessmen who bought food and drinks for the students, and the young workers who blocked the army troops sent to stop the marchers.
The last two weeks of demonstrations have been an extraordinary humiliation for the Government, and especially for Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, who personally ordered the repression of the student movement. 
But more fundamentally, they suggest that the Government may be losing its grasp on what the emperors called ''the mandate of heaven.''
Mr. Deng may be too good a Communist to believe in such a mandate, but in his lifetime he has already seen the Qing dynasty crumble in 1911 and the Nationalist Government collapse in 1949 because they lost the moral legitimacy to rule. 
While almost no Chinese expect the Communist regime to fall any time soon, many see in the vast protests a similar process: erosion of the Government's moral authority to rule.
''It has already lost the mandate of heaven,'' said A. P. Xia, a graduate student in politics who has taken part in the demonstrations. 
''Experience has proved that Communism is a failure, here and in other socialist countries.''
Mr. Xia foresees neither violence nor the overthrow of the Government, simply a long process of peaceful change. 
There is no force now in existence to replace the Communist Party, and the student demonstrators are still only loosely organized in at best a hazy alliance with workers. 
A crackdown is still a very real possibility.
Many Chinese have noted the parallels with 1949. 
Nearly four decades after the Republic of China was founded, the Kuomintang had lost popular support because of corruption, inflation, brutality and economic inequalities. 
Today, nearly four decades after the founding of the People's Republic, the Communist Party has lost a tremendous amount of popular support because of corruption and inflation, as well as brutality and economic inequalities.
Yet even such an outspoken critic of the Government as the dissident Fang Lizhi points out the enormous differences. 
In 1949, he notes, there was an alternative: the Communist Party. 
Today, no alternative exists, and that alone is likely to keep the Communist dynasty from crumbling, or at least to keep it from crumbling as quickly as the Kuomintang's.
Â 
Losing Authority, Losing Control
But the sense of discontent, even outrage, hangs in the air. 
On a bus recently, a woman cursed a man who bumped her. 
''Why are you cursing me?'' he asked loudly. 
''I'm not a murderer. 
I'm not a thief. 
I'm not a Communist.''
The bus roared with laughter.
As it loses much of its moral authority, the Communist Party is also finding that in some ways it is losing control over the country. 
The Government can still wield immense power, as it chose to when it crushed rioting in Tibet last month. 
But such power may be useless to enforce the central Government's will against more mundane and universal challenges.
Almost everybody seems to be defying Beijing in one way or another. 
The provinces refuse to halt building projects that the Government ordered stopped, and some have even set up illegal border checkposts at boundaries to prevent scarce goods from leaving the area. 
Cities buy condominiums in Canada rather than pass on their foreign exchange earnings to Beijing, as they are supposed to. 
Farmers refuse to hand over grain to the authorities, as required, and sometimes beat up tax collectors. 
Chinese couples violate the ''one couple, one child'' policy so routinely that the average couple can expect to have more than 2.5 children.
The striking achievement of last week's student protests was the outpouring of sympathy from workers, and an important question now is the extent to which that cooperation can be maintained. 
Students quote from the slogans of the American and French Revolutions, and are inspired by Patrick Henry's ''Give me liberty or give me death.''
They tend to want more liberalization, while workers are disgruntled in part because of liberalization - particularly the threats of inflation from decontrolling prices and unemployment from decontrolling jobs.
A test of whether the students can sustain worker support will come when they march next, perhaps tomorrow, the May Day holiday when workers might join in, or more likely on Thursday, the 70th anniversary of nationalist student demonstrations.
Chinese scholars have noted the difficulties that Mikhail S. Gorbachev is facing in the Soviet Union, and they sometimes say with a certain amount of condescension that Mr. Gorbachev's mistake was to open up the political system to complaints before he opened up the economic system to growth. 
Mr. Deng has taken another road to modernization, and he has been enormously successful over the last 10 years in opening up the economic system.
But Mr. Deng's failure to seize the initiative in political liberalization seems to have had a price: the students in the streets have come to see the leaders, including Mr. Deng, as opponents rather than apostles of change. 
Now, perhaps, Mr. Deng may be forced to join Mr. Gorbachev in prying off the lid of the political pressure cooker.
Crowd of Chinese students demonstrating for democracy (Sygma/Bill Pierce)

file: Economic Progress in China Has a Seedy Side.txt
text:
ï»¿
A petite Chinese woman, with a skimpy skirt and a blouse revealing more than it covered, walked daintily across the lobby of the best hotel in this city. 
A few yards away, several smartly clad women sipping tea in the coffee shop smiled alluringly at the male guests.
It is an open secret that here in Shenzhen, a special economic zone just across the border from Hong Kong, economic progress has brought with it the seedy side of the free market: prostitution, corruption, smuggling and even drug trafficking.
Shenzhen is China's best-known boomtown, and it is renowned throughout the country for its economic growth, high salaries, modern fashions and adherence to "bourgeois" morals, if any. 
To many people in the rest of China, Shenzhen is a lawless place.
The Government is reluctant to disclose information on activities that are not supposed to occur in a Communist country, and police officials declined to be interviewed. 
Still, the underside of Shenzhen has become an explosive factor in the debate over how fast China should develop and how much capitalism should be brought in.
The Government's hard-liners argue that the capitalist influence is responsible for the decline in morality and the growth in pornography, bribery and drug smuggling. 
Some elderly conservatives would prefer to see Shenzhen's development proceed with more careful monitoring. 
In Shenzhen, some disagree.
"Prostitution, drugs and smuggling, yes, all these have appeared here," said Zhong Yaohua, an official in the Shenzhen Economic Development Bureau. 
"But slowing down economic development won't solve these problems."
Other defenders of Shenzhen admit that the bribes may be higher than in the rest of China and there may be a buoyant black-market economy, but they say the city is not entirely lawless. 
One law prevails even here, they say: the law of the market.
Shenzhen, designated a special economic zone more than a decade ago, has only in the last few years matured into a vibrant business center. 
But as trade links expand between Hong Kong and China's southern coastal areas, the entry points become more difficult to patrol and many goods slip out of the reach of border guards.
Last year, Chinese customs authorities confiscated $125 million worth of goods in 11,600 incidents of smuggling, a significant rise over the previous year, China's official press reported.
Shenzhen officials insist that only a small portion of smuggling occurs across its closely monitored borders. 
Still, more than $19.8 million worth of goods were seized by Shenzhen's police in 1990, and in the first quarter of this year, more than $5.2 million in merchandise was confiscated.
All sorts of items -- from antiques to cigarettes to guns to computer parts -- are smuggled into China. 
More than 90 percent of an estimated 10 million videocassette recorders sold in China are brought in illegally, and about 40,000 boxes of cigarettes, worth $14.6 million, were seized by police in 1990, official Chinese press reports said. 
The aim is to evade high import duties.
Greater contact with Hong Kong and Taiwan businessmen has cultivated a booming prostitution industry. 
A prostitute can make anywhere from $25 to $250 a customer, amounting to several times more than the average worker makes in a month.
Of course, most Chinese women would be scandalized at the thought of selling their bodies. 
But many apparently are not, for there are about 20,000 prostitutes in this city of nearly 1.9 million, according to one police estimate.
Drugs are also sold here, although much more secretly than other smuggled goods. 
While these social ills virtually disappeared for the first few decades of Communist rule, they are hardly new to China. 
Prostitution and drug trafficking, in particular, were rampant before the 1949 revolution.
"The Communist Party got rid of these seedy professions, but the sickness was still there," said Wang Xinkuo, a senior manager at Catic Shenzhen Enterprise Group. 
"Some of the black-market practices came in with the open-door policy, but some are simply the vestiges of the old society."

text:

WHAT are the economic implications of the turmoil in the Communist world?
President Bush said this week that China remains a country of strategic importance to America but that a ''normalized relationship'' is impossible as long as the harsh crackdown on dissent continues. 
And Japan's decision to suspend aid to China dramatized the vulnerability of the Chinese economy to the shocks felt by both foreign government and business.
Capital from Hong Kong had been flowing so heavily into China that twice as many people are employed in Guangdong Province by Hong Kong manufacturers as in Hong Kong itself. 
That inflow of capital and technology from Hong Kong and other capitalist democracies could now cease, causing the collapse of Deng Xiaoping's efforts to modernize the economy.
His modernization drive was built on the theory that economic reform had to be combined with political discipline. 
Economic and political experts on China, from both capitalist and Communist countries, had long warned that the Chinese Government would not tolerate dissent. 
Silviu Brucan, a professor of social science at the University of Bucharest in Rumania, said two years ago, ''It is not a good sign that of Deng's four cardinal principles of modernization, the most frequently cited lately has been the people's 'democratic dictatorship.'
''
Mr. Brucan contended that ''while Gorbachev feels secure to advocate more democracy, having attracted most of the intelligentsia, scientists and engineers (numbering almost 15 million in the Soviet Union), Deng is fearful that the Chinese people, still beset by widespread illiteracy, are insufficiently prepared to withstand Western ideological influences.''
This refusal to countenance political dissent stemmed from fear of the unruliness of the Chinese people, as manifested in the Cultural Revolution; the wide disparity between living standards in rural and urban areas; anxiety about the speed with which the people could turn capitalist and reject their rulers, and the enormous development tasks Mr. Deng believed would require continued state capital and controls.
Yet, as one found on visiting China two years ago, the political ferment was as palpable, especially among young people, as the economic progress. 
Chinese leaders insisted that their repressive political actions - they had just cracked down on students protesting the removal of Hu Yaobang, a liberal, as General Secretary of the Communist Party - would mean no reversal of China's drive to reform the economic system. 
Today Chinese leaders are holding to that line - and the Bush Administration is trying to hold the door open to continued relations with China, apparently hoping that economic modernization will in the end bring political liberalization in its train.
In the Soviet Union, Mikhail S. Gorbachev is trying to carry out economic and political reform simultaneously. 
But he is trying to use political reform - especially the opening up of the system to the voices of economic criticism and dissent - as the lever for a deeper reconstruction of the Soviet economy.
But if the Soviet Union does not make faster progress in restructuring and improving its economy, Mr. Gorbachev's effort at political liberalization could fail. 
This week Leonid Abalkin, an economist who will be playing a leading role in the Soviet leadership, warned that there could be a ''right-wing swing'' unless rapid economic progress is made within two years.
Vladimir Tikhonov, another leading economist, said there could be ''famine in the very near future'' unless radical changes are made in farmers' ownership of the land. 
And a third economist, Gennadi Lisichkin, criticized the Government for printing money with little of value behind it - ''like putting an alcoholic in charge of a liquor shop.''
The huge budget deficit, amounting to 11 percent of the gross national product, is the heart of the Soviet plight. 
That deficit results in the profligate creation of money to support an inefficient industrial structure and vast misuse of labor - really just unemployment in disguise. 
The effort to use price controls has produced a vicious suppressed inflation, which results in worsening shortages of consumer goods including food.
Viktor Belkin, an economist at the Academy of Sciences, this week publicly called the Soviet system ''a cannibalistic economy, feeding on itself.''
It devours its capital stock, wastes its human resources and breeds corruption. 
These root causes of Soviet failure also apply to China, where, despite the initial successes in farming and industry, inflation and corruption helped bring on the recent popular uprising.
The turmoil in the Communist world creates both hazards and opportunities for the United States. 
Foreign capital, cut off from China by fears of repression and economic retrogression, is flowing to the United States, putting upward pressure on the dollar. 
Unless the Western countries reunite to stabilize the dollar, it could worsen the United States trade deficit and add to recessionary pressures.
On the other side, Mr. Gorbachev's efforts to restructure the Soviet economy by cutting military outlays and trimming the budget deficit to eliminate concealed inflation creates the parallel opportunity in this country for lower budget deficits, lower interest rates, stronger growth and a strengthened international trade position.

file: Economy Is a Pawn In China_s Power Game.txt
text:
