SECRETIVE power struggles have been a way of life here for millenniums, but now the jousting is growing particularly intense. 
China's octogenarian rulers must decide within the next few months on a political platform and a roster of leaders to be approved at the crucial 14th Communist Party Congress late this year.
Deng Xiaoping already has launched his campaign -- a virtual road show -- for swifter change across the nation, and he remains the single most important political figure in China even though he no longer holds any official posts. 
But there are a half-dozen other octogenarian leaders who collectively also have great influence. 
The result is a protracted bargaining process, now under way behind the scenes, to determine the outcome of the party congress.
A party congress occurs just once in five years or so, and this one may be the last that China's octogenarians will be able to control. 
Mr. Deng will be 88 next month, and his main rival, Chen Yun, has just turned 87. 
Both are frail. 
"This is the old man's last effort to push reform," a senior Chinese official said of Mr. Deng.
Mr. Deng has committed himself to the position that China can avoid the fate of the Soviet Union only by hastening economic restructuring and improving the standard of living. 
But his elderly colleagues, who include one nonagenarian, Peng Zhen, don't all agree. 
So Mr. Deng, who for years had virtually confined his movements to a few spots in China, has been traveling around the nation for support for his policies and proteges. 
"Deng doesn't really have any of his own people in the leadership now," said a Chinese economist. 
"He may have control, but he doesn't yet have full control. 
He has to fight against all the other old hard-liners to get the people he wants into the leadership."
Mr. Deng launched his campaign in January with a trip to the southern province of Guangdong, setting off a wave of enthusiasm across the nation for greater economic restructuring. 
But Mr. Deng himself has been frustrated at the ability of hard-liners to block his directives, and he is said to have scolded the younger leaders -- who hold the formal titles -- for failure to follow through on his speeches.
"Everyone says that I am the master planner for economic reform," Mr. Deng reportedly said during a two-hour visit in May to Capital Corporation, a steel mill in Beijing. 
"But no one seems to be carrying out anything."
The intrigues now under way were apparent a day after Mr. Deng's visit to the steel company. 
His comments there were recorded on videotape by the company, but the next day the Central Committee General Office sent an envoy to confiscate the tape, according to a Chinese with access to top officials. 
It is not clear what one should make of this: perhaps Mr. Deng's enemies were trying to block the distribution of the tape, or perhaps his supporters were planning to edit it for television. 
Or perhaps the Politburo members simply wanted to know what Mr. Deng was saying behind their backs.
There are many signs that Mr. Deng is gaining in the power struggles, although the disputes certainly are far from over. 
One such sign is that Ding Guangen, his bridge-playing partner, apparently is overseeing the preparation for the report that will be presented at the 14th Party Congress. 
Mr. Ding is believed to have peppered the draft with reformist phrases, such as "market economy" instead of the previously used "commodity economy."
Another sign that Mr. Deng is pushing ahead is that the Government has eased controls in many areas, such as prices, rents and stock ownership. 
Many intellectuals are also rejoicing at reports that He Dongchang, the hard-line party secretary and deputy director of the State Education Commission, is being pushed out. 
Still, while the political system is tilting toward Mr. Deng, there have been no purges of major hard-liners yet.
Mr. Deng himself is said to have three prominent hard-liners in his sights: Propaganda Minister Wang Renzhi, Acting Culture Minister He Jingzhi and the director at People's Daily, Gao Di. 
Mr. Deng criticized them by name in January, yet they remain in their jobs. 
Apparently they have support from other octogenarians.
The 14th Party Congress will approve the report, a platform for the next five years, and choose a new Central Committee. 
The Central Committee will then choose a Politburo to serve until 1997. 
Some reshuffling is expected, but the two most important figures -- Prime Minister Li Peng and General Secretary Jiang Zemin -- are generally expected to retain their Politburo seats. 
Mr. Li may be vulnerable, however, to being "promoted" out of his Government job next March when the National People's Congress meets.
Mr. Deng appears to be supporting two Deputy Prime Ministers, Zhu Rongji and Tian Jiyun, and they are among the possible candidates to succeed Mr. Li if he is pushed out as Prime Minister. 
Mr. Deng went out of his way to say that while he and most other leaders do not understand economics, Mr. Zhu does know something about the subject. 
Mr. Zhu was picked recently to head a new super-ministry called the Economic and Trade Office.
As part of Mr. Deng's campaign to boost reform-minded officials and promote economic change, the Politburo recently released a document that says Yangtze River cities and border areas will be opened up to the outside world in the same way that coastal cities already have been.
"Clearly at the moment we are in a Deng-ist high tide," said a Western diplomat. 
But no one knows whether the tide will go out again, particularly after Mr. Deng's death, leaving the landscape unchanged.

file: EDUCATION_ABOUT EDUCATION.txt
text:
ï»¿
What is the source of student power?
What, in the latest dramatic example, gave China's students the power to temporarily paralyze the Government and perhaps, despite the bloody rout by military firepower, change their country's course?
Some 30 years after American students marched in the forefront of the battle against racial discrimination, campuses across the nation are experiencing racial divisions and racist incidents.
Numbers alone are not what gives students power, even though the events in Beijing's Tiananmen Square were driven by the very mass of the protesters. 
Still, in China as in the United States and elsewhere, university students constitute only a fraction of the entire population. 
They command little economic power. 
Nor are they a significant part of their countries' political apparatus. 
What then is the source of their power?
Most likely, their power derives in large part from the advantages of youth: great energy and enthusiasm, faith in a better future (which many of their elders may think admirable but naive), fewer family obligations, none of the restrictions that will later be imposed by the economic establishment, which rules over jobs and careers.
All this gives students greater freedom for action; but despite this, the successful use of their power depends in large measure on support from the majority of the citizenry. 
It does not detract from the bravery of China's students that their sudden show of power depended, in addition to their own remarkable discipline and adherence to nonviolence, on open and tacit support from many quarters, even within a faction of the Communist Party and the Government.
All this does not automatically mark the Chinese students as by nature always virtuous. 
After all, another generation of Chinese students, a little more than 20 years ago, served as Mao Zedong's brutal shock troops of the Cultural Revolution.
History thus suggests that students reflect powerful trends in their society, sometimes taking the lead, perhaps because they consider themselves less vulnerable or because their idealism has not yet been dulled by adult caution. 
When the students interpret social and political trends accurately, their power is considerable.
If students' attitudes can shift so dramatically between generations, there is good reason for a critical look at the past and current mood among a vocal group of American students and what inspired it.
In the 1960's, the student voice rang out in support of civil rights. 
White and black students linked arms in the battle against discrimination. 
Faced by what seemed like an unyielding force of prejudice, backed by the sheriffs' guns and dogs, students drew strength from what had been the dream of rebellious youth through the ages: to be on the side of righteousness, while at the same time challenging the authorities.
Like today's students in China who are fighting for greater freedom and justice, they had joined, or even marched in the vanguard of, the noble cause of civil rights which, they sensed, was also the cause of the majority of righteous citizens.
In the late 1960's and early 70's, American students opposed the Vietnam War and incidentally also learned that governmental power can turn violent, though fortunately not in the manner of the Chinese troops this week. 
Still, when challenged by campus protesters, the police bloodied students at Columbia and Harvard and, in 1970, gunfire by the Ohio National Guard killed four students at Kent State University.
All of this stands in marked contrasts to current reports of new racial divisions and even harassment of minority-group students on American campuses.
Student demonstrations against apartheid in South Africa, which were prominent on the campuses and captured the media spotlight only two years ago, have been replaced by news of hostile incidents against minority-group students.
Student voices seem to echo new racist sentiments off-campus. 
Instead of Dr. Martin Luther King's non-violent drive for civil rights and a more perfect democracy, growing numbers of students now seem to reflect an era in which politicians shun the taint of liberalism. 
The students once again appear to mirror society's changing sentiments.
Some educators and civil rights advocates say those American students who use their power to protest affirmative action programs seem to reflect an adult neo-reactionary backlash that appears to say that democracy has gone too far. 
It is difficult not to judge their actions against those of the Chinese students who captured the world's admiring attention by mirroring a changing society's search for more democracy.

file: EDUCATION_Capitalism Course May Be Canceled.txt
text:
ï»¿
An American graduate degree program that teaches Western-style capitalism to students in China is in peril. 
But it is unclear whether the threat comes from Federal budget cutters or a White House sensitive to hard-liners in China.
Officials at the State University of Buffalo, which offers a master's degree in business administration in a program financed by the Chinese and American Governments, were notified on Feb. 
5 that $400,000 in United States Commerce Department money for the program was in jeopardy and would probably be canceled April 1. 
The Chinese Government provides the remaining $200,000.
Instead, university officials were told, the money would be diverted to Eastern European countries.
But The Buffalo News, quoting an unnamed diplomatic source, reported Sunday that the White House had ordered the program terminated because its free-enterprise curriculum had been increasingly criticized by hard-liners in the Chinese Government.
The diplomat said the Chinese Government had singled out the business course as ''highly subversive'' and a ''Western-oriented operation incompatible with the aims of the present Chinese leadership.''
Â 
Not Yet Canceled
A senior Bush Administration official said today that the program had not yet been officially canceled, but that the Administration was considering switching it to the more politically compatible ground of Eastern Europe.
''Given the atmosphere in China, with the Chinese reform movement not proceeding well,'' he said, ''and given the fact that there is a great need for similar programs in Eastern Europe, and given the fact that the Commerce Department is stuck holding the bill for this program, it might be better suited to change it to Eastern Europe.''
University officials have mounted a letter-writing campaign to the Commerce Department to protest the cuts and received support from some corporations represented on the degree program's board, including the Xerox Corporation, the General Electric Company and the Union Carbide Corporation.
''One could conjure up a scenario that the Chinese want to terminate the program but do not want to say so,'' said Dr. Joseph Alutto, head of the university's School of Management. 
''It's not any information we have received. 
Our continuing contacts with the Chinese Government say that is not the case.
''All the information we have says there are two issues involved. 
One is the budget problem in the Department of Commerce and the desire to respond to initiatives in the Eastern bloc. 
The second is a sense, perhaps, in the Department of Commerce that China may no longer be a primary area of interest.''
Â 
Temporary Halt in Classes
Dr. Alutto said Chinese Government officials have been questioning him about how soon the degree program would be back in full operation. 
The university had temporarily halted classes following Beijing's crackdown on students in Tiananmen Square last June. 
Students have recently returned to classes, but are expected to lose about a year of course work altogether.
The program, the only one at college level financed by both Governments, has awarded 131 M.B.A. degrees to Chinese students since 1984.
Currently 89 students are enrolled in the program, offered at the National Center for Industrial Science and Technology Management Development in Dalian, a seaport community in Lyaoning province. 
The classes, which originally were taught by both American and Chinese professors, are now taught by Chinese faculty, many of whom have done postdoctoral work at the Buffalo University.
Â 
Breach in Protocol, Some Say
University officials said a cut in financing by the United States would represent a breach of the protocol signed by the two Governments when the program was established in 1984. 
It stipulates that if a country withdraws from the agreement, it must pay to complete the educations of those students currently enrolled.
''I feel it would be unfortunate for all parties concerned to precipitously cancel the program,'' said Dr. Steven B. Sample, the university president. 
''Educationally, it would be a grave mistake.''
Dr. Alutto said: ''My only hope is that the long-term issue is kept in mind here. 
If the United States is at all serious about the modernization of China, it has to continue supporting programs like that. 
Essentially our graduates are providing the future economic leaders of China.''

text:
ï»¿
Among the contacts being renewed between China and groups in the United States is a collaborative effort in which American educators are to help China remodel its higher education system.
A five-member delegation from the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching visited China recently and found the Chinese still eager to proceed with a three-year agreement between the foundation and the Chinese Government.
The accord, signed in Washington last year, touched on China's major concerns. 
In talks at the time, Chinese officials said they were prepared to examine dramatic innovations like charging tuition and imposing some sort of education tax.
After Government soldiers killed demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in June, many contacts between the United States and China were suspended to protest China's suppression of human rights. 
The Bush Administration has come under heavy fire because of the secret trip to China in July by the national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, and the Deputy Secretary of State, Lawrence S. Eagleburger, and a second visit, on Dec. 
8, to mend relations between the two countries.
Nevertheless, some dealings between the Chinese and nonprofit American groups have been warily resumed.
Â 
Links 'Worth Maintaining'
''The cultural and academic view is that whatever the political atmosphere, these links which generally represent progressive forces for reform are worth maintaining,'' Winston Lord, former Ambassador to China, said yesterday. 
''However, there are some who feel that these contacts can be exploited, making it look as if it's just business as usual.''
Ernest L. Boyer, president of the Princeton-based Carnegie Foundation, said his group's trip from Nov. 
26 to Dec. 
6 was primarily a fact-finding one to test the political climate and see if the agreement on higher education should be sustained.
''We felt it was important to talk directly and received strong encouragement not only in the State Department but even among our China scholars that the agreement should not be discontinued,'' Dr. Boyer said.
The punitive aftermath of Tiananmen Square was evident to the Carnegie delegation at Beijing University. 
The freshman class is not taking an academic program but spending time in political indoctrination and military training. 
Departments in politically sensitive areas like political science and sociology have not been permitted to enroll new students.
Dr. Boyer said high Chinese officials expressed a desire to resume the Fulbright Scholarship program, which had been suspended after the Tiananmen Square killings.
Â 
Issue of Handling Diversity
He said Chinese officials wanted to talk about how to handle the diversity that exists among the two million undergraduates in Chinese universities. 
They were particularly interested in American institutions like the City University of New York with its numerous senior colleges and community colleges.
The Carnegie delegation visited half a dozen universities and met with officials, educators and scholars. 
Some meetings were formal, while others resembled the typical get-togethers of scholars all over the world.
''I was struck even more than in the past how completely American colleges and universities have penetrated that nation,'' Dr. Boyer said. 
''In every conversation, you talked to people who had been to one or more campuses here and who could talk about why Yale was better than Stanford or what were the top 10 universities in America with as much intelligence as you would find in any faculty club in America.''
The upshot of the visit is that the agreement will go forward and that Carnegie will develop a follow-up strategy.
Dr. Boyer said he told Chinese officials that if the Government was serious about sustaining a higher education system Chinese students must be reassured that they would be able to move back and forth in academic disciplines in a free climate.
Â 
'Respectfully Received'
''I'm sure I was being heard and respectfully received,'' he said. 
''I do not pretend to know the politics, but no one argued about this.''

file: EDUCATION_Scholar Exchanges Jolted by Tremors in Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
One casualty of the turmoil in China may be the scholarly and scientific collaboration that has enriched knowledge in the United States and China, opening up the geologic wonders of Tibet and the workings of the Chinese Communist Party for Americans while helping the Chinese fight off a potent crop disease.
The crackdown in China against pro-democracy demonstrators and the tensions in Chinese-American relations that have followed have deterred many American scholars from venturing to China and prevented many Chinese scholars from venturing out of their country. 
Even if travel continues unabated, Chinese scholars and officials may be less willing to talk freely in the less tolerant atmosphere now prevailing in their country.
The National Academy of Sciences has suspended its three major exchange programs with China to protest the use of Chinese troops against demonstrators in Tiananmen Square. 
The suspension affects about 200 American and Chinese scholars.
The academy has urged 30 American scholars in China under its sponsorship to come home. 
It also postponed a symposium in Shanghai on gene research that would have had 15 American speakers and 200 participants from all over China.
Â 
Exchanges in Doubt
Several other academy exchanges are also in doubt: a visiting scholars exchange program, for example, that annually sends 35 Americans to China and 30 Chinese to the United States for one to three months, and conferences on Chinese religion and philosophy, which would have brought 15 Chinese scholars to the United States in September.
Hundreds of other scholars travel on their own with university or private sponsorship, and many of these have also had to change their plans.
''Everybody who is involved in the exchanges with China in academic work is very upset at the negative impact this will potentially have on both American access to China and Chinese access to America,'' said David M. Lampton, president of the National Committee on United States-China Relations.
Mr. Lampton is a political scientist who, in 1982, studied Chinese river planning and discovered that, despite China's totalitarian system, regulation of the environment is not well centralized, a shortcoming that has resulted in polluted water supplies and wasted arable land. 
Such a study would not have been carried out, he suggested, had not Chinese officials been open and candid with him.
Though its numbers are uncertain, the exchange of scholars with China is the largest the United States has with any Communist country, said Peggy Blumenthal, a vice president of the Institute for International Education, the largest international exchange program in the United States.
Â 
Fears About the Impact
''Chinese scholars have important contributions to make in scientific and other fields and for us to cut off communications with them hurts our own scholarship and slows down the rate of scholarship everywhere,'' she said.
In the last decade of information exchanges between scholars in the United States and China, American scientists have helped China protect its pepper and tobacco crops against a devastating virus and taught the Chinese how to build an advanced collider to study subatomic particles.
In turn, the Americans have learned about a Chinese drug that reportedly has been effective in destroying cells containing the AIDS virus, and a Chinese graduate student working in the United States discovered a new material that can be used in high-temperature superconductors. 
American social scientists have been able to scrutinize the workings of the Chinese Communist Party.
Now, there is fear that a freeze in American relations with China may cut effectively sever links between these two communities, by limiting the travels of American and Chinese scholars and by making Chinese academics reluctant to speak freely.
Science and scholarship thrive on exchanges of information unimpeded by national boundaries. 
Journal articles are one way of communicating, but face-to-face meetings of scholars, informally, at conferences or in laboratories, are as essential.
Â 
No Substitute for Contacts
''There is no substitute for getting together on an informal basis with colleagues doing the same kind of work you are doing,'' said Dr. Jules B. LaPidus, president of the Council of Graduate Schools, which represents 400 graduate schools.
Just as important as formal conferences, he said, is ''what takes place in the hallways and restaurants where you find groups of people who don't usually see each other sit down and draw on the back of envelopes and write equations and talk about what actually happens in the laboratory and ask their colleagues, 'Have you tried this?' or 'Have you got any ideas about that?'
''
One group for whom access to China and its officials is vital are the American historians, geologists, anthropologists and others who study China, said Kyna Rubin, a professional associate with the National Academy's Committee on Scholarly Communications With the People's Republic of China. 
American political scientists have even been allowed to examine Chinese government operations and economists have been studying the economic reforms.
''One would suspect that's not going to be as easy to examine as it was before June 4,'' she said. 
''For Americans trying to learn about China, to be denied access to China takes us back to the 1950's, 60's and 70's when you had to study China from afar rather than first-hand.''
American scientists in China have been using the silkworm as a tool in genetic and other biological experiments. 
They have been studying erosion and the spread of deserts. 
''American geologists are crazy about Tibet'' and its distinctive, often inaccessible geological formations, said Jane Liu Jernow, who directs the Committee on Scholarly Communication's science program.
Chinese land specialists are still scheduled to come here to study satellite data that track erosion.
Â 
Reluctance to Speak Freely
All such research has been jeopardized by the current atmosphere in China that makes Chinese more reluctant to speak their minds.
There are no precise figures on how many people and programs will be affected, since hundreds of scholars come to the United States or travel to China on their own. 
China has not yet closed its doors to Americans. 
American universities are still urging Chinese colleagues who have trips scheduled for the coming academic year to show up on schedule.
Still, how readily China will let its scholars out of the country, and the willingness of those scholars to speak freely with Americans is in doubt.
''We are concerned about the scholarly environment in China, if it is conducive for American research or if there's an environment of intimidation against the Chinese academic community,'' said Ms. Rubin. ''How productive can our students and scholars be if libraries are closed, if the archives are closed, if Chinese colleagues are inaccessible?''
American research may also be set back simply by the loss of visiting Chinese graduate students and postdoctoral fellows, who are often some of the most able researchers at many university graduate mathematics, physics and chemistry departments, U.S. 
Workshops in China In scientific exchanges, experts say, Americans have probably been teaching Chinese scientists far more than the Americans have learned from them. 
Scientific research in China was practically halted during the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976 and China lost pace with the rest of the world. 
In recent years, Americans, taking their own equipment and chemical agents, have gone to China and run workshops on gene cloning and immunotoxins to acquaint the Chinese with newly developing areas of science.
Dr. Dean H. Hamer, a research scientist for the National Cancer Institute who arranged three such workshops in 1987 and 1988, said that Chinese scientists at the Institute of Microbiology in Beijing, using biological engineering techniques absorbed from the West, have produced an attenuated strain of a virus, the cucumber mosaic, that devastated crops. 
The new strain immunizes pepper, tobacco and some fruits against the virus. 
Thousands of acres of crops have been saved, Dr. Hamer said.
Americans have also capitalized on their contacts with China in experiments with drugs that might help fight AIDS and cancer.
Chou Wen-chung, a professor of musical composition at Columbia University, says the new atmosphere in China may impede the kind of cultural exchanges that brought the violinist Isaac Stern and the playwright Arthur Miller to China and enlightened American scholars about Chinese concepts and forms in music.
''The situation is rather tragic,'' he said, ''because it was happening at a time when things are changing both for Chinese intellectuals and Western scholars.''
Tsao Hu, left, a visiting scholar from China, and Dr. Dean H. Hamer, a research scientist, conferring on an experiment at the National Institutes of Health. 
The turmoil in China has threatened scientific and scholarly collaboration (The New York Times/Marty Katz)

file: EDUCATION_Scholars Creating Archives of China Unrest.txt
text:
ï»¿
Scholars and universities around the world are setting up archives to collect pamphlets, posters and other items created during the democracy movement in China last spring.
At least seven universities, including Yale, Harvard, Columbia, and the University of Chicago, are putting out calls for the material. 
Scholars involved in the effort say their aim is to collect materials of great historical significance and prevent the Chinese Government from denying the uprising ever happened. 
Outside the United States, the University of Leiden in the Netherlands, the University of Toronto and Australian National University have joined in the effort.
''The Chinese are trying to systematically stop their own people from knowing anything about it,'' said Jonathan Spence, the George Burton Adams professor of history at Yale University and a pre-eminent scholar of modern Chinese history. 
''They are denying any sort of witness to their own people. 
So in a sense, it might be the foreigner who becomes a custodian of Chinese information if they refuse to keep it themselves.''
Â 
Closing Off the World
China has a long pattern of closing the outside world from events within its borders, Professor Spence said. 
During the Great Leap Forward in 1958 and the subsequent famines, as well as during the Cultural Revolution, the Chinese Government tried to prevent news about the social upheavals from leaking out.
Despite the extensive foreign television coverage of the student demonstrations and the June 4 violence in and around Tiananmen Square, said Professor Spence, the Chinese Government has branded the students as hoodlums and insisted that they, not the troops, initiated the killings.
But material collected for the archives will show otherwise, the scholars involved said. 
The universities want to document the scope of the pro-democracy movement. 
In addition to pamphlets and posters, the archives will contain photographs, videotapes, bloody clothing and eyewitness oral histories.
Scholars have moved quickly to get the material, for much of the written record of the movement is ephemeral, said Katharine Morton, the head of manuscripts and archives at the Sterling Memorial Library at Yale. 
While official Chinese newspapers wrote straightforward accounts of the demonstrations for a few days in May, debate was primarily carried out in pamphlets, placards and wall posters, which can easily be destroyed.
Â 
Various Approaches Used
The material has been collected in different ways. 
Professor Spence at Yale and Prof. Timothy Brooke of the University of Toronto sent letters to newspapers around the world and have received some material.
Marsha Wagner, the director of the C.V. 
Starr East Asian Library at Columbia University, was in Beijing during the pro-democracy movement. 
She took photographs of many of the wall posters and carried the film out with her, she said.
Other foreigners in China at the time smuggled out political pamphlets. 
Some continue to make their way to the West through Hong Kong, said Qiu Zhong, who is involved with the archive set up jointly by the University of Chicago and the Chicago-based center for Psychosocial Studies. 
Oral histories of tourists and the survivors will also be important.
While the various archives are still in their early stages, the scholars involved already know security is a major concern. 
Some of the photographs and videotapes show Chinese in ''counterrevolutionary'' acts, which could be dangerous to them. 
Balancing the need to protect people's identities with the openness usually associated with academic projects will not be easy, the scholars said.
''We have to be extremely careful about who gets access to these materials,'' said Kandice Hauf, an associate in research at the Fairbank Center for East Asian Research at Harvard University. 
''People are still being arrested.''

file: Empire of the Day and Night Creams.txt
text:
ï»¿
YUE-SAI KAN, a 43-year-old celebrity television host who produced "One World," a Western life-style magazine broadcast in China from 1987 through 1990, is about to wield yet another potential tool of cultural revolution.
It was 9 o'clock one recent morning, just two days before Ms. Kan would leave Manhattan for China to introduce her own line of cosmetics, a line that will, she promised an Asian-American visitor, "make you gorgeous."
As she opened the door of her six-story town house on the Upper East Side -- which is equipped with an office, a sound studio, television monitors, two secretaries, one housekeeper (who makes chiao-tzu, or dumplings) and a husband (the industrialist James McManus) -- she apologized for not being dressed.
She was lying. 
Even in a most casual outfit, a bright red ("my favorite color") floral T-shirt and matching leggings, she was camera-ready. 
The skin, covered by her own foundation, was pale and blemish-free. 
The lips and fingernails were the same shade of red as her outfit. 
Her hair gleamed. 
In six hours, she would have a haircut. 
A casual observer couldn't imagine why.
She opened the first Federal Express delivery of the day. 
It was a photo of herself, which will soon be emblazoned on advertisements, shopping bags and, blown up to four feet high, window displays.
"It's a digital photo," she said, waving the picture. 
"It's expensive. 
But I think it's beautiful, don't you?"
She was happy. 
It seemed that yet a few more dollars of the $5 million she and her husband had invested in her new venture had been well spent.
A S she scampered up a staircase to her second-floor office, past a hallway hung with framed photos of her on the covers of Western and Asian magazines, she apologized yet again. 
"You are the only one privileged to see this mess," she said.
Ms. Kan (whose name is pronounced you-sigh con) may be personally tidy, but her suitcases were, indeed, pretty chaotic. 
Unzipped tote bags sprawled on the floor. 
Letters in English and in Chinese were strewn all over the sofa. 
Wads of paper blew about under a coffee table and chairs. 
She looked at the mess in dismay, picked up the telephone and, in Chinese, summoned Annie Xu, her housekeeper, to sweep up and make coffee.
The chaos was deceiving. 
In Shanghai, she plans to introduce her cosmetics line with the precision of a military general.
On Sept. 
28, she will hold a press conference in a hotel yet to be named, to announce the line of cosmetics and her new television show, "Yue-Sai's World," which will have 15-second commercials for the cosmetics. 
On Sept. 
30, the show will hit the air amid a blitz of the star's personal appearances on television talk shows, radio shows and interviews in magazines and newspapers. 
On Oct. 
1, she will formally introduce the line of 32 items: foundations, lipsticks, rouges, moisturizer, nail polishes, day and night creams (made with Chinese herbs) and a perfume called First Love. 
The line, most of it manufactured in China, will be sold at 10 department stores in Shanghai, a city of 14 million.
At each store, windows 12 feet wide by 8 feet high will be filled with the enlarged photographs of Ms. Kan and her products. 
The windows will be designed by Rolando Seinhart, creative director of cosmetics and fragrances for Bloomingdale's in Manhattan. 
Inside the stores, Ms. Kan will divide her army of 44 sales clerks, handpicked from 1,200 young women who sent resumes, photos and letters in response to a single advertisement in a Shanghai newspaper.
Ms. Kan plucked an applicant's letter from a suitcase and read it aloud: "I, Miss Chen, was born 1968, am 1.6 meters tall. 
I have a pretty good-looking face. 
My skin is nice, and since 1987, I graduated from high school, can speak some English and I work now in a clothing store since 1986."
The letter was covered with a half dozen pictures of Ms. Kan, who said, "She says she has collected every picture she has seen of me in different magazines."
The letter ended, "I hope Yue-Sai is my idol, and it would be my greatest pleasure in life to work for her."
Ms. Kan tossed the letter back into the suitcase. 
"We're not hiring her," she said.
LIKE Estee Lauder, Ms. Kan is selling her own image, as transformed into sophisticated products, packaging and advertising. 
Given the success of "One World" -- which she produced for China Central Television and which garnered an audience of 400 million people, many of whom still push, tremble and faint at the sight of her -- the sell shouldn't be a difficult one.
She is also waging a beauty price war. 
She has positioned her $6.50 lipstick above the Lifei brand ($4), which is made in China, and Avon (nearly $4), and below Max Factor (more than $35) and Christian Dior (more than $40).
"How can they sell the same stuff in Asia that they sell in the United States?" she asked, glaring at a segmented Avon eye shadow stick in varied shades of blue and green.
"Whatever's good for whites is wrong for Asians," she added. 
"We have puffy eyes; they have deep-set eyes. 
We have flat noses; they have tall noses."
"We call them 'big noses,' remember?" she said with a laugh, then continued: "Is it that they have the audacity for us to use the same products?
Or do we have the stupidity to use the same products?"
Her line offers nine lipsticks and matching nail polishes, divided among a red-orange family and a pink family, and a choice of two foundations. 
The brown eye shadow, she said, "extends the eyes and emphasizes the black of my eyes, not the blue of my eyes."
She named the colors after cities: Tokyo Pink, New York Red, Venice Orange.
"I gave them the world on TV," she said, "I'm giving them the world again."
"One World" traveled to 17 countries in the course of 102 broadcasts. 
One episode, titled "Denmark: Love, Marriage and Women's Roles," showed a dizzying array of couples being married and then, almost as rapidly, being divorced.
"Twenty-five thousand people get married every year," Ms. Kan said on the show. 
"Fifteen thousand get divorced every year."
In an episode of the new show, "Yue-Sai's World," she will introduce the Chinese to Michael Jackson's music video "Black and White," the whole six minutes.
Ms. Kan, who works 18 hours a day and is away from home a third of the year, is nothing if not global in her sensibilities.
Still, her sense of what becomes the Chinese woman is quite specific. 
Ms. Kan does make-overs with a fervor that is messianic.
She whipped out a bottle of foundation, and with the expert hands of someone who has spent 20 years in front of the camera (she first volunteered on a local-access cable show in Manhattan's Chinatown in 1972), smoothed the foundation on her visitor's face, chatting all the time. 
She took out a lipstick pencil and started outlining.
"The lips have to be balanced," she said. 
"God gave us two of everything, and they must be balanced."
Her visitor laughed, somewhat hysterically.
"Oh, I'm serious," Ms. Kan said, studiously working away. 
"Don't you feel beautiful?
You're going to be gorgeous!"
T HE idea for the line was born in 1986, after Ms. Kan had become friends with other Chinese television celebrities in the United States. 
Since 1980, she had been producing "Looking East," a cable television show that presented Asian life-styles to Western viewers, first in Manhattan and eventually across the United States. 
When she was sitting around with Kaity Tong, the Manhattan newscaster, Emerald Yeh, an anchor in San Francisco, and Linda Yu, an anchor in Chicago, the conversation didn't revolve around the fate of Deng Xiaoping.
"We talked about makeup," Ms. Kan said. 
None of them could find one brand that made everything they needed. 
But Ms. Kan didn't start her new empire then. 
"The time wasn't right then," she said, because "the people's living standards weren't high enough" in China.
She also had not yet met James McManus. 
In 1989, she was introduced to him by Mortimer Levitt, the owner of the Custom Shop chain of men's clothing stores in Manhattan. 
They married in February of the following year. 
"He proposed to me after six months," she said, giggling.
Ms. Kan was born to a wealthy family in Guilin, China, and moved to Hong Kong as a child. 
She went to college at the branch of Brigham Young University in Laie, Hawaii, and went to New York City after graduation. 
In 1971, she and her sister Vickie started Kanjin, a import-export concern doing business with China.
Her first show was "Looking East," and "One World," which showed Western life-styles to the Chinese, had its debut in 1987. 
She dated men like Ted Turner and George Lang, the Manhattan restaurateur. 
But it was Mr. McManus, who owns 12 companies, who put her in a position to become the cosmetics queen of China.
The wedding (her first, his second) took place at the Silver Palace Restaurant in Chinatown, where she hired 85 waiters ("from uptown") and rented silver, linen and crystal for 520 guests. 
"We chartered 100 limos to take people home," she said. 
"The logical thing is to rent buses, but my husband didn't want it, so what can I do?"
Soon after, she told him her dream. 
"If there's anything I want to do it's to design cosmetics," she said, "and he said, 'But, of course.'
"
For her trip to Shanghai, Ms. Kan was packing 32 suitcases. 
During her three-month stay, her husband will commute from Manhattan to Shanghai every two weeks.
But Shanghai is only the first market.
"I have 400 million potential buyers," she said.
Each one of them she wants to make gorgeous.

file: End Paper_ Letters from China_They Misjudged The Dragon.txt
text:
ï»¿
MOST OF MY 240 graduate and undergraduate students at the Beijing Institute of Chemical Technology were witty, wise, sweet and highly intelligent - sometimes brilliant. 
They were patriotic, with a deep-rooted love of their homeland, its ways and its people.
They also seemed to love America - and Richard Nixon, about whom they said with simple logic: ''He was a great man because he made our countries friends.''
''The heart of a teacher and the heart of a student are always linked to each other,'' one student wrote to me recently. 
He and others - Chinese university students, the men and women of Tiananmen Square of June 1989 - write to me still, their professor of English from September 1987 to July 1988 in the Chinese Government's ''foreign expert'' program.
As a teacher, I had few resources to carry forth a foreign-language program, having quickly discovered that these university students could speak little English despite years of studying it at middle, secondary and undergraduate levels.
Chinese education is archaic, relying mainly upon rote. 
Locked in my students' brains were a warehouse of English vocabulary and a wellspring of English grammar that had never been opened for regenerative speech.
I realized that we had to spend the year talking to each other and thinking in English. 
Consequently, our two-hour classes took on a simple format: They would tell me about China, and I would tell them about America.
They puzzled over America, the commonplace and the conceptual. 
I would describe an American scene, say a supermarket, and then ask them to enter it, walking down imaginary aisles to imaginary checkout counters. 
One student inevitably asked, ''But why would I need so much food?''
Helping my students overcome their shyness was a constant struggle. 
Initially charmed by their modesty, I resigned myself to their tradition of self-effacement when trying to get them to form ''English corners,'' groups of eight students that would meet after class on campus once a week to practice English. 
''Teacher Charles,'' one student explained, ''you must understand why we do not have English corners as you wish. 
No one wants to show off.''
They loved American music, especially tapes of Willy Nelson and folk rock, like Paul Simon's ''Graceland.''
They flocked to American films. 
The movie ''Breakdancing'' was big in Beijing that year and, thinking that all Americans could do breakdancing, they asked me to perform. 
I deferred to a student who, having seen the film many times, had perfected the slithering movements.
They added more and more Western touches to their clothing, which was already heavily denimed - loud shirts for the men, rather than the prosaic white ones, and sundresses or miniskirts for the young women, which must have made hearts jump even among the old men in the Politburo.
And they loved to talk. 
But because each of my classes was attended by an official ''class monitor,'' discussion of political topics was reserved mainly for office hours, which my students had not previously encountered. 
Though the office that was provided for me had little light and no heat, it had two couches, several chairs, a daily Thermos of boiled water for tea - and scores of students stopping by, eager for a word or two.
It was during these times that I, usually a nonpolitical person, inadvertently became a symbol and spokesman for democracy, a misty concept firing the students' imaginations.
To them, it was primarily a way of gaining a few choices in their lives. 
They wanted something to say about where they would be assigned to work, for example, complaining that too frequently students are sent to remote areas and jobs unrelated to their training, with nothing to do. 
One confessed: ''I fear that I will spend the rest of my life in Xinjiang Province only drinking tea and reading newspapers.''
They wanted choices, too, about basic conditions, such as where they could live and when they could marry; they had to reach prescribed ages - 23 for men and 20 for women - for government permission. 
Marriage was also prohibited while they were students, although some had been married before starting their programs.
They wanted to be free of corruption and profiteering of the kind I discovered when one student promised to invite me to the tiny apartment that he and his wife were scheduled to get from her work unit. 
With sadness and quiet anger, he later informed me that they were disgraced, being unable to fulfill their invitation: They could not afford the payoff for the apartment demanded by the Communist Party official in the work unit.
They wanted to be free to do as they wished in their own homes. 
That they weren't became clear when another student invited me home, saying that his family had decided it was time for Chinese people to be allowed to have foreign guests. 
When the head of his mother's work unit learned of the plans, however, the family was warned that the visit would bring heavy penalties, like the loss of both apartment and jobs.
My students desperately wanted more than their meager portion of books, ill-stocked libraries and ill-equipped laboratories; more than a small dormitory space where they had to live eight to a room and were permitted only one shower a week; more than their ration of food -rice dishes mainly, with occasional shreds of pork. 
(During the Tiananmen Square hunger strikes, I wondered how such undernourished men and women could survive.) Never did their limited vision of democracy call for changing China's form of government, and though they showed no love for the Communist Party, they expressed no desire to replace it.
The reforms they wanted seemed to them a natural progression within the many economic reforms already in motion. 
''It is a good time to be in China,'' one student told me. 
When I asked if a Cultural Revolution could happen again, they said that was not possible. 
''Chairman Mao is gone,'' they chided, ''and the party is no longer our parents telling us what to do.''
They misjudged the dragon.
''The younger generation has completely lost hope with our regime,'' says a letter delivered just a few weeks ago. 
''Almost every one of my friends intends to go abroad through different channels. 
Please don't think we are not patriots. 
On the contrary, we hope to save our homeland. 
If we remain here, no one knows what will happen to us. 
So if you are willing to and capable, help me please!''

text:
ï»¿
WERE YOU FOLLOWED?"
LIU XIANG ASKED anxiously, by way of greeting. 
It was a bright September day last year when we met for dinner at a restaurant in the center of Beijing. 
He hardly touched his food, spending much of his time looking over his shoulder. 
A fugitive from the law, Liu was very different from the easygoing physics student who, the year before, was at the center of the democracy movement at Tiananmen Square.
"They're closing in," he said in a whisper. 
"The police have been asking around town about me, and I've got to leave very soon. 
But this time I've got to get to Hong Kong safely. 
Otherwise, it's all over."
Liu Xiang (pronounced lee-o shahng) was haunted by the memories of the prison from which he had just escaped. 
Each night he had the same nightmare. 
"In my dream, they beat me, and I try to explain that I didn't really mean to escape, and they just keep on beating me and beating me."
Each night he would wake, his body in a cold sweat, his heart pumping wildly.
IT ALL BEGAN WITH A MIDNIGHT SNACK. 
LATE ON THE evening of April 18, 1989, Liu Xiang went out with some friends to eat and ran into a crowd of Beijing University students marching toward Tiananmen Square. 
Caught up in the excitement, Liu joined the march. 
That decision changed his life.
Gangly, with close-cropped hair, Liu was then a 23-year-old senior at Qinghua University, one of China's premier colleges. 
A member of the Communist Youth League, he was at the time a firm supporter of the Communist Party. 
He remained a supporter even as the democracy movement sucked him in, as it did millions of others around the country. 
But then came the crackdown, and Liu found to his horror that the Communist Party had no compunctions about declaring war on him and his fellow students.
Fleeing to southern China, Liu entered a world he scarcely knew existed -- a free-for-all zone of bribery, smuggling and criminal gangs. 
He escaped to Hong Kong in April 1990, requesting asylum from the British authorities. 
Instead, he was returned to China some days later. 
Thrown into prison, he learned to rely on his fists as well as his brains. 
He managed to escape and make his way back to Beijing. 
By then it was summer and the police were on his heels. 
He fled south once more and again sneaked across the border to Hong Kong. 
Last month, he arrived in New York to start a new life.
Liu Xiang's two-year odyssey affords an unusual glimpse of China's underside, where the regime's repressive apparatus is sometimes more pathetic than terrifying. 
Corruption, greed and passive resistance conspire to frustrate the hard-liners' ability to capture democracy movement fugitives like Liu Xiang.
In Maoist times, it probably would have been impossible for a political fugitive to escape China once, let alone twice. 
In past campaigns of repression, the party was able to mobilize the masses to turn in their neighbors, even their family. 
This time, ordinary Chinese sided with the fugitives.
Escape stories of the democracy movement activists may differ in the details but they all share one point: none of the activists would have been able to escape if it were not for the assistance of a range of people along the way, from peasants to Communist Party officials. 
Liu Xiang found that acquaintances everywhere were willing to lie for him, bribe for him and forge identity papers for him. 
These acquaintances showed him that, particularly in southern China, the security network is tattered. 
Liu found his way out through the holes.
What Liu's two-year ordeal also underscores is the way the British overseers of Hong Kong sometimes seem to be doing Beijing's bidding. 
Sending a democracy movement activist back to China, to face the possibility of a long prison sentence, is hardly in keeping with the professed British ideals of fair play and common decency. 
However, the British authorities hold the view that the best way to manage Hong Kong is not to vex China but to maintain stabilityI and allow for a graceful exit in 1997. 
Liu seems to have been a victim of that policy.
It was in Hong Kong, while hiding as an illegal immigrant after his second escape, in December 1990, that Liu recounted details of his life after the June 1989 crackdown at Tiananmen Square. 
Speaking mostly in Mandarin, his words punctuated here and there with prison jargon, sometimes drifting into the functional English he learned in school, Liu Xiang gave a Dantean account of his journey through the many circles of a Chinese Communist hell.
QINGHUA UNIVERSITY, A SPRAWLING CAMPUS nestled in the northwestern outskirts of Beijing, is the M.I.T. of China. 
In China, only a tiny elite pass the examinations to get into any university, and those who succeed tend to find higher education a liberating experience.
After slaving away in high school and struggling to pass college entrance examinations, they finally have the chance to fall in love (romance is banned in high schools) as well as the time to reflect on life and politics. 
One of the few burdens foisted on them is that of history: students have played an important role during China's major upheavals of the last 100 years, and they sometimes hold themselves responsible for the direction of their nation.
My wife and fellow New York Times correspondent, Sheryl WuDunn, met Liu Xiang while she was interviewing students at Tiananmen Square shortly after the democracy movement began. 
Liu was bright and articulate, one of a handful who would phone us with information about plans for demonstrations and other student activities. 
We met with him often, and he impressed us as courteous, gentle and eager to be helpful. 
Without appearing manipulative, Liu Xiang charms those around him.
One of his greatest skills is in cultivating guanxi (connections) -- a critical talent in China. 
China is not so much a market economy or a socialist economy as a guanxi economy. 
Everything from jobs to cars to videos is distributed largely on the basis of guanxi. 
Knowing this is how the system works, Liu would collect guanxi the way some people collect postage stamps.
Back in the spring of 1989, in his ramshackle dorm, with books and clothing strewn about, Liu and his five roommates complained about hard-line policies, but not about the system itself. 
On one visit, I asked Liu if he was anti-Communist. 
"Of course not," he said, a bit horrified. 
"We all support the Communist Party. 
We want to reform it."
Liu Xiang's father, an officer of the People's Liberation Army, had been killed during a gun battle in the Cultural Revolution and was later declared a martyr by the Government. 
Liu grew up in the ancient city of Xian, in north-central China, and was raised as a believer in Communism.
When the 1989 student democracy movement began, he didn't want to get involved. 
"It's very tough to get into Qinghua University," he explained, "and if you get in trouble then it's all down the drain."
Yet it was impossible to stay away from Tiananmen Square. 
First he watched from the sidelines. 
Then he helped carry to waiting ambulances those classmates who had gone on hunger strikes and had fainted. 
He stayed with them as they were revived, and he saw them pull the IV tubes from their arms to resume their fast. 
Liu was moved in a way he had never been before.
A radio buff, Liu was asked by several of his friends -- student leaders -- to help set up a loudspeaker system at Tiananmen Square to air news about their movement. 
Liu helped run the "broadcast station," as they called it, and also served as a liaison with a number of foreign journalists.
Then, in the early morning hours of June 4, his world was shattered. 
"We had expected tear gas that evening, but nobody thought the soldiers would fire on the people," Liu Xiang recalls. 
"We were shocked, and that was when my attitude toward the Communist Party changed. 
Everything we believed in suddenly collapsed."
At 4 A.M., heading with some friends for the area around Tiananmen Square, Liu found tanks burning and the People's Liberation Army behaving like an invading force. 
The students spent much of the next few days harassing troops and playing a dangerous cat-and-mouse game with them along the alleys around the main roads. 
Twice, bullets narrowly missed Liu, and once, he says, he helped set fire to an armored personnel carrier -- a capital offense in itself.
The Army quickly consolidated its control over the capital. 
Many students and workers were detained, and the security forces began daily interrogations of Liu Xiang on the Qinghua campus. 
Obliged to write day-by-day accounts of his activities during the democracy movement, Liu omitted any mention of his involvement in the broadcast station or his role in setting fire to the personnel carrier. 
The authorities knew nothing about those matters, and grilled him instead on his contacts with student leaders and with me and Sheryl.
The university refused to allow Liu to graduate, and the questionings continued all summer. 
The authorities were sure he wasn't telling the complete truth, but he had one advantage over them: they didn't know what he had actually done.
"I figured if I lied, I'd be able to get a diploma and resume a normal life," he says, and so he lied about almost everything. 
He denied any role at Tiananmen and insisted he had met my wife and me only casually and briefly. 
Yet even during that terrifying time, he managed to outwit the police, who were keeping us under partial surveillance, to meet with Sheryl and to brief her on the crackdown and the interrogations on the campuses. 
Beneath his affable exterior was clearly an iron resolve, a courage that sometimes bordered on the reckless.
As in almost every part of the country, the investigations at Qinghua were subverted by a massive cover-up by students, professors and even Communist Party officials. 
At the risk of their careers and their freedom, officials intervened and lied to protect those involved in the Tiananmen movement.
At Qinghua, some well-placed individuals secretly met with Liu and other students who were under investigation. 
"They would tell us, 'The authorities know this much, so tell them that, and no more,' " Liu says. 
One sympathizer helped Liu obtain a photocopy of his university diploma, so that he could pretend to have graduated.
There was, however, no sign that the investigation was drawing to a close. 
As the summer wore on, Liu Xiang began to worry that time was running out. 
When the regular Qinghua students returned to campus for the fall semester, the authorities would be able to question more people and might learn that he had been lying about his democracy movement activities.
After a number of student acquaintances were arrested, he became even more nervous and finally obtained some false documents from a friendly official. 
He then secretly arranged to flee to the southern city of Shenzhen, adjacent to Hong Kong.
TWELVE YEARS AGO, Shenzhen was little more than a farming community. 
But as soon as it was declared a special economic zone -- an area modeled on the frenetically capitalistic Hong Kong -- it was transformed almost overnight into a boom town. 
Hong Kong entrepreneurs found that they could save on labor costs by transferring their garment and toy factories across the border. 
Today, Hong Kong companies employ some 2 million Chinese workers in Shenzhen, which has a population of 1.9 million, and the surrounding towns of Guangdong Province.
In most of China, jobs and apartments are assigned. 
In Shenzhen, and to a lesser extent elsewhere in Guangdong, it is possible to find a job and rent an apartment on one's own. 
This has corroded the Government's control mechanisms and created a wealth of new opportunities -- for criminals as well as more conventional entrepreneurs. 
Among the concrete-block apartment houses and thriving shops are people who will supply ID cards to those who want a new identity. 
In Maoist China, there was nowhere to hide; now there is Guangdong.
Criminal gangs have also moved in. 
The gangs, known as Triads (derived from the Cantonese name for the Three in Accord Society, the "three" being heaven, earth and man), have a long history in China. 
Triads fled after the 1949 revolution to Hong Kong and Taiwan; there, in close proximity to China, they have remained powerful, providing "protection" to nightclubs, for example, and periodically getting into terrifying turf battles in which hoods go after one another with cleavers.
With the weakening of Communist controls over the last dozen years, the Triads set up branches in Shenzhen and other parts of Guangdong, running smuggling, gambling and prostitution rackets. 
(According to the Shenzhen authorities, in just the last five months of 1990 more than 60 criminal gangs were broken up.)
Liu Xiang thought that in such a free-for-all he could get a job with no questions asked. 
Ordinary Chinese are not allowed to enter Shenzhen without a special certificate, but Liu was able to go through guanxi and get the necessary documentation. 
Liu's new papers, which were under his own name, proclaimed him a worker who had never participated in the democracy movement and who was going to Shenzhen as a buyer for a factory.
Shortly after arriving in Shenzhen, in September 1989, Liu Xiang found a temporary position in an office assigning Chinese sailors to jobs on foreign ships. 
Liu told his employer he had not taken part in the democracy movement, showing the bootleg photocopy of his diploma as evidence. 
"If I had been involved," he declared, "how would I have the diploma?"
Struggling to rebuild his future, Liu systematically went about cultivating guanxi in Shenzhen. 
Through a network of new friends, he found someone with connections to the Public Security Bureau, and he managed to extend his length of stay in Shenzhen.
He also made connections with the criminal underworld. 
Those gangsters whom he met were not caricatures out of a kung fu movie. 
Some were well-educated and ambitious young people alienated from the system and were drawn to the easy money to be had from smuggling and other illegal activities.
As a final backup, in case the authorities caught up with him, Liu used his job to obtain an ID card in the name of a sailor whose papers he was handling for the agency.
Unfortunately, Liu Xiang did his job so well that his boss decided to hire him permanently. 
While on a trip to Beijing in early 1990, the boss dropped by Qinghua University to check Liu's file (all Chinese have a personnel file, whose contents they are not allowed to see) and was horrified to learn that his star employee was being sought by the university authorities for fleeing in the middle of investigations.
Upon returning to Shenzhen, the boss promptly dismissed Liu Xiang. 
Liu then joined the gangs, helping them trade currencies on the black market. 
"We made a lot of money in a short period," he says, grinning at the memory.
Meanwhile, Qinghua officials had informed the Public Security Bureau in Beijing that Liu was working in Shenzhen. 
Soon, two Beijing policemen were in Shenzhen, questioning people about Liu's whereabouts. 
Liu Xiang felt the net tightening around him. 
It was time to leave for Hong Kong.
OVER THE NEXT FEW weeks, Liu borrowed maps of Hong Kong, memorizing the street names and geography of the border area. 
He got Hong Kong currency, and he went to places frequented by Hong Kong tourists, to see what set them apart from mainland Chinese.
"I decided that the head and feet were most important," he says. 
"Hong Kong people have fancy haircuts and they wear imported shoes. 
Plus a lot of them wear blue jeans."
So Liu invested in a pair of imported athletic shoes and an expensive haircut. 
The only giveaway was a chipped and rotten front tooth, an obvious product of Chinese dentistry.
Hiring a boat to take him all the way to Hong Kong was too expensive, so Liu arranged to make his escape on Zhong-Ying Street, a shopping district straddling the border. 
One side of the street is China; the other, Hong Kong. 
It is an area crammed with shops selling everything imaginable, from gold jewelry to traditional medicines to pornographic magazines.
Residents of China need special permission to visit the street, but Liu and two friends used their guanxi to pay a bribe equivalent to $106 (several months' salary for a factory worker) so that the Chinese People's Armed Police would look the other way. 
Hong Kong police are stationed along the street to prevent residents of China from slipping into the British territory, and Liu and his friends sneaked through back entrances and alleys until they got to a gulf of water separating them from Hong Kong.
"We found a private boat that would take us across the water," Liu says. 
"When the marine police were changing shifts, we crossed the channel."
On April 22, 1990, after being dropped off on shore, Liu and his companions hiked across some hills and then flagged a minibus. 
They went immediately to Chinese University, whose student union had sent delegates to Tiananmen Square during the democracy movement.
Liu Xiang's problems seemed to be over. 
At Chinese University, he was treated as a hero, and he and his friends were put in touch with the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of the Patriotic Democratic Movement in China. 
The three subsequently turned themselves in to the Hong Kong Government and requested asylum.
Although Liu and his friends were kept at a detention center, they were treated courteously, and there seemed to be no problems. 
Liu had documents, including photographs and testimonials, confirming his role at Tiananmen.
On their seventh day in Hong Kong, immigration officers told the three to get their belongings ready, shook their hands and wished them well. 
Liu was elated. 
But then a long bus pulled up, and he froze. 
It was not the van used to take people back to the center of Hong Kong. 
Instead, it was the bus used to repatriate illegal immigrants to China.
"There must be some mistake," Liu protested, but the police forced him and his friends on the bus. 
Liu's voice hardens as he speaks of the Hong Kong Government's decision.
"It was contemptible," he says. 
"We'd been betrayed by the Hong Kong Government. 
We were so shocked and angry, and we figured we'd be sentenced to 10 years in prison."
The Hong Kong Government declines to discuss specific cases. 
The territory's British overseers have briefly, and as secretly as possible, provided refuge to some prominent democracy activists from China before sending them on to Europe or the United States. 
But the Hong Kong authorities have done this unenthusiastically, worried about the reaction from Beijing, and have systematically moved to curb criticisms about China that would upset its leadership. 
Hong Kong has not allowed some prominent Chinese dissidents living abroad to visit the territory. 
Films critical of China are censored.
In most parts of its former empire, from India to Africa, Britain tried to nurture democratic governments in the territories it was leaving. 
In Hong Kong, it appears to have done the reverse, and democracy forces in Hong Kong charge that British officials have done this so that London can maintain smooth diplomatic and trade relations with Beijing.
British and Hong Kong Government officials dispute such charges. 
They assert that Hong Kong cannot survive without China, and that openly supporting a small number of democracy activists would only hurt the great majority of Hong Kong residents in the long run.
THE FEW MINUTES on the bus as it returned to China were among the worst in Liu's life.
He knew that the Hong Kong authorities provide a list of all the illegal immigrants they repatriate. 
He also knew that the papers and photos he was carrying -- intended to document his involvement in the democracy movement and therefore win him asylum -- would get him swift punishment from China. 
He hid these under the bus seat, knowing that he was riding in a Hong Kong bus that probably would not be searched.
As many as 100 people are repatriated each day from Hong Kong. 
Most are illegal immigrants from Guangdong Province and are released, on payment of a small fine, once they can prove they are from the local area and have no criminal record. 
Those from distant provinces, like Liu Xiang, are interrogated to make sure they are not wanted for some crime. 
Sometimes they are sent back to the Public Security Bureaus in their hometowns, a process that can take months.
From the list provided by Hong Kong, the Chinese knew Liu's name, but he lied about his identity, claiming to be a worker from Xian and giving a false address. 
Eventually, of course, the police would realize that he had given a phony address and might beat the truth out of him, but he hoped to be free by then. 
He asked a detainee who was about to be released to phone a friend in Shenzhen and explain the situation. 
The Shenzhen friend promptly went to great lengths to bribe the guards to release Liu.
"The guards took the 'gifts,' but said that to release me they needed proof that I didn't have a criminal record," Liu says. 
"My friend tried to get that, but it was very difficult to get the necessary paper forged. 
In Guangdong, it's usually easy to get things done with money, but in this case we had some difficulties."
The friend did get one such forged document, but it didn't look authentic and the friend decided not to run the risk of using it.
Liu was transferred first to Zhangmutou Detention Center and then to Yangcun Detention Center, both in central Guangdong. 
The conditions were similar: up to 40 prisoners to a cell and up to 10 sleeping in a single, oversized bed. 
In addition to the beds, the cell contained a basin of water and a hole in the floor for a toilet.
Meals consisted of cold rice with warmed-over vegetables. 
"The biggest problem was that there wasn't enough food," Liu says. 
"If somebody spat out a rotten or disgusting vegetable on the floor, someone else would pick it up and put it in his mouth, even though the guards would beat us if they saw us doing that."
Liu, who is 5 foot 11, weighed 172 pounds when he entered prison and just 147 pounds seven weeks later. 
In addition to hunger, the prisoners constantly suffered from mosquito bites and a particularly ferocious kind of bedbug that left their legs covered with angry red welts.
At the detention centers, as in all Chinese prisons, order was established in each cell by the "boss" -- a prisoner who bullied his way to the top of the heap and ordered the other prisoners around. 
Liu felt frighteningly out of place, but he was lucky enough to be physically larger than most of the other prisoners.
At Yangcun, in another bit of good fortune, the boss in his cell was a fellow northerner and Mandarin speaker. 
"Big Brother, please take my watch," Liu told the boss as soon as he was in the cell. 
The boss warmed to such flattery (and no doubt would have taken the wristwatch in any case), and soon Liu became one of his strongmen. 
They would rough up new arrivals, looking for money hidden from the guards. 
The money would be used to buy cigarettes, food and clothing.
When the boss was moved to another prison, Liu Xiang took over. 
As though he had taken on the coloration of the jungle, the college boy was now a gang leader, forcing other prisoners to wash his underwear and give up their money and sometimes even their food. 
When they disobeyed, he ordered his strongmen to beat them up. 
One might expect Liu, formerly an advocate of democracy, to be embarrassed about his activities as a boss, but he is unapologetic.
"Originally, I didn't want to do it, but then I realized that in prison everything depends on this," he says, clenching a fist. 
"If you don't beat them up, then you'll get beaten up. 
And then you'll end up washing their underwear. 
In there, the only thing that matters is violence. 
There's no morality, just power."
That attitude reflects a general moral uncertainty of recent years. 
China's main sources of moral values -- traditional Confucianism and revolutionary Communism -- have largely collapsed, and many young people today speak of a crisis of faith. 
Some have turned to religion, others to drugs or various cults, to give their lives meaning. 
Even the outpouring of support for the 1989 democracy movement seemed to have stemmed partly from a popular yearning for a noble cause to believe in.
That student movement has given rise, in turn, to a new and powerful imperative: protect the student participants. 
Thus, while many young people are complaining about their nation's spiritual vacuum, there have been countless cases of ordinary people displaying enormous moral courage in protecting student dissidents. 
Even as Liu is matter-of-fact when he talks about beating people in prison, he is scrupulous about not getting anyone in trouble for helping him.
Ironically, it was Liu's assertion of brute force, not his principles, that got him in trouble in prison. 
Liu had ordered his henchmen to beat a newcomer suspected of hiding his money, but the guards broke up the fight and then decided to teach Liu a lesson. 
They beat him and locked him in a separate cell, with his wrists handcuffed tightly behind his back.
"I was left lying on the wet cement floor," he says. 
"There was nothing inside, just a hole for a toilet, and it was clogged and the floor was very wet. 
The handcuffs were terribly tight, and after 15 minutes I was sweating and my blood couldn't circulate. 
I called the guards, but they didn't come. 
I kicked the door, and kept kicking for an hour or so. 
Finally, a guard came and loosened the handcuffs a bit, but by that time I couldn't use my hands. 
There was no feeling in them."
After 20 agonizing hours, Liu was returned to his regular cell.
WHILE IN PRISON, Liu Xiang spent his time humming a popular Chinese rock song -- "I Have Nothing" -- and searching for a solution to his problems. 
"What I thought of most was getting out," he says. 
"What I worried about most was my Mom. 
If she heard I was in prison " -- he pauses and shivers -- "it would be terrible."
He thought his best opportunity to escape would be while working on the prison farm. 
"I decided the best time was when it rained, because then it's harder for them to drive their motorcycles around looking for you, and they won't try as hard to find you."
So on June 12, 1990, after a thunderstorm, Liu made his move.
He was working in a large vegetable field with seven other prisoners. 
Security is relatively lax in Chinese labor camps, because traditionally there is no place for an escaped prisoner to run. 
On that day, only three guards were on duty, and the prisoners were scattered about the field. 
Liu began to work near the guard who was paying the least attention.
"When the guard wasn't looking, I slipped behind a hedge," he says. 
"I was ready to say that I needed to relieve myself."
But the guard didn't notice and Liu crawled to the edge of the field and then through another hedge functioning as a kind of fence. 
Since Liu had not been convicted of any offense, he was wearing civilian clothes and was able to hurry along the road and hitch a ride on a truck. 
A sympathizer had smuggled a small amount of money to Liu, which enabled him to make his way to Canton, where he hid with friends.
He then made his way back to Beijing by train -- using tickets purchased by a friend -- and even though he was a fugitive from the law, he was welcomed by his buddies. 
Almost no one had qualms about seeing him or helping him. 
Yet to his friends, Liu seemed a changed man. 
He was no longer an idealistic university student but a prison-hardened young man who had had a taste of the fast life in Guangdong. 
He boasted of his underworld connections and of the invitations to join the gangs.
By late summer, Liu had regained some of his weight and had had his bedbug bites treated. 
But he also was getting increasingly edgy, terrified that the police were closing in on him. 
He decided to escape once more to Hong Kong.
Having jettisoned his documents while being repatriated to China in April, Liu Xiang had to spend $42 on a bribe to get a new pass to go in and out of Shenzhen. 
He arrived in Shenzhen in the fall of 1990 and renewed his underworld guanxi to see if they could help him flee to Hong Kong. 
But this time he found himself running into one obstacle after another. 
Some smugglers were willing to take him by boat to Hong Kong, but then they were arrested. 
His friends who had arranged the bribe for him to get to Zhong-Ying Street had also been arrested.
While waiting to work out a solution, Liu had his hair permed to look more like a Hong Kong resident. 
The best time to cross the border, he decided, was on a public holiday, when few Hong Kong police are on duty. 
He selected Christmas Day, which is a holiday in the British colony.
Working through his guanxi, Liu was able to join a group of Shenzhen residents visiting Zhong-Ying Street on Dec. 
25. As the other tour members gawked, Liu slipped through the back doors and alleys on the Hong Kong side of the street and made his way to the water. 
With his usual aplomb, he offered to help a group of elderly Hong Kong people carry their bags onto a ferryboat. 
He had a terrible moment when he saw that Hong Kong police were beside the ramp, looking for Chinese illegal immigrants, but he marched brazenly toward them. 
The police recognized the elderly people Liu Xiang was helping and let the group pass.
On the other side of the bay, Liu Xiang took a taxi to meet some friends, who gave him refuge. 
But inquiries to the Hong Kong Government ran into a stone wall. 
The highest levels were advised of his situation in detail, but they refused once more to grant him asylum. 
This left him an illegal immigrant in Hong Kong, subject to arrest and repatriation at any time.
Liu considered various ways to reach the United States, including smuggling himself on a freighter, but in the end another method was found (details of which cannot be revealed here). 
On April 12, Liu Xiang arrived in the United States and was admitted by the immigration authorities because of his political background. 
As this article goes to press, Asia Watch -- the human rights organization -- is trying to find a university to take Liu for the next academic year.
"I think I will love New York," Liu Xiang says exuberantly, a few days after arriving. 
"It's great. 
And after seeing police all over the streets in Hong Kong and China, and being afraid of them, I notice that there are very few police on the streets of New York. 
That leaves a very favorable impression."
