BECAUSE the Chinese words for fish and for prosperity or abundance are pronounced the same - yu - fish is one of the symbolic foods for the Chinese New Year celebrations that begin Saturday.
For this year's holiday banquets, an increasing number of chefs - especially in New York and California - will be scooping their fish live from tanks in the kitchens and sometimes in the dining rooms of restaurants. 
Cooks preparing fish at home can also buy fish live from markets in the Chinatowns of San Francisco, Los Angeles and New York -in Flushing, Queens, and the Sunset Park section of Brooklyn as well as Manhattan.
The trend reflects the growing influence of Hong Kong cuisine, the newest of Chinese cuisines to be imported to the United States. 
Restaurateurs in Hong Kong, anticipating the return of the British colony to China in 1997, have started establishing businesses in the United States, and more and more chefs are relocating.
In Hong Kong, restaurants with fish tanks are routine and shoppers in the city's Central Market often take their fish or shrimp home in plastic bags filled with water.
''As more chefs come here from Hong Kong, you'll see more restaurants with live fish,'' said Ken Hom, the author whose latest book, ''Fragrant Harbor Taste'' (Simon and Shuster, 1989, $24.95) is about the cooking of Hong Kong. 
He described the Hong Kong style as essentially a more elegant version of Cantonese cooking. 
The restaurants tend to be fancier and considerably larger than other Chinese restaurants.
''There is great emphasis on seafood because of Hong Kong's location,'' he added. 
''And whereas it may be easy to keep fish alive in a pond in a rural area in Canton, in a big city like Hong Kong it's expensive. 
That adds to its allure.''
Though his restaurants do not have tanks of live fish, Michael Tong has added a chef from Hong Kong to the staff of one of his establishments, Shun Lee Palace in midtown Manhattan. 
''Hong Kong cooking is the first really new Chinese style that has caught on in awhile,'' Mr. Tong said.
Several Hong Kong-style dishes, like gray sole on a bed of crispy, edible bones, are on his special New Year's menu at Shun Lee Palace, 155 East 55th Street.
Other restaurants in Manhattan that maintain tanks of live fish - usually freshwater varieties - include the Golden Unicorn, 18 East Broadway at Catherine Street, and Oriental Town Seafood Restaurant, 14 Elizabeth Street at Bayard Street.
The new Triple Eight restaurant, at 88 East Broadway at Forsyth Street, maintains tanks of both fresh- and saltwater fish. 
The fish are usually simply steamed with ginger and scallions so the freshness of the flavor can dominate.
Among the dishes at Oriental Town Seafood is steamed black carp with black beans. 
The Golden Unicorn serves live shrimp cooked at tableside in a broth.
Live shrimp is a delicacy that only a few restaurants carry. 
''They are very expensive - up to $20 a pound wholesale - and are so delicate that they can't be kept overnight,'' said Chuck Lou, one of the owners of Hy Fund, a fish market at 75 Mulberry Street in Manhattan, where at least six kinds of fish are available live on a given day.
The fish are freshwater varieties, like carp, buffalo fish, crappie and a type of large-mouth bass. 
Mr. Lou said the market does not carry live saltwater fish because maintaining the chemical balance in a tank is extremely difficult.
Some of the fish come from the Great Lakes and, increasingly, from fish farms around the country. 
Tank trucks filled with swimming white crappies, catfish, carp, blue gills and freshwater bass now make the 28-hour trip to New York from fish farms in Arkansas on a regular basis. 
At the New York Fish Exchange, a wholesaler at the Fulton Fish Market, several other varieties are available from time to time.
Prices in retail markets like Hy Fund in Chinatown range from $1.40 a pound for live carp to $8 a pound for large-mouth bass. 
The markets will dress the fish to order.
In the San Francisco area, live fish are kept in tanks at several Hong Kong-style restaurants, including Wu Kong, at 101 Spear Street near Mission Hill, Hong Kong Flower Lounge in Millbrae, North Sea Village in Sausalito and Suntung Lok in Burlingame. 
Markets in San Francisco that carry live fish include Wah Fat Fish and Sang Sang.
Bruce Cost, author of ''Asian Ingredients'' (William Morrow, 1988) and owner of Monsoon, a restaurant near the San Francisco City Hall that opened in November, is planning to install an aquarium for live fish. 
''For the time being I'm keeping live catfish in a couple of sinks in the kitchen, but I expect to install fish tanks between the kitchen and the bar where the customers can see them.''
The San Francisco restaurants and markets are supplied by fishermen who keep their catch in tanks on boats and by fish farms in Southern California and elsewhere. 
The fish, among them catfish, rock cod and striped bass are bought, cleaned and cooked the same day.
When Chinese cooks buy live fish in a market they usually steam it. 
One example suitable for a Chinese New Year's menu, is steamed buffalo fish with ginger and scallions, a recipe that Norman Weinstein teaches at his cooking school in Brooklyn, Hot Wok. 
Another is Mr. Hom's steamed fish with ham and vegetables.
Both these dishes are particularly appropriate for celebrating the Chinese New Year because they call for whole fish, a symbol of prosperity.
Â 
Sole, Carp and More
Â 
Gray Sole Fillet with Crispy Bones
(Adapted from Shun Lee Palace Restaurant, Manhattan)
Â 
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time: 15 minutes
Â 
1 whole gray sole, 3 1/2 pounds, filleted with skin on; reserve the carcass in one piece without the head
Â 
1 egg white
9 1/2 tablespoons cornstarch
1 1/2 teaspoons cold water
4 tablespoons chicken stock
1 tablespoon rice wine
1 1/2 teaspoons salt

8 to 10 cups vegetable oil
4 scallions, cut in 1-inch pieces
4 slices ginger root, 1/8-inch thick and cut in 1-inch sticks.
1.Place each fillet skin-side down and cut across the fillets to make four pieces of equal width from each.
2.Beat the egg white with 5 tablespoons of cornstarch in a bowl large enough to hold the fish. 
Add the fish pieces and turn them in this marinade to coat them. 
Refrigerate at least 30 minutes.
3.In a small bowl dissolve 1/2 tablespoon of the cornstarch in the water and stir in the chicken stock, rice wine, 1 teaspoon salt, sugar and sesame oil. 
Set aside.
4.Pat the carcass dry and rub with the soy sauce and remaining 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. 
Then rub with 4 tablespoons cornstarch. 
Set aside at room temperature.
5.Heat the oil in a large wok or deep-fryer until it reaches 375 degrees. 
Add the fish carcass and fry undisturbed until very crisp and golden, about 10 minutes. 
Remove, drain and place on a serving platter.
6.Reheat the vegetable oil to 300 degrees. 
Add the fish pieces one at a time, gently swirling them to keep them separate. 
Cook for about 30 seconds, then using a slotted spoon or skimmer, transfer the fish to a colander to drain. 
Pour the oil out of the wok.
7.Place the wok over high heat, add the scallions and ginger, stir for 10 seconds, then add the sauce mixture. 
When it comes to a boil add the fish pieces and turn in the mixture just enough to coat them with the sauce.

8.Transfer the fish to the center of the crisp fried bones and serve at once. 
Serve pieces of the crisp, edible bones with the fish.

1 2- to 3-pound piece buffalo carp with bone, or a whole largemouth bass or sea bass, 2 1/2 to 3 pounds
5 tablespoons Chinese rice wine or dry sherry

1 bunch scallions cut in 3- to 4-inch sections

1.Select a heatproof platter that will hold the fish and fit into a large roasting pan.

Place the fish on the platter.

3.While the fish is steaming, place the sesame oil, soy sauce and remaining wine in a small skillet.

4.Using heat-proof mitts, lift the fish platter from the roasting pan and drain off any accumulated liquid. 
Pour the sesame oil and soy sauce mixture over the fish and serve.
Yield: 4 to 6 servings.

Whole Sweet and Sour Fish
(Adapted from Monsoon Restaurant, San Francisco)
Â 
Preparation time: 1 hour
Cooking time: 20 minutes
Â 
1 whole sea bass or red snapper, about 3 pounds
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
9 tablepoons cornstarch
4 large dried black mushrooms
2 1/2 cups hot water
1 small onion, peeled and quartered

1 tablespoon light soy sauce

1.Butterfly the fish, slicing up alongside the bone, then pressing down on the fish to flatten it completely. 
Flatten the head as well. 
The butterflying can also be done with the whole fish boned, if desired. 
Cut slashes into the skin of the fish.
2.Blend the eggs with 1 teaspoon of the salt and rub over the fish.
3.Spoon about 2 tablespoons of the cornstarch into a sieve and sprinkle evenly over the fish, then rub it on. 
Allow the fish to stand, uncovered, for 15 minutes. 
Repeat twice again.
4.Meanwhile, soak the mushrooms in 1/2 cup hot water until they soften, about 20 minutes. 
Drain them, reserving the soaking liquid, and squeeze out any excess water. 
Cut off the stems. 
Quarter the caps and mix with the onion, ginger, garlic, red bell peppers and scallions. 
Set aside.
5.In a nonreactive saucepan combine the remaining 2 cups of water with the sugar, vinegar, soy sauces and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. 
Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring just until the sugar dissolves. 
Set aside.
6.Mix 3 tablespoons of the cornstarch with the reserved mushroom soaking liquid and set aside.
7.In a large (16-inch) wok, heat all but 1/4 cup of the oil until it is very hot, 375 degrees, but not smoking. 
Cook the fish for 5 to 7 minutes, until it browns. 
Lift the fish out of the wok and drain on paper towels. 
Leave the oil in the wok.
8.While the fish is draining, heat the remaining oil in another wok or a largeskillet. 
Stir-fry the vegetable mixture until the vegetables begin to soften, then add the vinegar mixture. 
Bring to a simmer. 
Stir the cornstarch mixture and add it, stirring. 
Cook until the sauce turns syrupy and clear.
9.Reheat the oil used to fry the fish, return the fish to the wok and fry again briefly to crisp it. 
Drain the fish, place it on a platter, reheat the vegetables and the sauce, and pour this mixture over the fish. 
Decorate with coriander and serve.
Yield: 6 servings.

(Adapted from ''Fragrant Harbor Taste'' by Ken Hom (Simon & Schuster, 1989)

Preparation time: 30 minutes
Cooking time: 8 to 10 minutes
Â 
8 dried Chinese black mushrooms
1 whole red snapper, sea bass or any firm white-fleshed saltwater or freshwater fish, 1 1/2 to 2 pounds
4 tablespoons rice wine
2 1/2 teaspoons Chinese sesame oil
8 thin slices peeled fresh ginger
8 thin slices Smithfield ham
Y cup chicken stock
Salt

.Blanch the broccoli in a small pot of boiling salted water and drain.

text:

After years of being spurned on the international weapons marketplace, there are signs that these days Taiwan is finding Western countries willing to sell it modern military equipment to defend itself against mainland China.
Taiwan's relative success in buying modern weaponry shows the extent to which it may be reintegrating into the international community even though scarcely any important countries recognize it as the legitimate Government of China. 
The weapons purchases are also likely to inflame relations between Taipei and Beijing and cause tensions between the Chinese Government and Western Governments willling to sell such equipment.
Weapons specialists say that since the Persian Gulf war and the warming of relations between the Soviet Union and Western countries, military contractors -- and perhaps Governments -- are under greater pressure to find new markets, like Taiwan. 
While they may not yet be selling jet fighters, companies are talking to Taiwan about a wider range of weaponry and electronic warfare equipment.
"The business for us is shrinking in the U.S., so we have to start looking overseas for business," said a representative of an American armaments company, who was displaying advanced military communications systems at an exhibition recently in Taipei. 
"That's why we're here."
Armaments companies have always been willing to sell to Taiwan, but in the past, Western governments have frequently denied export licenses. 
Not all weapons specialists agree, but many say that the United States and several European countries may now be reconsidering the benefits of selling certain modern equipment to Taiwan against the risks of Chinese retaliation.
They add that with the collapse of Communism in the Soviet Union, the strategic importance of China may be diminishing, so that countries may be willing to stand up to pressure from the Chinese Government.
"Before, Taiwan could never pay billions of dollars for weapons and the French would never talk to us before," said Hei Youlong, a business executive and weapons expert in Taipei. 
"Now, Taiwan has money and when it talks, people start listening."
For example, in a deal many weapons specialists say is nearly completed, France plans to sell to Taiwan six Lafayette-class frigates, worth $2 billion, according to local news reports, with an option to buy 10 more.
Nearly two years ago, the deal fell through when China protested to France and successfully blocked the sale. 
Not only is the sale expected to go through this time, but China issued only a mild criticism of the deal.
In contrast, in the early 1980's, when Taiwan purchased two submarines from the Netherlands, China downgraded its relationship with the Netherlands to consular status. 
The relationship has since returned to normal.
More recently, the United States has approved the sale of four E-2 Hawkeye early warning aircraft, manufactured by the Grumman Corporation.
Taiwan, however, apparently wants a more modern version that the United States so far has not agreed to sell.
Currently, Taiwan's ability to detect approaching aircraft flying at low altitudes is relatively weak, as is its air capability in general, weapons analysts say. 
In the last two years, 19 to 20 jet fighters have crashed, including a prototype for a locally built fighter plane that Taiwan is trying to develop through a co-production arrangement with an American company.
The United States has consistently refused to sell F-16 jet fighters to Taiwan because they could be used to attack mainland China. 
It has sold the aircraft to other Asian nations, including Pakistan, Thailand and Singapore.
Taiwan and the United States cut off formal ties in 1979, when the United States and mainland China established diplomatic relations. 
At the time, the United States agreed to provide Taiwan with defensive arms but in 1982, it issued a joint communique with the Chinese that essentially limited American arms sales to Taiwan in quality and quantity to the level of those supplied previously. 
The United States was then supplying about $800 million in arms to Taiwan.

file: Foreign Passports Tell of a Desperate Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
The term ''pregnancy leave'' is taking on a new meaning here, as shown by a successful Hong Kong Chinese banker who is negotiating an unusual sweetener before he takes a new job. 
He wants his employer to pay to send his pregnant wife to Canada to give birth, insuring that their child will be born a Canadian citizen.
In the latest triumph of Hong Kong ingenuity, and the latest sign of Hong Kong's desperation, hundreds and possibly thousands of pregnant women are traveling to Western countries to give their babies what is regarded here as one of the most important things in the world: a foreign passport.
''In Hong Kong, when people ask you where you are going to have your baby, they don't mean which hospital,'' said Frank Ching, a writer and local newspaper columnist. 
''They mean which country.''
It used to be thought that the moment of truth for Hong Kong would come in 1997, when the British colony will revert to China, but now many people feel that the crisis is already here.
Â 
Mounting Frenzy Expected
Pessimists are drawing parallels with the surrender to Communism of Shanghai in 1949 and Saigon in 1975. 
They expect a mounting frenzy to leave, a surge in corruption as people try to buy a new future, and a social breakdown as the civil service abandons its loyalty to the lame-duck British administration.
''Hong Kong will all be destroyed before 1997,'' said George Hicks, an Australian businessman and writer who seats himself firmly in the pessimist camp. 
''The upheaval and disintegration will come way before 1997, as everybody tries to beat their neighbor out. 
This is like a game of musical chairs in which everybody knows when the music is going to stop.''
Of course, there are also optimists who believe that Hong Kong's economy is well positioned to continue to prosper, and that ballooning bank accounts will help salve anxieties about the future. 
Hong Kong has faced bouts of pessimism in the past, and few places in the world have displayed such a remarkable resiliency in overcoming wars, strikes, riots and trade embargoes.
In 150 years, Hong Kong has transformed itself from a pirates' lair to the world's largest container port, from an impoverished colony abounding in opium and skeletal rickshaw boys to an international financial center where impeccably dressed young men and women race along the streets, their Rolex watches peeking from under their sleeves as they chatter into portable telephones. 
Hong Kong today is richer and healthier than much of Europe, and it has more Rolls-Royces per capita than anywhere else in the world.
Â 
Despair Over Basic Law
Yet Hong Kong's fate seemed to be sealed in early April, when China's legislature approved the Basic Law that will govern the territory after 1997. 
The passage by China's National People's Congress was a formality, but it had the ring of finality for many Hong Kong residents who had hoped for a more democratic document.
Ever since the rise of China's hard-liners and the killings in Beijing last June, the mood in Hong Kong has been bleak and angry. 
Survey Research Hong Kong, a polling business that has measured confidence in the future since 1985, says its latest survey recorded a new low in public confidence. 
''People in Hong Kong are very discouraged at this time,'' said Louis Tong, director of the company. 
#1,000 Leaving Each Week Residents are emigrating at the rate of more than 1,000 a week, more than twice the rate in 1986. 
The obsession with emigration has spawned a new magazine, The Emigrant, as well as books and counseling services to help Hong Kong Chinese obtain foreign passports.
In one of the most unusual cases, a few people even paid about $5,000 each as a down payment on a passport from Corterra, which a brochure and advertisement identified as a South Pacific nation. 
They discovered too late that there is no such country.
Hong Kong does not officially report figures for capital flows, but John G. Greenwood, chief economist of G. T. Management (Asia) Ltd., an investment company, has derived estimates that suggest that Hong Kong began to shift capital abroad in 1984, the year that Britain agreed to return Hong Kong to China. 
By his method of calculation, the capital outflow soared in 1989 to nearly $5 billion, or almost $1,000 per inhabitant.
The apprehensions have been compounded by Hong Kong's unaccustomed encounter with economic difficulties. 
Economic growth tumbled to just 2.5 percent last year, about one-third of the usual level, and hotel occupancy rates dropped to 74 percent, compared with 92 percent in 1988. 
Over the last decade, Hong Kong's economy became integrated with southern China's, and so China's woes spill across the border into the British territory.
Â 
U.S. and China Imports Fall
The cause of the economic downturn is fairly straightforward: slowdowns in Hong Kong's biggest export markets: China and the United States. 
Thus the optimists, like George Baeder, director of the Pacific Rim Consulting Group in Hong Kong, argue that those are cyclical slowdowns and that when economic growth returns, the problems of Hong Kong will seem much more manageable.
''Think what happens when the U.S. economy picks up, when China rebounds from its cyclical downturn,'' he said. 
Then, he continued, if the leaders in Beijing ease out some prominent hard-liners and turn toward more pragmatic officials, Hong Kong will again be on the move.
Another source of optimism in some quarters is the belief that hard-line rule in Beijing is unsustainable. 
Albert W. Y. Chan, a local politician in the New Territories part of Hong Kong, is guardedly optimistic for the long term.
''With the democratization of Communist societies around the world, I don't think that the Chinese Communist Party can keep control indefinitely,'' he said. 
''Sooner or later, probably before 1997, there'll be major changes that will benefit Hong Kong.''
Â 
The Pessimism Deepens
The conventional wisdom in the business sector used to be that China would pursue its own self-interest in insuring Hong Kong's continued prosperity -because Hong Kong is China's biggest outside investor and trade partner, and because successful reunification might encourage Taiwan to return to the mainland as well. 
Arguments about China's self-interest are heard much less often today, for today's China seems to measure its self-interest more in control than in prosperity.
The multinational companies that have regional offices in Hong Kong are weighing the arguments, and more than half of them are considering moving elsewhere, one recent survey shows. 
Singapore is the most likely beneficiary, particularly for companies that focus on Southeast Asia, but many companies say they intend to remain in Hong Kong.
One source of concern for the private and public sectors has been the growing assertiveness of labor groups, and the threats of strikes by firefighters, taxi drivers, nurses and other groups.
''Everybody's scrambling for more money,'' said a longtime civil servant. 
''Nobody wants to wait. 
I don't see how the society can operate that way.''
The official, a Briton who regards Hong Kong as his home, added glumly: ''And I don't think that the real panic has set in yet. 
That's still ahead of us.''

While no one has been seriously hurt, several people have been punched or beaten with clubs or rifle butts.

The Government's response to the complaints came this morning when the Foreign Ministry summoned James Munson, a Canadian television reporter and president of the Foreign Correspondents Club. 
A Foreign Ministry official, Liu Rucai, said any protest from the journalists would be utterly unreasonable and unacceptable.

He complained that some journalists had contact with Chinese people engaged in illegal activities.

file: Free-Market _Dragon_ Gains In the Fight for China_s Soul.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the struggle for China's soul, the hard-line leadership in Beijing seems to be losing ground to this southern Chinese region of fish farms, toy factories and private bars whose knack for free-market Communism has made it one of the fastest growing economies in the world.
Guangdong Province is China's greatest success story, and already it is becoming an international manufacturing center that in some ways recalls the early years of the "four dragons": Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan. 
While Guangdong used to be politically suspect within China for its laissez-faire ways, Deng Xiaoping and other Chinese leaders have recently praised it as a national model and called upon the province to become Asia's fifth "dragon."
Â 
The Bribes Help
That suggests that Guangdong has defeated Beijing, at least for now, in the competition to chart China's future. 
This could have enormous repercussions, for Guangdong represents a fundamentally different vision of China than Beijing.
"You can get anything done here," said an entrepreneur who found that bribes of $2,000 helped win commercial licenses and official support for his thriving business here in Guangzhou, also called Canton, the provincial capital. 
The businessman works 16-hour days, rakes in the cash, and has even bought a forged American passport for $20,000. 
He wants a foreign passport for ease of travel and for protection in case Chinese policy changes, but for now he prefers to remain in Guangzhou.
"There's more money to be made here," he said.
Guangdong (pronounced gwahng doong) is a symbol of aggressive restructuring, a place where people go to Paula Abdul concerts instead of Marxist study sessions, where entrepreneurs outnumber ideologues, where more people are rich than red. 
It is China's economic frontier, a magnet that draws the ambitious and restless from all over the country, and it is becoming a more important force than Beijing in shaping the values, fashions, economic understanding and social problems of the entire country.
Â 
The Underside of Success
A 25-year-old woman described her elation when she came down to Guangdong from Beijing in January and found a job as a secretary for a factory manager. 
Her salary was $190 a month, five times her previous wage.
But there were two problems. 
She was regularly exhausted by the long hours and heavy workload. 
And her boss made advances toward her and arranged for her to live in a room that was near to his and that had just a curtain for a door.
"So I quit," the woman said. 
"I got my old job back, and my parents ordered me never to leave Beijing again. 
But the pay and the opportunities were better in the south. 
Much better!
So I'm going to take the job as secretary again. 
I'll find a way of dealing with the boss. 
And if worse comes to worst. 
. . ."
Her voice trailed off and she shrugged.
Such social problems as sexual harassment, drug addiction and prostitution are more common in Guangdong than in most of the rest of China. 
But most people now accept that they are the inevitable underside of the economic integration of the province with Hong Kong and its rise as one of the world's major manufacturing bases for products like Mickey Mouse toys, Wendy Walker dolls, Adidas sweat pants, Yashica cameras, Accord watches and a cornucopia of sweaters, brassieres, purses and shoes.
The economic boom in Guangdong and Hong Kong may be one of the most important transformations under way in Asia. 
The boom, which is focused on the Pearl River delta towns nearest to Hong Kong, has lasted more than a dozen years and in many ways parallels the rise of the four dragons -- except that Guangdong's population of 68 million is about equal to that of all four dragons combined.
The Tiananmen crackdown and nationwide economic slowdown in 1989 caused a pause in the typical double-digit growth rates, but by last year Guangdong had rebounded: in 1991, the equivalent of gross national product jumped 13.5 percent, and industrial output soared 27.2 percent.
For someone arriving from northern China, the towns around here feel like the free world. 
Guangdong still has political prisoners -- including Wang Xizhe, a thoughtful democrat and essayist who is serving a 14-year sentence in solitary confinement -- but many fewer than Beijing. 
There is also less surveillance here, less intimidation, less political indoctrination, and less of a state sector.
In Guangdong Province, 38 percent of industrial production comes from private or foreign-financed businesses, while only about 35 percent is manufactured by the state sector. 
The remainder is produced by collective enterprises, which are often owned by the local townships.
Even the state-owned companies, because they must operate in a market environment, are far more competitive than state-run companies elsewhere in China. 
Bei Zhaohan, the chairman of the Baiyunshan Group Corporation, a state-owned conglomerate based in Guangzhou, seems not so different from Western business tycoons.
Â 
The Lure of Property
"We want to get into property development," said Mr. Bei, a dynamic 52-year-old man with a well-tailored suit and boardroom manners, "because I see that the richest people everywhere -- in the U.S., in Japan, in Hong Kong -- are all property magnates."
Guangdong's township enterprises are even more freewheeling, and many do without any Communist Party secretary. 
One prosperous township brimming with such companies is Houjie, a frenetic community about half-way between Guangzhou and Hong Kong.
Houjie has an official population of 75,000, mostly peasants who used to wade through the surrounding rice paddies, but it also is a temporary home to more than 80,000 migrant laborers who work on assembly lines in the township's 900 factories.
"There was nothing to do at home," Yan Jimei, a 20-year-old woman with long, neatly combed hair, said of her village in nearby Guangxi Province. 
"So I came here to look for a job. 
Life's much better here."
In a slightly squalid dormitory room in which 12 young women bunk together, 16-year-old Wang Zhiyin recalled that a year ago she was living quietly in the Sichuan Province countryside. 
Then several women returned to her village from their jobs in Guangdong and told of the wages they were making. 
A few days later, Miss Wang accompanied them back to Houjie and found an assembly line job making pink stuffed turtles for $50 a month.
American labor organizations have charged that Guangdong factories are inhuman sweatshops that frequently employ children. 
While some teen-agers do work in the factories, most are in their late teens and their dormitory living conditions are often better than those they left behind in their villages.
Wages are low by American standards, but extravagant by Chinese terms: $50 to $60 a month, more than some university professors earn. 
Almost all of the workers are women, who are regarded by factory managers as more responsible and adroit with their hands then men, and they typically work six days a week for up to about 10 hours a day. 
The women say this is far preferable to sloshing around the rice paddies.
The Communist Party Secretary in Houjie, a short, exuberant man named Fang Shuhui, is enormously proud of the town's progress and points out the sights -- the gleaming new movie theater, the mansionlike public toilet -- as he cruises around Houjie in the back seat of his chauffeur-driven gray Mercedes Benz 300 SEL. 
The car is nicer than those assigned to Cabinet ministers in Beijing, and Mr. Fang also has a cellular telephone, a beeper and other paraphernalia of a tycoon.
Communist Party bosses like Mr. Fang have nurtured a quasi-market economy, with 85 percent to 90 percent of prices in Guangdong determined by supply and demand, but the province is still a planned economy in one very useful way: the Government has devoted enormous resources to building bridges, roads, electricity plants and the like. 
The result is that some analysts believe that growth in Guangdong may be more sustainable than in places like Bangkok, where the economic boom of recent years has strained the infrastructure and led to constant traffic jams.
Â 
The News From Hong Kong
The opening up of Guangdong has created some risks for the local Communist leaders, however. 
News from Hong Kong, where newspapers and television report constantly and unflatteringly about the Chinese leadership, filters across the border more and more easily.
In the city of Dongguan, the local government even operates a cable television service for $7 a year, offering Hong Kong channels.
A major lesson of the south -- and one that Deng Xiaoping appears to have drawn, encouraging him to make Guangdong a national model -- is that the strategy of the moderates in Guangzhou appears to have been far more successful than that of the hard-liners in the north. 
The Communist Party seems much more likely to be toppled in Beijing than in Guangdong, and it was striking that during the Tiananmen democracy movement in 1989 the protests were far milder in southern cities than in the north.
As in Singapore and Taiwan, the ruling party here in southern China has won a measure of popular support simply by raising living standards.
"Folks complain here, too, but the volume is much lower than in Beijing," said a woman who abandoned a promising career in one of the most prestigious ministries in the central Government to come to Guangzhou to do business.
The willingness of such intellectuals to come to Guangdong to work, joining the uneducated peasants who hold assembly line jobs, reflects the rising status of Guangdong around the country. 
Increasingly, it is seen as China's economic frontier.
"There are more opportunities here," said Zhang Yanan, a 31-year-old university graduate from the central Chinese city of Wuhan who has just found work in a township. 
"Maybe there's not so much culture, but there's more money -- and with money, you can do a lot of things."

file: From China_s Provinces, Rare Voice of Dissent.txt
text:
ï»¿
While China's students and workers seem too intimidated to mount any new protests, the hard-liners who run the country are now facing a challenge from an unexpected quarter: the leaders of the nation's provinces.
Leaders of the 30 provinces gathered in the Jingxi Hotel in Beijing last week for a conference that was marked by a virtual rebellion against the hard-liners' plans to increase the power of the central Government, well-connected Chinese said. 
The local leaders complained bitterly about their economic difficulties and the Government's demands for more money.
Their comments were said to be implicitly critical of Prime Minister Li Peng and his stewardship of the economy. 
The Communist Party General Secretary, Jiang Zemin, addressed the meeting, but apparently tried to distance himself from Mr. Li. By one account, Mr. Jiang said that because the party has great confidence in the Cabinet run by Mr. Li, its leaders have not been closely involved in economic and financial matters.
The challenge from the provinces comes at a time when China otherwise seems remarkably quiet. 
Even recentincreases in the prices of basic items like sugar and coal have not stirred a hint of public protest, probably because of the climate of intimidation.
An indication of the scale of the government's surveillance over the population has been provided by the official Beijing Evening News, which disclosed that 650,000 people were involved in security work in the capital alone when the Asian Games were held here a month ago. 
Many of those agents have gone off duty since the Games closed, but security remains tight enough to discourage ordinary people from conducting protests.
The province governors and Communist Party secretaries are less apprehensive about getting into trouble. 
Many are members of the Central Committee, and a few of them -- like Ye Xuanping, governor of Guangdong province -- have reputations and power bases rivaling those of the national leaders. 
Even the less prominent governors apparently feel that they are safe so long as they stick together.
Diplomats and Chinese officials say that the first hint of the rebellion came late in September, when the governors were summoned to Beijing to put their seal of approval on China's next five-year plan, which goes into effect in January. 
Instead of approving the plan, the governors criticized it vociferously.
The governors, led by Mr. Ye, complained that the Government wanted to take back authority, like the power to approve investment projects, from theprovinces, and intended to adjust the taxation system so that the provinces would end up paying more.
In the meeting last week, which like the earlier one has not been reported in the Chinese news media, even the governors of minor provinces were reportedly outspoken and critical of the national Government. 
They complained that they and their enterprises were already squeezed dry, and had no more money to give Beijing.
More fundamentally, many of the governors are unhappy with the nation's retrenchment policy. 
A Chinese official who met recently with province leaders said he found them pugnacious and concerned mostly with how to evade the obstacles put up by the ideologues in Beijing. 
"If we run into an obstacle, we'll go around it," the official quoted a local leader as telling him.

file: From the Stone Age to Tiananmen Square.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA
A New History.
By John King Fairbank.
Illustrated. 519 pp. 
Cambridge, Mass.:
The Belknap Press/
Harvard University Press.
$27.95.
SLIGHTLY before the midpoint of John King Fairbank's latest and last book -- the eminent Harvard historian of China died last year at the age of 84 -- appears the only overtly autobiographical passage in the volume. 
It was in the early 1930's, Fairbank writes in "China: A New History," that he and his wife settled into Beijing life, and three things at once impressed the young newlywed graduate students as unusual. 
First, there was the extraordinary extent of their privilege as foreign residents; they were treated as members of the ruling-class elite from the first moment in China and were left unbothered by the ubiquitous police. 
Second, because of the incredible surplus of Chinese manpower the easiest form of transportation around the ancient city was by rickshaw: you lay back against the seats of the two-wheeled vehicle while the "intelligent human horse between the shafts" trotted and sweated his way to your destination. 
Third, in both city and country, all women of early middle age and over had bound feet, which left them "stumping about awkwardly on their heels as though the front sections of their feet had been amputated."
Why had this last practice in particular, Fairbank muses, been so little studied or discussed by either Chinese or Western scholars?
For close to a millennium, hundreds of millions of Chinese women had had the toes of their feet systematically bent under their arches, and the arches themselves strapped, tilted and broken, and then the women had performed the same protracted and agonizing ritual deformation on their own daughters. 
Why had no one tried to assess the "social and psychic repercussions" of this nightmare practice, reputedly performed for the sensual delectation of men, even though the physiological, esthetic or erotic effects of foot-binding were far from clear?
Perhaps, Fairbank concludes, Chinese scholars had dodged the topic because it would have forced them to confront the whole problem of women's subjugation; and perhaps the Westerners had dodged the topic as well because they were eager to avoid giving offense to Chinese sensitivities. 
Few scholars "are muckrakers by temperament," notes Fairbank, and since foot-binding was unique to China it was not a convenient topic for comparative sociological study. 
Furthermore, he observes, there is an "occupational quirk of sinologists, a secondary patriotism or sinophilia that may lead otherwise hard-headed scholars to want to say no evil of the object of their researches."
This last sentence is starred to a footnote on the same page, almost the only time in this entire history that Fairbank uses such a device, and the purpose of the starred note is clearly to deepen the autobiographical reflection further, and to carry it forward in time into another kind of dangerous psychic terrain. 
"For an outstanding example of sentimental sinophilia," Fairbank adds, "see my statement in Foreign Affairs, October 1972, that in a certain context the Maoist revolution was 'the best thing' that had happened to the Chinese people in many centuries."
In these brief passages we have a distillation of the historical stance that Fairbank adopted in the last years of his long and formidably productive scholarly life -- a stance that sought to present itself as both frank and skeptical, tackling the difficult questions and suggesting directions for new research, while making the author himself disarmingly vulnerable by his admission of past mistakes. 
Fairbank, this century's foremost promoter of Chinese studies, chose to bow out with a show of modesty.
I say show of modesty not with any intention to belittle this extraordinary man, but rather to underscore the incredible ambitiousness of his final work. 
"China: A New History" sets out to cover, in 432 pages of text, the entire span of China's history from the paleolithic cultures of 400,000 B.C. to the Tiananmen massacre of 1989, and it does so with a brisk and sprightly air but also with an awesomely thorough overview of the current scholarly work of scores of historians. 
The book is indeed a kind of reprise not only of Fairbank's life as a reader and teacher, but also of his long years as editor or co-editor of the many volumes of the monumental "Cambridge History of China," Volume 15 of which, on the People's Republic and Taiwan between 1966 and 1982, was published last year. 
Perhaps most surprisingly, for those who have followed Fairbank's extraordinary range of studies in the fields of Chinese-United States foreign policy, institutional history and missionary history, "China: A New History" is dedicated in large part to social history, to the infrastructures and daily life of the Chinese, and to the elusive world of "civil society" that obviously existed and flourished at many levels under the watchful eyes of the purportedly omnipresent autocratic state.
Despite Fairbank's attention to social movements in this volume, his intellectual energy seems still to be most concentrated on the problems of state power and dissonance that led -- among other things -- to those three aspects of exploitive hierarchy that he highlighted in the book's autobiographical musings. 
In one passage, arresting to the historian at once for its concision and for the vastness of the ideas tackled, Fairbank reflects on how a kind of unifying theory does seem to emerge from his lifetime's reading and research on China's long history, a theory that makes sense because it incorporates the rhythms of China's periods of fragmentation and conquest by others along with its own enduring institutional forms. 
In Fairbank's words:
"The hypothesis may be stated as follows: (1) that early China created a politicized state organized for purposes of central control both by bureaucratic methods of philosophic persuasion and by the imperial autocrat's use of violence; (2) that non-Chinese invaders from Inner Asia became integral participants in the Chinese polity by their military prowess and administrative skill; and (3) that the resulting Sino-nomadic imperial power continued to maintain the primacy of central political control over the subordinated processes of economic growth and cultural diversification."
Elsewhere in the volume, Fairbank produces a rather different formulation that he felt contrasted China succinctly with the main lines of Western development. 
Where the main line of Western national "style" had been "industrial-military-entrepreneurial," that in China had been "agrarian-nomadic-bureaucratic."
In many ways, as Fairbank's chapters on modern China show, both Chiang Kai-shek and Mao Zedong were caught in this cycle of values. 
Fairbank is distinctly unsympathetic to both these central leaders of 20th-century China, consistently with his earlier views in the case of Chiang, and perhaps seeking to bury the ghost of those 1972 "sentimental" deviations in the case of Mao.
Though the economic, educational and industrial reforms of Chiang's Kuomintang years are discussed fairly and thoroughly, Chiang himself emerges as a "vigorous Dr. Jekyll" who "metamorphosed" into a "sordid Mr. Hyde," and lost the civil war of 1946-49 through "stupidity" and "incompetence."
Similarly, though Communist attempts at national and rural reconstruction get their due, Fairbank writes that Mao's basic "organizational principle" was that of any traditional Chinese "bandit" who used "force and guile . . . to curry favor with the local people," before he emerged at last as an "updated emperor" whose final acts were to lead his people "up a mountain and into a volcano."
The only man to get an equally bad press is the leader of the massive mid-19th-century Taiping Rebellion, Hong Xiuquan, whose "bizarre and irrational" theocracy prompts Fairbank to search for parallels that range from Napoleon to Hitler. 
The invoking of such parallels is a device that Fairbank enjoys, and like his invocation of echoes from China's past it can be effective and arresting. 
Occasionally it illuminates the instant with a zany humor similar to that which did indeed bubble just beneath Fairbank's own often formidable public persona. 
One of my favorites is Fairbank's aside that the closest equivalent he can think of to Mao's massively publicized swim across the Yangtze River in 1966 would be "the news that Queen Elizabeth II had swum the Channel."
SUCH asides may not be good history, but they are good-humored and make a point. 
On other occasions, the aside can trivialize the moment. 
Thus to summarize the archeological finds of Stone Age Chinese skeletons with smashed-in skulls as showing that "Peking Man was a small-time cannibal or at least a head-hunter who savored brains" strikes me as a little tacky; to equate Han dynasty neo-Confucian imperial rituals with White House "foto-ops and sound-bites" is erratic; and to call the terrible famine that followed the Great Leap Forward "first-class" is truly odd.
Such ruminations aside, this book is an admirable achievement. 
And even if one cannot accept the idea that this history is entirely new, Fairbank has filled the analytic narrative with intelligent ideas and original contributions: on the long-term effect of the absence of early maritime trade in China, on frontier appeasement policies, on the inherent problems of translation of foreign texts into Chinese characters, on Confucian attitudes to the military, on the development of popular religion, on sweated labor, on the failures of democratic experimentation and the other quests of China's new elite of "Sino-liberals," on the politics of repression and the role of sycophancy. 
Fairbank dominated the field of China studies in the West for 50 years. 
In this volume, we see that even on the edge of death his hand had not lost its cunning.

file: Frustrated Chinese Look to U.S. as a Haven.txt
text:
ï»¿
''There are two kinds of people in China these days,'' said a worker in his 20's, continuing with a cheerful exaggeration. 
''First, there are those who simply want to go to the United States. 
And second, there are those who are already well along in their preparations to depart.''
Not everyone is afflicted by the ''emigration fever,'' as it is called here, but it is clear that the urge to leave has markedly increased since the army's crackdown on the democracy movement last year. 
That urge to relocate is motivated not only by political repression but by a far-deeper sense of frustration and discontent, as well as by rising economic expectations that China cannot meet.
''This place isn't stable, for all the official talk about stabilityI,'' said a woman in her 40's, who agonized over lists of English words to prepare for moving to the United States. 
''And everyone finds it stifling, with few opportunities to use your skills. 
What's more, Americans all have cars!''
Alarmed by the flood of students going abroad - compared with the trickle of people returning - the Chinese Government early this year imposed restrictions that on their face prevented college graduates from going abroad to study until they have worked for five years.
But ingenious young scholars are putting their minds to work evading the regulations. 
The most common method is to invent an aunt or uncle in Hong Kong or the United States, and take advantage of a clause allowing those with relatives abroad to pay fees instead of working for five years.
''We've had no significant change in the types of people who come in applying for student visas,'' an American diplomat here said. 
''We're still seeing lots of recent college graduates who come in. 
The number of applicants and the number of issuances are both up.''
In August, for example, the United States Embassy in Beijing received 1,550 applications for student visas, compared with 1,371 applications in August 1989 and 949 applications in August 1988. 
The portion receiving visas has also risen, to 60 percent from 43 percent two years ago.
There is no doubt that the new regulations have had an effect - many recent graduates say that they have postponed their plans to go abroad - so one explanation for the increase in the number of applicants is that it would have soared without the restrictions.
''Five members of my senior class are applying to American universities,'' a high school student in Beijing said. 
''I could do very well here, and join the Communist Party, and find a suitable husband, and get a good job. 
But there are lots of limits on what we can do here, and I think I'll be better off with training in America.''
A young business executive said that a few years ago, a Japanese executive offered to pay for her to study in Japan. 
She refused, and these days she thinks she made a terrible mistake.
''Now I can see that if you have talent here, you're suppressed and harassed,'' she said. 
She complained about her cramped dormitory room, which she shares with three roommates, and about her company's plans to send her to work in a factory to gain an appreciation for manual labor.
''I'm optimistic about my own future,'' she said, ''because I plan to go abroad, but I'm pessimistic about China. 
Anyone with talent is trying to leave. 
Absolutely everyone I know is looking for an exit.''

file: Furor Erupts Over Hong Kong Plan.txt
text:
ï»¿
Plans for a new airport here have led to a furor over who now speaks for this British colony's 5.7 million people -- Britain or China, which is scheduled to take control in 1997.
Hong Kong's British Governor is to visit Beijing on Monday and is expected to tell the Chinese authorities that the project will proceed, despite their angry objections.
Analysts and diplomats here say that while Beijing may have some justified concerns about the financing of the ambitious airport project, it also has decided to use the issue to assert control over Hong Kong, even before 1997.
In a war of words that has grown more and more bitter in the past two weeks, Chinese officials have insisted that Beijing has a right to a say in all important policies and projects that will affect Hong Kong after 1997. 
On Tuesday, in a statement that a prominent government analyst at the Chinese University here called "astonishing," the Deputy Premier of China asserted that "during the transition period, only the Central People's Government can, and is entitled to, speak on behalf of the people of Hong Kong."
Â 
Airport at Top of Talk List
Deputy Premier Wu Xueqian's remarks were quoted in official Chinese press reports. 
The Governor, Sir David Wilson, scheduled his trip before the latest exchanges began, but the airport is now expected to top the list of subjects to be discussed.
Today, Sir David was circumspect about the trip, saying only that Hong Kong wanted "a sensible relationship, a good relationship with China," adding, "That's the objective of my visit."
Sir David is expected to meet with Chinese Premier Li Peng and with Lu Ping, the new head of the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office.
An experienced political analyst at Hong Kong University said that the dispute over the airport has grown into such an important political issue that "it is very doubtful that the question can be resolved at the Hong Kong level, during the Governor's visit."
"This is an issue that must be negotiated by Britain, by top-level officials," the analyst said. 
At most, he added, "The governor may be able to soften them up and help prepare for the visit of Lord Caithness," the British minister with special responsibility for Hong Kong. 
He is to meet with Chinese officials later this month.
Â 
China Seeks Project Suspension
Newspapers here have reported the airport dispute in front page stories with bold headlines, and in editorials they have called China's statements "hostile" and "bullying."
One political columnist said that if Britain acceded to Beijing's demands for veto power over projects here, the Hong Kong administration would go from being a "lame duck" to a "puppet" government.
Western diplomats said when a Hong Kong government team went to Beijing a week ago for talks on the technical and financial details of the $10 billion airport package, they were told to suspend the project until China's objections were answered.
As the three days of talks bogged down in Beijing, China's Ambassador in London was summoned to the British Foreign Office on two separate occasions to explain China's opposition. 
The talks ended on Jan. 
12 with Luo Jiahuan, who heads the Chinese airport team, telling reporters that the current Hong Kong government was only "a colonial government," and did not represent the Hong Kong people, who should be consulted more on the airport and given more information about it.
Another member of the Chinese airport team, an official with the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office, Chen Zuoer, warned of "serious consequences" should the project proceed without China's full approval.
Â 
Total Cost Put at $16 Billion
Plans for a new international airport and an expanded shipping port, which the government now estimates will cost $16.3 billion, were announced in October 1989. 
Since then, China has bombarded the Hong Kong government with objections, but recently its criticism has grown more pointedly political. 
The project is still largely in the planning stages, though important contracts are scheduled to be announced soon, with work to begin before the end of this year and the first runway to be completed by 1997.

Cotton futures prices surged yesterday at the New York Cotton Exchange, bolstered by reports that Pakistan was halting all new export sales and by rumors of purchases by China.
The news from Pakistan, a leading cotton producer and exporter after China, the United States, Soviet Union and India, was the major factor in the cotton pit, said Ed Whitten, an analyst with the Balfour Maclaine Corporation in New York.
''Pakistan has issued an edict to not allow any more exports,'' he said, adding that rumors of Chinese purchases of American cotton also supported prices.

file: Gains Toward Cambodia Settlement Are Seen.txt
text:
ï»¿
Diplomats and Thai officials say the necessary elements for a comprehensive settlement in Cambodia are rapidly coming together.
The assessment is based on several developments: the first direct talks between the Vietnamese and the Chinese in more than nine years, the first visit of a Thai foreign minister to Vietnam in more than 12 years and the first summit meeting, expected next summer, between the Soviets and the Chinese in nearly 30 years.
''Everyone has pretty much decided that Vietnam has made its decision to extricate itself from Cambodia and get on with the business of rebuilding its economy,'' a Western diplomat said. 
''A lot of the old taboos are falling, the Soviets want to get on with the Chinese, and everyone is positioning themselves for new diplomatic and trading relationships.''
Over the weekend, the Vietnamese Deputy Foreign Minister, Dinh Nho Liem, flew to Beijing for the first direct talks between the two nations since Mr. Liem helped to negotiate a cease-fire in their February 1979 border war. 
That short, sharp clash was a self-described effort by the Chinese ''to teach Vietnam a lesson'' after Hanoi, supported by Moscow, invaded Cambodia in late 1978 and overthrew China's ally, the Khmer Rouge Government of Pol Pot.
Under the Khmer Rouge, who took power in April 1975, more than one million Cambodians died from starvation, disease, party purges and mass executions.
Â 
China to Cut Support
China has been the prime supporter of the Khmer Rouge, which it revived as a way to harass Vietnam and its patron, Moscow.
But in December discussions with the Soviet Union, China agreed to cut its support for the Khmer Rouge in step with Vietnamese troop withdrawals. 
The Chinese insisted on a firm timetable for final withdrawal. 
With Soviet prodding, Hanoi announced this month that its troops would be out of Cambodia altogether by September if a political settlement could be reached by then, a declaration quickly welcomed in Beijing.
In late December, the Vietnamese said they had completed the withdrawal of 50,000 soldiers in 1988, with 50,000 remaining. 
Western diplomats believe the Vietnamese still have about 85,000 troops in Cambodia.
As a sign of the political delicacy of the meeting between ancient enemies, Mr. Liem's visit to Beijing was announced by neither side at first. 
The experienced Mr. Liem, Vietnam's Ambassador in Moscow for four years, is thought to be preparing a visit to Beijing by Foreign Minister Nguyen Co Thach, perhaps before a regional conference on Cambodia scheduled for Jakarta, Indonesia, in late February.
Asian diplomats say the Soviets and the Chinese would like the major aspects of Cambodian deal settled by their scheduled summit meeting, the first since 1959.
Â 
Thais Promise Aid to Hanoi
The other related development in regional relations was exemplified by the sudden visit to Hanoi of the Thai Foreign Minister, Siddhi Savetsila. 
In four days of meetings with Mr. Thach that ended Thursday, Mr. Siddhi, accompanied by more than 60 businessmen and academics, announced that Thailand looked forward, after a Cambodia settlement, to helping Vietnam out of its economic morass.
Mr. Siddhi had regularly discouraged the business-oriented Prime Minister of Thailand, Chatichai Choonhavan, from opening relations with Vietnam. 
And he constructed what has been firm Thai policy, to which the Association of Southeast Nations has sometimes unhappily conformed: support for China and the Khmer Rouge and a boycott of Vietnam until it ended its occupation.
But a decade later, with less ideological leaderships in Moscow, Beijing and Hanoi and the boycott slipping, Thailand has clearly decided ''not to miss the train,'' a Western diplomat said.
Difficulties remain about the shape of an interim Cambodian government that is to oversee new elections. 
The Chinese have agreed that the Khmer Rouge should not return to sole power, but it is unclear how that can be insured or how a new civil war can be avoided.
Â 
Progress on a Formula
But here, too, there has been progress. 
In his talks with Mr. Siddhi, Mr. Thach said Vietnam agreed to an international control ''mechanism'' in Cambodia, an undefined compromise between the larger international peacekeeping force Thailand and China wanted and the smaller ''control commission'' Hanoi favored. 
They also agreed that the Jakarta talks should be expanded to include the Soviet Union and China.

file: GALLERY VIEW_A Painting Prodigy, but Still a Child.txt
text:
ï»¿
Wang Yani is a prodigy. 
She is largely self-taught. 
She paints rapidly in brush and ink. 
The earliest of the 69 paintings in ''Yani: The Brush of Innocence,'' at the Arthur M. Sackler Gallery, were made when she was 3 and 4 years old. 
She has spent her 14 years in the village of Gongcheng in Guangxi province in southern China, 50 miles from Guilin, which the catalogue says has been renowned since Ming times for ''the most beautiful mountains and waters under heaven.''
There is plenty of exuberance and delight in this problematical and even troubling show. 
The monkeys with which Yani was preoccupied between the ages of 3 and 6 are tireless in their willingness to perform for one another and for her. 
Her large, irked lion - painted when she was 8 - with monkeys pulling his tail and climbing over him like a party of kids on a sleeping father's back, opens one beady eye, turns down his red mouth, and bears them.
Almost everything in these episodic paintings is in a state of expectancy or resolution. 
A monkey with a fishing line has just hooked a fish. 
Trees not only flower but actually offer fruit. 
Wide-eyed birds seem to be waiting for orders to fly. 
Almost every animal is self-confident and proud. 
Only in the children - there are no explicit images of adults, although they are omnipresent in the mountains and trees - is there doubt that happiness is near.
Yani seems to have Chinese painting in her blood. 
Her feeling for every single thing she paints reflects the pantheism that runs like a river through Chinese art. 
Mountains and monkeys, as well as cranes and lotuses, are staples of Chinese painting. 
From the age of 3, Yani has had an awareness of solid and void and of the expressive possibilities of brush and ink. 
She is completely at home on paper.
The exhibition provides a great deal of information. 
According to Jan Stuart, the specialist in Chinese art at the Sackler, who installed the show, there is now in China a particular interest in prodigies. 
Artistic prodigies who are girls are no longer that surprising. 
Nor is the enthusiasm with which Yani has been greeted by a Chinese art establishment largely run by men.
What arouses that enthusiasm is the freshness and youthfulness of her paintings. 
After a period of artistic dogma and oppression, they seem to offer an assurance that new beginnings are possible and that childhood can have the irresistible force of a condition.
In her catalogue essay on ''Wang Yani and Contemporary Chinese Painting,'' the art historian Julia Andrews points out that Mao Zedong died in 1976, when Yani was 1, and suggests that Yani has given the Chinese an image of themselves they need. 
''Her emergence coincided with the severe disillusionment of many older artists in socialist realist art and with a desire to promote experimentation and exploration of other forms. 
The paintings of a child who knew nothing of politics offered a fresh vision that many artists sought in their own work.''
One of the pressures Yani has to live with, however, is that there is now an investment in her ''innocence.''
She is already something of a sideshow. 
''She is a national treasure, and people come from great distances to watch her at work,'' write Lynn T. Goldsmith and David Henry Feldman, developmental psychologists, in the catalogue. 
When the exhibition opened, Yani was in Washington to answer questions and demonstrate her freewheeling techniques.
Wang Shiqiang, Yani's father, formerly a narrative oil painter working in Western styles, wants to protect her from self-consciousness. 
Her feeling for painting has a great deal to do with him. 
When she was tiny, they roamed rivers and fields and visited the zoo where she first encountered the monkeys that made her howl and jump with glee. 
He bought her a pet monkey when she was 3. 
Ms. Stuart said that Yani considers her monkey her best friend.
It was on a trip with her father when she was 2 1/2 that Yani first painted. 
From the beginning, her images and methods were purely Chinese. 
In 1983, when Yani was 8, her father gave up painting. 
He works as a cultural-affairs officer. 
When Yani travels, he accompanies her. 
He keeps a diary of their travels. 
He will decide when she is ready for art books. 
He has kept almost all her paintings, which now number around 10,000. 
None has been sold.
All the family references in the catalogue are to Yani and Shiqiang. 
There is only passing mention of her mother, Tang Fongjiao, even though her presence can be felt throughout Yani's stories. 
She works in a department store. 
It is said that the money she earns buys Yani's art supplies.
There is no indication in the catalogue that Yani even has a brother. 
She does: Wang Qiangyu is 9 years old, and he, too, is exceptionally gifted as a painter. 
The family is considering discouraging him from painting. 
The fear is that his artistic development may inhibit Yani's spontaneity.
In short, this show of paintings made between the ages of 3 and 12 by a wonderfully gifted child needs to be approached with caution. 
There are many possible agendas in it. 
For example, the exhibition was organized by the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City, Mo., with the sponsorship of the Ministry of Culture of the People's Republic of China. 
This museum has been a force in Chinese art, and an exhibition on a contemporary Chinese artist unknown in the United States will help it remain one.
It is significant that a prodigy in a distant, semi-autonomous region of China can be seen in Japan, Europe and the United States when still a prodigy. 
This exhibition is a statement of the will that existed in China to make the world aware of at least some of its cultural energy. 
And it is a statement of the will of the international art world to penetrate every corner of the globe and show art when it is still fresh and hot.
Should this exhibition be taking place?
A number of Yani's paintings are astonishingly finished for a child, but they are not the paintings of an accomplished artist. 
In addition, they are weighed down by the museum setting and by their black frames. 
The best way to see the paintings is in the catalogue, where the rapid succession of images reflects the quickness and concentration with which they were made. 
What this show is, above all, is a fabulous children's book - imagined and painted by a child.
Yani is not ready for the art-historical treatment. 
When Ms. Goldsmith and Mr. Feldman write of the ''significant shift when she is about 6 or 7,'' a ''period'' that can be ''characterized by explorations of a broader range of technical and thematic issues,'' it is absurd.
So is the mythology of production. 
In a generally sensitive catalogue essay, Dr. Wai-ching Ho, a developmental psychologist and the project director for the show, writes that ''by the age of 6 Yani had produced 4,000 paintings'' - a statement proudly repeated in the press release. 
All this does is put pressure on Yani to produce, and turn her into a production machine.
Why is Yani a prodigy?
For one thing, she seems to have been born with an understanding of space and form. 
For another, she not only has the ability to fantasize, but her fantasies are totally accessible to her, and she has absolute faith in their goodness and worth.
The paintings in this show are functional. 
That is to say, what Yani painted was real to her, with real effects. 
In his essay, Dr. Ho relates, ''One day her father bought her a lovely red umbrella. 
Too impatient to wait for the rain to come, she painted a monkey holding a little red umbrella and playing happily in the rain.''
Ms. Goldsmith and Mr. Feldman write that in her paintings Yani ''fed'' her ink monkeys. 
''Sometimes her father would even hear her chiding the painted images to behave, because she was about to share (that is, paint) their fruit.''
These are the works of someone with supreme confidence in herself, in her subject matter and in painting, and who has the ability to make others believe in her magical powers. 
When a painting works, everything in it is personified. 
The smudges and blots of her cliffs and peaks loom like people and animals amid strange and not always friendly activities and games.
From the beginning, Yani has had a remarkable ability to digest psychologically loaded information. 
For example, when she was 4, she painted three images of intoxication. 
In ''Drunk,'' two furry monkeys with red faces are sprawled out on the floor alongside a phallic- and dragon-shaped wine pot made by her father. 
In ''Sniffing the Wine,'' a solitary monkey and the pot seem almost to be kissing each other while loquat fruit shaped like disembodied breast-eyes lie on the floor to one side. 
These images are already sexual and self-conscious. 
They are not innocent. 
Yani is clearly extremely observant, so it is not surprising that the strength of her paintings depends so much upon eyes. 
The most conspicuous aspect of her children are their big eyes. 
The eyes anchor her horses and egrets in space and make them human. 
Even the lotuses she loves so much look as if they can see. 
It is only the larger and more threatening forces, like mountains, that are deprived of sight.
What will happen to Yani?
Certainly she has tremendous resources. 
. Such an artistic prodigy may be conceivable now only far from a big city, in a secure world rooted in tradition. 
Yani still lives in Gongcheng, near mountains and rivers she continues to wander, and to which she feels she belongs. 
She clearly has remarkable intelligence, shrewdness and wit. 
She will need them. 
(After closing at the Arthur M. Sackler Gallery on Oct. 
22, the exhibition will travel to the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City [Dec. 
16 to Jan. 
28] and then to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco [March 7 to April 29]. 
Financing was provided by United Technologies Corporation.)

file: Games Offering China a Chance To Polish Image.txt
text:
ï»¿
With parachutists, panda balloons, 11,000 pigeons and 20,000 young Chinese dancers and martial arts experts, China opened the 11th Asian Games today as a mini-Olympics intended to win back international respect and domestic support lost during the military crackdown last year.
Flanked by other top leaders, President Yang Shangkun tonight opened the extravaganza before an international crowd of about 65,000 spectators in the Workers Stadium in the center of the capital. 
Determined that nothing should go wrong, the authorities arranged an enormous show of force and sent workers home this afternoon with the stern advice that they should stay off the streets and watch the ceremony on television.
Â 
Prelude to Olympic Bid
For China this has been far more than an athletic competition. 
It is the biggest international conference ever held in China, and more important it is an opportunity to rejoin the international community after the criticisms and isolation that followed the crackdown in June 1989. 
No effort has been spared to impress foreigners, from the new drug-testing center to the fake brick walls that have been erected around town to conceal the grim apartments that previously lined the roads.
If the Asian Games go smoothly, China intends to make a bid to be host to the Olympics in 2000. 
Officials from the International Olympic Committee arrived to see the Games, and they were treated as heads of state in the hope that they would back China's application to be host to the Olympics.
''This is my wish,'' the 83-year-old President Yang told Juan Antonio Samaranch, the president of the International Olympic Committee, in a meeting today. 
''If it is fulfilled, I shall be very happy, and China will build more stadiums and gymnasiums.''
The Beijing Asiad, which has been in the planning for eight years, is also intended to serve a domestic purpose: to unite the Chinese people behind a patriotic theme closely associated with the Communist Party. 
The torches used to light the Asiad flame were carried in an extensive relay race through every province in China, and some 180 million people were organized to line the route and applaud.
''China used to be called the 'sick man of East Asia,' '' the People's Daily declared today in a front-page editorial. 
''Over the past 40 years and more, ever since the establishment of the People's Republic of China, many Chinese athletes have made awesome achievements and now China has become host of the 11th Asiad. 
From a certain angle, this change reflects the great achievement of the Chinese people in socialist construction.''
Â 
Fear of 'Hostile Elements'
The Government's worst fear has been that ''hostile elements'' will take advantage of the international spotlight and create disorder, just as student demonstrators took advantage of the visit by President Mikhail S. Gorbachev of the Soviet Union in May 1989. 
But these days nearly everyone in Beijing seems cowed, and few people expect any significant unrest.
''We're not going to do anything at all during the Asian Games,'' said a member of an underground organization that grew out of the 1989 crackdown. 
''It's much too tense.''
After the crackdown, there were at first some calls for a boycott of the Asiad, but those soon fizzled and for a time it seemed that Beijing would be host to the first Asian Games ever in which every eligible country participated. 
Then the Gulf Crisis intervened, and on Thursday the Olympic Council of Asia voted overwhelmingly to exclude Iraq because of its invasion of Kuwait. 
It is not clear whether Jordan is sending athletes. 
54 Delegates From Kuwait Kuwait's 54 delegates were given a rousing welcome as they entered the stadium during a procession of delegations. 
While many Kuwaiti athletes were stuck in their home country and have not been able to participate, some had been training in Europe and were able to come to the Asiad.
Other enmities seemed mostly to have been forgotten today. 
South Koreans, thousands of whom have turned up for the Games even though Seoul has no diplomatic relations with Beijing, waved their flags and roared approval not only for their own delegation but also for that of North Korea. 
A Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister, the most senior official from Hanoi to make an official visit to Beijing since the two countries fought a border war in 1979, sat with top Chinese officials in the President's rostrum. 
And athletes from Taiwan and China, who grew up hearing tales of each other as dreaded ''Communist bandits'' or ''stinking capitalists,'' are mingling affably in the Asian Games Village.
While the level of competition in some sports may not be up to the highest international standards, Asian athletes are among the best in the world in diving, archery, shooting, judo, badminton, volleyball and table tennis, among other sports.
The 29 Asiad events will include, in addition to most of the typical Olympic sports, such Asian specialties as kabbadi, which has the advantage in poor countries that it requires no special equipment. 
The game is a bit like tag, except that attackers must continuously repeat the word ''kabbadi'' and are eliminated if they run out of breath.
Â 
Objective Is 100 Gold Medals
China, which takes sports very seriously, is hoping for about 100 gold medals, of the 308 possible. 
This will be a chance for China to redeem itself after a disappointing performance at the Seoul Olympics in 1988, when it won only five gold medals.
In the last Asian Games, which were held in Seoul in 1986, China won 94 of the 270 gold medals then at stake. 
South Koreawon 93 and Japan 58.
China's delegation of 838 athletes and officials is the biggest in the Games, followed by South Korea's with 757 delegates. 
Japan is third with 722, while Palestine - which many Asian countries recognize as a nation, and which is represented by Palestinian athletes living in various countries - has just two delegates.
Security was tighter than it has been in Beijing since the night of June 3 of last year, when protests erupted at Beijing University to mark the one-year anniversary of the killings of pro-democracy protesters.
Â 
Police Monitor Rail Stations
Tens of thousands of people without Beijing residence permits have been shipped out of the capital to their hometowns, and the police are monitoring the railway station and main roads to keep unauthorized people from coming to Beijing. 
University students have been subjected to bed checks to make sure they are not on the streets fomenting political mischief.
A large area around the stadium was sealed off in midafternoon, and everyone entering the stadium was searched with metal detectors. 
A helicopter hovered over the stadium during the ceremony, and thousands of police were in the nearby streets, but there was no hint of trouble.
It is difficult to gauge the attitude of Beijing residents to the games. 
In general, some intellectuals are contemptuous of the Asiad and complain that it is a terrible waste of money, while some children and workers are quite enthusiastic about the sports competition.
Â 
Cost Put at $530 Million
But the most common attitude seems to be one of only mild interest, mitigated somewhat by indignation at the forced contributions that were solicited to raise money for the games. 
China spent about $530 million preparing for the Asiad.
China's capital, normally a relatively drab city of endless apartment blocks whose color is measured in hues of gray, has taken on a new look for the games. 
Statues of Pan-Pan, an exuberant panda who has been chosen mascot of the Asiad, decorate the city just as portraits of Chairman Mao Zedong used to be the universal fixtures.
The most startling renovation has been the fake brick walls that have appeared along some major roads, to hide the dilapidated homes that used to line the way. 
Workmen even painted bricks on the outside of the new walls so that they appeared relatively elegant. 
But for Beijing residents, who sometimes have to wait a decade or more to be assigned an apartment, it has been galling to see such efforts dedicated to camouflage instead of to resolving the housing shortage.
Â 
New Buildings Draw Complaints
''Why don't they put those building materials into building us houses, instead of into hiding the problem?'' complained a worker in his 20's.
Officials have also made sure that shops are filled with merchandise to impress visitors. 
Nearly $900 million worth of merchandise - including eels from Fujian province, seedless grapes from Xinjiang Province and Phoenix brand bicycles from Shanghai - have been flown to the capital to lure visitors and startle longtime residents.
One problem, however, is that ticket sales to Asiad events have not been publicized much, even though they are an important source of revenue for the games. 
A Chinese American businessman complained tonight that he had been trying for days to purchase tickets to athletic events, and still had no idea where to buy them, or if they could be purchased at all.

With an area of about 600,000 square miles, Mongolia is slightly smaller than Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Louisiana combined. 
The capital is Ulan Bator, with a 1986 population of about 500,000.
Mongolians account for 90 percent of the population of about two million. 
Some 2 percent of the population is Chinese and another 2 percent is Russian.
In the early part of the 20th century, Mongolia passed back and forth from Chinese to Russian dominion; in 1924, it became, in effect the first Soviet satellite state. 
Until now, the country has been ruled by the 10-member Politburo of the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party Central Committee.
The People's Great Hural, or national assembly, meets about three days a year to enact the basic laws of the country.
Â 
Genghis Khan formed the first
Mongolian state from nomadic tribes in 1203, and went on to conquer much of Asia and European Russia. 
Mongol power declined after the Mongol dynasty in China was overthrown in 1368.
Â 
The Manchus, who conquered
China in 1644, brought the Mongols under their rule in 1691 and the country was a Chinese province for the next 220 years. 
In 1911, Mongol leaders declared their independence of Chinese rule.
Live animals and animal products account for half of Mongolia's output.
