file: Getting Out of China Harder Than Going In.txt
text:
ï»¿
Arranging a $175 million investment in a coal mine in China was hard enough. 
It took several handshakes with Deng Xiaoping and other top Chinese leaders to get Beijing's agreement.
But now, the Occidental Petroleum Corporation has set itself up for what may become an even tougher task: getting rid of the investment without a huge loss.
The open-pit An Tai Bao coal mine in China's Shanxi Province -- the dream of Occidental's late chairman, Armand Hammer -- is one of the biggest and most famous joint ventures in China. 
As Western investment in China boomed in the early 1980's, and board chairmen competed to sign agreements in the Great Hall of the People, the Occidental deal symbolized the hope that Chinese-American cooperation could be lucrative for both sides.
Â 
'Beyond China's Capability'
These days, as Occidental tries to withdraw from an apparently money-losing venture, the mine exemplifies the skepticism with which many foreign companies now view the Chinese market.
"The An Tai Bao case becomes symbolic of both the potential and the problems," said an American consultant familiar with the project. 
"China is a developing country, and a lot of projects were thought up that went beyond China's real capability."
China may be a huge market, but the economy is severely underdeveloped, with supply shortages, crumbling roads, antiquated trains and countless Chinese officials willing to wait forever rather than sign agreements that do not suit them perfectly.
More than three months after Dr. Hammer's death in December and more than two months after Occidental announced it was pulling out of China, the joint venture is illustrating another pitfall of foreign investment: the difficulty of withdrawing gracefully or profitably.
Â 
Sale to China Expected
One foreign business executive said Occidental had decided to sell its stake to the Chinese, possibly because of difficulties in finding an outside buyer. 
He added that Occidental was close to reaching a settlement with the Chinese, but this could not be confirmed.
Occidental could withdraw from the investment under terms in the contract, lawyers familiar with the project said. 
The Chinese side would pay for Occidental's holdings according to complex formulas in the contract. 
One lawyer in Beijing said the amount would be substantial enough so that the Chinese would want to find a buyer to help cover the payment.
In any case, bankers say, Occidental would have to offer its stake to its Chinese partners before it approached an outside buyer. 
An analyst said some companies had considered purchasing Occidental's interest, but none seemed eager to buy.
Â 
Chinese Said to Be Offended
Without a settlement, Occidental could probably find a buyer itself, but only at a depressed price. 
The Chinese partners must approve any transfer of Occidental's 25 percent stake in the mine, and analysts said some of the Chinese involved were offended by Occidental's sudden announcement of plans to pull out.
Those familiar with the mine said that because of economic factors, especially low coal prices, it could take a couple of years to sell the stake to an outside buyer.
"The overall investment climate is not conducive to people investing in a project of this size, and China projects are not famous for their quick returns and lack of operational problems," said Paul Y. Au, regional representative for China at the Royal Bank of Canada, one of the banks financing the deal.
Occidental executives declined to be interviewed, as did the Chinese partners. 
Most bankers and business executives associated with the project declined to be named, for fear of offending the Chinese.
Â 
New Investment Philosophy
Occidental has said that its decision to pull out reflects a new investment philosophy and not any disillusionment with China. 
Ray R. Irani, Dr. Hammer's successor, plans to sell about $3 billion in assets, including the company's 51 percent stake in the meatpacker IBP Inc., to reduce debts.
Bryan Jacoboski, an analyst at Paine Webber Inc., said that much of the $3 billion would come from the sale of many oil, gas, coal and chemical operations. 
He said that the disposal of Dr. Hammer's money-losing pet projects -- among them a Soviet petrochemical business, Arabian horses, Black Angus cattle, a film production company and the Chinese coal mine -- is likely to bring relatively little.
"The symbolism is more important than the financial impact," he said.
Occidental has said that it is prepared to write off much of its China investment, which analysts say has increased over the years to about $250 million.
Â 
Attempt to Save Face
Despite Chinese annoyance at Occidental and determination to bargain hard, they need to maintain the impression that Occidental was able to leave gracefully and that the mine is a success.
"The Chinese don't want to lose face," said a Chinese business executive familiar with the project. 
"If no one takes the deal, it's embarrassing for China, especially since Deng Xiaoping personally supported it."
But some bankers say it may be difficult for any company to turn a reasonable profit on the project in the coming years. 
Estimates of the mine's annual losses range from $25 million to $50 million.
A foreign businessman in Beijing said: "One question is whether they are serious about posturing for the Chinese or whether they are really willing to walk away from the project -- and what would that do for China if a company was willing to walk away and lose millions of dollars?
They've had their problems. 
How do you bring a bunch of West Virginia and Kentucky coal miners to a small town in Shanxi?
You're talking about a cultural conflict."
Â 
China's Largest Mining Project
Many companies interested in China would be intimidated by the sheer size and complexity of the mining project, analysts said. 
Already, the Americans and the Chinese have invested $700 million to $800 million. 
It is the largest mining project in China, and Occidental's one-quarter share is the biggest American investment in a single project there.
This huge operation comes on the market as foreign investors are becoming more cautious and more likely to favor smaller investments. 
Part of this caution results from China's economic difficulties.
The average value of new American investments in China has dropped from $2.3 million in 1989 to $889,000 in the first nine months of 1990, said China's Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade.
Occidental's coal mining venture has been tangled in bitter disputes and misunderstandings with local, provincial and central government officials ever since talks began about a dozen years ago.
Some of the project's difficulties stemmed from the very blessings by Mr. Deng and other top Chinese leaders. 
When the deal was negotiated in the early to mid-1980's, China was a command economy where orders from the central Government were easily carried out. 
But after the economic restructuring of the last decade, Occidental found that local authorities did not heed orders from Beijing.
One headache involved local wildcat miners, who began to steal coal from the mine. 
Occidental could not sink shafts in the most efficient ways for fear of crushing trespassers.
Bankers say they are confident that the project will generate the finances to repay a $475 million loan provided by a syndicate of international banks.

file: Getty Trust And Chinese.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and the Getty Conservation Institute today announced a joint effort to preserve two of China's largest and most significant cultural sites, where statues and paintings dating from the fourth century are decaying from harsh weather, pollution and damage by earthquakes.
The sites are the Mogao Grottoes on the edge of the Gobi in northwestern China and the Yungang Grottoes, 200 miles west of Beijing. 
Together, the sites contain 545 cave-like temples carved into cliffs. 
The temples contain more than 53,000 clay figures of Buddha, ranging from miniature bas-reliefs to a statue 108 feet high. 
The temples, popular among both Chinese and foreign tourists, also have 484,200 square feet of wall paintings.
The cost of the project has not been determined, but it will be shared by China, the Getty Conservation Institute and Unesco. 
The work is to involve at least 25 preservation specialists from the United States. 
The focus will be on arresting decay, not restoring art already damaged, said Luis Monreal, the director of the Getty Conservation Institute, a private foundation. 
He said the first step would be ''diagnosis'' of the sites and would take 18 months.
Â 
How It Happened
The announcement of the conservation project was made in Los Angeles by Ma Yuzhen, China's Consul General, and Harold M. Williams, the president of the J. Paul Getty Trust, a private foundation. 
The Getty Conservation Institute, a subsidiary of the trust, was created in 1982 and has collaborated with Egypt to preserve the tomb of Queen Nefertari and the royal mummies in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
The possibility of cooperation between China and the Getty was first raised in 1986 by China's National Administrative Bureau for Museums and Archeological Data. 
Last May, Getty representatives visited the sites.
Mr. Yuzhen said the sites contain ''evidence of the astonishing creativity of the ancient Chinese people.''
''The Mogao and Yungang Grottoes are the most magnificent storehouses of Buddhist art in the world,'' he said. 
''Both are national treasures of China.''
''We can provide resources of rescue technology not available now in China,'' Mr. Monreal said. 
''At the same time, field projects of this magnitude provide the international conservation community with valuable information on the application of new materials and technologies.''
Â 
What the Sites Contain
The Mogao Grottoes are near the town of Dunhuang on the edge of the Gobi, 1,100 miles west of Beijing. 
The site includes 492 rock temples with thousands of square feet of wall paintings and 2,000 painted clay figures of Buddha.
Hot summers and frigid winters and sand blown by fierce winds have eroded many of the statues and paintings, peeled off paint and washed out colors. 
Algae and fungus are also problems. 
The area also has frequent earthquakes of medium intensity.
Because of the damage and fears for safety, some of the temple caves are closed to the public, Chinese officials said. 
Although remote, the Mogao Grottoes are accessible by a new airport.
The Yungang Grottoes, near Datong, a coal mining city in northern China, face decay from pollution, salt deposits and the weather. 
There, 53 rock temples are carved into the face of a 1,000-yard-long sandstone cliff.
The Yungang temples contain 51,000 representations of Buddha, ranging from miniature bas-reliefs to statues 60-feet high, all carved directly in the rock. 
Most of the carvings, which date to the year 460, were restored in the Ming Dynasty from 1368-1644. 
The eroded carvings were covered with plaster, which was then redecorated.

text:

Every evening in the last week, the official television news, viewed by millions of Chinese, seems to have reverted to the kind of indoctrination techniques familiar in the Mao era.
In the past there was never such a broad visual diplay, but today the methods have been adapted to television. 
Every night there are scenes of horror stories that inspire pity for the soldiers of the People's Liberation Army and hatred for ''the small number of conspirators'' who began ''a counterrevolutionary rebellion.''
In the first days after the military crackdown against pro-democracy demonstrators on June 4, in which soldiers killed hundreds or perhaps thousands of civilians in central Beijing, the television showed Government footage of civilians throwing rocks and stones at tanks and soldiers.
The Government has now moved beyond that, using other scenes to nurture a sense of outrage against the ''thugs'' and ''hooligans'' who are accused of inflicting damage to the city.
Tonight's national television news program was fairly typical. 
Here is some of what the viewers saw.
Â 
Scene 1
The camera pans to a large, sparsely furnished hall where several hundred high officials have come to listen to a reading of a speech first delivered by Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader. 
The speech is introduced by Prime Minister Li Peng, who appears wearing a Western-style suit for the first time in recent days.
''Comrade Deng Xiaoping's important speech made a profound analysis of the cause and nature of the counterrevolutionary rebellion and the correctness of the measures we adopted,'' Prime Minister Li tells the gathering.
Mr. Li's voice fades out and the announcer explains that Mr. Li had urged everyone at the meeting to study Mr. Deng's words carefully and to ''unify the people's thinking on the basis of Deng Xiaoping's speech.''
The camera passes through the rows of officials sitting in folding chairs as the announcer lists the names of some of the more important officials. 
Some officials are taking notes, some are reading and at least one participant is looking sleepy.
Â 
Scene 2
The camera opens on a street corner, called Xidan, where a great deal of the violence took place in the early-morning hours of June 4. 
Xidan was also where a soldier was killed and his body disemboweled and burned by civilians. 
For the last few nights, the television news has shown scenes of the charred body of the soldier propped against a truck, or lying flat on its back.
A few days ago, the television news showed citizens placing small wreaths along the bridge at the intersection, in memory of the soldier. 
Now, the camera shows how the railings are brimming with large, colorful wreaths as parades of citizens continue to lay more flowers in the soldier's honor.
The announcer relates the Government version of the events of that June 4 morning, when the soldier, Liu Guogeng, was killed, supposedly while trying to rescue a man from a boisterous crowd.
The soldier was on his way to seek help from colleagues, the announcer says, but when he was about 200 yards away from the Communist Party headquarters, on the Avenue of Eternal Peace, or Changan Avenue, he was beaten to death by ''thugs'' who then doused his body in petroleum, disemboweled it and then burned it.
The picture then switches to Jilin Province, where Mr. Liu's mother, father and younger brother live.
''I ask his younger brother to learn from the older brother,'' says his mother, who is sobbing with sorrow and anger. 
''Go annihilate the thugs.''
His father, lying sick in a hospital bed with an undisclosed ailment, says: ''We must resolutely deal with these thugs. 
They deserve no leniency.''
His younger brother says: ''I feel honored. 
I will learn from my brother.''
Â 
Scene 3
An announcer reports that as of Tuesday, the Beijing Public Security Bureau has received 1,227 letters giving details about ''counterrevolutionary thugs.''
Â 
Scene 4
The camera turns to a meeting of 31 leaders of China's ethnic minorities, including a Tibetan Buddhist, who are all voicing their support for the Government's efforts to ''put down the recent rebellion.''
The announcer reads a few remarks by one of the leaders. 
''The scheme of those who wanted to create contradictions and stir up riots among the ethnic groups have failed thanks to the joint efforts of the minority people,'' the announcer quotes the leader as saying.
Â 
Scene 5
Two students who were named on Tuesday among the list of 21 ''wanted'' student leaders are seen being led into a police station for interrogation.
One of them is Zhou Fengsuo, a 22-year-old physics student at Qinghua University in Beijing, who was arrested in the central city of Xian, where his family lives. 
He was reportedly turned in by his older sister and brother-in-law.
The scene turns to a livingroom couch in Xian, where Mr. Zhou's sister, Zhou Yanrong, is sitting with a baby in her lap and her husband next to her.
Miss Zhou and her husband, Yang Yibo, who works at the Institute of Communications Engineering in Xian, says she saw the Tuesday television news that showed the woman's younger brother as a fugitive.
The couple say they discussed what to do next and came to what the television announcer thought was the correct conclusion.
''They contacted the security office of the institute, and the officers there cooperated with five policeman to go to the town of Three Bridges to arrest Zhou Fengsuo,'' the announcer says.
''Zhou Fengsuo confessed that he was a member of the standing committee of the Beijing autonomous student union and that on June 9, he took the train to Xian,'' the announcer adds.
Â 
Scene 6
The camera focuses on an old, heavy-set woman, standing in the Chongwenmen district on a bridge covered with wreaths to commemorate a soldier. 
The soldier was reportedly beaten up by ''thugs'' on the evening of June 3.
The old woman says she witnessed the ''thugs'' kill the soldier by throwing him off the bridge.
''I stand in front of the people of this city as a witness,'' the woman says, speaking into a television microphone. 
''The People's Liberation Army soldiers did not shoot people.''
''I went up to the People's Liberation Army soldiers with some other old women and we pleaded with them not to shoot the people,'' the woman says. 
''They told us: 'We are the people's army. 
We will not shoot the people.'
''
''But then the thugs spread a rumor, telling the people that the soldiers had killed the son of an old woman,'' she says. 
The woman explains how the ''thugs'' then beat up the soldier and threw him off the bridge.
''When I saw the dead soldier, I felt terrible,'' she says. 
''He was still alive when he was thrown off the bridge. 
I feel I should bear some responsibility for the death of the soldier because I took the lead with two other women to go after the soldier, and this gave the thugs the opportunity to follow us.''

file: GLOBAL DEALS_ THE FAUX PAS FACTOR.txt
text:
ï»¿
When United Technologies Sikorsky Aircraft began negotiations to sell two dozen helicopters to the Chinese government early in 1985, Marion P. Spigener bore the title of customer relations representative. 
But by the time a top-level Chinese delegation arrived that July to seal the deal at Sikorsky's headquarters in Stratford, Conn., Spigener was sporting a new title: chief of protocol.
''During the selling process,'' he recalls, ''we realized they had only a vague notion of what a customer relations man really does. 
But they knew what protocol meant. 
It's a proven set of rules that has worked for years - in fact, for centuries. 
They wanted to be working with a man who makes things happen, who brings things together.''
In a triumph of style over substance, Spigener's title was ''upgraded'' to a term more familiar in diplomatic circles than on Wall Street.
A seasoned practitioner in the art of Doing The Right Thing, Spigener books hotels, plans banquets, hires limousines, schedules plant tours, makes security arrangements and selects gifts (often, something from Steuben or Tiffany & Company). 
Above all, he prepares Sikorsky executives for a visit to foreign customers - from giving a briefing on current events, to providing a list of safe conversational gambits, to handing out sheet music for sing-alongs at Korean and Japanese banquets. 
In today's competitive global arena, Sikorsky Aircraft cannot afford to make a single faux pas in dealing with the Saudis, Brazilians or any other potential purchaser in the 16 countries in which the company is currently in negotiation.
Spigener is hardly flying solo in his role as protocol officer. 
Corporations such as A.T.&T., Boeing and the Chase Manhattan Bank also have protocol specialists. 
Many of these masters of the British title and the Japanese tea ceremony are now expanding their spheres to include Eastern Europe. 
Their mandate: to provide at least two of the three ingredients that Adlai E. Stevenson, when he was chief American delegate to the United Nations, listed as endemic to a diplomat's life - ''protocol, Geritol and alcohol.''
Forty-five-year-old Robert W. Frye, the debonair chief of protocol at New York-based A.T.&T., looks every inch the diplomat, from pocket handkerchief to gold cuff links. 
He carries a briefcase loaded with the tools of his trade: passport, 35-millimeter Ricoh camera, Franklin electronic Wordmaster (''So I'll spell right'') and aspirin. 
Like protocol officers everywhere, he stocks up on Cross pen-and-pencil sets embellished with the company logo. 
''My aim is to prevent distractions from getting in the way of constructive negotiations,'' he says, ''to make people feel relaxed and comfortable.''
As Frye tells it, much of his work is routine. 
He books ''senior customers'' from abroad into the Waldorf-Astoria, escorts their spouses to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the South Street Seaport and his company's Bell Laboratories in Murray Hill, N.J. 
After A.T.&T. built a telecommunications manufacturing plant in Thailand, as part of its on-going relationship with the Thais, Frye found himself squiring Professor Dr. Her Royal Highness Princess Chulabhorn on a trip to Disney World in 1988. 
(One of the instructions he was given: ''Never touch the Princess, unless she needs assistance or shakes your hand.'') And in his nine years as chief protocol officer, he has organized a host of events in foreign countries.
When A.T.&T. opened a new plant in Spain in 1987, Frye was in charge of the intricate seating chart at a company-sponsored state dinner. 
The potential for a high-level gaffe was daunting, particularly at the table that included James E. Olson, then A.T.&T.'s C.E.O.; King Juan Carlos of Spain; Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez, and leaders of Spain's banking and business communities. 
As a backstop, Frye asked that the Spanish order of precedence, an offical ranking of dignitaries, be translated for him.
Corporations like A.T.&T. that deal directly with foreign governments are natural breeding grounds for protocol officers. 
Aircraft manufacturers, for example, sell to foreign governments and national airlines. 
Executives from the large international banks have tete-a-tetes with central bankers, finance ministers, officials at the World Bank and directors of the International Monetary Fund.
Joseph Verner Reed, the 52-year-old chief of protocol for the White House, is the arbiter general of American decorum. 
The scion of a socially prominent Greenwich, Conn., family, Reed perfected his knowledge of international protocol as a vice president at Chase Manhattan Bank and assistant to its globe-trotting chairman, David Rockefeller, in the 1970's. 
One of Reed's more demanding assignments entailed helping Rockefeller find accommodations and transportation for the Shah of Iran and his entourage when they went into exile in 1979.
After a stint as Ambassador to Morocco and service at the United Nations, Reed was invited by his close friend and fellow Yale alumnus, President Bush, to head the White House protocol office's 60-person staff. 
''International business is increasingly aware of that peculiar word, 'protocol' - the order of doing business between governments, corporations, people,'' Reed says. 
Although at least one critic has derided his grand style of state entertaining as ''Cecil B. De Reed,'' Reed himself says that much of what he does simply reflects proper family etiquette: ''Do you stand up when your grandfather comes in?
Do you have your mother-in-law over for lunch?
It all requires protocol.''
Following in Reed's footsteps at Chase, Anne de la Morandiere has brought considerable elan to her job as vice president and director of external affairs and special events. 
De la Morandiere relishes the chance to influence a business deal with something as prosaic as a seating chart. 
''It's wonderful to hear afterwards that a deal was consummated,'' she says. 
''Would that happen if the right people weren't seated next to each other?''
Annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund in Washington or foreign locales - in 1991, the groups will meet in Bangkok - test de la Morandiere's staff with weeklong rounds of breakfasts, lunches and dinners.
Though the members of Chase's International Advisory Committee, who include Henry Kissinger, and the members of the board of directors are usually, Morandiere says, ''well enough traveled to know the ropes,'' she will occasionally slip in a reminder on protocol: ''On one occasion in London, I did warn them that they could light up a cigarette only after the Queen has been toasted.''
She adds, helpfully, ''That's usually just before dessert.''
De la Morandiere points out that protocol officers must be able to stand their ground with C.E.O.'s, customs officials and even caterers. 
''You can't crumble when the chairman says, 'That's a stupid idea,' '' she says. 
No matter how well-laid the plans or assertive the protocol officer, however, the unpredictable does happen. 
The entire Italian Government collapsed last summer just a week before Chase's board was due to arrive. 
Only Giulio Andreotti, now Prime Minister but then merely acting Foreign Minister, honored his appointment with the board.
De la Morandiere has also had some awkward moments in the Far East. 
''You don't number tables in China,'' she says. 
''You go to the primrose or the hollyhock table. 
The Chinese don't want to appear to rank guests, and how can you quibble with that?
You just wander around in a vast dining room, hunting for your seat. 
It's wild.''
At the Boeing company, the corporate image is closer to hot dogs than caviar. 
Letitia Baldrige, a corporate-etiquette consultant based in Washington, D.C., has an explanation: ''It's the aw-shucks attitude handed down from the Air Force military establishment.''
David C. Peterson, who retired as Boeing's director of customer relations in February, was in charge of a stream of foreign dignitaries who visited the aerospace company's Seattle headquarters. 
He traces Boeing's down-home attitude to a conservative corporate culture that has existed from the company's earliest days. 
''We couldn't be as social as Lockheed and McDonnell Douglas were down in Los Angeles. 
They had the glamour of Hollywood,'' he says. 
''We felt like green peas. 
So over the years we made a conscious effort to get to know customers, their wives and their families.''
It was routine for Peterson's wife, Sally, along with other Boeing spouses, to throw a barbecue for visiting dignitaries at an executive's suburban home. 
Boeing's customers included Jordan's King Hussein, who came to Seattle to see his country's jets rolled out and to take a tour of the 747 assembly plant. 
''It's the world's largest building, you know,'' Peterson says. 
Thornton A. Wilson, former C.E.O. at Boeing, referred to Peterson as the company's ''chief cookie pusher.''
People used to just barge over to foreign countries, without the right gifts, the right clothes,'' says Letitia Baldrige. 
''They lost deals because they put their foot in it. 
It's tough competition for Americans against the suave Europeans, who understand sophisticated customs and are used to crossing borders.''
In February 1989 a meeting was set up in Moscow between A.T.&T. brass and one of the largest distributors of telephones in the Soviet Union. 
The person who handled the arrangements was Aleksandr Kovaler, the 27-year-old deputy managing director for the U.S.S.R. and Eastern Europe for A.T.&T. 
International in Brussels. 
But Kovaler misjudged the gift to bring. 
''We gave them a large-button telephone - the kind for kids and older people - and they didn't know why we were giving it to them,'' says Kovaler. 
''They were puzzled, not amused.''
Alan W. Lukens, a former Ambassador to Congo and a consultant to the State Department on crisis management, points out the problem of sending someone who is not a protocol officer to act as goodwill ambassador. 
''Oil companies tend to send out geologists,'' he says. 
''They're good technicians but they have no ideas about relations with governments, and they get into trouble.''
C.E.O.'s who lack adequate coaching in protocol can also make mistakes on foreign trips. 
''They're big shots at home - but fish out of water overseas,'' Lukens says. 
''They get led around by local managers who don't always represent the real interests of the C.E.O.''
According to A.T.&T.'s Robert Frye, Americans new to the game often leap into intimate conversations with foreign executives. 
At a first meeting, he says, ''they'll ask 'How are the kids?'
You don't ask, 'How do you like your work?'
You ask, 'What is your favorite hobby?'
''
Stephen Blank, senior associate of Multinational Strategies Inc., a New York consulting company, says that in European companies ''executives know the right answers to protocol problems - they can tell you, 'This is how you do it in Nigeria.'
At most American companies, each division goes off on its own.''
Corporations tend to fill their protocol jobs with people who have backgrounds in public relations, marketing and meeting planning and who have a knowledge of the industry. 
Such candidates are preferred to foreign-affairs specialists with no industry experience. 
Says Charles Lahiguera, a senior career adviser at the State Department who helps foreign-service officers find jobs in the private sector: ''One of our people speaks Chinese and knows the Far East. 
But when he went out to Wisconsin to apply for a job, they said, 'What we want is someone who knows how to run a plastics factory.'
''
The remuneration for knowing the proper etiquette for drinking in Korea (fill your neighbor's glass as well as your own) or the correct presentation of bilingual business cards can run to six figures. 
Knowing a foreign language is not a prerequisite for the job, according to Frye, who speaks only English. 
''At A.T.&T. we're dealing with over 100 countries,'' he says. 
''You can rent language skills - interpreters, translators - if you need them.''
But anyone involved with corporate protocol - from secretary to executive assistant to meeting planner - must be knowledgeable about the fine points of gift giving. 
Among other things, they must be careful lest the gift be interpreted as a bribe under the strictures of the 1977 Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. 
Before the passage of the act, ''there were terrible bribes,'' according to William Proxmire, the former Democratic Senator from Wisconsin who was author of the legislation. 
''The Lockheed Corporation paid a bribe to Japan of more than $1.5 million,'' Proxmire says. 
''Bribery was wholesale. 
And it had an adverse effect on the market. 
You bought things because you got a bribe.''
In 1982, Boeing pleaded guilty to Federal charges of failing to disclose more than $7 million in payments by top-level executives to overseas agents in the early 1970's. 
Though none of the payments seems to have been made by protocol officers, Peterson, the former Boeing man, says that protocol officers these days are wary. 
''I've heard about giving cars,'' as gifts, he says. 
''We've never done that in our whole history. 
We're especially careful. 
Gifts under $25 is all.''
A.T.&T.'s Frye goes to great lengths to find - or create - appropriate gifts. 
A top Italian executive was scheduled to visit A.T.&T headquarters. 
Frye learned that the V.I.P. was a biking enthusiast. 
''I phoned his wife at their home in Italy,'' Frye recalls, ''and found out what bike he liked. 
She gave me its exact name and model number. 
Then I got in touch with the manufacturer, obtained a copy of the original mechanical drawing of the bike and had it etched on a beautiful piece of crystal. 
Do you think he'll ever forget A.T.&T.?''
Letitia Baldrige is bountiful in her praise for the many polished executive secretaries who often function as protocol officers - in fact, if not in name. 
''There's a vast interlocking network of secretaries out there,'' she notes. 
''They know who to call. 
If there's a lunch for a visiting lord from London, they'll phone the secretary to the British Consul General and get the lowdown on who should sit where, what the person likes to eat. 
Two of the best I've seen are Jim Robinson's assistant at American Express and Rand Araskog's at I.T.T.''
Barbara Neysmith, American Express's former assistant to the chairman, last fall moved on to become assistant corporate secretary. 
Katherine Condon, Araskog's assistant, serves as manager of the chairman's office.
Foreign nationals who work abroad for American companies may also find themselves pressed into service. 
In setting up overseas negotiations, Morgan Stanley & Company relies on its Tokyo staff, which is more than 80 percent Japanese, and its London staff, which is more than 90 percent British and European. 
Such advice is essential. 
''If John Reed is going to Sao Paulo,'' says John Maloney, vice president of media relations at Citicorp, ''the arrangements are going to be made right in Brazil.''
Thanks to the worldwide flow of information, and the increasing numbers of foreign executives who attend American business schools, doing business globally no longer requires an encyclopedic knowledge of foreign customs. 
''The Japanese are getting used to us,'' says a protocol officer with a major commercial bank. 
''They've adapted to an international language of behavior and habits and expectations. 
Everyone's beginning to act the same way - in Stockholm, Paris, New York, Singapore.''
There can be pitfalls in trying to master foreign ways. 
As a communications specialist in the investment banking field puts it, ''If you attempt to learn Japanese culture - and don't get it right - you look stupid. 
Why risk using the wrong protocol?''
The doubters have not discouraged entrepreneurs from setting up shop as cross-cultural protocol consultants. 
Sondra Snowdon, formerly a protocol specialist at Citicorp and author of ''The Global Edge: How Your Company Can Win in the International Marketplace,'' dispenses advice to such clients as Price Waterhouse and New York's Hotel Pierre. 
Two Stanford M.B.A.'s, Lennie Copeland and Lewis Griggs, have sold their ''Going International'' film and videotape series to 1,500 companies, from Aetna Life & Casualty Company to the Xerox Corporation. 
Brigham Young University published and sold 750,000 guides to foreign manners called ''Culturgrams'' last year, each pamphlet in the series written by a native or an American who has lived for five to ten years in the country.
Last Fall, when Marriott Hotels and Resorts opened a hotel in Warsaw, it called on International Planning and Analysis Center Inc., Washington-based consultants, to provide a crash course on Poland. 
Mark L. Raczynski, an I.P.A.C. vice president who had been a soldier in the Polish underground army in World War II, enlightened Marriott executives. 
The company should not invite the President of Poland to the ribbon-cutting, for instance: ''Would you invite President Bush to the opening of a hotel in America?
But go ahead and invite the Mayor of Warsaw, because of the importance of the joint venture.''And he cautioned the executives to be evenhanded. 
''Arrange appointments with both Solidarity and Communist Party leaders,'' he said. 
It was timely advice.
For American companies, the fall of the wall in Eastern Europe has introduced a new challenge. 
According to Baldrige, ''Eastern European businessmen are terribly naive. 
They haven't had a chance to get out and travel. 
They have a huge learning process to go through.''
In the sudden confluence of East and West, there is great potential for gaffes.
According to George Lorinczi, a partner in the Washington office of the New York law firm of Stroock & Stroock & Lavan, ''It's a terrific problem, the way Poles, Czechs and to some extent Hungarians have been isolated. 
Now they are inundated by business proposals and propositions.''
Lorinczi, who was born in Hungary, spends much of his time traveling in the Eastern bloc. 
''In Warsaw,'' he says, ''the Cabinet ministers had a waiting room full of people. 
And they couldn't tell who was who. 
They couldn't tell the difference between someone from Goldman, Sachs or Bear, Stearns - and Stanislas, a retired welder who has $600 to spend.''
Last fall, Stroock organized the First Hungary Fund, a closed-end mutual fund that was placed by Bear, Stearns & Company and the International Finance Corporation, an arm of the World Bank. 
In setting up the fund, Lorinczi says, there were ''plenty of moments when cultural and political differences ruffled deals and egos.''
Different legal customs and terms can be misinterpreted. 
''What is a perfectly normal thing to ask in a Western transaction - for a company to give 'representations and warranties,' for instance - can be an insult in Eastern Europe,'' Lorinczi says. 
''A Hungarian will say, 'You don't believe my company can enter into a contract?'
''
In the give-and-take of investing in a region hitherto out of bounds, like Eastern Europe, even the touchy matter of a nation's treasures can become a headache for corporate diplomats. 
''Take the case of Herend, Hungary's world-renowned porcelain factory - some 200 years old,'' says Lorinczi. 
''When Western interests made a proposal to buy it, the Hungarians went into a state of shock, just as we'd react if outsiders tried to buy the Smithsonian.''
That was where an instinct for diplomacy came in. 
''It had to be explained,'' Lorinczi says, ''that with a fresh infusion of capital and improved marketing, it would be better for everyone. 
It took a lot to get the notion across. 
We had to explain how both traditional and national interests would be preserved.''
And cross-cultural confusion can cut both ways. 
Americans have been puzzled to find themselves warmly received by Czechoslovakian businessmen for no apparent reason. 
''The U.S. 
Embassy would phone a Czech official to make an appointment for an American businessman - just as a courtesy,'' Lorinczi says. 
''The Czech would assume that the executive must be a well-connected figure. 
He'd think that someone who gets that kind of service must be George Bush's first cousin.''
Lorinczi's diplomatic solution to the misunderstanding: ''We have to explain present American realities, the apolitical nature of our business system, our decentralization, the minimal Government interference, the kaleidoscope of disconnected or unconnected businesses. 
We would explain that there is no American position on a business situation, that it's a happy chaos. 
And then the Czechs would ask, 'How can you operate in that environment?'
''

file: Going Above and Beyond the Call.txt
text:
ï»¿
One is an obstetrical nurse whose grateful patients have named at least nine babies in her honor. 
Another is a subway conductor whose cheerful patter leads passengers to applaud his arrival. 
Still another is a principal who uses her own money to take her handicapped students on special trips.
From New York City's largely anonymous municipal work force of 200,000 employees, seven individuals were singled out this week for honors and $5,000 prizes for outstanding performance.
The seven were named recipients of the 20th annual Sloan Public Service Awards, sponsored by the Fund for the City of New York, a nonprofit organization created by the Ford Foundation to promote civic improvement. 
The awards are financed by the fund and the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
"They are the city's unsung heroes, who deliver the highest quality of service but rarely are recognized for their commitment," said Mary McCormick, president of the fund. 
The winners were nominated by fellow employees, supervisors or New York residents; a panel of corporate and civic leaders made the final choice. 
The awards were presented at the recipients' work places on Tuesday, followed by a reception that night at the Hotel Roosevelt.
Â 
Mary McInerney
She decided to make a career of helping children with handicaps, she says, when she was about 8 years old and discovered that an older cousin had a disability that kept him from reading. 
She sat down to teach him.
Now, as principal of the Hungerford School on Staten Island, one of the city's special education schools, she offers an inventive program for teaching physically or mentally disabled pupils, kindergarten through age 21, that attracts children locally and from other boroughs.
She believes fervently that whenever possible, disabled students should attend classes with students without special needs. 
"They need to socialize and develop friendships with students we classify as 'normal,' and find role models outside their immediate circles," she said.
Because youngsters dependent on wheelchairs or special equipment often have to wait for available funds for repairs, she will use her $5,000 prize for a trust fund for equipment. 
She intends to name the fund for her father-in-law, Thomas McInerney, to "keep alive the memory of this generous Irish farmer."
Â 
Annie Shen
At Elmhurst Hospital Center in Queens, the obstetrical staff stopped counting the number of newborns called "Annie" after nine, including Egyptian, Ghanaian, Colombian and Chinese babies.
"I try to discourage it," said Annie Shen, an obstetrics nurse, with a smile, "but it's such an honor."
The bulletin boards in her office are covered with photographs of the babies she has tended.
The Elmhurst community has been inundated in the past decade with immigrant families and the hospital's patients are said to be the most multiethnic in New York.
Mrs. Shen, born in China and trained in Britain, alerted the medical staff at Elmhurst to the high incidence of diabetes among pregnant Asians, which she believes may be caused by their diet. 
The hospital gives her credit for rallying its response to the findings, enabling it to adapt rapidly to the new health-care needs. 
She is the co-author of two medical papers on diagnosing, treating and preventing the diabetes.
Mrs. Shen plans to use the award to fulfill a cherished dream -- a trip to China to "look for my roots."
Â 
Harry Nugent
For two decades, he has made it his mission to make the 17-mile long subway run between 242d Street in the Bronx and South Ferry in Manhattan a more civilized experience through his travel commentaries.
"I don't believe the public address announcements have to have the quality of graffiti," he said. 
Mr. Nugent added that he was gratified by the number of listeners who praise his diction and inquire where he was educated (New York city schools).
When his Broadway local train approaches 66th Street, he advises passengers where to find the exit for Lincoln Center and often tosses in a news item about performances at the Philharmonic or the ballet. 
At 28th Street, he is apt to inform riders they have reached the flower and fur district, or in Nugent style, "the street of flora and fauna."
He tries not to repeat his commentary.
His biggest satisfaction, he said, came from a homeless passenger. 
"He leaned into my window," he said, "to say 'thank you for 40 minutes of happiness and making me feel like a human being.'
"
Â 
Ellie Ludvigsen-Jennings
The program she created a few years ago to help the Department of Probation deal with the rising incidence of family violence cases in Queens died in the city's budget cuts. 
But the innovations of the program live on in a domestic violence manual that will soon be made available to all city agencies and some private ones for training officials to look for the danger signs of possible abuse.
Ms. Ludvigsen-Jennings had her first close-up look at violence among youth groups when she served as an Inner-City Peace Corps member in Brooklyn assigned to work on street-gang programs. 
She later joined the Youth Board and then moved to the Mayor's Office of Service Coordination as administrator of youth programs in Brooklyn and Queens.
Years spent coping with family violence have convinced her, she said, that people need to stop trying to control others and concentrate on controlling themselves: "People have to learn to live together, it's as simple as that."
Â 
Yolanda Bonitch
Her title is dry: Manhattan Borough Community Specialist in the New York Public Library. 
But her work is anything but: getting books into the hands of youngsters living in homeless hotels or shelters, group homes, hospitals and residences for AIDS patients.
One library official remembered Ms. Bonitch's visits to the bleak and forbidding Martinique Hotel in Manhattan, which other staff members were reluctant to even enter. 
"She knocked on every door on every floor," the colleague recalled, "enticing the kids to a newly installed library shelf, frequently changing the book collection to please their tastes and even persuading their mothers to dress them up for special events."
Because Spanish was her mother tongue, she is sensitive to the needs of Hispanic communities -- she was the guiding force behind a committee of children's librarians that produced a bibliography for Hispanic youngsters that is widely used in school districts. 
But she is no less attentive to other ethnic groups, particularly the homebound elderly who are comforted by a book or tape in their native German, Yiddish or Chinese.
She sees nothing extraordinary about her commitment, saying "It's a wonder we're paid to do work that is so dear to the heart."
Â 
Stephan Likosky
Mr. Likosky did not invent the idea of a prison library. 
But in his 12 years as an institutional librarian, he has helped develop libraries from New York City northward to the upstate prisons near the Canadian border, negotiating to secure needed space and persuading wardens that libraries have a calming impact on inmates. 
He was a prime mover in setting up a dozen libraries at Rikers Island.
A student of linguistics who once taught Russian at Harvard University, he has turned down promotions rather than leave prison work.
Even existing prison libraries need improvement, he maintains, because they offer limited opportunities. 
He advocates turning them into "learning centers" equipped to teach inmates about computers and to help them develop other skills that will give them job opportunities when they are released.
On Rikers, he argues, detainees need such programs to use their time constructively. 
"The government spends $56,000 in a year to keep a person in a city jail, often for a first offense," he said. 
"For much less cost, it could help prepare an inmate for rehabilitation."
Â 
James Gilmore
Years ago, his father walked the same beat in Washington Heights. 
Since then, drugs have become a major industry in the area, but Officer Gilmore has used techniques from his father's era to develop information used to smash two major drug operations.
An officer in the Manhattan District Attorney's office attests to his value in providing data he obtained from rival gang members "too frightened to talk with anyone but Jimmy."
Community residents provide another perspective on James Gilmore, citing his help in organizing a team to guide children to schools and to escort elderly people who were frightened to leave their homes to do their marketing.
"One of the things I learned from my father is that a policeman builds equity with his community by never shunning the smaller duties," said Officer Gilmore. 
"People truly appreciate it when you get rid of drunks on a stoop, break up a rowdy street quarrel, ticket triple-parked cars. 
That's also police work. 
It's now called improving the quality of life. 
I call it converting a neighborhood into a policeman's buddy system."

text:

Mikhail S. Gorbachev left China today after a four-day summit meeting that ended 30 years of estrangement between the Soviet Union and China, taking with him promises of expanded party and government contacts and a general reduction of military tensions in Asia.
The reconciliation of the two Communist giants was interrupted and finally eclipsed by huge pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing and other Chinese cities, dampening Mr. Gorbachev's hope of putting his policies on display to a wide Asian audience.
But the Soviet leader pronounced the summit conference an event of ''epoch-making significance.''
As Mr. Gorbachev concluded his visit with a side trip to Shanghai, the official Soviet and Chinese news agencies issued a joint communique promising new ties between the Communist parties of their two nations, which split in the late 1950's over ideology.
The agreements, which had been described earlier in general terms, included the reduction of military forces along the Soviet-Chinese border ''to a minimum level commensurate with the normal, good-neighborly relations between the two countries.''
Â 
Demilitarization Hoped For
Mr. Gorbachev said at a news conference Wednesday that he hoped this would eventually lead to full demilitarization of the border.
The Chinese and Soviet leaders also upgraded negotiations on several outstanding boundary disputes, now under the charge of deputy foreign ministers, to the level of foreign ministers.
The most extensive section dealt with the future of Cambodia, on which the two nations failed to overcome their remaining differences.
The Chinese repeated their call for the creation of a four-party transition government, including the Vietnamese-backed regime of Hun Sen and the three rebel factions headed by Prince Norodom Sihanouk. 
Prince Sihanouk would lead the government pending elections under this plan.
Moscow, which supports Vietnam in its 10-year-old war against the guerrillas, insisted that transition and elections were an internal Cambodian matter.
The two sides agreed that when Vietnam finishes withdrawing its troops in September, outside parties should gradually end military aid to any of the warring factions.
The communique declared that ''neither side would seek hegemony of any form'' in Asia or elsewhere.
Â 
Steers Clear of Protests
In Shanghai, Mr. Gorbachev steered clear of the student protests that have spilled into this city. 
He met with Mayor Zhu Rongji and the Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin, laid a wreath to the Russian poet Pushkin, and toured the Minhang Special Economic Zone, one of the areas China has created to attract foreign investment.
The Soviet Union is contemplating establishing similar zones.
Compared with his three days in Beijing, where his schedule was cut and juggled to avoid the legions of protesters occupying the city center, the Shanghai visit was peaceful.
The only mishap occurred at the administrative building of the free trade zone, when an elevator carrying Mr. Gorbachev, his wife, Raisa, Foreign Minister Eduard A. Shevardnadze and Aleksandr N. Yakovlev, another Politburo member, balked and refused to move. 
First Mr. Shevardnadze got out, then Mr. Yakovlev, and still the elevator would not function. 
Finally, The Soviet leader was forced to descend the stairs from the sixth floor.
When a reporter asked if the group was too heavy, Mr. Gorbachev said, ''No, it's your Western technology.''
Shortly afterward, Mr. Gorbachev toured a Chinese-Japanese joint venture - an elevator factory.
The Soviet leader apparently saw nothing of the demonstrations that filled the port and city center here.

file: Governmental Candor Now Shortwave Staple.txt
text:
ï»¿
From Radio Afghanistan to the Voice of Zaire, more official government radio stations than ever before are broadcasting abroad on shortwave, and many have started downplaying strident propaganda and overt ideology in favor of more candor in their official newscasts.
The trend reflects the recent movement toward greater political and cultural openness in the Soviet Union and China, which has encouraged other countries to follow suit. 
It is also a response to the proliferation of other forms of communication in the developing world, which has fostered greater competition for listeners, government and private analysts say.
''The winds of openness are blowing in more ways than one,'' said Lawrence E. Magne, the editor of Passport to World Band Radio, an annual publication for shortwave users published by International Broadcasting Services, a private company in Penns Park, Pa. 
''There's been a decline in hard propaganda and a rise in more objective news.''
But with about 100 countries broadcasting abroad, the shortwave spectrum is becoming so congested that countries are building more powerful transmitters and taking other steps to insure that their official voices are heard abroad.
Â 
The New Candor
People who monitor international shortwave radio say the new candor has been evident in several countries, especially in the Soviet Union and China.
''Both are now surprisingly frank when it comes to dealing with domestic problems,'' said Kim Elliott, the director for audience research of Voice of America, which is operated by the United States Government. 
''They're doing a much better job of talking about themselves.''
During the recent earthquake in Armenia, for example, Moscow radio provided extensive news coverage. 
Shortwave monitors say the coverage included not only detailed reports of the estimated damage but also criticism of the Government's response.
In general, criticism of official institutions in the Soviet Union, the result of Mikhail S. Gorbachev's attempt to implement a sweeping reform program, is most apparent in the two official stations charged with external broadcasts, Moscow radio and Radio Peace and Progress. 
The economy, with its lack of consumer goods and lethargic industrial sector, has also been a subject of recent critical newscasts.
Â 
Coverage of Nanjing Riots
Beijing radio, which once began broadcasts with quotations from Mao Zedong, has similarly moved away from heavily ideological broadcasts. 
Its recent coverage of the riots in Nanjing, where Chinese students demonstrated against students from Africa, suprised Western analysts of shortwave programming.
''They hinted that there was racism in China,'' said G. Alex Batman, who monitors broadcasts for International Broadcasting Services. 
''That would not have happened in the past.''
And Vilnius radio, the official voice of Lithuania, a Baltic republic in the Soviet Union, has recently broadcast calls for more political autonomy.
Apart from the new openness, competition from other foreign stations, cassette players, videocassette recorders and improved domestic radio and television has forced countries to adjust their programming abroad to ''provide an attractive alternative to domestic media and cater to the international interests of the listener,'' Mr. Elliott said.
In many cases, he said, listeners wanted objective news about a country and would listen to stations they thought were providing it. 
This, he added, explained in part the vast international audience of the British Broadcasting Corporation. 
''One reason it's so powerful is because it's credible,'' Mr. Magne said. 
''Propaganda doesn't sell anymore. 
People won't listen.''
Â 
Medium for Propaganda
But ever since the late 1910's, when Bolsheviks used radio to try to foment revolution among vastly dispersed peoples, addressing broadcasts to, as its announcers intoned, ''all, all, all,'' propaganda has been and remains a key reason for broadcasting. 
Because of shortwave radio's range, countries have used it to project their messages across geographic and often ideological and religious divides.
Some countries have not been affected by the trend toward more candid and self-critical programming. 
Extremely strident propaganda can still be heard on Albania radio and Pyongyang radio, the official station of North Korea. 
And analysts in the West stressed that Moscow radio has not abandoned propaganda in its broadcasts; its message has simply become more subtle, they say.
Despite the Soviet Union's decision to end jamming of the United States Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, radio warfare is not dead. 
The Soviet Union, for example, is still jamming foreign broadcasts aimed at Afghanistan in the Pashto and Dari languages, said Jonathan Marks, a Dutch shortwave expert at Netherlands radio.
Â 
A Crowded Spectrum
The medium's primary constraint, however, is the increasingly crowded shortwave spectrum. 
The number of national broadcasters has risen over the last 20 years to about 100; the number of hours broadcast has risen to about 30,000 hours annually, almost double the number in 1960. 
This has left too many countries competing for too few frequencies.
''It's a very crowded spectrum,'' said Mr. Marks. ''In order to be effective, countries are looking at ways to get their signal closer to their foreign audiences.''
Several countries, notably the United States and Britain, have embarked on ambitious programs to expand their broadcasting ability, building more powerful transmitters and establishing far-flung radio networks. 
But budgetary constraints will almost certainly delay the American expansion program.
Â 
Exchange Agreements
In addition, several countries have recently signed agreements to exchange radio facilities, essentially using one another as relay stations for broadcasting. 
A country transmits a program by satellite to another country's station, which then rebroadcasts the program by shortwave. 
This allows a country to broadcast from a position closer to its target.
''It's much cheaper than building a relay system overseas and then managing it,'' said Mr. Marks, who has counted more than 30 of these agreements, the majority of which developed in recent years.

file: GRUMBLING GROWS IN CHINA_S MILITARY.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's 3.1 million soldiers are enjoying a higher budget as their reward for crushing the democracy movement last summer, but Chinese officials say significant tensions are festering within the military leadership.
The influence of the army and its generals has increased in recent months, and some Chinese and foreign experts say the military could play a pivotal role in coming years. 
Indeed, few of these experts will rule out the possibility of a coup d'etat after the death of the senior leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Already, the army is partly reorienting itself from a mission of defense against the Soviet Union and other external threats to a growing role in insuring internal security. 
The army has created rapid deployment forces in each military region, and troops have also been transferred to bolster the People's Armed Police, which already had 600,000 members.
The clearest sign of the army's rising influence is its budget. 
The only official announcement so far is that the military budget will increase. 
Although the amount was not specified, a well-placed army officer said the 1990 budget was $850 million higher than last year's, a 16 percent increase. 
Another Chinese, who also has access to high-level military information, put the increase at $1.06 billion, or 20.3 percent, when riot control and other domestic security costs are included.
Â 
Increases Amid Austerity
Such increases will only keep pace with inflation, but they are striking because military spending had fallen 40 percent in real terms over the last four years. 
This year money is particularly tight because of an austerity drive. 
But even as university faculty members report that they have been told that the education budget is being cut by 5 percent, more money is being scraped together for the army.
The army remains the most secretive institution in China, but discussions recently with an array of Chinese officials, in and out of the army, suggest that there are a number of splits in the military.
The use of military force to crush the democracy movement in June sparked considerable discontent, the officials say, both among younger officers and among senior generals who are keenly aware of the army's image problem. 
In May, seven top military figures signed a letter urging that the army never be used to crush the students, and some of them are said to be still smoldering.
Vice President Wang Zhen, a hard-liner, recently urged the former Defense Minister, Zhang Aiping, to acknowledge that it was a mistake to sign the letter in May, one official said. 
While the conversation began politely, the official said, it soon became a shouting match when Mr. Zhang refused to change his views.
Â 
Shades of Old-Time Warlords
A large number of career military officers are said to be concerned about the rising influence of the family of President Yang Shangkun, who is also first vice chairman of the Central Military Commission. 
Mr. Yang's half-brother, Yang Baibing, is the Military Commission's secretary general as well as the army's chief political commissar, and he has been behind a broad campaign lately to re-emphasize political considerations in the army.
President Yang is 83 years old but appears very healthy; a well-connected Chinese said that Mr. Yang had a medical check-up a few weeks ago and amazed the doctors with his vigor. 
Thus some soldiers and civilians fear that after Mr. Deng dies, the Yang family will make a bid for supreme power.
Frictions are also reported between the army's central leadership in Beijing and the seven military regions. 
There are persistent rumors that the commanders and political commissars will be shuffled soon to prevent them from building independent fiefs.
Â 
Political Training Proves Irksome
One of the principal disagreements these days appears to be the extent to which the army should be ''red'' versus ''expert.''
Much of the military's younger leadership places its faith in technology and professionalism, and chafes when 30 percent or more of training is spent in political study to make soldiers more ideologically correct.
Even some official accounts have acknowledged the tensions. 
The official People's Daily granted that ''a handful of people'' in the military were ''stubbornly sticking to bourgeois liberalization.''
The official New China News Agency reported earlier this month that in the army ''some comrades are still quite confused on such questions as the superiority and future of the socialist system.''
So far it is striking that for all the disagreements, almost no one in the military is known to have been disciplined for hesitating in June. 
Only one commander, Xu Qinxian, who feigned illness rather than march against the students, is believed to have been court-martialed.
There are reports that the army disciplined 111 officers and a much larger number of troops for misconduct in 1989, much of it presumably related to the democracy movement. 
But Western diplomats say that such numbers are relatively insignificant.

file: Gulag Comes to Haunt Chinese Area.txt
text:
ï»¿
If Solzhenitsyn were Chinese, then the windswept plains here in Qinghai Province might be as notorious as Siberia, and the word "laogai" might be as common and ominous as "gulag."
Qinghai Province, the northeastern part of what was once Tibet, is a sparsely populated region of prairies and mountains, 10,000 feet or more in elevation with few trees or shrubs and bitterly cold winds that leave cheeks dry and cracked. 
Soon after the 1949 Communist revolution, it was made the centerpiece of China's gulag: the site of harsh, remote labor camps where "counterrevolutionaries" and criminals fought for survival and often lost.
Laogai" (pronounced lao-guy, the first syllable rhyming with cow) means "reform through labor," but that is a euphemism for the cold and starvation and illness that offenders faced. 
The first prisoners, in the early 1950's, were forced to build the mud walls that confined those who came later. 
Rations were so meager that felons working in the fields caught earthworms and regarded them as a great delicacy.
In the 1980's, the number of prisoners in Qinghai apparently declined and conditions improved, but Wei Jingsheng, one of China's most articulate advocates of democracy, was sent to a Qinghai laogai in 1984, where he suffered from altitude sickness. 
Mr. Wei, now serving the 13th year of a 15-year sentence, is believed to be in a prison in Hebei Province, and no one connected with the 1989 democracy movement is known to have been sent to Qinghai.
Â 
An Embarrassment to Officials
For officials in Qinghai Province, who are now trying to attract foreign investors and tourists, the province's history and reputation constitute a serious embarrassment. 
A room full of provincial officials erupted in indignation when a reporter brought up the topic of laogai camps.
"There's this prejudice against Qinghai," said Wang Yinhui, director of the Qinghai Foreign Affairs Office. 
"Sure we have laogai. 
But so does every country."
Suonan Tsering, a Tibetan who is in charge of minority affairs in Qinghai, said: "Qinghai people are unhappy about this prejudice. 
Some people in other places think that we're all criminals, all involved in laogai production."
Wu Zhengyun, vice chairman of the provincial planning commission, said there were fewer than 10,000 prisonzers in Qinghai's laogai camps. 
He added that since 1985, Qinghai had not accepted any more prisoners from other provinces.
"There are still a few prisoners from other provinces who were sent some time ago, but soon there will be none," Mr. Wu said. 
He added that while it was now impossible for foreigners to see a laogai camp, such a visit might be allowed some time in the future.
It is impossible to know whether the official figure of 10,000 prisoners is accurate. 
The reliability of the official national total of 1.26 million Chinese in prisons, laogai and re-education-through-labor camps is also uncertain.
The Chinese authorities do not normally invent economic and social statistics entirely these days, although they do manipulate them to their advantage, but the credibility of official information about prisons is particularly low.
During a tour of Beijing No. 1 Prison two years ago, for example, the authorities turned down a request to visit other prisons on the ground that there were no others in Beijing. 
Many former inmates can attest that this is untrue, and the official New China News Agency recently published references to the supposedly excellent care at Beijing No. 2 Prison.
By all accounts the overwhelming majority of prisoners are common criminals rather than political offenders. 
And a range of Qinghai residents interviewed privately over the course of a week agreed that there were many fewer inmates in the laogai system now than in the Maoist period. 
They said that camps remained but that treatment was now reasonably humane.
"They're fed well and they sleep on bunks now instead of on the floor," said a peasant who based his information on a fellow villager who was recently released from a laogai.

file: Gulf Crisis Stirs Concern on Asian Games_ Fate.txt
text:

The crisis in the Persian Gulf is truly a terrible thing, a Chinese writer complained the other day.
''With this new situation, Kuwait may not be able to attend the Asian Games,'' he added. 
''And maybe some other Arab countries won't come either. 
It really is terrible.''
These days conversations here are frequently turning to the situation in the Persian Gulf, but usually people focus on the effect of the conflict on the Asian Games, which begin in Beijing on Sept. 
22.
It is not that people discount the horrors of a possible war, or lack sympathy for Western hostages in the region, but in most conversations those topics seems secondary to the impact on the sports competition.
Â 
Appeals to the Nation
China has been preparing lavishly and frantically for the games, which are held every four years as a regional version of the Olympics. 
After the Army crackdown last year, the Government has tried to win back loyalty and pull the nation together again with nationalistic appeals to make the games succeed. 
The Chinese leadership also hopes that if the games succeed, they will win back respect internationally - as well as tourists for China - and lead the way for China to be the host of the Olympics in 2000. 
Until the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, China's diplomacy had seemed to be working, for all 38 countries in the region had said they would take part.
The dreams of a perfectly smooth event collapsed with the invasion of Kuwait. 
Among those killed was Sheik Fahd al-Ahmed al-Sabah, a Kuwaiti who was also the president of the Olympic Council of Asia, the group that coordinates the Games. 
The invasion thereby not only left the organization leaderless in the final month before the games, but also cast doubt on whether athletes from Kuwait would participate because of the annexation of Kuwait by Iraq.
Â 
Deadline for Lists
''Everybody's wondering about these questions, but our Government hasn't explained what's going to happen,'' a middle-age woman said. 
''We have no idea who's going to participate.''
One reason the authorities have not explained is that they apparently do not know. 
While all 38 countries said at first that they would in fact participate, the deadline for submitting name lists of competing athletes is tonight at midnight. 
It is not clear how many countries have submitted these name lists, and officials of the Asian Games have declined to be interviewed on the subject.
In recent days, the authorities have publicly expressed optimism that the Asian Games will succeed despite all the conflicts. 
Zhang Baifa, a Vice Mayor of Beijing, told a news conference on Saturday: ''We are confident that the Asian Games will surely be a meeting of unity, friendship and progress.''
Â 
Fans From Saudi Arabia
Despite the invasion, Kuwait might be able to send a team, as most of its athletes are said to be training in Europe. 
But other gulf countries may be too absorbed by the possibility of war to send teams, and even if they all do arrive in Beijing some teams may object to competing against political rivals. 
Saudi Arabian sports officials had advised China that if their soccer team reached the finals, they would send 3,000 fans to Beijing to root for their squad. 
Partly as a result, the Chinese authorities arranged the early opening of an unfinished expressway between Beijing and the nearby port city of Tianjin. 
The idea was that some fans could stay at hotels in Tianjin and commute to Beijing.
These days, however, some Chinese wonder whether there will be any Saudi Arabian entry at all.

text:

China and Vietnam announced today that Vietnamese leaders would visit China this year, in a meeting that is expected to lead to a normalization of relations between the two neighbors.
While they have a territorial dispute and have been at odds since a brief border war in 1979, the two countries have been drawn together lately by the collapse of Communism elsewhere around the world. 
Relations between Hanoi and Beijing have been improving rapidly, and the warming is likely to improve the prospects for a peaceful settlement of the Cambodian war.
The joint statement issued today, during a visit by the Vietnamese Foreign Minister, Nguyen Manh Cam, did not specify which leaders would visit China.

Vietnam also offered assistance to China in one crucial matter: the embalmers who had prepared Ho Chi Minh's body for exhibit flew to Beijing in 1976 and took charge of the effort to preserve Mao Zedong's body, after an earlier Chinese effort produced unsightly results.
