Vietnam ousted the Chinese-backed Khmer Rouge forces, and in 1979 China invaded Vietnam border areas as a punishment.
"Both sides agreed that a relationship of good-neighborliness and friendship should be restored between China and Vietnam," the statement said.
It continued, "Both sides expressed their readiness to take practical steps to restore the exchanges and cooperation between the two countries in the economic, trade, scientific, technological, transportation, cultural and other fields with a view to gradually normalizing Chinese-Vietnamese relations."
There was no public mention of the territorial dispute of the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea. 
Vietnam and China clashed in 1988 over their rival claims to the islands.

file: Hard Line in Beijing Fails to Kill Boom.txt
text:
ï»¿
Jiang Lianxiang has a modest living room, with a sofa, a television, a refrigerator that doesn't fit in her dollhouse-sized kitchen, and an abiding faith that her son will be richer than his parents. 
Here, it almost seems as if the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown on dissent had never happened.
"Our incomes are still going up," said Ms. Jiang, a relaxed and smiling woman of 41, as she sipped tea in her living room and watched her son practice his calligraphy in a corner. 
"We have most things we could want. 
Of course, the boy wanted an electric fan for the summer, but if you open the window it's really not so hot. 
And we talked about getting a video player, but then we were afraid that might disturb the boy from doing his homework each evening. 
So we pretty much have what we need."
This economic complacency is not what was expected after the army throttled the democracy movement 1,080 miles away in Beijing. 
Many Chinese and foreigners alike believed that with tanks crushing student tents at Tiananmen Square, the economy risked collapse as well, through a decline in foreign investment, a rollback of economic reforms and an increasingly disgruntled and uncooperative work force.
But none of that has happened, at least not so far. 
It is one of the paradoxes of the 1990's: China, with a hard-line Communist leadership, is booming along at a 6 percent growth rate, with low inflation, foreign investment up, and exports and foreign exchange reserves at record highs.
In contrast, democratic India, Asia's other third-world giant, is struggling along with a 4 percent growth rate, a trade deficit, and double-digit inflation. 
As for the Soviet Union, the other country with which China is most often compared, its economy has sunk further into chaos as the country fragments in the aftermath of the hard-liners' failed coup in August.
Of course, there are clear differences among the three countries, and no one seems to think that repression makes good economic sense. 
But so far, against most expectations, China has not paid any overwhelming economic price for pursuing a hard-line ideology.
"The doomsaying that went on a couple of years ago, on so many fronts, has not come about," said Nicholas Lardy, a specialist on the Chinese economy at the University of Washington. 
"In fact, I can't think of any negative forecasts that have come to pass."
To be sure, there is still deep bitterness toward the Government in many circles, and there is a common belief that the hard-liners are doomed. 
And for the economy the last few years have not been clear sailing by any means.
Beginning in late 1989, China endured its worst slump in more than a decade. 
The recovery is now well under way, but many Chinese economists worry that inflation will soon come roaring back. 
And the state-owned sector of the economy is still a disaster area: unreformed, inefficient and perhaps hopeless.
Yet over all, despite immense troubles in the state sector, the Chinese economy is enjoying far more vigorous growth than the economies of the United States, Japan, India or most other countries, rich or poor. 
This kind of steady economic growth is the crucial feature of Deng Xiaoping's strategy to preserve Communist Party rule in China. 
Mr. Deng, the ailing 87-year-old architect of present-day China, argues that if the party can raise living standards substantially, ordinary people will support Communist rule and overlook such matters as the army assault on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989.
"In the end, convincing those who do not believe in socialism will depend on our nation's development," the official Economic Daily recently quoted Mr. Deng as saying. 
"If we can reach a comfortable standard of living by the end of this century, then that will wake them up a bit. 
And in the next century, when we as a socialist country join the middle ranks of the developed nations, that will help to convince them. 
Most of these people will genuinely see that they were mistaken."
Â 
Expectations Rise Faster Than Income
Mr. Deng seems to be right that many ordinary Chinese are far more concerned with whether they can "fa cai" -- get rich -- than with repression of dissidents. 
But it is not at all clear that growing prosperity will make them more supportive of the Communist Party, for two reasons.
The first reason is that while incomes are rising, expectations are rising even more quickly. 
Consequently, many people seem dissatisfied with their stunning economic progress and some even insist -- absurdly -- that they are worse off financially than they were a few years ago.
The second reason is that many Chinese believe that they owe their fatter wallets not to Communism but to capitalism. 
And many economists here say they are right.
After a dozen years of economic restructuring, China sometimes seems more capitalist than Communist, and that is one reason why the country is doing so well. 
Most of the growth now is coming from private and collective enterprises, not from the state-owned behemoths. 
China's politics and oratory may be hard-line Communist, but brush aside the slogans and what emerges is that the economy's saving grace is that it is deeply pluralistic.
The state sector accounts for only about one-third of China's gross national product and 18 percent of the labor force. 
The goods and services purchased by the Government total only 6 percent of G.N.P., just one-half the level in India. 
China's 800 million peasants live in their own homes, work for themselves on individual plots of land that are more or less their own, and increasingly engage in small-scale capitalist ventures that make everything from tofu to ball bearings.
"Our policy is to talk all the time about socialism, while moving more and more toward the private sector," quipped a Chinese official who returned recently from a visit to the Soviet Union. 
"The Soviets are just the opposite. 
They're talking all the time about reform, but they still haven't changed anything. 
There, the state still owns everything."
Thus China sometimes seems to be repeating the slogan "Socialism Forever!" as it heads directly toward a market economy.
Important reforms are again on the Chinese agenda these days, although the leadership still balks at any rapid restructuring of the state sector. 
Despite protests from some of the nation's octogenarian leaders, like Vice President Wang Zhen, China is moving ahead on stock issues in the cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen. 
Canton may get a stock market by the end of next year, and foreigners will be permitted to buy special "B Shares" beginning early next year.
"Li Peng personally favors central planning," said an economist who has discussed economics with the Prime Minister. 
"But he knows that he has no choice. 
He's got to move toward the market, and that's what's happening in China now."
Â 
Shift to Market Continues Apace
Aside from the nurturing of stock markets, there are several other reforms now gaining momentum:
*The Government this year began to raise money by issuing bonds underwritten in part by securities firms, in place of the old system of issuing bonds that people were simply forced to buy. 
Chinese workers used to dread the automatic deductions from their paychecks to pay for bonds, but now the securities pay reasonable interest and can be sold before they mature.
*China, beginning this year and next, is inaugurating large-scale "housing reform," by raising rents from their present unrealistic levels (a few dollars per month or less) and by encouraging families to buy the homes in which they live.
*The Government this year raised prices of grain, cooking oil, bus fares, rail transportation and other goods and services to levels that more closely reflect their value. 
Already, most goods in Chinese shops are sold at market-determined prices, rather than at state-fixed prices.
*China is moving toward making the yuan a convertible currency. 
A 31 percent devaluation over the last two years has left the official exchange rate little different from the black market rate, and many companies and some individuals can now trade their foreign exchange at near-market prices at specially created currency markets in major cities.
While foreign economists applaud these moves to rationalize the Chinese economy, ironically many ordinary Chinese are far less enthusiastic. 
In particular, workers are alarmed by the freeing of prices and rents, because the upshot is that they will have to pay more for their apartments and more for food and other necessities.
Thus some Chinese economists say, with barely disguised glee, it will be the hard-liners who will be blamed for the costs of market liberalization.
Already in China, it is sometimes startling how enthusiastic many people are about anything that smacks of capitalism.
When a liberal American man married a Chinese woman who had graduated with a degree in economics, he was surprised to find her a disciple of Milton Friedman and an absolute believer in markets. 
In their dinner table discussions, it was left to him, the nominal capitalist, to defend the proposition that the Government sometimes has a role to play in the economy.
"You just look at our economy and it's pretty obvious," said an economics professor, looking over his shoulder to make sure no one will overhear his heresy. 
"What's the most vibrant sector?
Private business!
What's next?
The collectives. 
And which is least efficient and always manages to lose money?
The state sector!"
Yet most fundamentally, what is changing is not so much the policies as the attitudes toward markets and competition. 
These attitudes have yet to infiltrate state-owned companies in any concerted way, which is partly why the state conglomerates are in such trouble, but they have spread throughout society itself.
Â 
Business Careers Gain in Status
Until a few years ago, for example, many intellectuals held the traditional Confucian view that business was a low-status occupation and beneath their efforts. 
Consequently, many of China's entrepreneurs were ex-convicts who could get no other jobs and were forced to sell clothing or videos in small stalls.
In the last few years, however, more and more university graduates have also gone into business, largely because they can earn incomes many times greater than those if they work as Government officials. 
Most people expect that the boom in the private sector will continue, with at least the tacit approval of the Government, and entrepreneurs are enjoying rising status.
"It used to be a girl wanted to marry a guy who had a nice job as an official," said a 20-year-old woman in the town of Bijie in Guizhou Province. 
"But now a lot of girls say to heck with that. 
They'd rather marry a guy who's into business, and who can spend some money on them."
Joint ventures with foreign companies are particularly prized employers, and the most brilliant graduates of Beijing universities now often aim for jobs at such concerns in the way that students a few years ago used to seek jobs with the Communist Party Central Committee. 
Now there are more such companies than ever, and foreign investment has picked up particularly quickly in the last few months.
Even after the 1989 crackdown, foreign investment rose somewhat, against most predictions. 
Taiwan companies poured in cash to make up for the slowdown in investment by American and European companies.
And in any case, China gets far more hard currency from exports than from investments or tourism, and exports to the United States and other countries have been booming for the last two years. 
This export boom might collapse, however, if the United States revokes -- as Congress threatens to -- the trade benefits known as most favored nation status.
Â 
The New Breed Of Businessman
Zhong Hongru, a 47-year-old man with piercing eyes and thick hair brushed neatly back over a high forehead, is an example of the new breed of businessman in China. 
Until 1987, he was a doctor here in Guiyang, earning $40 a month. 
Then he left the hospital and started his own trading company, initially bringing sweaters from Shanghai to sell in local shops.
Last year, Mr. Zhang's company earned nearly $1 million in profit. 
He has diversified into everything from chopsticks to Maotai wine, and his apartment boasts a Japanese-made television and an enormous stereo system. 
As he relaxed on his couch on a recent afternoon, Mr. Zhang seemed confident that the Government would continue to tolerate private enterprises like his own -- if for no other reason than that they are too important to squelch. 
He notes that he pays $100,000 a year in taxes and employs 500 people.
"Look, I'm contributing to the state," Mr. Zhang said, with a twinkle in his eye. 
"So whatever the problems with this or that policy, I think the direction of reform will continue."
--------------------

file: HEALTH_ Medicine Abroad_In China, Billions of Bad Teeth but Just a Few Orthodontists.txt
text:
ï»¿
For an enterprising orthodontist, China may represent the ultimate challenge.
In this nation of 1.2 billion people, nutrition has been poor, dentists are scarce, and teeth come in at odd angles and in odd shapes. 
More to the point, there are only about 300 orthodontists in the entire country. 
That works out to about 4 million mouths per orthodontist.
For now, it is up to people like Dr. Fu Minkui to cope with the challenge. 
Dr. Fu is the elder statesman of China's orthodontists.
''In China most people don't even know we can correct teeth, and even medical school students have never heard of orthodontics,'' said Dr. Fu, vice dean of the Dental School at Beijing Medical Sciences University.
''Someday, I hope there will be an orthodontist in every Chinese village, but I know this is a long way off,'' said the orthodontist, who does not expect orthodontics to be common in China for 30 to 50 more years.
Â 
A Matter of Priorities
Although many people need orthodontia to correct bite problems, some of which may eventually cost them their teeth, many others want braces simply to look better. 
These prospective patients raise special questions in poor countries like China, where dentistry of any kind is scarce.
''Most of the money is spent on acute care and infectious diseases such as hepatitis, and very little goes to cosmetics,'' said Wang Dajue, a surgeon at the China Rehabilitation Research Center in Beijing.
Still, China's economic development over the last decade has produced a new class of people with money and the inclination to change how they look and, more important, to change how their children look.
''Now that many parents here have only one child, they are paying much more attention to that child,'' Dr. Wang said.
Â 
Fashion as Well as Function
Dr Fu observed: ''It's getting more fashionable for the young people to wear braces. 
They care about looks, we care about function, so it all works out.''
Dr. Fu is China's first orthodontist to continue his studies in America, attending Northwestern University in 1981-82.
In a clear sign that orthodontics has been given a push, the Government has allocated money for expensive X-ray machines and other large dental equipment that had to be imported. 
It has also financed a factory to make braces.
This investment has vastly reduced the costs of Chinese braces. 
One stainless steel tooth bracket now costs 50 cents to make in China. 
Although the quality is not as high as it is in the United States, orthodontists in Hong Kong are considering buying the cheap tooth brackets.
The cost for a complete program of braces in China is $100, which may be just a fraction of the cost in America, but it represents the equivalent of three to four months' salary for an average Chinese worker.
Comparison With U.S. 
[The American Association of Orthodontics, which is based in St. Louis, said the cost of braces and treatment varies considerably in the United States, according to severity of the problem and how well the patient cooperates. 
But it said ''typical braces'' usually cost from $3,000 to $5,000. 
The association also estimated that there are roughly 10,000 orthodontists in the United States. 
That means a mere 24,000 mouths for each specialist.] In Beijing, there are two major dental hospitals, but only about 40 orthodontists. 
Each year, Dr. Fu and his staff of 37 orthodontists and assistants at the Dental School of Medical Sciences University of Beijing accepts just 700 new walk-in patients, about all his offices can handle. 
Registration takes place just once each year on a first-come, first-served basis.
This March, before the day of registration, hundreds of parents accompanying children with crooked teeth camped for two days and nights outside the university's hospital.
''My parents brought me here,'' said Sun Yingchu, a 14-year-old patient at Dr. Fu's clinic. 
She spoke through a wiry night brace that seemed to envelop her face.
''They tease me at school,'' she confided. 
''But I don't think anything of it. 
Later my teeth will be pretty.''
The hospital receives another 700 patients a year through referrals, mostly because they are interesting cases that complement the department's research or teaching activities.
The number, however, hardly makes a dent in the millions of young children who apparently need the treatment. 
Dr. Fu estimates that of about 220 million school-age children, 40 percent need braces either for cosmetic reasons or to save their teeth.
''There are so many of these children who need braces,'' said Xu Baohua, 25, an intern in orthodontia, as he pointed to a row of children in their dental chairs at the Medical Sciences University of Beijing.

file: HEARINGS OPENED ON KOREA M.I.A._S.txt
text:
ï»¿
The top-ranking Republican on the Senate Select Committee on P.O.W.'s and M.I.A.'s asserted today that American prisoners had been transferred to China and the Soviet Union after the Korean War ended in 1953, and he suggested that some might still be alive.
The Senator, Bob Smith, Republican of New Hampshire, also said Government documents showed that United States officials knew about prisoners in the Soviet Union and North Korea and hid the facts from the public.
The Government "has covered up what it knew through a pattern of denial, misleading statements and, in some cases, lies," Mr. Smith said.
Other witnesses said the Senator misinterpreted the documents he had studied.
Â 
Aversion to Conflict
The Senator did not offer any reason why the Government would conceal the existence of prisoners. 
But one witness, Philip A. Corso, a member of the National Security Council staff in the Eisenhower Administration, suggested that Washington did not want to provoke a war with China or the Soviet Union by pressing them on the issue.
Mr. Corso said he believed that as many as 1,200 prisoners had been transferred to the Soviet Union during the Korean War.
Today's hearing, the first of two days the committee is devoting to missing service personnel from the Korean War, had the look and feel of recent sessions on Vietnam M.I.A.'s, with family members and advocates in the audience, some wearing satin jackets with "POW/MIA" emblazoned on the back.
Senator Smith released a sheaf of documents that he said provided conclusive evidence that at the end of the Korean War, North Korea failed to repatriate Americans it had captured.
"It's a document that shows in explicit detail that the Government of North Korea did not return a large number of American servicemen at the end of the war and that some of the men left behind were sent to Communist China and to the Soviet Union," Mr. Smith said.
Â 
'Bad Research'
But Paul M. Cole, a researcher from the Rand Corporation who was hired by the Defense Department to look into the issue, said much of the intelligence reports and other data that Senator Smith drew upon were flawed.
"What you're dealing with is bad research," Mr. Cole said. 
"I'm a university professor as well. 
You're dealing with C stuff in some cases."
Although the Government officially listed more than 8,000 Americans who served in Korea as unaccounted for, Mr. Cole said he doubted that more than 100 were moved to the Soviet Union or China. 
He said most of those were interrogated by Chinese or Soviet aides, returned to North Korean prison camps and later repatriated.
Still, Mr. Cole and Alan C. Ptak, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for P.O.W./M.I.A. 
Affairs, said they could not rule out the possiblity that Americans had been sent to Russia and that some might still be alive. 
The men said that until Moscow grants fuller access to its archives, it would be impossible to preclude that possibility.

file: Heirs to Mao See Markets Trickle Down.txt
text:
ï»¿
The dusty main street of this rural Chinese community is a flourishing free market, with peasants and townspeople jostling each other to sell everything from shoulder pads to pictures of Hong Kong actresses.
Now, in a tribute to the maneuverings of the leadership in Beijing, 600 miles north, local Communist Party officials are planning to put up a red banner over the street along the lines of "Struggle for a socialist market economy!"
More to the point, they are also planning to establish several more free markets and to devote more attention to the needs of local businesses.
A five-day journey through Anhui province, a relatively poor region of rice paddies and mud-walled villages in east-central China, suggests that even remote places like this one are digesting the call of the recent 14th Communist Party Congress for an economic revolution along market lines.
Â 
Getting the Message
Few rural party workers know much about the leaders in Beijing who were promoted or demoted, nor do they care much about the party's contortions that enable it to borrow from capitalism to advance Communism. 
But in rural areas, the congress's outcome is being read as a green light to push ahead with economic changes and not to worry about ideology.
"Our big impression of the party congress was that the leaders said that the reform policy won't change for 100 years," said Hong Congmin, the Deputy Mayor here in Sanhe, a township with a population of 20,000. 
"That lets us all breathe more easily. 
We can pay more attention to running businesses."
Dai Zhaoyin, the 45-year-old Mayor, looked a bit puzzled when he was asked if Sanhe was bothered by "leftists" -- the code word for hard-liners, against whom the country is now supposed to be on guard.
"Well, I'm not sure they're leftists," he said doubtingly, as if speaking of some rare species of wildlife. 
"But there used to be some old comrades who weren't so flexible in their thinking. 
Now things will go a bit more smoothly with them."
In many ways, townships like Sanhe have long been far ahead of the leadership in Beijing. 
Nobody knows quite what the party means when it calls for a socialist market economy, but it probably is something like Sanhe: a bustling free market, a sharply rising living standard, income distribution that by Chinese standards is egalitarian, a docile population and a Communist Party organization that is unquestionably in charge.
Indeed, in many ways China has been led in the last dozen years not so much by the old men in Beijing who appear to call the shots as by towns like Sanhe that speckle the countryside. 
It was the peasants in most places who took the initiative in breaking up the communes, and it was they and the townspeople who started building the quasi-market economies that the party congress finally got around to endorsing a couple of weeks ago.
Â 
And What After Deng?
Still, even after 14 years of economic restructuring, many ordinary Chinese continue to worry whether such policies might be reversed after Deng Xiaoping, the nation's 88-year-old senior leader, dies.
"What people here care about most is whether the policy will change," said Yang Chuanzao, Mayor of Maoqian, a village of rice farmers 100 miles north of Sanhe. 
"That's what people fear. 
So they thought it was great when the congress said that the policy won't change. 
Everybody felt relieved."
Emboldened by all the talk of change and of a market economy, many Chinese seem to have found an excuse to do all the things they already wanted to do. 
Mr. Yang, for example, is busy making plans for his village to start collectively run factories producing carpets, lamps and embroidered cloth.
In Bengbu, a city of 2.8 million in northern Anhui province, the local newspaper is full of lofty phrases borrowed from the party congress, and a group of city officials who had gathered over a banquet table the other day agreed that the talk of change would have practical effects on the city. 
But they had a bit of trouble identifying precisely what changes might occur, until one mentioned the increased financial opportunities.
"Officials can now go into business," said Wang Wei, director of the city's external-affairs office. 
"Of course, the business can't interfere with your official work, but cadres can be managers of enterprises now."
All the officials beamed at that thought, and the conversation drifted to the possibilities of going into business on the side and making pots of money.

file: Hijacking Prompts Beijing Shake-Up.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government acknowledged problems today in its handling of a hijacking last week in which 128 people were killed, and it suggested that it would dismiss some relatively low-ranking officials at the airport and airline involved.
But the results of an official investigation made public today did not address the crucial question in the incident: why did the plane's crew not obey the hijacker's demand and fly to Taiwan?
Instead, the plane continued on its scheduled course to the southern city of Canton, and crashed when the pilot and hijacker struggled over the controls as it tried to land.
The crash, on the morning of Oct. 
2, killed an American, 30 people from Taiwan and 3 from Hong Kong. 
There has been sharp criticism abroad of China's handling of the incident, including suggestions that the authorities were so determined to foil the hijacking that they risked - and lost - the lives of the passengers.
The hijacked plane also struck two other airliners, setting off an inferno in which passengers on a Shanghai-bound plane, waiting on the runway, were also killed. 
The authorities have offered no explanation for why the runway was not cleared and the passengers evacuated in the 40 minutes that the hijacked plane was circling overhead.
Â 
Changes in Management
The official New China News Agency, which has carried only brief reports about the crash, said today that the incident ''revealed the existing problems of the airport and airline company.''
It said a shake-up would be ordered in the management, apparently of Canton's Baiyun Airport and of Xiamen Airlines.
According to the agency, the hijacker - Jiang Xiaofeng, a 21-year-old purchasing agent from Hunan Province - forced his way into the cockpit after the Boeing 737 left the eastern Chinese port city of Xiamen in Fujian Province. 
Mr. Jiang, who was described as wanted by the police for absconding corporate funds, reportedly asserted that he had a bomb that he would detonate unless all crew members except the pilot left the cockpit.
The agency said that Mr. Jiang ordered the plane to fly to Taiwan, but it gave no explanation for why the pilot did not obey. 
The departure point, Xiamen, is much closer to Taiwan than it is to its destination of Canton.
Communications with the ground were cut until the plane established contact with flight control at Canton, the press agency reported. 
The ground control reportedly informed the plane that it could land anywhere, including Taiwan, but at that point the pilot responded that he had enough fuel to go to Hong Kong but not to Taiwan.
Â 
Instructions to Pilots
''In the end, as the fuel was running out, the pilot made an emergency landing'' in Canton, the agency reported. 
As it taxied along the runway, Mr. Jiang attacked the pilot and it veered out of control, the report said.
The bodies of the pilot and Mr. Jiang were found in the cockpit, but there was no sign of explosives, suggesting that he had been unarmed all along.
The official version of events seemed intended to suggest that it was the pilot, Cen Longyu, who made the decision to defy the hijacker and continue flying to Canton.
The Civil Aviation Administration of China has not disclosed what standing instructions it provided to pilots whose planes were hijacked. 
But on a number of recent occasions, airline crews have attacked and overpowered hijackers. 
Even if there were no formal orders to try to foil hijackings, Mr. Cen may have felt that his bosses would disapprove if he obeyed the hijacker without attempting to trick him.
In a statement today, the Civil Aviation Administration of China declared that passenger safety was its highest priority. 
For the first time, it also expressed sorrow at the loss of life.
The statement also welcomed the announcement from Taiwan a few days ago that it would henceforth return to the mainland any hijacker of a civilian airliner. 
That announcement will make it much less likely that anyone will again try to hijack a plane, especially as Japan has already returned a hijacker and Hong Kong almost certainly would do so as well.
The relatives of those killed have been upset not only at the handling of the hijacking, but also at its aftermath. 
There were long delays in releasing the names of those on the planes, and Taiwan residents were not allowed to visit injured relatives in the hospital for two days after the crash.

file: Hong Kong After 1997_ Blueprint for Rule Expected in March.txt
text:
ï»¿
As alarm mounts over China's tough attitude toward Hong Kong and hopes rise that Britain will introduce greater democracy here, there is a growing sense that Hong Kong's future will be largely determined in the next few months.
The final version of the Basic Law, the blueprint for rule here after 1997, is expected to be determined by March, and the end game of sorts begins on Wednesday, when Hong Kong's Governor, David Wilson, visits Beijing for the first time since the crackdown on pro-democracy protesters there June 4.
''Everything's at stake,'' said David J. Clark, a senior lecturer in political science at the University of Hong Kong. 
''From now until March is the last opportunity to influence the content of the Basic Law.''
Opinion polls suggest that confidence in the future is waning, and more and more skilled professionals are applying for a ''lifeline'' to leave before 1997, when the territory reverts to Chinese rule. 
Each time the Beijing authorities criticize Hong Kong - as they have frequently recently - the mood becomes more bleak, many residents say.
Â 
Meeting With British Minister
As soon as Governor Wilson returns from Beijing, he is scheduled to meet with Foreign Secretary Douglas Hurd of Britain in Hong Kong. 
The two apparently will discuss the results of the talks in Beijing and possible measures to boost confidence in Hong Kong.
At issue is the extent to which the people of Hong Kong will be able to elect their legislators. 
The debate is not just over the elections in 1997, when the territory reverts to Chinese rule, but also over those in 1991, which some Hong Kong leaders believe are pivotal for determining the pace at which greater democracy is brought to Hong Kong.
For nearly two years now, British and Chinese leaders have tried to devise a plan that would provide for a smooth transition in 1997. 
Thus, Hong Kong would move slowly toward the system that China intends to put into effect after 1997. 
Beijing believes that only 30 percent of legislators should be directly elected, so that would imply that Britain should not allow election of a higher proportion before 1997.
Advocates of faster democratization want a greater proportion of directly elected seats in 1991, even if the percentage exceeds what is stipulated for 1997. 
This way, they argue, when China assumes control over Hong Kong, it will have to unravel a relatively advanced democratic system in order to implement the more conservative one spelled out in the Basic Law, and this could be embarrassing for the authorities in Beijing.
Â 
Fears of a Legislator
If the pace of democratization is to quicken, it must be encouraged by the British, at the risk of reprisals from China.
''In the present climate, the chances are nil - that is, the Chinese will not give in,'' said Martin C. M. Lee, an outspoken legislator who was recently barred by the Chinese from the Basic Law drafting committee. 
''The question is, 'What will Britain do?'
And I fear that Britain will kowtow.''
One test of how far London will go against Chinese wishes will be the fate of a British Government proposal to give 50,000 Hong Kong families, or about 225,000 residents in all, the right to live in Britain. 
The plan was recently condemned by the Chinese as a ''gross violation'' of British commitment to the Chinese-British agreement signed more than five years ago.
When the British and the Chinese agreed more than five years ago that Hong Kong would be returned to the mainland and that a joint committee would help draft a Basic Law, there was a strong sense of opportunity: the Hong Kong people would become a part of their motherland and have a say in forming the laws that would govern it after the territory was returned to China.
Â 
Basic Law Assailed
But there is now widespread skepticism among Hong Kong's 5.7 million residents that China will abide by the Basic Law, according to local polls. 
For many of the territory's legislators and leading intellectuals, who have worked over the last three years to help shape or influence the Basic Law, there is little pride in the final document as they envision it. 
Many people believe the Basic Law was largely dictated by Chinese leaders on the mainland.
''To me, the Basic Law is a total failure, a tragedy, an irony in itself,'' said Albert W. Y. Chan, a regional councillor for the territory's Tsuen Wan district. 
''The declaration of the Basic Law should have been a joy to most Hong Kong people, that they could have a system determined by themselves. 
But that is not the case. 
Their system will be dictated by the Chinese Government.''
Instead, these people look to the future with a mixture of resignation and defiance. 
On New Year's Eve, a cold, damp, dark night a few thousand Hong Kong residents huddled together outside to light candles for the victims of the Rumanian uprising and to demand the removal of the ''Ceausescus in China.''

file: Hong Kong And China Get Closer.txt
text:
ï»¿
Eight years before the marriage of the century, when capitalist Hong Kong and Communist China will be united in a ceremony here, they seem already to be melting into each other's arms.
The ''bamboo curtain'' that once isolated Hong Kong from its vast neighbor has been trampled down by the millions of Hong Kong Chinese who cross the border each year to shop, to see a doctor, find a wife, take a vacation, or to die. 
Several hundred thousand mainland Chinese also visit Hong Kong each year, either as tourists or on business, and residents of Guangdong Province in southern China watch Hong Kong television programs and occasionally even read Hong Kong newspapers.
Many Hong Kong residents remain deeply suspicious about whether China's intentions toward the territory are entirely honorable, and tens of thousands of the most talented young people are fleeing each year rather than live in Hong Kong after it returns to Chinese rule in 1997. 
But the millions of residents who remain seem to feel that if there is nothing to be done about it, they might as well enjoy the benefits.
That has already resulted in a reintegration of Hong Kong with the motherland, nearly 150 years after they were split apart by the persuasive efforts of British gunboats. 
Economically and culturally, China and Hong Kong are becoming one again.
Â 
'Enlargement of Hong Kong'
''We see no boundaries,'' said Gordon Y. S. Wu, chairman of Hopewell Holdings, a Hong Kong company that has invested deeply in China. 
''It's basically an enlargement of Hong Kong.''
It is not so much that the territory is returning to Chinese control; in some respects, China is coming under Hong Kong's control. 
The territory is already the largest source of China's foreign investment and its largest trading partner. 
More than two million people in Guangdong Province work directly or indirectly for Hong Kong companies.
Hong Kong songs and movies are popular throughout China, and adventure books by Hong Kong authors such as Jin Yong are popular among young Chinese. 
More and more Chinese companies are putting up signs bearing the old-style Chinese characters that were banished from the mainland decades ago but are still used in Hong Kong and Taiwan.
Perhaps most important, Hong Kong is increasingly seen as a model - economically, socially and even politically - for China.
Â 
Imitating the Capitalist Side
''They are trying to imitate the capitalist side of Hong Kong,'' at least in Shenzhen, the free-wheeling city across the border from Hong Kong, said David K. P. Li, chief executive of the Bank of East Asia.
Su Shaozhi, one of China's most prominent social scientists, told a Hong Kong interviewer recently that ''Hong Kong has a lot of strong points from which we must learn.''
In particular, he stressed that China should try to copy Hong Kong's development of the rule of law.
Already Shenzhen has announced that it will try to adopt Hong Kong's commercial and trade law. 
The city has even hired a Hong Kong institution, Sun Hung Kai Securities, to advise it on setting up a stock market.
But for many people here, what matters most is that the reintegration of Hong Kong and China has changed their daily lives.

They also visit doctors and dentists across the border, where prices are much cheaper, and some send their children to university in China.

Brothels and Burial Plots
Burial plots are extremely expensive in Hong Kong, so families buy plots in Shenzhen. 
Some Hong Kong men regularly visit Guangdong's brothels; others find Chinese wives and install them in apartments in Shenzhen where they will be available for weekend visits during the 5-to-10-year wait for approval to immigrate into Hong Kong.
''Some Shenzhen women have a Hong Kong husband two days a week, and a local boyfriend five days a week,'' said Zhang Qingni, a Shenzhen lawyer sent by the Government to study Hong Kong's legal system. 
Miss Zhang recently represented a Hong Kong man seeking to divorce his Shenzhen wife.
Each year 27,500 mainland Chinese move legally to Hong Kong, and many more move illegally. 
In addition, more than 355,000 mainland Chinese visited Hong Kong as tourists last year, almost double the number in 1985. 
About two-thirds came on group tours, but many also came as business executives.
Just as Hong Kong is the largest investor in the mainland, so the mainland is the largest investor in Hong Kong, with $10 billion invested in the more than 2,000 mainland companies operating in Hong Kong. 
Many of them were set up by towns or counties in Guangdong as a way to shelter hard currency, and as an excuse for officials to visit Hong Kong regularly.

Some of them are also used to funnel investments back into China. 
That way, they get special incentives aimed at foreign investors that they would not receive as purely local investments.
Mainland residents often resent what they say is the trickery of Hong Kong people, while Hong Kong residents often say that mainlanders do not know how to work hard. 
Yet for all the resentment, the partnership is growing rapidly. 
It is also changing Hong Kong's role from a manufacturing base to a service center and hub for Guangdong Province.
Roderick W. Macneil, a lawyer who runs a China consulting company in Hong Kong, said, ''I really view Hong Kong now as the capital of Guangdong Province.''

After two bleak years in which it has lurched from one crisis to the next, exhaling confidence the way a punctured tire loses air, Hong Kong finally seems to be feeling good about itself again.
A new agreement was reached at the beginning of this month between Britain and China about a new airport to be built here -- and more broadly about how the territory will be governed until the hand-over to China in 1997 -- and it has elicited an enormous sigh of relief.
Spirits also rose today after the United States Senate vote Tuesday on trade benefits to China. 
Because Hong Kong depends a great deal on China for its economic livelihood, the vote, which makes likely the prospect of unconditional extension of the benefits, touched off even greater business optimism.
Â 
Stock Market at a High
For two straight days now, the Hang Seng stock market index has hit a new high, closing today at 4,028.77, up nearly 19 points from Tuesday's record. 
Housing prices are also estimated to have risen at least 10 percent since the airport agreement was announced on July 4. 
And for the first time since the Army crackdown in Beijing two years ago, there seems to be a measure of hope in the air here.
Hong Kong's confidence has been shaken not only by the political repression and ideological orthodoxy on the home turf of its future landlord, but also by the arrests of Hong Kong visitors on the mainland and a rising number of mainlanders sneaking into the territory and committing robberies. 
Emigrants continue to flee the territory at a pace of over 1,100 a week.
Now, with major uncertainties removed, politicians, business executives and bureaucrats here are turning to the nuts and bolts of the airport and port project, which is expected to dominate the economy until 1997 and cost more than $16 billion.

Caution and Foreboding
As with all bouts of optimism in Hong Kong in the last decade, however, this one is mixed with caution and a foreboding that China's verbal assaults may once again cloud the skies.
The agreement provides that China will support the construction of the airport in Hong Kong and will honor Hong Kong's debts after 1997. 
In exchange, Britain agrees to consult Beijing on all matters relating to the airport that will have an impact after 1997. 
Academics and politicians say the document is a crucial annex to the original joint declaration in 1984, which provides the basis for the handover of power. 
Some say it could set a precedent for power-sharing on all matters straddling 1997.
"China got what it wanted -- it got a formal acknowledgment of their role prior to 1997," said a diplomat in Hong Kong.

For instance, a construction boom could be inflationary, unless the Government allows the import of labor. 
Another major risk that investors and bankers must consider is that all the connecting parts, such as the rail link, the suspension bridge and the airport, must be completed before any one can be used.
For the moment, the general public is busy with Hong Kong's favorite pastime: making money. 
Last week, the first Government land sale since the memorandum brought a price that was more than double the one reached for a similar plot in the same area last November.

file: Hong Kong Empire_s _Junk_ Tactic.txt
text:
ï»¿
Li Ka-shing has built a multibillion-dollar fortune and a business empire by trusting his instincts rather than the crowd's. 
But for all his contrarian savvy, his attempt to burst into the United States by purchasing the $3 billion ''junk bond'' portfolio of the Columbia Savings and Loan Association is raising more eyebrows here than cheers.
For the time being, the United States Government has halted the transaction because regulators did not approve of the loan Columbia Savings, based in Beverly Hills, Calif., would be making to Mr. Li's group. 
But negotiations are continuing, and Mr. Li seems determined to buy the bond package. 
Through a spokesman, Mr. Li refused to be interviewed.
His determination highlights a sensitive challenge facing Chinese executives in this nervous British colony. 
As they spirit some, if not most, of their billions of dollars in capital out of Hong Kong before China takes over in 1997, will they also be able to export their money-spinning wizardry to the United States?
Periscope on Corporate America
''The big factor in the deal is that it would give us a periscope into corporate America,'' said Simon Murray, a wiry Briton with a dry wit who is group managing director of Mr. Li's flagship conglomerate, the publicly traded Hutchison Whampoa Ltd.
The United States has a far more competitive market, where the informal networks that tie together and control Hong Kong's economy do not reach.
Mr. Murray emphasized, nonetheless, that Mr. Li could not afford not to look to the United States as a potential home for some of his assets.
''We'd like to have a position in the U.S., but there are different rules in that game,'' Mr. Murray said, acknowledging that wandering outside the cozy confines of Hong Kong was easier said than done. 
''It sounds immodest to say that Hong Kong is getting too small for us, but the walls are getting close. 
We don't have much choice.''
Â 
Delicacy of the Situation
Making the situation even more delicate is that confidence in Hong Kong may be shattered if it appears that business leaders like Mr. Li are pulling up stakes.
''His options are limited by his profile,'' said John Mulcahy, an analyst at Peregrine Brokerage Ltd., a firm in which Mr. Li has an investment. 
''The impact on market sentiment if people thought he was really pulling out would be devastating.''
Undaunted, Mr. Li, who is 62 years old, has placed himself at the vanguard of those determined to gain a foothold in the largest, one of the safest and one of the most open economies in the world. 
That determination could eventually have a big impact on both Hong Kong and the United States, because of the tens of billions of dollars his companies control.
Mr. Li and various public and private interests he controls are a 50 percent partner in the group that won the bidding for Columbia Savings' junk bonds. 
With the market for such bonds nearly comatose, describing Mr. Li's move as being against the grain would be an understatement.
Â 
Potentially Attractive Terms
The deal, nonetheless, had potentially attractive terms. 
Mr. Li and his partner, Gordon Investment, a Canadian investment concern, would have put down just 10 percent, or $300 million, in cash. 
The remainder would have come in the form of a 10-year loan from Columbia, which lost $430 million in the first half of the year.
The $3 billion price tag was $70 million over the estimated market value at the time of the bid. 
At its peak, Columbia's junk bond portfolio had a face value of about $4.5 billion.
''I worry that they're going into something that they don't understand,'' said Marc Faber, an investment adviser here who previously ran the Hong Kong office of Drexel Burnham Lambert Inc., which sold most of the junk bonds to Columbia Savings. 
''They are very good, but what do they know about managing a junk bond portfolio?''
''I would prefer they stay in Hong Kong, where they have the expertise,'' said Steven So, an analyst here with Jardine Fleming Securities.
Â 
Further Drop in Bonds' Value
Joe Bencivenga, head of high-yield research at Salomon Brothers in New York and a former junk bond analyst at Drexel, said the value of the bonds had dropped another $200 million since the bidding. 
''They need to have a 5-to-10-year horizon to make this work,'' he commented.
As Mr. Murray emphasized in his office overlooking the Hong Kong harbor, this move would be not an investment play but an essential part of the group's future as it seeks to escape the uncertainty of Hong Kong.
It is also, Mr. Murray added, part of the testing of the next generation of leadership at the company; a key figure in it was Richard Li, Mr. Li's 23-year-old, American-educated son.
''Some people have expressed their doubts about the sons,'' Mr. Mulcahy said, ''but K. S. still has the final say. 
He's exposing them to the front line.''
Â 
Loans to 300 Companies
The acquisition would instantly make this canny entrepreneur a big lender to more than 300 large American companies, people familiar with the portfolio's contents said .
The companies, they said, range from RJR Nabisco to McCaw Cellular Communications, Pacific Lumber and Wickes. 
The deal would give Mr. Li access to potentially large amounts of inside data - as well as the responsibility for helping keep the companies afloat in difficult times.
''It is a good opportunity, but it will require an immense amount of manpower,'' said one Wall Street expert who had studied the portfolio. 
''There are going to be numerous workouts, bankruptcies and other negotiations associated with these securities.''
Â 
Possible Acquisitions Studied
Mr. Murray said Hutchison Whampoa had already studied possible acquisitions like Pan Am, Hilton Hotels and CSX, the transportation concern.
Despite its reputation as a bastion of free markets, Hong Kong's economy is actually a series of semi-monopolies and cartels, analysts contend. 
Much of Mr. Li's fortune was created from and is invested in such situations.
Mr. Li's background is like that of many Hong Kong entrepreneurs; he is a refugee from China. 
He left his family's home in southern China in 1940, and 10 years later had opened a factory, riding the crest of the first wave of industrialization in Hong Kong - making plastic flowers. 
That business provided him the capital to make his move, eight years later, into property investment, where he built his fortune, now estimated at $2 billion to $3 billion.
Â 
Member of Informal Cartel
By the early 1980's his principal real estate concern, the publicly traded Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd., in which he owns about 40 percent, was an industry leader. 
It is now a member of what analysts here describe as a sort of informal cartel that orchestrates the supply of apartments to the market every year to insure that supply will not slacken.
When Mr. Li bought control of Hutchison Whampoa - one of the old British trading companies, or hongs - he gained control of one of two leading retailers here and a more-than-60-percent share in the business of loading and unloading containers at what is one of the largest ports in the world. 
Later, Mr. Li acquired a large stake in a Government-sanctioned monopoly, Hongkong Electric Holdings, a power company.
In recognition of his position as a pre-eminent business figure, Mr. Li holds the title of non-executive deputy chairman of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, which dominates finance here.
Â 
Steps Taken Into Canada
Mr. Li has also taken several big steps into Canada, acquiring 43 percent of Husky Oil Operations Ltd. and buying a 204-acre site in downtown Vancouver, British Columbia, where the 1986 World's Fair was held. 
He is building, in a project in which his other son, 26-year-old Victor, is heavily involved, a $1.7 billion development at the site that will include more than 7,000 housing units and two million square feet of office space.
Recently, Hutchison has invested heavily in telecommunications. 
It now dominates the paging and cellular phone businesses here and is a big investor in Asiasat I, a satellite sent into orbit aboard a Chinese rocket earlier this year. 
Its signal will reach from Karachi, Pakistan, to Tokyo -more than two billion people.
It is an impressive history and array of businesses, but it has still been difficult to get American investment experts to take the company seriously, Mr. Murray complained. 
One of Mr. Li's problems in moving to the United States, he added, is that Wall Street investment bankers still do not bring him their best deals.
''We're an afterthought for some of these people,'' Mr. Murray said. 
''They say, 'There's this guy in Hong Kong named K. S. Li who has got a lot of bread. 
He'll buy anything.'
We have to find a way in that allows us to do the negotiated deals. 
That's what we hope this deal will do for us.''

file: Hong Kong Journal_A Plea to the Motherland_ Listen to Your Heart.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dame Lydia Dunn, a senior member of the colonial government here, is a seasoned politician as celebrated for her perfect British reserve as for her establishment views.
And so the colony was stunned recently when Dame Lydia broke into tears as she testified before a British parliamentary committee investigating the problems confronting Hong Kong as Britain prepares to return it to China in 1997.
Dame Lydia lost her composure when she began to speak on the emotional issue of nationality and the fact that while Hong Kong's residents are British subjects, and have been for almost 150 years, they have no special right to live or work in Britain. 
As one legal expert put it: ''A native of Hong Kong has no more chance of being accepted for permanent entry into Britain than, say, a Japanese. 
Colonial ties count for nothing.'
Each time China routs demonstrators in Tibet or harasses a human rights militant in Beijing, Hong Kong residents flinch, reminded of the future fragility of their own freedoms. 
Tens of thousands of people here have already begun to cast about for some kind of escape hatch should Hong Kong life collapse under the Communists.
Â 
'Colossal Bitterness' Found
David Howell, a Conservative Member of Parliament and the chairman of the visiting foreign affairs select committee, said he was surprised by the ''colossal bitterness'' he had encountered over the issue. 
As the committee left for Beijing to continue its inquiry, Mr. Howell told reporters that while Britain would never grant all of the 3.2 million people born here the right to settle in Britain, proposals to relax some restrictions on immigration should be weighed.
For years critics have charged that the restrictive nationality laws are racist, and there is a feeling here that Britain might be more apt to make immigration concessions if Hong Kong natives were not almost exclusively ethnic Chinese.
Angry Hong Kong officials, politicians and professionals argue that for the first time in its history, Britain is relinquishing a colony to another sovereign power, a Communist power at that, and because Hong Kong's fate is unique, its people deserve unique immigration concessions. 
They say that if the British Government is not prepared to grant full right of abode in Britain to all Hong Kong natives, which most concede is a political impossibility, officials should at least make more liberal use of their discretionary powers and permit more civil servants and those with strong family, educational or cultural ties to enter Britain.
Instead, Britain has maintained a hard, unbending attitude, even refusing recently to grant automatic right of abode to a handful of Hong Kong war widows whose husbands died defending the colony against the Japanese in World War II.
Â 
Concessions Are Urged
The hearings last month, and the loud, bitter calls for help from Hong Kong, appear to have created some momentum for change. 
In the last few days, several important British publications, including The Economist and The Sunday Times, have declared that Hong Kong-born residents deserve special nationality concessions.
Britain took away all residency rights for colonials through four nationality acts passed between 1962 and 1981. 
Most Hong Kong people, who had no need or desire to live in Britain, originally viewed the mounting restrictions as churlish insults, but now they are seen as vitally affecting their future.
Britain's refusal to bend its restrictive policies is now seen as one more indication that it is abandoning the 5.7 million people in the colony, 98 percent of whom are ethnic Chinese.
Even the colony's top officials, usually unswerving in their defense of the British Government, which appoints and employs them, have been uncharacteristically critical of the laws. 
Dame Lydia, a member of the executive council that advises the Governor, called them ''morally indefensible,'' while the Chief Secretary, Sir David Ford, vowed the Hong Kong government would continue to press London for changes.
Sir David, in his testimony, pointedly reminded the visiting parliamentary committee that residents of the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macau, which reverts to China in 1999, will have right of abode in Portugal, which means that under European Community rules they may also reside in Britain - unlike this colony's own British subjects.
Â 
Grades of Citizenship
William S. Clarke, a lecturer in law at Hong Kong University specializing in nationality issues, said Britain is the only democracy that has grades of citizenship with vastly different rights. 
A full British citizen, he said, has the right to live in Britain, while those born in a British colony are merely British dependent territories citizens, who have the right of abode in their own colony but not in Britain. 
When China takes over Hong Kong, residents here will be downgraded to British overseas citizens ''who have no right of abode anywhere in the world,'' he said. 
''Their passport is really just a travel document.''
Moreover, China has already declared that all ethnic Chinese here will be considered Chinese nationals in 1997.
To gain entry into Britain, he explained, a Hong Kong resident would have to apply for permission like any foreigner and would be given right of abode, eventually, only if he were independently wealthy or had special skills or a British spouse. 
Mr. Clarke said there are probably no more than 100,000 Hong Kong residents with that right.
Hong Kong people have begun seeking foreign passports as an insurance policy against a Communist calamity in 1997. 
Last year, conservative government estimates placed the number of emigrants at 45,000, with most going to Canada, Australia and the United States.
Â 
How a Passport Would Help
''I sometimes wonder what the British people feel when they read about Hong Kong British subjects scurrying around the world to find somewhere else to take them in,'' Dame Lydia told the bipartisan committee from the House of Commons. 
Then, her voice choked, she added, ''It would do so much to help families commit themselves to a future here if they could be guaranteed a hope of last resort in Britain.''
The British and the Chinese are now conferring on the basic law that will govern Hong Kong after 1997. 
But as one political analyst here said, ''The British confer, but it is the Chinese who decide.''
In the end, ''granting full passports is the one real, practical measure Britain could take to help protect Hong Kong's people,'' he said. 
''The Chinese might not like it, but they could not stop it.',

file: Hong Kong Journal_Colony_s Cold Shoulder for Democracy_s Goddess.txt
text:
ï»¿
When an obscure documentary, ''Mainland China 1989,'' was screened in an art theater here last week, Hong Kong censors cut 17 minutes from the 78-minute film, deleting interviews with a mainland dissident and several pro-democracy student leaders. 
Officials said that without the cuts, the film could ''seriously damage our relations with other countries.''
Hong Kong, which is to be handed back to China in 1997, is now quick to censor itself, and equally quick to criticize any word or deed that could upset or offend China.
While democracy is sweeping Eastern Europe, in this colony the democratic impulse that gripped Hong Kong in the hopeful, heady months of May and June is fading. 
British and colonial government officials, politicians and community leaders have grown more and more fearful of China since it crushed the democracy movement in Beijing last June and adopted a sterner, more intrusive attitude toward Hong Kong.
Time of Anxiety
On the surface, Hong Kong still has the flash and flair of a wildly successful Western city, sleek, rich and self-assured. 
But as residents hear repeated Chinese warnings that it will not permit the colony to become a base for ''subversives,'' and as they watch Beijing attack liberal leaders here by name and draw up new provisions to limit political dissent after 1997, the underlying mood has become anxious.
''For years Hong Kong was afraid to speak out, but for a few weeks last summer all taboos were forgotten and they stood up to support democracy and protest the bloodshed in Beijing,'' said Joseph Cheng, a political analyst who has edited books on Hong Kong and China. 
''Now, the self-restraint, the self-censorship is creeping back and it is a sad thing to watch.''
The Governor of the colony, Sir David Wilson, set the new political tone here in October when he advised Hong Kong residents to use their rights and freedoms ''with self-restraint.''
Â 
No Symbols, Please
Recently, in an effort to reassure Beijing, British colonial officials have denied several Chinese dissidents with valid visas the right to enter Hong Kong, bundling them off on return flights to the United States. 
Pro-democracy groups have been denied the right to put up a permanent Goddess of Democracy, symbol of the Beijing democratic movement, in Hong Kong.
When Chinese families who for years have celebrated Taiwan's National Day on Oct. 
10 put out their Taiwanese flags this year, the police removed them, saying they obstructed traffic. 
When students from the April 5 Action Group, who held a permit to protest, gathered outside the celebration to mark China's National Day in September, they were pushed back by the police, there was a scuffle and several were arrested.
This fall, furious that Hong Kong had allowed a mainland athlete to declare himself a dissident and go to the United States, China suddenly stopped taking back its own citizens caught sneaking into Hong Kong. 
The crowded colony has reason to fear being overrun by a wave of mainlanders. 
After intense negotiations, the Chinese asserted that Hong Kong had made suitable concessions and once again accepted the return of the illegal migrants.
Â 
Damning Evidence
Hong Kong officials adamantly denied making concessions. 
But in a secret letter written the day the dispute was settled, and later obtained by a local newspaper, the colony's political affairs adviser wrote the director of the New China News Agency, whose Hong Kong bureau serves as China's de facto embassy, that ''the Hong Kong government has no intention of allowing Hong Kong to be used as a base for subversive activities against the People's Republic of China.''
''N.C.N.A. will have noticed the arrest of members of the April 5th Action Group,'' the letter continued. 
''They will also have noted that the 10 October celebrations passed off in a low-key way, and that the Hong Kong government has recently rejected a proposal for a permanent site for a replica of the statue of democracy.''
''The Hong Kong Government,'' the letter concluded, ''will continue to have a prudent regard for the special circumstances of Hong Kong and the interests and concerns of the Chinese Government.''
While government officials insisted that the letter showed toughness in the face of China's demands that they ban all dissident activities, others said the tone and substance of the letter were deeply disturbing.
In fact, this week a court found the April 5th demonstrators not guilty of all charges. 
But even the most ardent reformers concede that most of the colony's new political will has dissipated.
The Chinese themselves seem satisfied that Hong Kong's new political will is dissipating. 
Last week, a senior Chinese official told reporters that the time was ripe to discuss details of the colony's future political system, saying: ''Hong Kong people were not so calm over a considerable period of time after June 4th. 
They were too emotional. 
Hong Kong people are getting more calm now.''
Among the Hong Kong Government's recent moves to appease Chinese officials was the rejection of a proposal for a permanent site for a replica of the Statue of Democracy, which now stands in Victoria Park.

file: Hong Kong Journal_For Gentry_s Old Home, an Outstanding New Face.txt
text:
ï»¿
One day before long, when Dame Lydia Dunn joins the House of Lords, a legislative institution that has symbolized British male gentry for centuries, she will stand out not only because she is a woman but also because she is Chinese.
''It's rather intimidating,'' Dame Lydia said in an interview in her spacious wood-paneled office, accented with two reproductions of large antique Chinese screens. 
''Whenever I think about being introduced into that august body, I often think, 'I wonder what they think to have someone like me in their midst?'
''
A 50-year-old executive director at Swire Pacific Ltd., a British-run Hong Kong conglomerate, and the leading member in Hong Kong's Executive Council, Dame Lydia was honored on the Queen's birthday list in June with a life peerage. 
Only two other Hong Kong residents, both men, currently hold the honor here, and the flurry over it is a reminder of how this territory blends Chinese and British styles and traditions.
Hong Kong is run by a Briton who serves as Governor and periodically dons formal uniforms that seem to have emerged straight from history books of imperial Britain. 
And while more than 97 percent of Hong Kong's population is Chinese, the judges and lawyers here still wear white-powdered wigs in the courtroom, and prominent executives and public servants are knighted and called Sir. 
The result is some Chinese names, like Sir Yuekong Pao and Sir Runrun Shaw, that raise a few eyebrows among the British aristocracy.
Â 
In the British Tradition
If there is any symbol of that mix of styles in Hong Kong, it is Dame Lydia. 
Her cautious, conservative diplomacy during the territory's transition to Chinese rule, while it has won her prominence here and in London, reflects the delicacy with which Britain has approached China.
Dame Lydia is one of the few Chinese women to have risen so quickly in Hong Kong's British-styled society, winning appointments in the Parliament for more than a decade and senior positions in several business organizations. 
Her immaculate attire, sometimes a bold yellow dress or a V-necked red frock, has been a mark of her elegance, as is her knack for tact and diplomacy in the debating halls and corporate boardrooms.
While her roots are as Chinese as those of China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping - both have the same family name, but use different Romanizations - Dame Lydia is very much a product of British tradition: she is married to a British man, she travels often to Britain, she works at a British company and has a second home in London.
Now, with her seat in the House of Lords - an honor often given to reward the Prime Minister's political allies - the Hong Kong people may gain a voice in the British Parliament.
But if this greater access to the British Government gives Hong Kong a bit more influence in Britain, it comes just as the territory is moving inexorably toward becoming a part of China. 
On July 1, 1997, Hong Kong will become a part of China, by agreement between London and Beijing.
''I don't think she'll have a political future in Hong Kong,'' said Frank Ching, a local columnist currently writing a book about Hong Kong. 
''Lydia Dunn has a reputation for sitting on the fence.''
Â 
'I Am Not a Politician'
Dame Lydia would not rule out the possibility of seeking the post of chief executive, the top job in Hong Kong after 1997. 
But Mr. Ching and others say that her seat in the House of Lords may preclude her from gaining the requisite blessing from the Chinese, who may view her as an emissary of Britain.
For all Dame Lydia's prominence in Hong Kong, her views on some key matters remain a secret, because she rarely expresses them. 
She has never held an elected office, and says she will not run next year for one of the new 18 directly elected seats in the Hong Kong Parliament.
''I am not a politician,'' Dame Lydia said.
If her career has stressed cooperation with the colonial rulers, it is far from the only path taken by Hong Kong's British-educated Chinese professionals. 
Dame Lydia is probably one of two most prominent Chinese in the territory, and the other is a perfect contrast: Martin C. M. Lee, a leading lawyer and Queen's Counsel who dresses in sober suits and speaks in a posh accent but regularly infuriates the British Government by demanding more democracy for the territory.
Currently, none of Hong Kong's members of Parliament are directly elected, and although freedom of speech and of the press is generally allowed, no one asserts that the territory is a democracy.
Â 
Expelled From Committee
Mr. Lee was expelled by the Chinese authorities from the drafting committee of the Basic Law, the constitution for the territory after it becomes part of China. 
The British have not welcomed him much more warmly, and he seems unlikely to become a lord any time soon.
''Mr. Average would like somebody like me to speak up on occasion,'' Mr. Lee said in an interview.
Even Dame Lydia has indirectly expressed criticism of his outspokenness, saying that political leaders have responsibility ''to take the consequences of their words.''
But Mr. Lee says he believes such criticism is motivated by a fear of China's reaction, and he brushes it aside.
''They are beginning to think like a slave already,'' Mr. Lee said. 
''I don't want to antagonize my master and I don't want another guy to antagonize him either for fear that they will get less bread from the master.''
But Dame Lydia's refusal to take a stand on an issue has sometimes frustrated even a few British officials. 
In April, when the British Foreign Affairs Committee visited Hong Kong to hold a hearing on the pace of democracy in Hong Kong, Dame Lydia summarized the two diverging views -one faster, one slower - among the delegates.
''I can personally see the case for both,'' she said, diplomatically. 
When a British official then pressed her to state her personal view, she replied, ''That is difficult to comment, and I would say that I have an open mind on the pace.''

text:
