In a bold proposal for change, three influential Chinese economists with close ties to the Government have called for China to abandon state ownership of industry.
The proposal would transfer ownership of all China's state-owned companies to shareholders that would include individuals, universities, institutions and local governments.
The economists, all Communist Party members in senior positions at Government institutions, presented their ideas in writing to the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang, about 10 days ago, said Hua Sheng, the most prominent of the three economists. 
He said the ideas had also been discussed with other high-ranking officials.
Ready for Publication
Mr. Hua, who spoke in a four-hour interview on Sunday night, is ensconced with his colleagues in a guest house belonging to China's State Council - the rough equivalent of a cabinet in Western countries - so that they can prepare their ideas for publication. 
Their proposal is to be published next month in an official journal and expanded into a book to be published in Chinese in May. 
An English-language edition is expected by the end of the year.
Mr. Hua said there had been no reaction from China's top leaders. 
He acknowledged that the plan would meet opposition and he said he doubted it would be adopted in the next six months, because China is focusing on how to stabilize its overheated economy.
But he said that when the economy has been stabilized, perhaps by the middle of this year, the proposal is likely to be considered and eventually to be adopted.
Â 
A Sign of Interest
In a sign of Government interest, the official newspaper People's Daily carried a long article today about Mr. Hua and his ideas. 
People's Daily, which is published by the Communist Party, did not directly include the suggestion that China abandon state ownership, but it did note approvingly that Mr. Hua had ''courageously pointed out that public ownership no longer is the premise of socialism.''
Separately, the English-language China Daily began publishing a four-part series on the ideas of Mr. Hua and his colleagues today. 
It also did not directly mention the privatization proposal.
Â 
A Record of Success
Mr. Hua, who at 36 years old is head of the Microeconomics Department at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of Economics, is considered a Wunderkind in Chinese economic circles. 
His education included a year at Oxford University, and he plans to return there this month to begin studies for a doctorate in industrial economics. 
His collaborators, in the current proposal and in several previous projects, are Zhang Xuejun, 34-year-old head of planning and statistics at the same institute, and Luo Xiaopeng, 41, a manager of national economics research in the State Council's Research Center for Rural Development. 
In the last five years, their proposals have led to several of China's most far-reaching structural changes.
This time, however, they are not just seeking greater economic efficiency but eventually political restructuring as well. 
Mr. Hua said the proposal would create a class of universities and corporations independent from the Government and able to exert pressure for greater democracy.
Â 
'Strongholds for Democracy'
''Right now universities are just like Government agencies,'' Mr. Hua said. 
''If they were economically independent, then universities could become strongholds for democracy.''
Mr. Hua said a new definition of socialism is needed, focusing on broad issues of social justice like equality of opportunity, instead of on public ownership of the means of production.
Mr. Hua asserted that while Marx was generally correct in the field of politics, he erred in economics by opposing private property.
Mr. Hua said that when companies are owned by the state, the Government interferes with managing them efficiently and the companies themselves try to maximize benefits to employees rather than profits and productivity. 
In the long run, he said, the society and the workers suffer because the economy is unable to grow robustly. 
Mr. Hua said that the companies would do best if they instead had owners whose sole interest was in seeing them perform efficiently and profitably. 
''The problem with many socialist reforms is that they try to reduce government intervention without creating an owner for each company,'' Mr. Hua said. 
''And every enterprise needs an owner.''
A Western diplomat in Beijing who specializes in economics noted that the Government has been very interested in ways to develop a shareholding system, and suggested that there probably would be high-level interest in the latest proposal. 
But he added that the idea would not only be opposed by many people for ideological reasons, but would also be extremely difficult to carry out because at the local levels there is bureaucratic resistance and inertia, and there is no legal groundwork for a shareholding system.
Mr. Hua first achieved general recognition in 1984, when he proposed what is known as the ''dual track pricing system.''
That plan, adopted the following year, stipulates that the Government should continue to fix prices for goods produced under the state plan, but that prices of goods produced above the quota can float freely.
Several other Chinese economists, most notably Li Yining, a Beijing University economics professor, have called on China to move to a system of shareholder ownership. 
The Communist Party has endorsed the idea, but even maverick thinkers like Professor Li say the state should retain a controlling interest of 25 percent to 51 percent in companies it spins off.
Â 
Going Further Than Others
In two respects, Mr. Hua and his colleagues go much further than others have gone. 
First, they call on the central Government to sell all its holdings. 
Second, the new proposal is the first to aim at broad political goals such as greater democratization, as well as at economic efficiency.
Financially, a huge amount is at stake. 
State-owned companies have fixed assets valued at about $190 billion, and they account for two-thirds of China's industrial output.
Because potential investors would not be able to afford to buy companies from the state, Mr. Hua would like the Government to issue ''asset certificates'' that could be used in place of money to buy shares in state companies. 
The certificates would be given to Chinese universities and other institutions, partly replacing the subsidies they receive from the Government. 
Certificates would also be given to local governments, in exchange for pledging to pay a fixed sum to the central Government each year. 
Finally, certificates would be given to individuals working at state-owned companies, in exchange for giving up their right to lifetime employment.

file: In Beijing, Wishful Whispers That Li Will Fall.txt
text:
ï»¿
The whispers among Chinese officials these days are all about power struggles or major reshuffles in the leadership.
Many of the whispers concern a possible demotion for Prime Minister Li Peng. 
The problem with assessing the rumors is that Mr. Li appears to be one of the most disliked people in China these days, many Chinese and foreign diplomats say. 
Thus it is difficult to tell whether the rumors are based on fact or on wishful thinking.
Whether or not Mr. Li falls, other senior leaders are widely expected to be replaced during the National People's Congress in March and April. 
Most accounts are that there will be one or two new deputy prime ministers, and perhaps a new vice president.
Those mentioned for the posts tend to favor economic liberalization, and if they are promoted, as is rumored, it would be a sign that perhaps China is returning to the path of economic restructuring that it pursued for a decade before the violent crackdown in June.
The rumors about Mr. Li are mostly traded among middle-level and senior officials. 
Even if they are not true, they could impair his effectiveness.
One official said he and other policy advisers were now unenthusiastic about providing information and recommendations for the Prime Minister because they believe that he might not be around much longer.
So far, no one says he has seen a document spelling out Mr. Li's resignation, and there is no clear evidence that he is in difficulty. 
Indeed, there is some evidence to the contrary. 
A friend of Mr. Li, Zou Jiahua, was named to the pivotal position of head of the State Planning Commission last month.
But some Chinese officials say Mr. Li was highly embarrassed at the fifth plenum of the Communist Party Central Committee, in November. 
They say he made a detailed proposal to the Central Committee, calling for rewriting the formula for how much money the provinces pass on to the central Government. 
The proposal would have called for higher contributions from the provinces; the Central Committee, which includes many provincial leaders, rejected it.
Those who believe that Mr. Li will lose his job note that China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, hinted at that on May 31 in a speech that has still not been officially released. 
''We should change the group of leaders,'' Mr. Deng said in the speech. 
''The new group of leaders should be a brand new one that conveys a new image to the people.''
Mentioned most often by Chinese officials to replace Mr. Li is Li Ruihuan, a 66-year-old former construction worker who is one of six members of the Politburo's standing committee. 
He is more popular than most top officials, and he is regarded as a centrist.
A senior Chinese cited an incident in support of the theory that a power struggle was under way. 
The official said the Prime Minister's office telephoned the national television headquarters to complain that the news clip of Li Ruihuan meeting with a foreign dignitary lasted longer than the one of Li Peng meeting with the dignitary.
Aside from Li Ruihuan, the most widely mentioned candidates for promotion are Zhu Rongji, the ruler of Shanghai, and Ye Xuanping, the Governor of Guangdong Province. 
Mr. Zhu and Mr. Ye, who are believed to be under consideration for deputy prime ministers, are regarded as among the strongest advocates of economic restructuring left in the leadership.

file: In Canton, Investors See Hong Kong After 1997.txt
text:
ï»¿
Throughout the 1980's, China's hottest growth area, and its biggest experiment in capitalism, was in Hong Kong's backyard: Guangdong province, a hotbed of entrepreneurial activity, economic experimentation and hundreds of Hong Kong-financed factories.
But Guangdong's reform-minded politicians and its soaring economic growth - 15.9 percent in 1988 -made it a prime target for Beijing's conservatives in the economic crackdowns that followed the Government's violent crackdown on the democracy movement last June. 
And when entrepreneurs in Hong Kong look at Guangdong, an area that includes the rich Pearl River basin and the former European trading outpost of Canton, they often feel they are staring at their own post-1997 future.
What they see today is a confused picture. 
The region is not the disaster that many predicted a year ago, nor is it enjoying the booming growth of the past. 
A Chinese Government campaign that started last summer to eliminate ''inefficient'' rural and township enterprises - hundreds of thousands of small companies and production centers in Guangdong alone - greatly slowed the region's output. 
So did a sharp downturn in China's domestic demand for the products Guangdong has become famous for: bicycles and color televisions, small washing machines, smaller refrigerators and sewing machines.
In recent months, the economy has shown signs of reviving, while other regions have ground to a standstill, or worse. 
''The reason is mostly subterfuge,'' said one foreigner living in the area who keeps close watch on the factories and small enterprises. 
''Many of the enterprises that the Government closed quickly merged or formed again, often using 'retained earnings' that were retained in big glass jars under the flood. 
And today the political pressure is easing up.''
In fact, on the streets of Guangzhou, as Canton is now called, Hong Kong's influence seems to be overshadowing Beijing's. 
Night markets are alive with a variety of products that one would rarely find in the capital, from fruits to locally produced Hitachi television sets. 
The Chinese-language newspapers are once again beginning, if cautiously, to hail the productivity of privately run factories, and local businesses have little interest in selling their raw materials to Government-run factories that are unwilling to pay market prices.
Nonetheless, there is a broad sense that Guangdong cannot again get too far ahead of the rest of China. 
''It creates too much jealousy and too many political tensions,'' said a Chinese banker based in Hong Kong.
Some development is going elsewhere, especially as Taiwanese entrepreneurs develop the coastal area closest to Taiwan itself, around the port of Tianjin. 
Other projects that a year ago seemed bound to fuel development are delayed until the direction of the political wind becomes clear. 
On nearby Hainan Island, where the Kumagai Gumi Company, a Japanese construction concern, paid a reported $30 million early last year for 30 square kilometers of land, the governor was ousted and the project has stalled.
The best news Guangdong has received in a year came last week, not from Beijing but from Washington. 
President Bush's decision to continue most-favored-nation trading status for China marks a reprieve for Guangdong, which is more dependent than ever on its exports.

file: In China, a Disdain for Taiwan Turns to Envy.txt
text:
ï»¿
Like many young Chinese, Cheng Lin grew up despising and even fearing the Nationalist Chinese forces on Taiwan. 
But these days, for Miss Cheng and probably hundreds of millions of other Chinese, loathing has faded into longing, and Taiwan is no longer the enemy but the model.
''Young Chinese envy Taiwan,'' Miss Cheng, one of China's most famous pop singers, said in her velvet voice in a recent interview.
''We used to think that Taiwan was a wretched place, but then we discovered it isn't like that. 
It is very rich and we envy it enormously. 
Life is so much better there.''
Miss Cheng, a 22-year-old who is married to a Taiwan singer now living on the mainland, is probably protected by her fame and is therefore bolder than most Chinese. 
An idol to many of China's youths, and probably a barometer of their views, she scarcely paused when asked if China should adopt Taiwan's free market economic system.
''Everybody thinks that in their heart,'' she answered.
Â 
Lessons From Taiwan
Not only pop singers, but also economists, journalists, student demonstrators and even Communist Party officials are searching for lessons in Taiwan's stunning economic development and in its political liberalization in the last few years.
Perhaps the reports of the Nationalists' defeat in the Chinese civil war four decades ago were exaggerated, for Taiwan's influence on the mainland is substantial and almost certain to increase. 
Contacts between the mainland and Taiwan are multiplying almost daily, leaving ordinary Chinese with a clearer impression than they have ever had before of an alternative to the Communist way that they have known for 40 years.
The most obvious sign of the growing ties between the onetime enemies is the presence this week in Beijing of Shirley Kuo, Taiwan's Finance Minister, who is here to attend a conference of the Asian Development Bank. 
Miss Kuo is the first Taiwan Government official to come here since the end of the civil war.
Â 
Coveting on the Mainland
The ''Taiwan fever'' on the mainland includes a tremendous interest in the way of life on Taiwan, including fashions, music, films and books. 
Potentially far more important, many mainlanders also covet Taiwan's economic system or increasingly competitive political system.
Above all, people are asking questions that Chinese leaders find embarrassing: Why is Taiwan so much richer than the mainland?
Why are Taiwan citizens now allowed more political freedom than their relatives on the mainland?
''Across the nation, many people think we should imitate Taiwan,'' Wu Jiaxiang, a leading Communist Party theorist, acknowledged in a recent interview. 
''But that is a very complicated matter.''
Mr. Wu said he thought that the mainland could learn some lessons from Taiwan's experience with opening up its political system, particularly its tolerance of public meetings and its use of voting to select officials.
''They've done better than the mainland in this,'' he conceded, ''although they have not done as well as the West. 
We should be able to do what Taiwan has done.''
Â 
Students' Awareness on Taiwan
Student leaders here generally say that while they are deeply interested in the liberalization on Taiwan, it has not been a direct inspiration to their movement for greater democracy.
But some students acknowledge that Taiwan's political development has been in the back of their minds, and they say it is relevant because of its similarities to the mainland. 
At least until recently, both were Chinese societies ruled in an authoritarian manner by a single party, yet Taiwan has found a path toward significantly greater democracy.
Taiwan officials are delighted by the island's growing influence on the mainland, and in the last two weeks a major debate has been under way in Taipei about how to react to the student unrest.
Jaw Shau-kong, a Taiwan legislator, sponsored a motion that drew support from 24 colleagues urging the Government to support the mainland students demonstrators, and the Nationalist Party central standing committee has also discussed the possibility of assisting the students.
''We're watching it very closely,'' Mr. Jaw said in a telephone interview. 
''We hope to help the students ask for more freedom and democracy.''
On how Taiwan could help the students, Mr. Jaw mentioned moral support, but he also did not rule out clandestine financial aid.
Â 
Influx of Taiwan Journalists
One area in which Taiwan's political impact is already felt is in the journalists it has sent to the mainland. 
The first Taiwan journalists came to the mainland less than two years ago, but now dozens are in town, and several publications plan to open bureaus in Beijing and other cities.
Freedom of the press has become an increasingly important issue in China, and one reason seems to be that intellectuals want to follow Taiwan's path toward liberalization.
''Look at what Taiwan did,'' a Beijing university professor said recently as he discussed strategies for getting greater democracy on the mainland. 
''They first expanded freedom of the press. 
That's what we need to do, too.''
Chinese economists are also casting an increasingly interested eye across the Taiwan Strait. 
Mainland journals, such as Comparative Economic and Social Systems, are publishing articles about Taiwan's economy, and many economists here say the mainland can learn a great deal from the economic miracle on Taiwan.
''For the present period, our economy should be like Taiwan's,'' Wu Jinglian, one of China's most prominent economists, said in a recent interview. 
''We have to build a system very close to Taiwan's or those of other newly industrializing Asian countries.''
Chinese lawyers are also looking at Taiwan's legal system for inspiration. 
Chang Hailong, a lawyer in the southern city of Shenzhen, said Taiwan had gained useful experience in commercial law that the mainland was studying to see what lessons could be learned.
In fact, the reverent gaze toward Taiwan is partly a vindication of the Nationalists' propaganda in the last few decades that they would serve as a beacon of inspiration to their brethren suffering under the ''Communist bandits'' on the mainland.
But Taiwan need not feel quite so smug, for almost no one here seems enthusiastic about the Nationalist Party itself, whose rule on the mainland before 1949 is widely remembered for its corruption, chaos and brutality.
Â 
A Fascination With Success
Aside from the use of Taiwan as a political or economic model, there simply seems to be a society-wide fascination with Taiwan's success.
Tapes of Taiwan singers like Su Rui, Wan Shalang and Pan Anbang are extremely popular on the mainland, and so are books by Taiwan authors. 
Dog-eared copies of the scathing indictment of Chinese culture, ''The Ugly Chinaman,'' by the Taiwan essayist Bo Yang, are cherished by university students here since the work was banned two years ago.
Some shrewd business people have already realized that a Taiwan connection is a big help in marketing books or videos.
A book bearing the subtitle ''An Exposure of Taiwan's Dark Society'' created a sensation recently and prompted demand for a companion video series that sold 10 times more copies than the average mainland video. 
The purchasers apparently did not realize that both the book and the screenplay were written by mainland Chinese who had never been to Taiwan.

file: In China, Capitalism Inches On.txt
text:
ï»¿
With the hard-line rhetoric blaring from the central Government these days, it may seem from abroad that China has abandoned liberalization in any form. 
But while the pace of economic change certainly has slowed significantly since the mid-1980's, in the last two years necessity has prompted leaders at all levels to take small but important steps toward a market system.
"There is reform, but it's regionalized," said a Chinese business executive. 
"It's coming from the bottom up. 
It's the local governments that are implementing reform, and they'll do as much as they can get away with."
Many of the visible changes are in trade, already much more unfettered than other areas. 
Export and import subsidies have been reduced, for example. 
But, Chinese economists say, there also have been a few price adjustments, advances in the bond and stock markets and city-by-city, county-by-county attempts to tackle the complex problem of urban housing, welfare and enterprise ownership.
Â 
'Moves Ahead Slowly'
"I wouldn't say reform is on the front burner, and Li Peng does not have a big appetite for reform," Nicholas R. Lardy, an economist at the University of Washington, said, referring to the Prime Minister. 
"But when faced with the alternatives, he moves ahead slowly."
China allowed its first government bond underwriting earlier this year and already the city of Shanghai and Shenzhen, the special economic zone created next to Hong Kong, have started modernized stock exchanges; Canton is waiting for approval. 
Scores of enterprises are hoping to raise money by obtaining a listing soon on these exchanges.
Shanghai, Canton and counties in poorer provinces like Anhui in central China, also have begun their own experiments in revamping housing. 
So far, however, there has been no nationwide attempt to overhaul urban housing, which is provided by employers.
One proposal supported by some Westerners is a national housing corporation that would buy homes and apartments from the various enterprises and manage them. 
Workers would turn to the housing corporation, rather than their employers, for mortgages and living accommodations. 
But so far, there seems to be no consensus on the concept.
Because of their financial burdens, as well as their overall inefficiencies, up to 38 percent of China's industrial state-run enterprises were losing money by the middle of this year, according to materials presented privately at a recent economic planning session. 
But China has been loath to make significant changes to loosen up government-run industry.
For this reason, some Chinese economists say that the last two years have been largely wasted from the standpoint of reform. 
They say that since the military crackdown in June 1989, central planners have regained control over much of the economy and that there is no longer much chance of a big change in the ownership system.
Proposals a few years ago to transform state-owned companies to shareholder-owned ones have been dropped or starkly scaled back because of accusations that this was the same as privatization -- an ideological taboo.
These economists also say that Chinese leaders missed an attractive opportunity to retool their economy, to raise prices during a period of low inflation, to close down money-losing enterprises and to literally force those enterprises to improve, instead of bailing them out with government loans.
"Parts of the economy show signs of improvement, but there has been no fundamental change," said a Chinese economist. 
"I don't think that in the next one to two years there'll be any major reform."
Â 
A Solid Exchange Rate
One of the more noticeable changes in the direction of a market economy has been in the foreign exchange markets. 
Since the 1989 crackdown in Tiananmen Square, China has devalued the renminbi, the local currency, by 43 percent. 
The rate of 5.3 yuan, as the unit of currency is called, to the dollar is generally thought to be not too far off from what it would be in a free market. 
Economists say a realistic exchange rate is very important in pricing imports and exports appropriately, and in this respect China is well ahead of many other developing countries that enormously overvalue their exchange rates.
A year ago, Prime Minister Li agreed to a plan to allow the Government's Administration of Foreign Exchange Control to make tiny, daily adjustments to the exchange rate, according to a Chinese official. 
The purpose apparently was to save companies from having to accommodate large jumps in the exchange rate.
But it also meant that China's exchange rate began to operate almost as a managed floating exchange rate. 
In fact, the rate has gradually risen another 2 percent in the last 10 months.
These days, many companies trade their dollars legally on the swap markets, where last month, 5.8 yuan could be changed for one dollar, essentially a market rate. 
Last year, a total of $13.16 billion was traded in 100 such official exchange centers, compared with $8.57 billion in 1989. 
In the first half of this year, $8.75 billion passed through swap centers, according to an article last month in the English-language China Daily.
Companies still have to give a portion of their foreign exchange export earnings to the Government, but now, much of those earnings are converted into local currency at the swap market rate, which offers a greater incentive to export. 
In return for this benefit, however, the Government this year began slowly reducing export and import subsidies, in part because it could no longer afford the swelling payments.
Â 
Price Revisions
Some of the most important measures in the last two years involved raising fixed prices for food and raw materials, which had been sold well below market levels. 
Economists regarded it as crucial to rationalize these prices and the Government has now obliged. 
But the main reason apparently was not so much an enthusiasm for markets but that the Government could not afford the subsidies.
China this year, for example, raised the prices of steel and cement, and it took a big step in May by raising the average price of grain by 71 percent and the average price of edible oils by 168 percent. 
For years, the Government had purchased grain and oils from farmers at prices much higher than it charged urban residents for them.
Such subsidies amounted to the equivalent of $7.5 billion in 1990, but the new price hikes will shave the burden by nearly a third in the case of grain and by more than two-thirds in the case of edible oils.
"They have been raising some prices, but in many cases it's been more for budgetary reasons rather than to rationalize prices," said Christine Wong, a China economist at the University of California at Santa Cruz. 
"It's hard to say they aren't moving forward on reform because they've done little things here and there. 
What's lacking is a comprehensive vision of where they ought to be going and what they need to do to get there."
Still, China's state sector is shrinking as a share of the economy and by the end of the 1980's, it produced less than 40 percent of China's national income. 
That is not far off from government contributions in Italy and France, according to Professor Lardy.
One Chinese business executive said he remained optimistic even though he expected few big reform measures from the nation's current leadership.
"The leaders?" he asked rhetorically. 
"It is not in their interest to reform. 
Their interest lies in planning, which means control and power. 
Power means better treatment, better living conditions."
But he added that 60 percent of the labor force, most of which is in the countryside, is essentially working for itself, and that even if China took no steps toward reform, the state sector would continue to shrink.
With a smile, he added, "The private sector will just keep expanding, and as long as more people are working for themselves, things will get better."

file: In China, Democracy Makes Yet Another Big Comeback.txt
text:
ï»¿
Like the bamboo shoots that emerge everywhere after a spring rain, to use a Chinese simile, democracy is sprouting again in China.
No one knows if it will take root any more than it has in the past. 
But what is striking this time is that the calls for a more democratic system are coming not just from students and intellectuals but from a new social class of wealthy entrepreneurs and from the Communist Party itself.
This time there is little of the fanfare of past crusades for democracy: the dissident posters pasted on ''Democracy Wall'' a decade ago, or the student demonstrations that ended with a crackdown on intellectuals in January 1987. 
But today's calls for more openness and democracy may also have more weight because some are coming from within the party itself.
'New Political Order'
No one expects the Communist Party to permit the emergence of a multi-party democratic system, at least for many years. 
But the party is tolerating criticism that not long ago would have been a ticket to prison, and there seems to be a growing view that political liberalization modeled to some extent on the increasing openness in the Soviet Union is in order in China today.
''We need not only a new economic order, but also a new political order,'' the Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, told Henan Province officials last month. 
Mr. Zhao did not elaborate, but it seems he may have had in mind a society increasingly founded on law instead of caprice, where institutions respond to popular opinion instead of signals from above.
Accompanying the debate about more democratic political institutions is a growing tolerance. 
On Sunday night, for example, about 50 young artists and dissidents openly gathered in a smoke-filled private bar to hear a discussion of human rights and sign a petition calling for release of political prisoners. 
The security forces did not intervene, and initial nervousness faded into joviality.
Â 
An Illegal Arts Magazine
''Now people can criticize the party quite openly,'' said Mang Ke, a poet who was active in the Democracy Wall movement a decade ago. 
''More and more people are daring to criticize the Government. 
People want more democracy.''
Mr. Mang is testing the limits of the new openness. 
He is editor of a new arts magazine that, although illegal, has aroused no reaction from the Government. 
And in a sign of the growing self-confidence of the dissidents, the staff members have decided to list their names in the second issue, which is due to be printed later this month.
An unauthorized new social science magazine with democratic leanings has also emerged in the last few months, and again the normally vigilant security organs have not reacted.
''The leaders don't like all this, but they can't control it,'' said Fang Lizhi, an astrophysicist who is China's best-known dissident. 
''There are too many people who are outspoken.''
One of the new features of the present steps toward liberalization, Mr. Fang says, is support from a new class of wealthy business entrepreneurs. 
Such people, who have come into existence only in the last decade, are helping to finance the incipient democratic movement and provide logistical support. 
Just in the last month, for example, owners of private businesses have twice underwritten gatherings of intellectuals to discuss democracy.
Mr. Fang said one businessman dropped by his home the other night to offer the equivalent of thousands of dollars to bolster democratic activities.
Â 
A Minority Concern
Still, only a tiny proportion of the population seems visibly concerned by the question of democracy. 
Supporters of political change admit they are frustrated by the many young people who seem much more interested in the opportunity to make money than the chance to vote. 
And even those who proclaim support for democracy often seem to have only vague notions of what it is that they want.
Among high officials, the new-found tolerance seems partly the result of a genuine feeling that pluralism is more respectable than repression, and that a measure of democracy and freedom can help economic modernization.
But perhaps no less important in explaining their tolerance is simply the crisis of confidence in which the Communist Party finds itself. 
In the last eight months, China has been mired in inflation and corruption that the party admits have tainted its image. 
Its image as a monolith has cracked, and people have felt free to rush into the vacuum to offer their own ideas.
The official press has suddenly become less official, with newspapers spewing out various ideas including greater democracy. 
People's Daily, the newspaper of the Communist Party itself, published the preface of a new book, ''On Democracy,'' including the assertion that lack of democracy has been the chief cause of many of China's failures, including the Cultural Revolution that shook the country from 1966 to 1976. 
The article added: ''Only when democracy is instilled in economics, culture and other fields, can reform of those areas succeed.''
Meanwhile, the Government seems to be trying to provide some new mechanisms to broaden its base and gain legitimacy by involving more people in decision-making. 
Officials have even said recently that up to one-third of leading posts in the central Government should be filled by people outside the Communist Party.
Â 
'Marxism Is in a Crisis'
The limits to the new openness seem to have been unintentionally defined by Su Shaozhi, a distinguished political theorist and Communist Party member, who strongly rebuked the party in a recent speech for failing to provide academic freedom.
''We should frankly admit that Marxism is in a crisis,'' Mr. Su said in the speech, which was reprinted in the World Economic Herald in Shanghai. 
''We should be aware of the grim situation that Marxism now faces. 
Because Marxism was dogmatized and glorified for a long time, and bolstered by those in power, Marxists were liable to rest content with the hackneyed and stereotyped expressions in textbooks.''
Other newspapers were immediately ordered not to reprint the speech. 
The World Economic Herald was reprimanded, and many journalists express fear that the newspaper's editor may be dismissed in a few months when the controversy dies down.

file: In China, Protest Proves Easier Than Organization.txt
text:
ï»¿
When thousands of cheering and banner-waving Qinghua University students left campus last week to join an enormous demonstration that crumpled police lines and forced the Government to agree to a discussion, they forgot one thing: their leaders.
Fearful of reprisals, Qinghua's student leaders had already resigned and declared that they would not take part. 
Only after the demonstrators marched down the street and attracted an enormous outpouring of popular enthusiasm did the leaders slink after the crowd and take up positions at the rear of the march.
The incident reflected the spontaneous, almost accidental nature of the students' pro-democracy movement, which is already hailed by many Chinese as having earned a major place in history by taking on the Government against all odds.
'Date Will Live in History'
''It was the first time in Chinese history that the ordinary people won a great victory,'' a journalist for an official newspaper said of last Thursday's march, in which 150,000 demonstrators were welcomed almost as a liberating army. 
''The date will live in history.''
Less obvious but just as important, the students for the first time showed signs of a capacity for organization that could become a major challenge to the Government. 
Chaos and ineptitude and rivalries are still the most striking features of their activities, but the shadow of an effective organization is emerging.
If it is not crushed, it could for the first time in four decades of Communist rule provide a coherent framework to muster sustained pressure on the Government for change. 
In other countries, non-Governmental organizations like the Catholic Church in Poland or the Shiite Muslim networks in pre-revolutionary Iran played essential roles in disseminating ideas and organizing opposition, but in China there was not even the hint of such an institution.
Â 
Not Easy to Find Leaders
Without money, telephones, photocopiers or permission, the student movement in less than two weeks has succeeded in establishing a loose network of universities in Beijing and the nearby city of Tianjin, and it is trying to establish links with other universities. 
An inter-university committee has been established and its decisions seem to be generally respected by most of the city's students.
But in what may be a sign of the difficulties of creating their own leadership, Beijing University students today postponed an election intended to select a new group of student leaders. 
They said the election needed better planning and would be held soon.
Students there have already set up their own loudspeaker system to broadcast news and they are talking about starting a newspaper.
Posters are also a prime way to communicate ideas. 
Today, students at Beijing University and other campuses erected new posters criticizing the Government's televised discussion with student leaders, held on Saturday, as inadequate and superficial. 
Most students said they planned to continue their protests.
Perhaps the greatest challenge of the student movement has been to find assertive leaders who dare to command the ranks. 
The newly formed student organizations still have no presidents, only committees that are so large that they are ungainly, and many of the most talented students are afraid to take an official position in an organization that is branded illegal.
At Beijing University, for example, the organizing committee has 63 members. 
Daily operations are managed by a standing committee of five people elected by the full committee.
Aside from prison, there are other risks: the Government still assigns jobs to college graduates, so if a student is marked as a leader he might be assigned to a dreary job in a distant city from which he can never escape.
Â 
The Young Are the Vanguard
When Wang Dan, a 20-year-old Beijing University history student who is the movement's best-known leader, was asked the other day what he planned to do after graduation, he laughed humorlessly. 
''My graduation itself is enough of a question mark,'' he said.
''But I believe that even if I am arrested and so unable to participate, there will be more and more people after me,'' added Mr. Wang, who appears to have been singled out by the Communist Party for attack in anonymous wall posters.
One of the consequences of this nervousness is that the student leaders are often relatively young and inexperienced. 
The natural leaders, those who are older and more respected among their peers, are apprehensive of being in the forefront of the movement. 
Some older students, including young teachers and graduate students, try quietly to advise the young leaders, but tensions are inevitable.
''Those who walk in the front row of the demonstration and get caught are not the most important leaders,'' said a third-year student who is playing a behind-the-scenes role at Beijing University. 
''They are young people in their first or second year. 
They are 17 or 18. 
For them it's not so bad. 
But those in their third or fourth year are more careful.''
Â 
Rivalries and Accusations
Students are reluctant not just to lead, but also to be led, causing further problems. 
The fractiousness and accusations have already split the movement, and unless a single president emerges the divisions are likely to get worse. 
Some leaders accuse each other of excessive ambition, or even of being Government plants.
The toll that the rivalries take was evident several days ago when Beijing University convened an open meeting of students to elect leaders and plan activities. 
More than 5,000 students initially gathered for the meeting, but almost all left when rival candidates began fighting over the microphone and calling each other Government stooges.
An unanswered question so far is whether a faction in the leadership is encouraging the demonstrations, or using them. 
Such speculation is inevitable here, because China is a country where historically the conspiracy theorists have usually been right.
While the overwhelming majority of students clearly rose on their own initiative, it is possible that some leaders who favor more rapid change are doing what they can to help the students succeed, in the hope that this will help create a mandate for change and hasten the retirement of elderly officials such as the senior leader, Deng Xiaoping. 
So far, however, there is no evidence that the student unrest is related to power struggles within the party.

file: In Corner of Tibet, Chinese Now Predominate.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the smoke from his cigarette whirled around the deep lines in his face, tan and textured like the old leather saddles on the horses grazing behind him, Namshin remembered the days when the plateau was inhabited only by fellow Tibetans, so that he lived his first 35 years without ever seeing a single Chinese.
"Now look at those villages over there," said the 68-year-old Mr. Namshin, who possesses 150 sheep but only one name, and he waved his hand beyond a herd of yaks at some hamlets on the prairie. 
"They're all Chinese. 
Now there's no place to raise our livestock down here, and we must go into the mountains to graze our sheep."
Four decades after the Communist revolution, Mr. Namshin's dismay seems to be shared by many other Tibetans who live here in Qinghai Province. 
The Communists have brought roads, trains, X-rays, television and a measure of prosperity. 
But they have also brought their own people, Han Chinese, who are remolding this part of the Tibetan plateau in their own image.
Â 
Minority in Their Land
This land of mountains and prairies historically was Amdo Province of Tibet, but it fell under Chinese control in the 18th century and was inherited by the Communists after their 1949 revolution. 
Today, when most people around the world speak of "Tibet" they refer to the "Tibet autonomous region" that China invaded in 1950 and still tightly controls. 
But to the Tibetan government in exile and to many Tibetans themselves, this too is Tibet -- the one forgotten by the West, the one that cannot call itself Tibet, the one in which Tibetans are now a minority in their own land.
Once this was a center of Tibetan learning, the birthplace of the Dalai Lama, the exiled spiritual leader of Tibetans. 
But now the Dalai Lama's photo cannot be sold on the streets to people who still worship him with a devotion that is luminous in their eyes.
The rights of Tibetans have been a matter of growing international concern, but this Tibetan area has been among the most remote and among the least visited by foreigners, with little information trickling to the West about conditions here. 
A rare, eight-day journey through Qinghai found many Tibetans chafing at religious and family planning restrictions, and alarmed that they were being submerged in a Chinese sea.
As a result of Government-backed migration, Qinghai Province's population of 4.5 million is now 58 percent Han Chinese, 20 percent Tibetan and 22 percent Hui and other minorities. 
In contrast, a 1950 handbook to China says Tibetans were then the largest group in Qinghai.
Yet there is little sign in Qinghai of political unrest or of the deep antagonisms that are immediately evident in the Chinese "autonomous region" of Tibet, particularly in the capital, Lhasa. 
Troops in Lhasa have fired on protesters and tortured monks and nuns, provoking outrage in the West and radicalizing the local population, but here the authorities are using gentler tactics and appear to have won acquiescence and sometimes support from a considerable sector of the Tibetan population.
"Relations among the nationalities are good here," said Wenchangtai, a 28-year-old Tibetan peasant, as he chewed on oily bread for breakfast in a room of his mud-walled home in Gonghe County. 
One indication that relations are indeed relatively good is his Han Chinese wife, Wang Guojin, also 28, who was sitting a few feet away on the "kang" platform bed nursing their baby.
"Our parents had no objection," Mr. Wenchangtai said. 
"Of course, some parents might not be happy, but it wasn't a problem with ours."
About 10 percent of the marriages in the area are between Tibetans and Han, local people say.
Suonan Dajie, an 18-year-old student walking down the dirt path to visit relatives, also seemed fairly typical of a younger breed of Tibetans who have few complaints about the system.
"I know that in Tibet there've been some separatist activities, but it's not like that here," he said. 
"Relations among the nationalities are good here, and we've got religious freedom."
Â 
Chinese Learned in School
Mr. Suonan Dajie and Mr. Wenchangtai, who spoke in the fluent Chinese they learned in school, were interviewed at random along with dozens of other Tibetans, mostly during several days of hiking along the trails of Gonghe County in central Qinghai Province. 
No one else was present for most of the interviews, although the security forces made considerable efforts to trace this reporter's steps and interrogate those Tibetans who were interviewed.
Local officials, who had previously refused to allow a visit to Qinghai, allowed this trip to an international conference in Qinghai. 
They protested vigorously when this reporter slipped away to roam the countryside, and they also assigned "tails" to try to determine who was contacted.
The jitteriness among officials contrasted with the bucolic scenes of yellow wheat and snow-capped mountains, and paradoxically most of the rural Tibetans seemed more content and less politicized or fearful than the urban middle class in cities like Beijing and Shanghai -- or Tibet itself. 
In Lhasa, many Tibetans are enraged by the shootings and torture and repression about them. 
But here in Qinghai there appear to be few detentions and little or no torture to radicalize the Tibetans, although conditions may not be so idyllic as the authorities claim.
"There've been no conflicts, not even one," claimed Suonan Tsering, a Tibetan who is director of the Government's nationality affairs commission in the provincial capital, Xining.
Â 
Confrontations Reported
In fact, however, there have been several confrontations since 1987 in the East Qinghai town of Tongren, and two Tibetan monks there were sentenced last year to prison terms of 12 months and 18 months for unfurling a Tibetan national flag on the street. 
Both presumably have now completed their sentences.
In Xinghai County, two young men were forced to flee to India last year when the police sought to arrest them for distributing 100 pro-independence leaflets, villagers said. 
And in Gonghe County, a young man was detained after he visited associates of the Dalai Lama in India. 
He was released and fled back to India.
Robert Barnett, coordinator of the London-based Tibet information network, an independent monitoring service, cited several past arrests in southern Qinghai, not far from the town of Yushu. 
But he said it was not known if there were now any Tibetan political prisoners in Qinghai.
Villagers in Qinghai said they were unaware of the new Tibetan-language broadcasts by the Voice of America, but they all knew of the shootings of protesters in Lhasa. 
They said the news had spread by word of mouth, rippling across the grasslands from hut to hut, tent to tent.
Â 
'Our Hearts Are Breaking'
"Our hearts were breaking," a middle-aged Tibetan peasant said in the privacy of his home. 
"We don't count as people here. 
We're becoming a minority, and the only way to protect ourselves is independence. 
People don't dare say it, but everybody feels it in their hearts."
That was far from a uniform view among Tibetans interviewed, but even those who opposed independence were deeply distressed by the violence in Lhasa and by restrictions affecting religion. 
While many young Tibetans said they had religious freedom, there are stark limits. 
A half-dozen shopowners said independently that they were not permitted to sell photos of the Dalai Lama.
The photos are enormously important to Tibetans, who revere the Dalai Lama and want to display photos of him in their shops, monasteries and on altars in their homes. 
In the Tibet autonomous region, repression is in many respects greater than in Qinghai, but there photographs of the Dalai Lama are allowed to circulate freely.
"We can display the photos in our homes, but not here at the monastery," said a young monk at Kumbum monastery, also known as Taer Si, in eastern Qinghai. 
As in Tibet, the monasteries function as an alternative university system, and what little resistance has surfaced in Qinghai has come largely from monks.
"That is the space of the picture of the Dalai Lama," said a lean old monk in Kumbum monastery. 
He pointed reverently to a blank space on a wall, as if it were one of the monastery's most precious possessions.
The authorities also place loose restrictions on the numbers of monks who can be inducted into any monastery. 
Kumbum, for instance, had 3,000 monks at the time of the Communist revolution, according to the American-published "China Handbook" of 1950. 
Now it is officially allowed to have 400 monks, although in fact there are about 500.
A common source of antagonism appears to be family planning restrictions in rural areas. 
The rules in Qinghai are similar to those in the rest of China: Han couples are allowed one child each, or sometimes two in the countryside, while Tibetans and other minorities are given special dispensation and are allowed two or three each. 
Fines equivalent to $100 to $200 are now imposed on those who have unauthorized births.
While many peasants all over China complain about family planning rules, here the grumbling sometimes takes on nationalist overtones because those who enforce the unpopular policies tend to be Han Chinese.
"They didn't sterilize anyone around here until recently," said a Tibetan peasant who already has more children than he was supposed to. 
"But now they're trying to sterilize women after they give birth to two babies. 
They keep coming to me and saying that unless my wife agrees to be sterilized, then they'll take our land and smash our house."
He shrugged his shoulders helplessly. 
"So we'll give in," he said. 
"She'll be sterilized."
Still, standards of living for Tibetans in Qinghai are unquestionably rising, as they are in all of China, and that may be one of the most important reasons why there is not more political and religious ferment.
While the villages visited were all accessible only by dirt path, they had electricity, bicycles, often tiny tractors and among young people, the first hints of an interest in fashion. 
A teen-age girl was toiling one evening in the fields, arranging stacks of grain -- a timeless scene, except that she was wearing a bright-red blazer.
"They control religion pretty tightly," said a 29-year-old Tibetan peasant who seemed to fit in the middle of the spectrum of opinion. 
"But life's getting a lot better for us. 
Most folks have televisions, and a few even have a color television. 
So life's getting more comfortable, and a lot of us are reasonably satisfied."

file: In Hong Kong, a Deepening Sense of Despair and Betrayal.txt
text:
ï»¿
The feeling of betrayal is heavy in the Hong Kong air, but when people here dissect the territory's crisis, they sometimes speak most bitterly not of hard-liners in Beijing but of Government officials in London.
One of the most graphic comparisons suggests that Britain's plan to hand over Hong Kong's 5.7 million inhabitants to China in 1997 is analogous to handing over 6 million Jews to Nazi Germany in World War II. 
Martin C. M. Lee, Hong Kong's best-known dissident and apparently the first to make that analogy publicly, said that the comparison may not be precise but it reflected the despair and betrayal felt in Hong Kong.
''The people of Hong Kong were led down the garden path by the British and Chinese Governments,'' Mr. Lee said.
A cartoon in The Hong Kong Standard, an English-language newspaper, captured the resentment: it compared British Foreign Ministry comments on the need for a popular government by self-determination in the ''dynamic, bustling, financial center, Afghanistan,'' with the calls for caution and continuity in ''backward, undeveloped, remote, illiterate Hong Kong.''
Â 
Discriminating About Democracy
The cartoon reflects one of the main complaints of people here - that while Britain has favored democracy in other parts of the world, including Eastern Europe and Namibia, it has refused to introduce a democratic system in Hong Kong and thereby create a chance for democracy under Chinese rule. 
Under great popular pressure, the colonial Government has agreed that a small number of legislators would be directly elected next year, but most legislators and all officials in the powerful executive branch would continue to be appointed.
It is not only ethnic Chinese but also Britons and other resident foreigners who make such criticisms. 
Anthony Rogers, the chairman of the Hong Kong Bar Association, was quoted in the Hong Kong press recently as telling a conference in New Zealand that the failure to allow self-determination for Hong Kong was ''one of the biggest denials of human rights by Britain in this century.''
Another prime complaint is that Britain has been cowed by Beijing into acting as its police in the territory. 
The Hong Kong Government, stressing the need to avoid offending Beijing, refuses to allow Chinese dissidents into Hong Kong and even censors movies that might offend the Chinese Government. 
One official, explaining censorship policies, suggestd that the Hong Kong Government had to be more aggressive in censorship after the rise of the hard-liners because China is more easily upset than it used to be.
''The perpetrators of 4 June 1989 were in effect given veto powers over liberty and democracy in Hong Kong,'' said the Far Eastern Economic Review, a Hong Kong-based news magazine that recently featured a cover story proclaiming the surrender of Hong Kong. 
Hundreds died on June 4 when Government troops moved against pro-democracy protesters in Tiananmen Square in Beijing.
Â 
A Varied Choice of Lands
Another common criticism is over London's refusal to allow greater numbers of Hong Kong Chinese to move to Britain. 
Simon Murray, a leading Hong Kong businessman, said in a speech last week that it may be a ''sublime conceit'' of the British to worry that millions of Hong Kong Chinese wish to move there, for most Hong Kong residents, he said, seem more interested in emigrating to the United States, Australia or Canada.
Many officials in the British and Hong Kong Governments are privately sympathetic to these sorts of criticisms. 
But in rebuttal, some officials suggest that Hong Kong poses special problems because it must be handed over to a foreign country. 
When Britain retreated from colonies in Africa or other parts of Asia, it could hold an election and pull down the flag, but in Hong Kong there has been wide acceptance of the view that Hong Kong cannot become independent and must be returned to China.
Barrie Wiggham, the secretary for the civil service in Hong Kong, defended the British position and said that London has always argued Hong Kong's case in meetings with Chinese officials and has sought greater democracy.
Because Hong Kong will become Chinese territory in 1997, Mr. Wiggham added, it would be counterproductive to develop democratic institutions that would last only a few years. 
While democracy proponents argue that Beijing would be politically embarrassed to dismantle a democratic structure it inherited, Mr. Wiggham suggests that China might dismantle such a system anyway, and the result would be a greater blow to Hong Kong's stabilityI and confidence.
''The reality is that we live alongside China, and so there are limits to how far we can travel down that road,'' he said. 
''It was a question of how much we could achieve in Hong Kong without upsetting the system or creating instability.''

file: In Hong Kong, a New Confidence.txt
text:
ï»¿
To the list of fictional acts of derring-do attributed to the Teen-Age Mutant Ninja Turtles, the popular cartoon characters, many in this British colony now add a real feat: helping rescue the Hong Kong stock market.
The stock of the Hong Kong company that manufactures these toy characters, Playmates International Holdings, became a standout this year and helped to fuel a stock market rally.
Playmates' demonstration of entrepreneurial flair was followed by two other developments that warmed Hong Kong's chill: President Bush's decision at the end of May not to suspend China's most-favored-nation status in trade, and China's decision to permit Fang Lizhi, the dissident who fled to the United States Embassy after the military crackdown in Beijing on June 4, 1989, to emigrate to Britain. 
The move was viewed as an indicator of a more open China.
Â 
Stocks Rebound
As a result, share prices in this beleaguered capitalist enclave, which plummeted after the crackdown, have rebounded sharply. 
They rose nearly 5 percent in June. 
Today, the key market indicator, the Hang Seng index, surged to a post-crash high of 3,385, up more than 44 percent from the period a year ago.
Many in Hong Kong still expect the worst when China regains control over Hong Kong in 1997. 
But resilient entrepreneurs here interpreted the success of the pizza-munching turtles as a sign that there are opportunities in the short time left to do what they do best: make money.
Playmates International is among the stock market's hottest performers. 
Its stock closed at $14.40 a share (Hong Kong) today, or $1.84 in United States currency, up from $1.60 (Hong Kong) at the beginning of the year.
''That was when Hong Kong started to feel good about itself again,'' Eric A. Rasmussen, an economist here for Jardine Fleming Broking, a regional securities firm, said of Playmates' success. 
''People felt they could still do it.''
Nonetheless, he added, ''One shock from a stupid move from China and the market could drop right through the floor.''
Â 
A Different Kind of Rally
He and several other economists also pointed out that this rally in Hong Kong has been different from others. 
The money fueling it is coming primarily from Hong Kong and other Asian investors, including Taiwan and Japanese institutions. 
Western capital has played a less important role than in the past.
These changes make Hong Kong less of a financial bridge between the West and Asia, its traditional role, and more of a regional hub. 
''Hong Kong has become more of an Asian financial center rather than a global financial center,'' said Alan A. McLean, chief economist at the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, the colony's dominant financial institution.
Much of the investment in Hong Kong is going into factories that take advantage of China's low wages. 
Hong Kong's economy has been slowly merging with that of neighboring Guangdong Province in China, economists say. 
For instance, two million Chinese work in Hong Kong-run factories on the mainland, Mr. McLean said, nearly triple the 780,000 who work in factories in the colony. 
More than 80 percent of Hong Kong's re-exports, the fastest-growing sector of the territory's trade, are coming from or going to China. 
A re-export is merchandise imported and then shortly exported to a third country, usually with new packaging and in only slightly altered form.
Â 
Tourism Hurt
But these links cannot counter the pessimism many in Hong Kong feel when they consider life under Communist rule. 
Stung by the harsh face the Chinese Government showed in last year's crackdown, Hong Kong's economy posted no growth in the first half of this year, and inflation is close to double-digit levels. 
Tourism and hotel occupancy are down significantly.
More than 1,000 people a week are emigrating from Hong Kong, in part to avoid living under Communist rule, causing a serious brain drain. 
Now there is a worry that commercial fraud, already a problem, may flourish as many accountants depart.
Improbable as it may seem, these serious problems have not completely squelched the territory's economic spirit. 
Nearly every conversation in Hong Kong is interrupted by the sound of jackhammers or other construction equipment as old buildings fall and new ones go up at a furious pace.
From the top of the new 70-story Bank of China tower, the famous harbor looks like a spoiled child's bathtub full of toys. 
The water last week was jammed with ferries, lighters, tugs, dozens of container vessels and an American aircraft carrier.
Making the best of a bad situation, one company has even been marketing Rice Paddy Babies, toy dolls dressed up as Chinese and described as Hong Kong residents seeking to emigrate and looking for ''sponsors.''
The stock market's sudden surge is regarded as similarly opportunistic. 
''We have been surprised by the strength of the market,'' said Mr. McLean of the Hongkong Bank. 
''We thought it would take the whole year to get back where it is.''
Â 
Many Are Cautious
Pleased as many are with the market's new life, there remains an unmistakable undercurrent of caution.
''It's a difficult feeling to come to grips with,'' said Philip L. Tose, chairman of Peregrine Capital Ltd., a merchant bank. 
''Sure, things are bubbly on the surface, but you crack that surface and just underneath there are real problems. 
Confidence today is very shallow. 
We are going to have more shocks in Hong Kong.''
Mr. Tose is among those who have benefited most from Hong Kong's revival. 
He founded Peregrine with some partners in January 1989 after leaving the securities unit here of Citicorp. 
The company weathered the stock crash after the June 4 crackdown in China, and went on to conclude two takeovers and several asset sales, reaping tens of millions of dollars in windfall profits and a listing on the Hong Kong stock market.
''We've made much, much more money than we thought we would,'' Mr. Tose acknowledged. 
''Frankly, luck is better than brains. 
But there's still a lot to do here.''
He added: ''Everyone was deeply shocked by what happened last June, and that won't go away. 
People are skeptical now, but on the whole they want to stay here. 
Hong Kong is a great place to do business.''
Â 
Trading Status Stressed
Many also emphasize the importance of President Bush's decision on China's trading status in rebuilding confidence in Hong Kong. 
There had been pressure on the United States to suspend favored-nation status for China because of the country's reported human rights violations. 
Many members of Congress, which must confirm the President's decision, still express those concerns.
The most-favored-nation listing sharply reduces tariffs and duties charged on products originating in China. 
Since so much of China's trade flows through the colony or is produced in Hong Kong-owned factories, a crimp in China's exports to the United States would have hit hard here.
What heartened many was the role Hong Kong played in the Administration's decision. 
''Were it not for Hong Kong, most people would have been in favor of suspension,'' said Representative Stephen J. Solarz, Democrat of Brooklyn, who held hearings on the matter in Congress and was in Hong Kong last week.
''For the first time since last June 4, we believe Beijing saw Hong Kong as a political asset, not just an economic asset,'' added John Kamm, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, which fought to keep the favored-trade status for China.
But perhaps the most comforting aspect of the decision was that it suggested that politics was taking a back seat to basic economic interests, analysts here said.
''The real question for people here is whether they feel China or the United States will be pragmatic,'' said Mr. Rasmussen, the economist. 
''They don't trust ideologies.''

text:

CHINA'S CRISIS, CHINA'S HOPE
By Liu Binyan.
Harvard University, $22.50.
"Things are seldom what they seem," goes a song in "H.M.S. 
Pinafore," and no one should know that better than Liu Binyan, a former reporter for the Chinese Communist Party newspaper, People's Daily. 
Mr. Liu was one of the intellectuals expelled from the party in 1987; his longtime criticism of official corruption had made him a hero to many of his readers. 
He was repeatedly refused permission to travel to the United States to accept invitations tendered through the Nieman Foundation at Harvard University. 
Yet he was allowed to accept a 1988 invitation. 
Why?
Mr. Liu thinks this reflected, even in so small a gesture, a fundamental transformation in China -- the will of the people growing as a political force, despite party policies, aged leaders and political events. 
The essays in "China's Crisis, China's Hope" (nicely translated by Howard Goldblatt) are based on lectures Mr. Liu gave at Harvard's Fairbank Center for East Asian Research in 1988 and 1989, before the death of the Communist Party General Secretary Hu Yaobang, the eruption of the democracy movement and the June 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre. 
The author has included two additional essays and a preface written after those events, assessing the great changes he sees in Chinese society and politics. 
His picture is not overly rosy. 
China faces serious problems -- its arable land, for example, has decreased by 50 percent since 1949 -- and even the eventual removal from power of the current leadership will be only one step forward. 
Despite Mr. Liu's pessimism, the underlying sense of these essays is one of optimism for "the flood that is China's reforms."

file: India Is Reportedly Ready to Test Missile With Range of 1,500 Miles.txt
text:
ï»¿
Indian scientists are preparing to test a long-range ballistic missile that would vastly enhance the country's military and political power, Indian and Western military experts say.
The officials said the test, to take place somewhere in Orissa or Andhra Pradesh states, was expected early this month. 
Western specialists said the Indian missile, called the Agni, would have a range of up to 1,500 miles and a payload of one ton.
The apparent success of the Indian program comes despite efforts by the United States and its allies to restrict the export of technology and goods to countries that might use the technology to buy or develop nuclear missiles.
Experimental, India Says
Indian scientists involved in the project said it was experimental. 
''The current strategic situation between India and its neighbors hasn't pushed us into this technology,'' an Indian defense scientist said. 
''The decision was taken years ago to build up an infrastructure for missile technology.''
Nonetheless, the move is seen as an effort to assert India's military dominance in the region and to show its determination to play a more prominent role in the world.
If India were successfully to develop a ballistic missile with a range of 1,500 miles, it would join a small group of countries with such capabilities. 
The nations with medium- and long-range ballistic missiles are the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France, China, Israel and Saudi Arabia. 
An Israeli Weapon Israel has tested the Jericho 2 missile, with an estimated range of 900 miles. 
Saudi Arabia bought the DF-3 missile, with a range of 1,200 miles, from China. 
Some third world countries have developed or bought shorter-range missiles. 
Those nations include Syria, Iran, Iraq and Egypt.
Last week, William H. Webster, the Director of Central Intelligence, predicted that 15 developing nations would be producing ballistic missiles by the year 2000, including North Korea, Argentina and Syria. 
He said the production was part of a worrisome trend that included the development of chemical and biological weapons in the third world.
Last year, India successfully launched the Prithvi, a short-range surface-to-surface missile with a range of 150 miles. 
The missile is described as a tactical weapon that can be fired from behind battlefronts into enemy lines. 
India has a separate civilian space program that is being assisted by the United States and France.
India has said it will not use nuclear warheads on its new rockets.
Â 
Pakistan's Program
Last January, Pakistan tested two short-range missiles built with Chinese assistance. 
Some Western experts say Pakistan may have developed the missile with technology from Western commercial rockets.
Western nations have pushed for guidelines that would prevent the West from aiding the development of long-range ballistic missiles that can carry nuclear warheads. 
Some Western experts say India has used technology from its space rockets, technology that predates the Western controls, to develop the weapon.
Defense officials said the test-launching would be a demonstration of India's military capabilities. 
They said they were aware that it could draw sharp reactions from the United States and its allies as well as India's neighbors, including Pakistan and China. 
China is far ahead of India in nuclear technology and missile production.
The Indian missile is to be fired into the Bay of Bengal from a military base and ''final checks are on,'' said a top official at the Indian Defense Ministry.
So far, about $300 million has reportedly been spent for the missile research program.
India says it has developed short- and long-range missile technology on its own, and without Soviet assistance, although India buys Soviet military hardware. 
Several smaller systems used for the Prithvi and for short-range missiles are imported from Western nations, including the United States.
India has declined to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, saying the treaty discriminates against poorer nations. 
It has said that it is committed to a peaceful nuclear program, although officials say it has the capability to produce atomic weapons.
Western nuclear experts say New Delhi has a secret atomic weapons program, a charge that India has strongly denied.

file: Industrial Countries to Aid Poorer Nations on Ozone.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Western industrialized countries and Japan agreed today to help developing nations adhere to a worldwide ban on a class of chemicals that is destroying the protective layer of ozone in the atmosphere.
They fell short of establishing a special international fund urged by China, India and a group of other developing countries, but did not exclude the possibility and ordered a report for consideration at an ozone conference in London next year.
Earlier this week, 80 nations adopted a declaration agreeing to phase out the production and consumption of chlorofluorocarbons by the end of the century. 
The chemicals, used in refrigerators, air conditioners and industrial solvents, rise into the atmosphere, where sunlight breaks them down. 
The resulting compounds destroy the ozone layer, which protects the earth from the sun's damaging ultraviolet radiation.
Scientific evidence presented to the conference, the first meeting of 37 signers of the 1987 Montreal Protocol on protection of the ozone layer, indicated that its destruction will continue to accelerate for decades, even if the whole world bans chlorofluorocarbons.
Â 
Waiting Seen as Unacceptable
As a result, increased ultraviolet radiation at the earth's surface will cause ''tens of millions of cases of skin cancer, cataracts and, possibly, serious immunological disease,'' 90 environment groups said in a statement.
In addition, they and many government officials pointed out, even the best available substitutes for the ozone-destroying gases will continue adding to the global warming effect, in which increasing levels of carbon dioxide and other gases combine with moisture to trap heat inside the earth's atmosphere, causing climate changes and a global rise in sea levels.
The participants agreed with Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain, who said last week that waiting and seeing is no longer an acceptable environmental policy. 
But what can be done, and to what effect, was far less clear.
Â 
Special Fund Urged
The Indian delegate, Ambassador Kalarickal P. Fabian, and the Chinese representative, Wang Yangzu, were among those urging the wealthier countries, which produce most of the 700,000 tons of chlorofluorocarbons used every year, to establish a special international fund to help developing nations acquire new technology themselves, instead of having to buy expensive modified refrigerators, air-conditioners, and silicon-chip factories from the West.
Neither India nor China has signed the Montreal Protocol, though Mr. Fabian said India was considering it and China helped draft the compromise resolution on aid to developing countries.
But, attending as observers, they agreed with representatives of more than 80 other countries, including the 36 that have ratified the Montreal Protocol, on the need for a ban on chlorofluorocarbons rather than the protocol's 50 percent cut in five of the substances by 1996.
The agreement does not cover carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform, used as cleaning solvents and fumigants, or require a phase-out of halon gases, used as fire extinguishers.
Â 
Severe Effects of Ozone
In 1987 British scientists found that 97.5 percent of the ozone above the South Pole had been eliminated during winter there. 
Similar but less severe effects have been observed over the North Pole, and scientists fear the northern latitudes between 40 and 60 degrees, where most of Europe and Canada and part of the United States lie, could be similarly vulnerable.
Even if the world does stop using all chlorofluorocarbons by the end of the century, it is estimated that the amount of chlorine compounds in the atmosphere will keep rising over the next 100 years. 
Unless other measures are taken, it would reach nearly four times its present level by 2100, according to a new study by the United States Environmental Protection Agency that was presented to the delegates.
Eileen Claussen, a deputy assistant administrator of the agency, said the study showed that other chemicals that deplete ozone, especially carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform, would also have to be universally replaced by safer substitutes to start a decline in chlorine compounds in the stratosphere.
