file: INFERNO IN CHINA_ FINALLY THE RAINS CAME.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE GREAT BLACK DRAGON FIRE 1
A Chinese Inferno.
By Harrison E. Salisbury.
Illustrated. 180 pp. 
Boston:
Little, Brown & Company. 
$17.95.
In terms of sheer destruction and ecological damage, the fires that swept the Hinggan forests of Manchuria and Siberia in May 1987 rank as one of the worst environmental disasters of this or any other century. 
The fires were more than 10 times the size of last year's fires in Yellowstone National Park. 
Yet little is known about them outside China and official circles in the Soviet Union. 
Even among experts, there is only sketchy information on possibly the world's largest forest fires in the past 300 years, conflagrations that blackened an area almost the size of New England.
Harrison E. Salisbury, the distinguished former New York Times correspondent and the author of, among other books, ''The Long March: The Untold Story,'' is one of the few foreigners to have visited the remote, devastated region. 
''The Great Black Dragon Fire'' is the sobering story of a catastrophe whose full impact has yet to be measured or understood. 
The Chinese are convinced that the fires affected their climate, and there has been speculation that they may have further damaged the fragile ozone layer.
The Greater Hinggan Forest was the world's largest stand of evergreens, stretching like a green velvet sea, approximately 500 miles long and 300 miles wide. 
It is bisected by the Heilongjiang, or Black Dragon, River (known in the West by its Russian name, the Amur), which forms the border between Chinese Manchuria and Soviet Siberia. 
Before the fires, the Manchurian part of the forest accounted for a third of China's timber reserves.
There had been a prolonged period of dry weather, and the danger of fire was high on both sides of the river in the spring of 1987. 
From Mr. Salisbury's description, it would seem that the Chinese fire prevention and detection methods and firefighting resources were primitive by American and Canadian standards. 
Despite the hazardous condition, people smoked in the forest, built campfires and used unsafe logging practices. 
From natural and accidental causes, a number of fires broke out about the same time in Manchuria and Siberia, quickly consolidating into several large ones.
One known cause was Wang Yufeng, an 18-year-old who was temporarily working as a brush cutter. 
Ironically, brush cutting is done to reduce the danger of fire, but the inexperienced teen-ager violated every safety rule and, as Mr. Salisbury notes, became a modern Chinese version of Mrs. O'Leary's cow. 
He overfilled his machine, spilling gas, which ignited from an engine spark and set the machine and the grass on fire. 
It jumped to the trees and flashed into a raging inferno that destroyed the town of Xilinji. 
(The hapless young man was whisked off to jail even as the alarms were sounding.) Thus began one of the largest Black Dragon fires. 
The monthlong battle was fought by Chinese Army troops, the local inhabitants and what appears to have been a small number of professional firefighters. 
Missing were the battalions of trained forest firefighters who are deployed in the American West and specialized apparatus, effective communications and airplanes that drop fire-retardant chemicals. 
There was no contact between the Chinese and Soviet commands that were fighting fires on each side of the river.
Mr. Salisbury's interviews with the people involved reveal the strength of the human spirit when faced with overwhelming tragedy. 
There were some notable cowards and incompetents, but there were more heroes. 
Most of the inhabitants of the Manchurian timber towns did the best they could as the fiery monster devoured their homes and livelihood and killed their families and neighbors. 
No one really knows how many died, but Mr. Salisbury believes the official Chinese report of only 250 is far below the actual toll.
As the Mayor of Xilinji, Wang Zhaowin took firm command, anticipated the tricks of the wind and saved thousands of lives by evacuating her people from the river - where they would have been trapped - to an open road junction. 
Incredibly, 18,000 people huddled at the crossroads as flames fanned by a 40-mile-an-hour wind engulfed the town. 
(Later, her bitter reward was to be relieved of her job by the provincial government.) The Black Dragon fires burned until it rained in early June. 
When they were over, China had lost more than three million acres of timber. 
The total damage is estimated at more than $4 billion. 
The long-range environmental impact has yet to be calculated, but the outlook is grim. 
It could be several generations before the dominant larch evergreens grow again, and the Hinggan forest may never be the same.
One can only guess at what happened on the other side of the river in Siberia. 
Between 9 million and 15 million acres are believed to have burned there - at least three times larger than the area destroyed in Manchuria. 
Despite glasnost, there has been no report from the Russians. 
What may have been the greatest forest fire in history remains a nonevent in the Soviet Union.
Mr. Salisbury's book penetrates some of that secrecy and provides a fascinating look at a remote pocket of the world. 
It is also a dramatic and compassionate account of the people who live there and the disaster that befell them. 
And ''The Great Black Dragon Fire'' is another warning to everyone who is concerned about what is happening to planet Earth.

file: International Bankers Told of Soviet Reforms.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Supreme Soviet is about to take up legislation giving the State Bank of the U.S.S.R., or Gosbank, authority to issue foreign-exchange licenses to domestic banks, Yuri Ponomorev, a board member of the bank, said at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank here today.
The Soviet Union is still not a member of the global lending institutions 45 years after their founding, but Mr. Ponomorev's attendance at these meetings is seen as in keeping with the perestroika, or restructuring, put in place by Mikhail S. Gorbachev. As one of his country's top bankers, Mr. Ponomorev has offered new details on Soviet banking reforms to finance officials from 152 countries as well as to thousands of commercial bankers who have been here for the weeklong meeting, which ended today.
The moves envisioned would enable many more Soviet institutions to handle their own currency transactions and provide new opportunities for Western financial institutions in the Soviet Union, Mr. Ponomorev said.
GATT Membership Sought
The Soviet Union wants to join the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and although Moscow was rebuffed when it initially applied in 1986, most analysts here see GATT membership remaining a high Soviet priority.
Ed A. Hewett, a Soviet affairs specialist at the Brookings Institution, noted that Moscow is making numerous changes in its way of doing business and could approach GATT as a market economy, as Hungary did in the early 1970's.
While Moscow has not yet applied to either the I.M.F. or the World Bank, it has been closely following the experience of two of its neighbors that are members, Poland and China, which are using the organizations to advance their own domestic economic reforms.
Poland has used the meeting here to mobilize international assistance. 
The Governor of the People's Bank of China, Li Guixian, said at the meeting that his country's annual average growth had reached 9.6 percent in the last 10 years since it joined the institutions, compared with 7.1 percent from 1952 to 1988. 
He said membership in the world organizations had ''injected vitality and dynamism into the Chinese economy.''
China has been a substantial borrower from both the bank and the fund. 
Until June, when a violent crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing led the World Bank to suspend seven loans, China had borrowed $7.64 billion from the World Bank since 1980. 
In addition, China has taken two loans from the I.M.F., one for $600 million and the other for $500 million.
Â 
Smaller Countries Joined
Although the Soviet Union was part of the postwar discussions at Bretton Woods, N.H., that led to the formation of the I.M.F. and World Bank, Moscow pulled out and has remained outside organizations that manage financial relations among capitalist countries. 
But smaller Communist countries, like Yugoslavia, Poland, Hungary and Rumania, have joined the organizations to try to give a lift to their economies. 
Now Mr. Gorbachev insists he wants to reintegrate the Soviet economy into the world economy.
''We think the Soviets want to come into a more cooperative posture,'' Barber B. Conable Jr., president of the World Bank, said at a news conference.
Michel Camdessus, managing director of the I.M.F., acknowledged at another news conference that Soviet membership could produce ''a world that is less dangerous and more stable,'' although he added, ''For me it is very difficult to enter into hypothetical scenarios.''
Â 
Opposition Called Softening
The United States continues to oppose Soviet membership in GATT as well as the bank and the I.M.F., although some Administration officials say that Washington's opposition to GATT membership is softening.
The main fears are that once in the international organizations, the Soviet Union would prove obstructionist, possibly reneging on repayment obligations to the fund and bank and packing the institutions with ideological Soviet staff members.
''Soviet participation in international economic institutions will be one big headache for everyone,'' said Senator Bill Bradley, Democrat of New Jersey, at a forum here held in connection with the annual meeting.
Others contend there could also be benefits, including a strengthening of the agencies' claim to be truly universal bodies.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_Airport Project Shows Hong Kong_s Unease.txt
text:
ï»¿
As planes land at Kai Tak airport here, they swoosh down close enough to the windows of buildings to make passengers feel like peeping Toms.
So it is not surprising there is widespread agreement that a new airport is needed. 
But as the Hong Kong Government moves into the detailed planning stages for a $16.2 billion replacement airport, the project is beginning to symbolize the kinds of problems emerging as Britain prepares to hand over Hong Kong to China in 1997.
Even though the airport will be one of the largest and most intricate construction projects in the world, Britain and China have not been cooperating. 
Critics worry that if the two Governments cannot work together to plan and finance something as basic as an airport, the transition to Chinese rule will be difficult indeed.
The most crucial element to the project's success is the endorsement of the Beijing Government, which will inherit the airport. 
Beijing was apparently not officially consulted in planning the venture. 
So far, Chinese officials have been cagey about their views. 
Indeed, they have expressed a deep concern that after Britain builds the project, they will be stuck with the bill - a large debt package without the money to pay it off.
''I think China has a right to be angry,'' said Martin C. M. Lee, a prominent lawyer and legislator in Hong Kong. 
''The airport is clearly something that can't go ahead without their support.''
The British have chosen 1997 as the date when the first of the new airport's two runways will open. 
Many business executives here say they think the British set an unusually tight schedule to meet that deadline in building a modern airport in what is now an expanse of water near Chek Lap Kok island about 17 miles from downtown Hong Kong.
Still, many economists and financial analysts say the project, announced last year just a few months after the military crackdown June 3 and 4 in Beijing, will significantly help the local economy in the years before the Beijing takeover. 
Construction companies, technical and engineering consultants and financial firms already are lining up for a piece of the business.
''Because of June 4, domestic confidence was pretty low,'' said C. K. Law, a senior economist at Bankers Trust Securities (Pacific) Ltd. 
''Then the Government thought it had to do something to prop up confidence -like build an airport.''
Â 
More Than Just an Airport
Actually, plans call for much more than just an airport. 
The overall project will include the world's longest single-span suspension bridge, a high-speed railway, two port terminals and numerous expressways and transportation links.
Kai Tak airport is expected to reach capacity by the mid-1990's. 
The Government began an analysis of the need for a new airport nearly a decade ago, but shelved the plans when the economy went into recession and London and Beijing began talks on the question of Hong Kong's future.
Now Hong Kong is moving with a sense of urgency and determination, having formed a management team that will include Government and outside consultants, as well as a newly formed provisional airport authority.
With plans under way, many engineering and development experts are skeptical that the series of projects can be finished within budget and on schedule. 
And some critics still object to the location, timing and cost.
Moreover, the scale and the number of parties involved will turn the projects into a giant, intricate jigsaw puzzle: all the pieces must fit together before they can form anything.
To get to the new airport, about nine times the distance from downtown Hong Kong as the current airport, passengers will take a high-speed rail line to cross three land masses and two waterways. 
Since the suspension bridge will be the only means to cross the main water channel, it must be finished before the airport can be used, and likewise, the railway must be finished before the vast majority of the public can get to the airport.
Â 
Financial Challenges
''The problem is time and money,'' said David R. Butler, a partner at Scott Wilson, Kirkpatrick & Partners, consulting engineers who are involved in building an expressway that can help serve as an airport link. 
''If it were just one engineer building it with a pot of gold, it wouldn't be a problem. 
Clearly, there are so many other people involved besides the Government. 
It'll be a massive organizational task.''
One fear is that the project will drain Government reserves, which now exceed $9 billion, and the benefit will go mainly to British and foreign contractors and consulting firms. 
So far, the major consulting contracts have gone to British or American companies.
The Government has said it would try to raise 40 to 60 percent of the financing, both direct investment and loans, from private sources, and the rest by digging into its own pockets or by public borrowing. 
Since it rarely borrows long-term money, the Hong Kong Government has a strong credit rating and should not have trouble raising cash in the financial markets.
While financial institutions, particularly Japanese ones, have expressed interest, raising such large sums of money without assurances from China will not be an easy task. 
The Government ultimately hopes the Chinese will help finance the project, either directly or indirectly.
''The greatest challenges are the finances,'' said Malcolm F. Williams, director at Kleinwort Benson Ltd., a British firm hired by the Government as financial adviser for the main airport links, including the railway. 
Mr. Williams would not estimate how much could be raised privately. 
He did say that equity investments would more likely come from corporate airport users like airlines or project contractors, rather than from third parties.
With the cost of building the main bridge alone estimated at $2.3 billion, some analysts say the price of a train ride to the airport could be $20, more than double the cost of taxi fare now to the current airport.
Â 
International Competition
Projecting how well the new airport may do in terms of air traffic and revenues is complicated. 
Substantial returns will not begin until the airport has been operating for some time, and by then, it will be in the hands of the Chinese Government. 
There also will be competition from international airports being built in nearby Macao and in Shenzhen, China.
China is evaluating the project and is said to have investigated cheaper alternative sites, including one suggested by a group of academics and another by Gordon Y. S. Wu, managing director of Hopewell Holdings Ltd., a large construction company. 
The Hong Kong Government says it will not change the site, something that would cause a great loss of face and shake confidence in the Government.
''Everyone is looking for a perfect structure, but life is not perfect and so you have to manage the process,'' said Henry D. Townsend, consultant project manager for the Bechtel Group, the advisers on the first phase of the project. 
''Time has come to put aside all alternatives and get on with the project.''

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_China Feels The Cuts in Its Economy.txt
text:
ï»¿
Displaying the bravado and ambition that have fired China's economic growth in the last decade, this little village had originally expected to increase its industrial production by 50 percent this year.
But such high hopes are becoming dimmer here and in thousands of other villages along China's coast, where the nation's striking economic growth has been concentrated in the last decade. 
In the country's economic retrenchment, imposed after the political upheaval and bloodshed of May and June, the coastal regions stand to lose the most.
While not all will suffer real economic declines, these regions are sure to see their supercharged growth rates cool down.
Effects of Austerity Program
The nation is already feeling the effects of Beijing's general austerity program. 
In October, nationwide industrial production fell 2.1 percent, compared with October of 1988. 
That was the first such decline in a decade. 
Yet, the central Government has said the austerity program will last at least until 1991.
Officials in Beijing said they decided to re-impose stronger central economic controls to deal with inflation problems, supply-and-demand imbalances, economic inefficiencies, overinvestment in certain industries and deficiencies in others. 
The inflation rate has dropped to 8.7 percent in October from 27 percent in January. 
But some Chinese worry that the program will lower the growth rate but not necessarily raise economic efficiency.
''In theory it sounds very reasonable, but in practice it will be co-mingled with politics so that nothing will get done,'' a Chinese businessman said.
This village of 2,850 people still plans to raise its economic output, and so far the austerity program has hampered but not crippled most of the 14 factories here making everything from champagne to chemicals. 
But in the surrounding area of Qingdao, about two-thirds the way up the coast, officials expect economic growth to drop to 12 percent this year from 24 percent in 1988.
Â 
Businesses Are Closing
That pace may still seem remarkable compared with growth rates in Western countries. 
But the sudden slowdown is causing thousands of small factories and businesses to close and could lead to grave economic problems in the coastal areas.
It is difficult to gauge the economic discontent among local officials, who do not feel free to speak out, and reliable statistics are hard to come by. 
But the austerity measures are beginning to result in business closings and a reduced flow of money to support new ventures, and this is likely to increase resentment against the central Government.
Just a few years ago, growth in the coastal provinces was vigorously trumpeted as a means to infuse the rest of the economy with a new spirit.
The leaders in these areas harnessed the energy of peasants pent up over years of rigid control, and small collective enterprises cropped up throughout the countryside. 
Their work in making consumer and exportable products in thousands of small factories resulted in double-digit growth rates.
Â 
Plan of '39 Stipulations'
But since the military put down the student democracy movement last summer, and particularly after the Communist Party Central Committee met in November to discuss the economy, the Government has reinforced austerity with a blueprint of ''39 stipulations'' for the economy. 
The effect is to shore up socialist bastions in the economy: central control and state-run enterprises.
The Government announced in November that in the first nine months of this year, one million rural enterprises were shut down and several hundred thousand others halted production or were forced to switch product lines.
The casualties may even be higher. 
The official China Daily referred in passing recently to three million rural enterprises being closed. 
Part of the discrepancy may be that the larger number includes planned projects that have been canceled or postponed as well as those that have been shut down, merged or converted.
Instead of the nationwide annual growth of about 10 percent over the last decade, China's leaders want 5 to 6 percent a year.
Â 
Tight Credit Policy
They have tightened credit to bring down inflation and slow down the economy, leaving many small collective enterprises severely strapped for cash.
Recently, the Government eased credit slightly, but local officials and business managers say a prolonged lending squeeze without economic alternatives could cause the localities to stop listening to central directives. 
As they have with previous policies mandated from Beijing, local officials could prove adept at skirting obstacles.
In Liaoning Province in the northeast, about one-third of the state-run enterprises are losing money, said a Chinese businessman with access to high-level information.
Nationwide, that figure is about one-fifth. 
But Liaoning is part of China's industrial belt, with many steel plants and machinery factories, the kind the Government wants to shore up.
Â 
Payroll Problems
Some factories have even had trouble covering their monthly payroll. 
One Chinese executive said 80,000 employees in a large city in Liaoning were not being paid. 
The situation was so severe, he said, that one factory manager reportedly wept as he pleaded with a Government banker to provide a loan to pay thousands of employees.
In Shandong Province, there are clear signs that the situation is not yet as bleak as the national statistics would suggest, although the area is probably an anomaly. 
Two Party members said economic planners considered the province's economy to be among the most stable and orderly in the nation. 
They say that means the local authorities may be able to dance around the tough measures without much backlash from the central Government.
Indeed, officials in Qingdao, one of the province's two coastal regions, say that only about 165 companies -mostly medium-sized collectives -were shut down or merged, and most of them were product distributors, not manufacturers. 
Over all, Qingdao has tens of thousands of collective enterprises, which produce 70 percent of the area's output.
Â 
'Efficiency Is Important'
One of the few rural collectives closed was a brick maker in Xiaowang village, but the local officials insist the closing was based on their own economic decisions and not forced by the austerity program.
''No one told us to shut it down,'' said Sui Lishan, the village party secretary in Xiaowang. 
''Efficiency is important to us. 
The land is important to us. 
And this enterprise ate up a lot of energy and land.''
As in the past when faced with directives from Beijing, local officials here also seem adept at turning some austerity measures to their benefit.
Officials said that before the austerity program was implemented, they had planned several projects to produce energy because the supply of electricity and other energy was not enough to accommodate their plans for industrial growth. 
Now with the retrenchment, they found they could cancel some other ventures and channel money to the energy projects to insure their completion.
A result is that the growth rate in Qingdao crept up again in November, said Zhang Rui, a deputy secretary general in the municipal government.
''But we don't expect it to reach 30 percent again,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''After all, 12 percent is not that bad.''
China's coastal areas, which enjoyed striking growth in the 1980's, may be the hardest hit by the Government's economic retrenchment. 
In the Shan dong Province, however, the the situation does not seem too bleak for some manufacturers like the Number Nine Rubber Factory in Qingdao. 
(NYT/Sheryl WuDunn); map of China showing location of Xiaowang (NYT)

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_China Opens Grain Market.txt
text:
ï»¿
In one of its few efforts this year to overhaul its economy, China opened a national wheat market last week to replace central allocation of the nation's 85-million-ton annual wheat harvest.
More than 200 grain trading companies started dealing at the Wholesale Grain Market in Zhengzhou, the provincial capital of Henan, China's wheat heartland, the official New China News Agency reported.
The market's opening was delayed for two years. 
But it was ultimately allowed to proceed because it may help the Government manage grain distribution, long a serious problem.
Although the Government buys most grain grown in China, it lacks a modern storage network, and in bumper years much grain is left to rot outdoors. 
Serious shortages have occurred in some regions while others have surpluses.
China still lacks wholesale markets for the 169 million metric tons of rice, its main crop, harvested annually.
A futures market allows buyers and sellers to negotiate a price for what they think a commodity will be worth at a future date.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_China Problems That Slow Economy Are Reflected in Lag for Port Project.txt
text:
ï»¿
Perhaps the boldest single project envisioned during the last decade of China's economic restructuring was a plan to copy the success of Hong Kong, 300 miles to the northeast, here on southern China's Hainan Island.
The Yangpu Port project, as it is known, came to symbolize the vaulting aspirations of Hainan, where a chunk of land was to be leased to a foreign company for a transformation into a duty-free port and a modern city of several hundred thousand people. 
The project was the centerpiece of a broad program to promote a market economy on Hainan.
But Hainan's progress has been stalled, along with the Yangpu project. 
There are several reasons for the slowdown, but they seem to add up to the clearest example yet of how Beijing's political crackdown has spilled over into, and put a damper on, some areas of the nation's economy.
Trend to Recentralization
Foreign investment was supposed to make the difference here, but getting it depended on the central Government's willingness to allow Hainan unprecedented autonomy. 
Since the June crackdown, many foreigners say, Hainan's autonomy may be evaporating in the general trend toward a recentralization of authority.
The Yangpu project has not yet been approved by Beijing and some officials say Premier Li Peng has rejected the idea that it become a free port. 
And while some foreign investors have come to take a look, they have been reluctant to put their money down.
Worst of all for Hainan, three of the most widely known supporters of the province's bold plans - Communist Party General Secretary Zhao Ziyang; his son, Zhao Erjun, a businessman, and Hainan's Governor, Liang Xiang - have all fallen from power in the last six months.
The island still has an industrial growth rate of more than 10 percent while most of the mainland is suffering a drop in industrial output. 
But Hainan officials are coming to realize that it may be difficult to get the foreign investment the island province of 6.7 million people needs.
''The central Government gives us lots of policies, but it's short of money,'' said Jiang Wei, an economic planning official. 
''So we depend on foreign investors. 
We have lots of good projects, but we need investors to develop them.''
Hainan, an agricultural backwater, lacks the basic roads, water and communication structures to develop a modern base that will attract Western-financed export companies.
In the early 1980's, the central Government plowed enormous sums into other special economic zones, like the town of Shenzhen, next to Hong Kong, but these are times of austerity, and Beijing is giving Hainan much less money than it gave Shenzhen.
''There's been some impact since June, and development will be a bit slower,'' acknowledged Li Huiliang, a Canton native who is now running Haikou's Southyang Footwear Factory, a Taiwan- and Hong Kong-financed company that exports athletic shoes to the United States.
But Mr. Li and others here are reluctant to accept defeat. 
Mr. Li says Hainan can still prosper, given its advantages over parts of the mainland. 
There is no electricity shortage, he said, and land costs are lower here than in some other coastal areas. 
Mr. Li says his company makes a profit of 30 to 40 cents on a pair of shoes and the profit would be 20 to 30 cents a pair if they were made in Taiwan.
Â 
Headaches for Executives
Another manager of a foreign venture, Rennie Velasco, is less enthusiastic. 
Miss Velasco, who is from the Philippines and runs the Haikou Lone Star Cafe, an American-financed fast-food restaurant, said that while Hainan might prosper if it became more flexible, for now it gives foreign executives the same headaches as the rest of China. 
''It's so difficult to do business here,'' she added. 
''It's so frustrating.''
To many foreigners, still waiting to see what will happen here, the Yangpu project is a barometer of the conditions in Hainan, and these days it is not a reassuring one.
The initial plan was for Kumagai Gumi Ltd. of Hong Kong, a 35 percent-owned subsidiary of a Japanese construction company, to lease 12.5 square miles at Yangpu. 
There, on the northwest side of Hainan, the company was to develop a free port, like Hong Kong.
Kumagai Gumi was to pay for the construction of local roads, power plants, water systems and other infrastructure projects. 
Foreign companies would then be expected to swarm to the area to take advantage of the cheap labor force.
Kumagai Gumi has already paid the equivalent of $6.75 million as the first installment on its lease. 
And the province's party secretary, Xu Shijie, and other leaders all insist the Yangpu project will go through.
Â 
'Won't Be Like Hong Kong'
But local officials and foreign business executives note that the project has yet to be approved by the State Council in Beijing. 
''There must be some differences between Yangpu and the rest of Hainan, but Yangpu won't be duty-free,'' said Mr. Jiang, the economic planner. 
''It won't be like Hong Kong.''
A foreign executive close to the project said that if Beijing did not allow the area to be duty-free, it might no longer be worthwhile for foreign investors.
Despite the Yangpu uncertainty, Hainan is still trying to arrange other long-term land leases, including 21.1 square miles near Haikou. 
Ye Zhanghe, an official in the province's economic cooperation bureau, said the province wanted the area to become a recreational zone with hotels, golf courses and other resort facilities.
''Certainly there has been an influence from June 4, but it hasn't been so great,'' Mr. Ye said, referring to the day Chinese troops moved against protestors and crushed the democracy movement. 
He added that since that time more than 100 foreign companies had come to Hainan to establish businesses.
But others, Chinese officials and foreign analysts alike, have less optimistic views, noting the apparent reluctance of foreign investors to commit themselves.
In addition, some Chinese and foreigners, contending that Hainan's dreams were never realistic, note that it lacks the geographic and developmental advantages of boom economies like Guangdong Province, which adjoins Hong Kong.
One of Hainan's clear natural advantages is its southern shore, which boasts beautiful palm-lined beaches. 
If the southern coast could be developed into a winter resort, it might attract residents of Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan who now go to Thailand.
Â 
Six Hours From Beaches
But the island's only international airport is here at Haikou, six hours by car from the southern beaches, and it will probably be at least five years before an international airport is built and resorts are put along the sandy beaches.
The province acknowledges that it is relatively new to the tourism business, and there are signs that it does not perfectly understand how to promote itself to attract foreign tourists.
''The scent is not obvious, not stirring, but internal, harmonious and penetrating in the air,'' reads an account about a suggested local culinary specialty. 
''Dog meat is superb if black or brown dogs with smooth skin and short fur are used.''

text:

The cautious process of rebuilding the strained relations between the Soviet Union and China have taken another modest step forward with a report here today that the first Chinese-Soviet joint venture in China will soon be established.
The China Daily reported that the countries are close to signing an agreement to build a linen mill in the remote town of Batou, Inner Mongolia, near the Soviet border.
The mill would produce four million meters of printed linen a year from flax, the article quoted Ji Jin, an official of the Ministry of Textiles, as saying.
Nearly two dozen joint ventures between the countries are in the Soviet Union, mostly restaurants.
The chill between the Communist giants, which has lasted about 30 years, began to thaw last year with the visit here of President Mikhail S. Gorbachev. Li Peng, China's Prime Minister, made the first visit by a Chinese prime minister to Moscow in 25 years in April.
The article said the Soviets were also considering a similar project in a small town in Sichuan Province, in western China. 
Such steps would be decidedly cautious, keeping the Soviets in remote regions of the country and away from the cities.
Nonetheless, trade between China and the Soviet Union has been growing steadily, enlivening border towns that were walled off from the other side for decades.
For instance, a new highway was opened in March connecting the Chinese town of Suifenhe, in Heilongjiang Province, making it one of the country's busiest trade centers. 
Last year, the town handled a quarter of the freight passing between the countries, and enterprises throughout China and the Soviet Union have set up offices there, according to reports in The China Daily.
