file: Japanese Edgy Over Emperor_s Visit to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two days before Emperor Akihito begins the first visit to China by a Japanese monarch, Tokyo is once again consumed by a familiar battle: how to avoid apologizing for Japanese war atrocities while still appearing deeply apologetic.
From the moment the trip was first proposed by Beijing, the Government here has tied itself in knots over how to phrase Akihito's first words to a nation where millions died at the hands of the Japanese. 
Influential right-wing politicians tried to scuttle the trip altogether, protesting that the Emperor, and with him modern Japan, will be humiliated by seeming to kowtow to China.
Publicly at least, Tokyo has tried to shrug off the problem, insisting that the trip, like the Emperor himself, is apolitical. 
But few seem convinced, especially after seemingly conflicting statements by the top officials dispatched to put their spin on the Emperor's comments.
On Tuesday, the Foreign Ministry's chief spokesman, Masamichi Hanabusa, told reporters that the Emperor "is not on a mission to make an apology."
That was all taken care of 20 years ago, he said, when the two countries resumed diplomatic relations.
Koichi Kato, the chief Cabinet secretary, who is reportedly presiding over the last-minute honing of the Emperor's every utterance, said, "The purpose of the Emperor's visit to China is not to issue a new apology," adding that Akihito would "invoke previous statements."
That was interpreted as a reference to past expressions of "regret" whose vagueness has angered many Asians, who say the comments typify Japan's continuing inability to face up to its past.
The Emperor's comments are the subject of particular scrutiny because of the tremendous symbolism: in the 2,000-year history of the monarchy, no emperor has been to China.
But despite the efforts by the Government to portray the trip as a mission of good will, it has been attacked by both the left and the right.
"The Chinese intend to reconstruct a bilateral relationship favorable to them by starting from 'the past,' " Seiichi Eto, a conservative member of the ruling party's delegation in the lower house of Parliament, wrote in a popular magazine recently. 
"We cannot disregard the worry that this kind of Chinese attitude could lead to a surge of antagonism and hatred in the Japanese public against China."
There is already considerable speculation that the right wing may try to force Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa from office if Akihito is viewed as paying homage to the Chinese.
"This whole trip is planned for the sake of China, not for Japan," said Toshiro Mayuzumi, a prominent composer who has led an opposition movement against the trip. 
"Japan did not invade China. 
It fought for the liberation of Asia. 
It is absolutely improper to send the Emperor to apologize."
Opponents on the other end of the spectrum have protested that Japan is legitimizing the authoritarian Government in Beijing and ignoring human-rights issues to placate its neighbor.
Akihito, of course, will refer specifically to none of that. 
In the post-war traditions of the royal family, the Emperor must remain studiously apolitical while still setting a tone, if not an agenda, for the nation. 
The Constitution specifies which acts he is supposed to carry out in Japan's name; none of them, strict constitutionalists point out, include missions to foreign nations.
The unknown factor, of course, is whether the Emperor himself feels moved to say something beyond Japan's usually elliptical references to the war. 
When Akihito ascended to the throne in January 1989, many expected that he would set a very different tone. 
Freed of the questions of responsibility that followed Hirohito to his grave, it seemed he would have a far freer hand to erase the trail of enmity that Japan had left throughout Asia.
But at a small news conference at the palace last week for reporters who will be traveling with him, the Emperor barely budged from his father's parlance. 
Speaking slowly and deliberately, he noted that "in recent times there was a period of unfortunate history" between the two countries.

file: Japanese Say Their Country Has Sold Its Soul.txt
text:
ï»¿
Japan's postwar mistake has been selling its soul to the West along with its cars and computers, several Japanese novelists and critics told an international literary conference here this week.
''With prosperity, the economic miracle, has come cultural and spiritual degeneration,'' said Masao Miyoshi, a critic and professor of literature at the University of California at San Diego, who moderated a panel of Japanese writers on Monday. 
''Japan has surrendered to Western cultural hegemony. 
We are represented in industry but not in cultural matters.''
The same point was made more informally by the novelist Kenzaburo Oe, a perennial candidate for the Nobel Prize. 
''You know why Honda is great,'' Mr. Oe told his American dinner companions at a gathering that opened the conference. 
''But we don't care about Honda. 
We care that our cultural life is unknown to you.''
Â 
A Shift in Focus
The panel discussion, one of a dozen here this week at the War Memorial and Performing Arts Center, was part of the Wheatland Foundation's fourth annual conference on world literature, which until this year has been dominated by Central European and Soviet writers. 
But in this most Asian of American cities, the conference organizers shifted the focus and, for the first time, invited novelists, poets, playwrights and essayists from Japan, South Korea, China and Southeast Asia.
The Chinese panel, scheduled for Thursday, is expected to be the most provacative because of last year's massacre in Tiananmen Square. 
Most of the participating Chinese writers, all living in exile, are members of the younger generation, but they were joined here by Liu Binyan, the eminent journalist who has twice been expelled from the Communist Party.
The Japanese panel was considered the most distinguished assemblage of the week, with several of the country's foremost writers. 
Among them were Mr. Oe, whose books include ''A Personal Matter'' and ''Teach Us to Outgrow Our Madness,''and Yuko Tsushima, daughter of the prominent novelist Osamu Dazai, who committed suicide shortly after World War II. 
Ms. Tsushima's novels include ''Child of Fortune'' and ''The Shooting Gallery.''
Â 
Prize for Translation
Mr. Oe's work is distinguished by twists of syntax and sentence structure more common in English and the European languages than in Japanese, said Van C. Gessel, a professor of Japanese literature at the University of California at Berkeley, who attended the conference. 
Ms. Tsushima's novels, he said, are full of the mundane details of domestic life and grapple with the struggles of a divorced mother in a country that is harsh on nonconforming women. 
Later in the week, Ms. Tsushima's translator, Geraldine Harcourt, will be awarded the Wheatland Foundation's translation prize, which has previously gone to Arpad Goncz, the new interim President of Hungary.
The Wheatland Foundation was established in 1984 by Ann Getty, the philanthropist who is married to the heir to the Getty oil fortune, and Lord Weidenfeld, the British publisher. 
Together, Mrs. Getty and Lord Weidenfeld bought Grove Press in 1985, subsequently losing millions of dollars. 
They put the publishing house on the market and found out last month that it was virtually unsalable because of its liabilities. 
Mrs. Getty lives here in San Francisco in a lemon yellow stucco mansion with sweeping views of the bay and is the hostess at the city's grandest dinner parties.
Â 
The Getty Touch
Mrs. Getty's touch was evident at the conference, held in the Green Room of the War Memorial and Performing Arts Center, a high ceilinged chamber that opens onto a stone loggia overlooking City Hall. 
It was here, in brilliant spring sunshine, that conference participants nibbled chocolate-dipped strawberries during the breaks between panel discussions.
The discussions, more often than not, left participants yawning, whispering among themselves like school children or trying to sneak a look at the baseball box scores without rustling the newspaper. 
But occasionally sparks flew, as they did when Mr. Oe made it clear that he did not think much of Yukio Mishima, Japan's most famous postwar novelist, who committed hara-kiri after a failed attempt to take over a military base.
Mr. Oe argued that Mishima shaped his life to ''live up to the image of Japan created by Europeans.''
Mishima's decision to die in the ''traditional way,'' Mr. Oe said, was the final proof of his ''perverted relationship with the image of Japan'' and ''a great betrayal of his fellow Asians.''
This incensed Pierre Mertens of Belgium, a novelist and lawyer who writes frequently about war crimes and totalitarianism. 
''Mishima is accepted in other countries as a great writer,'' Mr. Mertens sputtered into his microphone, calming himself with a sip of cool water. 
''I don't think the Japanese have a right to decide he's not a great writer. 
And once we've thrown the suicides out of literature, what happens to Primo Levi?
We'll be getting into cultural genocide before too long.''
Â 
Two Confessions
While Mr. Oe lamented that Japanese writers are too obeisant to the West, rather than ''turning our eyes to the Asian literature,'' his life and career follow the same pattern. 
He was 10 when the war ended and vividly recalls the truck full of American soldiers who rolled into his village with chocolate bars and chewing gum, copies of ''The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'' and ''Black Beauty'' and volumes of Walt Whitman and William Butler Yeats.
''This was the beginning of my literary life,'' Mr. Oe said, dipping his head apologetically. 
He went on to study French literature at Tokyo University and write a thesis about Sartre.
Ms. Tsushima, too, offered a contrite explanation for a lifetime spent reading Western literature in translation rather than indigenous Japanese works. 
''Women seemed so free and liberated in the foreign literature,'' she said. 
''There were very few books written by Japanese women and to read them made me feel I was going back to the olden days. 
That aspect within me has changed recently.''

file: Japan_s Emperor Tells China Only of His _Sadness_ on War.txt
text:
ï»¿
Emperor Akihito, opening the first visit to China by a Japanese monarch, acknowledged today that Japan's wartime occupation had "inflicted great suffering on the people of China," but he stopped short of the apology demanded by a growing number of Chinese.
The Emperor's statement, made shortly after his arrival, unambiguously placed the blame on Japan for its wartime aggression, marking the clearest acceptance ever by Tokyo of responsibility for its conduct in the 1931 seizure of Manchuria, the 1937 invasion of China and the brutal occupation that followed.
But the statement was also consistent with the position of the Japanese Government that no outright apology for Japanese actions was necessary. 
In addition, many prominent right-wing political groups in Japan had opposed issuing any kind of an apology on the Emperor's trip.
At a banquet tonight in the Great Hall of the People, the first of many to be held for the Emperor and his wife, Empress Michiko, the Emperor said: "In the long history of relationships between our two countries, there was an unfortunate period in which my country inflicted great suffering on the people of China. 
About this I feel deep sadness."
The Chinese authorities refused to say whether they considered the comments satisfactory. 
"It is up to the Japanese side to decide what remarks the Emperor will make during his visit to China," said Wu Jianmin, spokesman for the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
Â 
Beijing Seeks Economic Aid
The Emperor's arrival here, hailed by both countries as the first such visit in their 2,000-year relationship, was accompanied by a 21-gun salute and military bands that sent the strains of Japan's anthem once again wafting across Tiananmen Square. 
Eager for economic help and international recognition, Chinese officials said the visit represented "a new stage in relations."
The Japanese Government clearly hopes for the same, broadcasting videos on Chinese television this week to introduce Akihito as the symbol of a new, peace-loving and technologically advanced Japan.
The trip also has great import diplomatically. 
China is worried that Washington will take a harder line against Beijing on human rights issues if Gov. Bill Clinton is elected President, and it wants to show its appreciation for Japan's support while other countries have expressed disapproval.
Japan, on the other hand, is increasingly worried about signs of growing Chinese military strength and wants to improve the climate for greater economic and political cooperation with Beijing.
Â 
Limits on the Emperor
According to the Japanese Constitution, the Emperor has no independent powers and all of his statements on sensitive matters are prepared by the elected Government and the Foreign Ministry bureaucracy, which have made it clear that they hope his six-day visit will increase popular support for Japanese-Chinese friendship.
In recent months, the Japanese business community has become convinced that China's economic reforms are real and has revived its interest in investing in China. 
A consortium of Japan's biggest trading companies announced just before the Emperor's departure for Beijing that it was considering a $4 billion investment in a petrochemical complex in China, and other companies are investing heavily.
But the war issue always threatens to create strains, with some signs that Chinese popular animosity toward Japan has even increased. 
Indeed, there is a widespread feeling throughout East Asia that Japan has been slow to face its militaristic past.
Â 
Rejects Reparations for Women
In recent years, the Chinese have protested things like the way the war is described in Japanese textbooks, visits by Japanese political leaders to a shrine for Japanese war heroes and statements by some Japanese politicians that China has exaggerated the number of people killed in the war.
In recent months, Chinese feelings were inflamed by Japan's refusal to pay reparations to the families of Chinese and Korean women who have come forward after decades to silence to say that they were kidnapped during the war and forced to provide sex to Japanese troops.
Japan maintains that it settled the issue of the war with China in 1972, when it established diplomatic relations with Beijing. 
At that time, China dropped its demand for reparations but cleared the way for large amounts of investment and trade.
In the nearly four years since Akihito ascended to the Chrysanthemum Throne, Japanese officials have reluctantly edged the new Emperor beyond the vague locutions of his father, Hirohito, who often referred to the "unfortunate" and "regrettable" past, but never acknowledged Japan's specific responsibility for the invasions launched in his name.
Akihito has been more forthcoming, especially at a 1990 dinner with Roh Tae Woo, the President of South Korea, and during a tour last year that the Emperor took through Southeast Asia. 
But in China, where 20 million people were killed or wounded at Japanese hands, sensitivities are especially acute.
Â 
Echoes of Pearl Harbor Issue
The debate in Tokyo over how to word tonight's speech cast a shadow over the Emperor's departure for several weeks. 
It also echoed a similar debate on the 50th anniversary of the bombing of Pearl Harbor last Dec. 
7. At that time, Japanese officials said they were reflecting deeply on Japanese deeds but did not think an apology to the United States was appropriate.
Most younger Japanese say they see no reason that the Emperor should not apologize. 
Some express resentment at what they say is the tendency by Japan's neighbors, including China, to bring up the question of apologizing in order to embarrass Japan into giving more foreign aid or trade concessions.
But powerful voices in the right wing of the governing Liberal Democratic Party say an apology would humiliate the country and the new Emperor. 
They also say Japan did nothing worse in China than Britain, the United States or other colonial powers trying to carve up its territory.
Â 
No Signs of Protest
One of Japan's largest dailies, Mainichi Shimbun, noted today that the Chinese Government "has promised a nationwide welcome" and cleared the streets of dissenters seeking apologies and monetary compensation.
In fact, on the streets of Beijing today, few seemed to be paying much attention to the 58-year-old monarch. 
He was greeted at the airport by young Japanese students waving paper flags, and at the official guesthouse by 500 Chinese children.
Only small crowds gathered for the formal arrival ceremonies on Tiananmen Square. 
There were no protests, perhaps because some of those leading the campaign for Japanese compensation have reportedly been sent away on business trips or detained by the police.
Chronology: "A Century of War and Peace" 1895 -- Japan defeats China in Korea. 
China agrees to cede Taiwan to Japan, and Korea falls under Japanese influence.
1931 -- Japan, taking advantage of the Chinese Nationalist government's preoccupation with a Communist insurgency, seizes Manchuria, in northeast China, and eventually sets up a puppet state called Manchukuo.
1937 -- Japan invades the Chinese heartland and eventually captures nearly two-thirds of China's provinces. 
In eight years of war, Chinese casualties are estimated at upwards of 20 million.
1945 -- Defeated by the Allies, the Japanese withdraw from China.
1949 -- Communists take control of mainland China.
1972 -- After President Nixon's surprise opening to China, Japan establishes diplomatic relations with China. 
But business and investment are slow to develop.
1989 -- Hirohito, the emperor in whose name China was invaded, dies. 
After the crushing of the democracy movement in Tiananmen Square, Japan is relatively quick to restore aid to China.
1990 -- Prime Minister Toshiki Kaifu becomes first leader of anindustrialized democracy to visit China after Tiananmen.
1992 -- Emperor Akihito goes on a goodwill mission to China.

file: JIANG_S WARNING_ _NO FORGIVENESS_.txt
text:
ï»¿
The new head of the Chinese Communist Party has asserted that the leaders of the democracy movement should be ''severely punished'' and shown ''not an iota of forgiveness'' for their role in what he called a ''counterrevolutionary rebellion.''
The remarks by the party leader, Jiang Zemin, came on Wednesday in his first public appearance since he took over as General Secretary from Zhao Ziyang, who was dismissed on Saturday.
In the speech, which was published in the official press today, Mr. Jiang reiterated the policy toward dissidents, some 1,600 of whom have been arrested since the army crushed the protest movement on June 4.
While he said intellectuals and others who only gave verbal support to the protest movement should be given ''ideological education,'' Mr. Jiang said there would be no tolerance for the ''adversaries of socialism'' or for ''those who stubbornly stick to bourgeois liberalism,'' a code phrase for Western freedoms.
Mr. Jiang was speaking to a meeting of members of the non-Communist parties allowed to exist here. 
His comments tended to support the view of many specialists that China's leaders intend a thorough and harsh repression of the protest movement.
''We should thoroughly expose and mete out according to law timely and severe punishments to the plotters, organizers and behind-the-scene commanders'' of the protest movement, Mr. Jiang said.
''As for those cruel enemies of the people, we shouldn't have an iota of forgiveness or we are making a serious mistake in history,'' he continued. 
His remarks appeared to be a paraphrase from Mr. Deng's speech June 9.
For several days, China's leaders and press have been reiterating a distinction first made by Mao in the 1950's between those who are ''enemies of the people'' and those who merely made ''mistakes.''
The second category, Mr. Jiang seemed to be saying on Wednesday, amounts largely to the students and intellectuals who only took part in rallies and demonstrations.
In suppressing the movement, the leadership has so far been harshest with those it has accused of attacking soldiers during the military assault on Tiananmen Square on June 4.
As the Chinese press reported on Mr. Jiang's remarks, the Standing Committee of China's legislative body, the National People's Congress, opened a previously postponed meeting today expected to endorse the party's suppression of the protest movement.

file: Job Is Difficult But Pays Well In Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Christopher Patten was named Governor of this British colony, the British tabloid press -- and even the more staid newspapers -- gleefully detailed his impressive pay and perquisites.
As Governor of Hong Kong, Mr. Patten, a former Member of Parliament, will receive a tax free salary of $273,000 -- larger than the British Prime Minister's -- and be chauffeured about in a Rolls-Royce that bears a crown instead of a license plate. 
He will have a 90-foot yacht, a weekend villa, and a household staff of 56. 
The Governor's household will cost close to $1.5 million dollars a year.
The Sun newspaper in London said: "Now Patten is King of Hong Kong," and "Nice Work If You Can Get It."
Mr. Patten, who was offered the governorship after he lost his parliamentary seat last April, wryly conceded, "Sweet are the uses of adversity."
Â 
A Time of Transition
It is this colony, where 98 percent of the six million people are ethnic Chinese, that provides the sumptuous perks, sets the Governor's salary, pays it and exempts it from taxes.
If he serves out his five-year term, Mr. Patten will be here in 1997, when Britain hands over this capitalist center, with its glass office towers, cricket clubs, race tracks and yachts, to China.
And while many may envy his new life, few would covet his new job -- balancing the demands of leaders in London and Beijing while governing an anxious Hong Kong as it completes its transition back to China.
Â 
To Face a Range of Issues
People in Hong Kong have become vocal about wanting a Governor who is more than London's man in the colony. 
And Mr. Patten's appointment has created some new expectations.
The former Conservative Party chief, who directed his party's surprising victory in Britain's last elections, will not only head the colony's 190,000-member civil service and command the 8,000 soldiers in its military force. 
But he will also face a range of issues from a growing crime problem to constant questions and quarrels with China over the expensive new airport project, which Beijing fears may deplete the colony's coffers.
Then, too, there is the continuing demand by liberals here that Britain fulfill its promise of more democracy in the years before the handover, a demand China has rebuffed.
A smart, pragmatic politician who learned some of his earliest political lessons on the streets of New York as a volunteer for a John V. Lindsay mayoral campaign, Mr. Patten succeeds David Wilson.
Â 
Political Ties Welcomed
While Lord Wilson was a China expert, and Mr. Patten is not, most here welcomed the change to a sharp politician with strong ties to Prime Minister John Major of Britain.
John Walden, a political commentator and former Hong Kong Government official, said, "He will be a breath of fresh air, and many feel that's what we need."
Business interests here hope Mr. Patten will have more clout with the British political establishment. 
Those seeking democratic change hope he will be more sympathetic to their calls for more democracy.
The Joint Declaration, signed by Britain and China in 1984, spells out the general terms of the handover, and promises Hong Kong "a high degree of autonomy" as a special region of China, with Hong Kong people governing Hong Kong. 
But Beijing has begun to meddle in the colony's affairs more and more. 
In the meantime, Britain has been perceived as giving in to China's demands to limit democracy.
Â 
Caretaker or Best Hope?
Some cynics have said that Mr. Patten will merely be a caretaker charged with protecting British interests. 
But others say he may be the colony's last best hope.
"From all the reports on Patten, he's an experienced politician, a man of principles and ambition, and not a man to be content to act as a caretaker," said Mr. Walden. "He is one of Britain top politicians, and Major wouldn't send him here if it were a dead end."
Mr. Patten will step into a world in many ways as elegant and anachronistic as the dress uniform and swan-plumed pith helmet that Hong Kong governors traditionally don for ceremonies.
But there are signs that Mr. Patten, who is 47 years old, plans to change and update the office whenever he can.
He has already declined to wear the formal costume, and passed up the traditional peerage bestowed on Hong Kong governors. 
Both changes have been well received.

file: Journey to Isolation.txt
text:
ï»¿
As our caravan of air-conditioned tour buses lumbered into Chongjin, a port town in the barren northeast corner of North Korea, housewives and schoolchildren -- most of whom had apparently been ordered off the streets before we arrived -- stared in amazement from their windows and schoolyards. 
For the inhabitants of the world's most hermetically sealed nation, we were, without doubt, an odd sight: a hundred or so Japanese businessmen, a few American academics and journalists, even a couple of South Korea's leading industrialists thinly disguised as "academics" and "consultants."
But the biggest oddity was not us. 
It was our buses.
North Korea is so broke these days that buses are rarely seen. 
Not only are there virtually no tourists, but gasoline is so scarce there are few moving vehicles. 
Furthermore, conditions in the last few years have deteriorated so much that this notoriously secretive nation is doing the unthinkable. 
It is welcoming its traditional enemies, urging them to build megaports and factories in areas they would have been shot for entering a year ago.
For the North, this reflects the total failure of juche, the national religion of self-reliance. 
These days, the North Korean Government is busy amending its laws for international joint ventures and wooing many of those it has openly despised. 
Last month, it passed its first comprehensive foreign investment law, specifically aimed at drawing in South Korean investors and those from other "enemy" states.
"We want to develop our technology," Kim Dal Hyon -- the Deputy Prime Minister and a man believed to be in the vanguard of a tenuous reform movement -- admitted to us in a rare flash of candor in Pyongyang, the capital. 
"It is for our own survival."
Yet, with characteristic bravado, North Korea's officials also insist they can do what Eastern Europe could not: reform their economy without backing off an inch from the hard-line Communist ideology that has kept this nation tightly controlled since the division of North and South in 1945.
The harsh reality sweeping through this country is this: After 45 years, North Korea has been virtually abandoned by its longtime allies. 
Throughout the cold war, while the United States supported the South, the Soviet Union and China provided the regime of Kim Il Sung, who is now 80 years old, with food and fuel and technology. 
Every day freight trains rumbled across the single-track bridge spanning the Tumen River. 
But with the end of East-West hostilities, both Moscow and Beijing -- faced with their own economic problems and pragmatically preferring the capitalist South's steel plants and car factories to the North's Stalinist rhetoric -- have opened diplomatic relations with Seoul.
In late September, China -- the country that sent more than a million troops swarming over the border more than 40 years ago to crush the South -- welcomed South Korea's President, Roh Tae Woo, on a historic first trip. 
Roh brought what the Chinese wanted: news that this year South Korea's trade with the Chinese will double to more than $10 billion, and that even more South Korean-owned electronics factories and clothing plants would be built in the special economic zone of Guangdong Province, adjacent to Hong Kong. 
In a few days President Boris N. Yeltsin is scheduled to make his first visit to Seoul, and to talk about rebuilding Russia the way South Korea had transformed itself into one of Asia's industrial dragons.
No one knows for certain what kind of panic this is touching off in Pyongyang, but on North Korea's side of the Tumen, Li Song Pil, the spry stationmaster, can measure the country's isolation with precision. 
A few years ago, six or seven freight trains crossed the river every day. 
These days, he said: "Sometimes we see one. 
Sometimes, nothing comes."
But if this nation of 22 million is opening its door, it is opening it just a crack. 
The regime of the "Great Leader" and his son and heir apparent, "Dear Leader" Kim Jong Il, is determined not to let capitalists undo more than 40 years of rigid political training.
On our 10-day swing through the country several months ago, we were honored guests, even treated to a giant picnic on a beach along the northeastern coast near an area that North Korea hopes to turn into a thriving port. 
But an electric fence separated us from North Koreans living nearby. 
One morning, a group of us touring one of Chongjin's decaying shipyards wandered toward the shipyard entrance, hoping to get to the street and talk to people passing by. 
We never got the chance. 
As we approached the big iron gate, it slammed shut and armed guards emerged from their posts, shouting, "Seot!
Seot!"
("Halt!
Halt!"). One of our well-groomed guides, clearly annoyed by our temerity, explained that although the country is open, mixing with the populace "could be dangerous."
The regime seems equally insecure in its new international forays, alternating welcoming gestures with standard cold-war charges against the United States and its "puppets" in Seoul. 
Indeed, little that has happened in North Korea in the past year has eased fears that the regime might once again lash out, especially since it could soon gain nuclear capability.
There is far less of that fear than there was just a few months ago when the Central Intelligence Agency asserted that a 20-year effort by North Korea to build a crude nuclear device could be only months away from completion. 
American satellites had picked up a near-completed plutonium reprocessing plant, the last major hurdle before a bomb can be assembled. 
Under pressure from Washington, Tokyo and Moscow, Kim Il Sung was forced to let in international inspectors. 
Many believe that Pyongyang, surprised by the harshness of the West's reaction, may now have given up its nuclear card. 
Skeptics in the United States and Japan, however, note that the North Koreans are past masters of deception.
Oddly enough, among those who feel less threatened by Pyongyang's nuclear capabilities are the South Koreans, who appear confident that the end game in a four-decades-long conflict has begun. 
Even President Roh, in his last months in office, is talking like a general who sees victory on the horizon.
The North's "determination to develop nuclear weapons has become weaker," he told me in September at Blue House -- the giant new presidential palace on a hillside above Seoul, only about 35 miles from the border -- that is surrounded by elaborate defenses against possible North Korean terrorists. 
"North Korea is much more isolated this year than it was last year. 
Their economic situation is deteriorating, and their people are suffering from the lack of food. 
They have decided they must gradually open up. 
They have no choice. 
The waves of liberalization are rolling in."
In fact, the main fear in Blue House today is that the waves may crash in too quickly. 
Mindful of the enormous cost of creating an united Germany, Seoul still talks of achieving its dream of reunifying the Korean peninsula but seems in no rush to realize it. 
Some say that the price tag may be as high as $400 billion. 
And those who once argued for pressing the North to the wall are saying they want to avoid forcing a collapse.
South Korean companies are urging their Government to permit them to begin investing in the North, rebuilding its infrastucture and creating jobs and access to cheap labor, so that the South's economy will not be forced to absorb crippling costs when reunification arrives. 
Last month, even with the nuclear questions unresolved, the Government allowed a delegation of industrialists to visit the North to explore moving old textile factories and aging equipment to its industrial zones.
"We would like to encourage North Korea to change gradually, to change peacefully," one of Roh's most senior advisors says. 
"But this is not the kind of thing where you get to pick your timing."
Says Donald Gregg, the C.I.A.'s station chief in Seoul at the height of the cold war and now the American Ambassador there: "There is already a subliminal feeling of victory in the air -- that unification will come, and it will come on the South's terms. 
That is an enormous change. 
Three years ago, a Russian came to me here, one of the first who was allowed into Seoul, and he said with some surprise, 'You know, the South is scared to death of the North.'
That was true then. 
It's not true anymore."
In the tightly ordered world of Pyongyang, North Korea's show city, every Government project is a "gift" from the Great Leader. 
This year, marking the 80th birthday of Kim Il Sung and the 50th birthday of his son, Kim Jong Il, there have been a lot of gifts. 
Some are buildings, like the Reunification Housing Project apartments, functional two-to-four-room units that would be welcome public housing anywhere in New York -- save for the speakers in most hallways constantly blaring Government propaganda.
With basic necessities in shorter supply than at any time in memory, the most prized gifts are food and clothes. 
China celebrated the senior Kim's birthday in April -- a few months before giving diplomatic recognition to the South -- by sending several hundred thousand tons of pork. 
When our group visited the Pyongyang High Middle School No. 1, Li Chun Ran, a 17-year-old, removed her lab smock to show us her new blue school dress. 
She wears it every day. 
"Kim Il Sung and the Dear Leader, Kim Jong Il, gave me the dress," she said.
The school, a Government showcase, boasts of classrooms filled with Japanese personal computers, advanced science laboratories equipped with up-to-date microscopes and even a room for driver's education, complete with a Chinese car and a screen projecting scenery racing by on the road. 
The only hitch is that almost no one in Pyongyang can buy a car. 
Indeed, the only cars on the streets are Volvo taxis (priced so that only foreigners can hire them), a few aging Mercedes limousines for V.I.P.'s and some modern-looking trams made in Eastern Europe. 
At night, the city is virtually pitch-black, with only a few buildings lit.
In a city of grandiose Stalinist-style monuments, the biggest one is the 105-story Ryu Gyong Hotel, designed to be the tallest in Asia. 
A bit more than half-finished, the pyramid towers over the city. 
No official would comment on the project, but rumors abound that it is out of money, and it is visibly in need of structural repair. 
But clearly utility is not an issue. 
Only about 100,000 tourists visit North Korea each year, all on group tours and most from the dwindling family of Communist or socialist countries. 
Most of them could not afford the Ryu Gyong if it were open.
What strikes a visitor to Pyongyang, a city of two million, is the total absence of spontaneity. 
It is perhaps the only Asian city without the chaotic, open markets that are plentiful in other Communist capitals, from Hanoi to Beijing. 
The department stores seem well stocked; there are few, if any, shoppers.
"Anything of value is rationed," explained a diplomat stationed in Pyongyang. 
"You might have coupons to get a few things, but almost no one buys in the stores."
When two of us asked on a Saturday to go to a restaurant where ordinary Koreans eat lunch, our guide had to take us on a 45-minute drive around town until he found one that was open. 
When colleagues visited an off-the-tourist-path apartment building and found it run-down and filthy, they were brought in for questioning.
Although officials take great pains to keep visitors from seeing any sign of poverty in Pyongyang, they are unable to do the same in the countryside. 
Early one morning, not long after our train began its journey up the coast, we saw women hoeing the hard earth by hand in the villages passing by our window. 
Oxen were few and far between. 
According to diplomats stationed in Pyongyang, malnutrition is widespread, with many people not getting their full allotment of 4.4 pounds of red meat and chicken a month. 
Earlier this year, the regime adopted the slogan "Let's Eat Two Meals!"
Every few months there are reports from ethnic Koreans living over the border in China about food riots breaking out in remote towns in the North. 
The stories are impossible to check, but with so many accounts most experts believe they carry at least some truth. 
"What we think happens," says Kim Chang Soon, the director of the Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul, "is that people are supposed to receive rice every 15 days, but they get only enough for 10. 
So for the last 5 days they eat grass and vegetables and when the 15th day arrives, they go to get their rice. 
If it isn't there, they raid the warehouse."
Rice is not the only scarce commodity. 
From our train, we saw armed guards standing atop piles of coal at rail depots; later, North Korean officials conceded that theft had become a growing problem. 
Since 1990, Moscow has refused to deliver oil at what were called "friendship" rates, far below the market value. 
By some estimates, North Korea is getting only a third of the petroleum supplies it needs.
South Korean officials, who have an interest in painting a bleak picture, estimate that Pyongyang's economy shrank by 3.7 percent in 1990 and by 5.2 percent last year. 
Exports last year were about $1 billion -- roughly what the South exports in five days. 
Many economists, and the American intelligence community, estimate that things are actually much worse in the North. 
But because the North Korean Government guards most economic data as state secrets and because almost every economic "fact" is an extrapolation from anecdotes, it is easy for North Korean officials to issue blanket denials.
"We do not face any economic crisis that is not found in Russia or any East European country," one senior official insisted to us. 
The "only economic trouble we face," he said, was that "we cannot export or import any goods from the formerly socialist countries."
In most countries, sudden privation of the sort North Koreans are experiencing would be tinder for revolution. 
But North Korea is unlike most countries. 
So far, there is no sign of the kind of discontent that brought down Communism in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. 
Unlike East Germans a few years ago, who knew -- from television and from a steady stream of visitors -- about life in the West, North Koreans seem to know almost nothing about the heady prosperity in the South. 
There is no television from the outside world, only a few shortwave radios in the hands of the elite, and endless propaganda about the abuse of workers, crime and homelessness in South Korea, Japan and the United States.
In short, after 35 years of brutal Japanese occupation, followed by 44 years of strong-arm Communist dictatorship, few North Koreans are in a position to question what they are told. 
And what they are still being told is that North Korea remains a "socialist paradise on earth."
At the "mass games" for Kim Il Sung's birthday, where 100,000 schoolchildren performed precision gymnastics, a huge sign proclaimed "We Envy Nobody in the World!"
Public devotion to the Great Leader seems undiminished. 
If the South's economy was built on entrepreneurship and industrial policy, the North's has been built on a personality cult: a quasi-religious loyalty to the "great sun of mankind," Kim Il Sung. 
On the outskirts of Pyongyang, workers still line up to see North Korea's equivalent of Abe Lincoln's cabin -- the primitive thatched-roof house where the Great Leader was born.
When you ask North Koreans why they work so hard -- a national characteristic shared with the South -- the answer is predictable. 
"These buildings were made for us by the Great Leader, Kim Il Sung, who wants to give greatly to his people," Cho Ho Sun, a 35-year-old construction worker, said, pausing for a moment from his work planting trees around the just-completed Reunification Housing Projects. 
"They were built on rice fields," Cho continued. 
"By planting trees, we pay solicitude to Kim Il Sung and the Dear Leader, Kim Jong Il."
People in North Korea really talk this way. 
North Korean authorities -- unlike their counterparts in China, for example -- hardly blink when you walk up to almost anyone in the capital, where people seem accustomed to handling foreigners, and start a conversation. 
They have little reason to fear that something untoward will slip out.
Although the few people we managed to speak to -- always under the gaze of a Government functionary -- invariably spoke of the Great Leader and the Dear Leader almost as one, it wasn't clear during our visit if the succession from father to son was as certain as it once seemed. 
North Korean officials seemed hard-pressed to name even a few things the Dear Leader had done for his nation. 
We pressed one young official dining with us one night at the Communist Party's guest house in Pyongyang -- a 14-course meal, including quail soup and steamed piglet, followed by a Las Vegas-style floor show. 
He struggled for a few moments, said something vague about the Dear Leader's management of the economy, then came up with: "He is competent at many things."
In September, however, North Korea's Foreign Minister Kim Yong Nam, in New York to attend a session of the United Nations, reportedly told South Korean reporters that all power had been transferred to Kim Jong Il, and that the senior Kim, while he was still President, was playing only an "advisory" role. 
In a rare move, the younger Kim recently entertained a delegation of foreign businessmen on his yacht; until then, handling foreigners had always been his father's job.
Whether Kim Jong Il becomes the next Great Leader, though, depends largely on a segment of North Korean society about which little is known: the ruling elite. 
By most estimates, the 1.5 million or so members of the "intelligentsia" are the ones who have everything: education, social status, whatever wealth there is to go around. 
Within this group are 10,000 to 15,000 senior officials with access to the best medical care and special shops.
There is widespread speculation that many of the top military brass -- presumably the key figures in succession politics -- were deeply unhappy when Kim Jong Il was named head of the armed forces earlier this year. 
The younger Kim is reputed to be a spoiled playboy with a pronounced taste for liquor and women. 
(Japanese intelligence agents learn what little they can about him by seeking out the foreign "hostesses" he is said to import for "entertainment.") The most commonly discussed scenario for North Korea after Kim Il Sung is that the Dear Leader will be told that he can keep his cars and "entertainers" -- as long as he does what he is told.
NORTH KOREA'S Military ranks as the world's fifth- or sixth-largest, with about one million men, 710 ships and 850 combat aircraft (mostly older Russian-made MIG's) and a budget accounting for 21.5 percent of the country's gross national product. 
The military is also the country's most successful exporter: North Korean-made versions of the Scud missile are becoming a favorite among Middle Eastern nations.
American and South Korean commanders acknowledge in private, however, that respect for the North's military prowess is declining. 
Many of the troops spend their days putting up new buildings and rebuilding the fractured rail network. 
South Koreans, who for years based their enormous military budgets on the size and skill of their Northern enemies, are now cutting back the rate of growth.
Pyongyang's nuclear capability is quite another matter. 
Attention was suddenly focused on its bomb-building plans when post-mortems of the Persian Gulf war uncovered shocking intelligence lapses, chiefly the failure of the International Atomic Energy Agency to detect the scope or progress of Iraq's nuclear bomb project -- although Iraq had submitted itself to regular agency inspections.
Until a few months ago, North Korea had never let agency inspectors into Yongbyon, the sprawling, secret installation Kim Il Sung began building in the mountains north of the capital in the 1960's. 
The first part completed was a small, Soviet-supplied research reactor. 
A much bigger reactor opened in the mid-80's, capable of producing enough waste plutonium to build a crude bomb.
Around 1988, American satellite cameras began to pick up another giant building that seemed perfectly suited for reprocessing plutonium -- turning waste into bomb fuel. 
It is a complex technology that many thought was beyond North Korea's talents. 
But apart from satellite pictures, intelligence about the project was sketchy. 
"In Iraq we had oil people coming in and out, we had some scientific exchange, we had commerce," one American intelligence official with long experience in Asia said this year. 
"With North Korea, we had nothing. 
Zip."
Kim had long justified barring outside inspectors by saying he would not permit them as long as the United States kept nuclear weapons in the South. 
But last December the Bush Administration removed the remaining American nuclear weapons from South Korea. 
Under intense pressure from Washington, Seoul agreed to forswear any reprocessing of its own -- making it easier to demand that Pyongyang do the same.
Once the North Koreans allowed inspectors in, the atomic energy agency discovered a vast reprocessing center. 
But the C.I.A. had guessed wrong about the innards of the cavernous building. 
The reprocessor was less than half completed, the equipment unimpressive. 
The North Koreans admitted they had experimented with reprocessing tiny quantities of plutonium in laboratories -- far too little to make a bomb -- and insisted their work was part of an energy research project.
Early this year, however, before inspectors arrived, satellite photographs showed trucks pulling up to the reprocessing facility, perhaps to cart away equipment. 
Bolstering suspicions that critical equipment might be hidden, Hans Blix, the director of the atomic energy agency, noted in a report he circulated to several governments that the North Koreans may have built a "pilot plant" to process plutonium, out of satellite view, before taking the risky leap to the building at Yongbyon.
The United States and South Korea are still insisting on an agreement to allow South Korean teams to look around in the North, while North Koreans inspect sites in the South. 
Because South Korean inspectors speak the same language and share the same culture, it is hoped they might be able to uncover what the agency cannot. 
A nuclear-armed North could overturn the delicate balance that has kept the region in check for decades. 
If North Korea succeeds in producing a nuclear bomb, the South would be forced to build one of its own (it tried once in the 1970's, before the United States quashed the project) and Japan might be forced to rethink the wisdom of its own ban on nuclear weapons.
AS INSPECTORS WERE combing through the North's nuclear reactors in late July, a North Korean journeying to the South was escorted across the miles of tank traps and mine fields and barbed wire that make up the demilitarized zone and onto the highways that feed into Seoul. 
He was Kim Dal Hyon, one of the new breed of economic "pragmatists."
He was the one who had told us in Pyongyang two months earlier that the openings were "for our own survival," that juche had been a philosophy of necessity, not of choice. 
"We have been isolated by the world community," he had said, "because of pressure from certain superpowers."
In Seoul, Kim was given a tour of everything from advanced electronics factories to noisy markets overflowing with consumer goods. 
He visited the country's industrial heartland. 
When he was finally escorted to Blue House, his message to President Roh was simple: South Korea, for its own good and the North's, should allow its giant chae bol -- the industrial conglomerates like Samsung, Daewoo and Hyundai -- to invest in the North.
"I know that without prospects for profit, they will not come," Kim said. 
"I promise that they will make profits."
The energetic North Korean knew precisely what he was walking into: a quiet but significant split between the United States and South Korea over how to deal with the North. 
Meeting with North Korean representatives at the United Nations early in the year, Arnold L. Kanter, a senior State Department official, made it clear that the North would get nothing -- not even mid-level talks with the United States -- until the nuclear questions were completely resolved. 
South Korea, with far more at stake, has gradually moved toward a different view.
Scores of economists sent to study the obvious parallel -- the integration of East and West Germany -- had come back with the message that if Seoul wanted to avoid economic disaster, it better start now. 
"The best guesses are that it would cost $250 billion to $400 billion," says Kongdan Oh, a Korean-born policy analyst with the Rand Corporation, a research institute based in Santa Monica, Calif. 
"So there are a lot of contingency plans under way. 
If the South can get management know-how and technology into the North and begin to train people, it will bring the costs down."
Bowing to United States pressure, until recently President Roh resisted negotiating with the North while the nuclear issues remained unresolved. 
But with an election approaching, the pressure is building for a major initiative with economic promise. 
During Kim Dal Hyon's visit, Roh agreed to allow a team to visit the North and explore business opportunities. 
According to South Korean press reports, when Roh met recently with the heads of the South's largest conglomerates, Koo Cha Kyung, chairman of the Federation of Korean Industries, used the one argument that he knew would strike a nerve. 
South Korea, he said, "should consider investing in labor-intensive and consumer goods industries in the North because Japan is showing great interest in North Korea's labor pool."
In fact, no one has been more heavily courted by Kim Il Sung these days than the Japanese. 
It is hardly a natural alliance. 
In his recently published reminiscences, Kim's hatred for the Japanese is writ large in almost every chapter, as he recalled his early days battling the nation's occupiers. 
"While visiting various parts of the world," he wrote, "I have had the opportunity of seeing many former colonial countries, but I have never seen imperialism so hideous that it deprived people of their language and surnames and even plundered them of their tableware."
Now, though, North Korea looks across the Sea of Japan (in Pyongyang it is called the East Sea of Korea) and sees a giant bank vault. 
For more than a year, delegations from the former colonizer and the former colony have been meeting regularly -- and getting no place.
"The meetings are very strange," says one Japanese official involved in the talks. 
"The North Koreans send maybe 15 people, but most of them don't speak at all."
Although the negotiators claim to be diplomats, "most don't have any experience abroad," he says.
Pyongyang has also been making overtures to the business community of Niigata, one of Japan's major ports, which is a few hundred miles across the sea from the Tumen outlet. 
But even with the help of the United Nations Development Program, North Korea's initial presentations to potential investors in the Tumen have been rambling and vague. 
China and Russia are less than enthusiastic, because they view the project as competition for their own ports.
On our visit, Japanese executives who toured the region found that very little of the infrastructure had improved since the Japanese occupiers left in 1945. 
"The river is too narrow to carry ships," one executive of a major trading house said. 
"They are wasting our time."
WHEN ROH TAE WOO LEAVES office next February, he will go down in history as the man who brought the beginnings of democracy to South Korea. 
Just as remarkably, he brought about diplomatic independence. 
The "northern policy" that brought Pyongyang to the negotiating table was not hatched in Washington but in Seoul.
So far, though, the apparent progress is far greater than the reality. 
The "reconciliation and nonaggression" agreement signed nearly a year ago calls for regular exchanges of family members, air and mail links. 
But almost every effort to put specifics of the agreement into effect have failed. 
The North, for example, has blocked installing a military "hot line" until the United States and South Korea halt their joint military exercises. 
North Korea's rulers know that as soon as news and people move across the border the "paradise on earth" line will quickly wear thin. 
Meanwhile, diatribes and sometimes gunfire are still exchanged. 
Earlier this year, an apparently accidental incursion into South Korean territory led to the killing of three North Korean soldiers.
South Koreans have no doubts that managing reunification will be the task for the next decade. 
Managed well, it could turn Korea into the region's newest economic powerhouse, fusing the technology of the South with the eager, cheap work force of the North. 
Managed badly, it could bring chaos, with new battles along the DMZ -- a conflict that could involve China, Japan and the United States.
It is easy to forget that for all their common roots, North and South Koreans are virtual strangers to one another. 
They have grown up in different worlds, fought a war against each other and rebuilt vastly different societies. 
That has been driven home to South Korean negotiators who, visiting Pyongyang, have opened their hotel-room doors to long-lost relatives. 
Instead of a tearful embrace, they have gotten lectures on the wonders of the Great Leader's rule.

file: Just When Beijing Needs It, Farmers Have Bumper Crop.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yang Guojun, a tall, plump man who buys grain for the state, smiles shyly as he talks about the summer's bumper harvest that he and his crew collected over 10 days from the baskets of the local peasants.
''We worked through the night sometimes, just so that the peasants could go home the same day they came,'' the 45-year-old Mr. Yang said as he gestured to the seven storehouses reserved for this township in Henan province, in north-central China.
Grain buyers like Mr. Yang have been busy throughout China, for the nation has just completed its largest summer grain harvest on record. 
If expectations for the autumn crops come true, the year-end bounty may break the record previously set in 1984 at 407.3 million metric tons of grain.
Some estimates say that if the weather is good this fall, the harvest could total 420 million metric tons. 
If the weather is bad, the total is not expected to exceed 405 million metric tons.
This rosy outlook for the harvest comes at a crucial time for the Chinese Government, whose support has been severely weakened by the crackdown on protests in the capital and in 85 or so other cities throughout the country. 
While the bumper harvest reduces the danger of major peasant unrest, the Government, whose cash supply is diminishing quickly, still faces the daunting challenge of paying for the crops.
Last year, officials issued i.o.u.'s, or ''white slips'' as they are called here, instead of cash to pay for wheat, tea, cotton and other crops. 
Peasants have been understandably indignant, and there has been concern that they will simply refuse to turn over crops in the future unless they are paid in cash. 
Rural residents make up 59 percent of China's population.
There are no Government estimates for how many white slips were issued, although at least one economist put their total value at $19 billion, most of this apparently later redeemed. 
This year, in an effort to avoid a similar uproar, the state took greater pains to see that money set aside in its budget for grain was used precisely for that. 
It also called in the Chinese central bank to help finance grain procurement.
This summer's bumper harvest of more than 93.55 million metric tons of grain eases the pressure on the state, since farmers should have substantial amounts of leftover grain, after they fulfill their state quotas, to sell for cash in the market.
Even so, the Government has had to pay the value of $6 billion to $7 billion for the summer harvest and other seasonal agricultural products, according to statistics reported in the official press.
But the summer harvest, mostly grain, is less important than the fall crops, which make up three-fourths of the total harvest. 
Already, there are reports that this spring and summer, white slips were issued in Shandong, Sichuan and Zhejiang provinces.
It is often difficult to determine when these i.o.u.'s are issued, often because official press reports contradict each other and also conflict with what officials say.
Â 
Better Times Seen
For example, in Henan province, an official at the agricultural bank said the bank financed all three million metric tons of grain, at a cost of $486 million, through increased deposits, a reduction in loans to rural enterprises and a decrease in long-term construction loans.
''There will be no white slips this year,'' an official said. 
Last year, the province issued $135 million in white slips, which the aide said were cashed early this year.
But an article in the newspaper Peasant Daily late last month said that in Henan's northern county of Miyang, more than $55,000 in white slips had been issued to 1,000 peasants.
''I have been here four to five times for this cursed sum of about $11,'' the article quotes a peasant, Zhang Dongfa, who was trying to cash his slips at a grain-procurement center.
The farmers are forced to sell a certain percentage of their grain to the state, and the amount varies with the region, the crop and the harvest. 
In central Henan province, where Mr. Yang procures grain, the percentage is generally 17 percent of a farmer's production.
Â 
Tricks of the Trade
The farmers can then sell the leftover grain to the market, at market prices, which this year are generally twice the state price. 
But often, even this price is administered by the Government, which collects the ''market'' grain from the peasants to distribute and sell it to the market on their behalf. 
Only if a peasant transports the grain himself to the market, usually a long distance away, does he get a true market price.
While local governments are short of cash, the authorities acknowledge that there is another reason they issue white slips - because funds earmarked for grain are misappropriated and used for rural enterprises that bring in more cash for the locality.
Moreover, many small villages, especially those in mountainous areas, are far from the county and city centers, and so central and provincial authorities may not even know when white slips are issued.
''There is a question about whether they get accurate information filtering up,'' a Western diplomat in Beijing said.

file: KHMER ROUGE GET MORE CHINA ARMS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Despite public assurances by China that it has stopped sending military aid to the Khmer Rouge guerrillas since September, Chinese arms continue to flow across the Thai border to all the opposition factions fighting the Phnom Penh Government, including the Khmer Rouge, senior Western diplomats say.
It is impossible to tell whether these Chinese arms left China after September, the diplomats say. 
The arms supplies, they say, could represent shipments that were already on the way or had been previously warehoused in Thailand.
In any event, the diplomats say, the arms supplies seem intended more to keep up morale among opposition fighters as the peace process drags on into the dry season, when fighting usually intensifies, than to have a significant effect on the balance of forces.
China, like the Soviet Union, had previously said that it would stop all arms supplies in the context of a comprehensive peace settlement, but that it would not do so unilaterally.
Last month, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman, Li Zhaoxing, said, "Since the five member countries of the Security Council adopted the five documents on Cambodia, China has not provided any military assistance, including weapons, to the Cambodian resistance."
Â 
U.N. Council Offers Plan
The five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council agreed on the framework for a comprehensive peace plan for Cambodia on Aug. 
28. The permanent Council members include China, the United States and the Soviet Union, the main proxy powers of the conflict, as well as Britain and France.
Fighting the Vietnamese-installed Government in Phnom Penh, led by Prime Minister Hun Sen, are three opposition organizations that have formed a loose alliance: the Communist Khmer Rouge, under whose regime more than a million Cambodians died from 1975 to 1979; the followers of Prince Norodom Sihanouk, and the Khmer People's National Liberation Front of Son Sann, which groups rightists who overthrew Prince Sihanouk in 1970 and who were ousted by the Khmer Rouge in 1975. 
The Khmer Rouge were driven from power in 1979, after the Vietnamese invaded.
China has been the main backer of the Khmer Rouge, which has the strongest guerrilla army, and the two other guerrilla groups. 
The Soviet Union has backed Vietnam and the Cambodian Government. 
The United States gives nonmilitary aid to Prince Sihanouk's followers and to the Khmer People's National Liberation Front, but has withdrawn diplomatic support at the United Nations for the coalition of rebel groups.
"There is movement of arms, but we don't take it too seriously," a senior Western diplomat said. 
"Partly it's a definitional problem. 
Did the Chinese stop shipping that day?
Some may have been already at sea, and some in warehouses in Thailand, now being delivered."
Â 
Hurting Beijing's Image
But because China had announced a halt in shipments, he said, any supplies make Beijing look bad.
The Associated Press reported on Saturday that Western intelligence figures said the Khmer Rouge were loading "trucks and trucks of new Chinese ammunition" in violation of Beijing's pledge to stop military aid.
As usual, an Asian diplomat said, military claims and developments in Cambodia have to be evaluated in the context of the negotiations, which have been faltering.
In a conference on Sept. 
9 and 10 in Jakarta, after a secret summit meeting between Vietnamese and Chinese leaders, the Cambodian Government and the three guerrilla factions agreed to accept the United Nations peace framework in its entirety.
But since their September meeting, the four parties have been dragging their feet. 
With the support of the Khmer Rouge, Prince Sihanouk first rejected any role for himself on a Supreme National Council that would represent Cambodian sovereignty in a settlement. 
Then he insisted on being chairman of the council but said Mr. Hun Sen could not be the deputy chairman. 
Later he rejected any role for himself once again.
The United Nations plan calls for the national council to have a largely symbolic role. 
United Nations officials would monitor, control and, if necessary, run five important ministries -- finance, interior, defense, foreign affairs and information -- and insure that the elections for a new government are free and fair.
A meeting of the Cambodian factions this month in Paris, to discuss a draft of the peace plan, was inconclusive.

text:
ï»¿
Former Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger met today with three Politburo members and China's Foreign Minister in the first of a series of talks that both sides hope will help ease the strains between China and the United States.
In his remarks at a banquet given by the Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, Mr. Kissinger said that while China and the United States should work to improve understanding, American policy must reflect ''our historic democratic values as well as our national interest,'' according to a paraphrase by the New China News Agency.
Mr. Kissinger's trip comes as an important meeting of the Communist Party Central Committee is being held in Beijing. 
The meeting, expected to conclude on Thursday, may produce one dramatic development, according to a senior Chinese official. 
He said that Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, might resign as chairman of the Central Military Commission. 
That is Mr. Deng's only remaining official post.
The Kissinger visit, which is to end on Friday, follows a visit with Chinese leaders last week by former President Richard M. Nixon.
Like Mr. Nixon, Mr. Kissinger will probably meet with Mr. Deng, but he has not released details of his schedule.
He has been to China more than a dozen times since 1971, when he came on a secret mission to lay the groundwork for an official trip the next year by Mr. Nixon, who was then President.
Chinese leaders have always warmly received Mr. Kissinger, and his influence with some of them may even have risen since June, when he indicated sympathy for the Chinese leadership at a time when it was being widely criticized for the military crackdown on the democracy movement.
''Some in America feel that China should make the first move in the present situation, while some in China feel the United States should move first,'' the agency said in paraphrasing Mr. Kissinger's comments.
Since both sides have an interest in stabilityII and peace, the agency account went on, ''both countries should take steps together to put relations onto a smoother path.''
Mr. Kissinger, who arrived in Beijing on Tuesday evening, has met with Wu Xueqian, a Deputy Prime Minister and Politburo member, and with Li Ruihuan, a member of the Standing Committee of the Politburo.
President Kim Il Sung of North Korea was reported to have made a secret visit early this week to Beijing. 
North Korean Embassy officials denied that the visit took place, and officials at the Chinese Foreign Ministry were unavailable for comment.

file: KITCHEN BOOKSHELF_New Cookbooks That Fortify The Spirit as Well as the Palate.txt
text:
ï»¿
OUR sober national mood seems to have permeated the world of cookbooks, for the book list this holiday season looks as restrained as anything in recent memory.
Gone are the expensive, all-encompassing, how-to-cook books like Julia Child's and Anne Willan's that delighted gift givers and recipients last year. 
Gone too are the picture-packed coffee-table books that said more about the depth of the giver's pockets than they did about the recipient's needs or desires.
Still, even without the glitter, there are solid and worthy offerings available, possibly even something for everyone on your list.
For Sinophiles, THE TASTE OF CHINA (Simon & Schuster, $29.95) by Ken Hom, is a laudable exception to the usual coffee-table gift book. 
The indefatigable Mr. Hom, well known as an authority on Chinese food, set out to discover the state of Chinese cuisine today, after decades of upheaval.
He takes us into private homes; state-run, big-city restaurants; village eating halls, and market stalls. 
Along the way we are introduced to good chunks of Chinese history and culture, both ancient and modern.
The book is handsomely produced, with photographs that are both evocative and frank. 
Nothing is prettified here: hunks of meat displayed in the market, spare, dusty kitchens, waiters with stained and dirty aprons. 
But the distinctive current of delight, even joy, that pervades pictures and text creates enchantment from the humblest of scenes.
For the dedicated griller, the one who's out in the backyard under an umbrella, turning hamburgers while the snow drifts down, there is THE THRILL OF THE GRILL (William Morrow & Company, $24.95) by Chris Schlesinger and John Willoughby, full of wonderful ideas and recipes from grilled tuna steaks with a do-ahead nectarine-red-onion relish to instructions for different types of barbecue (North Carolina, Texas, etc.).
The tone is as relaxed as if Mr. Schlesinger, co-owner of the East Coast Grill in Cambridge, Mass., had pulled up a chair next to the cook: "You have to figure out your own personal refueling policy," he advises. 
"The one I like is one handful of coals or wood chunks to every beer."
Not all recipes require a grill, and many can be adapted to an oven broiler. 
My only quibble is the book's format (recipes and commentary are displayed side by side on the same page), which can cause confusion.
For Italophiles: The Italian food book category grows every season. 
This year's is a particularly fine crop. 
One of the most exciting is Carol Field's CELEBRATING ITALY (Morrow, $24.95), a look at Italy's still vibrant traditions of festivals and celebrations and the foods (and recipes) that form a significant part of them. 
These include Christian festivals like Christmas and Easter, as well as more obscure holidays like the Feast of the Redeemer in Venice in July.
There are also regional festivals, many with strong, if unstated, pagan origins: the Festa dei Serpari, a snake festival in an Abruzzese village east of Rome, or the magnificent Carnival battles in Ivrea in the Piedmont, in which bands of youths spend the days before Lent pelting each other energetically with oranges trucked in from Sicily, until the whole town reeks of fermented orange juice. 
"Not a single orange," Ms. Field writes, "is squeezed into juice or transformed into a ritual dish."
There are plenty of ritual dishes in the book, however, from breads and sweets to robust bean and lentil stews, pastas of all shapes and sizes and baked, roasted, grilled and braised meats, fish and sausages, all characteristic of one part or another, and of one season or another, of this country that is still as remarkably and intimately connected with its past as any place on earth.
Nancy Verde Barr's WE CALLED IT MACARONI (Alfred A. Knopf, $21.95) is a celebration of the Italian community in Providence, R.I., where the author grew up. 
Many of the recipes are "classic" Italian-American adaptations of traditional southern Italian foods, while others were developed from her trips back to the homeland. 
There are period photographs and interviews with members of this still very strong community.
LA CUCINA DI LIDIA (Doubleday, $24.95) by Lidia Bastianich and Jay Jacobs, is similar in tone, an affectionate memoir of the cooking of the author's youth in Istria, a remote region northeast of Venice where Italy and Yugoslavia meet.
Ms. Bastianich is the chef and co-owner, with her husband, Felice, of Felidia, an esteemed New York restaurant. 
Here she records the robust and rustic preparations of her home, where sauerkraut and soft-shell crabs are considered as authentically Italian as risotto and balsamic vinegar. 
The recipes are delightful, though sometimes rather labor- and time-intensive. 
Many are unusual regional preparations not found in standard Italian cookbooks.
Also in the Italian category is Giacomo Castelvetro's FRUIT, HERBS & VEGETABLES OF ITALY, written in 1614 and translated into English for the first time by Gillian Riley (Viking, $29.95), with handsome illustrations from period art.
As a Venetian exile in England, Castelvetro set himself the goal of persuading the British, even then known as prodigious consumers of meats and sweets, to eat more fruits and vegetables. 
There are no recipes as such, but his good humor and good sense are attractive, and his attitude toward food would not be out of place in Italy today.
For the culinary scholar who wants a cookbook that goes beyond recipes to tell an enthralling story, there is Jennifer Brennan's CURRIES AND BUGLES (HarperCollins, $25), subtitled "A Memoir and a Cookbook of the British Raj."
With affection and wit, Ms. Brennan, raised in India in the last days of Britain's empire, shares memories of prodigious hunt breakfasts, Christmases, birthday parties, regimental teas and ladies' nights, along with more everyday fare.
Recipes are both Anglo and Indian, with dishes like peshawari pasande (lamb marinated and simmered in yogurt and spices, cardamom, turmeric, saffron and coriander) sharing space with Karachi Club champagne cup and Granny Whitburn's Scottish whisky marmalade. 
The recipes are not as clear as one might wish and should be read with care before proceeding. 
But given that precaution, the fascination of the period and the author's endearing tone make the book worth savoring.
For fish-lovers, FISH: THE BASICS (Simon & Schuster, $24.95) by Shirley King, is possibly the last fish cookbook you'll ever buy. 
Even expert cooks will find this useful, while beginners who follow the book's wise and measured guidance will quickly feel comfortable with seafood, in the fish market, in the restaurant or at the kitchen stove.
The book includes advice about buying and storing different types of fish; an intelligent discussion of seafood's health benefits; basic cooking methods and individual recipes with variations. 
The book may appear dauntingly encyclopedic at first, but anyone with even a slight interest in fish should press on.
For irrepressible meat lovers there is THE USEFUL PIG (HarperCollins, $22.95), by Roberta Wolfe Smoler, a collection of traditional and unusual pork recipes from around the world, with a few of the author's own devising -- pork with Moroccan preserved lemons, for instance.
This is a savory compendium with one disappointment; I would have liked an acknowledgement that pork is peculiarly a subject on which the world is divided between adorers (Chinese, Europeans) and abhorrers (Jews, Muslims). 
No one has ever satisfactorily explained why.
For lovers of African-American food, an increasingly difficult cuisine to define, there is FAMILY OF THE SPIRIT COOKBOOK (Simon & Schuster, $24.95) by John Pinderhughes, a compendium of recipes from black cooks, along with portraits taken by the author, a New York photographer. 
Some of these are familiar: Verta Mae Grosvenor from National Public Radio and Leah Chase, chef and co-owner of Dooky Chase's Restaurant in New Orleans. 
Others are obviously much-loved relatives and friends.
What makes the food African-American seems to be simply that African-Americans cook it. 
From crab cakes to bread and butter pickles, this is more or less the traditional good food of country folk in the eastern part of America -- which is, to my mind, as fine a definition as any.
There are two books for bakers: Susan G. Purdy's AS EASY AS PIE (Collier Books, $14.95) details all manner of pies, sweet and savory, cream pies, fruit and berry pies, dumplings and cobblers, meat and fish pies, a few pizza recipes and even that old suburban standby, grasshopper pie, without a trace of the dreaded frozen whip. 
Recipes are clear, and there are enough basic pastry instructions to turn the most fumble-fingered neophyte into an expert pie maker.
KEN HAEDRICH'S COUNTRY BAKING (Bantam, $24.95) is a down-home book with recipes for breads and muffins, pies and tarts, pizzas, cakes, cookies and crackers. 
This is a back-to-the-land sort of book, with plenty of whole-grain preparations but not at all hortatory in tone. 
Reading through it, you might dream of installing Mr. Haedrich in your own kitchen; his recipes are the next best thing.
Finally, for Canadophiles: Here is A TASTE OF QUEBEC ( Macmillan of Canada , $21.95) by Julian Armstrong, food editor of The Montreal Gazette. 
Dishes like blueberry oat crumble and suet fruit pie might not be familiar to sophisticated chefs, but the book is a welcome introduction to the region and to comfortable, appealing foods that never forget their rural roots. 
More than a collection of recipes, the book is also a useful traveler's guide to foods and restaurants.
Â 
Sneak Previews of What's Inside All Those Pages
Â 
Cranberry Apple Pie (Adapted from "Ken Haedrich's Country Baking")
Â 
Total time: 1 hour, 20 minutes, plus time for cooling
Â 
Flour for dusting wax paper
Pastry for a two-crust pie, chilled
1 12-ounce package fresh cranberries
2 large Granny Smith apples, peeled, cored and chopped coarse
1 1/4 cups packed light brown sugar
1 1/2 tablespoons quick-cooking tapioca
Finely grated zest of 1 lemon
Juice of a half lemon
1/4 teaspoon ground cloves
1 teaspoon light or heavy cream.
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees.
2. On a sheet of lightly floured wax paper, roll half the pastry into a 12-inch circle and line a 9-inch pie pan with it, letting the edge hang over. 
Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate.
3. On another sheet of lightly floured wax paper, roll the other half of the dough into an 11-inch circle; set aside. 
Combine cranberries, apple, sugar, tapioca, zest, lemon juice and clove and turn into the refrigerated pie shell, then lightly moisten the outer rim of the shell with water. 
Invert the top crust over the filling and press around the edge to seal. 
Trim overhang to about 1/2 inch, then turn the edge of the pastry down and under, sculpting it into an upstanding ridge.
4. Brush top of pie sparingly with cream, then poke a few steam vents with a fork or paring knife. 
Bake 20 minutes, reduce heat to 375 degrees, then bake another 40 minutes. 
When done, the top of the pie will be a rich gold and the juices should bubble thickly. 
Transfer pie to a rack and cool at least 30 minutes before slicing.
Yield: about 8 servings.
Â 
Grilled Shrimp With Greens, Bacon and Sweet Potato (Adapted from "The Thrill of the Grill")
Â 
Total time: 50 minutes
Â 
16 medium-size shrimp (about 1 pound)
Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
1/2 pound slab bacon, cut into small cubes
1 cup cooked sweet potatoes (about 1/2 pound, diced)

Total time: 1 hour
