file: Microsoft Nails Some Pirates.txt
text:
ï»¿
When the Microsoft Corporation unveiled its updated MS-DOS 5 software operating system last June, it was confident that it had devised a way to thwart the loss of $1 billion a year from software piracy. 
Its packaging contains two one-of-a-kind holograms, one a circular image on the package box and the other a rectangular image pasted inside on the product manual, viewable through a window on the box. 
The multidimensional images bear the company's name or the MS-DOS logo and tell consumers that the product is the real McCoy.
Microsoft pamphlets said the holograms are "virtually impossible" to reproduce and "raise the counterfeiting barrier to a level previously unattempted in the software industry."
Yet within two weeks of the introduction, a Taiwanese counterfeiter commissioned a holographer in China to copy and produce the holograms. 
Over the next half-dozen months, Microsoft's counterattack took it to Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong and Melbourne. 
The idea was to track down the counterfeiters, mostly without the aid of foreign governments. 
Ultimately, the company helped bust a major Asian couterfeiting ring that may have produced up to $150 million worth of the company's hottest products.
But whether Microsoft can halt future clandestine activity there depends on talks this week with officials of the People's Republic of China. 
Beijing has not yet kept its promise to give the company valuable molds seized in the March raids that produce nearly exact fakes.
Alison Gilligan, one of Microsoft's antipiracy specialists, notes, "We're scared the molds will disappear out the back door and be sold to the highest bidder."
In the meantime, the company is trying to get the fakes off the market, an endeavor made difficult "because we still don't know the extent of what is out there," said David Curtis, head of international law and corporate affairs at Microsoft. 
So far, goods have been seized in the United States, Germany, Canada, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan and enroute to Venezuela. 
The company is attempting to get a search warrant to seize goods in Melbourne shipped from Taiwan.
The software industry loses up to $14 billion a year to piracy, including illegal copying by dealers, corporations and individual users. 
Fakes are so common in Taiwan that Microsoft estimates that only 20 percent of the software used there is legally obtained. 
About 90 percent of all counterfeiting worldwide comes from Taiwan.
Illegal competition for DOS projects is keen because nearly 80 percent of all personal computers worldwide are DOS based. 
Ms. Gilligan said Microsoft commands "a big chunk" of this market.
In this case, Microsoft caught wind of the operation last October when a salesman calling on a software store client in Taipai, Taiwan, saw an MS-DOS package that didn't look right. 
The salesman purchased a copy and sent it to Alix Parlour, the company's piracy attorney based in Hong Kong, who in turn forwarded it to Microsoft's headquarters here. 
Said Ms. Gilligan, "we were in shock. 
No one could believe it happened."
Ms. Parlour set up a corporate espionage team, using private eyes from the countries involved.. 
She wanted to control the investigation, instead of turning it over to a foreign government that might not consider piracy a serious crime. 
Microsoft also wanted to compile a list of suspects -- job shops, distributors, importers, exporters and buyers. 
It then would have evidence to pursue in civil suits in each country if local authorites refused to prosecute.
Investigators started checking out Taipei printers and binderies, asking if they had big orders or knew who did, hoping clues would lead to a "kingpin."
Work would likely be done through 15 to 25 shops.
A break came when trash found behind a bindery contained clipped-off edges of Microsoft manuals. 
An investigator watching the shop noticed Microsoft materials visible on the seat of a white van parked nearby. 
He followed the van as it visited several other contractors and discovered that it was registered to the brother of another suspect.
The assembly plant was identified because all the contractors were delivering goods there. 
An investigator concealed himself outside the plant and by watching which visitors were treated with the greatest respect, soon identified the ringleaders.
By January, Ms. Parlour had enough information to ask government trademark police to raid five locations. 
A prosecutor issued search warrants for three sites and the raids yielded 5,000 packages of products, thousands of holograms, 20,000 manuals and 13,000 diskettes, all fakes. 
Documents gave the names of players and indicated 75,000 to 100,000 products, including MS-DOS 5 and the Windows operating system, had been shipped monthly since October.
The fakes were produced in five languages -- English, French, German, Italian and Swedish. 
Microsoft had thought the copies were limited to English.
One of the storage sites was the home of the 80-year-old mother of a suspect. 
Investigators said she was was unaware that the boxes stacked ceiling-high in her house contained illegal goods.
But the prosecutor refused a warrant for the residence of the ringleader, saying he saw no grounds. 
Ms. Parlour said that after the raids, "our surveillance team watched helplessly outside the leader's home as he removed records and cartons containing an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 products worth $750,000."
The man remains outside of Microsoft's grasp although the company has sued Fong Shu Gwong, who they say is the No. 2 man. 
Said Ms. Gilligan, "we believe he may serve as the fall guy and in return, his family will be well taken care of during his possible incarceration."
To Ms. Parlour's frustration, the raids did not uncover the source of the holograms. 
For a while, the team was sidetracked to Japan but the path eventually led to a broker in Hong Kong. 
When Hong Kong investigators posed as businessmen attempting to buy Microsoft holograms, the broker said, "I think I know someone who can help you," and introduced them to the Shenzhen Reflective Materials Institute in China's most capitalistic, free-market province, Guangdong.
The institute, just 10 miles from the Hong Kong border, legitimately produces holograms for Chinese documents. 
It is affiliated with the Government-owned Shenzhen University.
In March, simultaneous raids at the Shenzhen Institute and the broker's office resulted in the seizure of the hologram molds, 10,000 holograms and documents showing filled orders for 450,000 fake holograms. 
An additional contract showed a standing order for 3 million more, a loss of $150 million to Microsoft if all have been produced and placed on illicit packages that may have been distributed worldwide.
Mr. Curtis of Microsoft said the company is pleased "that we were able to conduct a raid in the P.R.C. with the cooperation of local authorities, with the grounds based on trademark violations."
As he pointed out, "We've been talking about this for a long time."
In her May 18 meeting with officials from the People's Republic, the Shenzhen Institute and the Shenzhen Administration of Industry, Ms. Parlour will attempt to negotiate release of the hologram molds or their destruction. 
She'll have representatives from the Commerce Department with her.
This spring, China agreed to strengthen its copyright laws rather than face United States trade sanctions. 
In late April, Carla Hill, the United States Trade Representative, identified Taiwan, India and Thailand under the special 301 provisions of the Trade Act of 1974.
The 301 provisions call for identifying trading partners that deny adequate and effective protection for intellectual property. 
The Government can take action if disputes are not resolved. 
China is one of 22 countries that have been placed on a special "priority watch" list.
Ms. Parlour will be trying to bring those provisions to bear.

Mr. Bush, a former United States envoy to China who prides himself on having special insight into the world's most populous country, said Beijing's opposition to Iraqi aggression showed how much Washington had in common with "this very important country, China."

It is important, I think, to the Chinese side as well."

text:

The Chinese and Soviet Foreign Ministers met today in western China for a hastily called conference on the Persian Gulf crisis, and afterward declared in a joint statement that the world should work for a peaceful solution if at all possible.
While the statement emphasized the Soviet and Chinese view that every effort should be made to avoid war, it did not rule out military intervention. 
Indeed, it could be read as a final warning to Iraq that Moscow and Beijing might endorse the use of force if Baghdad did not change.
The statement suggested that the United Nations Security Council would pass additional measures and said the Soviet Union and China would continue to work to insure the strict implementation of resolutions already passed, which call for an Iraqi withdrawal.
China and the Soviet Union have been the most reluctant of the permanent members of the Security Council to endorse a resolution authorizing the use of military force to drive Iraqi troops from Kuwait. 
While the statement was ambiguous, the two countries appeared to be positioning themselves so that they could, if necessary, declare that there was no longer hope for a peaceful solution and that they had no alternative but to back the use of force.
Â 
More Than 3 Hours of Talks
The meetings between China's Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, and his Soviet counterpart, Eduard A. Shevardnadze, were held in the northwestern Chinese city of Urumqi and lasted more than three hours. 
Plans for the meeting were disclosed only on Thursday, suggesting that it was called on very short notice.
"Both sides stand for a political solution to the gulf crisis on the basis of relevant U.N. Security Council resolutons and support the positive efforts of Arab countries to resolve the conflicts," the joint statement said, according to a version released by the official New China News Agency.
"They strongly appeal to Iraq and demand that it withdraw its army from Kuwait unconditionally and immediately," the statement continued. 
"They hold that so far as there is still hope for a peaceful solution, the international community should continue to work to that end and try its best to avoid a war."
The statement was only a little bit different from a formula China has used in the last three weeks. 
But that formula is in itself a step away from China's initial reaction, which emphasized its opposition to force and seemed to offer no exceptions.
Â 
Political Credit for Support
A Western diplomat said he expected China to vote in favor of the Security Council resolution authorizing military moves against Iraqi troops. 
Mr. Qian is reported to have said that China would not veto such a resolution, and the diplomat said China believed that it would gain additional political credit in Western capitals if it voted for the resolution instead of abstaining.
"The two foreign ministers agreed that the two sides will continue to hold consultations with each other when the United Nations Security Council adopts additional measures, so as to insure that the relevant resolutions adopted previously by the Security Council will be implemented in real earnest," the statement declared. 
"The two sides are willing to work for a solution to the gulf crisis together with the other member states of the Security Council."
Mr. Qian and Mr. Shevardnadze had 90 minutes of private talks, accompanied by only one translator and assistant for each side. 
That meeting was followed by another 90 minutes of consultations in the presence of a larger group of Foreign Ministry officials. 
Mr. Shevardnadze returned to the Soviet Union late this afternoon.
The two foreign ministers also discussed bilateral relations, but the communique gave no details. 
Chinese-Soviet relations have improved dramatically in recent years, but a projected purchase of Soviet military equipment by Beijing has stalled in negotiations in recent months.
The statement said that Mr. Qian and Mr. Shevardnadze favored "further deepening of the good-neighborly and mutually beneficial relations in all the fields between the two countries."

text:

The Bush Administration announced today that China's Foreign Minister had been invited for talks in Washington on Friday, in what appears to be compensation to Beijing for not blocking the American-sponsored United Nations resolution authorizing force against Iraq.
The announcement by the State Department that Foreign Minister Qian Qichen will meet in Washington with Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d followed a meeting between Mr. Baker and Mr. Qian in Cairo on Nov. 
6. In those talks, Mr. Baker told Mr. Qian that any assistance Beijing gave for the American policy in the Persian Gulf "will not be forgotten and the meaning of that assistance will not be lost on the domestic audience in the United States," an Administration official said.
Hours after the Chinese Foreign Ministry announced in Beijing this morning that Mr. Qian had been invited to Washington, Chinese diplomats at the United Nations, who had been waivering on whether to support the proposed Security Council resolution authorizing the use of force against Iraq, signaled definitively that they would not oppose it.
[In Beijing, Mr. Qian on Wednesday labeled as "groundless" reports that China would support the resolution, Reuters reported. 
Asked if his remarks meant China would not vote for the resolution, Mr. Qian replied: "I think so."
He stopped short of saying that Beijing would use its veto to stop the resolution.]
While Mr. Baker has met with the Chinese Foreign Minister four times since the June 1989 killings of pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, it was always either at the United Nations or overseas. 
This will be the first time Mr. Qian, who will be in New York for the Security Council meeting, is being invited to Washington, and it seemed to symbolize an end to the 18-month-long official chill in Chinese-American relations that resulted from the Tiananmen Square incident.
The Deputy State Department spokesman, Richard A. Boucher, insisted that the invitation to Mr. Qian did not contravene the sanctions imposed by the Bush Administration on China, because those banned "official exchanges," such as military or commercial delegations from one country visiting another, but not "contacts."
"We've consistently said that we would hold meetings with Chinese officials in pursuit of vital U.S. interests," Mr. Boucher said. 
"While Minister Qian is in Washington we intend to explore ways to strengthen cooperation on global and regional issues and seek understandings on ways to achieve improvement in bilateral relations, including further progress in the area of human rights, that would permit a gradual return to normal high-level exchanges.
"We have vital issues with China right now, in the Persian Gulf and with the progress on Cambodia. 
We have always made the distinction between contacts and exchanges."
Mr. Boucher also noted that the Commerce Department Under Secretary, Michael Farren, has invited China's Deputy Minister of Trade, Gu Yongjiang, to come to Washington on Dec. 
10 and 11 for trade talks.

The Administration's efforts to enlist Beijing's support for its Persian Gulf policy, even at the price of warming relations before Beijing makes any fundamental change in its human rights policies, appears to have general support from Congress, even from among those lawmakers who were the strongest advocates of punishing China for Tiananmen Square.
Representative Stephen J. Solarz, the Brooklyn Democrat who is chairman of the House subcommittee on Asia, said: "We are now confronting in the gulf the most serious crisis since the end of the cold war.

We need the Chinese to support our efforts and if this is a price that had to be paid to secure their support, it is a price worth paying.
"I hope Baker uses the opportunity, though to remind the Chinese that progress on human rights will be indispensable for any continued improvement in relations."
The invitation to the Chinese Foreign Minister is only one of the many apparent ramifications of the Administration's decision to seek a Security Council resolution that will authorize the use of force against Iraq if it does not withdraw its forces from Kuwait by Jan. 
15.

Hamilton, the Indiana Democrat who chairs the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on Europe and the Middle East, said today that the imposition of this deadline made it incumbent on the Bush Administration to open up a dialogue, either directly or indirectly, with President Saddam Hussein of Iraq to make sure he understood that if he did withdraw from Kuwait he would not be attacked.
Â 
CHINESE SEEM DELIGHTED
BEIJING, Nov. 
27 (Special to The New York Times) -- A diplomat who met with Foreign Ministry officials today said they appeared delighted that Mr. Qian had been invited to the United States.

China hopes this new stature will be a prelude to normalization of commercial and official ties to the United States and other Western countries, the official added.

file: MIDEAST TENSIONS_Chinese Official Leaves in Doubt How He Will Vote on Iraq at U.N.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, suggested today that he would not vote in favor of a United Nations Security Council resolution authorizing the use of force against Iraq.
His comments were ambiguous. 
As a permanent member of the Security Council, China could veto the resolution, although most diplomats believe this is unlikely. 
An abstention by China would diminish the international support that President Bush would like to have before moving to drive Iraqi troops from Kuwait.
It is possible that Mr. Qian's comments were intended to increase his bargaining power in negotiations with the Secretary of State, James A. Baker 3d, before the vote. 
In exchange for supporting the resolution, China would like the United States to drop sanctions and its criticism of Chinese human rights violations.
Mr. Qian tried today to dispel any notion that China had promised the United States that it would vote for a resolution endorsing the use of force if Iraqi troops do not leave Kuwait by Jan. 
15. He said, "Such reports are groundless."
Â 
'You Will Know After I Vote'
In a brief meeting today with reporters at the airport before flying to New York for the Security Council session, Mr. Qian refused to specify whether China would veto the United Nations resolution or abstain. 
Asked whether he meant that China would not vote for the resolution, he replied, "I think so."
When pressed on whether China would veto the resolution, he replied, "I didn't say so."
Asked if China would abstain, Mr. Qian said, "You will know after I vote."
The United States will have one final chance to lobby Mr. Qian before the vote, as Secretary of State Baker is expected to meet Mr. Qian after his arrival in New York and before the Security Council session, expected on Thursday.
On Tuesday, Bush Administration officials said that Mr. Qian would make an official visit to Washington at the invitation of Mr. Baker. The official visit would symbolize an end to the 18-month-long chill in official relations since the military crackdown in Beijing in June 1989. 
But an Administration spokesman said Mr. Qian's visit would not constitute an "exchange" and would therefore not contravene the Administration's ban on exchanges with senior Chinese officials.
Â 
Regained Some Legitimacy
Mr. Qian, however, said he saw no difference between contacts and exchanges, and said that his visit would be a "fairly important" event in American-Chinese relations.
A deputy trade minister, Gu Yongjiang, is also scheduled to visit the United States, on Dec. 
10-14, at the invitation of J. Michael Farren, Under Secretary of Commerce for international trade.
China has gradually regained some of its legitimacy in the world after many Western countries scaled down ties in response to the crackdown. 
But China would welcome a return to normal relations with the United States because it would help restore lending and commercial ties as China's economy is in its worst slump in more than a dozen years.
The World Bank has resumed lending to China, but not at the levels that preceded the crackdown. 
Although Iraq is an ally, China has viewed the Gulf crisis with a bit of relief because attention has been diverted away from China's human rights issues.
Â 
Editors Charged With Sedition
Because of its position on the Security Council, China has been able to assume a significant role in United Nations actions toward Baghdad, and Mr. Qian recently concluded a few weeks of hectic diplomatic activity, visiting several Middle East capitals.
While China's recent role may help boost its profile in the world, there are signs that China is continuing a tough line against dissidents jailed after the crackdown in June last year. 
Two men, Wang Juntao and Chen Ziming, were charged last week with counter-revolutionary sedition and trying to overthrow the Government.
Relatives of the two men, who are well known for their peaceful efforts to promote democracy and economic change in China, were notified of the charges. 
But they were not told when the trial would be held. 
Hundreds or thousands of other people are still in Chinese prisons or labor camps for their role in the democracy movement.
So far, China has voted in favor of the United Nations resolutions against Iraq. 
Initially it emphasized its opposition to the use of force, but in recent weeks there has been a change of emphasis, so that officials now say that so long as there is a glimmer of hope, peace should be pursued. 
Mr. Qian echoed this position again today.
Diplomats have said that China could be positioning itself so that it could eventually announce that there is no longer even a glimmer of hope for a peaceful resolution and that thus it is obliged to endorse a use of force against Baghdad.

No Hurry for Force, China Says

text:
ï»¿
The United States is ready to seek a United Nations resolution this month authorizing offensive military action against Iraq, provided that final consultations with other members of the Security Council go as anticipated, a senior American official said today.
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d arrived in Brussels tonight to begin an intensive round of country-by-country conferences, involving at least 9 of the Security Council's 15 members. 
He is seeking the backing of a half-dozen small countries, and confirmation that the Soviet Union and China will also cooperate.
The meetings will conclude on Nov. 
24, with a meeting in Bogota with Foreign Minister Luis Jaramillo Correa of Colombia, and the resolution could be introduced at the United Nations two days later.
"We do not know yet whether we will be able or not to go forward, because we don't know for certain that a country might not say no," said the senior American official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. 
"We haven't yet heard from China and the Soviet Union finally."
Â 
Congress Weighs Special Session
But other Americans involved in the talks said Washington had strong indications that most of the pivotal countries were ready to go along, despite statements made today in New York by a top Gorbachev aide, Yevgeny M. Primakov, who called for a political initiative to persuade President Saddam Hussein of Iraq to give up Kuwait peacefully.
United Nations action would greatly help an operation led by the United States to drive President Saddam Hussein's forces out of Iraq. 
All of Washington's major European allies except Britain and all of its major Arab allies have made Security Council approval a precondition to taking part in such an operation, according to a ranking European Community official.
Leading figures in Congress from both parties have said they would back a special session, in the event of a favorable vote in the Security Council, to debate President Bush's policy in the gulf. 
But it might prove difficult for critics of the policy to vote against it with a United Nations resolution already on the record. 
Congressional leaders decided Wednesday not to call for a special session now but reserved the right to do so later.
The Bush Administration considers it crucial that any resolution be brought to a vote before Nov. 
30, when the United States yields the chairmanship of the Security Council to Yemen. 
That small Arab nation has seldom been an American ally in the Persian Gulf crisis and could tangle a new resolution in parliamentary complexities, the senior official said.
Â 
'Don't Act Like Cowboys'
Top Administration policy makers have said in the last week that despite Mr. Bush's deployment of about 150,000 fresh troops to Saudi Arabia and the surrounding region, no decision has been made yet to start an offensive. 
No attack is likely, they have said, before January or February at the earliest.
A United Nations resolution, like the troop deployment, would be part of the effort to persuade Mr. Hussein that his only options are retreat or destruction. 
But it, like the troop deployment, runs the risk of frightening the American people, too, and convincing many of them that a war is imminent.
The senior American official said that, following Congressional and other advice, the Administration was making an effort "to not move precipitously, don't act like cowboys, proceed through the United Nations to the extent that you can."
Under Security Council rules, approval of a resolution authorizing the use of military force requires at least nine affirmative votes, and all of the five permanent members -- the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China -- must either vote yes or abstain.
Â 
Soviet and Chinese Votes
The Soviet Union and China have given preliminary indications, the senior official said, that they will not block a resolution along the lines the United States seeks, although there has been no sign that Soviet forces would play an active role in an offensive. 
Mr. Baker will try to clarify the Soviet position at a meeting in Paris on Sunday with Eduard A. Shevardnadze, the Soviet Foreign Minister.
Another American official said a definitive statement from China is expected within the next few days. 
Mr. Baker, who met Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in Cairo last week, is said to be confident that the Chinese will not veto the resolution but is not sure they will vote for it rather than abstain.
A Soviet decision to vote yes would probably have a major influence on the Chinese vote.
Britain and France have already signed up, as has Canada. 
Mr. Baker made a hasty trip to Bermuda on Tuesday to win the agreement of Joe Clark, the Canadian Minister of External Affairs.
Â 
No Overture to Cuba
If the Soviets and the Chinese eventually go along, that would give the United States the votes of all the permanent members and that of Canada, for a total of six. 
On Sunday, Mr. Baker will seek the backing of Finland, which is considered a likely supporter, and of Romania, whose support is thought to be a bit less certain.
That same day, he will also meet Douglas Hurd, the British Foreign Secretary, and Roland Dumas, the French Foreign Minister.
The United States hopes to get commitments of another two to four votes, giving it a total of 9 to 12, at the meeting in Colombia and at Mr. Baker's session in Geneva on Saturday with the Foreign Ministers of three African countries -- the Ivory Coast, Ethiopia and Zaire. 
State Department officials said a substantial margin was important to impress on Mr. Hussein his isolation from almost all of the world's other countries.
The other three members of the Security Council this year -- Cuba, Yemen and Malaysia -- are considered the least likely to support the United States, and Mr. Baker does not plan personally to solicit their backing. 
But the Administration has written off only Cuba, which has voted for only the mildest of the 10 resolutions on the crisis adopted by the Security Council.
Mr. Baker, who will spend Friday in Brussels, will be joined in Paris on Sunday by President Bush. 
Both will be there for the 34-nation summit meeting of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, marking the end of the cold war, which runs from Monday to Wednesday.
After the summit conference, Mr. Bush will head to Saudi Arabia to spend Thanksgiving with American troops there and offshore, and then to Cairo.
Â 
BUSH PLAN FOR IRAQI ARMS
WASHINGTON, Nov. 
15 (Special to The New York Times) -- President Bush said tonight that an Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait should be followed by international guarantees that would eliminate Iraqi chemical weapons and halt that country's nuclear weapons program.
In an interview on Cable News Network, Mr. Bush stopped short of making the elimination of chemical and nuclear weapons in Iraq a military goal of the United States. 
He said any effort to control those weapons after the current crisis is over would have to be carried out under United Nations auspices.
Mr. Bush went somewhat further than he had been willing to go in saying that in addition to forcing an Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait, the United States was eager to eliminate Mr. Hussein's arsenal.
"Having demonstrated this recklessness," he said, "I don't think the rest of the world would say this is good enough, just what they call the status quo ante, going back to the way things were before the invasion."
Mr. Bush said that even if Iraq withdrew peacefully from Kuwait, "I think you'd see an understandable cry in the reinvigorated United Nations, under the peacekeeping function" to have controls on Iraqi weaponry.

file: Modern Dance Imbued With Mountain Spirit.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE modern dancer Yung Yung Tsuai has introduced us to her ancestral China and now she will bring us a view of a culture within our own country.
The founder of Yung Yung Tsuai and Dancers, who is also the artistic director of the Byrdcliffe Performing Arts Center in New Rochelle, has participated since last September in the Visiting Artists Program of North Carolina. 
Based at Isothermal Community College, about an hour's drive from Asheville in the Blue Ridge Mountains, she gave school and community lectures, presented modern-dance demonstrations and performances and led workshops.
One product of Ms. Tsuai's experience is a new dance, ''Blue Ridge Blues,'' which Ms. Tsuai and her company will present in its Westchester premiere next Friday and Saturday at 8:30 P.M. at the Emelin Theater in Mamaroneck.
Folk Ballads and Songs
The story depicts the way contemporary life has weakened the Southern American mountain culture, particularly its folk-dance tradition. 
It is danced to folk ballads and songs that will be performed by the husband and wife team of Lynn and Liz Shaw, fiddlers and singers from North Carolina. 
They are producing a folk-music series for the Public Broadcasting System to be broadcast next year.
As a cultural footnote, Christine Morris, a mountain clogger from West Virginia, will perform the traditional clogging steps upon which ''Blue Ridge Blues'' is based. 
(The work will also be presented outdoors, free of charge, at Untermeyer Park in Yonkers on July 8 at 8 P.M.) Other dances to be performed on the Emelin program will include Ms. Tsuai's autobiographical ''Song of the Great Wall''; ''Ekstasis,'' choreographed by Anne Tobias, and ''Trading Places,'' which the North Carolina choreographer Lynne Tanner created with Ms. Tsuai.
Â 
Where the Tradition Grew
''Blue Ridge Blues'' is a departure from Ms. Tsuai's past work, which has delved into East-West relationships. 
The dancer, a native of Taiwan, said she went south with only a vague idea of what she would find. 
A New York City-area resident for most of the 18 years since she came to this country, on a scholarship from Martha Graham, Ms. Tsuai said she felt it was time to explore. 
''I was looking for inspiration for other sources of creativity,'' she said.
Aware that ''bluegrass and clogging and the mountain-dance tradition came from this area,'' Ms. Tsuai set out at the beginning of her stay to find the region's folk musicians and dancers. 
It was a measure of their declining numbers that she spent three months looking.
''When I first heard I was going to meet a modern dancer from New York, I thought, 'Oh, sure - fine,' '' said Ms. Shaw, who conceded that she had been skeptical about finding anything in common with Ms. Tsuai. Speaking by telephone from North Carolina, she added that she did not know in advance the dancer was Chinese.
''When Yung walked in, carrying a little gift of two jade Buddhas in a glazed box, I thought 'Wow!'
'' said the fiddler, explaining that taking gifts to new acquaintances was a mountain custom as well as a Chinese one. 
It was the beginning of a collaboration that revealed surprising similarities in outlooks.
Ms. Shaw is a fifth-generation fiddler as well as a fifth-generation practitioner of shape-note singing - singing based on an 18th-century musical system in which each note of the scale is assigned a geometric shape. 
(''The harmonies break all laws of music, and have their own distinctive sound,'' Ms. Shaw said.) The shape-note tradition took hold and survived in parts of the South, and Ms. Shaw is determined to keep it alive. 
Ms. Tsuai, she said, understands this goal.
''Her culture respects her ancestors and traditions, and honors that in you that has lived before you,'' said the fiddler, who referred to the two of them as ''the Chinese lady and the mountain girl.''
The Shaws and others became Ms. Tsuai's teachers of mountain music and dance. 
''Here was this Martha Graham scholar asking me questions!'' exclaimed Ms. Shaw. She described Ms. Tsuai as ''unassuming'' and ''a great student.''
Ms. Tsuai stressed that she studied ''traditional'' clogging, as opposed to ''precision'' clogging, which was developed after 1920 and has become more ''commercial.''
She described clogging as ''similar to Chinese folk dance'' in its ''uplifting spirit'' as well as its ''rhythm.''
''The fire inside of you comes out,'' during the dance, Ms. Tsuai said. 
She added that clogging had its origins in Scotland and Ireland, but had also been influenced by the American Indian and black cultures.
Traditional cloggers wear hard soled, high topped shoes, but ''Blue Ridge Blues'' will be danced barefoot. 
The work ''is inspired by clogging but is still a modern-dance form,'' Ms. Tsuai said.
Movements based on such steps as ''ringing the cow's tail,'' where one leg goes around in a circle behind the other, and the ''shuffle'' will be danced to songs like ''Handsome Molly,'' ''Pisca'' (a shape-note song), ''Young Emily,'' ''Soldier's Joy'' and ''Kitchen Girl.''
The stage set has been created by James Byrne, an artist from Central Piedmont College in North Carolina, to show industry encroaching on the mountain way of life. 
Ms. Tsuai's 13-year-old daughter, Tysan, will be among the featured dancers.
While Ms. Tsuai noted that ''there is almost no trace of the Chinese'' in ''Blue Ridge Blues,'' many of her experiences in North Carolina resonated with her background. 
The dancer told of the time she visited a fox hunter, who called to his 80 dogs with a high-pitched song. 
''About 30 dogs showed up,'' Ms. Tsuai said. 
''It stirred up a lot of Chinese fox stories.''
The main impulse for the dance, however, came from her belief in tradition. 
''I feel sad about the cultures dying,'' she said, adding that there had been some progress in reviving the Blue Ridge art forms.
Ms. Shaw said Ms. Tsuai had ''captured the spirit'' of the mountains in her work. 
''This dance of hers has a special message for me,'' she said.

file: Mongols to Elect New Parliament With China Watching the Results.txt
text:
ï»¿
Mongolians go to the polls Sunday, in some areas by horse or camel, to vote in sharply contested parliamentary elections that are in part a referendum on the pace of the nation's transition to democracy and a market economy.
The campaign is a triumph of pluralism, with a dozen political parties representing the interests of everyone from shepherds to capitalists. 
But many Mongolians say they have lost the enthusiasm that they felt for the first competitive election, held two years ago in the aftermath of the democratic revolution that ended seven decades of Communist rule.
"I was very excited by democracy when it first arrived," Ninj, a 55-year-old housewife, said as she prepared dinner over a fire in her ger, the traditional white felt tent in which many Mongolians still live. 
"I thought everything would get better, but in fact not much has changed. 
I'm very disappointed."
Â 
At Issue: Pace of Change
While each party has a different platform, the main issue facing the new Parliament is the pace of democratic change. 
The governing party, the former Communist Party, is privatizing the economy and freeing the press, and seems committed to continue doing so, but an opposition victory would probably accelerate the process.
Ms. Ninj, who like most Mongolians uses one name, said she would vote for the former Communist Party, formally known as the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party. 
The Party had intended to modernize by dropping the word "Revolutionary" from its name, but in the meantime, a Buddhist monk registered his own party called the Mongolian People's Party and so the former Communists are stuck with their old name.
"I got used to the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party when I was young," said Ms. Ninj as she sat in her ger, which is 20 feet in diameter and has a smoke hole in the top. 
"And so that's who I'm going to vote for."
The generation gap cuts across this ger, as it does all Mongolia. 
Ms. Ninj's 25-year-old daughter, Ulziy, said she would vote for the newly formed Capitalist Party. 
Ms. Ulziy said she thinks the Capitalist Party will lower tariffs and allow the import of the food and clothing that Mongolia lacks.
Ms. Ulziy has another reason to support the new democratic forces: They helped overturn the Communist policy that banned abortion and all forms of artificial birth control. 
The Communists felt that Mongolia needed more than its 2.1 million inhabitants in a country about three times the size of Texas. 
But Ms. Ulziy already has two children and thinks that is plenty.
The voting here in Mongolia could reverberate across the border into the Inner Mongolia region of China, where nationalism has been rising among ethnic Mongols ever since Mongolia's free elections in 1990. 
The Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party won those elections after it renounced Communism, and China clearly hopes that it will win again on Sunday.
Â 
Beijing Aids Party Paper
Last year China even intervened in Mongolian politics, donating 500 tons of newsprint to the newspaper published by the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party. 
China apparently worries that if the former Communists are voted out of power in Mongolia, China's Mongols will be inspired to seek democracy or independence.
The elections will choose the members of a new 76-member Parliament, which will replace the previous, much larger legislature. 
President Punsalmaagiyn Ochirbat, a former Communist who says he has turned a new leaf, is not up for re-election.
The architect of the democratic revolution two years ago, Zorig, is today the chairman of the main opposition coalition. 
Mr. Zorig, who now teaches politics, is 29 years old and reflects the general youthfulness of the campaign. 
Nearly 40 percent of the 300 candidates are 30 years old or under, while only 25 percent are 46 or more.

file: More in China Willingly Rear Just One Child.txt
text:
ï»¿
Gong Daifang, a 36-year-old peasant, has made a decision that her ancestors probably would never have understood: her 10-year-old son is enough, and she will not have another child.
Even when local leaders in this brick-and-mud village in Sichuan province offered to allow her to have a second child, she decided that for practical economic reasons she would have only one, instead of seven like her own mother.
''My husband and I thought it over, but we believe that this way we can save money and lead a better life,'' Miss Gong explained. 
China's population, the world's largest at 1.1 billion, is still increasing. 
But there are indications of a revolution in attitudes, with more and more Chinese couples falling in line with the nation's one-child policy as a matter of choice rather than compulsion. 
In view of the changing attitudes, some experts are predicting that China's population will actually decline after peaking in the early 21st century.
Coercion still underlies the one-child policy, and the rationing of the right to become pregnant remains a source of tension and bitterness in many parts of China. 
Many peasants grumble that the policy is not always carried out fairly, or should not be applied to them until they give birth to a son. 
Even Government officials acknowledge that some women are probably still forced to have abortions, and that many parents would like more children than they are allowed.
But there is little doubt that young people's attitudes are changing and that China's family planning campaign has much broader support than it did.
Interviews over the last year with families in scattered parts of China, including rural areas in Sichuan, Hunan and Gansu provinces as well as in Beijing, suggest that many young people today want only one or two children and that the traditional Chinese enthusiasm for large families is rapidly declining.
Deng Daoyun, a 24-year-old peasant who lives in the picturesque Sichuan hamlet of Sancun, 40 miles north of the city of Chengdu, is proud of her 3-year-old son but said she was happy to stop where she was.
''One child is enough. 
More kids, more nuisance,'' she said, mocking the old saying that goes, ''More sons, more joy.''
Liao Zhenxiu, a housewife in Duanjiaba, pointed at her television set and tape recorder as the reasons for not having a second child. 
''If I had lots of kids, how could I afford these things?'' she asked. 
''If you have lots of kids, you're poor.''
Â 
The Bottom Line Is Money
Two factors underlie the changing preferences. 
The first is the emergence of a quasi-market economy, in which a mother can get a job and earn more money if she has fewer children. 
The second is the institutionalizing of the Chinese Government's system of incentives and penalties that give enormous advantages to those who have just one child.
The incentives vary by region, but often a couple with just one child will get more land, a better house, a reduction in grain taxes and a subsidy amounting to about $15 a year -equivalent to more than a month's income for many poor peasants. 
On the other hand, those who have children without permission must pay fines annually for 10 years, amounting each time to 5 to 10 percent of the parents' income.
The upshot is that there is much less need today to drag women to abortion clinics, because cool calculation of the penalties may well lead them to seek abortions voluntarily.
It is clear that without the system of incentives and penalties, there would be more children. 
In Qinmi in Sichuan, 24-year-old Tan Wenbi cuddled her 20-day-old son and said she would have no other child. 
But asked what would happen if there were no one-child policy, she thought for a moment and then said that if that were the case she would like a girl as well.
In Tongzhi, a village in Hunan, 28-year-old Rong Maozi said she was delighted to have one boy and one girl. 
But if there were no pressure whatever, she said, she would continue to bear children.
''I'd like more kids, boys and girls, but they won't let me,'' she said. 
But her voice held no rancor, suggesting that more than a dozen years of propaganda about family planning have had an effect.
Â 
Acknowledging the Problem
''The lessons really have sunk in,'' said Aprodicio Laquian, a Filipino who recently completed a five-year assignment in China as country director of the United Nations Fund for Population Activities. 
''If you ask a person on the street if China has a population problem, they'll immediately say 'yes.'
''
Despite the new attitude, however, foreign experts and accounts in China's official press say the family-planning program faces severe problems in meeting its short-term targets. 
Chinese officials acknowledge that it will be extremely difficult to meet their goal of holding the population to 1.2 billion by the turn of the century. 
China now has 1.1 billion people, and the number is growing by more than 15 million a year. 
The principal challenges are these:
* China's baby boomers, born after the famine at the beginning of the 1960's, are now in their reproductive years and will produce an echo of the earlier baby boom.
* Many young Chinese are now so prosperous that they can afford the fines for having a second or third child. 
In some areas these fines are called the ''extra baby fee.''
* The Government no longer has such tight control over the country as it used to.
In Sancun, the family planning official, a woman named Zhuang Dazi, keeps record books of the menstrual cycles of all women in the village, and there has not been an unplanned child in a decade. 
But control mechanisms are disintegrating in some other parts of the country. 
Some women now travel away from their hometowns when they become pregnant, and give birth without ever registering their baby. 
And because of the decline in control, it is also possible for women to bribe doctors to remove their intrauterine devices, or IUD's, the most common form of birth control in China.
Â 
Misguided Short-Term Goals
China's population goals are at risk partly because the Government relaxed the Draconian controls it began implementing at the end of the 1970's. 
Some foreign diplomats worry that the authorities could institute a new policy including forced abortions and other harsh measures. 
But officials here, recalling the bad publicity China received around the world for such measures, say that will not happen.
''The situation is rather grave,'' said Shen Guoxiang, a spokesman for the State Family Planning Commission. 
''But that doesn't mean we should tighten control over family planning.''
While China will almost certainly miss its target for the turn of the century, that goal is widely regarded as misguided. 
If China had been more successful in carrying out its one-child policy, experts say, a result would have been a rapid aging of the population and social strains as a relatively small number of workers supports an unusually large proportion of retired people. 
Concern about this problem appears to be one reason why China is not implementing the one-child policy as strictly as it used to.
China's continuing population increase has more to do with demographics - half the population is 25 or younger, and so is still producing children or is yet to produce children - than with family size. 
But after this demographic bulge reaches middle age and retirement, the population is expected to contract. 
Accounts in the official Chinese press even muse that the nation's ''ideal'' population is 700 million, implying that this figure could be a longterm goal.
Â 
A Closer Look at the Statistics
Chinese officials and foreign commentators frequently say that Chinese women still have an average of nearly 2.5 children, despite the one-child policy. 
But this is misleading, Chinese and foreign demographers say. 
While China's total fertility rate is about 2.3, this statistic measures births for all women in their reproductive years, ages 15 to 49. 
Thus the figure includes some women in their 40's who bore three or four children long before family planning controls were introduced.
A more accurate reflection of the present situation is the distribution of births. 
More than half of all births are of first children, and an additional 25 to 30 percent are of second children. 
Only 15 percent of all births are of third children.
The family planning rules that achieved the declines in fertility differ by province, but here in Sichuan, couples can apply to have a second child if the first is sickly or if the parents are disabled and need help. 
In remote areas, couples can normally have two children and occasionally they are allowed three. 
Partly because of this relaxation, there are scarcely any accusations within China these days about forced abortions.
''The Government absolutely doesn't allow forced abortions,'' said Tan Sushun, director of the Sichuan College for Family Planning Professions. 
''When a woman is pregnant outside the plan, we give her education and tell her not to give birth. 
But if she really wants to, she can.''
Miss Tan acknowledged that some village officials do resort to force, against the rules, but villagers interviewed said they did not know of such cases. 
Indeed, force is usually unnecessary, for even the most strong-willed couple will normally wilt and agree to an abortion after months of reprimands and threats from village officials.

file: More Soviet Workers at U.N. Are Really Working for U.N.txt
text:
ï»¿
The 430 or so Soviet citizens who work for the United Nations Secretariat got a welcome New Year's gift this year: Starting Jan. 
1, they are no longer expected to hand over a chunk of their salaries to the Soviet Mission.
The change is one of several introduced by the Soviet Union since President Mikhail S. Gorbachev achieved power there. 
And while Chinese staff members are still forced to give part of their pay to the Chinese Mission, the events of the last year have meant changes not only for United Nations workers from the Soviet Union, but also for their colleagues from Eastern Europe and even for the Chinese.
One change is in the nature of United Nations assignments. 
Most countries believe the United Nations should be staffed by an independent, international civil service loyal only to the principles of the United Nations Charter. 
They encourage their citizens to take lifetime career posts.
During the cold war, Moscow, its East European satellites and China sent workers to the United Nations for limited periods, frequently housing them in diplomatic missions. 
Many were intelligence agents and all were Communist Party loyalists expected to follow government orders at work.
Â 
Discarding 'Obsolete Approaches'
In some cases they were made to surrender a part of their pay that varied with rank and marital status but was intended to leave them with as much spending money as a diplomat of equivalent rank.
Two years ago, the Soviet Union agreed to allow staff members to live outside the mission compounds in New York and elsewhere and promised to reconsider its policy on personnel.
Last October Deputy Foreign Minister Valentin M. Nikiforov told the General Assembly that Moscow was discarding "obsolete approaches to personnel problems" and that Soviet workers for international organizations would be treated in a manner "fully -- I repeat, fully -- consistent with international norms and standards."
Moscow has said it will now allow those who wish to take career posts. 
But it will continue making some short-term appointments, arguing that these bring expertise and new ideas to the United Nations.
Â 
New Permanent Contracts
In 1990, 84 Soviet and East European staff members, including 65 Soviet citizens, came to the end of their fixed-term contracts. 
Instead of being replaced by other Soviet citizens or receiving other short-term positions, 16 of the 84, including 9 Soviet citizens, were given permanent or probationary permanent contracts by the United Nations, which informed their governments without asking their permission.
Another 13 got new fixed-term contracts after saying they did not want the permanent jobs the United Nations offered them. 
A further 37, all Soviet citizens, have been given short-term extensions while the United Nations decides whether to offer them permanent posts.
And the United Nations plans to begin awarding permanent posts to competent Chinese employees without consulting Beijing.

file: MOSCOW IS SELLING WEAPONS TO CHINA, U.S. OFFICIALS SAY.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a move that is undercutting efforts to stem the spread of arms, Russia is selling missile-guidance technology, rocket engines and other advanced weapons systems to China, its onetime adversary, American officials say.
The exports to Beijing worry Bush Administration officials, who fear that a main reason the Chinese are acquiring the technology is to develop new weapons to sell to the third world.
"Re-export is a big problem," a Pentagon official said. 
"You don't know what the Chinese will do with the stuff once they get the high-tech capabilities."
Russia's arms sales have become a growing worry for Washington even as its military threat has shrunk. 
Moscow's reduction in military spending, combined with a desperate need for hard currency, has led arms factories and military-related institutes to look abroad for orders to survive. 
At the same time, conversion of military industries to civilian production has proved difficult.
Â 
Enriching Uranium
In addition to weapons, a senior Bush Administration official said, Moscow is selling technology to the Chinese that can be used to enrich uranium. 
Washington is concerned that Beijing will use the technology to improve the design of its nuclear power plants, making them attractive to third-world buyers and further undermining efforts to stop the spread of nuclear arms.
Despite a cooperative relationship with non-Communist Russia, the United States has so far been unable to stop the Russian sales. 
Russian officials seem to have decided that the proceeds from arms and technology sales are worth the risk of irritating American policy makers.
The Administration, for its part, seems to have concluded that supporting reform in Russia is more important than drawing a firm line against weapons sales and threatening a reduction in financial assistance.
Â 
U.S. Formally Complains
Moscow is proceeding with the sale of diesel submarines to Iran, and a Russian company, Glavkosmos, is selling a rocket booster to India in violation of an agreement restricting technology for ballistic missiles. 
A senior American official said the Administration had complained to Russia and China about the sale, apparently with no effect.
Undermining its leverage, the protests by Washington have come as Western nations, including the United States, have shown little restraint themselves in selling arms. 
The Administration, although it has exhorted governments of other industrial nations to control the spread of destabilizing weapons, appears to have placed emphasis on competing with its allies for arms deals as it faces a faltering economy and a difficult election campaign.
Two such deals -- the sales of combat jets to Saudi Arabia and Taiwan totaling $14.8 billion, announced in September -- exceed the value of American arms sales to all nations of the third world last year. 
Administration officials say that the Russians would be selling weapons to Iran and China regardless of American sales. 
But Russian officials have cited such deals to justify their exports.
The pattern of Moscow's arms sales has changed considerably since the cold war, when it provided billions of dollars in arms to nations like Cuba, Iraq and Libya, often at concessionary terms, in an effort to extend or maintain its military influence.
What the Russians are after is cash, not influence. 
That, plus the defeat of Iraq in the Persian Gulf war, which effectively removed Baghdad as a potential client, has limited the number of prospective customers. 
Two of the major customers are Iran and China.
Â 
Risky Business
"In absolute figures Russian exports have gone down," an Administration official said, "but the reality is that the customers that still want to buy from them are questionable."
And Richard F. Grimmett, an expert on conventional arms sales at the Congressional Research Service, observed: "The Russian focus is on those countries that are willing to pay cash. 
There is a tremendous focus on Iran. 
China has picked up, too. 
The Chinese cannot get high-technology weapon systems from other suppliers. 
What you have there is a marriage of convenience."
Russia has sold diesel submarines and SU-24 and MIG-29 aircraft to Iran, and is providing spare parts for some of the Iraqi aircraft that were flown to Iran during the gulf war -- planes that the Iranians have said they will not return. 
And along with Czechoslovakia, Russia has sold T-72 tanks to Syria.
Â 
Better Guidance Systems
American officials say Moscow has sold missile-guidance technology, rocket engines and rocket technology to China. 
China's air-to-air missiles are not well equipped to seek out enemy planes, and Russian technology is expected to enable Beijing to improve them. 
China's surface-to-surface missiles are also considered to have inferior guidance systems and could benefit considerably from Russian exports, American officials said.
Moscow has sold S-300 surface-to-air missiles to China, the officials say. 
The S-300 is a Patriot-like system designed to shoot down planes and missiles.
In addition, Russia has sold 24 SU-27 fighters to China. 
American officials believe that Beijing is buying the planes in hope of acquiring production technology so that future aircraft can be assembled at home. 
Adding to the American concern, there are indications of discussions between Russians and Chinese officials about the joint production in China of tactical missiles and other weapons systems, an Administration official said.
Russia is also selling tanks and tank technology to Beijing.
A further worry, a senior Administration official said, is the sale of advanced Russian dual-use technology, which can be employed to enrich uranium for nuclear power plants. 
The United States is worried that this technology transfer will help China modernize its nuclear power plants and make them more marketable in the third world.
Both Russia and China have recently announced the sale of nuclear power plants to Iran, a transaction that disturbs Washington. 
The Administration believes that even ostensibly peaceful nuclear programs will enhance Teheran's expertise and help it develop nuclear weapons.
Â 
Yeltsin Lays It Out
The Russians have not been secretive about arms sales. 
In February, President Boris N. Yeltsin said weapons exports would be a cushion for the Russian arms industry as the country tried to make the transition to a civilian economy.
More recently, a Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman justified the sale of three diesel submarines to Iran in blunter terms, saying it was a way of raising cash during a difficult period.
"Russia cannot in principle, taking into account the economic situation in this country, give up the receipts of freely convertible currency through the sales of armaments abroad," the spokesman said.
Whatever the rationale, Moscow has been stepping up sales efforts. 
In August, it held a major air show and used the occasion to promote arms, displaying surface-to-air missiles and self-propelled artillery. 
Signs in Russian and English said customers could buy military aircraft out of existing inventories or purchase specially configured planes off production lines. 
Chinese and North Koreans were among the foreign officials examining the weapons systems.
Norman Friedman, an American military expert, remarked, "They have got one product that is worth buying and they are selling it."

file: Muscovites Welcome Peace But Lament Lack of Dessert.txt
text:
ï»¿
The most immediate tangible result promised here today from Mikhail S. Gorbachev's Beijing visit was Peking duck and a dozen other dishes. 
The arrival of 29 Chinese chefs is being expedited because of the summit meeting, according to officials working on the refurbishing of Moscow's dowdy, long-Russified Chinese restaurant.
Aside from that tidbit, Muscovites were stolidly unoptimistic in interviews about any short-run hopes for additional consumer goods from Mr. Gorbachev's mission. 
But they were genuinely relieved about the pledges of greater tranquility on the border after 30 years of hostile relations.
''We're tired of quarreling with the Chinese and I pray to God relations get better,'' said Olga M. Strepikheyeva, a 79-year-old retiree whose main point was that it is a long way from the Beijing talks to the empty shop shelves here.
Â 
The Fruits of Heroism
''Gorbachev is taken as a hero in China, but here his heroism has brought us nothing in the stores,'' she said. 
Then spotting a group of Chinese tourists passing her on Gertsena Street, the tiny woman smiled cherubically under her spring babushka and gestured to them with mock gaiety, ''Yes, let them see our fabulous life under Mr. Gorbachev.''
Muscovites were outspoken and well informed about the trip, but only within the limits of the official Soviet news reports on the Beijing events. 
These were notably deficient in explaining the mammoth size and libertarian politics of the Chinese demonstrations that disrupted Mr. Gorbachev's itinerary.
''The line people like to say about Gorbachev is that he is the stormy petrel of perestroika,'' said Yuri Bospalko, stressing the troubled seas that bring change. 
Word From the U.S. 
Mr. Bospalko was one of the few Muscovites to have an accurate idea of the street scenes in Beijing because he is deputy chief editor of the American news desk at Tass, the Soviet press agency, and privy to foreign dispatches not circulated here.
''I know about the one million demonstrators because we get Cable News Network on the dish upstairs and our correspondents fax us summaries of the American press,'' he said in the street outside the Tass office, asserting that fuller reports on the demonstrations would be made available in the Soviet press tomorrow. 
''I think Gorbachev is handling things in Beijing about as well as he handles things here in the Central Committee,'' he said admiringly.
Aleksandr G. Davidov, a construction engineer, said it was important to understand that the summit meeting was about ''more serious global problems'' and ''certainly not'' about the Soviet consumer's relentless troubles with scarce goods and the current panic buying of such commodities as matches and salt.
''To tell you the truth I have only a very vague idea about the demonstrations by the Chinese,'' he said when asked, reflecting the fact that Soviet television has been showing fleeting and colorfully serene pictures of the street crowds.
Â 
'I Am a Capitalist'
It was not until Mr. Gorbachev's televised news conference Wednesday night that viewers could tell from the emphasis of Western correspondents' questions that the Soviet leader was in a delicate position, being identified with the demonstrators' demands for political change.
''I know all about the demonstrations and I praise the students' reason,'' said Arkady P. Zorkin, who said he was a devotee of Western radio news broadcasts here. 
''They should get rid of their bureaucracy just like here.''
A retired veteran, Mr. Zorkin smiled and proclaimed, ''I am a capitalist,'' as he showed a dozen telescopes he has set up so visitors to the Lenin Hills promenade can rent peeks at the Moscow skyline below, an enterprise that was forbidden not too long ago. 
Such entrepreneur's savvy is what Mr. Gorbachev's summit meeting is all about, he said, predicting impressive economic growth from the visit, ''especially in the Far East.''
Farther up the hill wends Friendship Street, no longer an ill-fitting name for the address of the Chinese Embassy compound.
''There were awful incidents, tense relations,'' Valery I. Lukyanenko recalled of the cross-border fistfights and fatal shootings 20 years ago between the two nations' soldiers. 
''But now all around the world things are becoming more normal,'' he said in the sunshine.
''It's a revolutionary visit, a step beyond all the old problems and troubles,'' said Sergei A. Zhdanov, another passer-by outside the embassy.
Â 
A Time for Fantasies
Downtown at the Peking Restaurant, which saw its last Chinese chef over 30 years ago before the Chinese-Soviet troubles, Galina F. Gorinova, was preparing for a visit to Beijing on Saturday with five other Russians to make final arrangments for the 29 Chinese chefs and assorted restaurant managers who will be moving to Moscow. 
''The summit has expedited everything,'' she said. 
''And these chefs will be participating in the joint venture with a personal stake in the enterprise.''
Out on the street, Yuri Bychkov and Arkady Kostrolitin allowed themselves post-summit fantasies.
''Carpets, towels, sprinting shoes, hats,'' said Mr. Kostrolitin, summarizing what China means to him. 
''Remember those good raincoats in the old days?''
Both were curious about the demonstrations in Beijing. 
''Political freedom?''
Mr. Bychkov said when told what they were about. 
''We're also demanding political freedom,'' he said, smiling. 
''Some of the great Taiwan sound equipment would also be all right.''

text:
