Karen A. Krusich earns less than the other M.B.A.'s in her class back home, just $200 a month, but in her current job she does get plenty of respect. 
The first time she walked into a classroom here, the students applauded.
"Around here, they're not bitter and know-it-all," she said. 
They tend to be adoring -- and persistent.
"Every time I'm on my bike, people say, 'Hello, can I talk to you in English?'
" Ms. Krusich said with a grimace. 
"Sometimes I love it. 
Sometimes I want to scream."
Thousands of Americans like Ms. Krusich are getting respect, if not a lot of money, teaching English for a year or two at colleges throughout China. 
They leave an indelible mark.
In some cities, people sometimes cannot identify the Mayor but gossip knowledgeably about the foreign teachers. 
And English-speaking officials or academics often reminisce about American professors who taught them how to pronounce the "th" sounds, which are not found in Chinese, or introduced them to ideas of democracy.
Â 
An Experience to Relish
About 30,000 "foreign experts," including 9,000 or so Americans, work in China. 
Most are teachers, but their ranks also include doctors, crop specialists and even editors who polish English-language translations of Chinese propaganda.
Here in Nanchang, a provincial capital in east-central China, about 30 foreigners teach English in colleges.
"At first the little children here cried when they saw me, and ran away," said Ms. Krusich, a 42-year-old businesswoman from Chicago. 
"But then I started giving them candy, so now they're very friendly."
Now the children call Ms. Krusich "Auntie," and like most Americans she says she relishes the experience in China. 
Still, there seem to be two frequent minefields for foreign experts: romance and politics.
Many of the American teachers are single and in their early 20's, hormones coursing through their arteries in the same way that the veins of Chinese officials pulsate with prudishness and paternalism. 
While foreigners sometimes date and even marry local Chinese without difficulty, officials in some areas try to swat Cupid away.
Such officials tend to feel that when around foreigners, Chinese should never let down their guard, much less their clothes, and they fear infiltration of relative Western casualness about sex as much as Western seriousness about democracy. 
Such officials sometimes act as match-breakers and punish the Chinese involved.
Two years ago, a Chinese woman in Beijing was imprisoned on accusations of prostitution because of her steady relationship with a British boyfriend.
Today's foreign teachers are the latest in a long line of Western adventurers -- at least since the Jesuits of the 16th century -- who have come to China to teach Western ideas, technologies or languages. 
Early in this century, many Christian missionaries taught in schools throughout China, and then too some Chinese were suspicious of "foreign devils," as well as apprehensive about any intimacy.
Another delicate subject is politics. 
During the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement, many foreign experts took to the streets with their students, but now most teachers and students alike seem to try to avoid direct criticisms of the Government, except in private conversations.
Still, teachers often introduce Western ideas in more subtle ways. 
Yingling Chin, a Chinese-American from Illinois who teaches in Nanchang, said that when he had a choice of two American films to show the class he asked the students to take a vote. 
Initially confused by the idea, the students have now caught on.
"It's an exercise in democracy," Mr. Chin said with a grin.
Salaries for teachers range from $120 to $200 a month. 
Most say they came because they wanted to experience life in an exotic foreign country, or because they wanted to learn more about China in particular.
They normally get rent-free apartments, with a telephone and often a maid. 
The accommodations are palatial by Chinese standards, but Westerners are often put off by the power failures, water shortages, and doormen who make Chinese visitors register their names.
"They tend to complain when they're there and rave when they come back," said Robert M. Pease, the executive director of the Princeton-in-Asia program, which has placed 25 college graduates in China in each of the last two years. 
"I don't think anybody regrets doing it."
Â 
The Numbers Are Up Again
Mr. Pease said the number of Americans in the China program peaked at 43 in 1988-89, right before the army fired on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing. 
The killings caused a sharp drop in applications, but now the numbers are up again.
Some foreign experts come through university programs like the one Mr. Pease administers. 
Others get in touch with Chinese embassies to volunteer their services, or write to the Foreign Affairs Office in the city or province where they want to work.
Chinese officials go out of their way to make their visitors feel at home. 
Some years ago, a group of American experts in the city of Chengdu were planning a grand Thanksgiving dinner and searched the region for a turkey, with no success. 
To universal delight, the Chinese hosts presented them on Thanksgiving Day with two turkeys, which were consumed with great merriment.
"Finally, someone asked them where they got the turkeys," recalled Jane Kenyon, a New Yorker who was then teaching English in Chengdu and who attended the dinner. 
"They said, 'The zoo.'
"

file: NATIONAL NOTEBOOK_ Atlanta_Asian Square, For Shopping.txt
text:
ï»¿
CONSTRUCTION of an $8 million, 109,000-square-foot shopping center begins next month to serve a growing Asian population here.
The project, Asian Square, is scheduled for completion in mid-1992, said Roger Lin, general partner in a group of Chinese businessmen developing it. 
Space is being leased or sold, and so far 30 percent of it has been committed, he said.
The shopping center will have a supermarket as an anchor that will carry specialty foods appealing to Asian tastes. 
It will rise just northeast of Atlanta, in the town of Doraville, home to many of the Asian immigrants moving to the Atlanta area. 
The architect is Gerald Tirella of Atlanta.
The partners are financing the project themselves, said Mr. Lin, a native of Taiwan who has lived in Atlanta for eight years.
Although the Atlanta region has a glut of retail space, Mr. Lin said the partnership was encouraged to pursue the project because of the growing Asian population and the success of a similar shopping center nearby.
About 70,000 Asians -- among them immigrants from Taiwan, Hong Kong, Korea and Vietnam -- live in the Atlanta area. 
The population is expected to jump to about 82,000 by 1995.
The smaller Asian shopping center, China Town, built by another group of Chinese businessmen, is almost fully leased. 
The center, which includes a bank, a newsstand, a video store and several restaurants, attracts large crowds, particularly on weekends.
"There certainly is a need for another Asian shopping center," said James Yeh, president of the Atlanta Taiwanese Chamber of Commerce.
Although Asian Square may struggle initially because of its large size, Mr. Yeh said the project should be successful in the long run. 
The vacancy rate for retail space in Atlanta is 15.7 percent, according to a study by Jamison Research in Atlanta.
Mr. Yeh said Asian businesses are now scattered along a corridor between Doraville and Chamblee, another Atlanta bedroom community northeast of the city. 
Business leaders hope that the shopping centers will concentrate merchants in a Chinatown arrangement of the sort found in other major cities.
Kim Nguyen, a clothing store owner who plans to move to Asian Square, said several Asian businesses had outgrown their current space and were looking for new locations.
"I think it's going to be a good place to have a business," said Mr. Nguyen, a native of Vietnam who has lived in Atlanta for about 10 years.

file: NATIONALISTS WIN TAIWAN ELECTIONS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The governing Nationalist Party won a major victory today in Taiwan's first full election in more than four decades, as voters appeared to rebuff opposition calls for a declaration of independence from China.
Communist leaders in Beijing, who had been intensely concerned about the election and had warned that they would attack if Taiwan declared its independence, are expected to be as relieved as their adversaries in the Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang.
The election, a milestone in the political restructuring of Taiwan, means that the Kuomintang will have the votes it needs to control a Parliament that will convene in March to revise the constitution and perhaps ordain a new system of government.
The Nationalists won 71 percent of the vote, on the high side of expectations. 
The main opposition group, the Democratic Progressive Party, which advocates independence, received 24 percent of the vote, well below its goal and also below its performance in national elections in 1989.
Â 
Two-Party System Seen
The rest of the votes were cast for smaller parties, but these groups did so poorly that Taiwan seems likely to continue as a two-party rather than a multi-party political system.
"We're very pleased that we've been endorsed by the electorate, in that they want stabilityI and development," Jason C. Hu, the chief Government spokesman, said tonight. 
"I hope that we can put aside the issue of reunification and independence and build up the country. 
The voters have seen no need to push an extremist position that may put us in danger."
Both the Nationalists here and the Communists in Beijing insist that Taiwan is an inseparable part of China, although each claims sovereignty over the other part. 
Taiwan formally calls itself the Republic of China, but the Democratic Progressive Party campaigned for a constitutional conference to formally decree the birth of a new "Republic of Taiwan" that would be fully independent of China and would apply for membership in the United Nations as a new country.
Â 
Looking to Next Election
The Democratic Progressives, at least initially, did not appear subdued by the election results.
"We think that Taiwan independence will still be an issue and that we can do better in the next election," said Yang May-sing, a spokeswoman for the party. 
"This is the first time that the issue has come up, and people are sensitive to it. 
But we think we can do better next year."
Analyzing the party's poor showing, Miss Yang cited an institutional tilt in Taiwan toward the Kuomintang, including a tendency by the three Government-controlled television networks to support Kuomintang positions. 
She also asserted that there had been vote buying by Kuomintang candidates.
Vote buying is a long tradition here, even though officials formally condemn it and there are rewards for turning in anyone who tries to buy a vote. 
Typically, a campaign worker offers $10 to $30 in expectation of a vote of thanks. 
In rural areas, farmers are sometimes made to swear on a statue of Buddha that they will vote for the candidate who provides the money.
Â 
All Parties Buy Votes
Local journalists and neutral officials say that while candidates of all parties buy votes, the Kuomintang perhaps does more of it because it has more money.
Parris H. Chang, a political science professor from Pennsylvania State University who is visiting here, said the opposition would have to do some soul searching about its strong backing for independence.
Of the 325 National Assembly candidates who were elected today, 254 were from the Kuomintang and 66 from the Democratic Progressive Party. 
Five were independent or non-aligned. 
Including 78 members who were elected in 1986 and who also will participate in the constitutional conference, the Kuomintang will have 79 percent of the seats. 
That will give it the three-quarters control it needs to approve a revised constitution.
Â 
Fewer Mainlanders
In a sign of the generational transition under way in Taiwan, less than 22 percent of the new legislators are originally from the Chinese mainland. 
In contrast, politics for most of the last 40 years -- ever since 1949, when Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek fled with the Kuomintang to Taiwan after his defeat by the Communists -- have been dominated by mainlanders.
The Kuomintang has threatened in recent months to disband the Democratic Progressive Party for supporting independence, which is nominally illegal. 
However, a government spoksesman gave no hint today whether the ruling party's election victory would make such a crackdown more or less likely.
Miss Yang, the opposition spokeswoman, said that the Democratic Progressives were not very worried about this possibility and that they could quickly reorganize even if they were disbanded.

file: Neighborhood Politics_ Choosing the Council - An occasional look at the races for New York_s new Cit.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hussein Jaber, a Palestinian who moved from Jerusalem to Brooklyn 12 years ago, has creatively adapted himself to life in Sunset Park -- one of New York City's most ethnically diverse neighborhoods -- by hanging a sign in his bodega's window, which caters to the area's large Hispanic population, saying "Mexican grocery."
A few blocks to the north, along Eighth Avenue, a thriving community of recent immigrants from China have created New York's newest Chinatown, replete with dim-sum restaurants, Asian groceries and -- merchants uneasily acknowledge -- Chinese and Vietnamese gangs bent on extortion.
This rapidly changing polyglot community is the heart of the new 38th City Council District, created this spring by the city's Redistricting Commission. 
The ethnic mix is just one of the district's complications and contradictions.
The district -- which meanders along the waterfront from the edge of Brooklyn Heights south to Red Hook and Sunset Park and includes a substantial number of Irish-American, Italian-American and black residents -- has torn apart adjacent, traditionally close-knit neighborhoods, incorporating slivers of Park Slope, Cobble Hill, Carroll Gardens, Windsor Terrace and Bay Ridge.
Â 
'It's Been a Wash'
All of which conspires against the expectation of the city's Redistricting Commission that a Hispanic candidate would be elected from the 38th District. 
A principal goal of redistricting, which will expand the City Council from 35 to 51 members in this fall's election, was to increase minority representation. 
Hispanic leaders have been particularly unhappy with the way district lines were redrawn, asserting that many districts like the 38th, intended as Hispanic, may not be represented by Hispanic Council members.
Although many City Council races have large fields of candidates, the field is particularly large in the 38th District, indicating the level of interest and the degree of jostling to shape the agenda for New York City in the 1990's.
Most of the nine candidates for the Sept. 
12 Democratic Party primary and many district residents complain loudly about how redistricting has divided neighborhoods and pitted one ethnic group against another.
"The redistricting butchered communities," said Robert Acito, the district manager of Community Board 6, which represents the neighborhoods of Red Hook, Carroll Gardens and Cobble Hill, and is now divided between three City Council districts: the 33d, the 38th and the 39th. 
"And if the ideal was to promote minority participation in government, it's been a wash."
Mercedes Pagan, the director of Unidad Latina, a Hispanic community organization in Sunset Park, is also pessimistic that redistricting will bring new power to Puerto Ricans, Dominicans, Mexicans and other Hispanic residents, who are most heavily concentrated between Fourth and Seventh Avenues in Sunset Park.
"Minority people just don't vote," she said, because they feel that city government cares little about them or their neighborhoods.
In District 38, statistics seem to bear her out. 
Of the district's 140,000 residents, 99,000 are of voting age. 
Just over 50 percent are Hispanic, about 30 percent are white, 11 percent black and 7 percent Asian. 
But among registered voters, Hispanic and white residents each account for about 40 percent of the population. 
Only about 10,000 people -- or roughly 10 percent of the electorate -- are expected to vote, most candidates and others in politics say.
The area was originally settled by Irish immigrants in the 1840's, who were followed by waves of Scandinavians and Italians drawn to the thriving waterfront at the turn of the century. 
Since the Depression, waterfront industry has slowly declined, and many descendants of these European immigrants have moved. 
They have been supplanted by Puerto Ricans, Chinese, Palestinians and Latin Americans.
Â 
As Few as 2,000 Votes
Among the candidates, three are Hispanic, one is black and five are white. 
Most have roots in Sunset Park or Red Hook -- the two intact communities within the district. 
Yet several have either recently moved into the district in order to run, or are creatively calling themselves Sunset Park residents despite their Park Slope or Windsor Terrace addresses.
The race could be close; a candidate may need no more than 2,000 or 3,000 votes to win. 
The favorite, even other candidates acknowledge, is Louis Valentino, an official with local 1814 of the International Longshoremen's Association, which still wields considerable power on the Brooklyn waterfront. 
Other candidates are Joan Griffin McCabe, an education lobbyist from Windsor Park who has been endorsed by much of Brooklyn's Democratic Party establishment, and Ann English, another longtime party figure.
The three Hispanic candidates are Pedro Velazquez, Javier Nieves and Ismael Morces, all involved in community activities. 
Beatrice Byrd, the president of the Brooklyn chapter of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, is the one black candidate. 
The two other white candidates are John Kennedy O'Hara, a lawyer and unsuccessful candidate for the State Assembly, and Martin Krongold, a political newcomer.
Candidates and residents generally agree on the major issues. 
At the top of the list are drugs and crime, the need for affordable housing for the district's largely poor and working-class population and the future of the decaying industrial waterfront.
Â 
Drugs in Sunset Park
"This community's in bad shape," said Julio Torrez, a barber at the Park Barber Shop on Fifth Avenue near 44th Street in Sunset Park, and one of many Puerto Ricans who settled in the community a generation ago. 
"There are drugs and vandals all over."
Areas like Fourth Avenue between 59th and 61st Streets and Fifth Avenue near 49th Street have become prime areas for drug dealers, attracting suburban buyers coming over the nearby Verrazano Narrows Bridge -- much as Washington Heights' proximity to the George Washington Bridge has made that upper Manhattan neighborhood one of the city's most drug plagued.
"Several years ago, a lot of middle-class suburban kids started coming over the bridge looking for safe neighborhoods like Sunset Park to buy drugs," said Tony Giordano, the president of the Sunset Park Restoration Committee and Mr. Velazquez's campaign manager. 
"The more customers who come, the more suppliers who show up, and the crime rate has soared."
Crime is also an issue in the burgeoning Chinese community near Eighth Avenue. 
In the last five years, tens of thousands of Chinese immigrants have poured into Sunset Park, opening restaurants, groceries and other shops along the avenue and transforming the area into New York's third Chinatown, with Manhattan and Flushing, Queens.
Â 
Prisons, Garbage and Prostitutes
"This area has been growing so fast because Manhattan's Chinatown is too crowded and unsafe," said Danny Tsoi, the owner of the Ocean Palace restaurant on Eighth Avenue and 55th Street. 
"But the Chinese and Vietnamese gangs see this area as a golden goose" for extorting money from merchants.
There are other festering issues: a Federal prison proposed at Third Avenue and 29th Street, a city garbage-processing plant proposed in Red Hook, noisy truck traffic serving waterfront industries and warehouses, a concentration of prostitutes between the Gowanus Expressway and the waterfront and schools that are overcrowded even by New York City standards, because of the number of large Hispanic families, community residents say.
"It's a shame what they're trying to throw down our throats," said Mr. Velazquez, the president of the United Democrats of Sunset Park, whose redistricting proposal was largely adopted by the city.
But issues like crime and education have become somewhat overshadowed by mudslinging, much of it at the frontrunner.
Â 
Mudslinging and Lie Detectors
Several candidates have charged that Mr. Valentino is only running to protect waterfront jobs controlled by his union, which has previously been tied to organized crime.
A New York State Commissioner for labor affairs in the 1970's, Mr. Valentino testified at the 1979 trial of Anthony Scotto that he took a $50,000 cash contribution from Mr. Scotto for Mario M. Cuomo's unsuccessful 1977 mayoral campaign. 
Mr. Scotto, a leader of the Brooklyn longshoremen's union, was convicted of racketeering and served three years in prison.
But Mr. Valentino has denied the allegations against him, offering to take a lie-detector test and vowing, "If I fail, I'll buy a suit for every man, woman and child in this district."
Â

file: Nepal_s Economy Is Gasping as India, a Huge Neighbor, Squeezes It Hard.txt
text:
ï»¿
A dispute with India is forcing Nepal, one of the world's poorest and least accessible countries, to fight for its economic survival, a fight that is also testing its political stability.
New Delhi cut most of the landlocked kingdom's vital trade links to the outside world more than two weeks ago, and Nepal was shaken by student demonstrations on April 3 and 4. 
The protests became as anti-Government as they were anti-Indian. 
Universities in the Katmandu area were closed amid conflicting reports of casualties as the police suppressed the riots.
Lines at gas stations are long, straining tempers. 
The streets of Katmandu, the capital, are nearly devoid of cars, and travel around Nepal by air or bus is becoming more difficult. 
Forests are being stripped for cooking fuel.
In an interview Sunday, Nepal's Foreign Minister, Shailendra Kumar Upadhyaya, said Katmandu wanted to end its special relationship with India, which had become one of economic dependence.
''It is in our interest to let interdependence grow,'' he said of ties with India. 
''It is in our interest to see that our dependence on one country does not grow.''
Â 
Border Crossings Closed
Nepal, wedged between China and India, the world's two most populous nations, has only one reliable outlet to the sea, overland through the Indian port of Calcutta, more than 700 miles away.
On March 23, after a dispute over how to renegotiate lapsed trade and transit treaties, New Delhi suddenly closed 19 of 21 border crossings with this Himalayan nation, severing links not only to the port but also to northern Indian cities.
The Indians want a single pact. 
The Nepalese want two, as they have had since 1978, to separate their important transit rights from trade and commercial ties to India. 
The two accords were a concession made by a previous Government in New Delhi under Prime Minister Moraji Desai.
Foreign Minister Upadhyaya said Nepal had in the last few days proposed a new trade treaty that would include no special concessions but only most-favored-nation status, putting economic relations with New Delhi on a more equal footing. 
Indian officials have not responded.
At the end of March, two more agreements expired, covering Nepal's imports of petroleum products and coal through India. 
Almost immediately, there was a sharp drop in supplies of kerosene for cooking and gasoline for the buses and trucks that link remote villages to sources of food, medicine and other necessities.
Â 
Trees Cut for Fuel
Rationing of petroleum products has been introduced. 
Prices of other commodities like sugar, salt and processed foods, many imported from India, have risen.
Even protected trees have been cut to meet fuel shortages. 
Trucks arrive daily, bringing precious logs to be burned in cooking fires.
Chirin S. Thapa, a principal adviser to King Birendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev, called the damage to forests ''an unfortunate part of this emergency.''
He said the emergency measures could endanger the survival of Nepal's 18 million people.
Deforestation in Nepal, apart from eroding local hillsides, is contributing to flooding in India and Bangladesh as swollen Himalayan rivers rush down to the plains.
Interviews with Nepalese and Indian officials here and in New Delhi, Nepalese businessmen and journalists, and Western diplomats in Katmandu reveal a complex interaction of causes and perceptions that led to what the Nepalese say was a completely unexpected blockade by India.
Â 
Links With China a Factor
It is almost universally believed in Katmandu that the trade dispute was only a pretext for New Delhi to vent its displeasure with Nepal for an accumulation of grievances. 
Growing Nepalese-Chinese cooperation, culminating in Katmandu's purchase in August 1988 of Chinese antiaircraft guns, is a major factor.
The presence of Chinese contractors working on World Bank or Government aid projects in Nepal, especially near the border with India, has led to protests, Nepalese officials say.
Many Chinese consumer goods are on sale in Nepalese bazaars. 
Some, like small appliances and crockery, have displaced Indian products, although Nepalese officials say the trade gap with India continues to widen.
In addition, the fast-developing Nepalese tourist industry - a vital hard-currency earner - has in recent years ceased to be an appendage of Indian tourism. 
With direct air links to Europe, Southeast Asia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Burma and Hong Kong, Nepal is bypassing Indian travel agents, airports and airlines.
Personal relations between King Birendra and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi are reported to be frosty. 
The 43-year-old King, who inherited the throne from King Mahendra in 1972, saw India annex the neighboring kingdom of Sikkim in 1974, and later, in Nepal's view, reduce the King of Bhutan to an Indian vassal.
Â 
A Martial Tradition
Diplomats say that the royal family, which dominates a party-less Government, is sensitive to the fate of Sikkim and Bhutan and concerned about Katmandu's independence. 
Nepal is the oldest nation in South Asia, with its own architecture, language and distinctive forms of Hinduism and Buddhism.
''They are proud of their martial tradition,'' a diplomat said. 
''Beneath this placid, gentle exterior, there is a determination there.''
Indian officials, who acknowledge their annoyance with Katmandu's Chinese arms purchases, say they are also perplexed by what they see as a new and inexplicably uncompromising attitude in Nepal, which has benefited from nearly 40 years of Indian aid and special trade concessions and an open- door policy for millions of Nepalese job seekers.
Indians say Nepal, apart from resisting a combined trade and transit treaty, refuses to reverse decisions that New Delhi regards as violations of a 1950 treaty of friendship between the two capitals that has been the base of their relations ever since. 
These violations include the levying of tariffs on Indian goods and the introduction of work permits for Indian nationals in Nepal. 
Nepalese in India are not required to have them.
A new trade treaty, initialed by Nepal and India last November, was rejected by New Delhi when the Nepalese would not withdraw tariffs, an Indian official said.
Â 
Government Is Criticized
If the economic crisis in Nepal is prolonged, the King and his Government will have to rely on the willingness of the Nepalese to stand behind their decision to defy New Delhi, and to make adjustments to lives that are already borderline for many.
Most Nepalese interviewed said they were strongly opposed to the large Indian presence in Nepal and to any attempts by New Delhi to dictate this country's policies.
But they were also critical of the Government, which they said has failed to develop the country or allow people effective democratic rights. 
Nepalese are limited to voting in party- less elections for local councils. 
Open criticism of the monarchy and the Government is rarely tolerated.

file: New Goddess of Democracy To Haunt Beijing_s Leaders.txt
text:
ï»¿
Over the next month or so, China is expected to have to deal with a new irritant: the Goddess of Democracy, a 225-foot ship that is preparing to broadcast a stream of pro-democracy news and commentaries to the Chinese people.
The ship is expected to reach Taiwan within a few days, and then to take on supplies and a transmitter so that it can begin its broadcasts.
But the project encountered an unexpected obstacle today, according to reports from Taiwan, when Taiwan declared that while the ship could dock now, it would not be allowed to return if it made unauthorized broadcasts to the mainland. 
That could create major problems, for the ship will need to take on supplies, and there are few other ports in the immediate area.
Music, News, Democracy Reports
The ship, a former oceanographic vessel with a French crew of nine and a group of journalists, will broadcast music, news, and reports of last year's democracy movement. 
The project is sponsored by a coalition of 19 publications from around the world, the Federation for Democracy in China.
The coalition, headed by the French news magazine Actuel, estimates that it will cost about $200,000 per month to broadcast from a stationary point in the ocean. 
It is not clear how long the money will last.
The Chinese Government has issued some blistering criticism of the plan to operate the radio ship, and it has refused to rule out the use of force to stop the broadcasts. 
Western diplomats and Chinese themselves say Beijing's response will be an important test of the Government's tactics and an indication of the extent to which it feels constrained by international opinion almost a year after the Tiananmen Square crackdown on the student democracy movement.
Taiwan announced today that an unidentified submarine, presumably Chinese, was spotted near the Goddess of Democracy off the southern tip of Taiwan. 
That raised suspicions that Chinese forces might be considering an attack on the ship. 
Officials in Taipei have pledged to defend the ship if it is attacked near Taiwan, but not if it is raided on the high seas.
Â 
What China Might Do
If the Chinese Navy were to seize the ship at sea or sink it, the result would almost surely be a new wave of international outrage as well as prolonged isolation for the hard-liners in Beijing.
An attack on the ship would also greatly increase the chance that the United States would revoke most-favored-nation trade status, which gives Chinese exports the same relatively low tariffs that the United States imposes on goods from most other coutries. 
The status is now under review, with a decision from the Bush Administration expected by June 3.
''If they do something stupid like that, it would shatter the relationship,'' a Western diplomat said. 
''I don't think they'll do that.''
The alternative for China is to jam the transmissions of the radio boat, in the same way that it now jams Chinese-language transmissions of Voice of America and the British Broadcasting Corporation. 
But jamming is expensive and not entirely effective, for many Chinese continue to listen to the VOA and BBC broadcasts despite the interference.
Â 
Immense Aggravation for Beijing
The Goddess of Democracy's planned broadcasts are likely to be an immense aggravation to the Chinese Government. 
Not only will they provide a rival source of information, but they will suggest that the hard-liners' victory has not been complete and that there is an organized opposition. 
So far the exiled democratic movement has not been very visible or effective within China, but that could change if its views can be broadcast into living rooms throughout much of the country.
''We're all waiting for the ship's broadcasts,'' said a university teacher in Beijing. 
''Quite a few people are talking about it.''
Already, the ship has caused a ripple of diplomatic embarrassment in the region. 
Hong Kong's British Government, which is often accused of kowtowing to Beijing, refused to let the ship dock in its harbor, saying that the territory should not become ''a battlefield for other people's political battles.''
Taiwan has said it will let the ship dock, but it is clearly concerned that the incident not interrupt the warming relations with the Chinese mainland.
''We have not and will not be involved in any activities of the democracy ship,'' The Associated Press quoted Taiwan's chief Government spokesman, Shaw Yuming, as saying in Taipei. 
''As a member of the international community, we do not support the ship's unauthorized broadcasts in international waters.''
Â 
Law on Broadcasting at Sea
The 1982 Law of the Sea Convention permits a country that is the target of unauthorized broadcasts from international waters to ''arrest any person or ship engaged in unauthorized broadcasting.''
While the convention has not yet taken effect, China could argue that the provisions simply reflect existing customary international law.
The United States has taken a similar action. 
In 1987, American officials boarded the Sarah, a pirate radio ship that was operating Radio New York International from the high seas off the East Coast. 
The station was closed, and the operators were taken to the United States and charged with the crime of broadcasting from outside the national territory.
But there were some differences. 
The Sarah was a commercial radio station, and the United States first obtained permission from its flag country, Honduras, before staging the raid. 
The Goddess of Democracy is not a commercial station, and it carries the flag of a Caribbean country, St. Vincent, which would have to be asked whether the Chinese authorities approved of plans to board the vessel.

file: New Strategy Suggested in Battle on China Trade Status.txt
text:
ï»¿
Anticipating that President Bush's decision to renew trade benefits for China this year will ultimately survive any challenge, opponents in Congress have started lining up behind legislation that would impose human rights conditions before similar benefits are granted next year.
The strategy was disclosed at a hearing today of the House Ways and Means Committee's Trade Subcommittee, where members of the international business community warned that should China lose most-favored-nation trading status, China would retaliate by not buying $6 billion of foodstuffs and other products it now purchases from the United States.
The warning had resonance. 
Representative Beryl J. Anthony, Democrat of Arkansas, said he did not want to see ''innocent producers of farm commodities punished'' by retaliation. 
Many farmers in his district grow soybeans.
Others Will Pick Up Business
Representative Frank J. Guarini, Democrat of New Jersey, said that since no other countries were contemplating any kind of trade action against China, ''our allies will simply pick up the business that we lose.''
Noting that the United States gives the preferred status to Iran, Iraq and South Africa, he added that ''to single out China is hypocrisy.''
Representative Robert T. Matsui, a California Democrat, said that a majority of the Chinese in his district ''tell me that by continuing trade there would be a more positive atmosphere.''
The trade status, which China has enjoyed throughout the last decade, provides the lowest available tariffs. 
Many members of Congress want to deny renewal this year because of Beijing's crackdown on dissent.
Resolutions of disapproval of the President's action have been introduced and will probably clear both chambers. 
But legislative analysts say that opponents did not have the two-thirds support in either chamber needed to override an almost certain Presidential veto.
A leader of the opposition, Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, acknowledged as much when she predicted that one of the compromise bills ''I believe will have a good deal of support in the Congress.''
She was alluding to legislation proposed by Representative Donald J. Pease, Democrat of Ohio, which postpones the China trade battle until next year.
Under the Pease measure, before such trade status is extended, Beijing will have to show ''significant'' improvement in human rights, end martial law in China and Tibet and suspend support for the Khmer Rouge of Cambodia.
''I view this as a middle course between stopping trade altogether and making harmless and meaningless statements,'' Mr. Pease said at the hearing. 
He said that among his co-sponsors are 6 fellow members, of 36 on the Ways and Means Committee.
Â 
Extension Suggested
On a parallel track is a bill of Representative Peter J. Kostmayer, Democrat of Pennsylvania, that would grant a six-month extension, again on condition that China improve human rights.
But members of the business community today took exception to this approach. 
''Conditionality creates insurmountable problems in practice,'' said Roger W. Sullivan, president of the United States-China Business Council, representing American multinationals in China.
''The fundamental problem is that the Chinese leadership, by its intransigence over the past year, has made clear that it is unlikely to make fundamental changes in internal policy to accommodate U.S. concerns.''
Last year two-way trade between the United States and China amounted to $18 billion. 
American investment in China, in place and planned, exceeds $4 billion.
If Congress decides to withdraw the trade status, said Howard Lewis 3d, vice president of international affairs at the National Association of Manufacturers, business decision-makers in this country ''will conclude that China is just too risky.''
He added. 
''They may also conclude that other countries in transition are also too risky, from Poland to the Soviet Union to certain Latin American countries.''

file: New Tension Over Trade With China.txt
text:
ï»¿
As China's trade surplus with the United States rises sharply, diplomats and business executives say relations between the two countries could worsen because of China's import restrictions, software piracy and other issues.
"The tremendous growth in the trade deficit, and the proliferation of Chinese measures to restrict access to the market for imports, taken together, constitute a meaningful, significant trade problem," Joseph A. Massey, assistant United States trade representative, said at a news conference Friday night after two days of talks with Chinese officials on intellectual-property issues.
Â 
A Soaring Trade Surplus
China's trials of pro-democracy demonstrators seem to be largely completed, and so the human rights issue is expected to subside after two years in which it was the focal point of contention between the two countries. 
But since the Tiananmen crackdown in 1989, China has enjoyed a soaring trade surplus with the United States.
Kenneth G. Lieberthal, a China scholar at the University of Michigan who is visiting Beijing, said, "There is good reason to be concerned about the potential deterioration in Sino-American relations in the coming months."
While Beijing and Washington have differences on a range of issues, as well as in their ideologies and vision of the emerging international order, most people believe that trade disputes will be crucial in determining relations in coming months.
The United States trade deficit with China reached $10.4 billion in 1990, up from $6.2 billion in 1989. 
The only larger United States deficits are with Japan and Taiwan. 
By some estimates, the deficit with China will soar to more than $15 billion this year.
American imports from China include clothing, toys and shoes, with the value of the footwear more than double the level in 1989, according to figures for the first nine months of 1990. 
But while American imports were increasing sharply, American sales to China dropped sharply, from $5.8 billion in 1989 to $4.8 billion in 1990.
This trade imbalance, coupled with continuing indignation in the United States at the Chinese human rights situation, is expected to lead to another effort on Capitol Hill this year to withdraw China's "most favored nation" trade status. 
The effort failed last year, after the Bush Administration moved to quash it, but some experts say that Congress will try harder this year and that the Administration may devote less energy to the issue.
"Most favored nation" status is the key issue likely to emerge in coming months, executives say, and in the end most think it will be preserved after a fight. 
But they do not rule out the possibility that it will be revoked. 
That could cause a sharp drop in Chinese exports to the United States, retaliation by China and a significant chill between Washington and Beijing.
Â 
Property Rights at Issue
Another trade issue under negotiation concerns intellectual-property rights, which were the focus of Mr. Massey's talks with the Chinese. 
China has always ignored copyrights, to the point that pirated copies of President Bush's autobiography are available from a number of Chinese publishers.
American software manufacturers are particularly concerned and estimate that pirated software in China may cost them $400 million a year in lost sales. 
Mr. Massey said the piracy problem in China was one of the most serious in the world.
To address the criticism, China has adopted its first copyright law, to take effect in June. 
But its effectiveness will depend on carrying out regulations that have still not been published or completed.
If the United States is dissatisfied with Chinese progress on the issue, the Office of the Trade Representative could initiate an action under section 301 of the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988. 
After an investigation, that could lead to imposition of retaliatory tariffs against Chinese exports to the United States.
Â 
'Dumping' Charged
There are also disputes about Chinese garment exports, and allegations that China breached its quotas limiting such exports to the United States. 
China is also accused of "dumping" certain products, at unfairly low prices, in the United States market.
John Frisbie, director of China operations for the United States-China Business Council, said that in the last few months China had begun to increase its imports and that this may help ease trade frictions.
Underlying the disagreements, Washington and Beijing seem to have fundamentally different perspectives on where the fault lies. 
In the United States, China is often viewed as recalcitrant, deceptive and repressive, as well as determined to adopt a mercantilist policy of bolstering exports and curtailing imports.
In China, officials complain that the United States is trying to subvert the Chinese Government and has ignored positive steps Beijing has taken, like the release of many dissidents from prison and the adoption of a copyright law.

file: New Yorkers Try to Defend Students Hunted in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the struggles and torments of Chinese students in China became increasingly more vivid for New Yorkers over the last month, people in the city have begun exploring ways to defend the lives and views of those who are being hunted, arrested and imprisoned.
In Chinatown, the center of one of the largest Chinese communities in North America, young women have been stopping tourists to ask them to write to their representatives in Congress urging greater sanctions against the Beijing regime. 
At the Public Library on 42d Street, a Chinese graduate engineer sells T-shirts with the slogan ''Democracy or Death'' to raise money to open an office.
At a restaurant near Columbia University, scholars from China meet with American political scientists to discuss how far they should go in lobbying for international ostracism of the Beijing Government. 
And in SoHo, an auction is held of contemporary Chinese art works, with the money to be used to publish a book memorializing the soldiers' brutality.
Identifying a Criminal
And in one of the more dramatic responses, Chinese students in the metropolitan area joined hundreds of others throughout the United States in a campaign to call and overload special police numbers in Beijing that were set up to take details from people seeking to turn in participants in the student demonstrations.
''There were many thousands who called from here,'' said Dr. Fu Xin Wuan, a chemist at the Rockefeller University. 
''Our idea was mostly to tie up the exchanges,'' Dr. Fu said. 
''But some people who called from here said first that they could identify a criminal, and when they were asked who, they said, 'Deng Xiaoping.'
'' Dr. Fu added that other callers tried to talk seriously about democracy and liberty with the people on the other end. 
The campaign ended after a few days.
Dr. Fu was a founder of the Chinese Human Rights Organization, which united several hundred visiting scholars and scientists even before the students in Beijing began to occupy Tiananmen Square. 
After the protests and, more particularly, after the army's attack, the group turned its attention from theoretical to practical goals, forming links with other student groups, Chinese-American organizations and human rights advocates.
''The most important thing we are doing is getting information about what happened and leting the world know about it,'' said Dr. Fu, who conceded that it has been hard to determine facts among the many rumors. 
''We are talking with people who just came from Beijing or tracing reports of names of people who were killed or are arrested. 
We have lists of names. 
A friend will say that somebody is missing. 
We will check with other friends and relatives.''
Another project that the rights group is working on is the publication in seven languages of a book of photographs documenting the killings. 
His group has been working closely with Asia Watch, one of several organizations working out of offices at 485 Fifth Avenue that monitor human rights.
The director of Asia Watch, Sidney Jones, who was in Beijing early in the protest, has been collating the material gathered by several groups, including Dr. Fu's organization, into daily releases, noting such items as the names of those arrested.
One recent release noted that a report from London said that a young student who had been shown facing down a moving tank as the students held the square had been arrested and identified as Wang Weilin, a 19-year-old son of a factory worker.
Â 
A Positive Tradition
Ms. Jones noted that expressions of anger and indignation in the United States seemed to her to be more muted and confused than those that followed such events as the use of martial law and the suppression of Solidarity in Poland or the overthrow of President Salvador Allende Gossens in Chile.
''One reason people have been slow to react,'' Ms. Jones said, ''is that there never has been a tradition of China-bashing here, as there has been with Soviet-bashing, and the negative side of the Chinese political system has not been demonstrated here. 
Since relations with China were restored, it's been just mutual admiration, and the dark side has not really emerged.''
She also said the muted outcry could be partly explained because the Chinese here had not been a ''high-profile political community like the Poles are in Chicago.''
Finally, she said, the lack of an identifiable figure among the protesters, someone like Lech Walesa, had made it hard to project the conflict in terms that Americans could easily grasp.
Dr. Fu and other Chinese said that they understood that and that they had tried to use the image of the young man and the tank as a symbol of their struggle. 
''We have designed a T-shirt with the picture on one side and the plea for democracy on the other,'' the chemist said. 
''We are selling them on the street for $8 though some people are giving us much more.''
Another fund-raising effort is being planned by Ethan Cohen, whose Art Wave gallery at 52 Greene Street has shown the works of Chinese artists who abandoned and defied socialist realism.
The 28-year-old Mr. Cohen has spent long periods in China, where his father, Jerome Cohen, directed the codification of laws. 
Now, with Chinese artists, he is planning to put on a daylong street fair in SoHo this summer calling attention to the protest.
One artist in the show, Ai Weiwei, recently ended an eight-day hunger strike. 
He is also a member of a recently formed group called Solidarity for China, which, he said, was made up of artists, scientists and professionals from China, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
Â 
'We Want to Bear Witness'
''We are contacting all human rights group to prepare for a renewed democracy movement,'' he said. 
''We want to bear witness to what really happened and we want to pressure the Chinese Government to be less brutal, because we know that the Chinese Government wants relations with the West and, especially, with the United States.''
As for the appeals for broad economic sanctions, Mr. Ai said the issue was extremely tricky. 
''We need sanctions to show our moral stance, but we cannot push too far.
''China's relationship with the West is what really keeps the hope of democracy alive, and we do not want to encourage anyone to go back to the old ways that existed under Chairman Mao. 
That would be too terrible.''

text:

Former President Richard M. Nixon met with Education Minister Li Tieying today for what the Chinese described as ''frank and sincere'' talks on China's policy toward its students in the aftermath of the crushing of the student-led democracy movement.
Mr. Nixon, on the second day of a private visit as a guest of the Government, was briefed on China's ''practice of being kind-hearted toward the students while setting strict demands on them,'' the official news agency said.
Since the Government crushed the pro-democracy movement in early June, Mr. Li and other officials have said they will ''understand, educate and unify'' most of the hundreds of thousands of students who took part in the protests, and will punish only a small group of leaders. 
All students have been required to report their activities during the protests and undergo intense political education. 
Hundreds have been arrested.
The press agency did not say how Mr. Nixon responded to Mr. Li's briefing, but in diplomatic parlance, ''frank and sincere'' often are used to describe talks where the sides disagree.
Mr. Nixon's spokesman, John Taylor, said the former President did not intend to try to mediate a solution to the standoff between Washington and Beijing over China's crushing of dissent.

file: Nixon Tells of China at White House Dinner.txt
text:
ï»¿
The White House was not exactly trumpeting it to the world, but Richard M. Nixon was back in the Presidential residence Sunday night, giving his former protege in the world of Chinese-American relations a firsthand report on his trip to China.
Mr. Nixon, who appointed Mr. Bush as the first American representative to Beijing since the Communist revolution in China, gave the President a confidential memorandum on his visit, on his view of Chinese-American relations after the crackdown on dissent and on the prospects for their improvement, Administration officials and associates of the former President said. 
Nixon aides and White House officials declined to make the report public.
But Marlin Fitzwater, the White House spokesman, and other officials suggested that the Bush Administration was not uncomfortable with Mr. Nixon's harsh comments to Chinese officials about the crackdown on dissent in May and June.
Mr. Nixon, who warned the Chinese against sinking into a ''backwater of oppression and stagnation,'' was much sharper in tone than Mr. Bush, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and other senior American officials had been in public.
Mr. Nixon spoke at length about his visit during the two-hour dinner in the White House residential quarters and then took questions from Mr. Bush, his wife, Barbara, Vice President Dan Quayle, Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser, William H. Webster, the Director of Central Intelligence, and other top officials.
Â 
Crackdown 'Excessive'
The dinner was not announced in advance and was reported at the White House briefing today only in response to a question about Mr. Nixon's visit. 
During his visit to China, Mr. Nixon told his hosts that ''many in the United States, including many friends of China, believe the crackdown was excessive and unjustified.''
''The events of April through June damaged the respect and confidence which most Americans previously had for the leaders of China,'' he said during a banquet given by President Yang Shangkun in Beijing last Wednesday.
In response to the Chinese crackdown, the Bush Administration suspended sales of weapons and military visits and promised a sympathetic response to Chinese students who wanted to extend their stay in the United States. 
Critics in Congress and elsewhere called the response weak and, over the Administration's objections, both houses of Congress voted by large margins to impose stiffer sanctions. 
The Bush Administration and Mr. Nixon himself have been careful to note that Mr. Nixon was making a personal visit to China last week and was not representing the United States Government or Mr. Bush.
Â 
'Special Credibility'
But Mr. Bush has made a practice of taking relatively moderate stands on a variety of issues while letting surrogates deliver harsher messages. 
And Administration officials said they were aware that Mr. Nixon's comments carry a special weight, since his visit to China in 1972 paved the way for resumption of American diplomatic relations with that country.
''A tough message takes on special credibility when it comes from an old and very respected friend,'' one official said. 
''You may have noticed that we haven't said much about China since June, but I haven't heard any negative feelings about what Nixon said. 
Generally, my sense is that it was positively received.''
Asked about Mr. Bush's view on what Mr. Nixon told the Chinese, Mr. Fitzwater said: ''You know that the former President had some very direct things to say to the Chinese leadership about American reaction to what happened there. 
But we wouldn't want to embellish on those statements.''
Asked whether Mr. Bush agreed with Mr. Nixon's statements during his trip that China and the United States should put aside their differences and resume normal relations, Mr. Fitzwater replied, ''The President found those views quite interesting and productive but our general policy has not changed.''
Correction
In my previous column, I had President Nixon sending George Bush to China as envoy in 1974; it was President Ford.
An article yesterday about Richard M. Nixon's visit to the White House, where he discussed his recent trip to China, misidentified the President who sent George Bush to Beijing as chief American diplomat. 
It was Gerald R. Ford.

Three people were arrested over the weekend in New York City on charges of heroin trafficking that officials said resulted from an unusual tip by law-enforcement authorities in China.

Ka Yiu Mak, 35, was arrested near his home in Elmhurst, Queens.

text:

Poet in Full Rig
While Jean Cocteau thought of himself as a writer, his real talent was social gesture, in which he successfully combined outrageousness and a passion for French pop. 
Here is his induction into the French Academy, from ''Confessions of a Literary Archaeologist'' by Carlton Lake (New Directions).
At that moment a drummer began a deafening roll, the guards drew their sabres, and through the rear entrance filed the not-quite-forty immortals. 
Most of them were wearing dark business suits, but when Cocteau passed by, I saw that he was resplendent in his full Academy regalia: the embroidered green uniform (not actually green but midnight blue, with green facing), cape, cocked hat (all by Lanvin), and sword. 
Cocteau's sword was not the usual academician's sword. 
Executed by Cartier, its hilt bore various symbols relating to Cocteau's life and work. 
I was unable to make out all of them as he passed, but I could see the hand guard, at least - a profile of Oedipus - and, at the top, the ivory lyre, symbol of the poet.
His Bed Too Was a Canvas
Vincent van Gogh could find homely appeal in almost anything - in this case a streetwalker. 
He's quoted in ''Van Gogh: His Life and His Art'' by David Sweetman (Crown).
I hadn't far to look. 
I found a woman, not young, not beautiful, nothing remarkable, if you like, but perhaps you are somewhat curious. 
She was rather tall and strongly built; she did not have a lady's hands like Kee, but the hands of one who works much; but she was not coarse or common, and had nothing very womanly about her. 
She reminded me of some figure by Chardin or Frere, or perhaps Jan Steen. 
Well, what the French call une ouvriere. 
She had had many cares, one could see that, and life had been hard for her, oh, she was not distinguished, nothing extraordinary, nothing unusual. 
. . . Did we spend much money together?
No, for I did not have much, and I said to her, Listen you and I don't need to make ourselves drunk to feel something for each other; just put what I can spare in your pocket.
Â 
Table Manners of the Avant-Garde
W. H. Auden and Christopher Isherwood went to China during the Sino-Japanese War in 1938. 
This is a not untypical dispatch from them in ''Journey to a War'' (Paragon House).
We kept swapping specially dainty morsels with our neighbours. 
Auden and I developed a private game: it was a point of honour to praise most warmly the dishes you liked least. 
''Delicious,'' Auden murmured, as he munched what was, apparently, a small sponge soaked in glue. 
I replied by devouring, with smiles of exquisite pleasure, an orange which tasted of bitter aloes and contained, in its centre, a large weevil. 
On the whole the food was very nice, but our hosts disparaged it out of courtesy - and of course we had to protest: ''Horrible stuff, this. 
We must apologize. 
. . .''
''No, no!
Not horrible. 
Wonderful!''
''Very poor after your English cookery.''
''English cookery disgusting!
Chinese cookery marvellous!''
Â 
The Poem as a Put-Up Job
Students have every right to distrust a teacher who reads them his own poems. 
This is from ''Memories and Hallucinations: A Memoir'' by D. M. Thomas (Penguin).
I am frightened by the coincidences that seem to cluster around art - even bad art or non-art. 
Once, I was reading to a class of students a poem I'd written about a nestling. 
Our cat, grey Lucina, had mauled the baby bird before we could interfere. 
The poem was new, I thought it better than it was; it would later go into the wastepaper basket. 
As I was reading the weak verses to my class, my voice full of compassion and vanity, there was a knock on the classroom door. 
One of my colleagues entered, his hands cupped around something tiny. 
''I found this outside,'' he explained, in a troubled voice; ''can anyone suggest what I can do with it?''
My students gasped; he was showing us an injured nestling.
The students thought it was a put-up job. 
As though we'd have conspired to maim a nestling in order to amaze them.
Â 
Heaven Hangs On
Though contemporary life lends itself more easily to ideas of hell, a surprising number of Americans still believe in heaven. 
This is from ''Heaven: A History'' by Colleen McDannell and Bernhard Lang (Vintage).
In a Gallup Poll published in 1982, 71 per cent of the American public answered ''yes'' to the question: Do you think there is a heaven where people who have led good lives are eternally rewarded?
This figure was only one per cent less than in 1952, and showed a small increase since 1965. 
Those who believed in heaven outnumbered those who believed in reincarnation by more than three to one. 
When the pollsters, however, tried to ascertain what one actually does in heaven, the polls revealed that the images of the modern heaven, in existence since the eighteenth century, had greatly faded. 
While 54 per cent of those polled assumed that they would be in the presence of God or Jesus Christ in heaven or an afterlife, only 19 per cent believed that people would have responsibilities there. 
Less than half assumed that they would see their friends, relatives, or spouses. 
Although one third believed they would grow spiritually, only 18 per cent thought that they would grow intellectually. 
. . . Only 5 per cent of those polled thought that eternity would be boring.

file: Notes on China_Beijing Hopes To Stamp Out The _6 Evils_.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has started a new campaign against ''six evils'' in its latest attempt to restore a glow of revolutionary virtue to the national complexion.
The evils are prostitution, pornography, the sale of women and children, narcotics, gambling, and profiteering from superstition.
The official People's Daily and other newspapers have had front-page articles and editorials about the dangers of the ''six evils'' and the risk that they will subvert socialism and national stabilityI. 
A national conference in Beijing on the crusade has called for local authorities to place high priority on the campaign. 
What's Behind the Crusade?
''The duty of the Communists is to fight every form of evil and wipe it from the face of the earth,'' People's Daily declared in a front page editorial recently, adding: ''These are the vicious ways in which subversives and saboteurs will corrupt our party, our cadres and our socialist system.''
Fathoming the real reasons for China's campaigns is never easy, and most political analysts say there are at least two possible explanations for what is happening.
One possibility is that the campaign reflects an escalation of the crackdown on Western influences, a tightening of control on society.
The alternative explanation, they say, is precisely the opposite: that some leaders are trying to take the sting out of the political crackdown by changing it into a law-and-order campaign.
In any case, the latest crackdown captures the political spirit of the moment. 
China's history in the last four decades is punctuated by number-based slogans, which are as important to officials here as acronyms are to their Western counterparts.
Communist China has been a blur of them: the four modernizations; the five things to heed and the four beautifuls; the five black categories of people; and many others. 
The Eighties have been relatively free of such slogans, aside from folk ditties such as ''the three biggies'' - color television, radio-tape player, and refrigerator -that people want to acquire.
Â 
'4 Haves' or '5 Great Loves'
Now, numbers are again in the air. 
In their political classes, for example, some Beijing residents are being told to cultivate the ''four haves'': idealism, morality, culture and discipline. 
Others are diligently memorizing what are supposed to be their ''five great loves'': the motherland, the Communist Party, the socialist system, the capital city and their work.
Study sessions are likely to take up the ''six evils'' very soon.
The party's standard slogan also seems to have undergone revision during the central committee meeting last week. 
Before it was ''rectification of the economic environment''; now it is ''retrenchment of the economic environment and deepening of the reforms.''
What does this mean?
There is no explanation in the speeches or editorials that use the new formula.
The mystery is doubly confusing because some Chinese intellectuals regard ''retrenchment'' and ''reform'' as opposites. 
Embracing both seems to them nonsensical.
On the other hand, supporters of retrenchment deny that they are ''anti-reform. 
''Thus the revision of the slogan is seen by some as a compromise that serves both factions. 
It gives new hope to those who yearn for greater change, while it clothes the retrenchment in a blanket of respectability by suggesting that it is ''pro-reform.''
So far there has been little evidence that the extra lip service to ''deepening of the reforms'' will have any practical significance.
Â 
Lying, and Enjoying It
''I know every trick in the book,'' says a character in a 1980 short story by the Chinese writer Shen Rong. 
''Skirting issues, fancy intellectual footwork, turning issues on their head, spinning a yarn; if all else fails I'll just start admitting all ideological errors I can think of. 
By now we're all used to lying.''
Miss Shen's short story concerns a self-criticism session by a group of intellectuals and their wrenching discontent with the process. 
Now her story has sprung to life throughout the nation, as citizens meet in compulsory sessions to express their feelings and show support for the party.
''We sit around the room, and the leader asks people to comment,'' said a middle-aged intellectual. 
''At first the group is silent for a few minutes, and then the leader calls on someone. 
The leader doesn't want to, but he has pressure from his superiors. 
And then the lying begins.''
Â 
Bubbling With Sorrow
One common approach, for those who despise the sessions, is to go off on tangents. 
For example, some people bubble with sorrow at the deaths of young soldiers during the crackdown, without expressing their view on the protests themselves.
Another strategy is to make a game of it, and to flagellate oneself so enthusiastically that it becomes a joke. 
Indeed, where the leader of the session is thought to be only going through the motions, then the self-criticism sometimes becomes so exaggerated that the audience begins to titter.
''We all learn to lie,'' said one young businessman, ''and to enjoy it.''

file: Now Beijing Blames a Single Villain for All Its Ills.txt
text:
ï»¿
As China fills out its official version of the crushed democracy movement, a single villain has emerged who is held responsible for the student turmoil and virtually all of the country's economic woes: Zhao Ziyang, the ousted chief of the Communist Party.
Last week, virtually every newspaper here was jammed with front-page attacks on Mr. Zhao, who has not been seen since late May, when he had a tearful encounter with the students in Tiananmen Square. 
By week's end, China's leadership had openly joined in the fray, rarely missing an opportunity to heap more blame on the purged party leader.
Not surprisingly, then, the chief topic of conversation in Beijing these days -second only to the constant speculation over whether Deng Xiaoping, the country's foremost leader, is alive and active - is Mr. Zhao's fate.
Many believe that the torrent of articles and speeches is simply setting the stage to put Mr. Zhao on trial, in what would be the first formal charges against a top party leader since the Gang of Four - Mao's widow, Jiang Qing, and three radical colleagues -were tried in 1980 for their roles in the Cultural Revolution.
But many others say they believe the Government will stop short of formal charges because Mr. Deng, too, is closely tied to economic changes that Mr. Zhao undertook, changes that are now being scaled back.
''To put Zhao on trial is to put on trial the whole past decade of economic reforms,'' a Western diplomat said the other day. 
''That may be a little more than they bargained for.''
Indeed, the attacks are coming just as China is greatly scaling back a number of changes that occurred under Mr. Zhao. Many private businesses he helped allow to flourish are being disbanded or consolidated by the Government, or being labeled tax cheats.
The latest attack came on Friday as Qiao Shi, a member of the Communist Party leadership, said at a ceremony to mark the beginning of the autumn term of schools and colleges that ''international hostile forces have never given up their attempt to subvert the socialist system.''
Â 
Bourgeois Connivance
''For a period, Zhao Ziyang's connivance with and weak attitude toward bourgeois liberalization resulted in a surge of ideological attacks against socialism and the leadership of the Communist Party.''
The attacks have not gone so far as to roll back all that Mr. Zhao stood for, especially the encouragement of joint ventures and technology transfer from foreign companies.
Instead, they have consistently held him accountable for diluting the power of the party by turning more economic decisions over to local governments and private enterprises, and for suggesting that Western economies provided a good model for China to emulate in some respects.
In fact, in his public speeches, Mr. Zhao rarely sounded themes too far out of line with those of other leaders, especially as the economy expanded at a rapid pace. 
But examining his speeches in retrospect, the official Chinese press has concluded that the party leadership had a counterrevolutionary in its midst.
''Zhao Ziyang often told some people that capitalism was actually better and our socialist system had problems,'' Workers' Daily said the other day. 
Many articles have reconstructed Mr. Zhao's role in the days leading up to the student occupation of Tiananmen Square, accusing him of violating the party's constitution by advocating reduced economic interference, and of deliberately ''escalating the turmoil.''
The People's Daily said Thursday that Mr. Zhao ''betrayed us all'' when he addressed student demonstrators sympathetically on May 4, a month before the crackdown, and said his speech played the role of ''supporting the enemy, confusing the masses, suppressing the cadres and splitting the Central Committee.''
In an article on Friday, by indirection, Mr. Zhao was blamed for virtually everything that is wrong today with the Chinese economy: rampant speculation, the shortages of raw materials, tax evasion.

Official China Mostly Hears A Party Line.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Chinese official was expounding the other day on the glories of the present hard-line Government as his two lieutenants sat beside him, nodding solemnly as if they agreed with everything he said.
But when the official stepped out for a moment, the assistants began to mock the Communist Party, until the boss returned. 
Then they resumed their posture of approval as the official declared that in his experience virtually everyone supported the Government.
Many Chinese say they believe that their highest leaders, like the official in that meeting, delude themselves about public opinion. 
They suggest that because no one dares to disagree with a superior, the propaganda spun by the Government ends up deceiving the leaders themselves.
"It's a major problem for China," said the daughter of a senior party official. 
"The leaders can get good statistics on material conditions, but it's very difficult for them to find out what people are thinking."
The fundamental problem is common to authoritarian governments: when expression of disagreement risks punishment as heresy, how can the Government find out what is going on?
Â 
Problem for Emperors, Too
China's emperors faced similar difficulties in cutting through the pomp and flattery to discover what was really happening outside the palace walls. 
The Ming Dynasty emperors employed young agents to go out in the provinces and act as their eyes and ears, and some emperors even disguised themselves and went about on their own fact-finding trips.
Since the military crackdown in June 1989, China's top leaders have emphasized the need to "go to the grass roots," and one Politburo member or another is constantly shown on television, gravely walking through a factory or strolling through a village in a remote province.
These visits are always choreographed by local officials, who accompany the leaders and insure that everything follows the script.
Â 
'Sound and Light Show'
"They never see anything at the grass roots," said an official in a provincial government that has seen its share of visits by national leaders. 
"It's very difficult for them to know what's really going on."
The "sound and light show" put on by provincial governors for a leader's visit do not necessarily suggest that everything is working perfectly. 
The current battle between the central Government and the provinces over taxes, for example, may lead local officials to point to financial difficulties to back their arguments for more money.
"The governors may exaggerate the problems, to try to squeeze more money out of the center," said an economic official in Beijing. 
"They may want to show how bad things are."
Â 
A Disastrous Strategy
Still, local officials are unlikely to acknowledge problems like political unrest, widespread evasions of family planning restrictions or local protectionist barriers that violate central Government policy. 
And even if a top official strayed from his escorts and asked ordinary people about their views, it is unlikely that people would respond.
Authoritarian traditions lasting thousands of years have taught most Chinese that outspokenness is a disastrous strategy. 
In the West a squeaky wheel may get the most oil; in China, a squeaky wheel is normally hammered until it stops squeaking.
"Those trips are just for show, because the leaders are only allowed to see the good things," acknowledged a relative of a senior Politburo member. 
But the relative added that the top leaders find other ways to stay well informed, and in particular that they use their staffs to keep a finger on the popular pulse and report to them in confidential memorandums.
A catastrophic instance in which China's leaders misled themselves came after Mao Zedong's attempt beginning in 1958 to try to catch up with the industrialized world. 
Responding to absurdly high production targets, local officials falsely reported that agricultural production had doubled, when in fact it had dropped. 
This obscured the beginnings of a famine in which about 26 million people died.
Â 
Videotapes Help Fill Need
The leadership has tried to develop several channels for obtaining accurate information from the provinces, including the establishment of a series of classified information summaries that appear each day and carry articles too sensitive to appear in the daily press. 
Top leaders are also said to receive updated summaries by fax, as well as a half-hour videotape each morning -- including film clips lifted from Cable News Network and other satellite transmissions -- to keep them up to date on news that is deemed inappropriate for television broadcasts.
Senior officials also rely on classified statistical summaries to follow economic and social conditions. 
Chinese businessmen say that Li Ruihuan, a Politburo member who used to be head of the city of Tianjin, even designed a system so that he could tap into his office computer and find the latest figures for Tianjin crime rates and other unpublished information.
But the public mood is not so easy to assess. 
One of the classified information summaries recently told of a gang of hoodlums who cut off the fingers of their victims -- an item that would never appear in the newspapers -- but these summaries would never report the mockery that intellectuals express for Prime Minister Li Peng.
In the absence of any reliable channel for information about the public mood, the children of the top leaders have sometimes taken on the job of advising their parents about popular opinion.
