file: Pastimes_Coins.txt
text:
ï»¿
Some money just goes up in smoke. 
In Chinese communities around the world joss money does just that. 
It's burned in honor of the dead so the deceased can make ends meet in the afterlife and at 50 cents for a hundred notes, joss money is a bargain.
N.T. Wang, a senior research scholar at Columbia University's East Asian Institute, says that there are two worlds in Chinese belief - the yin and the yan. 
The living reside in the yan and the dead in the yin. 
And although the two are separate, some commerce exists between the two. 
Chinese believe that dead ancestors continue to care for their living descendants and guard them against misfortune. 
In return, the living continue to offer food, money and other necessities to their ancestors.
At a spring festival, called Qing Ming, families gather to pay homage to their ancestors. 
Meats and fruits are left for the dead, paper houses and paper banknotes are burned. 
In the past gold- or silver-colored foil was shaped into bullion bars and burned.
In autumn, another festival honors ghosts of the nether world. 
Called Da Jiao, it is a chance to appease spirits other than those of the family. 
Professor Wang explains that the world of yin also has ghosts who are rogues and gangsters. 
They must be appeased in the nether world just as they are in this one so fake gold and silver coins are sprinkled at funerals.
Classical Chinese belief describes the passage from the world of the living to the world of the dead as a one-way street. 
But Hindu and Buddhist influences have made inroads into that belief and some Chinese now feel that reincarnation is possible. 
Those Chinese think that offering joss money will help the dead do good deeds in the afterlife and then be reborn into a better life.
Funeral notes come in various colors; in the United States green is popular. 
On the front is a picture of the Lord of the Dead - Yen Wang. 
Two of his assistants supervise the receipt of all offerings and their signatures appear. 
Different spellings occur but those printed in Shen Zhen, China, appear as Yin Low and Yuk Wong. 
Joss money can be purchased in packets of 100 notes in denominations from one dollar to 50 million dollars. 
If the thought of carrying around a packet worth five billion dollars appeals, this reminder is offered as a public service - banknotes are only redeemable at the Bank of Hell.

file: PASTIMES_NUMISMATICS.txt
text:
ï»¿
One of the strangest and most popular coins munches coral and algae on the bottom of the Indian Ocean. 
The shell of the Maldive cowrie, Cypraea moneta, has been used as money by the Chinese, the Hawaiians, the West Africans and Ojibwa Indians. 
It was considered money 4,300 years ago and is still used today.
Even when the cowrie is not money, it makes a popular ornament and a potent fertility talisman. 
The cowrie filled a need for small change among the poorest people of the world. 
In Nigeria, for example, an English penny was worth 120 cowries.
The cowrie shell first surfaced as money in China in the 24th century B.C. The Chinese character pei, ''sea creature living in a shell,'' is still a part of many Chinese words associated with money. 
The cowries could not be counterfeited or defaced. 
The Chinese Emperor Wang Mang decreed that cowries would be the coins of the realm since copper coins were prey to clipping. 
Marco Polo noted the existence of cowries as money in Yunan and called them porcellani, a diminutive of porco, Italian for pig. 
The shells became the origin of the word, porcelain.
The people of the Maldives traded the cowrie for rice in Bengal, where 15 cowries bought a pound of rice. 
Later the cowrie was brought to Africa by Arab slave dealers and was in use in the Mali Empire 500 years ago.
King Gezo of Dahomey found the cowries the perfect coin - they could not be counterfeited and any worthwhile amount of them could not be hid from the royal tax collector. 
Popularity of the cowrie became spectacular when it was used by Dutch and English in the West African slave trade.
The English and the Dutch competed for the Maldive cowrie, each seeking to find favor with the king and queen of the Maldives. 
There the cowrie trade was a royal monopoly. 
Palm branches were floated on the ocean and removed once cowries started eating the leaves. 
Live cowries were placed in pits, then removed weeks later. 
They were washed, sorted and loaded as ballast aboard English and Dutch ships bound for London and Amsterdam. 
There the cowries were sold to the West African slave dealers. 
In the early 1500's an English slave dealer could purchase an adult slave for 16 pounds of cowries, about 6,400 shells.
By 1667, a slave cost 100 pounds of cowries and by 1772, 450 pounds. 
The reason for the inflation is found in the two species of cowries residing in the Indian Ocean. 
Another cowrie, Cypraea annulus or ring cowrie, is more numerous than the money cowrie, Cypraea moneta.
Only in the Maldives are the money cowries numerous enough to be culled profitably. 
On the shores of East Africa, the ring cowrie can be picked off the beach, which is exactly what the British did. 
When the ring cowries - they have a small reddish-orange circle on top of the shell - were introduced into the slave trade, they debased the other currency, the money cowries.
In the early 1900's the cowries began to disappear from international trade. 
Colonial authorities decreed that cowries would no longer be imported or be accepted as tax payments. 
And finally coins of extremely small denomination were minted.
The cowries are still in use in some remote areas of Ghana and Nigeria, especially in places where national boundaries cross tribal areas. 
There the cowries, without national insignia, are used for small transactions and the legend of the Cowrie Mother still exists. 
Living in the bush covered in cowries, she'll bring riches to the person who catches her. 
In Ghana the modern coin, the cedi, is a direct descendant of the old cowrie, called a sedie.
In the southern part of the United States, some houses still have a cowrie or two, their owners oblivious to the cowries monetary origins.

file: PATTERNS(2).txt
text:
ï»¿
An Eye on China
Americans in the clothing business are viewing the upheaval in China with deep concern.
In 1988 China was America's third- largest apparel trading partner, behind Hong Kong and Taiwan, exporting nearly 800 million square yards of clothing and textiles, worth $2.2 billion in all, to the United States. 
But in terms of number of garments, China is the No. 1 supplier to the United States.
Chinese-made clothes represent approximately 6 percent of all garments sold in this country, said Carl Priestland, the chief economist of the American Apparel Manufacturers Association. 
Chain retailers like K Mart and J. C. Penney and manufacturers like Liz Claiborne have become heavily involved with Chinese manufacturers in the last several years.
''There is no doubt there will be some effect, some late deliveries,'' said Bernie Ozer, a vice president of Associated Merchandising Corporation, which has an office in Hong Kong and representatives in China. 
''We're monitoring the situation in every way possible. 
Right now nobody knows.''
Mr. Ozer said there will almost certainly be delivery problems for early fall clothes.
''So far there has been no interruption of the flow of merchandise,'' said Herbert Rounick, the chairman of Hero Industries Inc., which imports women's dresses, suits, sweaters and blouses from China for its Oleg Cassini licensed apparel line.
Mr. Rounick pointed out that little garment manufacturing is done in Beijing and that he had experienced no communications problems with his Shanghai office. 
''If it's contained in Beijing, we foresee no problems,'' he said. 
''There's not much happening in the countryside, where most of the textile factories are.''
Beyond that, Mr. Rounick said he was hopeful that the ''new moves will bring in younger people who are more astute in pursuing businesses.''
Â 
Garment District Expansion
Real estate in the garment district has been undergoing a transformation, reflecting trends in manufacturing and retailing. 
On Broadway in the high 30's, a short block away from the true glitz of Seventh Avenue where the top designers have their showrooms, several buildings are being changed from combination office and textile showrooms to what realtors call ''first class'' ready-to-wear showrooms.
The movement toward larger, modernized showrooms mirrors changes in apparel retailing, where mergers and acquisitions of the last three years have resulted in centralized buying offices and, consequently, a reliance on fewer - and larger - clothing manufacturers. 
At the same time, retail sales have slumped, driving manufacturers out of the city or out of business.
''The marginal garment center tenants don't have the staying power,'' said Michael Kornblum, a senior partner of Catalano Kornblum Development Corporation, which is renovating 1412 Broadway, at 39th Street. 
''But for tenants who hit it big, 3,000 square feet is no longer enough. 
Some of the buildings do not accommodate lateral expansion.''
Catalano Kornblum has signed up Escada, a large German apparel company, to lease 35,000 square feet in the renovated No. 1412 building. 
Other Broadway renovations for first-class showrooms include Nos. 
1450, 1386 and 1372. 
A new office building at 115 West 39th Street, the first new construction in the garment center in two decades, will also be primarily for fashion showrooms.
''Seventh Avenue was once known as the better-price area and Broadway the cheaper,'' said Sidney Winoker, the president of Winoker Realty, the renting agent for 1450 Broadway, whose new tenants include Cherokee and Giorgio Armani men's hosiery. 
''But that distinction is starting to break down.''
Meanwhile, offshore production has shrunk the domestic textile business and forced the survivors to seek less expensive rents. 
''The problem is bolts of fabric take up a lot of room,'' said Peter Catalano, Mr. Kornblum's partner. 
''There has been a lot of octopussing out to the side streets,'' he added.
''A lot of manufacturers moved out of the city because of retailers going into private label,'' Mr. Kornblum said. 
''I see people outside of fashion moving in.''
He mentioned law and real-estate firms as the kind of nonfashion tenants who have been moving into the garment district.
Â 
Scarfs for AIDS Benefit
Beginning tomorrow, Bergdorf Goodman will exhibit a series of 69 scarfs by designers and artists like Geoffrey Beene, Bill Blass, Hubert de Givenchy, Stephen Sprouse, Roz Chast, Paul Davis, Maurice Sendak and Kenny Scharf. 
The designs also appear in a new book, ''The Scarf'' (Stewart, Tabori & Chang), by Andrew Baseman.
The one-of-a-kind silk squares will be on display in the store's 57th Street windows for one week; then they are to be auctioned off in a benefit for the Design Industries Foundation for AIDS. 
(This gives the foundation a major plate-glass presence in New York: costumes produced by Metropolitan Home magazine for its Love Ball benefit are in the windows of Barneys New York.) The auction of the designer scarfs is a silent one. 
Throughout the week sealed bids will be accepted in excess of $250, which is not a bad floor price considering that a regular Hermes scarf retails for about $175.

file: PEACE_S PROSPECTS IN CAMBODIA GROW.txt
text:
ï»¿
After more than a decade of unrelievedly vicious fighting and months of stalled peace talks, there is now a possibility that the end of the Cambodian civil war is imminent.
Probability is not the word, at least not yet. 
The Cambodian Government and rebels seeking to overthrow it have accused each other of violations of the cease-fire they agreed to only last month, and Western and Asian diplomats have been embarrassed before in predicting a quick end to the war.
Some diplomats say they still do not understand how there can be peace in Cambodia as long as there is the threat of a return to power by the Khmer Rouge, the Communist guerrillas whose radical attempt to remake Cambodian society resulted in more than a million deaths in their four-year reign in the 1970's.
But later this month, China, the patron of the Khmer Rouge, is scheduled to sponsor a new round of peace talks in Beijing that will bring together representatives of the Vietnamese-backed Phnom Penh regime and the three major rebel factions.
Â 
Shifts by Hanoi and Sihanouk
Chinese leaders are thought to be ready to use their influence at the talks to insist on new progress toward peace in Cambodia, a nation whose reputation acquired over centuries as a land of bounty and of a gentle grace has been sullied in a war often fought between soldiers young enough to be considered children.
There are other elements to the new optimism about prospects for a lasting settlement in Cambodia.
One is the Government of Vietnam, which seems willing to give up much of its influence in neighboring Cambodia in order to improve its relationship with China. 
There is also the stated desire of the exiled Cambodian leader Prince Norodom Sihanouk to die in peace in the land he ruled as a god-king until 1970.
"I want to die on Khmer soil," the mercurial 68-year-old Prince told a news conference last month in the Thai beach resort of Pattaya, where he was host of what may have been the most fruitful round of peace talks since the Vietnamese launched their invasion of Cambodia in 1978.
Â 
The Go-Ahead From Beijing
At the Pattaya talks, the Cambodian Government and the three major rebel groups -- the Khmer Rouge, the followers of Prince Sihanouk, and a faction faithful to former Prime Minister Son Sann -- agreed not only to an indefinite cease-fire, but also to a cessation of foreign arms supplies.
The agreements were reached under a framework drafted last year by the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.
"The progress last month in ending this stalemate is due directly to the actions of Sihanouk," said a Western diplomat in Bangkok. 
"It appears the Chinese have given him the go-ahead to make peace, and his willingness to set aside past differences was the magic of Pattaya."
Temperamental, impishly charming and a man of shifting loyalties, the Prince remains a revered figure to many in his homeland, and diplomatic observers and Cambodian participants described the air of reconciliation fostered by Prince Sihanouk at the talks as remarkable.
Â 
Air of Reconciliation
For example, during earlier negotiations, the leader of the Vietnamese-backed Government in Phnom Penh, Prime Minister Hun Sen, and the Khmer Rouge negotiator, Khieu Samphan, were said to barely acknowledge the presence of each other in the same room.
But at Pattaya, Mr. Hun Sen, who rose to power in Phnom Penh after defecting from the Khmer Rouge, turned to Mr. Khieu Samphan at one point and described him as "my beloved excellency."
To an extent not yet clear, the success of the Cambodian talks was being determined hundreds of miles away, in Vietnam's capital, Hanoi, where the governing Communist Party was meeting the same week in its first party congress in five years.
While pledging continued support for the Government in Cambodia, the party made clear its desire for closer ties to Beijing and its intention to put an end to military interventions like the 1978 Cambodian invasion.
Â 
Reining In the Khmer Rouge
In what appeared to be a signal to China, the party ousted Vietnam's Foreign Minister, Nguyen Co Thach, who had long been seen in Beijing as China's chief adversary in Hanoi.
"I think the Chinese feel that with Thach gone and with the Vietnamese bowing out as the sponsors in Phnom Penh, it's time to restore some sort of peace in Cambodia," said an Asian diplomat. 
"You'll see China willing to rein in the Khmer Rouge."
The other superpowers are playing a more limited role in forging a peace agreement in Cambodia.
The United States has provided what is officially described as nonmilitary aid to Prince Sihanouk's followers and the Son Sann faction, and it has put pressure on Vietnam to end the war in exchange for normalized relations with Washington.
The Soviet Union has aligned itself diplomatically with Vietnam and with the Cambodian Government but, consumed by its internal problems, the Kremlin has indicated a desire to end all military involvement in Indochina.
The intentions of the feared Khmer Rouge remain the principal mystery in the peace negotiations.

file: PEARL HARBOR REMEMBERED_History_s Refraction Illuminates 2 Views Of a Date of Infamy.txt
text:
ï»¿
On Japan's airwaves this week, the battleship Arizona has sunk a dozen times, the aging Zero pilots have been interviewed so many times that dedicated viewers know their exploits by heart, and a stream of commentators have talked -- and talked, and talked -- about how the United States and Japan must seize this weekend to reaffirm the most critical alliance linking East and West.
But in subtle and telling ways, the images and explanations being offered here and in the United States to explain how two great powers came to battle each other are strikingly different.
For many Japanese, this has been a long week of trying, once again, to find comfort in a carefully sculpted interpretation of history that overarches the country's memories of the war. 
In dramas and documentaries, the Japanese have watched this week as their fathers and mothers made a futile effort to steer the country away from war, as a small group of military leaders drove a peaceful people to ruin, and as their country rose from its defeat to be as technologically powerful as the nation to whom it eventually surrendered.
Perhaps the clearest cleavage of interpretations came in the studios of NHK, the giant semiofficial broadcaster, which struggled for months with producers from ABC over a documentary that was aired this week in both countries. 
Although American and Japanese viewers saw nearly identical film, they heard very different scripts, and they were differences that went beyond the imprecision of translations.
Â 
2 Views of Rape of Nanking
In an 18-second clip about Japan's 1937 capture of Nanking, the then capital of China, ABC reported that "Japan's claim it was liberating China was ludicrous to Americans, particularly when hundreds of thousands of Chinese men, women and babies were murdered in what was called the Rape of Nanking. 
The U.S. sent China $50 million in war relief."
But in Japan, where the Rape of Nanking is not mentioned in textbooks and the country's right wing contends that the incident was a fabrication, viewers heard nothing about war atrocities.
Though NHK's version of the documentary showed vivid footage of Chinese being shot in a ditch, the voice-over said simply, "In a totalitarian attempt to grab land and wealth, the Japanese military had led the country into an eight-year war in Manchuria and China," an invasion that caused tension with the United States.
At a luncheon with foreign correspondents on Friday, Mikio Kawaguchi, the chairman of NHK, said there had been no effort to rewrite history for a Japanese audience, simply an attempt to explain things differently to American and Japanese viewers, who "have a different way of looking at history and life."
"Even though both sides were sincere in their efforts, the methods they wanted to employ to portray what they saw as truth were different," Mr. Kawaguchi said of his company's joint venture with the American network. 
"There were perception gaps. 
The two sides had such disagreements that they feared they might be headed into a second Pearl Harbor."
Â 
A Weeklong History Lesson
Without question, Japan learned a lot of history this week. 
Many young people said that until the flurry of programs, they had not been certain why Pearl Harbor prompted such strong emotions in America. 
At the same time, the tone of much of the coverage paralleled the tone of the little that is taught about the war in schools: Japan was more a victim than an aggressor.
Several broadcasts explored the internment of Japanese-Americans in the United States. 
Several reported arguments that President Roosevelt had known about the attack in advance and done nothing to stop it. 
Others found a simple answer for Japan's ultimate defeat: The country was simply outproduced by the United States. 
A lengthy program today, "The Secret Story of the War Over Steel," showed how the giant American steelmakers that provided the hardware for Japan's defeat later fell to Japanese competition.
Japanese television warmed to another popular theme here: that the Japanese military, rather than the Japanese people or even political leaders, was solely responsible for plunging the nation into war.
On Friday night, for example, viewers tuned into a vivid drama called "Defeat in Showa 16," a title suggesting that Japan lost the war as soon as it began in 1941. 
The Japanese calendar begins anew with the ascension of each new emperor, and 1941 was the 16th year of the Showa era, Emperor Hirohito's reign.
Â 
Shouting at the War Institute
Based on fact, the drama was the story of a railway executive, a bureaucrat and other Japanese who were drafted into the Government's "Total War Research Institute."
The institute was charged with determining what would happen if the country gave everything -- from its steel works to its samurai spirit -- to the cause of "liberating" the country from encirclement by Dutch, British and American colonialists.
In the show, the young men of the institute concluded that the Government's war plans were madness. 
There were frequent shouting matches with the military brass, but the young men's voices were drowned out. 
Many historians and older Japanese say that the spirit of such dramas is accurate.
"Everyone knew that relations were at a critical position, even though there was no indication war would be coming so soon," said Junnosuke Ofusa, who joined The New York Times bureau in Tokyo in 1930 and helped guide the newspaper's coverage of Japan for the next five decades. 
Mr. Ofusa, who retired several years ago, said that "no one said outwardly that it was a bad idea, because the military police were everywhere. 
But the Japanese people knew there was little chance of winning the war."
At the same time, some Japanese bridle at placing all of the blame on the military, because the argument is often used to absolve the rest of the country.
"Of course the military had much of the power," Seiki Nishihiro, a former Deputy Defense Minister, said the other day, discussing the coverage of the anniversary. 
"But the mass media and everyone else followed, so not only the military was responsible."
Bubbling just beneath the surface of the coverage was the question of whether, and how, Japan should apologize for the Pearl Harbor attack.
Government spokesmen, who have spent much of the last year fretting about the anniversary celebrations, were openly distraught. 
While they were issuing statements of "regret" or "remorse" or "self-reflection" -- a great deal of time was spent trying to figure out which word best described Japan's position -- Parliament was going in the other direction, scuttling any parliamentary apology altogether.
"Why should we fling mud at the history of Japan?"
Masayuki Fujio, a senior politician, asked the other day, in a remark that was quoted in the Japanese news media throughout the weekend.
But the week was so painful that this country, which planned no formal events to commemorate Pearl Harbor, seems eager to have the anniversary behind it. 
"In a sense it is a kind of Pearl Harbor week anyway," said a weary-looking Taizo Watanabe, the Foreign Ministry's chief spokesman. 
"So many questions asked, so many answers and apologies from us."
With one more apology on early Sunday morning here, after President Bush's address at Pearl Harbor, the Japanese hope it will be all over, so they can go back to topics that are easier to discuss.
"Ask me about anything else," a senior Government official said the other day. 
"Ask me why the trade deficit is getting bigger again. 
Ask me about why we are so slow to open the rice market. 
Just don't ask me about Pearl Harbor."

file: Perils of America as Seen in a Chinese Novel.txt
text:
ï»¿
Wang Qiming, a violinist from Beijing, grew up thinking of America as a paradise. 
Then he arrived in New York and had his luggage stolen at the airport. 
That was only the beginning of his troubles: he lost a small fortune gambling and his daughter became a drug addict before she was kidnapped and murdered.
Mr. Wang is a fictional character, but his creator, Cao Guilin, is a Chinese emigrant who lives in Queens and says the character is based on his own experiences.
In any case, his book, "A Beijing Man in New York," is the talk of the Chinese capital these days. 
It has been serialized in Beijing Wanbao, the most-read newspaper in the capital. 
A radio play based on the book is now being broadcast daily at lunchtime across the country, affording the public a tour through the seamy side of New York.
Many ordinary Chinese are reading with fascination about the experiences of a fellow Chinese who makes it to America and who initially strikes it rich by opening a small garment factory. 
Figuring out how to get to the United States is almost an obsession for many young Chinese, and Mr. Guilin's novel seems to offer a glimpse of what life might be like if they succeeded. 
At the same time, the Government is delighted to publicize how cruel life can be under capitalism.
Chinese newspapers have no shortage of reports about murders, rapes, robberies and homelessness in America. 
But many Chinese say they discount the reports as exaggerated or distorted. 
The novel, however, has captured the public imagination, and many readers seem genuinely surprised at its portrayal of the hardships faced by immigrants there.
"I picked it up accidentally and since then I've read every episode," said a college-educated restaurateur in Beijing. 
"Life in America is not a heaven, and this shows the ups and downs of an immigrant's life."
When the novel was first printed in a magazine, all 120,000 copies sold out immediately. 
Then it was published in book form in September, and that sold out. 
Now another magazine has published it, and it is being serialized in the China Press, a Chinese-language newspaper in New York.
"From a literary point of view, the craftsmanship is not very good, but the emotion is real," said Wang Hongxian, the magazine editor who first printed the story. 
"A number of students overseas write about their experiences. 
Some focus on the difficulties, some focus on the good things. 
This is not like those. 
It's more real, more objective."
In the novel, after Mr. Wang loses his luggage, he gets a job as a dishwasher while his wife knits for a garment factory. 
They are able to buy an old car and move into a decent apartment in their first year. 
Then Mr. Wang and his wife borrow money to start a knitwear factory. 
They become rich and buy a few buildings and a better car.
But life for the Wangs starts to turn sour when their daughter, corrupted by New York City schools, leaves home, turns to drugs and is kidnapped. 
Meanwhile, the factory goes bankrupt and Mr. Wang loses $40,000 when he gambles away the last of his money in the hopes of making enough to pay his debts. 
In the end, the kidnappers demand a ransom, which Mr. Wang cannot afford, so they kill his daughter.
"New York, ah, it really is a heaven in hell, a hell in heaven," moans the fictional Mr. Wang.
Mr. Cao, who was a violinist in Beijing before he left a decade ago for the United States, said he wrote the book because he wanted to dispel the fantasies that many young Chinese have about America. 
He admits he spiced it up to make it "more readable."
"You can achieve the American dream, but you can't just step off the plane and get it," Mr. Cao, who is himself a successful knitwear manufacturer, said in a phone interview. 
"You must go through a hard, bitter struggle that might make your heart bleed, but this cultural shock, you must go through all this before you can achieve the American dream."
Mr. Cao said he is surprised at the stir his novel has created in Beijing. 
Royalties, Mr. Cao said with a laugh, are no more than enough to cover a plane ride to Beijing. 
But he said he plans to publish another book soon.

file: Pessimism Is Growing on Saving Pandas From Extinction.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN a quiet enclave in the heart of Sichuan Province, two giant pandas ambled playfully among the rocks and bamboo, oblivious to the growing fear that their species could become extinct within decades.
Millions of dollars have been spent to preserve panda habitats and save the animals from hunters who kill them for pelts. 
But the efforts have been stymied by red tape and in-fighting among Government ministries. 
The result is that the panda is losing its competition with humans.
"I'm rather pessimistic about the giant panda," said Yin Lin, a technician who conducts artificial insemination in the panda at the Chengdu Zoo. 
"There is a very strong trend toward extinction."
According to China's official statistics, there are only about 1,000 pandas left in the wild, and another 100 in zoos all over the world. 
Privately, some experts say the number of pandas in the wild is as low as 700.
Â 
Loss of Food Supply
Pandas eat bamboo, but their digestion is so poor they must eat practically all day long to get enough nourishment. 
But in China, where arable land and wood are scarce, both local residents and the Government have cut down substantial areas of bamboo forests.
Many specialists say the panda's best chances for survival are in the wild, rather than in the zoos, but the wild panda reserves do not necessarily get the funds, and when they do success is limited.
"Our hearts are aching with anxiety," said Pan Wenshi, a panda specialist at Beijing University. 
"We know the panda must rely on man to survive. 
But man has not yet offered a good way of helping it."
Researchers and officials are often limited in what they can do: they lack funds, they do not have enough decision-making power or they are overruled by the bureaucracy.
Sometimes the panda projects are bogged down by petty jealousies and proud bureaucrats, both Chinese and foreign experts say. 
Money and time are often wasted on repetition of effort, and more money does not necessarily mean better results.
For example, at the Wolong Reserve, a large panda preservation about 90 miles northwest of Chengdu, officials built a research site with $1 million donated a decade ago by the World Wide Fund for Nature. 
Experts envisioned a program to breed pandas and put them back in the wild. 
In the past decade, however, the center has bred only one panda, and it died.
One problem is that China's reserves and zoos do not work together to share specialists, resources or even good breeding pandas. 
Specialists at the Chengdu Zoo have not been welcomed at Wolong, and panda experts from Beijing have been turned away, researchers say.
Part of the reason is that pandas in the wild are controlled by the Ministry of Forestry, while pandas in captivity are managed by the Ministry of Construction.
"We do have some contact, but there are some administrative obstacles," said a panda researcher under the Ministry of Construction. 
"It's a problem. 
But if we had a leading group overseeing panda work, who would lead it?"
This year Wolong appears to be opening up to outside researchers, and the Chengdu Zoo sent its first male panda to the center for mating this spring. 
Academics say that while this is progress, there are still many turf wars and problems.
"It's territorial behavior," said Wang Song, a biologist at the Academy of Sciences in Beijing. 
"The Smithsonian and the American Government departments cooperate very well. 
Under socialism, we should be better but we're not."
China's 14 panda reserves also face other challenges. 
They are isolated from each other, and sometimes they have so few pandas that the fertile ones have difficulty finding mates. 
As a result, there are problems with inbreeding as well as relatively low reproduction rates. 
The World Wild Fund for Nature has proposed linking the reserves together to address these problems, but some experts say this is often not feasible.
Another problem is that even in the reserves, the pandas have two-legged neighbors. 
Frantic researchers at Qinling Reserve in Shaanxi Province are trying to raise money to relocate the reserve's 2,200 human residents, who have slowly encroached upon the bamboo forest.
In Wolong Reserve, new houses have been built for 3,000 residents, but the residents refuse to move unless they are fully compensated for farming income they would lose. 
Meanwhile, the authorities built a power station to prevent them from further destroying bamboo trees for fuel.
"Everything about pandas gets mired in politics and sometimes it's forgotten that the main purpose is to save the pandas," said George B. Schaller, director for science at Wildlife Conservation International in New York.
Many experts say the panda population has dwindled to 700 to 900 over the past decade, although Chinese officials have been unwilling to announce the results of a panda census completed three years ago, and the official Government estimate remains about 1,000. 
In any case, some experts say the census faced enormous obstacles and was not very thorough. 
Some say it is possible there are more than 1,000 pandas.
The previous census, in the late 1970's, counted about 2,000 pandas, experts with first-hand knowledge say. 
But the Government announced that the panda population was about 1,000, apparently because it anticipated a decline and did not want to be blamed for it. 
Some experts believe that the authorities reported a lower number to attract more attention and funds to help the pandas.
Scientists say poaching is the principal reason for the population decline. 
In Wolong, the panda population dropped by half: from 145 to 72 in the 12 years to 1986, according to a recent report by the World Wide Fund for Nature.
Â 
Death Penalty for Poaching
"Hunting is the most serious immediate problem," said Mr. Schaller. "If poaching isn't checked, the panda will disappear."
Pandas have become so prized that the value of a pelt has risen to more than $10,000 to $20,000 in some parts of China, according to various Chinese and foreign reports. 
The pelts make their way through a long chain of underground dealers before they end up abroad, especially in Taiwan and Japan.
China recently decreed the death penalty for poaching and trading in panda pelts, and so far at least four men have been sentenced to death. 
A recent report in the official Public Security News said that in Sichuan alone there have been arrests in about 200 cases of trafficking in panda pelts in the last few years.
The impact of poaching is particularly serious in light of the panda's poor reproductive abilities. 
A female panda ovulates once a year, and may raise about half a dozen babies in her lifetime if she is lucky. 
Breeding in zoos has been difficult because not all researchers know how to tell when a panda is ovulating. 
Even if a panda is born, it frequently dies in the first few weeks or months, either because the mother accidently crushes it to death, or because it is not fed properly.
"In the best of worlds, the panda reproduces at an incredibly slow rate," said Devra G. Kleiman, a zoologist at the National Zoological Park of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. 
"That's why the loss of even a single breeding period of a single panda is a real loss."
For this reason, some experts say that among pandas in captivity, all efforts should be concentrated on breeding, rather than putting them up for exhibition. 
But pandas for exhibition have become an enormously lucrative business for the Chinese zoos or institutions that control them.
A Chinese zoo can make more than $500,000 on the loan of a single panda for a few months, and the drive to make money often interferes with panda breeding.
Peter Karsten, director of the Calgary Zoo in Canada, also asserted that Chinese zoos sometimes loaned mismatched panda couples -- either pairs of the same sex or pairs that are unlikely to breed -- to avoid being embarrassed if a foreign zoo was able to arrange a mating that had eluded the animals' home zoo. 
He also said that China tries to control the supply of pandas outside China, perhaps for commercial reasons.
At a broader level, experts complain that there is a fierce competition among institutions that control the pandas, and the result is that zoos and ministries guard, rather than share, pandas as well as knowledge about how to care for them.
Thus, after nearly 20 years of panda breeding in China, only 28 pandas have been bred and raised successfully in captivity there, Chinese panda experts say.
Because of the poor track record, some specialists are skeptical about breeding programs, and more broadly, about panda preservation in China. 
Even Chinese experts have some difficulty in waxing optimistic.
"It will take several generations of researchers before we have success," said Hu Jinchu, a panda expert at the University of Nanchong in Sichuan. 
"This may be 100 to 200 years. 
But if the Government policy is good, the economy is good, the educational level is improved and we get international cooperation, then maybe there will be hope."

file: Political Sway of the Military Is Subtly Spreading in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
While China's political leaders have removed themselves from sight to engage in a bitter struggle for power, there are signs that the military may be accumulating a larger role in the Chinese political process.
It is still too early in the power struggle to determine the consequences of the political crisis, but some scholars and diplomats see the outlines of two trends: a greater military influence during a prolonged period of political instability, and less certainty that the army will carry out orders from political leaders.
Some fear that the leadership may increasingly be vulnerable to military pressure, and even to a coup. 
But they say that the army is genuinely trying to become a more professional organization and that it may not be interested in taking advantage of weakness in the Government.
Pattern of Strength
''The military gains strength whenever the political leaders depend on them to tackle unrest,'' said an Asian diplomat in Beijing. 
But he and other diplomats noted that there were competing trends and that the military may not necessarily want to play a pivotal political role.
Some Chinese are worried about hints of an greater military role because of suspicions that it could be misused by the family of President Yang Shangkun, the 82-year-old veteran military figure who took a hard line against student demonstrators.
Many students and intellectuals are suspicious of Mr. Yang and believe, without real evidence, that his next target is Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader.
Â 
No. 2 to Deng in Army
Mr. Yang is vice chairman of the Central Military Commission and subordinate to Mr. Deng, who is chairman of the commission.
In addition, Mr. Yang's younger brother, Yang Baibing, is head of the general political department of the People's Liberation Army. 
And Chi Haotian, the chief of the General Staff, is widely rumored to be President Yang's son-in-law.
A young official at Communist Party headquarters said President Yang took his post in exchange for giving up his influence over the military, and that his younger brother was elevated as part of the arrangement. 
But the official said the Yang family was doing what it could to accumulate more control over the military, with an eye toward gaining more political power.
''By the time old Deng realizes what's going on, it'll be too late,'' the official said.
Â 
Zhao as Obstacle
An obstacle to Mr. Yang would have been the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang, who was also the first vice chairman of the Central Military Commission and the intended successor to Mr. Deng as chairman of the commission. 
But Mr. Zhao has already been stripped of his power to order the movement of troops, a senior party official said, and he is now being criticized in internal documents in preparation for an attempt to dismiss him as party leader.
With Mr. Zhao out of the way, only Mr. Deng would rank ahead of President Yang on the Central Military Commission. 
And only Mr. Deng has greater prestige and influence over the army than the Yang family.
Beijing is thick with intrigue these days, and the military fits into all of them. 
There are disputes about who has ordered some of the troop movements, and there are those who say that President Yang ordered some of the troops without informing Mr. Deng. What Role for Troops?
In addition, there are doubts about why the troops have been called to the capital. 
It was originally believed that they were summoned to intimidate and suppress the democracy movement.
Most officials acknowledge that that was one reason, but they say that it was at least as important to provide a show of force to intimidate Mr. Zhao and his supporters in the Beijing Military Region. 
A more important role for the army would reverse the trend of the last decade, in which the military has lost soldiers, money and prestige.
The People's Liberation Army, which includes all services, has seen its share of the national budget drop from 17.9 percent in 1979 to 8.2 percent last year, and about 1.5 million soldiers have been demobilized.
Few of the present Central Committee members are army officers, and none of the obvious candidates to lead the Government or the Party in the future have much military experience.
Â 
Unrest Leads to Power
Yet whenever there has been unrest in recent Chinese history, the military has gained strength. 
In 1969, after three years of the chaos of the Cultural Revolution, army officers composed a full 45 percent of the newly chosen Central Committee.
The influence of the military in those years was cut back after concerns about the army's reliability, and especially after a murky incident in 1971 that apparently was an attempted coup by the top military figure, Lin Biao. 
Now, too, there are growing doubts about the military's reliability, but in a different sense.
The fear used to be that the military might seize power for itself. 
That remains a concern, especially after Mr. Deng ultimately leaves the scene.
But the more obvious sign of unreliability has been the army's apparent reluctance to enforce martial law in any strict way. 
Convoys of troops were easily stopped on the outskirts of Beijing by crowds of people who sat in front of the trucks, and some soldiers tearfully withdrew.
Â 
Orders Reportedly Ignored
The head of the 38th Army is said to have refused to march on Beijing, and the Beijing Garrison Command is also widely believed to have been unwilling to carry out martial law. 
''The army has proven itself a most unreliable tool of the Government,'' said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
''It was a quasi-rebellion. 
This time it just refused. 
Next time, it might turn on the Government.''
In fact, the army eventually did enter Beijing and take up positions in places like the train station and the airports, but only after clearly establishing that it was not going to harm citizens.
Some people think that was the result of a careful negotiation: the army effectively agreed to obey instructions if the instructions were amended so that they stipulated that no violence would be used against Beijing citizens.
''More and more of the military leaders are independent of the party and the leaders,'' said Thomas Chan, a China scholar at Hong Kong University. 
''They may not be so easily used in the future as the personal army of the leadership.''

file: POPULATION POLICY IN ASIA IS FAULTED.txt
text:
ï»¿
Serious flaws in family-planning programs in China and India make it unlikely that the world's two most populous nations will be able to stabilize growth until well into the next century, by which time they may have added more than 1.5 billion people to the world's population, according to findings published this week by the independent Population Crisis Committee.
The problem is especially acute in India, the research group says. 
India, with a population of about 882 million that is growing 2.1 percent a year, is likely to overtake China as the most populous country by 2035, the committee says; India's population may reach 2 billion before leveling off.
China, with about 1.165 billion people, is likely to stabilize at about 1.5 billion, the group says.
The world's population is estimated at 5.4 billion.
Â 
Burdens on the Environment
The continued growth in India and China contributes to an intensifying crisis in ecological and human resources in large areas of Asia, where land is being rapidly degraded by overuse, water supplies are under strain and agriculture must struggle to stay ahead of soil and water depletion.
Throughout Asia, there is no longer time to let economic development lead to smaller family size, as happened in industrial nations. 
Some Asian nations, led by South Korea, Thailand and Indonesia, have made significant reductions in population growth through effective family planning.
"For people who are concerned about problems like global warming, ozone-layer depletion or world poverty, we just have to be vitally interested in the success or failure of the Chinese and Indian programs," said Sharon L. Camp, senior vice president of the Population Crisis Committee.
Copies of the reports are available for $5 each, including postage, from the Population Crisis Committee, 1120 19th Street, Washington, D.C. 
20036.
Â 
India 'Most Critical'
The studies of China and India conclude that the success of China's much-publicized population-control efforts have been "exaggerated," and that most couples have not one, but two or three children.
The situation in India is more dire.
"From a demographic perspective, India may be the world's most critical country," the Population Crisis Committee says. 
Nearly half the illiterate people in the world live in India, where a third of the people suffer from malnutrition.
The studies -- "India's Family Planning Challenge: From Rhetoric to Action" and "China's Family Planning Program: Challenging the Myths" -- call for more international assistance to the two countries, and more receptivity in Beijing and New Delhi to outside advice and help.
Â 
U.S. Angry With China
Under the Reagan and Bush Administrations, however, Washington has denied family-planning aid to China because of coercive population-control programs, including forced abortions.
Under the influence of Republican conservatives, Washington also halted its contributions in 1985 to the United Nations Population Fund, citing its involvement in programs like China's. 
Washington supplied 20 percent of the fund's resources, and its withdrawal has hobbled the fund's work in both Asia and Africa.
The United States policy took shape in 1984, just before an international population conference in Mexico City, where Washington took a strong stand against abortion and population control in general. 
Abortions are used frequently in poor nations to regulate child-bearing.
Although Congress has been generous in appropriating money for programs in many other countries, and the United States Agency for International Development is a major contributor to family-planning programs worldwide, the policies on China and contributions to international organizations continue.
The reports on China and India, written by Ms. Camp and Shanti R. Conly, the committee's director of population policy analysis, fault both countries on the limited options available to women seeking contraception.
Â 
Flawed Technology
In India, sterilization (mostly of women) accounts for 70 percent of contraception. 
Because of the near finality of the method and the risks to health from unsterile operations, many women wait until they have had four or more children, Indian experts say.
In China, an outdated and often risky steel-ring intrauterine device is used by 60 million women, the study says. 
About 36 percent of women rely on tubal ligation.
The roots of the problems are different. 
In India the Government has pledged a renewed effort to slow population growth, but many earlier efforts have been undercut by cultural resistance and a lack of political will. 
Conversely, in China, the determination of the Government to cut growth drastically led to Draconian measures that also aroused opposition.
But the Population Crisis Committee study found similarities in the shortcomings of the two nations' programs.
"Local programs in China and India are typically characterized by poorly trained personnel who lack both the interpersonal skills and technical knowledge necessary to adequately counsel clients on the risks and benefits of contraceptive measures," the committee said.

file: PRACTICAL TRAVELER_Rerouting Asian Trips Away From China.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHEN the first tanks rolled through Tiananmen Square on June 4, ''tourism to the People's Republic of China was crushed for the foreseeable future and probably for many years to come,'' Linda Ball, editor of the trade publication Tour and Travel News, wrote after she returned from China. 
Although her colleagues may dispute her on how long tourism to China will be eclipsed, people in the trade agree that a decade of effort by Chinese officials and Americans with commercial and personal investments was blown away in a matter of hours.
Take the flights of Northwest and United Airlines. 
Until the crackdown by Chinese authorities on the protesting students, Northwest was providing twice-a-week service into Shanghai from Osaka, Japan, on 747's with a capacity of 400 passengers. 
According to Bob Gibbons, a spokesman, the flight now goes only once a week - in on Monday and out on Tuesday - but there are only 150 passengers. 
Before the crackdown, Mr. Gibbons said, all of Northwest's flights in the Pacific were nearly twice that, about 70 percent full.
United, according to Sara Dornacker, a spokeswoman, had been sending three flights a week into China since February 1986. 
In the week of June 18, this was cut to one flight a week - into Beijing from Tokyo on Friday and out one hour later. 
On Friday, June 23, this flight, also using a 747 with a capacity of 400, carried just 72 fare-paying passengers into China. 
''And that's up from what it had been,'' Ms. Dornacker said.
Some of the impact was not felt for a few days. 
''I had one person who canceled June 21 on an October departure,'' said Howard C. Smith, president of the Chinasmith travel agency in New York. 
''They were willing to wait and see until the executions started. 
Then they said 'no way.'
''
That harsh ''no way'' undoes the long labor China began in 1978 when it opened its portals and began to seek dollars from tourism. 
The first tourists in almost 30 years went to worthwhile but dull places, in what is called hard class, but the Chinese moved to adapt to tourists' demands with the establishment of hotels and airline service with names familiar in the West. 
Northwest Airlines began flying into China again for the first time since the 40's on May 2, 1984.
By 1988, according to officials of the China National Tourist Office in New York, the trade contributed $2.2 billion to the gross national product. 
In the first four months of 1989, the trade publication Travel Weekly said, China was host to 93,000 United States tourists.
The negative impact of the Chinese Government's move to halt the demonstrations was felt quickly. 
United flew two evacuation charter flights for the State Department on June 8, in addition to its three scheduled flights that week. 
The line filled 1,290 seats of the 2,000 it had available on the five flights, Ms. Dornacker said. 
Mr. Gibbons said that in the rush, Northwest at first thought that more charters would be needed, but ''it was one person with 18 reservations'' who created the illusory demand.
Â 
Cruise Ships
Pearl Cruises dropped all its cruises into China for the rest of 1989: ''China Dynasty'' for June 23, as an example, became ''Highlights of the Orient,'' with calls in Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Taiwan. 
On June 22, Royal Viking Line discarded its China schedule for the fall; ''China in Depth,'' scheduled to depart Sept. 
10, became ''Shogun Autumn,'' with calls in Japan, South Korea, Okinawa, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
Pacific Delight, which describes itself as the biggest packager of tours to China and the Orient, canceled all its trips to China up to early August and began amending 60 or 65 of its 94 itineraries, according to Lythia Rousseas, a spokeswoman. 
Tour operators everywhere have done the same.
June was not over when Chinese authorities began to try to repair the damage. 
The China International Travel Service in Beijing said it was guaranteeing the safety of tourists and it was safe for everyone to return. 
''Now we are getting telexes and faxes from China agencies asking us please to send our people back,'' Mr. Smith, the president of Chinasmith, said on June 22. 
''They say they are offering 20 percent discounts across the board, and that is only the start.
''Of course, I have to reply that no one is asking to go to China. 
My reaction is that I cannot send people under the circumstances. 
For me, the tea is bitter because I always enjoyed going - I don't like what's going on.''
When Mr. Smith was interviewed, he said his agency was spending 90 percent of its time processing refunds. 
Clients who requested them were getting full refunds, he said, unless some of the money had already been sent to China, in which case a service fee of $150 was deducted. 
Most of his clients, he said, were accepting reroutings to Southeast Asia. 
For those who remained determined to go to China despite State Department warning against it, he said he was considering having them sign a risk-waiver form.
A Pacific Delight client who wants to shift to a new itinerary receives a discount of $100, Ms. Rousseas said. 
Pacific Delight is giving full refunds, on request, to all those booked on canceled trips. 
But like all the organizations interviewed, Pacific Delight said it weighed the situation day by day, considering how far ahead to cancel or maintain plans.
Most agencies and packagers, including the cruise lines, are giving full refunds to clients, and the fiscal health of an agency may hinge on how much money had already been remitted to China. 
Ms. Rousseas said that Pacific Delight was discussing with the Chinese authorities what might be recovered on deposits for tours. 
She said that the New York office laid off four out of 45 employees as a result of the drop in tours to China.
Â 
Ethnic Market
The most immediate impact was felt in the so-called ethnic travel market: Chinese families planning to visit friends and relatives in China. 
George Chen, president of C. L. Thomson Express, a big ticket wholesaler, said: ''Chinese visits to their friends and relatives in China dried up right away. 
And the ethnic travel agents are dead in their tracks now.''
Mr. Chen, who has offices in San Francisco but who began building his business in Hong Kong, said that one problem was Chinese-Americans' fear that they might be prevented from leaving China if there was further upheaval.
Mr. Chen does not sell his consolidator tickets to the public, only to travel agencies, so he is particularly sensitive to business failures. 
He said on June 22 that he had heard of no closings yet. 
''They don't react that quickly,'' he said of agencies. 
''They don't want to shut even though it might be the smart thing to do.''
Hong Kong tourism has been affected as well; 26 percent of its visitors are usually estimated to be on their way into or out of China. 
Hotel occupancy rates are down but, according to Douglas J. King of the Hong Kong Tourist Association, it is hard to assess because 4,500 rooms have been added in a year, and more are under construction. 
Before the troubles in China, 36 Hong Kong hotels were offering a promotional price for the summer: six nights for the price of four. 
Mr. King did not expect any new discounts but acknowledged that a further drop in tourists is expected in July and August. 
He did say, however, ''We expect the U.S. trade back, we have had setbacks before.''
At Oriental Clipper Travel, at 217 Park Row in New York, Andi Yu said on June 28 that a rebound was on the way. 
With the discount offered on land arrangements by China, Miss Yu said that her agency was selling a nine-night trip leaving Aug. 
10 to Beijing, Xian and Shanghai at half price. 
Including round-trip air fare from the West Coast, it will cost $1,277 - rather than $2,500. 
''It will be a one-shot, just to show the public that it is safe to go,'' Miss Yu said. 
Asked who was interested in the 45 places on this tour, Miss Yu said that many American students had called.
Nonetheless, most travel agents are less sanguine about prospects for renewed traffic to China. 
At Chinasmith, Mr. Smith said: ''Tourism is not normally thought of in conjunction with martial law.''

file: Practicing Acupuncture Made Easy.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dr. Doreen Chen first studied acupuncture 40 years ago in rural Chinese villages. 
She did not press her first silver needle into a patient's skin until her teachers were satisfied that she understood the philosophies of harmony and equilibrium that guided the needle. 
And she did not receive her license in to practice acupuncture on her own until she had completed a long and rigorous apprenticeship.
Now, she says with quiet but obvious outrage that New York State "wants to call someone an acupuncturist after some classes and a test."
The state Department of Education has changed the requirements for licensing acupuncturists and those who already have their licenses are angry. 
Among other things, acupucturists will no longer need 10 years of experience to qualify for a license.
The easing of the rules has prompted petition drives, letter writing campaigns and a rally in New York City, at which nearly 100 acupuncturists and their patients carried placards warning "Save Us From Quacks."
The acupuncturists describe their battle to reverse the new rules as a defense of their patients' health and their professional pride.
"This is not a 5 cents, 10 cents profession," Dr. Chen said during an interview in her Upper West Side office, where a closet is crammed with Tupperware filled with seaweed, lily flower, chrysanthemum and red peony that she blends to create medicinal teas.
She said that the current regulations mean nearly all acupuncturists are also medical doctors and can recognize serious underlying diseases, like diabetes or cancer, which require more modern treatment. 
The new regulations, she said, would grant licenses to acupuncturists who do not have the training to make those judgments.
"This is medicine not folk craft," said Dr. Chen, who also has an M.D. degree. 
"I'm worried that patients will get hurt."
The state officials who developed the new regulations, however, say other states with similar rules have not seen the problems Dr. Chen predicts. 
The real fear of practicing acupuncturists, state officials say, is not the loss of respect or quality but the loss of income.
Acupuncture has become popular in recent years, riding the wave of patient interest in "natural" medicine. 
This new popularity means new business and, state officials say, those who already have their licenses are reluctant to share.
"It's not uncommon for people who've been through a strict licensing process to feel territorial," said Ronnie Hausheer, acting executive secretary to the State Board for Acupuncture. 
"But there is enough business for everyone."
Until last year, when the rules were officially changed, New York State had the toughest licensing requirements of the 20 states that license acupuncturists. 
The original law, passed in 1974, required acupuncturists to be trained in both Western and Oriental medicine and already have a license outside of New York. 
In addition, acupuncturists had to prove that they had actually practiced acupuncture elsewhere for at least 10 years.
Â 
'Standards Were Hard'
"The standards were hard but they should be," said Dr. David P. J. Hung, who trained in China and Japan and was the first acupuncturist to be licensed in New York. 
"Some Westerners think this is just stick the needle in and take it out. 
That is wrong."
In the years since Dr. Hung received his license, acupuncture has become increasingly accepted. 
It has been recognized by the American Medical Association. 
Many hospitals, including several public hospitals in New York City, have acupuncture clinics. 
It is used to ease the side effects of chemotherapy, to bolster the immune system of AIDS patients and to stem the cravings of smokers and drug abusers.
"Before, when patients came to me, they came in secret," said Dr. He-Hon Lao, who came to the United States in 1985 after practicing acupuncture in China for 20 years. 
"Even a few years ago they were afraid to tell their medical doctor. 
They were afraid their doctor would say, 'That's silly, don't do it.'
Now their doctors send them here."
In some circles, acupuncture has become downright chic in this age of holistic and natural medicine. 
"My massage therapist recommended it," said Joanne Rubin, a 37-year-old advertising consultant who is seeing Dr. Chen for digestive problems. 
"I recommend it to all my friends."
Ms. Rubin, who first had acupuncture eight years ago has her own personal measure of how much more accepted the practice has become. 
"My mother doesn't think it's weird anymore," she said.
This new acceptance of acupuncture means new business for acupuncturists. 
After Dr. Chen received her New York license in 1982, she said had about 80 patients a month, working five days a week. 
She now treats 150 patients a month and works only three days a week. 
Next month she will open a second clinic in Tarrytown, N.Y. 
She charges $80 for her initial consultation and $50 for each subsequent visit.
Dr. Hung has three separate clinics, one in Manhattan, one in Queens and one outside of Rochester. 
Most of his patients are Westerners, he said. 
He estimates that he sees from 20 to 30 patients a day.
Dr. Lao, too, sees mostly Western patients at a rate of 150 a month. 
She opened her first office in Brooklyn last January. 
Three months later she opened a second office on the Upper East Side of Manhattan.
While the acupuncture business has grown in recent years, the number of acupuncturists has remained fairly constant. 
Since 1974, 218 acupuncturists have been licensed in New York. 
At the moment only 140 are practicing, Ms. Hausheer said.
The plan to change the licensing requirements was at first supported by those who already had their licenses.
"We worked to get the new rules passed," said Charles P. Wang, an adviser to the American Acupuncture Association. 
"We agree that the 10 years' experience requirement is too long."
But the response of the board was not what the acupuncturists had expected. 
Rather than reducing the experience requirement, the board eliminated it altogether. 
Under the new rules a candidate for a New York State acupuncture license must complete at least two years of college, a three-year training program, and pass an examination.
The test, which is scheduled to be given for the first time in New York in March, was developed by the National Commission for the Certification of Acupuncturists and is used in 18 of the 20 states in which acupuncturists are licensed. 
Most New York acupuncturists, however, do not feel the exam is tough enough.
"Any one can pass this," Dr. Hung said. 
"If you study three months, four months, you can pass that test. 
People won't trust acupuncture anymore."
Because the test is "too easy" Dr. Hung said, "thousands of people will get a license."
"Three thousand, maybe four thousand," Dr. Hung said.
Ms. Hausheer disagreed. 
"There's a lot of fear that patients will be hurt and that thousands of people will apply for licenses but those fears are not substantiated by what's happening in other states that do it this way," she said.
Other states, she said, have not seen an increase in complaints against newly licensed acupuncturists.
Her office, she said, has "heard from maybe 100 people who will be applying for licensure and it's far from clear that all of those will qualify."
Ms. Hausheer says it is a safe guess that the new rules will encourage more Western-trained acupuncturists to apply for licenses, and that, she says, is the cause of much of the disapproval from the veteran acupuncturists.
Of the 140 acupunctursists currently registered in New York, 74 percent are Chinese, 11 percent are Korean, 7 percent are American, 2 percent are Japanese and 6 percent are of other nationalities.
Many of those trained in China admit they are concerned about the skills of those trained elsewhere.
"Acupuncture came from China," Dr. Chen said. 
"The root comes from China. 
It's Oriental medical practice. 
You can't just turn it around and upside down and say this is American acupuncture."

text:

President Bush today strongly defended his decision to send two senior aides to Beijing last weekend, rejecting criticism that he has forgiven Chinese leaders for the killing of democracy demonstrators there in June.
Mr. Bush's comments came as lawmakers and independent experts on China stepped up their condemnations of the surprise high-level visit as proof of the Bush Administration's willingness to sacrifice democracy and human rights in return for the normalization of relations with China.
The Senate majority leader, George J. Mitchell, condemned the American overture as ''embarrassing kowtowing to the Chinese Government.''
He added, ''These actions make a mockery of our profession of concern for human rights and our inconsistent with our stated ideals.''
The Democratic Senator from Maine also said that he will lead efforts to override Mr. Bush's Nov. 
30 veto of legislation to permit any Chinese student fearful of reprisal at home to remain in the United States beyond his visa's expiration.
Â 
Assurances on Missiles
It was the first high-level American visit to Beijing since President Bush banned such contacts after the military crackdown.
In defending his decision to send his national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, and Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger to the Chinese capital, Mr. Bush said that Mr. Scowcroft won assurances from the Chinese that they would not sell missiles in the Middle East, and praised an announcement in the Chinese press to that effect as ''a very sound development.''
What Mr. Bush did not say was that there was no urgency on this issue since the missile, the M-9, is still under development, or that he had received the same assurances during a trip to China last February.
Mr. Bush, a former United States envoy to China who had previously said that Beijing must make the first move to improve relations, acknowledged to a group of editors that China has not apologized for the crackdown. 
But, he said, ''I don't want to see that China remains totally isolated.''
Mr. Bush said that relations with Beijing remain strained, but added, ''I don't want to make it any worse.''
The President also noted that the United States deals with a number of countries which violate human rights, suggesting that China should not be the exception. 
''We have contact with countries that have egregious records on human rights, so I am going to keep looking for ways to find common ground,'' he said.
Â 
Need to Brief Beijing Is Cited
Mr. Bush argued that the visit did not constitute a normalization of relations with China and criticized those who said so as people who ''simply do not know what they are talking about.''
He said that he planned no further sanctions against Beijing for its campaign of repression, which did not end with the crackdown on student demonstators last June but continues with executions and arrests of workers and students who participated in the democracy demonstrations.
Mr. Bush sought to justify the visit as a way to brief Chinese leaders on the results of the Malta summit talks. 
But the high-level nature of the briefing struck China experts as rather unusual. 
China was briefed on a higher level than some of the closest allies of the United States, including Australia and South Korea.
The President's remarks came amid criticism that the visit illustrates a continuing double standard in the Administration's approach to human rights.
''We don't expect the Chinese to be democratic and we don't hold them to the same standards that we hold the Soviets or the East Europeans,'' said Merle Goldman, professor of Chinese history at Boston University.
Representative Stephen J. Solarz, Democrat of Brooklyn and chairman of the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific, said: ''We have to ask ourselves what our reaction would be if Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev were to unleash ther Red Army on demonstrators in Red Square. 
In such circumstances the President would hardly send his national security adviser to Moscow.''
Â 
Rejects Charges on Killing
Although Administration officials had discussed ways to brief the Chinese for some time, Mr. Bush made his final decision only last Thursday, cutting short a visit to Washington last week by James Lilley, the United States Ambassador to Beijing, senior Adminsitration officials said. 
The delegation was dispatched in secrecy to Beijing on Friday.
In other remarks, Mr. Bush denied charges that agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation had mistreated a potential witness to the killing in El Sal vador of six Jesuit priests. 
He said that he had investigated claims by Salvadoran Archbishop Arturo Rivera y Damas that American officials had tried to brainwash the witness, Lucia Barrera de Cerna, a Salvadoran housekeeper, to discourage the investigation of the crime.
''I have confidence that our attorney general would not permit the kind of inquisition process that was alluded to,'' Mr. Bush said. 
Mr. Bush also said he hoped to attend a February drug summit meeting with South American leaders in Cartagena, Colombia, despite security agency fears he could be a target of the drug cartels.

file: Project Helps China Modernize Eye Surgery.txt
text:
ï»¿
Project Orbis, a program that uses an airplane equipped as a teaching hospital to train eye surgeons in developing countries, has reached an agreement with China to establish a permanent relationship.
The pact, signed earlier this week by the Minister of Public Health and the executive director of Project Orbis, would send at least three ground-based surgical and nursing training groups a year to locations in China.
Next year Project Orbis plans to start 5- to 10-day training sessions away from the plane in Beijing, Shanghai and Chengdu. 
It already has held surgical programs on planes in each of the three cities since Orbis first visited China in 1982.
Project Orbis is financed primarily by the United States. 
Typically, a team of doctors conducts demonstration surgery on a patient in a DC-8 jet, where it has an operating room and a small viewing room. 
Closed-circuit cameras allow a larger audience of local doctors to watch the surgery in the airport where the plane is parked.
China is eager to improve its techniques of eye surgery to help some of its seven million blind people. 
Oliver Foot, executive director of Orbis, said that when the plane last visited China in 1985, only 10 percent of the eye surgeons used microscopes to perform operations but that the proportion rose to 80 percent this year.
''They read all the journals and soak up as much information as they can,'' he said. 
''During the surgery, there is absolute silence. 
Then afterwards there are continuous questions.''
Most of the training focuses on routine operations like cataract extraction, retina surgery and corneal transplants. 
But equipment and surgical instruments are scarce, except in major cities, and tradition discourages the donation of eye parts for transplant. 
As a result, the project has performed transplants in China with corneas supplied from North America.
So far, the project has focused on the major cities, but China hopes that under the new agreement the sessions will move to more rural areas.
For their part, Orbis doctors in China have learned about eye diseases that they have not encountered elsewhere, such as ocular leprosy, and they have picked up nuances in technique. 
In 1982, for example, Orbis doctors discovered that Chinese doctors were using a silica bead that soaked up a cataract as the bead was rolled across the eye. 
It is an inexpensive method and was later used by Orbis in other developing countries.
Orbis spends about $400,000 on programs in China from its annual budget of $6 million.

file: Prominent Dissident Is Freed by Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities have released Wang Ruowang, a prominent writer and dissident, after 16 months of detention, but he remains subject to some restrictions, his wife says.
Mr. Wang's wife, Feng Suying, said in a telephone interview from her home in Shanghai that Mr. Wang could not come to the phone because he needed rest, and that in any case he was probably not permitted to speak to foreign journalists. 
But she confirmed that Mr. Wang had suddenly been released from a detention center on Monday, without any explanation from the authorities.
A prolific essayist and widely respected social critic, Mr. Wang is 72 years old and yet has retained the admiration of much younger intellectuals throughout the country. 
His influence and reputation seemed to gain when he was criticized and expelled from the Communist Party at the beginning of 1987, along with Fang Lizhi, the astrophysicist, and Liu Binyan, the journalist.
China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, personally ordered Mr. Wang's expulsion from the party. 
In a speech on Dec. 
30, 1986, which was later leaked to foreign reporters, Mr. Deng declared: "Wang Ruowang is indeed wayward. 
I said he should be expelled long ago. 
Why has this not been done?"
Â 
Accused by Beijing
Mr. Wang supported the 1989 democracy movement, but there is no evidence he was a leader of it. 
Nevertheless, the leadership in Beijing accused him of helping to inspire and spread the protests in Shanghai, where he was living, and accused him of being "a representative of bourgeois liberalization."
"Beijing Turmoil," a Government-sponsored book published this year, accuses Mr. Wang of taking part in street demonstrations, giving interviews to foreign reporters and wearing a sign reading: "Save the country, save the people, save the students."
After the crackdown on June 4, 1989, Mr. Wang was kept under house arrest at first, and in September 1989 he was formally detained in a prison that was nominally called a detention center. 
Ms. Feng said he had not been beaten or otherwise mistreated while under detention.
"They were rather humanitarian toward him," she said. 
"He's fattened up a bit, but he's not fit and he doesn't have any strength. 
When he writes, his hand shakes. 
His eyesight has deteriorated, and it's difficult for himto climb the stairs. 
If he exercises, he'll get better."
Â 
To Report Twice a Month
Ms. Feng said Mr. Wang would spent his time at home "studying" and would have to report twice a month to the authorities on his "ideological state."
He must receive approval to leave Shanghai, and it probably would be impossible for him to travel abroad, she said.
It is not clear why the authorities suddenly released Mr. Wang, without making any announcement. 
Ms. Feng said the authorities had given no reason for the release, but she suggested that her husband might have acknowledged making some errors -- which could give the Government an excuse to release him. 
The Shanghai Foreign Affairs Office and the Shanghai Public Security Department both declined to comment.
Ms. Feng said that there was no news on whether other dissidents would also be released soon. 
Shanghai's Mayor, Zhu Rongji, has said that only two other dissidents remain in prison in that city: Zhang Weiguo, a journalist, and another whom he did not identify. 
In addition, there may be hundreds of others who were sentenced to prison in Shanghai for taking part in violent protests after the crackdown, and whom the Government does not regard as political prisoners.
Throughout the country, hundreds or thousands of Chinese remain in prison or in detention centers for their involvement in protests and riots at the time of the crackdown. 
In addition, some political prisoners are still serving sentences from the Democracy Wall movement a decade ago.

The authorities today detained a prominent dissident who was released from prison in January and whose treatment had previously been an issue in Chinese-American relations.
The official New China News Agency said the dissident, Yang Wei, a 33-year-old biologist, was detained in Shanghai for conducting ''demagogical propaganda for counterrevolutionary ends.''
Mr. Yang earned a master's degree from the University of Arizona and planned to return there to earn a doctorate, when he was arrested in January 1987 for his involvement in student demonstrations in the winter of 1986-87.
The United States Congress approved an amendment to an appropriations bill in December 1987 calling for Mr. Yang's release and saying he had broken no American or Chinese laws.
Mr. Yang served a two-year prison sentence, but after he was released in January 1989 he remained deprived of his ''political rights'' for another year, meaning that he could not leave China.
''Yang didn't show any penitence and continued to provide information for the reactionary organization,'' the press agency said today, referring to the New York-based Chinese Alliance for Democracy, with which Mr. Yang has had some links.
It is not clear what penalty Mr. Yang might face. 
But he might be expected to face an unusually stringent sentence because he would be regarded as a repeat offender.
