text:
ï»¿
TO ALL APPEARANCES A LADY
By Marilyn Bowering.
336 pp. 
New York: Viking. 
$18.95.
Those who think of Canada as a staid and proper place will have their misconceptions swept away by Marilyn Bowering's historical novel of the bad old days in Vancouver, British Columbia. 
Back then, vigilantes and smugglers, restless sea captains and idealistic reformers, Chinese gangsters and opium traders made the city as colorful and violent a community of misfits as could be found anywhere.
Ms. Bowering tells two linking tales: one of a modern half-Chinese bachelor seeking to discover his parents' true identities, the other of his mother's and father's adventures during the late-19th-century period of colonial expansion in the Far East and British Columbia. 
In 1957, Robert Lam sets off on a sea voyage with a briefcase full of just-discovered family documents. 
He is leaving behind, he thinks, his 100-year-old stepmother, who has just died and left him free to travel. 
But Lam Fan, the irascible old lady, appears on board as a ghost. 
She is determined to lead him - by guile if necessary - to understand the hard life his family once lived as immigrants to Western Canada, and to be proud of both his Chinese and British ancestors.
India Thackery, Robert's English mother, and Lam Fan, her Chinese adoptive sister, came to Vancouver from Hong Kong at the turn of the century, following a stormy voyage on a clipper ship via Kowloon and Saigon. 
Robert's father emigrated from China, driven by memories of mass famine and cannibalism. 
His mother's husband, Robert Haack, washed up in Canada from California.
All these people were in various ways sustained and undone by the opium trade that flourished quasi-legally in pioneer North America. 
Miss Thackery, a kind, idealistic Victorian lady, was quietly employed as a bookkeeper in an opium factory; Lam Fan was a lifelong addict of the factory's wares; and the hapless Robert Haack was a would-be opium smuggler who made enemies both among the Chinese who controlled the business and the white vigilantes who sought to exclude the prosperous immigrants.
Haack is the novel's most fully developed character, a drifter capable of both courage and cowardice, decency and hypocrisy, sentimentality and cold-bloodedness. 
His chance meeting with Robert Louis Stevenson and his love for the tender India Thackery inspire him to try bettering himself, but the impulsive ways he tries to gain respectability often land him in jail or worse. 
India Thackery, too, is appealing, as ingenuous and thoughtful as her young Chinese half sister is sly and impulsive. 
When the thieves who rob the opium factory maroon India on an island of quarantined Chinese lepers, she reacts to her predicament with great resourcefulness and charity.
Is this story beginning to sound melodramatic?
Well, it is, but that's all right. 
The 19th-century part of the novel is a tale of the times, featuring improbable plot twists and a cast of broadly drawn characters reminiscent of the fiction of Charles Dickens or Mark Twain. 
As fanciful as the story is, it provides a vivid picture of life in frontier Vancouver, which, like London slums or Mississippi River towns, could be as brutal as it was hospitable to newcomers.
Ms. Browering, an accomplished Canadian poet, has researched her material thoroughly and reports it with an eye to evocative details. 
When India and Robert go in search of a child prostitute India is intent on rescuing, they visit the makeshift lodging of some out-of-work settlers - ''a group of men sitting on an ice-covered floor around a small pile of leaves, which one man was attempting to blow alight. 
Another man was being shaved by a companion, and another lay on straw, smoking a pipe. 
They nodded politely to [a visitor] but had eyes for the food in his hands. 
In a corner, a man wrapped in rags and newspapers tried to hide the rat he'd been skinning with his fingers.''
The modern scenes, which take up about a quarter of the novel, are less successful. 
For one thing, they are overresearched; we learn a lot more about navigating the waterways of British Columbia than necessary. 
Also, neither Robert Lam nor Lam Fan develop well as characters in these sections. 
Robert has but one note to sing, that of a confused truth-seeker. 
Lam Fan is not a very interesting ghost; her one note is shrill and pedantic. 
Both characters seem willed into place as plot devices to give the book a complicated structure that it doesn't need.
Rather than holding the novel together, they constantly interrupt its flow. 
Juxtaposing stories from different centuries with their contrasting world views doesn't work. 
The technique almost forces the reader to skip over the present-day adventures of Robert and his ghostly stepmother in order to find out what will happen next in the much more compelling tale they are unfolding about their ancestors.
Marilyn Bowering does have a fascinating story to tell. 
If only she had told it more simply!
Still, ''To All Appearances a Lady,'' though not a completely satisfying novel, is ambitious and often enjoyable.
Â 
'DIRTY, DIRTY ROBERT!'
I sat on the broken steps and looked out into the darkened world I had known since childhood: the ghosting apple trees, the tilted greenhouses, and surmounting all the dark face of Christmas Hill. 
In this International Geophysical Year, in which nations had joined harmoniously together to observe the marvels of the earth, atmosphere, and space, in which boys in their twenties handled millions of dollars' worth of rocketry, I, Robert Louis Lam, three years from retirement, had quarrelled with a one-hundred-year-old woman over my future.
I sighed and thought about the Rose and what it would be like to set sail in her and never come back. 
And as I did, an icy hand gripped my shoulder and a voice shrill with anger cried out, ''Dirty Robert Lam!
Dirty, dirty Robert!''
I turned at that to see Fan standing there in her nightgown, holding a knot of papers in her shaking hand. 
. . .
I stood up and put my arms around her. 
Her head touched my chest, her arms felt like small dry sticks. 
She tried to say more, but her mouth was dry, and I could smell on her breath the sour fume of opium.
From ''To All Appearances a Lady.''

file: Q&A.txt
text:
ï»¿
Jumping Chinese
Q. If all the people in China were to jump up and down all at once, would it affect the Earth's orbit?
A. The Earth's orbit would be unaffected, though a simultaneous hop by the 1,133,687,501 people reported to live in China on July 1, 1990, would release approximately as much energy as the magnitude-4 earthquake in Westchester County, N.Y., six years ago, according to calculations by the seismologists at the Lamont-Doherty Geological Observatory of Columbia University.
Using just a round billion people weighing an average of 50 kilograms jumping one meter in the air, they came up with an energy release of 1018 ergs, or 1 followed by 18 zeros, said Nano Seeber, one of the seismologists. 
An erg is the force required to move one gram by one centimeter.
Even a jump by the whole population of the world, about five billion people, would not alter the Earth's orbit, Mr. Seeber said. 
The only things that would do so would be the loss of a large piece of the Earth or the impact of a large outside agent, he said. 
The hop's action and reaction would cancel each other.
Â 
Eliminating Alcohol
Q. How long after a person stops drinking does it take for all alcohol to be removed from the body?
A. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism of the National Institutes of Health estimates that alcohol is cleared at a rate of approximately 100 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per hour, or about half an ounce of pure alcohol every two hours, so that if a person ingested approximately three drinks in a half-hour period, it would take about six hours for that alcohol to leave the body.
Dr. T. K. Li, an alcoholism researcher at the Indiana University School of Medicine, emphasized that the speed could vary widely, as much as threefold, because of the range of individual variation in factors like body weight and blood alcohol levels.
Readers are invited to submit questions about science to Questions, Science Times, The New York Times, 229 West 43d Street, New York, N.Y.

file: Quiet Tibetan Influx_Devout, Exiled but Kept Out by U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
Pema Tsering's escape from Tibet began 30 years ago with a nighttime trek through the Himalayan mountains and ended three weeks ago on an Alitalia jet to Kennedy International Airport. 
With hot buttered tea and steamed beef dumplings, New York's entire Tibetan community turned out to help him celebrate, fitting comfortably into a small East Side restaurant.
For the 500 Tibetans in the United States, Mr. Tsering's arrival was a very big deal, the beginning of a wave of Tibetan migration to the United States that will ultimately quadruple their minuscule but passionate exile community. 
It was made possible when Congress authorized 1,000 special visas for Tibetans.
Although Tibetans have been fleeing the Chinese occupation of their homeland for 40 years, the United States has never granted them refugee status. 
Like tens of thousands of other Tibetans in India and Nepal, Mr. Tsering, who is 42 years old, lived for decades in a refugee settlement, stuck in an odd sort of limbo with no country to call his own.
Tibetans register only a blip in the great human drama of international migration, but immigration experts say their story highlights just how political, and how arbitrary, the refugee policy of the United States really is.
Â 
Working With Dalai Lama
The resettlement of the 1,000 Tibetans, scheduled to arrive over the next 3 years, also represents an unusual effort, organized and financed not by a government but by a national network of volunteers -- a small subculture of Tibetans and friends of Tibet working with the Dalai Lama's exile administration in Dharamsala, India.
"I personally see the resettlement project as a fantastic gift from America to Tibetans, which has been very late in coming," said Losang Gyatso, president of the Tibet Association in New York. 
Mr. Gyatso is a senior vice president at Lintas New York, an advertising agency, where he works as a creative director on the Diet Coke account.
Early this month, gazing upward at "enchanting skyscrapers," Mr. Tsering stood on a Manhattan street corner in the Murray Hill neighborhood that could be called Little, or Tiny, Tibet. 
It was far from the jungly Tibetan village where he was born, far from the mountainous Nepalese terrain where he labored on road gangs as a boy and far from the refugee camp in India where, until last month, he worked at a Tibetan school.
As the ever-present sirens of New York wailed, he spoke with calm about his childhood vision of the United States, taking a metaphorical step beyond the typical immigrant's dream of streets paved with gold.
"When I was little, in my village, we believed that America had made a spiral staircase from the Earth reaching to the moon," Mr. Tsering said. 
"And each stair was extremely wide, planted with a wild field of crops. 
And beyond each stair there was another, waiting to be developed."
It was a plain, linoleum-covered staircase that Mr. Tsering climbed that first night to the new apartment in Murray Hill he was to share with Tashi Dorjee, the second of 18 Tibetans to arrive in cities across the country last month. 
The apartment is still largely unadorned, but Mr. Tsering and Mr. Dorjee have constructed a colorful altar to the Dalai Lama, whom Tibetans call His Holiness, on a mud-brown bureau from the Salvation Army.
New York City's Little Tibet, where the new immigrants live, is so petite as to be mostly invisible to others in that part of Manhattan -- the 30's between First and Third Avenues. 
Besides the apartments of individual Tibetans, it consists of two restaurants and a brownstone, which houses the Office of Tibet, Tibet House and a bookstore. 
A sign on the brownstone door typifies the mellow Tibetan style: "While opening the doors, please be gentle with the door handles."
The 120 New York-area Tibetans, the biggest Tibetan community in the United States, are scattered from Murray Hill through Long Island, New Jersey and Connecticut. 
They get together several times a year, particularly for Tibetan National Day on March 10, when they demonstrate for Tibetan independence at the United Nations, and for the Dalai Lama's birthday on July 6, when they retreat to the mountains for an extended picnic, draping their leader's portrait with multicolored scarves.
Â 
Immigrants and Advocates
Unlike other immigrants they are not linked by churchgoing; their practice of Tibetan Buddhism tends to be a very private affair. 
But they are fiercely cohesive in their politics, and they see the new arrivals, first and foremost, as colleagues in advocacy for a free Tibet. 
That is also how the new immigrants see themselves. 
"Our mission here is not to get rich -- well, who doesn't want to get rich?
-- but to speak up and enlighten the American people about the Tibetan situation," Mr. Tsering said.
The Tibetans have been displaced for decades by Chinese rule, which, they say, has resulted in a million dead, 120,000 in settlement camps, and a population in Tibet itself outnumbered by the Chinese, 6 million to 7.5 million. 
But the United States, unlike India, Nepal, Canada and Switzerland, does not allow Tibetans into this country as refugees.
Technically, this is because they are coming through another country -- Nepal or India -- willing to grant them residency. 
Politically, it is because the United States Government has been unwilling to offend the Chinese by acknowledging that Tibetans could have a "well-founded fear of persecution," as refugees must under Federal law. 
China claims historical sovereignty over Tibet predating its military occupation of that country in 1950 and the Tibetan uprising, bloody and failed, in 1959.
Mr. Tsering's group of Tibetans is being allowed into the country not as refugees but as "qualified displaced Tibetans" under a special provision, sponsored by United States Representative Barney Frank, Democrat of Massachusetts, in the 1990 Immigration Act.
Â 
Fans, Gurus and Mormons
"It didn't make any difference to us what they were called, as long as they were provided haven," Mr. Frank said in a recent interview. 
He described their special status as "semantic" politics by the State Department intended to keep China happy.
The Tibetan U.S. 
Resettlement Project, based in New York City, is working to establish 19 "clusters" of Tibetans across the country, in cities including Minneapolis, San Francisco, Salt Lake City, Ithaca, N.Y., Portland, Ore., and Amherst, Mass. 
The project brings together an unusual assortment of volunteers, from Tibetan political enthusiasts to New Age gurus to Mormons.
Some volunteers spoke of the project with political fervor, like the national project coordinator, Tenzin Taklaj, a 26-year-old Tibetan-American in New York. 
"It is up to us here in exile to preserve our culture because it's being destroyed in Tibet right now," he said. 
"The more we are, the stronger we will be."
And others sounded idealistic on a more cosmic level, like a volunteer, Jed Miller in Amherst, Mass., a chiropractor who said he uses Buddhist meditation to reduce his patients' stress. 
He referred to the value of the new immigrants' "highly developed inner technology."
The volunteer network was constructed over the last few years, as the organizers of the project persuaded members of Congress to support their effort. 
Since two earlier intiatives had failed to earn the Tibetans refugee status, the organizers -- Tenzin Tethong, now a minister in the exile Government of the Dalai Lama, and Edward J. Bednar, an American friend of Tibet since discovering the Tibetan Book of the Dead after "a near-death experience" -- decided to go another route. 
They promised to bring Tibetans in at no cost to the U.S. government, which spent about $7,000 a person to resettle Indochinese refugees.
Congress agreed to grant the Tibetans something every immigrant wants: an instant "green card," allowing permanent residence in the United States, and full work authorization. 
The 500 Tibetans already living in this country arrived separately, on student visas or after marrying an American. 
The new immigrants, when joined by their families, will quadruple, at least, the Tibetan-American population.
"The Tibetans' situation has always been a clear illustration of the connection between immigration and foreign policy," said David Reimers, a New York University history professor and immigration expert. 
"But it also shows how immigration policy is made up of a whole series of weird things. 
Someone gets the ear of someone in Congress and these flukes happen, like instant legalization for 100 Burmese students, or, in this case, 1,000 Tibetans."
The State Department authorized the Tibetan Central Administration of the Dalai Lama to choose the immigrants from 47 refugee settlements in India and Nepal. 
Half will be poor refugees, including those who recently left Tibet; the other half will be more educated and considered likely to succeed in the United States.
Â 
'Big Smiles, Open Faces'
Across the country, the Tibetans are sponsored by families with whom they live. 
Volunteers find them jobs before they even arrive in the United States. 
The Minneapolis coordinator, Tara Dadak, an American whose husband is a former Tibetan Buddhist monk, said, "Tibetans come at you with big smiles, open faces and an ultra-American work ethic very pleasing to employers."
After they adapt to life in America, which other Tibetans say won't take long, the new arrivals will face something familiar to all Tibetan-Americans: They will be considered exotics.
"A lot of people project onto Tibetans their own fantasies about Tibet," said Mr. Gyatso. "Older Americans, in particular, who have known Tibet through National Geographic and 'Lost Horizon,' see Tibet as a very special place, like a crack in space or something. 
Which is terrific, in a way. 
But the negative side is that they don't want to confront the reality that the paradise has been shattered. 
They'd rather remember the Shangri-La."

file: REFORM MOVEMENT GROWS IN MONGOLIA.txt
text:
ï»¿
The revolutionary changes in Eastern Europe appear to have swept eastward into Asia, with the Communist leadership in the remote nation of Mongolia preparing for a meeting on Monday that may lead to the ouster of its Politburo.
Wedged between the Soviet Union and China, Mongolia has only two million inhabitants, about half of them herdsmen who roam the nation's vast grasslands. 
It has long been under Soviet domination, but in the last three months an increasingly vocal democracy movement has pressed for more independence from Moscow and for the replacement of many top officials.
Responding to ever larger demonstrations and to hunger strikes by dissidents in the central square of the capital, Ulan Bator, President Zhambyn Batmonh announced on television Friday night that the Communist Party Central Committee would meet on Monday and consider the replacement of the entire Politburo.
Mr. Batmonh indicated that the Central Committee would move up the date of a party congress, which would elect a new leadership and institute policy changes. 
The President also said that leaders might call at the meeting on Monday for a national referendum to measure public confidence in the People's Great Hural, a rubber-stamp legislature.
Â 
Prospects for Change Unclear
A diplomat in Ulan Bator, reached by telephone from Beijing, said it was unclear whether changes in the Politburo would come as early as Monday or be delayed until the party congress. 
Nor is it clear whether the entire Politburo will be replaced or if some members, like President Batmonh, will remain on the new committee.
The diplomat said that Ulan Bator was quiet today, and that the hunger strike had ended Friday night after Mr. Batmonh's speech. 
A general strike proclaimed by the democracy movement also appeared to have been called off, the envoy said.
The democracy movement in Mongolia may have influence beyond its borders, in the Chinese region known as Inner Mongolia. 
The three million ethnic Mongolians living on the Chinese side of the border are said to be aware of the protests in Mongolia, and the authorities in Beijing appear to be nervous that unrest might spread. 
Prime Minister Li Peng already has called for vigilance against separatists among China's ethnic minorities.
A front-page article last month in China's official People's Daily praised officials in Inner Mongolia for spreading socialist ideology, and Beijing announced in January that it would boost investment in Inner Mongolia to create an industrial base.
Â 
Movement Born in December
Mongolia's democracy movement began in December with a few demonstrations of only a few thousand protesters, but it has gained momentum with its demands for greater political change, more prosperity and more assertions of Mongolian nationalism. 
The leadership has reacted with some criticism but primarily with accommodation, even giving live television coverage to a convention last month that brought the birth of Mongolia's first opposition party.
Prime Minister Dumaagiyn Sodnom said last month that he did not rule out the possibility of a multiparty system in Mongolia. 
But it is not clear to what extent the leadership as a whole is willing to give up power. 
Tserendashiyn Namsray, a Politburo member, was quoted on Radio Ulan Bator last month as saying there were differences of opinion within the Politburo on these subjects.
The second-oldest Communist regime in the world, behind the Soviet Union, Mongolia is unlikely to duplicate the changes in Eastern Europe, according to diplomats in Ulan Bator. 
They say that the bitterness in Mongolia is not as deep as it was in Romania or Poland. 
And while Mongolians are resentful of Soviet domination, the diplomats say, they also are wary that they might be vulnerable to pressure from China if they entirely leave Moscow's orbit.

file: Reporter_s Notebook_ Turmoil in China_Seeing Shadows Where Once There Were Leaders, Facts and Inform.txt
text:
ï»¿
Writing about China's leadership these days must be a bit like covering the afterlife: Even if one is convinced it exists, confirming the details can be tough.
Indeed, covering China's leaders may well overlap with writing about the nether world, for there is some dispute about which world Deng Xiaoping now resides in. 
Mr. Deng, the country's senior leader, is variously said to be dead, dying or in even closer control of China than he has been in years.
In the last few weeks reporting about China has turned upside down, just as interest is exploding in what is going on in China. 
It used to be that there were leaders, and facts, and sources; now there are only shadows.
Take the simple question of who is in control in China. 
It should be easy to figure out who a country's leaders are; now, it is a puzzle. 
Aside from Prime Minister Li Peng, who appeared on television today and before that on May 25, no top leader has been seen in nearly three weeks.
The Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, almost certainly has been stripped of his power, and Prime Minister Li at least has the influence to get on television and to get some of his hard-line policies adopted. 
But does that really mean that his position is secure, or just that he has control over the television station?
Is Mr. Deng, assuming he is still alive, simply using Mr. Li as an instrument or does the Prime Minister have an independent power base?
Is President Yang Shangkun staging a coup against the Government, or is he working with other officials to reassert hardliner control?
Most Western diplomats and Chinese officials can make educated guesses to answer these questions, and journalists inevitably have to address the questions. 
But always there is uncertainty, because sources in China are increasingly fallible. 
Some journalists and diplomats have better sources than others, but probably none is regularly briefed by a Politburo member.
Instead, sources tend to come from a range of people: children of high officials, those who work for high officials and diplomats. 
The party is very careful about letting documents out of its possession, so most information comes not from leaked documents but simply from what people remember from meetings or from documents they have read previously. 
Confirming information is extremely difficult or impossible.
Â 
Witnessing Clashes
Covering the reports of skirmishes between military units has been particularly difficult, because probably no reporter has personally witnessed any of the reported clashes. 
Instead, reporters have relied on accounts from Chinese witnesses and from foreign diplomats, but almost inevitably there is uncertainty in the stories.
What was known was that army forces took up defensive positions with tanks, in a manner not normally associated with defense against civilians. 
In addition, artillery shells could be heard in the distance and occasional bursts of machine gun firing. 
Sometimes soldiers reported that they had been engaged in minor clashes with other troops, although they were usually vague on details.
Convoys of troops could be seen rushing around main roads, but it was often impossible to identify them. 
License plates of trucks are a clue -V11 plates mean that a military truck is from the northeastern city of Shenyang, for example - but it was then difficult or impossible to distinguish a group of Shenyang soldiers from the 39th Army from the Shenyang soldiers in the 40th Army.
Keeping track of soldiers was doubly difficult because they tended to shoot in all directions from their convoys, and they had a particular distaste for binoculars. 
Following along behind a convoy, in a car or on a bicycle, was impossible. 
Thus it became crucial to have a network of friends around the city who could report the latest troop movements.
Writing about the reports of skirmishes reflects a judgment that the accounts appear correct, and that they signify underlying tensions in the military that could be very significant. 
Many Chinese and foreigners have indeed feared that a civil war is a possibility, and that is consistent with the evidence. 
On the other hand, it is plausible that the skirmishes are many fewer than have been reported, and were not so serious as initially believed. 
Perhaps they were mostly bluffing, and attempts to scare and deter other armies instead of to attack them directly.
Â 
Friendships at Risk
Confirming information has been particularly difficult lately because sources are drying up in a time of political retrenchment. 
Many journalists an diplomats had friends and sources in the Zhao camp, and they have suddenly found themselves without information, or else too afraid of arrest to want to see any foreigners.
And even when Chinese friends are willing to maintain friendships with foreigners, there are agonizing questions about whether it is right to put them to risk. 
Thus the tendency has been to call on them much less, or not at all, for fear of inadvertently sending them to prison.
There are similar worries about quoting people by name. 
Most Western journalists like to use the names of ordinary people they quote: it adds a ring of authenticity, even when it is unpronouncable. 
It used to be that most Chinese never wanted to give more than their surname, even when they made the most inoccuous remark. 
Then, in the last few months, more and more seemed to find the courage to allow their full names to be printed in criticizing Beijing.
A few took an intermediate approach: they agreed to use their surname and initials, because that would make it more difficult to determine their Chinese characters and find them.
Now, since the expectations of a crackdown in the last few weeks, the mood has changed and nobody is willing to have their names used.
''Are you kidding?'' one young worker responded when he was asked if a reporter could use his name. 
''It's easy for you to get on a flight out of here. 
I'll be in jail for years.''
Â 
Getting Around Town
Even getting around the capital to find out what is happening has been difficult, for reasons of safety and transportation. 
Earlier this week, citizens erected barricades at many intersections, so that driving cars around Beijing became a nightmare. 
The result was that bicycles again became fashionable, and foreign correspondents rushed around town on bicylces.
However, bullets have become a major reason to stay away from some areas. 
On the first day of the shooting, many reporters were near the front lines, and two - one Japanese, one French - were shot and wounded. 
Since then, and especially after all the reporters visited the hospitals and wrote second-day stories about those who had been less lucky than themselves, many journalists have been more prudent.
Photographers have been particularly hard-pressed, because the soldiers have made it clear that they do not want their pictures taken. 
Some of the Chinese who were killed were shot because they were trying to take photos of the carnage.
Journalists have had to deal with the added problem that they are not really supposed to engage in journalism these days. 
Special martial law regulations ban coverage of what either the democracy movement or the troops are doing, and so there is no way to explain away one's presence as simply that of a journalist.
As a result, foreign correspondents have suddenly proven scarce in the capital, but a large group of foreigners has suddenly appeared who roam around the capital and pass themselves off as tourists. 
Their claims are belied by their notebooks and questions that few tourists would pose: ''So are the soldiers there from the 38th Army, and are they ready to fight with the 27th Army?''
Most ordinary residents seem fiercely supportive of foreign journalists, as well as curious about how foreign newspapers are covering the events in China. 
Workers or housewives sometimes guide journalists away from trouble, and everyone delights in the opportunity not to speak Chinese but to practice execrable English.
They push a journalist toward the most gruesome scenes, to drum into him what they regard as the Government's brutality. 
If there is a bloodstain from the attack earlier this week on civilians, the local residents will virtually drag a reporter to inspect it.
''Tell the world about it,'' a young worker said today as he pointed toward a trickle of blood on the ground from an old man who was shot by mistake near Tiananmen Square. 
''Make sure the world knows what is happening here.''

file: Reporter_s Notebook_Deng to Retire in the U.S., And Other Chinese Rumors.txt
text:
ï»¿
Of all the rumors that have swept Beijing in the last week, perhaps the most astonishing was that in a nefarious attempt to kill demonstrators the Chinese Government had electrified the metal grates over the city's subways.
Students carefully walked around the grates for a day or two, until they saw that others were walking over them with impunity. 
Then the rumored danger was that the army planned to drop paratroopers into Tiananmen Square to deal with the students, and demonstrators carefully searched the skies for this new threat from above.
Â 
Deng Is the Topic
Perhaps it is inevitable that with the newspapers and television stations carefully avoiding the real events, people should rely on rumors. 
In any case, some of the rumors are so unfavorable to the Government -but repeated with such absolute conviction - that the authorities may be worse off with the rumor mill than with an independent press.
''Did you hear?'' a businessman asked the other day. 
''Deng Xiaoping is going to retire in the United States. 
He's got a lot of money there.''
One of today's rumors was a generational variation: it said American bank accounts of Mr. Deng's eldest son, Deng Pufang, had been frozen by American banking officials.
Â 
A Germ of Truth
Some of the rumors begin accurately, but get better each time they are handed on. 
One rumor started out that Mr. Deng, China's senior leader, had declared that it was worthwhile to bring out 150,000 troops in the capital if that would bring China 20 years of stabilityI. 
That may or may not have been true, but at least it was plausible. 
Unfortunately for Mr. Deng, a somewhat embellished version was the one that stuck.
It quoted Mr. Deng as saying that to achieve 20 years of stabilityI, it was worth killing 200,000 students.
Â 
The Birth of a Rumor
It is easy to see how rumors start in Beijing. 
This conversation took place Sunday night on the street:
A middle-aged Beijing woman speaks to a young man in civilian clothes who had a military haircut.
WOMAN: Are you a soldier?
MAN: Yes, I am.
WOMAN, astonished: Where did you come from?
MAN: Xian.
WOMAN, shouting to the crowd: The troops have come!
The soldiers are already here!
They are from Xian!
A large crowd gathered around, and the woman asked the man triumphantly: So how many of you are there?
MAN, looking puzzled: Just two of us. 
We wanted to come and see the capital.
Â 
A Measure of Success
Another conversation, overheard in the Western district on Sunday morning:
A young man, to a small crowd: ''The American President, Bush, has said that if the Government can't implement martial law within 24 hours, then it isn't effective.''
(The attribution was inaccurate.) Another young man: ''Yes, I've heard that too. 
And I believe that 24 hours is the accepted international standard. 
People always say that if martial law isn't implemented within 24 hours, then it can't take effect.''
Young man No. 1: ''Well, we should wait until 10 A.M. Then it will be 24 hours, and we will prove by international standards that martial law has failed.''
Â 
Awaiting the Troops
Throughout the capital, neighborhood residents have taken charge of local intersections. 
The people stay up all night, passing the time by exchanging increasingly implausible rumors about the imminent arrival and undoubted brutality of enormous numbers of troops.
Most of the corner-watchers are people who live nearby, but a few are sent by the central student organizing committee to make sure that all intersections are covered. 
The main strategy, if the troops come, is to block their path with people and obstructions like bicycles, bricks and anything else available. 
They also speak to the soldiers and try to convince them that they should not attack their fellow countrymen.
The students' latest concern is that the Government will use soldiers from remote areas because they speak different languages and may be unable to understand the students' pleas for retreat. 
So the student organizing committee now sends members of minority nationalities to all the major roads where it expects troops may arrive, so that they can function as translators and persuade soldiers to leave in any tongue.
''We can convince any group of soldiers not to attack us,'' Pa Hardin, a member of the Uighur minority, said the other day as he waited in front of the Beijing Train Station. 
He had been assigned to stand there in case Uighur soldiers emerged from the station to attack the students.
Another tactic has been adopted by the ''Kamikaze'' group of workers who roam around the capital all night looking for invading army convoys to halt. 
Many of the Kamikazes now carry knives, so they can puncture truck tires, and they often travel with their wives or girlfriends. 
The idea is that the woman will distract the soldiers while the man slashes the tires.
Â 
What's Good for Leaders
In some ways the students imitate the nation's leaders.
Before the Communist victory in China in 1949, Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai were famous for their accessibility and common touch.
When they conquered Beijing, they moved into the walled Zhongnanhai compound in the center of the capital, but for the first few years, ordinary Chinese could still stroll around the leaders' compound. 
As time passed, not only were ordinary Chinese barred, but a complex system of passes was devised so that permission was required to go from one part of the compound to another.
The students on Tiananmen Square have adopted a similar system. 
The outside of the square is cordoned off by students, supposedly to protect those who are resting inside. 
Then there are several inner circles, each cordoned off by student guards who demand a pass to go through. 
To see the student organization's top leaders, a visitor must be escorted through four different checkpoints and present identification at each.
''We need to have a good system of discipline and organization,'' a student leader explained this evening. 
''Otherwise the Government will say we encourage chaos.''

file: Reporter_s Notebook_Spies Learn Students Can Be Stern Teachers.txt
text:
ï»¿
A young secret policeman, or perhaps he was just an innocent student, held a banner the wrong way during today's demonstration.
Other students noticed he was holding the banner strangely, with one hand on the pole and the other cupped on the bottom. 
They decided he must be a police spy and pounced on him.
While he claimed to be from Anhui Province in central China, he had no student identification. 
These days students know that their ID cards mean free train rides, cut-rate soda and other benefits, so they always carry the cards with them.
The students took the suspect to a tent at their headquarters in Tiananmen Square for interrogation.
''What will you do with him?'' an onlooker asked. 
''We will release him after we put him through some education,'' came the reply.
Â 
The Tactics of Their Elders
The students have not only taken control of the streets during demonstrations, but have also picked up a few survival tactics from their Communist Party elders. 
They keep a careful eye out for provocateurs who might discredit the movement, and have no compunction about temporarily detaining the suspects.
The students, of course, do not have prisons at their disposal, but they try their hand at the ''re-education'' that is a central part of the Chinese prison experience.
Students are aware that secret agents are always milling around and listening in on conversations, even at the universities. 
It is not unusual for a stranger with a tape recorder to walk up to two people engaged in conversation and stick a microphone in front of the speaker.
Normally the intruders are only curious students, but the possibility they may be spies tends to put a damper on the conversation as well as on the student movement. 
The practice explains why the students are becoming experts in counterespionage.
Â 
Long-Distance Calls
Some of the banners carried in today's demonstration in Beijing suggested that the protesters had made a particular effort to reach sympathizers overseas.
Students wrote their banners in several foreign languages, not only to show their sophistication but also in the hope they would be seen in film clips shown by foreign television networks.
One banner read, ''Of the people, by the people, for the people.''
Chinese posters have always homed in on the people factor - ''people power'' and ''The People's Liberation Army shouldn't be used against the people'' are common slogans - but the reference to Lincoln's Gettysburg address was clearly meant for an American audience.
For the French, another poster read, ''Le 1789 de la Chine,'' referring to the hope that this year will be the Chinese equivalent of the French revolution of 1789.
And for Chinese all over the world, many of the banners were written in ''complex'' characters that normally are not used within China but are common in Hong Kong, Taiwan and American Chinatowns. 
After the Communist revolution, China simplified its writing system to improve literacy, and the simplified characters now used cannot always be understood by overseas Chinese.
Â 
Martial Notes
Just as the protesters in the United States in the 1960's incorporated music in their demonstrations, so have the Chinese. 
Throughout the protests they have sung the revolutionary Internationale as well as the Chinese national anthem. 
The latest rage is a mocking song incorporating the names of the Prime Minister, the senior leader and the President to the tune of ''Frere Jacques'':
Down with Li Peng, down with Li Peng Down with Xiaoping, down with Xiaoping There is another scoundrel, there is another scoundrel, Yang Shangkun, Yang Shangkun.
Many protesters have displayed portraits of Zhou Enlai, the former Prime Minister who died in 1976. 
That a pro-democracy movement should worship a leader of the China of Mao Zedong, in which where there was no democracy at all, may seem strange, but today Mr. Zhou symbolizes not Maoism but honesty in government and care for the will of the people. 
Mr. Zhou lived a simple life and is believed to have interceded to curtail the excesses of Mao.
Â 
A Slight to the Leaders
The posters of Mr. Zhou seem intended to slight China's current leaders by hinting that no one today is nearly as good as he was. 
The other innuendo is aimed directly at Prime Minister Li Peng, who was looked after in childhood by Mr. Zhou.
The idea is that they are entirely different kinds of leaders.
''Zhou came out to talk to students,'' said a recent graduate student. 
''He was wise and had good manners. 
Li Peng does not come out much to talk with students and he is not wise and has no manners.''
The anger against the Prime Minister has taken various forms. 
In today's demonstration, students held up pictures of Mr. Li with swastikas painted on them.

file: Reporter_s Notebook_Tourist in China_ Akihito Does a Political Tiptoe.txt
text:
ï»¿
China is a big country to survey in six days, even if you are an emperor, travel on a personal Boeing 747 with an army of fretting chamberlains and speed to the Great Wall with thousands of Chinese paramilitary police lining both sides of the road for 50 miles.
But the challenge is even greater for Emperor Akihito of Japan, because every stop on his itinerary must serve an unstated agenda: to set aside China's fear that Asia's other great superpower still harbors the sense of cultural superiority, one that led it a generation ago to try to conquer the Middle Kingdom.
So on the first visit a Japanese emperor has ever paid to China, Akihito's handlers have taken care that every moment resound with deep cultural significance, preferably one that will remind China of the arduous days centuries ago when Japanese envoys came here to learn at the feet of China's masters.
So today, while his hosts pondered the roles that the likes of Toyota and Sony might play as Chinese-style Communism begins to look more like Japanese-style capitalism, the Emperor had something else in mind: the Tang Dynasty.
Spending the day inside the giant walls of Xian, the eastern end of the Silk Road, the 58-year-old Emperor sought out some of his roots. 
He visited the Shaanxi Provincial Museum to see the stone tablets where scholars and Chinese emperors had first etched the pictographic symbol for the word pronounced in Japanese as "heisei," or achieving peace. 
Three years ago, hours after the death of Akihito's father, Hirohito, "Heisei" was chosen as the name for the new imperial era.
The Emperor spent a considerable time at the tablets (there are more than a thousand, bearing everything from Confucian classics to a cure for stomachache), asking detailed questions about the calligraphy.
"It is all very interesting," a Chinese official traveling with the Emperor said as he stood outside the building. 
"So tell me, do you think this visit will increase Japanese investment in China?"
The museum is not the only place where the Emperor has driven home the connections between two countries that, on the surface at least, seem among the most dissimilar in Asia. 
An accomplished student of certain types of fish, the Emperor visited the Chinese Academy of Science and talked about how his eighth-century ancestor, Emperor Shomu, used medicines from China. 
He has quoted from famous Chinese poets whose work he studied as a child.
So enamored was the Emperor of finding proof of the centuries of exchanges between the two countries that he skipped the one attraction virtually everyone else comes to Xian to see: The giant terra-cotta army, uncovered in the mid-1970's, whose thousands of soldiers and horses guard the burial mound of a Chinese emperor.
"It is something popular among the Americans and Europeans, I think," Hideo Kagami, the Emperor's spokesman on the tour, said Sunday. 
"I believe His Majesty has a stronger interest in stone tablets."
Â 
He Who Would Have Been
For most of the Emperor's trip, his schedulers have taken care to glide past sites that millions of Chinese remember with bitterness, places like the Marco Polo Bridge, where Japan staged an incident that prompted its full-scale invasion of China in 1937. 
But there was one moment, out of sight of most of his hosts, when there was a brief reunion with a figure from Japan's colonial control of parts of China.
It came on Sunday, just before the Emperor and his wife, Empress Michiko, left Beijing. 
At a reception by the Japanese Ambassador to China, Akihito was approached by a slight, elderly man in a tailored Mao suit. 
He was Pu Jie, the younger brother of Pu Yi, the "last emperor" of China and the central figure in the epic film by that name.
Pu Yi became a willing ally of the Japanese, who installed him as emperor of their puppet state, Manchukuo, in 1935. 
Pu Jie was trained to be the next emperor, sent to Japanese schools and married to a member of the Japanese aristocracy. 
But he never got to the throne: Japan was defeated and the Chinese sent Pu Jie for "re-education."
Today he is a member of the National People's Congress and a frequent visitor to Tokyo to promote bilateral relations.
Pu Jie left no doubt that he has a warm spot in his heart for Japan's royals. 
Asked what he told Akihito, Pu Jie did not hesitate: "I said today is one of the happiest days for the Chinese people."
Â 
The Non-Best Seller
Perhaps so, but many Chinese seemed a little confused about whose motorcade was blasting past bicyclists and farmers in their fields. 
And the Japanese seem to have a way to go before they change their image among the Chinese people, most of whom know Japan only as a one-time invader.
Biographies of the Emperor, on sale at major bookstores around Beijing, were not exactly leaping off the counters. 
The stores seem to have sold a few more than 2,000 copies, or one for every 500,000 Chinese.
Â 
No Sex Please, We're Royal
Pity the Japanese reporters who cover the Emperor every day!
First, by strictly enforced tradition, Japanese emperors never say much. 
Second, unlike the British royals, the people who surround the Chrysanthemum Throne do not seem given to sex scandals and failed marriages.
The biggest story at the palace these days is whether the Crown Prince, the heir to the throne, will succeed in his seemingly endless search for a bride. 
But the Japanese press cannot write about it: They agreed earlier this year to stop writing about the search because the speculation was driving away many potential candidates.
It is hardly surprising that Japanese reporters analyze every word for a glimpse at the Emperor's life. 
So a round of wondering began when, in the Forbidden City, the Emperor was taken to the bedroom of his former Chinese counterparts. 
Akihito, getting right to the heart of the matter, asked whether Chinese emperors and empresses had separate bedrooms. 
(It seems they did.)
This was quickly flashed back to Tokyo, raising the obvious question about the sleeping arrangements in the Imperial Palace. 
The Emperor did not say, and the Japanese reporters, polite to their core, did not ask.
Â 
Lost, Maybe, in Translation
The other utterance still under debate is how exactly what the Emperor said when he placed the blame on Japan for attacking China.
According to the English translation provided by the Japanese Foreign Ministry, he said: "In the long history of relationships between our two countries, there was an unfortunate period in which my country inflicted great suffering on the people of China. 
I deeply deplore this."
But in Japanese the comments seem far less judgmental. 
Though the words he used could be stretched to mean "deplore," a more literal translation would be, "About this, I feel deep sadness."
Japanese is a vague language, and it gets vaguer when the war comes up, but there was considerable suspicion that the Tokyo Government might have deliberately used phrases that could be spun differently in different countries.
Japanese officials deny this: "We did the best translation we could," a senior Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
Â 
My Wall's Bigger Than Yours
The Emperor was whisked past some of the most obvious evidence of Japanese influence in China (a new Matsushita electronics plant in Beijing, the Red Lips Karaoke Bar) to see the Great Wall. 
His guide was Chen Xitong, the Mayor of Beijing, and as they walked a considerable distance the Emperor remarked again and again on how large and impenetrable the wall seemed.
Mr. Chen shrugged it off.
"In time of emergency it was useless," he said, recalling invaders who sidestepped it. 
Then, reciting a lesson that the Emperor of a mere 120 million Japanese hardly needed, he added, "The real great wall is the people."

file: Restaurants.txt
text:
ï»¿
When you tire of mashed potatoes and roast chicken, which should be any second now, a trip to Hong Kong may be just what your blanded-out taste buds require.
Fortunately, since Hong Kong restaurants have come to New York City, you won't have far to go. 
Triple Eight Palace, tucked away on the second floor of an all-Chinese shopping mall, is just under the Manhattan Bridge between Market and Forsythe Streets in Chinatown. 
And parking is right around the corner.
A vast Hong Kong food palace, slightly frayed around the edges, it has all the splendor of a Las Vegas casino: the glitter of gold embroidery on Chinese red fabric, twinkling neon lights, the sparkle of crystal chandeliers.
Triple Eight caters to the Chinese community: there were never more than two other Westerners there on any of our three visits. 
Toddlers arrive in strollers, infants in carriages along with their pre-adolescent siblings, parents and grandparents. 
Whatever the reason, we were the beneficiaries of the last remaining bastion of that wonderful old custom:that children should be seen and not heard.
If you would also like to take in a Chinese wedding celebration, Sunday evening is recommended. 
Along with our dinner one night, we were happy observers at the festivities of a beautiful young bride in a glittering red dress and a handsome, even younger-looking bridegroom. 
Their musical selections were ecumenical: Chinese words to Western music; country-and-western music in English, and Chinese music with Chinese words.
Perhaps because so few Westerners come here, not all of the staff is fluent in English. 
But all seem eager to warn you about the pricey dishes.
Patron: "Do you have bird's nest soup?"
Waiter: "Yes. 
Very expensive."

text:

The way for peasants to get rich, Wang Hongjun used to think, was to raise more livestock and plant more grain and potatoes.
Then Mr. Wang, who heads a rural county in Sichuan Province, was sent three years ago to the State Training Center for Cadres from Poor Areas.
In the six-week course in Bejing and other parts of eastern China, Mr. Wang learned that in some parts of the country peasants had tripled their incomes by beginning small businesses, and he concluded that the road to wealth laynot in more farming but in running sideline businesses.
Upon his return to his county, Mr. Wang persuaded peasants to set up a silk-making cooperative. 
Instead of selling silkworm cocoons to Shanghai factories, they would process the silk right there. 
The factory has prospered, and Mr. Wang and other Sichuan Province officials describe it as an enormous money-maker for the county.
The Training Center is proud of the factory, and of other innovations that have resulted from its seminars. 
The center is part of a broad anti-poverty campaign in China that has shown considerable success in eliminating theproblems that afflict large numbers of people in other parts of the third world: malnutrition, epidemic disease and abysmal health care.
These days almost all Chinese have food to eat and roofs over their heads, so increasingly the trend in anti-poverty work is in spreading education and information rather than arranging income transfers.
"The Government used to try to spend money primarily on relief efforts," said Liu Yitao, deputy director of the training center. 
"If there wasn't enough grain in an area, then the Government would send grain. 
But these days the effort is mainly to help peoplehelp themselves."
Such efforts at education and assistance are aimed at the 110 million people, nearly 10 percent of the population, who are classified as poor because they earn less than $62 a year. 
Such people will not starve to death, but their lives are bleak: they live in mud huts or caves, eat meat only on festivals, and have trouble paying the fees to keep their children in school.
While China has been quite successful in alleviating the most dire forms of poverty, it has had little success in stimulating local markets and equalizing the opportunities among various parts of the country. 
While all China benefited immensely during the last dozen years of the open-door policy, the richer coastal areas gained the most. 
The gap between rich and poor areas has grown considerably in that period.Funds are limited, as is the effect the Training Center alone can have on the lives of the vast numbers of poor people. 
But since the center's founding in 1987, some 17,000 local workers have taken part in its programs.
Typically they spend about 45 days, partly in seminars in Beijing and partly touring parts of coastal China that have turned to agribusiness to help their economies.
Many of the officials in poor areas are peasants, and the tour of more prosperous regions comes as a revelation to them.
In particular, the program aims to show them how their villages can start rural enterprises -- everything from making shoes and buckets to processing tofu and sausage -- as a way to supplement the income from traditional agricultural products.

file: Salaxi Journal_For Chinese, an Ancient Scourge Loses Its Terror.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Du Dayi found out that he had leprosy, the short, soft-spoken peasant was as worried about his neighbors as about the disease. 
In those days, more than four decades ago, Chinese villagers sometimes burned leprosy patients alive in an attempt to destroy a disease that they loathed like none other.
"People were afraid of us then and looked down at us," said Mr. Du, who has lost an eye as well as his nose to the disease, the latter affliction apparently distorting his speech. 
"But now it's no problem, and I can go around easily. 
I can even go to the bank!"
A hundred-odd villagers clustered around Mr. Du as he spoke and seemed a testimony to a monumental change in attitudes toward leprosy. 
The peasants in this remote village in south-central China were unconcerned about touching him and were staring wonderingly not at his severely disfigured face but at something they found even more astonishing: the face of an American interviewer.
Leprosy, which for thousands of years has been a scourge mainly of regions with warm climates, still afflicts some 4 million to 10 million people around the world, and hundreds of thousands of new cases are reported each year. 
But the number of victims around the world appears to have declined by more than half over the last decade, and in China and many other countries the progress has been enormous -- in fighting the disease and the fear that surrounds it.
"The struggle is being won; there's no doubt about that," said James A. Gittings, an officer of American Leprosy Missions, which fights leprosy in China and other countries. 
A multidrug treatment regime that became widely used in the 1980's has played a key role in the decline of leprosy, and doctors hope to conquer the disease by the year 2000 so that it is only a relatively minor problem in the third world.
Â 
An Energetic Campaign
In poor parts of China like this one, political issues like freedom of expression seem to many peasants remote and hazy compared with concerns of health and poverty, for villagers are far more likely to have seen a leprosy patient than to have seen a dissident. 
Responding to such concerns, the Chinese Government is campaigning energetically against leprosy and appears to be enjoying great success, for this is the kind of activity that the Communist Government does best.
If it sometimes outrages the West by mobilizing people against dissidents, it is also impressive in its ability to mobilize people against disease and other common threats. 
The authorities force doctors to work in remote areas, and while this may offend Western ideals of freedom it is nonetheless helpful in fighting a disease like leprosy.
"What they've managed to achieve is to reduce leprosy to a level where it's not really a public health problem any more, not a major contagious disease," said Dr. B. P. Kean, the representative in China of the World Health Organization. 
"They've done extremely well, especially in recent years."
China claims to have only 30,000 reported cases of patients now undergoing treatment, down from about 100,000 a decade ago. 
Four decades ago, it says, there were 500,000, although all the figures in China and elsewhere are uncertain and not particularly reliable. 
There are often variations in methods of counting and in estimating the number of people who carry the disease but whose condition has not yet been diagnosed.
The rural-based attack on leprosy is evident here among the rock-littered hills of Guizhou Province, one of the poorest in the country. 
Doctors hike from village to village, explaining the symptoms of leprosy and looking for patients. 
Most victims are now caught in the early stages and are treated, free of charge, before they are disfigured.
"The biggest problem we face is that leprosy victims don't go to the doctor soon enough," said Liu Fangmin, the deputy director of the Salaxi Leprosy Hospital here. 
"We tell them that the faster they come to us, the easier it is to cure. 
But the biggest headache is still finding the leprosy patients."
To overcome this problem, the medical authorities have begun to provide cash incentives, and consequently the easiest way to make a bundle of money in this poor area is simply to turn in a person with leprosy. 
The local government will pay the equivalent of $20 to anybody who reports such a person. 
Sufferers can even turn themselves in and claim the money, or doctors can turn in their patients.
The reward amounts to half a year's income for many peasants, and those who supply names are guaranteed secrecy -- because some villagers might resent it if they discover that a neighbor has fingered them.
Leprosy is an infectious disease that causes changes in skin color and deadens the sensation in various parts of the body. 
Because they do not feel pain, patients often injure themselves and as a consequence in later stages sometimes lose their fingers.
Despite an ancient misconception, leprosy is not easily spread and most healthy people seem to have a natural resistance to it. 
In any case, these days drugs can cure the disease in a period ranging from a few months to many years.
"When they are first diagnosed, the patients are afraid and feel they've been robbed of their dignity," said Wang Yongjuan, the health director for Bijie Prefecture, a poor region that encompasses Salaxi village. 
"But we tell them that they can be cured quietly, that we won't tell anyone about it. 
And they get their self-confidence back."

file: Salem_s Seafaring Legacy.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the early-morning mist comes in from the harbor in Salem, Mass., the most pleasant place to be is on the Common. 
This wide expanse of green is both a cultural and physical hub of the coastal town north of Boston, and the odd geometry of its criss-crossing paths is a product of habit and time. 
Today, morning joggers may have replaced the pasturing cows and military parades of former times, but still there is a feeling in this setting, surrounded by fine Federal houses, of the orderliness and peace that gave this Essex County town its name (from the Hebrew word shalom, meaning peace).
With a population of 38,000, Salem is still a thriving everyday sort of place, which is part of its charm. 
And although its historic center is intact - from Chestnut Street to the Common - there is nothing now in the bustle of its waterfront streets to indicate anywhere near the density of commerce along its wharves and warehouses that made Salem in 1800 the richest city per capita in America.
It is thrilling to think of those merchant captains setting out from the small New England town to ports all over the world and bringing back not just cargoes of tea, spices and textiles but a whiff of the exotic that made every home in Salem a cosmopolitan place. 
''From father to son, for above a hundred years, they followed the sea,'' wrote the Salem native Nathaniel Hawthorne in his vivid introduction to ''The Scarlet Letter,'' entitled ''The Custom House.''
What made these merchant captains unusual was the additional mandate - be collectors - passed on to them by their professional association, the East India Marine Society, founded in 1799. 
No present-day auction house aficionado can hold a candle as a collector to the enthusiasm of a Salem sea captain who with untutored eye would find on those far-flung shores of China, Japan, India, Africa and the Philippines curiosities of both the natural and artificial world, which became the basis of the oldest continually operated museum in the country, the Peabody Museum of Salem. 
And because, in most cases, they were the first Westerners to sail into certain ports, what they collected was the real thing - a first-contact item - unadulterated by market expectations that developed later.
Although these items may have represented only 5 percent of the cargo, they are what survive in the showcases of the Peabody in displays that include rarities of the East, divided by country of origin - ivory boxes from India, porcelain cups in their original straw packing from China and packets of snuff from Zanzibar.
And for anyone fortunate enough to have just read ''Moby Dick,'' the maritime history division is a veritable gold mine of whaling memorabilia, including the actual art works depicting whales described by Herman Melville and scale models of harpooning paraphernalia and the try-works, or furnaces, used to melt down the blubber.
Situated on Essex Street, the Peabody's original structure is an 1825 quasicommercial building in the late Federal style, with a high granite gable pierced by a round window framed by radiating keystones set over seven high arched windows. 
It has been added to several times over the years, most recently in 1988, by a sleek, skylighted wing with a handsome interior floating circular staircase; there are 30 galleries.
Allied to the main collections of ethnology, natural history and maritime history is the newest division on Asian Export Art, a result of a 1984 merger with a collection at the Museum of the American China Trade in Milton, Mass. 
Headed by Dr. H. A. Crosby Forbes, whose great-grandfather Capt. Robert Bennet Forbes made 10 trips to Canton in the 19th century, these collections of ceramics, furniture, silver, paintings, textiles and metalware, made over a period of five centuries for the foreign market, fulfill the museum's purpose, which is to be a place to study the fine arts as cultural history.
In the contemporary wing, with views into an Oriental garden featuring Yingde rocks from the rivers of Hangzhou, Boston's sister city, are reflections of the classic lines of the museum's 1825 East India Marine Hall. 
Most of the exhibits - from China, Japan and India -can be appreciated for their color and form, but there is always a point to be made by the arrangement. 
Porcelains, divided by type - including blue and white, rose palette and white wares - showed the evolution of the Oriental style and European copies. 
One of the surprises of the furniture exhibit is to discover that the American ball and claw motif may be an old Chinese form, a reflection of the dragon's paw grasping the pearl of wisdom in the Ming dynasty. 
And even more than the paintings of foreign ports, the photographs of cities like Shanghai make the merchantile world come vibrantly alive.
A continued commitment to contemporary crafts from Asia, including one exquisite 1987 Khmer wedding costume, gives the museum a renewed link with Asia and the recent influx of Asian immigrants. 
But still it is those proud ship figureheads that line the walls of the East India Marine Hall that recall the great thrust into the unknown.
Not that anyone was the poorer for it. 
As the ships unloaded at Derby Wharf, the merchant princes of Salem, including Elias Hasket Derby, the new country's first millionaire, began to live in a style that raised building crafts to a level of perfection during one of the finest periods in American architecture. 
Today visitors can explore a historic area roughly 6 blocks by 10 blocks, encompassing a 17th- and 18th-century waterfront area as well as a grander 19th-century residential district. 
The main practitioner of this elegant Federal style was Samuel McIntire, whose houses of red brick with white-columed porticos still line the streets of Salem.
Walking down Chestnut Street on a spring afternoon, with side views into blossoming gardens, one is struck by the fact that this elegant neighborhood is still a place where people live and children play rather than simply a restored district of the kind that loses its character at the price of preserving its architecture. 
The townspeople deserve credit for having kept these handsome homes in shape without the benefit of profitable international commerce - the last ship sailed from Salem in 1880. 
For the rest, Salem is a typical American town, with small neighborhoods and public parks weaving in and out of the historic areas. 
And in the downtown shopping district, whose turn-of-the century buildings are also undergoing restoration, many new buildings blend with the old.
One of the grandest of the 20 or so historic properties open to the public is McIntire's Gardner-Pingree House (1804), recently reopened after a re-restoration conducted according to the latest technologies and under the guidance of the Essex Institute and its chief curator, Dean Lahikainen. 
The results give a sense of how the house would have originally been furnished - more open and spare and in brighter colors than was believed during an earlier restoration, which took a more romantic view. 
The three-story brick house, divided horizontally by two marble bands and crested by a balustrade, has an elliptical portico with delicate Corinthian columns. 
A master woodcarver, McIntire employed a signature form that consisted of a carved basket of fruit and flowers, a prosperity motif that adorns both fireplace surrounds and furniture.
By using period inventories and paint analysis, the restorers have come up with solutions that include a palette of seagreen, terra cotta and light blue, and floor coverings of Brussels carpet and a Turkey-pattern painted floor cloth. 
Rather than purchase substitute antiques for chairs and settees still known to be in family hands, they commissioned Allan T. Breed, a Maine cabinetmaker, to make reproductions from the originals. 
Although this is a controversial approach, the goal of restoring the rooms' integrity has been achieved.
In the garden, also newly restored by Lucinda Brockway, a 1790's plan from the Derby family has been followed; it called for ''an airy irregularity'' and a row of tall poplar trees behind a summer house at the foot of the garden. 
A Derby garden pavilion, which has been moved there, is a veritable dictionary of classical architectural forms. 
Painted a stone color, it is shuttered, swagged and festooned, and the roof balustrade is topped by urns with flame finials. 
In addition to myrtle, forget-me-nots and creeping thyme, there is a pear tree in the garden that is an offshoot of a 1629 pear tree in nearby Danvers.
In the Essex Institute next door, one can see versions of period rooms designed earlier in this century by the curator, George Francis Dow, when, to quote the label, they ''saw the Colonial period as an era of simplicity and virtue.''
In contrast to the Peabody, the Essex is a temple to local culture and crafts, including a stageful of chairs showing the evolution of certain decorative motifs. 
Elsewhere on the grounds and on nearby streets are other restored houses from the 17th to the 19th centuries, administered by the institute.
Closer to the old wharves is the world that Nathaniel Hawthorne, the son of a sea captain, knew. 
So vivid were his fictional accounts of old Salem that one senses in those pasts another present. 
The recently refurbished 1819 Custom House on Derby Street, where Hawthorne worked as surveyor of the port between 1846 and 1849, is still as he described it: ''Ornamented with a portico of half a dozen wooden pillars, supporting a balcony'' and ''an enormous specimen of the American Eagle with outspread wings, a shield before his breast.''
His own little office, overlooking the harbor, with a stool and high desk spread with ledgers and a fanlight window, is remarkably like his own description of it except that the newly painted mustard-colored walls are no longer ''cobwebbed, and dingy with old paint.''
Seeing the Custom House in functioning order - a Customs officer worked there as recently as last December - is an argument for restoring other custom houses along the coast for maritime use, even if only for regulating pleasure craft.
Not far from the Custom House on Turner Street is the most famous literary house in America, the 17th-century House of the Seven Gables, a clapboard house stained a dark brown with high triangular walls bounded by the roof slopes that give the house its name. 
It overlooks the water in a nondescript neighborhood of mostly clapboard houses, some with two-story balconies, painted red, green, yellow, gray and brown.
Readers are never disappointed, for here is a case where the reality comes very close to the fictional image. 
This is because Hawthorne hewed closely to the house as he knew and loved it on his visits to his distinguished cousin, Susannah Ingersoll, whom he nicknamed the Dutchess. 
In May 1840, in a letter to a friend, Hawthorne wrote, ''The day after the great storm in March, I went with David Roberts to make a call on the Dutchess at the old house in Turner Street, to learn how she weathered the gale. 
I had a more than ordinary pleasant visit, and among other things, in speaking of the old house, she said it has had in the history of its changes and alterations Seven Gables. 
The expression was new and struck me very forcibly; I think I shall make something of it.''
The house has been furnished to the period of Hawthorne's visits, and whether completely accurate or not, the rooms, the secret staircase, the tea set and even the penny-candy and notions shop all convey something magical - a cozy darkness overlooking a gnarled horse chestnut tree and the sea. 
The garden, of a geometric Colonial-revival style, lacks the irregularity and intimacy of the one Hawthorne describes, but never mind, wisteria covers the arbor, and the scarlet runner pole beans climb the trellises to attract the hummingbirds that so delighted the fictional party. 
Standing at the water's edge, one realizes that though the neighborhoods on land may have changed over the centuries, the view over the sparkling water is the same as it was for the first ship that set out to sea.

A visitor to this city's North Beach neighborhood could easily assume that the traditionally Italian community and its recently arrived Chinese neighbors have settled into the most harmonious blending of cultures since Marco Polo helped turn the Orient's noodles into Italy's spaghetti.
Near Broadway, which once marked a boundary between North Beach and Chinatown, it is possible to buy pasta or dim sum, focaccia bread or fortune cookies. 
Strolling past first-floor apartments on the way to the boccie court near Washington Square, the tiny park at the community's center, passers-by can hear the clicking of mah-jongg tiles through open windows.
And in the early mornings in front of Saints Peter and Paul Catholic Church overlooking Washington Square, Chinese immigrants silently exercise in unison to the ancient discipline of tai chi.
But a closer inspection discloses jagged scars left by rapid demographic change.
White residents at a bus stop in North Beach complain that the recent rerouting of a bus line to ease congestion in Chinatown was done for the convenience of ''those people'' at the expense of ''us.''
Others make jokes about the way Chinese drive cars. 
And half a block from Washington Square, the wall of a health center serving Chinese-speaking clients was spray-painted on the Chinese New Year: ''Kill You All Soon.''
''There's a lot of tension, a lot of animosity,'' said Henry Der, the executive director of Chinese for Affirmative Action, a civil rights and research group. 
''No matter how liberal we may be here, people still derive great comfort from having people like themselves living in their neighborhoods.''
It has been more than 100 years since anti-Chinese hysteria erupted here and unemployed whites led attacks against Chinese laborers, brutalizing them and vandalizing their stores and laundries. 
Since then tensions have seldom been evident until the last decade, when successive waves of immigrants from Asia burst the boundaries of what had long been a rigidly circumscribed Chinatown.
By the time of the 1990 census, the population of San Francisco is expected to be one-third Asian, half of them of Chinese descent. 
The growth is partly a result of Hong Kong's capitalists moving and investing their wealth on the West Coast in anticipation of the reversion of Hong Kong to control by China's mainland Government at the end of the century.
As this population has expanded, Chinese have bought up commercial and residential property in North Beach, jumping the psychological border at Broadway and sometimes, as landlords, bringing with them high rents that forced out established businesses.
Cultural differences are also causing friction. 
Some longtime North Beach residents complain about laundry hanging from balconies and the bins of bok choy on the sidewalks. 
They shake their fists at each home newly painted in the colors that signify good luck to the Chinese, pink with blue or green trim. 
The Chinese, meanwhile, wonder how their neighbors, many of them descendents of Genoa fishermen, could have come to prefer their homes in white or pale gray.
''The Italians perceive they are being driven out by the Chinese,'' said Dr. Grace Pung Guthrie, director of a study of North Beach financed by the Ford Foundation. 
''But the Chinese have an interest in preserving the unique quality of the neighborhood too.''
Thus it is especially irksome to the new residents that the old-timers are reluctant to acknowledge their contributions to the neighborhood, like the award-winning rehabilitation by a Chinese nonprofit group of a dilapidated hotel into 65 units of low-cost housing.
There are tensions within the Chinese community as well; one of Dr. Guthrie's findings is that established Chinese-Americans report feeling hostile toward the newly arrived Chinese. 
''They hate the rudeness of these newcomers, the shoving on the bus, spitting in the street,'' Dr. Guthrie said.
There are signs in North Beach of attempts to work together. 
The neighborhood association recently elected its first Chinese-American president.
But answers are not always simple. 
For example, nearly all of the dozens of Chinese businesses in the area were left out of a recent Chamber of Commerce guide to North Beach shops and services. 
Marsha Garland, founder of the North Beach Chamber, said she tried to make sure the Chinese were included by hiring a young man of Chinese descent who could speak Cantonese to approach the owners about paying to be listed in the guide as other businesses had done.
''They thought he was part of an extortion racket and they were afraid to talk to him,'' Ms. Garland said.
In the meantime, Chinese immigrants are bearing the burden of the racist stereotyping that occurs behind their backs and angry verbal attacks directed at them on the streets.
''They are bowing, smiling, saying, 'Sorry, so sorry,' to deflect aggression from Caucasians,'' Dr. Guthrie said.
Mr. Der agrees. 
''They don't confront, but they don't forget,'' he said. 
''It widens the gap.''

text:
