file: Searching for America_s _Big Money_.txt
text:
ï»¿
The casino buses arrive every two hours from 9 A.M. until 11 P.M. at the Confucius Statue on the Bowery in Chinatown. 
Men and women in tattered coats and worn sneakers scurry out of bakeries and snack shops, jostling to get on the bus. 
After a week of hard work, they are off to risk their week's pay at the blackjack and baccarat tables of Atlantic City.
These natives of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia, who arrived in New York hoping to make the "big money" America had given their friends and relatives, live in communal apartments to save money. 
They work 12 hours a day, six days a week, in restaurants and sewing factories, making $300 to $450 a week.
For them a day in the casinos of Atlantic City is often the one release from their hardscrabble lives, a place where a week's salary can be won or lost in 15 minutes. 
Their sheer numbers and willingness to gamble make them valuable to the casinos. 
One expert, Paul Siu, estimates they might bring in as much as 10 percent of Atlantic City's $4 billion in annual revenue.
To make the casinos more appealing to the Chinese, two of the new games approved by the New Jersey State Legislature this year are Chinese -- Sic Bo, a dice game, and Pai Gow Poker -- said Stephen Richer, president of the Greater Atlantic City Convention and Visitors Bureau.
Although gambling dens are scattered throughout Chinatown, many Chinese still choose Atlantic City because they are afraid of tongs, loan-sharking and police raids, according to Mr. Siu, who is executive director of Far Eastern operations for Caesars World Marketing, a subsidiary of Caesars World Inc.
Â 
A National Obsession
Culturally and historically, gambling has played a large role in the lives of Chinese who have little education. 
It is popular in Hong Kong, Taiwan and other Southeast Asian countries with large Chinese populations. 
Indeed, a campaign in Shanghai by Communist Party officials earlier this year against mah-jongg that included mass self-criticisms by 4,300 party members, a bonfire of 400 mah-jongg sets and the unleashing of 5,000 "anti-gambling squads" failed to stamp out the national obsession with the game.
Chow Yin Kung, a cook and a weekly gambler, lives in a 10-by-14-foot room in a two-bedroom apartment in Flushing, Queens. 
Three mattresses take up most of the space. 
A 20-inch television set, two red milk crates, three black plastic shelves and a hot pot complete the furnishings. 
A photo album is full of pictures of his daughter and son, 21 and 20 years old, left behind in Malaysia. 
Mr. Chow says he misses them terribly: "When I have nothing to do, I think about them and go crazy."
On his day off, Mr. Chow gets up earlier than usual to go to Atlantic City, to the glittering chandeliers, sleek smoked-glass pillars with brass columns, pink plastic cranes and palm trees. 
The clanking of slot machines, the flashing of roulette signs and the shouting of bets make him forget his problems. 
"Isn't this nice?" he grinned as waitresses in low-cut minidresses and high heels strutted by.
Another gambler, Mr. Pan -- like most of those interviewed, he declined to give his first name, which is what would identify him in the Chinese community -- says he does not feel comfortable in his own home because he does not have much in common with his two sons, who grew up in America. 
"They prefer to hang out with their English-speaking friends and go to ball games," said Mr. Pan, who came to America in 1984 from Taiwan. 
"What else is there for me to do?"
Mr. Pan, a cargo hauler for an international airline, said he hides his gambling from his children. 
"My sons have no idea where I am now," he said on the bus ride home.
Â 
Secret Sojourns
Many of these gamblers ride to Atlantic City in secret. 
Compulsive gambling conflicts with moderation, order and family stabilityI, Confucian principles that helped shape Chinese society, according to experts like Lee Feigon, chairman of the department of East Asian culture and languages at Colby College in Waterville, Me., and the author of several books on China.
Mr. Chow said he had seen little outside Chinatown and Flushing, which has recently become home to many Chinese immigrants, since he arrived in the United States five years ago. 
"I'm scared to go anywhere," he said shyly. 
"I hear there is a park in the city that's really nice. 
But I feel awkward because I wouldn't understand what people say."
Mr. Chow said he does not have that problem in the casinos, where he is surrounded by other Asian gamblers and Chinese hosts and hostesses who often speak more than two dialects. 
"I feel at home there," he said.
But Mr. Chow seemed lost when he left the gambling floor. 
In Cafe Roma at Caesars, where he is entitled to a free meal, Mr. Chow pointed to the menu listings for creole gumbo and steak.
Until recently, when he made a point of memorizing a few dishes by their positions on the menu, Mr. Chow's orders were a game of suspense. 
He would point at random and wait for his surprise. 
Many times his main course turned out to be an ice cream sundae or a piece of cheesecake. 
"I hope they don't change the menu," he said with a grin.
Â 
Concentrating on Winning
Not everyone bothers with the free meals, though. 
They concentrate on one thing: winning money.
"When you eat their food, you feel like you owe them something," Mr. Pan said. 
"I don't want the casinos to think they have a hold on me."
Mr. Pan pocketed his $900 in winnings and headed for the bus stop.
Casinos offer special incentives to attract Asians. 
Hotels advertise special room rates in Chinese-language newspapers. 
Casinos often bring in famous entertainers from Asia. 
Buses to the casinos are often free after cash rebates and special coupons. 
Caesars charges $12 for a ticket ($10 at night), but gives each gambler $15 in cash in the casino and a $5 coupon good for the next trip.
After 14 hours of gambling with only one short tea break in which he devoured a roll in three bites, Tsoi Leung Choy, 46, and his 72-year-old father were still going strong in the baccarat pit at Bally's Park Place, fanning the cards and blowing away the bad luck with their mouths.
At Trump Plaza, C. S. Yeoh rubbed his chips on his pants and kissed them before betting on the Players.
At a blackjack table in Caesars, with a glass of milk by his side, Mr. Chow, who speaks little English, knew just what to say to his dealer. 
"More, more," he knocked on the blue felt table. 
"Big one!
Big one!" he screamed as the dealer threw him a card. 
"No more!" he waved his hand. 
"Thank you," he said, smiling as the dealer threw him some chips.
After winning $200 in less than 15 minutes, Mr. Chow called it quits. 
He knew that the casinos always win in the long run. 
"See this?" he pointed to a naked statue of David near the wall and then a topless Cleopatra perched from the ceiling. 
"They stayed in here for too long."
At the end of the day, Mr. Pan kept to himself on the bus, his brows furrowed despite his winnings. 
Luck will reverse for those who have no self-control. 
"Lose, I shall not cry," he said. 
"Win, I shall not rejoice."
"Greediness is the debacle and moderation the virtue," Mr. Chow said, referring to his 15-minute battle at the blackjack table. 
The winnings will go to New York Telephone to pay for the calls he made to his two children in Malaysia.
Mr. Tsoi worried over what to tell his wife. 
It took him all week sewing suits in a midtown garment factory to earn the $400 he lost. 
"She'll be upset," he muttered. 
"Very upset."
Mr. Yeoh complained of a severe headache after losing his whole month's salary, $2,000, during his 24-hour binge. 
He says he must find a way to pay his rent for the next month.
"Maybe," he said hopefully, "I'll win it all back next week."

file: Secretly, Dissident Workers In China Press Their Cause.txt
text:
ï»¿
Only when the sun goes down do they dare to congregate, and even then they speak in hushed voices as they discuss their plans to develop an underground movement for greater democracy.
Now there are no loudspeakers, printing presses or financial contributions, as there were in the flowering days of May. 
Only seven men remain of the hundreds of people who once were active in a workers' union that pressed for greater democracy.
They meet secretly, in considerable danger, and scribble their appeals for change on crackly, cheap pieces of paper and wait until twilight before they furtively paste up the messages on lampposts and signboards. 
They almost never say the name of their organization, the Workers' Autonomous Union, in public.
'Furious and Frustrated'
''You don't understand what it's like to live here in China,'' the union member said to a visitor. 
''Why do we keep pushing for democracy, even when we risk arrests?
We are furious and frustrated. 
The Communist Party and the Government is so corrupt, and yet it controls us all so completely. 
The officials skim off the country's money and there's hardly anything left for the workers.''
The group decided, after much discussion, to contact a foreign reporter to tell the world that their struggle for democracy was continuing, and to solicit assistance from foreigners, especially people on Taiwan.
So far the union's activities have been scarcely noticeable in Beijing, but if it is able to attract more participants and form a small underground organization, it could become a more significant embarrassment and nuisance for the Government. 
The union spokesman disclaimed any involvement in periodic attacks by snipers against the martial law soldiers who patrol the streets in Beijing. 
However, diplomats do not rule out the possibility of the formation of a sometimes-violent underground resistance to the authorities, and the union could become the core of such an organization.
Â 
Speaking Among Friends
''Do foreigners know what happened?'' the spokesman asked. 
Then, he abruptly proceeded to describe how he saw a young woman and two men killed just south of Tiananmen Square in the early hours of June 4, when the Chinese Army suppressed the democracy movement in Beijing.
''We are still continuing our fight for democracy,'' said the spokesman. 
''There is no democracy in China. 
We have so little choice in our lives here. 
The Government and the Party decide where we work, where we live, how many children we can have and when.''
They discuss democracy among their close friends, but not a word with fellow workers. 
The spokesman refused to divulge even the regularity of their gatherings, let alone the location.
Each of them has been writing essays on democracy and posting them in alleyways, residential lanes and occasionally on major streets throughout the city. 
At their meetings, they debate how to spread their message. 
At times they despair that their voice will not be heard.
Â 
Less Repression Than Feared
While martial law and the current political atmosphere have severely hampered their activities, they believe the repression may not be as severe as they had anticipated two months ago.
''I went to Tiananmen Square many times,'' the union member said. 
''I gave many speeches and I must have been filmed many times, but they haven't arrested me, have they?''
Some workers, he noted, had only been detained for interrogation, particularly about leaders of the union, and then released.
The group believes there have been about 40 arrests and detentions of members belonging to their unofficial, loosely formed union that had begun to expand its network throughout the city during May. 
The number, however, may be wrong because they have not been able to contact many colleagues. 
Some may have been arrested secretly, and some of those who they think were arrested may actually be in hiding.
Â 
Few Recent Court Sentences
Many workers and intellectuals who had been outspoken during the may protests have been frightened about being jailed or dismissed from their jobs if their role in the demonstrations were discovered. 
The Government has announced the execution of 12 people so far in connection with the turmoil, and nearly all of them have been workers.
Few additional court sentences have been announced since then, but the television images of people being sentenced to death still chill many workers.
''Many people are afraid to come out, but we know they support us,'' the worker said.

file: Senate Backs Curbs On Beijing_s Access To Markets in U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
Responding to China's human rights record, soaring trade surplus and continued arms exports to the Middle East, the Senate voted today to impose conditions on the renewal of China's favorable trade status with the United States in June.
The vote sends the legislation to President Bush after nearly three years of political maneuvering. 
The Administration has repeatedly threatened to veto the legislation, and the 59-to-39 vote today fell 8 votes short of the two-thirds majority that would be needed to override a veto if all senators voted. 
But the margin was wider than in last summer's vote on the same issue, when the Democrats also prevailed, 55 to 44.
The bill, a compromise between separate measures approved by the House and Senate last year, is the first penalizing China's growing exports to emerge from Congress since Beijing'scrackdown on dissent in 1989.
It would condition the renewal of China's most-favored-nation trade status on the Chinese Government's accounting for and releasing from prison all citizens accused of expressing their political beliefs nonviolently. 
It would also require as a condition of renewal that the President certify to Congress that China has made substantial progress in observing human rights, opening its markets to American goods and curbing exports of missile and nuclear technology.
The Senate's Democratic leadership insisted on the vote today to force the President and Republicans into the politically awkward position of publicly supporting the Chinese Government in an election year.
Several senators who changed their votes cited concerns about Chinese arms exports. 
Among them was Senator Jim Exon, a Nebraska Democrat who voted against the legislation last summer because he feared that China might retaliate against American corn exports. 
He said he voted in favor today because a recent Central Intelligence Agency report made him worry that China sought to replace the former Soviet Union as a superpower and the United States' leading adversary.
Arms exports are "the way you get to be a superpower," he said in an interview after the vote. 
"You surround yourself with a lot of your supporters, you give them a lot of nuclear armaments and then you become Mr. Big."
Senator George J. Mitchell of Maine, the majority leader and chief sponsor of today's bill, also cited China's occupation of Tibet and its $12.69 billion trade surplus with the United States last year, the second largest surplus after Japan's. 
Ten conservative Republican senators voted for the bill.
Â 
Five Democrats Vote No
Only five Democrats, all from farm states, crossed party lines to support the Administration. 
Their leader, Senator Max Baucus, the Montana Democrat who heads the Subcommittee on International Trade, said he supported the use of existing trade laws against specific Chinese exports.
Supporting the bill "is the politically easier course to take," he said. 
"It's easier to beat up on the Chinese and, for some Democrats, to beat up on the President in an election year."
The Administration lost today's vote despite weeks of strenuous lobbying to persuade Republican senators to vote with it. 
That effort concluded today with Republican senators meeting over lunch with Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser.
Yet so reluctant were Senate Republicans to defend China that Senator Bob Packwood, the Oregon Republican who led the bill's opponents, was unable to find enough senators to fill all the time allocated this morning for speeches criticizing the measure. 
Mr. Packwood yielded the extra time to Democrats.
Senator Bob Dole of Kansas, the Republican minority leader, had argued for weeks without success for a voice vote, which would have allowed Republican senators to support the President without being identified individually as having done so.
Legislation to revoke China's trade status was introduced shortly after the army crackdown in Beijing in June 1989, but no action was taken. 
The House approved a bill in October 1990 to impose conditions on the annual renewal of China's trade status, but the Senate took no action before that session of Congress expired two months later.
New bills imposing conditions were introduced in the House and the Senate and approved last July, although only in the House were Democrats able to assemble the two-thirds majority needed to override a Presidential veto. 
It was a compromise bill combining and slightly watering down the two bills that passed the House by a vote of 409 to 21 on Nov. 
26 and came before the Senate today.
The most-favored-nation trade status is misleadingly named, referring to very low tariffs imposed on most imports from all but a handful of countries like North Korea and Albania. 
Under legislation enacted in the early 1970's, the most-favored-nation status of China and other countries that had Communist governments at the time requires annual renewal by the President.

file: SENATE RESTRICTS TRADE WITH CHINA_ BUSH VETO LIKELY.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Senate voted today to impose conditions on trade relations with China, but sponsors of the legislation failed to muster the two-thirds majority needed to overcome a likely Presidential veto. 
As a result, the day's action was a victory for the Bush Administration.
The 55-to-44 vote for trade restrictions was a setback for the Senate Democratic leadership. 
The legislation was sponsored by Senator George J. Mitchell, Democrat of Maine, the Senate majority leader.
The bill would attach conditions to any renewal of China's most-favored-nation trade status, as of next July, but would allow the President's recent renewal of the low tariffs to continue until then. 
The conditions would include an end to certain Chinese arms sales, the release of some political prisoners, and a halt in exports of products produced by prison labor to the United States.
Â 
Some Cross Party Lines
The Administration prevailed by retaining the support of 37 Republicans and persuading 7 Democrats from farm states to cross party lines. 
Only 6 Republicans voted against the Administration, led by Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, whose state has been particularly affected by a surge in textile imports from China.
Mr. Helms criticized China's human rights record and asserted that China continued to export products to the United States that were made with prison labor, a violation of American law. 
"For more than 40 years, these leaders have maintained themselves in power by the same means," he said.
Senator Bob Dole of Kansas, the Senate minority leader, said the 55-to-44 vote insured that a Bush veto would not be overridden. 
"This legislation is not going to become law," he said.
Â 
What the Status Does
The term "most favored nation" is a trade term that actually applies to almost all United States trading partners, including Iraq and Libya. 
Countries awarded this status ship goods to the United States at the lowest tariffs available for each category of import.
The House of Representatives voted two weeks ago to pass a similar bill. 
The House vote was 313 to 112, more than the two-thirds majority needed to override a Presidential veto. 
The bills must now be reconciled in a conference attended by members of both houses of Congress. 
The legislation will then go to President Bush, whose advisers say they will recommend a veto of any bill not providing for unconditional renewal of China's trade status.
As recently as two weeks ago, the Administration was still unsure whether it could muster the 34 votes needed to give it a strong chance of sustaining a veto. 
China's opponents and advocates alike focused their lobbying efforts on the Senate as the key battleground.
The Administration stressed party loyalty in a last-minute lobbying blitz and made limited concessions to fence-sitting Democrats and Republicans.
The Administration said it would back Taiwan's application to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, a move calculated to win support from anti-Communist lawmakers and free-trade advocates. 
The Administration said it would take legal action against Chinese import barriers if negotiations did not yield results in several months.
A combination of heavy lobbying and a package of limited concessions sent to Congress on Friday helped the Administration win a dozen or more votes in the last week. 
Business interests, led by grain and aircraft exporters and textile importers, joined the Administration in its successful lobbying effort over the last several weeks.
China was the largest importer of wheat from the United States last year. 
Grain exporters estimated that if China halted those imports in retaliation for action by the Congress, wheat prices could fall by 10 percent.
A group of mostly farm-state senators led by Senator Max S. Baucus, Democrat of Montana, chairman of the Senate subcommittee on international trade, sent a letter to President Bush on June 19 asking for concessions in exchange for their support. 
The President made some of the concessions but did not outline new initiatives on human rights or China's arms exports.
Senator Kent Conrad, Democrat of North Dakota, one of six Democrats to sign Mr. Baucus's letter, criticized the President's response today. 
"I found the President's response to be very weak," he said.
But Mr. Conrad said in the debate that he would still vote against the bill because modifying China's trade status was not an appropriate way to respond to address his concerns about China's record on human rights.
Mr. Baucus said the question facing Congress was how much China could be pushed to change its practices without persuading its leaders that the changes were impossible or involved an unacceptable loss of face. 
The conditions in Mr. Mitchell's bill are so extensive that Chinese leaders would rather cut themselves off from the United States than comply, Mr. Baucus said.
Backing Mr. Mitchell was an eclectic alliance of anti-Communists, human rights advocates and protectionists. 
Senator Donald W. Riegle, Democrat of Michigan, was one of several senators who focused on the growth in China's trade surplus with the United States, which reached $10.3 billion last year.
But Senator Lloyd M. Bentsen, Democrat of Texas, the chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, posed the same question as Mr. Baucus and reached a different answer. 
Recent changes in the Soviet Union, particularly a huge increase in emigration, show that conditions can foster change in Communist countries, he said.
Senator Dale Bumpers, Democrat of Arkansas, assailed the decision of the Chinese leadership to use force against demonstrators in and near Tiananmen Square in June 1989. 
Instead of arresting demonstrators, he said, "They chose to start mowing them down with guns and machine guns."
Before the final vote, the Senate added four amendments to Senator Mitchell's bill that made Chinese compliance more difficult. 
These amendments made it harder for Mr. Mitchell to gather votes.
An amendment introduced late in the evening by Senator Bentsen modified a provision in Senator Mitchell's bill that would have canceled the trade status immediately if China exported certain arms at any time in the coming year. 
The cancellation would instead take effect on July 3, 1992.
The amendment was a last-minute bid to soften the language of Senator Mitchell's bill and win support for it.

file: Seoul Gets Some Diplomatic Backing in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
South Korea's President, Roh Tae Woo, said on Tuesday that China's top leaders had endorsed his policy of persuading North Korea to abandon its nuclear-weapons program in return for a promise of normal relations with the West and substantial economic assistance from Seoul.
This morning, the two countries issued a joint declaration, and the South Koreans indicated they had received the sort of public endorsement they wanted.
Korean officials had reported that China's head of state, Yang Shangkun, warned Mr. Roh in a meeting here on Monday that while his Government was eager to ease tensions on the Korean peninsula, it felt that too much pressure on the hard-line Communists in Pyongyang might be self-defeating.
On Tueday, President Roh met with two top Chinese officials -- Prime Minister Li Peng, and the head of the Communist Party, Jiang Zemin. 
Afterward, the South Korean leader was careful to say that "the preference is not to press but to persuade" North Korea to meet the terms of an earlier agreement allowing mutual inspections of nuclear sites.
Mr. Roh has insisted that until the North agrees to such inspections, relations cannot move forward.
A Chinese endorsement of the South Korean policy would be significant, since Beijing remains the last ally of Pyongyang and is believed to have more influence on the North Koreans than any other country.
Â 
Recent Establishment of Ties
Mr. Roh's landmark visit comes just a month after China and South Korea opened diplomatic relations, ending four decades of cold war hostility. 
Chinese troops joined North Korean forces in fighting the South Koreans and other American-led United Nations forces from 1950 to 1953. 
The war left the South devastated, and for more than a decade, mired in desperate poverty.
But on Tuesday, the South Korean President made it clear that his country was prepared to embrace China without looking back.
"No region in the world suffered more than the Korean peninsula due to the cold war," Mr. Roh said. 
"My visit at this time has put an end to the cold war between us and has opened a new era of reconciliation and cooperation."
He emphasized his country's economic achievements over the last quarter-century, hinting that the kind of affluence and success it now enjoys could be shared by the North if it takes the necessary steps toward building relations.

file: Seoul Looks North, Balancing Hope and Anxiety.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Roh Tae Woo said here not long ago that he wants to be remembered as the man who fulfilled South Korea's "aspirations for democratization."
But for Asia and the United States, perhaps most important has been his paramount role in isolating North Korea, a three-year diplomatic campaign that has left one of the world's most menacing powers bereft of its cold-war allies and on the defensive about a nuclear-weapons project that ranks among the biggest threats in Asia.
Yet in Seoul, only 35 miles from the mines and tank traps of the demilitarized zone that divides Korea, South Koreans are hardly celebrating. 
As President Roh (pronounced NO) leaves office, the former general who was once feared as a military strongman in a business suit is now often criticized for going soft, signing empty agreements with the North rather than speeding its collapse.
Â 
The Generation Gap
A rising generation of educated young South Koreans, with no memory of families fleeing across the border, have begun to question whether their parents' preoccupation with reunification is even worth the price. 
Mindful of Germany's experience, they fear that unification could nearly bankrupt the South, derailing the nation just as it begins to focus on the cold realities of competing with Japan and China.
How Mr. Roh's successor, who is to be elected on Friday, manages relations with North Korea may well determine when and how peacefully the cold war ends in Asia. 
For all their new-found prosperity and democratic values, South Koreans are acutely aware that for most of the last century, their peninsula has served as a battleground for far larger powers maneuvering for strategic advantage -- first Japan, then the Soviet Union, China and the United States.
If the Koreas reunify peacefully, the nation could become a regional powerhouse of 70 million people. 
If relations between North and South collapse totally -- and many American military officials and diplomats fear they easily could -- that could rekindle the first battle the United Nations ever tried to settle with force.
Â 
Question for Clinton
"North Korea could explode or implode," said Gen. Robert W. RisCassi, the commander of the 40,000 United States troops who remain here. 
As the Stalinist Government of Kim Il Sung is driven further into a corner, its economy shrinking and its people running short of food, General RisCassi contends, "it is a debatable matter" whether the country will change peacefully or lash out as it did once before.
That question, endlessly debated these days in Washington and Seoul, is at the heart of the question of how many American troops the Clinton Administration will decide to keep here, and for how long. 
On the streets, where radical students, nationalists and political opposition leaders once demanded an American pullout, all three candidates for President of South Korea are now urging the United States to stay.
"It's true that America's presence here has sometimes hurt our standing in the international community and hurt the pride of the people of South Korea," said Lee Chul, a former student leader who is now a top official of the opposition party headed by Kim Dae Jung, a leading contender in the presidential race. 
"But when you look at the growing military power of Japan and other countries, it is important to have balance. 
If America pulled out, it would be very destabilizing."
The other candidates for President are Chung Ju Yung, the founder of the Hyundai manufacturing comglomerate, and Kim Young Sam, of the Democratic Liberal Party.
Â 
Finding Allies in East Europe
When Mr. Roh took office in early 1988, the North and the South were locked in the same standoff they had been in since an armistice was signed in July 1953, and foreign policy was low on the national agenda.
But a year after he took office, Koreans watched on television as the Berlin wall fell, seeing it all through the prism of the DMZ.
"There was a wistful period for a while," Donald P. Gregg, the United States Ambassador, said recently. 
"Everyone thought it could happen as quickly as it did in Germany. 
Then they watched, and added up the costs, and that was sobering."
President Roh, by his own account, seized the moment.
Instead of surrounding himself with his old military advisers, he gathered academics and foreign policy specialists advocating a vast change in South Korea's strategy.
Working quietly, he began to court several Eastern European nations and then the former Soviet Union, eventually welcoming Mikhail S. Gorbachev to a country where Russians had been barred. 
In return he offered Russia $3 billion in aid, a figure North Korea angrily denounced as a huge payoff.
Â 
Melting the Ice
But the effects were clear: After nearly two decades of silence, the Prime Ministers from North and South began to meet regularly, though the talks always seemed on the verge of foundering, with both sides often shouting accusations at each other.
Mr. Roh, following a path charted largely by his national security adviser, Kim Chong Hwi, began to dangle the investment carrot in front of the North, whose economy is a tenth the size of South Korea's. 
Eventually he even allowed South Korean business leaders to travel North to talk about potential factories.
A year ago this week, the two sides finally struck what seemed like a historic accord on "Reconciliation, Nonaggression and Exchanges and Cooperation."
It fell short of a peace treaty, but it seemed bound to break down the isolation, calling for a military hot line, regular exchanges of news, even telephone, mail and rail service between nations and families that had been totally cut off from one another.
Â 
Just a Piece of Paper
So far, though, no major provisions have been put into effect. 
To Mr. Roh's critics, the agreement was an empty gesture that allowed North Korea the appearance of compromise while still building its bomb.
"In the past year, Roh's Government was in far too much haste to put together an agreement," said Cha Young Koo, the director of the security policy division of the Government-financed Korea Institute for Defense Analysis. 
Mr. Cha attributes the agreements to "personal ambition" on the part of those surrounding President Roh. 
"They pressured to make something happen in the hope that the North would change," he said.
Government officials defend their approach, saying there is evidence the "pragmatists" are in the ascendency in the North. 
Last week North Korea dismissed the Prime Minister who led the talks -- some speculate because he was moving too slowly -- and promoted several officials who have talked about copying China's combination of limited economic freedom and strict political control.
Â 
Pleas for Patience
"It takes time," said Lim Dong Won, the vice minister of National Unification Board in Seoul and a key figure in the talks. 
"North Korea is not so weak that it will collapse suddenly. 
North Korean people have been poor for so many years that they are accustomed to it. 
They can eat one meal a day and not be tempted to revolt. 
You can't use a Western yardstick of progress. 
You have to use a North Korean yardstick."
Most United States officials seem to agree: A recent Defense Intelligency Agency report said, "This measured approach may hold more promise than more publicized attempts to twist the economic levers ever more tightly against Pyongyang."
"They are moving away from isolation," President Roh said in a recent interview. 
"There are a number of indications they are opening their doors."
Asked whether it would last, he paused. 
"The fact is that Kim Il Sung is the decision maker in North Korea and the only decision maker," he said.
But to many South Koreans, Mr. Roh is fighting the last war.
"My kids, they don't know where North Korea is," said Park Yung Chul, a professor at Korea University and one of the millions who left family in the North when they fled as war approached in 1950. 
"When pictures of life in North Korea come on the television, they flip the channel. 
They focus on Japan -- they read Japanese comics and watch Japanese movies."
Mr. Park, a member of a Government advisory board on unification, says he is coming to agree that South Korea should focus its attention elsewhere. 
"We are wasting our time and energy," he said. 
"We should be building factories, exporting to the States. 
We have a lot other things to do."
In fact, polls and interviews suggest that South Koreans are unwilling to pay their share of the $200 billion to $400 billion that many private analysts say unification will cost. 
Government officials acknowledge that the younger generation shares little of its parents' interest in building a single nation.
"I know there is such a view, especially among young people in Seoul," said Chung Won Shik, who was Prime Minister until a few months ago and headed the South Korean delegation to the talks. 
"But unification is the goal and the fate of this nation. 
Our young people don't always see the agony of 10 million separated families."
Â 
Nervousness at the Pentagon
For the United States military in Asia, North Korea remains the region's biggest potential diaster.
The Pentagon's classified five-year "Planning Guidance" describes several situations in which North Korea could lash out, even without Chinese and Russian help. 
The paper warns that United States troops should be "prepared to fight in a nuclear environment" and face a ground force of 1.2 million soldiers. 
It estimates that it would take 106 days of intense combat to defeat Kim Il Sung's forces.
Nonetheless, all the momentum seems on the side of reducing the United States presence. 
Every year the South Korean forces take more responsibility for defending their homeland. 
The Bush Administration reduced the troops here by 7,000 -- more cuts are to come -- and removed tactical nuclear weapons. 
The latter was largely a gesture to the North because nuclear-armed submarines could come right up to the coast.
Increasingly, South Koreans acknowledge that a smaller conventional United States force would also serve the purpose. 
"We are well enough trained and armed now that you could probably withdraw all but a few regiments of ground troops," Mr. Cha said.
Â 
Then, There's the Bomb
What is likely to turn the debate for the new Administration are the continuing doubts about the North's nuclear program. 
Under tremendous pressure from Seoul, Washington and Tokyo, Pyongyang allowed in international inspectors. 
But in recent weeks officials here and in United States intelligence have suggested that new evidence has turned up hidden arms sites.
One senior Bush Adminstration official said last week that North Korea already had enough plutonium to build a crude nuclear weapon. 
The fear is that a nuclear-armed North would force Japan, Taiwan and the South to follow the same path, something each is capable of.
All this has helped fuel one of the periodic swings toward fear -- fear that the country that has bombed airliners and tried to kill the South Korean Cabinet would make one last lunge for survival.
"The events of the past several years have encouraged optimism," the American commander, General RisCassi, said recently. 
But, he added, "there is certainly an equal, if not stronger, case for pessimism."
Â

file: Session on Rights in China to Be Test for U.N.txt
text:
ï»¿
An international campaign to have China condemned by the United Nations for human rights violations in connection with its suppression of the democracy movement is expected at a meeting opening on Monday in Geneva.
The drive, spearheaded by private human rights organizations around the world and supported by most Western governments, is widely seen as a critical test of the United Nations human rights enforcement machinery as its effectiveness is being questioned.
Over the last few weeks United Nations officials here and in Geneva say they have received more than 100 formal complaints about the Beijing Government's actions from rights groups outside the country and from individuals in China.
At the Geneva meeting, the petitioners will ask the 26 independent members of a United Nations human rights subcommission to condemn China for human rights abuses. 
Such a resolution would be sent for approval by the 43 governments represented on the full Human Rights Commission when it holds its annual worldwide review of human rights abuses next spring.
The New York-based International League for Human Rights plans to bring two Chinese student leaders who fled the country to Geneva to testify before the subcommission, the league's executive director, Felice Gaer, said.
The student leaders, Wuer Kaixi and Chai Ling, will be joined by Yan Jiaqi, a former adviser to the ousted Chinese Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang.
Other rights groups planning to press the case against China include Amnesty International and the International Commission of Jurists.
After the subcommission meeting, Western governments are expected to attack China's rights record at the annual session of the General Assembly, the top United Nations decision-making body, which opens in New York in mid-September.
Although the United Nations cannot force governments to respect the Universal Declaration on Human Rights, it can try to press them to do so by focusing attention on abuses through resolutions, reports and investigations.
The campaign to condemn China is certain to encounter fierce resistance, diplomats say, with Beijing pressing third-world countries on the subcommission to oppose critical resolutions.
Â 
Composition of the Panel
The panel is made up of experts nominated by their governments. 
Most of those from the developing world are civil servants or others likely to obey official instructions. 
Western governments generally appoint judges or private lawyers, who are considered politically independent.
China has been highly sensitive to criticism of its internal policies. 
At the last Human Rights Commission meeting in March, it persuaded third-world members to block criticism of its actions in Tibet.
But Western diplomats say China must not be allowed to escape United Nations criticism for its suppression of the democracy movement, even though it is has a permanent seat on the Security Council and is a nuclear superpower. 
''The U.N.'s credibility is at stake,'' said Reid Brody of the International Commission of Jurists.
At the meeting last March, developing countries agreed to end investigations into the human rights practices of Iraq, Syria, Zaire and Honduras, and they blocked a Western attempt to condemn Iraq for using poison gas in its war against Iran. 
Among the few countries regularly criticized by the Commission are Israel, South Africa, El Salvador, Chile and Rumania.

file: Shaky Numbers Behind China_s Rosy Economic Picture.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA appears to be easing out of its worst economic slump in a dozen years, but Chinese and foreign economists say the recovery will be slow and painful and that there is no sign of any significant move toward a market economy.
Just a few months ago, there were some tentative hints that China might lift price controls and adopt other market-oriented changes.
But these days the central planners are again dominant, and drafts of the country's five-year plan that will take effect in January reportedly contain little in the way of a commitment to change.
"They talk about reform, but there are no specifics," said a Chinese economist. 
"It's a blank when it comes to reform."
Still, Chinese officials, in public at least, are emphasizing the good news: industrial production is rising again. 
At the beginning of this year, some diplomats and Chinese thought that the economy might continue to deteriorate and lead to large numbers of factory closures and new protests, but that risk seems to have receded.
"The economy is now taking a turn for the better, thereby promoting political and economic stabilityI," Zhang Zhongji, spokesman for the State Statistical Bureau, said at a news conference last week.
He noted that industrial output in September climbed 7.5 percent from the same period a year earlier -- the best performance since July 1989, a month after the army crackdown helped push the economy into a slump.
Mr. Zhang also noted other good economic news:
* A bumper harvest, including a record 420 million tons of grain, is expected this year.
* Inflation has been subdued, and the index of retail prices stood last month only 1 percent higher than a year earlier.
* China's foreign exchange reserves are rising because of a strong trade surplus, which totaled $4.9 billion in the first nine months of this year.
Yet some official reports acknowledge that the situation is still grim, and most ordinary Chinese apparently feel the same way.
Beijing workers say that in recent days they have been summoned to meetings in which officials have read to them a document announcing hefty price increases in coal, cooking gas, natural gas, electricity and other necessities.
The price of the ubiquitous cakes of coal that are used as fuel in Chinese homes all winter also soared, by 50 percent, the document discloses.
"Of course, we're unhappy," said a worker in his 20's. 
"But what are we to do?
The Government spent so much money on the Asian Games that they have to get it back somehow."
The price increases have invited some sarcastic comments at these worker meetings, but no strikes or other significant indications of rebelliousness have been reported.
THE Asian Games, a mini-Olympics, concluded successfully in Beijing early this month, and the authorities apparently felt that security was tight enough and the atmosphere calm enough that they could introduce the price increases -- which have not been disclosed in the news media -- without provoking unrest.
But diplomats here and Chinese economists say there is much more to the story. 
For most of this year, the increases in industrial output simply went into ever-higher mountains of inventories. 
The inventories continued to increase even last month, the diplomats and economists note, and they will impede the recovery that may now be under way.
Moreover, part of the reason for the industrial growth is a statistical fluke: China calculates each month's growth as a comparison of the same period one year earlier. 
Since the latter half of last year was severely affected by the slump, it is therefore easier to show growth now in comparison with that period.
Seasonally adjusted production figures, developed by Rock Creek Research Inc., an American consulting firm, also show China's industry generally improving since March of this year. 
But Rock Creek's figures underscore the problems that remain: its models suggest that industrial growth slipped badly in July and August of this year.
Likewise, inflation is subdued now, but the Government has sharply eased credit this year -- $20.4 billion in additional loans in the first eight months of 1990 -- to stimulate the economy. 
Government payments to farmers for the grain harvest in coming months will also expand the money supply and perhaps lead to inflationary pressures, after a lag of six months or more.
"There'll just be more inflation down the road, and we'll be back to the cycle of boom and bust," said a Chinese economist.
One of the main reasons for the economic slowdown was that consumers simply stopped buying goods, apparently in part because of the turmoil in the capital and uncertainties about the future.
Refrigerators, televisions and electric fans piled up at stores around the nation, and some store managers resorted to desperate measures to clear their stocks: they promised to refund the sale price in full, after five years. 
That brought in some cash, but no one knows the extent of this liability or how it will be paid off.
NOW retail sales are gradually picking up again, but companies that make household appliances are still in desperate shape.
In the first three quarters of 1990, production of washing machines was only 69 percent of the level in the same period of 1989, and output of refrigerators was at 64 percent of the level of 1989.
What pains many economists -- Chinese as well as foreigners -- is that the Government has not made use of the slowdown to remove price controls and introduce a restructuring. 
Freeing prices might have been accomplished relatively easily earlier this year, when inflation was subdued, but will be much more difficult as the economy picks up.
Moreover, the economic purpose of a recession, to weed out inefficient companies, is neglected in China because the state always protects companies from bankruptcy.
"There hasn't been any fundamental structural change accompanying this recession," said a Western economist in Beijing. 
"The fundamental problems are still here. 
I don't believe state enterprises are one iota more efficient now than they were two years ago."
Indeed, they may well be less efficient. 
The state-owned sector of the economy is a disaster area: one-third of state-owned companies are losing money, and the total losses in the first three quarters of this year were double the total losses in the same period last year.
WITH state enterprises on the ropes, the recovery is coming from the sectors that have been most pummeled by the central planners over the last year, but that have still managed to maintain a measure of vitality.
Of the 7.5 percent industrial growth in September, for example, the state sector saw growth of only 3 percent, while rural collective enterprises grew at a rate of 9.4 percent, and the tiny sector that includes private businesses and joint ventures soared 57.7 percent.
"There are all these conflicting strains in the economy, in terms of regions and in terms of types of ownership," said a Western diplomat. 
The diplomat noted that growth was strongest in the coastal areas of China that already are richer than the interior.
Many economists would be more optimistic if they saw signs that the Government was embracing proposals for structural change. 
But instead the Government apparently intends to postpone any major changes for at least a year or two.
The only changes that apparently have been agreed upon involve modifications in the contract system that governs most Chinese enterprises.
Chinese and foreign economists say the leadership has agreed that new contracts will include a more systematic method of taxation in which enterprises' taxes will be paid as a proportion of revenues. 
The taxes will also be the companies' first obligation.
A second change is that payments of principal on certain loans will no longer be deductible from the companies' taxes.
These are minor adjustments compared with the sweeping economic changes that many foreign economists recommend and that some Chinese officials have been lobbying for in recent months.
Â 
Â 
THE UNEMPLOYMENT RISK
ONE of the principal political risks for the Chinese Government is rising unemployment, in part because it is the employer that has prime responsibility for monitoring and controlling workers. 
Unemployment not only distresses workers, but it also makes it easier for them to act with impunity.
"The unemployment situation is very grave," Economic Reference News, an official newspaper, reported last month. 
It said the unemployment rate has risen to 4.4 percent, from 2.5 percent, "greatly surpassing the warning level of 3 percent."
In China, however, statistics are often at odds. 
Zhang Zhongji, spokesman for the State Statistical Bureau, said the unemployment rate was unchanged, at 2.6 percent.
In any case, these figures do not include large numbers of young people who are officially "awaiting assignment."
In the next five years some 92 million people are expected to enter the ranks of the labor force, and the Government will be hard put to provide jobs.
Perhaps as a result, the leadership has already stopped criticizing private and collective enterprises and is now hailing them and the "free markets" where private traders sell their goods.
"The leaders know that they can't solve the employment problem through the state sector or the agricultural sector," said a Western economist in Beijing.

file: Shanghai Editor Now a Rallying Cry.txt
text:
ï»¿
In his lifetime, Qin Benli has been buffeted by a Nationalist purge, the Communist revolution, the anti-rightist campaign, the Cultural Revolution, the campaign against spiritual pollution and the campaign against bourgeois liberalism.
Now the deceptively frail-looking editor in the gray Mao jacket finds himself at the center of China's latest social storm.
The Communist Party's attacks on his plucky, Shanghai-based weekly newspaper, The World Economic Herald, more than any other event, have enlarged the Chinese student uprising to include a substantial segment of the country's journalists, and have enshrined the notion of press freedom on the list of popular demands confronting the Chinese leadership.
Mr. Qin, who is in his 70's, picked his way through the chanting crowds on Huaihai Zhong Street today and revisited his office for the first time since April 26, when the Shanghai party organization suspended him and put his newspaper under the censorial supervision of a five-member ''rectification committee.''
Roses and Handshakes
He shyly accepted roses and elated handshakes from his staff, and vowed that his independent weekly would resist the censors in its battle to publish what it wants - which is a broad range of interesting ideas pressing the limits of what is officially acceptable.
''This is a special opportunity,'' he said. 
''We are just one little newspaper, but if we win we can contribute to a free press in China.''
Although he has not been reinstated, Mr. Qin's unflappable optimism does not, just now, seem as outlandish as it might have a few weeks ago.
Like the Chinese leaders in Beijing, the Communist authorities here in China's largest city are showing signs of bending under the pressure of a mounting public siege.
Today, demonstrators in the scores of thousands - a local journalist claimed several hundred thousand -clogged the promenade along the Huangpo River where Western financiers held sway in colonial times; sat in the streets and trees around city hall; occupied Peoples' Square, and marched in small battalions through the narrow streets.
Â 
Gorbachev Skirts Protests
Their banners and chants called for greater democracy, the removal of the local Communist Party leader, the complete retirement of the country's 84-year-old paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, a clean-up of official corruption and, invariably, an end to the official hounding of Mr. Qin's newspaper.
The wave of protests stemming from a student hunger strike in Beijing reached here on Tuesday, and today the first few clusters of blue-collar workers were evident among the throngs of students and intellectuals.
Their marching eclipsed a visit by Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, who skirted the scenes of protest to meet local officials and tour an elevator factory before returning home to Moscow from four days of overshadowed Soviet-Chinese summitry.
''We welcome Gorbachev, but our parade has nothing to do with him,'' said Wu Qangsui, deputy editor of the evening newspaper Xinmin Wanbao and a member of the Chinese Parliament, who marched with a column of journalists past city hall this morning.
''We want to print the truth, but because the way is not smooth for us we are out here today,'' he added. 
''The World Economic Herald is an example for us.''
Â 
Paper Was Disciplined Before
The Herald, housed in a scuffed and flourescent-lit former French missionary school that now belongs to the Academy of Social Sciences, has had periodic brushes with the authorities since Mr. Qin founded it in 1980. 
Officially tolerated but not affiliated with the party or Government, his paper has a modest circulation, by Chinese standards, of 300,000, mostly among intellectuals.
Twice before the party has imposed short-lived rectification committees after the newspaper's pages scandalized the official ideologists.
''This is the third time we've been rectified, so I'm sort of used to it now,'' Mr. Qin said in an interview today. 
The immediate cause of the latest and harshest crackdown was apparently the Herald's six pages of reminisence and discussion after the death April 15 of Hu Yaobang, the ousted Communist Party leader who is revered by protesters and intellectuals as a strong proponent of political liberalization. 
Mr. Hu's death was also the spark for the initial outbreak of student unrest in mid-April.
Employees at the paper say another major factor leading to the crackdown was its publication in January of an article by a Beijing scholar criticizing the Communist Party.
Â 
Censors Review All Material
The team of censors, made up of three local Communist Party functionaries, a retired editor and a journalism teacher, insists on reviewing all material before it goes to press. 
The second issue presented for its inspection was deemed unacceptable because it included a letter from the All-China World Economic Association defending the Herald.
Mr. Qin's deputies agreed to cut the offending material, but for the following issue, due out last week, they assembled two full pages of similar letters. 
The censors balked, and this time the Herald staff held its ground.
''If they want the Herald to publish at all, this time they must give in,'' said Chen Hansheng the international news editor.
One Herald reporter said the party had invited Mr. Qin to return to his post, but the editor has refused to do so unless the local party leader, Jiang Zemin, admits he was in the wrong.
Â 
Journalists Offer Support
Tacked to the newsroom wall are supportive letters, telegrams and petitions signed by journalists at most of the other major Chinese newspapers, including those of the local Communist Party.
Mr. Qin, who has spent much of his career in disgrace and a few years of it in a labor camp, hardly seems a firebrand. 
An underground Communist during the 1949 revolution, he retains his party membership and loyalty.
He defends Mr. Deng, a target of the students' protest, saying, ''China still needs him for direction.''
And he does not approve of the students' hunger strike, a tactic that has sent many to the hospital.
But he supports what the students stand for, and believes that their protest signals something healthy ahead for China - perhaps including a Chinese version of glasnost.
