text:
ï»¿
The largest population in the world is proof that it must go on, but sex in China is still laced in secrecy more than sensuousness.
Only recently have social scientists shed light on what happens in the Chinese bedroom -- or, given the acute housing shortage, the living rooms, kitchens, closets and fields to which couples must sometimes resort.
The new research suggests that many young Chinese are enjoying their own sexual revolution. 
That tends to be confirmed by the incidence of venereal disease, which by some official accounts is rising by about 70 percent a year.
A mammoth new survey, already described as the Chinese "Kinsey Report," has led the way in charting the changing mores of the post-Mao period. 
The study, which is expected to be published as a book at the end of this year, profiles a society that remains fundamentally prudish, yet one that is becoming more free-wheeling at the youthful and intellectual fringes.
Â 
Interviews With 23,000 People
To be sure, "free-wheeling" in a Chinese context may mean little more than removing one's clothes. 
The new survey, which was based on interviews with 23,000 people of all ages and backgrounds, in 15 provinces, found that 60 percent of those surveyed "often or sometimes" were naked during sex. 
The researchers thought that was surprisingly high.
"This is quite different from how it used to be, suggesting that with the reform and opening policies, people are more liberal about sex," Liu Dalin, a Shanghai sociologist who is the architect of the survey, wrote in a recent unpublished essay.
Foreplay is often rudimentary or nonexistent, the survey found, perhaps because many couples keep as much clothing on as possible. 
Among peasants, 34 percent engaged in less than one minute of foreplay.
Â 
'How to Conceive a Son'
"Older people don't understand the idea of foreplay," Professor Liu, one of China's best-known researchers into the erotic, said in an interview.
Mr. Liu has written some 41 books, including many recent best sellers about sexuality. 
But Chinese publications are very tame by Western standards, and the priority of many peasants seems to be less along the lines of "The Joy of Sex" than something like "How to Conceive a Son."
Partly because of the hasty and purposeful manner with which sex is apparently conducted, more than a third of women reported pain during intercourse. 
The survey did not ask about female orgasm, for fear that many respondents would not understand the concept, but only a third of urban women and a quarter of rural women said they "very often" felt pleasure during intercourse.
"We don't know how to estimate, but we think that female orgasm is very rare," Mr. Liu said. 
"One reason is that traditionally women are very modest and suffer from closed minds and pressure not to feel too much pleasure. 
Another reason is that husbands engage in little foreplay and lack the knowledge and skills to elicit orgasms in their wives."
Shanghai and some other cities now offer "School for Newlyweds": a special class in which new couples are given a basic introduction into sexuality and contraception. 
Giving satisfaction to the woman is among the topics now addressed.
While Mr. Liu's survey is one of the largest conducted anywhere in the world about sexual behavior, he acknowledges that there are flaws in it.
Perhaps the most important is that the sampling often has not been very scientific, and that rural respondents accounted for only one-quarter of the total -- even though they make up about three-quarters of the population. 
In addition, those rural areas chosen for the surveys were somewhat more prosperous and educated than the Chinese countryside as a whole. 
As a result, China as a whole may be even less sensuous in its sex life than the report would suggest.
China has no Judeo-Christian tradition associating illicit sex with sin, and rather seems to regard sex less as a matter of morality than as an issue of propriety and decency. 
In ancient times, China was much more open about sex, and one of the great works of ancient literature, "The Golden Lotus," brims with explicit descriptions of the under-the-covers activities in a wealthy household. 
China recently published the first unexpurgated version of "The Golden Lotus" since the Communist revolution, but only scholars may buy it.
Â 
The Times Are Changing
"We never used to talk about sex, but there has been a dramatic change," said Hu Jinhua, the editor of Shanghai Public Health News, a daily newspaper. 
"In the 1980's sex education was even introduced in the schools, with Shanghai in the lead. 
The change has been very rapid."
The shift in attitudes is most pronounced among young Chinese, especially university students. 
More than 78 percent of the students questioned in Professor Liu's survey approved of premarital sex, and 90 percent of the students said China's sex education policies are too conservative.
Fewer than 11 percent of the students said they had any sexual experience, but this may reflect opportunities more than appetites. 
University students are often housed six or eight to a room, so arranging a rendezvous is difficult, and in any case students risk expulsion if they are caught sleeping together.
"We've been pretty much Westernized," said a woman who graduated recently from one of Shanghai's best universities. 
"Sex was regarded as no big deal, and while the school authorities discouraged us from falling in love, most of us had boyfriends."

file: Shanghai Journal_New Challenges for a City of Hope and Past Glory.txt
text:
ï»¿
Below the reconstructed Long Bar, where the foreign taipans, or big bosses, used to sip their pink gins and chat about the women with gowns slit up the leg past the waist, or about rogues of the underworld like Big-Eared Du and Pockmarked Huang, a symbol of the new Shanghai is taking shape.
It is a Kentucky Fried Chicken restaurant, the first here in China's biggest city, and it will cheer up the ground floor of the former Shanghai Club, now known as the Dongfeng Hotel. 
The bustle of the workers completing the interior of the restaurant, under Colonel Sanders' frozen grin, reflects the kind of foreign influence that Shanghai is seeking these days.
The restaurant is a world apart from the establishments that characterized this city before the 1949 Communist Revolution: the dim bars and brothels along Blood Alley, the opium dens and movie houses where sozzled sailors recuperated from their voyages, with limousines parked outside next to sleeping rickshaw boys and dying beggars.
The legacy of past glitter and fame - as well as notoriety - are engraved on Shanghai's psyche, and today no city in China is more self-consciously sophisticated, or more aware of the last four decades of stagnation. 
Only in the last few years, residents say, have they felt some hope that the city can succeed in a vigorous campaign to redevelop its economy and restore its relations with the rest of the world.
Â 
'Never Recover Its Glory'
This strenuous effort to recover a measure of its past greatness, and to keep workers satisfied so that they do not provoke political unrest, is Shanghai's paramount mission, but these days it is running head on into the central Government's economic and political retrenchment. 
Vitally needed foreign loans and investment have slowed since the crackdown in Beijing in June, and industrial growth declined in September for the first time on record.
''Shanghai's golden age was in the 1930's, and it will never come back,'' a young teacher said as he stood in front of the old Shanghai Club. 
''This is the most fashionable city in China, the center of the country, but it will never recover its glory.''
The most worrying problems for the moment are economic, particularly falling industrial output. 
In September, industrial production was 2.6 percent below the figure for August and 1.8 percent below the figure for one year earlier. 
The New People's Evening News, a Shanghai newspaper, reported in October that 72,000 workers had been laid off because of factory closings.
''You've got a situation that can't go on,'' said a Western diplomat here. 
''The problem of factories closing hasn't eased; it has gotten worse. 
And if it continues to get worse, the situation will look pretty grim.''
Â 
Austerity Policy a Factor
The immediate cause of the difficulties is primarily the austerity policy imposed by Beijing a year ago, and tightened further this summer. 
The retrenchment has hurt Shanghai, like most of the country, by squeezing credit and investment and by slowing retail sales.
The longer-range cause of the difficulties is the decade-long program of economic liberalization, which helped many parts of China but caused enormous dislocations in Shanghai, Western diplomats and economists say.
It used to be that other parts of China would produce raw materials, including silk, cotton and coal, that ran Shanghai's factories. 
But in recent years, other provinces have been allowed to set up their own factories, and they refuse to sell their raw materials to Shanghai.
Shanghai's former Mayor and party leader, Jiang Zemin, took over as national party leader in June, but there is no sign that he is showing favoritism toward the city. 
''It may help Shanghai a little bit to have him in Beijing,'' said a young Chinese worker. 
''But now he has his own concerns to think about, rather than Shanghai's.''
For all the economic difficulties, diplomats say that life in Shanghai is not so tense or repressive as in Beijing. 
A Chinese dissident here estimates that fewer than 100 intellectuals have been detained in Shanghai since the nationwide crackdown on the student-led democracy movement began in June, and says that almost all were seized on orders from Beijing rather than on the initiative of the local authorities.
Â 
Newspaper Is Suspended
The best-known institutional casualty is the World Economic Herald, a weekly newspaper that was circulated nationally and won a reputation as the best and boldest newspaper in China. 
It was suspended in May and will be formally disbanded at the end of this year, Chinese here say.
Those Chinese say the newspaper's editor, Qin Benli, has been ordered to stay at home and avoid contact with foreigners or with several of his former colleagues. 
Four other staff members have been arrested.
Chinese officials and foreign diplomats who have recently been in both cities say the resentment and bitterness in Shanghai do not run so deep as in Beijing. 
They say the economic challenges may have had the advantage of protecting Shanghai to some extent from purges and political repression. 
Partly for fear of making the economic crisis worse, and partly because Shanghai's Mayor and party leader, Zhu Rongji, is an advocate of political and economic change, Shanghai has been relatively gentle in dealing with protesters.
''Zhu's job is to keep state enterprises producing,'' the Western diplomat said. 
''It is not to lock up dissidents.''
Shanghai sees its mission as the recovery of a measure of its former glory, but China's economic and political retrenchment and the continued closing of local factories has hampered the redevelopment of the city's economy. 
The No. 1 Department Store, above at right, is the most fashionable shop in what a resident says is still ''the most fashionable city in China.''
(The New York Times/Nicholas D. Kristof)

file: Shanghai Journal_Will Houses Blossom Along Capitalist Road_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yu Muqiao must stride over the gaping crack in the wooden floor of her two-room house, scurry down a narrow pitch-dark hallway cluttered with wet clothes and stray beams, then down a flight of broken steps and around the corner 20 yards to get to the newly built public toilet that her family uses.
Her son must pull out a thin mattress every night to sleep on the kitchen floor. 
Still, Mrs. Yu, the 62-year-old matriarch who lives with her household of seven in this cubbyhole, pays a monthly rent of just $1.22. 
That sum is split among six salaried adults, and after the family pools its rent subsidies, it takes in more money than it pays out for the home.
Mrs. Yu's experience -- paying virtually nothing for miserable housing -- is duplicated in cities throughout China. 
But now the Government is moving to revolutionize housing allocation, and with Shanghai in the lead, it is starting a national housing program that is expected to be one of China's most important economic and social initiatives of the 1990's.
The housing privatization program -- nobody uses the word privatization, but that is a major component of the plan -- is an indication that China is ready to take important steps to liberalize its economy and move toward the market. 
And for ordinary people in the cities, many of whom are aghast at the idea of rents rising to market levels, the housing plan will perhaps affect daily lives as much as any other single step since the end of the Maoist era 15 years ago.
"If we don't change the way we allocate housing and people continue to pay so little money for housing, this would simply be unacceptable," said Wu Zhengtong, a researcher at the Shanghai Municipal Housing Authority. 
"We must reform the housing system because it affects the stabilityI of society."
China has talked boldly before about housing reform, only to back down in the face of ideological resistance, public apprehension and the magnitude of the task. 
In the late 1980's, the authorities vigorously promoted housing reform and conducted experiments in several cities. 
But those programs withered with the rise of the hard-liners in 1989, and only now is China returning to the course of home privatization.
This year, the Government agreed to conduct the reform nationwide. 
Some cities, including Shanghai, are focusing on raising rents to market levels. 
Others, particularly in the south, are promoting home ownership. 
For instance, in the city of Jiangmen, in the southern province of Guangdong, 76 percent of the citizens live in apartments they own.
"We'd love to buy a house," said Tang Yinmei, a 63-year-old retiree who lives with her husband and her son's family in a one-room house with a loft in the Old City of Shanghai. 
"But my husband's work unit has no houses available."
While her family's housing subsidies more than compensate for the $1.07 monthly rent, the apartment is tiny and there is no running water. 
A nightsoil collector comes to their house every day to empty the chamber pots.
Â 
Employers Provide Homes
Most Chinese live in homes provided by their employers. 
Because rents are so low, companies have little incentive to build, and there is a chronic shortage of housing. 
In addition, few repairs are made, and workers are tied to their employers because changing jobs would mean losing a home and having to wait years to get a new one.
At present, rents typically amount to less than two percent of an average family's income. 
The real burden, of course, is borne by the employer or Government, which built the house and maintains it for the family.
Each year, the Government spends about $7.5 billion on building new homes and repairing old ones, according to a Chinese news report.
In Shanghai, rents were doubled in May. 
But the Government was clearly concerned that this would upset workers, and so it gave out subsidies that nearly covered the increase in rent. 
The authorities hope to reduce the subsidies as rents rise. 
Many employers in Beijing also have begun to tell their workers that rents will rise, beginning next year.
Still, a rational housing market is a long way off. 
In Shanghai, the Government expects to take 10 to 15 years before it raises rents to the level of the cost of the housing. 
Even at this price, housing would still come to only about 10 percent of the average worker's pay, according to Mr. Wu at the Shanghai Housing Authority. 
The average urban worker earns about $30 a month.
In May, Shanghai also announced that one-fifth of new homes available would be offered for sale at subsidized prices, with the purchaser gaining the right to resell after five years. 
Buyers will be able to buy only one house at the subsidized price.
One stumbling block in the past has been that China was loath to permit the ownership of private property, which it saw as a violation of a fundamental tenet of socialism. 
But a bit of fancy semantics has made the buying and selling of houses more acceptable to the leadership.
"Privatization or marketization, it's the same thing," a Chinese reporter said. 
"But the first word grates on the ears of the leaders."
As a result, the preferred term for the housing program is shangpinhua, or "creating a commodity market."
For Shanghai workers, the new housing policy has meant not only higher rents, but also a five percent deduction from their monthly wages to go to a housing fund. 
The amount is matched by the employer and can be used when the worker decides to purchase a house. 
In the meantime, the money from the fund is used to build new houses for needy people.
A small housing market for individuals is developing, and the prices are rising rapidly. 
Thus, if one can buy a house at the special Government rate -- about one-fifth the market price -- then the purchase option becomes more attractive.
One problem is that unless the Government dares to raise rents sharply, incurring public wrath, most people will prefer to continue renting rather than to pay large sums of money and obtain ownership -- which perhaps will mean little difference except the obligation to repair the building.
"There aren't enough homes sold at the cheap prices, and the market-priced houses are unaffordable," said a Chinese economic reporter. 
"Besides, if you buy a house on the market, who will do home repairs for you?
China doesn't have any private electricians or repairmen."

file: Shanghai vs. Mah-Jongg_ What Odds_.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the evening, after folks here have emptied their rice bowls and put down their chopsticks, the criminal instincts overwhelm the most unlikely people -- high-school students, white-haired old women, even longtime Communist Party members. 
As if by compulsion, someone locks the door and they prepare for an evening of law-breaking.
It is mah-jongg time.
The Communist Party has tackled tough assignments before, like the 1949 Revolution. 
But these days, the leadership of Shanghai, China's largest city, has set itself a truly daunting task: to eradicate mah-jongg, the game that is a national craze.
The crackdown conducted over the last few weeks has been about as effective as a campaign against office football pools would be in the United States.
Â 
Nothing Better to Do
The campaign seems to illustrate two fundamental truths about Communist Party rule in China.
The first is that the party seems so remote these days that it has an unerring talent for annoying ordinary people without really meaning to. 
Probably more Chinese peasants care passionately about mah-jongg than about freedom of the press, and the result is that even those unconcerned about persecution of dissidents profess irritation at endless political study sessions, at requirements that they "volunteer" to buy Government bonds, and at denunciations of mah-jongg when there are no better entertainment options.
The second fundamental truth is that the party has lost much of its ability either to inspire or to terrorize, and so its edicts are frequently ignored.
"It's no use to try to regulate mah-jongg," said a young woman here. 
"Nobody pays attention to the campaign. 
The Government babbles, and the people play."
"The Government has no authority anymore," she said, pointing to a group of bicyclists careering across the street through traffic. 
"Look at those people -- that's illegal too. 
But the law doesn't matter."
Â 
Gambling Is the Target
The authorities are trying to stamp out mah-jongg because play is usually accompanied by gambling. 
Most mah-jongg enthusiasts bet only small amounts, often the equivalent of just a few cents. 
But some people become hard-core gamblers and fritter away all their savings, occasionally even staking their wives on a game.
Consequently, many Chinese regard mah-jongg as a dangerous vice -- but an exceedingly fun one -- with much the same ambivalence that some Americans might feel for alcohol or blackjack or double helpings of chocolate cake.
The United States and other countries also control gambling, and sometimes even office pools, but Shanghai is one of the few places that tries to change social habits and ban small-scale betting in the privacy of the home. 
In Hong Kong, in contrast, mah-jongg is legal at social gatherings or in the abundant parlors that have licenses from the Government, which has sought to keep the game out of the hands of Chinese gangs.
The Taiwan authorities allow social mah-jongg betting in the home, while Macao offers all kinds of gambling, including casinos, and consequently attracts large-stakes gamblers from all over Asia.
One reason for the authorities' zeal in Shanghai may be that privacy is not a well-known concept in China. 
Even the Chinese expression for privacy is usually used in a pejorative sense to hint at selfishness or secretiveness. 
Still, even if they don't always value privacy, many ordinary Chinese treasure their small-stakes mah-jongg.
"There's no way you can succeed in banning mah-jongg," said a college-educated woman who supports the Government. 
"You might as well try to ban knives because they can sometimes be used to kill people."
Mah-jongg, which had its origins in the Song Dynasty more than 700 years ago, is played with 144 domino-like tiles with names like West Wind and Red Dragon. 
In the 1920's the game became popular in the United States and Britain, and Chinese who saw the movie "Driving Miss Daisy" were astonished to see a scene in the film in which Americans were playing mah-jongg.
Whether in America or China -- or in other countries like Japan and Korea where mah-jongg is popular -- the rules are essentially the same. 
Four people normally play at a time, each player keeping a "hand" of tiles and leaving the rest in the center of the table. 
The players take turns putting some down and taking up others, with the aim of building up a set of matching tiles. 
The rules are something like gin rummy, but played with tiles rather than cards.
Â 
Shanghai Gets Tough
China banned mah-jongg during the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976, but there was a resurgence in the 1980's and now it is normally tolerated, even though it is frowned on. 
Mah-jongg sets are available in stores -- Beijing Department Store has 10 kinds on sale, at prices ranging from $5 to $156 -- but mah-jongg gambling dens are strictly banned and the game is normally forbidden in the workplace and in schools.
While in most of China the Government does not bother people who play in their homes, Shanghai for some reason has been particularly determined to uproot mah-jongg.
"Playing mah-jongg is an ugly social trend," Wenhui Bao, a Shanghai newspaper, declared several months ago. 
"People wallow in it so that it saps the energy and seriously affects production, work and studies. 
Gambling over mah-jongg causes crime and considerable social harm. 
We must absolutely eradicate this mah-jongg craze."
In the latest campaign against mah-jongg, which began around the turn of the year and was timed for the Chinese New Year celebrations, when people have time on their hands and are prone to gamble, the authorities created 5,000 "anti-gambling squads" to prowl the suburbs.
In addition, 270,000 rural Communist Party members in Shanghai were summoned to meetings to watch as 4,300 party members publicly gave self-criticisms and renounced mah-jongg.
One county head in the Shanghai suburbs called a mass meeting and started a bonfire of 400 mah-jongg sets. 
Shops in the outskirts were told to stop selling mah-jongg games, according to official newspaper reports. 
But in central Shanghai, stores continue to sell mah-jongg sets and the police have been restrained.
"If you're just playing at home with the old lady and the kids, then the cops will just give you a warning," said a middle-aged mah-jongg enthusiast.
"But if you've got some friends over, then they'll probably figure you're gambling and confiscate all the money in your pockets."
Shanghai residents said that while the police might enter a house if they heard the sound of tiles from the street, most police officers were too lazy to bother and would hurry on. 
But if a neighbor reported that mah-jongg was being played, the police would almost certainly raid a private house, they said.
Many mah-jongg players said that the real problem in Shanghai was that there was nothing else to do in leisure time that was fun and affordable.
"We need more ways of having fun," said Zhang Weiguo, a Shanghai journalist and dissident. 
"On TV we see these things from the West -- skiing, water slides, hang gliding and so on -- but the only thing that people here have to turn to is traditional old mah-jongg. 
So it's gotten to the point that out of 1.1 billion Chinese, maybe 900 million play. 
Only a melon-head doesn't play."
"The problem is the Communist Party management," Mr. Zhang said. 
"It's true that more people are playing mah-jongg and that this is hurting the economy and harming the society. 
But the reason people play is that they don't have alternatives."

file: Shenyang Journal_A City That Undoes Mao Under His Steady Gaze.txt
text:
ï»¿
This drab, Dickensian city, where a statue of Mao presides over the snow-covered central square, is best known for its soot and industry.
Now, relying on an imagination that rivals Dickens's own, it has found a new product to earn it recognition: ideas about how to make China work.
No one knows quite why Shenyang has become a prime battlefront in the struggle to revitalize China's economy, but there is little doubt that this wintry city 400 miles northeast of Beijing has become a testing ground for the entire country.
''We are proud that we can contribute to our country's reform process,'' said Han Yaoxian, a city official who wrote the nation's first bankruptcy law - and then applied it to several companies that until then had cheerfully been losing money for years.
Shenyang was the first city in China to open a securities market, the first to float shares in a large state-owned company, the first to allow a company to go bankrupt, the first to propose selling stock to foreigners, the first to institute wide-scale job transfers and layoffs, and the only one to open an office in South Korea. 
#5.3 Million People In effect, this city of 5.3 million is pioneering the next big task for China's economic development: revitalizing the state-owned companies that produce more than two-thirds of the nation's output.
Guangdong Province in the south pioneered the system of special economic zones and joint ventures with foreign partners. 
Jiangsu Province pioneered the development of rural enterprises that have flourished in the last decade. 
And now the greatest challenge - to foster incentives in the country's heavy industrial base and inject dynamism in state-owned companies that dominate the economy -is being confronted in Shenyang.
''Shenyang is on the leading edge of reform in many different areas, in housing, foreign trade, stocks, management and development of the private sector,'' said Carl Eugene Dorris, the United States Consul General in Shenyang.
Part of the reason, Mr. Dorris said, is that Shenyang has some leaders who are unusually capable, and some factory managers who are unusually upset with the status quo. 
''These people have become real radicals,'' Mr. Dorris said about the factory managers. 
''They're tired of the dead hand of the state on their businesses.''
Some of Shenyang's experiments, such as the securities exchange and a proposal to sell stocks to foreigners, already have been copied in other cities. 
Others, such as large-scale sales of housing to private individuals, are scheduled to be carried out around the country before long. 
But it still is too early to know how successful the city will be in its most important experiments, those seeking to improve the efficiency of state-owned industries.
Â 
Opening Ties With Seoul
In the last few months, Shenyang's pioneering spirit has been most evident in its relations with South Korea. 
Officially, China recognizes only North Korea, not South Korea, and while Beijing sees immense opportunities for business with Seoul, officials are cautious about proceeding too openly for fear of offending North Korea.
Yet in August, the city of Shenyang opened an office in Seoul and sent a senior Deputy Mayor, Zhang Rongmao, to the ribbon cutting. 
This is the first Chinese office in South Korea, and it is not clear if Beijing was consulted. 
The central Government had designated a different area, Shandong Province in the east, to open the first office in Seoul and to lead the way in forging ties with South Korea, but those negotiations have dragged on and Shandong still has not exchanged offices with Seoul.
In a sign of the sensitivity of the issue, Shenyang's Foreign Affairs Office disclaims any knowledge of the Seoul office. 
While the city set up the office so that it formally does not represent the city of Shenyang but simply the ethnic Koreans who live in the area, it was a daring move - particularly since North Korea's only diplomatic mission in China outside Beijing is in Shenyang.
Liaoning Province, which encompasses Shenyang, has even set up a concern called the Bohai Company to specialize in trade with South Korea.
One man often credited for Shenyang's dynamism is Li Changchun, the 44-year-old Governor of Liaoning Province and former Mayor of Shenyang. 
Mr. Li, an electrical engineer and former factory manager who is the nation's youngest Governor, has a reputation for being unusually open to new ideas.
Perhaps Shenyang's most risky undertaking is its plan to shuffle 300,000 workers, 15 percent of the city's work force, out of their jobs. 
The plan is a direct attack on the ''iron rice bowl,'' the system in China of lifetime employment, where it is common for companies to have more workers than they know what to do with. 
Streamlining the work force will make industry more efficient, but it could spark unrest among workers who fear being laid off.
Â 
'Way of Increasing Production'
''Removing surplus workers is a way of increasing production,'' said Guan Weiguo, the executive director of the Economic Restructuring Commission in Shenyang.
While the experiments in Shenyang amount to undoing Mao's work, one of the few changes apparently not being contemplated is tearing down the statue of Mao in the center of the city.
''Mao was a great person, respected by people all over the world, so we couldn't tear down the statue,'' Mr. Guan said, carefully adding: ''Mao had many, many ideas. 
Some of them we can draw upon for reforms, and some of them we can ignore.''

file: Shevardnadze Flies to Beijing to Prepare Summit.txt
text:
ï»¿
Foreign Minister Eduard A. Shevardnadze of the Soviet Union arrived here tonight, saying he was ''full of good expectations and great hopes'' for three days of discussions with China's top leaders.
The talks are expected to prepare for the first Chinese-Soviet summit meeting in 30 years.
The summit meeting between Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, and Deng Xiaoping, the senior Chinese leader, now seems all but certain, and plans for it are expected to be the principal topic of Mr. Shevardnadze's meetings. 
But other issues are also to be raised, including the withdrawal of Vietnamese troops from Cambodia.
An Eastern-bloc diplomat said earlier that Mr. Shevardnadze would bring with him a team of experts on Cambodia for separate discussions with a team of Chinese officials. 
The talks on Cambodia are to focus on the method of international supervision of the Vietnamese withdrawal and of elections that would follow, the diplomat said.
''We hope to take a step forward in our discussions with our Chinese friends,'' Mr. Shevardnadze told reporters as he arrived here. 
He said in a statement issued on his arrival, ''We are convinced that the summit will open a new chapter in the history of our two neighboring countries.''
The dates of the summit meeting, which will formally end the 30-year Chinese-Soviet split, may be announced this week. 
If the dates have already been largely decided, they are a closely guarded secret - or, rather, various Chinese officials and diplomats mention so many dates that no one is sure who is right. 
But the meeting is expected to be set for no earlier than March and no later than June, and almost certainly will be in China.
Before leaving Moscow, Mr. Shevardnadze told the official press agency Tass that the prospects for Chinese-Soviet relations are ''great.''
He said the summit preparations would include the signing of agreements, discussions of principles to settle border disputes and cooperation to resolve regional conflicts. 
He did not indicate what agreements might be signed.
In addition, the Foreign Minister said topics during his visit to Beijing would include disarmament, Asian security issues and international cooperation to deal with problems of debt and the environment.
Mr. Shevardnadze is scheduled to meet with Mr. Deng, Prime Minister Li Peng and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen. 
Mr. Deng is in Shanghai with his family, and so Mr. Shevardnadze is to fly there to meet with him.
Strains between the two countries' Communist parties existed before China's Communist revolution in 1949, and continued below the surface in the 1950's, when China and the Soviet Union were nominally close friends.
By 1959, Nikita S. Khrushchev, the Soviet leader at the time, regarded China as unpredictable and perhaps dangerous, while Mao Zedong was fiercely critical of the Soviet reconciliation with the United States.
Â 
Deng's Warning in 1960
The rift opened in 1959, when the Soviet Union scrapped a defense agreement under which it was to give China technology relating to an atomic bomb. 
The split became inevitable a year later, when Moscow recalled the 1,390 Soviet specialists working in China. 
By 1969, relations had worsened to the point that the two countries fought brief skirmishes along their border.
Mr. Deng played a role in the split when he represented China at a conference in Moscow in late 1960 and warned that China might be obliged to lead a Communist movement separate from Moscow's. 
Mr. Deng is said to be less friendly toward the Soviet Union than some other leaders, but even he apparently believes that after 30 years it is time to repair relations.
Negotiations between the two countries began again in 1982, but progress was slow because of what China called the three obstacles to normalization: the Soviet military presence in Afghanistan, the Soviet troop concentration along China's border, and the occupation of Cambodia by Vietnam, an ally of the Soviet Union. 
Now each of those problems is on the way to being resolved.

text:

BEFORE the Great Revolution, the Cultural Revolution and the Beijing Spring of 1989, Shanghai was China's most Westernized city, supplying foreigners and Chinese alike with the finest in handmade clothing. 
Somber-hued pajamas and gray serge Mao jackets were not enough to keep Shanghai's custom tailors in business during the succeeding decades, and a number emigrated to Hong Kong, where many of the best tailors are Shanghainese. 
But Shanghai has managed to hold onto its market for silk underwear, hand-embroidered silk blouses and bed and table linens, presumably in part because they are highly transportable and do not depend on multiple custom fittings for perfection. 
And according to the Hong Kong Tourist Association, Hong Kong department stores expect to be able to continue to stock silk underwear from China.
Hong Kong shops, particularly the numerous department stores, blossom with silk underwear of varying degrees of quality and charm. 
The overwhelming majority of the stock is in sets of camisoles and pants. 
Some stores offer a rich variety of shapes, decorative styles ranging from a simple overcast edge to hand embroidery, lacelike drawn work and appliques in flowery or Art Deco-flavored geometric patterns and colors. 
There is usually a smaller selection of pants sold separately, from string bikinis to tap pants. 
Full slips are much harder to find; the selection is usually limited in color and style, and the slips are often not as flattering or as up to date as the camisole sets; once in a while one comes across a real beauty. 
Half slips, too, are scarce and unimaginative, but something basic in a standard length is usually available. 
Bras are almost nonexistent, with the exception of one small independently owned shop.
The fabric of choice these days is crepe-backed satin, sometimes referred to as charmeuse, which has the slicked, glossy surface of satin with the softness and drape of crepe. 
All items should be cut on the bias - on the diagonal grain of the fabric - for give. 
Occasional novelty fabrics crop up, too - figured satins in which the background is satin and a repeated design, of polka dots or hearts, for example, appears in crepe or other textured silks. 
Crepe de chine, a very delicate, lightweight crepe is rarely available.
Workmanship is consistently good. 
Seams should be double sewn; French seams are sewn once with the raw edges on the outside, then sewn again like a regular seam with the first seam enclosed, leaving no raw edges exposed. 
Slips that are entirely handmade, with French seams of tiny hand-sewn stitches and occasional faint pencil marks (guidelines for the embroiderer that come out when washed), might be old stock in the department stores, or found in shops for custom-made goods. 
Embroidery, drawn work and applique are still done by hand. 
Colors range from white and palest champagne, ice blue and pink to classic peach, celadon green and richer tones like garnet, sapphire and emerald as well as, of course, black.
Recently an excellent selection of silk underwear could be found in Hong Kong at the Star House branch of Chinese Arts and Crafts Ltd. 
(weekdays 10 A.M. to 6:30 P.M., Sundays noon to 6 P.M.; telephone 3-674061); it is immediately to the left when you disembark from the Star Ferry on the Tsimshatsui side. 
A bewildering array of camisole sets meets the eye, averaging $35 (at 7.8 Hong Kong dollars to the United States dollar), and adequate dressing room facilities are provided. 
There tends to be a wider selection in small sizes (P, S and M) but L and XL as well if you search for them. 
Pants range from $6.25 to $15.50, depending on the style and amount of embroidery. 
At the lower end of the price range were silk jersey or crepe de chine bikinis. 
Slips were poorly designed and limited in color.
Yue Hwa (301-9 Nathan Road at the corner of Jordan, Yaumatei; 3-840084; 10 A.M. to 9:30 P.M.) had the double disadvantage of a smaller selection and a no-try-on policy for underwear, but some of their camisole sets, in the standard colors of black, white, pink, or peach had unusually beautifully embroidery ($37), and a few entirely hand-sewn crepe de chine slips ($25) with delicate floral embroidery, in a silvery gray-beige as well as black and peach, but in limited sizes.
Next to Nothing (31 Star Ferry Concourse, Central; 5-238704; 10 A.M. to 7 P.M. daily) is a tiny shop inside the Star Ferry terminal (after you pay your fare) on the Hong Kong side. 
Both merchandise and the shop itself are different in style from the mainland-Chinese department stores. 
Mary Reynolds, the proprietor, has all of the things in her shop (mainly crepe-backed satin) manufactured in Hong Kong itself. 
All are 100 percent silk, made with French seams and, on shirt tops, real shell (not plastic) buttons; the garments will not shrink, but lack the hand detailing of the Shanghai-made goods.
The most appealing items are the simple, no-frill slips ($45) and chemises ($32) several inches longer than the camisole tops sold with pants), bra and pants sets ($26; a string bikini alone is $9.50). 
Deluxe nightshirts ($70), pajamas (either single-breasted with shawl collar or double-breasted, $109 or $122) and full-length robe and gown sets ($154) have the same tailored elegance. 
Colors range from white, gray, peach, pale green and black to jewel tones like ruby and emerald before the holidays. 
There are also men's boxer shorts, available in crepe de chine in a few geometric prints ($17).
Â 
NO HEAT, PLEASE
The Chinese make silk underwear to last; seams and fabric hold up well. 
The deepest colors (except black) have a tendency to bleed, and should be washed separately. 
Silk fibers, animal protein like human hair, become frizzled and desiccated by heat. 
So wash by hand in lukewarm water, preferably with real soap powder rather than detergent, and rinse thoroughly to remove all traces of soap. 
Dry away from direct heat and sunlight - never in a dryer - and iron with a medium-warm iron.Â Â Â Â -Â Â A. 
M. S.

text:
ï»¿
AMERICAN visitors to London have always counted on finding and taking home the best in certain kinds of goods: china crafted according to centuries-old tradition, rain gear that will last a lifetime, wool suits tailored to fit royalty. 
They also know that here they will find cashmere clothing of exquisite quality and style.
Nearly all of the cashmere goods sold in London come from Scotland, home of Dawson International, the world's largest importer and processor of raw cashmere. 
Most of Dawson's - and the world's - supplies of raw cashmere, in turn, come from China, and the story of its passage from goat to garment reads like a chapter from an adventure-travel guide.
From the Chinese hinterlands, the rare wool may travel by yak, raft, sampan, even Chinese air force carrier, to the ship that ferries it to Dawson's factory in Bradford, England, where it is checked for quality, washed and dried, then checked again to insure that no long, coarse hairs remain. 
Next it travels to Dawson subsidiary Todd & Duncan in Kinross, Scotland, where it is dyed and spun, then distributed to knitwear manufacturers. 
Finally it arrives in London, where it receives a welcome worthy of any traveler back from an exotic journey.
Cashmere has always been a luxury item. 
During the first half of this millennium in Kashmir (from which cashmere gets its name), it was woven into shawls and scarfs that were bought by merchant traders for the courts of the Roman emperors. 
The shawls, and the wool itself, were introduced to the French fashion world in the 19th century by Empress Eugenie. 
The basic reason for the high cost is that one Kashmir sheep yields only a few ounces to a pound of down fibers in a year, and only a fraction of this raw material ends up as cashmere threads after an elaborate refining process.
Over the past 18 months this cost has risen by an estimated 60 percent, says Michael Gilbert, sales and marketing manager at Todd & Duncan. 
The culprit here, he adds, is the sort of economic, if not social, perestroika that China has undergone in the past few years. 
Now China's cashmere trade, once under total government control, is being run in part by individual entrepreneurs who have bid up prices.
Though inexpensive cashmere clothing can be found, it may not be much of a bargain. 
If you find coarse and discolored hairs in the wool, it was not subjected to the same rigorous sorting and cleaning procedures as fine cashmere. 
Also, cheap cashmere clothing is often knitted with a slacker and longer stitch, causing it to wear quickly. 
Finely knit cashmere, on the other hand, should improve and soften with washing and age.
Cashmere garments come in single-ply, knitted with single strands of cashmere, or multi-ply, knitted with two or more strands twisted together. 
Contrary to a popular belief, ply does not determine quality, merely weight; indeed, faults are harder to hide in single-ply garments.
Intarsia sweaters, those with decorative images and patterns, tend to cost a bit more than unadorned sweaters, and hand-intarsia sweaters a bit more than machine-laid intarsias. 
The designs of hand-intarsias are often sharper, more precise, as the different colors are laid in by hand. 
The more complicated a pattern is and the more colors it has, the more likely it is that it is a hand-intarsia.
In London, cashmere clothing and accessories are sold at department stores like Fortnum & Mason in Piccadilly and Harrods in Knightsbridge. 
Many other shops specialize in cashmere, most stocking well-known brands - such as Scotland's Pringle, Peter Scott and Ballantyne - as well as their own.
THE Scotch House's main store in Knightsbridge is a common first stop for Americans in search of cashmere. 
Popular with the tartan trousers and button-down-collar crowd, the Scotch House stocks classics in unadventurous but popular colors like wine, light gray, navy, red, camel and pastel pink and blue, as well as a few updated styles.
Probably the trendiest of the Scotch House's offerings are found in the second-floor women's cashmere department. 
A red mock-turtleneck mini-dress with a fitted waist sells for $727. 
A knee-length peach dress with shoulder pads, cable trim and scooped neck costs $829. 
One woman's intarsia sweater that, according to Ms. McKenna, ''Americans go mad for'' is a navy-and-red argyle crewneck, selling for $355. 
Also popular are Chanel-style golfer sweaters - gold-buttoned, two-toned boxy cardigans - which sell for $363.
In the men's department on the ground floor, near the domed tartan room, a chunky, eight-ply Aran-stitch pullover sells for $711. 
A crewneck intarsia sweater printed with a camel, navy and green argyle, crisscrossed with golf clubs, costs $553. 
The children's department has basic crewnecks and V-neck pullovers, priced according to size.
Also in Knightsbridge, just off Brompton Road, is the small but elegant Shirin Cashmere boutique, named after the designer whose chic clothes it showcases. 
For Shirin, who has another shop in Paris, there is more to cashmere than twin sets. 
Colors are striking, cuts stylish and prices not for the faint-hearted.
An azure tunic with a stiff white collar and large diamond shapes in fuchsia, khaki, yellow and black sells for $671. 
The collar and sleeves of another azure sweater, this one ribbed and fitted, are trimmed dramatically with jet beads. 
The sweater costs $679; a matching jacket, $987.
In khaki, a miniskirt sells for $314, and a fitted sweater sparkling with red, green and white rhinestones and tiny gold beads costs $569. 
For a mere $103, you can pick up two-toned neckpieces in color combinations like yellow and black or azure and black, which can be worn with plain crewnecks to dress them up.
Like Shirin, N. Peal & Co. specializes in high-fashion cashmere. 
With a design studio in Savile Row and three shops in Piccadilly's swank 19th-century Burlington Arcade, where beadles in top hats and gold-corded coats still stand guard, N. Peal has room for experimental styles. 
It also has shops in New York City and San Francisco, but Americans who buy at its London shops will find not only a better designer selection but better buys - foreign visitors who make purchases in Britain are refunded value-added tax (15 percent of the total value of goods purchased, though in some cases this is offset in part by service charges imposed by the shop) as they leave the country.
At N. Peal, traditionalists will find all the classics; a utilitarian turtleneck sweater costs $292, a sensible V-neck cardigan $371. 
But the shop distinguishes itself with items like an ocher cashmere women's jogging suit - more for apres-jogging - for $932 and mod black leggings for $410. 
For the truly extravagant, there are unlined wraparound dressing gowns with shawl collars for $1,027. 
For men, a green and navy cardigan with leather buttons and a mighty 10-ply sweater each sell for $656.
Also in Burlington Arcade are three Berk shops, with a mix of classic and designer cashmere clothing. 
The shops sometimes run special offers and sales of closeout items and small sizes. 
On one day I visited, some women's single-ply sweaters were on sale for $205.
Definitely not on sale were an elegant red sweater with lace-stitch sleeves and mock turtleneck ($1,077) and snazzy red palazzo pants ($706). 
For those who want to be up to their elbows in cashmere, Berk had charming creamy white lace-stitch evening gloves with silver-and-pearl buttons for $199. 
For men, Berk had blazers, navy with gold buttons, for $940 and a gray V-neck intarsia sweater with a polo scene for $638.
On Regent Street near the Cafe Royal is Estridge of Piccadilly, a small shop that sells mostly predictable classics in standard colors and some intarsias. 
It should be called Sweaters in the Round, for its main room is circular. 
Half the shelves are stacked with lambswool sweaters and the other half with cashmere.
FOR women, a camel-colored golfer cardigan with gold buttons sells for $332. 
The raciest sweater on display was an azure cowl-neck at $261. 
For men, a charcoal, white and black intarsia argyle sweater costs $379, and a royal blue V-neck, $313.
Far from the madness of Piccadilly in quiet, bookish Bloomsbury is Westaway & Westaway, a massive woolen-goods store that sells classics only, leaving designer cashmere to other shops. 
There are some intarsia sweaters but not a shoulder-padded piece in the place.
''You only have to look at the decor,'' says knitwear buyer Julian Sayers, standing in the middle of Westaway's utilitarian basement cashmere department. 
''You wouldn't come here expecting to find cashmere suits. 
You'd come here expecting lower prices.''
And lower prices are what you get - significantly lower if you are willing to forgo better-known labels for Westaway's own. 
For men, a pair of cashmere socks costs $28, a V-neck sweater with a Westaway label $150, a Peter Scott V-neck $189 and a sturdy, four-ply cable-knit sweater $276.
For women, a basic Westaway & Westaway crewneck costs $141, and a Westaway twin set sells for $276. 
A Pringle cable-knit golfer cardigan with gold buttons is $294.

file: SHOPPER_S WORLD_Good Prices, and Caveats, in Hong Kong Pearls.txt
text:
ï»¿
RUBIES blaze, diamonds sparkle, pearls glow from the windows of hundreds of Hong Kong jewelery shops. 
Hong Kong is a serious competitor in the world's jewelry markets, offering values unmatched in New York or in Europe.
But all that glitters here is not gold. 
Fakes proliferate, along with charlatans and second-rate workmanship. 
As in all comparative shopping, it is important to learn something about the kind of jewelry you're going to buy before going if you're going to make any major expenditures, or to shop with someone who is knowledgeable. 
Mistakes in jewelry are expensive.
Because Hong Kong is a free port, its manufacturers pay no import duty on gems or precious metals, enabling them to keep prices low. 
Demand has been so great for Hong Kong jewelry, which at its best can rival the world's finest, that industry publications report a shortage of skilled craftsmen. 
Jewelery is Hong Kong's fifth largest export.
To increase public confidence, the Hong Kong Tourist Association, which has offices in the United States as well as Hong Kong, promises ''prompt rectification of justified complaints'' in disputes involving its members, which display a red ring logo. 
On a recent trip to Hong Kong I shopped for cultured pearls, keeping in mind that, as with gems, quality can double the price. 
Before traveling, I got useful advice on how to evaluate pearls from Clare Richter, a Manhattan pearl importer who has been in business at 680 Fifth Avenue for 39 years.
Pearls, she explained, are valued by luster, color, roundness, size and surface smoothness. 
After looking at several qualities and sizes, I decided that, if I had to sacrifice anything, it would be surface perfection. 
Small dimples are impossible to detect at a distance, whereas luster, size, color and roundness are more discernible.
Europeans like pink-toned pearls, Mrs. Richter said. 
The Chinese favor white ones. 
This is simply a matter of taste, although white pearls are, therefore, more expensive in Hong Kong. 
I shopped for the best buy in large, perfectly round, lustrous white pearls.
Next, I called a knowledgeable Chinese friend who said, ''You must bargain and be very patient to get a good buy. 
Start bargaining for 50 percent less than the jeweler's price. 
Then, walk out and come back later.''
She warned of poor workmanship. 
''If the setting catches in your stockings, don't buy,'' she said.
Hong Kong offers a wide range of jewelry shops, from crammed storefronts to luxurious boutiques. 
Friends in Hong Kong said that the best, and not necessarily the most expensive, tended to be in luxury hotels and upscale malls. 
Finally, I compiled a list of a half-dozen jewelers, recommended by friends, that conformed to these criteria and were members of the Hong Kong Tourist Association.
Once there, my first stop was the Trio Pearl Company, in the Peninsula Hotel, where my mother has been a customer for 30 years. 
Prices are very high, there is no bargaining and the Hong Kong Chinese do not shop here - all reasons to avoid Trio. 
But quality and reliability are excellent. 
Jimmy Chow, one of the owners, delights in talking shop.
Cultured pearls range in size from 1.5 to about 10.5 millimeters (about four-hundreths to a third of an inch), he noted. 
As pearls get larger, their price jumps geometrically. 
A 16-inch strand of 7.5- to 8-millimeter perfectly round pearls cost $1,400 at Trio, while a strand of 8.5- to 9-millimeter pearls cost $4,000. 
A 9.5- to 10-millimeter strand was $9,000.
''You must look at pearls in the daylight against a white background,'' Mr. Chow counseled. 
''Everything under lights in this shop is to my advantage - and against yours.''
We called on Avanti Jewelry in the New World Shopping Mall, the jeweler of my Chinese friend. 
Two strands of 8.5- to 9-millimeter pearls of excellent quality cost $3,700, less than one-half Trio's price. 
Often, two strands can be bought at a cheaper per-strand price, and two strands can be worn long or in two short necklaces. 
A charming antique-style diamond brooch, outlined in emeralds, was priced at $5,600 at Avanti.
The jeweler I preferred, for price, quality, reliability and design, was K. S. Sze & Sons in the Mandarin Hotel, suggested by a Chinese friend in Hong Kong. 
There, gold bow earrings cost $415. 
Similar ones at Tiffany & Company in New York were five times as expensive. 
A 1920's-style bar pin set with diamonds and a two-carat emerald was priced at $5,000. 
Rhonda Lung, who has worked there for 25 years, told me that she did not have the size and quality of pearls I was looking for at that moment, before the Chinese New Year.
Traditionally, jewelers let their stock run down, and prices are lowered as well, just before the Chinese New Year, like our after-Christmas sales. 
Thus, you might find good buys but a smaller selection.
We went to Henry Jewelry, 43-45 Queen's Road Central. 
Eric Lam showed us two magnificent strands of 9- to 9.5-millimeter pearls for $11,000. 
Two strands of slightly less fine pearls were $5,000. 
The only visible differences to me were a few bumpy spots on the less-expensive strands.
Clasps are extra and can double the price of a necklace. 
A beautiful Italian-made, round diamond-studded clasp shaped like a pearl, with .453 carats of diamonds, cost about $1,000 in Hong Kong. 
In New York, the identical item cost $1,500. 
If you bought a double strand of pearls and wanted them fully convertible from one long strand into two fitted chokers, you would require two clasps. 
Thus, you would save $1,000 on the clasps by buying in Hong Kong.
At Falconer Jewelers, in the Regent Hotel Lobby, I saw a lovely strand of pink-hued pearls, 9- to 9.5-millimeters, for $2,700. 
When I returned to New York, I dropped into Falconer's American branch at 1 West 47th Street. 
I was assured that prices were similar to those in Hong Kong. 
But a strand of the same size pearls, of lesser luster, cost $4,000. 
According to Mrs. Richter, a strand of perfectly round 9- to 9.5-millimeter pearls would cost $7,500 at most places in Manhattan.
Richard C. Reuter, a past president of the Cultured Pearl Association of America and president of Leys Christie & Company, a leading cultured pearl importer, cautions against buying in Hong Kong. 
''If you make a mistake 5,000 miles away, there's no way to recover,'' he said, adding that he believes Americans should buy from reputable American jewelers.
Hong Kong jewelry becomes even more of a bargain when you have things custom-made; jewelers will follow a photograph or drawing and will incorporate your own stones. 
A pair of large, 14-carat gold earrings copied from a pair of costume jewelry ones cost $380 from Mrs. Lung at Sze. 
A reasonably priced New York jeweler estimated his cost for making the identical thing at $850, in one to three days.
Since copying is a Hong Kong strength, bringing favorite costume jewelery to be copied takes some of the uncertainty out of having it made from a sketch.
When buying watches, remember that fakes abound and that one should buy only from authorized distributors of the top brands. 
Demand a receipt and the manufacturer's guarantee from the dealer.
I bought a slim gold Rolex man's watch with an alligator band for $1,800. 
After three days, it didn't work. 
My husband took it to Rolex in New York. 
He had the manufacturer's warranty, so Rolex repaired it free of charge. 
The same watch cost twice as much in New York.
Jimmy Chow of Trio Pearl examining a string priced at $54,000; pearl necklace with a gold and diamond clasp, $6,500 at Avanti (pg. 
6); K. S. Sze & Sons, a jeweler in the Mandarin Hotel (Ray Cranbourne/Black Star) (pg. 
24)

file: SHOPPER_S WORLD_In Hong Kong, Antique Silks Evoke a Patrician Past.txt
text:
ï»¿
ANTIQUE Chinese textiles are enjoying a great new popularity. 
One reason is that even casual shoppers quickly become intrigued with these highly personal bits of history -- imagining the aristocratic Chinese woman who slipped her bound foot into a tiny pair of four-inch silk shoes, or picturing the pampered Chinese boy who wore embroidered silk earmuffs, each one sliding over an ear like a glove on a hand.
In Hong Kong, shoppers can choose from a fascinating array of antique textiles, from a pair of child's earmuffs for $30 (prices are in United States currency at 7.8 Hong Kong dollars to one United States dollar) to an embroidered rank badge worn by a Mandarin official that sells for $150 to a magnificent dragon robe costing $12,000.
"I think in the United States you are more likely to see either very costly robes, or little bits of embroidery that are pretty and inexpensive but have no historical importance," said an art expert in Hong Kong who does not sell textiles but follows the market. 
"Here, dealers have a wider range of items for sale, and they pay more attention to the history of the pieces."
Valery M. Garrett, a Hong Kong collector and a lecturer and writer on Chinese textiles, said that while they are sold in New York, London, Taiwan and occasionally Singapore, Hong Kong has the greatest concentration of these pieces.
Generally, items will be less expensive in Hong Kong because there is no sales tax and, because they are antiques, no duty is charged when the textiles are brought back to the United States. 
Most of the pieces for sale date from the Ming (1368-1644) or Ching dynasties (1644-1912), although some earlier pieces are available.
These textiles are interesting works of art that are highly decorative. 
The colorful Chinese robes look striking when mounted inside a large plexiglass frame. 
The antique earmuffs, collars, sleeve bands and other pieces also make handsome decorations, matted in silk and framed, or framed in plexiglass.
Dealers say the rank badges, one of the newly popular collector's items, are sought after because they have an interesting history, are relatively inexpensive (prices begin under $200) and look very handsome when framed. 
"These badges were worn by imperial officials and by the military during earlier dynasties, but the wearing of the badges was really formalized during the Ching dynasty," said Ms. Garrett, who has written a book on the badges, "Mandarin Squares: Mandarins and Their Regalia," published by Oxford University Press.
The nine civil service rank badges for officials used different birds to symbolize ranks, while the military badges featured beasts such as dragons or lions. 
Ms. Garrett said that by the mid-19th century, wealthy merchants began to buy ranks, the way some Westerners purchased European titles.
"You could also buy a rank for an ancestor, so a merchant might buy a high civil service rank for his grandfather, who was really an illiterate farmer," Ms. Garrett said. 
"Then he would commission a portrait that would show the relative in fine robes decorated with his important rank badge."
Though Hong Kong borders on China and the mainland is easily accessible, buyers here say few antique fabric pieces are coming out of China now. 
The damp climate and even the politics of the mainland -- all kinds of antiquities were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution there in the late 1960's -- work against their preservation.
In fact, Ms. Garrett said, "Generally, it has been the Westerners, the foreigners in China, who revered these pieces and collected them."
Today, there are many sources outside the mainland, from sons and daughters of Chinese families who left China to the relatives of missionaries, merchants and other colonial officials who once lived and worked there.
While a number of stores now carry some kind of antique textiles, three highly regarded shops here are particularly worth visiting because their salespeople are adept at explaining the history of the pieces they offer and the symbolism of the designs.
Taken together, the shops offer a good indication of what Hong Kong has to offer. 
At Teresa Coleman Fine Arts, a small, bright gallery on hilly Wyndham Street in central Hong Kong, the long, narrow wooden drawers hold all kinds of treasures: embroidered fan cases (long, thin triangles of silk), delicate women's shoes and small purses, sleeve bands that once encircled the wide sleeves of Chinese robes, rank badges, earmuffs, robes and shawls. 
This shop offers the greatest array of antique textiles in Hong Kong and is a perfect place to visit for an introduction to the market.
A tiny pair of deep pink silk shoes here, dating from about 1870 and made for a woman with bound feet, is barely four inches long. 
Foot binding began as a court custom and as tiny feet became the vogue and were deemed beautiful and erotic, the painful practice eventually spread to all but the poorest classes in China, becoming popular toward the end of the 11th century and continuing into the 1930's. 
Little girls would have their toes broken, bent back and tightly bound between the ages of three and five, so that the foot developed as a small stump.
Belinda Winard, a salesperson at Teresea Coleman, said three and a half inches was considered the ideal length of a bound foot, though that was not always achieved. 
These pink shoes, which sell for $282, are embroidered with blue lotus flowers with a ribbon border of red and gold.
A lovely cream-colored silk collar from the 19th century with a black ribbon border, made to wear with a woman's robe, has four distinct gourd-shaped sections, each embroidered with a garden scene depicting one of the four seasons. 
The collar is priced at $256.
A pair of military rank badges worn by a fifth-rank officer, worked in petit point, with the beast, a bear, appliqued on top, sells for $614. 
The badges, which are the usual size of 12 by 12 inches, have a sky blue background; the bear is done in yellows, greens and reds, his eyes facing a bold red sun. 
The bear stands on the waters and waves pattern, surround by swastikas, ancient symbols for infinite good luck.
The large, airy Plum Blossoms gallery in central Hong Kong's glittering Exchange Square carries a smaller, more expensive collection of Chinese textiles. 
Stephen McGuinness, the managing director, has sold to private collectors and to museums around the world, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. 
Currently, one of his prized pieces is a 10th-century tapestry fragment priced at $120,000. 
The tapestry features prancing lions woven in greens, purples, reds and blues on a black background. 
The rectangular piece of cloth is thought to have come from a robe, he said. 
This piece came from a monastery in Tibet, a country that has recently become an important source of rare old textiles.
"THE monasteries in Tibet were virtual treasure troves, and they are the source for most of the pieces coming from China today," Mr. McGuinness said. 
"Tibet is high and dry and its climate helped preserve textile pieces. 
Its monasteries, which had Chinese wall hangings, silk curtains and robes, had thick stone walls that kept the articles at constant, cool temperatures."
Moreover, he said, the monasteries were repositories for Chinese clothing, because the style-conscious aristocracy donated what were considered unstylish clothes.
A later, less expensive piece is a curtain panel that dates from about 1760. 
It is 10 feet of midnight blue silk and gold brocade, the gold design featuring pairs of dragons chasing a pearl, which was the wish-granting gem of the Chinese. 
That piece is priced at $7,000.
A late-19th-century Chinese tablecloth studded with little round mirrors is embroidered with the Hundred Antiques motif, which includes bronze vases and platters. 
It sells for $800.
"This altar cloth was the kind of thing usually presented to wealthy Chinese at their 60th or 70th birthday party," Mr. McGuinness said. 
"It symbolizes their wealth, their importance."
At Charlotte Horstmann & Gerald Godfrey, one of Asia's most respected antique galleries, there are baskets full of small Chinese purses, earmuffs and sleeve bands in the shop at Ocean Terminal Center on the Kowloon side of the harbor. 
A six-inch royal blue silk purse from the 19th century, with a lovely garden scene, sells for only $19. 
The tiny stitches, each as small as a pinpoint, are known as blind stitches because the close work involved was said to inevitably lead to blindness in the seamstress. 
Hiroko Wilde, a salesperson, explained that for this reason, very young people sewed this stitch because by middle age their eyes failed. 
The work was also known as forbidden stitches because until the late 19th century they were reserved for members of the court.
A pair of cream-colored sleeve bands are decorated with geese, butterflies and peonies in beige, browns and blues, all embroidered in the blind stitch. 
They are mounted in plexiglass frames and priced at $1,126. 
Horstmann's also has what it calls a warehouse of antiques downstairs from the shop, where serious collectors can look at more robes and tapestries.
"Chinese gowns were once regarded as decorative objects to be worn, cut up or remade in another style, but today people have a new respect, a new awareness of their beauty and worth," said Gerald Godfrey.
In a recent visit, the warehouse had a beautiful 19th-century gown in a rich yellow-gold silk. 
Made in China for a Tibetan monk, it was lined in soft sea otter fur. 
The silk woven covered in small stylized bats, which symbolize happiness to the Chinese. 
The robe sells for $7,400.
Â

All three shops are closed on Sunday.
