file: Taiwan_s Mainland Efforts Widen.txt
text:
ï»¿
For four decades, one of the world's most bitter rivalries has magnified the distance between the island of Taiwan and the Chinese mainland 90 miles away. 
While the political conflict remains unresolved, thousands of Taiwan businesses are flooding into China and establishing important economic links.
Most foreign investors were frightened away from China after the bloody suppression of the democracy movement in June. 
But Taiwan investors, who themselves lived for decades under martial law, seemed less alarmed. 
They are continuing to open factories on China's east coast.
''Textiles, electronics, plastics - so far, they have all invested in mainland China factories, but not directly,'' said Kao Chunlee, research department manager at the Taiwan International Securities Corporation.
Direct investments in the mainland are still illegal under Taiwan law, but mom-and-pop enterprises have often ignored the restrictions or evaded them by channeling money through companies in Hong Kong.
It is more awkward for large corporations to ignore the rules, but they, too, have their methods. 
For instance, Tuntex Group, a prominent textile company, is considering a project in China. 
It said that the actual investment would come from an Indonesian entity, but Tuntex acknowledged that it would then build the factory, provide the equipment, install it and run the plant.
Like Tuntex, Taiwan's other large corporations are hoping to move production to the Chinese mainland, and they are forcing the Government to rethink its most fundamental policy toward its longtime enemy across the Taiwan Strait.
Tired of waiting for the Government, more and more of Taiwan's executives have traveled to China in search of an answer to the problems of rising costs at home. 
In response, the Government seems to be easing restrictions on contacts with the mainland.
Taiwan's leaders found themselves in a particularly awkward position in January, when news broke that Y. C. Wang, chairman of Taiwan's largest conglomerate, the Formosa Plastics Group, made a secret trip to the Chinese mainland in October. 
Even by international standards, Formosa Plastics is a titan, with operating revenues last year of $5.8 billion, and Mr. Wang is perhaps the single best-known executive in Taiwan.
Instead of grounding him, as the Government might have done in reaction to a public trip by a less prominent person, the authorities issued new regulations to allow business trips to the mainland.
Â 
Bowing to the Inevitable
''Capital outflow is inevitable,'' said Ma Yingjeou, chairman of the Government's Research, Development and Evaluation Commission. 
''If not to the mainland, they will go to Southeast Asia. 
It's a trend we can't ignore.''
How to accommodate the trend is an extremely sticky problem for the island's leaders, whose one overarching plan has shaped the last four decades of remarkable economic development: strengthen Taiwan against the threat from the mainland. 
Any direct official contact with China is banned, and all trade and investment with the mainland is supposed to go through other places, like Hong Kong.
One stopgap measure the Government settled on was to allow selected groups of Taiwan's declining industries to conduct trade and investment directly with China. 
Later this year, the Ministry of Economic Affairs is expected to issue a list of industries barred from going - presumably those considered crucial to Taiwan's security - while allowing all others to do as they wish.
Â 
Hopes for Direct Routes
Business executives are hoping for direct air or shipping routes from Taiwan to Xiamen, across the Taiwan Strait in Fujian Province, but the Government denies that it has immediate plans for such a step. 
This month, executives from private Taiwan airlines are expected to visit China to discuss the prospects for such links. 
A spokesman for the Chinese Government airline, however, declined to comment on the visit.
Such changes are only incremental, but they are expected to pave the way to closer links between Taiwan's 20 million people and the mainland, just as the Government's decision in 1987 to allow its citizens to visit relatives on the mainland led to greater business links.
As they contemplate Taiwan's economic future, some officials are becoming alarmed at the prospect of growing dependence on China. 
Last year, trade with China through third countries soared above $3 billion, about 30 percent more than 1988, and investment reached about $400 million, according to official statistics from China and Taiwan. 
Other estimates are higher.
Â 
Taiwan Authorities' Concerns
What concerns some officials is that if Taiwan authorities do not control the investment in the mainland, the island could lose important industries to China - as well as profits that would not necessarily be repatriated. 
If Taiwan has not yet improved its industrial base, their argument goes, there will not be any new money-making industries to replace the old industries fleeing to the mainland, and the ultimate result could be harmful to Taiwan.
''China and Taiwan have a political conflict,'' said Hong Chichang, a legislator and member of the opposition group, the Democratic Progressive Party. 
''Although China may not attack Taiwan, China still has the strong intention of taking over Taiwan. 
If we don't limit Taiwan's investment there, this could hurt Taiwan.''
Most investment so far has gone in small amounts, coupled with old equipment, from hundreds of small factories making shoes, purses, umbrellas, textiles and apparel. 
Industry executives said more than half of Taiwan's 1,500 shoe manufacturers, for instance, have already moved operations to the mainland to escape Taiwan's rising costs and strong currency, which appreciated more than 40 percent against the American dollar in 1986 and 1987.
Â 
Effects of Economic Success
The change also in a sense reflects the success of Taiwan's economy: As living standards soared, so did wages, and it no longer was economical to produce labor-intensive products in Taiwan. 
Because of its success, the economy was forced to turn in other directions, and the manufacturers of low-technology products found that to compete they had to transfer production to low-cost countries.
Bankers expect the trade links to grow. 
To capture some of the business, Credit Lyonnais opened a branch last year in the Xiamen special economic zone in Fujian. 
And Citibank is sending a China specialist to Taipei to try to develop that market.
If small manufacturers went to China for survival, the larger Taiwan companies are interested in China to help them remain competitive, and even expand.
Â 
Big Project Seen at Tuntex
Bankers and industry executives said Tuntex had already embarked on a project that could eventually amount to between $100 million and $200 million, which would be the largest single investment so far. 
The company, which would not comment on the amount, said an agreement had not yet been signed.
Other businessmen said Formosa Plastics has plans to invest, but the company said any projects on the mainland were still under investigation.
''I don't think there is any magic -it's driven by economic factors,'' said Chang Liang, president of Shearson-Global Financial Services Company in Taiwan. 
''If somehow they make Fujian an export processing zone and provide good facilities, move the military 10,000 miles away, and if Taiwan would allow direct sailing from here to there, then we're talking big.''
Â 
Advantage for South Korea
Formosa Plastics said its longtime customers in Taiwan had been pressing it to build a plastics factory in China to supply their Fujian offshoots with necessary raw materials. 
Some are buying from other countries, including South Korea, that can ship goods to China more cheaply.
To ship a container from Taiwan to Hong Kong, for instance, Formosa Plastics said it cost $400, and then another $800 for shipping to Fujian; South Korean companies, they argued, can ship the same container from Seoul to Fujian for about $400.
''If we don't go, some company will go to build factories in Fujian to supply our customers,'' said Wang Wenyoung, Y. C. Wang's son and a general manager at Formosa Plastics. 
''Then we lose market, and what happens to Formosa Plastics in the long run?
It's very dangerous.''

file: Taiwan_s New President Signals Major Softening in Relations With China.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Lee Teng-hui said today that he would soon revoke his Government's 40-year-old declaration of a ''Communist rebellion'' on the Chinese mainland, and would immediately restore the civil rights of nearly 30 dissidents, including 2 of the Government's most prominent opponents.
With the announcement, on the day of Mr. Lee's inauguration as the country's first Taiwanese-born President, the Government signaled its intent to end the formal state of war that has existed with the Communist Government since Chiang Kai-shek led the Nationalist retreat to Taiwan.
But the move will also chiefly have a domestic effect, because it will end the Government's reliance on emergency powers that took precedence over Taiwan's Constitution, a much-awaited milestone in the country's transition from authoritarian rule to a multiparty system.
By restoring civil rights for dissidents, Mr. Lee is permitting leaders of the country's fledgling opposition, the Democratic Progressive Party, to run for office.
Dissidents Gather in Protest
Mr. Lee's inauguration came as students and intellectuals pressed their protests for democratic reforms and in opposition to the appointment of Gen. Hau Pei-tsu, Taiwan's hard-line, conservative Defense Secretary as Prime Minister. 
Though General Hau has said he would resign his military posts and has begun wearing business suits instead of his uniform, 5,000 students and shoppers gathered today at the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial to protest against his appointment.
Mr. Lee has served as President since the death two years ago of his predecessor, Chiang Ching-kuo, the son of Chiang Kai-shek. 
In that time, he has presided over rapid changes in Taiwan's relationship with the mainland, including a startling number of Taiwanese business ventures in the People's Republic and a flood of more than a million Taiwanese visitors there.
But so far, those contacts have been indirect - mostly funneled through Hong Kong - because of the Taiwanese Government's insistence on maintaining its policy of ''three no's'' toward China: no direct contact, no negotiation and no compromise on the question of which is the legitimate government of China.
President Lee today appeared to back away from that policy, which has already been eroded by the widening network of business and family contacts across the Straits of Taiwan. 
He said that Taiwan wanted to establish direct ''channels of communication'' with the mainland, calling to ''completely open up academic, cultural, economic, trade, scientific and technological exchange.''
Â 
An Offer Likely to Be Refused
But President Lee presented conditions that Beijing has already said it would reject, including an opening of the Chinese Government's economy, a move toward democratic changes, and negotiations between the two governments on an equal basis. 
Beijing has said it would only negotiate party-to-party, treating Taiwan as a provincial government.
Even though few expect that Mr. Lee's overture will draw the two governments together for talks anytime soon, many saw it as a signal to Beijing of a softening of Taiwan's official line. 
It was a message, a Government official said, ''intended for the next generation of leadership'' in Beijing.
''What the President announced today is a big change,'' said Wu Wen-Cheng, a professor at Soochow University here, ''because it means that for the first time the Government is not insisting on the three no's policy. 
We are moving to a more flexible and pragmatic age.''
Three years ago, Taiwan ended martial law, touching off the beginning of a liberalization move that has in many ways closely paralleled South Korea's. 
But the Government still had broad powers under the ''temporary provisions'' in effect since Chiang Kai-shek led the retreat to Taiwan four decades ago.
Seeming to address the protesters who have been calling for quicker democratic change, Mr. Lee said today that ''if we proceed gradually, one step at a time, our system of party politics will naturally become sounder over time, our foundation of democracy will naturally become firmer, and the time when the country is well-governed and enjoys lasting stabilityI will naturally be in sight.''
Â 
Uncertain Political Climate
Despite the announcements today, President Lee still finds himself in a precarious political position. 
There are disagreements over what form of government Taiwan should adopt, including whether it should have a strong president.
Mr. Lee is being pressed by entrepreneurs who seek greater direct access to mainland China and reformers, including the students, who are seeking to acknowledge the reality of two separate Chinas, something neither government formally acknowledges.
On the other side, Mr. Lee needs the support of the far more conservative mainland-born politicians who dominate the political scene here. 
The legislature and electoral college are dominated by men in their 80's and 90's who represent regions of the mainland that have not been in the Taiwan Government's control for decades. 
Therefore,the Taiwanese themselves are vastly underrepresented in their own government. 
While the ruling Nationalist Party has asked the elderly mainlanders to step aside in the next two years, the party has stopped short of requiring them to do so.
Included among the 10 dissidents whose release was announced today are Shih Ming-teh, who has served 25 years in jail on two separate charges of sedition, most recently for his role in a 1979 anti-Government protest.
Â 
A Pardon Reportedly Refused
Mr. Shih, who has been hospitalized for four years since a hunger strike harmed his health, was reported by Chinese-language papers here to have refused the pardon, saying he wanted President Lee to apologize for the treatment of political prisoners in Taiwan.
Others involved in the 1979 protest, which turned into a riot in Kaohsiung had their rights restored today. 
They can now run for office and resume their work.
Also among those pardoned is Hsu Hsin-liang, perhaps Taiwan's best-known dissident, who spent most of the 1980's in exile in the United States. 
For years Taiwan blocked his return, sometimes sparking clashes between the police and Taiwanese waiting for his arrival at the airport. 
Mr. Hsu was arrested last year after he was caught trying to enter the country, and in December, he was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
Many dissidents accused of trying to undermine the Nationalist Government have been released in the last two years. 
With the latest group Taiwan appears to have relatively few political prisoners left. 
Many received pardons today, including top officials of the opposition Democratic Progress Party who are likely to run for election.

file: TALKING TO HIMSELF, BUT VERY LOUD.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE SECRET SPEECHES OF CHAIRMAN MAO
From the Hundred Flowers to the Great Leap Forward.
Edited by Roderick MacFarquhar,
Timothy Cheek and Eugene Wu.
561 pp. 
Cambridge, Mass.:
The Council on East Asian Studies/
Harvard University Press. 
Paper, $15.
Two Chinese texts for the day: ''It's good to have a bit of disturbance. 
Students making a disturbance is not equivalent to rebellion. 
. . . I say let them agitate to their hearts' content. 
. . . Make the process of the disturbance serve as an educational process, serve as a political course.''
And: ''The People's Liberation Army is for dealing with imperialism, not for dealing with the people. 
The People's Liberation Army is the son of the people. 
How could the son [of the people] ever oppose the father of the people?''
These observations, so poignant in light of the demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in May and June and the subsequent Beijing slaughter, were made by Chairman Mao Zedong 32 years ago, in February and March 1957. 
Mao was trying to get support for what became known as the Hundred Flowers Movement, a broad-based airing of views on the problems facing China, which he believed would dissipate the tensions that had arisen since the suppressions of the Hungarian and Polish risings in 1956. 
The reassurances Mao offered to intellectuals, party workers and students, in many informal speeches and off-the-record discussions, had the effect desired. 
By the spring of 1957 the movement was in full swing, and a deafening chorus of complaints was surfacing in every available forum.
Unfortunately for Mao, the complaints were directed not only at shortcomings in the political, economic and intellectual life of China, but at the Communist Party as an entity, and at Mao himself as an authoritarian and incompetent leader. 
Bitter and chagrined, Mao backed off from his support of the Hundred Flowers and joined forces with more conservative cadres who had never wanted the campaign in the first place. 
By the summer of 1957 the party was conducting a full-fledged ''Anti-Rightist Campaign'' against those who had been most outspoken. 
At least half a million Chinese were punished for having answered the chairman's call.
Mao gave hundreds of informal speeches, containing phrases and thoughts similar to those quoted above, but very few of them made their way into the five volumes of his official collected works. 
For the Mao canon was too important to be left to Mao, and batteries of senior comrades and editors were at hand to tidy up his work, remove indiscretions and try to reach a point of view consistent with whatever the party line of the time happened to be. 
However, for over 30 years Mao was the most revered and most feared person in China, and his words were stored in countless ways by those who heard them - in secret party archives, internal memos, private notebooks, tape-recorded transcripts. 
When the young Red Guards were encouraged by Mao in 1966 and 1967 to lash out at the senior officials in the party, the bureaucracy and the educational establishment, they customarily ransacked the homes and offices of their victims. 
In the course of these raids, much confidential material came to light. 
Some of it was used as evidence against the senior personnel concerned. 
If the words were Mao's, they were transcribed by Red Guards and circulated in various published or informal ways, as evidence - if more was needed - of Mao's creative originality as a thinker. 
Occasionally bits of these collections reached scholars in the west and were translated there; two important examples were the pieces published by Jerome Chen in 1970 as ''Mao Papers'' and by Stuart Schram in ''Mao Tse-tung Unrehearsed'' (1974).
Now, in ''The Secret Speeches of Chairman Mao,'' Roderick MacFarquhar, a professor of government at Harvard University, together with Timothy Cheek of Colorado College and Eugene Wu, the librarian of Harvard's East Asian collection, have edited a remarkably comprehensive collection of these informal Maoist texts. 
Wisely, I think, they have chosen to focus on just two key events in China's recent history, rather than using a scattershot approach that would give a little taste of many topics.
Their focus on The Hundred Flowers Movement of 1957 and the Great Leap Forward of 1958 is particularly apt, because each presents such a different side of Mao's character and his approach to politics. 
The Hundred Flowers texts show Mao almost as a petitioner among his own people, ''a wandering lobbyist,'' as he described himself in a talk to army cadres in Nanjing. 
He is genial, relaxed, sharp in comment but open to give and take. 
The Great Leap Forward texts, by contrast, show a much darker side of his character - angry, impatient, visionary, uninterested in arguments that might have brought him back to earth.
Obviously, these texts, by such a major political actor, collected in such informal ways, raise complex problems of authenticity. 
Mr. Cheek, in an opening essay called ''Textually Speaking,'' confronts this problem directly, reflects on the pros and cons of the authenticity of different texts, collates various speeches from different editions with their variant forms and with official published versions where possible, and concludes the speeches published here are genuinely the words of Mao. 
Mr. Cheek knows the field extremely well and has had the help of an international array of Chinese analysts, along with the bibliographic skills of Mr. Wu (who directs an essay of his own to similar problems), so I accept this judgment, especially since Mr. Cheek is not dogmatic about the works in question and tells us when he has doubts.
As Mr. Cheek nicely phrases it, in Mao's earlier official collected works, Mao himself accepted the need for a ''consensual approach to his own deification,'' whereas in the official collections published by the Communist Party since Mao's death in 1976, one gets a kind of ''academic theology'' in which '' 'scientific,' linguistic and historical analyses seek to contribute to a living faith.''
In contrast, the Red Guard editions that never ceased praising Mao, ''genius'' editions as Mr. Cheek calls them, provide both ''a gold mine of political and psychological data for Mao studies'' and ''a cesspool of run-on sentences, obscure grammar, and simple nonsense for the translator.''
Three other essays by eminent China scholars help to give us a valuable set of contexts in which to read Mao's informal texts. 
Mr. MacFarquhar's opening essay, as one would expect from the leading expert on both the Hundred Flowers Movement and the origins and implementation of the Great Leap Forward, gives an excellent overview of Mao's state of mind as he argued with his senior party colleagues over the need for change and criticism at the center. 
Benjamin I. Schwartz gives a moving analysis of Mao's ''deep anxieties, soaring exaltations, injured pride, deep resentments, and unexamined complacencies.''
Mr. Schwartz concludes that the ideas behind the Great Leap were more central to Mao's being than those of the Hundred Flowers, and presented an apocalyptically utopian view of the fusion of his mind with those of China's masses (as opposed to the bourgeois intellectuals) that represented Mao's ''final spiritual resting place.''
Merle Goldman, looking at the Mao of the late 1950's from the vantage point of her deep familiarity with the manifestations of political and literary dissent in China, explains how the Hundred Flowers slogans sprang from Communist Party intellectual history - specifically, from an earlier 1951 Maoist analysis of the Beijing Opera tradition and from the roots of a historiographical academic debate that Mao refused to pass judgment on. 
She also shows how Mao was enraged with his propaganda chiefs and newspaper editors, and concludes, forcefully, that Mao comes across in these talks as ''contradictory, repetitious, and obsessed.''
What, then, are the central contributions made by this new collection to our knowledge of China?
Perhaps the greatest is that they show us how much frank discussion was in the air during this strange period of Chinese history, and how difficult it sometimes was for Mao to get what he wanted despite his immense prestige. 
The final impression is that Mao felt so far above the fray, even while so grubbily absorbed in it, that he ceased to have any clear sense of the country's terrible suffering. 
People really had become ciphers to him, mere details on the way to some ultimate colossal goal. 
''In the past during the revolution numerous people died without asking anything in return. 
Why can't it be like that now?''
Mao asked his senior colleagues in August 1958 as he discussed the Great Leap. 
Maybe they should think of letting the peasants have two days' rest a month, he ruminated a little later, but then at once modified the thought: ''during the busy season, rest a little less,'' he said, and eat and sleep at the work site too, to save precious time. 
''This point should be written in the documents but not be talked about too much,'' he told his colleagues. 
Sometimes Mao's thoughts strayed to stranger zones: to great wide roads in every commune with no trees on their verges so that every road would be an airport; or to a world of Chinese so healthy that physicians would have no patients, and could go till the fields and do research.
Almost everything Mao was saying in 1957 was something students and workers wanted to discuss with their own Government in 1989. 
Perhaps most ironically, it was presumably Hu Yaobang, then directing the Communist Youth League, who tried to give Mao accurate information on student unrest. 
Hu Yaobang's own death in April 1989 was the initial spark that culminated in the June tragedy, even though the deeper causes had been smoldering a long time. 
As Mr. MacFarquhar says, this 1989 Tiananmen crisis ''would almost certainly have the same numbing effect on China's intellectual elite as the Anti-Rightist Campaign, and could deter rural and urban entrepreneurs and foreign investors.''
As we can now see, thanks to these texts, the paradoxes at the center of this Government were paradoxes that lay also at the heart of Mao's being. 
Or, as Mr. Schwartz puts it so beautifully in his essay: ''In the end, on the level of his final abstract vision, Chairman Mao may be not so much 'alone with the masses' as alone with himself.''
Â 
THE CHAIRMAN, UNEDITED
One added richness in this strange and absorbing book is that if we so choose we can take any one of Mao's off-the-cuff draft speeches and then see how it compares with the final party version (if there is one). 
To do this in the case of one of Mao's most famous speeches, ''On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People,'' is a fascinating exercise. 
The history of this speech is more than usually devious, since Mao initially delivered it on Feb. 
27, 1957, to a large group of nonparty intellectuals and bureaucrats, whom he was trying to persuade to join in the Hundred Flowers Campaign. 
It was not published at the time, to Mao's anger. 
But after he himself swung against the protesters, he apparently acquiesced in the publication of a totally revised version in The People's Daily of Peking on June 19, 1957. 
This latter version was doctored to make it appear that Mao wanted the Hundred Flowers Campaign to serve as a vehicle of class struggle, and that he anticipated trouble from the start.
The ''speaking notes'' for the original speech that have now surfaced bear almost no relation at all to the mood or content of the dogmatic and tedious June 19 version. 
The newly discovered version occupies 58 pages of ''The Secret Speeches of Chairman Mao,'' and there is a surprise on nearly every page. 
Some examples must serve for the whole: Mao's frank discussion of the troubles in Poland and Hungary, his sense that the people wanted two news agencies in competition with each other, his analysis of the way China's national bourgeoisie is not an enemy, his frank announcement that 770,000 Chinese were killed in the mass campaigns of 1950 to 1954, his portrayal of the constructive role of student protests in modern Chinese history, his analysis of problems in China's cooperatives and his estimate that in some areas 15 percent of the households were ''lacking grain,'' his mention that many Chinese now feel ''disgust with Marxism.''
Among other important things Mao discussed in February that never made it to the June text were the urgent need for birth control in China, the fact that 40 percent of school-age children had no schools to go to, and the fact that during 1956 China had been troubled by a mass of protests and strikes: 7,000 students protesting in 28 different cities, according to Communist Youth League figures, and 50 strikes conducted by urban workers, some involving over 1,000 workers, according to statistics Mao admitted were still incomplete.
Â 
JONATHAN D. SPENCE

file: Talks in Taiwan Urge a Popular Presidential Vote.txt
text:
ï»¿
After five days of strenuous national debate, a national conference on this island's future concluded today with a call for popular presidential elections.
The endorsement of popular elections by the 150 delegates seemed to give a considerable lift to proposals that would restructure Taiwan's political system along much more democratic lines in coming years. 
President Lee Teng-hui had chosen all the delegates and given them a mandate to grapple with the intensely emotional question of Taiwan's future.
It was the first time that the Government and its opponents had openly discussed on a public stage some critical questions about Taiwan's future. 
They included: Should the nation revise its Constitution or draw up a completely new one?
Should the Government adopt a presidential or parliamentary system?
How should the 20 million people on Taiwan build economic links with 1.1 billion Chinese on the mainland?
''This is a fantastic thing,'' said Kang Ning-hsiang, a prominent member of the Democratic Progressive Party, the opposition group. 
''To bring all these people together to talk about our future is the greatest political event.''
With bells ringing every so often to signal the end of a speaker's floor time, delegates stood up one by one on podiums to state their views on various issues. 
The conference delegates included a student, a Mongolian, a Tibetan, a handful of previously jailed dissidents, and Chinese scholars from the United States.
The conference has no legal authority, and so it is not clear how their conclusions will be carried out.
''Everyone feels a little funny,'' said Jaw Shau-kong, a legislator from the governing Nationalist Party and a delegate to the conference. 
''This is outside the legal system.''
The agreement on popular presidential elections was the most important decision at the conference. 
Currently, the President is elected through the National Assembly, an electoral college that is made up mostly of elderly men, who purport to represent constituencies on mainland China.
Â 
Charter Revision Proposed
While they agreed on presidential elections, delegates were divided on whether citizens should elect the President through an electoral college or bypass that step and hold direct elections.
The delegates also debated ways to restructure the island's legislature, which has passed only one minor law in its current session, which ends in a few weeks. 
President Lee and other Nationalist leaders have indicated that Taiwan needs a constitutional overhaul, but that that may not be easy to achieve.
In one move that will make Parliament more democratic, Taiwan's highest court ruled recently that those aging legislators - unelected in decades - must resign by the end of next year. 
Opposition members want an earlier deadline.
President Lee said in March that he would revoke within about a year the Government's 40-year-old declaration of ''Communist rebellion'' on mainland China. 
Changing that condition, which vests the President with special powers, would require altering Taiwan's Constitution, and there was no consensus on how to revise it.
The opposition party is demanding that the Government scrap the Constitution and write a new one. 
And while the party's voice has been more influential than its 30,000 membership would suggest, it is not clear that it has much support on this issue.
Still, delegates agreed that constitutional changes are inevitable and some hoped the conference would deepen the sense of urgency.
''We can keep the momentum of reform, and not just of the Constitution,'' said Ma Ying-jeou, a Nationalist Party delegate and Cabinet-level official. 
''The party structure has to be democratized to cope with new constitutional democracy.''
Probably the most delicate and emotional issue of the conference focused on Taiwan's policy toward mainland China. 
During the last couple of years, relations between China and Taiwan have warmed dramatically.

text:
ï»¿
HONG KONG
By Jan Morris.
Illustrated. 359 pp. 
New York: Random House. 
$19.95.
Fewer than nine years remain before Hong Kong will cease to exist as a British colony and become part of the People's Republic of China.
Never before have several million people been handed over to Communism. 
Jan Morris's unarticulated question in ''Hong Kong'' is: will Hong Kong continue to flourish as a bastion of capitalism, one of the world's leading financial centers, or will it slowly degenerate, turning into just another seedy and tacky Chinese city?
The story of Hong Kong, as Ms. Morris tells it, is full of drama, beginning with its birth as a colony a century and a half ago as the result of an encounter between the two dominant powers of the day, the Manchu dynasty, then in an advanced state of decline, and the expansionist British empire, which had yet to reach its zenith.
The colony was wrested from China in stages: first Hong Kong island was ceded in the aftermath of the Opium War in 1842; next, the Kowloon peninsula was seized in 1860; and finally, in 1898, the New Territories (the hinterland of the penisula and the rocks and islands immediately around Hong Kong) were added, enlarging tenfold the colony's area.
However, the last treaty contained the seeds of the colony's destruction, for instead of taking the land outright, Britain obtained a 99-year ''lease'' for which it did not pay any rent. 
No doubt, at the time, 99 years appeared to be close to eternity.
In the early 1980's, as the deadline loomed closer, the British asked for an extension and were sternly rebuffed. 
In 1984, Britain agreed to return the colony to China on July 1, 1997, along with its five and a half million people.
Ms. Morris, a historian, travel writer and author of the ''Pax Britannica'' trilogy, is fascinated by the story of Hong Kong, the last major colony not only of Britain but of any of the former colonial powers of Europe. 
She approaches the subject of Hong Kong ''as a student of British imperialism.''
She sets herself the task of portraying ''the last of the great British colonies as it is in its last years.''
She does a superb job.
Ms. Morris confesses that as recently as 1982 her sentiments toward Hong Kong were characterized by ''unmitigated dislike.''
Now, however, she finds a sense of poignancy as the territory faces a future that can be described, at best, as uncertain.
Ms. Morris alternates chapters of themes or analysis with chapters of historical description. 
She lovingly describes the historical setting, painting in broad strokes the colony's rise from a settlement of a few thousand fishermen to the present.
In the early years, she recounts, ''the Chinese Secretary was a Pomeranian clergyman, the Treasurer a former ship's mate, while in 1849 the Registrar-General dropped everything and joined the Gold Rush to California.''
Today, she says, tiny Hong Kong is the world's largest exporter of textiles, toys and watches. 
It has more Rolls-Royces per capita than any country in the world, makes more films per year than Hollywood and the pay of the Governor of Hong Kong is more than double that of the British Prime Minister.
One of the book's best historical chapters is on the Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945. 
The Japanese tried to eradicate all vestiges of the British presence, to the extent of changing the name of the Peninsula Hotel to the Toa, of Jimmy's Kitchen to the Sai Mun Cafe and of Queen's Road to Nakameiji-dori.
Many in the Chinese community were compromised, Ms. Morris says. 
Some of the best-known Chinese citizens joined Japanese puppet bodies, such as the Rehabilitation Advisory Committee, the Chinese Representative Council and the Chinese Cooperative Council. 
''Some Chinese'' she writes, ''at least in the beginning, supported the Japanese simply as fellow Asians.''
But she concludes that, in general, ''they were not traitorous.''
For more than a century Hong Kong was essentially a transient community, offering haven for refugees from China who either returned home when things quieted down or who used the colony as a springboard from which to seek greener pastures abroad.
Only in 1981 did the census show a majority of the people actually born in Hong Kong. 
''Only recently,'' says Ms. Morris, ''has the emergence of a new, educated Chinese middle class, born and bred in the colony, made one feel that Hong Kong is approaching some kind of social equilibrium, becoming a real, balanced city - and with 1997 closing fast, perhaps it is too late.''
Only history will tell whether it is too late. 
So far, the signs are not good. 
Earlier this month, a China-appointed committee responsible for drafting the Basic Law that will govern Hong Kong after 1997 rejected demands for greater democracy and imposed additional hurdles to make universal suffrage unlikely even in the next generation.

By SUSAN MERNITd wonders of Oriental cuisine, bao bing, a simple fruit dessert, has long stood out as one of the most ubiquitous in Asia. 
Yet it is almost unknown in the West.
A sweetened froth of seasonal fresh fruit and finely shaved ice topped with flavored sugar syrup and condensed milk, bao bing, or bing, has always been immensely popular throughout Asia. 
Now it is beginning to gain popularity in the United States as more Asians settle in this country.
Made with regional fruits like mangoes, litchis and rambutans, bao bing is ''Asia's answer to the ice-cream soda,'' said Gim Yee, owner of the Bamboo Garden, a restaurant in New York's Chinatown. 
In Taiwan, Malaysia, China and Vietnam, bao bing stalls do a brisk business; in Hong Kong, bakeries sell bao bing along with custard eclairs and pork bao.
Bao bing (pronounced bow-BING) can be traced back more than 1,000 years. 
According to Reay Tanahil, the author of ''Food in History'' (Stein & Day, 1973), bao bing, which means ''shaved ice,'' was eaten in China as early as the seventh century A.D. In 1972, when President Richard M. Nixon made his first visit to Beijing, bao bing was served during state dinners with Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai.
Not surprisingly, the dessert has evolved over the years. 
Nina Simmonds, the author of ''Classical Chinese Cooking'' (Houghton, Mifflin, 1982), said modern bao bing reflected westernization in Asian cuisine.
''The bao bing Asians eat today uses condensed milk and sweeter syrups, and is often served in tall paper containers,'' she said. 
''Classical bing skips the condensed milk, uses sugarcane juice and is served in a shallow bowl.''
Today, restaurants in Asian communities across the United States offer bao bing on their menus. 
Alfred Shu, owner of Memories of China, a Chicago restaurant, said bao bing is as popular with Asians in the United States as it is in Taiwan or Hong Kong.
Ten years ago, only one restaurant in New York's Chinatown sold bing. 
Today, more than 40 do. 
In Elmhurst and Flushing, Queens, and the Bay Ridge section of Brooklyn, restaurants catering to Asians make and sell bing, as do those in other large cities with Asian communities.
At the Bamboo Garden, at 22A Bowery between Pell and Bayard Streets in Manhattan, Mr. Yee and his staff sell 40 to 100 orders of bao bing a day. 
Mr. Yee, who was reared in New York, said he began to serve it only after customers began to request it. 
''A lot of the new immigrants, especially people from Hong Kong, really like bings,'' he said.
But Asian and Western tastes can differ. 
Red bean and custard are two of the most popular flavors in Taiwan, said Tony King, director of the China Council of the Asia Society in New York, while in New York, watermelon and litchi are favorites. 
Henry Hugh, a chef for a Manhattan investment house from Flushing, Queens, said many of his Asian-born friends prefer Malaysian-style bing, made with corn, green taro gelatin, starch beans and strawberry syrup.
Fortunately, there are many varieties of bao bing that please Western palates. 
Mango, litchi, mixed fruit and watermelon bing all have their Western devotees. 
''I have litchi bing at least once every two weeks,'' said Spencer Jarrett, an audio-visual producer based in New York. 
''I go to Maria's or Yuen Yuen Tea Parlor and get one to take out.''
There are signs that bao bing is gaining favor with an increasing number of Westerners. 
The Stony Wok, a Chinese restaurant in Flushing, Queens, has been serving bao bing to its customers every spring and summer for five years. 
The manager, Pai Kang, said: ''At first, customers ordered the ices out of curiosity, but then, they taste them and get hooked. 
Now, many people order them every time they come in.''

text:

ALMOST A REVOLUTION
By Shen Tong with Marianne Yen.
Illustrated. 342 pp. 
Boston:
Houghton Mifflin Company.
$19.95.
THIS account by the Beijing student leader Shen Tong is one of the first of an expected flood of memoirs about China's democracy movement in the spring of 1989. 
This deluge marks a major setback for the Chinese Government's longstanding attempt to erase the Chinese people's historical memory. 
It is clear that Chinese intellectuals are no longer so willing to participate in a conspiracy of silence to save face for the motherland they love so painfully. 
For this reason alone, the appearance of "Almost a Revolution," written with the help of Marianne Yen, a former Washington Post reporter, is cause for celebration.
While the book is frustratingly thin on description and analysis of the movement itself, it does make three contributions: it is one of the first portrayals of the political shaping of a member of the post-Red Guard generation of activists; it provides an insider's record of the day-to-day events of the spring of 1989 (Mr. Shen was an organizer of the "dialogue delegation" whose goal was to negotiate with the Government); and it describes the slaughter at Changan Avenue and Xidan, the site of one of the worst blood baths of the June 4 crackdown, which also happened to be the doorstep of Mr. Shen's home.
The first half of the book, "Beginnings," provides a rebuttal to those who are concerned that members of China's new generation want to surrender themselves to materialism, self-interest and indifference to their country's pain. 
True, compared with the tumultuous, bitter childhoods of the members of China's Red Guard, the so-called lost generation, who sacrificed everything for a revolution that betrayed them, Shen Tong's youth in China's well-supplied capital was easy. 
It consisted of a happy progression of girlfriends, adventure and comparatively free access to information. 
Indeed, he describes himself as a popular and precocious youngster who short-circuited the neighborhood's electrical lines with his science experiments and renounced "women" at the age of 10 for all the trouble they caused him.
Yet because Shen Tong grew up a stone's throw from Tiananmen Square, China's symbolic political center, and was the child of thoughtful intellectuals, he could not help being exposed to deeper concerns. 
He reports clear memories of the 1976 Tiananmen incident, a brutal suppression of an antitotalitarian demonstration, which occurred when he was in first grade: his parents, to avoid being caught with the notebooks in which they had laboriously copied democratic poems and appeals posted in the square, dissolved the pages in water. 
In the winter of 1978-79, Shen Tong remembers, his father often took him to visit Democracy Wall, which was a five-minute walk from home. 
He recalls, "I watched in amazement as people stood before sheets of white paper pasted on the wall, biting their index fingers to write and, whenever the blood ran dry, biting their fingers again so they could continue writing."
In high school, Shen Tong became involved in the sale of the iconoclastic experimental writings of the lost generation's "misty poets," and began to read banned Hong Kong magazines, in which he found the transcripts of the defense of the famous dissident Wei Jingsheng. 
He was fortunate to attend the prestigious Beijing University during the 1980's, "probably the years when the Chinese people enjoyed the most intellectual freedom they had had since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949."
It is clear from his book that Shen Tong and his fellow students absorbed many of the lessons of the recent tragic past, particularly the idea that blind obedience is dangerous. 
But unlike their parents, they were arrogant and rebellious: "We thought of ourselves as the smartest students in the country and believed there was nothing we couldn't do. 
. . . We were brash, willful, and dared to have our own thoughts and to speak our own minds."
However, the students' motivations for their activism in the spring of 1989 are as fuzzy in Mr. Shen's account as they were in life; nowhere does he mention the ghastly dormitory and study conditions, now widely believed to have been a primary source of student discontent, nor does he recognize the irony that, despite their cries for democracy, one of the student movement's primary demands was to gain recognition from the very Government it was criticizing.
The second half of the book, "Movement," is an inside view of meetings, speeches, demands, strategies, factionalism, euphoria and defeat. 
Unlike the engaging account of Mr. Shen's youth, this section is often tedious. 
Nevertheless, his recital of the now-familiar events of that dramatic spring is poignant: the April 15 death of the scapegoated party leader Hu Yaobang; the intoxicating early marches; the April 26 editorial in The People's Daily denouncing the demonstrations; the euphoric rally of May 4 and the reform-minded party leader Zhao Ziyang's sympathetic speech to the Asian Development Bank; Mikhail Gorbachev's visit on May 15; Mr. Zhao's apologetic visit to the hunger strikers on May 19; the May 20 declaration of martial law; the emotionally charged waiting time before the clearing of the square; and the massacre itself.
IT has been China's fate to swing back and forth between near-total repression and an outpouring of energy and expression that ends in chaos and blood. 
In 1989, the pattern recurred. 
"I felt that we had started a car that was now driving off in a dangerous direction," writes Mr. Shen. "We all felt powerless to do anything."
The "dialogue delegation" he led failed to produce meaningful negotiations. 
Despite repeated attempts by some student leaders and older intellectuals to rein in the movement, the more radical approach of the hunger strikers came to dominate the protest. 
The student leadership became ridden with factions. 
And a desire for self-immolation seemed to be in the air. 
That this "dare to die" student movement led to the downfall of Zhao Ziyang's reformers makes the deaths of the protesters particularly tragic.
Throughout his account of the democracy movement, Shen Tong follows a subtheme, his parents' quandary: although they had an even deeper understanding of the price a country pays for totalitarianism than he did, their fear for their son's safety outweighed their wishes to support him in his protests. 
Mr. Shen recalls his sister begging him to withdraw from the movement and reminding him to pick up his passport and apply for a United States visa. 
And in the final days of the demonstrations, Mr. Shen writes, he was too busy with politics to spend time at his dying father's bedside.
Finally comes the description of Bloody Sunday. 
Leaving the university, Mr. Shen headed toward Tiananmen Square and then took refuge at home as the violence unfolded. 
In the doorway, a man bled to death before his eyes. 
As the tanks rolled forward, Mr. Shen records flatly, "it was odd to see people picking up anything, even a little pebble, and throwing it at the metal monsters coming toward us."
He went into the streets and pleaded with soldiers not to fire; the face of a young woman standing next to him was blown off. 
A soldier was stoned to death. 
A young man was shot to pieces against a white fence, and "a piece of his skull landed on the gold metal ball on top of the railing."
Shen Tong makes no attempt here to participate in the debate on casualty figures. 
Rather, his earnest record is an important, if inconclusive, contribution to China's newly discovered historical memory.

WHEN an Asian wakes up in the morning and wants to eat the breakfast of his dreams (and of his ancestors), it's usually not bacon and eggs.
A Chinese reaches for a bowl of porridge of soybeans or rice, a Japanese sips miso-thickened broth and a Korean might eat beef dumplings in broth. 
On the side are little dishes of pickled cabbage, lettuce and radish. 
Breakfast, washed down by tea, is savory, not sweet; seldom greasy, and to an Asian palate tasty. 
It is a meal thousands of years old.
But to the Western palate, an Asian breakfast is an acquired taste.
After 24 years of marriage, Stuart Bloch, a lawyer in Washington, is still astonished by what his Chinese-born wife, Julia Chang Bloch, has for breakfast. 
Watching Mrs. Bloch, the American Ambassador to Nepal, eat Chinese rice soup with pickled lettuce and slivers of dried pork, he said, "I wouldn't touch that stuff with a 10-foot pole."
But by noon, he was ready for Chinese food.
Theodore Bestor, an associate professor of anthropology at Columbia University and a specialist in Japanese culture, said: "It's a personal observation, but people's food preferences are the least flexible parts of their culture. 
People will experiment with dress and child rearing, but with food, when they haven't woken up yet, they want something familiar."
In Manhattan, at the Essex House Hotel Nikko, Japanese guests order a foreign -- Western, that is -- breakfast on the first morning of their visit, said Kazunobi Takita, the assistant general manager. 
"Then on the second day their ethnicity comes out, and they order a Japanese breakfast," he said. 
"They must talk to the rice. 
They cannot talk to the bread."
In Manhattan, a traditional Japanese breakfast is also served at the Plaza, Hilton, Marriott Marquis and Rihga Royal hotels, as well as at Menchanko-Tei, a restaurant.
What Japanese eat in restaurants and in their homes, whether in New Rochelle, N.Y., or in Tokyo, is what their ancestors ate at least as far back as the seventh century, said Elizabeth Andoh, an anthropologist and cookbook author whose books include "An Ocean of Flavor: The Japanese Way With Fish and Seafood" (Morrow, 1988). 
The typical breakfast, she said, is soup, rice and pickles. 
"Anything you have in addition, like grilled fish, relates to circumstance -- wealth or geography -- rather than an era," Ms. Andoh said.
The soup is usually miso based, and may include cubes of soft bean curd, slivered seaweed and scallions. 
The pickles include white radish, cucumber, cabbage, seaweed and carrots.
Beyond those basics, Essex House also serves grilled salmon; a dumpling filled with minced carrots, seaweed and fish cake, and side dishes of Japanese omelet, seaweed flavored with sesame oil, and julienne strips of burdock and carrot.
At Menchanko-Tei, the basic dishes are augmented with grilled mackerel and fresh bean curd topped with shaved bonito flakes and sprinkled with soy sauce. 
On the side is a tiny packet of five slices of seaweed to wrap around rice and pickles.
China has two traditional breakfasts, northern and southern, dictated by local agriculture. 
The breakfast of northern China, where soybeans and wheat grow, is eaten in Beijing, Shanghai, Taiwan and, authenticity intact, in Flushing, Queens.
On a recent Sunday morning, Chinese families were lined up at the People's People Restaurant in Flushing to eat a northern Chinese breakfast, served Tuesday through Sunday. 
The restaurant, which seats 90, was packed. 
Most of the patrons were from Taiwan; it was for them that Chung King, the owner, opened the restaurant in November.
Until he opened his restaurant, Mr. King said, "they ate Western breakfasts, fried a couple of eggs, or ate dim sum."
(Dim sum is southern Chinese steamed, boiled and fried dumplings and buns.) But what they really wanted, Mr. King said, was soy-milk soup. 
And so each day his chef makes 100 gallons of it.
The bowls of soy-milk soup being served at People's People had flecks of white soybean curds drifting in a broth whose surface was dappled with floating droplets of hot chili oil. 
An assortment of fried and baked breads was served alongside.
What looked like a bread-and-bread sandwich was a deep-fried nonsweet cruller tucked in a toasted envelope of bread sprinkled with sesame seeds. 
The crisp sesame bread was flaky, while the cruller was soft, airy and faintly chewy inside and crisp outside. 
It is best piping hot.
There was su bing, flaky buns filled with slivered cooked white radish, or with scallions lightly sauteed in lard. 
A fried bun contained chives and scrambled eggs; other buns had minced pork and cabbage. 
The food, Mr. King said, can be made at home, but making it is time consuming.
Peter Kwong, the author of "The New Chinatowns" (Hill & Wang, 1987), said that "in China, you dash out, and stop at shops, and eat it on the way to work."
The southern Chinese counterpart of soy-milk soup is congee or jook, a soup made by cooking rice for two hours, until the grains amalgamate into the broth. 
Because rice is scarce in the north, the soup there is served thin, but in the south, where rice is plentiful, the jook is thick.
Jook is to the southern Chinese as chicken broth is to Jews. 
"Jook is truly ancient, and dates at least to 171 B.C.," said Bruce Cost, the chef and owner of the Monsoon restaurant in San Francisco, and the author of "Bruce Cost's Asian Ingredients" (Morrow, 1988). 
He added this somewhat bland soup, sometimes cooked with chicken broth, is a medium in which the Chinese boil bits of beef, chicken and pork balls. 
Some people eat the jook by itself; some with side dishes of peanuts, pickled lettuce or slivered ginger.
"What's great is that even in one simple little meal, you get different little taste sensations," said Nina Simonds, the author of "China's Food" (HarperCollins 1991).
Although dim sum is part of a southern Chinese breakfast, the starting point is jook, served at tea parlors from huge cauldrons on rolling carts. 
It is made plain, but diners add to it tiny balls of fish, pork or beef; slivers of beef or chicken, or sliced preserved duck egg. 
Condiments to sprinkle on top include flakes of dried preserved pork, pickled lettuce, pickled cucumber and finely slivered scallions and ginger. 
By 11 A.M. the jook is usually sold out, confirming its place as a breakfast food.
In Manhattan, devotees of jook can be found at the two Big Wong restaurants in Chinatown, where people line up five deep at the takeout counters, shouting out their orders. 
The jook is offered with preserved duck egg as well as pork, chicken and beef balls. 
Long twists of fried dough are eaten with the jook, either cut up and dropped into the bowl, or on the side.
Although the Chinese and Japanese have special breakfast food, Koreans do not. 
"We eat the same food for breakfast, lunch and dinner," said Young Choe, the manager of Woo Chon Restaurant in Manhattan, which is open 24 hours a day. 
What makes Korean meals special is not the foods, but the ritual, where family hierarchy prevails. 
"The eldest person takes the first dish," Mr. Choe said, "and then it's passed."
The meal can be as simple as a bowl of steamed rice, a side dish of pickles and a bowl of beef broth. 
Or it can be more elaborate, with dumplings floating in the broth, and many little dishes of pickled vegetables.
"If you have breakfast in a Korean inn, you get the rice, the soup, a bit of fish, often grilled, and as many side dishes as people have the imagination to give you," said Laurel Kendall, the associate curator of Asian ethnographic collections at the American Museum of Natural History in Manhattan. 
In Korean kim chi, or pickles, she said, "there are pickled cabbage and, in the summer, pickled cucumbers, little red beans preserved in sugar and soy, and pickled bean sprouts."
Not to mention radish, bell flower, carrots and seaweed. 
Then there are the soups, which come with beef or pheasant dumplings, beef ribs, crab, clams or fish.
But when Mr. Choe eats a Korean breakfast, he eats an austere dish, seol rong tang, a beef broth with thin wheat noodles and rice. 
Why?
"It is very gentle and soothing," he said.

A series of earthquakes rattled northern China late Wednesday and early today, killing at least 18 people and flattening about 8,000 houses in a largely rural area, the authorities said.
Officials of the State Seismological Bureau said the quakes were not related to the tremor in Northern California on Tuesday.
The bureau said that five tremors, registering up to 6.0 on the Richter scale, shook an area along the Shanxi-Hebei provincial border and that at least 28 people had been injured.
The first quake, measuring 5.7, was felt in Beijing, about 135 miles to the east, but there were no reports of injuries or damage in the capital.

text:
ï»¿
In recent weeks Chinese have learned just how effectively the Government can keep an eye on each one of them.
For a long time, large and small cameras have been fixtures on lampposts and traffic lights in Tiananmen Square and in areas like Government and diplomatic compounds. 
And many foreigners and some Chinese presume that their telephones are tapped.
But as the Communist society in recent years seemed to embrace a greater pluralism and freedom of movement, Chinese and foreign visitors alike began to ignore the mechanical eyes in the street and went about with their ordinary relatively free-spirited activities.
Now, as the Government public security machine is propelled into motion throughout the country, ordinary Chinese are beginning to see how efficiently the authorities can maintain surveillance over them. 
#13 Arrested as Spies for Taiwan Today, for example, the television announced that the Chinese security authorities had arrested 13 Chinese as spies for Taiwan. 
It showed extensive film clips of some of them carrying out their suspected illicit activities all over China.
Some of them were trailed on Tiananmen Square conversing with workers and bystanders, the heads of the suspects barely visible in the sea of faces. 
Occasional sun spots on the film suggested that the cameraman was in a car nearby.
In another instance, the midriff of a suspect was filmed apparently with a camera from the pocket of a security agent. 
Other angles suggested the security agent, possibly posing as a photojournalist, filmed shots with a video camera on Tiananmen Square.
Of course, it is expected that security agents monitor suspected spies. 
But the television news programs have made clear that security officials have also been busy filming student leaders. 
When one student leader had a meal at a Beijing hotel recently, for instance, three video cameras were apparently used to produce secret footage that was later shown on television.
The Government also seems to have a large collection of footage of the entire democracy movement, which has enabled it to present a visual account of its version of events on June 4, when soldiers gunned down unarmed civilians.
Ordinary Chinese are discovering that even as hundreds of thousands of citizens filled the area of the square during April and May to watch pro-democracy demonstrators parade with their banners, the Government security apparatus could virtually single out a casual conversation or hearty exchange of political views.
Â 
Journalists Photographed
Throughout the two months of the democracy movement, many foreign journalists noticed men, presumably security agents or policemen, snapping pictures of them, scribbling notes about them or taping their conversations.
When the first posters went up at Beijing University and other schools in the capital, it was common to see people reading the texts of posters into tape recorders. 
Some were obviously students, but others looked older and would not say who they were when approached.
After students protested in front of the Communist Party headquarters, where China's leaders live and work, senior officials and their families saw videotapes of the dramatic pushing and shoving match between students and soldiers at the doorstep to the walled-in compound, said a Chinese who saw the film clips.
When outspoken citizens mounted their soap boxes on Tiananmen Square to tell the crowd of their views on democracy, it was probably clear to them that their public speeches were noted by the authorities. 
But beyond that, it seems as though those speeches were documented and filed into dossiers on each of the citizens.
Now, their words have come to haunt the speakers, as recent articles in the official press have quoted from some of those earlier speeches. 
A long article in Beijing Daily relayed parts of a speech given by Ren Wanding, an essayist and dissident, on Tiananmen Square during a long series of speeches.
Â 
Denunciations by Citizens
But one of the more remarkable aspects of the crackdown has been the contributions from citizens, mainly in the form of denunciations. 
The Government asserts that it has received more than a thousand letters that help to identify ''thugs.''
Newspapers have printed articles by professors and even a Beijing University student criticizing his fellow students' democracy movement.
Â 
Some Fugitives Turned In
Zhou Fengsuo, a 22-year-old student leader, was turned in by his sister and brother-in-law. 
One ''rumor-mongerer'' wanted by the police was turned in by two shop assistants. 
And peasants and workers in suburbs of Beijing, which are not under martial law, have turned in to the police at least two foreigners who were seen in the village asking questions.
Denunciations were characteristic of China in the Mao era, so it is not that surprising to see the activity reappear, although at a more moderate level.

file: The Group of 7 Statement_ Concern From East Europe to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Following is the official text of the political declaration issued today by the Group of Seven major industrialized democracies:
Â 
EAST-WEST RELATIONS
1. We, the leaders of our seven countries and the representatives of the European Community, reaffirm the universal and supreme importance which we attach to freedom, democracy and the promotion of human rights.
2. We see signs of this same desire for greater freedom and democracy in the East. 
The people there, including the young people, are reasserting these values and calling for a pluralist democratic society. 
Some of their leaders are aware of the positive contribution that greater freedom and democracy can make to the modernization of their countries and are starting to make changes to their laws, practices and institutions. 
Others are still endeavoring to resist this movement by taking repressive measures which we strongly condemn.
3. We hope that freedom will be broadened and democracy strengthened and that they will form the basis, after decades of military confrontation, ideological antagonism and mistrust, for increased dialogue and cooperation. 
We welcome the reforms under way and the prospects of lessening the division of Europe.
4. We call upon the Soviet Government to translate its new policies and pronouncements into further concrete action at home and abroad. 
Military imbalances favoring the Soviet Union, both in Europe and in Asia, remain an objective threat to each of us. 
Our governments must therefore continue to be vigilant and maintain the strength of our countries. 
For the foreseeable future, there is no alternative for each of us, within existing alliances, to maintaining a strategy of deterrence based upon an appropriate mix of adequate and effective nuclear and conventional forces. 
In order to hasten the advent of a world in which the weight of arms and military strength is reduced, we recommit ourselves to the urgent pursuit of a global ban on chemical weapons, a conventional forces balance in Europe at the lowest possible level consistent with our security requirements, and a substantial reduction in Soviet and American strategic nuclear arms.
5. We offer the countries of the East the opportunity to develop balanced economic cooperation on a sound commercial basis consistent with the security interests of each of our countries and with the general principles of international trade. 
We have noted developments of relations between the E.E.C. and countries of the East, in particular the conclusion of an agreement with Hungary, the progress already achieved during the current discussions with Poland and the opening of negotiations with the Soviet Union.
6. We welcome the process of reform under way in Poland and Hungary. 
We recognize that the political changes taking place in these countries will be difficult to sustain without economic progress. 
Each of us is prepared to support this process and to consider, as appropriate and in a coordinated fashion, economic assistance aimed at transforming and opening their economies in a durable manner. 
We believe that each of us should direct our assistance to these countries so as to sustain the momentum of reform through inward investment, joint ventures, transfer of managerial skills, professional training and other ventures which would help develop a more competitive economy.
Each of us is developing concrete initiatives designed to encourage economic reforms to promote more competitive economies and to provide new opportunities for trade.
We agreed to work along with other interested countries and multilateral institutions to concert support for the process of reform under way in Hungary and Poland, in order to make our measures of support more effective and mutually reinforcing. 
We will encourage further creative efforts by interested governments, the public and the private sectors in support of the reform process.
Concerning concerted support for reform in Poland and Hungary, we call for a meeting with all interested countries which will take place in the next few weeks. 
We underline, for Poland, the urgent need for food in present circumstances.
To these ends, we ask the Commission of the European Community to take the necessary initiatives in agreement with the other member states of the Community, and to associate, besides the summit participants, all interested countries.
7. We are in favor of an early conclusion of the negotiations between the I.M.F. and Poland. 
The strengthened debt strategy is applicable to Poland, provided it meets the conditions. 
We are ready to support in the Paris Club the rescheduling of Polish debt expeditiously and in a flexible and forthcoming manner.
8. We see good opportunities for the countries of West and East to work together to find just solutions to conflicts around the world, to fight against under-development, to safeguard the resources and the environment and to build a freer and more open world.
Â 
CHINA
We have already condemned the violent repression in China in defiance of human rights. 
We urge the Chinese authorities to cease action against those who have done no more than claim their legitimate rights to democracy and liberty.
The repression has led each of us to take appropriate measures to express our deep sense of condemnation, to suspend bilateral ministerial and high-level contacts, and also to suspend arms trade with China, where it exists. 
Furthermore each of us has agreed that, in view of current economic uncertainties, the examination of new loans by the World Bank be postponed. 
We also have decided to extend the stays of those Chinese students who so desire.
We look to the Chinese authorities to create conditions which will avoid their isolation and provide for a return to cooperation based upon the resumption of movement toward political and economic reform and openness.
We understand and share the grave concern felt by the people of Hong Kong following these events. 
We call on the Government of the People's Republic of China to do what is necessary to restore confidence in Hong Kong. 
We recognize that the continuing support of the international community will be an important element in the maintenance of confidence in Hong Kong.
Â 
TERRORISM
1. We remain resolutely opposed to terrorism in all its forms. 
We confirm the commitment each of us has undertaken to the principle of making no concessions to terrorists or their sponsors and to cooperating, bilaterally and in all relevant international fora, in combatting terrorism. 
We reiterate our commitment to the policies agreed at previous summits; in particular we condemn state-sponsored terrorism. 
We are determined not to let terrorists remain unpunished, and to have them brought to justice within the framework of international law and in conformity with the rule of law. 
We call upon those states which have supported or encouraged terrorist acts to demonstrate by their actions that they have renounced such policies. 
We reaffirm in particular our absolute condemnation of the taking of hostages. 
We call on those holding hostages to release them immediately and unconditionally on those with influence over hostage-takers to use it to this end.
2. Deeply concerned for the safety of all travelers and outraged by the murderous attacks perpetrated against international civil aviation and the frequent threat to air transport safety from terrorist groups, we reaffirm our commitment to the fight against all forms of terrorism affecting civil aviation. 
We reiterate our determination to contribute to reinforcing internationally agreed measures for protection against aircraft hijackings and sabotage.
3. We particularly condemn the recent attack on an aircraft over Scotland, which killed 270 people. 
We have agreed to give priority to preventing such attacks by further strengthening security measures. 
We attach importance to the implementation of the work plan recently adopted by the I.C.A.O. 
Council for this purpose.
4. We have also agreed on the need for improved methods of detecting explosives. 
We endorse efforts currently under way in I.C.A.O. to develop, as a matter of high priority, an appropriate international regime for the marking of plastic and sheet explosives for detection.
Â 
HUMAN RIGHTS
In 1789, the rights of man and of the citizen were solemnly proclaimed. 
Just over 40 years ago, the General Assembly of the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which have been further developed and codified and are now embodiesd in the Covenants on Civil and Political Rights and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
We reaffirm our commitment to freedom, democratic principles and human rights. 
We reaffirm our belief in the rule of law which respects and protects without fear or favor the rights and liberties of every citizen, and provides the setting in which the human spirit can develop in freedom and diversity.
Human rights are a matter of legitimate international concern. 
We commit ourselves again to encouraging and promoting the universal respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Looking toward the future, we see opportunities as well as threats; this impels us to pledge our firm commitment to uphold international standards of human rights and to confirm our willingness to reaffirm them and to develop them further.
We stress the protection of freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and of freedom of opinion and expression; for without these freedoms, other rights cannot be fully realized.
We stress also respect for the rule of law and the plurality of opinion, for without them there can be neither representative government nor democracy.
We believe equally in freedom of association in a pluralist society.
We hold that the right of each individual to physical integrity and dignity must be guaranteed. 
We abhor and condemn torture in all its forms.
We believe that all human beings must act toward each other in a spirit of fraternity.
We believe that everyone has a right to equality of opportunity as well as to own property, alone or in association with others. 
Extreme poverty and exclusion from society violate the dignity of everyone enduring them. 
Those who suffer or are in need should be supported.
We stress that the rights of the child, the disabled and the elderly require special protection.
We consider that developments in the human sciences, for instance the progress achieved in genetics and organ transplantation, must be applied in accordance with all human rights if the dignity of human beings is to be preserved.
We, the present generation, have an obligation to ensure that future generations will inherit a healthy environment.
We reaffirm our belief that these rights and freedoms cannot be properly safeguarded without the rule of law, impartial justice and genuine democratic institutions.
