file: THE LAW_Echoes of struggle for rule of law in China reverberate on Columbia campus.txt
text:
ï»¿
On a balmy summer day, the Columbia University campus seems as remote from Tiananmen Square psychically as it is geographically. 
But in the office of Professor R. Randle Edwards of Columbia Law School, the recent tremors in China have registered clearly and profoundly.
Professor Edwards is chairman of the Committee on Legal Education Exchange with China, a six-year-old group dedicated to bringing Chinese lawyers, law students and legal scholars to American law schools, and sending Americans to China. 
Through such cross-pollination, the committee hopes to ease China's painful evolution from renzhi to fazhi - that is, from the rule of man to the rule of law.
In the past decade, China's legal system, largely shut down during the Cultural Revolution, has experienced a Great Leap Forward. 
The number of law students has grown from 50 to more than 15,000, with commensurate growth among professors, judges and practitioners. 
The committee, which is based at Columbia, has made its own small but important contribution: since 1983, it has sponsored 127 Chinese scholars at 32 different American universities.
When the tanks of the 27th Army rolled into Tiananmen Square on June 3, did they flatten China's incipient legal institutions as surely as they crushed the Goddess of Democracy?
Last Saturday, committee members from U.C.L.A., Berkeley, Georgetown, the universities of Michigan and Minnesota and CUNY Law School at Queens College joined Professor Edwards in considering that question, along with the future of their own program.
The group has already canceled its annual summer session in Beijing, in which Justice Antonin Scalia of the United States Supreme Court was among those to have taught. 
More broadly, the committee now has to re-examine the wisdom and morality of its mission: whether, essentially, continued exchanges help legitimize the forces of reaction and lawlessness now in control.
For Professor Edwards, the massacre in Beijing had a more personal dimension: His two sons, Lee and Jon, were in the city at the time; Lee was on the edge of Tiananmen Square when the troops entered. 
He plans to enroll in Columbia Law School this fall, a resolve undoubtedly strengthened by what he witnessed, and experienced, there.
The most immediate concern of Professor Edwards and his colleagues was the status of Chinese scholars now in United States. 
Then they had to consider the Chinese scheduled to arrive for the coming academic year, and whether it was still safe for them to come.
The committee resolved to help those Chinese already here to extend their stays. 
It also decided to move forward with next year's exchanges, but with greater caution. 
This fall, for instance, three or four professors from the group will travel to China to see whether any of their alumni have suffered because of their participation in the program.
To Professor Edwards, the wisdom of continued exchanges is obvious. 
''Should we quit because we're collaborating with the enemy?'' he asks. 
''Or should we continue because most of the beneficiaries are people whose hearts are in the right place, who will help give China the chance to develop the rule of law over the next decade?''
If anything, his resolve is heightened by what happened on Tiananmen Square - not on June 3 but before. 
In the actions, the oratory, the banners of the demonstrators lay proof of how quickly notions of due process had seeped into the Chinese consciousness. 
Professor Edwards noted placards like ''Patriotism cannot be illegal'' and the banners carried by Beijing law students stating clauses from the Chinese constitution.
Many of these banners were photographed by Lee Edwards, who had spent the past two years living and working in Beijing, part of that for an English-language sports magazine. 
Fearful that it could provoke shooting, Professor Edwards's son, who is half Chinese, tried to stop a crowd from beating a fleeing soldier. 
Mistaken for an informer, he was beaten by the crowd with a shovel and club and hospitalized for three days.
Professor Edwards is reluctant to speak about his son's ordeal, partly to protect his privacy, partly because he remains in Beijing, partly because he thinks it detracts from the significance of what happened on Tiananmen Square - a process, he submits, in which the committee should continue to play its part.
''The real story is that the people in the world's oldest continual civilization have demanded control over their own lives,'' he said. 
''They've been evolving for 3,000 years, and in the last 10 years have made incredible progress. 
What they did in April and May eclipses all of the evil and viciousness done to them in June.''

file: THE MALTA SUMMIT_Bush Rejects Bill on China Students.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Bush today killed legislation that would have allowed Chinese students to stay in the United States after their visas expired. 
He said he was taking administrative action to give equivalent protection to the students.
Mr. Bush said that the legislation, passed with overwhelming support in Congress, was ''wholly unnecessary.''
The President said he already had ''sufficient authority to provide the necessary relief'' for the 40,000 Chinese students in the United States.
Chinese student leaders immediately criticized the decision. 
''We are disappointed, surprised and very puzzled by President Bush's action,'' said Haiching Zhao, chairman of the National Committee on Chinese Student Affairs, and a postdoctoral fellow in biochemistry at Harvard University.
Â 
Pressure From Beijing
White House officials met today with Chinese student leaders and urged them not to criticize Mr. Bush's action.
Beijing had repeatedly urged Mr. Bush to veto the bill, warning that otherwise it would terminate all student-exchange programs with the United States.
Senator Edward M. Kennedy, Democrat of Massachusetts, said, ''The President should have stood up for the courageous Chinese students instead of bowing to the cruel Chinese regime.''
Representative Bruce A. Morrison of Connecticut, chairman of the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, said in an interview tonight, ''I am appalled that the President, right on the eve of his meeting with President Gorbachev, knuckled under to the demands of the Chinese Government.''
Â 
The Validity of the Veto
In a ''memorandum of disapproval,'' Mr. Bush said he was rejecting the bill by means of a ''pocket veto'' because Congress had adjourned for the year. 
But he said he was returning the bill to the House, because Federal court decisions raised questions about the validity of a pocket veto between two sessions of the same Congress.
Congress reconvenes Jan. 
23. It is not clear whether Congress will try to pass a similar bill or try to override the President's veto.
The House majority leader, Representative Richard A. Gephardt, Democrat of Missouri, said: ''Overriding the President's veto will be the first item of business on the Congressional agenda when we return in January. 
The Chinese students deserve the full protection of American law.''
The students say they would face persecution if forced to return to their homeland. 
But Mr. Bush said, ''I will always adhere to the principle that no one will be returned forcibly to a country where he or she faces persecution.''
Â 
Grace Period of Four Years
Mr. Zhao asked, ''If the President thinks that administrative action is just as good as a new statute, why couldn't he have signed the legislation?''
Regulations, he said, are not the same as statutes ''in terms of fully protecting Chinese students.''
Under the bill, introduced by Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, Chinese students in the United States could have stayed here and applied for new visas without going home for the two-year waiting period normally required for foreign students. 
The bill would have given the Chinese students up to four years to apply for other types of visas or to seek status as permanent residents of the United States.
Mr. Bush said he had directed Attorney General Dick Thornburgh and Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d to arrange ''effectively the same protection'' for Chinese students as they would have received under the bill.
He ordered an ''irrevocable waiver of the two-year home-country residence requirement,'' and he said that Chinese students could apply for such clemency until Jan. 
1, 1994.
Â 
Threatened With Reprisals
Chinese Army troops crushed the democracy movement and killed hundreds of protesters in Beijing in early June. 
Since then, students at Chinese universities have been required to attend classes on Communist Party doctrine and ideology. 
Chinese students in the United States say they have been harassed by representatives of the Beijing Government and threatened with reprisals if they express support for the democracy movement in their homeland.
In a statement tonight, Mr. Bush promised ''continued lawful immigration status'' for Chinese students who were legally in this country on June 5. 
He said that the United States would not move to deport the students and would allow them to take jobs while they were in this country.
The Pelosi bill was approved in the House of Representatives by a vote of 403 to 0 and in the Senate by voice vote.
Seventy-one senators and 105 members of the House of Representatives signed letters this week urging President Bush to approve the bill. 
The House letter said: ''The Tiananmen Square mentality persists in China. 
Although the Chinese Government claims that it will deal leniently with those who opposed it, the reality is that the crackdown continues.''
Â 
Offending China's Leaders
Members of Congress said that Mr. Bush, a former chief of the American mission in Beijing, was afraid of offending China's leaders. 
For his part, Mr. Bush said he hoped that China would object less to his administrative action than to the legislation, even though he asserted that the two types of protection were equivalent.
Mr. Bush said his action achieved ''the laudable objectives'' of Mrs. Pelosi's bill while preserving the President's authority over foreign affairs against encroachments by Congress.
Explaining why he rejected the bill, Mr. Bush said: ''My Administration has opposed Congressional micro-management of foreign policy. 
Such legislation puts America in a straitjacket and can render us incapable of responding to changing circumstances.''
The House and the Senate both contend that the pocket veto is not appropriate between two sessions of the same Congress.
Â 
'Constitutional Prerogative'
Under the Constitution, if a bill is passed by both houses of Congress in precisely the same form, it is ''presented'' to the President. 
He can sign it, making it law. 
He can veto it by returning it to Congress within 10 days. 
If the President neither returns nor signs the bill within 10 days, the Constitution says, it becomes law - ''unless the Congress by their adjournment prevent its return, in which case it shall not be a law.''
To preserve its ''constitutional prerogative'' to reconsider vetoed legislation, Congress this year designated the clerk of the House and the secretary of the Senate to receive veto messages from the President while they are not in session.
Thus, Congress contends that its adjournment from Nov. 
22 to Jan. 
23 does not prevent the President from returning vetoed bills for reconsideration.

file: THE MEDIA BUSINESS_A Bookseller Gives Up Its Stores to Focus on Publishing.txt
text:
ï»¿
The traditional, if vanishing, role of the book publisher as bookseller has been further eroded by an established company's decision to close its three stores and concentrate on publishing.
China Books and Periodicals, the largest American retailer of publications about China, closed its bookstores in New York and San Francisco on Oct. 
7 and will close its Chicago store on Dec. 
1.
But the company, founded as a bookseller in 1960, plans to expand its activities as book publisher, a direction it first took in 1984 with one book. 
It hopes to publish to 20 in the current publishing year.
A Business Decision
The about-face from full-time retailer to full-time publisher was a business decision that was not related to the change in China's social climate since the political crackdown in June.
''Bookstores are not usually great sources of revenue,'' said Vicki Chabra, the book division's marketing director. 
''We have been keeping them open as a service.''
''When we started, there were no other distributors of books about China,'' she said. 
''Now you'll find them in many bookstores.''
China Books was founded by Henry Noyes, the son of missionaries in China, and it is now headed by his son, Chris Noyes. 
In the beginning, it specialized in books of fiction, history and scholarly research, mostly in English, that were imported from China.
The company in time expanded to a complete line of language and travel guides and art books from China. 
It attracted much attention and wide sales in 1967 when it imported the English version of ''The Little Red Book'' of quotations by Chairman Mao Zedong.
Â 
Company's First Publication
In 1984, the company's first publication, ''Two Years in the Melting Pot,'' received good reviews. 
It was an account, in English, of American life as perceived by Liu Zongren, who had been sent here to study English and journalism. 
China Books has just published a fiction work by Mr. Liu, ''6 Tanyin Alley,'' about life in a Beijing courtyard.
Nancy Ippilito, the head of the book division, said China Books would publish ''Crisis at Tian'anmen,'' a compilation by a Chinese journalist, Yi Mu, in November.
Only a few publishers still operate bookstores in the United States. 
At one time Charles Scribner's Sons operated several bookstores, including the highly regarded store on Fifth Avenue near 48th Street in Manhattan. 
The store was bought by Rizzoli International Bookstores Inc. in 1984 and closed last January.
Last December, Harper & Row discontinued its New York store, which sold publications of its own and associated imprints. 
''It has never been a financially viable operation,'' said William Shinker, senior vice president and publisher of the adult trade division.
McGraw-Hill Inc. still has a bookstore at its headquarters at Rockefeller Center, and its books are part of the stock of 18,000 titles by several different publishers.
Â 
Doubleday's Stores
The Doubleday Book Shops and the Bantam Doubleday Dell Publishing Group are both owned by a West German concern, Bertelsmann, but their operations are separate. 
''There is no problem in maintaining our independence,'' said Gary Del Vecchio, president and chief executive of the bookstore operation. 
''Actually, no one publisher has enough books to keep a store going by itself.''

file: The Mystique of Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
TIBET is manifest proof of the smallness of human beings. 
The Himalayan landscapes are so vast, so bereft of any inhabitants except the odd nomad, that here it is the land that has shaped the people instead of the other way around. 
When Tibetans die, they do not build tombs; they leave the corpse for the vultures to devour. 
Occasionally the Government makes an effort to tame the plateau, to show who is boss, by carving a road through the emptiness, but nature gets its revenge by bogging down vehicles in snow or mud.
It is from the roof of the Potala Palace, where the Dalai Lama as a boy rigged a telescope to study ordinary people as they strolled among the yaks on the streets below, that Tibet is at its most magnificent. 
As Tibetan pilgrims shuffle by, turning prayer wheels and mumbling chants before disappearing into little chapels to light yak-butter candles, the mysticism and beauty of the land are simply overpowering.
Tibet inspired the notion of Shangri-La, and it retains a remoteness and exotic quality now rare elsewhere in the world. 
The Tibetan pilgrims who prostrate themselves in the dust have nothing but their faith, but they count themselves as very rich indeed -- for they have been able to make the holy journey to Lhasa. 
The pilgrims clutch prayer wheels as they walk clockwise around the Jokhang Temple, according to ritual.
In recent years, to be sure, Tibet has been an unhappy sort of Shangri-La. 
It had links over the centuries with the Chinese empire, and in 1950 the newly installed Communist Chinese Government used those relations to justify sending its army to "liberate" Tibet, which it claimed was part of China. 
These days there is a Tibetan Government in exile, but the United States and other Western governments recognize Chinese sovereignty over Tibet -- while urging Beijing to halt the torture and repression there.
In the mid-1980's there seemed to be some hope for a compromise between the exiled Dalai Lama and the Beijing authorities, but then pro-independence demonstrations erupted in September 1987 and were bloodily suppressed. 
Tensions rose, and the unrest culminated in clashes in March 1989 that left at least a dozen dead and led to the expulsion of all tourists and the imposition of martial law. 
China lifted martial law in May 1990, and since then the region has been largely quiet. 
As a result, the Chinese Government is again encouraging Western tourists -- so long as they come in organized groups and do not encourage Tibetan separatists.
The groups are escorted to a limited number of places where tourists are welcome. 
Last year, 10,375 foreigners visited Tibet, including 1,441 from the United States. 
Tibetan tourism officials say they expect 13,000 visitors this year, including about 1,400 from the United States. 
In general, there seems little risk for Westerners, partly because most Tibetans regard them as allies.
Tibet can be reached from Nepal -- there are two flights a week -- but most tourists arrive on the daily China Southwest Airlines flights from Chengdu, China. 
In my case I went as a journalist rather than as a tourist, but my itinerary was similar to what a tourist might see. 
I spent a week there, and it seems foolish to stay less than that.
Lhasa is 11,830 feet high, and most visitors feel some shortness of breath at first. 
In Andean cities like Cuzco, Peru, foreigners often deal with similar altitudes by drinking coca tea, which contains a raw ingredient that goes into cocaine. 
In Tibet, there is no such exotic remedy, but the Lhasa Holiday Inn -- by far the best hotel in Lhasa, and the place where most foreigners stay -- does offer an oxygen hose in each room to assist those with breathing difficulties. 
Occasionally a new arrival has to fly out by the first available plane to a lower altitude.
Tibet is not a place of luxury, but the hotels and food are adequate. 
Most hotel restaurants serve principally Chinese and Western food, with a certain Tibetan influence: yak burgers, for example, at the Holiday Inn. 
Guides vary enormously, from local Tibetans who are one with the land to Chinese who have only lived in Tibet for a short period.
The pride of Lhasa is the Potala Palace, the former home of the Dalai Lama. 
Since Tibet's spiritual leader fled into exile in 1959, the palace has been turned into a museum and it is one of the most spectacular sights in Asia. 
I find it far more impressive than the Chinese Imperial Palace in the Forbidden City in Beijing. 
While the Forbidden City is sterile, the Potala oozes faith. 
It is the Tibetan version of Versailles: 13 stories tall, 1,300 feet by 1,150 feet, with 16-foot walls protecting a warren of more than 1,000 rooms. 
The Government regards the Potala as a museum, but many Tibetans still regard it as one of the holiest spots in the world. 
They come not so much out of curiosity as out of reverence, which is seen in their eyes as they shuffle from room to room, lighting candles and praying before the jewel-studded tombs of past incarnations of the Dalai Lama.
They wind up narrow stairs, little more than ladders, and emerge on an open roof with views of all of Lhasa.
The rooms in the Potala have names like Chapel of Immortal Happiness and Chapel of the Stages on the Path to Enlightenment. 
The contents are as vivid as the names: altars and carvings are everywhere, all weighed down with gorgeous pieces of cloth of every conceivable color. 
White scarves, left by pilgrims to show their respect, adorn many of the altars. 
The entire Potala is a celebration of color, and clothes and books and carvings and tombs seem to be crammed wherever there is space.
THE Potala was built mostly during the rule of the fifth Dalai Lama, and the regent concealed news of his death in 1682 for a decade because of fear that the mourning would halt construction of the palace. 
Only when it was virtually completed did the regent announce the Dalai Lama's death and launch the search for his reincarnation. 
By the time the successor was found he was already a teen-ager, and he proved to have a strong and rather ungodly interest in the opposite sex. 
The sixth Dalai Lama disappeared in 1706, but he is still fondly remembered for his poetry and sometimes roguish behavior.
Most visitors to Lhasa also tour the Jokhang Temple and the surrounding Barkor Market. 
This area is the political and religious focal point of Tibet, the gathering point of pilgrims who come from hundreds or even thousands of miles -- these days usually by bus, instead of by crawling and prostrating. 
It is also the site of most pro-independence demonstrations in the last few years, but if there is a prospect of a protest then your guides are almost certain to keep you away.
The entrance to the Jokhang is crowded with pilgrims, prostrating themselves, and with vendors who peddle prayer wheels, bugles and other souvenirs. 
The atmosphere is half carnival, half mystical. 
Inside, the oldest part of the temple supposedly dates from the seventh century and houses an ancient Buddha that was carried to Lhasa 1,300 years ago from the Chinese capital of that epoch, Changan, now called Xian. 
This holy of holies is in a cramped, dark room that magnifies the spiritual intensity: pilgrims are shoulder to shoulder, murmuring prayers as they edge their way around the statue.
The Chinese are sometimes reluctant to arrange visits to the monasteries that surround Lhasa, because the monasteries function as an alternative university system and as centers of opposition to the Government. 
If a visit is permitted, it is well worth the trip. 
These used to be the largest monasteries in the world -- Drepung Monastery near Lhasa once had nearly 10,000 monks -- and they are still influential in Tibetan society.
In addition to Drepung, alternatives are Sera Monastery, on the outskirts of Lhasa, and Ganden Monastery, 45 miles by rough road from the city. 
Ganden is one of the most poignant sights in the area: the monastery was devastated in the Maoist period, and most of it today is only rubble. 
It is as if Notre Dame had been bombed. 
The destruction helps explain the bitterness that many Tibetans feel for the Chinese authorities.
In the evening it is well worth taking a bicycle-rickshaw to the area around the Jokhang Temple and perhaps popping into one of the small bars. 
Studying English is the rage in Lhasa, and it is likely that someone will approach to start a conversation. 
I remember a doctor who spoke to me for more than an hour about the political situation. 
He was torn in his emotions: he wanted to get his anger at the Chinese off his chest, but he was also terrified of being arrested for his candor. 
Speaking in Chinese, he repeatedly said he risked being beaten and imprisoned for years for talking to a foreign journalist.
Tourists are allowed to travel to certain other parts of Tibet, and I relished a three-day circuit that encompassed the towns of Shigatse and Gyantse. 
The trip begins with a six- or seven-hour ride along a newly constructed highway that still has a few rough edges: a truck became stuck in a patch of mud, blocking traffic in both directions.
Shigatse was the traditional seat of the Panchen Lama, who ranks second in the religious hierarchy to the Dalai Lama. 
The 10th Panchen Lama died in 1989, and visitors to Tashilhunpo Monastery in Shigatse stroll around the glass case in which his embalmed body is seated. 
A dozen or so monks constantly pray for a rapid incarnation of the Panchen Lama in the form of an infant.
The monastery is built against a hill, and the tombs of past Panchen Lamas are on display, as is the site where the tomb of the 10th is now being prepared. 
The monks consult oracles and study divine lakes for hints about where to find the infant 11th Panchen Lama. 
A few candidates will presumably be selected within the next year or two, and in theory the child who recognizes the personal belongings of the last Panchen Lama will be pronounced the new one. 
There is considerable room for manipulation of the process, and many Tibetans fear that the Chinese authorities will try to select a boy whom they can control and turn into a spokesman for the regime.
AS I wandered through the lanes and corridors of Tashilhunpo, admiring the sculptures and altars, I chatted with Barsan, who came to the monastery in 1947, when he was 7 years old. 
Then there were perhaps 3,000 monks at the monastery, now there are 800, and Barsan says there will never again be as many as there used to be. 
In the Cultural Revolution, he was forced to work for five years as a construction worker and farm laborer, but today he hides what bitterness he may feel.
From Shigatse it is less than two hours by car to Gyantse, a small town whose claim to fame is the Kumbum, part of the Palkhor Monastery on the edge of town. 
The Kumbum, built in 1427, is the largest stupa, a kind of Buddhist tower, in Tibet: built with a dome, it soars heavenward and dominates the arid landscape for miles around. 
A few monks will show you around the dim interior, illuminated by yak- butter candles and crammed with ancient manuscripts.
In the evenings, after the official tourist itinerary is completed, it may be possible to take a four-wheel vehicle and drive independently to a nearby village. 
Traveling without any Chinese official, I found that villagers were extremely friendly and happy to show me around their crude homes.
One of the best reasons to visit Gyantse is simply to enjoy the road connecting it to Lhasa. 
Yes, the dirt road is miserable after rain -- on my trip, many trucks were stuck in the mud, and my four-wheel-drive vehicle frequently had to drive across open fields rather than the road itself -- but the scenery is spectacular. 
The terrain is the classic image of Tibet: a vast emptiness full of mountains and glaciers and occasional herds of yaks. 
The emptiness is broken only by a telephone wire that goes along the road. 
Because of the absence of trees, the telephone poles are not made of wood but of mud bricks.
Â 
SIGNPOSTS FOR A VISIT TO LHASA
Â 
The Border
While the police sometimes tolerate individual tourists who sneak into Tibet by overland routes, the only legal way to enter is as part of an organized tour -- even if it is a tour of one. 
The difference between an illegal individual tourist and an authorized tour group with one person is that the latter has a schedule and an escort and pays hefty fees.
A tour agent will arrange for the Chinese visa and the permission slip to travel to Tibet, both of which are essential. 
Backpackers who cross the border without permission, mostly by bus from Sichuan or Qinghai Provinces, often stay at the budget Yak Hotel in the center of Lhasa. 
On occasion the police have taken to seizing some of these unauthorized visitors, and detaining them rather roughly at the airport until the next flight. 
Budget travelers have made daring midnight escapes from the airport, even swimming a river to avoid soldiers.
The Chinese Government is very concerned about tourist involvement in the independence movement, and so it is illegal for foreigners to give out photos of the Dalai Lama; everywhere you go children will ask for his photo. 
Tibet is generally very safe, but tourists of Asian ancestry, who might be mistaken for local Chinese, should be somewhat cautious about roaming the Tibetan quarter at night. 
A Japanese friend had pebbles tossed in his direction at a monastery; some monks believed he was Chinese.
Â 
Tours
A number of travel agents can arrange the tours, as can Holiday Inn, which manages the best hotel in Tibet. 
Information is available from the Holiday Inn sales office, (800) 331-3831, or from Holiday Inn Lhasa, No. 1 Minzu Lu, Lhasa, Tibet, China (telephone 222-21; telex 68010 HILSA CN). 
The Government tightly regulates tour costs and keeps them high. 
The Holiday Inn's weeklong tour of the Lhasa area, excluding the air fare to Lhasa, costs $1,475 for a single traveler, or $860 each for a couple, meals included. 
Discounts grow as the size of the group grows, with 10 people paying just $590 each.
Some cheaper package tours stay at the nearby Tibet Hotel. 
The Tibetan decor in the rooms is charming, but guests say that service leaves much to be desired. 
There is one tourist hotel each in Shigatse and Gyantse; neither meets international standards.
Â 
Weather
Most tourists visit in the warmer months from April to October. 
In winter, there is some snow and the days are shorter, but Lhasa becomes a more interesting city as the nomads leave the hills and roam the streets of the capital. 
In December, the coldest month, the temperature averages 32 degrees. 
Because the weather is changeable, travelers should take clothing that can be worn in layers -- such as sweaters. 
Sunscreens are also useful, because of the altitude. 
You should not count on being able to buy anything at all other than food in Lhasa, so take film.
Â 
Reading
Partly because of the limitations of the guides, it makes sense to buy a guidebook or two for the journey. 
Perhaps the best is Stephen Batchelor's comprehensive and beautifully illustrated "Tibet Guide" (Wisdom Publications, London); other useful ones include the Lonely Planet guide, "Tibet: A Travel Survival Kit," and Passport Books' "Tibet: A Complete Guide."
The Dalai Lama's autobiography, "Freedom in Exile," is fascinating, although for a more objective version of political events I would strongly recommend an essay by Melvyn C. Goldstein on Tibet in "China Briefing 1990," published by the Asia Society and Westview Press. 
-- N. D. K.

file: The New China -- A Special Report._Chinese Communism_s Secret Aim_ Capitalism.txt
text:
ï»¿
To listen to some Chinese, one of the best-kept secrets in the world is this: Here in the land of Mao, where red banners with propaganda slogans still dangle from tall buildings, Communism has collapsed.
It's quite a state secret, but some Chinese believe that's essentially what has happened. 
Indeed, the joke making the rounds among Chinese intellectuals is this: "Under the leadership of the Communist Party, we're advancing from socialism to capitalism."
It is true that one can spend days rummaging through the free markets of cities like Guangzhou or Shanghai and find little trace of Communism. 
Yet Deng Xiaoping, the 88-year-old senior leader, has no intention of creating the kind of democratic capitalist society that exists in the West.
Â 
Looking for a Hybrid
Rather, there is growing evidence that his aim is to build a hybrid along the lines of capitalist totalitarianism, or free-market authoritarianism.
Mr. Deng is willing to free prices but not the press, to loosen controls over companies but not citizens. 
The Communist Party Congress, which today dismissed several leading hard-liners in choosing a new Central Committee, underscored Mr. Deng's readiness to abandon central planning in the economy but not in politics and society. 
[Page A7.]
The party congress, which closed its weeklong session tonight, called for an economic "revolution" along market lines. 
But the congress also reaffirmed the leaders' determination to crush opposition and pursue socialism -- a term that they have shorn of most economic meaning, so that today "socialism" seems to signify little more than that they retain power.
Â 
Party Leadership Stressed
"The core principle these days is Communist Party leadership," said Zhang Weiguo, a Shanghai journalist and dissident. 
"Preserving Communist Party rule is all that socialism means now. 
It's a game."
Socialism is such a flexible concept for the Chinese leaders that they are studying the experience of the super-capitalist "four dragons" of Asia: Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea and Hong Kong. 
The attraction of the four dragons is that for many years they experienced economic miracles without the hubbub and chaos of Western-style democracy.
The upshot is that just as Mao Zedong took the Soviet Union as a partial model for China in the 1950's, Mr. Deng seems to take the four dragons as a partial model in the 1990's.
If China succeeds over the next few decades in duplicating the successes of Taiwan and South Korea, then the economic impact on the world can scarcely be exaggerated. 
China, with nearly 1.2 billion people and a nuclear arsenal, could make Japan seem like a lightweight.
Yet the stakes of failure are equally awesome. 
Few experts rule out the possibility of civil war and tremendous upheavals, and it was only three decades ago that millions of Chinese died in the worst famine ever recorded in world history.
Already in a number of ways China is increasingly resembling Taiwan and South Korea as they existed in the 1970's: thriving economies, authoritarian governments, and societies in which rising prosperity and educational levels sow a yearning for a more open and tolerant government.
Â 
How Evolution Might Unfold
Most Chinese intellectuals appear to believe that the Government here will change dramatically, one way or the other. 
Many believe that one of the most hopeful prospects is an evolutionary process of change similar to that in Taiwan.
According to this script, China would continue to pretend to be a Communist country. 
But in practice it would increasingly resemble a market economy, and it would gradually ease restrictions on the press and on dissent.
Sometime after the death of Mr. Deng and the other revolutionary leaders, the Communist Party would try to recover a bit of legitimacy by expelling hard-liners and by offering voters more choice in local elections. 
It might change its name, while keeping most of the same people. 
Meanwhile, China would experience a continuing economic boom, allowing the party to "buy off" voters and win their support.
Then, like Taiwan, China would make elections more meaningful and stop torturing dissidents. 
Newspapers would become bolder, contacts would grow with the outside world, and a middle class would emerge.
After a decade or two, China would still be dominated by a single party but it would no longer talk much about ideology. 
The Communist revolution might still be part of its legacy but only in a general way, just as people in France can continue to be proud of the French Revolution without wanting to set up a guillotine in a downtown square.
The Communist Party denounces this kind of change as "peaceful evolution," supposedly a plot by Western powers to corrupt China's revolutionary virtue. 
But for many Chinese, who see the alternative as catastrophic turmoil, such a course of events is about the best outcome they can reasonably expect.
"Socialism is ridiculous," said a Chinese economist who often advises the party. 
"Our only hope is peaceful evolution. 
Otherwise, we die."
Â 
Will It Work?
Hope Persists
To be sure, it is far from clear that the Chinese Communist Party can succeed in taking this path, even if it wants to. 
It may well be that the Government here, like Iran's Government under the Shah or the Soviet Union's under Mikhail S. Gorbachev, has antagonized so many people that it cannot survive any opening up of the system.
But whether or not it works, many Chinese and foreigners believe that the strategy at least has some chance of succeeding. 
And for now they believe that it is the direction in which China is going.
"I believe the Communist Party is going to concentrate on the things it thinks it can do best -- presumably political control, media, education -- and allow the economy to function by some of its own logic," said Thomas B. Gold, a sociologist and China specialist at the University of California at Berkeley.
"As the society becomes increasingly complex, and as a new type of person moves into the party hierarchy, there has to be some kind of a loosening," he said. 
"One question is the degree to which they can guide it and avoid an explosion."
It may sound odd that the Government should still fill the airwaves with tributes to socialism while plodding step by step toward a market economy. 
But ideology in China has declined to little more than a decorative art, a way of arranging banners and beautifying whatever the Government wants to do.
The emptiness of the slogans was evident when a couple of foreigners visited Mao's hometown in central China and interviewed Wen Huikang, the vice president of the Mao Zedong Thought Society. 
Mr. Wen spoke glowingly about the continuing relevance of Mao's writings, and finally a visitor asked a softball question: Which was his favorite essay by Mao?
Mr. Wen paused. 
He searched for a way to answer the question, and he began to look panicky. 
It became clear that he could not name a single work by Mao.
Â 
Few Believers In Communism
It is difficult to find any Chinese official or Communist Party member who believes in Communism or socialism. 
A few years ago, When an American graduate student met his Chinese girlfriend, an economics graduate from Beijing University, he discovered that she and her classmates were fervent believers in laissez-faire.
They were so alienated by the Chinese experience with central planning that it was left to him, a product of American universities, to suggest that governments could occasionally play a useful role in the economy.
The son of a prominent Central Committee member was asked recently if his father believed in Marxism. 
He looked surprised by the question.
"Oh, Dad used to believe in that stuff," he said. 
"But that was a long time ago."
Some of the octogenarian leaders apparently still keep the faith. 
But in 1976, when Mr. Deng was last purged, People's Daily quoted Mao as saying Mr. Deng "knows nothing of Marxism-Leninism."
That appears to have been unfair, for Mr. Deng still shows a profound understanding at least of Leninism. 
While he pays little attention to Marxist economics, he appears deeply committed to Lenin's teachings about one-party rule.
In that sense, China may gradually move away from Marxism while trying to remain a Leninist state.
Â 
Defining Socialism Is a Stumper
Of course, the Government insists that it is perfecting socialism, not abandoning it. 
But nobody here seems to know just how to define socialism -- particularly in an age of stock markets, private millionaires and horse racing.
"We've been practicing socialism for several decades, and yet nobody can figure out just what it is," Zhao Ziyang, the former Communist Party leader, acknowledged shortly before he was purged in 1989. 
The remark was used against him, but these days some reformist officials offer exceedingly vague definitions of socialism.
Mr. Deng's view, the official New China News Agency reported on Saturday, is that "the essence of socialism is to liberate and expand the productive forces, eliminate poverty, avoid polarization in wealth distribution and finally acquire common prosperity."
The advantage of that definition is that China can do virtually anything and remain socialist. 
The drawback is that by that standard, Taiwan -- which is both wealthy and egalitarian -- is more socialist than mainland China.
"It seems to be a very elastic concept," said Nicholas R. Lardy, an economist at the University of Washington.
Foreigners often find it disconcerting that the airwaves should be so full of Communist slogans while the streets are so full of entrepreneurs. 
But China's officials have been mouthing empty slogans for so long that they rarely let them interfere with daily life.
Before the 1949 revolution, Mao reportedly once gave a speech in which he used a phrase meaning "from masses win respect."
The party's press agency transmitted the speech to other Communist-held areas, but the phrase was garbled and came out "from fog win treasure."
This was meaningless, but no one noticed. 
A party newspaper dutifully published an editorial about the importance of the treasure in the fog.
Â 
State Economy Is Dwindling
In the same way, few Chinese pay much attention to the party's insistence that it is following the socialist road. 
Indeed, the economic restructuring since the end of the Maoist era 14 years ago has already left the economy not very Marxist.
The state sector now accounts for only about one-third of economic output, according to Mr. Lardy. Farming is now mostly quasi-private, and retailing and other services are increasingly outside the state sector as well. 
Even in the industrial sector, state-owned companies accounted for only 53 percent of output last year, compared with about 36 percent for collectives and 11 percent for private businesses.
Since Mr. Deng opened China to the outside world in 1978 and began what is sometimes called the nation's "second revolution," gross national product has soared at an annual rate of 8.7 percent. 
At that pace, incomes double in a bit more than nine years.
To be sure, about 70 percent of all Chinese live in villages, but for them the stakes of economic growth are greater than for anybody else. 
For the first time in hundreds of generations, some families have been able to send children to school, to build a brick house, to eat meat regularly, to have a doctor present for childbirth.
Yet for all the economic changes under way, China is not necessarily adopting the vision of Adam Smith.
The true private sector is very small, with the bulk of the economy falling in a hazy zone that defies easy labels. 
Agriculture, for instance, is not quite private, since peasants must contract with the state to get farmland.
Likewise, the collective sector is an ambiguous catch-all category that includes some genuine private businesses but also many factories run by township governments. 
And all companies, public or private, run into constant interference from government officials and tax collectors. 
No matter what happens, the Government is likely to continue to play a substantial role in the economy.
Â 
Growing Corruption Feeds Discontent
Another major challenge for private businesses is the growing corruption, especially demands for payoffs from local officials. 
This is not only an impediment to economic efficiency, but also a major reason for public discontent.
Thus some skeptics fear that China, instead of blossoming into an oversized Taiwan, will become bogged down by inefficiency and corruption and will rather resemble something like Mexico or Nigeria. 
Many Chinese note parallels with the end of the Qing Dynasty at the beginning of this century and other past epochs and believe that Communism is a dynasty about to collapse.
"Parts of China, like the coastal areas, can take the road of free-market authoritarianism," said Antonio Chiang, a Taiwan magazine publisher now visiting China. 
"But I don't see it happening in the entire country."
If the economic boom can be sustained, a crucial question is whether Chinese can be "bought off" by their economic prosperity so they have a stake in the system and do not challenge the Government. 
That is in part what happened in Taiwan, where the ruling Kuomintang massacred thousands of Taiwanese in 1947 and subsequently governed with considerable brutality until it eased restrictions in the 1980's.
Because the Kuomintang engineered the economic miracle -- and because it eventually responded to the middle class and eased the repression -- it has survived the transition to free elections. 
Today it remains in power.
The challenge will be much greater for China. 
Memories of Communist brutalities -- like the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown -- are still fresh. 
And while incomes are growing rapidly, many Chinese remain dissatisfied because they now realize that people in Taiwan and Hong Kong are even wealthier.
Â 
How to Release Political Steam
Most importantly, the Chinese authorities seem unwilling to follow the Taiwanese example and ease restrictions in response to growing aspirations for political freedom and participation. 
Some Chinese and foreigners worry that if there is no mechanism for releasing political steam, eventually the pressure cooker may explode.
"You simply cannot postpone political reform and assuage political demands through economic prosperity alone," said Michel Oksenberg, the president of the East-West Center in Honolulu. 
"You have the beginnings in China of an urban middle class, and we see no movement in the political sphere to cope with the increasing occupational differentiation, the changing locus of where people live."
The obvious explanation for why Mr. Deng and his octogenarian colleagues do not want political change is that they are afraid of it. 
But there is another, more charitable explanation.
They grew up in a China that was torn apart by warlords, famine and foreign invasion, and perhaps as a consequence they are passionately concerned with maintaining order. 
They find democracy not only personally threatening but also divisive and unstable, and prone to the kind of weakness and chaos that wracked China in the decades before the Communist revolution of 1949.
Yet while Mr. Deng apparently believes that resisting political change will preserve the order, few others see it that way.
"The problem is that at the highest level, the old politicians are still clinging to power," said Chen Yizi, a former economic official who fled to the United States after the Tiananmen crackdown. 
"That fundamental problem can't be solved, and so I think the road they're taking now is a dead end."

text:
ï»¿
Despite turn-of-the-century photographs of hollow-eyed Jewish and Italian children gazing at their teachers with gratitude and zeal, history presents a less rose-tinted picture of immigrants in the New York public schools.
The swarms of children in the Lower East Side ghetto were often crammed into classrooms of 60, and truancy and delinquency were rife. 
Reading and math scores plummeted and history classes were curtailed so more English could be taught. 
A 1911 Teachers College study shows that only 60 percent of elementary school children went on to high school; even the most ardent pupils had to work to support their families.
But history also shows that waves of immigration have enlivened New York's schools at the same time as they have overwhelmed them. 
The news two weeks ago that 120,000 immigrant children from 167 countries have entered the city's schools over the last three years was greeted as a sign of renewal as robust as the cherry and apple blossoms coloring the cityscape.
During the 1970's and 80's, the city's schools had seemed doomed to fade slowly, hurt by the middle class's steady exodus to the suburbs, by fiscal cuts, decaying buildings and a growing population of poor youngsters from chaotic families.
Now immigrant families from the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Russia, Guyana, China and other countries have rejuvenated some floundering schools.
Many families are fleeing political oppression or poverty. 
"Every time there's an upheaval anywhere in the world, the schools in New York are the first to absorb it," says Mitchell L. Moss, director of New York University's Urban Research Center.
Some arrive illiterate even in their native languages. 
But others, says Dr. Emanuel Tobier, an economics professor at N.Y.U., are among the most ambitious and best educated of their compatriots, with an enormous craving to make it and an energizing fear of catastrophe if they don't.
Seward Park, the Lower East Side's neighborhood high school, was for a long time a place to avoid, but an influx of Chinese and Latin American students has brightened its academic tone. 
The annual dropout rate, for example, fell from 13.5 percent in the 1982-83 school year to 10.7 percent in 1989-90.
The prestigious Westinghouse national science competition is still dominated by New York City schools, as it has been since it began in the 1940's, but the faces have changed. 
Winning often requires working after school in a laboratory for two years, and many of the recent winners hungry enough to do that have been the children of immigrants from China, India and the Soviet Union.
Soundings like these, says Dr. Tobier, buoy many executives, who have long despaired about the quality of the city's work force.
Also, countries like South Korea and Thailand are gaining new prominence in the world economy. 
Today's immigrants raised in New York will be well-positioned for international commerce.
"This is a multicultural world, and we're rich in terms of who is in our system," said Joseph J. Saccente, who is retiring as the Board of Education's chief executive for monitoring and improving schools.
But an influx of immigrants brings problems too. 
District 6 in Washington Heights is so crowded that students are sent to the east Bronx. 
In District 24 in Queens, classes are held on the auditorium stage and two assistant principals moved into the principal's office so classes could be held in their offices.
Â 
Hunting Albanian Teachers
Schools are scrounging around for bilingual teachers, and not just in Spanish and Chinese. 
District 11 in the northeast Bronx is considering hiring teachers of Albanian, but they are hard to find. 
Most immigrants who don't speak Spanish must take their classes entirely in English, and some educators fear they will suffer in mathematics and science classes.
The debate over bilingual education, settled legally but not philosophically, is being stirred up by the new wave of immigrants. 
Some teachers complain that students are being funneled into bilingual classes to furnish jobs for bilingual teachers, and say immigrants would learn more English the old-fashioned way -- by breaking with their own language cold turkey.
But others who grew up in the old system argue that it forces students to endure years of feeling stupid in subjects like mathematics when their handicap is linguistic, not arithmetical.
Â 
Ambition, Pluck and Pressure
"I was competent in my own language," recalls Angel Villarreal, the Puerto Rican-born assistant principal of Junior High School 98 in the Bronx.
Schools are also being asked to revamp their curricula to take account of the cultural backgrounds of newcomers. 
Such sensitivity, says David Reimers, a historian of immigration, was never shown the Irish and German immigrants of the mid-19th century.
And experts like Mr. Moss believe that new immigrants have injected the system with ambition, pluck and pressure for better schools. 
He says Asian families in the Forest Hills neighborhood where he grew up are joining longtime residents in demanding improvements.
Perhaps cognizant of that emerging constituency, Mayor David N. Dinkins last week decided to restore $600 million of almost $1.5 billion he had taken out of a $4.3 billion school construction plan. 
Overcrowded District 24 is already building one elementary school, has a junior high school on the drawing board, and has five other additions in the works.
"It's more or less the way my family arrived in this country a generation or so ago," said John Falco, the district's deputy superintendent. 
"You have industrious people who come to this country for all the benefits our family came for -- freedom and economic prosperity -- with children eager to learn."

file: THE REGION_A Traditionally Insular Community Begins to Reach Out.txt
text:
ï»¿
YU KIM LY was buried last week in his faded blue jeans. 
At his wake, near his coffin, the photograph of the winsome-looking 16-year-old and the small crowd of black-clad teen-age mourners offered few hints of the violent death he met the previous week on a street in lower Manhattan.
The boy was shot three times in the head along with two other teen-age friends, all members of the Vietnamese gang Born to Kill, a violent group that has increasingly encroached on the territory of established Chinese gangs, terrifying the Chinese, Vietnamese and Korean communities throughout New York.
Although law-enforcement officials said the three deaths were not officially gang related, the murders galvanized more than 20 Asian community groups, traditionally wary of outsiders, to meet recently with the police and protest increased gang violence and insufficient police protection.
Their protest differed from similar protests in past decades. 
Not only did it demonstrate a new pan-Asian solidarity, but it also appears to have been ignited by the changing random pattern of gang violence and the rise of the drug trade. 
The meeting also pointed up the chasm between Asian-Americans and the police department -- as well as conflicts within their own communities.
"Now is the time to fight back," Paul Mack, the executive director of the Brooklyn Chinese-American Community Association, said. 
"But without any assistance from higher up, we just can't do it. 
But also look at it this way, without cooperation from the community, there isn't much police can do."
The dramatic rise in the number of Asian immigrants over the last 20 years has been reflected by an increase in gangs. 
"The stakes are higher now," said Ko-lin Chin, a senior research analyst at the New York City Criminal Justice Agency, a private nonprofit organization, who wrote "Chinese Subculture and Criminality" (Greenwood Press, 1990). 
"More immigrants mean more business, more money, more power. 
There's more heroin trafficking. 
And when the gangs in the 90's now send a message, they kill people."
An estimated 300,000 Chinese live in New York, 150,000 in Chinatown. 
In the 1980's, as new groups from Taiwan and Hong Kong flowed in they settled in Flushing in Queens and along Eighth Avenue in Brooklyn, each area with Chinese populations of over 60,000. 
More recently, Chinatown has felt the influx of a wave of 30,000 undocumented immigrants, mostly from China's Fukien Province, according to Virgo Lee, the director of Mayor David N. Dinkins's office of Asian Affairs. 
The Vietnamese population has jumped from 5,000 to 40,000 since 1980.
A possible indication of increased gang activity is reflected in police statistics for Chinatown. 
The data for the first six months of 1990 show robberies up by 30 percent over 1989. 
In the Fifth Precinct, which patrols Chinatown, 13 people have been murdered so far, compared with 12 homicides for all of 1989. 
This month alone, five gang members were murdered in three separate incidents in lower Manhattan.
At the heart of the violence is Born to Kill and its rivalry with more traditional Chinese gangs. 
The gang, made up of young Vietnamese immigrants, is extremely unpredictable and violent and primarily involved in robbery, extortion and burglary of Chinese retail stores and restaurants.
"One merchant in Brooklyn was hit six different times in one day by gang kids who wanted money," Mr. Mack said, referring to different gangs.
The Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese gangs are linked to their community's social and economic life. 
The Chinese gangs especially rely on their relationship to certain large, established social and political associations. 
These groups use the youths to protect illegal activities like gambling, Mr. Chin said.
The leaders of the groups that have an association with the gangs "have an ambivalent and very subtle relationship with their gangs," said Mr. Chin. "They cannot dismiss them because they are the nuclear power of the adult organization. 
If they let them go, another will recruit them, and they will be left without street soldiers."
Â 
A Little Progress
The communication gap between the police and the community only assists the gangs. 
The police claim that Asians are easier victims because they are scared or unwilling to report crimes; the community groups say the only solution in the short term is more police on the streets and in the long term school programs to discourage children from gangs.
The language barrier and the innate distrust of authority add to the unwillingness of the Asian community to work with the police or even appear in court. 
The police say they cannot make arrests and prosecute unless the attitudes change.
"The community has to make a difference," said Sergeant Michael Collins of the Fifth Precinct's Asian Gang Intelligence Unit. 
"They have to report the crimes. 
They have to stop participating in extortion. 
They have to be willing to follow through the system."
Community leaders, like Paul Yee, president of the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, a group of more than 60 community organizations, argue that the legal system quickly frees criminals, who take revenge on their victims, who lack police protection.
"We feel the system is just too ridiculous," Mr. Yee said. 
"The police blame the community people. 
They don't blame the crime."
Both law-enforcement officials and community leaders claim some progress. 
The police say they are increasing the number of uniformed patrol officers in the precinct and upgrading the gang surveillance unit.
Still, many present at the meeting were skeptical. 
To some, it recalled the old Chinese saying, "When alive don't go to authority. 
When dead don't go to hell."

text:
ï»¿
The Chinese press announced the ousting of President Mikhail S. Gorbachev promptly and factually on radio and television news programs on Monday, with no sign of the glee that some Chinese hard-liners may feel for their apparent reprieve from the time when their Soviet "Big Brother" in the Communist movement would slip into political pluralism and capitalism.
Chinese leaders have long appeared to feel a deep animosity for Mr. Gorbachev, based on the view that he has undermined Communist governments in other countries as well as his own. 
While Beijing did not publicly criticize Mr. Gorbachev, China's hard-liners have characterized him in conversations and internal documents as a dangerous revisionist who had betrayed Eastern Europe and abandoned Leninist principles.
"The changes in the Soviet Union are the internal affairs of that country, and China hopes that the Soviet people will solve their own problems by themselves and maintain political stabilityI," the Beijing Government said in a statement issued this morning.
"I think they're thrilled," Merle Goldman, a China scholar at Boston University who is visiting Beijing, said of the Chinese leaders. 
"It only proves that political reform leads to chaos and instability. 
They can just say, 'I told you so!'
"
Still, Chinese leaders may well worry about how events will develop in the Soviet Union and in particular that any Soviet unrest could spill across the border. 
For example, if the ouster of Mr. Gorbachev intensifies rather than eases the demands in the Islamic regions of the Soviet Union, that could also stir pro-independence feelings in the Islamic northwest of China.

file: The Transition_ Political Memo_New Tune for Clinton_ Sounds of Compromise.txt
text:
ï»¿
As if trading in the saxophone of the election season for a cello, Bill Clinton seems to be modulating the direct and even brassy oratory of his campaign into a Presidential tune.
As a candidate, Mr. Clinton's task was to distinguish himself as sharply as possible from President Bush. 
Listening to him this week on his first trip to Washington as President-elect, it was clear that as President, his aim will be to prevent conflict abroad and build consensus at home so he can concentrate on the economy.
After meeting with Congressional leaders he played down his campaign demand that Congress slash the size of its staff and that he be given new powers to veto spending, which Congress complains would diminish its authority. 
He offered to negotiate on his plan to lift the ban on homosexuals in the military in the face of opposition from Gen. Colin L. Powell, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. 
And after a session on foreign policy in the Oval Office with Mr. Bush, he sounded a less aggressive note about getting tough with China.
John Brummett, editor of The Arkansas Times Magazine, said Mr. Clinton seems to be adapting his style in the Governor's Mansion for the Oval Office.
"He does have a tendency to promise as a candidate and then once elected, suddenly become very realistic," Mr. Brummett said. 
"It is bravado versus realism, and it is a pretty clear pattern we have seen before. 
It is just the difference between getting elected and governing."
Â 
Room for Compromise
This style has its obvious risks: it could simply reinforce Mr. Clinton's image as a politician who has a tendency to dance around sensitive issues to get the support of all sides. 
But it could also allow him to stake out a far-reaching position while leaving room for a compromise down the road.
During the campaign, for instance, Mr. Clinton lacerated President Bush for "coddling" the "tyrants" in Beijing and promised he would never do that. 
On Thursday, when he had to speak about China as President-elect instead of Presidential wannabe, Mr. Clinton chose his words carefully. 
He repeated his support for human rights, but gave Mr. Bush credit for making progress with Beijing when he got "tough" on the Chinese and said he did not want to "isolate" China, the very formulation Mr. Bush has often used.
Mr. Clinton may have been signaling that he took too absolute a position in this area as he was fighting to get elected and is now using the grace period of his transition to retreat a bit. 
The last thing he wants during his first days in office, after all, is a fight with China or with Congress over his China policy.
In a similar manner, and perhaps for a similar purpose, Mr. Clinton has lowered his voice about Congress cutting Congressional staffs and cutting middle-class taxes. 
He is on the record for both, but can push them loudly or quietly depending on what tradeoffs he needs later.
Â 
Feeling His New Role
Beyond political calculations, there may be something unconscious going on. 
The American public is watching as Mr. Clinton absorbs the weighty reality of the office he is about to inherit. 
When he arrived to meet Mr. Bush at the White House this week, he seemed intent on striking a Presidential stance, rather than giving in to the natural instinct to crane his neck and look around at his new house.
Mr. Clinton spent almost two hours with President Bush in the Oval Office on Thursday. 
According to a Clinton aide, Mr. Bush gave the President-elect a tour of each problem spot in the world. 
Mr. Clinton then asked Mr. Bush how he would respond if events spun out of control in each area. 
It may have been no accident that after this conversation, Mr. Clinton found a softer voice on China.
Similarly, Mr. Clinton began his transition period with a strong statement of his intent to lift the ban on homosexuals in the military. 
As Democrats in Congress and generals in the Pentagon protested, Mr. Clinton backed off just a bit, saying he still intended to carry out his campaign promise on the issue, but was prepared to discuss it and find common ground. 
Last week, Mr. Clinton met with General Powell and said wryly that the nation's highest-ranking uniformed officer did not hold back on any subject.
Â 
A One-Man Polling Operation
In both cases, Mr. Clinton seems to have been displaying one of his particular managerial traits. 
Clinton aides during the campaign often complained about his democratic style of decision-making -- how he would ask the opinion of everyone from his top strategists to the flight attendant on his campaign aircraft before making up his mind.
Mr. Brummett said, "Sometimes he is just too prone to agree with the last person he talked with."
Several years ago in Arkansas, the Arkansas legislature was considering a bill granting tax credits for private donations to Arkansas's badly underfinanced colleges and universities. 
Mr. Clinton was torn between wanting to support higher education and not wanting to drain his budget of tax revenues.
The bill was passed and he had five days to decide whether to veto it. 
He agonized for five days, consulting with all sides, and on the evening of the fifth day he finally decided to veto the bill, stamping on it in big black letters: "DISAPPROVED."
A Clinton aide was sent over to file the veto with the House clerk and slipped it under the door of her office. 
Mr. Clinton then and telephoned Arkansas college presidents to explain what he had done. 
Instead, they persuaded him to change his mind.
So the Governor summoned a state trooper in his security detail and asked him to go back to the clerk's office and retrieve the vetoed bill. 
The trooper could see through the locked glass door that the bill was lying on the floor. 
He took a coat hanger, slipped it under the door and slid the bill out. 
He brought it back to Governor Clinton, who simply crossed out a few letters and sent it back as "APPROVED."
"The most unnerving thing about Clinton," said a long-time friend, "is knowing when he's made a decision. 
He'll look you in the eye to get your advice and for that moment, it seems like you're the only person in the world whose opinion he cares about. 
And then a second later, he'll turn to the waiter here and ask him his opinion."

file: The Universal Dumpling (Dough, A Little Filling, A Lot of Ancestry).txt
text:
ï»¿
THE term multicultural has been deployed with such abandon lately that Joseph Ben-Moha, the owner of the Roxy Deli, began to take a more philosophical view of dumplings.
"I look at my kreplach and I say, 'What makes you different from my pirogi?'
" he said. 
"And then I must think, 'What makes a wonton not a kreplach, a kreplach not a pirogi, a pirogi not a wonton?'
"
He decided to pursue these questions by sponsoring a dumpling derby in his deli on Broadway at 47th Street. 
Last Thursday, nine cooks and four judges met to cook and compete and appraise. 
They also debated whether a dumpling is a dumpling is a dumpling.
"They're all dough," Mr. Ben-Moha reasoned. 
"The only difference is the insides."
Greeting the wonton contingent, he said, "If people ask me what is a kreplach, I tell them it's like a wonton."
Janny Leung, a pharmacist who lives in Flushing, Queens, smiled politely. 
She didn't recall ever having used the term kreplach. 
Tony Yep, a dim sum chef at Shun Lee West in Manhattan, crinkled his brow until it resembled the top of a steamed dumpling. 
"Wonton are spicy," he said. 
"Sichuan wonton are very spicy."
"Small, wrapped food is a universal concept," said Dan Lenchner, who owns Manna, a kosher catering company in TriBeCa. 
His wonton stuffed with Mexican fried beef and chili was a beacon of pluralism. 
"I tend to stay away from traditional kosher forms," he said.
His decision resonated with one judge, Michael Klenfner, a record industry executive. 
"I grew up in Brighton Beach, Little Odessa on the Atlantic, where every restaurant had pirogi, which they called vareniki, and they all had kreplach," he said. 
"But everybody went to the New Deal Chinese restaurant to eat dumplings."
The wonton contingent quietly chalked this preference up to the paper-thin dough that is sold in packages of 100 and used to wrap wontons. 
In China, wontons are considered noodles, not dumplings. 
Stuffed with pork, chicken or shrimp, the triangular packets can be fried, steamed or boiled and are generally served with noodles in broth.
In New York, however, the line between wontons (of which there are Peking, Cantonese, Shanghai and Sichuan versions) and Cantonese dumplings has been blurred. 
Dumplings are shaped like fat Hershey's Kisses, stuffed in a manner similar to wontons, steamed or fried, and served as dim sum. 
There is some speculation that in New York, wontons slipped into the dumpling category before wonton skins were available here, when local Chinese cooks used the heavier egg roll skins to wrap their dumplings.
Both Ms. Leung and Mr. Yep waved aside the semantics. 
They consider themselves dumpling makers.
Kreplach competitors, on the other hand, are shy of the dumpling nomenclature. 
To most, kreplach is kreplach: heavy dumplings shaped like lumpy round pillows, stuffed with meat and onions, boiled and usually served in chicken soup.
"Kreplach is religious, symbolic," said Olga Gurwitz, a 70-year-old retired businesswoman who lives on the East Side. 
The dough enveloping her amorphous beef pillows is thicker than a wonton skin. 
"It is handmade," she said. 
"The dough symbolizes the protection we have from a harsh world. 
We eat it on religious holidays."
Considering the paucity of cross-cultural influence in kreplach as compared to the abundant variations on wontons, she said, "It's easier to improvise when you don't feel you are meddling with something sacred."
Beatrice Kusnetz of Far Rockaway, Queens, concurred that changes in the kreplach form are rarely whimsical, though she conceded that health concerns have modified her recipe.
"I don't fry my onions in chicken fat anymore," said the 78-year-old retired nurse, another competitor.
"No, that was a hundred years ago," Mrs. Gurwitz agreed. 
"Who can eat like that anymore?
But you need a stronger soup for the flavor."
"I never noticed the soup," said Ms. Leung, who said that her family eats wontons with noodles in a subtle chicken broth. 
"I taste the scallion, and the cilantro," she said.
"Spicy," Mr. Yep said, smiling.
But Ms. Leung said the communal tradition surrounding her family's dumplings remains intact among her, her parents, and her brother and sister. 
"On Saturdays it takes the five of us two hours to make 100 dumplings," she said. 
Family dumpling-making seems to remain stable across shifting ethnic lines. 
"This is the way you maintain your past," said Bea Lewis, another judge who said she is a kreplach expert by dint of having recently become a grandmother. 
"A Jewish grandmother has to know everything about kreplach so she can teach her grandchildren," she said. 
"This is the way your past becomes your future."
Bozenna Mcaward, a 37-year-old pirogi contestant who was born in Poland and moved to Brooklyn two weeks ago, agreed. 
Her cousins encouraged her to enter the contest. 
"I need my family to make pirogi," she said.
Faina Merzlyak, a contestant who lives in Brooklyn, said Polish pirogi are generally shaped like a half moon and stuffed with meat, potatoes, mushrooms or farmers' cheese. 
They can be boiled and served in soup, or served with sour cream, caramelized onion or applesauce as a first course. 
Pirogi can also be fried. 
The Russian vareniki is shaped the same and can be filled with anything from sauerkraut to sour cherries.
Ms. Mcaward registered, in shy and recently acquired English, her amazement at finding pirogi-making a competitive activity on Broadway. 
She expressed amusement at the presence of wontons in the derby. 
"In this country anything can be pirogi," she surmised.
She nodded approval of the flavor of the wonton, but expressed reservations about incorporating soy or ginger, scallion or cilantro in her pirogi. 
"In potato pirogi?" she said dubiously.
Gus Kavis, another pirogi contestant who is the manager of the Odessa Restaurant on Avenue A in Manhattan, told Ms. Mcaward that few American pirogi-philes still make their own. 
"They come to me in cars from New Jersey and Connecticut and buy them," he said. 
"They take the pirogi home and cook it."
Miss Mcaward shook her head. 
The purity of pirogi, she suggested, can only be preserved by making one's own. 
This opinion seemed to be shared by all contestants.
When asked whether he could envision using kreplach dough to wrap a Hong Kong-style dumpling, Mr. Yep replied that this would be tantamount to placing a hamburger in a hot-dog roll. 
Improvisation, like Mr. Lenchner's Mexican wonton for kosher audiences, seemed ephemeral rather than enduring. 
"Interesting to taste," said Ms. Mcaward, in a tone that said "not destined for the heirloom recipe file."
Considering their dumplings, the contestants voiced a separate-but-equal point of view. 
Actual dumpling-making, they said, is a time-honored tradition whose essence is repetition: the grandchild who best mimics the matriarch's version stands to become the next dumpling queen. 
And, as with architectural icons, it is no small undertaking to change these little bits of culinary ballast.
Nevertheless, the dumpling duelers found common ground. 
No matter what its ethnic persuasion, they said, dumpling-making is a deliberate thing, complicated and time consuming. 
Despite this, the little swaddled nuggets are forever adjuncts -- pillows floating in soup, soft pyramids steamed in bamboo for an appetizer -- rarely a main course.
The dignity of any dumpling is difficult to capture in a recipe. 
"It's a touch," Mrs. Gurwitz said. 
"It is something you are born with."
The other contestants vigorously agreed. 
Which may explain why, when she was awarded first prize in the kreplach category, Mrs. Gurwitz cried.
Ms. Leung, who took the wonton prize, wasn't as visibly moved, nor was the city's pirogi king, Mr. Kavis. But both seemed to empathize with Mrs. Gurwitz. Like a latter day Miss America, she accepted her prize of $100 and a dozen roses, waved to the audience and said, "I've waited my whole life for this moment."
Mr. Ben-Moya got a little misty-eyed, too. 
But his dumpling musings weren't abated. 
"We must address the ravioli issue," he said.
