3 Doughs, 3 Fillings
Â 
Potato and Mushroom Pirogi
(Adapted from Faina Merzlyak)
Â 
Total time: 1 1/2 hours, plus 2 hours for sitting
Â 
For the dumplings:
Â 
16 ounces fresh yogurt, preferably homemade, or one with a high-fat content, like Brown Cow
1 egg, lightly beaten
1 teaspoon salt
2 1/4 cups flour.
Â 
For the filling:
Â 
1 large potato, about 1/2 to 3/4 pound
4 tablespoons unsalted butter
1 medium-size onion, chopped
16 ounces mushrooms, trimmed and minced (2 cups)
Salt and freshly ground pepper to taste.
1. To make the dumplings, lightly beat the yogurt, egg, and salt together in a mixer. 
Slowly add the flour, beating until smooth. 
Knead the dough on a floured surface until smooth. 
Add water only if needed. 
Form into a ball, wrap in a kitchen towel and set aside in a cool place for 2 hours.
2. For the filling, peel and quarter the potato. 
Cover with cold water, bring to a boil, lower heat and simmer 15 to 20 minutes until it offers no resistance when pricked with a fork. 
Drain and set aside. 
Slowly melt 2 tablespoons of the butter. 
Whip the potato with the butter until it is fluffy and creamy. 
Set aside.
3. Heat the remaining butter in a pan. 
Add the onions and saute until they are translucent. 
Add the mushrooms, salt and pepper and continue to saute until the mushrooms are tender and the moisture has evaporated, about 5 minutes. 
Remove from pan and let cool slightly.
4. Mix the mashed potatoes with the mushroom mixture.
5. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. 
Roll out the dough until it is 1/8-inch thick, then cut it into 3-inch rounds with a cookie cutter or the top of a glass. 
Put 1 heaping teaspoon of filling on one side of the circle of dough. 
Fold the other side over the filling so the pirogi looks like a half moon. 
Press the edges together and seal with thumb and index finger.
6. Lower heat until water gently simmers. 
Carefully place pirogis in the water one at a time, in batches of 4 to 6, for 5 to 7 minutes. 
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels in a warm place. 
Serve with fried onions or sour cream.
Yield: 30 pierogis.
Â 
Kreplach
(Adapted from Olga Gurwitz)
Â 
Total time: 2 1/2 hours
Â 
For the dumplings:
Â 
3 eggs
1/2 cup safflower oil
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 3/4 cups flour
1/2 cup water.
Â 
For the filling:
Â 
1/2 cooked chicken, 1 1/2 to 2 pounds
1 egg
1/2 onion
Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste.
1. To make the dumplings, gently beat the eggs, oil and salt together in a large bowl. 
Slowly add the flour and water as needed. 
Transfer to a floured board and knead until smooth and loose. 
Cover with kitchen towel and set aside for 2 hours.
2. To make the filling, remove chicken meat from bones, remove skin and grind meat with the egg, onion, salt and pepper. 
Taste to correct seasoning.
4. Roll out dough, a portion at a time, to between 1/8- and 1/4-inch thick. 
Cut it into rounds 3 inches across. 
Place a heaping teaspoon of filling in center of dough rounds and fold edges over to make a half moon. 
Press to seal. 
Refrigerate until ready to cook.
5. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. 
Lower to a simmer. 
Gently place kreplach in the water, one at a time, in batches of 6 to 8 and cook for 20 to 25 minutes, or until the dough is cooked through. 
Drain and serve in chicken soup or plain.
Yield: About 30 kreplach.
Â 
Wontons
(Adapted from Janny Leung)
Â 
Total time: 1 1/2 hours
Â 
75 wonton skins, fresh or frozen
1 1/4 pound fresh medium-size shrimp
1 egg, separated
2 scallions, washed, chopped
1 tablespoon sesame oil
1 tablespoon salt
1/2 teaspoon freshly ground pepper
3/4 pound ground beef
5 dried shiitake mushrooms or 1/4 ounce Black Forest mushrooms, soaked for 20 minutes, drained and minced
4 stalks fresh cilantro, washed, leaves chopped.
1. If using frozen wonton wrappers, defrost them unwrapped in the open air for about 1 hour. 
Carefully peel them off, one by one, and refrigerate until ready to use them. 
It is best to defrost in a colander so air can circulate around them. 
Discard any that are waterlogged.
2. Peel the shrimp. 
Make sure entire shell is removed, including the tail. 
Chop them coarsely by hand.
3. In a large bowl, lightly beat the egg yolk. 
Add scallions, sesame oil, salt and pepper. 
Mix well. 
Add the shrimp, beef, mushrooms and cilantro and mix well with hands.
4. Lay out a wonton skin and lightly brush the edges with the egg white. 
Place about 1 tablespoon of the filling in the middle. 
Fold into a triangle. 
Seal edges with the tip of a fork, pressing down around the border. 
Brush with a little more egg white and refrigerate. 
Continue until all the wontons are stuffed.
5. When it is time to serve the wontons, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. 
Lower heat to simmer and gently place a few wontons in the water so they are not touching. 
Cook 5 to 7 minutes. 
Drain on paper towels.
Yield: 75 wontons.

file: The Versatile Allure of Japanese Noodles, Served Hot or Cold.txt
text:
ï»¿
AKIHIDE YONEHAMA has eaten a bowl of noodles every day since he was 3 years old. 
He is now 49. 
Mr. Yonehama, the owner of Menchanko-Tei, a Manhattan restaurant whose name translates as "a house of mixed noodles," is not alone in his passion. 
In fact, noodles may become Japan's next great food export, after sushi.
Slinky, slippery noodles are popular for two reasons: versatility and cost, said Elizabeth Andoh, author of "An Ocean of Flavor: The Japanese Way with Fish and Seafood" (William Morrow, 1988).
The noodles -- made from eggs, wheat or buckwheat -- can be served hot or cold, in broths that are steaming or chilled. 
In summer a bowl of chilled noodles, topped with a bit of meat or seafood and fresh vegetables, is a perfect one-dish meal. 
Cold beer or sake are the perfect accompaniments.
Ms. Andoh says the Japanese have probably been eating noodles for more than 1,500 years.
Toshiko Takahara, a staff member of the Japan Information Center in Manhattan, said: "Some Japanese eat noodles for lunch once a day, sometimes for dinner every few days. 
And men -- after they have dinner and go out and drink, they eat noodles late at night."
In Manhattan, a number of noodle restaurants serve delicious cold noodles through September; others serve them all year. 
Three in particular are continuing a history of Japanese noodle-making. 
They are Mr. Yonehama's Menchanko-Tei, at 39 West 55th Street; Omen, at 113 Thompson Street (near Prince Street), and Honmura An, 170 Mercer Street (near Houston Street).
What distinguishes one place from the other are the secret flavors of the noodles and their broths. 
The restaurateurs are not unlike the Japanese heroine of "Tampopo," Juzo Itami's movie, who is obsessed with making the perfect broth for noodles.
The newest noodle restaurant, Honmura An, specializes in soba, a noodle made from buckwheat. 
When the noodles are served cold and dipped swiftly into a hot broth, they remain firm, but when they arrive submerged in the broth, "you have to slurp the noodles quickly," said Koichi Jun Kobari, the restaurant's owner. 
"Soba soaks up water, losing texture. 
The cold noodles are the best."
With an etched memory of soba-making and three generations of recipes, Mr. Kobari opened Honmura An in February. 
Its namesake original was founded in Tokyo 65 years ago by his grandfather Yoshizo Kobari.
The 30-year-old Mr. Kobari imports shelled buckwheat kernels from Japan and has them stone-ground at his restaurant.
Each day, a noodle-maker makes the soba by hand, mixing the dough in a lacquered bowl. 
He spreads sheets of dough on a wooden board and cleaves it into fine pale beige noodles. 
They are then ready to be boiled and chilled, to be served cold or immersed in a hot broth.
The restaurants use the same basic ingredients in their broths -- bonito (dried flakes of young tuna), mirin (sweet, rice-based cooking wine) and soy sauce, but the owners are shy about disclosing names, measurements or cooking times of other ingredients.
At Honmura An, kamo seiro is cold soba served with a rich chicken broth flavored with duck. 
But Mr. Kobari would say only that the duck is added "briefly" to the broth.
For a quick lunch, Japanese might eat only a bowl of noodles. 
At dinner, appetizers precede the noodles. 
One Honmura An appetizer is tataki, fillets cut from a steak that has been marinated in soy sauce and stock.
Like Mr. Kobari, Mikio Shinagawa, the 36-year-old owner of the restaurant Omen, is also a descendant of noodle fanciers. 
His mother is from Kyoto and his father is from Gunma, near Tokyo. 
There, Mr. Shinagawa said, "people have the custom of eating noodles once a day; if they have it for lunch one day, they will have it for dinner the next."
Twenty-five years ago, his parents opened the first of three Omen noodle restaurants in Kyoto. 
In 1979, when Mr. Shinagawa's parents came to visit him in Manhattan, he didn't know where to take them to eat.
"As a joke," he recalled, "my friends said: 'Why don't you open a restaurant here in New York?
We have no place to go.'
"
So, in 1981, he opened Omen, named for a thick, wheat-based noodle. 
At this time of year, he also offers somen, a very thin noodle imported dried from Japan. 
"In the summer, people come here just to eat the somen," he said.
Somen is cooked for a few minutes in boiling water and placed in a chilled broth. 
It arrives in a round ceramic bowl topped with boiled shrimp sliced lengthwise, slivers of shiitake mushrooms, scallions and julienned strips of scrambled egg.
The broth, Mr. Shinagawa said, is made of seaweed, mirin, bonito and ginger juice and is light with just a hint of sweetness.
Year-round the signature dish of Omen, is, appropriately, omen. 
Served on a tray, the noodles are accompanied by a hot broth, a bowl of toasted sesame seeds and a ceramic plate of vegetables that are boiled, shredded and served cold. 
They may include white radish, carrots, scallions or Chinese cabbage.
The noodles are preceded by peanut-ae (pronounced peanut-EYE) a dish of cooked spniach and tiny scallops moistened with a peanut-sesame sauce. 
In tribute to his Buddhist training, Mr. Shinagawa serves a smooth, silken black tofu, a vegetarian dish served at Zen Buddhist temples in Japan. 
The color is from black sesame seed; to eat the tofu is an experience newer to the eyes than to the tongue: It tastes like bean curd but doesn't look like it.
On some days, a crowd representative of Manhattan's Japanese community fills Menchanko-Tei, waiting to enter the 42-seat restaurant. 
Chauffeurs polish windows; in line areexecutives, Buddhist monks and crews from TV Nippon. 
On a hot, humid day, many customers eat hiyashi chuka, chilled Japanese noodles in a broth topped with slivers of cucumber, egg, Chinese-style roast pork and tomato.
Ms. Andoh calls the dish a chef's salad over noodles. 
The noodles, which are made in San Jose, Calif., are wheat-based but are bound with egg, like those that Japanese cuisine borrowed from China.
Hiyashi chuka is one of four noodle dishes that Mr. Yonehama offers at Menchanko-Tei, his "house of mixed noodles."
His favorite is menchanko topped with fresh shrimp, rice cakes, bean curd and Chinese cabbage. 
To the chicken-based broth, he has added some seafood and a mysterious shellfish.
"We do not know the name," Mr. Yonehama said through an interpreter, smiling. 
It is "some sort of clam."
Then, smiling more broadly, Mr. Yonehama said, "In Japan, for every family and every restaurant, the soup is a secret recipe."
To precede the noodles, there is oden, geometrically shaped food that has been simmered in broth: triangular wedges of fried bean curd; round fluffy fish cakes; circles of white radish.
In Japan, oden is served outdoors on pushcarts, as the chestnut vendors do in the streets of Manhattan. 
At night, appetizers like yaki-zakana (broiled fish) are served. 
Pods of soybeans boiled in salted water arrive in a small bowl. 
The pods are peeled and popped into the mouth.
Menchanko-Tei is the happy result of Mr. Yonehama's miserable early experiences as a restaurateur. 
From 1970 to 1975, he and his four brothers opened 29 different restaurants in Kyushu, southern Japan. 
"The only one that succeeded was noodles," Mr. Yonehama said.
He now has two restaurants in Kyushu and one in Manhattan, an office in Tokyo and a 20,000-square-foot factory in Kyushu where his soup bases are made. 
The soup concentrates are used in his three restaurants and sold to supermarkets in Japan.
Mr. Yonehama is planning to open other Menchanko-Tei restaurants for homesick Japanese in Honolulu in 1992, and eventually in London and Paris. 
"I try to make people from Japan feel at home," he said.

text:
ï»¿
AS the sun rises along a deep and smooth bend in the Huangpu River, where the boats known as sampans tie up at the mouth of the Suzhou Creek, the river bank already shows signs of bustle. 
On the main street, Doric columns, Gothic windows and plaster friezes adorn the grand buildings towering above the rest of the city's low, flat-roofed houses and hint at the past presence of European brokers in the opium trade. 
But now the street overflows with Chinese workers - officials, bankers, shippers, dumpling vendors and cart pullers.
The Bund, the long, winding embankment along the river in the eastern part of Shanghai, welcomes dozens of freighters and hundreds of sampans every day. 
It is a crossroads where American executives run into martial arts experts, where canvas-covered skiffs glide close to Mercedes limousines, where Tudor-style buildings overshadow common brick houses and where foghorns muffle the murmur of busy pedestrians.
In some ways it is as Western to the Chinese eye as it is Oriental to the foreign visitor. 
The Chinese inhabitants have shaped the Bund to their own needs - sellers of hot pork buns scout for hungry passers-by, brightly clad Tibetan women offer cow horns and herbal roots for sale and tip their tall headdresses to anyone who glances at their wares. 
Policemen in khaki uniforms make their patrols, wide-eyed children stare off at the water as their mothers point to the huge ships and lovers stroll hand-in-hand.
Yet to the Chinese visitors, who come to this waterfront by the thousands every day, the city's Bund represents a world of finance, a place where Shanghai's shrewd merchants meet the rich businessmen of the West. 
Unlike the simple houses or small inner-city flats that most Chinese live in, the buildings here are grand, stark reminders of Western imperialism, yet symbols too of Shanghai's old opulence, of its history and of its industry when it outshone the rest of China.
The Huangpu River, the source of Shanghai's riches, was named after a prince, Huang Xie, who more than 2,000 years ago mobilized thousands of laborers to dredge the river. 
In Chinese ''pu'' refers to an area where a river flows into the sea. 
Three tributaries feed into the river, which from the Bund runs 50 miles to the East China Sea and then blends into the Pacific Ocean. 
This river gateway has made Shanghai's port the busiest in China. 
Scores of cargo ships anchor near the tall cranes that lift gigantic containers onto shore. 
Sampans ferry goods from land to boat or from boat to boat. 
Vessels pause only long enough to exchange goods between China and the rest of the world.
In its heyday, beginning with the opium trade in the 1830's and lasting until 1949 with the Communist victory in China's civil war, the Bund was the enclave for the British, American and French Consulates, the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, as well as companies like Jardine Matheson & Company, David Sassoon Sons and Dent & Company. 
These were the hongs, the foreign trading companies that grew on the opium trade in the last century and today thrive on international trade from their Hong Kong bases.
The Chinese people had used opium as medicine for years, but in the 1830's and 40's its use as a drug expanded. 
The astute European traders smuggled thousands of chests of opium from India to the coastal areas of China in exchange for tea and silk. 
After legalization in 1860, which brought regulation, the trade began to decline; in the first decade of this century it was abolished. 
By then the hongs, which had diversified into many other kinds of merchandise, had already settled along the Bund.
This stretch of magnificence had muddy origins. 
Nearly a century and a half ago the wide space along the water was reserved for trackers towing boats and mooring ships. 
The shore became crowded with sheds and workshops and later infested with dirty kitchens, latrines and refuse. 
The British, French and Americans had staked out territories along the river to house their merchant traders, officials and missionaries. 
They helped transform this wide embankment from a muddy towpath, whose shape varied with the tide, into a beautiful esplanade. 
Their name for it comes from an English-Indian term, band, for embankment or dike.
In the latter half of the 19th century the Chinese authorities allowed the embankment to be cultivated and the dirt path filled. 
With the aid of Chinese laborers, the British built a garden on the shore front, across the wide street from their consulate. 
The garden overlooks the creek spilling into the Huangpu River and is site of the infamous, although probably apochryphal, sign declaring, ''No dogs or Chinese allowed.''
One legend even has it that the youthful Mao Zedong was inspired to revolution in part after seeing the sign. 
For all the legends, however, no such sign apparently existed.
F. L. Hawks, in ''A Short History of Shanghai,'' published in 1928, said, ''All respectable and decently clad Chinese were admitted'' to the parks in the Western concession areas, ''but when it was found that coolies used the benches for siestas, notices were posted on the benches restricting their use to foreigners.''
Another author, Pan Ling, in a 1982 book, ''In Search of Old Shanghai,'' said there were two separate regulations on a long list, one banning dogs and another excluding Chinese unaccompanied by foreigners.
The garden has become Huangpu Park, where fathers come to snap pictures of their little girls, where couples from the countryside toting newly-purchased televisions and radios come to rest, and where rustic Chinese tourists come to marvel at the rock gardens and fountains. 
The park has an entrance fee of less than a penny. 
Gatekeepers are unlikely to be able to change the large bills that foreigners usually carry, so bring small change from your hotel. 
The old British Consulate, a longtime symbol of foreign imperialism, now houses the Shanghai Foreign Investment Commissions: a site that once represented the evils of foreign encroachment now reflects China's attempt to woo foreign investors back.
By the entrance to Huangpu Park, cruise boats leave to take visitors north up the river for a view of the vast harbor and a glimpse of the East China Sea. 
The wind blows fiercely, so take a warm jacket. 
On board is a 64-year-old magician, Ye Mafei. 
Accompanying him might be his son and daughter, magicians in their own right who have performed with him in several countries. 
The boats leave for the three-hour trip at 8:30 A.M., 1:30 P.M. and 6:30 P.M. First-class tickets cost $4.70. 
Every day at dawn, the aging masters of tai qiquan, a meditative form of kung fu, and wu shu, or martial arts, come to the Bund and sometimes to the park to practice. 
By seven in the morning, the bank along the river is lined with more than a hundred exercisers, some engaging in slow breathing routines, others taking a sword or spear in hand to perform sparring dances. 
As a visitor looks on, a wiry old man stretches his legs in a ballet split, his head bent to the ground in line with his legs. 
Nearby, a white-haired master leads a middle-aged student through the high kicks and hard punches of a wu shu routine. 
A group of men and women perform their tai qiquan movements in unison in an area of the walkway where the sun shines between tufts of trees. 
For at least an hour in the morning, the sounds of the traffic are deadened by the blast of rock music as a team of men and women begin their day with disco dancing. 
Across from Huangpu Park on Beijing East Road is the Friendship Store, which sells everything from local chocolates to silk rugs to wood-carved screens to candy to Chinese paintings. 
Souvenirs include contemporary vases, jade and jewelry, even furniture.
Turning the corner onto Zhongshan East Road, the main strip along the Bund, and crossing the creek brings the visitor to the territory on the right that more than a century ago was part of the American concession. 
The territory changed hands several times. 
It passed to the Japanese after the Sino-Japanese War began in 1937 and then a part of it was used by the Soviet Union as its Shanghai Consulate at the base of the old drawbridge, known as the Bridge of the Outer Ferry. 
Later the consulate, an old-style mansion with bay windows and cupolas breaking through a red-brick roof, became a club for sailors. 
With relations between China and the Soviet Union warming again, the Soviets last year regained the building and renovated it as their consulate once more.
Two hotels flank the consulate on Suzhou Road: Shanghai Mansions, a tall red modern building with a good Chinese restaurant, and a cheaper alternative, the Pujiang Hotel.
Back on Zhongshan East Road, past the Greek columns of the Shanghai Textile Industrial Building and the granite-block Bank of China Building, the visitor should turn the corner on Nanjing East Road. 
On both sides of the street are the two buildings of the grand old Peace Hotel, where limousines line up outside waiting for wealthy businessmen negotiating deals over dinner banquets inside. 
Noel Coward reportedly finished the draft of ''Private Lives'' in this hotel. 
The older building on the south side of the street was formerly the Palace Hotel.
Farther south along the Bund is the Tudor-style Customs House, where giant spools of thick cables cover the floor in front of the large doors, seemingly unnoticed by customs officials and shippers scurrying about or engaged in disputes over goods. 
On the southern tip of the Bund, where the old French concession used to be, is the Dongfeng Hotel. 
Here was housed the Shanghai Club - for men only, and serious tipplers at that. 
The members used to come for a drink at the mahogany bar, which stretched 100 feet. 
It has now been shortened to fit comfortably in the popular Suzhou Restaurant, but in the late afternoons a smaller bar upstairs opens for seamen. 
The old hotel has been converted into government offices, and a Cantonese restaurant on the first floor there also serves dim sum or dumplings at lunchtime.
Nanjing East Road, a slight detour from the Bund, takes a visitor through the bustling shopping strip that gave Shanghai its worldly and avant-garde reputation before the Communist revolution. 
In those days the nearby Fuzhou Road was the red-light district, where teahouses and bordellos teemed with singsong girls whose lilting dialects lured clients. 
Now Western modernity with a Chinese flavor continues to pervade the streets, which are lined with shops selling all sorts of wares from radios and watches to ''lotions for the aged'' to pianos and silks. 
Children gather around a Japanese video recorder display that shows them and the street scene on a large television.
Farther down, by an overpass crowded with people looking down at the river of people below, lies Shanghai's No. 1 Department Store, a far cry from Bloomingdale's but worth a visit. 
The store sells televisions and other electrical appliances, sporting goods and winter and spring clothes.
On Sunday couples stroll and window-shop, parents chase their wandering children and visitors cart away their new purchases. 
Store lights glitter as darkness descends and still the crowds of pedestrians pour out onto what has been called the ''great white way.''

SOME HOTELS TO CONSIDER
Among the hotels worth considering in Shanghai are these:
Hua Ting Sheraton Hotel, 1200 Caoxi North Road; telephone 386000. 
Double room $94 plus 10 percent service charge. 
Try the Chinese restaurant, which serves Sichuan and Cantonese food, for about $27 a person.
Peace Hotel, 20 Nanjing East Road; 211244. 
Double room $62 and $49. 
On the eighth floor of the north wing, completed in 1928, there is a large banquet hall and a parlour restaurant that offers very good Shanghai-style food (about $10 a person) and a splendid view of the Bund.
Pujiang Hotel, 17 Huangpu Road; 246388. 
Double room $16.
Shanghai Hilton International, 250 Huashan Road; 550000. 
Double room $135 plus 10 percent service charge. 
Hotel has a Western-style buffet that is a treat for travelers who yearn for American gourmet salads and cold cuts as well as hot food and desserts. 
The hotel also has a Shanghai-style restaurant.

text:
ï»¿
When Robert M. Gates talks, people listen. 
But it can be risky for the nation's top spymaster to go public.
Since he took over as Director of Central Intelligence four months ago, Mr. Gates has made five public appearances before Congressional committees, lacing his bleak world view with tantalizing bits of secret information -- intelligence with the bark off, as he likes to call it.
A complicating factor is that by having his independent say in public rather than in closed sessions, Mr. Gates has sometimes offered views that appear to run counter to Administration policy.
For example, when he told the House Foreign Affairs Committee last month that North Korea could possess a nuclear weapon from within a few months to "a couple" of years, Mr. Gates irritated much of the State Department bureaucracy, which felt more time would be needed for the North Koreans to develop a bomb and that Mr. Gates's assessment undermined the sensitive diplomatic effort to open North Korean facilities to inspection.
When he told the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee in January that there were "a thousand or two" designers of nuclear weapons in the former Soviet Union, he puzzled much of the Administration's non-proliferation establishment, which scrambled to figure out where he got the figures and then concluded they were probably meaningless.
On the other hand, if Mr. Gates too closely echoes the views of the Bush Administration, he opens himself to criticism that he is slanting intelligence to serve the agenda of policymakers. 
When he suggested to the House Foreign Affairs Committee last month that China was complying with the Missile Technology Control Regime, the international accord that bans the sale of missiles and related technology, he incurred the wrath of Senator Joseph R. Biden, the Delaware Democrat whose bete noire is Chinese proliferation. 
"We have no indication that I'm aware of that they are selling technologies now that would be a violation of the agreements they've signed up to," Mr. Gates said.
On the same day that Mr. Gates was testifying, Mr. Biden was briefing the Senate, in a rare closed session, on China's recent sales of missile technology to the Middle East -- sales, he suggested, that clearly violated the spirit if not the letter of the accord. 
He got his information in part from private briefings provided just days before by Gordon Oehler, Mr. Gates' chief aide on proliferation. 
(The Senate voted 59-39 on Feb. 
25 to deny favored-nation status, but failed to override the Presidential veto.)
Â 
A Question of Propriety
The apparent discrepancy between the testimony of Mr. Gates and the view provided by Mr. Oehler prompted Mr. Biden to send Mr. Gates a classified letter that raised the issue of politicization. 
In an angry speech on the Senate floor on March 18, the Senator said: "On the same day that we in the Senate were convened in closed session to discuss the disturbing implications of intelligence reports about Chinese arms sales, Director Gates was over in the House giving China a clean bill of health. 
His testimony that day raises questions of both propriety and accuracy."
After a meeting to iron out their differences, the Senator said in a statement that he was convinced that there was no effort by Mr. Gates to "distort the intelligence," but they agreed that part of his testimony on Chinese arms proliferation practices could have been misinterpreted. 
Other senators noted that as an intelligence official, Mr. Gates was supposed to leave to policymakers the issue of compliance with international agreements.
Sensitive to charges during his confirmation hearings that he tailored intelligence as a senior official in the 1980's, Mr. Gates has accepted the recommendations of a C.I.A. task force on polticization. 
On March 16 he told analysts, "We must engage in a candid discussion of the issue, devise effective measures to prevent it from occurring, and resolve to deal decisively with any circumstances that may foster distortions."
C.I.A. officials insist that they would be happier if Mr. Gates's testimony could take place in private. 
"We like to think of ourselves as the Administration's ultimate think tank, but not its ultimate spokesperson," said Gary E. Foster, the C.I.A.'s new chief spokesman. 
"We try to keep intelligence pure and straight. 
We are uncomfortable with open sessions because we don't know where they're going to go."
In a speech last month, Mr. Gates said that he and the agency's senior officials will be making more speeches, more public appearances before Congress and, most likely, more news. 
But perhaps more alert to the pitfalls of going public, Mr. Gates in testimony before a House panel last week delivered a cautious prepared statement about regional threats around the world. 
All he would say about the timing of North Korea's becoming a nuclear power was that it's "close, very close."
In fact, the testimony included little new information and committee staff members said Mr. Gates declined to answer lawmakers' questions except behind closed doors.

text:
ï»¿
SOME years ago, when three Red Guards tried to carry the Cultural Revolution to a village inhabited by the Yao ethnic minority, the Yao peasants dealt with the annoyance in a traditional way: they bound the Red Guards and prepared to slaughter them as a human sacrifice. 
Yao elders eventually managed the release of the young revolutionaries, but the incident left a lasting impression of the delicacy of relations with China's ethnic minorities.
While China is often regarded abroad as a homogeneous nation, some 8 percent of the population is made up of members of 55 minorities. 
Tibetans are the best-known minority -- and an often-cited example of acrimony and repressiveness in the Government's handling of relations with minority groups. 
But the Xishuangbanna District of southwest China is perhaps more representative, and certainly more successful, in the way it has managed ethnic minorities.
The villages around the local capital of Jing hong are full of members of various ethnic groups, wearing distinctive bright clothing and speaking their own languages. 
Fights sometimes erupt when one village believes another is trying to steal its land or its women, but none of the groups is known to have formed a political underground or to have called for independence.
In general, relations with the 25 significant ethnic minorities here in Yunnan Province in Southwestern China appear to be relatively trusting.
"There are a lot of minority problems here, but they're not political as in Tibet," Shen Qirong, a spokesman for the Nationality Affairs Commission Yunnan Province, said in an interview in the provincial capital of Kunming. 
"There've been no calls for independence or separatism, and the problems that arise are in isolated areas, and then they pass. 
They're not systemic."
In Tibet and the far western region of Xinjiang, ethnic tensions have led to clashes with the authorities and to independence movements. 
But many diplomats say that in general, China has managed its other ethnic minorities in an enlightened manner, granting them special privileges to co-opt them into the system. 
Two years ago, at about the same time that students demanding democracy were shot, Chinese Moslems demonstrated to protest a book that they said defamed them. 
The authorities responded not by crushing the demonstrations but by arresting the author and banning the book. 
To be sure, the Moslems were demanding not democracy but suppression of another viewpoint, but the fact that the Chinese listened to the protest at all is an indication of how seriously the ethnic groups are treated.
Outside of Tibet and Xinjiang, where some diplomats expect the separatist movements eventually to triumph, China's policy toward minorities has been quite effective. 
The largest ethnic minority, for example, are the Zhuang, with a population of 15.5 million concentrated in south-central China, but the Zhuang have been partly assimilated and do not cause problems for the Government. 
The 4.8 million Mongols have also been politically quiet, despite concerns that upheavals in the neighboring country of Mongolia would trigger unrest among them.
"China is much more conscious of minorities as groups than most developing countries," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"They have an amazingly well defined minority policy and program. 
You can criticize it, because they don't have real power or because it's often window-dressing. 
But there are efforts to bring minorities into high-profile positions, which has its own value because then they begin to serve as role models."
In Yunnan, one reason for the relative contentment seems to be the preferential treatment given to members of minority groups. 
Typically, ethnic minorities are allowed to marry earlier than members of the Han ethnic majority, and, most important, to have more children. 
Their children can also get into universities with lower examination scores than are required of Han students, and model members of minorities are chosen to fill prominent Government posts. 
The Governor of Yunnan Province, for example, is a member of the Naxi minority.
Because of the affirmative action policy, some families that in the past had tried to assimilate into the Han majority are now applying for declarations that they are members of a minority, and not Han, so that their children will have a better chance of getting into the universities.
In Jinghong, a young man who was registered as Han, and was thus allowed to have only one child, was disappointed when the child was a daughter. 
He checked his geneology, found some Dai minority ancestors, and re-registered himself as a Dai so that he could try to have a son.
Some Han complain that the preferences are unfair, but there is little noticeable resentment against affirmative action policies in China.
A main source of tension in Xishuangbanna in recent years has been the establishment of state-owned rubber plantations in minority areas. 
Nearby villages complain that the plantations take their land, and village children get in fights with the children of the Han Chinese plantation workers. 
The fights escalate, and the police sometimes are beaten when they try to intervene.
"Those tensions have declined dramatically," said Tian Jiaxiang, who is a Dai and deputy governor of Xishuangbanna. 
He said, and some local villagers agreed, that the disputes had been reduced by readjusting land and giving villagers a share of the income from the plantations.
Some members of ethnic minorities grumble that the fundamental problem is that many Han are arrogant and look down on other people. 
The authorities acknowledge that this is a problem, but they also note that there is growing intermarriage between Han and the minorities and suggest that this shows an increasing mutual respect.

text:
ï»¿
The aging Mao Zedong, feeling frustrated with the Communist Party bureaucracy in the 1960's, traveled south and used provincial newspapers to launch his calls for change. 
The result was the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, and nothing in China was ever quite the same.
When the aging Deng Xiaoping felt frustrated with the Communist Party bureaucracy in the 1990's, he too traveled south -- this January -- and used provincial newspapers and television stations to shake up the regime. 
But Beijing is still locked in a power struggle, and it is unclear whether Mr. Deng's efforts to impose his will will have the sweeping effects that Mao's did.
Mr. Deng has criticized several hard-liners by name, and he declared that "anyone who isn't a reformer must leave the stage."
But a political stillness hangs over the capital so far, and the bureaucracy is waiting for the other shoe to drop. 
Those whom Mr. Deng criticized remain in their posts, although at least one has checked into the hospital with what appears to be a political illness.
This is widely expected to be a decisive year in Chinese politics, in part because this fall a party congress is to convene for the first time in five years. 
But the power struggles and prospects are exceedingly murky. 
"There's a lot of speculation about what will happen, but nobody really knows," said a Chinese official who circulates among the leaders. 
"Even Deng Xiaoping doesn't know yet how it will all come out."
Some Chinese are giddy with hope that there will be tremendous change: that Prime Minister Li Peng and other hard-liners will be dismissed, that political prisoners will be freed, and that ousted figures like the former party leader Zhao Ziyang will make a comeback. 
For now, however, the evidence does not support such expectations. 
Mr. Deng's speeches during his trip to the south suggest that while he would like accelerated economic change he has no intention of easing political controls significantly.
"We must not be soft-hearted," Mr. Deng declared, and he said that the regime would have to "exercise dictatorship against our enemies" for perhaps several dozen generations to come. 
The speeches, which were circulated among Communist Party members as Central Committee Document No. 2, reiterate that China's leaders acted correctly in June 1989, when they ordered tanks and troops to crush the democracy movement at the cost of hundreds of lives. 
Mr. Deng also urged that officials watch for "the initial symptoms" of anti-government activity, so it could be wiped out more easily.
Â 
Frank and Consistent
Few world leaders have been so consistently misunderstood as Mr. Deng. In the 1980's, his advocacy of economic liberalization was widely mistaken as an indication that he was a closet capitalist who might tolerate democratic reform as well. 
Then, after he helped destroy the democracy movement in 1989, he was reviled as a brutal hard-liner. 
But in fact Mr. Deng has been reasonably frank and consistent about his views for the last 30 years: He believes firm dictatorial control is essential to manage China and preserve stabilityI, but he differs from the ideologues in that he will try almost any form of agricultural and industrial management that seems likely to promote economic growth and raise living standards.
"Reform and opening up require greater boldness and courageous experiments, and must not proceed like a woman with bound feet," Mr. Deng urged in Document No. 2. Officially the document is confidential, but Hong Kong publications have obtained and published it.
Document No. 2 also makes clear Mr. Deng's visceral fear of the instability of democracy. 
He says that if the army had not crushed the democracy movement "there would have been a chaotic situation which might have led to civil war."
Still, Mr. Deng's campaign to promote economic liberalization has left the hard-liners in trouble. 
The Communist Party Discipline Inspection Commission is believed to have sent work teams to investigate three bastions of the hard-liners: the Culture Ministry, the People's Daily and the Propaganda Department. 
The leaders of those three units are expected to be dismissed later this year.
One difficulty in gauging the impact of Mr. Deng's campaign is that so far it is virtually all talk rather than action. 
"There's a risk that the winds of reform will blow for a while, but then they'll die down and the landscape will be pretty much the same as before," said a Chinese with close ties to the reformist faction in the leadership that lost power in 1989.
There also are mixed signals. 
Four weeks ago the Politburo denounced Bao Tong, a reformist official who has been in prison since the Tiananmen democracy movement, and expelled him from the Communist Party. 
Zhu Rongji, a Deputy Prime Minister, was in Hainan Province last week quietly telling officials to scrap the stock market they started a month earlier.
Still, even the oratory about bolder change has an impact at the local level, in that local leaders -- especially in southern China -- use it as an excuse to push a little harder for their pet projects. 
Local officials often have little patience for Communist ideology and simply want to promote economic growth, and now some think they can get away with a bit more. 
Some are forcing state-owned enterprises to face the discipline of the market, even if that means layoffs, and Guangzhou, Shanghai and Shenzhen are all imitating Hong Kong and trying to introduce the bourgeois pastime of horse-racing.
"Whatever you want to do these days, you cite Deng Xiaoping," an official says. 
"If you want to start a brothel, then you say, "Well, comrade Xiaoping says we should take bolder steps!"

file: The World_As Ideology Recedes, The U.S. Rearranges Its Global Struggles.txt
text:
ï»¿
Viewing American foreign policy these days can seem a bit like watching a badly dubbed and poorly edited foreign movie. 
The actors often seem to be speaking the wrong lines and their actions often seem to be all out of order.
Consider the last two weeks. 
One day the United States intervenes in Panama and the next day it virtually invites the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact to invade Rumania to support the democracy movement there. 
One day the Administration sends two senior officials to Beijing to patch up ties with China, apparently out of concern that the Chinese leadership, if alienated, might rush into an embrace with Moscow, and the next day it invites the Soviet Foreign Minister to visit NATO headquarters. 
For years the United States railed against the Marxist Sandinista Government in Managua, but it turned out that the threat deemed worthy of an invasion was from a 19th-century-style tinpot dictator in Panama.
Is there a method to this melange?
Actually, yes. 
The ideological competition between East and West, so prominent in global politics in the last 40 years, is giving way, making what was unimaginable a year ago, such as a visit by Foreign Minister Eduard A. Shevardnadze to NATO headquarters, almost routine. 
At the same time, more traditional power politics is becoming more apparent.
In the classic form of power politics, ideologically inspired actions take a back seat to basic territorial and economic imperatives. 
Dominant powers assert themselves in their own regions or spheres of the world while competing for mastery in areas where there is an opportunity for a contest. 
This is the real meaning of the Panama invasion, and of Moscow's insistence on keeping Eastern Europe in the Warsaw Pact, even while allowing it to retreat from Communism.
The object of this game of nations is not necessarily a freer world or a workers' paradise, but survival of the fittest and everything this requires: influence, resources and allies.
When the glow over the end of the cold war fades, watch for Washington and Moscow to go on competing for advantage on the Eurasian land mass, just as they have for nearly a half-century. 
''The end of the cold war does not mean an end of a global competiton between the superpowers,'' said Michael J. Sandel, a political theorist at Harvard. 
''Once the ideological dimension fades, what you are left with is not peace, harmony and sweetness, but old-fashioned global politics based on dominant powers competing for influence and pursuing their national interests.''
But, at least in the view of some critics, it seems that not everyone in the Bush Administration - particularly the President - is alive to the subtleties of this transition and the new opportunities it may be opening. 
President Bush has never fully explained his decision to send his national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, on two secret missions to China, except to say that for geopolitical reasons he did not want to isolate Beijing by punishing its leadership too harshly for the murders in Tiananmen Square. 
Some in the Administration argue that such a policy is the essence of ''realist'' power politics.
To the critics, though, it seems a bad imitation. 
To be sure, it might not be in America's interest to be isolated from China, both because China is the biggest power in Asia and because of the potential for a Moscow-Beijing alliance against Washington. 
But the question is not whether links between the United States and China should be maintained but on whose terms and, in the wake of Tiananmen Square, with what timing. 
And with whom should these ties be maintained - with the current aging Chinese leadership or with the next generation of the Chinese people?
Given the changes in Moscow, Beijing's leaders are not in the same pivotal position in the superpower contest that their predecessors enjoyed two decades ago. 
And given the alienation of today's leaders from their people, their future tenure is questionable. 
Therefore, the critics argue, catering to the sensibilities of Deng Xiaoping and his colleagues isn't realism, but an anachronism.
''The Scowcroft China mission is a classic case of cultural lag: a President applying 1970's thinking to a 1990 situation,'' said Edward N. Luttwak of the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. 
''The United States-China relationship in the 1970's was a natural coalescence against a dynamically expansive Soviet Union. 
With Soviet activism in decline, the importance of the Beijing-Washington strategic relationship declines as well. 
Certainly Washington need not worry that Beijing will be driven into the arms of Moscow. 
Today it is the economic relationship that is increasingly important, and in that relationship the United States is the giver and China the taker.''
In addition to traditional power politics, something more is emerging as the ideologically driven East-West competition wanes. 
Moral concerns like human rights could take on new force, while the environment, terrorism, drugs and above all economics rise as factors in international relations. 
In the days when power depended on who had the biggest army and navy, it was easy to identify which country was predominant. 
Today, a country's balance of trade is becoming as important an indicator of its status as its place in the balance of power. 
In this economically interdependent world, America's place will increasingly depend as much on how it deals with its trade deficit with Japan as on how it coexists with the Soviet Union in Europe.
''In many third world areas, we will find ourselves both competing with and cooperating with the Japanese and not the Soviets,'' Geoffrey Kemp, a senior associate at the Carnegie Endowment, argued. 
''The Russians just are not going to be players. 
Aside from military equipment, the Soviets have nothing to sell. 
Not only are they unable to compete with Europe, Japan and the United States, but also with their own former satellites in Eastern Europe - which is naturally going to draw Eastern Europe westward and leave the Soviets with a shrinking pie.''
As long as the world economy continues to expand, there will be room for the United States, Europe and Japan to act in cooperation, Mr. Kemp noted. 
But, he added, if there is a global recession ''one would be foolish to assume that this will remain the case.''
President Bush leaving the Pentagon last week after a briefing on Panama (Associated Press)

text:

A UNIVERSAL joke in socialist countries is that employment in state-owned companies is a matter of make-believe: "We pretend to work, and they pretend to pay us."
In China, this game is carried to extremes. 
Employees in state-owned companies receive only about $30 a month, and some quip that they don't even deserve that much, what with late arrivals, tea breaks, lunch breaks and early departures.
But these days the situation is becoming less humorous: The state sector is losing ever-increasing amounts of money, to the consternation of the hard-liners who run the country.
One-third of state-owned companies are losing money, another third earn negligible profits, and only a third earn any money for the state. 
The total losses in the state sector doubled in the first nine months of this year, compared with the same period of last year.
This is helping to provoke a fiscal crisis, both because there are fewer profitable enterprises to hand over earnings to the state and because there are more failing enterprises to subsidize. 
In China, inefficient companies are subsidized because of the fear that if they closed, disgruntled workers would foment unrest.
"We should waste no time or effort in boosting the economy," Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader, said early this month. 
"Without economic growth it would be difficult to maintain political stabilityI."
The crisis in the state sector is, paradoxically, perhaps one of the most important forces left for reform here. 
The hard-liners, fearful that they will be blamed for the economic slump, already have eased up on their initially tough economic policy. 
The leadership has relaxed its retrenchment policy and ended attacks on collective and private businesses.
"They are terrified of a recession," said a Chinese businessman. 
"They are becoming a lot more flexible than they used to be, because they want practical measures to get the economy going. 
They know that's the only way they'll get popular support and survive in office."
Provincial leaders, showing unusual gumption, are said to be rebelling against the central government's plans to make them hand over more money. 
And the shortage of money has driven the leadership to a course of action it had long shied away from: raising prices for necessities such as coal, sugar and even bus fares.
Ordinary people are muttering, but so far there have been no major protests.
"Everybody's angry about the price increases," said a middle-age woman as she returned from the market. 
"But there's nothing we can do but complain to each other."
Some Chinese intellectuals chuckle that such price rises are terrific. 
On the one hand, they make the economy a bit more rational by bringing price levels closer to the market. 
On the other hand, they cause widespread indignation at the central planners who now dominate the Government. 
When change comes, these Chinese say, it will be all the faster because central planning is being so thoroughly discredited.
Over all, the economy is showing signs of recovery. 
Industrial production in October was 12.7 percent higher than it was in October 1989 -- the best performance in more than 18 months.
But most of this resurgence is coming not from the state sector but from other parts of the economy. 
In September, the last full month for which figures are available, the state sector enjoyed a growth rate of only 3 percent, while collectives (mostly in rural areas) grew at 9.4 percent and private companies and joint ventures soared at a 57.7 percent growth rate.
"The most interesting thing about the economy is that for all the favoritism shown to the state sector, it's been greatly outperformed by rural enterprises," said a Western economist in Beijing.
That leads to what may be the lesson of the Chinese experiment that is most relevant to other socialist countries. 
China's economic restructuring has lasted much longer and in most cases gone further than the economic changes in Eastern Europe, and it has achieved breathtaking results -- per capita incomes have approximately doubled since the process began at the end of 1978.
But the most glittering parts of this massive accomplishment were supplied by the non-state sector: in private agriculture, private business, and especially in rural collective enterprises. 
All the experiments and changes have not enabled state companies to become more profitable.
"China has made virtually no progress toward systematically putting the state sector on some kind of legal, independent basis, as they had intended to," said Barry Naughton, a specialist in the Chinese economy at the University of California at San Diego. 
But he added that he was not as critical of China's state sector as many Chinese economists are, and that part of their difficulties are simply the natural result of a cyclical downturn.
The Government is hoping to save its state sector through what it bills as a "reform" program. 
Among the elements are the merger of failing companies into healthy ones to create enormous conglomerates, and a more rigorous tax system, so that tax obligations would be a matter of law and not of negotiation.
The southern city of Shenzhen is pioneering the auction of Government enterprises to anyone with the cash and inclination to take them over. 
And both Shenzhen and Shanghai are competing to be the first to open a modernized stock exchange, in the hope that stock in state enterprises can be sold to shareholders.
A couple of years ago, some Chinese officials hoped to get rid of most of the state sector. 
They never used the term privatization, but rather a variety of euphemisms that amounted to much the same thing. 
These days, however, "ownership reform" is ideologically impossible on any large scale, and even share ownership is now intended to supplement rather than supplant state ownership.
That is the nub of the problem, many Chinese officials complain. 
They say that tinkering with state ownership will not succeed, so the Government should scrap the system altogether. 
Their advice to Eastern European countries now considering what to do with inefficient state sectors is not to copy Chinese experiments, but to try to dump the companies on anyone who will take them.
"Most people know that state ownership is the root of the problem," said a Chinese economist, "but for now, it's ideologically impossible to do anything about it."

For years, this outpost of Europe behaved like a standoffish neighbor to the Asian community it lived in. 
Instead of cultivating ties with the community, it relied on its own natural wealth and its political, economic and cultural links to Europe.
But now, fearful that it will lose European markets after the European Community is fully established in 1992 and aware that its Asian neighbors' economies are flourishing, Australia is accepting, even embracing, its geographic location, hoping to share in the regional growth.
''In the sense of being a true part of the growth in this region, developing ourselves in the rapid pace of Southeast Asia, we're a sort of hanger-on-er, rather than a full participant in the growth,'' said Paul W. McCarthy, chief economist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
In the two years since Prime Minister Bob Hawke traveled to Seoul and announced a drive for closer economic cooperation within the Pacific region, Australians have been shaking the hands of more Asian officials, business executives and tourists than ever before. 
There are more Hong Kong Chinese immigrants mingling in Australian society, and in the last three years Australia has run trade surpluses with Japan, which now accounts for more than one-fifth of Australia's total trade.
Japanese investment, which exceeded $26 billion in the end of the 1989 fiscal year, has been the fastest growing source of foreign investment in the country. 
Britain and the United States, however, still have higher levels of investment.
Yet many Australians say more needs to be done, especially economically, to integrate their island with Asia. 
Trade with Southeast Asia, for instance, has grown only slightly in the last three years.
While Australians still crave American imports, Japanese businesses have become such a dominant influence in trade that 4 of the top 10 largest Australian exporters are Japanese companies. 
After Broken Hill Property Group, Australia's largest industrial corporation, the No. 2 exporter is Mitsui & Company (Australia) Ltd. 
Most of the exports are commodities, such as wood chips, ore and coal, and many of them go straight to Japan, which receives more than twice the value of exports of Australia's second-largest market, the United States. 
For Australia to become a larger force in Asia, many economists and business executives say, the country must restructure its own economy.
Â 
Plyboard, Not Chips
''Instead of sending wood chips, we should be sending plyboard, and where they take paper pulp, we should send paper,'' said Paul A. Everingham, a corporate lawyer.
He said one concern is the Australian view of Asia. 
''One of our problems is that Australians think of Asia in terms of Japan and China, and they think of the other countries as places they can go to for holidays.''
Japan and China have been the focus of Australia's ties to Asia. 
In a dramatic turnaround from the White Australia policy, which essentially shut out Asian immigrants until the early 1970's, Mr. Hawke this June granted 19,000 Chinese students the right to stay for four years in Australia. 
And Australian businesses have called on China for years.
Japan, on the other hand, sends not migrants but money. 
Japanese companies operate throughout Australian financial and trading circles, and more and more Japanese honeymooners are coming to Australia to eat steak and play golf. 
In Brisbane and the nearby sunny Gold Coast, Japanese corporations have purchased nearly a dozen resort hotels to cater to large Japanese tour groups. 
In 1989, nearly 350,000 Japanese tourists came to Australia, buying large blocks of seats on the planes and paying for spaces on the golf courses.
The area has always been a Shangri-la for Australian retirees, but now some Australians are finding that the Japanese presence involves a price: some Australians are priced out of the market as purchases by Japanese companies push up property values.
While some Australians fear or criticize the influx of foreign capital, others are calling for measures to develop the export of services in which Australia is strong, such as education, health and advanced technology. 
These may be areas of opportunity for trade with neighbors like Indonesia and Malaysia.
Â 
A Joint Venture
In Adelaide, Japanese and Australian business executives and politicians are planning together the construction of a high-tech metropolis, where tiny villages would be linked to a modern network of communications, a research university, a science and industrial park and other commercial facilities that would attract investors.
But the move toward Asia has been bumpy, because Australia still values its historic ties to Europe. 
More students are studying Japanese, but many Australians still aspire to attend Oxford. 
More trade delegations are going to Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, but the country remains part of the Commonwealth and Australians still celebrate the Queen's birthday.
''No doubt we have to come to grips with becoming a part of Asia,'' said William J. Shields, executive director of Macquarie Bank Ltd. 
''But it's dangerous to see us as an Asian country. 
Culturally we have other links.''
Some Australian companies find it difficult to break into Asian markets, and many do not speak the languages or know the local customs. 
Moreover, most of the economies are still viewed as developing ones, compared with Australia's rather mature economy, where per capita gross domestic product was $17,100 in the last fiscal year. 
Australia is trying to develop its manufacturing base and looks upon certain Asian countries as stronger competitors, with their cheap labor.
''A lot of people claim that Japan, Hong Kong and Taiwan are catching up to us'' in output, said Saul Eslake, chief economist at McIntosh Hamson Hoare Govett Ltd., an investment firm in Melbourne. 
''And there's a lot of angst about all that.''

text:
ï»¿
THERE wasn't much publicity. 
The subject was not at the top of the news. 
But when a distinguished Soviet academician on a diplomatic mission was persuaded recently to give an informal talk on Central Asia, there was standing room only in the hotel banquet hall that a local scholar booked.
Central Asia is an old idea taking on new life, not only in Pakistan but also in the Asian Muslim world beyond the Middle East - as far east as China's Xinjiang region. 
As fissures appear in the Soviet Union, and the superpowers seem ready to pull back from Afghanistan, a region that for more than a century had been pulled apart by outsiders - Russians, British and Chinese among them - is beginning to stitch back together its common history.
The search for roots has been made possible by the evaporation of East-West tensions, in much the same way that other parts of the world also feel freer these days to define themselves in terms other than pro-Moscow, pro-Washington or non-aligned.
No one expects a new Central Asian empire to stir the ghost of Tamerlane, certainly not in an age when nationalisms are fragmenting rather than enlarging geographical domains. 
But a process, however tenuous and exploratory, of rediscovering old cultural, historical, religious and commercial bonds is under way, perhaps most of all in Pakistan, the nation in the middle that looks both east and west. 
The Lahore Museum, the country's most distinguished repository of archeologly and art, has put on a show about Central Asia with exhibits from a Moscow collection, and a new institute has sprung up to publish bulletins on the region.
Enter the bemused Soviet scholar, Yuri Gankovsky. 
After taking the lectern in Islamabad, he was peppered with questions by an audience hungry for information. 
He was also buffeted by accusations that Moscow was turning its harshest face south to subdue its Islamic republics -''Flowers for Estonia and tanks for Azerbaijan'' is how one questioner phrased it. 
Hands were still waving when question time came to an end.
''Tashkent is far closer to Islamabad than Islamabad is to Karachi,'' said Ijaz S. Gilani, director of the Center for Asian Studies in Islamabad, referring to the Soviet city 500 miles away and Pakistan's capital more than 650 miles south.
Before the colonial British came, before first Russian and then Soviet might intervened to close the borders, and long before Islamabad cast its lot decisively with the West, large areas of Pakistan inhabited the world of the silk roads, where Orient and Occident collided in the bazaars and sometimes on the battlefields.
Throughout the region, as urges from the past stir from Xinjiang to the Soviet Central Asian republics, news travels quickly across the mountains and plains. 
Pakistanis discuss rumors of the desecration of Chinese mosques. 
Analysts speculate on whether a revolutionary situation is developing in the Soviet south.
Pakistanis who visit Soviet Asia say they are met with warmth and curiosity. 
''My mother and I just wanted to see these places we had heard so much about,'' said Abida Hussain, a member of Parliament. 
''People first thought we must be Indians, and treated us with reserve. 
But when we told them we were Pakistanis, they were delighted, and welcomed us as one of them.''
A close relationship with the Muslim-majority nations of West Asia - Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey - has always been part of Pakistani policy. 
It is a theme Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto stresses, just as her Government looks forward to the prospect of increased cultural ties with Soviet Central Asia once there is an Afghan settlement. 
Soviet diplomats in Islamabad are keenly aware of this potential, both as a source of opportunity and as a source of concern.
Â 
Reasons to Worry
Not all the interest in Central Asia is benign or cultural. 
William Maley of the Australian Defense Force Academy, who has toured the Pakistan-Afghanistan border area, says some Pakistani generals would like to extend their strategic borders into Soviet territory through Afghanistan. 
For this reason, some Pakistanis were pursuing secondary aims in the Afghan war, hoping to weaken the Soviet underbelly. 
And thoughts of a new community of interests unsettle India, which fears it may one day confront a bloc of conservative Islamic lands from its western borders to the horizons of Europe.
To some extent, Kashmiri nationalists battling to separate their largely Muslim valley from India are encouraged by what they see as an inevitable coalescing of Islamic Central Asia. 
At this point, it is convenient for them to overlook the deep divisions of the Islamic world. 
Shiites, Sunnis, Sufis and Ahmadis cannot live in peace even within Pakistan. 
Ethnic rivalries could break out among Soviet Tadzhiks, Uzbeks, Kazakhs and Turkic people as easily as they have among warring Afghan communities.
But for now, Kashmiris want nothing more than to break down the border that separates them from brothers across the mountains. 
With the wider region in flux, anything can seem possible.
''Our old Central Asian trade routes were active right up until 1926, when the Soviet state closed the borders,'' Mr. Gilani said, adding that cultures as well as commodities traveled these caravan trails. 
''Some routes are still there, and we have new ones. 
Four busloads of Pakistanis cross the border on the Karakoram highway into China every day as traders.''
Coming the other way at this time of year are groups of Chinese Muslim pilgrims with bundles, heading for Mecca. 
For them, the Haj - the pilgrimage each Muslim is expected to make at least once - begins in Pakistan.

text:

DENG XIAOPING is gambling again. 
The 85-year-old Chinese leader, who has proved an astute political oddsmaker, is betting that by ending martial law Beijing will reap economic and diplomatic benefits without risking further unrest.
Avoiding new turmoil is crucial, and the hope here is that foreigners will take the lifting of martial law, announced last week, more seriously than will the Chinese. 
It seems that the action is an effort to expunge some trappings of repression without ending the repression itself.
China's leaders had hoped for a more enthusiastic response abroad. 
True, the Bush Administration agreed - on the very day of the announcement, although it said there was no connection - to allow World Bank loans for relief after earthquakes and other calamities. 
President Bush had earlier sent his national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, on two missions to Beijing, and the Administration suggested that the lifting of martial law was a dividend. 
But Japan has said that it wants to see further liberalization before resuming negotiations on a $5 billion loan package. 
In Washington, Congress may well vote for new sanctions against China after convening later this month.
China's leaders had hoped for a more enthusiastic response abroad. 
Martial law and the bloody victory over the democracy movement last June carried with it tremendous costs. 
The Bush Administration's overtures notwithstanding, the Government has become a virtual pariah in the world. 
The sharp drop in tourism and foreign investment has hurt the economy and risks sparking further unrest. 
And the military presence during martial law deepened the hostility of many Chinese toward the Government.
Army troops remain in the capital, and the police have been ordered to intervene at the first sign of trouble. 
Unauthorized demonstrations are still illegal. 
On Tiananmen Square, even speaking loudly is an offense.
Until last May, the Communist Party might have gained some popular support with political liberalization, many Chinese intellectuals and foreign scholars say. 
While in Eastern Europe, Communist parties were generally reviled as Soviet-installed instruments of oppression and stagnation, the Chinese party still had a modest reservoir of good will based on its successes in the 1950's in reorganizing society and reviving the economy, as well as on the more recent economic boom of the early 1980's.
Â 
The Path Not Taken
Some young party officials here believe that when the leadership came to the crossroads last May and June, it could have chosen greater pluralism over violent repression. 
They say that if China had held elections, partly free, partly rigged, as in Taiwan and many developing countries, the Communist Party could have relied upon rural support to win.
But even these party members say that the Communists have so outraged the country over the last nine months that liberalization will be far more complex and dangerous than ever before. 
A famous pop singer, Hou Dejian, who has some protection because of his fame and Taiwanese origins, put it this way: ''In Eastern Europe, the regimes sacrificed one or two persons and protected the whole party. 
China was the opposite. 
China sacrificed the whole party and government to protect one or two persons.''
Economic pressures are crucial in this respect. 
A year ago, many Chinese were upset about inflation. 
Now inflation has been tamed, but unemployment and slow growth have emerged to make people more upset than ever.
Industrial output grew by only 6.8 percent in 1989, the Government announced last week, down from 17.7 percent growth the previous year. 
More alarming, most of the growth came early in the year; in the last quarter, industrial output grew only seven-tenths of 1 percent.
Because of a tight monetary policy, rising debts and a shortage of energy and raw materials, countless factories have been closed across the country - up to 8 percent of factories in some cities, the Government spokesman acknowledged. 
The Chinese people as a whole may not have seen their real standard of living drop, but they certainly have fallen far behind their expectations of continued improvement.
By late last year, the Government seemed to realize the political risk of further austerity, and monetary policy was sharply relaxed, though this may mean a resurgence of inflation later in 1990. 
The authorities also disclosed that all workers at state-owned enterprises will get a wage increase by the Chinese New Year holiday later this month.
It is not clear that the lifting of martial law will bring many of the expected economic benefits. 
Foreign business executives interviewed last week said that the move by itself made relatively little difference, and that economic prospects and the investment climate remain inauspicious. 
Tourism will improve, but is expected to remain subdued.
Most Chinese seem to believe that the party will try to consolidate its position through economic relaxation - a move intended to improve its popularity on pocketbook issues - while maintaining political controls that remain as strict as ever. 
But Chinese officials and foreign diplomats interviewed also maintain that hostility to the leadership is so great, particularly in cities and even within the party itself, that the hard-liners will be taking considerable risks if they try to rely on anything but the barrel of a gun.
Significantly, while the end of martial law brought no immediate economic benefits, it did ignite some minor political incidents. 
In several cases reported Thursday and Friday, people were hauled away from Tiananmen Square after shouting slogans or trying to present wreaths to honor the dead.
Â 
'When the Overthrow Will Come'
''Everybody is talking about when the overthrow will come,'' said a Government official. 
His own prediction is that it will take 10 years, but he acknowledged that his guess is unusually conservative. 
When asked, most people say two to five years will be enough. 
They do not so much forecast the end of socialism in China as simply a shift to a more moderate set of economic and political policies, probably under new Communist leaders. 
They see the changes coming either because of new street demonstrations or from a military coup or a power struggle within the Communist Party.
As the Government tries to heal the wounds of June and win a measure of support, it is stressing ''political study'' sessions intended to show that, as a huge billboard proclaims in the center of Beijing: ''Only socialism can save China. 
Only socialism can make China develop.''

text:
ï»¿
IN the 1950's Chairman Mao declared: "The Soviet Union's today is China's tomorrow."
Now it would be a counter-revolutionary offense to say that in public. 
But in searching for a country to emulate, Deng Xiaoping, China's 87-year-old senior leader, has come up with a partial model, one that in many respects runs counter to China's original revolutionary principles.
That model is Singapore.
When Mr. Deng traveled to southern China early this year to squeeze the hard-liners and campaign for faster economic liberalization, he mentioned only three countries by name: Japan, South Korea and Singapore, all cited for their sound development. 
One of the most illuminating statements he made was this:
"Singapore's social order is rather good. 
Its leaders exercise strict management. 
We should learn from their experience, and we should do a better job than they do."
While it may seem odd for a Communist government to take as its model a monument to free enterprise, Mr. Deng's comment reflects a fascination with the practical accomplishments of Asia's "four dragons": Singapore, Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea.
Mr. Deng explicitly called upon Guangdong Province to catch up with the "four dragons" over the next two decades, "not only catching up with them in terms of economic prosperity but also in terms of social order and public conduct."
Mr. Deng has also called for China to build "several Hong Kongs" along its coast, and Wu Bangguo, the Communist Party leader in Shanghai, was recently even more explicit. 
Mr. Wu reportedly told a visitor that China aimed to learn from the policies of South Korea and Singapore in developing their economies.
The emulation of Singapore, an island-state whose population of 2.7 million is 77 percent ethnic Chinese, reflects a growing consensus among China's leaders that prosperity and order are more important than Marxist ideology. 
Singapore is attractive in that it has enjoyed an economic miracle with political stability in a system dominated by a single political party that the voters regularly return to power by overwhelming margins.
"The talk about Singapore says a lot about what Deng wants," said a Chinese economist. 
"He would like to free up the economy, but he wants tight political control."
Â 
Clean and Orderly
Singapore not only has very few street protests; it has a cleanliness and orderliness that critics find dreary and antiseptic but that Mr. Deng regards as inspiring. 
There is no pornography, no extreme poverty, little corruption and not much spitting or littering in public. 
Bubble gum is prohibited, and critical foreign publications are sometimes banned.
"Of course old Deng likes Singapore," said a young Chinese Government official. 
"It's run by Chinese, it's efficient, it's rich, and no one jabbers about human rights."
The point is that Mr. Deng increasingly seems to regard Communist economic dogma -- state ownership and central planning -- as details that can be fudged. 
On the other hand, the bedrock of Chinese Communism, on which no compromise is allowed, is continued political control and maintenance of social order. 
This conception of government rests less on Marx than on Confucius. 
The sense of continuity from earlier Chinese dynasties, less visible in the Maoist era, has become more apparent in the last decade. 
The core convictions of "Emperor Deng" seem to have little to do with economic ideology. 
Instead, what Mr. Deng is passionate about is the Communist dynasty's right to rule and the need for a strong central government.
The redesign of the Communist road is evident when officials are asked what kind of a country they are trying to build. 
Officials sometimes describe their work as "mozhe shitou guo he" -- crossing the river by feeling with one's feet for the stones to step on. 
But there tend to be long silences when they are asked what is on the other side of the river.
Lei Yu, a prominent reformist who is now vice chairman of the Guangxi region in southern China, ventured an answer to that question in an interview earlier this year. 
Whatever changes, he said, the fundamental aim of Chinese socialism is collective prosperity and the absence of large income gaps between the rich and poor.
"If people live better, without big income gaps, that's the important thing," Mr. Lei said.
By that definition, however, bastions of free enterprise like Taiwan are more socialist than mainland China. 
Taiwan is far more prosperous than the mainland and by some calculations enjoys a more egalitarian distribution of wealth.
By standard measures, China's economy already has veered off the Communist road. 
The state sector now accounts for only half of industrial output, and its share is dropping steadily. 
A report prepared by China's National Information Center predicted a few weeks ago that by the year 2000 the state sector would account for only 27 percent of industrial output, with collectives making up 48 percent and private enterprise producing 25 percent. 
The economic flexibility -- which is almost certain to accelerate after the death of Mr. Deng and the other first-generation revolutionaries -- will not necessarily lead to democracy and greater respect for the human rights associated with it, however.
China's leaders seem much more envious of Singaporean wealth than of its voting system, and some of the "four dragons" in the past combined bustling markets with brutal repression. 
That deft combination may be what China's leaders hope to adopt for themselves.
