text:
ï»¿
'WE'RE tired of being second-class citizens,'' declared a large poster erected illegally last week by Chinese students at the Beijing Languages Institute. 
In a sense, that seemed to be what China's racial unrest of the last two weeks has been about.
The confrontations between Chinese and black African students reflect the deep-seated contradictions in Chinese feelings toward foreigners and the historical indignation at preferential treatment for foreigners. 
It was this indignation that helped carry the Communist Party to power 40 years ago, and the authorities' cautious approach acknowledged its continued potency.
Decades ago, foreigners dominated key areas of China and enforced special privileges for themselves. 
Now, it is the Chinese Government itself that enforces special treatment for foreigners, and resentment is rising. 
On trains, for example, the Chinese passengers obliged to travel ''hard class'' stare through the windows at the ''soft class'' cars reserved for foreigners and high officials.
And on university campuses, Chinese students seethe when they see their government providing special dormitories, cafeterias and scholarships to African students - particularly when the Chinese students feel they should be looking down on the Africans.
The latest troubles started when two African men brought Chinese dates to a Christmas Eve dance in the eastern city of Nanjing, touching off a brawl that has led to racial confrontations in at least four cities.
Initially the unrest seemed to be motivated largely by sheer racism, for there are few other ways to interpret such slogans as ''beat the blacks,'' which thousands of demonstrators in Nanjing shouted in the aftermath of the initial brawl. 
Racial stereotypes of blacks are very openly expressed in China.
While the latest unrest has focused on Africans, in a larger sense it spotlights the growing resentment in China of special treatment accorded to foreigners in general. 
Particularly for white Americans or Europeans, a foreign face has been magic in China in the last 10 years.
The civility was sometimes embarrassing: Chinese women would give up a seat on a crowded bus to a young white man. 
Longtime foreign residents say they think that attitude has changed, perhaps because of generally rising tensions arising from the rapid changes in society and the economy. 
Now when a foreign driver sideswipes a Chinese bicyclist, the bicyclist will not apologize as in the past but is likely to cling to the hood of the car and scream until a suitable payment is arranged.
An electronics student at Beijing University remembered that when the open-door policy was inaugurated a decade ago, Chinese marveled at the wealth and technology that foreigners enjoyed.
The Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976 had destroyed the self-confidence of many Chinese, and they were awed by the inscrutable Occidentals who rode in taxis and snapped photographs of each other in front of Mao Zedong's mausoleum.
''Now this is changing,'' the student said. 
''we have more contact with foreigners, and we see that they aren't all such wonderful people after all.''
This question of relations with foreigners resonates in Chinese history like no other.
China's psyche is still raw from the way one Western country after another humiliated China in the last 150 years, defeating it, seizing chunks of Chinese territory, overturning Chinese customs and grinding China's dignity into the dust under its heel.
The European arrogance still engraved on China's soul was typically expressed in a letter that an Englishman wrote home in 1842: ''It seems quite useless to kill the Chinese. 
It is like killing flies in July.''
The historical sense of humiliation is what makes the current resentment against the favoring of foreigners so political. 
The 1,500 African students in China are particularly resented, partly because of simple racism and partly because they receive special scholarships and living quarters from the Chinese Government.
Americans are more likely to be excused when they live lavishly in China, perhaps because they are likely to pay their own way and partly because it is felt that they live lavishly at home as well.
Higher stipends for foreign students or other signs of preferential treatment increasingly seem to touch a raw nerve.
The Communist Party is clearly concerned about such sentiments. 
The authorities in Nanjing have openly sympathized with the students, perhaps partly to placate them. 
Indeed, the authorities in some cases have seemed scarcely more restrained than the racist demonstrators. 
While the government denied the charge, the Africans reported being beaten and tortured by the police.
''Throughout the ages, the Chinese have had only one way of looking at foreigners,'' the famous Chinese social critic Lu Xun wrote more than 50 years ago. 
''We either look up to them as gods or down on them as wild animals.''
It was an exaggeration, but to many Africans in China at least the latter alternative rang true this week. 
For other foreigners, the tensions are not so volatile nor attitudes so extreme. 
But the lesson of China's recent demonstrations may be that preferential treatment of foreigners has become a political issue, and that many Chinese are fed up with seeing foreigners in their own land treated as gods.

text:
ï»¿
DENG XIAOPING gave up his last office in the Communist Party last week, but it remains to be seen whether he will give up power. 
Mr. Deng's authority has come not from his titles, but from his eminence and from the Confucian-style respect that other leaders give him. 
The 85-year-old Mr. Deng has not surrendered this status with his job as chairman of the party's Central Military Commission.
Power in China has never been so dependent on titles as in the West. 
The Empress Dowager Ci Xi ruled China at the turn of the century, even though the Emperor should have been in charge. 
When the Emperor made a move, Ci Xi had him imprisoned and his followers executed.
''Imagine what it would be like if every time George Bush wanted to make a decision, he had to consult and get approval from Ronald Reagan, Jimmy Carter, Gerald Ford and Richard Nixon,'' a Chinese intellectual said recently. 
''That's the problem in China today.''
Yet these shackles on leaders, binding them to consult their elders, are cultural ones, and they constrain all sides.
Even if Mr. Deng wanted to withdraw from all decision-making once and for all, it would be difficult. 
Inevitably, he will be consulted, for he is China's patriarch. 
Officials unhappy with the leadership are likely to pass on their complaints to Mr. Deng, in the knowledge that so long as he lives he remains the ultimate arbiter of disputes. 
And if Mr. Deng disagrees with the way the country is being run, he will probably speak out, and his successors will probably feel an obligation to obey.
Mr. Deng's departure from the party's commission is only the latest step in his gradual retirement. 
The major move came in 1987, when he left the Politburo and Central Committee. 
Now he has only one post -chairman of the Government's Central Military Commission, essentially the same as the party commission. 
He said that he would resign from that job next spring.
The retirement from the Politburo was a calculated one, intended to force the resignation of other elderly colleagues of his generation. 
The resignation from the commission was equally calculated. 
It enabled Mr. Deng to install Jiang Zemin, his intended heir as paramount leader, as the top military leader. 
This was a major accomplishment, for Mr. Jiang had no army experience.
Thus the shuffle may have more meaning for Mr. Jiang than for Mr. Deng. Mr. Jiang will be in a better position to build a national base, which he lacks, having become the national party leader only in June. 
Previously, the 63-year-old Mr. Jiang was the party boss of Shanghai.
Mr. Jiang will have to tread carefully. 
One possible source of rivalry, particularly after Mr. Deng dies, is President Yang Shangkun and his family. 
Mr. Yang was promoted to first vice chairman of the military commission, and his brother, Yang Baibing, was installed as the commission's secretary general as well as elevated to the Central Committee's secretariat. 
So long as Mr. Deng lives, he can protect Mr. Jiang, but after that anything might happen.

file: THE WORLD_For Vietnam, The Price Of Progress Is Cambodia.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE are two Southeast Asias, Prime Minister Chatichai Choonhavan of Thailand is fond of saying: one thriving and capitalist, the other socialist and stagnant.
So it should be no surprise that even the famously stubborn Vietnamese leadership, despite its divisions over the pace of change, has realized that it must join the development race now or be forever left behind, floundering in a politically unstable swamp of unemployment and inflation.
That is the prime reason Vietnam finally decided to cut a deal on Cambodia and withdraw the bulk of its troops after an occupation of 11 years -- to end its international isolation and attract Western investment. 
And it is the prime reason that Vietnam's Foreign Minister, Nguyen Co Thach, went to Washington recently, the highest-ranking Hanoi official to do so since the north became independent in 1954.
That year, when the French left Vietnam, Hanoi was the most modern city in Southeast Asia. 
In 1975, when the Americans left, the region's most advanced city was Saigon. 
Both cities today have a sort of aspic charm, with moldy French provincial buildings in Hanoi and American DeSoto buses still grinding through the streets of Ho Chi Minh City.
The isolation and stagnation have been the price of both war and ideology. 
But now Hanoi, like the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, needs the West, and seems more willing to pay the price.
Vietnam eased central controls on the economy beginning as early as 1987. 
But a Cambodia-related embargo on aid, investment and trade with Vietnam, led by Washington, has successfully blocked vital loans from multilateral agencies like the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.
While more countries now trade with Vietnam, the American veto on the lending agencies has forestalled significant Western investment and stifled domestic development, particularly as Soviet aid declines.
A settlement in Cambodia, much more than the emotional and easily manipulated issue of the American M.I.A.'s, has always been the key to economic and diplomatic normalization between Washington and Hanoi. 
And only normalization will open Vietnam in a serious fashion to the West.
So it is Washington's main card with Vietnam, and even the American Chamber of Commerce, eager to do business with Vietnam, should not be surprised that the Bush Administration will continue to play it, at least until a Cambodia settlement is ratified.
Cambodia is also the main obstacle to normal relations between Hanoi and Beijing, whose support for Vietnam's revolution soured quickly over its Cambodian adventure. 
Hanoi's expulsion in 1979 of China's allies, the Khmer Rouge, no matter their crimes, was an insult for which the Chinese, especially Deng Xiaoping, were eager to extract the severest pain.
But China's own isolation over the killings near Tiananmen Square, coupled with the collapse of Eastern Europe and Moscow's sudden retrenchment everywhere, have also pushed Vietnam and China closer together.
Both leaderships are intensely aware of being socialist holdouts, but hope that Asian socialism will be a more lasting brand. 
They cite the communitarian nature of Asian societies and the fact that Communist rule rose from revolution and nation-building, and was not merely imposed, as in Eastern Europe, by a conquering army.
Still, there is an element of whistling in the dark. 
Vietnam's aging leaders, like China's, hope to embrace Western aid, investment and private enterprise while preserving the one-party nature of the Leninist state. 
But increasingly, younger intellectuals and those with more experience in southern Vietnam are expressing doubts that economic and political development can be separated -- or that the country can walk with one leg shorter than the other, as one Politburo member, Tran Xuan Bach, put it before being purged in March.
All this is taking place in the context of a leadership struggle. 
The party General Secretary, Nguyen Van Linh, has begun the reforms but lacks the time and strength to see them through. 
He has said he will retire at the next party congress, probably in May, and the battle between conservatives and reformers has gathered bite.
The conservatives, who had been grouped around Le Duc Tho, who died two weeks ago, and his brother, Interior Minister Mai Chi Tho, have used the collapse of Eastern Europe to try to brake any move toward even a Soviet-style multiparty system.
In the last five months, the Vietnamese have had a security crackdown, arresting as many as several hundred people, some for just a few days, especially in the south. 
They include retired soldiers of the old National Liberation Front, religious figures, businessmen and others with what the Government calls "too much" contact with Westerners.
While the internal crackdown has now eased somewhat, there continues to be a public campaign about the reported efforts of "reactionary forces overseas" to sabotage the state and socialism. 
Two weeks ago, a court in Hanoi convicted 38 people of trying to overthrow the Government with the help of Thailand and of Vietnamese exiles based in the United States.
While these people represent no real threat to the regime, the trial is apparently being used to justify the crackdown and serve as a warning to others, including the Western-leaning reformers in the leadership, among them the urbane Mr. Thach.
But while some might see his international prominence as a stepping stone of sorts, he will almost assuredly not be Vietnam's next General Secretary. 
Even in a collective leadership, there are other, less congenial forces at play.

file: The World_How Tiananmen Square Helped Rally Support for Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN an odd way, the only people who have done about as much as the Dalai Lama in the last few years to galvanize support for Tibetans are Deng Xiaoping and the other octogenarians who rule China.
Not intentionally, of course. 
But the leadership's crackdown on demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in June 4, 1989, and the repressive measures taken since then, while raising the issue of human rights in China generally, have also given a thrust to concern over abuses in Tibet. 
And it has helped to land Tibet, a sparsely populated plateau region north of the Himalayas, firmly on the international agenda.
"Tibet has come out of nowhere," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"There were always a small number of people interested in Tibet. 
But before June 4, they were drowned out by the rest of the people with their love affair for China."
The authorities in Beijing insist that Tibet has been a part of China for many centuries, but Tibetans dispute this and point out that the region was left alone by the Chinese early this century. 
That changed in 1950, when the new Communist Government invaded Tibet, and even more so after the Chinese crushed an abortive rebellion in 1959 and imposed much tighter control.
The United States and other Western governments regard Tibet as a part of China. 
But these days, animosity in the West for the hard-line regime in Beijing has translated into mounting support for the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled leader and foremost advocate. 
Some believe that irritation at China was a factor in the awarding of the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize to the Dalai Lama.
The Dalai Lama's status was further bolstered by his meeting with President Bush earlier this year, intended as a symbol of the Administration's distaste for Chinese repression. 
Likewise, Western ambassadors in Beijing seem much more interested than before in making trips to Tibet, and their No. 1 destination there these days is Drapchi Prison in Lhasa, the capital, where some political offenders are housed.
Potentially the most significant recent move was the launching in the spring of a Tibetan-language service of Voice of America. 
Visitors to Tibet say that the 15-minute daily broadcast has an enormous audience. 
The broadcasts not only provide news and information, but are also apparently taken -- or mistaken -- as a symbol of American support for Tibetan independence.
"The strong feeling in Lhasa is that more and more the U.S. is supporting Tibet," said a foreigner in Tibet. 
He added that the policy may contain a pitfall: the Tibetans may come to believe, as the Kurds did in Iraq, that if they rise up and demand independence then the United States will back them. 
While Western governments are pushing for human rights for Tibetans, there is no indication that they favor Tibetan independence.
Within Tibet, the Chinese authorities had a relatively conciliatory policy from the early 1980's through 1987. 
But for the last four years they have taken a much tougher line in Tibet and on several occasions troops have fired on protesters. 
The violence appears to have radicalized the population of Lhasa and strengthened the yearning for independence.
Diplomats and scholars often regard as exaggerated propaganda the assertions of Tibetan exiles that China is practicing genocide or a policy of forced sterilization and abortion to curb the number of Tibetans. 
But almost no one doubts the Tibetans' desire for independence. 
And human rights abuses -- torture of monks and nuns, killings of protesters, and long spells of imprisonment for advocates of independence -- are well documented by rights monitors like Asia Watch and Tibet Information Network.
The crackdown in Beijing's Tiananmen Square came three months after clashes in Lhasa between Chinese troops and anti-Government demonstrators in which at least 12 and perhaps more than 100 people died. 
By extension, the scenes from Beijing seemed to crystallize what had been for many people little more than just a notion of the tensions in Tibet.
"People had heard about what had happened in Tibet, but they didn't quite believe it until it became so real on TV and they realized, 'My God, this is also what's happening in Tibet,' " said John L. Ackerly, the legal counsel for the International Campaign for Tibet. 
The organization, which is based in Washington, has with the London-based Tibet Information Network played a major role in placing Tibet on the international agenda.
Â 
A Proprietary Feeling
Few people these days seem optimistic about a reconciliation between China and the Tibetan government-in-exile. 
Partly because they now see their movement gaining ground, the Tibetans have little incentive to compromise with Beijing. 
And the Chinese have now so embittered the Tibetans that -- rather like the Shah of Iran in his later years -- they would risk new upheavals and protests if they relaxed their repression.
Moreover, to a degree perhaps unappreciated in the West, suppression of the Tibetan independence movement is one of the few policies of Beijing's hard-liners that appears to draw broad support from Chinese. 
Even young intellectuals in Beijing, who disdain Communism and yearn for human rights for themselves, often say that Tibet is Chinese and should remain so. 
The reasons have much to do with Chinese nationalism, and with a grim resolve that the nation must never again endure the humiliation of a century ago, when China was carved up by more powerful countries and lost territory at its extremities.
"You might have a relatively democratic government" in China in the future, said Guocang Huan, a China scholar at Columbia University, "but such a government probably would not compromise much on Tibetan independence."

file: The World_In the Trade Wars, China Has Learned Guerilla Tactics.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHEN a truck from China pulled into the neighboring Portuguese enclave of Macao late last year, American officials happened to be on hand to take a peek at the cargo. 
They were surprised to find Chinese-manufactured ski jackets bearing labels reading "Made in Macao."
Business executives in both China and Macao were clearly trying to evade the limits imposed by China's quota of garment exports to the United States. 
American officials say that it was one incident in a pattern of unfair trading by China, and that in 1990, such practices brought China $2.5 billion in extra sales to the United States that were not counted in the bilateral trade statistics. 
"They got away with this for years and no one did anything about it," said an American official. 
"They thought they could continue getting away with it."
While all nations cheat on free trade to some degree, China is a socialist country that has put up barriers to imports so brazenly that it hardly makes a pretense at advocating free trade. 
One theory has it that China may be displaying a passion for building up net exports to accumulate foreign exchange -- what economists call a mercantilist streak. 
From missiles to textiles, exports have become a top priority. 
The pressure has led many companies to evade international rules, and the result is likely to be a protracted struggle between Washington and Beijing over China's trade behavior.
Last year, the United States's trade deficit with China was $10.4 billion -- the third largest, behind only Japan, with which the United States had a $41.1 billion deficit, and Taiwan, with which the deficit was $11.3 billion. 
China, whose exports have more than tripled in the last decade, is the only non-market economy that has become a major exporter to the United States.
And while most Western countries say they would like China to abandon more of its Government control of the economy, they are finding that China is maintaining socialism while also learning some of the ways that exporters like Japan and Taiwan cause headaches for foreign industrial countries.
In many ways, China is a picture-perfect unfair trader. 
Just ask anyone who wants to sell cars here. 
Not only must a foreign auto company pay stiff duties; it must also give two cars of each model to the Government, pay $40,000 for "testing" and finance a Chinese delegation's trip to "inspect" the factories overseas.
While the United States has had disputes with Japan over rice and with Taiwan over turkeys, the barriers in China are in many respects more comprehensive and fundamental. 
The exchange rate here is fixed, most big companies are state-owned, Government permission is needed for most imports, and in many cases tariffs have been raised and barriers added in the last few years.
Â 
Export Promotion
A big export promotion effort, coupled with curbs on imports, has pushed China's overall trade balance from a deficit of $6.6 billion in 1989 to a surplus of $8.7 billion last year. 
And trade is likely to continue to do well -- unless Congress cuts off most-favored-nation trade status for China, against President Bush's wishes -- partly because China is gradually devaluing its currency.
While they admit that Chinese enterprises often engage in illicit practices, some Chinese economists disagree that China's trade machine is basically unfair. 
They say the central Government has tried hard to curb some unfair practices, but that decentralization and the boom in capitalist enterprises in southern China -- just the kind of things Westerners want to see -- are thwarting the effort. 
"China is a developing country, and there is a cost to free trade," said a Chinese economist. 
"It must protect some of its industries. 
Is that unfair?"
American businessmen are much less sympathetic. 
To many, China's economy is a giant maze, with dead ends at every corner and booby traps that lead to dense tangles of bureaucracy and high costs. 
For instance, beyond extensive tariffs, quotas and other restrictions, China has a set of secret regulations that foreigners cannot even see. 
Often companies learn about them only through trial and error: sometimes a shipment is allowed into the country, sometimes it is not.
Nicholas Lardy, a specialist on the Chinese economy at the University of Washington, said that while China has curbed imports and boosted exports in the last two years, it is not clear that it will sustain its apparent passion for accumulating foreign exchange through the unbridled sale of exports. 
He noted that for most of the 1980's, China imported more than it exported, and he suggested that last year's trade surplus was an anomaly -- explainable partly because China faced economic uncertainties and restricted access to foreign capital and loans.
Prudence and caution, some Western economists say, thus may be enough to explain China's recent trade surplus. 
China is getting rid of export subsidies, and allowing imports to rise again. 
Its domestic economy is also rebounding and this may increase demand for imports. 
Still, in the first four months of this year, its overall trade surplus rose to $2.34 billion, up from $1.31 billion for the same period last year. 
Similarly, the United States deficit with China expanded to $2.19 billion in the first quarter, compared to $1.88 billion in the same period last year.
"I think it comes from a very deep-rooted ambivalence toward opening to the West and distrust of foreigners and capitalism," said another American economist who specializes in China. 
"Maybe some of those dirty tactics are engaged in because everyone is under so much pressure to generate revenues."

file: THE WORLD_Now, the People_s Army Has Fewer Friends, More Power.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA'S favorite hat used to be the army cap. 
As recently as this spring, young boys wore them everywhere and doting parents beamed their approval.
These days, most boys go bareheaded. 
Scarcely anyone is willing to be seen in an army cap, and a vendor acknowledged that sales have slowed greatly since the army's violent repression of the democracy movement in early June. 
''Chinese don't buy these caps now,'' the vendor said. 
''Now I try to sell them to Japanese visitors.''
The changing fashions point to the problems the Chinese army faces these days. 
The television propaganda of recent months has not erased the memories of troops firing on protesters. 
And in Beijing, which remains under martial law, the army has been further discredited by what is perceived as an arrogance on the part of the troops, most of whom come from the countryside and feel a certain contempt, readily reciprocated, for city residents.
The army must deal not only with the public dislike but also with the knowledge that even its repression was not handled well: if the army lost more than a dozen troops and scores of vehicles when taking on unarmed civilians, what would have happened if it had faced armed opposition?
Beyond that, the army is searching for the role it wants to play in China, according to many diplomats and other experts on the Chinese military. 
They say that many elements of the army resent being used as an instrument of repression and favor a professional force that would be on alert at the borders rather than in the capital.
Yet if the army has rarely been so burdened with difficulties, it has rarely been so important in recent years. 
Deng Xiaoping, China's 85-year-old senior leader, is trying to arrange a transition to a circle of younger leaders headed by Jiang Zemin, the new Communist Party chief. 
But Mr. Jiang is relatively weak and is likely to face a power struggle as soon as Mr. Deng is no longer able to protect him. 
At that point, the army, one of the few relatively cohesive forces left in China, could step forward and help choose the next generation of leadership.
''The army has seen its power grow whenever there have been periods of chaos or uncertainty or transition, and I think that is still true today,'' said a Western diplomat here.
If the army does gain greater influence, the generals might tend to favor hard-liners like Prime Minister Li Peng. 
But that is not certain. 
The politics of top officers are scarcely known, and much would depend on which general comes out on top. 
It is possible that a deal would be worked out, with the military offering support in exchange for a commitment to spare it from further budget cuts.
The last two party chiefs, Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang, were doomed in part by the reluctance of military leaders to accept them on the Central Military Commission. 
The absence of such support left them particularly vulnerable when Mr. Deng and others of his generation chafed at their unwillingness to crack down on protesters.
Â 
Misgivings in the Ranks
This time, Mr. Deng seems to be trying to help Mr. Jiang by installing him as either chairman or vice chairman of the military commission, an attempt to give him a chance to consolidate his power. 
Beijing is full of reports about shifts in the commission and in the army itself, changes that could shape civilian politics.
The increasing influence over the political struggles is just what many younger officers want least, diplomats and other analysts say.
These misgivings about its political role - and especially concerns about a role in repression - were behind the cracks in the military monolith in May and early June. 
The commander of the 38th army, General Xu, took sick leave rather than move his troops into Beijing in late May, Chinese officials say. 
The commander, the son of a famous General, Xu Haideng, had been thought absolutely reliable. 
In addition, military units took up defensive positions that suggested they feared attack from other units.
Chinese officials also say that a mutiny in Inner Mongolia in late June resulted in the execution of about 20 officers. 
No further information is known about that incident. 
Still, it now seems that the threat of civil war was not so great as it seemed at the time. 
While some skirmishing apparently took place among units, this may have been the unintended result of nervous troops stumbling across one other in the darkness.
''There was never an open split,'' said a Chinese official with contacts in middle and high levels in the army. 
''The officers generally agreed with their mission, but there was disagreement on how to do it, and many thought that it wasn't handled very well and was unnecessarily bloody.''
Today, the worst disagreements within the army seem to have been resolved, but conflicting ambitions still exist. 
One problem is that the generation of civilian leaders after Mr. Deng has had very little military experience. 
Many diplomats expect that the ascendancy of leaders without such ties will mean more pressure on the army to cut spending, after a decade in which it already has faced austerity and the demobilization of more than a million troops.
The army also must come to terms with its inadequacies. 
In 1979, China was shocked by the punishment it took from the Vietnamese Army during a brief border war, and that embarrassment led to efforts to modernize the military. 
China's generals are said to be aware of the shortcomings and to favor continued cooperation with the West to gain the equipment and technology they need. 
Western sanctions on military aid are likely to increase the army's distaste for political interference, diplomats say.
The military's needs are now as obvious as ever, for the crackdown against the democracy movement was the military's first big test since the Vietnam clashes, and few people were impressed.
Said a Western diplomat here, ''Even aside from the killing, it wasn't a performance to be proud of.''

file: THE WORLD_Restlessness Reaches Mongols In China.txt
text:
ï»¿
RELATIONS between the Chinese and the Mongols have been a bit strained ever since Genghis Khan slaughtered millions of Chinese in the 13th century. 
By one account, the Mongols considered converting all of northern China into a vast pasture; they relented when an adviser pointed out that the Chinese, if spared, could be taxed.
The tradition of mutual distrust is again bubbling to the surface in Chinese-controlled Inner Mongolia, a desert region more than twice the size of California. 
More and more Mongols there are reasserting their ethnic heritage, establishing links with the outside world, and even organizing underground networks to press for democracy and autonomy.
"This is our last chance to achieve democracy, to reassert our culture," Huhehada, a 29-year-old leader of the underground movement, said recently. 
"Mongols need their own culture, their own history -- recorded in their own hands. 
Or else they'll face the fate of American Indians or of Tibetans."
Mr. Huhehada was interviewed in exile in Ulan Bator, the capital of the neighboring independent nation of Mongolia, from which he and other Inner Mongolian dissidents are orchestrating their campaign. 
They say about 2,000 people, half of them living in Inner Mongolia, have joined their newly formed General Coordination Committee of Inner Mongolian Rejuvenation Movements. 
The group is banned within China and the dissidents fear that Beijing will now press Ulan Bator to ban it as well.
Mongolia itself abandoned one-party Communist rule in 1990, and has since seen a tremendous flowering of traditional Mongol religion and culture. 
Mongolian radio can be heard in Inner Mongolia, and the growing contact across the border seems to be a major reason for the surge of nationalism among China's Mongols. 
In addition, Beijing has just announced that it will open the entire border to trade, and that is certain to multiply links with Mongolia and perhaps the demands for change.
Inner Mongolia so far is not nearly as much of a headache for the Chinese leadership as is Tibet, where Buddhist monks and nuns regularly protest for independence and human rights. 
Nor is Inner Mongolia even as much of a concern as oil-rich Xinjiang, the Muslim region of northwest China where there was an abortive armed uprising in 1990. 
But many of the same pressures -- resentment at Chinese arrogance and immigration, yearning for self-rule and prosperity, and outrage at repression -- seem to be at work in Inner Mongolia.
"Our economy is based on colonialism," said Tsenglet, another of the Mongol leaders exiled in Ulan Bator. 
"Our land is rich, but the Chinese take our resources and leave us poor. 
We see that!
And there's been pressure from immigrants. 
We're now a minority in our own land. 
Life for our people is worse than ever."
Â 
Resentments Grow
The statistics do not bear that out: Ethnic Mongols in Inner Mongolia have rising incomes and improving health conditions. 
But living standards are not rising as fast as those of most Chinese, and resentment seems to be growing. 
As in Tibet, Chinese immigration to Mongolia is a particular irritant.
The Han, the main ethnic group in China, began to migrate to Inner Mongolia 200 years ago. 
By the time of the Communist revolution in 1949, the Han reportedly outnumbered Mongols 5 to 1. 
The 1990 census found a total population of 21.5 million, of whom 3.4 million were Mongols -- a ratio of 6.4 to 1. 
It would be even more skewed, except that the Mongols have more children than the Han, and many families of mixed heritage have reclassified themselves as Mongols to win educational benefits and other advantages available to minorities.
There are periodic reports of large anti-Government demonstrations in Inner Mongolia, but many foreign diplomats and Chinese alike are skeptical. 
The situation is murky in part because China normally will not let foreign journalists visit.
The Chinese Government denounces reports of unrest as lies and fabrications. 
But most foreigners who have visited have reported modest signs of discontent, and dissidents are forging links with the West to get out documents and information on human rights. 
"It's been a long-overlooked corner of China," said Robin Munro, a researcher for Asia Watch, a human rights organization that has published two reports about Inner Mongolia in the last 12 months. 
"Until recently, dissident activity there met the fate of being repressed in obscurity and isolation. 
Nobody would know about it. 
But there has been this link forged now with international channels of communication, so that repression in the region is reported on. 
When it's published outside China, it filters back in through international radio stations, the Inner Mongolian dissidents hear about it, and it basically emboldens them to continue."
As everywhere in China, dissidents face considerable risks. 
At least 17 people are known to be in Inner Mongolia's prisons for their political activities; the true number may be much higher.
While many of the dissidents would like to see Inner Mongolia reunite with Mongolia, they acknowledge that this would be difficult to achieve because of the preponderance of Han Chinese. 
Some say they would like to expel the Han, or at least relocate them, while others say they would settle for a solution short of reunification.
"In any case, the first thing we need to get is the freedom to speak out, to express our grievances," said Uringkhai N. Tumen, a 27-year-old in Ulan Bator who heads an underground cultural organization in Inner Mongolia. 
"At the least, we need real autonomy -- real autonomy, not what we have now."

file: THE WORLD_Taiwan Becomes a Tiger With an Identity Crisis.txt
text:
ï»¿
LIKE a compulsive overachiever who impresses everybody but himself, Taiwan has enjoyed stunning successes in recent years but is gripped by an identity crisis. 
Despite having engineered an economic rise that makes Japan look like a slowpoke, and despite having introduced free speech and free elections, Taiwan still seems full of anxiety about itself and uncertainty about what it is.
Until five years ago, when four decades of martial law gave way to a sometimes tempestuous political free-for-all, the answer was clear: Taiwan was an inseparable part of China. 
The Nationalist Government here claimed to be the ruler of all China, and in school children spoke Mandarin Chinese rather than the Taiwan dialect and learned about the history of mainland China rather than Taiwan.
These days, however, few Taiwanese seem enthused about identifying themselves with a largely peasant Communist society where people spit on streets and the army shoots student protesters. 
On the other hand, Taiwanese fear that if they try to establish an independent country, mainland China will attack.
Few countries recognize Taiwan, its top leaders aren't invited to the United States or other major countries, and citizens sometimes find that immigration officials at distant airports are puzzled by their Republic of China passports. 
"We don't know who we are," said Antonio Chiang, a magazine publisher in Taipei. 
"The uncertainty is enormous. 
We don't know what we'll be in the future, an independent country, a part of China or whatever. 
It's an unreal existence, and it's related to the lack of self-confidence."
For four decades, the 15 percent of Taiwan's 20 million people who are mainlanders -- whose families came from China with Chiang Kai-shek -- dominated Taiwan and sometimes seemed contemptuous of local culture and history. 
But in the last few years, after Taiwan allowed visits to the mainland for the first time since the Communist revolution of 1949, many people came back shaking their heads and exchanging tales of relatives demanding expensive gifts and of awful trains and shortages of toilet paper.
Â 
A Change of Vision
Rather than seeing themselves as exiled mainlanders, many came back as confirmed Taiwanese. 
One survey found that only 36 percent of Taiwan people who visited the mainland wanted to do so again.
Yet because of the fear of inviting military attack from Beijing, a National Assembly election last month -- the first full election on Taiwan in four decades -- led to a crushing defeat for the opposition party after it proposed a declaration of independence from China.
"Most people in Taiwan don't have much confidence in the future," said Tim T. Y. Ting, a leading pollster. 
"It's unpredictable. 
Anything can change tomorrow and destroy everything you have."
This uncertainty, coupled with the rapid change, seems to have provoked a malaise in some circles. 
People complain about crime, corruption, politicians, disintegrating moral values -- and this in a society that until recently played down discord and did not acknowledge uncertainty about national identity.
Diane Ying, publisher of a business magazine called Commonwealth, which recently devoted a special issue to Taiwan's history, cited a litany of concerns about the future and added: "All this is because of the uncertainty. 
There's nothing you can control about the future. 
Everything seems to be out of control."
Nowadays, some Taiwanese react by trying to forge their own identity and culture. 
The Taiwan dialect is having a renaissance, though it is still sometimes thought of as less cultured and sophisticated than Mandarin.
Democracy is speeding this, because with voters overwhelmingly Taiwanese, politicians try to portray themselves as Taiwanese as well. 
Thus, during the campaign, the opposition tried to portray the ruling Nationalists as carpetbaggers from the mainland, while the Nationalists used Taiwanese dialect in their campaign advertisements.
In any case, for younger people the distinction between mainlanders and Taiwanese is fading, and intermarriage is frequent. 
"I don't find any difficulty," said Jaw Shau-kong, a 41-year-old Taiwanese-speaking mainlander and a popular politician. 
"It doesn't matter if you're a mainlander or a Taiwanese, so long as you work for Taiwan."
Other Taiwan inhabitants also say that whatever one's background, a new Taiwan identity is slowly emerging that embraces everyone who lives here, and that this perhaps will foster more self-confidence.
"Before I entered university, there was no doubt about identity," Yvonne Yang, the 32-year-old administration manager at Taiwan's English-language radio station, remembers. 
"We were Chinese and we would go back to the mainland. 
But then I started to talk to some friends and I discovered that the textbooks had many errors. 
I thought that maybe they were lots of lies. 
But then I started to work and I really loved this country. 
I created my own sense of belonging."

file: THE WORLD_Taking the Measure of A _Measured Response_.txt
text:
ï»¿
EVERY time President Bush and Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d have spoken with the press in the last two weeks, they have been badgered with the same question, ''Why aren't you saying and doing more about China?''
Each time, with increasing exasperation, they have answered, ''Look at all we have said and done.''
Mr. Baker himself said: ''We think a measured response is just that. 
It calls for a response which clearly expresses our outrage, but does not resort to an overly emotional response which involves inflammatory rhetoric.''
But one person's inflammatory rhetoric is another person's poetry, and because the Administration's declarations on Tianamen Square have contained no poetry, no memorable language, nothing seems to have stuck in the public's mind.
While the President seemed to find the perfect combination of words and deeds to express the nation's desire for progress with Moscow on arms control on his recent swing through Europe, his attempts to strike a similar balance in relation to Beijing have left many unsatisfied.
The Administration has been criticized as being neither forceful enough in its condemnation of what happened in Tiananmen Square nor convincing enough in its articulation of what it calls the ''countervailing geopolitical considerations,'' which require a maintenance of ties with Beijing.
As a result, Congress put forth its own sanctions and declarations last week, which the Administration rejected as superfluous.
Presidents shape their policy environment through their words. 
''We often think of political rhetoric as a bad word, as pandering, as mere talk - it's action that counts,'' said Michel J. Sandel, a political theorist at Harvard University. 
''But that is a mistaken idea and one that the President seems to share. 
At the level of the Presidency, there is no sharp distinction between words and deeds. 
Talk is action. 
Words are deeds.''
He added, ''The President's measured policy response on China was very reasonable, but because he did not at the same time articulate the importance of the moment, give clear expression to the principles and ideals at stake, his deeds were lost.''
Ronald Reagan's ''genius,'' argued Mr. Sandel, was his ability to articulate a clear moral message vis-a-vis the Soviet Union. 
As a result, Mr. Sandel said, people were confident that they knew where he stood and therefore they were ready to accept a nuanced policy toward Moscow, including sweeping arms control agreements.
Â 
The Larger Themes
While Mr. Bush has a policy on China full of nuances, he has not managed to gain much support for it because he has failed to sound the larger themes.
''No one would have paid much attention to the details had the President given broad thematic expression to public feelings,'' Mr. Sandel said.
It was Mr. Reagan, in a speech in London last month, who voiced what was on many Americans' minds about China. 
''You cannot massacre an idea,'' he said. 
''You cannot run tanks over hope. 
You cannot riddle a people's yearnings with bullets.''
Some experts theorized that Mr. Bush's seeming reluctance to use such language may be connected to his stint in Beijing as ambassador. 
It is difficult to summon a poetic outrage against people whom you basically liked and once considered friends.
''President Bush, like most people who have dealt with the Chinese over the last decade, was captivated by them,'' said Charles William Maynes, editor of the journal Foreign Policy.
Administration officials, though, have been equally reserved when it has come to explaining all the ''countervailing'' strategic considerations that they say require them to react to the killings in China in a way that will not totally alienate Beijing.
There is a logic to this, said Robert W. Tucker, professor of diplomacy at Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.
To go into detail on such matters, he said, ''They would have to admit that the cold war with Moscow really isn't over, and because it isn't over we still need a strong relationship with China to counterbalance the Soviet Union.''
After having been battered for the first four months of his Administration for not being responsive enough to Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the last thing Mr. Bush wants to do now is start making speeches about why the Soviet Union remains a fundamental threat.
Again, though, something more compelling than ''countervailing considerations'' might have bought the Administration more room to maneuver. 
Maybe something along the lines expressed by the man who sent Mr. Bush to China as Ambassador in the 1970's.
As Richard M. Nixon wrote in an article last week: ''China has a limitless capacity to fascinate. 
But it is not Disneyland. 
It is, as it has been since 1949, a Communist dictatorship held together by brute force. 
Those who insist on romanticizing relations between nations will always be disappointed when the realities of national interest and survival inevitably intrude.''
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d defending the Administration's China policy before a House committee last month (The New York Times/Jose R. Lopez)

file: THE WORLD_The People_s Republic at 40, at Odds With the People.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE People's Republic of China prepared to mark its 40th anniversary today with splendid dragon dances and fireworks, but with little joy.
The brooding Chinese public appreciates the sea slugs and other delicacies doled out by employers for the birthday party, but the atmosphere is tense. 
The Communist Party displayed a clenched-teeth determination to celebrate the occasion, but under security so tight that people without proper residency permits were ejected from Beijing, and many residents of the city were ordered to stay indoors today.
Most telling, the leadership's suspicion of the common people is such that only a carefully screened elite was to be allowed into Tiananmen Square to hail ''People's China.''
To many Chinese, the need for rigid security is simply the latest evidence of the party's dissipation of its 40-year-old mandate and its crisis of legitimacy.
It was very different on Oct. 
1, 1949, when Mao Zedong mounted the rostrum of Tiananmen Gate and before a crowd of hundreds of thousands of supporters proclaimed in ringing tones the formation of the People's Republic. 
''From this moment,'' he declared, ''the Chinese people have stood up!''
Since then, Communist China's achievements and errors have been colossal, etched in history on a truly Chinese scale. 
The party emancipated hundreds of millions of peasants from the hopeless misery in which they had eked out an existence for hundreds of generations. 
It provided opportunities for women. 
The country won respect in the world, and the last decade of economic change created a new prosperity for much of the population.
Yet the gains were achieved at a staggering price. 
In redistributing land and consolidating control, Mao later admitted, 700,000 people were killed. 
The Great Leap Forward, a catastrophic attempt at rapid industrialization, combined with bad harvests to produce tens of millions of deaths in the early 1960's. 
Political upheavals like the anti-rightist campaign of 1957, the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976, and the crackdown now under way against supporters of this spring's democracy movement have cost the lives or ruined the careers of unknown numbers of Chinese who dared seek change.
With each violent oscillation, with each purge, the party has lost some of the good will with which it began its rule. 
At first, the regime was widely regarded as a genuine people's government, fundamentally different from the warlords and emperors of the past. 
Now, ordinary people seem to regard the party as an adversary. 
Intellectuals are even more bitter; they recall what the Chinese writer Lu Xun had to say about the first Chinese revolution that in 1911-12 toppled the Qing Dynasty. 
''Before the revolution, we were slaves,'' Lu Xun wrote. 
''Now we are slaves of former slaves.''
The Communists began with tremendous popular support. 
Opium was eradicated, brothels were closed, land was distributed, roads and railroads were built, literacy campaigns were launched, health care was expanded and an industrial base was developed.
Older people sometimes still express appreciation for the revolution and the improvements it brought in their lives. 
But now, half the population of China is 23 or younger, and 74 percent were born after the revolution. 
Young people have been deluged with statistics in the last few weeks purporting to show how much Communism has helped China, but many seem to resist to the extent that they do not even acknowledge the regime's real accomplishments.
Per capita incomes have multiplied 5 to 10 times in the last 40 years, depending on who does the calculating, to about $350 a year. 
Life expectancy has nearly doubled, from about 35 years to 69 years. 
China exploded a nuclear bomb in 1965 and launched a satellite in 1970, showing remarkable technical skill for so poor a country.
''There have been tremendous accomplishments,'' said Kenneth G. Lieberthal, director of the Center for Chinese Studies at the University of Michigan, ''but they have not kept up with the even more tremendous accomplishments elsewhere in Asia.''
Â 
Open-Door Policy
Therein lies the problem for the Communists. 
The majority of the population is less interested in contrasts with conditions 40 years ago than in the contrasts with life in neighboring countries today. 
The open-door policy of the last decade has increased the well-being and opportunities for most Chinese, inspiring a certain gratitude, but this has probably been outweighed by the destabilizing influence of allowing people to learn how much better off Taiwan and Hong Kong are than China.
Many Chinese feel they enjoyed the gains of the Communist revolution long ago, but are still paying the price in terms of despotism, economic inefficiency and corruption. 
They complain that the revolution has degenerated into cycles of too brief liberalization and longer repression, of some hope and greater hopelessness.
The last great emotional trough came in 1976 after the death of the beloved Prime Minister, Zhou Enlai, the leader credited with steering China away from the excesses of the Cultural Revolution. 
Demonstrations of mourning followed Zhou's death, an outpouring that in fact was meant as a show of support for Zhou's protege, Deng Xiaoping. 
The demonstrations were crushed, and Mr. Deng was purged - a parallel with the present repression and purges engineered by Mr. Deng.
But after an interregnum of two years, Mr. Deng returned to power and introduced sweeping changes. 
The nation once more was on the move, and seemed to be growing less repressive. 
Mr. Deng and the party were at the peak of their popularity five years ago, in the 35th anniversary celebration, when university students hailed their favorite leader with a large banner: ''How are you, Xiaoping!''
Yet the successes and exposure to the world created rising expectations that Mr. Deng could not meet and political demands that he would not meet. 
The economic changes ran into difficulties, as the Government and party bureaucrats seemed unwilling to cede more of their power and privilege. 
Inflation soared, corruption spread and income inequalities widened. 
Most important, Mr. Deng proved no less able than Mao to plan a smooth succession. 
Both of Mr. Deng's heirs apparent, Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang, were dismissed in disgrace.
The party's decision to use force to crush this spring's democracy movement was a catastrophe for the country and for the party's legitimacy. 
Hundreds of people were massacred and the country's educated young people were humiliated by requirements that they work at the ''grass roots'' and by political study sessions in which they were forced to profess their faith in the party. 
The reformist wing of the party was gutted, but Mr. Deng is still in command and there are mixed signals about who is rising and falling. 
For now, however, the accent is on central planning and political repression, worsening the crisis of confidence in which ''People's China'' finds itself during its birthday celebration.
In secret documents now circulating among officials, Mr. Deng seems to acknowledge the difficulties, and he says he chose Jiang Zemin to be the new party chief partly to provide a fresh image. 
But few find in Mr. Jiang a sign of broad vision or new initiative. 
Indeed, in a press conference on Tuesday, Mr. Jiang seemed to go out of his way to appear rigid, declaring that the shootings on June 4 were not a tragedy.
The alienation is much lower in the countryside and in provincial cities than in Beijing, and if the Government can keep people happy economically - an uncertain prospect - it may be able to avert a further crisis in the immediate future. 
Dwight H. Perkins, a Harvard economist, suggests that if the peasantry is kept happy, it can supply the army recruits to keep the regime in power.
Yet many Chinese and foreigners believe the present leadership is precarious, and will be more so after Mr. Deng's death. 
They say that the new relationship of antipathy and even contempt between the people and the leaders at some time will produce change. 
Once more, they cite the words of the writer Lu Xun early in this century: ''Lies written in ink cannot obscure a truth written in blood.''
Â 
LIFE OF A REVOLUTION
Early euphoria: 1949-1955.Â Â Communists seize power, driving Chiang Kai-shek and his Nationalists to Taiwan. 
Land is redistributed, inflation is controlled, and the economy seems to improve. 
But the Korean War cuts China's links with the West and leads to more radical policies. 
By Mao's count, 700,000 ''counter-revolutionaries'' are killed.
Catastrophes and consolidation: 1956-1965.Â Â In 1956 and 1957, intellectuals are urged to speak out and ''let a hundred flowers bloom.''
Soon afterward, an anti-rightist campaign punishes those who did speak freely.
Impatient with economic performance, Mao launches the Great Leap Forward in 1958. 
The result is a deep depression that combined with natural disasters leads to tens of millions of deaths between 1960 and 1962. 
Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping reintroduce incentives to repair the economy.
Cultural Revolution and Mao's death: 1966-76.Â Â Mao unleashes Red Guards to attack his rivals. 
Many party leaders are ousted and sometimes tortured and killed. 
Mao calls on the army to restore order. 
In 1976, both Mao and Prime Minister Zhou Enlai die, and the extremist Gang of Four tries to consolidate power. 
They are overthrown, and power formally lies in the hands of Mao's weak successor, Hua Guofeng.
Deng era: 1977-89.Â Â Hua loses influence, and Deng Xiaoping maneuvers his way back to power. 
Mr. Deng allows decollectivization of agriculture and private businesses. 
Tens of thousands of Chinese go abroad for higher education. 
Mr. Deng chooses as his heirs Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang, but he purges Mr. Hu in 1987 and Mr. Zhao in May 1989.
Hundreds of protesters are killed June 3-4, 1989, after Mr. Deng orders troops to crush the democracy movement. 
Mr. Deng indicates that his heir will be the new party leader, Jiang Zemin, but the leadership seems paralyzed by uncertainty and conflict.
Oct. 1, 1949: Mao declares founding of People's Republic (Magnum/New China Pictures); June 4, 1989: crackdown on pro-democracy movement in Tiananmen Square (Sygma/Jacques Langevin)
