text:
ï»¿
JUST 10 years ago, a group of American Congressmen touring the Soviet Union were startled when a provincial politician launched into a remarkably candid and seemingly heartfelt tirade about the menace of China.
''Today they are attacking Vietnam, tomorrow it will be India, then the Soviet Union, and maybe even the United States,'' the official reportedly warned, reflecting a phobia not uncommon then in the Soviet Union.
The provincial official was Eduard A. Shevardnadze, now the Foreign Minister and chief executor of the new pragmatism that, on Monday, brings Mikhail S. Gorbachev to the first Chinese-Soviet summit meeting in 30 years.
Mr. Gorbachev's visit will ratify a process of normalization that is already well under way, marked by an expansion of trade and lessening of tension along the 4,600-mile border, by Soviet concessions on several issues of mutual discomfort, and by a respectful fascination among Soviet intellectuals with China's more advanced economic reforms.
Vladimir A. Myasnikov, a leading Soviet expert on China, says that with this summit, ''We are closing a page of the cold war, the last page of the volume: Asia.''
A few years ago, such a reconciliation would have been seen by the United States and its allies as an alarming development. 
Since President Nixon's visit to China in 1972, the West has regarded the triangular relationship of Washington, Beijing and Moscow as the stable foundation of superpower relations. 
Now, it seems generally accepted that whatever military resources are freed up by rapprochement between the Chinese and Soviets will not be turned against the West, but against domestic impoverishment.
For one thing, no one believes that this meeting will mean a return to the Communist fraternity of the 1950's. 
Where Stalin saw China as a potential ally against the imperialists, Mr. Gorbachev sees normalization as a prerequisite for economic cooperation with the other Asian countries that have so far resisted his charm. 
Soviet and Chinese economists both talk of development schemes that would pool Soviet natural resources, Chinese labor and Japanese and South Korean capital. 
Moreover, the Soviet Union remains the principal arms supplier to two of China's rivals, Vietnam and India, while China continues to finance guerrillas warring against the Soviet-backed regime in Afghanistan.
Still, Mr. Gorbachev is eager to lay aside a legacy of tensions because China is the linchpin of a broader Asia strategy. 
Rapprochement means the demobilizing of border garrisons, the advance of his disarmament campaign in Asia and the Pacific, and a climate of good will that the Soviets hope will let a thousand joint ventures bloom. 
In Beijing, the Soviet leader will be playing to an audience that includes Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and other up-and-coming Asian nations whose capital and technology the Soviet leader hopes can be wooed to the assistance of his anemic economy. 
Chinese-Soviet detente should also give Moscow more flexibility in its dealings with North Korea and such wary Southeast Asian nations as Thailand.
China, for its part, relishes the prospect of increasing border trade and the chance to relax the standoff along its northern border. 
Chinese leaders welcome a chance to decrease the strategic influence of the Soviet Union and its ally, Vietnam, in Asia. 
Some Chinese, including the restive students, hope that Mr. Gorbachev's visit will inspire broader democratization of their society, although that prospect seems to cause considerable ambivalence in the leadership.
As Mr. Shevardnadze's remarks 10 years ago demonstrated, the two neighbors have a history of mistrust, ancient and contemporary, bloody and ideological, mutual and deeply ingrained.
Russian children learn from school days of the Mongol hordes that swept across the border from China in the 13th century. 
Chinese children are taught that more than a million square miles of what is now the Soviet Union was hornswoggled from the Chinese empire by Russian rulers centuries ago. 
Since their respective revolutions, the two countries have also stockpiled resentments, beginning with Stalin's alliance of convenience with Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists before and during World War II. 
Even in the 1950's, when Stalin and Mao huddled together against the capitalist world, the relationship was out of balance, with the Soviets unabashedly condescending to ''our little brothers.''
The Chinese endured their role as junior sibling until 1956, when Nikita S. Khrushchev's destalinization campaign collided with the growth of Mao's own Stalinist cult. 
When Khrushchev arrived in Beijing for the last Chinese-Soviet summit conference in 1959, there was already an unmistakeable chill in the air. 
The Chinese public took their indignation out on Soviet advisers and technicians until Khrushchev abruptly withdrew them, leaving hundreds of joint projects half-built.
Â 
Relaxing Old Dogma
In 1969, Soviet and Chinese troops engaged in a series of bloody border skirmishes. 
Chinese children in Beijing pelted the cars of Soviet diplomats with stones and shouted ''Down with the Soviet revisionists,'' while in Moscow an actor brought down the house at the Taganka Theater by interrupting a play about Soviet village life to cry: ''Something must be done about China!''
Now, with the ascent of Mr. Gorbachev, China and the Soviet Union have found themselves, for once, moving in the same direction - away from the failed Stalinist model of Communism toward a more pragmatic socialism. 
In both countries the grip of old dogma has been relaxed.
Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese eminence, has made Mr. Gorbachev work for his meeting. 
The Soviet leader has withdrawn Soviet troops from Afghanistan, and Mr. Gorbachev's pledge last December at the United Nations to cut half a million troops from the Soviet armed forces included 200,000 soldiers in Moscow's vast Asian domain. 
The withdrawal of three-fourths of the Soviet contingent in Mongolia is scheduled to begin the day Mr. Gorbachev arrives in Beijing.
In Beijing in February, Mr. Shevardnadze proposed that the Soviet Union and China both reduce ''offensive components'' of their forces along the border, limit military exercises and exchange monitoring teams to build confidence. 
Moscow has also prevailed on Vietnam to promise the removal of its forces from Cambodia by September, while hinting flexibility on a formula for the future of Cambodia, one issue awaiting the leaders in Beijing.
Through all of this, the Chinese have been careful to assure that the meeting does not spook Japan or the United States, both now far more important trading partners with Beijing than the Soviet Union. 
About the time Mr. Gorbachev heads for home after a stopover in Shanghai, a flotilla of American warships is due to steam into Shanghai harbor.
The Soviets, for their part, disavow any attempt to alienate China's affections toward the West. 
''The policy of the triangle belongs to the 20th century,'' said Mr. Myasnikov, ''and it exits with this century.''
Â 
A CYCLE OF TRUST AND DISTRUST
Since China came under Communist rule in 1949, Chinese-Soviet relations have gone through a cycle of friendship, growing mistrust, border fighting and, now, renewed warmth. 
Here is a history.
Â 
1949-1954: Close cooperation.Â Â China takes the Soviet Union as the model for reorganizing its society, with aid and advice from Moscow. 
The first meeting between Khrushchev and Mao, in 1954, is a high point. 
But the Soviets' condescending attitude toward the Chinese plants seeds of resentment.
Â 
1956-1966: Growing rift.Â Â Khrushchev's de-Stalinization collides with Mao's personality cult. 
They clash over Moscow's claim of pre-eminence in world Communism, and later Mao derides Brezhnev's quest for detente with the United States. 
Mao and Khrushchev meet for the last time in 1959. 
In 1963, talks on Chinese-Soviet relations break off, and Soviet aid is halted.
Â 
1967-1979: Open estrangement.Â Â In 1967, ambassadors are withdrawn. 
In 1968, China condemns the Soviet intervention in Czechoslovakia. 
In 1969, Soviet and Chinese troops clash along the border. 
In 1972, China invites President Nixon visit and reopens ties to Japan. 
In 1979, China fights a border war with Vietnam, a Soviet ally.
Â 
1982-1989: Efforts to reconcile.Â Â In the early 1980's, Soviet peace overtures run up against China's declaration of three obstacles: the Soviet Union's presence in Afghanistan, its troops along the Chinese border and its support for the Vietnamese in Cambodia. 
But gradually, steps are taken toward warmer relations: two trade agreements; Chinese acceptance of a Soviet proposal for a summit meeting if Moscow helped end the Cambodian conflict, and talks on the border dispute. 
In February 1989, they agree to the summit meeting in Beijing.

file: THE WORLD_There_s a New World Order in Asia_ The U.S. Will Have to Catch Up.txt
text:
ï»¿
A handful of Asia-based diplomats are willing to give President Bush the benefit of the doubt. 
They are willing to believe that he canceled his trip to Asia this month for reasons that go beyond opinion polls suggesting that the President's globetrotting habits have cut into his approval rating among voters.
In fact, some diplomats say, President Bush may have been well advised to stay home until he knows with certainty how Washington should respond to the political and economic changes that are sweeping across the Far East, and that appear destined to alter the American role. 
"Everything is fluid in the region right now," said a senior European diplomat in Bangkok. 
"Perhaps now is not the moment for the President to visit Asia. 
The United States needs time to absorb it all."
Since World War II, American policy in Asia has centered on -- indeed, tens of thousands of Americans have sacrificed their lives over -- the two great land masses on the Pacific rim of China: Indochina and the Korean peninsula. 
But consider the news from the region in just the last few weeks: Cambodians announced the end of their 12-year civil war; Vietnam restored full diplomatic relations with its chief adversary, China, in hopes of concentrating on economic development; North and South Korea reported the first substantive progress on a framework to resolve more than four decades of brotherly hate.
Any one of those developments would have been startling a few years ago. 
Taken together at a time when the cold war is all but over, they could be important evidence of a new era of peace and prosperity, even amid reminders of lingering suffering like that of the Vietnamese boat people now resisting forced repatriation from Hong Kong..
Last week Mr. Bush and the other NATO heads of state met in Rome to chart a new role in a Europe without the Soviet threat that had defined the alliance's reason for existence. 
It was a get-together that Mr. Bush, who considers himself a sort of honorary chairman of the club of world leaders, might well have relished not only for its reassuring pomp but also for its comparative lack of ambiguity.
The Bush Administration has made its own Asia headlines in recent weeks by announcing its willingness to open talks with Hanoi to normalize diplomatic and trade ties 16 years after the war's end, its plan to remove tactical nuclear weapons from the region, and its intention to send Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d to Beijing this month. 
Mr. Baker would be the highest-ranking American official to visit China since pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananman Square were put down in a bloody confrontation by Chinese soldiers two years ago.
The American Century in Asia is not over yet, but already the United States is facing what could be the starkest policy choices since 1898, when President William McKinley invaded and colonized the Philippines even though he knew it as little more than a group of islands "somewhere away around on the other side of the world."
The question for the United States is whether it should continue in the role of policeman and mediator in a region that is increasingly able to resolve its own conflicts and that, far from being the home of "little brown brothers" of old, is now America's fiercest economic competitor. 
The Bush Administration insists that the choice has already been made, and that the United States military will remain in Asia indefinitely, although the Pacific force, which last year numbered about 140,000 men and women, will be cut by more than 10 percent as part of worldwide Pentagon reductions.
Defense Secretary Dick Cheney says a complete military withdrawal would almost surely result in a "series of destabilizing regional arms races, an increase in regional tensions and possibly conflict."
Yet that has not silenced forces on Capitol Hill and private defense analysts in the United States who argue that, at a time of domestic austerity, there is no need to continue defending nations that are able to do it themselves. 
They say, too, that American military forces in Asia are seen increasingly as a paper tiger, since it seems unlikely that the United States, still traumatized over the war in Vietnam, would ever allow itself to be drawn into another large regional conflict in Asia.
"This isn't Kuwait -- there's no oil here for the United States to rush in to protect, and the threat of Communism is dying here as it is everywhere in the world," said a Thai official. 
Selig S. Harrison, a senior associate of the Carnegie Endowment, argues that the American military umbrella in Asia has subsidized the economies of booming East Asian nations, particularly Japan, by freeing them from large military expenditures. 
"We are helping to make Asia safe for Japanese investment," said Mr. Harrison, who estimates that the United States spends $42 billion a year in direct and indirect costs for its Far East military forces. 
"It's a ridiculous expenditure."
There is one important area of agreement between analysts like Mr. Harrison and the Bush Administration, and that is over the need for a continued American military presence in South Korea, which faces an isolated and unpredictable enemy to the north. 
Pyongyang is believed to have an active program to develop nuclear weapons and in the near future could have the bomb. 
Even in the Koreas, however, there is hope of finally making peace. 
Late last month, the two nations agreed on the broad outlines of a peace plan reported to include a non-aggression pact, a pledge of respect for each other's political systems and provisions for reuniting families across the border.
Â 
China and Vietnam
In Indochina, the optimism about peace is greater still. 
Despite apprehension among their neighbors that China and Vietnam might be contemplating a destabilizing military alliance, diplomats say the recent warming between Beijing and Hanoi is instead a marriage of convenience between two still-bitter rivals wishing to put aside their differences for now to focus on economic progress.
Closer ties between China and Vietnam may also be the factor that prevents Cambodia from collapsing into civil war again. 
Beijing has broad control over the genocidal, Chinese-armed Khmer Rouge, responsible for the deaths of more than a million Cambodians in the 1970's, while Vietnam retains influence with the government it helped install in Phnom Penh under Prime Minister Hun Sen. Under a United Nations peace treaty, the Khmer Rouge, Mr. Hun Sen and his political allies, and two other Cambodian factions will share power in what amounts to a coalition government.
In the expectation that the United States military will gradually reduce its presence in Asia, countries now living under the American defense umbrella have begun putting forward proposals for stepped-up regional military cooperation.
Several of the more ambitious proposals have come from Japan, which last summer recommended to the members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations that they begin regular consultations on military issues. 
Last week, the new Japanese Prime Minister, Kiichi Miyazawa, expressed his hope that Japan would soon rewrite its defense laws to permit the use of its troops outside Japanese borders, as part of United Nations peacekeeping forces.
But with only a month to go before ceremonies to mark the 50th anniversary of the attack on Pearl Harbor and with memories of Japanese occupation and atrocities during World War II still vivid across Asia and the Pacific, Mr. Miyazawa's suggestion met with a decidedly unenthusiastic response outside Japan.
Said an American diplomat: "Given a choice between an Asian defense umbrella provided by the United States and one offered by Tokyo, you'd better believe that we're going to remain the more popular option."

file: THE WORLD_To Beijing_s Surprise, the Tibetans Are Still Restive.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ever since Chinese troops ''liberated'' Tibet in 1950, the Communist authorities have tried to pressure Tibetans into submission. 
But these days many Tibetans seem more eager than ever to pry themselves from the Chinese embrace, and there are signs that time is running against Beijing.
Government officials acknowledge that they face a long-term struggle against what they describe as ''a tiny number of separatists.''
Yet the very trend of economic and social development seems to be running against the Chinese. 
The worldwide pattern since the early 19th century has been that nationalism increases rather than diminishes as peasants earn more money, drift to cities and become more politically aware. 
In Tibet, as peasants buy televisions and radios to plug into the modern world, they may be swayed by the independence movement and nationalism that already flourish in Lhasa.
Economic factors may provoke even greater discontent. 
Incomes are rising in Tibet, but not as fast as in the rest of China. 
While the region has some natural resources, it is difficult to see how Tibet could catch up with the rest of China - unless it went all-out to attract foreign tourists, a strategy that the Government has judged too risky politically.
''The city dwellers are better off than in the past, but they're not satisfied,'' acknowledged Hu Jinan, the deputy head of the Tibetan Government's Cultural Bureau. 
''They know it's better elsewhere.''
Tibet is officially an ''autonomous region'' of China, but the Government's legitimacy has been in doubt at least since the Dalai Lama, the traditional leader of the region, fled into exile in 1959. 
There is little armed resistance to Chinese rule, partly because Tibetans are Buddhist and generally pacifist, but the Dalai Lama has set up an exile government and many Tibetans would like him to return and lead Tibet as a sovereign state.
Government officials here often seem amazed that Tibetans should resent Chinese rule. 
Indeed, there is little doubt that Beijing has been, by its standards, not only very repressive but also very generous in Tibet. 
Torture is said to be common, and the Government has expelled politically active monks from monasteries and planned new limits on the number of monks. 
But Tibet is materially better off than it used to be, and health and educational standards have risen - although the same would have been expected without Chinese rule.
Each year the central government not only excuses Tibet from its tax obligations but also provides about $275 million in subsidies. 
About one-third goes to salaries, but much of the rest is used for schools, hospitals and infrastructure projects. 
The Chinese seem to feel that they are owed a bit of loyalty and gratitude, but the distrust is so great that they get little credit either in Tibet or outside of it.
Outside of Tibet, the Dalai Lama and those around him have tried to build support by telling of forced sterilization of Tibetans, huge influxes of Chinese and a deliberate policy of either genocide or forced assimilation. 
But many diplomats and other experts regard the anti-Chinese propaganda from the Dalai Lama as little more reliable than the Chinese propaganda about Tibet. 
With access tightly curtailed, the debate about Tibet has been waged more with polemics than with information.
Among the most poignant claims by the Dalai Lama is that Tibetans have become a minority in their own land because of large-scale Chinese immigration. 
But the exile movement's estimate of a Tibetan population of 6 million Tibetans and 7.5 million Chinese is considered misleading because it refers to a vast area of China that extends far beyond present-day Tibet. 
The official Chinese figures for Tibet's population are often viewed as more relevant: 2.12 million ethnic Tibetans and 79,000 permanent Han Chinese inhabitants, not including tens of thousands of Chinese cadres, soldiers and entrepreneurs without permanent residence permits.
Chinese immigration into Tibet has accelerated, but this seems to be a result not of a conspiracy by Beijing but of economic subsidies to the region. 
Chinese traders say they find it more profitable to do business in Tibet than in their home provinces.
Despite rumors about Chinese hospitals killing Tibetan infants, the family planning policy seems to be much more relaxed for Tibetans than it is for Chinese. 
Peasants interviewed said they were allowed to have as many children as they wanted, and most couples seemed to have three to five.
It is also striking how little assimilation has occurred after four decades of Chinese rule. 
Even in Lhasa only a minority of Tibetans speaks any Chinese, and in the countryside it is virtually impossible to find Chinese speakers. 
The Chinese language is not even taught in rural elementary schools, which is as far as most Tibetans pursue their education.
This strategy of trying to buy friends in Tibet with subsidies and various benefits showed some promise of succeeding in the 1980's, but in Lhasa it already seems to have collapsed. 
The last three years of protests, each time brutally crushed, have led to new bitterness on each side.
Despite the repression and mistrust, many Tibetans are optimistic that they will gain independence in the coming decades. 
They are inspired partly by the collapse of Communism in Eastern Europe and partly by signs of a weak and unpopular central Government in Beijing. 
Tibet has turned out to be fairly indigestible, and they hope that Beijing will eventually spit it out.
''We don't like the Chinese,'' a Tibetan in his 20's explained the other day. 
''They've turned to repression and terrorism to keep us down, but most people still want independence and want the Dalai Lama to return. 
Independence is a real possibility.''

text:
ï»¿
CHINA'S six-decade civil war may be ending. 
The bearer of the olive branch was Shirley Kuo, Finance Minister in the Taiwan Government, who last week became the first Nationalist official to return to China since the Communist victory in 1949.
But the visit by Miss Kuo, who was in Beijing to attend the annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank, was only a symbol of a peace process that has been unfolding for two years.
Not everyone thinks reunification will occur, but it is no longer out of the question. 
And even if the two societies do not merge politically, they are likely to have peaceful relations and maintain a close economic and cultural relationship. 
In any event, the final result appears likely to be peace and a close relationship.
It was in 1927 that the Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek ended an uneasy association with the Communists by slaughtering every leftist they could find. 
The ensuing civil war, briefly suspended during the cooperative battle against the Japanese invaders, was marked by enormous bitterness and brutality. 
The enmities smoldered after the Communists sent the Nationalists fleeing to their bastion on Taiwan 40 years ago. 
Many on Taiwan are still appalled by the brutalities of the anti-rightist campaigns and the Cultural Revolution in the 1950's and 1960's. 
And the two sides shelled each other as recently as a decade ago.
A Communist leader like Mao could not forget that the Nationalist forces tortured to death one of his wives and executed both his brother and adopted sister. 
Nor could the Nationalists who fled to Taiwan forget that many relatives who had stayed behind were executed or driven to suicide on the mainland. 
The vehemence and distrust is still sharp in the minds of older Chinese, especially in Taiwan, but younger people on both sides worry less about historical sins than about present opportunities.
For now the opportunities are largely economic. 
Trade through Hong Kong surged 80 percent last year, to $2.8 billion, and more and more Taiwan manufacturers are moving entire assembly lines to China. 
The economic partnership and cultural ties seem almost certain to grow. 
People from Taiwan already are the second most numerous tourists in China, slightly trailing the Japanese.
The fundamental question, therefore, is whether the economic and cultural ties will lead to political integration. 
No one dares to respond to the question flatly, but most people are increasingly skeptical.
''There's not much advantage in reunification for Taiwan,'' said Byron S. J. Weng, a China scholar at Chinese University in Hong Kong. 
''It can reap the advantages without reunification.''
Taiwan officials are blunt on this point. 
Maps printed in Taiwan still depict the Nationalists' dream of a Republic of China encompassing Taiwan, China and Mongolia, but the hope seems to be dying. 
The humiliation of having been sent fleeing to a tiny island four decades ago has been replaced by the self-confidence of having engineered an economic miracle and, in the last two years, an incipient democracy.
Â 
Long-Lost Relatives
A Taiwan businessman who was born on the mainland compared the island's situation to that of a prosperous family that suddenly discovers long-lost relatives in nearby slums. 
The family feels attachment and responsibility, but is not ready to ask the relatives to move into the same house. 
Nevertheless, few Taiwanese seem interested in creating an independent country that they would call Taiwan. 
They prefer to continue calling their island the Republic of China. 
Most seem prepared to wait for a resolution. 
In China, most people also seem prepared to wait - so long as Taiwan does not declare its independence from the mainland. 
That is the one eventuality that might lead China to attack Taiwan. 
Aside from such remote possibilities, most people in China simply regard Taiwan as a rich island whose economic success and political liberalization they want to replicate. 
For all the changes in China in the last decade and for all the hopes raised by the pro-democracy demonstrations of recent weeks, a deep self-doubt exists in the intellectual psyche about whether Chinese culture is even capable of sustaining a democratic society. 
Now, as people learn more about Taiwan, they are beginning to look to the East as well as the West for political inspiration.
Â 
Politics and Pride
In the meantime, the two sides are edging toward dialogue. 
Jaw Shau-kong, a Taiwan legislator, said in a telephone interview that the next step may be for unofficial representatives of both sides - telecommunications technicians, maybe - to meet. 
Later, perhaps, the two societies' leaders will sit down together. 
More distant moves toward harmony seem vaguely possible. 
Some Communist officials have suggested that China might even be willing to change its name, constitution and ideology - and to share power with the Nationalists - as part of a deal to merge with Taiwan.
This would be difficult now, as long as old revolutionaries are still around. 
But in a decade or two, younger leaders may be more interested in recovering Taiwan than in maintaining their public faith in Communism. 
''Before, the nation was defined by the party in power,'' said a young Communist Party official who favors sharing power with the Nationalists. 
''But national pride transcends politics. 
First we are Chinese, and only second are we Communist or Nationalist.''
So much has changed that it is difficult to forecast what might happen after the old revolutionaries are gone. 
Perhaps nothing will happen politically. 
But there is at least the possibility that what for so many decades has been a great regional quandary could be resolved in one way or another.
''What is fascinating is that you cannot safely predict the limits of what might happen,'' said Kenneth G. Lieberthal, director of the Center for Chinese Studies at the University of Michigan. 
''Almost anything is possible.''
A symbol of change: Taiwan's Finance Minister, Shirley Kuo, arriving in Beijing last week to attend a meeting of the Asian Development Bank (Agence France-Presse)

file: THE WORLD_Why China_s Students Aren_t Ready for the Masses.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA is glorifying manual labor again, this time as a way to deal with troublesome young intellectuals. 
Last weekend, the Government announced that college graduates who want to enter graduate school - useful for getting good jobs and especially for arranging an opportunity to study abroad -should work first for one or two years. 
A separate and so far unpublished requirement will oblige those who have graduated from college since 1985 to work at the ''grass roots,'' typically at a factory or farm, for a year before taking white-collar jobs in the city, say Chinese with access to official information.
More significant, the plan also calls for college freshmen to go through full-time military training - a few weeks at most institutions but perhaps a full year at Beijing University, the vanguard of the democracy movement this spring.
In some ways, the new campaigns are reminiscent of the Cultural Revolution, when 17 million Red Guards were sent to the countryside to learn from peasants.
But there is an important difference. 
Early in the Cultural Revolution, when Mao urged students to go to the villages, many went because they thought it was the right thing to do. 
Today's students are antagonists of the leadership, and they are certain to do everything they can to avoid the yoke of military service or manual labor.
Talk about a national public service requirement was heard well before the June 4 massacre at Tiananmen Square. 
For several years, many adults were saying that such service might acquaint university students with the hard work and deprivation that for most Chinese are a way of life.
But coming now, the new programs inevitably are seen as punishment and propaganda. 
The most worrying aspect, for many, is that the work in the countryside or factories will involve the transfer of residency permits, and that many students will be left in fear that if they make political mistakes they will lose forever the right to live in Beijing or any other city.
In fact, many people doubt that the current programs will be carried out, because of resistance from an unenthusiastic bureaucracy. 
But if they are implemented, they could create logistical nightmares and aggravate the surplus of labor in the countryside as well as the sense of unfairness among intellectuals.
Perhaps most significant, compulsory manual labor or military service for this generation of students could well prove counterproductive. 
Instead of persuading young people to abandon their dreams of democracy, it could confirm their bitterness toward the regime and their belief that Western-style changes are needed all the more urgently.
Students working on a farm during the Cultural Revolution (Magnum/Marc Riboud)

file: THE WORLD_Why Japan_s Influence Doesn_t Match Its Economic Power.txt
text:
ï»¿
In East Asia no less than anywhere else, the collapse of the Soviet Union and Communism was supposed to lead to vast new influence for Japan, the region's economic superpower. 
But recent months have shown, instead, just how deeply Japan remains mired in the debates and anxieties of the past.
At least to its neighbors, the new Japan looks suspiciously like the old Japan. 
And in Japanese eyes, Asia is still a place for caution, if not paralysis. 
"The cold war is at an end, but Japanese don't really know how to disengage from it," said Terumasa Nakanishi, professor of international relations at the University of Shizuoka. 
"We lack any kind of national consensus on how to act."
Some of Japan's self-confidence has been deflated, in any case, by its poor economic performance recently. 
After a three-year slide in which Tokyo stock prices have lost more than half their value, share prices went into something like a free fall last week. 
Despite a rebound Friday, fears persist that the current mild recession could deepen and drag down the world economy. 
Privately, Japanese leaders say this may be a bad time for bold actions, especially costly ones.
Toward Russia, for example, financial concerns are an impediment to direct Japanese participation in an economic bailout. 
But the main concern here is still political. 
The same dispute over four tiny islands in the Kurile chain that has blocked improvement of relations since the end of World War II, when the Soviet Union seized them, has resisted all recent attempts at a settlement. 
Though negligible in strategic value, the islands are a powerful symbol of past unresolved grievances.
Japanese politicians, especially nationalists, say the final chapter of the country's climb back to legitimacy after defeat cannot be written until the islands are returned. 
But diplomats have begun reluctantly to conclude that with Russian nationalism flaring anew in Siberia, President Boris N. Yeltsin may find it more difficult to give up the islands than even Mikhail S. Gorbachev did.
The practical effect is that Japan continues to be a reluctant partner in the Western scramble to assemble a package of assistance to help Mr. Yeltsin out of his economic problems. 
The $24 billion aid package announced 10 days ago by the United States and Germany made Japan decidedly uncomfortable. 
Japanese diplomats said it was inappropriate to announce the package because all the details had not been worked out, and because a premature announcement might send the wrong signal to the Russians: that they had the money in hand and could ease up on austerity.
Â 
'Political Constraints'
Japanese leaders said that although Tokyo would join multilateral efforts to stabilize the ruble, Japan would not increase its own aid beyond what it announced last year after the failed coup against Mr. Gorbachev. "We face political constraints," said Finance Minister Tsutomu Hata.
There has also long been talk here of investing in the exploration of natural gas and oil in eastern Russia or other parts of what was the Soviet Union. 
But it remains just talk. 
Japanese industrialists, cautious in normal times, are not about to invest during the current recession in a resource for which there may not be a need until well into the 21st century. 
They also look to the Government for insurance or guarantees, and Japanese leaders are not ready to cooperate until the territorial issues are resolved.
But Russia is not the only place over which Japan is showing caution. 
Many people had expected Tokyo to play a role in rebuilding Cambodia. 
Indeed, Yasushi Akashi, a United Nations diplomat who heads the peacekeeping efforts there, expects his country to pay for at least one-third of the cost of stationing troops. 
But for now it looks as if Japan will not send its own troops, despite the best efforts of Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa. 
As in the Persian Gulf war last year, Japan will help foot the bill without putting its people on the line.
The Cambodians say they would like Japanese troops, if only in a logistical role, but other Asian nations are less sure. 
Last week, Jiang Zemin, the Chinese Communist Party General Secretary, visited Japan and, in diplomatic language, recommended caution. 
The idea of Japanese troops going overseas for the first time since World War II was a "sensitive" issue for "well-known reasons," he said.
If Japanese officials were disappointed that Mr. Jiang was not warmer to Japan's playing a more robust role in the region, Japanese relations with other Asian countries are also troubled. 
A growing trade imbalance with South Korea is rankling President Roh Tae Woo and other leaders in Seoul. 
And three years of intensive efforts to improve ties with South Korea have resulted in more tensions than ever, this time over Japan's dismissal of claims for compensation by South Korean women who say they were kidnapped from their communities and forced to become sex slaves for Japanese front-line troops during the war.
Because it continues to be dogged by the past, Japan has had a hard time implementing its pledge to join a "global partnership" with Washington to combat poverty and tyranny in the world. 
Not only does Japan refuse to criticize China on human rights, but it has also looked the other way when Burma and Thailand suppressed their democratic stirrings.
Japan had pinned a lot of its hopes for a new order in Asia on a long-planned visit by Emperor Akihito to China later this year. 
But because of lingering Korean and Chinese resentments, the visit is now uncertain. 
What was to have been a symbol of the progress Tokyo had made in being accepted has thus instead become a victim of the lingering doubts in Japan's own backyard.

file: Three From Hong Kong Are Jailed by China.txt
text:

A Chinese court convicted three Hong Kong residents today on charges of helping pro-democracy campaigners and sentenced them to prison terms of four to five years, a Chinese newspaper reported.
The three were the first Hong Kong residents sentenced by China for involvement in the democracy movement that was crushed in China in June 1989.
The Yangcheng Evening News in nearby Canton said the three were charged with collaborating with a Hong Kong group in attempting to smuggle Wang Juntao and Chen Ziming, two well-known dissidents, out of China.
The dissidents were convicted on Feb. 
12 in Beijing of plotting to overthrow the Government. 
Each was sentenced to 13 years in prison.
The newspaper said the Canton Intermediate People's Court sentenced Lo Hoi-sing, a 42-year-old businessman, and Lai Pui-Shing each to five years in prison and Li Lung-hing to four years. 
The newspaper provided no further information on Mr. Lai and Mr. Li.
The paper said Mr. Lo supplied details of Mr. Chen's whereabouts to John Shum, a Hong Kong actor who is a member of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of the Patriotic Democratic Movement in China. 
Beijing has branded the alliance "subversive" for helping wanted dissidents escape the country.
Mr. Lo's wife, Chau Mat-mat, said in Hong Kong that the sentence was harsh. 
She said she would appeal to Chinese authorities to reduce the sentence.
She said her husband, formerly a Hong Kong trade representative to Beijing and later a businessman specializing in China trade, was only involved in passing messages from some one in China to Mr. Shum, a friend of Mr. Lo for years.

file: Tiananmen Killings Not a _Tragedy,_ Chinese Party Chief Says.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin, said today that the army's suppression of the democracy movement in early June, in which hundreds of people were killed, was not a ''tragedy,'' and he refused to rule out more death sentences for the movement's leaders.
In a news conference broadcast live on the national television, Mr. Jiang sounded a hard line. 
A 63-year-old technocrat who has been named by Deng Xiaoping to succeed Mr. Deng as senior leader, Mr. Jiang was formally designated General Secretary of the party in late June, and this was his first meeting with reporters since then.
When an Italian reporter asked Mr. Jiang whether the ''the Tiananmen tragedy'' could have been avoided, the party leader responded: ''First, I'd like to correct you in your use of the word tragedy. 
We do not believe that there was any tragedy in Tiananmen Square. 
What actually happened was a counterrevolutionary rebellion aimed at opposing the leadership of the Communist Party and overthrowing the socialist system.''
'Motivated by Discontent'
Mr. Jiang refused to say how many people were arrested or executed in the crackdown after the suppression of the democracy movement, and he said he could not rule out further death sentences because that would be political intervention in the judicial process. 
He said all cases would be handled according to law.
Asked for details of arrests and executions, Mr. Jiang said that aside from a small number of leaders, ''The great majority of students who took part in demonstrations or hunger strikes were motivated by discontent or by concern about corruption, and we can understand that.
''Our policy toward the students is to try to educate them and unite them,'' he added. 
''I have said on many occasions recently that youth are the future and the hope of the country.''
Among the Chinese who listened on radios and watched on television, the question that seemed to resonate most deeply came from a French journalist who told Mr. Jiang of a Chinese friend, a woman who was wounded in Tiananmen Square and then arrested and sent to a prison farm where she was raped three times in her first week. 
Was this the way to educate and unite the hope of the country, the journalist asked.
Â 
Belittles 'Fairy Tales'
Mr. Jiang emphasized again that the party had dealt leniently with most students, and he warned against believing ''fairy tales from the Arabian Nights.''
A former Mayor and party leader from Shanghai, Mr. Jiang reasserted that China would not change its open-door and economic reform policies.
By televising the full news conference, the leadership risked embarrassing itself and exposing the Chinese audience to foreign skepticism about the official account of the repression. 
But most of the 19 questions were tame, and the moderator called on few Western journalists. 
Only one American was allowed to raise a question.
Â 
Zhao's Fate Still Unknown
The Politburo members criticized the former party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, several times. 
They said he committed the mistake of supporting the student and worker turmoil and splitting the party. 
Mr. Jiang said that investigations of Mr. Zhao are continuing but that the party was taking a ''down to earth'' attitude toward its former leader. 
That wording, and the announcement that Mr. Zhao was being paid his salary and leading a comfortable life, seemed to suggest that Mr. Zhao would not face criminal charges of trying to overthrow the Government.
Mr. Jiang confirmed that the party Central Committee was planning a session soon to discuss economic issues in coming years, but he did not say whether Mr. Zhao's fate would be decided at the meeting, as has been expected. 
He said the leadership had not decided on when to convene the Central Committee.
In what may be a signal that Mr. Deng will retire from his last remaining official position, chairman of the Central Military Commission, Mr. Jiang said that Mr. Deng was eager to withdraw but that it would be up to party and Government organizations to decide when he could retire.

file: Tiananmen Protest Leader Credits _Lots of People_ for Escape to West.txt
text:
ï»¿
A leader of the Chinese student movement that was crushed in Tiananmen Square in June said here today that she was able to avoid arrest for 10 months thanks to the help, protection and encouragement of ordinary Chinese citizens.
The student, Chai Ling, a 23-year-old psychology major who played a central role in the democracy movement, and her 24-year-old husband, Feng Congde, who is also on the Beijing Government's list of 21 ''most wanted,'' said they were finally able to slip out of China two weeks ago.
In their first interview since arriving in France, where they have requested political asylum, the couple called on the West to adopt tougher sanctions against China. 
They said it was also important to keep the Chinese people informed about events abroad.
Miss Chai said a ship that will soon be used for broadcasting news into China from off-shore international waters would bring great encouragement. 
The ship, the Goddess of Democracy, set sail from the French port of La Rochelle on March 17 with several exiled Chinese dissidents on board.
Â 
Secret Groups Aid Dissidents
Beijing was rebuffed this week when it asked France to outlaw A Boat For Democracy, the foundation that is financing the broadcast ship. 
China also formally protested the French Government's decision to allow Miss Chai and her husband into this country. 
Their request for asylum is under consideration.
Miss Chai said she went into hiding immediately after the Tiananmen Square movement was crushed, staying first in Beijing and then moving to places she refused to identify. 
''All this time, I had the support of lots of people,'' she said. 
''People who had their own problems of family and work to worry about, but who helped and protected us with their own resources.''
She said secret organizations sprung up after June to help the dissidents, while those who hid her always knew her identity and assumed the risks. 
She said the same people helped her and Mr. Feng to leave the country, although she would not disclose how they escaped or where they first arrived.
Speaking in Chinese through a French interpreter, Miss Chai said her worst moment was when she thought her husband had been captured. 
''My friends said I had to move places, but I felt very bad,'' she said. 
''I thought I would never see him again. 
If at that moment someone from security had found me, I would not have had the strength to react. 
I saw the limit of my will.''
Â 
'We Did Not Go Far Enough'
After one week, she said, she learned that Mr. Feng was safe, but she did not see him again for four months. 
She said that occasionally she was accompanied by other fugitive students and dissidents, but that ''most of the time I was hidden alone and I had lots of time to reflect on what happened in Tiananmen Square.''
''Today my feeling is that I am not 100 percent satisfied with what we did,'' she said. 
''We did not go far enough, take our actions far enough. 
For example, we were not in contact with people abroad and had little understanding of the impact we had. 
But I think that, after 40 years of repression, this was the most pacific and reasonable revolt imaginable.''
She is believed to have been in charge of protests in Tiananmen Square during the final days of the movement, but she was unable to cast much light on the continuing debate over how many people died when the army tanks and troops moved in shortly before dawn on June 4.
''I was in the center of the square, but all around I heard shots being fired and ambulance sirens,'' she said in response to a question noting that the Chinese authorities assert no one died in the square. 
''We sent out observers and some came back with blood stains on their clothes.''
Â 
Darkness of Tiananmen Square
Mr. Feng said that since all lights were switched off in the square, it was difficult to know what was happening. 
''Those who were in the square can only testify to what they saw around them,'' he said. 
''I don't think even the army or the Communist Party know how many people died.''
It is now generally accepted that most of the killings in the crackdown took place not in the square but on the north side, along the Avenue of Eternal Peace, and in other parts of the city.
Miss Chai said that she would continue the fight to emancipate China, but that first she needed time to adjust. 
''I feel very disturbed,'' she said. 
''Every time I close my eyes, I see nightmarish scenes that prevent me from sleeping. 
I feel the souls of the dead are seeking my help. 
I need time to recover.''
She said she was helped by ordinary Chinese citizens. 
(The New York Times/Alan Riding)

file: Tibet After Martial Law_ Whispers of Protest.txt
text:
ï»¿
Five months after martial law was lifted here, a sullen calm has returned to the narrow lanes of this holy city. 
But Chinese marksmen are still perched on the roofs of buildings overlooking the central square, and many Tibetans suspect that their guns have not been silenced for long.
Here among the snow-swept peaks and glacier-fed rivers to the north of Mount Everest, nationalism is forging a significant challenge to the Communist leaders 1,600 miles away in Beijing. 
This is Deng Xiaoping's Lithuania, and some fear it will become his Beirut - except that Tibet is more vast, amounting to two-thirds the size of Western Europe. 
If China ever crumbles, Tibet is likely to be the first piece to break off, with reverberations across Asia.
A weeklong visit to Tibet - one of the first permitted by a foreign journalist since martial law was lifted May 1 -found no evidence of widespread or serious unrest in the majority rural population, for most peasants and nomads absorb themselves not in politics but in the practical matters of their barley and yaks.
Yet in Lhasa, the discontent and repression seem pervasive in the wake of martial law, which was declared after widespread protests in 1987. 
The mood suggests a dangerous cascade of bitterness that threatens to overwhelm the land that inspired the notion of Shangri-La.
Â 
'We Hate China'
''Everybody wants independence and the return of the Dalai Lama,'' a well-educated Tibetan in his 30's whispered late one evening, after ducking into a building near Jokhang Temple to take refuge from police spies. 
''We hate China and what it has done.''
He spoke in a mixture of terror and fury, and he extended his arms as if handcuffed to suggest what he thought would happen if he were caught. 
A moment later he fled in fright when a jeep pulled up outside and someone shined a flashlight through the window.
While the man was more outspoken than most, he seemed to represent the antagonisms and distrust that are nearly overflowing in Lhasa. 
While the police and troop presence has been reduced since the end of martial law, anti-Chinese protests continue on a small scale and the authorities acknowledge that they face a long-term struggle to subdue what they describe as ''a tiny handful of separatists.''
Â 
Violent Suppression And Rising Distrust
Tibet, now an autonomous region, was ''invaded'' or ''liberated'' by Chinese troops in 1950 - the term depends on the speaker. 
The Dalai Lama was the supreme figure in a theocratic Government, and even though he fled to India in 1959 after an abortive uprising, his influence is everywhere. 
After his flight China consolidated its hold on Tibet, which had been claimed by all Chinese governments since the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, although the western two-thirds of Tibet had been effectively independent since 1912.
In the early and mid-1980's, a conciliatory policy by the Chinese authorities seemed to be winning results, and tensions eased in Tibet. 
But protests beginning in 1987 were violently suppressed, with the police firing on crowds of demonstrators around the Jokhang Temple, and many Tibetans say that since then discontent has risen dangerously.
The Chinese authorities will face a test next Thursday, the third anniversary of the beginning of the recent wave of unrest. 
Posters already have gone up on brick walls around town, calling for demonstrations on that day or on Oct. 
1, China's national day.
Word about the proposed protests is whispered from ear to ear among Tibetans who mingle in the narrow lanes around the Jokhang Temple, but no one knows if people will take the risk and respond.
There have been a few minor incidents in recent months. 
About a dozen monks and nuns were arrested last month during a peaceful protest at the Dalai Lama's old summer residence near Lhasa, and about six more were seized on Sept. 
14 when they marched around the Jokhang Temple and chanted pro-independence slogans.
Â 
Harsher Policies After Martial Law
''Those who try to split the motherland will, if they dare to violate the Constitution and laws, surely be opposed by the broad masses,'' said Mao Rubai, the vice chairman of Tibet's Government. 
He is a member of the Han race, which accounts for 93 percent of all Chinese, while the Tibetan people are of Mongolian stock.
There are some signs of a tougher policy since the end of martial law, including the appointment on May 31 of a new chairman of Tibet's Government, Gyaincain Norbu, a law-and-order man with long experience in the courts and prosecutors' offices.
By official count, there are a few more than 100 people now imprisoned for engaging in illegal separatist activities. 
But most independent estimates are higher.
Officials deny that those imprisoned have been tortured, but most Tibetans say that physical abuse is routine. 
The six people arrested on Sept. 
14 were briefly taken into a police station near the Jokhang Temple, and when they were led out 10 minutes later to be bused away, they were already said to have been beaten.
A comprehensive report earlier this year by Asia Watch, an American human-rights organization, detailed treatment of prisoners that included attacks by trained dogs, assaults with electric cattle prods, suspension by ropes, scalding with boiling water and rapes of nuns.
Â 
Tibetans Express Views on China
Official Chinese publications have occasionally written about Tibetan prisons - describing them as so idyllic that offenders are almost sad to leave - but the authorities refused repeated requests to visit a prison on this trip.
But Gong Liefu, the deputy director of Tibet's Foreign Affairs Office, said that it was illegal for a foreign journalist to ask people whether they favored independence, and that it might be illegal for Tibetans to respond in the affirmative.
Nevertheless, Tibetans made their views known. 
At dusk, as shops closed and most Chinese police withdrew from the streets, they sometimes approached a foreign reporter to speak their mind. 
And even in officially arranged interviews, Tibetans sometimes refused to go along with the official line.
In the heart of the Jokhang Temple, as pilgrims kowtowed in the dust not far away, a senior monk named Tudeng Renqing criticized the expulsion from the temple of eight monks who had taken part in a protest. 
In the presence of about 10 people, including Han Chinese officials, he was then asked for his views about independence, and a silence settled over the room as he paused and thought for several minutes.
''From a religious point of view,'' he finally responded delicately, ''I'd like all believers as well as the general population to act peacefully.''
A reporter suggested that in the circumstances, that sounded like an endorsement of peaceful efforts for independence. 
The lama laughed and beamed.
Â 
Beijing's Backers Offer Reasons
A yearning for independence is common in Lhasa, but it is not universal. 
Some Tibetans insist that independence would be a disaster for the region's development and assert that only a tiny fraction of young people oppose links with the ''motherland.''
Most of the top positions in the Government administration are held by such Tibetans, who point to improved health care and rising prosperity under Chinese rule.
In addition, there seems to be a broad stratum of urban Tibetans who recognize the improvements but are also resentful of Chinese domination. 
They are moderately discontented, but see little alternative to Chinese rule and in any case are afraid of getting in trouble if they oppose the regime.
''We don't thnk about politics,'' said a Tibetan university student over a beer in a privately owned bar. 
''We don't dare. 
We just study.''
Darchi, a 40-year-old peasant interviewed at random as he harvested his barley in a mud-brick village near the city of Shigatse, said: ''We don't want independence. 
Before we had a difficult time and now life is getting better. 
I want to buy a television, and then I can sit back and drink barley beer and watch TV.''
Yet even those, like Mr. Darchi, who are wary of independence adore the Dalai Lama. 
Most homes and temples have photos of the Dalai Lama on the wall, and ordinary people are moved nearly to tears as they touch a Dalai Lama photo to their head when it is given to them.
Â 
Failing Economy Under China's Rule
As China's leaders try to win over the Tibetan population and earn the appreciation of local residents, their challenge is compounded by economic difficulties. 
Despite enormous subsidies from Beijing - some of which go to pay the salaries of Han Chinese officials rather than to benefit local Tibetans - industry in Tibet has grown by only about 6 percent per year over the last decade, compared with about 12 percent annually in the rest of the country.
Officials concede that the economic gap between Tibet and coastal China is growing, not diminishing, and that adds to the perception that the Chinese authorities are mismanaging the local economy.
Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader, visited Tibet in July and pledged even greater subsidies over the next decade to build the local economic base. 
But the region's greatest economic resource, tourism, may not be exploited to the full because of fears that large numbers of individual tourists could help provoke further unrest. 
Ngaphu Rinchen, the director of tourism in Tibet, said that while visits by tour groups would be expanded, it would be ''difficult'' to allow individual tourists to return within the next two or three years.
In Tibet all those problems tend to overlay and reinforce the main gulf in the society: that which separates Tibetans and Han Chinese. 
While Chinese complain that Tibetans are lazy and ungrateful, and more likely to show hospitality to a foreigner on the street than to a longtime Chinese colleague, the Tibetans resent what they regard as a superior attitude and colonial policy on the part of the Chinese.
''Life has settled a bit since the lifting of martial law, but it's still tense,'' said a Tibetan in his 20's who has spent the last dozen years in Lhasa. 
''This is a volcano, and someday it will explode.''

file: Tibet Without Going There.txt
text:
ï»¿
AT the end of the world, where the Tibetan plateau suddenly teeters off a cliff in one direction and collides against snowcapped peaks in the other, the Xinsi Monastery looms unexpectedly from the golden wheat fields to preside over the landscape. 
The red-robed monks come bustling out, the dough on their hands an indication that they have been interrupted in their chores rather than their prayers, and they break into welcoming grins as magnificent as the scenery.
It is a scene from Tibet, more Tibetan than Tibet itself. 
Here there are no Chinese troops prowling in the background or Chinese tour leaders curtailing contacts with the monks.
This is Qinghai Province in the west of China, but it used to be the northeast part of Tibet until it fell under Chinese control centuries ago. 
The Tibetans regard Qinghai as part of Tibet, but the Chinese Government's restrictions on travel to Tibet do not apply here. 
Tourists are allowed into Tibet only as part of a costly organized tour -- although this can be a one-person tour -- while foreigners are free to fly to Xining, the provincial capital, from Beijing.
Qinghai -- pronounced ching-hi -- was opened to foreigners only in 1983, and it still is among the least visited parts of China. 
Only about 1,200 Americans go to the province each year, slightly fewer than visit Tibet, and the sight of a foreigner still turns heads even in Xining.
The single greatest splendor in Qinghai is the Kumbum Monastery, better known today by its Chinese name, Taer Si. 
Fifteen miles southwest of Xining, the Kumbum is a stunning collection of temples and compounds set against a hillside, the buildings all painted red and other bright colors, with pilgrims praying and spinning the large prayer wheels and prostrating on the ground. 
The monastery is as noteworthy for the Tibetan pilgrims who come to worship as for the architecture itself. 
When I visited in August, I came across a group of four sturdy young Tibetan men in bedraggled clothing.
We chatted for a bit in Chinese and they said they had come from their homes in Sichuan Province, by way of Lhasa. 
I asked how they had traveled. 
They looked puzzled.
"By foot," said the oldest of them, about 18 years old.
"How long have you been traveling?"
"Two years," the young man said. 
"But we'll be home in another six months."
The monastery was built in the last quarter of the 16th century on the instructions of the third Dalai Lama. 
The site is the birthplace of the founder of the Gelukpa order of Buddhism, Tsongkhapa. 
This was a center of learning -- one of the Tibetan Ivy League, so to speak -- for Tibetan and Mongolian monks, and at the time of the Communist revolution there were still 3,000 Tibetan monks. 
Now the Government has set a limit of 400 monks for the Kumbum, but this is not strictly enforced and there are about 500.
The most unusual sight in the monastery is the 50-foot-long carving made of yak butter. 
The workmanship may not be at the level of the Parthenon frieze, but there are elephants, flowers and religious figures, all in brightly colored deep relief. 
The carving is newly-sculptured each year.
XINING itself is of limited interest: a traditionally Chinese city of cement blocks whose hues are all shades of gray. 
The only important sight within the city is the Dongguan Mosque, which was built in the 14th century and is one of the largest mosques in China. 
The entrance arch is elegant and the plaza-like open space inside is picturesque. 
There is a large Muslim community in Xining -- the province was even ruled by a Muslim warlord immediately prior to the Communist revolution in 1949 -- and the mosque fills to capacity on Fridays for prayers.
Few people in Qinghai speak English, but if you have an evening free you might wander over to the English Corner on Sheng Li Road. 
This is where Chinese men and women gather, particularly on Sundays, to speak English to each other in a caliber ranging from a few words to fluency, and a genuine American is richly prized and quickly surrounded.
The best part about Qinghai is the Tibetan areas, and in general any road south or west will take you to Tibetan villages. 
The current Dalai Lama's native village, Takster, meaning Roaring Tiger, is apparently only about an hour or two by car from Xining, but the authorities told me that the area was closed to foreigners and refused to allow me to visit. 
Other foreigners have gone with impunity, however, and one may well be able to make arrangements with a taxi driver for a day trip. 
Foreign tourists who are caught in closed areas and who act surprised, innocent and apologetic are normally scolded and sent away. 
Occasionally a fine is negotiated, but normally there is no punishment.
One Tibetan area that is often recommended to tourists is Qinghai Lake, an immense body of water that is China's largest salt-water lake. 
Bird Island in the lake is supposed to be particularly beautiful and full of migratory birds in April and May. 
I didn't visit Bird Island, but I found Qinghai Lake itself about as interesting as one would expect a big salt lake to be.
THE highlight of my visit was simply a few days roaming the Tibetan villages around Qiapuqia, a town of about 30,000 in Gonghe County south of Qinghai Lake. 
Most of the townspeople are Han Chinese, but many of the nearby villages are Tibetan and the people are extremely welcoming.
"Uncle, are you a foreigner?" asked an eight-year-old girl who was startled to encounter me on a dirt path near her village. 
I explained in Chinese that I was a genuine foreigner. 
Since I was the first one she had ever seen, she led me to her home. 
Her family was enormously excited at my arrival, and pressed tea and bread on me, but the town was sufficiently remote that all they knew was that I was not Tibetan.
"Are you Han Chinese?" the grandmother asked me, after peering for several minutes at my face, which does not look in the least Chinese. 
I explained that no, I was an American. 
She nodded sagely, to show that she had heard of Americans, but I'm not sure she distinguished in her mind between Americans and Martians.
The best way to make friends in such areas -- in any Chinese village for that matter -- is to take a Polaroid camera. 
Few peasants own a camera, and if you can take some instant photographs and pass them around, the entire village will cluster around and observe in amazement, and peasants will compete to invite you into their homes. 
Of course, none of the villagers speak English, but sign language can be quite eloquent when necessary. 
If a non-Chinese speaker gets somewhere where sign language is insufficient, someone will get the school's English teacher to translate.
About 10 miles from Qiapuqia is the Xinsi, a Tibetan monastery that gets only a few foreign travelers a year. 
The path is not quite wide enough for a car, but it makes a nice all-day hike, or else you may be able to get a lift on a motorcycle.
There are about 100 monks at the monastery, ranging from 7 years old to the late 70's. 
The setting is spectacular: snowy mountains in the background, and an abyss and valley in the foreground. 
It really does seem to be the end of the world. 
The monks speak no English, and not much Chinese, but they were eager to show me around the many temples as well as the kitchens and living quarters. 
There are several courtyards and temples with large carved Buddhas. 
Each of the temples is surrounded by the familiar red prayer wheels.
I hiked back to Qiapuqia from the monastery in about six hours, stopping to talk to Tibetan villagers on the way, and found it an exhilarating walk. 
But one word of caution: the local police were aghast at my activities, because I was a journalist (as I had told everyone I had talked to), and later sent policemen to retrace my steps and interrogate everyone I had chatted with.
This was probably a special case that wouldn't affect an ordinary tourist, but it is a reminder that this is a sensitive region. 
The worst that can realistically happen to you is that you'll be fined and expelled, but it is possible to get local Tibetans in deep trouble if the authorities believe they are engaging in pro-independence activities. 
So avoid meeting in places like your hotel -- where local people may be questioned about why they are talking to a foreigner -- and be discreet in your conversations with Tibetans.
Â 
Â 
Â 
A REMOTE, LITTLE-VISITED AREA
Getting There
Air China has flights every Friday from Beijing to Xining and back, all seats economy class, for $133 each way. 
First class trains are also available, but the journey takes 44 hours from Beijing. 
If flights are full, it is possible to fly to Lanzhou, and take a train, bus or taxi for the half-day ride to Xining.
It is possible to travel from Qinghai to Tibet, by bus or by hitching rides on trucks, but this is technically illegal unless you have a permit to enter Tibet. 
In fact, youthful Westerners do this regularly, and despite occasional crackdowns the authorities seem to tolerate it most of the time. 
The trip, by bus or truck, takes a minimum of three days from Xining to Lhasa.
Even in the summer, Qinghai can be chilly because of the elevation -- Qiapuqia, for example, is more than 9,000 feet above sea level. 
But if you forget warm clothes, yak wool sweaters are available for about $25 in Xining. 
Winters are cold but tolerable, with temperatures below freezing but little snow.
Â 
Accommodations
The best hotel in Xining is the Qinghai Guesthouse, $32 a day for a double, and it is reasonably good, with a working bath in the slightly musty rooms, a television, and fair restaurants. 
Phone (971) 44-888. 
Wang Bingxi of the Qinghai Tourism Bureau, 42-721, can arrange to have you picked up at the airport for a fee. 
The second best hotel in Xining is the Xining Guesthouse, $15 a night for two, 215 Qiyi Road, phone 42-701.
A taxi to Kumbum Monastery costs about $9 round trip, including a wait of up to three hours at the site. 
The entrance fee at the monastery is $1.50, including a guide, or $1 without.
Â 
Excursions
Mr. Wang of the tourism bureau can arrange tours of various sites including Qinghai Lake and Gonghe County. 
A two- or three-day car trip taking in Gonghe County and coming back by Qinghai Lake would cost a bit less than $200 for the vehicle, if arranged through him. 
A taxi could probably be negotiated for significantly less, and the uncomfortable bus that runs daily to Gonghe costs about $1.
In Qiapuqia, the best place to stay is the Gonghe County Communist Party Committee Guesthouse, which is perfectly tolerable, with private rooms with baths, but no telephones, and costs just $6 a night. 
Phone is 2773. 
The guesthouse restaurant offers local meals, such as tsampa -- roast barley flour kneaded into dough. 
Most restaurants in Qinghai are run by Han Chinese or Hui Muslims, and food tends to be spicy, somewhat like Sichuan food. 
Restaurants are mostly small, somewhat dirty, not particularly good and incredibly cheap.

file: Tibetan Asks Deng to Lift Martial Law.txt
text:
