The Dalai Lama appealed today to Deng Xiaoping, the senior Chinese leader, to use his influence to lift martial law in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.
In a letter delivered to the Chinese Embassy by his office here, the Dalai Lama, spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhists, also renewed his call to Beijing for talks on Tibet.
Beijing declared martial law in Lhasa on Tuesday, sending in thousands of troops to restore order after three days of anti-Chinese protests described as the worst unrest since an uprising in March 1959. 
By official count, 16 people have been killed in the unrest; Tibetans say the toll is higher, according to Western travelers.
The anniversary of the 1959 uprising was observed today, but the Dalai Lama, who is in his exile headquarters in the Indian hill town of Dharmsala, did not come to New Delhi to take part in protests mounted by Tibetans. 
Beijing crushed the 1959 revolt and ultimately declared Tibet an integral part of China, leading to the Dalai Lama's flight from the country.
Â 
'Chinese Atrocities'
Today, several hundred exiles demonstrated at India Gate, about a mile from Parliament, carrying placards that denounced ''Chinese atrocities'' and called for Tibetan independence.
The demonstrators, many belonging to youth and women's groups impatient with the lower-keyed efforts of the Dalai Lama and his willingness to talk with Beijing, burned a Chinese flag and an effigy of Li Peng, the Chinese Prime Minister.
The Dalai Lama suggested negotiating with China in a speech last September to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. 
He proposed talks in Geneva in January of this year. 
The Chinese did not accept the invitation.
Tashi Wangdi, the Dalai Lama's spokesman and a member of his exile cabinet, said today that there have been several meetings here between the Chinese Embassy and the Tibetans to discuss this and other issues. 
But he added that Beijing has major objections to be overcome before formal talks can open.
Mr. Wangdi said the Chinese objected to the composition of the team the Dalai Lama had proposed sending to formal talks. 
The Chinese also say that the Dalai Lama's suggestion that Tibet become an associated state of China - it is now called an autonomous region - was unacceptable.
In his letter to Mr. Deng today, the Dalai Lama said he hoped ''the Chinese leadership will have the wisdom to realize the true feelings of the Tibetan people and the strength and courage to rectify past mistakes.''
Â 
REPORTS OF NEW ARRESTS
BEIJING, March 10 (AP) - Official Chinese reports said today that Tibetans peacefully celebrated the ''30th anniversary of democratic reforms in Tibet'' - Beijing's characterization of the 1959 uprising. 
But Tibetans reached by telephone spoke of large-scale roundups and pervasive fear in Lhasa.
''There are new arrests,'' a woman said. 
''There are many, but we don't know how many.''
A man came on the line and said: ''Don't talk a long time. 
There are a lot of police. 
We can't talk long.''
China's nightly news said martial law stopped a riot planned for today in the capital. 
State television said more than 30 Tibetan ''rioters'' surrendered to police and admitted to taking part in disturbances this week in Lhasa.

file: Tibetans Fear Loss of a Safe Haven in Nepal.txt
text:
ï»¿
Tibetan exiles in Nepal, fearful that their country of refuge will grow more dependent on China because of an Indian economic blockade, say they are worried about their future in this land, where they are prohibited from taking part in anti-Chinese activities.
Some Tibetans are also concerned that their role in revitalizing Buddhism in Nepal, the world's only Hindu kingdom, may come in for unwelcome scrutiny. 
There are thought to be about 14,000 Tibetan refugees in Nepal, most of them the families of people who fled here from Lhasa in 1959, when the Chinese suppressed a revolt.
A refugee who works with newcomers arriving in Katmandu from Nepal's border with Tibet said immigration officials have been tightening controls as the country begins to feel the effects of India's closing of most of Nepal's southern trade routes.
This aid worker, who asked not to be named, said that Tibetans who reached a Nepali-Chinese border town, Kodari, were given visas for 12 months until about a year ago, when the validity was reduced to three months.
Recently, he said, Tibetans were being told they could stay only 30 days. 
Most Tibetans, who now travel legally on Chinese exit permits and passports, want to visit the Indian town of Dharmsala, where their exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, is based. 
The 30-day limit poses problems for these visitors, who travel a circuitous overland route to India and back.
Radhe Bista, a spokesman for the Nepalese Government, said in an interview that there was no blanket 30-day regulation covering visas for Tibetans, who are regarded as Chinese citizens. 
He said that the immigration officials at Kodari, the only land border crossing, have discretion in granting entry.
Mr. Bista said there was no intention of curbing the activities of Tibetan refugees, who have enjoyed wide freedoms to move about and engage in business. 
Tibetans are credited with starting and building an export trade in woolen and cotton carpets, which is earning much-needed hard currency for Katmandu. 
They also dominate the manufacture and sale of handicrafts to tourists, Nepalese say.
Â 
Indian Embargo
At the Tibetan refugee center of Jawalakhel, south of Katmandu, where many carpets are made for export, exiles said that their business was suffering from the inability to get raw wool and cotton because of the Indian embargo, which began on March 23. 
India says it will allow only essential supplies to enter Nepal.
Nepalese and Tibetans say that most exports are also blocked because of the trade blockade and the Indian decision to stop supplying Nepal with petroleum products needed to transport the goods to Calcutta port by trucks.
The Tibetans' role in advancing the cause of Buddhism in Nepal is just beginning to be noticed, Nepalese and Tibetans say. 
The Tibetan Buddhists do not proselytize. 
But they are devout people who give a large part of their earnings to the building of monasteries and temples, to which Nepalese also come to study and worship.
Nepal has two distinct Buddhist communities. 
The Newaris, original settlers of the Katmandu Valley, are often Buddhist or practice a combination of Hinduism and Buddhism. 
On the Nepal-Tibetan border, there are other Buddhists who follow Tibetan schools of Buddhist teachings.

file: Tibetans Protest Chinese Leader_s Visit to India.txt
Tibetan_s Tale_ Unrest, Explosion, Crackdown.txt
text:
ï»¿
The first Tibetans to leave Lhasa for Nepal since the Chinese imposed martial law in the city a month ago say several weeks of growing public protests, culminating in attacks on Chinese residents and shops, led to Beijing's action.
In a series of demonstrations in late February and early March, Tibetan nationalist flags were unfurled and emotional crowds chanted ''Independence!
Independence!'' a monk among the 42 Tibetans said in an interview. 
Mobs set Chinese businesses on fire, he said.
The recently arrived Tibetans, including children, traveled overland on Chinese exit permits allowing them to visit relatives in Nepal. 
They left Lhasa two weeks ago and reached Katmandu last week.
Since the early 1980's, China has allowed international travel to and from Lhasa through the Nepalese border town of Kodari. 
Until the recent imposition of martial law, tourists were also able to fly between Katmandu and Lhasa. 
Travel agents here say they have been told that tourist flights may resume as early as Saturday. 
This may indicate that martial law will soon be lifted.
The Tibetan monk, who asked that his name not be used to protect his family and religious colleagues in Tibet, said public disaffection in Tibet, which China formally absorbed after the Communist revolution in 1949, entered a new phase in December.
Â 
A Call to Demonstrate
Other Tibetans in the group have given Tibetan exiles here similar accounts of recent events.
The monk, a follower of the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, said signs began to appear during the night in Lhasa in early December, urging Tibetans to come out on Dec. 
10, International Human Rights Day. 
When protests materialized within a few days, a 31-year-old monk who tried to parade through the streets with a Tibetan flag was intercepted by the Chinese police, who tried to wrench the flag from his hands before finally firing, killing him.
When students came out on Dec. 
18 to demand greater human rights for Tibetans, the monk said, Chinese officials made a major effort to talk with them about their grievances. 
The officials spent more than six hours with the students, lecturing them on loyalty. 
There were no arrests.
On Feb. 
7, the eve of the Tibetan New Year, posters went up overnight in Lhasa asking every family to send one member to a demonstration the next day at the Jokhang Monastery, the focal point of city life. 
The monk said as many as 10,000 people went to hang khatas, white ceremonial scarves that are a sign of honor, on a Tibetan flag that was unfurled there.
After March 1, the monk said, the protests became increasingly regular, and larger. 
In early March, Tibetans marked the anniversary of the unsuccessful 1959 revolt against the Chinese, after which the Dalai Lama went into exile in India.
Â 
Protesters Throw Stones
On March 5, thousands were in the streets, the monk said, and they threw stones at the police, who fired tear gas and then bullets at the crowd.
Tibetans say 104 bodies were found that day by relatives and friends.
The monk said foreign tourists -''especially backpackers,'' he added through an exile interpreter - taught Tibetans how to dip cloths in water and breathe through them to mitigate the effects of tear gas, an act that infuriated the police.
On March 6 and 7, the monk said, enraged mobs, ''their spirit at its peak,'' began to attack Chinese residents of Lhasa and set fire to their shops and other businesses. 
At 4 P.M. on March 7, announcements were read all over Lhasa ordering people to go home. 
Tibetans say the announcements warned that anyone who tried to assemble again would be shot.
At midnight that night, martial law was officially declared.
Since then, the monk said, Tibetans have been required to buy daily permits to go out, even for shopping. 
People on bicycles passing Chinese policemen or troops have to stop and produce these permits or be pulled off the cycles.

file: To Cantonese, A Little Graft Is Forgivable.txt
text:
ï»¿
Lei Yu charges into the room, his extraordinary energy a fitting reflection of one of China's fastest-changing cities.
Mr. Lei, the Deputy Mayor of this frenetic and prosperous city, is one of a growing number of sharp and shrewd local officials who shun the Communist bureaucrat's life of long lunches and snoozes. 
Some people see him as a local hero who bucks the system; others accuse him of glaringly corrupt practices.
Guangdong province, of which Canton is the capital, is famous both for bucking the system and for its corruption, so it is not surprising that after being removed from a senior post for violating regulations, Mr. Lei has been able to climb his way back into one of the most powerful and busiest jobs in town.
"Compared with us, the life of New York's Mayor is light and easy," said Mr. Lei, 56 years old, who typically leaves home at 7 A.M. and returns about midnight.
Â 
Local Booster
Mr. Lei does not campaign for election, but he lobbies for Canton's needs -- like a new stock market, foreign bank branches, greater efficiency in enterprises, higher exports and more economic restructuring. 
Leaders like him are rare in China, and he seems highly regarded and popular.
"He's very clearly a reformist, full of ideas of what he wants to do," a foreign analyst here said. 
"He's someone who is a real activist for getting things done."
It is a tribute to his ability and political skills that Mr. Lei has been able to return to power after being disgraced and dismissed from his post as administrator of Hainan Island in 1985. 
Mr. Lei and his assistant had taken advantage of the island's special privileges to import foreign cars duty-free and resell them at a high profit on the mainland. 
They ultimately approved the import of nearly 80,000 cars, in what became one of the biggest scandals of China's reform era.
The scheme was widely denounced as an example of corruption at the time, but Mr. Lei apparently did not benefit personally. 
On Hainan Island, which has since split away from the rest of Guangdong and been made a province by itself, Mr. Lei is remembered as a folk hero who took advantage of every loophole to buoy the local economy and paid with his job for his dedication to his constituency.
"All men are fallible," Mr. Lei said, dismissing the incident. 
"I'm not a saint. 
When I make a mistake, I correct it."
Â 
A Pragmatic Decision
But early in 1988, less than three years after the car scandal, the province government decided that Mr. Lei's talent was more important than the tarnish of his recent past. 
Guangdong, which is not necessarily bothered by an official flouting the rules from the capital, welcomed him back to the fold.
"The mountain is high and the emperor is far away" goes a saying that many people say explains why Guangdong province has been able to shape a freewheeling economy -- it is simply too far from Beijing for the national Government to maintain close scrutiny. 
Guangdong is already China's economic showcase with growth of about 10 percent last year, twice the national rate.
But Mr. Lei denies that the province's leaders scurry around the guidelines set down by Beijing.
"It is not that we don't respond to the call of the party Central Committee, but that our cadres should not be the kind who blindly obey," Mr. Lei said. 
"If our cadres are not resourceful and they appear helpless in the face of something, would you call them good cadres?
If they can't do anything, would you like to have them?
I wouldnot."
Guangdong, however, still has a great deal of catching up to do if it wants to move beyond the level of a developing country. 
Although per-capita income in Guangdong was more than 40 percent higher than the national figure last year, it was only $430.
Â 
Progress, Not Perfection
Not everything here moves as fast as Mr. Lei and his colleagues would like, and many economic changes, for example in prices and housing, have been adopted only slowly in Canton.
Moreover, hard-liners say that negative Western influences, like pornography, prostitution and other crimes, are much more evident in Guangdong than elsewhere in China. 
Prostitutes linger at the city's best hotels looking for customers, and taxis now have gratings to protect drivers from robbers.
As problems like these irritate local leaders, Canton continues to compete with nearby cities, such as Huizhou, Shenzhen and Zhuhai, for foreign investments. 
Mr. Lei adds that the entire province is battling with Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines for consumer markets in the United States and other prosperous countries.
"There is a Chinese saying: Sailing against the current, you must forge ahead or be driven back," Mr. Lei said, his eyes dancing about. 
"The present reality is just like this. 
Aside from stopping, if you drop your speed, you will fall behind."

file: To Chinese These Days, _Comrade_ Is Gauche.txt
text:
ï»¿
The decline of ''comrade'' and the return of ''Miss'' is but one of the ways that ordinary Chinese are shedding the revolutionary trappings of the last four decades. 
While the airwaves mount a propaganda blitz for Communist values, people are each day moving more in the other direction: wearing more cosmetics and shorter skirts, studying more English, trying ever more frantically to go to the West -and, perhaps most basic of all, reverting to pre-Communist era ways of speaking and writing the Chinese language.
After the 1949 revolution, the Communists replaced forms of address like Mr., Mrs. and Miss in favor of the egalitarian ''comrade.''
Indeed, in Mao's time, a woman would have been deeply alarmed to be hailed as ''Miss,'' for it implied a sneer and meant that a young woman was putting on airs.
Age Distinctions
''Comrade'' is still used, but much less than before. 
These days, a young woman might be addressed as ''Miss,'' and an older person as ''Old Granny'' or ''Old Granddad,'' but hailing other people is a bit of a problem. 
To fill the gap, Chinese have seized upon the term ''shifu,'' which originally referred to a master worker.
Bit by bit, ''Mr.'' is making inroads. 
And the traditional way of saying wife - ''tai-tai'' - is also occasionally heard in place of ''lover,'' which was the revolutionary way to refer to a spouse.
''The language is always changing,'' a Chinese journalist said, ''but never so much as in the last five years.''
One of the most important reasons for the changes is the stream of visitors from Hong Kong and Taiwan, who use prerevolutionary ways of speaking. 
Mainland Chinese often display an immense fascination with these wealthy tourists and executives and emulate them in speech, clothing, literature and personal habits. 
Many Chinese express a deep yearning to shed backward ways, and to them Taiwan and Hong Kong represent all that is modern, fashionable and desirable.
Television ads sometimes feature sales pitches by people speaking Chinese with a Cantonese accent, suggesting that the speaker is from the prosperous region of southern China that envelops Hong Kong. 
The idea is that if a sophisticated person from the highly developed south admires the product, it must really be good.
The mainland normally uses Chinese characters that have been simplified, to make them easier to learn, but it is increasingly common to see on name cards and shop signs the traditional, complex characters that are still used in Hong Kong and Taiwan.

file: Tokyo Faults U.S. Sanctions For Chinese.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the United States and other Western countries impose sanctions and condemn China for its crackdown on the democracy movement, Japanese officials have begun sounding a note of caution that such steps could backfire and deepen Beijing's ''isolation'' from the rest of the world.
Senior Government officials said today that as a result, a modest difference of perspective had emerged between Washington and Tokyo on how best to respond to recent actions in Beijing, including the arrest and execution of Chinese accused of taking part in protests.
''Sanctions by definition mean punishment,'' a senior Foreign Ministry official said in an interview. 
''But even if you want to punish the Chinese, you don't get the results which you wish. 
We don't think sanctions are an appropriate response for the Western democracies to make.''
The comments of Japanese officials came a day after the Bush Administration announced another round of sanctions in Washington, suspending participation in all high-level contacts with Beijing. 
The United States had earlier suspended military sales and cooperation with China.
Â 
Muted Criticism by Japan
Japanese officials said Foreign Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka would put forward the Japanese concerns about sanctions in talks next week in Washington with Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d.
Since the Chinese crackdown began two weeks ago, Japan has criticized Beijing's actions but in a far more muted tone than other countries. 
In part, that was attributed by officials to Tokyo's concern about reviving anti-Japanese feelings dating from Japan's subjugation of China in the 1930's.
A senior official said today, however, that the motivation was also to avoid reinforcing ''xenophobic'' tendencies of China, causing Beijing to feel surrounded by enemies.
Japan has not withheld criticism of China, and today Prime Minister Sousuke Uno deplored China's execution of three young men who were accused of setting fire to a train during the recent turmoil, declaring the executions to be ''not acceptable.''
Â 
Tokyo's Aid to Beijing
Japan has also suspended new economic assistance to China. 
But Japanese officials appear to be emphasizing that that step was being taken until China ''stabilizes'' its situation, and that aid could be resumed if China's economic liberalization program is restored, even if political freedoms do not return.
Today, for example, Finance Minister Tatsuo Murayama told Parliament that ''we should bear in mind that China is unquestionably an important neighbor'' and that ''both economic and political considerations'' should be weighed as Japan decides whether to resume aid.
Japanese officials acknowledge that Tokyo's position could be criticized by some as insufficiently concerned about human freedoms and too eager to continue lucrative business relations. 
That criticism was heard when Japan maintained business relations with Iran in recent years, citing the need to avoid ''isolating'' Teheran.
Japan is the largest aid donor to China, and its assistance is widely considered crucial to China's hopes for economic growth in the years ahead. 
Japan is now at the end of a $3.3 billion seven-year aid program, and Tokyo announced last year that it would be renewed by a $6 billion program. 
Talks for that renewed program are what were suspended this month.
Â 
'Like a Thief at a Fire'
Japanese officials and businessmen here say that no clear picture has emerged on the future of private-sector cooperation between Japan and China. 
Japan is a major trading partner of China, with total trade at $6.6 billion last year.
By comparison, Japan's private investment in China is considered relatively small, only about $2 billion, or about 1 percent of Japan's overseas investments. 
Business officials say that current investment is likely to remain but that future investment is in doubt.
Some businessmen have begun traveling to China on tourist visas to talk about trade and investment, drawing criticism from the Tokyo Government and abroad.
Foreign Minister Mitsuzuka, noting criticism from abroad, said last week that people are saying that ''Japan is trying to make money like a thief at a fire'' and that businessmen should not be so eager to make deals in China.
But officials said today that those views were being expressed to give Japan ''credibility'' abroad, whereas its basic point of view was that Japan should try to sustain economic relations with China.

file: Tokyo Issue of China Bonds.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Bank of China has issued nearly $145 million in bonds in Tokyo in its first such financing outside China since the 1989 military crackdown on the pro-democracy movement, a Japanese underwriter said Friday.
"All of the funds to be raised by the bond issue will be used for projects in developing China's petrochemical industry," said Shen Yue, an official with the Yamaichi Securities Company, the leading underwriter on the financing.
The bonds, with an issue price of 100.8, will mature in five years and carry a coupon of 7.7 percent, Mr. Shen said, adding that the sale was the seventh such issue by the Bank of China in Japan since 1984, with the last occurring in April 1989.
Japan joined many Western nations in imposing sanctions to protest Beijing's military crackdown in June 1989, which left hundreds of people dead. 
But last year, Japan said the economic assistance would start flowing again as China worked to regain international good will.
Ten Chinese banking institutions have been authorized by the Chinese Government to issue bonds overseas. 
Between 1982 and 1989, they floated $4.25 billion in bonds in Tokyo, Hong Kong, Frankfurt, London and Singapore.
China's Government does not plan to issue bonds itself this year, according to The China Daily newspaper.

file: Tokyo Journal_Akihito_s Travel Plans_ No Kowtowing to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yosuke Kuwabara took a taxi to Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa's house in a residential neighborhood of Tokyo on Tuesday morning, began shouting slogans, and then did what a dedicated rightist is supposed to when he believes the Emperor of Japan is about to be humiliated: He took out a knife and began slitting open his stomach.
Mr. Kuwabara did not get very far with his attempt at ritual suicide. 
The police say the wound was not deep and he will live. 
But his protest was vivid enough to force an embarrassing dispute into the headlines. 
The issue is whether to send Emperor Akihito for a brief visit to China, even if he is obliged to apologize before the cameras for deeds Japan committed, in the name of his father, a half-century ago.
Any time a Japanese emperor visits a neighboring country that was part of the Greater East Asian Co-Prosperity Sphere, this country's politicians and bureaucrats begin months of hand-wringing over the issue of apologies, carefully fine-tuning the wording to fit the political climate of the moment.
But a visit to China is unchartered territory. 
Japanese officials who keep track of such things say there is no evidence that any Japanese emperor visited China back to the first occupant of the job, the possibly mythic Emperor Jimmu, who is said to have acceded to the throne in 660 B.C.
Â 
Deliberations a Sham
Officially, Mr. Miyazawa says he has yet to make up his mind about whether the Government will accept an often-repeated Chinese invitation to send the Emperor to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the beginning of diplomatic relations between Japan and the People's Republic. 
"My basic feeling is that if Our Majesty is to visit China, it should be in an atmosphere where all our people are happy to see him off," he said the other day.
In fact, Mr. Miyazawa has been meeting wth all of the top leaders of the governing Liberal Democratic Party and today they reportedly reached a final agreement to go forward. 
Arrangements are already under way for a trip to Beijing, Xian and Shanghai in October.
But there is a critical if unwritten understanding with Beijing that if the symbol of modern, peaceful Japan is to ride through Tiananmen Square, he will do so with only minimal and vague apologies for Japan's wartime actions.
"It is a very, very delicate issue on both sides," a senior official of the Japanese Foreign Ministry said recently. 
"But I think we are finding a way to go ahead."
An announcement is expected sometime in the next two weeks, after Mr. Miyazawa is finished having polite lunches with everyone who thinks this visit may be a bad idea.
Â 
Some Want Visit Abandoned
For months the prospect of the visit has been the subject of considerable controversy in both Tokyo and Beijing. 
In Japan, influential right-wing politicians within the Liberal Democratic Party have insisted that no visit take place if the Emperor is forced to kowtow to the Chinese in public.
Though none of them seem willing to go to the extremes Mr. Kuwabara did, they say the day should be long past when Japanese officials had to begin toasts at state dinners with references to past aggression. 
They feel that particularly strongly in the case of China, which depends heavily on Japanese aid and investment.
But that day still seems a way off. 
So a group that calls itself the People's Council for the Protection of Japan submitted a petition to Mr. Miyazawa a few weeks ago to abandon the visit altogether.
Many Chinese, who are becoming more vocal in demanding reparations from Japan, are also upset by the trip. 
Beijing has been reluctant to silence those who are making the demands for fear of seeming to be lackeys of Japan, even though officials there seem eager for the issue to go away before it threatens economic ties.
The 1972 accord between Beijing and Tokyo, establishing relations, seemed to rule out compensation, but some Chinese now say that as individuals they can still pursue their claims. 
The movement was begun by a scholar in Beijing last year, without official backing, and it seems to have taken on a life of its own.
Some Chinese now insist that they are entitled to $200 billion or more in compensation for the suffering inflicted by Japan. 
Japan denies that they are entitled to anything at all. 
But if the Japanese Government finds a way to compensate Korean women who were forced to have sex with Japanese soldiers during the war -- which now appears likely -- it may open the way for others who suffered at Japanese hands to submit claims of their own.
Â 
A Welcome and a Warning
The man whose voice is missing from the debate, as always, is Emperor Akihito's. 
He is formally Japan's head of state, but under the postwar Constitution he holds virtually no political power. 
Therefore he has little voice in the question of when he goes to China or what he says there.
Nonetheless, a visit would abound in symbolism. 
Emperor Hirohito died in 1989, and the arrival of his son in China's capital, before he visits Washington, would be regarded as a critical turning point in relations between the two powers.
As word of the agreement with China has spread, even some of Japan's more conservative voices have come to support the trip, though some with all the enthusiasm of going to the dentist. 
The Mainichi Shimbun, one of the nation's largest dailies, said in an editorial the other day that with trade between the two nations exceeding $20 billion, "we cannot afford to offend the Chinese."
But it also issued a warning. 
The visit would be successful, it said, only if Beijing "guarantees that the Emperor will receive a nationwide welcome, without being subjected to problems or embarrassment."
It added, "We can safely assume that the Chinese leadership has extended the invitation in full appreciation of the Emperor's constitutional status and his position in the minds of the Japanese."

file: Tourists Threaten Buddhist Murals in Ancient Chinese Caves.txt
text:
ï»¿
Miles and miles from nowhere, carved into a cliff here in the arid desolation of northwestern China, are 492 caves lined with some of the finest Buddhist art in the world.
For up to 1,600 years, the dry desert air has preserved the vivid painted murals that fill the cave interiors, along with hundreds of painted statues ranging from life-size to 108 feet tall.
These days, however, the caves face a new threat: enthusiastic visitors. 
Some 150,000 people visited the grottoes in 1988 - nearly as many as in the entire four decades since the Communist revolution. 
The overwhelming majority of visitors are from other parts of China, but the number of foreigners is also soaring: from just 462 in 1979, when the Government opened the area to foreigners, to 30,000 in 1988.
''It's a wonderful thing and it's a terrible thing,'' said Duan Wenjie, the 72-year-old director of the Dunhuang Research Institute, who has lived here 44 years. 
''If people come in large numbers, then they risk hurting the treasures they have come to see.''
So Mr. Duan and his colleagues have agreed to a painful solution: they will build eight cave replicas and sharply curtail access to the originals. 
As it is now, only 30 of the caves are open to the public; after the mock-ups are completed by 1993, only a few of the originals will remain open. 
All the others will be padlocked to protect them.
Â 
A Familiar Dilemma
The same dilemma is faced by curators all over the world: how to allow people to enjoy artistic treasures without harming them. 
The compromises vary: putting glass over fine Rembrandts; installing a plexiglass shield in front of Michelangelo's ''Pieta'' and roping off the area in front of outstanding works.
The paleolithic caves at Lascaux, France, were closed after deterioration to the outstanding paintings there. 
And admittance to the paleolithic paintings in the Altamira Caves in Spain is restricted, although a simulation of the caves has been opened to the public in Madrid.
''Our method solves the dilemma of protecting the caves, while still allowing people to appreciate them,'' asserted Fan Jinshi, the deputy director of the Dunhuang institute. 
''The eight copies are representatives of the very best caves. 
You can't say that visitors will see less.''
The Dunhuang caves, also known as the Mogaoku Grottoes, were painstakingly carved into a cliff a mile long. 
The first caves were dug in A.D. 366, and the finest examples probably date from the Tang Dynasty, a golden age in China lasting from 618 to 907. 
In most cases the entire interior is brightly painted: portraits, geometric designs and murals depicting famous Buddhist scenes. 
The murals cover an area equivalent to more than one and a half football fields, and the caves also house some 2,000 painted sculptures.
Â 
'Discovered' in 1900
The artwork was paid for by wealthy Buddhists and by the imperial court, for in those days Dunhuang was a stopping point along the silk route, and a far more important city than it is today. 
But as the silk route faded, so did Dunhuang. 
The last caves here were carved during the Ming Dynasty, which lasted from 1368 to 1644.
Local monks guarded the caves continually, but the treasury was only ''discovered'' by the world in 1900, after a Taoist monk accidentally found a sealed-off cave containing 40,000 to 50,000 documents from eight dynasties. 
Foreigners made their way to the area and carried away not only the priceless manuscripts but also some outstanding examples of sculptures and murals that are now in Britain, France, India and the Soviet Union.
After the Communists took over in 1949, Prime Minister Zhou Enlai became a great patron of Dunhuang. 
He authorized money to buttress the cliff face with cement and install locked doors on all the caves, changing the site's appearance but also protecting it from erosion and earthquakes.
The opening to foreign tourists led to the construction of a small airport nearby and to growing numbers of visitors, both domestic and foreign. 
The overseas tourists, 60 percent of whom are Japanese, are particularly valued because of the money they spend. 
They have been a tremendous boon to the local economy - per capita income is about $100 a year -but unfortunately, the tourists breathe. 
The moist carbon dioxide they exhale is thought to be unsettling to murals that for centuries have been accustomed to desert air.
Â 
Long Trip for the Reward
A crucial question, of course, is whether foreigners will be willing to travel so far - 1,150 miles west of Beijing, approximately as far from the capital as Omaha is from New York - to see mostly reproductions, and a small but so far undetermined number of real caves. 
Local officials, who have relatively little experience with overseas tourists, are optimistic; indeed, they seem surprised even at the question.
They emphasize that conditions in the copied caves will be much better than in the real ones: not only will these be among the best examples of the artistic treasures at Dunhuang, but lighting will be better and there will be special audio-visual presentations to explain the history of the caves. 
The mock-up caves will be in an exhibition hall facing the cliff.
''There won't be much impact on tourism,'' said Ying Guangling, an official of the local tourism bureau in the modern town of Dunhuang, whose 10,000 residents live 25 miles across the desert from the caves. 
''Visitors will still see some of the real caves, so they'll be satisfied.''

file: Trade Gap Grows Slightly As Exports Remain Strong.txt
text:
ï»¿
The nation's trade deficit widened slightly in May for the second straight month, the Government said today. 
But the $4.6 billion imbalance reflected strong exports and was the third-best showing in eight years.
The gap with Japan, long the largest segment of the deficit, narrowed to $2.4 billion for the month. 
The figure was the slimmest difference with Japan since a $1.8 billion gap in February 1984. 
In May, imports of Japanese cars dropped by $302 million from the previous month.
The Commerce Department report showed that the May imbalance was up 1.5 percent from a revised April gap of $4.5 billion. 
The April figure was originally reported at $4.6 million. 
The deficit had fallen to $4.1 billion in March, the lowest since it reached $3.96 billion in June 1983.
Exports in May were off nine-tenths of 1 percent, to $35.3 billion, but still posted their second-best showing on record after April's $35.6 billion pace. 
Imports totaled $39.9 billion, down six-tenths of 1 percent from the previous month and well below the $44.5 billion record set last October.
The Bush Administration and many private analysts look to exports to help pull the economy out of recession. 
Exports account for more than 16 percent of the United States economy and represented about 40 percent of its growth in 1990.
Â 
Strong Trade With Europe
Some fear, however, that a weakening global economy will reduce foreigners' ability to purchase American goods. 
They also fear a stronger dollar, which makes American goods more expensive overseas.
But Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, cited the $1.3 billion surplus with Western Europe in May.
"Exports to Europe continue to lead the charge despite the recession in the United Kingdom and a slowing of European growth," he said.
Michael K. Evans, head of a Washington economic forecasting firm, agreed. 
"It's most impressive," he said. 
"Exports pretty much kept up their pace," despite the dollar and the world economy.
While the global economy may threaten exports, the weak United States economy apparently cut into American purchases of foreign-made goods. 
The sluggish economy "continues to hold imports down," Mr. Jasinowski said.
Â 
Under $100 Million for '91
For the first five months of 1991, the overall deficit has been running at an annual rate of $62.5 billion, better than the $90 billion forecast by the Bush Administration earlier this year.
If the forecast proves true, it would be the first annual deficit under $100 billion since 1983. 
The trade deficit peaked at $152.1 billion in 1987 and totaled $101.7 billion last year.
Contributing to the slip in exports was an $800 million drop in capital goods exports, including $400 million in aircraft. 
Exports of consumer goods also fell. 
Exports of industrial supplies, motor vehicles and grain increased.
America's foreign oil bill rose 15.3 percent in May to $4.6 billion. 
The volume of oil imports was up 13.9 percent, while the price rose 15 cents, to $16.55 a barrel.
Also contributing to the decrease in imports were drops in purchases of capital and consumer goods and of motor vehicles, which fell $280 million over all.
Â 
Deficits With Taiwan, China
In addition to its deficit with Japan, the United States ran an $800 million gap with Taiwan and a $700 million imbalance with China.
Some members of Congress are trying to force President Bush to remove China's most-favored-nation trade status until the country improves its human rights, trade and labor policies. 
Removing most-favored-nation status, would lift the prices of many Chinese goods, reducing United States imports. 
The trade deficit with China totals $3.6 billion so far this year.
In addition to Western Europe, the United States posted surpluses of $200 million with both Mexico and Egypt and $100 million with the Soviet Union.

file: Trial Nears for Ex-China Aide, Held 2 1_2 Years.txt
text:
ï»¿
For more than two and a half years, Bao Tong has sat alone in a cell in Qincheng Prison, his stomach troubles worsening and his white blood cell count dropping, as the nation's leadership struggled to decide what to do with him.
Now the regime is finally preparing to put Mr. Bao on trial, in a case that will be perhaps the most sensitive of any held since the crushing of the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement. 
Mr. Bao is not a student firebrand or worker organizer, but a 59-year-old member of Communist Party Central Committee who until 1989 was the political secretary to the Standing Committee of the Politburo.
A lean, bespectacled man, Mr. Bao is by far the highest official to have been jailed in connection with the 1989 upheavals. 
As the right-hand man of Zhao Ziyang, the former Communist Party leader, Mr. Bao was an ardent proponent of political change, and he had a quiet but crucial effect on the nation's domestic and international policy.
On Jan. 
15, Mr. Bao was told that he was formally arrested, a procedure that usually signifies a trial will begin within a few months. 
That same afternoon his family was also notified of the arrest, according to three Chinese familiar with the case. 
He is accused of leaking state secrets and of spreading counter-revolutionary propaganda.
The formal arrest, after Mr. Bao had been in detention for more than two years and seven months, suggests that the Government has decided how to dispose of the case. 
But while the leadership will almost certainly advise the court what sentence to impose, it is still unclear what the penalty will be.
The complication is that Mr. Bao is not behaving the way Chinese prisoners are supposed to, not even the way Chinese leaders are supposed to. 
Normally, purged leaders -- like Deng Xiaoping in the past -- issue self-criticisms to win clemency, and then try to claw their way back to power. 
But Mr. Bao is refusing to acknowledge any guilt, according to two Chinese with firsthand knowledge of the case.
"I haven't done anything wrong," one of the Chinese quoted Mr. Bao as saying. 
"I haven't violated the law nor breached party discipline. 
So what is there to include in a self-criticism?"
On Jan. 
20, his wife, Jiang Zongcao, along with his son and daughter, issued a bold and critical letter to top party, Government and judicial officials. 
They demanded an explanation for what they described as the unlawful detention of Mr. Bao, and called for an investigation into whether the authorities had abused their power.
"This whole unusual process of first detaining the person and then gathering materials and determining the crime can't help but make one suspect that this is a frame-up," the family's letter said.
Mr. Bao was summoned on May 28, 1989, supposedly to meet with the Standing Committee of the Politburo. 
Instead, on Politburo orders, he was incarcerated in a part of Qincheng Prison that was euphemistically called the "guest house."
He was fed fairly well, allowed family visits once every month or two, and could receive clothing and food. 
Still, his white blood cell count has fallen to about 2,000, well below normal levels of 5,000 to 10,000. 
But the cause of this condition was not immediately clear.
Despite rumors that he had been moved, he was never allowed out of Qincheng Prison, according to the Chinese familiar with the case. 
While in Qincheng, officials from the Organization Department repeatedly interrogated Mr. Bao about Mr. Zhao, apparently in an attempt to get evidence against the former party leader.
The case of Mr. Zhao, who still is mostly confined to his house and has not been allowed to receive guests, has been handled as a party matter rather than as a criminal investigation. 
The results of the investigation have not yet been publicized, but many Chinese believe that it is unlikely Mr. Zhao will be severely punished.
After his formal arrest last month, Mr. Bao was moved from the "guest house" to Qincheng's No. 1 Lockup for prisoners awaiting trial. 
Newly sent clothing was returned to his family, and he was refused permission to see family members during the Chinese New Year holiday a few days ago.

file: Trial Starts for Tiananmen Dissident.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government put a leading democracy advocate on trial today for "conspiracy to overthrow the Government," an offense that can bring the death penalty, and barred his wife from attending the trial.
The defendant, Chen Ziming, a 38-year-old social scientist and newspaper publisher, has reportedly been on a hunger strike, and today he appeared thin and weak, said a Chinese who saw him.
"I am tired," Mr. Chen told the court several times, the witness said.
Foreigners are barred from such "public" trials and this morning were even kept from reading the announcement of the trial on a bulletin board outside the court. 
The witness said the trial was adjourned at the end of the day but is expected to reconvene.
Â 
Praised for 1976 Tiananmen Role
Mr. Chen's mother and sister were allowed to attend the trial, as were a number of court and security officials, but the family members were not allowed to speak to Mr. Chen and will not be allowed to attend the next session when the trial resumes, the witness said.
Mr. Chen has been actively pursuing democracy in China since the 1976 Tiananmen protests against the now-discredited "Gang of Four."
Excoriated at the time on national television for his rousing speech against the Gang of Four, Mr. Chen was later praised by Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, as one of the "heroes of the Tiananmen incident," according to a report last month by Asia Watch, the human rights organization.
In the late 1980's, Mr. Chen pushed vigorously for policies that would promote political and economic liberalization, and his newspaper, Economics Weekly, became a widely read forum for intellectuals yearning for change.
Â 
Charged for Aiding 1989 Uprising
He backed the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement, playing a crucial role in an intellectual support group for the students, but after martial law was imposed, he called on the students to withdraw from Tiananmen Square to avoid bloodshed.
According to the trial notice, which Chinese were allowed to read, Mr. Chen is charged with both "conspiracy to overthrow the Government" and "counterrevolutionary incitement and propaganda."
The first charge is more serious and normally carries a minimum sentence of 10 years, and in severe cases it can bring the death penalty. 
No intellectual is known to have been sentenced to death for involvement in the Tiananmen movement, however, and execution is thought to be unlikely.
Mr. Chen and his wife, Wang Zhihong, fled Beijing after the crackdown but were arrested in southern China in the fall of 1989, along with a large number of Chinese from that area and from Hong Kong who had tried to help them escape. 
Ms. Wang was later released.
In trials so far, the most severe sentence announced was seven years for Ren Wanding, a human rights advocate. 
But not all sentences have been disclosed."

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_ Reporter_s Notebook_Civil Warfare as a Spectator Sport.txt
text:
ï»¿
When the cacophony of submachine-gun fire broke out for a solid five minutes two blocks away from him, the old vendor turned his back, pushed his cart toward a small crowd, and went on selling his wares.
He was not interested in watching anyone be shot, and he had work to do. 
The back of his bicycle wagon was covered with neat piles of broccoli, peppers, zucchini and scallions, and there were three more burlap sacks of green vegetables by his feet.
''My luck has been good so far,'' said the old man, a shiny green pepper in one hand and a wad of cash in the other. 
''As long as I stick to selling vegetables, I won't be bothered.''
A man selling watermelons nearby complained, ''I wish I were selling soy sauce. 
That stuff is really in short supply now.''
Life goes on in Beijing. 
It is a different kind of life than it was a few days ago, before troops entered the center of the capital and massacred hundreds or thousands of demonstrators, but people are finding ways of coping with the city's paralysis.
For those who cannot get to work because there are no buses, they have turned their absence from work into a holiday. 
One couple was playing badminton on the street today, laughing with their children, and another strolled, hand in hand, through the park.
''I walked to the office today, but we had no work to do so I just came back,'' said a short, thin man smoking a cigarette. 
''But life is boring. 
There's nothing but lies on the television these days, and we can't go where we please.''
The young man says that he has not dared to walk two blocks to look at the troops, and that by dusk, he is back at home. 
During the day, he wanders on the streets near his home and talks to his neighbors, or just stands in silence watching the odd car or bicycle go by.
Â 
Essential Services Vanish
The capital is in a state of suspended animation. 
This is a week of Sundays, in which most of the city is closed down. 
The doors have not opened this week at most banks, schools and large stores, and even though the newspapers continue publishing, not many people can read them because they are not being distributed.
Postal service has been disrupted, and there is no public transportation in a city that depends on buses and subways to move people to their work places. 
Fear also keeps people indoors.
''I'm afraid to go out now,'' a middle-age man said. 
''If they tell you to stop and you take a step forward, then they shoot you.''
As for food, people are hoarding all sorts of goods when opportunities arise. 
When a gasoline station opened for a few hours, the line stretched around the corner. 
People not only filled their gas tanks, but also spare gas cans.
Station attendants could not guarantee that they would be open the next day because they feared they would run out of fuel.
Taxis are also scarce so that when someone finds one, he tends to cling to it the whole day. 
A shopper found himself in a dilemma. 
He had found a grocery store that was open, but he was afraid that if he purchased a few bagfuls, he would not find a taxi and would have no way of getting the groceries home. 
He ended up finding a taxi, but not buying the food.
Rail service also appears to have been disrupted, at least for students. 
When two students from an eastern province, Shandong, tried to purchase train tickets to go home, they said they were told that only students with Beijing residence cards were allowed to buy tickets. 
They said they were sure that the reason was that the authorities did not want people to go to other cities and spread word about the killings of students in Beijing.
Another group of non-Beijing students was able to purchase tickets to the provinces. 
But when they showed up at the train station, which has been guarded by troops since last week, they were escorted to freight trains. 
Fearing that they might never emerge from those freight cars, they abandoned the thought of travel and went back to their university friends.
Â 
Rooftop Strategists
A recent pastime in Beijing has been troop-watching: climbing to the rooftops of tall buildings to peer at the soldiers and tanks below. 
At first it appeared to be a relatively safe hobby. 
Diplomats, journalists and even business executives brought their cameras, binoculars and even supplies of beer to the rooftops of the Jianguomenwai diplomatic compound and discussed the puzzling movements of the troops below.
''They must be the 27th Army, you know, the one that did the damage on Tiananmen Square,'' a diplomat said.
''No, I heard they were the 40th Army,'' a journalist replied. 
''That's what everybody down there is saying.''
When gunfire is heard in the distance, the military attaches flick out their walkie-talkies and communicate with their colleagues on rooftops throughout the city, as well as with their embassies.
''Sounds of machine-gun fire due east about three kilometers,'' one man barked into his walkie-talkie.
The experts also exchanged their analysis and intelligence on the troops, for what it was worth.
''There must have been more than 200,000 troops to retake Tiananmen Square from the students,'' an attache said.
Another disagreed. 
''You don't need that many troops to retake Tiananmen Square,'' he said. 
''A few thousand soldiers with submachine guns will get the message across.''
The building maintenance people were furious when they found out that foreigners were peeping from the rooftops. 
They locked the doors to the roofs and pulled away the wooden stepladders. 
But the foreigners kept coming. 
They punched a hole in the door and jumped where the ladder had been taken away.
Then the maintenance authorities put on stronger locks. 
And just to be sure, the doors to the rooftops are now constantly guarded.
Â 
Rumors and Guesswork
Many journalists and diplomats normally resent the armed police who guard the diplomatic compounds and restrict Chinese guests from walking in freely. 
But today, they could hardly have been more relieved when People's Liberation Army soldiers carrying AK-47's closed the gates and sealed the entrances to the compound.
A few hours earlier, troops had fired on two of the diplomatic compounds as they marched down the major thoroughfare just outside the compound. 
As the troops arrived, many residents were asking the question: Should we have evacuated yesterday?
''They're probably going to escort us all to the airport,'' a resident said. 
''Go pack your bags.''
''Fill the bathtubs with water, lest they cut the water supply,'' a journalist suggsted.
''Don't take the elevator. 
The troops may shut off the electricity, and you won't be found there for weeks,'' another said. 
Then the phones started ringing. 
''They are looting Building No. 12,'' a caller from a hotel nearby said. 
''Those troops haven't eaten and they are famished. 
They know foreigners have a lot of good food. 
They're not rational and will shoot. 
Lock your doors and keep quiet.''
In fact, the tale of looting was apparently unfounded. 
The troops maintained that they were looking for a sniper. 
But not many people knew that at the time.
Another caller said: ''Those troops shot at the buildings facing the highway, so don't go poking your head out of the terraces.''
''They also robbed some diplomats at gunpoint along the third ring road,'' she added.
A few brave foreigners marched up to the gate and politely asked why they were being locked in their residences. 
''It's just a temporary measure,'' came the reply.
The phone lines at the embassies were tied up as residents all began at once to dial for help. 
Some of the embassies were mildly reassuring.
''We've sent out a team of negotiators,'' a diplomat said. 
''Everyone should meet in front of Building 6 and try to walk in a group to the embassy. 
We don't know if it will work, but we will try.''
Other embassies were less comforting. 
''We just got word of this and haven't yet decided what action to take,'' a diplomat there said. 
''Call us back soon.''

file: Turmoil in China_2 STUDYING IN U.S. DISAPPEAR IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two Chinese graduate students in the United States, one traveling with her infant son, disappeared this week while visiting China to lend support to pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing.
The husband of one of the missing students said he had learned that his wife and infant son and the second student were arrested by plainclothes police as they were about to leave Beijing International Airport on a return flight to the United States. 
The 1-year-old was born in Chicago and is an American citizen traveling with an American passport.
Word of the incident has spread among Chinese students in the United States and alarmed many who were considering returning to China. 
They expressed fear that they may be subject to retaliation for any activities here sympathetic to the demonstrators. 
There are more than 29,000 Chinese students at American colleges.
The two missing students are Yu Cheng, 30 years old, a doctoral student in education at the University of Chicago, and Tong Boning, a mathematics student at the University of California at Los Angeles. 
Ms. Cheng is 4 months pregnant and was traveling on a Chinese passport with her son, Payton Lee.
Â 
Joined Tiananmen Protests
Li Sanyuan, Ms. Cheng's husband, said in a telephone interview from Chicago that Ms. Cheng left for China on May 19 because she was upset by the imposition of martial law and wanted to show Chinese demonstrators ''our solidarity with them.''
During her two-week visit, she joined protests in Tiananmen Square and passed out funds collected in the United States.
When the military began a crackdown over the weekend, she decided to leave and, on Monday morning, said goodbye to her mother, three sisters and three brothers-in-law at the airport's restricted departure area.
Mr. Li, a 32-year-old political science student who met his wife in Chicago, said his wife was supposed to call him when her C.A.A.C. airplane arrived in San Francisco at 11:40 A.M. Monday. But he received no call. 
''I didn't receive the baby in the United States,'' he said, his voice breaking.
He telephoned C.A.A.C. and was told that his wife and son were not on the passenger list and had never boarded the plane in Beijing. 
An employee at the airline, he said, confided that other passengers on the flight had seen the police arrest a man, a woman and a baby in the boarding area. 
The man, he said, was Mr. Tong, who was acquainted with Ms. Cheng through an informal student network.
Â 
Embassy Is Asked for Help
Friends of Mr. Tong at U.C.L.A. confirmed that he too had not returned to the United States. 
He had been active in drafting pro-democracy appeals to the Chinese Government.
Mr. Li, 32, said the State Department had sent a cablegram to the American Embassy in Beijing asking the embassy to search for his family.
''This is a kidnap of an American citizen by the Chinese Government,'' Mr. Li said. 
''Now the life of my wife and son are in danger. 
If they were in the hands of soldiers who exercised the massacre, than they might already have been killed.''
Ms. Cheng's father, who died 20 years ago, was a Governor of Hunan Province, Mr. Li said.

file: Turmoil in China_2 TV Networks Are Sending Top Anchors to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Top anchors from NBC News and ABC News will report from Beijing next week. 
The move provoked excitement at those networks yesterday and skepticism from their competitors, who questioned the value of sending the anchors at a time when television reports are being increasingly restricted by the Chinese Government.
Tom Brokaw, the anchor of ''The NBC Nightly News,'' flew to China yesterday, said a spokeswoman for NBC News, Peggy Hubble. 
He is to report from Beijing indefinitely.
Ted Koppel, the anchor of the ABC News program ''Nightline,'' is to fly to Beijing this weekend to complete a special report on the continuing events in China. 
In addition, he is expected to file reports for ABC's regular news broadcasts. 
A spokeswoman for ABC News said Mr. Koppel had been preparing a special report on the turmoil in China for several weeks.
Â 
Citizens 'Hesitant to Talk'
While expressing admiration for any attempts to bolster television news coverage, executives at CBS News and Cable News Network yesterday questioned the actions by NBC and ABC. 
In the latest move to restrict coverage, a satellite transmission dish used by CNN in Beijing was unplugged yesterday, ending one of the last live links to the events there.
There have been no transmissions of live video reports from Beijing since May 24. 
The networks have relied mostly on reports by telephone and on videotaped reports shipped out of the country and transmitted from Hong Kong.
''Gradually the vise tightens,'' said Ed Turner, the executive vice president for news gathering at CNN. 
''But we continue to be able to broadcast live over the telephone and it's astonishing they've allowed that to go on,''
Tom Bettag, the executive producer of ''The CBS Evening News,'' said that the restrictions were ''a major inhibiting factor'' in the decision by CBS not to send its anchor, Dan Rather, back to Beijing. 
''You have to pick your time very carefully,'' Mr. Bettag said. 
''The story is changing pretty fast and clearly the Government is exerting great control. 
Citizens are very hesitant to talk with foreign journalists.''
ABC and NBC did not send their evening news anchors to cover the meeting last month between Chinese and Soviet leaders, while CBS and CNN did.
Mr. Brokaw received his visa last month when the Soviet President, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, visited China. 
Mr. Brokaw did not cover that event. 
The visa was good for one entry over a 60-day period and is still good.
Mr. Brokaw will use the NBC crew already in China.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_A Dialogue of Dissidents of 2 Worlds.txt
text:
ï»¿
Their pain and despair obvious, a group of young Chinese studying in the New York area spent yesterday afternoon earnestly questioning three dissidents from Eastern Europe. 
They asked how the dissidents and their colleagues had managed to bring on the erosion of Communist totalitarianism in their countries and to survive deadening terror, the kind that came when troops fired on students in central Beijing.
The East Europeans - a Pole, a Hungarian and a Russian - were brought together with the Chinese students by Helsinki Watch, an international human rights-monitoring organization, at its headquarters at 485 Fifth Avenue, near 42d Street. 
Altogether, about 25 people were present, including journalists, human rights workers and a dozen or so Chinese.
All the East Europeans, who are visiting the United States, emphasized that there were great differences in the struggles for democracy and against Communism in each of their countries, let alone with the recent upheavals in China. 
Yet they said there were some striking similarities.
Â 
Earlier Uses of Force
''What comes most to mind is that the crackdown in Beijing recalled earlier crackdowns by Communists,'' noted Miklos Haraszti, a Hungarian dissident who founded an independent journal, Beszelo. 
''It is like what happened in Budapest in 1956, in Prague in 1968 and in Poland in 1981,'' when the Solidarity free trade union movement was apparently crushed in martial law.
Grzegorz Boguta, a Polish biophysicist, was one of the intellectual supporters of the Solidarity movement who was arrested in December 1981 and detained for months. 
In halting English, he told the Chinese students that as he was put into prison with thousands of others, he despaired. 
''But the Polish people have had a tradition of conspiracy,'' he said, ''and we were able to work to remove the monopoly of information from the full control of the Government.''
Mr. Boguta, a slight 34-year-old, did not go on at length about his own experience, apparently for fear of seeming immodest. 
But in fact, immediately after his release, he played a key role in organizing Nowa, the largest of more than 100 underground publishing houses bringing out the works of prominent writers and creating a network of illicit print shops and clandestine newspapers.
''With newspapers and books we were able to challenge the Government control over information and propaganda,'' said Mr. Boguta, stopping just short of urging Chinese students to do the same. 
The publishing house he founded is now fully accepted, if not legal, and since Solidarity's return to legal status this year, it has helped publish the union's new daily in editions of more than 500,000.
Â 
Not Just a Tactical Matter
Mr. Boguta was prepared to tell how his colleagues had gained the confidence and knowledge under martial law to begin acquiring newsprint and hiding duplicating machines and making contacts with foreign benefactors. 
But his Chinese questioners seemed more concerned with broader issues.
''In China, propaganda is the most important instrument of control,'' said one of the young Chinese, adding that he could not see how the Government's stranglehold on information could be loosened all over the country. 
He noted that in Poland, as he understood it, the Roman Catholic Church had provided sanctuaries for dissidents. 
''I know that when you provide some democracy, the people will want more, and that gives strength,'' he said. 
''But what can you do when there is no democracy at all?''
Another Chinese student emphasized what he thought to be a substantial difference. 
''You know our Communist leaders are different,'' he said. 
In China, it is still the generation of the revolution that is in charge, he said, while in Eastern Europe the Communist parties have passed into the hands of ''technocrats and bureaucrats,'' who were perhaps less ideological and more pragmatic.
Mr. Haraszti, who is returning to Budapest this week to attend the ceremony at which the unmarked grave of Imre Nagy, the Prime Minister executed after the 1956 uprising, will be decorated, said he viewed the events in Beijing as a typical response of Communist leaders who ''think they can reform Comunism but keep a one-party system.''
''That is the first stage,'' he said.
Â 
Views on Coercion
Lev M. Timofeyev, a Soviet dissident who was released from prison after Mikhail S. Gorbachev came to power in 1985, observed that unfortunately the kind of sacrifices that were extracted from the protesting Chinese students in Tiananmen Square was ''a necessary payment of blood for bringing about democracy.''
A major area of concern reflected by the Chinese was how the East Europeans, notably the Solidarity movement in Poland, had forged links between intellectuals and workers. 
''Can you tell us how Soldarity was seen by the common people?'' asked Fu Xinyuan, a chemist doing postdoctoral research at Rockefeller University in New York.
Mr. Haraszti, who is the author of a book called ''Worker in a Workers' State,'' noted that in Hungary, and presumbly in China, the authorities had traditionally sought to exploit differences between workers and students. 
He said he saw similarities between Chinese attempts to blame a few intellectuals for the democracy movement and events in his own country after 1956.
Mr. Boguta noted that in Poland, the links established through Solidarity came after long periods of mistrust. 
He said that during a Polish student rebellion in 1968, workers were sent to beat up students. 
Conversely, in 1970, when workers were killed during a strike at the Gdansk shipyards, students failed to answer their call for help. 
Only in 1976, when groups of intellectuals founded KOR, the Workers Defense Committee, did workers and students begin to talk and listen to each other.
One point made repeatedly was that the first responsibility of students and intellectuals is to testify to killings and terror. 
''If the terror succeeds to keep everybody quiet, then nothing else will make any difference,'' Mr. Haraszti said. 
''This is what intellectuals have to do. 
They have to say what is happening and keep as many people as possible from copping out. 
That is our responsibility.''

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_ARTILLERY FIRING IN SUBURBS ADDS TO TENSIONS IN BEIJING_ MYSTERY ON LEADERS GROWS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Artillery fire reverberated through the capital Tuesday, and there were continued reports of clashes among rival military units.
The security situation seemed to continue to deteriorate, and today there were the first direct moves against foreign residents of the capital. 
Troops fired at the Qijiayuan Diplomatic Compound, where many diplomats and foreign journalists live, witnesses said, but no one was known to be injured.
This afternoon, troops sealed off the nearby Jianguomenwai Diplomatic Compound, which also houses thousands of foreign diplomats and journalists. 
Several soldiers with submachine guns guarded each entrance and refused to allow people to enter or leave.
Embassies of several countries were trying to arrange evacuations of their nationals in the compound, but it was not immediately clear if they would be successful.
Witnesses also said that soldiers had stopped two diplomatic cars on Beijing's third ring road, forced the foreign occupants of the car out at gunpoint and robbed them of all their belongings.
The sounds of artillery fire appeared to be coming from the western outskirts of the city, the general direction of the headquarters of the Beijing military region. 
But it could not be determined if the headquarters was involved in the fighting or who was firing the shells. 
Most diplomats and Chinese said they assumed that the shelling involved competing army units seeking a military solution to China's power struggle.
The evening news program denounced as ''purely rumor'' the reports of fighting between military units near the military airport in southern Beijing. 
It also offered an unusual denial of a report that Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, had died.
Â 
No Explanation on Deng
''That's a sheer fabrication intended to poison people's minds,'' the newscaster said, without shedding any light on Mr. Deng's situation or whereabouts.
Not since the end of the Maoist period more than a dozen years ago has there been such confusion about the situation in the world's most populous nation. 
Today, even the most basic information - such as whether anyone at all is running China, or whether Mr. Deng is alive - is contested. 
None of China's leaders have been seen for 12 days or more, and there have been rumors of coups or assassination attempts against both Mr. Deng and Prime Minister Li Peng.
Late this morning, several thousand soldiers left the Jianguomenwai Bridge, traveling east in trucks and on foot out of the city center. 
They fired continuously into the air for several minutes, sending civilians running for cover and diplomats in their apartments diving for the floor.
It was not clear if the troops, who were singing and seemed in excellent spirits, were withdrawing from the city center. 
Nor was it certain where they were going.
Â 
Cryptic Message
This morning's radio news programs offered a hint that a little-known Politburo member in charge of security matters, Qiao Shi, may emerge to lead the Communist Party. 
The news broadcasts reported matter-of-factly that the Supreme People's Court had sent a message to ''Comrade Qiao Shi and the standing committee of the Politburo to express support for the actions to suppress counterrevolutionary riots.''
By singling out Mr. Qiao as representing the five-member standing committee, the message gave him a special status and could be interpreted as suggesting that he will succeed Zhao Ziyang as Communist Party General Secretary. 
Mr. Zhao is believed to have been stripped of his powers, though not of his post, more than two weeks ago.
The selection of Mr. Qiao, a 65-year-old proponent of strict law and order, would have to be ratified by the party's Central Committee. 
The reference on the broadcast, however, might merely have cited Mr. Qiao because of his special responsibility for security.
Chinese Communist Party officials say that Mr. Qiao has pushed for an end to the current turmoil while also trying to avoid violence as much as possible. 
He ordered the police and soldiers not to use force against a large student demonstration on April 27, and it is not clear what role he has played in the violent suppression of the democracy movement.
Â 
Talk of New Class Struggle
On Tuesday night, in a comment sure to alarm an already jittery population, one of Prime Minister Li's closest aides, Yuan Mu, appeared on television and implied that China should pay more attention to ''class struggle.''
In the Maoist era, a call for class struggle usually heralded large-scale purges in the party and often mass arrests.
The concept of class struggle is now tainted in China because millions of people were either killed or were badly disadvantaged in their careers because they were deemed to be members of a social class that had to be struggled against in the first three decades of Communist rule.
''For a long period of time,'' Mr. Yuan said, ''no one has paid attention to class struggle, or even to political struggle - as if there is no class struggle at all and the world is filled with love. 
But the fact is, there are bad elements.''
Mr. Yuan, whose appearance suggested that Mr. Li is still in power, also estimated today that 300 people had been killed and 6,000 wounded in the military crackdown in the capital. 
Most independent estimates are higher, ranging from several hundred to 1,500 or more, and the accepted wisdom among many Chinese is that tens of thousands of civilians were shot or beaten to death since troops attacked Tiananmen Square, in the heart of Beijing, early Sunday morning.
The official estimates were also regarded as suspect because Mr. Yuan said that most of the injuries were suffered by troops, rather than by the civilians whom the soldiers raked with submachine-gun fire. 
[A White House official said that Government cables from Beijing report the death toll at anywhere from 1,000 to 5,000, and that without knowing a specific figure, the Administration assumes that several thousand were killed.] There was further shooting Tuesday and early today in several parts of the capital, and some casualties were reported, but the numbers of deaths and injuries seemed barely more than a dozen. 
The troops seemed much more intent on defending their hold on the capital from rival units than attacking civilians.
Â 
Tanks in Place
More than 25 tanks continued to hold the bridge. 
A few tanks covered northern and southern approaches, but most faced east. 
They were carefully spaced, one behind the other, as if they intended to use their cannon rather than their machine guns.
Early this morning, five tanks escorted about 70 troop trucks, each carrying 16 to 20 soldiers, east from the bridge along Jianguomenwai Avenue. 
A few gunshots could be heard, but it was not clear who was shooting at whom.
The tanks were apparently used to open path for the trucks through barricades that neighborhood residents had put up on the road, using concrete blocks, trees, burned-out army vehicles and anything else on hand.
The tanks returned after 15 minutes and resumed their positions on the bridge. 
But other army vehicles then scoured the surrounding streets and seized about 25 pedestrians in the area. 
Although there has been no prohibition on walking outside at night, the pedestrians were forced into the center of the road and made to squat with machine guns digging into their backs. 
They were later put into army vehicles and driven away to the north. 
It was not clear what became of them.
The night in Beijing is eerie these days, with a deathly stillness because almost no one ventures out after darkness. 
Gunfire occasionally breaks the quiet, and blazes light the sky where citizens have seized and burned a military vehicle. 
But the strongest sensations are of stillness and tension.
The unrest is spreading to other Chinese cities, although reports are scattered and incomplete.
The northeastern city of Shenyang on Tuesday was the site of a demonstration involving tens of thousands of people - estimates ranged from 30,000 to 100,000. 
It was believed to have been the biggest demonstration in Shenyang, an important industrial city, in more than a decade, and many workers joined in.
Â 
Violence in Chengdu
But the most violent incident occurred in Chengdu, a large city in central China where there were protest demonstrations on Sunday and Monday against the killing of civilians in Beijing. 
Some reports have suggested that 300 people were killed by troops in Chengdu on Monday, but they appear to be exaggerated.
Jan de Wilde, the United States Consul General in Chengdu, estimated that 10 to 20 people may have been killed and several hundred wounded on Sunday and Monday. 
He said that most or all the casualties were from fighting and beatings rather than bullet wounds, and that the turmoil principally involved young hoodlums rather than pro-democracy demonstrators.
The incident included an attack by the hoodlums on the Jinjiang Hotel, which houses the consulate, Mr. de Wilde said, but he added that they were not looking for Americans. 
He said that he was satisfied with the Government's handling of the consulate's security.
A lull in the fighting in the center of Beijing left an atmosphere of nervous expectation. 
''We're in the eye of the storm,'' a Western diplomat said, suggesting that the conflict between the army and the citizens was about to be replaced by a conflict between army units.
The mood in Beijing seemed mixed. 
Some people are convinced that ''people power'' will eventually triumph and the Government will be overthrown. 
But perhaps the majority seem to believe that guns will triumph over ideals, and that the democracy movement is finished.
''We aren't very optimistic,'' a factory worker said as he gathered with his neighbors in northern Beijing to discuss the latest rumors. 
''If the present leadership falls, then maybe we will just get more chaos. 
There would be no leaders at all, and China would have warlords again.''
Â 
Reality Proves Elusive
The air of unreality in the capital has been increased by the mysteries in the press. 
The newspapers have not appeared in several days, and state television has been growing increasingly peculiar. 
Tuesday's evening television news program never showed the faces of the news readers, for example, as if they were embarrassed to be seen. 
The English-language news was cancelled, and all programming ended early.
Nobody interviewed seems to believe the Government propaganda, and it is so discredited that it seems to make most people even angrier than they were.
Mr. Yuan, the Government spokesman, said in his estimate of casualties that more than 5,000 soldiers had been wounded, compared with 2,000 citizens wounded. 
He said that the number of 300 killed included ''troops, thugs and spectators,'' but did not indicate which were most numerous. 
But he said that only 23 students were known to have died.
In the first sign of a hint of contrition from any official, Mr. Yuan said that the Government would assist with funeral arrangements of spectators who had been killed by mistake. 
He also offered the first comment on the international reaction to the bloodshed, saying China could put up with any consequences, like foreign sanctions.
''We are not afraid of this,'' he said. 
''We Chinese people will not allow them to interfere in China's domestic affairs, either by condemnations or by sanctions.''
Â 
LEADERS CANNOT BE FOUND
WASHINGTON, June 6 (Special to The New York Times) - The White House said today that it assumes that Chinese leaders have left Beijing, but does not know where they are.
Marlin Fitzwater, the President's spokesman, told The Associated Press that the United States Embassy in Beijing has had ''no contact with the top-level people, and we've tried.''
He added: ''The assumption has been that the top-level people have moved out to other locations. 
We tend to believe it.''

file: Turmoil in China_Beijing Ousts 2 American Correspondents.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today ordered the expulsion within 72 hours of two Beijing-based American journalists, including one from the Voice of America.
The Government accused the two reporters, Alan W. Pessin of the Voice of America and John E. Pomfret of The Associated Press, of violating martial-law regulations in Beijing.
China also issued its official version of the ''shocking counterrevolutionary rebellion,'' as the democracy movement is now labeled, and announced new arrests throughout the nation of students and workers who had been leaders of the movement.
Â 
In Reaction to U.S. 
Criticism
The expulsion order against the two reporters was widely interpreted as an extension of the Government's campaign of criticism against the United States in the last few days. 
The campaign began after the Bush Administration condemned the violent suppression of the democracy movement and then offered refuge to the dissident Fang Lizhi in the American Embassy in Beijing.
Because the Voice of America is an arm of the United States Government, the expulsion of Mr. Pessin is particularly likely to affect relations between Beijing and Washington.
