text:
ï»¿
As gunfire continues to echo in the capital, thousands of foreigners are preparing to leave and the United States Embassy here is urging all Americans to get out of the country.
Tourists, diplomats and business executives and their families have left their homes and hotels for the eastern part of the city, which is near the airport. 
Throughout the city today and Monday, convoys of embassy cars of many nations could be seen shuttling their citizens around barricades and down deserted streets.
Although the city seems to have quieted down a little since the military crackdown over the weekend, constant shuffles of troops and columns of rumbling tanks suggest that there could be clashes between military units. 
This seemed to be a factor in the decision of several embassies to urge their citizens to leave.
An advisory issued by the United States Embassy this evening said, ''Because of the deteriorating security situation in Beijing, the American Embassy urges American citizens in Beijing to make every effort to depart China at the earliest possible opportunity.''
The State Department earlier had been warning Americans against travel to China.
The embassy said that even with the advisory, its embassy staff will remain in Beijing. 
The British Embassy issued a similar statement.
Â 
Embassies Collecting Students
There are an estimated 1,400 Americans living in Beijing who are not associated with the United States Government and 8,800 in all of China. 
There are also 428 diplomatic personnel and dependents in China, as well as about 4,000 American tourists on normal days.
Several embassies have begun collecting students of their countries from universities here because it was rumored that troops were planning to enter the schools.
Prominently displaying their national flags, convoys of embassy cars from Japan, West Germany, the United States and Australia drove across the city to the university district in the west.
The United Nations has ordered its staff to relocate from diplomatic compounds to a hotel in the eastern part of the city, and to fly to Hong Kong on Thursday.
The Philippine Embassy has ordered an evacuation of its citizens, including some of its embassy staff, and it will charter a plane to fly citizens back to the Philippines.
The Canadian Embassy said that in addition to advising its citizens to leave, a majority of its staff will also depart, leaving a small group of 15 diplomats.
Even without the warnings, many citizens seemed anxious to leave.
Â 
'Like the Twilight Zone'
''It's like the twilight zone here,'' said Michael J. Petron, a 40-year-old New Yorker who has been teaching English in Beijing for the last nine months. 
Eight Chinese students at the school where he teaches have been missing since the weekend, and Monday night, he said, troops shot someone on the streets outside his room just half an hour after he had left the scene.
''At least if people shoot you in the Bronx, you can go out and buy a gun on the street corner and shoot back,'' he said. 
''But you can't do that here.''
Mr. Petron, unlike other Americans who already had plane reservations, was waiting for a Chinese official to return with his ticketing arrangements.
''I'm ready to go to Karachi,'' he said, ''anywhere but Teheran.''
When rumors spread that troops were going to invade the university district, a group of European high school students attending a Chinese school nearby unanimously decided they would evacuate their premises, a diplomat said.
They marched about a mile to one of the most expensive hotels in Beijing, the Shangri-La, and told the hotel that their embassy would pay the bills. 
After settling in, they called their ambassador to come pick them up. 
The embassy sent its cars, paid their bills and put them up at the ambassador's residence.
Foreigners throughout the capital have turned to their embassies for guidance and safe passage out of Beijing.
Â 
Ticket Offices Packed
''We watched as all the other embassies came to pick up their students at the schools,'' said a 21-year-old student from Bangladesh. 
''So we called up our embassy and asked them to take us away.''
Foreigners packed into the airline ticket offices of hotels, and some made their way past the thicket of burned-out cars to the main office of China's airline, near where some of the shooting has taken place. 
But most flights to destinations like Hong Kong and Tokyo are fully booked, so some foreigners are buying plane tickets to any city for which a seat is available.
''I've been waiting here for three hours and I haven't even been able to get into the door,'' said a middle-aged man who was standing outside the ticket office of the Polish airline. 
The office, normally empty, was full and there was a long line outside, as people who could not get tickets to Hong Kong developed an interest in Warsaw.
The lobby of the Lido Hotel this morning was frenzied as people sat with their suitcases around them, waiting almost desperately for their tickets to come through. 
Women clutched their babies, and some weeped as families came to the hotel for refuge.
Down the main road outside the hotel was a unit of troops, their trucks clustered in the field by the roadside and almost camouflaged by the tall grass and trees. 
As most of them rested, chatting with each other, several others remained on guard, their automatic rifles in ready position.
Â 
Buildings Facing Tanks Vacated
As more than 25 tanks pointed their cannons in every direction off a bridge near the Jianguomenwai diplomatic compound, foreigners were making preparations to vacate buildings with windows facing directly toward the troops.
Foreigners so far have not been singled out by the troops or by ordinary Chinese, except when they take pictures. 
At the Beijing Hotel, just east of Tiananmen Square, foreigners have been searched for film, and if any is found it is confiscated. 
One photographer was roughed up when he refused to give up his film.
In the last two days, foreigners have rushed to verandas and the rooftops of the tall buildings in the diplomatic compound to peer at the troops, tanks and armored personnel carriers below.

file: Turmoil in China_Foreigners Tell of Fear And Chaos.txt
text:
ï»¿
Foreigners fleeing Beijing are returning to their homes with terrifying stories of the killings they saw and the chaos they left behind.
They flew to Tokyo, Hong Kong and other cities after several countries ordered their citizens to leave the Chinese capital, where soldiers have killed or wounded thousands of people in crushing a pro-democracy movement.
''I saw a soldier's body, burned, hanging from the bridge,'' an Australian tourist, Jimmie Reid, said in Hong Kong. 
''That made me get the hell out of there.''
He said people told him the soldier had killed children and women.
'Anything That Moved'
Yves Robert, a French tour guide who arrived in Paris with a group of 40 tourists, said: ''We were shot at by the tanks at the Beijing Hotel doorway. 
They were shooting at anything that moved,''
Another foreigner, Ryoichi Kikukawa, a Japanese businessman, said in Tokyo, ''I came out to the veranda of the Minzu Hotel to see what was happening and gunfire from a tank hit the veranda about 20 inches above my head.''
Peter White, an English teacher from Ithaca, N.Y., got up before dawn yesterday to line up for a ticket on the same Japan Airlines flight.
As he was about to enter a taxi in front of his hotel, Mr. White said, he threw himself to the ground because of gunfire from soldiers, which shattered windows on upper floors. 
''I think it was their way of telling us to get back inside,'' he said.
Â 
Some Left Behind
Mr. White expressed concern for 20 American friends, including a pregnant woman, who he believed were still in Beijing.
In Frankfurt, Donald Pierre-Louis said: ''There's chaos, even panic, at the airport. 
Everybody is trying to leave'' Beijing.
Mr. Pierre-Louis, a 34-year-old native of Haiti, arrived with his wife, Danielle, and their two young children. 
He said they kept up with events by watching American cable television at their hotel.
''They cut off our phones for nearly two days but for some reason they left the television on,'' he said. 
''The more we saw the more afraid we got.''
Carol Benedict, a graduate student at Stanford University who was doing research in Beijing, said in Tokyo, ''Gasoline is a problem.''
She said her taxi driver said he had only enough for one more trip ''and all the gasoline stations are closed.''
Â 
Killings in Dormitory
One American woman who arrived in Tokyo yesterday had been in a dormitory where soldiers entered firing guns, killing a number of students, according to her friends. 
She was too upset to talk to a reporter.
''The airline offices were just two blocks from our hotel, but with all the tanks out there and gunfire it was too long a walk to risk,'' Ms. Benedict said.
Ms. Benedict told of a group of seven American students who tried to stick together in their efforts to escape, helped by a Japanese student who found them airline tickets. 
But he could get them only three tickets, and ''we had to leave the other four behind,'' she said.
''The last we knew they were out on Changan Avenue trying to get to the airline offices, but that was where the heaviest fighting was going on,'' she said. 
''I don't know what happened to them.''
Â 
Information Was Scarce
She said the lack of reliable information was the main problem. 
''It was very difficult to get phone calls through,'' said Ms. Benedict, who moved around trying to find a safe spot in Beijing clutching a shortwave radio to get BBC reports on what was happening in various parts of the city. 
''People were getting hysterical.''
''There were hordes of people at the airport,'' she said. 
''It was hot and humid, kids everywhere, people near panic, thinking, 'Today I have to get out at all costs.'
'' She said she had heard loud booms that sounded like artillery fire within range of the airport.
Some embassies, under gunfire, seemed overwhelmed with the task of evacuating their citizens, leaving some feeling stranded.
''The American Embassy made it very clear that transportation arrangements were up to us,'' said Mr. White, who said he was worried as other embassies pulled out their students, leaving him at his university as the last foreigner, with no clear directions from the embassy whether to stay or leave.
The embassy sent a convoy to bring American students to safety Monday, but some students, unsure whether they were safer on campuses, where army units were rumored to be preparing to attack, or downtown where gunfire was already erupting, stayed behind.
Chinese cheered the American convoy of a half-dozen vehicles led by a limousine flying an American flag, and flashed victory signs as it wound through the city trying to find a safe route, Ms. Benedict said.
''Chinese people are clearly looking to the American Government and the American people for support, and that seems to put American citizens at risk,'' she said, because the Chinese Government ''will try to suppress that kind of thinking.''

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_From the Security Apparatus, An Obscure Leader Emerges.txt
text:
ï»¿
Qiao Shi, the Communist Party leader whose major role was reaffirmed by the Beijing radio early today, has had a long career in the shadowy Chinese security apparatus and is believed to be close to old-guard conservatives.
Before the crisis in Beijing, Mr. Qiao was officially listed as the third-ranking member of the standing committee of the party Politburo, following only Zhao Ziyang, the General Secretary, and Li Peng, the more orthodox Prime Minister. 
With Mr. Zhao reported to have been stripped of his post for taking too conciliatory a line toward student demonstrators and Mr. Li widely despised, Mr. Qiao could be in line for the top party or Government jobs.
Some analysts say that may have been what elderly party hard-liners had long planned as they maneuvered over the last few years to place the 65-year-old Mr. Qiao in a highly unusual combination of powerful positions.
While Mr. Qiao is little known to foreigners and had an obscure early career, his current roster of titles suggests he may have been groomed for power.
Â 
Top Internal Security Officer
Qiao Shi (the name is pronounced chow shur) is the Communist Party's top internal security officer, as head of what is known as the Leading Group for Political and Legal Affairs under the Central Committee. 
This agency oversees the work of the Ministry of Public Security and all the police and courts in China.
It was apparently because of this job that the Supreme People's Court sent him the message broadcast by Radio Beijing. 
This post was formerly held by Peng Zhen, one of the leading conservatives.
To some analysts, the message to Mr. Qiao also suggested the possibility that China's current leaders may be moving toward a new stage of the crackdown involving trials of some of the student demonstrators or even party leaders accused of joining with them.
Mr. Qiao, a native of Zhejiang Province near Shanghai, is also head of the Personnel Leading Group of the Central Committee, which oversees the party organization department and is responsible for making all promotions and demotions in the party.
Moreover, Mr. Qiao is secretary of the Central Discipline Inspection Commission, which investigates corruption within the party and any violations of party rules. 
He succeeded Chen Yun, another elderly conservative, in this post and may have been placed there by Mr. Chen, analysts think.
Â 
Underground Agent in the '40's
In addition, Mr. Qiao is president of the Central Party School, where he oversees the party's theoretical journal, Seeking Truth.
Chinese familiar with Mr. Qiao's early life say he was an intelligence agent in the Communist underground in Shanghai during the civil war against the Nationalists in the 1940's. 
His official biography says he attended college in Shanghai. 
Few senior Chinese officials have college or even high-school degrees.
In the 1960's Mr. Qiao worked in the International Liaison Department of the Central Committee, which has responsibilty among other things for foreign intelligence and subversion. 
He disappeared in the Cultural Revolution, but later was promoted to deputy director and then director of the International Liaison Department.
Little is known about Mr. Qiao's family or personal life.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Gorbachev Expresses Regret on China Strife.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Mikhail S. Gorbachev expressed regret today over the violent culmination of the mass student protests in China. 
But he also defended Moscow's ''balanced'' response, asserting that the information was still vague and that the priority was to safeguard the fledgling Chinese program of change.
Mr. Gorbachev's comment at a news conference at the end of his visit to West Germany was his first extensive statement on China, to which he made a milestone visit last month when the protests were already under way.
After the crackdown in early June, the Soviet Congress of People's Deputies condemned outside attempts to put pressure on Beijing and termed the army's violent crushing of the demonstrations an internal affair.
''We don't know everything yet, neither we nor the West German Government have full information, so I believe that for now we must display great responsibility and balance in our assessment,'' Mr. Gorbachev said.
''I believe we are all worried, we are all concerned not to break the process of reforms in this enormous state. 
I think we all understand that this would cause major damage to the whole process of recovery in the world.
''So however we view this, we want the Chinese people and Government to find a solution that would answer the expectations of China and of us.''
Mr. Gorbachev said that these consideratons, ''and no others,'' determined Moscow's ''balanced, responsible and serious position.''

file: Turmoil in China_Gorbachev Mutes His Voice in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
With the tumult in China continuing, the separate theaters of the new Soviet candor - adventurous at home, strategically crimped abroad - have never been clearer.
As President Mikhail S. Gorbachev returned today to the international stage, arriving for a summit meeting in Bonn, he left behind the jarring, exhilarating novelty of domestic outspokenness in the name of democracy in the new national congress. 
But this only underscored his own painstakingly uncritical view of China's violent repression of its pro-democracy demonstrators.
President Gorbachev was the most talkative man on the Soviet television, day in and day out, no topics barred, for two weeks of give and take on domestic issues. 
But he shunned the same garrulousness over China, as if glasnost were not for export.
Won't Risk New Opening
''He will stick to this policy, without a doubt,'' said an experienced Asian ambassador here.
''He's worked too long and too hard to rebuild the China tie to risk it now with a critical remark,'' said the diplomat, who estimated that Mr. Gorbachev personally weighed each word in the resolution adopted last week by the Soviet congress that defended China and condemned outside critics for stirring ''passions'' over Beijing's internal affairs.
In private, some Foreign Ministry officials concede their discomfort about the repression in China, but mainly in ways as pragmatic as Mr. Gorbachev's policy. 
One ranking official said that by attracting the world's news organizations to Beijing for his mid-May summit meeting there, Mr. Gorbachev may have unintentionally increased the stakes of civil demonstration and made the problem more difficult for the Beijing regime in the early stages.
Â 
Cautious and Terse
Unlike some Western leaders who condemned the violence, Mr. Gorbachev has been cautious and terse, declining even to match the restrained criticism of President Bush, which was accompanied by American military sanctions.
''Let Bush speak for himself,'' Mr. Gorbachev declared. 
He has remained resolute in his policy of noninterference, whatever the outrage of other nations, as he works toward links with China that could help to resuscitate the despairing Soviet economy.
In the view of a Western expert on Chinese-Soviet relations, Gorbachev's approach seems like basic, time-tested Machiavelli. 
But it is uncharacteristic Gorbachev after all the plain-spoken and world-stunning initiatives he has made in the name of disarmament and democracy.
''He's got to know he copped out on Beijing after all his months of talking about progress on human rights,'' the expert said. 
''And it's shameful, even if his reasons can be seen.''
Â 
A Call for 'Dialogue'
The most Mr. Gorbachev has allowed was a mention of concern about the violence and a hope that ''dialogue'' would settle it. 
But he never acknowledged the bloodshed inflicted on civil demonstrators by Chinese troops, and neither have Government-controlled news organizations here.
Instead, Soviet newspapers and television have presented what seems, in these giddily forthright days, like an exercise in the nostalgia of Communist censorship: a 1950's-steeped sympathetic parroting of official Chinese press reports about a responsible government dealing properly with ''reactionary forces'' who were supported by the ''incitement to hatred'' of foreign voices.
Lacking the shocking television coverage of the Beijing bloodshed, the Soviet public has spared Mr. Gorbachev moral pressure at home, making it far easier for him to stand strictly by the noninterference policy that has been one of the tenets of his laborious rapprochement with the Chinese after 20 years of bad relations.
Â 
Sakharov Plea Ignored
He stood fast particularly in the face of withering complaint in the final moments of the new congress's inaugural session from Andrei D. Sakharov, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate, who refused to be silenced and demanded in the name of humanity that the congress denounce the killings by the Beijing regime. 
''Enough, enough,'' Mr. Gorbachev said firmly, preferring the congress's resolution of support for Beijing.
''Remember that the Soviets did the most of the work to get back into China, and it was hard work,'' a Western diplomat said, speculating on Mr. Gorbachev's intensity in not seeing the new ties broken by one violent episode. 
''Still, you can question his strategy in the long run if moderates finally do gain control in China.''
Another diplomat stressed ''the glass house'' caution of Mr. Gorbachev. His full domestic realm, whatever the excitement over free-wheeling declarations in the congress, includes persistent, explosive mixes of civil demonstrations, grass-roots violence and martial-law standoffs in outlying republics and among ethnic groups.
Â 
Bush 'No Less Strategic'
''President Bush has been no less strategic in his approach,'' a pro-Gorbachev diplomat commented, saying that the White House criticism could have been more sweeping, considering public outrage in the United States, and that the White House also stopped short of altering commercial and ambassadorial ties to China.
''No doubt the violence took Gorbachev by surprise when he came back from Beijing,'' the diplomat said. 
''But he has to stick with his policy. 
He wants relations with China to be his model of normalization, of noninterference with other nations.''
The diplomat said the defensible denominator in both glasnost and Soviet policy in China was Mr. Gorbachev's overriding need to do anything it takes to rouse the Soviet economy.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Hard-liners Seem to Control Politics, But the Economy Is Another Matter.txt
text:
ï»¿
While China's leaders tighten their grip over the political situation, they now face the even more complicated task of controlling the economy after their military crackdown shook the confidence of Chinese and foreigners alike.
For the Government to consolidate its control and win popular support, it needs to demonstrate that the economy is stable and that everyone will enjoy economic gains. 
But diplomats and others say the crackdown has already eroded confidence that had been carefully nurtured over a decade, and it will be an immensely difficult challenge to restore this confidence and achieve broad economic satisfaction.
Even before the pro-democracy demonstrations began two months ago, there were signs that the country's economy was facing difficulties, and some say that these contributed to the public dissatisfaction with the leadership.
''The economy is in very serious trouble, which is partly why people took to the streets to begin with,'' said Christine Wong, a specialist in the Chinese economy at the University of California at Santa Cruz. 
''There are many structural problems.''
#3 Areas of Difficulty Diplomats and economists suggest at least three areas in which the economy faces severe new difficulties as a result of the crackdown:
* Foreign investors and lenders will be wary of providing the capital and expertise for China to sustain its export-oriented development strategy in coastal areas.
* Tourists, who have been a growing source of hard currency, will be frightened away for some time, and in the meantime the many tourist hotels around the nation are likely to lose money. 
This may also shake the confidence of investors.
* The Government will be tempted to buy support from workers by increasing wages and bonuses, making it tougher to enforce the austerity plan to which it is committed. 
Without austerity, inflation is likely to rise and create new political problems.
These challenges could create major political difficulties for the leadership, which some diplomats say could prevent Prime Minister Li Peng and others in power from holding on to their positions for very long.
The June 4 crackdown, in which the army opened fire on civilians, led almost all foreign business executives to leave the country. 
Many of the executives have no specific date for their return, and many tour agencies have canceled trips to China until mid-summer.
International organizations like the World Bank, as well as foreign governments and private lenders, have postponed approvals for loans and are reviewing their credit assessments of China in light of what has happened. 
Eroding Confidence In Chinese Intentions Growing tensions with the United States will also make American companies think twice about how the business climate will be affected, especially if the tensions lead to anti-American sentiment in China.
Most fundamentally, the confidence around the world that China was really entirely committed to economic restructuring has been eroded. 
Some of the elderly leaders who seem to have reasserted control during the crackdown may be less enthusiastic about change than those who had been in power, and this could significantly reshape the landscape for foreign businesses.
''People had convinced themselves that China was heading for capitalism,'' said William H. Overholdt, director of research at the brokerage arm of Bankers Trust Company in Hong Kong.
''There's been a great disillusionment. 
If they had listened to what the leaders were saying, they would have understood that there was a very important market-oriented reform, but a very limited one and democracy is not what they had in mind.''
In a sign of concern at the economic consequences of the crackdown, senior officials have begun to reaffirm the open-door policy and stress that they will protect foreign investments. 
For example, Mayor Li Ruihuan of Tianjin said today that China would not only maintain its reform and open-door policies, but even carry them further.
Â 
'Could Mislead Investors'
Localities have also announced that their policies toward foreign investment will be unchanged and that their regions are safe for foreign tourists.
For businesses that already have operations in China, there is little talk of leaving, especially if they have been profitable up until now. 
The problem the Chinese will have to grapple with is persuading companies to make new investments in China.
''Some foreign businesses are likely to come to the conclusion that a Government that tells its people and the world that there were no students fired on in the square could also mislead potential foreign investors,'' said Stanley B. Lubman, a lawyer who specializes in China at Thelen, Marrin, Johnson & Bridges in San Francisco.
It is not clear exactly what it will take to reassure investors. 
Some say it will take a clear indication that the policies of liberalization, like enterprise restructuring, experiments with joint-stock companies and price liberalization, will continue. 
Some say it will take a long period of calm to reassure investors.
China's Business Begins to Suffer ''There will be some risk-takers,'' an investment analyst in New York said. 
''But for now, 90 percent of them will be scared away.''
Others are more optimistic, and they have begun to compare the crackdown in Beijing with incidents like the suppression of a rebellion in the South Korean city of Kwangju in 1980. 
At least 191 people died then, but business bounced back and is now stronger than ever.
Business in China, however, was beginning to suffer even before the pro-democracy demonstrations began. 
Foreign businesses were feeling the pinch from China's retrenchment policies that began last fall, and Prime Minister Li has said the next few years are to be those of austerity. 
The tightening of credit had local companies short of liquidity, and this had affected some joint ventures whose payments were delayed.
Â 
Regional Variations
But a great deal also depends on where the investment is. 
Guangdong and the coastal areas, for instance, seem to be affected less by the demonstrations, although there were some in major cities. 
As long as those areas are allowed to exercise the economic freedoms they have been given, then investors will probably continue to move in, diplomats and economists say.
''Western companies are faced with a moral dilemma,'' a Western resident in Guangdong said. 
''Headquarters may have instructed them not to continue with talks and ordered them to leave because they felt it was not appropriate to be in China when the Government massacres its people.''
''But like the Cantonese themselves, the joint ventures have a real stake in the economy,'' he added. 
''They are here to make money and to expand their share. 
It is hard for them to walk away.''
11,535 Tourists Who Won't Show Up So far, China's travel industry has been hit the hardest. 
Pacific Delight Tours Inc., based in New York, says it canceled tours through mid-July, a move that affected ''several hundred'' travelers.
The authorities here reported that 11,535 potential tourists had their trips to the capital canceled, and that for the month of May, the tourism bureau lost about $4 million, or 10 percent of its annual projected earnings, the English-language China Daily said today.
China's economic landscape is complicated by the task of restructuring the national economy and shedding rigidities and inefficient institutions. 
Many economists say China needs to focus on building institutions - like its banking system, tax system, legal system and physical infrastructure - but there are doubts about whether the leadership can concentrate on these tasks when it is preoccupied by political turmoil. 
10% Growth a Year in Economy ''This is a very complicated process that they were right in the middle of,'' said Albert Keidel, who runs Rock Creek Research, Inc., an economic consulting firm in Washington, D.C. 
''It involves some masterful combinations.''
There is no question that China's economy has been growing at a remarkable pace - about 10 percent per year over the last decade - so that even if it suddenly were cut in half, the economy's growth still would be respectable. 
Indeed, China's difficulties arise from growth that is too fast, rather than too slow.
But some of the measures for controlling an overheated economy -tightening credit and investment spending, holding down wages, at the same time finding new sources of raw materials and energy - are unpopular, and this can be politically risky when people have already demonstrated discontent with the Government. 
Trying to Beat Galloping Inflation Already the rate of inflation in the first quarter of this year reached 27.5 percent on an annual basis, among the highest rates the country has seen since 1949, and some unofficial estimates put the number much higher. 
While this number is small compared with some other developing countries, the Chinese are sensitive to inflation not only because they have never experienced such high inflation in the recent past, but also because one of the platforms of the Communist Party is stable prices.
In many ways, inflation is a necessary product of economic restructuring, especially price liberalization, so that the problem facing the leadership is largely one of managing the perception of inflation.
One ineffective but tempting way to manage this perception is to ''buy off'' workers by giving them higher wages and bonuses, Western economists say. 
Even before the crackdown, factories were paying their workers to keep them indoors and off the streets when pro-democracy demonstrations were taking place. 
And the television news this week has shown scenes of soldiers distributing grain to citizens when there were shortages last week.
Â 
'More of a Squeeze Later'
The intention has apparently been to appease workers by giving them material benefits. 
But paying more money to workers means expanding the state budget, and this could lead to new inflationary pressures if the Government needs to borrow or print more money.
''Anytime you get political turmoil, you get a kick to inflation,'' said Mr. Overholdt of Bankers Trust. 
''And obviously it is a kick to inflation that was already very bad, and that means more of a squeeze later. 
The question is whether it is an ongoing process or a one-time kick.''
Buying people's loyalty is a major challenge for another reason: the central Government is desperately short of cash, and this could lead to unrest in both rural and urban areas. 
Some one-third of state enterprises are in financial difficulties, according to official estimates, and the lack of funds has also begun to affect the peasants who make up about two-thirds of China's population. 
A Harvest at Hand, But So Little Cash The shortage of cash is an urgent problem because the harvest season is near. 
The Government already says it lacks nearly $3 billion needed to pay for about half of the grain, oil, tea and raw silk that will be harvested this summer.
Moreover, the price at which the farmers are forced to sell their grain to the state is about one-third the market price, so that farmers are reluctant to turn over a portion of their grain to the state, when they can fetch much higher prices on the market.
Local governments in many parts of the nation have been forced this year to give ''white slips,'' or I.O.U.'s, to farmers instead of cash to pay for pigs and tea and other commodities sold to the Government. 
These slips of paper are likely to be prevalent this year, official press articles have said.
A recent article in Peasant's Daily described how much the farmers dreaded the visits by local government officials who came to collect the grain. 
In some villages last year, the article said, children were given large bells and told to hide in tree tops, and when they saw the grain officials approaching, they would ring the bells as a signal for the farmers to run home and lock their doors. 
What of Rural Areas?
Thus, for the Government, paying low prices and then not giving farmers cash for their crops will create greater political risks at a time when urban populations have already shown their dissatisfaction, diplomats say.
The recent political turmoil, which occurred mainly in the cities, will probably not have a direct effect on peasants, who tend to be scattered across a vast amount of land, specialists say. 
But unless the Government cashes in the ''white slips,'' the farmers are unlikely to show much enthusiasm for the Government.
''The peasant dissatisfaction is certainly real,'' a Western diplomat in Beijing said. 
''But it is unlikely that peasant discontent could turn into resistance. 
They are spread out, so it is hard to organize resistance.''

file: Turmoil in China_Hong Kong Cancels Mourning Rallies.txt
text:
ï»¿
Plans for a series of rallies to mourn the victims of the Chinese crackdown were canceled here today after a violent confrontation between the police and a group described as provocateurs from the mainland.
But pro-democracy organizers, who canceled the rallies, continued their call for a token strike today, and many Hong Kong people shut their offices and shops or halted work to observe a moment of silence for the slain Beijing protesters. 
Schools were closed and many factories were idle.
Throughout the colony, people marked the deaths in Beijing with small personal tributes: flowers placed on Hong Kong's stone war memorial, a bit of black cloth draped along a window or tied to a car.
Violence Before Dawn
In its account of a predawn riot in the Chinese neighborhood of Mongkok, one of the most densely populated areas in the world, the Hong Kong Government said it was inspired by provocateurs from the mainland, assuring residents they were on the alert.
Several hundred police officers were called to Mongkok at 1:30 A.M. after a peaceful demonstration degenerated into a riot, with ''unruly hooligans'' hurling bottles and cans and battering storefronts with bamboo poles, the authorities said.
It was the first crowd violence since rallies and marches in support of China's pro-democracy movement began in Hong Kong several weeks ago. 
'These culprits were not those demonstrating in support of the Beijing students,'' a police official said. 
''They were criminal and nnruly elements who tried to exploit the situation.'
He added he had ''no information regarding their political motives, but I can't rule out any possibility.''
Â 
Organization of Crowd
Martin Lee, a legislator and a leader of the pro-democracy movement, said he believed the disruptive crowd ''was definitely organized,'' adding, ''In the beginning there may have been people having some fun, but toward the end we have witnesses who said they saw people brought in, carloads of people.'
He said there was a ''distinct possibility'' that the trouble was provoked by those wishing to discredit the demonstrations.
But the Secretary for Security, Jeffrey Barnes, said rumors that mainland agents had infiltrated the movement here, as they did in the 1960's in the Cultural Revolution, were unfounded. 
He said the Hong Kong Government was monitoring the situation closely. 
Another security official later said the riot was ''in no way political.''
A police spokesman said 'unruly hooligans in the crowd first tried to smash their way into a bank owned by China, and then turned to other shops and buildings on Nathan Road, later setting fire to a van. 
The police, wielding nightsticks, charged into the crowd, then set off tear gas to disperse the mob. 
Officials said the size of the crowd grew from 500 to about 7,000. 
The police said 15 people were arrested and 5 police officers were wounded.
Â 
Carnations for the Dead
Regina Lau, who was on strike from her job in a small trading company, said she was disappointed and very bitter that some people were not responsible and disrupted the demonstrations.
She had a small bunch of white carnations as a makeshift memorial for the students and citizens who died in the violence in Beijing. 
On the paper around the flowers she had written, ''We will miss you forever.''
The British colony, 98 percent ethnic Chinese, will revert to China in 1997, and the people here have been obsessed with the democratic movement in China, holding vigils, marches and demonstrations at first to express their hope and support for the cause and now, to show their anger and sorrow.
Despite the wilting heat, thousands of people stood in a line that stretched for more than a mile, waiting to sign the condolence book for China's dead that demonstrators have placed near the New China News Agency, the mainland's unofficial consulate here and the focus of many protests. 
Like Miss Lau, many brought flowers, and most wore black arm bands or head bands.
Â 
Many Shops Are Closed
In the business district, banks and the stock exchange remained opened but most of the fashionable boutiques like Gucci, Christian Dior and Baccarat were closed, as were beauty shops, computer and camera stores, tailor shops and dry cleaners.
Organizers had stressed that they did not want to disrupt commerce in the colony, but were simply calling for workday gestures to honor the dead.
Taxis, minibuses and limousines bore bits of black mourning cloth on their aerials, and many cars and trucks carried hand-lettered signs supporting the democratic cause in China and deploring the violence used to suppress it. 
Several thousand trucks and cars formed a caravan and paraded pass the New China News Agency.
The sleek new Bank of China tower, the tallest building in Asia and the pride of official Beijing, had two long slender black banners draped from its mirrored windows. 
The banners read: ''We are saddened for the thousands who were killed fighting for democracy,'' and ''We hate the wolves who betrayed the people.'

file: Turmoil in China_Shanghai Issues an Appeal for Calm, and a Warning to Go With It.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Mayor of this city appealed in a televised address for an end to the ''chaos'' that he said has prevailed here for several days, warning that anyone causing disturbances or interfering with efforts to restore Shanghai's transportation system would be ''dealt with by the police in accordance with law.''
Mayor Zhu Rongji's speech on late-night television was one of several indications today that the authorities here are preparing to toughen their response to a student-led protest movement in Shanghai.
Earlier today, local newspapers carried an editorial warning that those causing disturbances would be severely punished. 
Nonetheless, in several small rallies and marches around the city, students called today for a mass demonstration Friday to protest the bloody repression of the democracy movement that took place in Beijing last weekend.
The warnings and the continuing efforts of an apparently dwindling number of students to maintain the protest were the latest development in a war of nerves between the Government and protesters that has been constant and intense in China's largest city since the crackdown in Beijing on Saturday and Sunday.
Since then, students and their supporters have succeeded in virtually blocking public transportation by commandeering buses and using them to barricade streets. 
Absenteeism at factories has been high and there has been a mood of near insurrection among many here outraged by the central Government's handling of protests in Beijing.
With foreign companies and some consulates evacuating their personnel, flights out of Shanghai have all been full. 
Foreign students at the universities, fearing violence there, have been leaving their dormitories and living in hotels in the city while they make their plans to leave. 
An emergency charter flight organized by the Australian Consulate took 400 people to Hong Kong this afternoon.
Â 
A Partial Return to Normalcy
Still, while anti-Government feelings clearly run high among local people, there have been many signs that, even without tough government measures, many elements of life in Shanghai began returning to normal today.
For the first time in almost a week, bus service on several main streets was restored. 
Visits to factories indicated that absenteeism, estimated at times to be as much as 50 percent of the work force, has diminished. 
There were indications that rail service, all but completely disrupted for two days, would resume soon.
All along, commercial life has been little affected by the protest movement. 
Stores have remained open; the shopping streets have continued to be crowded; students have allowed food to pass through barricades and there have been no reported shortages.
There were reports that many students, including many of the most politically active, have left their campuses in recent days and returned home, apparently in the belief that they have lost the struggle for now and would do better to work behind the scenes for a renewed pro-democracy movement in the future.
The Government's strategy seems to have been to avoid direct confrontations with local protesters, a policy that, by removing the police from the streets, often gave the impression in the last few days that large parts of Shanghai were entirely in the hands of the students and their supporters.
Â 
Rally at Party Headquarters
Even today, for example, students held a rally in front of Communist Party headquarters here during which they read a statement demanding that the United Nations expel China because of what they called its human rights abuses. 
There were about a dozen unarmed soldiers guarding the entrance to the building, but, even though the demonstration filled up the broad avenue that runs along the harbor here, there was no effort to stop it.
Similarly, students have circulated freely around the city, giving speeches, putting up posters, marching down city streets and commandeering buses. 
The police have made virtually no effort to interfere with them.
But the government has, particularly in the last couple of days, used that absolute control of the news media to mount a propaganda campaign, both in the newspapers and on television, appealing to the desire for order and accusing a ''very small number'' of people of trying to foment disorder.
Television stations, for example, have repeatedly shown footage of a train set afire two nights ago by Shanghai residents. 
Students and many others say the train driver, ordered by the police here to ignore a human blockade, plowed into a group of people, killing six of them. 
The television news has portrayed the train burning as an act of sabotage by ''bad elements,'' and its repeated reference to the incident seems aimed at persuading people of the costs of continued protests.
Â 
'Do You Want Chaos?'
Mr. Zhu's unscheduled appearance on television at about 11 P.M. tonight seemed aimed at encouraging the move toward the restoration of normal life here by combining warnings against the students with an appeal to trust the local government and the Communist Party to solve Shanghai's problems.
''Do you want chaos in Shanghai?''
Mr. Zhu, wearing a Western-style jacket and tie, said. 
Then, addressing what he called ''a very small number'' of ''unlawful elements,'' he said, ''the broad masses of Shanghai citizens can no longer tolerate your illegal activities.''
He said the city had organized major efforts to clear blockades across streets and to resume normal transportation. 
He said any efforts to interfere with the restoration of normal service would be ''punished by law.''
He blamed the disorder on unspecified ''foreign rumors,'' by which he presumably meant reports by foreign news organizations, particularly the Voice of America and the BBC, both of which are widely listened to in China, on the crackdown in Beijing.
While the foreign news reports have generally put the numbers of dead in the Beijing crackdown in the thousands, the Chinese news media have lately been reiterating a statement by Yuan Mu, the spokesman for the State Council, that about 300 people died in the army's action, most of them soldiers.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Shanghai Reports Dissidents_ Arrest.txt
text:
ï»¿
The state-controlled local radio and television stations reported today that nine labor dissidents and an undisclosed number of other people had been arrested for their roles in the protests that have swept this city in recent weeks.
The arrests, which followed official warnings two days ago that ''bad elements'' would be ''punished in accordance with the law,'' indicated that the roundup of protesters under way in Beijing was spreading to other cities.
Shanghai, China's most populous city and most important economic center, has been the scene of an active student-led protest movement since the army's savage crackdown in Beijing nearly a week ago. 
Earlier this week, it brought the public transportation system to a halt, and on Friday it brought tens of thousands of anti-Government demonstrators into the streets.
But today, in a move that seemed to signal at least a temporary move away from open protests, students from at least one university, the East China Teachers College, were reported to have voted to disband the autonomous student union formed early in the pro-democracy movement to coordinate student activities. 
Students elsewhere said they expected the unions at other universities to follow the East China Teachers College example.
Â 
'Don't Have the Strength'
''We simply don't have the strength to do more now,'' said a student union member from Fudan University, adding that many students ''feel that further activism now would get us nowhere. 
They think it would be better to reflect on our experience and to renew the movement sometime in the future.''
Still, several dozen students from Fudan University staged a sit-in today in front of the Shanghai police headquarters, protesting the arrest of nine members of the Autonomous Workers Union.
The Shanghai radio reported this morning that the nine were taken in by the police on Friday. 
There was no information on their identities or the charges against them, but their arrests were seen here as a sign that the crackdown against the democracy movement was intensifying.
While many workers have taken part in the last few days of protest, the Autonomous Workers Union does not seem to have played a major role in the pro-democracy movement. 
There are no officially recognized trade unions in China.
Â 
Others Reported Arrested
The state press also said today that several other people, described as ''hooligans,'' have been arrested in the last couple of days. 
The evening television news today showed footage of some of them being led to vans by the police and of others being interrogated, apparently at police headquarters.
The Shanghai radio, meanwhile, has been broadcasting almost continuous accounts of the ''counterrevolutionary'' and ''reactionary'' activities of students and others that ''brought great harm'' to the city. 
The radio has asked those who have engaged in ''illegal demonstrations'' and who have ''disrupted transportation'' to register with the police. 
So far, however, there have been no reports that any student leaders have been arrested.
It was unclear whether the crackdown in Shanghai would extend to intellectual circles.
Officials in Shanghai, in contrast with their counterparts in Beijing, have generally taken a moderate approach to the protest movement.
The authorities apparently have not wanted to arouse the anger of a population already seemingly bitter and shocked by the military operation in the capital six days ago.
At the small sit-in in front police headquarters today, for instance, there was no attempt by the police to remove demonstrators by force. 
After several hours, the students sent a small delegation inside police headquarters, presumably to discuss their grievances, while the rest of them returned to their campus.
Still, there have been signs of a toughening attitude on the part of the authorities here toward protesters. 
Brigades of workers militia, hastily organized by the authorities to aid the police, were visible at various points around Shanghai today. 
Their presence at major intersections and near the universities was evidently designed to forestall any resumption of efforts to disrupt the transportation system or to set up new street barricades.
Today for the first time local television showed footage of Friday's mass demonstration, characterizing it as illegal and charging that student demands against the Government were ''unreasonable.''
The students' demands were that flags be flown at half-staff in mourning for the students slain in Beijing, that the local governments agree to a ''dialogue'' with students and that videotapes of the army's operation in Beijing be made public.
At the demonstration on Friday, student speakers warned that if their demands were not met within 48 hours, they would step up their protests. 
Today, however, it seemed unlikely that the students retained the strength needed to follow up on the ultimatum.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_State Dept. Making Plans for Airlift of Americans.txt
text:
ï»¿
The State Department began making arrangements today for a charter airlift of Americans from Beijing should commercial flights be halted, while defense planners drew up contingency plans for a possible military evacuation.
Under the present conditions, American officials said any sudden evacuation could be handled by the commerical carriers Northwest Airlines and United Airlines supplementing their regular service to China with charters.
''Right now there is not a need to lay on charters,'' the State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, said. 
''But the State Department and our embassy have been in touch with both airlines. 
Both airlines will make 747's available to us if needed.''
The Chinese authorities, Ms. Tutwiler said, have already approved such charter flights.
Â 
Americans in China
There are 1,400 Americans in Beijing who are not associated with the United States Government and 8,800 in all of China. 
There are also 428 embassy and consulate personnel and dependents in China, as well as about 4,000 American tourists on any given day.
At the same time, United States military forces in Japan have been making contingency plans for an emergency evacuation of American diplomats and citizens from Beijing, but have not received orders to begin any operations, Administration officials and military officers in Tokyo said.
The officials said that for several days Marine and Air Force personnel stationed in Okinawa and at Yokota Air Base, near Tokyo, have been making plans to fly up to 2,600 United States citizens from Beijing.
''At this point we are waiting to see if the conflict between the Chinese troops heats up,'' said a United States Embassy official in Tokyo. 
If fighting increases, he said, ''we expect that an evacuation might be ordered.''
Â 
Airport Reported Jammed
In all likelihood, the Americans would be brought to Japan, although officials said they had not yet consulted the Japanese Government about how to handle a large influx of foreigners based in Beijing. 
Travelers arriving at Narita Airport near Tokyo from China today reported that the Beijing airport was already jammed, as travelers without reservations tried to get aboard flights.
While officials would not comment about the details of any evacuation plans, one military officer said there were several ones under consideration. 
Under most, the United States would request China's permission to land aircraft there to evacuate Americans. 
But the official suggested that some scenarios include ''rescuing Americans under hostile fire.''
Two months ago, Marine troops in Okinawa were training how to evacuate an embassy, including one under fire. 
But no large-scale rescue effort has been undertaken from Asia since the Communist takeover of Saigon at the end of the Vietnam war. 
Last year, during the intense street fighting in Rangoon, troops moved into Thailand to prepare for a rescue operation in Burma, but it was called off.
Should the embassy have to be evacuated, it might not be only Americans flying out. 
A State Department official said a leading Chinese dissident, Fang Lizhi, and his wife, Li Shuxian, a physics professor, sought refuge in the embassy on Monday and are being allowed to stay.
Â 
Considering Delaying Agreement
The official said Mr. Fang, a 53-year-old astrophysicist who had been denied permission by the Chinese authorities to attend a dinner with President Bush when he visited China in February, ''took refuge for his own safety,'' but would not elaborate.
At the same time, Administration officials said the Administration is considering holding up an agreement to launch American satellites into space on Chinese rockets.
Under the agreement, approved by the Reagan Administration last year, American satellites would be sold to two foreign consortiums, which would arrange for the launching of the satellites by the Chinese. 
The consortiums are Asiasat of Hong Kong, a British-Chinese consortium, and Aussat, an Australian company.
Â 
President's Measures
In fleshing out the measures announced Monday by President Bush, the Administration has also decided to allow all Chinese nationals - not only students - in the United States to remain in this country after their visas expire, Ms. Tutwiler said.
Attorney General Dick Thornburgh later issued a statement saying that the visas of all Chinese nationals in the United States had been extended for one year. 
This would affect about 73,000 Chinese students attending American schools and nearly 250,000 Chinese visitors or business executives now in the United States, he said.
On Capitol Hill, the House voted 406 to 0 to condemn the Chinese Government's ''excessive and indiscriminate'' use of force and express sympathy for the victims.

file: Turmoil in China_Student Recounts 5 Days of Questioning by Police.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Chinese graduate student who disappeared last week on a visit home has returned to the United States and reported that Chinese police interrogated her for five days about American organizations aiding the pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing.
Cheng Yu, a 31-year-old education student at the University of Chicago, said she was also struck by the sympathetic attitude among some of the half dozen Chinese police who questioned her. 
She said one policewoman had mocked a Government television broadcast that said Chinese citizens were enthusiastically welcoming the soldiers who cleared Tiananmen Square.
Ms. Cheng, her 1-year-old son, Payton, and a friend, Tong Boning, a graduate student at the University of California at Los Angeles, disappeared last week while on a two-week visit to China to help pro-democracy demonstrators. 
They were supposed to depart China on June 5 and were escorted to the airport departure area by relatives and friends, but they did not arrive on schedule in the United States and their worried relatives notified the State Department that they were missing.
In a telephone interview from their home in Chicago, Ms. Cheng and her husband, Li Sanyuan, gave a vivid account of her five days in captivity.
Ms. Cheng could not relate the story entirely on her own because she had to leave the telephone to console her baby, who, she said, has been upset by the ordeal. 
Mr. Tong could not be reached in Los Angeles yesterday to relate his account.
Â 
Under Constant Surveillance
Ms. Cheng, who is four months pregnant, her son, and Mr. Tong were arrested in the departure area of Beijing International Airport by police officers who had evidently kept track of them during the two-week visit, she said. 
They were taken to a guest house in a Beijing suburb that, Mr. Li said, is popular with Chinese officials who use the nearby golf course.
At the guest house, the two students' bodies and belongings were searched and they were interrogated for five days in separate rooms by a half dozen police women and men. 
Ms. Cheng said two policewomen accompanied her each time she went to the bathroom and remained in her room as she slept. 
Generally, Ms. Cheng indicated she was treated well but she said she broke down once because the authorities were refusing to notify her husband or her mother, a Beijing resident, of her whereabouts.
''I imagined how he must feel, and my mother, who is 70 years old, and I cried,'' she said.
Ms. Cheng said she had refused food for a day to press her demand that the police obey the law requiring notification of relatives.
Much of the interrogation, she and her husband said, centered on her knowledge of American organizations in China that may be sending money and providing other support for pro-democracy students within China. 
Ms. Cheng had brought into China more than $3,000 in donations she collected from Chinese students studying in Chicago and elsewhere. 
She distributed the money to people in Beijing who were helping the students camped in Tiananmen Square buy food and maintain sanitary conditions.
Â 
Questioned About Donations
''They wanted to know how the donations are collected,'' she said. 
''They think there must be an organization of some people who are in charge.''
Ms. Cheng said she told the police that she had collected the funds ''spontaneously'' and did not represent any organization.
''They wanted to find that I am the connection between some political organization in the United States and the student movement in China,'' she said. 
Her husband added, ''They wanted to know whether there was a conspiracy or any sort of organization behind her.''
Ms. Cheng has written articles for China Spring, a Chinese magazine published in the United States, and her interrogators asked her about the magazine's operations.
The police focused on a diary Ms. Cheng kept during her 15 days in China. 
In the diary, she described encounters in Tiananmen Square with the leaders of the protests there and with ordinary students. 
Ms. Cheng said she kept the diary because she wanted to let Chinese students in America know of the bravery of the protesters in Tiananmen Square. 
When she and Mr. Tong left for the airport, he warned her that it would be dangerous to try to bring the diary through passport control, but she rejected his urgings.
''She didn't take enough precaution,'' her husband said. 
''She thought she might get it through customs. 
After all it was a notebook. 
It was not a document.''
Â 
'The End of a Nightmare'
Ms. Cheng said that at one point policewomen guarding her watched a news program on the crackdown in Beijing and laughed when a reporter declared that Chinese citizens were welcoming the troops.
''One of them said, 'Why don't you show it to us?'
'' Ms. Cheng said. 
''There were no pictures on the screen and she said it very sarcastically.''
At another point, when pictures failed to back up the message, a policewoman scoffed, ''The TV has turned into a radio station.''
''I think they were sympathetic,'' she said. 
''They feel real concern for the baby. 
They told me: 'Don't be pessimistic. 
Things cannot be that bad.'
''
Ms. Cheng said she noticed that one policewoman was reading a book by an American author whose title she remembered as ''Tolerance.''
Ms. Cheng and her baby were released Friday night, and she promptly called her husband and alerted him that she would be returning on the next plane to San Francisco. 
She arrived in Chicago on Saturday night.
''It's the end of a nightmare,'' Mr. Li said yesterday, ''because no one knew where my wife was and what could happen to her next.''
Ms. Cheng said she had no regrets about her mission to China. 
''I have a personal mission,'' she said. 
''I want to be with my people at this historic time. 
It was worthwhile even if I had been there longer than five days.''

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Students in Shanghai Wage War of Buses With Officials.txt
text:
ï»¿
First there are several disabled buses blocking the road to traffic and then, at the entrance to Fudan University, whose students put up the barricade, there are the signs of rebellion.
A Chinese flag is marked with a black band and under it the words ''China is Dead.''
Another sign hangs from a building declaring, ''National Disaster.''
Covering glass cases where school notices are usually posted are photocopied pages of Hong Kong and American newspapers showing pictures, not available in the Chinese press, of the violent crackdown over the weekend in Beijing.
Like most of the 40 or so institutions of higher learning in this city, Fudan, the most prestigious, is engaged in a strangely indirect battle with the local authorities, one that reflects the tension and unease in this city, China's largest, since the army's move on protesters in Beijing.
Â 
To Topple the Government
''Our goal is no longer, as it was before, merely to promote democracy,'' said one student, who gave only his surname, Wang. 
''Now, it is to encourage strikes, to disturb traffic and to help bring about the fall of the Government.''
Mr. Wang was standing next to a mobile speaker's unit, complete with microphone and loudspeakers, which students said is one of several being taken around this sprawling urban area so that the students' point of view can be spread, particularly about the brutality of the army's move in Beijing.
But a more intense battle has been taking place over the city's buses. 
They have been commandeered by students and supporters among the city's working class who let the air out of their tires so they can be used to disrupt the city's traffic and prevent people from showing up at work.
The crippling of the city's buses, which has all but eliminated public transportation in this city of about 12 million people, took place in broad daylight in the two days since the Beijing crackdown.
Â 
Counterattack at Night
The Government's counterattack takes place in the small hours of the morning when, presumably, most of Shanghai's aroused citizenry is asleep. 
Tonight, in fact, the state-controlled local television news showed a nocturnal police operation to tow the disabled buses off the streets and into repair yards.
A spokesman for the city transportation department, interviewed on the air, said 236 disabled buses had been recovered in this way, though he said they had not yet been put back into service because of a need for repairs and a lack of spare parts. 
Another view is that the city does not dare to restore bus service for fear that the buses will be commandeered and used as barricades again.
The students say the use of buses to make barricades is justified by the need to fight against a brutal Government. 
The action has the support of a large majority of people, they say, and the police have not interfered with their operations in what the students say is an effort to avoid arousing the people's anger. 
By contrast, the official propaganda machine attributes the sabotage of the buses to ''a very small number of bad elements'' who are seeking to use the current instability in China to stir up even more trouble.
Â 
No Public Transportation
Whatever the case, even as many of the barricades set up since Sunday have disappeared and the buses recovered by the city administration, there is still no public transportation in Shanghai.
The intensity of distrust here, and of the indirect conflict, could be seen when a train plowed into some people blocking the tracks a mile or so from the central station on Tuesday night, killing six and injuring six.
People who gathered about the scene of the accident said they believed that the train crew had been told by higher authorities to ignore the human blockade. 
They were so angry that they not only set the train's nine passenger cars ablaze last night, but also burned six police sidecar motorcycles parked on a road parallel to the tracks.
During a visit to the site this afternoon, a reporter discovered a large crowd of people, mostly workers in nearby factories, supporting the theory that the train accident was, like the Beijing army action, another instance of the reckless disregard by the authorities for the lives of ordinary people.
Â 
Tracks Blockaded
''All of the tracks have been blockaded for several days,'' said a man in the irate crowd examining the charred wreckage of the train and the heap of burned motorcycles. 
''So they knew there were people on the tracks, and yet they ordered the train not to stop.''
The official news accounts of the incident acknowledged that six people were killed in the accident but did not specify the cause. 
The account, carried on the local television news, along with pictures of the train engulfed in flames, went on to blame the arson on the ''very small number of bad elements'' who have been sabotaging the buses.
The Government's effort to quell the brooding crisis in Shanghai is, on the one hand, to try quietly, in the dead of night to repair the damage being done to the city's transportation system while, on the other, to portray its opponents as tiny, isolated bands doing harm to the people's welfare.
Â 
Mood of Defiance
The strategy also seems based on the hope that the student movement will die away, and indeed perhaps a half of the students have left the universities to go home, depleting their forces. 
Nonetheless, the mood at the partially depopulated Fudan today was defiant and even optimistic.
''The Government has lost its right to rule,'' said a student who, like virtually all of his colleagues, preferred not to give his name. 
''We are confident because we have so much support among the Chinese people. 
If we remain united in our effort, maybe we can succeed in forcing the Government to step down.''
Another student took a visitor on a tour of the campus slogans, drawing particular attention to one that made an allusion to a past martyr in the fight against tyranny.
According to legend, the student explained, a hero named Jing Ke tried to assassinate the cruel and ruthless first Emperor of China in the third century B.C. Before he set out on his doomed task, Jing Ke wrote a short poem reproduced at Fudan in black characters on red paper. 
It said:
Â 
The wind blows.
The river is cold.
The hero sets forth.
He may never return.

file: Turmoil in China_U.S. CHIDES CHINA OVER 2 EXPULSIONS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Bush Administration protested to the Chinese Government today over its expulsion of two American journalists, saying the move would not keep ''the truth about what is going on in China from being heard.''
The Chinese Ambassador to Washington, Han Xu, was summoned to the State Department this afternoon to hear a protest from Robert M. Kimmit, Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, over the expulsion of the journalists, John E. Pomfret of The Associated Press and Alan W. Pessin of the Voice of America.
In what is becoming an almost daily tit-for-tat exchange of allegations or punitive measures between Washington and Beijing, the White House spokesman, Marlin Fitzwater, said:
''Actions such as this, the harassment of journalists trying to do their jobs and attempts to jam Voice of America broadcasts, will not succeed in keeping the truth about what is going on in China from being heard in that troubled land or throughout the world. 
We find the quest for truth to be a process that cannot be thwarted. 
Where one voice is silenced another will take its place.''
All the Facts Are Not Known
Mr. Fitzwater said the State Department was still trying to ascertain all the facts surrounding the expulsions, and he declined to speculate whether Washington would order home some Chinese journalists in retaliation.
''In terms of any actions, we'll have to have a little more time so we are aware of the facts of each of the cases in terms of their activities, visas, permits, what can be done, and what we should ask,'' Mr. Fitzwater said. 
''The initial action is a protest to the Government.''
The State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, pointed out that there are 25 journalists from China in Washington, representing 10 news organizations, and 13 in New York, representing four organizations.
