file: Turmoil in China_U.S. Says 200,000 Troops Are Near Chinese Capital.txt
text:
ï»¿
An Administration official estimated today that up to 200,000 troops of the Chinese People's Liberation Army are now in or around Beijing and that troop movement into the vicinity of the capital ''has apparently not yet ended.''
The official said the estimate was based on ''calculations made from a variety of sources,'' implying that this included satellite coverage. 
The official declined to say whether the troops were reinforcements for units already there, or new units.
On Tuesday, officials in Washington estimated that the number of troops in and around Beijing was between 100,000 and 150,000. 
Officials said today that the new estimate did not necessarily mean there was a sharp rise overnight. 
It could be that troops already there had just been identified, one official said.
Few Further Details on Troops
The official would not give the origins or extent of the troop movement or their mode of transportation. 
Both State and Defense Department spokesmen have officially declined to give estimates of numbers or troop dispositions.
On the broader, politial front, the White House conceded today that it has no idea who is running the Beijing government, and urged Americans to leave China ''at once'' because the situation was becoming ''increasingly dangerous.''
Administration officials said they have no reason to believe that the senior Chinese leader, Deng Xiaoping, is dead or seriously ill, as some reports have suggested. 
Some official analysts even believe that Mr. Deng himself may have spread such rumors to make it appear as though he could not have been responsible for the bloody crackdown in Tiananmen Square Saturday.
As long as Mr. Deng is alive, Administration officials assume he is exerting influence, but whether he is predominant any longer and how he is interacting with the other senior leaders in the Chinese hierarchy is simply unknown.
Â 
'Who Is Making the Decisions?'
''Decisions are being made in China,'' the White House spokesman, Marlin Fitzwater, said during a briefing with reporters. 
''Announcements are coming forth every day of Government actions and decisions. 
Obviously they have a structure for doing that. 
The question is, do we know who is making the decisions and how?
The answer to that is, we do not. 
That is very clearly the design of the Chinese. 
They simply don't want anyone to know.''
Members of the United States intelligence apparatus explained that there were several reasons for the Administration's lack of knowledge.
''All of the top leaders have gone underground to their bunkers,'' said one official. 
''Satellites can take pictures of tanks but not individuals who are hiding. 
Add to that the fact that the situation is confusing even for the Chinese. 
They don't know what is happening themselves, so why should we?''
Decisions in Beijing are apparently being made at small meetings between and within factions, leaving little opportunity for electronic message interception, the officials said. 
Moreover, because power has been fragmented to such a degree, and the normal flows of inter-governmental information interrupted, even those informants the United States may have cultivated in the Chinese bureaucracy cannot speak definitively about what is happening overall.
Finally, even if the United States had a source in Deng Xiaoping's inner circle, it would probably be impossible to contact him now, the officials said, given the way in which the leadership has disappeared.
Â 
'We Don't Know Where They Are'
Mr. Fitzwater said that as far as he knew the Embassy has been unable to talk to any ''top leaders.''
''The truth is,'' said Mr. Fitzwater, ''we don't know where they are. 
We simply surmise that based on historical patterns that some of the leaders have gone to other locations within the city or on the outskirts of the city. 
But we have no confirmation of that.''
A senior White House official said the President was trying to stay abreast of developments in Beijing through intelligence briefings, contacts with the embassy, live news reports and discussions with allies.
Much of what the White House knows, Mr. Fitzwater told reporters, ''is dependent on the news organizations. 
In fact, you have more people there in more key positions and in more areas of the city that are able to watch than the U.S. 
Government.''
Â 
Official Visit Canceled
The Administration lost what might have been its best opportunity to get a first-hand report on the situation from the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, who was scheduled to visit Washington June 12. 
The Chinese Embassy informed the State Department Tuesday night that the visit was canceled and gave no explanation, the State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler said.
''The visit would have given us the opportunity to convey to the Chinese leaders our view of the tragic and brutal actions that have taken place and to urge that a policy of restraint and dialogue be reinstated,'' said Ms. Tutwiler. ''However, under current circumstances, we agree that such a visit should not take place.''
Mr. Qian arrived in Cuba today for the first official visit by a Chinese Foreign Minister to that country. 
The Cuban Government has expressed support for the Chinese crackdown on the pro-democracy movement, which Havana has described as ''counterrevolutionary.''
In view of the fact that the situation in China has become, in the State Department's words, ''volatile, uncertain and increasingly dangerous,'' the Administration decided to evacuate all dependents of United States government employees and non-essential government personnel, Mr. Fitzwater said.
Â 
U.S. Charters Planes
''We have urged all other Americans in China to leave at once,'' he added. 
To aid their departure, the Administration has chartered commercial aircraft to fly to Beijing and Shanghai. 
The first two charters, a Boeing 747 from United Airlines and a DC-10 from Continental Airlines, will arrive in Beijing Thursday.
The State Department said its 24-hour China Task Force has been receiving about 8,000 calls a day from Americans with friends and relatives in China, where about 8,800 United States citizens were living before the latest crisis.
Â 
U.S. Rejects Chinese Protests
On the diplomatic front, the Administration rejected a Chinese Foreign Ministry declaration that President Bush's decision to stop arms sales and military contacts was a ''detriment to bilateral relations.''
''The Chinese statement is unwarranted,'' said Ms. Tutwiler. ''Human rights violations, such as the ones that occurred in Beijing, are properly the concern of the entire international community, including the United States.''
The Administration also dismissed Beijing's condemnation of Washington for providing refuge in the American Embassy to Fang Lizhi, a physicist and prominent dissident. 
Mr. Fang and his wife, Li Shuxian, a physics professor, have been residing in the United States diplomatic compound since Monday. 
In February, the 53-year-old Mr. Fang was barred by Chinese authorities from attending a dinner given by President Bush during his February visit to Beijing.
''Mr. Fang came to our Embassy and asked for temporary refuge,'' said Mr. Fitzwater. ''He indicated that he was fearful for his safety. 
Our embassy accepted him on those terms.''

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_U.S. Suggests Way Out Of Dispute on Dissidents.txt
text:
ï»¿
In an effort to resolve the dispute over two Chinese dissidents who have taken refuge in the United States Embassy in Beijing, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d has suggested that the couple be allowed to go to a third country for asylum, Admnistration officials said today.
The idea of suggesting to the Chinese that they permit the dissidents, Fang Lizhi and his wife, Li Shuxian, to go to an unspecified third country originated with the United States Ambassador to Beijing, James R. Lilley, the officials said.
Mr. Baker accepted the proposal, which was one of several put forward by Mr. Lilley, and formally broached it with the Chinese Ambassador to Washington, Han Xu, during their discussions over the last three days. 
Mr. Lilley did the same with his contacts at the Foreign Ministry in Beijing.
Administration officials said that the Chinese have not responded to the American suggestion, but that an answer could be forthcoming at any moment. 
Repeated requests to the Chinese Embassy in Washington for a comment on the matter went unanswered.
'Left Ball in Chinese Court'
''We left the ball in the Chinese court,'' an Administration official said. 
''We have basically told the Chinese: You write the scenario and we will sign off on it. 
We want to find a quick solution. 
Our only bottom line is that we are not going to turn the Fangs over for arrest.''
Administration officials said the logic of the third-country proposal was that it would satisfy Washington's requirements that the dissident couple not be turned over for arrest, and spare Beijing the embarrassment of the couple's coming immediately to the United States for a media extravaganza.
Administration officials said they had no illusions that it would be easy to persuade the Chinese to accept such a compromise, particularly because the Beijing authorities put out an arrest warrant for Mr. Fang and Miss Li on Sunday and accused them of ''crimes of counterrevolutionary propaganda and instigation.''
The Chinese couple, both physicists, sought refuge in the American Embassy on June 4, after the military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.
Â 
Protection, Not Asylum
The embassy granted them temporary sanctuary on the ground that their lives were in danger. 
The couple made it clear at the time that they came to the embassy for physical protection and not in an effort to seek political asylum, which cannot be granted by the United States on foreign soil.
They insisted that they were Chinese patriots who wanted to remain in their home country, if at all possible. 
Given the position of the Chinese authorities, however, that is apparently no longer an option, unless they want to go to jail.
Administration analysts say they believe that the Chinese leadership remains divided on a variety of issues, including how to handle the Fang affair. 
It is known that Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, and President Yang Shangkun have a personal, visceral dislike for Mr. Fang, whose persistant and public demands for greater freedom in China have made him a folk hero among Chinese university students and an inspiration for the pro-democracy movement as a whole.
In addition, Administration officials believe that some circles in the Chinese leadership would like to use the Fang affair as a tool to worsen already tense relations with the West in general and the United States in particular.
Depicting Mr. Fang and Miss Li and their supporters as part of a broader ''conspiracy'' by foreigners to interfere in Chinese affairs might also be a useful way for Chinese authorities to undermine the legitimacy of the pro-democracy movement, the officials said.
Â 
The Economic Incentive
At the same time, the Administration is convinced that other elements of the Chinese leadership, possibly even Mr. Deng, have a powerful economic incentive not to damage ties with the United States and its Western allies any further and, as a result, might be ready to swallow their antipathy to the couple to get the matter behind them.
The State Department, though, showed no signs today of mincing its words or restraining its response to developments in China.
In a move that could itself inject further acrimony into Chinese-American relations, the State Department signaled today that it intended to expand and speed up processing of both immigrant and non-immigrant visas to accommodate those Chinese seeking to leave their country in the wake of the current wave of repression. 
Long lines of visa applicants are reported at the American Embassy in Beijing and American consulates elsewhere in China.
The State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, said: ''We will be monitoring the requirements to assure that staffing levels are adequate to provide the full range of consular services, including visa issuances. 
We will do whatever it takes to process visas in China.''
After the June 4 shootings in Beijing, President Bush ordered a halt to all military sales to China and extended the visas of Chinese nationals now in the United States until June 1990.
An inter-agency task force charged with preparing an additional list of possible sanctions the Administration might impose on China, should the situation there deteriorate further, has completed its work and presented its ideas to Mr. Baker. Officials said the options consist primarily of a variety of economic sanctions and limits on technology transfers.
Ms. Tutwiler cautioned, however, that this list of options was not presented to Mr. Baker ''in the form of recommendations.''
She added, ''They are merely a laundry list of possible options should the need arise.''
She declined to specify what actions by the Chinese authorities would prompt imposition of these additional punitive measures.
In light of the manhunt the Chinese police have begun for 21 fugitive leaders of the pro-democracy movement, and the mass arrests that have already taken place, Ms. Tutwiler once criticized the Beijing Government.
''Chinese media have reported the arrest of hundreds of persons,'' she said. 
''These arrests are very disturbing. 
Detention or arrest of people for exercising basic human rights of freedom of expression and free association is contrary to internationally recognized standards. 
We continue to believe that the solution to the problems in China lies not in repression and arrest, but in dialogue.''

file: TV VIEW_On Tiananmen Square, Echoes of Chicago in _68.txt
text:
ï»¿
If they are not pushed too far, there are astounding parallels between the Chinese students demonstrating for democracy in Tiananmen Square in recent weeks and the American students demonstrating for an end to the Vietnam War at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago in 1968, before most of those Chinese students were even born.
The most obvious is their shared conviction that ''the whole world is watching.''
That August in Chicago, 21 years ago, it was the slogan most often repeated. 
In Beijing, one American journalist reported its use, but that may be skeptically attributed to persistence in memory. 
More important were the outward signs. 
There were banners in English, surely not for the local population. 
There were plenty of competent English speakers available for interviews. 
There were volunteers to help identify who were the hunger strikers, who were the medical students, who were the demonstrators from the far provinces playing to the television cameras.
Playing to the television cameras was conscious, deliberate and fundamental. 
The presence of cameras alters the shape of events; there need be no more argument about that. 
But is that necessarily bad?
Should television cameras therefore stay away?
Does it make things better to keep them away?
The cameras did not create the anger; they shaped the protest. 
Removing them would make no difference, except it might intensify the anger, which would have found other ways to express itself, perhaps more destructive ways because they would have to be more secret ways.
But it was the physical presence of the cameras that shaped the events, not the journalists who accompanied the cameras. 
The big thing, in Beijing as it had been in Chicago, was that the cameras were there. 
In both cases, moreover, they had not been brought there to show the protest. 
They came to Chicago to cover the Democratic National Convention. 
They came to Beijing to cover the reconciliation of the two Communist giants after three decades of hostility, that is, to report the visit of the Soviet Union's Mikhail Gorbachev. 
The demonstrators knew the cameras would be there and planned their demonstrations to be where the cameras already were.
There is a serious danger of reading too much future portent into this. 
Such live coverage is possible under only the most specialized conditions. 
The site must be small enough to fall within the scope of a few cameras, and it must have boundaries, Tiananmen Square or Michigan Avenue. 
(In 1968, the demonstration in Chicago's Grant Park the night before the convention opened, vigorously broken up by the police, was out of range of live cameras and was not shown on television, except for some snippets of film on the next morning's news programs.) Sports provide paradigmatic live television - a baseball or basketball or football game, a horse race. 
They, too, must be within encompassable boundaries. 
The race for the America's Cup is within boundaries that are too vast. 
As a result, no picture ever tells you at a glance who is winning. 
It would be the same for live coverage of land or sea battles, the horrible prospect so often deplored by those whose chief interest in television is to deplore it. 
Fighting on land quickly boils down to company or platoon action, while in modern sea battles everything is over the horizon from everything else.
Nor can equipment be hastily deployed for live coverage of future demonstrations. 
Logistical plans for television coverage of the 1968 convention were complete to the smallest detail at least a year before the event; months before Mr. Gorbachev arrived in China, networks planning to be there had received permission for camera locations and transmission facilities, submitted detailed lists of equipment complete to serial numbers of camera lenses, and identified by name and passport number every reporter, technician and gofer who was coming. 
The storming of the Winter Palace by the Bolsheviks in March 1917 could have been covered on live television only if someone had attended to the planning no later than May Day 1916.
Both CBS and CNN are properly proud of having had their cameras in Tiananmen Square. 
And it was the presence of those cameras that mattered. 
What was important to the demonstrators was that they present their case to television, which they were thus able to do. 
But the Chinese authorities were aware of the subtle implications of being seen on television in a way that the authorities of Chicago in 1968 were not.
The Mayor of Chicago thought demonstrators were coming to disrupt the convention or start a revolution or both. 
To frustrate them, he took advantage of a strike of union telephone installers that applied to all television except that in the Convention Hall itself. 
As a result, there could be no live coverage of action in the streets. 
Television, however, was far enough advanced to put live cameras in the streets, record their pictures on videotape and supply the necessary power for both with portable generators. 
It was those tapes that America saw - the suppression of the demonstrators which was called by the subsequent official inquiry ''a police riot,'' the first time that term was ever used.
What much of the world saw in 1989 were live pictures of hunger strikers and their supporters in Tiananmen Square. 
It also saw official representatives of the Chinese Government, embarrassed and clearly aware that they were losing face on live television, order all transmissions shut down, a process exquisitely covered and painfully dragged out by the American television staffs themselves. 
The medium, which had been the message, was becoming the masseuse. 
Next there were news reports, presumably from inside the Government of China itself, of hard-liners versus moderates, that is, those who wanted to stop all this nonsense by force against those who were sure that in time the students would tire and the viewers get bored. 
That was as much as the outside world could see when the transmissions were stopped, but the news has plunged on. 
History is not limited to the eye of the beholder.
The physical suppression of the 1968 demonstration by the Chicago police certainly disrupted the Democratic Party's convention and may have defeated its candidate in the Presidential election that followed. 
It was many years, however, between the police being shown clubbing demonstrators on Michigan Avenue and the end of the war in Vietnam. 
We do not yet know whether the demonstrations in Tiananmen Square for more democracy will have parallel results.

file: U. S. EASING CURBS AS CHINA DECLARES MARTIAL LAW OVER.txt
text:
ï»¿
China lifted martial law in Beijing today, and within hours the United States announced that it was easing its blanket opposition to World Bank loans to China.
Prime Minister Li Peng, who announced the lifting of martial law in a nationally televised speech, warned against unspecified foreign and domestic ''hostile forces'' that he said were working to subvert Communism in China. 
But he said that by and large, China had returned to normal.
Despite the official end of martial law, the Chinese authorities retain the ability and apparently a desire to suppress any signs of political unrest, experts on China said. 
[An article and excerpts from Mr. Li's speech are on page A10.] Administration's China Policy Vice President Dan Quayle said the lifting of martial law vindicated Mr. Bush's efforts to re-establish normal diplomatic ties with China. 
But experts on China challenged the Administration's assertion that Mr. Bush's policy had helped persuade China to lift martial law.
The Chinese action did not quell Congressional anger over the crackdown, in which hundreds of Chinese civilians were killed. 
Nor did it seem likely to mute Congressional criticism of President Bush's policy, which many lawmakers consider excessively sympathetic to the Chinese leadership.
The White House and the State Department praised China's decision to lift martial law as ''a positive step.''
Neither publicly acknowledged that strict laws banning dissent remained in force in China.
The State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, said that in ''a partial change of policy'' the United States would examine loans on a case-by-case basis.
Â 
Support for 'Human-Needs Loans'
Proposals for seven loans totaling $780 million have been held at the World Bank since the beginning of the crackdown in June.
Mr. Bush does not want economic sanctions to ''hurt the Chinese people,'' Miss Tutwiler said. 
''Our view is that basic human-needs loans - for instance, earthquake relief - should be permitted periodically to go forward,'' she said.
Miss Tutwiler said the United States' revised position had been under consideration for months and was ''not connected'' to the end of martial law. 
The timing, she said, ''is sheerly, honestly coincidence.''
Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, said the lifting of martial law was ''an empty gesture.''
''Beijing can lift martial law because it does not need martial law to crush dissent,'' she said, noting that China had adopted a series of measures outlawing anti-Government demonstrations and authorizing security forces to stop protests.
Mrs. Pelosi is the author of a bill that would prohibit the United States from sending Chinese students back to China. 
Mr. Bush vetoed it on Nov. 
30. Congress is likely to override the veto soon after it reconvenes on Jan. 
23. Congress is also likely to approve a package of economic and military sanctions banning arms sales to China and suspending Federal insurance for private investments in the country.
Â 
Quayle Sees Policy 'Dividends'
Martial law was imposed in parts of Beijing on May 20, after more than a million people filled the streets of the capital to support demands for greater democracy.
Sweeping restrictions were imposed, including total bans on rumor-mongering, boycotts of classes, petitions, meetings and anything else that was deemed threatening to what Beijing called ''the normal order.''
After the June 3-4 military crackdown on the democracy movement, the Government banned all dissident organizations and gave the police the right to shoot demonstrators. 
Thousands of arrests and scores of executions followed.
It is not clear if China made a commitment to lift martial law when Mr. Bush's national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, visited Beijing last month.
Mr. Quayle said today that the lifting of martial law illustrated the ''dividends from the President's policy toward China.''
A White House spokesman, Roman Popadiuk, said the Administration would like to think that the trips to China by Mr. Scowcroft, in July and December, ''played a part'' in China's decision to lift martial law.
Â 
Repression Said to Continue
But outside experts expressed doubt. 
A professor of Chinese history at Boston University, Merle Goldman, said ''the Chinese have been suffering economically'' and need financial assistance from the World Bank.
''The lifting of martial law is essentially a cosmetic or symbolic gesture to show that things are back to normal and to impress the outside world,'' she said in a telephone interview.
If China released student leaders, intellectuals and workers imprisoned in the crackdown on the demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, that would provide tangible evidence of political liberalization in China, Mrs. Goldman said.
Senator Claiborne Pell, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, said the lifting of martial law was ''a small step in the right direction.''
But Mr. Pell, a Rhode Island Democrat, said, ''It does not change the fundamental circumstance of repression in China or the many serious issues that remain - human rights and freedom for arrested students and workers, human rights and an end to martial law in Tibet, and a halt to Chinese arms for Pol Pot and the murderous Khmer Rouge in Cambodia.''
Mr. Popadiuk said: ''We are pleased with the lifting of martial law and see it as a positive step.''
He said that the lifting of martial law was ''another in a series of positive steps'' by China. 
In the last few weeks, he said, the Chinese Government has readmitted a reporter from the Voice of America, has discussed renewal of a student-exchange program suspended since June and has curtailed criticism of the United States in Chinese newspapers and broadcasts.
Mr. Popadiuk also said the Chinese had ''announced that they would not be selling medium-range missiles to the Middle East.''
But an Arabic-language newspaper published in London said this week that Syria had ''officially received assurances from the Chinese Government of its commitment to military cooperation between the two countries.''
The report said that China had rejected American pressure to stop selling weapons to Syria.
Â 
Pledge to Halt Missiles Sales
Chinese officials concluded that they needed to maintain the military capabilities of Syria and Israel's other Arab neighbors because ''Israel is being armed with the most technologically advanced weapons,'' the report said.
Asked about that report, Miss Tutwiler affirmed that China had announced that it ''would not be selling medium-range missiles to the Middle East.''
She said she did not know if the Administration was monitoring China's adherence to its pledge.
It was not immediately clear what types of World Bank loans would be acceptable to the United States. 
Miss Tutwiler said that though Washington might support some ''basic human needs loans'' to China, it would continue to discourage ''project loans.''
A spokesman for the Asia division of the bank, Pastor B. Sison, said the distinction was not obvious, because loans for specific projects could also serve basic human needs.

file: U.N. Panel Backs 3 Translators Ousted at Beijing_s Request.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a ruling likely to have far-reaching consequences for Chinese and Soviet staff members here, a United Nations tribunal has said the organization had no right to dismiss three Chinese employees at the Beijing Government's request earlier this year.
The United Nations Administrative Tribunal ordered Secretary General Javier Perez de Cuellar to reinstate the three translators or pay them three years' salary as compensation.
The ruling, made public on Thursday, was hailed as a victory in the fight to end the Chinese and Soviet practice of sending their nationals to the United Nations for fixed periods instead of allowing them to become career international civil servants.
The United States and other Western countries have complained that this practice prevents the emergence of an independent international civil service, as called for in the United Nations Charter.
China and the Soviet Union have also made their nationals serving with United Nations organizations hand over part of their salaries to their governments.
Â 
Decision Is Praised
''This is an important decision which will strengthen the concept of an independent international civil service and also strengthen the hand of the Secretary General in resisting pressure from member governments over staff,'' said Lowell L. Flanders, the President of the union of United Nations employees.
The tribunal, which adjudicates disputes between United Nations employees and the Secretary General, said governmnents may only legally send their nationals to the United Nations for a fixed period of time if all the parties concerned make a formal agreement to this effect.
The three Chinese translators were among nine Chinese staff members whose contracts were not renewed by the Secretary General earlier this year after Beijing said it wanted them sent home. 
All nine had protested the Chinese Government's suppression of the pro-democracy movement last June and refused to surrender part of their salaries to China's United Nations mission as required. 
The other six are also appealing their dismissals.
Mr. Flanders said that about 700 United Nations Secretariat employees were on temporary assignment from China, the Soviet Union and some Eastern European countries and that many may now seek career appointments as a result of today's ruling. 
The Soviet Union has already said it intends to end its assignment policy.

file: U.N. Panel Puts China on List Of Human Rights Defendants.txt
text:
ï»¿
A United Nations panel today placed China on a list of countries accused of seriously violating their citizens' human rights.
The panel, a subcommission of the United Nations Human Rights Commission, voted 15 to 9, by secret ballot, to have the full commission examine charges that China brutally suppressed the student pro-democracy movement in violation of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. 
It also appealed for clemency for those arrested in connection with the student demonstrations that were put down in June.
The 26-member subcommission is preparing a list of countries that it considers guilty of human rights offenses. 
The full commission will consider the charges at its annual meeting next March. 
Both bodies can do no more than exert moral pressure on accused governments to mend their ways by investigating the charges against them and publishing their findings.
Other countries accused of human rights abuses by the subcommission today included Iran, Indonesia, Guatemala, El Salvador, South Africa and Israel.
Â 
A First for a Big Power
But experts said the condemnation of China was particularly significant. 
It was the first time that a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council has been censured for its human rights performance in a United Nations forum. 
It was also the first time that a United Nations body assigned to enforce respect for human rights has passed judgment on the Chinese Government's suppression of the democracy movement this year.
On Wednesday, Amnesty International, the human rights watchdog, said it had evidence that China had decided to execute many leaders of the pro-democracy movement in secret and had announced only a few of the death sentences that were passed.
The document approved by the subcommission, which is composed of nominally independent experts appointed by their governments, said the panel was ''concerned about the events which took place recently in China and their consequences in the field of human rights.''
It asked the United Nations Secretary General to transmit information provided by China and ''other reliable sources'' to the full commission and appealed for clemency toward those ''deprived of their liberty.''
China's expert on the subcommission, Tian Jin, angrily rejected the resolution, saying his Government was acting within its sovereign rights in ''suppressing a rebellion.''
He accused Western countries of trying to ''blacken China's name.''
He also warned that if the resolution was passed, Western countries would then ''attack'' other developing countries. 
''The consequences will not be limited to China and this merits attention everywhere,'' he said.
Â 
Third World Seeks More Seats

file: U.N. Passes Voluntary Register to Curb Arms Sales.txt
text:
ï»¿
At a time when the international arms trade may be starting to grow again after a sharp decline, the United Nations General Assembly voted overwhelmingly today to establish the first register of international arms sales.
The aim of the register, which won strong support in the wake of the Persian Gulf war, is to curb the international traffic in arms by publicizing transactions and identifying potential trouble spots by showing where arm stocks are increasing.
Although the resolution calls on all nations to provide the world organization with an annual list of all imports and exports of arms, it does not require them to do so. 
Nonetheless, diplomats say most countries are likely to comply with the register because of the overwhelming support it has received and particularly because of its support from Britain, the United States, France and the Soviet Union, which together account for about 70 percent of the international arms trade.
The register will initially apply only to sales of heavy arms, like tanks, armored fighting vehicles, artillery pieces, combat aircraft and attack helicopters, that can be used to seize and hold territory.
China, a major arms producer, refused to take part in today's vote, even though it participated in talks with the other four permanent members of the Security Council in Paris last summer on curbing arms sales to the Middle East. 
China offered no explanation for its stand. 
But some diplomats said the Chinese action might reflect the importance that arms sales has acquired for China as a source of foreign currency as well as resentment at the pressure to go along with the register from the United States and other Western supporters.
In today's vote, 150 countries approved the resolution establishing the register and procedures for gradually expanding its scope to cover not only heavy arms shipments but also lighter weapons, arms production and national weapon stocks. 
While no nation voted against, Cuba and Iraq abstained.
During the debate in committee, many developing countries complained that the register would discriminate against poorer nations, which import their arms, by requiring them to disclose their purchases while protecting richer nations with indigenous arms industries against revealing their military strength.
As a result, the resolution calls on the Secretary General to set up an expert group to report next year on ways of extending the register to include lighter arms as well as production sites and national weapon stocks. 
This could transform the register from a list of arms sales into one for conventional arms that includes transfers.
Purchases by developing countries account for about 75 to 80 percent of the international arms trade, which peaked at $57 billion in 1987 before declining, according to the latest report of the United States Arms Control and Disarmament Agency.
The United States earned $14 billion from selling arms overseas in 1988, the last year for which Government figures are available, accounting for 29 percent of the world market. 
According to the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency, world arms exports fell 13 percent from $57 billion in 1987 to $49 billion in 1988, the lowest level in 10 years. 
But in average terms, the agency says, sales have been declining 3 percent a year since 1983.
"For the first time in history, perhaps, the favorable prospects for controlling the transfer of conventional weapons appear to outweigh the negative," Prof. Stephanie Neuman, an arms control expert at Columbia University, said in a paper for the American Association for the Advancement of Science. 
Professor Neuman attributes the downward trend to the increasing sophistication of weapons, deteriorating economic conditions and "the new political order."
But at a recent meeting of arms control scholars at Wisconsin University, Michael Klare of Hampshire College said Iraq's defeat in the gulf war might encourage developing countries to shift from their preference for large tank and infantry formations to a greater emphasis on aircraft, helicopters and precision-guided munitions.

file: U.N. Population Plan for China a Test for U.S.txt
text:

This will be the first time the United States, which is a member of the council, has been asked to approve a new plan for China since 1985, when Congress cut off all American contributions to the agency, claiming it was helping China run a population control program that employed compulsory abortion and sterilization.
''There is a new President and a new program so I hope we will also have a new policy and the United States will resume its support for us,'' said Dr. Nafis Sadik, the agency head.
Dr. Sadik said that when she visited Beijing in January, Chinese leaders admitted that ''overzealous'' family planning officials had forced women to have abortions against their wishes.
But they insist that this is against official policy requiring voluntary abortions.
Dr. Sadik, who is from Pakistan and the only woman to head a United Nations agency, said the Chinese told her they are now trying to improve the image of their population policy abroad, cracking down on officials involved in family planning abuses, including coerced abortions.

This year the fund will have a record budget of just over $190 million to spend on controlling population growth.
Under the 1985 law, the President must determine annually whether China's population control program includes forced abortion.

[Page D2.]

China also agreed to extend patent protection to 20 years from 15 years and to eliminate most requirements that force multinational corporations to license production of their inventions to local Chinese companies instead of exporting directly to China, said the official, who insisted on anonymity.
The last issue settled concerned the protection of pharmaceutical and other chemical products already patented but not yet available for sale.

After initially insisting that only future inventions be covered, the Chinese agreed to protect products patented since Jan. 
1, 1986, the senior American official said.

file: U.S. Bars Chinese Role At Talks on Air Pollution.txt
text:

To avoid violating sanctions imposed on China last year because of its crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators, the Administration has excluded Beijing from an international conference on air pollution and climatic change, even though the Chinese burn more industrial coal than any other country, officials said today.
The conference, to be held here on Tuesday and Wednesday, will include the rest of the world's most industrialized or populous nations, and White House officials said they normally would have considered Chinese participation an important element of such a meeting.
The White House Conference on Scientific and Economic Research Related to Global Change is part of President Bush's effort to spur research into the way pollution may be changing the global climate and to allay criticism of his environmental policies. 
Mr. Bush will address the gathering on Tuesday morning and Wednesday afternoon.
The conference is to focus on the kind of research the industrialized and developing nations should conduct on the theory of global warming, which postulates that certain kinds of pollutants are causing the Earth's temperature to rise. 
The burning of coal is the primary source of carbon dioxide, a chemical that is believed to be a major cause of this phenomenon.
Criteria Explained
In drawing up the guest list for the conference, the White House selected countries ''that have substantial populations, large land masses, industrial economies or heavy future energy needs,'' said Stephen Hart, a White House spokesman.
China, which has the world's largest population, about 1 billion people, burns more coal than any other country and is expected to increase its consumption dramatically in an industrialization drive. 
At present, it is the third largest producer of carbon dioxide in the world, after the United States and the Soviet Union, according to United Nations statistics.
''China has the potential to emit a lot of carbon dioxide as they continue to develop, as well as chlorofluorocarbons, and under different circumstances they probably would have been invited to this meeting,'' Mr. Hart said.
Scientists say chlorofluorocarbons, chemicals used for such purposes as propellants in aerosol sprays and coolants in refrigerators and air conditioners, damage the ozone layer, increasing the amount of harmful radiation reaching the earth's surface.

High-Level Exchanges Banned
But Mr. Hart said China was excluded from the list because of the sanctions Mr. Bush imposed against the Beijing Government last year after its nationwide crackdown on political dissent, which culminated in the violence in Tiananmen Square last June.
Among those measures was a ban on high-level exchanges between the two nations. 
Mr. Hart said the White House determined that the rule would apply to the conference since the invitations went out to government officials of ministerial level.
Officials said that even if China's participation might have been useful, the Administration wanted to avoid the kind of severe criticism it drew last year after it was disclosed that Brent Scowcroft, the President's national security adviser, and Lawrence S. Eagleburger, the Deputy Secretary of State, had made two trips to China after the sanctions were imposed. 
The White House took the position at the time that the Scowcroft-Eagleburger mission was not an exchange.
The United States signed the 1987 Montreal Protocol, which called for a reduction of 50 percent in the production of chlorofluorocarbons. 
The 80 nations that signed the document are now negotiating a deadline for a complete ban on the chemicals. 
China has not ratified the protocol.
Sending delegations to the conference besides the United States are Australia, Brazil, Canada, West Germany, France, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, the Netherlands, Nigeria, Norway, Poland, the Soviet Union, Britain and Zaire, as well as the European Community and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d told South Korea today that Washington considered North Korea's suspected development of nuclear weapons a matter of urgent global concern and that it was now actively exploring with Japan, China and the Soviet Union ways to curtail the move.

8 that both nations agree to forego development of any weapons of mass destruction.

Last Major Benefactor

file: U.S. Companies Consider Options for Business in China.txt
text:

Amid the uncertainty created by the unrest in China, American companies with operations there are being urged to consider a variety of options.

Signs of Normality
Daniel L. Spiegel, a partner with the law firm of Akin, Gump, Strauss, Hauer & Feld, said his clients were asking what signs to look for to show that the situation was returning to normal.

But Charles J. Conroy, a partner at Baker & McKenzie, a law firm in New York, said he has advised clients at least to think about how to suspend or end operations if the situation worsens.
Albert Y. P'an of Transcapital International Inc. said he has told clients not to postpone any activities that are under way but not to start new ones.
Jack T. Huang, a senior associate at Jones, Day, Reavis & Pogue, a law firm in New York, said that it was too soon to talk about ending business relationships but that the Army's attack against students in Tiananmen Square would ''set things back for a number of years.''

'Lingering Uncertainty'
''The most terrible situation is the lingering uncertainty,'' he said.

Michael C. Oskenberg, a professor of political science at the University of Michigan and a senior adviser to Akin Gump, said a number of things had to occur in China before business relations could return to normal.

Mood in Hong Kong
Also important, Professor Oskenberg said, is the mood in Hong Kong, the British crown colony that is supposed to revert to Chinese control in 1997.

If Contracts Are Suspended

''These people have many spokesmen within the Administration.''
Â 
Exports to Communist Nations
The State Department officials said the Boeing deal had been been held up because the plane's navigation system was on the State Department's munitions control list that applies to exports to Communist countries. 
The Bush sanctions blocked the sale of all items on that list.
But the officials said the navigation systems would be used in civilian aircraft and would have no important military value for the Chinese. 
''Our decision is in keeping with the President's intent not to disrupt nonmilitary commercial trade,'' a State Department spokesman said.
A State Department official said the McDonnell Douglas Corporation, Boeing's principal rival, has also applied for a waiver of President Bush's sanctions, so that it might ship its navigation systems to Shanghai, where it is building its MD-82 midsize aircraft in a joint venture with the Chinese.
The State Department also authorized Honeywell Inc. to maintain navigation equipment in planes sold to China, arguing that this action was needed to protect the safety of Chinese airline passengers.
The four Boeing 757's are narrow-body 200-passenger planes, with a total value of about $200 million. 
They are part of an 11-plane order, but Administration officials said the exemption applies only to the four planes, which were scheduled for delivery in June.
Delivery of the remaining planes in the order depends on developments in China, the officials said. 
Boeing has already sent five 757's to China under a previous order, a company spokesman said.
The State Department officials said Boeing, which is based in Seattle, had pressed hard for a waiver, provoking some criticism in Congress.
Â 
Action With Allies Urged
Representative Lantos said the Administration should try to work out sanctions with allies to block the sale of commercial jetliners to China.
Such a move would ''exact a price,'' he said, adding, ''The Chinese must understand that massacres will not go unpunished.''
A State Department official said it would be a mistake to block American companies from selling planes to China, allowing airplane manufacturers from other countries to make the sales.
Representative Gerald B. H. Solomon, a Republican from Glens Falls, N.Y., who had also called for sanctions tougher than the Administration's, complained about the waiver, saying it sent the wrong message to the Chinese.
''We ought to be going to our allies to get them to join us in putting our foot down with the Chinese, instead of just saying that if we do not sell airliners to the Chinese somebody else will,'' he said.
Mr. Solomon said the decision to allow the sale might be a sign that the Administration also plans to allow the export of American communications satellites to China for launching on Chinese rockets under an agreement reached last year.
Â 
Also on Control List
The sanctions prevent the export of American-manufactured satellites to China since they are also on the munitions control list although do not have military use. 
An Australian consortium and a British-Chinese consortium, both of which arranged the Chinese launchings, are asking for exceptions from the sanctions.
Mr. Solomon has sponsored an amendment that would prohibit the export licensing for the satellites because of China's crackdown on the democracy movement. 
China has drawn customers for its launching of satellites because its prices are cheaper than those of American and Western European companies.
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, which is based in St. Louis, have been competing for China's aircraft market.
Last month, China announced that it would buy 90 planes in the next four years to add to its commercial fleet of 420.
Boeing has sold 61 planes to China since the early 1970's for about $2.35 billion.
Some experts said China is significant more as a potential market than as a immediate purchaser of American planes.
''There is no doubt China represents a potentially huge market,'' said Jack A. Modzelewski, vice president of research for Paine Webber Inc. 
''But we do not see China as a major source of buying potential for aircraft in the next three to five years.''
Â 
Constraints on Purchases
Mr. Modzelewski said aircraft purchases would be constrained over the next several years because of slow economic growth in China and China's limited supplies of hard currency.
In response to questions, Boeing said in a statement that the company did not believe that the licenses for the navigation equipment on the four 757-200 planes should have been suspended. 
It said it had ''discussed that issue at length with appropriate Government agencies.''
An Administration official provided one example of Boeing's activity on the issue. 
He said Boeing helped draft language that was included in House legislation that stated items on the control list intended for civilian use should not be blocked.
It said the four planes would be delivered to Guangzhou Airlines and Shanghai Airlines as soon as possible.
