text:
ï»¿
From a sunny second-floor suite of five offices, a copying machine and telephones that ring almost constantly, word has just gone out that the Bank of China is honoring its letters of credit and that most of China's ports, with the exception of Shanghai, are operating normally.
Since the bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square on June 4, the Commerce Department's equivalent of a China desk, has served as a crisis management center for the more than 350 American companies that in the past 10 years invested $3.5 billion in China - more than a third of the total foreign investment there.
Among the investors are General Foods, which makes coffee products in Guangzhou; Gillette, razor blades in Shenyang; Ingersoll Rand, air compressors in Shanghai and Nabisco, bakery products in Beijing.
''Basically, we're telling them to sit tight, and if they were contemplating an investment to hold off for a while and see how things shake out,'' said Christine L. Lucyk, who is Commerce's top China hand.
Daily Contact With China
Other Cabinet departments - State and Treasury, and the Central Intelligence Agency - have their own experts, who concentrate on their department's areas of expertise. 
Mrs. Lucyk's team of seven keeps up on developments affecting American-Chinese commercial relations through daily telephone calls to commercial officers at the Beijing Embassy, principally Lyn Edinger, commercial counselor, and Tim Stratford, commercial attache, and through contacts with scores of executive suites.
This is not to suggest that Washington's clusters of China-watchers work in isolation. 
Over the last two weeks, at the urging of State's desk, Commerce's has been telling companies to get their American personnel out of China. 
There are 1,000 there now, as against 9,000 before June 4 .
''They were very reluctant to leave,'' said one of Ms. Lucyk's aides, David K. Schneider. ''They were concerned about the fate of their Chinese employees, and about what would happen to their business.''
''In some cases,'' he said, ''their Chinese partners were telling them they shouldn't go because there was nothing wrong. 
Now we're trying to help some companies develop approaches to their partners to explain to them why they had to leave.''
Â 
Advice to Companies
The Commerce desk has also been offering advice to companies on how to deal with shipments of machinery and other goods needed to keep plants operating in China or fulfill contracts under the more 600 joint ventures American companies operate with Chinese partners.
The desk has also focused on such day-to-day matters as the state of mail service (the main Beijing post office is open but many branches are closed) and transportation (Japan Airlines has just resumed service to Beijing but with reduced frequency).
Although corporate aides often have not been pleased with what they hear, they are not reluctant to praise the messenger. 
''They're doing an awfully good job for the task at hand,'' said Richard E. Gillespie, vice president of the U.S.-China Business Council, representing 300 American multinationals with China operations.
Before martial law was imposed late in May, Commerce had a number of diplomatic and other activities planned for China. 
On the commercial side, Roger Severance, the Deputy Assistant Secretary for East Asia and the Pacific, was about to lead a delegation to China to take up a growing list of individual corporate problems with national and provincial leaders. 
These chiefly related to bureacratic interference in joint ventures and the inability of Chinese customers to obtain needed foreign exchange for payments.
Â 
Interrupted Operations
Also in July, the U.S.-China Joint Commission for Commerce and Trade, a high-level organization of the two governments created in the 1970's thaw, had been expected to meet to give new impetus to the commercial relationship.
This would have brought the Commerce Secretary, Robert A. Mosbacher, together for the first time with his counterpart, the Chinese Minister of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade, Zheng Tuobin.
When China reopened to the West 10 years ago, many business leaders had romantic notions about the huge market, with visions of 1 billion Chinese buying tube socks or other American miracle products.
But with many projects canceled in 1982 and with economic retrenchment last September, Americans now have a ''much more realistic view of doing business in China,'' Ms. Lucyk said.
''In China,'' she observed, ''we long ago lost our innocence.''

text:
ï»¿
Two months ago the story would have provoked shouted inquiries to the President as he boarded his helicopter and hasty news conferences by members of Congress eager to take a stand. 
But on Aug. 
28, 1989, the report provoked only silence.
The State Department prepared special guidance for its spokesmen on the report, but when no journalists asked about it at the daily briefing, the department did not volunteer a comment.
The report was brief: The Associated Press said a student in Beijing had been sentenced to nine years in prison for allegedly spreading rumors to the Voice of America. 
Attributing the report to a Chinese newspaper, the news agency said it was the first sentencing of a student to prison for participating in the spring democracy movement.
Through television Americans survey a vast world from their living rooms. 
With every new crisis, their attention turns and last week's news begins to fade out. 
As democracy bloomed in Poland and the drug war exploded in Colombia, China seemed to fade out. 
What ever happened to American outrage over the repression of the democracy movement?
To begin with, the Chinese are learning the lesson of South Africa: what American news organizations cannot see, the average American will not feel. 
Although the arrests and repression in China today are far more sustained than the fleeting explosion of violence in Tiananmen Square, they are taking place beyond the glare of television cameras. 
It is hard for Americans to summon outrage from file footage.
''The Chinese will never make the mistake again of allowing television cameras to show their tanks running over people in Beijing,'' an Asia expert in the State Department said. 
''What is happening there today may actually be worse - the slow dribbling out of arrests and convictions -but it lacks drama. 
It's not on television. 
It's not in Beijing. 
It is people being arrested in the middle of the night.''
Indeed, television has both cultivated and reflected the very short attention span Americans have toward foreign news. 
Stories on television, unlike in real life, always contain bold dramas and quick endings. 
The viewing public has become accustomed to news packaged in this format. 
When it cannot be packaged this way, the channel gets changed.
China's democracy movement attracted Americans' attention as a rare glimmer of democratic possibilities, like Hungary in 1956. 
But such moments lack staying power. 
At best they become memories that inspire the long boring haul of reform and institution building, which make for good history and awful ratings.
There are other explanations. 
With China, Americans seem to be experiencing the humility that comes from discovering that a nation they thought they knew was actually a stranger. 
It was as though the United States awoke one morning and realized that it did not know China, that it was not, as many hoped, on a steady course toward Westernization.
Americans learned the hard way that they would have to wait for China to sort out its own path, that this regime has much more staying power than many would like to believe and that its leaders have no intention of paying for American friendship with their own power. 
As that became more apparent, the policy debate on China assumed a new modesty.
This was reinforced from above. 
No one has more power to shape a debate than the President. 
But instinctively, President Bush seemed to realize that the students were never going to capture power, so he dampened expectations about the democracy movement.
In addition, strategic interests dictated that he not abandon the implicit Chinese-American alliance against the Soviet Union simply because so many students were gunned down. 
So Mr. Bush flashed just enough anger to appease the momentary sense of outrage and to prevent Congress from legislating its own sanctions, but not so much anger as to break relations with China or to keep its drama in the headlines an extra day.

file: We Must Change Our Lives.txt
text:
ï»¿
FREEDOM IN EXILE
The Autobiography of the Dalai Lama.
Illustrated. 288 pp. 
New York:
A Cornelia & Michael Bessie Book/
HarperCollins. $22.95.
Â 
MY TIBET
Text by His Holiness
The Fourteenth Dalai Lama of Tibet.
Photographs by Galen Rowell.
162 pp. 
Berkeley: Mountain Light Press/
University of California Press.
Â Â $35.
Perhaps the time has come when the world will lend a more sympathetic ear to the message of the Dalai Lama. 
His two main concerns for the last four decades have been the same: nonviolence as a way of relating to others - even to nonhuman sentient beings - and an attitude toward life that involves care for the environment. 
These were the messages he brought with him to the West to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989; they are the messages he develops in ''Freedom in Exile,'' his autobiography. 
The world may be ready to listen because more people are convinced today that such messages are needed if the future of this planet is to be assured. 
The timing of the autobiography is perfect. 
What may have seemed too idealistic and naive in the past is now seen by many as the only way to assure peace and preserve life on earth.
The timing of this volume is important also because of the new euphoria over the freedoms acquired by many nations in Eastern Europe in the past year. 
There is a solid hope that this phenomenon of the human spirit reaching toward freedom is but a glimpse of the beginning of even more manifestations of ethnic, racial, national and religious aspirations. 
Could Tibet finally hope for new freedom too?
There is every reason to expect that world pressure will mount in that direction, even though some Western nations fear that China will be offended by such a move. 
The Dalai Lama's book is a political one. 
For three decades he has traveled the globe to keep alive the world's interest in his nation's plight. 
This book is a call for freedom.
Tibet's loss of freedom is the most dramatic event in the life of the 14th Dalai Lama. 
When he was born to a family of small farmers on July 6, 1935, as he explains, there was no way for anyone to know he would become the Dalai Lama. 
However, two years before his birth, the 13th Dalai Lama had died. 
Several years later, according to custom, a search party of high-ranking Buddhist monks, guided by the state oracle and acting on what they saw as special signs, fanned out through Tibet looking for a child whom they could recognize as the previous Lama's reincarnation (as the Dalai Lama says in his book, he is believed by his followers to be the reincarnation of all 13 of his predecessors, the first having been born in 1351).
His explanation of these matters is forthright. 
And the writing is remarkable in that he says at the outset that he wrote directly in English, a difficult task, he adds, since ''my ability to express myself in this language is limited. 
Furthermore, I am aware that some of the subtler implications of what I say may not be precisely what I intended. 
But the same would be true in a translation from Tibetan.''
His story of how he was recognized as the new Dalai Lama and of his installation in the mighty Potala Palace in Lhasa as his nation's leader is well known from the memoirs of several Europeans who were there at the time. 
But he has retained much of the freshness of the child's view of what was happening to him, and his account is moving. 
It is also often amusing, especially when he tells of his famous fascination since childhood with everything scientific and technical - a passion that has led him to become an expert at repairing watches since he was 8 or 9. 
It also led to a hilarious collision with a tree when, as a boy of about 13, he sneaked into the palace garage and took one of only four motor vehicles in all of Tibet out for a private joy ride.
He had not much more time for such carefree fun. 
After the Communists came to power in China in 1949, one of their first moves was to make a claim on Tibet. 
Tibetan officialdom ended the regency that operated the Government on behalf of the youthful Dalai Lama, and, at an age when most Americans are in high school, he became the absolute ruler of Tibet. 
His book tells an impressive story of the education of this young monk-monarch as he tried to negotiate with the Chinese and to save his country. 
Finally, in 1959, with Chinese forces lobbing shells inside the compound of his summer palace, he consulted his oracle, and then he and a group of his closest advisers made their way across the Himalayas into India. 
Through the years they were to be followed by more than 100,000 escaping Tibetans, and today they occupy the Indian town of Dharmsala, where the Dalai Lama has his headquarters, and 50 other refugee centers.
The enormous destruction of Tibetan religion and culture wreaked by the Chinese is well attested to by many refugees, and by visitors to Tibet. 
But there are things no conqueror can obliterate, as is immediately evident in ''My Tibet,'' a volume of photographs taken in recent years by Galen Rowell, with a text drawn from interviews with the Dalai Lama or essays written previously by him. 
Mr. Rowell has caught the natural beauty of that nation as no other photographer has done before. 
Its mystical qualities are a combination of ruggedness and serenity. 
The pictures also testify that the faces of the Tibetan people have not changed from past years. 
They remain fresh and wholesome, shy and inward looking, full of fun and hidden sentiments. 
Mr. Rowell's rich color pictures of the people can be profitably compared with the collection of black-and-white historical photographs to be found in another volume, ''Tibet: The Sacred Realm. 
Photographs 1880-1950,'' first issued seven years ago and recently reprinted by Aperture. 
The conditions of life for Tibetans may have changed, but the great human qualities of these people have not; they glow from the pictures. 
Mr. Rowell's photographs, whether of nomads or the abundant animal life or landscapes and town scenes, reveal changes but they also underscore the idea found in the Dalai Lama's comments on each one - that there are hidden and enduring truths to be found here.
In the three decades since his escape, the Dalai Lama has traveled throughout the world studying, teaching and conferring with members of many religions - and always seeking the world's help in restoring his country to its people. 
But even if more political freedom should come to it, the road to liberation for Tibet will not be an easy one. 
''Freedom in Exile'' shows that the author is aware of the cultural gaps between traditional Tibetan Buddhism and the scientific approaches of the West. 
The long isolationism of Tibet is now over, but the struggle to come to terms with the advances in science and psychology that have occurred in the world is only beginning. 
How much of the old ways can survive not only the Chinese Communist domination, but the scientific and psychological pressures of the whole of Western culture?
It will be more difficult to vindicate rule by oracles, for example, in an age that seeks psychological examination and scientific proof for all such phenomena. 
The rest of the world is unlikely to be convinced that a society and its government should be based on the search for reincarnations of the great leaders of the past. 
Though one admires the foresight of the Tibetans in the past, in raising up and training leaders from childhood, one is struck by the difficulty of combining this method with the democratic ideals that now permeate Western culture and that will continue to dominate the world. 
The Dalai Lama is aware of these problems; to his credit he states that he is not afraid to face them squarely. 
It is evident to him, as to everyone, that even if he is allowed to return to Tibet and lead his people again, there will be no return to the old ways. 
One would hope, however, that the Tibetan experiment of trying to relate the spiritual to the concrete political realities of the world today would come to benefit all nations and all cultures.
There are some trenchant criticisms in this book of the West, for its lack of spiritual roots like those that nourish Tibet, and it is wholesome for us to hear them. 
But there are also some acknowledgments that Buddhists, and especially Buddhist monks and nuns, have something to learn from Western religions about translating the contemplation of goodness into practical action. 
It is the wish of the Dalai Lama, and, one would hope, of all genuine spiritual leaders, that religion can continue to give to all human beings a sense of the value and dignity of life, of the need to treat the world as sacred and of the desire to live in peace and harmony. 
The vision he has brought down from the roof of the world to the world he is exiled to has been broadened, but not lost.
It is good that the Dalai Lama has found currents in the West, including Western monasticism itself, that are points of contact with his own culture. 
Although the anthropology and the concept of the deity that lie under the two kinds of monasticism are different, the concept that the inner workings of the human spirit must be a part of the full equation of what human existence is all about, and that the human person cannot rely totally on materialism and external stimuli for fullness of life, forms a common ground in all monasticism. 
And it is to be hoped that more contacts between these two traditions will take place. 
Those that have already occurred - I presided over the first international meeting of Catholic and Buddhist monks, in Bangkok in 1968 - have enriched members of religious communities on both sides.
On the other hand, the total domination of intellectual life by monasticism that so characterized old Tibet will, I can safely say, never return. 
Studies for all monks must now go beyond the philosophical and mystical to the scientific. 
By the end of his autobiography it is clear that the Dalai Lama recognizes, as many religious leaders in the West do, that the education of people whose lives are dedicated to religion must change greatly. 
The challenge, for him and the Tibetan Buddhists, as for us in the West, is to retain the best from the past and find new freedom for it to evolve.
Â 
'THERE IS TOO MUCH DEVOTION TOWARD ME'
The Dalai Lama wrote ''Freedom In Exile,'' his autobiography, ''to counter Chinese claims and misinformation they spread about Tibet's history, culture and religion,'' he says, ''and to tell the truth about Tibetan independence.''
In an interview this month at Middlebury College in Vermont, where he was attending a conference on religion and environment, the winner of the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize said: ''Tibet has always been a separate, independent country from China. 
Sun Yat-sen, the father of Chinese democracy, considered Tibet a foreign nation, as did the Chinese Communists before their invasion began in 1949.''
Looking forward to a day when the Chinese occupation of Tibet might end, the Dalai Lama, who wants people to see him as ''a simple Buddhist monk,'' said he would step aside as ruler: ''If I return as the leader, it would be an obstacle to developing a genuine democracy in Tibet. 
There is too much devotion toward me. 
It would be better if I remained outside the Government.''
But, he added, the position of himself and other religious leaders, who traditionally governed the country, ''would be up to the Tibetan people.''
Soon after he fled Tibet in 1959, he wrote an autobiography, ''My Land and My People.''
But in the 1980's a British journalist, Alexander Norman, suggested it was time for a more complete account. 
They worked together on the book. 
Mr. Norman taped the Dalai Lama for several hours at a time and prepared a manuscript from the tapes, which they later rewrote together.
The Dalai Lama now has his headquarters in Dharmsala, India, where he tries to keep abreast of events in his country, in part by personally interviewing every refugee who manages to escape about the fate of families and villages under the Chinese occupation. 
He says there has been a massive deforestation as the Chinese have clear-cut millions of acres of Tibetan forests to sell lumber on the export market; and they are grazing dense herds of sheep on the fragile Tibetan grassland, causing rapid erosion. 
But more devastating has been the continuing oppression of the Tibetan people and suppression of religion and culture. 
Refugees say advocates of independence are routinely jailed and tortured, including many Buddhist monks and nuns.

text:

COME tomorrow, for the Chinese and some of our other friends in Asia, it will be another Year of the Snake.
I was born in China more than 70 years ago and each year around the time of the Chinese New Year, I become somewhat sentimental. 
Often I think about my boyhood days in Beijing. 
Celebrating the New Year in those days was the biggest event of the year, especially for the children.
I remember when I woke up on New Year's Day, I would find some money wrapped in red paper under the pillow. 
This was good-luck money put there by parents and grandparents while the child slept. 
It was a great thrill to open the red wrapper and find a few shining silver dollars.
But the next few days it got even better. 
Whenever you saw a relative or friend who was at least one generation older than you, he or she would give you a red wrapper with some money in it. 
In return, you would bow or prostrate yourself on the floor, wishing him or her a Happy New Year. 
It would become a game, involving physical contact: you trying not to accept the wrapper (it was only an act!) and the other person trying to prevent you from prostrating yourself on the floor.
It usually concluded with a happy ending, with you getting the money. 
Those were the good old days when silver dollars were plentiful in China. 
Beginning in the early 1930's, we got only paper money during the New Year holidays. 
But no one complained. 
In any case, the money usually ended up in a bank account opened by the parents and later used for the education of the children.
When my grandparents were living, there were feasts during the first few days of the New Year. 
Grandpa loved to see all his friends and relatives, and it was not unusual to have 20 or 30 people for dinner at our house. 
There was shark-fin soup, roasted duck, sauteed carp, red-cooked pork and many other delicious dishes. 
We children all wore new clothes and ate candies, fruits and cakes all day long!
The family fortune went downhill after my grandparents passed away, however, and with them also went the big feasts in the house. 
Now only memories linger.
The Chinese zodiac has a 12-year cycle. 
Beside the snake, there are 11 other animals in whose year you could be born. 
They are horse, sheep, monkey, cock, dog, boar, rat, ox, tiger, hare and dragon. 
In 12 more years there will be another Year of the Snake.
If some Chinese tell you in which animal year they were born, you could generally guess their age, provided you remember the order of the animal years. 
For example: before snake it is dragon; after snake it is horse, and so on. 
If they tell you next year that they were born in a Year of the Snake, their age may be 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84 or 96. 
Generally you can tell which age would be most realistic for that person.
Among the famous people born in the Year of the Snake are the actress Brooke Shields, the architect I. M. Pei, John F. Kennedy and Imelda Marcos. 
Many people do not think kindly of the snake. 
Perhaps the Adam and Eve story gave the snake a bad name. 
Yet it has been said that people born in the Year of the Snake are considered to be gentle, tender and generous. 
They are also supposed to be compatible with people born in most of the other animal years.
I was born in the Year of the Hare and my wife in the Year of the Snake. 
We have been married for almost 40 years and, believe it or not, we have argued only three times. 
At least that's what I remember. 
But then, people born in the Year of the Hare are sometimes said to have poor memories. 
Don't you believe it!

text:
ï»¿
Li Ying raised her slender arms and lowered them slowly, gracefully, like a wave falling from its crest, as a flurry of lithe dancers swished back and forth and around her.
For the Chinese audience, accustomed to acrobatics and theatrical drama, it was unusual to see such gentle, understated movements. 
But the audience seemed to absorb this American-style ballet willingly, as they have welcomed many other things Western.
''You can't compare it with what we usually see,'' said a Chinese man who has been interested in ballet for nearly a decade. 
''But it's not bad.''
This work, a simple romance called ''In the Mountain Forest,'' was conceived by an American choreographer, Norman Walker, in what is probably the first cultural exchange between the United States and China since the military crackdown in Beijing on June 3-4. 
Public performances began Thursday and end today.
After the crackdown, the Chinese Government harshly condemned the influence of ''bourgeois liberalism,'' a code-phrase for things Western, particularly American, and several academic and cultural exchange programs were suspended.
Â 
Politics Is Put Aside
The visit by Mr. Walker, a dance professor at Adelphi University in Garden City, L.I., risked being canceled, especially when money for it fell through last summer. 
But this exchange survived, partly because of the decadelong relationship between the Central Ballet of China troupe and Mary Yung Kantor, a Chinese-American who helped organize and pay for the visit.
Both sides have also been careful to leave politics out of any discussion of the exchange. 
''It's a pure cultural exchange,'' said Zhang Heqing, an official with the Central Ballet. 
''The technique is from the West, and the cultural style is from the West, but it's nothing political.''
Both Mr. Walker and Mrs. Kantor said there also was self-censorship on the American side. 
Mr. Walker has excluded sensuous or shocking movements that might offend Chinese artistic sensibilities. 
Moreover, the plot is simple. 
The first act begins with a magnificent spring, and the young girl and boy maturing into adults. 
The second act reveals a romantic summer night encounter between the couple, and finally, in the third act, they wed.
Â 
Talk of Return Visit
''Sensual ballets are not always received well here,'' Mrs. Kantor said. 
''We understand their needs. 
They needed to learn more movements and different pieces.''
Many artists have read the signs of tighter control of the arts, and it has been a cold, dry winter for most of them. 
But in the small circle of Chinese ballet, Mr. Walker's visit has brought new techniques and a new concept of ballet to the 44 dancers -two casts of 22 - who have been working with him since Dec. 
25, when rehearsals for ''In the Mountain Forest'' began.
The score, which concludes with a string of particularly unusual rhythms, has made it difficult for the Chinese dancers to master the ballet. 
But the dancers have absorbed the new techniques eagerly. 
There already have been discussions about having Mr. Walker return this summer.
''They have been trained in the Russian style, so the dance has a sense of presentation,'' Mr. Walker said. 
Thus, the Chinese dancers are accustomed to presenting their gestures in full view of the audience. 
Mr. Walker had to explain to them that their gestures can point inward, even away from the audience.
Â 
Other New Techniques
They have picked up other Western techniques as well.
''He teaches us to use the body to command the movements of arms,'' said Miss Li, a lead dancer. 
''In the past, when we wanted to raise the arm, the arm rose of itself. 
Now the body is directing the movements of the arms.''
Sometimes the Chinese dancers reproduced movements differently from the way Mr. Walker envisioned them, but the revisions were just as suitable. 
''They are capable of a lot of subtlety,'' he said. 
''Chinese people are not direct. 
There's a little bit of a turning away, of not presenting things so squarely. 
It's hard for Americans to get that subtle turn of the body.''
Indeed, Mr. Walker said he had discovered remarkable similarities between Chinese folk dance and American modern dance: the sense of the spectacular, the tricks, turns, leaps, falls and spirals.
Chinese acrobatics are popular, and there is a sense of the acrobatic in the dance as well. 
In another ballet choregraphed by Chinese, two dancers twirled for nearly a minute - a feat that brought an unusual burst of applause from the audience.
Officials involved in the program seemed encouraged by the blend of Chinese music and American choreography. 
The Chinese dancers said Mr. Walker's teaching had helped them develop their own sense of style, especially in an art that had been totally imported.
''He has his own peculiarity in choreography, his own style,'' Wei Tongsheng, a 23-year-old lead dancer, said of Mr. Walker. ''It is necessary to mix what is Chinese with something of the West to form our own.''

text:

OUT of the teapot comes more than the soothing or ceremonial cup. 
Tea can add subtle flavor and rich color to a variety of foods.
While Westerners generally think of tea only as a beverage, the Chinese have used it as a seasoning for centuries. 
And now as more American and French chefs are blending Asian flavors and techniques into their cooking, they too have discovered the pleasures of flavoring with tea.
Perhaps the most traditional use of tea in Chinese cooking is for tea-leaf eggs, a specialty often served on the Chinese New Year because eggs represent rebirth and good fortune.
After hard-boiled eggs are prepared, their shells are gently cracked all over but not removed. 
The eggs are then simmered for about an hour in a mixture of water, soy sauce, star anise and tea leaves. 
The dark, flavorful broth penetrates the cracked shells so when the eggs are finally cooled and peeled they have the look of marbelized porcelain.
Today tea is most frequently used for smoking poultry. 
Nina Simonds, the author of ''Classic Chinese Cuisine'' and ''Chinese Seasons'' (Houghton Mifflin, 1982 and 1986), said the smoking technique originated as a way to preserve foods in the warmer provinces of Sichuan, Hunan and Hubei. 
''A number of flavoring and coloring agents were used,'' she said in a recent interview, ''and among them were camphor, cyprus, bamboo and tea.''
She added that the use of smoke in China has evolved strictly as a flavoring now.''
Among the Chinese restaurants in New York that serve tea-smoked duck are Chin Chin on East 49th Street and Shun Lee West on West 65th Street.
Charles Palmer, the chef and a co-owner of Aureole in Manhattan, serves tea-smoked squab. 
''I do it differently from the Chinese,'' he said. 
''I don't cook the squab first. 
I smoke raw squabs for about 40 minutes, then roast them.''
Mr. Palmer said he first tasted classic tea-smoked duck at Chin Chin. 
''I liked the flavor because it was not as pungent as the taste you get from wood smoking,'' he said. 
''I didn't know exactly how the Chinese did it so I experimented.''
He uses branches of green Greek mountain tea that he buys in Astoria, Queens.
Ken Hom, an author and cooking teacher, said he saw a lot of young American chefs experimenting with tea smoking because ''it's new for them and different from using hickory chips.''
The type of tea used is extremely important. 
''It should be fresh, not old, so it imparts the best flavor and color,'' Ms. Simonds said. 
She prefers China black tea but also said that Lapsang souchong, which has a smoky taste, was very effective.
Not only are smoked foods more popular than ever, but the ease and simplicity of the Chinese technique adds to its appeal. 
It can be done on the kitchen stove in a wok.
The wok is lined with aluminum foil and in it are placed the tea leaves and, usually, some sugar. 
Some recipes also include raw rice with the tea leaves. 
Star anise, dried tangerine peel or cinnamon sticks may also be included for flavor. 
Whole duck, chicken or squab that has been steamed or poached in an aromatic broth is set on a rack over the tea mixture. 
The wok is covered tightly. 
Within minutes after the heat is turned on the tea mixture begins to smoke, seasoning the food and deepening its color.
After 10 to 15 minutes, the heat can be turned off and the food left in the wok to cool.
Occasionally tea leaves are used for stir-frying. 
A specialty of Hangzhou in southern China is stir-fried shrimp seasoned with fresh green dragon well tea leaves. 
In her book ''Chinese Cooking for the American Kitchen'' (Atheneum, 1976), Karen Lee includes a recipe for stir-fried beef with black tea. 
She also uses steeped black tea in sesame paste when making sesame noodles as well as in marinades for barbecuing.
Regardless of the cooking technique, Mr. Hom said it was important not to overdo the tea flavor. 
''It should add subtle depths but not overwhelm,'' he said.
Delicate teas can season rice. 
Yannick Cam, the chef and owner of Le Pavillon in Washington, sometimes uses jasmine tea instead of water for cooking rice to serve with Thai curries. 
In Elizabeth Andoh's first book, ''At Home With Japanese Cooking'' (Alfred A. Knopf, 1980), a dish of rice and chicken or fish is served moistened with hot green tea.
Tea even adds exotic perfume to desserts. 
Green tea has become a standard ice-cream flavor in Chinese and Japanese restaurants. 
Using tea in dessert is also popular among French and American chefs.
Jasmine is used to season a custard at Restaurant Troisgros in Roanne, France. 
Alain Senderens, chef and co-owner of Lucas Carton in Paris, steeps prunes in brandy and black tea. 
A parfait of tea and raisins with warm praline-champagne sauce is also on the menu at Beau Geste, a new French restaurant on the Upper West Side in New York.
In ''Chez Panisse Desserts'' (Random House, 1985), Leslie Remolif Shere includes a recipe for fruit poached in sauterne and seasoned with Darjeeling tea. 
Mr. Palmer uses jasmine tea and tangerine to add subtle flavor to ice cream.
''I think tea is an interesting flavor,'' he said. 
''There's such variation in teas. 
And the funny thing is I never particularly drink tea, but now I use it for cooking.''

text:
ï»¿
As his two children run about his small apartment, dodging his easel and smearing their fingers across his palette, Song Bin paints ''Mona Lisas'' - more than 100 of them so far.
Nearby, in a studio about as big as a queen-size bed, two Chinese artists have been painting European masterpieces by the hundreds. 
Like many other artists who fled from China to Hong Kong, they have given up hope of painting masterpieces of their own and earn money by reproducing the works of others. 
It has become a local cottage industry - copying the tranquil countrysides of Winslow Homer, the Tahitian beauties of Paul Gauguin and the famous works of other well-known painters, to the dot, stroke and hue.
Each year this city, tapping a cheap army of talented artists from the territory of Hong Kong or the neighboring Chinese province of Guangdong, exports thousands of copies of European masterpieces to Europeans and Americans, who choose what they want in mail-order catalogues. 
Patterns and samples are toted across the border to Shenzhen or Canton, and the painted replicas are carried back.
Usually, the artistic result is an adequate replica. 
Buyers know they are not getting the real thing, and the paintings would not fool experts, but the replicas cost a tiny fraction of what the original would bring. 
And if an exact copy seems too kitschy, the buyer can ask the artist to add a tree or a road to tailor the scene to the local environment or even the living-room furniture.
''Americans like the Renoirs, van Goghs and Manets, and they like big paintings,'' said Daniel Chui, the owner of Ultra Art, a Hong Kong company that deals in commercial art. 
''In England, they like Constables or Turners. 
In Germany, they like small portraits and dark paintings of animals and still lifes of flowers.''
A few years ago ''Mona Lisas'' were extremely popular, but the demand seems to have subsided. 
Since last year demand for the great masters has been declining, restricted mainly to buyers in Europe. 
Meanwhile, interest in commercial art - anything from a picture of a puppy to a swirl of lines and dots - has risen, particularly among Americans.
This trend can prove disappointing for the young Chinese artists who may want to paint ''Mona Lisas''; if the buyers want California landscapes, the copyists' study of the old masters suffers. 
Xu Zhicheng, a 28-year-old artist who escaped from China to Hong Kong a decade ago, has been painting more replicas of American landscapes and seascapes than of Turner seascapes.
Copying masterpieces over and over may seem less peculiar to a Chinese artist than to a Westerner. 
It is what Chinese painters have historically done, painting tree after tree and waterfall after waterfall to develop an artistic style. 
On the other hand, artists trained solely in traditional Chinese methods and esthetics might find it difficult not only to adapt to oil paints and Western brushes, but also to understand the enthusiasm of European artists for biblical scenes, fruit, Gothic churches and even nudes. 
Still, they tend to adapt quickly.
''When you look at a masterpiece for the first time, you won't know how to paint it,'' said You Zhong-Ping, who shares the cramped workshop with Mr. Xu. But painting a piece the second time around is much easier, Mr. Xu chimed in, adding that he often retouches the first copy: ''I don't completely understand their way of thinking or their ideology. 
I just paint until it looks right.''
Song Bin believes that an artist must understand the subject he or she is painting. 
Life in Wenzhou, the eastern Chinese city where he was born, differed fundamentally, of course, from the Western life style. 
He studied traditional Chinese painting and woodcut engraving at the Zhejiang Arts School in eastern China and graduated in 1966, on the eve of the Cultural Revolution, an upheaval that eviscerated the country's artistic expression for a decade. 
He came to Hong Kong in 1978.
Now 45, he still tries to bone up on the mores of the European upper classes and the history of the Renaissance and reads library books on art. 
He asks for the best possible pictures of the paintings he is to produce and scours the galleries of Hong Kong for original oil paintings in order to pick up tips on brush strokes, texture and blends of paint. 
''My training in watercolors didn't help much,'' he said.
Having painted the ''Mona Lisa'' so often, Mr. Song said he has learned how to apply the subtle touches of color for her face: a light layer of red, then a bit of yellow highlight and then a thin layer of white, which brings out a slight glow in her cheeks.
The corners of her mouth, he said, are still the hardest to portray because her smile has a feminine and maternal quality that is hard to capture. 
''You can't paint her smile too broadly,'' he said. 
''It's got to be delicate and subtle. 
You must understand her status in society, her personality.''
Copy artists are paid by the piece, according to the type of painting and the quality produced. 
Mr. You explained that a medium-size painting might take three to five days and bring about $200. 
Prices also vary according to genre. 
''French Impressionist paintings are cheaper than the Michelangelos,'' said Song Bin, ''even though the Impressionist works are harder to paint.''
Mr. Song, who calls himself a modern realist painter and relies on copying to support his family, earns about $960 a month, producing about 10 copies a week. 
But it takes him at least a week to paint a ''Mona Lisa,'' he said, and longer if the customer wants a good replica. 
He earns about $250 for a ''Mona Lisa,'' which is sold in Europe or America for much more.
The Hong Kong artists have faced stiff competition recently, as companies have gone directly into China to recruit artists for less money. 
An artist there can earn the equivalent of a month's salary in a week by copying.
Moreover, those artists, too, are eager to learn the Western style of painting. 
Only at China's best academies are artists encouraged to express their emotions and feelings, and to develop a personal style in their art. 
Any training in oil painting is generally scanty.
''They learn about light, color and shading as a set of rules,'' said Wang Yang, the director of the Institute of Chinese Painting and Calligraphy at Shenzhen University, ''but actually it should not be thought of in those terms.''
By copying masterpieces, he said, his students are forced to try to understand the thinking and the spirit of the original artist. 
''The original artist interpreted nature in a certain way. 
By copying, the Chinese artist must also delve into his mind and his own personality to re-create the work.''
Mr. Wang said he also tells his students that although they must absorb Western methods, they must be prepared to discard them in order to create a style of their own. 
Nevertheless, many artists who have been copying for a while acknowledge that though they tire of masterpieces they have painted dozens of times, they are drawn to the European tradition. 
After months or years of immersion in bright yellows and oranges, cathedrals and ballet dancers, copy artists turning to their own work find it hard to revive the simple line and form of the Chinese style and to tone down the brilliant colors favored by Western schools.
For Mr. Song, the daily mimesis of a masterpiece reminds him constantly that his work is not an art but a trade. 
Yet he said the Western style is already so much a part of him that he couldn't abandon it and return to traditional Chinese styles. 
Thedeep colors and splashes of light of Western art challenge him more than does Chinese painting, with its reverence for the line.
''Someday,'' he added, ''I'd like to be able to bring together the drawing of the line with the technique of light and shade.''

text:

President Bush can always count on hundreds of millions of fans in China this fall. 
People here regard him as an old friend and still talk about how he and his wife, Barbara, used to ride their bicycles around Beijing when they lived here in the early 1970's.
Friendship aside, the Government also has another reason to support the incumbent: President Bush will fight Congress to keep China's unconditional "most favored nation" trade status, despite human rights abuses. 
Bill Clinton probably would not. 
That makes this, from China's point of view, a one-issue race.
One indication of Mr. Clinton's thinking is that two exiled dissidents that Beijing considers "counter-revolutionary criminals," Chai Ling and Li Lu, were invited to speak at the Democratic Convention.
Beyond that, most Chinese are not familiar with the campaign issues, and newspapers have devoted little space to the race. 
For example, on the convention's third day the People's Daily published 190 words about the opening ceremony. 
For balance, it also carried a 277-word article describing a Tibetan arts troupe's visit to New York.

The Bush Administration secretly renewed high-level contacts with China in early July, shortly after imposing sanctions over Beijing's crackdown on dissent in June. 
Here is the text of the statement on the sanctions issued by the White House on June 20.
The President today directed that the U.S. 
Government suspend participation in all high-level exchanges of Government officials with the People's Republic of China, in addition to the suspension of military exchanges previously announced. 
This action is being taken in response to the wave of violence and reprisals by the Chinese authorities against those who have called for democracy. 
The United States has supported the legitimate democratic aspirations for freedom of peoples throughout the world. 
The United States will continue to voice its concern and its support for these aspirations.
The United States hopes that the current tragedy in China be brought to a peaceful end and that dialogue will replace the atmosphere of suspicion and reprisal. 
China is an important state with which we hope to continue productive relations.
In addition to the ban on exchanges, the United States will seek to postpone consideration of new international financial institutions' loans to China. 
The situation in China is of international concern, as witnessed by the variety of voices that have spoken up on the issue. 
We urge continued international expressions of concern.

file: WHAT_S DOING IN_ Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
As it sheds the chilly sandstorms and its wintry pall of coal dust, Beijing seems to go through a metamorphosis: the trees and grass in the parks and the bustling activity at temples and monuments and marketplaces light up the place the way color brightens up a drab black and white picture.
Ten million people, winding by on bicycles, jamming their way into buses, and eating noodles as they stand in the streets, is as much a symbol of this country as are the grand Ming palaces, the traditional garden houses, or the imposing memorial to Mao Zedong.
Much of China's precious art and many of its rare books were taken to Taiwan by the Nationalists after their losing war with the Communists in 1949. 
Over the next two decades, many of the capital's grand monuments were pulled down by the Communists or defaced in the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976.
A glance at the city's wide and barren streets and the scores of plain low-roofed buildings belies the grandeur of China's 4,000-year history. 
Behind some of the walls lies China's spiritual past: magnificent temples, grand old houses and the halls of the Chinese emperors. 
Tips of pagoda roofs peep out over their surrounding red walls. 
High arches and red-topped buildings dot even the smallest of public parks.
The central square, a vast plaza of gray pavement highlighted by large meeting halls and groups of statues, is not only the emblem of the state's power but also a reminder that this is a city with layers of history and a place that time and again has endured rampage and reconstruction.
China is not quite a land of plenty, but Beijing has some of the country's best museums, temples, imperial residences, hotels and restaurants.
As a city, Beijing appears to sprawl, but its design has the logic of a chessboard, with main streets running north to south or east to west. 
Tour buses are a convenient way to see the sights, which would otherwise take several days to cover in even a cursory way. 
Aside from the city's center, walking will not take a visitor to too many places.
Bicycling is the best way to see the life of the city. 
Many hotels rent bicycles, and the visitor should take time to ride through the back alleyways, where the people live and the children play.
Â 
What to See
In the central square is the imposing Tian An Men, or the Gate of Heavenly Peace, where Mao stood on the balcony and proclaimed the People's Republic of China on Oct. 
1, 1949. 
A large Mao poster hangs from the ledge near where he stood. 
For much of this century the square has been the focal point of China's political life, the scene of riots and political protests. 
These days the crowds are more likely to gather there to watch foreigners throw a Frisbee around than to start a demonstration.
From the square, the visitor should pass through the Gate of Heavenly Peace. 
Here, in the Forbidden City, the expansive, maze-like old imperial palace of the emperors, it is easy to lose oneself in time and space. 
Hundreds of thousands of laborers took 14 years to build the palace in the early 15th century.
Although many of the jewels and precious art objects were removed this century, the palace's 9,000 decorated rooms, the wide-open grounds and the traditionally ornate yet simple architecture are impressive. 
An exhibit on the last Emperor, Puyi, will last through the year. 
Admission to the Imperial Gardens is 54 cents, $1.35 for the Palace Museum. 
There are also small fees for other exhibits. 
The palace is open daily except Monday, 8:30 A.M. to 4:30 P.M. As with most such sites, visitors should carry small change.
Facing the Gate of Heavenly Peace, across the square, is the Mao Zedong Mausoleum. 
The hall is bordered on the southern side by the Front Gate. 
Free admission; open daily 8 A.M. to noon.
To the west side of the square is the Great Hall of the People, where the National People's Congress meets and where visiting dignitaries are entertained at banquets. 
If the congress is not in session visitors can take a look inside. 
Admission: $1.35; open daily 8:30 A.M. to 11 A.M., 1 P.M. to 3:30 P.M. Opposite the great hall are two of the city's largest museums on Chinese history and the Communist Revolution. 
Admission: 8 cents; spring and summer hours are 8:30 A.M. to 3:30 P.M., closed Monday.
South of the Front Gate is the Temple of Heaven, where the Emperor journeyed in procession from the Forbidden City to pray before the winter solstice. 
Admission: 27 cents.
On Yonghegong Street, in the northeast, is the Palace Temple, a large and elegant Tibetan Buddhist shrine. 
Built in the early Qing dynasty as an imperial residence, it was converted in the mid-18th century to a lamasery for monks from Mongolia and Tibet. 
In the last and largest hall, a four-story Buddha carved from sandalwood and draped in yellow satin towers over fruit offerings and yak-butter candlesticks that are lighted in ceremony. 
Admission: 27 cents; open 9 A.M. to 4:30 P.M., closed Monday.
Day trips to the Summer Palace and the Great Wall, outside the central city, are well worthwhile. 
Most hotels can arrange bus tours to them.
Â 
Where to Shop
Shopping in Beijing falls short of the delights of sightseeing, but by strolling through the handful of free markets, opened only in the last few years, the visitor glimpses a livelier side of Chinese society. 
Foreigners are supposed to use an official currency, called the foreign exchange certificate, which is different from the common renminbi used by the Chinese. 
Bargaining is possible in some of the free markets, but when discussing prices, remember that the certificates are worth up to 70 percent more than the renminbi.
Liulichang, southwest of the Front Gate, is a long street flanked by state-run antique shops where many travelers pick up a few Chinese-style vases or calligraphy works. 
Even window-shoppers may marvel at the thousand-year-old coins, the elaborate golden clocks or the watercolor landscapes. 
Fakes are said to abound, so the visitor should be careful, even if the shop offers certificates of authenticity. 
Prices are high and fixed. 
A seemingly simple calligraphy may cost $1,000.
Nearer to the Front Gate is Dazhalan, or the Big Fence, an old, narrow but lively street that used to be the only place where the local Chinese shopped for shoes, silk, toys, acrobat accoutrements, or just went to see the movies. 
The street has lost its monopoly as other stores around the city have opened up, but it is still full of crowds and color.
Wangfujing, the street east of the Beijing Hotel, has many specialty stores, as well as the city's largest department store, offering everything from scarves to shoes to furs, silks and candy. 
Similarly, the Friendship Store, on Jianguomenwai Street, near the Jianguo Hotel, sells wood carvings, paintings, books, chocolates and vases.
Â 
Where to Eat Beijing has some of the best restaurants in China, but visitors should remember that the Chinese tend to eat early. 
A hotel employee should be asked to write down the name and address of a restaurant in Chinese and visitors might have to pay the taxi driver to wait through dinner if they want a ride back to the hotel.
Travelers should not leave the city without tasting the famous Peking duck. 
Quanjude Duck House, 24 Qianmen West Street (701-1379), at the Peace Gate, is the best of its kind. 
A few side dishes can also be ordered, but menus tend to follow a set plan, with all parts of the duck - hearts, kidneys, livers, legs and tongues - offered as preludes to the main dish. 
The meal usually ends with candied apples and fresh oranges. 
Your hotel can make reservations for you in Chinese.
The spacious Dongfang Mingzhu Restaurant, also known as the Beijing Orient Restaurant, offers a modern atmosphere and the best variety of Cantonese dim sum (about $7 a person) as well as very good dinner dishes, mostly Cantonese (about $9.50 a person). 
The restaurant, 4 Zheng Yang Market, Qian Men West Street (301-6668), will help call a taxi for the ride home.
For delicious Shandong-style dishes in a classy thatched-roof setting, try the Beijing Du Yi Ju Restaurant. 
Shandong cuisine has influenced much of Chinese food as we know it today and this spot's manager is one of China's top chefs. 
Fixed menus are the custom ranging from about $16 to $150 a person. 
Reservations are recommended and the restaurant can order a taxi for your trip back to the hotel (Qi Jia Huozi on De Sheng Men Wai Street, tel. 
449-471 or 449-313).
Windows on the World, on the 28th floor of the Citic building on Jianguomenwai Street (500-2255), is also a delightful Cantonese restaurant where dinner costs about $10 a person. 
The fried milk is worth a try. 
For more elegance, taste the Cantonese food at Shang Palace at the Shangri-La Beijing Hotel ($15 a person; 831-2211) or the Sichuan dishes at Yuntai Restaurant at the Great Wall Sheraton ($23 a person; 500-5566).
Â 
Where to Stay
The new east wing of the Beijing Hotel (33 East Changan Street; 513-7766, extension 444), which used to be the only spot where foreigners were allowed to stay, is in a central location. 
A small double room costs $66.50, plus a 10 percent service charge, which all hotels in China customarily add. 
Standard rooms at the Zhaolong Hotel (2 Gongti North Road; 500-2299), in the northeastern area of the city, are $86. 
Double rooms at the Jianguo Hotel (5 Jianguomenwai Street; 500-2233), not far from the city center, cost $100. 
A short walk away is the Hotel Beijing-Toronto (Jianguomenwai Street; 500-2266), where standard rooms are $110.
The hotels with the best service (and the highest prices) are managed by foreigners. 
Standard rooms are $120 at the Holiday Inn Lido (Jichang Road; 500-6688), which is close to the airport, $140 at the Great Wall Sheraton (Donghuan North Road; 500-5566), and $165 at the Shangri-La Hotel Beijing (29 Zizhuyuan Road; 831-2211).
Â 
Night Life
Night life for the Chinese has recently centered around the television set, a new possession for many families. 
Chinese do not tend to drink much alcohol, but in the past year a couple of Chinese-run bars have opened up that offer imported liquors, beer and wine. 
Customers can also sing along to recorded music, Japanese-style. 
The Beijing Haiwei Wine Bar, on the third floor of the small shopping center on Hualong Street in the Nanheyan district, offers a modern sound and video system where many Japanese and Chinese go to sing their hearts out. 
Admission: $2.70; telephone 512-5146.
The Beijing Opera is still a popular spectacle among visitors, even though the drama of sing-song cries and whispers is a dwindling tradition among the younger generation here. 
Three opera houses cater to visitors: Changan Theater, 126 Changan Street, 655-915; Tianqiao Theater 30 Beiwei Road, Xuanwuqu, 330-513 or 330-300, and the Ji Xiang Theater, 14 Jinyu Hutong, 555-501. 
Schedules tend to be made known only at the last minute.
Most major hotels also have discotheques. 
The Cosmos Club is at the Great Wall Sheraton (cover charge $9.50; 8 P.M. to 1 A.M., closed Monday), Xanadu at the Shangri-La Beijing (cover charge $6.75; open every day 8:30 P.M. to 2 A.M.) and the Glass House at the Kunlun Hotel (cover charge $8.10; open every day 8 P.M. to 1 A.M.). 
Local Chinese are allowed only at the Kunlun.
Night markets have become bustling events, especially the one east of the Beijing Hotel on Changan Street, where even observers are pulled into the action by white-uniformed vendors trying to lure customers to their stalls for a dime or quarter snack. 
Whether it is spicy Sichuan noodles, fish ball soup, fried chicken legs or stuffed salty cakes, the local Chinese eat their fare standing up. 
Most foreigners tend to prefer the delicacies at more established restaurants, but the scene is lively.

text:
ï»¿
It is this time of year, as winter slips into spring and residents shed their furs and overcoats, that Hong Kong's eternal bustle accelerates a bit. 
Instead of hurtling about inside their office towers and shopping arcades, people careen along the sidewalks in their rush to get somewhere. 
The frenzy moves outdoors, to the markets, to the parks and to the harbor with its European yachts and Chinese junks.
Defining Hong Kong is a bit like defining a stew, for this is a territory with a bit of everything. 
Mirrored skyscrapers, sprawling mansions in the hills and spacious shopping malls with water-splashing fountains create a picture of modernism. 
I. M. Pei's stark, geometric monument for the mainland's Bank of China juts out in the skyline, as below, specks of white that are the yachts of the wealthy glide silently through the ''fragrant harbor,'' as Hong Kong is called in Chinese.
Just a few blocks away the image shifts to an older, poorer Hong Kong, where fish and vegetables are sold in the street, where fruit and meats are offered to the ancestral gods and where English is barely understood.
Hong Kong's 5.7 million people fit snugly onto this 413-square-mile territory off the southern coast of China, and yet while it is crowded - overwhelmingly so at times - it is a good spot for walking. 
Streets are small and the shops, which line them everywhere, make the streets more lively to walk through. 
A taxi can easily be hired, but it is more fun to walk and cars often seem to be too big for the roads one wants to go down. 
Buses are also convenient, and the subway system embarrasses the American varieties with its combination of efficiency and low cost. 
The cost of a bus or subway ride varies depending on the length of the trip, but it is generally between 20 and 85 cents.
Shopping is perhaps the prime activity in Hong Kong. 
But there are other things to do in the city, where the flavors of ancient customs still linger in the back alleys, the hidden temples and old teahouses.
Â 
Things to See
The Peak is far more than just a tall, pointy mountain. 
It is physically beautiful, even when the mist wafts in during the sunsets; on a fresh, clear day it offers one of the most expansive views of Hong Kong. 
By day, a sharp-eyed visitor may be able to see the New Territories to the north; by night the sparkling lights of the city glisten against the water in the still harbor below.
Such views have made the Peak one of the most coveted residential areas, a symbol for many of the rich local inhabitants that this is an enclave one attains through accomplishment. 
It is also a place where many foreign expatriates live and the home of elegant dinner parties, small private swimming pools and beautiful gardens.
For those who want to exercise, there are plenty of small roads that wind through small woods and grass. 
Try Mount Austin Road, where one can stroll - and perspire a little - and peer out over the mountainside at the expanse of the surrounding colony. 
The Peak Tram, more than 100 years old, will make you grab for a handle because of the sensation that the back is where the feet should be. 
The tram station is one block above the Hilton Hotel in the Central district, and the ride up, about every 15 minutes, costs around $1.70.
Hong Kong is divided into districts, among them Central, Tsim Sha Tsui and Wanchai. 
The subway, or Mass Transit Railway, stops at each of these places, but if you want to get to Tsim Sha Tsui from Central (or vice versa), take the Star Ferry. 
The stark contrast between the modern glass buildings and the strong, salty breeze during this short trip across the harbor is one of the hallmarks that keeps Hong Kong from being just another big city. 
The Star Ferry, which costs about 13 cents, leaves from the terminal by the docks in Central.
The south side of Hong Kong Island is very scenic, and its sandy beaches attract hundreds of people.
A visit to Stanley Market, Repulse Bay and Aberdeen would make a pleasant afternoon. 
Catch Bus No. 6 or 260 to Stanley at the Exchange Square Terminal in Central (a taxi would be a bit more than $6). 
Although Stanley is a residential area with long, sandy beaches, its main attraction for tourists is the sprawling street market. 
A patient shopper should enjoy walking through the narrow streets packed with stalls and stores, where famous-brand jeans (often less than $20), sweaters and all sorts of cheaper clothing are sometimes piled up on a counter. 
The clothes may be overruns, imitations or irregulars from the many factory outlets, so be careful.
One of the most interesting temples is the Wong Tai Sin temple, near the M.T.R. 
Wong Tai Sin Station on the Kowloon side. 
There on a weekend people can be seen praying to Taoist gods. 
It is a large smoke-filled complex, with several different halls, where people present all sorts of elaborately prepared meats and other offerings to the deities.
Â 
Shopping
It is often fun just to wander through the small shops or the large malls in Tsim Sha Tsui, or the Japanese department stores and clothing boutiques in Causeway Bay. 
Individual shops have their own business hours but generally close around 8 P.M. here, and after they close there is always the night street market on Temple Street, near Jordan Road.
A shopping guide is invaluable. 
There are several books on the subject, but the Hong Kong Tourist Association puts out a free publication, ''The Official Guide to Shopping and Eating Out,'' which lists shops as well as restaurants approved for membership by the association. 
Virtually anything can be found on sale, from Chinese art to Indian rugs to furs to computers to furniture to watches to jewelry.
Hong Kong is one of the world's major markets for diamonds and other gemstones, partly because there is no tax or duty on jewelry. 
In general, shoppers should be wary, especially when buying jewels or antiques, and it may be better to stick to the more reputable stores, even if their prices are a bit higher. 
The tourist association book is a good guideline, and make sure that the receipt shows a full description of the precious metal or gem. 
All the top hotels should have reliable jewelry shops. 
One good place to visit is Town and Country Jewellery (31 Queen's Road Central, in Central; 5225843).
Women's clothes are sold virtually everywhere. 
Some of the best buys can be found in the factory outlets upstairs in the Pedder Building, 12 Pedder Street, in Central. 
The shops across the street in the Landmark Building, and then farther east in the Prince's Building and Mandarin Oriental Hotel also have designer wear, at designer prices. 
For lower quality goods at rock bottom prices, try Li Yuen Street East and Li Yuen Street West, which brim with leather purses and bags, scarves, watches and blouses.
Hong Kong is full of tailors, most of whom specialize in men's suits. 
A tailored suit will cost somewhat more than a comparable suit off the rack at home, but the fit is usually much better. 
Tailors generally require a week and at least two fittings to make suits. 
Try A-Man Hing Cheong (unit M10, mezzanine floor of the Mandarin Oriental Hotel in Central; 5223336). 
Wool men's suits at A-Man start at about $450.
Â 
Eating Out
Hong Kong offers both Western and Asian food, but naturally, Chinese food is its specialty. 
It is best to make reservations at the best places, and even so, one may have to wait. 
Cantonese food, stir-fried quickly at high heat, is the most widely available, but all kinds of Chinese cuisines are represented. 
Try the roast duck at the Grand House of Yung Kee Restaurant, which is usually full, even though it has floors and floors of space (36-40 Wellington Street, in Central; 5221624). 
About $12 to $15 a person. 
The seafood at Tai Woo Restaurant, just across the street, is very tasty (15-19 Wellington Street; 5245618). 
About $15 a person.
For some of the best Shanghainese cuisine try the Wu Kong Shanghai Restaurant (27 Nathan Road, Alpha House Basement, Kowloon; 3667244). 
About $10 a person. 
Cleveland Szechuan Restaurant is good for the spicy Chinese cooking - especially the sizzling prawns - from Sichuan Province in the heartland of China (6 Cleveland Street, Flat C, Causeway Bay; 5763876). 
About $13 a person.
For Cantonese dim sum, which are dumplings served at lunchtime, try the Luk Yu Tea House and Restaurant (26 Stanley Street, in Central; 5235464). 
This is a favorite spot for old Chinese. 
There are no carts, which is what many dim sum houses use to bring around the food. 
If there isn't an English-speaking waiter available you may have to point, but the culinary experience is worth it, and costs only about $6 a person.
For a quieter atmosphere, try the Rainbow Room at the Lee Gardens Hotel (Hysan Avenue, Causeway Bay; 8953311). 
About $13 a person.
Â 
Where to Stay
Accommodations are not cheap, but they are generally excellent. 
The two most convenient districts are Tsim Sha Tsui and Central. 
Hotel rates change frequently, and visitors should ask for special winter rates, which some places offer. 
Add a 10 to 15 percent service charge and 5 percent government tax to all regular hotel rates. 
All prices quoted are for a standard double room.
The Regent, perhaps the most luxurious hotel, is a clay-red modern building with a spectacular view of the harbor. 
Rooms are $190 without a view, $256 with a view (Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 7211211).
Across the way is the grande dame of Hong Kong hotels, the Peninsula, oozing charm and history. 
Parts of it will be renovated this spring. 
Standard rooms are $276 (Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 3666251); The Mandarin Oriental (5 Connaught Road, Central; 5220111) is often ranked among the top three in the world. 
Rooms run from $192 (standard) to $308 (deluxe). 
At the well-located Hilton, rooms run $185 (2 Queen's Road, Central; 5233111). 
For those who want to stay as close to the shopping as possible, and yet save some money, try the Royal Garden, where excellent accommodations are $135 (69 Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui East, Kowloon; 7215215).
It may be a little out of the way, but the newly opened Grand Hyatt offers standard rooms for about $140 (1 Harbour Road, Wanchai; 8611234). 
Standard rooms at the New World, by the harbor right next to the Regent, run about $154, but there are smaller, cheaper rooms for $101 (22 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 3694111). 
At the Y.M.C.A. 
(Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 3692211) rooms cost $62. 
Book as far in advance as possible.
Budget choice: Harbour View International House (4 Harbour Road, Wanchai; 5201111) Rooms are $64.

file: WHAT_S DOING IN_ Singapore.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a remarkable combination of will, foresight and happenstance, what began as a swampy island only 85 miles from the Equator has been transformed into the most modern, efficient and simply the cleanest city of Southeast Asia. 
The last is not a bad attribute in a part of the world where sanitation is more talked about than practiced.
Singapore, a city-state of just 2.6 million people and possessing almost no natural resources except its harbor, rides along on a swift current of capital and financial services. 
It is, with Hong Kong, the most unashamedly materialistic society in the region - status conscious, a touch insecure, eager to taste, hear, see or drink what someone, usually in the West, has decided is ''the latest.''
So everything from Indonesian batik to Italian designers, from Chinese silk to the newest Japanese electronic devices, is available here, and usually at low, open-to-bargaining prices comparable to Hong Kong's.
A multiracial society of immigrants, Singapore's mosaic of Asian cultures can be enthralling, with significant contributions from the Chinese, the Malays and the Indians, who, respectively, make up 76 percent, 15 percent and 6.5 percent of the population. 
Conveniently for the American visitor, however, this variety is in the context of a largely English-speaking society, and people live amid a low degree of racial tension.
Altogether, then, Singapore is the easiest introduction any foreigner can have to Asia, a comfortable place with fine hotels, transportation and tourist services, with lots of stuff for the kids, restaurants of nearly every recognized cuisine and yet still the living embodiment of some of exotic Asia's most important cultural and religious influences.
Slowly, even a paternalistic Government obsessed with modernity and convinced that any problem can be solved by ''twiddling the knobs'' of social control has learned to try to preserve the city's cultural and architectural heritage - and just in time, too, before the last Chinese shop-house died for the 100th skyscraper.
Singapore's paternalism also has an element of social control and collective propriety. 
For the residents, this includes restrictions on the kinds of dogs allowed in public housing and fines for littering, not flushing the toilet or urinating in elevators.
For tourists, however, these are not normally major difficulties, though there are increasingly stiff restrictions on where one can smoke. 
In addition one risks the death penalty for drug use, and long hair on men has been sometimes known to create difficulties at immigration counters.
But the pleasures of picking at Singapore's contradictions, which are, of course, as fascinating as its felicities, can wait for a second or third visit.
It's a place where you can shop till you drop, eat till you pop and then plop into the swimming pool. 
Then you can do penance by seeing a Chinese temple or a Malay cultural show, or by taking the kids to one of the best zoos (cageless, in the modern style) or bird parks in Asia. 
The Singapore Zoological Gardens is on Mandai Lake Road and is open 8:30 A.M. to 6 P.M. daily. 
Admission: $2.65, $1.30 for children under 12; telephone 269-3411. 
The Jurong Bird Park is on Jalan Ahmed Ibrahim, open 9 A.M. to 6 P.M., with shows at 10, 10:30, 3 and 4, featuring swooping eagles, hawks, owls and even a condor. 
Admission is the same as the zoo; 265-0022.
Â 
Things to See
Two popular attractions, the National Museum and the eccentric Tiger Balm Gardens, a Chinese Disneyland built by the Aw brothers with their fortune from Tiger Balm, the the liniment, are closed for renovation, at least until the middle of next year.
Empress Place, one of the most successful renovation projects in Singapore, is worth a morning. 
It was built in 1854 as a courthouse, and has been carefully transformed into a museum and exhibition center. 
Until March the museum is showing artifacts from China's Qing dynasty, its last, on loan from the Shenyang Palace Museum. 
Open 9:30 A.M. to 9:30 P.M. daily. 
Admission $3.15; children $1.60.
Singaporeans love birds, and another nice diversion are the songbird cafes, which are less hokey than they sound. 
At the corner of Tiong Bahru and Seng Poh Roads is an unassuming coffee shop, its lot surmounted by poles. 
Handcarved wooden and wicker cages hang from them, while the songbirds inside go through their paces, apparently learning from their neighbors.
Don't forget to note the grasshopper vendor near the coffee shop who provides the birds' munchies. 
The coffee isn't great, but it's a nice way to spend part of a morning. 
The times are roughly 7 A.M. to 11 A.M.; Sundays at 8 A.M. there is a sort of concert.
Â 
Neighborhoods
Given Singapore's size, a standard city tour will provide good orientation and it barely takes a morning. 
Tours cost about $11, $6 for children; most include a sort of ''instant Asia'' cultural show. 
Ask at your hotel or the Singapore Tourist Promotion Board, Raffles City Tower, 250 North Bridge Road (339-6622). 
There is also a potted ''Contrasting Culture'' tour that will take you through what's left of the ethnic neighborhoods.
You'll see Arab Street, in the southeast, a Muslim sector, Chinatown and Little India, along Serangoon Road.
But go back on your own to chat and browse, particularly in Chinatown. 
On Telok Ayer Street is a favorite temple, Thian Hock Keng, the Temple of Heavenly Happiness, where new migrants to Singapore came to pay their respects to Ma Chu Poh, the goddess of the sea.
What began as a josshouse is now a relatively stately temple, with an iron gate imported from Glasgow. 
But the grounds also served as a place of rest and refuge for weary immigrants from Hokkien, many of whom used to smoke opium to relax after a long day of aching labor. 
They would smear opium on the mouths of the goddess's guardians, two statues that flank her own, and give them more to smoke.
Opium, like all such drugs, is illegal now in Singapore. 
Yet even today, what appears to be fresh opium is found smeared on the mouths of the guardians. 
Sometimes, in the evenings, from the rear of the temple grounds, comes the sickly smell of burning opium, tolerated still, or so it seems, for a founding generation quickly passing.
Â 
Getting Around
Singapore has a new subway system, called the M.R.T., or Mass Rapid Transit, and it is clean, quiet and cheap, with fares from about a quarter to 75 cents. 
It works with a magnetic ticket, rather like the Washington, D.C., subway. 
Sometime next year all 42 stations will be in operation.
Recently more stations opened on the east-west lines, so residential areas for the Malay community are accessible. 
One such district, on the east coast, is known as Geylang Serai. 
If you get off at the Eunos Station, you can look at the local market, a lively emporium where the prices are cheap, bargaining is good-natured (and hence serious) and the tour buses don't go. 
It's a good place to meet people and talk to them about their lives, while picking up some batik.
The bus system offers Explorer tickets good for one ($2.60) or three days ($6.30), available at hotels, tour agents and the bus authority (205 Braddell Road; 287-2727).
Taxis are also reasonable, and all are metered and clean. 
And in this carefully regulated city the taxi drivers are honest, or else.
Â 
Orchard Road
One of Singapore's most genuine sights, of course, is the area around Orchard Road, which is devoted to shopping, eating and people-watching. 
The place to start bargain hunting is the Tangs store at No. 320. Swiss watches, gold jewelry, perfume, cosmetics and electrical items are especially good buys. 
Also, surprisingly, Oriental carpets. 
Stay away from the cheap tailors - go to Hong Kong or even Bangkok for that.
It is perfectly legal, by the way, to change money with the many money changers, and the rates are better than at the bank.
Â 
Where to Stay
The days of ready discounts in Singapore hotels are over, at least until a lot more rooms are added in 1991. 
It's worth getting your travel agent to ask, but don't expect miracles. 
All hotels charge a 3 percent tax, soon to be 4 percent, and a 10 percent service charge on top of rates. 
They discourage further tipping but that doesn't mean you can't.
For Orchard Road shopping trips, the Hilton is almost ideally situated at No. 581 (737-2233). 
Doubles go for about $126, and it's a decent, well-run place. 
In roughly the same area and price category, the Hyatt Regency, at 10-12 Scotts Road (733-1188), offers doubles for $131.
Also on Scotts Road, at No. 22, is the Goodwood Park Hotel, a whimsical-looking building, formerly the German Club, that has pleasant public spaces and excellent Asian food.
The Shangri-La Hotel, 22 Orange Grove Road (737-3644), offers some doubles for $121. 
It's a fine hotel, but a bit far to walk from Orchard Road.
For a slightly cheaper stay: the pagoda-like Dynasty Hotel, attached to Tang's at 320 Orchard Road (734-9900). 
Doubles start at $110.
Bargain choices: The Ladyhill Hotel, 1 Ladyhill Road (737-2111), owned by the Goodwood Group, with doubles at $63, or the Cockpit Hotel, 67 Oxley Rise Penang Road (737-9111), with doubles at $74. 
The Cockpit has the sanction of Raffles Hotel, now closed for renovations until mid-1991, to make the original Singapore Sling, which is better than the imitations.
Â 
Where to Eat
For a good Malay meal in a cozy setting: Aziza's Restaurant, 36 Emerald Hill Road; 235-1130 or 732-9491. 
A meal for two with wine or beer: $40.
For Indonesian-Malay food, try the Sanur Indonesian Restaurant, fourth level, Centrepoint Shopping Center, 176 Orchard Road; 734-2192 or 734-2249. 
Meal for two: $20.
The Hyatt Regency has a nouvelle-American restaurant, Nutmegs, that can make a nice break from a long bout of Asian cuisine. 
Good crab cakes and ice cream, especially a mango sorbet of unmatched texture and perfume. 
Dinner for two, with wine and sorbet: about $95.
At the Goodwood Park Hotel, the Min Jiang is thought by many to be the best Sichuan restaurant in Singapore (about $50 for two, with beer). 
A new and elegant Shanghainese restaurant at the same hotel, the Chang Jiang, still has some teething problems, but a compelling menu (about $65 for two, if you stay away from shark's fin and abalone).
For excellent and inexpensive North Indian food, try Moti Mahal, 18 Murray Street (Food Alley); 221-4338. 
A meal for two with wine or beer: $25.
