file: WHAT_S DOING IN_Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
Wintertime in Hong Kong is cool and clear and generally sunny. 
And while this is not a peak season for tourists, it is nevertheless a wonderful time to visit, because the colony is at its most festive, decked out in lights and flowers for Chinese New Year next month, welcoming performers from around the world for its annual arts festival, and adding special exotic winter dishes to its restaurant menus.
Indeed, while January brings some markedly lower hotel rates and big sales in department stores and boutiques, those savings don't signal a colony suffering from the winter doldrums. 
The Arts Festival, the centerpiece of the winter season here, has grown into an important cultural institution, which gets grander each year. 
The Festival, which opens on Jan. 
19 and runs through Feb. 
10, features Asian and Western performers. 
And as this is still a British Crown Colony -- until it reverts to Chinese control in 1997 -- British performers are always well represented.
This year's highlights include performances of Mozart's " Marriage of Figaro" with an international cast, produced by Stephen Lawless, who has worked with Sir Peter Hall on productions for the Glyndebourne Festival Opera. 
"Figaro" will be performed on Jan. 
19, 21, 23, 25 and 27. 
Britain's Royal Shakespeare Company will present its acclaimed production of "Les Liasons Dangereuses" Jan 20 to 25 and Cheek by Jowl, a noted British touring company, will present "Hamlet" from Jan. 
27 to 31. 
Music lovers can hear the City of Birmingham Orchestra from England, conducted by Simon Rattle, from Jan. 
30 to Feb. 
1, as well as a number of other groups, including the Orpheus Chamber Orchestra from New York (Jan. 
24 to 26), and the Early Brass Ensemble of Toulouse, France (Feb. 
4 and 5).
Asian offerings include the Shanghai Symphony Orchestra (Feb. 
4), Pro Musica Nipponia performing the classical music of Japan (Jan. 
27 and 28), and the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra playing new works on traditional Chinese instruments (Feb. 
8).
This year's event also features a special U.S.A. 
Dance Series, including performances by the Joffrey Ballet (Feb. 
1 to 3) and the American Ballroom Theater (Jan. 
27 to 29), where beautifully costumed dancers glide, spin and boogie through a host of ballroom styles.
Many of the performances will take place in the colony's new Cultural Center, which sits on the harbor, just a block from the Star Ferry Terminal in Kowloon. 
Ticket prices range from a high of $64 (best seat for the opera) to $3.80. 
Tickets and performance information are available at a number of outlets, including the Cultural Center, and, on the Hong Kong side of the Star Ferry, at City Hall. 
For Festival booklets and information on ticket outlets, call the Hong Kong Arts Festival Society (529-5555) or the Hong Kong Tourist Association (801-7111; 35th Floor, Jardine House, 1 Connaught Place, Central District). 
In the United States, the association has an office at 590 Fifth Avenue, New York, N.Y. 
10036; 212-869-5008.
Chinese New Year is a three-day holiday, which this year (the year of the sheep) falls on Feb. 
15, 16 and 17. 
Anyone planning to visit Hong Kong should try to come before or after those days, as most Hong Kong stores and restaurants shut down then. 
The airport and the train stations are very crowded at that time, too.
Â 
Sights and Walks
The cool weather makes this an ideal time for hiking around one of the 236 out-islands that make up Hong Kong, and this year thousands of visitors will be making their way to Lantau Island to see what the Buddhist monks there say is the largest outdoor bronze Buddha statue in the world, a statue that is seven stories high and was just recently completed. 
Choose a sunny weekday (Lantau is jammed with day trippers on weekends), buy a first-class ticket at the pier in Central District ($2 round trip) and sit out on the deck and watch Hong Kong's fascinating harbor slip by.
Buses from the ferry terminal take visitors up a narrow winding mountain road to the Po Lin Monastery, a collection of traditional red buildings with ornate gold roofs set in a tranquil mountaintop garden. 
Visitors can take their own lunches and eat in the garden or share the monk's vegetarian meals -- the crispy egg rolls are legendary -- for just a few dollars. 
The Buddha, cast in bronze in China, is just up the road.
Twice the size of Hong Kong Island, but with only 16,000 people, Lantau has some breathtaking mountain and coastal views, and in spots, one can see real rural Chinese life in its little farming and fishing villages. 
There are miles of marked mountain trails and stone paths laid down by villagers hundreds of year ago; the remains of several 18th-century stone forts built to protect against pirates and opium smugglers; a tea plantation and a Trappist dairy farm that supplies milk to the Hilton Hotel in Hong Kong. 
Visitors can explore the island on their own or opt for a tour package offered by private operators.
Back on frenetic Hong Kong Island, new attractions include the towering Bank of China Building (1 Garden Road, Central) designed by I. M. Pei, all glass and glitter and angles, with two big radio antennas on top that help make it, at 1,034 feet, Asia's tallest building. 
The bank dominates the skyline, and is seen as a symbol of China's future dominance of the colony. 
The Chinese control access to the top of the tower, which is closed to the public, so for a sweeping view of the colony, the best place is still the top of Victoria Peak, just behind Central Hong Kong. 
The Peak Tram funicular is a bargain at $1.66 round trip. 
A free observation desk is in the Tram Station at the top of the Peak.
Â 
Hotels
The outstanding hotels here have put together some winter packages that unless indicated include tax and service charges. 
At the legendary Mandarin Oriental Hotel (5 Connaught Road, Hong Kong; 522-0111) a Winter Break package, at $466, consists of two nights in a superior double room, $202 for each additional night. 
Valid to March 31.
The Regent Hotel (Salisbury Road, Kowloon; 721-1211), consistently ranked as one of the top hotels in the world, is offering a special package from Feb. 
1 to March 3, with two nights in a double room at $400, extra nights $200 plus 15 percent service and tax.
The Ramada Renaissance (8 Peking Road, Kowloon; 311-3311) in the heart of the Tsim Sha Tsui shopping district is offering a two-night package for $294, and $130 for each additional night. 
Valid until March 31.
Budget choice: The Harbor View International House (4 Harbor Road, Wanchai, Hong Kong; 520-1111) is a clean, bright hotel not far from Central. 
It offers a double room with a harbor view for $83 a night plus 10 percent service charge.
The Y.M.C.A. 
(41 Salisbury Road, Kowloon; 369-2211) is a sparkling new building with one of the best locations in Hong Kong. 
A double room is $66.60 plus 10 percent. 
No room service or gym, however.
Â 
Restaurants
Hong Kong is justly famous for its food, and indeed is a place where dining out is the preferred form of entertainment. 
Generally, even the priciest places here are much less expensive than their New York counterparts. 
It is advisable to make reservations.
For a splurge, and a taste of Cantonese haute cuisine, try the elegant Man Wah Restaurant atop the Mandarin Hotel (522-0111). 
Special winter dishes include braised supreme snake soup ($11.50 per bowl) and a wintry hot pot that the restaurant calls Chinese fondue. 
That meal features 13 ingredients, including fresh prawns, scallops, crab claw and fresh vegetables, which you cook at your table, dipping them into a pot of hot broth, and costs $36 per person. 
Dinner for two with a glass of wine runs to about $70.
Cleveland Sichuan (6 Cleveland Street, Causeway Bay; 576-3876) is a comfortable restaurant with good spicy food and a number of sizzling dishes that the local Chinese love -- hot, hot metal platters of fish, meat or chicken that sizzle and smoke when doused in a sauce. 
The sizzling beef with spring onions and garlic is excellent. 
Dinner for two with drinks about $50.
Another fine Sichuan restaurant is the Red Pepper (7 Lan Fong Road, Causeway Bay; 576-8046) a plain, family run eatery with good spicy food like eggplant with hot garlic sauce, and chili and garlic prawns. 
Dinner for two with drinks about $40.
Spring Deer (42 Mody Road, Kowloon; 366-4012) is a homey, second-floor Peking restaurant justly noted for its delicious Peking Duck, which can be ordered on the spot. 
Dinner for two with drinks about $45.
Sun Hung Cheung Hing (45A Kimberley Road, Kowloon; 369-3435) is a real working-class restaurant that offers a Mongolian barbecue. 
Each table is equipped with a big metal hot plate. 
Order plates of chicken, beef and squid and prawns. 
They come with a half-dozen small plates of fresh vegetables, together with coriander, leeks and spring onions, great spicy barbecue sauce, soy sauce and oil. 
Pour oil on the hot plate, dip the meat in the sauce and throw it on the hot plate with the vegetables. 
Dinner for two with drinks about $25.
Â 
Shopping
January is the month of big sales, and one great bargain spot for women is the TakPac Shop (Room 301, Peddar Building, 12 Peddar Street, Central District), which offers Ann Klein II clothes at about a third less than in the United States, and in January, fall and winter clothes are marked down another 30 to 50 percent. 
A wool blazer, part of this season's line, sells for $64 to $128, while a longsleeved silk blouse is priced from $50 to $77.
For a man, no trip to Hong Kong is complete without a visit to a custom tailor, and there are literally hundreds. 
Seasoned travelers know to visit the tailor as soon as they arrive, so that the work can begin and the necessary fittings (a minimum of two for a suit) can be arranged. 
Prices for a man's suit begin at about $275, and the bargain part of the purchase is that you can select the fabric and style and have the suit custom fitted. 
At W. W. Chan & Sons Tailor (Burlington Arcade, Shop 2F, 9294 Nathan Road, Kowloon; 366-9738) a wool suit will run about $540, but the fabrics are beautiful, the selection of materials extensive and the quality and workmanship outstanding. 
For fine suits at very reasonable prices, De-Luxe Tailor (Room 704, Modest Building, 58 Stanley Street, Central; 522-9645) is a good choice. 
A wool suit here costs about $275.
For custom tailored shirts, David's Shirts offers a wide range of fine fabrics and excellent workmanship, with cotton shirts at $60. 
David's shops are in the Mandarin Oriental and the Wing Lee Building, 33 Kimberley Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon. 
William Cheng & Son (Han Hing Mansion, Eighth Floor, 38 Hankow Road, Tsim Sha Tsui; 366-0709) offers well-made men's cotton dress shirts for only $23, though his selection of fabrics is not as extensive as in some shops.
Â

file: WHAT_S NEW IN DIAPERS_For Delivery Services, Buying From China is Cheaper.txt
text:
ï»¿
Although diaper delivery vendors may have gained some market share from disposables last year, American producers of cloth diapers did not reap much of the benefit. 
A surge in imports from China in 1986 all but drove American cloth diaper producers from the delivery market. 
Imports of heavy-ply cloth diapers from China climbed to 1.06 million pounds that year, up from just over 82,000 pounds in 1985. 
The bulk were purchased by delivery vendors.
Faced with the onslaught, American producers concentrated on the retail sale of cloth diapers. 
That $35 million business, which consumes four million dozen cloth diapers a year, is three times as large as the diaper delivery sector. 
Thanks to its distribution requirements, it is also harder for importers to crack.
Unwilling to forsake the delivery business entirely, however, American producers petitioned for import restrictions. 
But by the time they were granted in late 1987, the sole American supplier serving the deliverers was Soft Care Apparel of Pelzer, S.C., a subsidiary of Gerber Products.
The quota drew criticism. 
Environmentalists feared that it would lead to higher prices for cloth diapers, which they favor over disposables. 
Free trade advocates objected to protecting a single company in a tiny market.
In the final analysis, last year's quota of 1.34 million pounds proved of only modest value to Gerber, which markets its diapers under the Curity brand name. 
''The quota was set at such a high level that the Chinese could keep 70 percent of the diaper service market,'' said Dan Pezold, director of marketing for Gerber's children's wear.
Nevertheless, the quota helped Gerber hang on to most of its business while it designed a heavier diaper comparable to the Chinese imports. 
Orders have picked up since it introduced the new diaper last fall, Mr. Pezold said.
The quota has also encouraged others to enter the market. 
Dundee Mills, Gerber's main rival in the delivery market before withdrawing in 1987, has designed a new diaper of its own and plans to re-enter the market. 
''We are doing it in a limited way for now,'' said Clarence McMerty, Dundee's vice president of marketing.
Intera Ltd., a producer of adult diapers based in Cleveland, Tenn., told the annual meeting of the National Association of Diaper Services last week in Dallas of its plan to introduce a cloth diaper for babies.
Yet the outlook for imports is now less predictable than ever. 
This year diapers became part of the larger Infants Wear category for Customs purposes, enabling the Chinese to import five million pounds of infant wear in total.
''Now the Chinese may have to choose between things like diapers and infants' sleepwear,'' said Knox H. White, an attorney with Haynesworth, Marion, McKay & Guerard, of Greenville, S.C., who represented the American companies in the quota case. 
''We have no idea whether it will mean more or less diaper imports.''

file: Wife of Jailed China Dissident Is Left Homeless by Eviction.txt
text:
ï»¿
The wife of one of China's most prominent dissidents says the authorities have evicted her and her sick daughter from the family home, leaving her nowhere to live.
The woman, Zhang Fengying, wife of Ren Wanding, a 48-year-old accountant who is serving a seven-year sentence for his role in the 1989 Tiananmen Square democracy movement, said she returned home on Wednesday to find her apartment door nailed shut. 
She had been away since January trying to seek medical treatment for her teen-age daughter.
"They're shutting me out of my house so that now I'm homeless," Ms. Zhang said. 
"Who can live without shelter and food?"
Mr. Ren's work unit formally dismissed him after his arrest, and since it owns the apartment, it wants to force Ms. Zhang out, presumably so it can reassign the place to another worker. 
In China an eviction is far more serious than in the West, because nearly all housing here is assigned by employers, and there is almost no rental housing available to individuals.
Â 
Human-Rights Campaigner
The eviction reflects the difficulties endured not only by Chinese dissidents but also by their families. 
Wives, siblings and children of dissidents sometimes encounter discrimination in getting jobs, in getting permission to go abroad and in finding a place to live.
Ms. Zhang said that she is now living temporarily with friends but that she cannot stay for long. 
She said she has no steady income -- she has no Beijing residency permit and thus no right to work in Beijing -- and no idea what she will do.
Ms. Zhang said the authorities would not even allow her to remove her money and other belongings now locked in the apartment.
Her husband, Mr. Ren, was one of the first Chinese to emphasize the need for human rights, as distinct from democracy. 
In the winter of 1978-79, he was a leader of the Democracy Wall movement in Beijing and consequently served four years in prison -- where he held out against pressure to repent, writing voluminous protests on toilet paper, the only paper he could find.
In late 1988, Mr. Ren re-emerged in the public eye, giving interviews and drafting essays calling for more democracy and attention to human rights. 
He is now serving his prison sentence in Beijing No. 2 Prison, sharing a cell with three ordinary criminals who reportedly sometimes take Mr. Ren's food from him.
Â 
Limits on Visits and Food
In another sign that the authorities are putting pressure on family members of political prisoners, the wife of another prominent dissident says jailers are cutting back on her visiting hours and the amount of food she can give to her husband.
That woman, Hou Xiaotian, the wife of Wang Juntao, who is serving a 13-year sentence for supposedly masterminding the 1989 Tiananmen Square movement, said jailers were also cutting the food supplements that her husband is allowed because of the hepatitis he suffers.
Ms. Hou said that when she visited her husband last Monday, jailers told her that her monthly visits would be limited to 30 minutes and that she could not bring more than 4.4 pounds of food for her husband. 
Prison rules dictate that visits be half an hour, but the guards had previously allowed longer visits.
The reason for the crackdown, Ms. Hou said, is that the authorities are trying to punish her for suing the court system and Qincheng Prison for illegal confiscation of property and for infecting her husband with the hepatitis. 
The courts have not processed her lawsuits, and there is no indication they ever will, but the Government was apparently still angered and embarrassed by her audacity.
The authorities have also repeatedly denied Ms. Hou a passport to travel overseas. 
In November, after Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d visited Beijing, Chinese leaders gave assurances that those with no criminal record would be allowed to travel overseas. 
Chinese Foreign Ministry officials insist that the assurances still hold but do not explain why Ms. Hou and others have not yet been given passports.

file: With Difficulty, China Moves to Regain Business.txt
text:
ï»¿
China is mounting a high-pressure campaign to lure back foreign businessmen who fled after the military crackdown on the democracy movement this month.
But while some executives are trickling back, many are wary of returning and are afraid of being used as pawns in the Communists' propaganda campaign to prove that everything is normal.
These fears were compounded today when a Chinese Government agency invited foreign businessmen in Beijing to a meeting to hear what was advertised as an important announcement. 
But there was no announcement, a West German businessman said.
Instead, the participants were filmed by a Chinese television crew, apparently for use on a Chinese news program to prove the Government's contention that life has quickly returned to normal after the army's killing of demonstrators and onlookers in central Beijing this month.
The meeting was sponsored by the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, which licenses foreign businesses. 
A similar meeting has been called for Wednesday by the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, and some American business executives say they will stay away from it for fear of being used.
Â 
'Don't Want to Get Caught'
''A lot of American businessmen don't want to get caught in this situation,'' said Lucille A. Barale, the president of the American Chamber of Commerce of Beijing.
''A lot have been told by their companies not to get caught,'' said Ms. Barale, a lawyer for Coudert Brothers, the New York-based international law firm. 
She returned to Beijing on Monday after fleeing two weeks ago to Hong Kong with her two children.
Beijing's effort to draw foreign businessmen is critical for China, both to stabilize its suddenly troubled economy and to prove that Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, is right in proclaiming that the Communists can simultaneously repress students and maintain their open-door policy.
Before Mr. Deng began his economic initiatives in 1979, China's foreign trade was negligible. 
But it has grown enormously in recent years, and now accounts for nearly a third of China's national income, a high proportion for so big a country. 
Mr. Deng has counted on foreign investment and technology to help achieve his goal of making China a modern state.
But in recent months China has been hit by both inflation, running at an annual rate of nearly 30 percent, and by a severe credit shortage. 
One sign of how this credit squeeze may affect foreign trade came last weekend when a Government-owned corporation, China National Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation, aborted its purchase of New Zealand's largest steel maker, New Zealand Steel Ltd.
Â 
A Flurry of Calls and Telexes
Diplomats here and in Beijing say the Communist leadership has given the highest priority to getting foreign businesses back to China. 
The Foreign Investment Leading Group, a high-level Communist Party agency, has been charged with the task of enticing or coercing businessmen to return, the diplomats say.
A result has been a blizzard of phone calls and telexes to offices in Hong Kong, where many of the executives of the 175 American companies that have offices in China fled. 
The message has been simple: The shooting is over.
As an added allure, some companies have been promised meetings with Chinese officials who had been unavailable for months or offered favorable new terms.
Jamie Horsley, the managing partner of the Hong Kong office of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison, said one of her firm's clients had ''miraculously'' received a telex last week saying their contract to manage a hotel in China had been approved. 
Chinese agreement on the deal had been stalled for a year.
There have also been threats. 
One large American company was called by a Chinese Government ministry and threatened with a lawsuit if its executives did not return to China promptly, a businessman involved in the dealings said.
The Chinese campaign has divided American business executives here, posing difficult financial and ethical questions. 
Many executives are anxious to return, worried about contractual obligations, the size of their investments and the fate of their Chinese employees.
Â 
Decade of Thinking Is Shattered
But after a decade of thinking China had broken its pattern of political convulsion and repression, these businessmen were also shattered by the shootings. 
The offices of Citibank, Combustion Engineering, Coca-Cola and Occidental Petroleum's $650 million joint venture coal mine were all shot up by the Chinese Army.
A Chinese colleague of Eric Kalkurst, a consultant who has been doing business in China for 15 years, was shot dead by soldiers when he went out early one morning to the local communal toilet near his house in an area of Beijing reserved for officials.
Mr. Kalkurst is now advising his clients to stay away from China. 
''I'm not sure there is a government there to really deal with,'' he said.
''If they can lie about the killings, what is to stop them from lying to businessmen?'' he asked, referring to the Communists' version of the shootings in central Beijing.
The Dow Chemical Company, which has four representative offices in China, withdrew its six foreign managers by company order and is keeping them out because of the continued State Department advisory against travel to China, a spokesman in Hong Kong said.
The company is also ''worried about the tense state of U.S.-China relations,'' with the possibility for something bad to happen, like a kidnapping, the spokesman said.
Â 
Depends on Nature of Business
Companies' reactions also depend on the type of business they were doing. 
Those companies engaged only in trade, buying or selling in China, have not been badly hurt yet. 
But with China's shortage of foreign exchange and the slowdown in production over the last month in many factories because of the turmoil, some traders may start looking to buy goods like toys or textiles in Southeast Asia, businessmen here say.
Those companies just starting to negotiate ventures in China may now be more cautious, and some companies with small investments have been inquiring over the last week whether their political risk insurance allows them to pull out entirely, an American lawyer in Hong Kong said.
But the larger operations, like Occidental's coal mine in Shanxi Province, are too expensive to just stop. 
Occidental withdrew the dependents of its 40 foreign employees at the mine, a 30-year joint venture with the Bank of China, but the managers and engineers stayed on.
Last week a Chinese television crew turned up to film them.
Â 
BUSINESS COUNCIL COMMENTS
WASHINGTON, June 20 (Special to The New York Times) - Small numbers of American corporate officials are going back into China, chiefly technical representatives sent to maintain quality control and otherwise keep plants from grinding to a halt, the vice president of the U.S.-China Business Council says.
The official, Richard E. Gillespie, whose organization represents 300 American multinationals with China operations, noted that Japanese companies are sending their officials back in greater numbers.
The American companies are worried that the Chinese ''will propagandize the issue,'' and that the return will be looked upon unfavorably in the United States, where there is Congressional pressure for additional sanctions, Mr. Gillespie said.
''Although some Americans are going back in, it won't be business as usual for some time,'' he said.

file: With Its Population Still on Rise, Beijing Pushes One-Child Family.txt
text:
ï»¿
Throughout China's vast countryside, it is often not so much democracy that stirs emotions as it is the desire to procreate, and few policies cause more heartbreak than the Government's family planning measures.
These days there are signs that the one-child policy will be carried out more rigorously. 
The number of women of child-bearing age is climbing dramatically, leading China to exceed its population targets, and the Government is now calling for tougher enforcement of family planning measures.
Â 
'Many Women Are Scared'
Here in Sichuan Province, as in most of the nation's countryside, population control has caused a mixture of anger, support, frustration, enthusiasm, deviousness and pain. 
Many Chinese intellectuals endorse the policy and believe it has given new hope for their country's long-term development, but it has also ruined marriages, intensified sexist attitudes and led to murder, bribery, abandonment and countless battles between mothers and daughters-in-laws.
"Sometimes the women cry, sometimes they don't," said a woman from Chuan Shi village, here in Guangan County, as she described the pressure on women to have abortions. 
"They dispatch more than a dozen people to your house all at once. 
They don't beat you, but they scold you, and many women are scared and just go to the hospital."
The case of Qi Yongxin, a peasant in Donglou village in Henan, shows how deep passions can run. 
When his wife became pregnant a year ago with his fourth child, a neighbor reported her to the authorities. 
The officials then pressured her to abort it, and Mr. Qi, his father and sister were so enraged that they beat the neighbor to death and crippled his wife and three-year-old child.
Mr. Qi was sentenced to death in March, according to the Peasants Daily, which reported the incident.
There have long been criticisms abroad of China's one-child policy, and the United States has suspended its contribution to the United Nations Family Planning Program because of allegations that the program was bolstering a coercive policy in China.
But the family planning policy has made substantial progress over the last dozen years, with the average number of babies per woman dropping from five or six in 1970 to two or three now. 
Without population control, 240 million more Chinese babies would have been born over the last two decades, official reports say.
Soaring populations and insufficient farmland are a major problem in many developing countries, and supporters of the program say that China has come to grips with the problem better than most -- giving its present and future generations a greater opportunity to rise above the poverty and misery that traditionally was often their lot. 
Most urban Chinese now seem to accept the idea that they can have only one child, and even in the countryside people desire fewer children than their parents had, although they still frequently want more than the Government allows.
Some Chinese describe the policy in terms that Americans might use about the income tax: fundamentally necessary, but they would rather it not apply to them personally. 
Still, others say that in many rural areas, where people are less educated, the policy is simply unpopular.
Â 
2.25 Children Per Woman
The one-child policy is a misnomer in many cases, because there are many exceptions and Chinese women have, on average, 2.25 children. 
Partly because the average is so much higher than one, the Government has had to abandon its original projections.
China is now expected to break the 1.2 billion barrier by 1995, and to approach 1.3 billion by the year 2000, the official newspapers announced in April. 
In contrast, the Government originally planned to keep the population below 1.2 billion by the year 2000.
China's population is now about 1.14 billion, in a territory slightly larger than the United States, but with far less arable land.
Will the missed targets prompt a new crackdown?
So far, the Government has called for tighter controls, and there seems to be a greater attempt to raise fines for evasion and to limit the number of cases where second and third children are allowed.
Official press reports have also called for more spending on family planning, which currently receives less than one percent of the central budget. 
But so far officials deny that a new crackdown is imminent, and there is no sign of another "high tide" of the kind that a decade ago led to many forced abortions in Chinese villages.
Peasants, officials and others interviewed during a weeklong tour of Sichuan Province, and in other parts of China in recent months, said that it was quite rare for the authorities to drag a woman to the hospital to undergo an abortion, but that it still happened.
"Last year there was a forced abortion in my village," said a young woman from Hongjiang Village in Sichuan. 
"More than a dozen cadres went to the woman's house and forced her to go to the hospital for the abortion."
Officials do not disclose national statistics on forced abortion, but Zeng Jian, the director of family planning for Guangan, said that in 1990, the county had "about 100 forced abortions."
This represented about 3 percent of 3,200 abortions that took place in the county in 1990. 
The phrase in Chinese that Mr. Zeng used normally suggests compulsion or physical force, rather than simply pressure tactics.
He added that last year, Guangan, with 1.09 million people, had only 200 unauthorized births, compared to 15,000 within the plan.
Â 
Other Government Tactics
Peasants also described other tactics, such as demolishing houses, confiscating furniture or electrical appliances, or beating the husbands of those who violate the policy.
"They dig a hole in the wall of your house, stick your head through and beat you on the backside," said a peasant from a Shandong Province village wih about 600 families. 
"It happened twice this year in my village."
In recent interviews, Chinese from Sichuan, Anhui, Shandong and Fujian Provinces all reported that demolition of houses was one method that officials sometimes used to deal with peasants who would not or could not pay the heavy fines for breaching the policy.
"It happens every year, but not that much," said a 23-year-old woman from Qingkang village in Guangan County.
Both officials and many peasants, however, say such methods are used infrequently. 
Indeed, visits to villages in many parts of China suggest that unauthorized children are far more common than destroyed houses. 
It is common in some rural areas to see couples with three children, occasionally even four, and local officials are often willing to charge a fine and look the other way.
Â 
Pursuasion, More Than Force
"If they refuse to pay the fine, their radio set and TV may be taken as mortgage -- yes, I've seen this in some places, but it is quite rare," said Shen Guoxiang, the spokesman for the State Family Planning Commission in Beijing. 
"It is quite common to persuade a woman not to have another baby when she wants to have it. 
But it is rare to drag the woman by the hand and force her to have the abortion."
The most common way of persuading couples to have fewer children is simply to offer a series of incentives and fines, and if these fail, to turn to pressure tactics aimed at making people feel guilty if they breach the policy. 
Here in Sichuan, which has a population of 108 million, one-child families get a wide range of benefits. 
These vary but can include monthly subsidies of $1, higher retirement pensions for the parents, greater allocation of land, lower grain taxes and easier access to good schools.
A fine for a child born out of the plan can amount to up to two year's income, but villages tend to set their own fines. 
Some even offer installment plans for families that cannot pay the fine in one lump sum.
Â 
Monitoring System
The incentives are linked to an efficient monitoring system -- which includes about 13 million volunteers -- intended to detect pregnancies as soon as possible. 
In Guangan, villages and townships keep lists of all the women of child-bearing age, and oblige them to undergo gynecological check-ups every three months -- apparently to insure that no one conceals a pregnancy.
One of the most effective methods of preventing unauthorized pregnancies is obligatory sterilization of couples who have already had two or more children. 
But it is common for mothers to flee their villages when they are summoned for sterilization or when they are expecting a baby outside of the plan.
In Guangdong's Wuhua County, last July's census workers discovered that over the years nearly 38,000 children had secretly been born and not registered with the authorities, according to a recent report in the Nanfang Daily.
The most common reason for couples to breach the policy is that they want a son, to continue the family name and ancestry. 
In Chinese tradition, daughters are married out of the family, while sons remain to care for their parents in their old age. 
So parents often keep having children until they have a son.
In some areas, family planning is loosely implemented because the officials themselves do not consider population control a priority or because their family members protest. 
Some peasants say that local officials set an example of evading the family planning controls, so that no one else wants to adhere to the rules either.
In Sichuan's Bai Mao township, Liu Anxiu, the 26-year-old daughter of the village Communist Party leader, acknowledged that she had given birth to two children -- she had to pay a fine of $153 after the second one. 
Ms. Liu's father was in a tough position to urge other villagers to have only one child.
Then, because her children were both daughters, Ms. Liu considered trying again for a son. 
Eventually her relatives dissuaded her, saying it would reflect badly on her father if she had a third child.
"They kept telling me that the children of officials shouldn't have more children," said Ms. Liu. "So I had to listen to them."

text:

It is the prospect of increasing business with China that brings more foreign companies here each year, and it is the threat of China's eventual dominance over business that drives away their potential employees.
Finding and keeping Chinese employees is developing into a major problem as companies with offices here seek to strengthen ties to China.
''We've said goodbye to a lot of people,'' said Robert J. Schmitt, regional marketing manager at the Digital Equipment Corporation in Hong Kong. 
45,000 Emigrated Last Year Some 45,000 Hong Kong Chinese emigrated last year, out of a labor force of about 2.8 million - worsening the problem of an unemployment rate that is so small it can barely be calculated. 
Many Hong Kong Chinese leave because of concern about what will happen to the territory after 1997, when Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule. 
Most people expect the numbers of emigrants to grow, particularly among white-collar professionals who are not convinced that the Chinese Communist Party will keep its promises to let Hong Kong continue its capitalist ways.
On the other hand, with economies in Asia expanding and costs rising in other financial centers like Japan, companies are moving support staff to Hong Kong, or fortifying or relocating their regional headquarters here.
Yet, as their offices here grow, banks, software companies, accounting firms and other corporations are watching the pool of skilled Chinese professionals shrink. 
They are seeing a territory once famed for its cheap, hard-working labor turn into an expensive auction house for bright Hong Kong professionals.
Â 
Measures to Combat Emigration
While some employers do not think there are any measures to combat effectively the tide of emigration, others have revised their compensation systems, enhanced company perquisites and replaced manpower with machines.
The Hong Kong offices of some American companies are advertising in newspapers in the United States and Canada, not for Americans or Canadians but for skilled Hong Kong Chinese who have already emigrated.
''If someone has another passport, that is an added positive aspect in the total evaluation of the person,'' said Eoghan M. McMillan, regional managing partner at Arthur Andersen & Company in Hong Kong.
Knowing that companies value a foreign passport highly, the Chinese who return to work in Hong Kong can command higher salaries as they shop for employers.
Â 
'Incessant Job Hopping'
''The marketplace is characterized by the most incessant job hopping I've seen here in the region,'' said Vangell Rafael, managing director of Paris-based Econocom Far East Ltd., which sells computer software and hardware.
In some cases, companies are paying as much as 50 percent more than last year in salaries for trained experts or middle-level managers.
Mr. Rafael said that a few months ago when he was at his former company, he hired a computer analyst with a United States passport at a salary of $50,000. 
A year earlier, he would have paid about $35,000.
''We bite the bullet and pay more money,'' Mr. Rafael said.
Â 
Creating a Buffer
Companies also try to hire 10 percent to 15 percent more employees than they actually need to create a buffer against people who leave on short notice.
Technology, finance and engineering companies have been experiencing turnover rates as high as 25 percent a year. 
More significantly, those who emigrate tend to be critically important employees with five to eight years' experience.
''In general, the quality of systems might have gone down,'' said Stephen Lau, a member of the Hong Kong Computer Society. 
Mr. Lau, who is director of information technology at Citicorp in Hong Kong, said that as a result, work is sometimes shifted to other offices in the Pacific Basin.
Â 
Working Through Headhunters
To lure employees, some companies are working though headhunters, while others are plucking talent directly from competitors. 
The incentives include service awards and prizes, intensive training and preferred mortgage rates.
''Some companies are using financial incentives like the 1997 handshake,'' said John C. Wilson, managing director of Russell Reynolds Associates Inc., a New York-based executive recruiting firm in Hong Kong. 
''A multinational would say to someone that if you stay with us until 1997, you will receive 'X' amount of U.S. dollars.''
Citicorp in Hong Kong said it is trying to raise morale by adding merit badges and monetary prizes pegged to performance and by improving training of junior employees.
Â 
Transfers to Other Locations
When possible, companies transfer or rehire Hong Kong Chinese in other locations. 
Digital Equipment, for instance, has 44 former employees from Hong Kong in its Toronto office.

Not only a call for democracy, but also anger over inflation and corruption, seemed to impel the tens of thousands of workers who joined students today in demonstrating in Tiananmen Square in the center of the capital.
So far most of the workers seem bitter enough to be willing to join the students, but not so angry that they will stage demonstrations or strikes of their own.

'The Economic Risk'

''If they fail to appear at their factory in the morning, they won't get their day's bread.''
Few seemed to care deeply that today's march also marked the 70th anniversary of the nationalist demonstrations that later influenced democratic and radical thought in China. 
Some complained that the real lesson of the demonstration was that the demands for democracy were still unrealized after seven decades of struggle.

''Any reform won't be successful until the masses receive benefits,'' said Wan Zhicheng, a 25-year-old factory worker. 
''We say we oppose corruption, but ultimately, it is the entire system.''
''Before an earthquake, small animals know it and run for cover,'' he said. 
''They are the intellectuals,'' he said, referring to the thousands of Chinese who have gone abroad to study and perhaps live.

file: Workers_ Resistance Lags in Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Zhang Quan slipped out of work several times earlier this month to join pro-democracy rallies, and he donated $27, two-thirds of his monthly salary, to the student demonstrators.
But like tens of thousands of other workers, he bowed out of Sunday's demonstration. 
He said he was too busy.
''The students and the citizens are tired,'' the 23-year-old cake seller said. 
''The movement has lasted for so long and we citizens have done our best to support the students. 
We have given them bread rolls, clothing and quilts. 
But as ordinary citizens, we are not rich. 
We are exhausted and we are disillusioned.''
The challenge for China's university students is to reawaken the enthusiasm of workers like Mr. Zhang. Such workers added a new dimension to the movement and vastly increased its scale, but now many seem to be settling back into silence.
Â 
Fear and Exhaustion
For a brief moment two weeks ago, workers and citizens, like Mr. Zhang, by the hundreds of thousands, seemed to come out of nowhere to support the hunger-striking students. 
But since martial law was declared nine days ago, the citizens seemed to be steadily disappearing from the streets.
The first few nights after martial law was imposed, citizens poured out in waves to block the troops from entering the city center. 
But during the week, many large work units have issued stern warnings against taking part in demonstrations, or even watching them, and some units have apparently promised bonuses for workers who stay inside and deductions for those who do not.
This seems to have frightened many workers, especially those with families to support. 
Mr. Zhang has no wife or children, but he still lives at home with his parents, who constantly urge him not to go out to the square.
Mr. Zhang says that the nature of his work often takes him out of the office, so that marching with the students was not that difficult. 
But as the papers and errands piled up he fell behind in his work.He spent Sunday settling his accounts and clearing up paper work.
Â 
'They Were Not Selfish'
Nonetheless, Mr. Zhang has not abandoned the movement. 
In fact he has been the most active of the workers in his unit.
''One reason I supported the students is that they were not selfish,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''They don't stand to gain anything for themselves, like food, drink or jobs, from the movement. 
Why did they stage it?
For the citizens. 
And the movement has awakened our people.''
Mr. Zhang went to Tiananmen Square for several demonstrations, but after martial law was declared, he passed all his evenings except one at home.
Now, he says that the movement is at a lull, that thus far it has failed and dampened the spirit among the citizens and workers. 
But he says he expects the tide of protest to rise as June 20 approaches, the date when the standing committee of the National People's Congress, China's legislature, is scheduled to meet.
Â 
'Shall I Continue to Donate'
Still, like so many others, he is willing to take part only if the masses do, and so when a smaller crowd of students shows up for a demonstration, as happened on Sunday, he is hesitant about risking his job. 
And if there are going to be arrests, he said, the police will arrest citizens before students.
''I've already donated $27 of my April salary to the students,'' said Mr. Zhang, who says he only makes about $40 a month. 
''And now, I'm wondering, shall I continue to donate?
What's the point?''
Mr. Zhang insists that he has not switched sides, and opposes a crackdown by the Government. 
But as he listens to the rumors about the downfall of the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang, and the apparent rise of Prime Minister Li Peng, he insists that the Government under Mr. Li cannot last for long since it does not have the support of the people.
Â 
Not Organized Enough
But at the same time, he acknowledges that the people are not organized enough to make a difference.
''The problem with Chinese is that we are not so united. 
About 30 percent would simply prefer to stand on the sidelines with their arms folded, and about 20 percent simply don't care. 
The remaining 50 percent want do something, but they still have a hard time uniting among each other.''
The fundamental problem, he said, is that Chinese are simply too tolerant.
''We Chinese can tolerate almost everything,' Mr. Zhang said. 
''As long as we have something to eat and to drink, we will not rebel unless there is nothing left for us to eat but leaves.''

The World Bank today approved the first loan to China since the student uprising last year that goes beyond the confines of meeting basic human needs.
The approval of the $114.3 million loan marked the first time in more than a year that the Bush Administration did not object to other than humanitarian assistance to China.
The World Bank's approval of the loan for technological improvements in rural industry had been expected for weeks, but it was uncertain whether the United States would vote against it. 
Such a move would have been largely symbolic, because both the European Community and Japan have resumed normal economic relations with China and both supported the loan.
Â 
Bush Met With Beijing Aide
The decision comes less than a week after President Bush met last Friday for the first time since the crackdown with the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen. 
The meeting occurred a day after China abstained, rather than opposed, a vote by the United Nations Security Council authorizing the use of force to expel Iraq from Kuwait.
While the World Bank is owned by 155 member Governments, an American has headed it since it was founded in 1945 and the United States has a 20 percent vote on all major issues. 
The bank makes loans and helps countries in other ways to strengthen broad economic sectors by building such projects as dams, fertilizer plants, irrigation works, ports and highways.
Before the military crackdown on the democracy movement in June 1989, China had been receiving World Bank loans of more than $2 billion annually.

Hostility on Capitol Hill
Since then, World Bank loans to China had shrunk to $650 million, primarily in the form of rural credits and assistance to small cooperative business enterprises in towns and villages.
The American position against non-humanitarian aid reflected opposition from Capitol Hill, where many lawmakers had been hostile to Beijing. 
But that opposition has been steadily softening since Iraq took over Kuwait in August and the Bush Administration began reaching out to a wide range of allies and other nations for support in challenging the invasion.
The package approved today consists of a $50 million loan and $64.3 million in credit.

As the Bush Administration gingerly moves to repair economic ties with China, the World Bank seems likely to soon resume lending programs suspended after the crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in June, say officials of the bank, the United States and foreign governments.
To resume its lending, the bank needs formal approval from its 152 stockholders, including the United States, which holds 20 percent of the shares. 
The bank and Administration sources say the loans could be made as early as next month.
Â 
A Step Toward Approval
The Administration officially insists that its policy against World Bank lending to China remains unchanged. 
But the lifting of some American sanctions against China on Dec. 
19 was seen as a step toward Administration approval of such lending in the near future.
''That's the kind of talk we're hearing around the bank,'' said a senior World Bank official. 
A World Bank mission has just returned from two weeks in China.
Criticism of any new China loans is likely in Congress, where some members are seeking tougher sanctions against Beijing because of what they consider continued represssion of human rights.
But Administration officials plan to argue that new lending should encourage liberal forces within the Chinese leadership pressing both for a greater opening to the outside world and more respect for human rights, an Administration economic official said.

14 by the bank's president, Barber B. Conable Jr.: ''It is our hope that in the not too distant future we can resume lending to China, but we do not have a specific date.''
Mr. Conable had also said the bank would be guided by China's economic performance, not political considerations.
Â 
Others Would Also Make Loans
Because of the World Bank's prestige as the biggest lender to the third world, approval would encourage lending by others, like the Manila-based Asian Development Bank and Japanese commercial banks, which also stopped loans after the June crackdown on dissent.
The World Bank, which is based in Washington, has provided $8 billion to China since 1981. 
It suspended $750 million of loans last June.
Since fall 1988, Beijing has moved toward central planning and away from the market-oriented policies that over the decade had attracted $14 billion of investment from industrial countries, of which $3.5 billion came from the United States.
An Administration official said Washington is trying to use a promise of World Bank lending to get the Chinese back to market-oriented policies.

Cloudy Prospects
Business representatives said that despite the recent moves by both sides to improve the climate, the prospects for business remained cloudy.

file: World Markets_Out of China, a Boost for Hong Kong.txt
text:

ORDINARY Chinese must be wondering what could have happened in their country to have sent the Hong Kong stock market bouncing to new heights this week. 
For while their markets, in the cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, were creeping downward, the Hong Kong market rose to a new record, mostly on the news from China.
The prime shaker in the Hong Kong exchange is not a central bank. 
It is a coterie of elderly men, most in their 80's, who rule China and who with a cough or a stumble can send the markets reeling. 
They essentially determine the pace of China's economic growth -- the direction is invariably up -- and therefore the action in Hong Kong.
Last week, the action was in the Hang Seng index, which surged to a peak of 6,329.12 on Thursday, dropped by 66.58 points on Friday to 6,262.54, but even so was up 277.21 points, or 4.6 percent, for the week.
Underlying the market's rise is a change in perceptions about Hong Kong's relations with China. 
For years, Hong Kong's proximity to China and its scheduled return to Chinese control in 1997 have provoked anxiety, dampening investor confidence and lowering price-earnings ratios in Hong Kong.
But these days, a growing number of investors see China as an opportunity, rather than a threat. 
They argue that Hong Kong companies are able to participate in one of the greatest economic booms anywhere, and that the boom will continue for many years.
"Hong Kong is always a proxy to China," said Wai-keung Wan, sales director at the Jardine Fleming brokerage house. 
"China is embarking on a long-term growth trend. 
In the 1990's, any country that can produce economic growth can reasonably command a premium. 
Therefore, people feel very positive about China."
Hong Kong's stock exchange, once a wayward cowboy market of which Americans were wary, has been rising on and off since the beginning of this year. 
A buying frenzy in Hong Kong seized investors last week because they thought China had cleared a number of political and economic uncertainties.
Investors were reassured by the new leadership team that the Communist Party announced a week ago, feeling that the seven members of the new Politburo Standing Committee are reform-oriented. 
In fact, the appointments were largely expected, but the market seized upon the news to leap ahead.
In the process, the market ignored some bad news: China's Communist leaders criticized and snubbed Hong Kong's new Governor, Christopher Patten, signalling that relations may become tougher between Hong Kong and China. 
Mr. Patten had come to China to discuss his proposals for broadening democracy in Hong Kong and for financing a $16 billion airport. 
"On the face of it, it was quite negative," said James K. Osborn, assistant director at Baring Securities (Hong Kong) Ltd. 
"But on sheer fact, it was not a worse surprise than what was expected."
On Friday, however, after Mr. Patten departed for Hong Kong, China said it would retaliate if Mr. Patten's proposals for democracy and the airport were implemented without Beijing's consent. 
China's comments are certain to influence the direction of the market next week. 
Disappointment with the trip -- coupled with profit-taking -- accounted for the market's fall on Friday.
The underlying reason for the Hong Kong market's euphoria recently has been the 14th Communist Party Congress, which culminated Monday with the announcement of the new leadership team. 
The congress declared that China would develop a "socialist market economy" with the emphasis on "market."
Moreover, China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, who is 88 years old and holds no posts, appeared on public television on Monday. 
Investors took that as good news -- dispelling fears that he was virtually on his death bed -- instead of focusing on the fact that his health seemed much worse than the last time he appeared on TV, in February.
Mr. Deng exerts the greatest influence in the country, and now he is determined to lock China onto a course of building a market economy. 
The congress hailed him and his commitment to economic reform.
The previous week also brought news that lifted the market. 
Chinese and American trade negotiators broke a stalemate in discussions over American exporters' access to the Chinese market. 
The result was that China agreed to import more American goods, thereby avoiding punitive duties on as much as $3.9 billion worth of Chinese exports to the United States.
Money has been pouring in these last couple of weeks from the United States, as well as from Asia, analysts said. 
Although trading is conducted in Hong Kong dollars, the currency is pegged at a rate of about 7.8 Hong Kong dollars to the United States dollar. 
"One beauty of the Hong Kong stock market is that it is really a U.S. dollar market because of the peg," said Allan Ng, a senior analyst at S. G. Warburg Securities (Far East) Ltd. 
"No matter what happens, there's not currency risk."
Many of Hong Kong's large companies have shed the undeserved fly-by-night reputation they had a decade ago. 
The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation recently acquired the British bank Midland Bank P.L.C. 
Among the major China plays in the market are Hopewell Holdings Ltd., a construction firm building a highway in China.
Not surprisingly, most of the buying focused on blue chip companies, such as the Hong Kong Bank, and on Cheung Kong, Hong Kong's largest conglomerate, run by its richest man, Li Ka-shing.
