Cable and Wireless P.L.C., the British-based telecommunications company with a presence in 50 countries, pleased investors earlier this month when it reported pretax profits up 15.5 percent for the fiscal year ended March 31. 
And this in a recession year.
Moreover, more than 60 percent of the company's revenues are dollar based, so the strong rally of the dollar in the last five months sent analysts back to their calculators to raise their earnings forecasts for the current fiscal year. 
Although its headquarters are in London, the company's heart is Hong Kong where the currency is tied to the dollar. 
Cable and Wireless has a 58.4 percent controlling stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications, which provided 43 percent of the company's revenue and 59 percent of its profit last year.
Company officials, including its group managing director, Gordon M. W. Owen, and finance director, Rodney J. Olsen, crowed about these numbers on a recent visit to New York City. 
They waxed enthusiastic about the company's global digital "highway," including an American link with US Sprint. 
The highway is a fiber-optic cable system linking major financial centers and offering business customers such things as high-definition television and video-conferencing, high-speed data transmission and faxes. 
Cable and Wireless also owns Mercury Communications, the first and only competitor to British Telecommunications, the Government-owned phone company.
Despite its good looks last year and prospects in the current year, there are questions about Cable and Wireless which, at current prices, make the stock less attractive.
The stock's volatility reflects some of this uncertainty. 
In June alone, its price fell to 490 pence ($9.08 at Friday's exchange rate) and then rallied to 560. 
It closed Friday at 529. 
The company's American Depository Receipt which trades in New York has moved from a low of 24.875 to 26.875. 
It closed Friday at 25.50.
The stock already trades at a 13-to-20 percent premium to the British market as a whole, based on earnings projections.
Then there are the questions about the quality of Cable and Wireless' earnings. 
The company has had a good stream of average earnings over the last decade, but the yearly numbers are subject to big hits from exchange rate moves. 
Last year, for example, the company estimated that pretax profits would have doubled to 31 percent if the dollar had not been so weak. 
Now the high hopes for the current fiscal year are based on the current strong dollar retaining its strength.
Some of the pretax profit last year was based on special factors that should vanish this year. 
One was the sale of a managing director's house in Hong Kong that added 9.2 million pounds ($16 million) to the books.
In addition, the sale of 20 percent of Cable and Wireless' stake in Hong Kong Telecommunicatons to the Chinese Government reduced the company's borrowing needs in 1991, dropping the bank loan level from 59.9 million pounds ($104.2 million at the end-of-March exchange rate) in 1990 to 16.3 million pounds in fiscal 1991. 
Company executives acknowledge that borrowing will pick up again this year.
Such things accounted for a swing in the company's net-interest and other-income line from a 46.9 million pound deficit in 1990 to a 31.2 million pound surplus the following year. 
The 78.1 million pound shift accounts for all but 3.7 million pounds of the increase in profits before taxes.
All of these considerations must be weighed against larger questions about the future of Hong Kong, which reverts to the control of China in 1997. 
Hong Kong Telecommunications is not only Cable and Wireless' main business but also a source of money needed to expand Mercury back home in the United Kingdom, enhance the global digital highway and eventually make the company much less dependent on Hong Kong.
Cable and Wireless, as well as analysts like Robert B. Morris 3d of Goldman Sachs in San Francisco, are not worried about the takeover by China. 
Mr. Morris is more concerned, at least in the near term, about how a tax increase in Hong Kong will eat into Hong Kong Telecom's earnings this year.
"The investment program we have in Hong Kong would not be going on there unless we had confidence," said Mr. Owen, the group managing director for Cable and Wireless. 
But Hong Kong's future will still hang over the company and the stock for some time.
Finally, there is the fallout from recent government decisions about how the British telecommunications industry should be regulated. 
Analysts have generally concluded that the new regulatory approach gives breaks to both Cable and Wireless and British Telecommunications. 
But how they sort out to the bottom line in the next few years is still being debated.
Negative interpretations, like that of Partick Wellington of County Natwest Securities in London, emphasize that new costs Cable and Wireless could incur for access to the B.T. network and the price restructuring that will enable B.T. to lower prices to business customers could hurt the company. 
Postive views, like that of Michael Armitage of Morgan Stanley & Company in London, conclude that what is good for B.T. is good for Cable and Wireless.

file: Writers in China Are Asked to Write, But Not Subversively.txt
text:
ï»¿
Literature is like groceries, says Ma Feng, the earthy ''old revolutionary'' who is China's new literary czar: in both cases the government should encourage what is nutritious and ban what is poisonous.
These days it is largely up to Mr. Ma, a lean man of 68 who joined the Communist rebellion in 1938 at the age of 16, to enforce that regulatory vision. 
It is a formidable task because many authors loathe the regime and develop a writer's block when they are asked to ''serve socialism.''
This leaves Mr. Ma in an awkward position as the effective head of the Chinese Writers Association. 
He comes from a different world - the countryside of north-central China - and he made his name writing short stories and film scripts about peasants who brim with decency and enthusiasm for the Communist Party. 
Nothing could be further from the urban frustration and alienation that inspire many Chinese writers today.
''I don't like Beijing - too many people,'' he chuckled the other day while puffing on his beloved Zhongnanhai cigarettes in an interview. 
Mr. Ma was living in his native Shanxi Province, 260 miles southwest of Beijing, when the crackdown on democratic impulses came last year and led to his summons to Beijing.
Early this year, Mr. Ma was formally named vice chairman and party secretary of the Chinese Writers Association, meaning that he would take charge of it. 
The nominal chairman, the writer Ba Jin, lives in Shanghai and is 86 years old and infirm. 
He had few responsibilities even before he lost his influence by supporting the student demonstrators seeking democracy.
Â 
Not Just a Club
There is no parallel to the Chinese Writers Association in the West, for it is far more than simply an authors' club. 
In China, the association is the work unit of the country's 3,500 authors: it is the employer, the source of housing and salaries, the organizer of political study sessions and the arbiter of who can travel abroad. 
Chinese publishers pay royalties, but these are less important than the association's salaries, and in any case it is difficult to be published without the association's blessing.
Mr. Ma sounds a conciliatory line, asserting that Chinese writers can write about whatever they choose, but they must not criticize their country or subvert Communism. 
His catechism is taken from the works of Mao Zedong, who argued that art is inseparable from politics and must serve the proletarian revolutionary cause.
''Writers should serve socialism and they should serve the people,'' Mr. Ma said, adding that authors should leave the ivory tower to understand the land they write about.
''If you write about society, you must study it,'' he said. 
''If you write about a factory, you should work in a factory. 
If you write about the countryside, you should spend time in a village, rather than sitting around the house writing blindly.''
Â 
Justifying Curbs
In the last few years, a group of young writers very different from the ''old revolutionaries'' has won prominence and acclaim for their attempts to probe the spirit of post-Mao China, but Mr. Ma asserts that they had only a small following. 
Asked about Bei Dao, a highly respected poet who was one of this circle of younger authors, Mr. Ma said he found such writers unimpressive.
''They had an impact on some younger arts circles, but if you go to a factory in Shanxi Province, no one will have heard of them,'' Mr. Ma said, adding that ordinary people do not want to read such books.
''They were just a small group of people,'' Mr. Ma said. 
''Many good writers are needed by the people, but in the late 1980's only their writings could be published. 
Now we want to publish books needed by ordinary people in factories and farms.''
Â 
Talk of Revenge
Many others see it differently and believe that the ''old revolutionaries'' behind the cultural purges - leaders like Vice President Wang Zhen and Acting Culture Minister He Jingzhi as well as Mr. Ma himself - now are relishing the opportunity to strike back at those who in recent years looked with contempt at their orthodox Marxist view of culture.
''It's revenge and it's petty,'' said Geremie Barme, an Australian scholar who recently visited China.
One Western diplomat said he thought the general attitude toward someone like Ma Feng was one of contempt. 
He said that Mr. Ma had stuck to his ideological line for many years and suddenly been vindicated, and that he was an opportunist turning that to his own advantage.
Some other diplomats and Chinese are not so harsh, portraying Mr. Ma as a decent man placed in an impossible position. 
They say he is among the better revolutionary writers but that he has never been an intellectual, in the sense of possessing a doubting or inquiring mind, and that he is out of touch with the main current of writers today.
Â 
A Conciliatory Sound
Mr. Ma, well aware of the antagonisms in the field, takes pains to sound a conciliatory line. 
He even explained the ousting of Liu Binyan, a dissident who was vice chairman of the association, not on the basis of Mr. Liu's heretical views but on the ground that Mr. Liu is in the United States and does not seem likely to return soon.
''In our association, some people took part in the turmoil,'' Mr. Ma said. 
''They won't be punished; they will be educated. 
I'm sure they will change their minds.''
''We've received many manuscripts for publication, criticizing various writers,'' Mr. Ma added. 
''But we don't want to publish them and crush the writers. 
We want to join forces with them and help them write more things that people want to read. 
If we criticize them, who will write for us?
What will be left of the Writers Association?''
Â 
The Purge Proceeds
Still, the authorities are going ahead with their purge in cultural circles. 
The top executives of several publishing houses and journals, including the most prominent, People's Literature, have been replaced. 
Some writers reportedly may not be published, although Mr. Ma denies the existence of any blacklist, and others have had trouble going abroad. 
And there has been a yearlong process of investigations, self-criticisms and political study sessions to return writers to the straight, narrow and sometimes winding path of Marxist orthodoxy.
So far this crackdown has had mixed results. 
In general, there is less experimentation and less writing about the problems of urban, alienated young people and about political discontent. 
But some works, like Harvest, a Shanghai literary journal, are still remarkably bold, and recent books are probably more lively and interesting than the leaders might have in mind.
''The new policies have had the effect of making people miserable and angry, and it's harder to get things done,'' said a Western diplomat. 
''But at the end of the day similar things end up being written and published.''
Â 
A Broader Effort
The selection of Mr. Ma to head the writers' association appears to be part of a broad effort to evoke the glories of the Communist Party in its heyday in China in the 1950's and early 1960's. 
To read People's Daily, watch television or listen to official speeches is to find a resurrection of the themes that emerged in Maoist days. 
Lei Feng, a model Communist and heroic soldier, is again an object of official adoration; songs like ''Good Socialism'' have been re-released, and industrial heroes like ''Iron Man Wang'' have been dusted off and hailed in the newspapers.
Mr. Ma fits neatly into this backdrop. 
After joining the Communist revolution at the age of 16, he won fame in 1944 with a novel about Communist troops, ''Heroes of Luliang Mountains.''
While his father was a scholar who won success in the old imperial examinations, Mr. Ma's characters are largely simple, decent peasants who evoke tu - the earth and an agrarian charm that goes with it. 
One of his books, a collection of short stories, has been translated into English.
These days, however, Mr. Ma says he is too busy to write any new stories.

file: Wuhan Journal_At 102, He_s Back in School, With Many Like Him.txt
text:
ï»¿
Qian Likun is a model university student, the kind of diligent scholar-athlete who joins in foot races, excels in his studies and is never distracted by a woman's short skirt.
Mr. Qian is also five times older than most university students. 
He is 102 years old, and while ordinary students study the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 and the fall of the Ching Dynasty in 1911, Mr. Qian has no such problem: he remembers them.
The University for the Aged, where Mr. Qian studies, has 8,000 students here in Wuhan, a major city on the Yangtze River of central China. 
Founded five years ago, it is part of a network of more than 800 such institutions for the elderly in China, all founded in the last eight years.
China has traditionally revered the aged, and this nation's programs for the elderly are very impressive for a developing country. 
Some Chinese villages have a special "house for the aged," where senior citizens can live if they have no children to depend on, and most cities have a range of physical fitness, entertainment and educational programs for retired citizens.
Â 
Questions for the U.S.
One question that Chinese often ask Americans is why families sometimes put their parents in institutions, why such a rich country cannot do more for its elderly. 
The questions include a hint of reproach, but mostly wonder at the breach of filial piety.
"We want to help the elderly help themselves, so that they can reduce their dependence on their families and on society," said Lu Jianye, the vice president of the Wuhan University for the Aged. 
"We also want to help them increase their contribution to society, and to develop hobbies such as art, calligraphy or even massage, so that they can enjoy their later years."
The university here, which charges tuition of less than $5 a term, offers courses in 123 subjects. 
These include painting, disco dancing, calligraphy, bridge, cooking, English, literature and health care for the elderly.
Â 
Canes Beside the Chairs
Most people in Wuhan are literate, but the university also arranges classes in some neighborhoods to teach reading and writing to the elderly, mostly women who never went to school.
China, with a population of 1.1 billion, has some 115 million people over the retirement age, which is normally 60 for men and 55 for women. 
The proportion of the aged will rise sharply in coming decades as baby boom generations grow older and family planning policies reduce the number of young people.
On a recent visit, the classrooms of the Wuhan University for the Aged were full of animated students, some with canes beside their chairs, enthusiastically commenting on each other's paintings, reciting standard phrases of English and dissecting ancient poetry.
"We don't want to get senile," said Yan Bin, a 56-year-old woman who retired recently as a professional singer. 
She was sitting around a table with three partners, working on her skills at bridge, the card game favored by Deng Xiaoping and countless other elderly Chinese.
"I never studied bridge before," said Mu Youqing, a silver-haired woman of 64 years who is a retired doctor. 
"But it's very highbrow and cultured, and it has a long history in China."
Â 
A Boost for the Brains
The baby of the foursome, 56-year-old Shao Kanfu, a lean, tall man who retired early, added, "I wanted to look after my health and give my brains a boost."
Most elderly people in China live with their children, and often they are responsible for caring for their grandchildren. 
So the University for the Aged holds classes in the midmorning and again in the early afternoon, when the students' children are at work and their grandchildren are at school.
In addition, because some of the old people cannot get around easily, the university has set up 13 branches around the city in residential areas. 
The university depends for money on tuition fees and also on generous grants from the city government. 
The faculty consists mostly of professors at nearby universities who are delighted to moonlight for a small fee.
"The teaching level isn't as high as at a regular university, and we don't go into as much depth as we would with younger students," said Zhou Wu, a junior high school instructor who teaches Chinese literature on the side at a branch campus of the University for the Aged. 
"But some of the older folks bring a good deal of enthusiasm as well as diverse experience to the classroom, so it's often more interesting to teach them than to teach my regular students."
Â 
Along for the 'Fun Run'
One of Mr. Zhou's most diligent students is Mr. Qian, the 102-year-old. 
A retired agricultural researcher, Mr. Qian diligently prepares for each class session and offers some pointed views.
"This poem isn't very good by Tang Dynasty standards," he said the other day as Mr. Zhou dissected a poem on the blackboard. 
"But it's better than anything we have today."
Mr. Qian manages to walk to the class on his own, and he hears and sees well enough to follow the teacher most of the time. 
The first class he took was on health care for the elderly, and he says he found it very useful in looking after his wife, who died a few months ago at the age of 100, and his daughter, who is 81 years old and in fading health.
When the university held a "fun run" this spring, some 300 old people ran about 2.3 miles to complete the race. 
Mr. Qian was ong them, but the university staff acknowledges that his pace was more of a hobble than a jog.
A lover of traditional poetry, Mr. Qian scarcely paused when asked for a few lines of his favorite poem. 
The room fell silent as he recited from memory this ancient Chinese poem:
The clouds are wispy this morning, the breeze is light.
As I pass the pond, I see flowers and willow trees.
The passers-by don't know the joy in my heart.
I'm like a kid at play.

file: Xiamen Journal_Chinese Isle Bewitched (and Bothered) by Taiwan.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a tiny electronics shop in this coastal Chinese town, on the poor side of the thin stretch of water called the Taiwan Strait, the proprietor is exploiting the longing to be like the Wangs and the Chens across the waterway.
His lure is a video of a young woman singing into a microphone, her gown rippling as she dances, and it seems to work. 
A crowd gathers inside the shop, eyes fixed on the singer, whose style and dress shows that she is from Taiwan.
As with many stores in this special economic zone, a Taiwan signature helps draw business, just as it has helped transform this once-backward tiny island of Amoy, as it used to be called, into a bustling metropolis.
But in a back room of the electronics shop, away from the music and the Taiwan glitter, a handful of Chinese explained their feelings about their Taiwan compatriots, revealing sentiments that were not entirely loving.
Â 
'Dregs of Society'
"They may be rich, but they aren't very polite," said a customs official who was helping the shop owner. 
"Lots of the Taiwanese who come here are the dregs of society. 
They bring over the worst of their world, and when we see them smuggling or going out with hookers, naturally we're turned off."
Xiamen is absorbed by the love-hate relationship that many Chinese feel toward their Taiwan brethren. 
Mainland Chinese and Taiwan Chinese may share the same forebears, but with more and more Taiwan residents visiting the mainland, the clash of ideologies, styles and levels of wealth has created headaches for Chinese leaders.
"It is true that the local people resent us a bit," said a Taiwan businessman who has been in Xiamen for several years. 
"The smugglers and boatmen came over here before the businessmen, and they were very crude people. 
This left a deep impression on the locals."
Tsay Mingshan of Taiwan, who is senior manager at a wholly owned Taiwan enterprise called Eupa, said: "Many Taiwanese thought that this was a 'yellow earth,' a new playground that you could dig into as you pleased. 
They didn't realize that if they came over here, people would watch their behavior and form opinions."
Trade between China and Taiwan for the first 11 months of last year reached $5.15 billion, up 41 percent over the same period in 1990, according to Taiwan statistics. 
Taiwanese investment in the mainland was $840 million for the first nine months of last year, nearly as much as for all of 1990, Chinese statistics show.
The relationship, which is much closer than it has been for most of the four decades since Chiang Kai-shek and his army fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the civil war to the Communists, seems bound to get better. 
China is thirsty for Taiwanese capital, just as Taiwan is eager to use the mainland's cheap labor and raw materials. 
China is also trying to forge closer ties as a means to bring Taiwan back under its territorial domain.
The Communist Party General Secretary, Jiang Zemin, visited Xiamen in December to commemorate the 10th anniversary of the special economic zone. 
Many businessmen say this was partly to impress the Taiwanese. 
But his visit also seems to have unleashed a spirit of expansion in Xiamen, which has lagged somewhat behind China's four other special economic zones.
"If Deng Xiaoping called for faster development, now that would be even better," said Zhang Zongxu, the Deputy Mayor of Xiamen, referring to the Chinese leader. 
Mr. Zhang, a former Chinese Consul General in Houston, said that Taiwanese investment had certainly helped Xiamen develop, but added that the audacity of some Taiwanese behavior rubbed him the wrong way.
"They play around with women, or one week they go around with one secretary and the next week it's another one," he said. 
"Or they go eating and drinking at the nightclubs. 
Afterward, they walk over to the singer and stuff a big tip into her bra."
Local residents have been overwhelmed in the last three years by the flood of rich Taiwan visitors. 
Some of the businessmen have come flashing their thick wallets and expensive tastes. 
These are the very "bourgeois" influences that China accuses Westerners of spreading and that, in fact, the Taiwan Chinese are probably even better at disseminating because of the common language.
Â 
Taiwan's Influence Is Strong
Moreover, to the Government's dismay, the island is an enclave for prostitution and smuggling. 
Scores of boats go back and forth across the strait, often carrying contraband like cigarettes, videotapes, books and other goods from Taiwan. 
Last year, security officials caught more than 200 people involved in prostitution rings, Mr. Zhang said.
Xiamen's economic development is still at least two decades behind that of Taipei. 
But Taiwanese investment is the fastest growing source of foreign capital, and when the Taiwan Government approves direct air and shipping links, perhaps in the next couple of years, Xiamen could become, in many ways, a virtual colony of Taiwan.
Meanwhile, Taiwan music, videos, books and fashions have almost become a way of life here. 
Multisystem televisions, which enable viewers to receive Taiwan stations, are among the hottest purchases.
Residents here speak the same Chinese dialect as about 80 percent of the people in Taiwan, and half a million Taiwan tourists have visited the island in the last four years. 
"Xiamen is turning into a Little Taipei," said a Chinese involved in trade with Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao.
Until the middle of last year, the Chinese military still broadcast Communist propaganda from the tip of Xiamen through a dozen huge loudspeakers aimed at nearby Taiwan-controlled islands.
Taiwan doubled the decibels, broadcasting its Nationalist propaganda from at least two dozen loudspeakers on the nearby island of Quemoy. 
Today, the Taiwanese speakers are still there, but the Taiwan Government seems to have discovered a more effective means of propaganda: they often play Taiwan pop songs.

file: Yangpu Journal_Months or Millennia After Flood, the Poor Endure.txt
text:
ï»¿
The only solution to her family's problems, Wan Ziyu said glumly, was for her to die.
"Every day I live is a burden for my son," said Ms. Wan, her white hair and wrinkled face betraying her 80 years. 
She looked down at her four-inch long feet, bound and crippled when she was a child, and said, brooding, "It's better for me to die as soon as possible."
The family has always lived on the edge of poverty; what pushed them over was a disastrous flood in eastern China in the summer of 1991. 
The flood, the worst in 100 years in Anhui Province, killed more than 5,100 people, caused $14 billion in economic losses and disrupted the lives of 220 million people.
Â 
Resilience Amid the Debris
The Chinese authorities promptly banned foreign reporters from the area, so the flooding attracted little attention around the world. 
But even now, 15 months later, in what local officials say is the first visit by a Western journalist, it is obvious that the area was devastated and that many peasants will not be able to recover for several more years.
The flooding is also testimony to the legendary resilience of the Chinese peasantry, for some villages are resprouting from the mud and will soon be sturdier than ever. 
International aid experts give the Chinese authorities good marks for organizing relief efforts, and there were no epidemics of disease among the tens of millions of people who lost homes.
Still, that is small consolation for Ms. Wan. She lives with her son and grandson in a mud hut that was supposed to be their temporary quarters to get them through last winter. 
It will have to shelter them this winter as well, and the family has no idea when they will have the $2,000 needed to build a brick home.
Â 
House Is Beyond Reach
"It's far more than we can afford," said her son, Wang Daoyun, who is 44. 
"There's no way we can build a permanent home until my son grows up."
The problem, Mr. Wang said, is that he has less than one-sixth of an acre and he is the only able-bodied person to provide for his mother and his child.
That was bad enough, but then the floods destroyed his home and virtually everything he owned. 
Now even an education for his son, a fourth-grader, is becoming a luxury.
"Already, the boy's school fees are 70 yuan a year," Mr. Wang said, "and next year it'll be 100 yuan. 
I can't pay that much."
(Seventy yuan is equivalent to about $12.75.)
Flooding is an integral part of Chinese history: one of the earliest names in the fog where history emerges from legend is the Great Yu, a heroic emperor who supposedly tamed a great flood in the 23d century B.C. the most capricious river is the Yellow River, which silts up and overflows the dikes to find a new course to the ocean.
When nonstop rains beginning in May 1991 made it clear that flooding in Anhui was inevitable, the Government opened floodgates and cut through dikes so the worst damage would be absorbed by villages like this one rather than by big cities downstream.
This almost certainly minimized the cost in lives, but it also meant that those who suffered most were those who had the least to start with.
"The flood left my rice paddy covered with sand, so that all I can plant is sweet potatoes and rape seed," Hu Changcui, a woman of 56, said as she stood in a crude brick shelter that serves as living quarters until the family can rebuild a home.
"And my son is 23 years old and not yet married!
Of course, we'll have to wait until we can build a house before he can think of getting married."
Â 
The Money Is Running Out
Throughout Anhui Province, 600,000 people are living in temporary housing: straw shacks, mud huts, brick shelters or canvas tents. 
About 700 clinics have yet to be rebuilt, along with 300 schools.
"We still have plenty of needs, but we're about out of funds," said Ye Ruqiang, deputy director of Anhui Province's flood disaster office.
The Government almost certainly could have attracted more foreign aid if it had allowed foreign news coverage. 
But instead the authorities seemed embarrassed, and chose to turn the floods into a huge propaganda effort to improve the image of the army, whose reputation had been sullied when it fired on crowds of pro-democracy protesters around Tiananmen Square in 1989.
The People's Liberation Army played a central role in flood relief and unquestionably saved thousands of lives, and special television programs hailed the soldiers' heroism.
Some families have already bounced back and seem in better shape than ever.
Â 
Now, Let's Find Wives
Miaoqian, a village of 8,000 in in an old lack bed in northern Anhui, has risen anew less than a mile from the old site.
"This is much better than my old house," Li Decao, a 36-year-old peasant, said as he showed off his new two-room house, with a pig and a few hens in the back yard.
Yang Chuanzao, the 30-year-old Mayor, said that soon after the disaster, the number of marriages dropped, because local people could no longer afford to hold a wedding festival and set up a new house. 
But he figures local youths will have more luck finding partners once they are settled in their new homes.
"It's definitely a bit easier for the young men to find a wife now," he said. 
"You're more attractive when you live in a brick house than when you live in a grass shack."

file: Year Later, Chinese Father Grieves and Fears.txt
text:
ï»¿
A year after soldiers shot dead his only son, the father's own odyssey through faith, heartbreak, bitterness and disillusionment with the Chinese Communist Party still leaves him confused and fearful.
The atmosphere in his shabby, simply furnished three-room apartment changes from bickering and laughter, when the 14 family members and relatives gather together, to a ghostly quiet, as memories turn to the son of this house and that time during the June 4 military crackdown when his life ended at 21 years as he rode a bicycle to his part-time job in a garage.
While most of the dead were killed while protesting against the attacking troops, this young man was shot in the back while bicycling to work on a side street four miles from Tiananmen Square. 
People who saw the shooting told his family that a small group of soldiers was on the street and apparently shot him at random. 
Neither he nor his family was active in the democracy movement, and family members agreed to be interviewed on condition that they not be identified, for fear of reprisals from the authorities.
Long Silences at Dinnertime
The father, a Communist Party member, is 61 now - his newly graying hair betrays the real aging that has taken place over the last 12 months - and the immediate despair over his son has faded into long silences at dinnertime. 
He tries to fend off the memories by channeling his energies into raising the 18 pigeons he keeps in a large cage outside his living-room window.
Since the day his son was cremated and the appropriate certificates turned over to the authorities as proof of his son's innocence when he was killed, no one from the Government has sent a letter of acknowledgment or sympathy or even come to ask about him, either to brand him a counterrevolutionary rebel or a martyr.
''The Government never said we were counterrevolutionaries or not,'' one of the son's relatives said. 
''They never said we were good or bad. 
They never asked us.''
Throughout Beijing and the rest of the country, hundreds of families are remembering their loved ones who were killed on June 4 last year, when troops opened fire on crowds of demonstrators in the center of Beijing.
Last year, the Government said it would compensate the families of victims innocently killed in the crackdown. 
It also prepared a list of the victims for possible release, but then said it would not release the list because of objections from the families.
Â 
No Compensation Evident
Each time such announcements were made, the father waited for a visit, but so far, he has received neither compensation nor consultation on the release of his son's name. 
The Government did not disclose how much the compensation would be, and apparently has not paid it to any of the victims' families.
It is this silence from the authorities that stirs anger in the father, the mother and four sisters. 
Some families have received visits by the authorities, especially if the victims were students who took part in the movement. 
This family does not even know if the son has become a statistic.
''This child was too young,'' the father said. 
''He wasn't even old enough to make his contribution to the nation. 
He had just started working. 
Such a small life, terminated, just like that. 
Such a loss.''
For the father, the death of the son was especially distressful. 
The son had pleaded with the father not to venture out, but the father adamantly insisted on going to work that early morning on June 4. 
The son followed the example, setting out to work on his own.
Â 
Fury Replaced by Fear
Yet, for the father, the fury has subsided slowly, and in its place is more fear than cynicism or courage borne out of pain. 
He has not complained to his ''work unit,'' where he is partly retired, and he has not tried to contact the authorities. 
He rarely speaks against the Government, only sometimes around family members.
His distance from the party has grown considerably, since the early days when his hope for China lay in the party, and he did not take part in any political study sessions during the year. 
The party is carrying out its nationwide re-registration for its members, and those whom it deems unsuitable may be expelled. 
The father says he will not officially resign from the party, nor will he officially re-register.
Like many Chinese whose anger over the crackdown has blended into their daily lives, the family is waiting for the Government to change, but in the meantime, their disaffection is turning into indifference.
''They are too busy to come see us,'' the father said, his voice soft and calm. 
''For a common man like me there is only patience and hope.''
Later, he added, ''The time of hope has already passed.''
The mother has taken to fits of craziness, talking in a rambling manner, family members say, and they have removed all of the son's belongings from the house because of the memories they inspire. 
She retired late last year, and then sought a part-time job after two weeks at home. 
She was spending her time at home thinking about her son.
Â 
His Ashes Are Visited
In honor of the son, the family has followed a Chinese tradition of burning fake paper money many times in the last year, and it has refrained from setting off firecrackers, because they symbolize happiness. 
Now, his ashes are kept at a state funeral parlor, and the family often goes to pay its respects.
''We go there to burn paper money and to burn the things he used to like to eat, like shrimps, apples, oranges and fish,'' said the mother, a thin woman, whose coarse, wrinkled skin makes her look older than her 51 years.
When a classmate of the son stopped in to pay his respects and to ask about visiting the funeral parlor, the parents jumped up to tend to him. 
The father returned to the living room, his face showing a mixture of pain and appreciation.
''My spirit is better these days,'' he said. 
''But I dread the visits of his classmates.''

file: YELTSIN CUTS VISIT TO BEIJING SHORT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Saying he needed to "restore order" and protect the reformist core of Russia's Government, President Boris N. Yeltsin cut short his visit to China this morning and headed back to Moscow.
His new Prime Minister, Viktor S. Chernomyrdin, whom Mr. Yeltsin chose this week after parliamentary pressure forced him to abandon acting Prime Minister Yegor T. Gaidar, was on his own visit to Kazakhstan, and Moscow itself seemed quiet early this morning.
But Mr. Yeltsin, who has a flair for the dramatic gesture, announced that he had been informed overnight of a concerted effort to replace the reformist core of Mr. Gaidar's team of young, Westernized economists, some of whom accompanied Mr. Yeltsin to China.
"They have begun too early to fight for portfolios, to pull apart the Cabinet, and so the master must return and restore order there," Mr. Yeltsin said at Beijing airport.
Â 
Core Must Remain
"Gaidar brought his own team with him, his young inner core," Mr. Yeltsin said. 
"The new prime minister wants to bring in his own team but the core of Gaidar's reformers must not under any circumstances be pulled apart."
Some Cabinet posts can be changed, he said, but most of Mr. Gaidar's team must remain.
Out of 30 people or so in the Cabinet, Mr. Yeltsin said, "three, four or five can be replaced."
But "the rest of the main figures" must remain, he said.
Earlier, China's official Xinhua News Agency mentioned Mr. Yeltsin's early departure, citing only his "busy schedule at home."
He was scheduled to leave later today in any event. 
The statement added that Yeltsin's visit to China "has been very smooth and successful."
There have been reports in Moscow that Arkady Volsky, the lobbyist leader of the main opposition grouping, Civic Union, had said on a visit to Tokyo that he was pushing Mr. Chernomyrdin to replace Mr. Gaidar's team with more conservative economists closer to industry. 
But Mr. Volsky said on Friday that he had been misquoted.
But there was a sense on Friday that Mr. Chernomyrdin was trying to make a fast start. 
He began making good on his promises to help industry in just the manner Western economists feared, proposing to a compliant Russian Pprliament an additional 200 billion rubles (about $480 million) in immediate credits to the energy sector he used to run.
Before flying to Kazakhstan for talks to promote better cooperation with Russia, especially in oil and gas, Mr. Chernomyrdin added an amendment to the 1992 budget law calling for the new credits this year. 
The Supreme Soviet, which had approved the budget law in principle earlier this week, passed it Friday with the new funding, pushing the budget deficit to 1.17 trillion rubles ($2.8 billion) for the year.
Finance Minister Vasily Barchuk had argued that the higher deficit would increase inflation and could damage Russia's ability to pay for needed imports.
Mr. Gaidar has encouraged his "team" of young, Westernized, like-minded economists to remain in the Cabinet if they could pursue and protect economic reform, and Anatoly B. Chubais, the deputy prime minister in charge of the crucial privatization policy, has already agreed to stay on. 
He extended the period in which Russians may pick up their free privatization voucher, with a face value of 10,000 rubles, another month, until the end of January.
Â 
Gaidar Team Open to Staying
In Beijing, where he was accompanying Mr. Yeltsin, another deputy prime minister, Aleksandr Shokhin, told Interfax that the Gaidar team would not "slam the door" if Mr. Chernomyrdin wanted them to stay on. 
But they wanted assurances about "the core of the Government and its policies."
Mr. Shokhin said he was encouraged that Mr. Chernomyrdin did not campaign to be Prime Minister and got the job "unexpectedly."
While Mr. Chernomyrdin "is a very experienced economist who worked in a key branch of the economy," Mr. Shokhin said "it is one thing to be a director and quite another to be a Prime Minister."
On Friday the Russian President announced that Moscow and Beijing had agreed in principle to cooperate on military and technological projects as part of an array of accords intended to deepen the relationship between the two countries.
The agreements, though overshadowed by Mr. Yeltsin's assertion that he would meet with President Bush next month to sign a new strategic arms reduction treaty, appear to broaden Russia's contacts with China, a former adversary, and sweep aside ideological differences in the relationship.
On the second day of what was to have been a three-day trip to China, Mr. Yeltsin and his entourage signed 24 agreements covering cultural, trade and scientific exchanges, food credits, the construction of a nuclear power plant and the reduction of troops along the Russian-Chinese border.
"An important step has been made in the development of bilateral relations and a new page has been opened in our friendly relations," Mr. Yeltsin told reporters tonight at a press conference. 
"Let's talk less and do more."
The two sides cemented their budding new relationship with the signing of a joint declaration of friendship, renouncing the use of a nuclear first strike against the other country and pledging not to enter into treaties "prejudicing the sovereignty and security interests of the other party."
Mr. Yeltsin said that at the last-minute insistence of the Chinese Prime Minister, Li Peng, the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding that laid down the general principles for closer cooperation on military and technological projects.
Mr. Yeltsin would not say what kinds of projects would be covered under the arrangement, but he said a "real agreement" would be worked out within a month by the two countries' defense ministers.
China would not comment on the agreement on military cooperation. 
It did, however, make public the text of the joint declaration, which says that China and Russia will set up exchange programs that will help build "cooperation in the military field."
A Russian Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksandr N. Shokhin, said that Moscow would extend a long-term $2.5 billion credit to finance the building of a nuclear power station that would conform to international standards. 
He added that restrictions on the secondary transfer of the technology would be very strict. 
The loan for the power plant, which is to be built in the northeastern province of Liaoning, would be spread over 10 to 12 years.
Mr. Yeltsin said that China had agreed to extend a credit worth about $52 million, mainly to allow Russia to buy food and feedstock. 
He added that China planned to sell 10 million tons of grain to Russia at world prices.

file: YELTSIN STARTING 3-DAY CHINA VISIT.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Boris N. Yeltsin of Russia arrived here today for a three-day visit that is intended to cement economic ties with China and reassert a working relationship that was thrown into doubt by the collapse of the Soviet Union and the abandonment of Communism there.
"We have to open a new era in relations between Russia and China,"
Mr. Yeltsin told reporters after he and his entourage of 100 Russian officials stepped off three private jets at a Beijing airport this morning.
Mr. Yeltsin will meet with the Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin, but he comes to China as an economic broker, not a political one, and as a head of state, not as a Communist Party leader. 
His task is to boost economic relations, beginning with plans to sign about 20 agreements that seal cooperation between Beijing and Moscow in a range of fields, from military matters and nuclear power pacts to cultural and scientific exchanges.
The last Russian leader to visit was Mikhail S. Gorbachev, who arrived in May 1989 to mark the formal end of the three-decade-long Chinese-Soviet split. 
Mr. Gorbachev's visit was particularly significant because it came during the Tiananmen Square democracy movement, which welcomed him as a hero.
Â 
Past Criticism of Yeltsin
Indeed, Mr. Gorbachev's visit gave a new stimulus to the democracy movement. 
The Chinese Army crackdown a few weeks later, and the rise of the hard-liners in Beijing, led to the resurgence of mutual suspicion between Moscow and Beijing. 
Chinese leaders have been especially scathing -- in private -- about Mr. Yeltsin's role in the disintegration of Soviet Communism.
Today, however, Mr. Yeltsin does not represent a bubbling democracy for young Chinese intellectuals and students, as Mr. Gorbachev did. 
While some Chinese admire him, others regard him as a symbol of the dangers of overthrowing a Communist system. 
When they look at Russia today, they see not so much freedom and democracy as chaos and economic decline.
For now, China is much more economically robust than Russia, and Mr. Yeltsin is likely to press Chinese officials for greater financial assistance, more weapons purchases and ample supplies of meat, shoes, warm coats and other consumer goods.
The nominal centerpiece of the visit is the signing of a joint declaration that will lay down the principles of the new friendship. 
No longer will the relationship be based on Communist brotherhood, but rather on a more pragmatic interaction between two governments.
China is expected to extend a small loan of tens of millions of dollars during the trip. 
Russian officials have also said their Government plans to continue selling weapons and other military equipment to China. 
The Chinese have already paid $1 billion for two dozen SU-27 jet fighters and are reportedly interested in MIG-31 jets, Kilo-class submarines and bombers.
Among the most visible signs of the growing economic relationship is the increase in trade, which totaled $3.9 billion for 1991. 
In Beijing, for instance, Russian entrepreneurs crowd the free markets jams as they stroll along the streets with their giant bags stuffed with clothing.

file: _Bolder Approach_ Is Urged for China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Li Peng called on China to "take a bolder approach to reform" today and said that its foremost task was to restructure the economy to stimulate economic growth.
Mr. Li, delivering his annual Government work report to lawmakers, suggested that the nation's rising living standards were the crucial factor that allowed Communist rule to survive in China instead of collapsing as it has in other countries. 
He indicated that the Government would make every effort to make people richer in order to repel capitalist subversion.
"To make China a powerful socialist country standing firm as a rock in the East, we must concentrate on our domestic affairs -- above all, on more rapid economic development," the Prime Minister said.
Â 
Address to Parliament
Mr. Li's speech was delivered to 2,500 delegates at the opening session of the annual National People's Congress, China's rubber-stamp Parliament. 
The address had been eagerly awaited for any light that it might cast on the power struggle that is believed to be under way between moderates and hard-liners within the leadership.
Instead of taking a clear position, Mr. Li seemed to take both sides. 
He called repeatedly for bolder reforms, but emphasized the need for stabilityI. 
He took a far more cautious line than the attitude suggested in a recent series of official articles that have gone so far as to recommend adopting elements of capitalism.
In the more audacious parts of the speech, Mr. Li borrowed from comments and proposals offered by Deng Xiaoping, the country's 87-year-old paramount leader, during a trip to southern China in January. 
Mr. Deng has engineered the latest push for more economic liberalization as the best way to preserve Communism in China.
Â 
'Emancipate Our Minds'
"We must further emancipate our minds, dare to innovate and take a bolder approach to reform and opening up," Mr. Li said. 
He called for more stock markets and for state-owned factories to compete in the market.
Though he said the focus of reform would be efforts to make state-owned enterprises competitive, Mr. Li did not offer many specifics about steps the leadership would take in its "bolder approach."
He also bowed in his speech to the hard-liners' demands for ideological campaigns and vigilance against subversion.
"We must be on the watch for any ideological trend toward bourgeois liberalization, checking it the moment it appears and never allowing it to run rampant," Mr. Li said. 
"Otherwise, there will be serious consequences."
The Prime Minister also called for dealing harshly with criminals, presumably alluding to democracy campaigners as well as to thieves and murderers.
"If we are too tenderhearted, we shall come to grief," he said.
Mr. Li also called repeatedly for buttressing political education programs, especially for university students. 
He said that social scientists "should continue to take Marxism, Leninism and Mao Zedong thought as their guide."
Â 
Dam Project Approval
This year's work report was less dismissive of human rights than in the past, and Mr. Li said that countries should discuss human-rights concerns. 
But he gave no indication that China was prepared to release political prisoners or tolerate dissent.
"It is not acceptable for a small group of countries to impose their human-rights criteria or models upon others," Mr. Li said. 
"Nor is it permissible to use human rights as a pretext for interfering in other countries' internal affairs."
Mr. Li called on the National People's Congress to approve the proposed Three Gorges Dam, a controversial project on the Yangtze River that has been under discussion since the 1920's.
Proponents of the Three Gorges dam say the project would generate huge amounts of electricity and reduce the risk of a catastrophic flood that might kill one million or more people. 
Critics say the project would flood one of China's most scenic areas, would offer only limited flood-control benefits, and is too costly and complex for China to tackle now.
Mr. Li's comments indicate that the Congress is almost certain to approve the Three Gorges project.

file: _GOING TO DEMOCRACY_.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA IN SEARCH OF ITS FUTURE
Years of Great Reform, 1982-87.
By John Woodruff.
Illustrated. 218 pages. 
Seattle:
University of Washington Press.
$19.95.
This is not a book filled with personal reflections on the splendor and mystery of China. 
It is a soberly analytical account by a correspondent whose observations probably were limited by the bureaucratic obstacles that the Chinese Government places in the paths of writers for powerful American newspapers.
But if he misses the daily simplicity and beauty of China, John Woodruff, The Baltimore Sun's Beijing correspondent from the fall of 1982 to the summer of 1987, gives social scientists, China scholars and historians an excellent, insightful look at the political, economic and social reforms under Deng Xiaoping, successor to Mao Zedong, who for 27 years ruled the lumbering land of one billion.
''China in Search of Its Future'' chronicles five years of reform in what likely has been the most peaceful, prosperous and politically stable decade China has experienced in the 20th century. 
Mr. Woodruff does not linger on the devastating damage - material, cultural and psychological - wrought by Mao's impassioned young Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution, which lasted from 1966 until Mao's death 10 years later. 
Instead, he describes how the Chinese in the 1980's find themselves teetering between Marxist dogma and a craving for a democracy that recently has inspired mass demonstrations in the streets of Beijing, Shanghai and other cities.
In fact, some of the more revealing chapters in this book - when Mr. Woodruff puts aside the dry but obligatory details on factories and farming - deal with China's future by describing its youth. 
The author's detailed account of student demonstrations leading up to New Year's Day in 1987 foreshadows this spring's chaotic upheaval. 
Mr. Woodruff tells of one foreign correspondent who asked a student during the demonstrations of 1987 where he was headed. 
''The student looked puzzled for an instant, then grinned as if delighted by his own cleverness. 
'I'm going to democracy,' he said.''
Those demonstrations provoked the veterans of the Communist Party to oust their leader, Hu Yaobang, blaming him for a lax atmosphere that allowed such freedom of expression. 
The demonstrations of today were spawned in part by the recent death of Hu, a man since lionized by the students as an avuncular figure of progressive reform.
The book contains plenty of detail on the inner wranglings of the six-member Standing Committee of the Politburo, and Mr. Woodruff cleverly uncovers the machinations of the ''dirty business'' of politics through dialogue with the ''born Red'' - the privileged children of China's revolutionary elite, the vanguard of the Long March in 1949. 
Fang Xiuqing, the 31-year-old daughter of an old revolutionary, explains to Mr. Woodruff that her coveted Beijing apartment was won through guanxi - a word as widely used as glasnost and perestroika are in the Soviet Union today. 
It simply means Ms. Fang has connections. 
Her father had known an elderly Politburo member, formerly a marshal in the People's Liberation Army during the civil war.
In a startling attempt to prove to the masses that special treatment of the ''born Red'' generation would not be tolerated by the party's Central Committee, three young sons of high-ranking Shanghai officials were executed in 1986. 
They had been convicted of gang-raping women, of using their fathers' names to lure women to parties and of extending promises of foreign study and job transfers. 
The executions, and the unusally extensive publicity given them in the Chinese news media, ''were, in effect, a brutal form of official apology for how far the party had permitted its officials, and their sons and daughters, to use and abuse their positions,'' Mr. Woodruff writes.
The Chinese have a saying, that their women ''hold up half the sky.''
However, as Mr. Woodruff writes, women in China still are forced to retire five years earlier than men. 
The nation's controversial one-child policy - an effort to curb the population - has caused some rural couples hoping for male heirs to practice the ancient atrocity of killing infant girls. 
The picture for women in China today would appear to be a bleak one. 
''But most of the women I knew seemed, for the moment, to be preoccupied with how much better life is now than it was a few years ago,'' Mr. Woodruff writes. 
''They were not much inclined to ask themselves whether men had it even better.''
Mr. Woodruff, now chief of The Baltimore Sun's Tokyo bureau, concludes that he is reluctantly optimistic about the progressive reforms he observed during his nearly five years in China. 
''My sense is that the rapid and dramatic changes I saw are indeed potentially historic, but that the key word in the sentence may yet prove to be 'potentially.'
It still seems too soon to feel certain that the Deng Xiaoping years will prove, in retrospect, to have been more than the greatest in a long line of ambitious starts.''

file: _KILL THE FOREIGNER!_.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA JOURNAL, 1889-1900
An American Missionary Family
During the Boxer Rebellion.
With the Letters and Diaries of Eva Jane Price and Her Family.
Foreword by Harrison E. Salisbury.
Introductory notes and annotations by Robert H. Felsing.
Illustrated. 289 pp. 
New York:
Charles Scribner's Sons. 
$22.50.
When I was a child in China, the closest things we had to grandparents were two elderly saints known to our whole missionary community as ''Uncle'' Jimmy and ''Aunt'' Sophie Graham. 
The Grahams and their son James had lived through the Boxer Rebellion. 
My mother told me the story of how an armed mob, inflamed by the sinister Boxers, surrounded the walls and battered on the gate of the mission compound. 
The Grahams had barricaded themselves in an upstairs bedroom trying to delay the massacre that seemed certain.
At last the gate gave way, and the Grahams could hear the screams as the mob surged into the courtyard. 
Without thinking what she was doing, Sophie lifted James from his cradle and carried him to the window. 
The baby, entranced by the mass of people below, laughed aloud and began to wave his arms.
Someone looked up, saw the happy child and waved back. 
Another waved and another until, unbelievably, the violent mob was transformed into a smiling, waving crowd. 
A few minutes later, the would-be assassins waved their final goodbyes and quietly left the compound. 
James was a grown man and a missionary himself when I knew him. 
But he never ceased to be known as the baby through whom God had wrought a miracle of deliverance.
What I wasn't told as a child was how precious few such miracles had been during the summer of 1900 in north China. 
More than 200 foreigners and an estimated 30,000 Chinese were brutally murdered during the Boxer Rebellion. 
Many of the victims were infants and children.
The I Ho Chuan, or Righteous, Harmonious Fists (nicknamed Boxers by Europeans), got their name from paramilitary rites that, they claimed, made them invulnerable to foreign bullets. 
They began as one of the many secret patriotic and religious societies that flourished in late 19th-century China, fed by the anger caused by the Opium Wars and related acts of humiliation imposed on China by the Western powers and Japan.
The missionaries had come in the wake of and under the protection of foreign gunboats. 
They and their early converts were particularly hated by the Boxers, who circulated rumors that these foreign devils and their secondary devils poisoned village wells, sold baby girls into prostitution and slavery, caused natural disasters by their magical incantations and grossed enormous profits by exporting human body parts.
In contrast to the Boxers' furious motto - ''Protect the country, kill the foreigner!''
- the patriotism and religious fervor of Eva Jane Price, a Congregationalist missionary from Iowa, seems touchingly naive. 
In ''China Journal, 1889-1900,'' a collection of letters and diaries, she often sounds uncomfortably patronizing, a Midwestern housewife who does indeed hold cleanliness near to godliness: ''I wish I could send you a picture of the crowd that comes in [to Sunday services] just as we see them - some men half naked, children nearly nude, women nursing their babies with not even a handkerchief to cover their breasts, an occasional boy with a hen or basket of eggs to sell (which we do not buy of course on Sunday), some dirty, lousy fellows but with souls to be saved.''
Usually Eva Price seems very much of her own time and place, but here and there are hints that she is more: ''Hurrah for China!
A place where the women can wear the breeches and be fashionable!''
And as the years pass her compassion for the Chinese seems more evident than in her early descriptions of their filth and ignorance: ''The dust is deep, deep, and I do not know what these poor people will do. 
There is suffering now and what there will be by spring is hard to say. 
They are poor, poor as Job's turkey. 
It makes me begrudge the food I eat when I know so many around us have so little to eat.''
In his foreword to the book Harrison E. Salisbury compares the Prices' story to a Greek tragedy. 
It is in some ways an apt comparison. 
The death of the Price family at the hands of the Boxers is known from the beginning, and Eva, playing out the tragedy, does not know how her story will end and cannot hear our warnings. 
She has no notion of herself as a tragic heroine. 
She is simply a devoted daughter far from home, seeking through her descriptions and commentary on life in this distant land to bind herself to those she has left behind.
I began reading ''China Journal, 1889-1900'' as I would begin to read Sophocles - with a feeling of dread that always lurked in the background. 
But despite all, I came to love Eva, whose letters remind me not of Antigone's oratory but of my own mother's letters from China - by turns funny, earnest, sad, exasperated, lonely, brave, depressed.
How brave those missionary women were. 
They truly went out like Abraham, not knowing whither they went. 
They tried against great odds to make a home for their husbands and children in an inhospitable land. 
They wanted to do good, and they never ceased to be homesick. 
In the late 19th century it took three months for a letter between China and the United States to travel in one direction. 
So when the grief-stricken Eva writes to tell of the death of her baby son, it is six months before her mother's word of comfort arrives.
I wonder if ''China Journal'' would have been published 20 years ago by anyone but some small denominational press. 
Even in the church the missionary endeavors of a generation or two ago have been regarded with some embarrassment, if not suspicion. 
The annotator of Eva's letters, Robert H. Felsing, shares this negativism. 
''Despite the murder of over 200 of their comrades in 1900,'' he writes, ''few missionaries ever grasped the ugly possibility that their activities in China may have been truly harmful to the Chinese.''
The Boxers are not simply exotic villains to us today. 
We understand all too well the ominous combination of wounded nationalism and fanatic religion. 
Still, it is too easy for us to judge the errors of another generation. 
Perhaps it was hubris rather than a divine call that led to the deaths of the Prices and thousands of their fellow Christians. 
If so, the story is a tragedy in the classic sense. 
However, if we let Eva speak for herself, she would not consider her life a tragedy, but a small part in the universal drama whose ultimate end is joyful.

file: _Meddling_ by Chinese Is Worrying Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
A bit more than six years ago, when Britain agreed to hand over this territory to China in 1997, the Chinese leaders pledged that Hong Kong could continue to revel in its capitalism, vices and freedoms. 
Most Hong Kong people then seemed relieved by the agreement, for they thought they could tolerate such a marriage based on separate bedrooms.
But these days, at the halfway mark between that 1984 Joint Declaration on Hong Kong's future and the actual turnover to China, there is growing doubt about the value of the Chinese pledges.
In particular, a flurry of recent attempts by the Chinese authorities to influence Hong Kong policy has led some people to ask this question: If China insists on interfering with Hong Kong affairs now, when it is British, then how can Hong Kong hope to remain unmolested after 1997?
The latest development began this month when Lu Ping, the newly appointed Chinese official in charge of Hong Kong affairs, asserted several times that the British authorities were being deceptive in their public statements about how construction of a new Hong Kong port and airport development would be financed.
Mr. Lu was apparently alarmed that the British were planning to empty Hong Kong's coffers with the $16 billion development project, saddling China after 1997 with a burden rather than a benefit.
Â 
Lectures Seen as Puzzling
The details are murky, but some Hong Kong residents thought that Mr. Lu's comments betrayed a confusion about the projects and about the territory's financial system. 
More fundamentally, it struck some people as bizarre that Chinese leaders should be lecturing Hong Kong on either finance or open government.
A cartoon in The Hong Kong Standard showed Prime Minister Li Peng, in a dilapidated office that suggested China's economic backwardness, declaring, "We'll have to show Hong Kong how to run an economy."
"If China is already interfering, in such a vocal manner, with such high-ranking officials, now when the Brits are still here, what chance is there that the people of Hong Kong will be left alone and allowed to exercise 'a high degree of autonomy' as promised after 1997?" asked Martin C. M. Lee, a leader of the democratic forces in Hong Kong.
He added: "There are more and more breaches of the Joint Declaration, breaches in spirit and breaches in letter. 
That's why so many people are leaving. 
Why, even the bank is leaving."
Â 
Passport for a Bank
He was referring to the announcement last week that the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, the local bank whose history has been intertwined with the territory's for 125 years, was creating a parent company with a legal domicile in Britain. 
The bank's action may further undermine confidence and raise emigration, already running at about 1,200 a week.
"If the bank is getting a foreign passport, then I guess I should too," said a Hong Kong Chinese who works for the bank.
To be sure, the mood is not unreservedly bleak. 
The stock market is weak but steady. 
The property market is firm, and money continues to be made, more here than in most parts of the world. 
Hong Kong still has more Rolls-Royces per capita than anywhere else in the world, and there are some signs that as time passes since the military crackdown in China in June 1989, the fear and the urgency with which people sought foreign passports may have diminished.
The 1984 Joint Declaration stipulates that after 1997, Hong Kong will be able to govern its own affairs, keep its own currency, and maintain its capitalist system for at least 50 years. 
China will manage foreign affairs and defense, but otherwise the future Special Autonomous Region is supposed to be left to itself. 
Chinese officials once even attended the ribbon-cutting of a hostess nightclub, where prostitutes meet and then go home with customers, to show their open-mindedness.
Â 
Long Lines at Consulates
"There were very high expectations created by the Joint Declaration that have not been met, but I think some of those expectations were unrealistic," said George Baeder, director of the Pacific Rim Consulting Group in Hong Kong.
Referring to the furor over Mr. Lu's comments on airport financing, he added, "It's inevitable that we'll see more of these explosions, rather than fewer, and this won't send very encouraging signals."
The six years since the signing of the Joint Declaration have seen momentous changes that testify to Hong Kong's resilience as well as trauma. 
There are long lines in front of foreign consulates, as residents seek immigration visas, but frenetic construction is continuing to alter the skyline in the background.
At the half-way mark on the way to 1997, the social changes are also manifest. 
Words have taken on new meanings: "astronaut" is one who leaves family behind to live abroad and win a passport. 
Fortune tellers are now called on to advise on questions of emigration as well as marriage.
Â 
Crime Is on the Rise
Strikes and crime are on the rise, and some people fear that the greatest danger for Hong Kong is not Chinese policies after 1997 but emigration and the social breakdown that comes with the rush to the exits before then.
Perhaps the most fundamental structural change since the Joint Declaration is the growing economic and social integration of Hong Kong with the Chinese province of Guangdong to the north. 
Hong Kong companies subcontract with low-wage factories across the border, while Hong Kong people routinely cross the border to save money on everything from vegetables to funeral plots.
While Mr. Lu's comments are the latest example of what some in Hong Kong see as Chinese "meddling," there have been many previous such incidents. 
Some were obscure -- like Chinese comments about urban planning in the New Territories part of Hong Kong -- and others were more direct, like demands that people in Hong Kong stop any attempts to subvert Communism in China.
Particularly since the 1989 crackdown, there has been apprehension that the Chinese authorities will try to stamp out "subversion" in Hong Kong even if that means ignoring the freedoms guaranteed in the Joint Declaration -- many of which are also guaranteed in the Chinese Constitution, to little effect.

file: _New Authoritarianism_ Seen in Chinese Actions.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Bush had an embarrassingly conspicuous front-row seat here Sunday to a spectacle that may have been inspired by a new theory that has come to be known as ''new authoritarianism.''
The spectacle, which ended up souring his visit, included a lecture from China's Communist Party leader about how democracy could ruin China's new policies, and sharp warnings against United States support for China's incipient human rights movement.
The finale was the use of more than 100 policemen to prevent China's best-known dissident, Fang Lizhi, and a prominent American scholar, Perry Link, from joining a banquet to which they had been invited by Mr. Bush during his 40-hour stay in China. 
Mr. Fang, Mr. Link and their wives were not allowed to board taxis or buses and were obliged to trudge through Beijing streets for one and one-half hours before two Canadian diplomats came to their assistance.
China expressed regret late tonight that the United States had made a ''fuss'' over the incident, and suggested that it was inappropriate for Mr. Bush to invite Mr. Fang without first consulting with Chinese officials. 
The statement followed a meeting between Ambassador Winston Lord and a Chinese Deputy Foreign Minister called to discuss the issue.
'Bush Was a Little Weak'
Mr. Fang, on the other hand, said today Mr. Bush's decision to raise the issue was ''a good beginning.''
But when pressed by reporters, he indicated that he thought ''Bush was a little weak'' in his handling of human rights matters on his visit, and he added that the United States appeared much more willing to criticize rights abuses in the Soviet Union than in China.
The police action to exclude Mr. Fang from the banquet and the Chinese condemnations of democracy surprised almost everyone here.
Part of the explanation for the actions may lie in the doctrine of new authoritarianism, which for the last two months has been hotly debated in official circles here.
Oddly, the theory is inspired not by Marx or Lenin, but by the experience of China's capitalist neighbors. 
Critics of socialism have often pointed out to Chinese officials the success of economies like those of Taiwan, South Korea, and Singapore. 
Some officials duly cited their use of market incentives, but also noted that they relied for most of their development on one-party authoritarian Governments.
''Authority is essential in modern economic life,'' a commentator wrote this month in People's Liberation Army Daily. 
In the present ''chaotic economic order,'' he continued, ''we should stress authority, strictly enforce orders and prohibitions and consciously safeguard overall interests.''
Of course, new authoritarianism is only one of the current fashions. 
Democracy is even more fashionable, not only among intellectuals and artists but even among Communist Party officials.
Moreover, many Chinese and foreign analysts doubt that the new doctrine can prevail. 
Mr. Fang said in a recent interview that while there will be ups and downs, democracy will be the trend in China. 
And Mr. Link said today that in the last decade whenever the Government had clamped down on intellectual freedom, intellectuals had quickly wriggled away and become even more outspoken than before.
Â 
Some Criticize Theory
Indeed, it is striking that the debate over new authoritarianism has been conducted in largely democratic fashion. 
Some newspapers have printed articles lauding it and urging greater stabilityI and order. 
Others have criticized the theory. 
The disagreements suggest that the official press is less monolithic than it used to be.
Workers' Daily, for example, this month lambasted new authoritarianism as ''an unrealistic prescription to save the world.''
Guangming Daily concluded in a long commentary that ''democracy involves a cost, but the cost of rejection of democracy would be even higher, such as the Cultural Revolution.''
New authoritarianism has various shades. 
One of the mildest is espoused by Wu Jiaxiang, a Communist Party official and protege of the party's General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang. 
Mr. Wu argued in the World Economic Herald last month that the doctrine should still be centered around respect for individual rights, at the same time that it rejects democratic decision-making for now. 
That tends to be a common theme among intellectual supporters of the new doctrine, but for others there does not seem to be much difference between new authoritarianism and any other kind.
Some foreign diplomats and many Chinese believe that Mr. Zhao shares the idea of new authoritarianism, but it almost certainly is not his alone. 
The chaos and turmoil that China has seen in this century have impressed upon many senior Chinese officials that one of the greatest threats to development is disorder.
The senior Chinese leader, Deng Xiaoping, has often cautioned that too much freedom could incite disruption, and he told Mr. Bush as much on Sunday. 
In their meeting, Mr. Deng said that without stabilityI, the achievements of recent years could be lost, a Foreign Ministry spokesman reported.
Such concerns have become increasingly common in recent months, as it becomes clear that the Government's orders often are simply ignored. 
Provincial leaders have refused to halt construction projects as ordered, for example, and some farmers are refusing to turn over their grain to the state, as they are supposed to.

EVENING CHATS IN BEIJING
Probing China's Predicament.
By Perry Link.
321 pp. 
New York:
W. W. Norton & Company. 
$24.95.
WHEN a young Chinese introduced Perry Link to his friends a few years ago, he offered perhaps the most flattering tribute he could muster. 
Beaming as he presented Mr. Link, the young man said, "The Communist Party hates him."
It will hate him even more after "Evening Chats in Beijing."
Mr. Link, a Princeton University professor of Chinese literature who angered the Chinese leadership in 1989 by repeatedly helping the dissident leader Fang Lizhi, marvelously captures the gloom prevailing among many Chinese intellectuals. 
Relying mostly on conversations with his Chinese acquaintances in 1988 and 1989, when he lived in Beijing, Mr. Link portrays better than anyone I know the sense of crisis and despair shared by many Chinese scholars in the capital.
What is the worst job in China today?
Night-soil collector?
Bricklayer?
Goatherd?
No, according to a young poet, the most painful job is teaching nursery school students.
"What do you teach the little ones?" the poet is quoted as saying. 
"To tell the truth?
If you do that, you are dooming them. 
Do you have the right to doom them?
But what, on the other hand, is your alternative?
Can you teach them to speak falsely?
Could you face yourself as a teacher if you did that?"
Few tribes anywhere in the world brood so much and so despairingly (or so articulately) as Chinese intellectuals. 
In part, the melancholy derives from disappointment that one of the world's oldest and greatest civilizations has produced nothing more than another third world dictatorship. 
And if China's intellectuals sometime seem particularly neurotic, one reason is that for decades they have been cowed into submission. 
They force back the bile and go on working for a system that oppresses them.
"Evening Chats in Beijing" is a lively survey of today's China as seen by these brooding intellectuals. 
Mr. Link speaks and writes Chinese about as well as any foreigner, and he ranges knowledgeably over plenty of terrain. 
He discusses the shortage of housing, the irritation at corruption, the uses and abuses of history and the dichotomy between reality and the China that smilingly presents itself to the outside world in meetings, speeches and newspapers. 
To study China is to search constantly for the relationship between reality and that official China.
"There is truth in Chinese newspapers, but you have to know how to find it," one person advises Mr. Link. "This often means reading upside down. 
If they say great strides have been made against corruption in Henan, you know that corruption is especially bad in Henan. 
If they say dozens of police were hurt in a clash with students, you know hundreds of students were injured if not killed."
More journalistic than scholarly, "Evening Chats in Beijing" benefits from numerous pithy comments by Mr. Link's friends, almost all of whom remain anonymous. 
In a discussion of how the Chinese adapt to cramped housing, which often forces several people to share a room, a young writer says, "I didn't know that sex could include sound until I saw American films."
This is a terrific book, but one should recognize that it offers a slice of China rather than a general introduction. 
One of the fundamental trends shaping China -- the economic boom of the last dozen years -- gets scant attention, and the peasants who account for the bulk of the population are scarcely mentioned. 
Though the voices in this book are among the most eloquent in China, they are not typical. 
Most Chinese are not anguished scholars who worry about the nation, but peasants whose concerns are directed at the harvest and their families.
Senior intellectuals in Beijing are a tiny and incestuous, if influential, elite. 
Indeed, they are such a small coterie that in many cases I was able to guess who the speakers were, based on Mr. Link's brief descriptions (I hope the security forces are more easily fooled).
Still, the discussions are frank and incisive. 
One can't help being impressed by the thoughtfulness with which China's brightest minds ponder their fate and castigate themselves along with everyone else. 
The Chinese in these "Evening Chats" are brilliantly and brutally honest, and it is a pleasure to eavesdrop.
